units.la: CREDO ego Reuerende pater, plerosque qui hunc librum viderint, admiraturos, quid nam permouerit opt. meum patrem Petrum Martyrem summum Theologum, vt cum ante maximam aetatis suae partem in sacris literis cognoscendis & interpretandis posuisset, in ipsa demum senecta, Commentarios scriberet in philosophicos Aristotelis de Moribus libros. Praesertim cum ea sit opinio multorum consensu confirmata, esse inter Christianam Theologiam & Aristotelicam Philosophiam, non modo discrimen ingens, verum perpetuum quoque dissidium, & bellum quodammodo ἀκαταλλακτον[?]. Quibus animo sic affectis Martyris nostri institutum vix probari poterit. Tibi vero Reuerede Pater, cui Martyris consilia & studia nota fuerunt, & qui de omni literarum genere optime iudicare potes, tui quoque similibus viris doctis & moderatis amantibus studia humanitatis, Martyris nostri institutum probari non dubito. Etenim, quod te non latet, sacrarum literarum & verae ac syncerioris Philosophiae, non est adeo magnum & perpetuum dissidium, vt non haec studia optime coniungi possint, sic vt sua cuique dignitas maneat. Quod autem plerique aliter senserunt, factū est non reiipsius sed hominum vitio, qui philosophia ad quaestum et inanes contentiones abusi sunt. Patrū enim memoria & adhuc nostra quoque aetate regnauit in Theologicis scholis pro vera philosophia contentiosa & rixatrix Sophistica, et ita regnauit, vt ipsas sacras literas graui tyrānide pene eiecerit e Theologorū scholis. Quis enim nostrum ignorat fuisse aliquando in theologicis scholis non minorem fere authoritatem Aristotelis quàm Mosis aut Pauli[?]; Mentio certe eius fuit magis assidua. Atque cùm religionis dogmata authoritate scripturarum con-firmanda fuissent, Aristoteleis rationibus ea probare conati sunt: rursus si Aristotelis dogmata ad iudicium & norman[?] rationis examinanda essent, toti ab eius authoritate pendebant, & ipsis placebat vetus illa Pythagorea probatio, αὐτὸς ἔφα. Commouit huius rei indignitas multos præclaros viros, qui theologiam ab erroribus repurgare cœperunt. Itaque asperius nonnulla in philo-sophiam omnes, & in ipsum etiam Aristotelem scripserunt. Vide-bant enim rixatricem hanc sophisticam, quæ sese philosophiæ ti-tulo uenditabat, matrem & nutricem fuisse præcipuorum erro-rum in ecclesia. Veruntamen ipsorum dicta non ita accipien-da sunt, quasi ideo omnem syncerioren Philosophiam damnent, & Aristotelis scripta e manib. studiosorum excutere velint. Nam aliam eorum fuisse sententiam, hinc apparet, quod in scholis quas instituerunt philosophiam & præsertim Peripateticam curarunt tradi. Et præterea ipsi, quod scripta illorum testantur, diligenter Platonis, Aristotelis & aliorum philosophorum libros euolue-runt. Quare si quid durius contra philosophiam scripserunt, id non intelligendum est de uera & syncera philosophia, sed derixa-trice & garrula sophistica, philosophiæ æmula, & de philosophia quæ humanis rationibus res diuinas & cœlestes diiudicare cona-tur, de illa inquam philosophia, quam hominum peruersum studi-um theologiæ & permiscuit & anteposuit. Illa autem uera & ge-nuina philosophia non modo studio sacrarum literarum non ad-uersatur, sed ad illud magna adiumenta adfert & multum orna-menti addit. Nam ut de reliquis philosophiæ speciebus nihil nunc dicamus, hæc de moribus philosophia, cuius plerisq; nullus uide-tur usus esse inter Christianos, propterea quod sacræ literæ abun-dè uitam & mores hominis Christiani informent, quantas quæso utilitates, quæ nam ornamenta affert homini theologo? Vnde e-nim melius cognosci potest quid humanæ uires absque spiritu Dei efficere aut non efficere queant? Ex quanam alia disciplina affectuum humanorum ratio & descriptio moralium uirtutum, quam ex hac ipsa petitur? Hæc autem & alia plura maiora, quæ in hac disciplina traduntur, quā sint theologis cognitu necessaria, nunc explicare me non necesse est, cum hæc omnia in his Com-mentarijs à Martyre erudite & perspicue explicata sint. Atque hæc non ideo ad te scribo Reuerende pater, quasi existimem Martyris scripto defensione aliqua apud te opus esse, cum me non latet constans tua erga Martyrem voluntas & exactum iudicium de omni hoc studiorum genere. Sed illis potius respondere per te volui, qui de his rebus minus exacte iudicant, & ita sacras literas excolendas esse existimant, ut uniuersam philosophiam penitus aspernentur, quibus libenter hoc damus, theologicam disciplinam omnibus aliis artibus, facultatibus & scientijs longe anteponendam esse: interim tamen philosophiam suo loco & ordine theologiæ non ut parem, sed ut modestam & obtemperantem pedisequam[?] reginæ ac theologiæ adiungimus. Atque ut apud veteres merito reprehensi fuerunt sophistæ, qui eloquentiam à sapientia seiunxerunt, & rursus non satis polita eorum scripta iudicantur: qui philosophiam omni eloquentiæ studio neglecto professi sunt: ita etiam iure reprehendendos arbitramur sophistas, qui philosophiam in sacrarum literarum locum quodammodo substituerunt, uti plerique Scholasticorum fecerunt. Rursus multa quoque in eorum scriptis desideramus, qui absque omni philosophiæ & bonarum artium cognitione sacras literas interpretari, & graves quæstiones explicare conati sunt. Aristotelem vero, ut omnes merito admirantur ac laudant, qui philosophiam & eloquentiam simul docuit, ita etiam iure ego hoc nomine Martyrem meum laudare possum, qui non tantum philosophiæ cognitionem cum sacrarum literarum studio coniunxit, uerum etiam simul & philosophiam & theologiam publice docuit. Nam cum Argentorati sacras literas profiteretur, & eo tempore schola ido-neo professore theologiæ careret, libenter hoc onus philosophiam docendi in se recepit, partito tamen hoc opere cum collega suo viro doctissimo & amicissimo Doctore Hieronymo Zancho, ita ut hic physicos Aristotelis libros, ipse vero eos qui de moribus ad Nicomachū conscripti sunt interpretaretur. Progressus autem est in huius operis interpretatione in tertium usq; librum, & deinde Tigurum uocatus certis & gravibus de causis tibi non ignotis Reverende pater eò se contulit, relicta Argentina. Cùm vero in ea schola philosophiam doceat Conradus Gesnerus, vir (ut omnes norūt) in omni philosophia & arte Medica exercitatissimus, Martyr noster onere philosophiæ docendæ liberatus est, i-deoq; etiam scriptionem commentariorū omisit, eaq; tantum nobis reliquit, quæ partim ipse Argetinę conscripsit in privatū usum, partim amici eo legente exceperunt, quæ etsi imperfecta adhuc sunt & non in eum finem conscripta ut in publicum ederentur, di-gna tamen visa sunt multis bonis & doctis viris apud nos quæ in lucem edantur. Dicebant enim illi etsi nō in omnes decem libros commentaria absoluerit, tamen si solum in primū scripsisset, edenda esse, propterea quod hic omniū interpretum consensu fit inter omnes decem difficilimus. Addebant hæc commentaria imperfecta præbere nihilominus pene perfectum exemplar interpretandi philosophiam. Neque enim dubitandū esse quin verus interpres habeatur, quicunq; hac methodo, qua Martyr in his commentarijs usus est, reliquos Aristotelis libros interpretatus fuerit, ita scilicet ut non tantū Aristotelis sententiam perspicuè & diserte exponat, verum etiā singula cum sacris literis conferat, & omnia ad hanc certissimam normā examinet. Hoc ergo iudicium optimorū virorū, quibus merito plurimum tribuo, sequutus, commentaria in publicum edidi, eaq; tuo nomini, Amplissime Præsul, inscripsi, primum quòd cum opus sit & imperfectum & ab ipso authore non recognitum, videbatur opus habere tali patrono qui de reipsa iudicare posset, & simul etiam quod approbasset nō grauaretur ab aliorum calumniis afferere: quorum utrumque Reverende pater optimè præstare potes. Nam quia ab ineunte ætate philosophiam omnem cognouisti, & præterea sacras literas diu iam magna cum laude, ut pote verus episcopus, docuisti, potes optimè iudicare de his Commentarijs, in quibus philosophia cum theologia conferatur. Quia vero Martyrem, quamdiu vixit, singulari amore prosequutus es, eiusq; labores in scholam & ecclesiam perpetuò probasti, non graue erit tibi hunc illius posthumum fœtum a maleuolorum hominum calumniis vindicare: idq; eo commodius facere potes, quòd beneficio Dei optimi maximi ad Episcopalem di-gnitatem gnitatem evectus, & ornatissimũ locum in ecclesia consequutus, ad huius causæ defensionem summam authoritatem affers. Accedit his singularis tuus in me amor, & multæ nec obscuræ significationes optimæ tuæ erga me voluntatis. Cui cum alia ratione respondere non queam, hoc publico scripto meam erga te observantiam vicissim declarare volui. Et quia mei fundi fruges nullas proferre potui, ob fortunæ iniquitatem, quæ hactenus non modo messem, verum ipsam satiationem multis rebus impediuit: hunc libellum in amplissimis latifundijs Martyris enatum ad te mittere volui: quem rogo ut gratum & acceptum habeas, cum propter ipsum Martyrem, cuius etiam mortui amor apud te non est mortuus: tum etiam propter Iulium tuũ qui hunc animo tui amantissimo ad te mittit, acrogat[?] ut hanc tenuem significationem suæ erga te observantiæ boni consulas, & uti consueuisti, perpetuo amore ipsum prosequaris. Deus Amplitudinem tuam ecclesiæ suæ incolumem quàm diutissimè feruet. Ti-guri pridie Idus Augusti.
units.tr: I believe, Reverend Father, that many who see this book will wonder what moved my dear father, Peter Martyr, the most learned theologian, to spend the very end of his life writing commentaries on Aristotle's philosophical books on morals, after he had devoted the greater part of his life to studying and interpreting Holy Scripture. This is especially so since many people hold the opinion, confirmed by general agreement, that there is not only a huge difference but also a perpetual quarrel, and a sort of irreconcilable war [ἀκατάλλακτον], between Christian theology and Aristotelian philosophy. Those who think this way will hardly approve of our Martyr's undertaking. But you, Reverend Father, who knew Martyr's plans and pursuits, and who can judge every kind of learning very well, I do not doubt will approve of it, as will men of learning like you who are moderate and love the studies of humane letters. For, as you know, there is not such a great and perpetual disagreement between Holy Scripture and true and purer philosophy that these studies cannot be combined very well, each keeping its own dignity. That many have thought otherwise has happened not through the nature of the thing but through the fault of men, who have abused philosophy for gain and empty disputes. In the memory of our fathers, and even in our own age, a contentious and quarrelsome sophistry, posing as true philosophy, has reigned in the theological schools, and it has reigned in such a way that it has nearly thrown Holy Scripture itself out of the theologians' schools by its heavy tyranny. For which of us does not know that at one time in the theological schools the authority of Aristotle was almost no less than that of Moses or Paul? His name was certainly mentioned more often. And when the doctrines of religion were to be confirmed by the authority of the Scriptures, they tried to prove them by Aristotelian arguments; and again, if the teachings of Aristotle were to be examined by the judgement and standard of reason, they depended entirely on his authority, and that old Pythagorean proof, ipse dixit [αὐτὸς ἔφα], pleased them. The unworthiness of this state of affairs stirred up many outstanding men, who began to purge theology of errors. Accordingly, some of them wrote rather harshly against philosophy in general and even against Aristotle himself. For they saw that this quarrelsome sophistry, which was boasting of the title of philosophy, was the mother and nurse of the chief errors in the Church. Yet their words should not be taken as if they condemned all purer philosophy and wished to snatch the writings of Aristotle from the hands of students. That their view was otherwise is clear from this, that in the schools they founded they took care that philosophy, and especially Peripatetic philosophy, should be taught. Moreover, as their writings attest, they diligently read through the books of Plato, Aristotle and other philosophers. So if they wrote anything rather harsh against philosophy, it is not to be understood as aimed at true and pure philosophy, but at the quarrelsome and garrulous sophistry, the rival of philosophy, and at that philosophy which tries to judge divine and heavenly things by human reasoning; I mean that philosophy which the perverse zeal of men has both mixed with theology and placed above it. That true and genuine philosophy, however, not only does not oppose the study of Holy Scripture, but brings great help to it and adds much ornament. For, to say nothing for now of the other kinds of philosophy, consider this moral philosophy, which seems to be of little use to most Christians, because the Holy Scriptures amply shape the life and morals of a Christian man. What advantages, I ask you, and what ornaments does it bring to a man who is a theologian? For from where can we better learn what human powers can or cannot accomplish without the Spirit of God? From what other discipline is the account of the human passions and the description of the moral virtues drawn, if not from this one? But there is no need for me now to explain these and many other greater things handed down in this discipline, how necessary they are for theologians to know, since all of them have been learnedly and clearly explained by Martyr in these Commentaries. And I write this to you, Reverend Father, not because I think that Martyr's writing needs any defence before you, since I am not unaware of your constant goodwill towards Martyr and your exact judgement on every kind of this learning. Rather, I wanted to answer through you those who judge these matters less exactly, and who think that Holy Scripture is to be cultivated in such a way that all philosophy is utterly despised. To them we gladly grant that theological discipline is to be placed far above all other arts, faculties and sciences; yet meanwhile we join philosophy, in its proper place and order, to theology as its humble and obedient handmaid, not as an equal. And just as among the ancients the sophists were rightly criticised, those who separated eloquence from wisdom, and their writings are again judged not polished enough, so too we think that those sophists are rightly to be reprehended who, in a sense, substituted philosophy in the place of Holy Scripture, as most of the Schoolmen did. Again, we also miss much in the writings of those who tried to interpret Holy Scripture and explain its weighty questions without any knowledge of philosophy and the liberal arts. But Aristotle, whom everyone rightly admires and praises because he taught philosophy and eloquence together, so for this reason I too can rightly praise my Martyr, who not only joined knowledge of philosophy to the study of Holy Scripture, but also taught philosophy and theology publicly at the same time. For when he was professing Holy Scripture at Strasbourg, and the school at that time lacked a suitable professor of philosophy, he willingly took upon himself the task of teaching philosophy, sharing this work with his colleague, the most learned and most friendly Doctor Jerome Zanchi, so that the latter interpreted Aristotle's physical books, while he himself interpreted those written on morals and addressed to Nicomachus. He progressed in the interpretation of this work as far as the third book, and then, being called to Zurich for certain serious reasons, which are not unknown to you, Reverend Father, he went there, leaving Strasbourg. Since Conrad Gessner, a man (as everyone knows) most experienced in all philosophy and in the medical art, now teaches philosophy in that school, our Martyr was relieved of the duty of teaching philosophy, and so he also omitted to write out the commentaries, and left us only those things which partly he himself wrote at Strasbourg for private use, and partly his friends took down while he was lecturing. Although these are still unfinished and were not written with the aim of being published, they seemed worthy to many good and learned men among us to be brought to light. For they said that, even if he had not completed commentaries on all ten books, yet if he had written only on the first, they should be published, because by the agreement of all interpreters this first book is the most difficult of all ten. They added that these incomplete commentaries nevertheless offer almost a perfect model for interpreting philosophy. For there is no doubt that he should be regarded as a true interpreter who, by the method Martyr used in these commentaries, interprets the remaining books of Aristotle, so that he not only expounds Aristotle's opinion clearly and eloquently, but also compares each point with Holy Scripture and tests everything by this most certain standard. Following, then, the judgement of these excellent men, to whom I attribute much, I have published these commentaries, and I have inscribed them to your name, most distinguished Prelate: first, because, since the work is both unfinished and not revised by the author himself, it seemed to need such a patron as could judge the matter itself; and at the same time, because, having approved it, you would not be burdened in defending it against the calumnies of others. You, Reverend Father, can do both of these things excellently. For since from your early youth you have known all philosophy, and moreover have for a long time taught Holy Scripture with great praise, as a true bishop should, you can judge these Commentaries very well, in which philosophy is compared with theology. And since you have followed Martyr with singular love as long as he lived, and have always approved his labours for the school and the Church, it will not be burdensome for you to defend this posthumous offspring of his against the calumnies of ill-disposed men; and you can do this all the more readily because, by the favour of God the best and greatest, you have been raised to the episcopal dignity and have attained a most distinguished place in the Church, and so you bring the highest authority to the defence of this cause. To these things is added your singular love towards me, and the many clear signs of your excellent goodwill towards me. Since I cannot answer you in any other way, I have wished by this public writing to declare in turn my respect for you. And because I have been unable to produce any crops from my own estate, owing to the unkindness of fortune, which until now has prevented not only the harvest but even the sufficiency of many things, I have wished to send you this little book, born on the broad estates of Martyr. I ask you to receive it kindly and gladly, both because of Martyr himself, whose love, even though he is dead, has not died in your eyes, and also because of your Julius, who sends it to you with a heart most fond of you, and asks that you kindly accept this slight token of his respect for you, and, as you are accustomed to do, continue to embrace him with constant love. May God keep your Dignity safe for his Church for as long as possible. At Zurich, the day before the Ides of August.
COMMENTARIES

units.la: COMMENTARIA D. PETRI MARTYRIS VERMILII, Florentini, in Primum librum Ethicorum Nicomachiorum Aristotelis.
units.tr: COMMENTARIES OF THE LORD PETER MARTYR VERMILI, OF FLORENCE, ON THE FIRST BOOK OF ARISTOTLE'S NICOMACHEAN ETHICS.

units.la: OMNIS nostra noticia vel est revelata vel acquisita: in primo membro Theologia, in altero Philosophia. Nomẽ Philosophiæ compositum est. Sapientia dicitur à nonnullis omnium rerum quæ sunt notitia. Sed cum Sapientia non comprehendat nisi certam & indubitatam cognitionem, haud potest esse omnium: nam singularia ignorantur, fortuita & contingentia propter illorum inconstantiam sciri non possunt. Aiunt alii eam esse diuinarum & humanarum rerum scientiam: verum inter diuina & humana multa reperiuntur, cœlorum orbes, astra elementa, meteora lapides, mineralia, stirpes, bruta. Sed cœlum referunt ad Deum, quòd sit immortale: inferiora dicunt ad homines attinere quòd sint corruptibilia. Sed quo loco habebunt Mathematicam? Sed videtur definienda, vt sit, Habitus mentibus humanis à Deo concessus, industria & exercitio auctus, quo comprehenduntur omnia quæ sunt, quà certò et firma ratione comprehendi possunt, vt ad felicitatem homo perueniat. Omnia sunt hic genera causarum. Forma quæ est habitus. Materia in qua inhæret, mens inquam & ratio humana, & illa circa quæ vt obiecta versatur, nempe circa omnia quæ sunt, haud simpliciter & absolutè, sed quà certò cognosci possunt. Agens attingitur, quòd nimirum Deus ponatur auctor: is enim lucem inseruit nostris mentibus, & semina indidit quæ principia sunt omnium scientiarum. Vnde Cicero prima Tusculana dicit Philosophiam donum & inuentum Deorum: quod item concedit Lucretius, licet fuerit Epicureus. Et quoniam certa notitia omnium rerum magis optari potest quàm sperari, & facilius amatur quàm possideatur, ac quo magis in eam incumbimus eo plus erga illam incendimur, idcò appellata est Philosophia. Nominis huius auctor fuit Pythagoras, is cũ Philon-tem veniesset, loqueretur, cum Leonte qui erat ibi tyrannus, is admiratus hominis ingenium & eloquentiam, de illo quæsiuit quam artem seu scientiam profiteretur, is noluit dicere se esse sapientem, sed sapientiæ studiosum, id est philosophum.
units.tr: All our knowledge is either revealed or acquired: the first belongs to Theology, the second to Philosophy. The name Philosophy is compounded. Some call wisdom the knowledge of all things that exist. But since wisdom comprehends only certain and indubitable knowledge, it cannot be of all things: singular things are unknown, and chance and contingent things cannot be known because of their inconstancy. Others say it is the science of divine and human things. But among divine and human things there are many: the orbs of the heavens, the stars, the elements, meteors, stones, minerals, plants, animals. They refer the heavens to God, because they are immortal, and say that the lower things pertain to human beings, because they are corruptible. But where will they place mathematics? It seems that wisdom should be defined as a habit granted to human minds by God, increased by industry and exercise, by which all things that exist are comprehended, insofar as they can be grasped by a certain and firm reason, so that man may attain happiness. Here are all the kinds of causes. The form is the habit. The matter in which it inheres is the mind and human reason, and the things with which it is occupied as its objects, namely all things that exist, not simply and absolutely, but insofar as they can be known with certainty. The efficient cause is touched on, since God is plainly posited as the author: for he kindled light in our minds and sowed the seeds that are the principles of all the sciences. Hence Cicero, in the first book of the Tusculan Disputations, says that philosophy is a gift and discovery of the gods, which Lucretius also concedes, although he was an Epicurean. And since certain knowledge of all things is more to be wished for than hoped for, and is more easily loved than possessed, and the more we apply ourselves to it the more we are kindled toward it, it was therefore called philosophy. The author of this name was Pythagoras. When he came to Phlius and spoke with Leon, who was tyrant there, Leon, admiring the man's talent and eloquence, asked him what art or science he professed. He refused to say that he was wise, but said he was a lover of wisdom, that is, a philosopher.

units.la: A Sic definita secatur in partem Agentem & Contemplantem, quarum utramq; Aristoteles tractauit prout subiectu erat capax. Ista sic differūt quod Θεωρητικὸν solum spectat, πρακτικὸν agit cognita. Finibus igitur discrepāt: Θεωρητικὸν in ipsa rerum contemplatione quiescit, quoniam eas facere non potest: τὸ δὲ πρακτικὸν ideo contemplatur, ut cognita exprimat opere. Ac certè in homine duo videmus opera: intelligit enim, deinde agit. Quemadmodum Deus non solum intelligit seipsum, sibi felix est & perfectus, verum etiam sua prouidentia creat et producta gubernat. Sic & hominis duplex habetur felicitas, una quàm πρακτικῶ dicere possumus, & de ea scribit Aristoteles primo libro: alteram contemplantem, & de illa decimo disputabit, quæ est longè perfectior & exquisitior. Unde patet hominem, si perficiatur hac gemina felicitate, nonnihil accedere ad Dei similitudinem. Quare Plato dixit in Phædone, Philosophiā esse ὁμοίωσιν θεῷ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἀνθρώ[?]πῳ. Neq; datur ista distinctio Practici & speculatiui, ut quidā sentiunt, per intellectus & voluntatis nostræ opera: hoc enim fieri non debet, quia scientiæ per obiecta distinguuntur. Sed si quis rem diligentius excutiat, videbit penes res quæ intelliguntur accipiendam. Nam ipsæ aut causas habent Deum & naturam: & tunc ad Speculatiuum genus pertinent, quoniam talia nos electione nostra haud possumus facere. Aliæ verò sunt quæ nos habent pro causis, quas volumus & eligimus: & huiusmodi sunt Practicæ facultatis.
units.tr: Philosophy, thus defined, is divided into the active and the contemplative part, and Aristotle treated both of these as far as the subject allowed. They differ in this way: the theoretical [θεωρητικὸν] looks only to the object, while the practical [πρακτικὸν] acts upon the things known. They therefore differ in their ends: the theoretical rests in the very contemplation of things, since it cannot make them; the practical contemplates in order to express what it knows in work. And certainly we see two operations in a human being: he understands, and then he acts. Just as God not only understands himself and is happy and perfect in himself, but also by his providence creates and governs the things he has produced, so also man has a twofold happiness: one we may call practical, and Aristotle writes about it in the first book; the other contemplative, which he will discuss in the tenth book, and which is far more perfect and exquisite. Hence it is plain that a human being, if he is perfected by this twofold happiness, comes somewhat closer to the likeness of God. Therefore Plato said in the Phaedo that philosophy is "likeness to God as far as is possible for a human being" [ὁμοίωσιν θεῷ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἀνθρώπῳ]. Nor is this distinction between the practical and the speculative, as some think, made by the works of our intellect and will: for this should not happen, because the sciences are distinguished by their objects. But if one examines the matter more carefully, one will see that it must be taken from the things that are understood. For some things have God and nature as their causes, and these belong to the speculative kind, since we cannot by our choice make such things. Other things, however, are those which have us as their causes, which we wish and choose; and of this kind are the practical faculties.

units.la: Utra vero istarum sit præstantior videndum est. Vulgata & recepta opinione Speculatiuum præfertur Practico. Siquidem Agens ad Contemplans ordinatur, & non secus. Id autem quòd in aliud ordinatur, esse illo indignius nemo ambigit. At se rursus opponunt Θεωρητικὸν genus ad Actionem spectare, ideo enim contemplamur naturam ut eius auctorem amemus, & Deum ideo quærimus, agnoscere, ut eum colamus, & nostra Theologia ista de causa dicta est à nonnullis Practica. At isti sic ratiocinando vehementer falluntur: non enim propterea dicitur aliqua scientia Practica, quòd ad illam notitiam consequatur opus, sed si illud idem perficiatur quod prius est cognitum. Quando naturam & cœlum contemplamur, etiamsi consequatur inde cultus & dilectio erga Deum, non debet dici talis noticia Practica: siquidem id non efficitur quod contemplamur: nemo enim est qui naturam & cœlum possit facere & alia opera quæ inde sequuntur, per accidens dicuntur consequi: non enim omnes qui hæc contemplantur, Deum amât aut colunt, imò ab eo sunt frequenter longè alienissimi. Deinde opera quæ consequuntur illam noticiam & etiam Theologiam nostram, eò spectant ut Deum magis ac magis gis cognoscamus, quoad ipsum in patria possimus à facie ad faciem intueri. Et Christus seruator noster hanc sententiam confirmauit, dicens: Hæc est vita æterna, vt agnoscant te solum verum Deum & quem misisti Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Which of these is the more excellent must be considered. By the common and accepted opinion, the speculative is preferred to the practical. For the active is ordered to the contemplative, and not the other way round. Now that which is ordered to another is admittedly less worthy than that to which it is ordered. But on the other side it is objected that the theoretical kind looks to action: for we contemplate nature so that we may love its author, and we seek God so that we may know him and worship him; and for this reason some have called our theology practical. But those who reason thus are greatly mistaken: for a science is not called practical because knowledge of it is followed by a work, but only if the very thing that was first known is itself carried out. When we contemplate nature and the heavens, even if worship and love of God follow from this, such knowledge ought not to be called practical, since what we contemplate is not thereby made. No one can make nature and the heavens; the other works that follow from them are said to follow only incidentally. For not all who contemplate these things love or worship God; indeed they are often very far from him. Moreover, the works that follow that knowledge, and also our theology, tend to this, that we may know God more and more, so that in our homeland we may be able to see him face to face. And Christ our Saviour confirmed this opinion, saying: "This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" [John 17.3].

units.la: Nec solum hæc duo membra diuidunt Philosophiam, sed etiam nostrū intellectum, unde unus vocatur Practicus & alter Speculatiuus, nō quasi sint duæ vires aut facultates animi, sed quia vt circa ista vel illa versatur intellectus, aut speculatiuus aut practicus dicitur.
units.tr: Nor do these two parts alone divide philosophy, but also our intellect: hence the one is called practical and the other speculative, not as if they were two powers or faculties of the soul, but because the intellect is called speculative or practical according to whether it is occupied with these things or those.

units.la: Philosophia speculatiua secatur in tres partes: quoniam aliqua vel avulsa & secreta sunt prorsus à materia, vt Deus & intelligentiæ, atq; habentur τὰ μεταφυσικὰ: aut in materia sic inhærent vt absq; illa nec definiri quidè possint, & ita sunt φυσικά: vel medio se habent modo, non enim esse possunt citra materiam, ferrcam aut lignem, &c. & tamen absq; illa & definiri possunt & intelligi, vt Mathematica.
units.tr: Speculative philosophy is divided into three parts: for some things are wholly separated and set apart from matter, such as God and the intelligences, and these are called the metaphysical; others are so present in matter that they cannot even be defined without it, and these are physical; others stand in a middle way, for they cannot exist apart from matter, such as bronze or wood, etc., and yet they can be both defined and understood without it, as in mathematics.

units.la: Possunt hæc vlterius distingui, sed supersedeo, & τὰ πρακτικὰ sic diseca-bo, vt præcepta ibi tradantur quoad vitam & institutionem vel vnius vel multorum. Si vnius, est liber Ethicorum: si multorum, vel illi sunt numero plures aut pauciores: Si sint pauciores, Oeconomica fiunt: sin complures, τὰ πολιτικά. Sed Artes vbi relinquemus? Comprehenduntur sub ter-tio genere Practici & pertinent ad Politica, nec à genere Sapientiæ sunt excludenda. Ars enim est σύστημα ἐκ καταλήψεων ἐγγεγυμνασμένων πρὸς τι τέλος δύναμιν τὴν ἐν τῷ βίῳ. Duo in ista definitione patent. Primum quòd Ars sit habitus pertinens ad noticiam, qua certò comprehenduntur aliqua, nimirum per exercitationem & experientiam. Unde à Sapientia non potest excludi. Neque dubitandum est veteres appellasse sapientes illos qui has artes adinuenerunt, vel in eis excelluerunt. Unde Bezeleel & Aoliab dicti sunt in sacris literis sapientes. Alterum quod dicimus est, Noticiam hanc esse practicam, nam per exercitationem ista noscuntur, & aliquid his habitibus præstatur & efficitur, quod ad vitam iuuandam conducit: quare funambuli, præstigatores, & alij huiusmodi qui nihil præstant quod humanæ vitæ sit vtile, non artifices, sed impostores & nugatores dici debent.
units.tr: These may be divided further, but I pass over this, and I will divide the practical [τὰ πρακτικὰ] thus: that precepts are delivered there concerning the life and conduct of either one person or many. If of one, it is the book of Ethics; if of many, these are either more or fewer in number: if fewer, they become Economics; if more, they are the Politics. But where shall we leave the arts? They are comprehended under the third kind of the practical and pertain to Politics, nor are they to be excluded from the kind of wisdom. For an art is "a system of well-exercised grasps toward some end, a power in life" [σύστημα ἐκ καταλήψεων ἐγγεγυμνασμένων πρὸς τι τέλος δύναμιν τὴν ἐν τῷ βίῳ]. Two things are evident in this definition. First, that an art is a habit pertaining to knowledge, by which certain things are grasped with certainty, namely through practice and experience. Hence it cannot be excluded from wisdom. Nor should we doubt that the ancients called wise those who invented these arts or excelled in them. Hence Bezalel and Oholiab are called wise in the sacred letters. The other point we make is that this knowledge is practical, for these things are known through exercise, and by these habits something is accomplished and effected that helps and advances life; therefore juggler-tricksters, conjurers and others of this kind, who produce nothing useful to human life, ought not to be called artists, but impostors and triflers.

units.la: Possunt autem diuidi artes in eas quæ aliquod opus producunt, & eas quæ in ipsa consumuntur actione. Apparet iam ex his quidnam de Dialectica existimandum, quandoquidem & ipsa inter artes censenda est, & res in vita vtilissimas efficit: unde non est à Sapientia diuidenda, præsertim cum [illegible, ~6 letters], organum & via qua vindicamus nobis sapientiā: neq; via praecidenda est à termino. Quin et Cicero distinxit Philosophiae partes, vt sit partim de vita & moribus, partim de natura & rebus occultis, aut de arte differendi: in primo Academ. quod ex Platone refert. Neq; Galen. ab ista sententia dissidet. De auctoribus autem Philosophiae sciendum est, quòd plus orbi profuerunt quàm Ceres quae fruges invenit, quà Bacchus à quo vina sunt reperta, quàm Hercules qui monstris orbem repurgavit: nam haec ad vitam corporis tuendam pertinent, sed Philosophia ipsum animum alit & instruit.
units.tr: Arts may be divided into those that produce some work and those that consist entirely in the action itself. It is now clear what must be thought of Dialectic, since it too is to be counted among the arts and produces things most useful in life. Therefore it should not be separated from Wisdom, especially since [illegible] is the instrument and the way by which we claim wisdom for ourselves, and the way should not be cut off from the goal. Indeed Cicero also distinguished the parts of philosophy, so that it is partly concerned with life and morals, partly with nature and hidden things, or with the art of disputing, as he reports from Plato in the first Academica. Nor does Galen dissent from this view. Concerning the authors of philosophy, it must be known that they have benefited the world more than Ceres, who discovered grain, more than Bacchus, by whom wines were discovered, and more than Hercules, who cleansed the world of monsters. For those pertain to preserving the life of the body, but philosophy nourishes and instructs the mind itself.

units.la: In istis autem libris Philosophiae Practicae primus quem habemus pra manibus, nimirum Ethicorum sic se habet ad reliquos, vt liber de physico audi tu: nam vt ibi traduntur elementa naturalium tractationum, ita hic Oeconomica & Politica prima videas contineri principia: ideo ipsum ante omnes alios interpretabimur. Et licet fateamur hanc facultatem quandam sumere à Physico, vt est distinctio partium animi, quodque effectus in eisdem animis reperiantur, ex quibus principijs multa instituit & efficit, non tamen potest iudicari ex numero scientiarum subalternarum, quoniam physica & ethica toto genere distant, quod non oportet esse in subalternis, vbi est necessarium vt subiectum scientiae superioris comprehendat subiectum inferioris.
units.tr: In these books of Practical Philosophy, the first that we have in hand, the Ethics, stands in relation to the others as the book On Physics does. For just as there the elements of natural investigation are handed down, so here you may see the first principles of Economics and Politics contained. Therefore we shall interpret it before all the others. And although we grant that this discipline takes a certain element from Physics, namely the distinction of the parts of the soul, and that the effects found in those same souls are the principles from which it establishes and accomplishes many things, nevertheless it cannot be judged by the number of subordinate sciences. Physics and Ethics differ entirely in kind, and this ought not to be the case in subordinate sciences, where the subject of the higher science must comprehend the subject of the lower.

units.la: Ethica dicitur ἀπὸ τοῦ ἤθους, quod est mos. ἠθικὴ vero ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐθίζειν[?] in conversatione: non enim mores & bonos habitus adipiscimur nisi consuetudine. Versatur autem totus iste liber circa hominem, quà praeditus fiat virtutibus, & felicitatem quam hic haberi potest assequatur. Quare Plato in [illegible, ~9 letters] hanc partem philosophiae μεγιστὴν ἠθικὴν[?] appellavit, non quasi agatur hic de sonis, vocibus aut fidibus, verum de concordia partium animi cum ratione. Qua vero ratione docendi utatur Aristoteles in hoc libro, videre non est difficile. Diuidit & definit, & omnibus fere argumentorum generibus utitur, nonnunquam exemplis, aliquando inductione, interdum enthymematis, aliquando ratiocinatione perfecta, quam syllogismum appellant, eoque demonstrativo, sed raro, quoniam instabilis et incerta est natura morum, ideoque verisimilibus frequenter utitur, & demonstrationibus aliquando sed a posteriori per causas autem & priora nunquam fere aut quam rarissime.
units.tr: Ethics is so called from ἦθος [ēthos], which means custom, and ēthikē [ēthikē] from ἐθίζειν [ethizein], to accustom, in conversation. For we acquire good morals and good habits only by custom. This whole book is concerned with man, insofar as he is endowed with virtues, and attains the happiness that can be had here. Hence Plato called this part of philosophy megistēn ēthikēn [μεγιστὴν ἠθικὴν] in [illegible], not as if this treats of sounds, voices or lyres, but of the harmony of the parts of the soul with reason. How Aristotle uses the method of teaching in this book is not hard to see. He divides and defines, and he uses almost all kinds of arguments: sometimes examples, sometimes induction, at times enthymemes, and sometimes complete reasoning, which they call syllogism, and that demonstrative, but rarely, since the nature of morals is unstable and uncertain. Therefore he frequently uses probabilities, and sometimes demonstrations drawn a posteriori, but almost never, or very rarely, demonstrations through causes and prior things.

units.la: Inuentores philosophiae huius partis dicuntur fuisse Pythagoras, Socrates, & Plato. Quoniam antiquiores Parmenides, Melissus, Anaxagoras, Democritus, Empedocl.s[?], Hippocrates, toti fuerunt in natura rerum excutienda. Socrates primus animum serio appulit ad mores & vitam instituendam. Ante quem illi septem Graeciae sapientes aliqua sane dixerunt quae ad vitā componendam facerent, vt Solon, Pittacus & alij, sed tantum quæ dixerunt erant sententiæ quædam, elegantes quidem & celebres, in quibus tamen nihil fuit absoluti aut perfecti. Post Platonem vero successit Aristoteles vir ingenij acutissimi, qui omnia huc spectantia in methodum quandam redegit & accuratissime conscripsit. Natus est post septem annos quam Roma fuit à Gallis recuperata. Stagyras habuit patriam in Thracia: obscuram alioqui ciuitatem nisi tantum habuisset ciuem. Patrem item habuit Nicomachum artem medicum, & propter illam artem Amyntæ regi patri Philippi charissimum. Audiuit Aristoteles aliquandiu Socratem, sed viginti annos totos Platonem. Discipulum instituit Alexandrum Macedonem, qui dicere solebat, se Aristoteli plus debere quam Philippo regi à quo fuerat procreatus, quòd Philippus tantum sibi dedisset vt esset, Aristoteles autem vt bene ac feliciter esse posset. Is[?] in sui præceptoris gratiam Stagyras, quæ fuerat à Philippo diruta, instauravit, & in meliorem formam Reipublicæ redegit quàm antea fuisset quàm euerteretur. Ab hoc Aristotele secta Peripateticorum est orta, quæ minus habet errorum quàm ulla alia secta, & usque in hunc diem floret.
units.tr: The inventors of this part of philosophy are said to have been Pythagoras, Socrates and Plato. Earlier were Parmenides, Melissus, Anaxagoras, Democritus, Empedocles and Hippocrates, who were wholly occupied with examining the nature of things. Socrates was the first to apply his mind seriously to forming morals and life. Before him those seven sages of Greece did indeed say some things that would serve to order life, such as Solon, Pittacus and others, but what they said were only certain maxims, elegant and famous indeed, in which nevertheless there was nothing complete or perfect. After Plato, however, came Aristotle, a man of most acute genius, who reduced everything bearing on this to a certain method and wrote it out most accurately. He was born seven years after Rome was recovered from the Gauls. His homeland was Stagira in Thrace, otherwise an obscure city, unless it had had only this one citizen. He also had as his father Nicomachus, a physician, and because of that art he was most dear to King Amyntas, the father of Philip. Aristotle heard Socrates for some time, but Plato for twenty whole years. He trained Alexander the Macedonian as his pupil, who used to say that he owed more to Aristotle than to King Philip, by whom he had been begotten, since Philip had given him only that he might exist, but Aristotle that he might live well and happily. For the sake of his teacher, Aristotle restored Stagira, which had been destroyed by Philip, and brought it back to a better form of commonwealth than it had before it was overthrown. From this Aristotle the school of the Peripatetics arose, which has fewer errors than any other school and flourishes down to this day.

units.la: Hæc Ethica dicuntur Nicoma-chum, vt Cicero libros de officijs: præclara sanè duo scriptorum genera, quorum doctrina & fama neuter istorum filiorum parentibus responderit. Scio esse nonnullos qui putarint Nicomachum ipsum filium Aristotelis hos libros conscripsisse, quasi à patre doctrinam prius acceperit, postea ipse collegerit ac in vnum volumen redegerit. Et Suidas testatur Nicomachum scripsisse De moribus 10. libros, sed an illi sint isti, plurimum est incertum. Quin & Cicero sentire videtur Nicomachum hos libros conscripsisse libro 5. de finibus. Extant & Magna moralia, & quæ vocantur Eudemia, sed cum istis non sunt conferenda.
units.tr: This Ethics is said to be addressed to Nicomachus, as Cicero's books On Duties are addressed to his son. Truly these are two distinguished kinds of writings, of which neither of those sons lived up to the teaching and fame of their parents. I know there are some who have thought that Nicomachus, Aristotle's son himself, wrote these books, as if he had first received the teaching from his father and afterwards collected it himself and reduced it into one volume. And Suidas testifies that Nicomachus wrote ten books On Morals, but whether those are these is very uncertain. Indeed Cicero seems to think in the fifth book On Ends that Nicomachus wrote these books. The Magna Moralia also exist, and the so-called Eudemian Ethics, but these are not to be compared with those.

units.la: Quoad ordinem huius facultatis Moralis ad alias scientias, ita veteres constituerunt, vt qui Grammaticam Rhetoricam & Dialecticam iam didicisset, ad Moralia statim animum appelleret: quoniam si animus æstuet affectibus, & vitijs obruatur, non est idoneus ad Mathematica, diuina & naturalia contemplanda, cùm ea tranquillum & sedatum animum requirant. Inter hæc verò Moralia primum locum habent Ethica, deinde Oeconomica, postremò Politica: in quo ego ordine circulum animaduerto. Quoniam primum per Ethicam fiunt boni singillatim qui eius studiosi fuerint: qui si probi euadent, bonas reddunt familias: atque familia cum rectè fuerint institutata, bonas efficiunt respublicas: in quibus rursus et leges & magistratus nil aliud spectant quam ut boni fiant singuli cives: non enim tantum corporibus prospectum volunt sed animis, atq; id curant ut cives ex virtute vivant.
units.tr: As to the order of this moral discipline in relation to the other sciences, the ancients arranged it so that one who had already learned grammar, rhetoric and dialectic should at once turn his mind to moral subjects. For if the mind boils with passions and is overwhelmed by vices, it is not fit for contemplating mathematical, divine and natural things, since these require a calm and tranquil mind. Among these moral subjects, Ethics has the first place, then Economics, and lastly Politics; in this order I notice a circle. For first through Ethics individuals become good, those who are diligent in it. If they turn out upright, they make their households good, and households, when they have been rightly instituted, make good commonwealths. In these again both laws and magistrates aim at nothing other than that individual citizens become good. For they wish to provide not only for bodies but for souls, and they take care that the citizens live by virtue.

units.la: De methodo autem horum decem librorum sic accipite. Primū de fine humanæ vitæ agitur, & is definitur in Primo, vbi traditur felicitatem esse operationem virtutis perfectæ. Quare sequitur ut natura virtutis consideretur, quod fit in secundo, vbi primum de virtutib. agitur, non quidem intellectus, sed quæ pertinent ad affectus moderādos, & declaratur talis virtus esse habitus inter excessum & defectum. In Tertio principia virtutū traduntur: nā ibi de voluntario, involuntario, electione atq; huiusmodi agitur: et à Fortitudine singillatim inchoatur virtutum particularium tractatio: & deinceps in ea re totus Quartus & Quintus consumitur. Postea in Sexto de his habitibus disputat Aristoteles, qui rationem seu intellectū ornāt, ut est, Prudentia, Industria, Solertia, ut huius ordinis complures alij. Septimo de virtute heroica, quæ iam descriptas longe superat, & de Continentia seu Incontinentia quæ ad virtutes & vitia perfecte non attinent. Octauo & Nono de amicitia. Decimo vero permulta scribuntur de voluptate, ac denique sermo est de vera & absoluta felicitate, quæ in rerum præsertim diuinarum contemplatione si-ta est. Ego vero sum interpretando rationem ac formam hanc persecuturus. Primum partiar propositum Aristotelis textum: secundo scopum & propositionem loci assumpti exponam cum eius probatione: tertio sensum & verba excutiam, quæ visa fuerint expositione indigere: quarto quæ dubia fuerint, ostendam: & ad extremum pro locis communibus admonebo quid cum diuinis literis, quæ allata fuerint consentiant vel dissentiant.
units.tr: Concerning the method of these ten books, take it thus. First the end of human life is treated, and it is defined in the First, where it is taught that happiness is the operation of perfect virtue. It follows that the nature of virtue must be considered, which is done in the Second, where first of all virtues are treated, not those of the intellect, but those which pertain to moderating the affections, and it is declared that such a virtue is a habit lying between excess and deficiency. In the Third the principles of the virtues are handed down, for there the voluntary, the involuntary, choice and such things are treated, and the treatment of the particular virtues begins singly with Courage. Thereafter the whole Fourth and Fifth are consumed with that matter. Afterwards, in the Sixth, Aristotle disputes about those habits which adorn reason or the intellect, such as Prudence, Industry, Shrewdness, and several others of this order. In the Seventh he treats of heroic virtue, which far surpasses those already described, and of Continence or Incontinence, which do not pertain perfectly to virtues and vices. In the Eighth and Ninth he treats of friendship. In the Tenth very many things are written about pleasure, and finally the discourse is about true and absolute happiness, which lies especially in the contemplation of divine things. I, for my part, in interpreting shall pursue this plan and form. First I shall divide Aristotle's proposed text; second I shall set out the aim and proposition of the passage taken up, with its proof; third I shall examine the sense and words which seem to need explanation; fourth I shall show what is doubtful; and at last, for the commonplaces, I shall point out what agrees or disagrees with the divine letters that have been adduced.

units.la: Nunc ad exponendum Aristotelem facile possem descendere, nisi remora quædam prius esset amolienda. Ea vero est, quòd Paulus 2. ad Colossenses dicit, Videte ne quis vos deprædetur per philosophiam. Quibus sanè verbis Christianos viros à philosophiæ studio videtur absterrere. Sed vos animaduersò Apostoli sensu, certo scio, nil turbabimini. Vera philosophia cum ex notitia creaturarum colligatur, & multa concludat ex his propositionibus de iustitia & rectitudine quæ Deus naturaliter mentibus hominum inseruit, iure accusari nō potest: est enim Dei opus & absq; illius munere singulari ab hominibus haberi non potuit. Sed Paulus eam philosophiam reprehendit quæ hominum inuentis et ambitiosis certaminibus Philosophorum est vitiata. Quòd si cōstitissent intra limites, & de his tantū pronunciassent quæ notitia creaturarū de Deo & natura certissimis rationibus indicabat, à vero non aberassent. Unde ait de ait Apostolus, διὰ τῆς φιλοσοφίας[?], & per ἐπεξήγησιν, κενῆς ἀπάτης[?], vanâ inquam deceptionem: & subdit, quæ sunt secundum hominum traditionem & elementa mundi. Mundum æternum esse tradiderunt homines, non creatum. Mundum ex atomorum concursu ac temere constare natura non ostedit, sed vanæ cogitationes confinxerunt. Stoicorum fatum & ἀπάθειαν[?], Academicorum perpetuam dubitationem, Epicureorum deitatem otiosam & nihil agentem, fuisse vanam huiusmodi deceptionem quis dubitet? rerum communitatem, promiscuas uxores in rebus publicis, uoluptatem summum bonum, et deos esse more vulgi colendos homines somniarunt, non autem ex naturali lumine, ac propositionibus practicis quæ per seipsas notæ sunt, certis rationibus cognouerunt. Ista sanè venena sunt & corruptiones quibus diabolus donum Dei Philosophiam per malos homines corrupit, eamq; sic in quinatam[?] & corruptam vitari Paulus voluit.
units.tr: Now I could easily proceed to expound Aristotle, were it not that a certain obstacle must first be removed. It is this: Paul says in 2 Colossians, "See that no one spoils you through philosophy." By these words he seems to frighten Christian men away from the study of philosophy. But I am sure that, if you grasp the Apostle's meaning, you will not be troubled at all. True philosophy, when it is gathered from knowledge of creatures and draws many conclusions from those propositions about justice and righteousness which God has naturally implanted in the minds of men, cannot rightly be accused. For it is God's work, and without his singular gift it could not have been had by men. But Paul rebukes that philosophy which has been corrupted by the inventions and ambitious contentions of philosophers. If they had kept within limits, and pronounced only on those things which knowledge of creatures indicated about God and nature by most certain reasons, they would not have strayed from the truth. Hence the Apostle says "through philosophy" and, by way of explanation, "empty deceit" [κενῆς ἀπάτης], vain deception, I mean; and he adds, "which are according to the tradition of men and the elements of the world." Men have taught that the world is eternal, not created. That the world consists of a chance concourse of atoms, nature does not show; vain thoughts have invented it. Who could doubt that the fate and apathy [ἀπάθεια] of the Stoics, the perpetual doubt of the Academics, and the idle God who does nothing, of the Epicureans, were such vain deception? Men have dreamed up the community of goods, wives held in common in commonwealths, pleasure as the chief good, and gods to be worshipped after the manner of the crowd; they did not come to know these things by the natural light and by practical propositions which are known through themselves, by sound reasons. These are indeed poisons and corruptions by which the devil, through evil men, has corrupted philosophy, the gift of God, and Paul wished it to be avoided in this polluted and corrupted state.

units.la: At iam videndum est quonam modo sacris literis respondeant quæ hactenus diximus. Habemus ibi quoq; Practicam & Contemplatiuam. Quæ credimus & in articulis fidei continentur, pertinent ad θεωρητικὸν, quoniam illa notitia percipimus sed non facimus, & quauis scientia non comprehenditur, sed nihilominus intelliguntur: ad Practica referenda sunt quæ in legibus, consiliis & adhortationib. continentur. Hucusq; ista consentiunt: differunt attamen, quoniam in philosophia θεωρητικὸν antecedit πρακτικόν, quia, ut dictum est, neq; Deum neq; naturam possumus contemplari humanis uiribus, nisi prius affectus nostri pacati fuerint. At in sacris literis priori loco Speculatiuum occurrit, quantumprius credendum est & fide iustificamur, postea sequuntur bona opera, idq; magis & cumulatius quo à spiritu sancto plus indies instauramur. Ita Paulus in Epistolis demonstrat: prius enim tractat dogmata, postea descendit ad morum instructionem & ad vitam componendam. Sic & filij Israel prius in Aegypto sunt collecti sub fide unius Dei seruatoris, postea in deserto leges acceperunt quæ ad practicam notitiam faciunt. Et in Decalogo idem ordo seruatur: primò enim dicit, Ego sum dominus Deus tuus: quod attinet ad fidem seu speculatiuam notitiam: postea consequuntur præcepta quæ ad opera spectant a Deo requisita. Discriminis huius causa est, quòd humanæ contemplationes acquiruntur indagatione atq; industria meditandi, & ideo sunt necessarij moderati affectus. Verum quæ credimus, afflatu Dei recipiuntur. Quare illis præparationib. nō est opus. Atq; humana ratione prius oportet homines iusta facere, quâ ut iustificentur. At diuinæ sanctificationis ordo longè aliter instituitur: prius n. credimus, postea iustificamur, deinde spiritu et gra-
units.tr: But now we must see how the things we have said so far agree with the sacred letters. There too we have a practical and a contemplative part. The things we believe and which are contained in the articles of faith belong to the theoretical [θεωρητικόν], since we perceive that knowledge but do not make it, and it is not grasped by any science, yet is nonetheless understood. Those things which are contained in laws, counsels and exhortations are to be referred to the practical. So far these agree. They differ, however, because in philosophy the theoretical comes before the practical, since, as has been said, we cannot contemplate God or nature by human powers unless our affections have first been calmed. But in the sacred letters the speculative comes first: we must first believe, and we are justified by faith; afterwards good works follow, and the more abundantly as we are renewed by the Holy Spirit day by day. Paul demonstrates this in his Epistles: for he first treats the doctrines, and afterwards descends to the instruction of morals and to ordering life. So too the sons of Israel were first gathered in Egypt under faith in the one God, the Saviour; afterwards in the desert they received laws which pertain to practical knowledge. The same order is kept in the Decalogue: for first it says, "I am the Lord your God," which pertains to faith or speculative knowledge; afterwards follow the precepts which concern the works required by God. The cause of this difference is that human contemplations are acquired by inquiry and by the diligence of meditation, and therefore moderated affections are necessary. But what we believe is received by the inspiration of God. Hence there is no need for such preparations. And by human reason men must first make themselves just, and only then are they justified. But the order of divine sanctification is instituted quite otherwise: for first we believe, afterwards we are justified, then the powers of our mind are restored by the Spirit and grace

units.la: Collatio iam-dictorum cum sacris literis. tia vires animi nostri reparantur, deniq; sequuntur iusta & honesta facta. Finis praeterea philosophiae est, vt illam assequamur beatitudinem seu felicitate quae hic viribus humanis potest acquiri: at pietatis Christianae, vt in nobis ea reparetur imago ad quam sumus conditi in iustitia & sanctitate veritatis, vt in agnitione Dei quotidie crescamus, quoad perducamur ad videndū illū, sicuti est reuelata facie. Ad haec non sumus in his Ethicis audituri de remissione peccatorum, non de timore ac fiducia Dei, nec de iustificatione per fidem Christo aut similibus: ista enim Dei voluntate patefiunt, quae non possunt per naturalem cognitionem ex creaturis vllis elici. Neq; inficiamur saepe contingere vt res eadem hic in Ethicis laudetur, et in sacris literis à Deo praecipiatur, verum tunc illa materia sunt eadem, non etiam forma, proprietatibus & principijs: diuersa enim in ipsis est ratio, diuersae proprietates, nec eadem principia. quemadmodum aquae pluuiae & alicuius fontis materia est eadem, sed vires, proprietas & principia longe diuersa. nam illa fit à calore coeli & nubibus & frigiditate mediae regionis aeris: ista vero vel à meatibus terrae elicitur à mari & colatur ita vt dulcis euadat, aut per conuersionem aeris in aquam ob frigiditatē loci vbi fons oritur. Ita quae facit Christianus, à spiritu Dei impulsus facit: nam qui aguntur spiritu, hi sunt filij Dei. Quae philosophi agunt iuxta ethica praescripta, rationis humanae ductu faciunt. Illi ad haec agenda incitantur quod sic iudicant honestum & rectum esse: at Christiani quod sic Deus censuerit. Illi se putant proficere ac perfici si sic agant: isti quod sit numini obediendum. Illi sibi ipsis credunt: isti Deo & verbis legis quam ipse tulit. Illi φιλωτι[?] laborant, isti vnius Dei amore impelluntur. Ex ista vero multiplici diuersitate fit vt eadem res quod ad materiam attinet, Deo paceat & eius iudicio damnetur. Haec de his differentijs & consensu tum diuinae scripturae tum humanae Philosophiae.
units.tr: Comparison of the aforesaid with the sacred letters. and finally just and honest deeds follow. Moreover, the end of philosophy is that we attain that blessedness or happiness which can be acquired here by human powers; but the end of Christian piety is that in us that image be restored to which we were created, in justice and the holiness of truth, that we may grow daily in the knowledge of God, until we are brought to see him as he is, face to face. In addition, in these Ethics we are not going to hear about the remission of sins, nor about the fear and trust of God, nor about justification through faith in Christ, or similar things; for these are made known by the will of God, and cannot be drawn from any creatures by natural knowledge. Nor do we deny that it often happens that the same thing is praised here in the Ethics and commanded by God in the sacred letters; but then the matter is the same, though not the form, properties and principles. For there is a different reasoning in them, different properties, and not the same principles. It is as with the matter of rainwater and of some spring: the matter is the same, but their powers, properties and principles are far different. For the one is produced by the heat of the sky, the clouds, and the coldness of the middle region of the air; the other is drawn from the veins of the earth, filtered through the sea so that it becomes sweet, or formed by the conversion of air into water because of the coldness of the place where the spring rises. So what a Christian does, he does impelled by the Spirit of God; for those who are led by the Spirit are the sons of God. What philosophers do according to the precepts of ethics, they do by the guidance of human reason. The former are incited to these actions because they judge them honourable and right; Christians, because God has so decreed. The former think they advance and are perfected if they act thus; the latter, because the will of God must be obeyed. The former trust themselves; the latter trust God and the words of the law which he himself gave. The former labour from love of honour [φιλοτιμία]; the latter are impelled by love of the one God. From this manifold difference it comes about that the same thing, as far as its matter is concerned, is pleasing to God and yet is condemned by his judgment. These things I have said about these differences, and about the agreement of both divine Scripture and human philosophy.

units.la: Sed vt ad id redeamus unde sumus digressi, nēpe an ista facultas pietati repugnet, affirmo non magis ei aduersari quàm astrologiam, rem nauticam, militarem, piscationem, venationem, & denique iuris humani prudentiam, quàm omnes intelligunt vt rebus publicis administrādis sit necessaria. ea vero suas leges & iustituta elicit ex propositionibus de iusto & recto mentibus nostris insitis, quas nihilominus easdem philosophi morales excutiunt & exquisitissime versant, ita vt non solum ista cognoscat quàm manifestime, sed etiā vt alijs tradere magna perspicuitate queant. Inde fit vt σοφία apud Graecos dicatur quasi σαφία & σοφὸς quasi σαφής, nempe quod illustret & quae tractat quàm perspicacissima faciat. Itaque ista ratione iurisperiti facile tuerentuerentur suam scientiam partem esse philosophiæ : quamuis de virtute, probitate atque iustitia non tam seuerter suis legibus statuant, ut philosophia de illis eisdem disputat. Nam philosophia, exempli gratia, ingratitudinem quoad omnem hominum statum detestatur: iura vero illam non puniunt nisi ergaparentes à liberis committatur, & à libertis ergapatronos. Humana iura neminem adigunt ut sua det egentibus: at philosophia libera-litatem & munificentiam erga omnes commendat. Quid plura? In laudem philosophiæ huius generis Cicero ita exclamat Tuscul.5. O vitæ philosophia dux, ò virtutis indagatrix expultrixq; vitiorum, quid non modo nos, sed omnino vita hominum sine te esse potuisset? Tu urbes peperisti. Tu dissipatos homines in societatem vitæ convocasti. Tu eos inter se primo domicilijs, deinde coniugijs, tum litterarum et vocum communione iunxisti, tu magistra morum & disciplinæ fuisti, &c. Quàm præclarum sit herbarum, lapidum, metallorum & pharmacorum vires nosse omnes intelligunt, quod & nos minime inficiamur: sed ex hoc nonne consequitur hanc facultatem eximiam esse, quà actus, electiones, artes, methodi, ingenia, virtutes & vitia hominum deprehenduntur? Quid præclarius haberi potest quàm seipsum nosse, & id quàm maximè hinc cognoscimus. Id præterea in memoriâ est reuocandū quod Plato dicebat, facile posse fieri, vt in nobis vehementes amores erga virtutem excitentur, si aliquod eius simulachrum in nostros oculos interdum incurreret. Et è diuerso nostrorum uitiorum bona est causa, quod illam de prope nusquam conspeximus. Non parua est voluptas ex hac scientia, nosse intra quos fines lumen naturæ se debeat continere, ac quousq; suo iure proferre se queat. Et vehemens accenditur Christianismi cultus ex Ethnicorum Ethicis animadversis: nam per collationem intelligimus quàm philosophicis præstent quæ in diuinis literis traduntur: nam sententia est vulgò iactata, Opposita cum simul conferuntur, maiori luce fulgere. Neq; possunt errores euitari commodè, nisi prius noti fuerint: idcirco qui nouit vtranque istarum facultatum, facilius alterius errata cauebit, nimirum humanæ philosophiæ, præsertim cum suis locis fuerint demonstrata.
units.tr: But to return to where we digressed, namely whether this faculty is opposed to piety, I affirm that it is no more opposed to it than astrology, the art of navigation, of war, fishing, hunting, and finally the prudence of human law, which everyone understands is necessary for administering commonwealths. Yet law derives its laws and institutions from the propositions about the just and the right which are implanted in our minds, and these same propositions moral philosophers nonetheless examine and handle most exactly, so that they not only know these things most clearly but can also pass them on to others with great clarity. Hence among the Greeks wisdom is called sophia [σοφία] as if from saphia [σαφία], clarity, and the wise man sophos [σοφὸς] as if saphes [σαφής], clear, namely because it illuminates and makes most perspicuous the things it treats. Therefore by this reasoning jurists could easily claim that their science is a part of philosophy, although they do not lay down laws on virtue, probity and justice as strictly as philosophy disputes about the same things. For philosophy, for example, detests ingratitude toward every condition of men; the laws, however, punish it only when it is committed by children against parents, and by freedmen against patrons. Human laws compel no one to give what is his to the needy; but philosophy commends liberality and munificence toward all. What more? In praise of this kind of philosophy Cicero exclaims thus in the Tusculans, book 5: "O philosophy, guide of life, seeker of virtue and expeller of vices, what could not only we, but the whole life of men, have been without you? You founded cities. You called scattered men together into the fellowship of life. You joined them first by dwellings, then by marriages, then by the common use of letters and speech; you were the teacher of morals and of discipline," and so on. How excellent it is to know the powers of herbs, stones, metals and drugs, everyone understands, and we by no means deny it; but does it not follow from this that this faculty is outstanding by which the acts, choices, arts, methods, talents, virtues and vices of men are discerned? What can be thought more excellent than to know oneself, and this we learn most of all from it? Moreover, it must be recalled what Plato used to say, that it can easily happen that vehement loves of virtue are aroused in us if some image of her should now and then fall before our eyes. And conversely, a good cause of our vices is that we have scarcely ever caught sight of her. No small pleasure comes from this science: to know within what limits the light of nature ought to keep itself, and how far it may rightly extend itself. And the worship of Christianity is kindled more vehemently when the ethics of the Gentiles are observed; for by comparison we understand how far the things handed down in the divine letters surpass the philosophical ones, for the saying commonly tossed about is that opposites, when set side by side, shine with greater light. Nor can errors be conveniently avoided unless they have first been known; therefore he who knows both of these faculties will more easily guard against the errors of the other, namely of human philosophy, especially when they have been demonstrated in their places.

units.la: Nunc iam propius ad rem accedamus, inducendo quandam aliam bre- viorem diuisionem tractationis Aristotelis. Primò agit de fine, secundò de his quæ sunt ad finem, ad extremum operis de ipso rursus fine, sed exquisitius. Rationes verò cur de fine primùm omnium agatur multiplices assi-gnantur: Primùm quòd ex illius cognitione oritur materia omnium rerum quæ posthac scribentur. Et quia necessarium est homines habere scopū propositum in quem suas omnes actiones tanquam sagittas ad signum dirigat, quam rationem haud multo inferius audiemus Aristotelem adducere. De-inde ut addit Eustratius, adipisci virtutes est laboriosissimum: est igitur operae precium mercedem proponere. Unde licet finem postremo loco assequamur, illam tamen convenit primum omnium utcunq; cognoscere. Agendo de fine multa inducit: primum, An sit. Deinde de forma qua constituit de ea agere, & auditorum conditione. Tertio Quid sit in quibus consistat bonis. Quarto de modo assequendi finem huiusmodi. Postremo Qualis sit.
units.tr: Now let us come more closely to the matter, introducing another, shorter division of Aristotle's treatise. First he treats of the end, second of the things that relate to the end, and at the close of the work again of the end itself, but more exactly. The reasons why the end is treated first of all are many. First, because from the knowledge of it arises the material of all the things that will be written hereafter; and because it is necessary for men to have a goal set before them, at which they may aim all their actions as arrows at a mark, a reason which we shall hear Aristotle adduce not much further on. Next, as Eustratius adds, to attain the virtues is most laborious, so it is worth the effort to set a reward before us. Hence, although we reach the end last, it is nevertheless fitting to know it first of all, at least in some measure. In treating of the end he brings in many things: first, whether there is one; then, the form in which he has decided to treat of it, and the condition of his hearers; third, what it is and in what goods it consists; fourth, the way of attaining such an end; lastly, what kind it is.
CHAPTER ONE

units.la: Omnis ars, omnis methodus, omnis actio & electio bonum aliquod expetere uidetur. Pro-pterea pulchrè dixerunt ipsum bonum quod omnia expetunt.
units.tr: Every art, every method, every action and choice seems to aim at some good. Therefore those who said that the good is what all things seek spoke well.

units.la: PROPOSITIO est, Humanis rebus est praestitutus aliquis finis. Probatur, Quoniam omnia humana bonum aliquod appetunt: & bonum illud in quod tendunt habet rationem finis: igitur Humana finem praescriptum habent. Boni autem ideò mentionem facit, quòd sit summum praedicatum Felicitatis, & quia rationes boni & finis propinquissimæ sunt, ita ut quidam existimarint bonum & finem conuerti, de qua re inferius dicemus. Unde antiquum pronuntiatum laudat, Omnia bonum appetere. Quod non est intelligendum de uno aliquo: id enim fieri non potest, ut rerum omnium sit unus aliquis finis: verū qualibet res proprium expetit: non enim equus bonum summum hominis, neque canis equi perfectionem expetit, sed unumquodq; suam. Ratio Aristotelis, ut ad euidentem syllogismum reducatur, sic habet:
units.tr: The PROPOSITION is: some end is set for human affairs. It is proved thus: since all human beings seek some good, and that good towards which they tend has the character of an end, human things have an end prescribed to them. He mentions the good because it is the highest attribute of happiness, and because the notions of good and end are very closely related, so that some have thought the good and the end to be the same, a matter we shall discuss further below. Hence he praises the ancient saying that all things seek the good. This must not be understood of one single good, for it cannot be that all things have one single end. Rather, each thing seeks its own proper good: a horse does not seek the highest good of a human being, nor a dog the perfection of a horse, but each seeks its own. Aristotle's reasoning, reduced to a clear syllogism, runs thus:

units.la: Quæcunq; bonum expetunt, finem habent sibi praestitutum.
units.tr: Whatever seeks the good has an end set for it.
Human beings seek the good.
Therefore human beings have an end set for them.

units.la: Maior est manifesta: quoniam appetendo bonum, cùm ad ipsum venerint, conquiescunt: cumque ibi terminetur motus & actio, ibi dicimus finem. Minor probatur: quoniam omnia humana comprehenduntur arte, methodo, actione & electione. Incipit à minori, more solito, & ista quatuor ait bonum appetere. Facit autem propositionem uniuersalem, ut firmior sit. Nam certè hinc fundamentum habemus uniuersæ huius doctrinæ. Superest modò vt singula definiamus: inde enim patefiet finem aliquem omnia ista sectari.
units.tr: The major premise is plain: when things seeking the good reach it, they come to rest; and since motion and action end there, we call it the end. The minor premise is proved thus: all human things are comprised under art, method, action and choice. As is his custom, he begins from the minor, and he says that these four seek the good. He makes the proposition universal so that it may be firmer, for certainly from this we have the foundation of this whole doctrine. It remains now to define each of these things singly, for from that it will become clear that all of them pursue some end.

units.la: Ars est, vt supra definiuimus, ordo seu comprehensio propositionum exercitatione cognitarum, ad aliquem finem vtilem atq; commodum humanæ vitæ: hinc vides finem illam persequi. Dicitur præterea Ars naturam imitari: quare naturam sibi proponit quasi finem, cum ad eam exprimendam tendat. Postremò Ars materiam assumit, vt lapidem, ferrum, aut lignum, eique formam inducere adnititur, quæ forma finis artificiosæ actionis habetur. Possemus etiam Artem definire, vt Aristoteles in 6. Ethicorum, vbi ait, illam esse habitum aptum ad aliquid faciendum cum ratione: Quibus verbis etiam finis demonstratur: eò enim spectat omnis Ars, vt quippiam vel agatur vel fiat. Et Cicero inquit Artem esse certiorem ducem quàm sit natura.
units.tr: Art, as we defined above, is an order or collection of propositions known through practice, directed to some end useful and beneficial for human life; you see from this that it pursues that end. Moreover, art is said to imitate nature, so it sets nature before itself as an end, since it strives to express nature. Finally, art takes up matter, such as stone, iron or wood, and strives to impress a form upon it, and this form is regarded as the end of the artificial action. We could also define art, as Aristotle does in Book 6 of the Ethics, where he says it is a habit concerned with making something, joined with reason. In these words the end is also shown, for every art looks towards something being done or made. And Cicero says that art is a surer guide than nature.

units.la: Methodus, si credimus Eustratio, est ἕξις ἐδλοπουτικὴ [?] μετὰ λόγου, viam facit & parat cum ratione: non enim sinit vt procedamus temere. Vnde Galenus in primo libro De methodo medendi ait, Inquirere & inuenire methodo, opponitur ex aduerso ei quod est fortuitò & temerè: & vti methodo, est via quadam & ordine quippiam inuestigare. Et subdit, Experientiam esse ἀμέθοδον [?], quandoquidem non desiderat artem aut ordinem, sed fauorem fortunæ ad inueniendum quod quæritur. Atque idem scribit libro nono De methodo medendi, Methodum in vniuersalibus esse sitam, exercitationem verò in particularibus: & sicuti nemo consequitur quod vult, nisi se exerceat, ita nemo potest bene seipsum exercere, nisi per methodum. Neq; ars vlla est quæ recte habeatur absque methodo. Μέθοδος [?] Cicero dicit, docendi viam atque rationem. Quidam vertunt istam vocem doctrinam, non male vertunt. Nam in partitionibus ita loquitur Cicero, Quot in partes distribuenda est omnis doctrina dicendi, id est ἡ ἐκ τοῦ ἐκτοπικοῦ [?] μέθοδος. Dicimus itaque methodum seu doctrinam esse habitum qui cum ratione viam facit vel ad cognoscendum vel ad agendum.
units.tr: Method, if we believe Eustratius, is a habit [ἕξις] ... with reason; it makes and prepares a way with reason, for it does not allow us to proceed rashly. Hence Galen in the first book of On the Method of Healing says that to inquire and discover by method is opposed to what happens by chance and rashly, and to use method is to investigate something by a certain way and order. And he adds that experience is without method [ἀμέθοδον], since it does not desire art or order, but relies on the favour of fortune to find what is sought. He writes the same thing in the ninth book of On the Method of Healing: method lies in universals, but practice in particulars; and just as no one attains what he wants unless he exercises himself, so no one can exercise himself well unless by method. Nor is there any art that is rightly held without method. Cicero says that method [μέθοδος] is the way and reasoning of teaching. Some translate this word as doctrine, and they do not translate badly. For in the Partitions Cicero speaks thus: "Into how many parts must all the doctrine of speaking be divided," that is, the method [ἡ ἐκ τοῦ ἐκτοπικοῦ]. We say, therefore, that method, or doctrine, is a habit which, with reason, makes a way either for knowing or for acting.

units.la: Et Galenus de placitis Hippocratis & Platonis triplicem methodum tradit, scilicet primam compositionis & diuisionis, alteram sequentium & pugnantium, tertiam verò maioris & minoris, æqualis et similis. Et in eodem libro inquit Platonem in Phædro & Philebo dicere, diuisionem esse cum incipiendo à summo diuidimus quæcunque occurrunt per differentias, quoad perueniamus ad species atomas: compositionem verò cum è diuerso incipiendo à formis postremis, hoc est speciebus atomis, colligendoq; oēs differētias que ad summum genus vel prædicamentum ascendimus, quo pacto habemus plenam & perfectissimam definitionem. Et certè his qui methodis utũ[?]tur, magnæ sunt agendæ gratiæ: ut enim bene de Republica meritus est Trajanus, qui, ut refert Galenus in libro 9. de methodo medendi, per universam Italiam vias strauit et refecit collapsas, ita qui de methodo aliquid tradunt vehementer studiosos adiuvant. Unde Galenus ibidem inquit, se quiddam accepisse ab Hippocrate, sed rude admodum, quod ipse methodo facile & perspicuum reddidit.
units.tr: And Galen, in his book On the Opinions of Hippocrates and Plato, hands down a threefold method, namely the first of composition and division, the second of sequence and opposition, and the third of greater and less, equal and similar. In the same book he says that Plato, in the Phaedrus and the Philebus, speaks of division as starting from the highest genus and dividing whatever comes to hand by differences until we arrive at the indivisible species, and of composition as starting from the last forms, that is the indivisible species, and gathering all the differences by which we ascend to the highest genus or category, by which means we have a full and most perfect definition. Certainly those who make use of methods deserve great thanks. For just as Trajan deserved well of the commonwealth, who, as Galen relates in the ninth book of On the Method of Healing, laid out roads throughout all Italy and repaired those that had fallen into ruin, so those who hand down something about method greatly help eager students. Hence Galen says in the same place that he had received something from Hippocrates, but in a very rough state, which he himself made easy and clear by method.

units.la: πρᾶξις[?] est humana actio quæ ab electione pendet & regitur. Unde excluditur intellectus operatio, non enim regitur electione, cum sit naturalis, neque aliter esse possit quàm res cognita patiatur.
