units.tr: Practice [πρᾶξις] is human action that depends on and is governed by choice. Hence the operation of the intellect is excluded, for it is not governed by choice, since it is natural and cannot be otherwise than the known thing allows it to be.

units.la: Electio est cum duobus propositis unum alteri præferimus: quare Perionius qui vertit studium & institutum, propriæ significationi minimè satisfecit, quoniam illa duo citra collationem possunt locum habere, & absq; eo ut unum præferatur alteri.
units.tr: Choice is when, of two things proposed, we prefer one to the other. Therefore Perionius, who translates it as "study and purpose," has not satisfied the proper meaning, since those two can exist without comparison and without one being preferred to the other.

units.la: Inquit Videtur, quoniam non semper in verum feruntur bonum, sed interdum apparens persequuntur.
units.tr: He says "seems," because they do not always tend towards the true good, but sometimes pursue the apparent good.

units.la: Non dicit bonũ simpliciter, sed aliquod: quoniam quilibet persequitur quod magis adlubescit atque ubi felicitatem arbitratur sitam. Bonum definiit Seneca quod impetum animi ad se mouet secundum naturam, & bo-num est quod est secundum naturam. Quatuor ista iam hic ab Aristotele commemorata finem aliquem dicuntur appetere, quoniam ea sunt quibus appetimus fines.
units.tr: He does not say "the good" simply, but "some good," since each pursues what pleases him most and where he thinks happiness lies. Seneca defined the good as that which moves the impulse of the mind to itself according to nature, and the good is that which is according to nature. These four things, now mentioned by Aristotle, are said to seek some end, since they are the means by which we seek ends.

units.la: Propterea pulchrè dixerunt ipsum bonum quod omnia appe-tunt.) Confirmat illa quatuor bonum expetere, quia scilicet omnia testimonio antiquorum in bonum ut in finem feruntur. Putant nonnulli sensum esse propterea quoniam illa quatuor bonum expectunt ideo verum esse quod omnia bonum appetant, quasi hoc inductione sit planum. Verum in hanc sententiam ego non discedo, siquidem non est perfecta inductio, quando tantum quatuor sunt allata. Unde potius contra oportet dicere, confirmari quatuor illa bonum appetere quia omnia bonum appetunt, & erit argumentatio ex propositione universali ad particularem, nam et illa quatuor inter ea quæ sunt connumerantur, ideoq; si cuncta bonum desiderant, illa quoque ipsum appetunt. Sed Aristotelis locutio videtur obstare: nam inquit Dio[?], quasi ex dictis inferat. Verum non ita est, nō enim ex dictis hoc infert Aristoteles quod sequitur: verum sensus est: Ideo iudico ad istud quod posui confirmandum pulchrè facere quod omnes antiqui dixerunt bonum, quod appetunt cũcta.
units.tr: Therefore they rightly said that the good itself is what all things seek.) He confirms that these four seek the good, because, by the testimony of the ancients, all things are carried towards the good as towards an end. Some think the sense is that because these four seek the good, it is therefore true that all things seek the good, as if this were made plain by induction. But I do not agree with this view, since it is not a complete induction when only four are adduced. Rather, one ought to say the opposite: that these four are confirmed to seek the good because all things seek the good, and the argument will be from a universal proposition to a particular one, for those four are also among the things that are included, so if all things desire the good, these four also seek it. But Aristotle's wording seems to stand in the way, for he says "Dio[?]," as if inferring from what has been said. But it is not so; Aristotle does not infer from what has been said what follows. The sense is rather: "I judge that to confirm what I have laid down it is well done to say what all the ancients said, that the good is what all things seek."

units.la: Verbum ἀπεφώνατο[?] quidam sunt interpretati. Dixerunt, alij Definierunt: & certè verbum ἀποφαίνομαι vtrunq; significat. Non tamen censenda est haec definitio perfecta, quandoquidem transcedentia definiri non possunt, nihil enim supra se habent quod loco generis queat accipi. Quin & Eustratius ait non esse hanc definitionem, sed descriptionem, verùm suae sententiae non meam affert rationem, sed quod per posteriora datur, quod interpretor, quia oportet prius aliquid esse quàm appetatur & desiderium moueat. At huic malo possumus facilè mederi, quoniam si appeti sumas actu, verum est quod Eustratius dicit: at si potentiam significet quae ipsi bono addatur, ne pe quod habet vim alliciendi & incitandi appetitum, vt sit sensus, Bonum est quod sua natura est expetendum, vel vt dicunt expetibile, non video quin ista possit esse descriptio vera & propria, & illa non raro vsus est Aristoteles.
units.tr: Some have translated the word [ἀπεφώνατο]. Some said "pronounced," others "defined," and certainly the verb [ἀποφαίνομαι] means both. Yet this should not be regarded as a perfect definition, since things that transcend cannot be defined, for they have nothing above them that could be taken in the place of a genus. Indeed Eustratius says that this is not a definition but a description; but he gives his own reasoning for his view, not mine, namely that it is given through what comes later, which I interpret thus: because something must first exist before it is sought and moves desire. But this difficulty can easily be remedied, since if you take "sought" in the sense of actual, what Eustratius says is true; but if it signifies the power that is added to the good itself, that is, that which has the force to attract and stir up appetite, so that the sense is "the good is that which by its nature is to be sought," or as they say, "desirable," I do not see why this cannot be a true and proper description, and Aristotle often used such descriptions.

units.la: Illud τ' ἀγαθὸν aliqui vertunt summum bonum. Et aliqui sunt eò vsq; progressi vt hoc de ipso Deo dictum putent. Qui summum bonum hic accipiunt, ideò mouentur, quòd sentiunt articulum Graecum semper significare quod summum est & praecipuum. Et certè Leonardus Aretinus it a vertit summum bonum, quam sententiam & Trapezuntius est secutus. Qui eodem errore adductus Aristotelem existimauit summam Trinitatem cognouisse quam nos colimus, propterea quòd in primo libro de coelo & mundo trinitatis meminit, adiecto articulo, ἡ τριάς[?]: quem coarguit Bessarion Cardinalis Nicenus, vir sanè inter neotericos Graecos doctissimus, & ait Trapezuntium scire debuisse articulum Graecū dictioni cuipiam adiectum triplicem vsum habere. Nam quandoque indicat rem summam & praecipuam eius generis, de quo sermo institutus, vt si dixerim ὁ αὐτοκράτως[?], Imperatorem significo, non quemuis aut vulgarem ducem belli, sed summum cuiusmodi fuit Augustus, Vespasianus. Alter vsus est, quando ratio & forma designatur absq; particularibus conditionibus, in qua singularia multa conueniunt, vt cum dicimus, ὁ ἄνθρωπος λογικὸς, vbi non sermo fit de isto vel illo singulari homine, verùm de natura & forma communi quae definitur, & quam Socrates, Plato & alia individua participant. Quòd si voluero certum hominem designare, dicam, ἄνθρωπός τις. Denique tertius est vsus, cùm de ea re agitur quae illi est notissima cum quo loquimur, vt cum discipulus condiscipulo suo ait ὁ διδάσκαλος, praeceptorem intelligit bene notum illi cum quo loquitur. Verùm Trapezuntius sic articulum accipit, quasi semper primam vim habeat, atque arbitratur hac ratione summam Trinitatem inuenisse, cùm tamen pro secundo significato verba eius accipi debeant. debeant:nam sensus eius est, ex eo quod omnes res naturæ, principio, medio & fine perficiuntur, antiquos fuisse adductos ut numen colerent in ceremo-niis ἁγιστείαις[?]: trinitatem intelligens naturam et formam communem ternarii numeri, quam omnia quæ tria fuerint participant. Atq; tria designat in unoquoq; rerum genere, principium scilicet, medium & finem cuiuscunq; rei naturalis, quibus singula quæq; perficiuntur. Neq; unquam Aristoteles vel per somnium Patrem, Filium, Spiritum sanctum, quæ sunt tres personæ beatissimæ Trinitatis, cognouit.
units.tr: Some render τ' ἀγαθὸν as "the supreme good," and some have gone so far as to think this was said of God himself. Those who take it as "the supreme good" are moved by the thought that the Greek article always signifies what is highest and pre-eminent. Certainly Leonardo Aretino translates it "the supreme good," and Trapezuntius followed this opinion. Led by the same error, someone supposed that Aristotle knew the supreme Trinity which we worship, because in the first book of On the Heavens and the World he mentions a trinity with the article added, ἡ τριάς. Bessarion, the Cardinal of Nicaea, a man truly most learned among the modern Greeks, refuted this, and says that Trapezuntius ought to have known that the Greek article added to a noun has three uses. For sometimes it indicates the highest and most pre-eminent thing of the kind under discussion: if I said ὁ αὐτοκράτωρ, I would mean the Emperor, not any ordinary general, but the supreme one of that sort, such as Augustus or Vespasian. The second use is when the reason and form is designated without particular conditions, in which many individuals agree, as when we say ὁ ἄνθρωπος λογικός, where the discussion is not about this or that particular man, but about the common nature and form which is defined, and which Socrates, Plato and other individuals share. If I wished to designate a certain man, I would say ἄνθρωπός τις. Finally, there is a third use, when the matter concerns something very well known to the person with whom we are speaking, as when a pupil says to his fellow pupil ὁ διδάσκαλος, meaning the teacher well known to the one he is addressing. But Trapezuntius takes the article as if it always had its first force, and thinks that by this reasoning he had found the supreme Trinity, though his words ought to be taken in the second sense. For his meaning is this: because all things in nature are perfected in a beginning, a middle and an end, the ancients were led to worship a deity in their sacred rites [ἁγιστείαις], understanding by the trinity the common nature and form of the number three, which all things that are three participate in. And he designates three in every kind of thing, namely the beginning, middle and end of each natural thing, by which each thing is perfected. Nor did Aristotle ever know, even in a dream, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are the three persons of the most blessed Trinity.

units.la: Et hac eadē ratione Cardinalis inquit nō esse hic vertendū τ᾽ ἀγαθὸν summū bonū sed quemadmodum Argyropylus vertit ipsum bonum. De ratione quippe atq; forma cōmuni boni loquitur Aristoteles, quā rectè describi affirmat quòd ab omnib. appetatur: multa enim bona sunt quæ appetūtur & cōueniunt in hac forma & natura cōmuni quæ modò est descripta. Et certè cū multa sint genera rerū, multæ etiam sunt bonorum differentiæ, et quodlibet sui generis bonum appetit. nam equus hominis bonū non expetit, neq; canis bonum leonis: sed quæq; natura bonum sui generis expetit. Unde plurimum illos admiror, qui non tantū summum bonū hic intelligunt, verum etiam ipsum Deū arbitrantur describi, quē unū bonum ab omnib. rebus aiunt expeti: atque hanc ratione adferunt, quòd Deus ipse sit qui omnia bona offerat quæ à rebus expetuntur, & ea omnia in Deo perfectissimè continentur: propterea nemo potest ea cupere quin Deum ipsum desideret. At quis non vi-deat hoc esse per accidens, quod à scientiis prorsus remouetur, cum ea non tradunt quæ per accidens contingunt. Et hac ratione, si valeret, conficere-mus libidinosos[?] homines, quando alicuius formam seu speciem capiuntur, Deum appetere: quod esset ridiculum. Damus & quidem libenter in Deo comprehendi omnia bona quàm perfectissimè, quemadmodum septenarius numerus omnes priores complectitur, quod etiam sacræ literæ testantur: siquidem in Exodo ait Deus Mosi petenti divini vultus aspectum, Ostendā tibi omne bonum: verum Aristoteles desideria huius coniunctionis[?] cum Deo ignorauit: propheta Dauid intelliexit[?] qui dicebat in Psalmis, Mihi adhærere Deo bonum est. Eum autem sensum esse loci huius quem expresimus, consequentia demonstrant: agit enim philosophus de beatitudine, quam licet omnes homines appetant, quia tamen in diversis rebus eam collocarunt, hoc est divitiis, honoribus, voluptatibus, virtutibus, hinc factum ut diversi ge-nera bonorum diversa cuperent, quæ tamen omnia rationem et formam boni communis participarent. Quin & philosophi hoc idem spectantes de finibus bonorum & malorum quando scripserunt. Iam exposuimus quid vox illa τὰγαθὸν isto loco significet: nunc id confi- deremus quod sequitur, Omnia inquam bonû appetere, quod facile conce- demus de rebus vniuersis, quib. conuenit vt agant, fiue fuerint elementa, fiue lapides, fiue stirpes, fiue bruta, fiue homines. Et superius cū affirmauimus, illa quatuor, nepe artè, methodum, actionem & electionè, non appete- re proprie, sed ea esse quib. homines appetunt finem, id spectauimus quod i- sta sunt accidentia neque subsistunt per fe, vnde pot us sunt facultates & vires per quas homines agunt: & cum illa dixit Ariftoteles bonum expete- re, fuit perinde ac fi dixisset homines per hac bonû desiderare, catera vero quæ recensuimus, quandoquidem per fe subsistunt, bonum expetunt. Neq; mouet nos quod aliqui aiunt non debere appetitum concedi vbi defuerit no- titia: quare lapides, herbas, frutices, elementa & quæcunq; destituuntur co- gnitione dicunt non appetere. Sed hoc est falsum, quoniam diuersa sunt ap- petitus genera. inuenitur enim Rationalis qui hominibus attribuitur. Ani- malis & is conuenit brutis, Naturalis qui omnibus inest quæ à natura mo- uentur: in quibus tametsi noticia non reperiatur, fatis est Deum naturæ au- thorem atq; regem illa esse præditum, nanq; optimè nouit ad quos fines ista velit tendere, atq; cū finem præscripserit sua noticia, pondera inclinationis & proprietates adiecit, quibus omnia hæc ad suos fines incitatur. Unde Ari- ftoteles primo physicorum dicere non est veritus, materiam quæ alioquin rudis & stupida est, appetere formam, sicuti fœmina expetit marem.
units.tr: And for this same reason the Cardinal says that τ' ἀγαθὸν should not be rendered here as "the highest good," but, as Argyropulus rendered it, "the good itself." For Aristotle speaks of the reason and common form of the good, which he rightly says is described as that which all things desire; for there are many goods that are desired and agree in this common form and nature just described. And indeed, since there are many kinds of things, there are also many differences of goods, and each kind desires its own good. For a horse does not desire the good of a man, nor a dog the good of a lion; rather each nature desires the good of its own kind. Hence I greatly marvel at those who understand the highest good here, and even think that God himself is described here, as the one good that all things desire. They bring forward this argument: that God himself is the one who offers all the goods that things desire, and all of these are contained most perfectly in God; therefore no one can desire them without desiring God himself. But who does not see that this is an accident, which is entirely excluded from the sciences, since they do not teach what happens by accident? And by this reasoning, if it held, we would conclude that lustful men, when they are captivated by the form or appearance of someone, desire God, which would be ridiculous. We do willingly grant that all goods are comprehended in God most perfectly, just as the number seven contains all the earlier numbers; and the sacred letters also bear witness to this, since in Exodus God says to Moses, who asked to see the face of God, "I will show you all good" (Exod. 33). But Aristotle was ignorant of the longing for this union with God; the prophet David understood it, who said in the Psalms, "It is good for me to cleave to God" (Ps. 73). The consequences show that this is the sense of the passage we have set out. For the philosopher is treating of blessedness, which all men desire, although they have placed it in different things, namely riches, honours, pleasures and virtues; hence it came about that different kinds of goods were desired differently, and yet all of them share the reason and form of the common good. Indeed, the philosophers, looking to this same thing, wrote about the ends of goods and evils. Now we have explained what the word τὰ ἀγαθόν [ta agatha] means in that place; now let us consider what follows, namely that all things desire the good. This we readily grant of all things in the universe, which are fit to act, whether they be elements, stones, plants, brute beasts or men. And above, when we affirmed that those four things, namely art, method, action and choice, do not properly desire, but are those by which men pursue an end, we had in view that these are accidents and do not subsist by themselves; therefore they are rather faculties and powers by which men act. And when Aristotle said that these desire the good, it was just as if he had said that men desire the good through them; but the other things we listed, since they subsist by themselves, desire the good. Nor does it trouble us that some say appetite should not be granted where there is no knowledge; hence they say that stones, herbs, shrubs, elements and whatever lack cognition do not desire. But this is false, since there are different kinds of appetite. There is the rational appetite, which is attributed to men; the animal appetite, which belongs to brute beasts; and the natural appetite, which is present in all things that are moved by nature. In these, although no knowledge is found, it is enough that God, the author and king of nature, endows them with it; for he knows most well to what ends they are to tend, and when he has prescribed the end by his knowledge, he has added the weights of inclination and properties by which all these things are urged toward their ends. Hence Aristotle, in the first book of the Physics, did not hesitate to say that matter, which is otherwise rude and dull, desires form, just as the female desires the male.

units.la: Quænam vero causa fit in omnibus rebus, propter quam bonum expe- tant, ex Symposio Platonis cognoscitur, vbi ostendit amorem filium esse [illegible, ~18 letters] id est paupertatis & copiæ: bonum enim quod appeti- tur copia est, ad quam fertur quicqnid ea fit destitutum expeditum cum fit. Et notum καλὸν & ἀγαθὸν apud Græcos tria significare, utile, honestum & pulchrum, & unumquodq; istorum trium magnam vim habet ad affectu alliciendum: quod etiam etymologia istarum vocum ostendit, quemadmodum Plato docuit in Cratylo, quandoquidem καλὸν dicit ἀπὸ τ καλεῖν, & ἀγαθὸν ἀπὸ τ ἄγειν.
units.tr: What is the cause, however, in all things, on account of which they desire the good, is known from Plato's Symposium, where he shows that love is the son of [illegible] poverty and abundance; for the good that is desired is abundance, toward which whatever is deprived of it is carried when it lacks it. And it is well known that among the Greeks καλὸν [kalon] and ἀγαθὸν [agathon] signify three things: the useful, the honourable and the beautiful; and each of these three has great power to attract the affections. The etymology of these words also shows this, as Plato taught in the Cratylus, since he says that καλὸν comes from καλεῖν [kalein, to call], and ἀγαθὸν from ἄγειν [agein, to lead].

units.la: Istis iam expositis quod ad textus interpretationem, descendendum est ad dubia, & primum quærimus, cur Aristoteles tantummodo illorum quatuor mentionem fecit. Respondemus, quoniam institutum eius erat de humanis rebus agere, quæ omnia his quatuor capitibus continetur: quippe vel agimus intelligentia, vel appetitu: artes & methodus ad notitiam pertinet, actiones atq; delectus ad appetitum. Præterea ea quib. agimus ita fe habet vt vel regant vel pareant: ars & methodus & electio regunt atq; imperant, actiones autem reguntur & parent.
units.tr: Having set out these things, as far as the interpretation of the text is concerned, we must now come to the questions. And first we ask why Aristotle mentioned only those four things. We answer: because his purpose was to treat of human affairs, and all of these are contained under these four heads. For we act either by understanding or by appetite; art and method pertain to knowledge, while actions and choice pertain to appetite. Moreover, the things by which we act stand in such a relation that some rule and others obey: art, method and choice rule and command, while actions are ruled and obey.

units.la: Sed quæris quare naturam tacuerit, cum ea sit principium motus. Id fa-ctum est, quoniam humana tradit, & natura latius patet quàm humana: quoniam & bruta & quæ non sentiunt naturæ sunt participia. Deinde naturæ ipsius hominis non meminit, quoniam de felicitate scribendum erat, quæ natura non obtinetur, sed studio atq; diligentia: neq; omnes qui naturæ sunt participes, felicitatem assequuntur. Ad hæc illa pertinent ad hunc librum, quæ moralibus virtutibus possunt regi, sed natura si deficiat, non à morali philosopho sed à medico instauratur.
units.tr: But you ask why he said nothing about nature, since nature is the principle of motion. The reason is that this treatise deals with human matters, and nature extends more widely than the human. Brute animals, and things that do not perceive at all, also share in nature. Nor does he mention nature in man himself, because he was to write about happiness, and happiness is not obtained by nature but by zeal and diligence. Nor do all who share in nature attain happiness. Moreover, those things that belong to this book can be governed by the moral virtues, but if nature fails, it is restored not by the moral philosopher but by the physician.

units.la: Dubium quoq; est quare sileat scientias, quæ tamen in fines eò magis feruntur quàm artes, quòd sint eis certiores: & in posterioribus Analyticis dicitur, Scire esse rem per causam cognoscere: unde apparet inventionem causæ finem esse Scientiæ. Respondet Eustratius relictas esse Scientias, quòd per se notum fuerit eas in suas fines tendere: nam si hoc habent artes quæ longè sunt inferiores Scientijs, illæ multo magis id sibi vendicabunt. Non multum rationi huic acquiesco: nam dicerem fuisse quoque per se notum, Electiones tendere in aliquem finem. Respondet aliter, affirmans in Methodo Scienti-am intelligi, quam ego responsionem probo, maximè propter illa quæ superius de Methodo induximus: nam doctrinam Methodum esse concedebamus.
units.tr: There is also doubt about why he passes over the sciences, which are nonetheless directed to ends all the more than the arts, inasmuch as they are more certain. In the Posterior Analytics it is said that to know is to know a thing through its cause, whence it appears that discovering the cause is the end of science. Eustratius replies that the sciences were left out because it was self-evident that they tend towards their own ends; for if the arts, which are far inferior to the sciences, have this property, the sciences will claim it all the more. I do not greatly assent to this reasoning, for I would say it was equally self-evident that choices tend towards some end. He gives another answer, asserting that by method science is meant. I approve this answer, chiefly because of what we brought up above about method, for we conceded that method is teaching.

units.la: Tertiò conatur Eustratius docere hoc propterea factum, quoniam quæ hic traduntur, ad practicum genus pertineant, nimirum ad affectuum moderationem, scientias verò spectare omnes ad contemplationem. Duo hic mihi displicent: primum, quòd neget in isto libro agi de contemplatione, cùm in decimo ea ponatur ut summa perfectio nostræ felicitatis. Deinde longè minus id approbo, scientias universas esse contemplatrices: nam si hoc sequeremur, ista facultas non esset scientia, Musica item & Medicina, cùm hæ omnes ad praxim pertineant.
units.tr: Thirdly, Eustratius tries to show that this was done because what is handed down here belongs to the practical kind, namely the moderation of the affections, whereas all the sciences look to contemplation. Two things here displease me. First, he denies that this book treats of contemplation, although in the tenth book it is placed as the highest perfection of our happiness. Second, I approve much less of the claim that all the sciences are contemplative, for if we followed this, that faculty would not be a science, nor would music or medicine, since all these pertain to practice.

units.la: Dubitant ad hæc alij cur affectuum & virtutum non meminerit. Sed causa fuit, quia virtutes ad electiones & actiones pertinent. Et affectus quid aliud sunt quàm impulsus ad agendum? Unde non immeriò adiun-gentur actionibus.
units.tr: Others, moreover, wonder why he makes no mention of the affections and virtues. But the reason was that the virtues pertain to choices and actions. And what are the affections but impulses to act? Hence they are not improperly joined to actions.

units.la: Videndum item est, quare Aristoteles hoc ordine processerit, ut postremo loco posuerit Electionem, quæ tamen prima videbatur esse: nam ab eo statim deriuantur actiones, ex actionibus artes consurgunt, post artes venitur ad methodos. Est attamen observandum, in docendo ea priori loco debere poni, quæ nobis fuerint notiora, ea verò sunt magis imperfecta, ideò artes prius collocantur, deinde methodi et doctrinæ. Neque dubium est actiones prius à nobis cognosci quàm delectus: notitia enim recta & quæ à sensu oritur oritur actiones cognoscimus, postea cogitationem flectimus ad ipsam electi-onem, unde actio proficiscitur. Cum igitur voluerit a notioribus progredi, ordine usus est decentissimo.
units.tr: It should also be considered why Aristotle proceeded in this order, placing choice last, although it seemed to be first. For actions are derived immediately from it, arts arise from actions, and after the arts we come to methods. Yet it must be observed that in teaching, those things should be placed first which are better known to us, and those things are more imperfect; therefore the arts are placed first, then methods and doctrines. Nor is there doubt that we know actions before choice. For by correct perception, which arises from the senses, we know actions; afterwards we turn our thought to choice itself, from which action proceeds. Since therefore he wished to proceed from the better known, he used a most fitting order.

units.la: At cur priori loco Artem posuit & Methodum, posteriori vero Actio-nem & Delectum? Quia duo priora notitiae sunt, quemadmodum posteriora voluntatis et appetitus. Nemo autem ignorat cognitionem priorem esse; quia non possumus amare incognita.
units.tr: But why did he place art and method first, and action and choice afterwards? Because the former two belong to knowledge, as the latter two belong to will and appetite. Yet no one is unaware that knowledge comes first, since we cannot love what is unknown.

units.la: Quæri etiam solet de arte venefica, quomodo expetat bonum. Hic censeo[?] dicendum, venenum, ut doctiores aiunt, & in bonam partem et in malam posse accipi. Nam id venenum dicitur, quod naturam mutat eius cui adhibetur: unde interdum fit ut ægroti qui a iusto temperamento discesserunt, ad ipsum restitui non queant nisi violentiora medicamenta sumpserint, quæ per seipsa venena sunt, licet arte medicorum temperentur, attamen sanis plurimum nocerent.
units.tr: It is also commonly asked about the art of poisoning, how it seeks the good. Here I think it should be said, as the more learned say, that poison can be taken in a good sense as well as a bad. For that is called a poison which changes the nature of the one to whom it is applied. Hence it sometimes happens that sick people who have departed from the right balance cannot be restored to it unless they take more violent medicines, which in themselves are poisons, even though they are tempered by the physician's art, yet would greatly harm the healthy.

units.la: Quod idem sentiendum est de de voce Græca φάρμακα. Unde Caius Iurisconsultus in pandectis ait, si venenum dixeris, debes addere vel bonum vel malum.
units.tr: The same must be thought of the Greek word pharmaka [φάρμακα]. Hence the jurist Gaius, in the Pandects, says: if you call it a poison, you must add either good or bad.

units.la: Quare si veneficia eo tendant, ut ægrotus restituatur sanitati, dubium non est quin ars illa bonum appetat: verum si ad perniciem hominum venena instruantur, proprie ad Artem non pertinent, quoniam (uti definiimus[?]) Ars prosine habet aliquam commoditatem vitæ humanæ. Neque mihi quis obiciat consuevisse Athenis venena temperari, & præsertim cicutæ, ad interficiendos qui capitis damnabantur: quæ sane actio non magis erat iniusta quam hodie sit nostrorum carnificum. Quis enim ignorat ad iustitiam pertinere atq; Reipublicæ conducere ut sontes occidantur? Posset etiam esse casus, ut quemadmodum licet ferro & flammis hostes punire in bellis iustis & legitimis, ita etiam venenis eos perdere non sit interdictum. Atq; de hoc semel fuit requisitus Hippocrates, quod tamen facere noluit, quoniam exercitus qui erat perdendus ex Græcis constabat. Hæc inquam me non movet: quoniam tunc, si Artem velimus hic ponere, dicemus perniciem illam malorum hominum quoad iustitiam & rempublicam habere boni rationem, sed venefica, ut vulgo male audiunt & legibus damnata sunt, minimè ad Artem pertinent.
units.tr: Therefore if poisonings aim at restoring the sick to health, there is no doubt that this art seeks a good. But if poisons are prepared for the destruction of men, they do not properly belong to art, since art, as we have defined it, has some benefit for human life. Nor let anyone object to me that at Athens poisons were customarily mixed, and especially hemlock, for killing those condemned to death. That action was certainly no more unjust than the work of our executioners today. For who does not know that it belongs to justice, and profits the commonwealth, that the guilty be put to death? There could also be a case where, just as it is lawful to punish enemies with sword and fire in just and lawful wars, so it is not forbidden to destroy them with poisons. Indeed, Hippocrates was once asked to do this, but he refused, since the army to be destroyed consisted of Greeks. I say that this does not move me: for then, if we wish to place it here as an art, we will say that the destruction of evil men has a reasonable account in relation to justice and the commonwealth; but poisoning, as it is commonly ill spoken of and condemned by the laws, does not pertain to art at all.

units.la: Accedit huc (ut habetur ex divinis literis) esse à Deo condita, & ideo ut inquit Augustinus de civitate Dei lib. xi.[?] cap. 22. suas habent utilitates, quas a nostro ingenio imbecilli vix unquam possunt deprehendi: tractatio itaq; illorum ut ars fabrilis & rhetorica censeri posset, quorum materia utilis & damnosa potest esse, pro ingenio & proposito utentium.
units.tr: Add to this that (as is taught in the divine writings) these things were created by God, and therefore, as Augustine says in the City of God, book 11, chapter 22, they have their uses, which can scarcely ever be grasped by our weak understanding. The handling of them could therefore be counted as a craft like smithing or rhetoric, whose matter can be useful or harmful according to the disposition and purpose of those who use it.

units.la: Reuocatur etiam in dubium an bonum & finis æqualia sint, & inter se ita habe habeant vt retrò commeent & vt vulgò dicitur conuertantur,ita vt quic quid est bonum sit finis,& quicquid est finis sit bonum. Hic ego iudicare ni-hil posse finem esse, quod rationem boni non habeat, cùm tamen sint multa bona quae fines dici non possunt: vt medicina, quae alioqui amara est & mi-nimè sapit, bona dicitur, quae tamen finis non est, eam quippe sumit aegrotus propter sanitatem consequendam: ita etiam sunt incisiones, adustio & alia id genus quae solent partibus corporis putridis et tumentibus à peritis medi-cis adhiberi. Quamuis Plato in Philebo secus videatur sentire: nam bonum id inquit esse ad quod alia referuntur: sed quae referuntur ad aliud, non ad bonorum ordinem, sed ad alium quendam sunt reducenda. Vnde fortasis quae nos commorauimus antea, bona non vocaret, sed media quibus adipi-sceremur bonum. Verum doctrinae Peripatetica hoc aduersatur: nam illi bo-num distinguunt, vt quoddam sit propter se, quoddam propter aliud. Quod Aristoteles in Rhetoricis deserte adfirmat. Quid verò dicetur de i-stis quatuor facultatibus ab Aristotele connumeratis, quando id quando-que expetant, vt malum aliquod euitemus, quoniam tum in bonum non videntur ferri. Imò tunc etiam bonum appetunt: quoniam abesse à malo est non paruum bonum, sicut habetur in eiusdem Philosophi Rhetoricis. In quem sensum Christus aiebat de Iuda, Bonum esset homini illi, si natus nu-quam fuisset: quibus verbis euitationem summi mali, hoc est aeternae damnationis, bonum appellat: et alio loco iubebat scandalizantem oculum eruere, atq; identidem manum, si quidem longe melius est vt his careas, quàm vt integer ac totus mittaris in gehennam.
units.tr: It is also called into question whether the good and the end are equal, and stand to one another so that they reciprocate and, as is commonly said, are convertible, so that whatever is good is an end, and whatever is an end is good. Here I judge that nothing can be an end which does not have the character of good; yet there are many goods which cannot be called ends. For example, medicine, which is otherwise bitter and tastes of nothing pleasant, is called good, and yet it is not an end, for the sick man takes it for the sake of obtaining health. So too incisions, cauterising, and other such things, which skilled physicians are accustomed to apply to putrid and swollen parts of the body. Although Plato in the Philebus seems to think otherwise, for he says that the good is that to which other things are referred; but things that are referred to another are not to be brought under the order of goods, but to some other order. Hence perhaps he would not call those things we discussed earlier goods, but means by which we attain the good. Yet the Peripatetic doctrine opposes this, for they distinguish the good, so that one thing is good for its own sake and another for the sake of something else. Aristotle plainly asserts this in the Rhetoric. But what shall be said of those four faculties enumerated by Aristotle, when they sometimes seek something in order to avoid some evil, since then they do not seem to be carried towards a good? Indeed, even then they seek a good, since to be free from evil is no small good, as is stated in the same Philosopher's Rhetoric. In this sense Christ said of Judas: It would have been good for that man if he had never been born; by these words he calls the avoidance of the supreme evil, that is, eternal damnation, a good. And in another place he commanded that a scandalising eye be plucked out, and likewise a hand cut off, since it is far better to lack these than to be cast whole and entire into Gehenna.

units.la: Nunc postremo loco superest vt quaeramus, vnde nam sit petendus mo-dus ac mensura huius desiderij quo cuncta bonum appetunt. Habetur au-tem quandoq; penes quantitatem boni ad quod res feruntur: prout enim vel maius vel minus id fuerit, studium erga ipsum vehementius est aut re-missius: nonnunquam vero prout perfectius vel obscurius cognoscitur, nam fieri potest vt bonum sit magnum, sed quia imperfecte cognoscitur minus desideratur, ac è diuerso minima bona, si ob oculos fuerint atq; perpetuò co-gitata & intellecta, vehementer mouent: adducimur etiam saepius vt maio-ri studio in aliquod bonum feramur, vel quia multum indigemus, vel quia sic assueuimus, vel propterea quòd temperamentum corporis eo stimulat, vel deniq; quòd alios aemulemur à quibus id vehementer expetitur, ne ab ipsis videamur superari.
units.tr: Now finally it remains for us to ask whence the measure and degree of this desire is to be sought, by which all things seek the good. It is sometimes taken from the magnitude of the good toward which things are carried: according as the good is greater or less, the pursuit of it is more vehement or more lukewarm. Sometimes it is taken according as the good is known more perfectly or more dimly. For it can happen that a good is great but is desired less because it is imperfectly known; and conversely, the smallest goods, if they are kept before our eyes and constantly thought about and understood, move us vehemently. We are also often led to pursue some good with greater eagerness, either because we are in great need, or because we have become accustomed to it, or because the temperament of the body spurs us on, or finally because we envy others by whom it is eagerly sought, lest we seem to be surpassed by them.

units.la: Verùm iam expendamus, quomodo ea quae dicta sunt diuinis literis con-gruant. Primum quod omnia bonum expetant, videtur imitatio quaedam esse Dei Opt. Max. authoris creaturarum: is enim dum conderet singula quaq; in bonu finem ferebatur, sicut libro Geneseos dicitur, Deum vidisse lucem, luminaria coeli, stellas, herbas & plantas, et alia quod essent bona, deniq; septimo die quievit cernens cuncta quae fecerat fuisse admodum bona. Hoc itaq; studium bonorum in omnibus rebus vestigium & character est divinae proprietatis. De artibus autem & doctrinis facile dabitur quod appetant bonum per seipsum atq; suopte ingenio, quamvis id in malum cedat & peccatum his qui non sunt in Christo renati, et propterea sapius fit ut hominib. cultis & ornatis bonis artib. & scientiis abscondatur arcana salutis, & rudioribus patefiant, iuxta illud, Abscondisti haec a sapientibus, & revelasti ea parvulis: & Paulus ad Cor. 1[?]. Videte vocationem vestram fratres, quoniam non multi sapientes, sed stulta mundi elegit Deus, ut pudefaciat sapientes. Quae locum non haberent, si artes & doctrina vera bona & quae Deo nos gratos facerent consectarentur[?]. Verumtamen ea quamvis genere atq; natura sua bona sint, nobis attamen si fuerimus infideles & arrogantes in malum vertu-tur. Quoad electiones & actiones ait scriptura libro Geneseos cor hominis pronum esse ad malitiam, idq; iam inde a prima pueritia: & Paulus in eundem fermè sensum dicebat ad Romanos, Scio enim quod non habitat in me, hoc est in carne mea bonum: quare dicendum est id esse naturae vitium per Adamum contractum, ut homines non regenerati per Christum, sint ad ea proni quae revera prava sunt, iniusta & turpia, ac legi divinae quam maxime repugnant: atq; si postea formentur disciplina praeceptorum et moralibus virtutibus, aut egregia indole fuerint praediti, superant quidem turpiores appetitus, & in bona quaedam civilia & moralia feruntur suo delectu, sed quae illis, ut antea dicebamus, & peccata sint & in perniciem cedant, quaob-rem constanter affirmandum est, nondum renatorum delectus & actiones (ut scribitur in Genesi) pronas esse ad malum. Quod tamen Aristoteli non adversatur: quoniā ea mala sub ratione bonorum apprehenduntur. Quin & regenerati fere perpetuo vel[?] nolentes rapimur ad peccata & illa praecipites expetimus, verum per gratiam & spiritum desideriis illis adversamur, ut denique per fidem in Christo victores efficiamur. Reliquas autem Dei creaturas bonum expetere non dubitamus, quoniam reguntur divinis legibus, et pro-ut à lege naturae ducuntur, agunt quaecunq; faciunt: quamvis & ipsa pro-pter hominis peccatum cogantur vanitati subiici. Fidei autem Spei & Charitatis nec non Gratiae ac impulsus divini spiritus non meminit Aristote-les, quoniam ea non novit, quae tamen verissima bona expetunt. His ita expositis reliqua videamus.
units.tr: Let us now consider how the things that have been said agree with the divine writings. First, that all things seek the good seems to be a certain imitation of God the best and greatest, the author of creatures. For in creating each single thing he directed it toward a good end, as it is said in the book of Genesis that God saw the light, the heavenly luminaries, the stars, the herbs and plants, and the other things, that they were good; and finally on the seventh day he rested, seeing that all the things he had made were very good. This zeal for the good in all things is therefore a trace and mark of the divine property. Concerning arts and doctrines, it will easily be granted that they seek the good through themselves and by their own nature, although this turns to evil and sin for those who are not born again in Christ. And so it often happens that the hidden mysteries of salvation are concealed from men who are cultivated and adorned with good arts and sciences, and are revealed to the cruder, according to that saying: "You have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little children"; and Paul, 1 Cor. 1[?]: "Consider your calling, brothers, that not many are wise, but God has chosen the foolish things of the world to shame the wise." These things would have no place if the arts and true doctrine pursued good things which would make us pleasing to God. Nevertheless, although these are good in their kind and nature, yet for us, if we are unbelieving and arrogant, they are turned into evil. As for choices and actions, Scripture says in the book of Genesis that the heart of man is inclined to wickedness, and that from earliest childhood; and Paul, in nearly the same sense, said to the Romans: "For I know that there dwells in me, that is, in my flesh, no good." Therefore it must be said that this is a defect of nature contracted through Adam, so that men not regenerated through Christ are inclined to those things which are truly depraved, unjust and shameful, and most strongly oppose the divine law. And if afterwards they are formed by the discipline of precepts and moral virtues, or are endowed with an excellent disposition, they indeed overcome the more shameful appetites and are carried toward certain civil and moral goods by their own choice. But these, as we said before, are also sins and turn to their destruction. Wherefore it must be constantly affirmed that the choices and actions of the not yet regenerate (as is written in Genesis) are inclined to evil. Yet this does not contradict Aristotle, since those evils are apprehended under the appearance of goods. Indeed, even the regenerate are almost continually carried off to sins, though unwillingly, and rush headlong into them; but through grace and the Spirit we oppose those desires, so that at last through faith in Christ we become victors. As for the other creatures of God, we do not doubt that they seek the good, since they are governed by divine laws, and whatever they do, they do as they are led by the law of nature; although even they, on account of man's sin, are compelled to be subjected to vanity. But Aristotle does not mention faith, hope and charity, nor grace and the impulse of the divine Spirit, since he did not know them, yet these seek the truest goods. With these things thus set out, let us look at the rest.

units.la: Videtur autem quædam esse differentia finium: nam earum quædam sunt actiones, aliæ vero præter ipsas quædam opera. Et illa quorū fines aliquæ sunt præter actiones, in his opera sunt meliora ipsis actionibus. Cumq; plurimæ sint actiones, artes & scientiæ, multæ quoque sunt fines. Medicinæ nanq; finis est sanitas: artis extruendarum nauium, nauis: facultatis rei militaris, victoria: & familiaris rei gubernandæ, diuitiæ.
units.tr: There seems, however, to be a certain difference among ends: for some of them are actions, while others are certain works beyond the actions themselves. And in those whose ends are some works beyond the actions, the works are better than the actions themselves. And since there are very many actions, arts and sciences, there are also many ends. For the end of medicine is health; of the art of building ships, the ship; of the faculty of war, victory; and of the management of household affairs, riches.

units.la: Scopus huius loci est, docere, Humanas res non tantum habere finem præstitutam, ut iam docuimus, verum finem illam esse multiplicem, & in ea finium varietate alias esse præstantiores aliis, quandoquidem ista multiplicitas est ex illarum rerum genere quæ ordinem inter se habent. Neque alia de causa nunc agit Aristoteles de his, nisi ut queat ex multis finibus præstantissimam deligere, quam ostendat humanam felicitatem. Erit igitur horum verborum ista propositio: Fines humani sunt multi: & unus est alteri præferendus. Probatio prioris partis est, Quoniam finium aliæ sunt actiones, aliæ vero præter actiones opera: & diuersarum artium & doctrinarum non eadem est finis. Sic demonstratur multitudo finium, partim a natura diuersa illarum, partim a diuersitate principiorum, prout ab aliis artibus & scientiis expetuntur. Altera propositionis pars erat, Unam finem esse alteram præstantiorem: quod ostendit, quoniam fines artium & scientiarum præcipuarum, quas vocant ἀρχιτεκτονικὰς[?], sunt multo nobiliores finibus aliarum facultatum quæ ad ipsas ordinantur: quod exemplis in textu confirmabitur. Poterunt igitur esse duo syllogismi. Primus:
units.tr: The purpose of this passage is to teach that human affairs have not only one end set before them, as we have already taught, but that this end is manifold, and that within this variety of ends some are more excellent than others, since this multiplicity arises from the kind of things which stand in an order among themselves. Aristotle now treats of these for no other reason than that he may choose from many ends the most excellent, which he may show to be human happiness. The proposition of these words will therefore be this: human ends are many, and one is to be preferred to another. The proof of the first part is: since some of the ends are actions and others are works beyond actions, and the ends of different arts and doctrines are not the same. Thus the multiplicity of ends is demonstrated, partly from the diversity of their nature, partly from the diversity of the principles by which they are sought by different arts and sciences. The other part of the proposition was: one end is more excellent than another. He shows this since the ends of the chief arts and sciences, which they call architectonic [ἀρχιτεκτονικὰς], are much nobler than the ends of the other faculties which are ordered to them; this will be confirmed by examples in the text. There can therefore be two syllogisms. The first:

units.la: Quæcunq; diuersam naturam habent & spectant ad diuersas facultates, non sunt eadem.
units.tr: Whatever have a different nature and relate to different faculties are not the same.

units.la: Fines humani diuersam naturam habent: nam aliæ earum sunt actiones, & aliæ opera, & spectant ad diuersas facultates: nam diuersæ sunt artes, actiones & scientiæ.
units.tr: Human ends have a different nature: for some of them are actions and others works, and they relate to different faculties, since the arts, actions and sciences are different.
Therefore there is not one end.
The second syllogism, hypothetical:

units.la: Si facultates ordinem inter se habent, ut una sit præstantior altera, fines quoq; illarum erunt ita comparatæ, ut una sit melior altera. Sed facultates ita se habent, ut una præferatur alteri.
units.tr: If faculties stand in an order among themselves, so that one is more excellent than another, their ends also will be so related that one is better than another. But the faculties are so arranged that one is preferred to another.
Therefore the ends will have the same order.

units.la: Iuxta huius probationis partes textus distribuitur: primò enim ostendit multiplices esse fines: deinde unam altera meliorem. Primum tradit usq; illum locum, Quot autem sunt huiusmodi, sub aliqua una potentia sunt. Iam de priore agamus parte.
units.tr: According to the parts of this proof the text is divided: for first he shows that the ends are many, and then that one is better than another. He sets out the first as far as that passage, "But as many as are of this kind are under some one faculty." Now let us deal with the first part.

units.la: Interposuerat sententiam vniuersalem de omnibus rebus, quod bonum appeterent. Sed cùm prius cœpisset agere de humanis rebus, nunc ad eas redit, nempe ad artes & methodos, ut illa quæ sequuntur declarabunt. Uti-lissimum est Aristotelis propositum: nam hinc ostendet facultatem hanc pro fine habere actionem, & eam quidem optimam, ideoq; curat, ut Eustratius inquit, intelligi non esse perfectiores actiones illas quæ habent opus permanes cùm desierint, imò potius è diverso accidere quā sæpissimè, ut postea demonstrabimus. Et certè si quis opinaretur facultates esse meliores quæ post actiones opus aliquod relinquunt, quàm illæ quæ tantum actione consumun-tur[?], is existimaret felicitatem hominis imperfectiorem eiusmodi operibus, cùm in actione tantum consistat: quare scire debetis quandoq; unum quandoq; alterum accidere, nempe ut interdum præstantius sit opus quod relinquitur, interdum vero actio. Nam finis medici est opus, nimirum sanitas, quæ in homine relinquitur cùm fuerit curatus: qui finis si conferatur cùm saltatione, quæ finis est artis saltatoriæ, multò est melior. E diverso artis ædificandi naues finis est navis, opus nimirum quod relinquitur post ædificationem: at hac finis collata cùm navigatione, quæ actio est & finis artis nauticæ, est imperfectior. Proinde quod attinet ad dignitatem, nihil refert an finis fuerit opus, an fuerit actio: nam quandoq; unum est melius, quādoq; alterum. Hoc tamen certum est, ut inquit Aristoteles, quod ubicūq; opera sunt fines, actiones quæ illa præcedunt & quibus fiunt, dignitate vincuntur: atq; ratio est, quoniam ad aliud ordinantur.
units.tr: He had interposed a universal statement about all things, that they seek the good. But since he had first begun to treat of human affairs, he now returns to them, namely to arts and methods, as what follows will make clear. Aristotle's proposition is very useful, for from this he will show that this faculty has an action for its end, and indeed the best action. Therefore he takes care, as Eustratius says, that it be understood that those actions are not more perfect which leave behind a lasting work when they have ceased; rather the reverse happens very often, as we will show later. And certainly if anyone supposed that faculties are better which leave some work after the action than those which are used up only in the action, he would judge human happiness to be more imperfect, being of such works, since it consists only in action. So you must know that sometimes the one, sometimes the other, happens: that is, sometimes the work which is left behind is more excellent, and sometimes the action. For the end of the physician is a work, namely health, which remains in the man when he has been cured; if this end is compared with dancing, which is the end of the art of dancing, it is much better. On the other hand, the end of the art of shipbuilding is the ship, a work which remains after the building; but this end, compared with navigation, which is the action and end of the art of sailing, is less perfect. Therefore, as far as dignity is concerned, it makes no difference whether the end is a work or an action, for sometimes one is better, sometimes the other. This, however, is certain, as Aristotle says: wherever works are ends, the actions which precede them and by which they are made are surpassed in dignity. The reason is that they are ordered to something else.

units.la: In verbis Aristotelis notabimus, quid posuit primum ἐνεργείας, postea πράξεις: quæ diversitas vocum, diversitatem nō indicat actus humani. Sed ποίησις & πρᾶξις differunt, ut dicetur in 6. Nam πράξεις, sive, ut nos diceremus, actiones hæ sunt quæ post se nec relinquunt opus: at ποιήσεις, quas (ut ita dicam) factiones dixeris, opus aliquod efficiunt quod post remanet, & extans potest demonstrari. Atq; hanc distinctionem inter agere & facere observavit Aristoteles. Neq; mirandum est, illum de finibus hic tam diligenter scribere quandoquidem mores, virtutes, electiones, affectus & alia humana sunt adeò diuulsa & diuersarum naturarum ac generum, ut nisi coniungantur aliqua scientia vel methodo tradi non possint, nec alia qua- piam re ordinantur & iunguntur nisi per fines.
units.tr: In Aristotle's words we shall note what he put first, energeias [ἐνεργείας], and afterwards praxeis [πράξεις]. This difference of words does not indicate a difference in human action. But poiesis [ποίησις] and praxis [πρᾶξις] differ, as will be said in book 6. For praxeis, or, as we would say, actions, are those which leave no work behind them, whereas poiesis, which we might call making (if I may put it so), produces some work that remains afterwards and can be pointed to. Aristotle observed this distinction between acting and making. Nor is it surprising that he writes so carefully here about ends, since morals, virtues, choices, affections and other human things are so scattered and of such different natures and kinds that they cannot be taught except by some science or method, and they cannot be ordered and joined together by anything except through ends.

units.la: Nunc vero ex dictis Philosophi vnam duntaxat habemus vniuersalem & constantem regulam, Omne opus quod extat post confectionem ea esse dignius, quare non oportet vt opus alijs conferatur actionibus, sed illi tantummodo praxi per quam est confectum. Et vt res melius teneatur, sciendum est quod post opera iam confecta sequuntur alia actiones: etenim cùm domus est aedificata, inhabitatur, & cùm sanitas restituta est aegrotanti, agere incipit expeditè iuxta suam naturam: unde cùm opus ad hæc posteriora fuerit relatum, indignius est eis, nam ad illa ordinatur. Sed quædam actiones nobilissimæ quæ opera artificiosa nec antecedunt nec sequuntur, vti sunt actiones virtutum: nisi dixeris frequentes actiones rectas ac iustas opus tandem relinquere, id est habitum in animo, ad quem postea sequatur actiones virtutum: quod si dixeris, non multum pugnabo, quamuis Aristotelem videam alio spectare, neq; habitum quod sciam vnquam appellauit opus.
units.tr: From the Philosopher's words we now have only one universal and fixed rule: that whatever work exists after it has been completed is more worthy, so that the work should not be compared with the actions but only with the practice by which it was completed. To hold the matter more firmly, we must understand that after completed works, other actions follow. For when a house has been built, it is lived in, and when health has been restored to a sick man, he begins to act readily according to his nature. Hence, when a work is referred to these later things, it is less worthy than they, for it is ordered to them. But some most noble actions, such as the actions of the virtues, neither precede nor follow artificial works, unless you say that frequent right and just actions finally leave behind a work, namely a habit in the mind, to which the actions of the virtues afterwards follow. If you say this, I shall not contend much, although I see that Aristotle is aiming at something else, and as far as I know he never called a habit a work.

units.la: Sed quando tot dicuntur de finibus, operæprecium esse arbitror vt definiatur quidnam sit finis. Vocis etymologia duplex adfertur. Vna est à verbo Græco τελέω vel τελέω quod est perficio aut finio, unde deriuatur τέλος, quod sit perfectio quædam eorum quæ ad ipsum referuntur: accipitur etiam pro termino & extremo rei, unde mors etiam dicitur finis, non quòd eam expetamus aut illa perficiamur, sed quia terminus est & extremum vitæ. Altera est etymologia, vt sit ἀπὸ τοῦ τέλλειν quod est oriri, quia ὥσπερ πάσης πράξεως [?] ante quamlibet actionem vel confectionem præluce t instar Solis orientis. Definitur autem ab Aristotele, quòd ὅρος ὁρίζει τ' ἄκρα, αὐτὸ δὲ ἡ [?] Vel, [illegible, ~12 letters].
units.tr: But since so much is said about ends, I think it worth while to define what an end is. Two etymologies of the word are offered. One is from the Greek verb teleo or telleo [τελέω], which means to perfect or to finish, whence telos [τέλος] is derived, meaning a certain perfection of those things which are referred to it. It is also taken for the limit and extremity of a thing, whence death too is called the end, not because we desire it or are perfected by it, but because it is the limit and extremity of life. The other etymology is that it comes from apo tou tellein [ἀπὸ τοῦ τέλλειν], to rise, because, hōsper pasēs praxeōs [?], it shines forth before any action or completion, like the rising sun. Aristotle defines it thus: a boundary bounds the extremes, and itself... [?] Or, [illegible, about twelve letters].

units.la: Cum autem multæ sint artes, actiones & scientiæ, multi sunt fi- nes.) Prius diversitatem finium ostendit à naturis eorum, nunc ex eo quod sunt diversarum facultatum. Divitias dicit fines œconomiæ juxta vulgarem opinionem, cùm in œconomicis & politicis dicat divitias potius instrumentum esse ad aliquod aliud bonum comparandum. Potuisset alteram partem interpretari quomodo fines ita se habeant ut unus altero sit præstantior, sed prius adversus ea quæ diximus proponentur dubia, nam cùm ista recens au- dieritis [?], ea facilius intelligetis quam si diutius ea differremus.
units.tr: Since there are many arts, actions and sciences, there are many ends. Previously he showed the diversity of ends from their natures; now he shows it from the fact that they belong to different faculties. He says that riches are the end of economics according to common opinion, although in the Economics and Politics he says that riches are rather an instrument for acquiring some other good. He could have explained the other side, how ends stand in such a relation that one is more excellent than another, but first the doubts raised against what we have said will be put forward, for since you have heard these things just now, you will understand them more easily than if we deferred them for longer.

units.la: Revocatur in dubium quomodo Aristoteles duo genera finium posuerit, nimirum actionem & opus: videtur enim relinquere τὸ θεωρεῖν, quam tamen commemorauit in Topicis ut finem, & Quintilianus in divisione artium lib. 2. cap. 9. triplicem finem constituit, opus, actionem & contemplationem, & ipse demum Aristoteles in Ethicis ad finem de contemplatione agit, ac eam procul dubio bonam partem esse docet humanæ felicitatis. Proinde manca esse videbitur hæc distinctio cum tertium membrum omittatur. Sed ad hoc respondemus, nomine θεωρίας[?] contemplationem ipsam contineri: ac diligenter notandum est Aristotelem non dixisse θεωρητικὸν[?] sed ἐνεργειαν[?] quia nomine θεωρήσεως[?] non comprehendisset contemplationem. Unde partitio non est mutila, neque secum pugnat Aristoteles, neque aduersatur Quintiliano: nā quamuis tres istæ fine, connumerentur, duæ tamen earum comprehenduntur unica voce.
units.tr: It is questioned how Aristotle could posit two kinds of ends, namely action and work. For he seems to leave out contemplation (to theorein), which he nevertheless mentioned in the Topics as an end. Quintilian, in the division of the arts in book 2, chapter 9, lays down a threefold end: work, action and contemplation. And Aristotle himself in the Ethics treats contemplation in connection with the end, and teaches that it is undoubtedly the better part of human happiness. Therefore this division will seem defective, since a third member is omitted. But to this we reply that under the name of theoria contemplation itself is contained. And it must be carefully noted that Aristotle did not say theoretikon [θεωρητικὸν] but energeian [ἐνεργειαν], because under the name theorēsis [θεωρήσεως] he would not have included contemplation. Hence the partition is not mutilated, nor does Aristotle contradict himself or oppose Quintilian: for although these three ends are enumerated, two of them are nevertheless comprehended under a single word.

units.la: Quæritur præterea, quia rationem adduximus quare opus præstantius ea sit confectione qua efficitur, quoniam ordinatur ad opus, num hoc verū sit in universum, quod quicquid in aliud tanquam in finem dirigitur, sit eo ignobilius: quod non videtur esse dandum: nam opilionis finis est curare oues ut bene habeant, hoc sua studet arte consequi, cum tamen ouibus longe præstet: quis enim dubitet hominem pecudibus anteferendum? quin & angeli, ut dicitur ad Hebræos, sunt spiritus administri salutis electorum, cum tamen ipsorum dignitas & natura homines antecellat: & deniq; Aristoteles de generatione & corruptione dixit finem corporum cœlestium esse ut generetur homines, cum tamen nulli Peripatetico dubium sit cœlos dignores esse hominibus. Quidam putarunt euasisse dubium, dicendo quòd commemoratur fines tantummodo esse actionum, sed non illorum, efficientium, scilicet cœli, angeli & opilionis. At hoc nihil iuuat, efficientia enim suas non assequuntur fines nisi per actiones, ideoque finis idem assignandus est efficienti & operi eius. Sed sciendum est quod ut habetur in secundo de anima 35. & 37. est duplex finis, unus dicitur Cuius gratia, alter Cui, Græci ἕ & ᾧ. Ut animal generans habet finem Cuius gratia, æternum illud scilicet & diuinum, nempe perpetuitatem, quam vellet assequi, quam quum absolutè non possit habere, saltem generando sibi vendicat. Finis Cui est res quæ generatur: & naturæ finis in plantis est, ut fructus aut flores producat, estque id finis Cuius, sed hominum usus est finis Cui: Tunc bene fieri potest ut finis Cui sit ignobilior, eoque ad ipsum refertur: finis autem Cuius est dignior, ut materia quæ ad formam dirigitur, & nemo ignorat formam præstantiorem esse materia. Verum è diuerso accidit, quando ad id quod est finis Cui aliquid dirigitur, non ut ipsum ex eo perficiatur sed ut ipsum perficiat, quoniam tunc finis Cui est indignior, eo quòd est ad talem finem. Ita de angelis & de cœlo, cœli finis Cuius, est assimilari Deo & alia perficere, quod est melius, nam [illegible, ~3 letters] cœlum dignius est hæc faciens quàm si non faceret. Similiter angelis finis est obedire Deo & nos seruare, quòd faciendo sunt digniores seipsis quàm si non facerent. Et opilio finem habet Cuius causa, suam ipsius copiam & vbertatem, cum qua melior est, quàm si ea destitueretur, & familiæ ac ciuitatis copia. Sed finis Cui, sunt ipsæ oues ad quas ordinatur vt illas perficiat. Et exemplū huius quod aliquid ordinetur ad aliud, vt ipsum perficiat et sit eo dignius, habetur, quando à Regibus & monarchijs constituuntur aliqui præfecti seu vicarij, & dirigūtur ad populū vt illū regant et curent, ad quā finē non referuntur vt ignobiliores plebe, sed vt qui ab ea obseruentur: & honorētur sed in his finis est Cui: verū si respiciamus Cuius gratia hæc fiat, semper agnoscemus finem esse præstantiorem. Atq; ista distinctione soluuntur instantiæ iam adductæ de corporibus cœlestibus, de angelis, de opilione: nam ista quamuis digniora sint fine Cui, non tamen fine Cuius gratia. Quibus enim præstantior est opilio, sed non seipso vel domino suo, si fuerit mercenarius, vel sua familia, vcl ciuitate: nam vel in gratiam suipsius, velin gratiam domini, aut familiæ aut ciuitatis curat oues. Identidem angeli faciunt & corpora cœlestia, quia ministrant nobis haudquaquam nostra ipsorum causa, sed partim vt Deo satisfaciant, partim vt suam ipsorum perfectionem exerceant. Sed opus cum refertur ad præcedentes actiones, neque vlterius respicit, est finis Cuius causa, vnde actiones antecedentes sunt illo, quemadmodum ait Aristoteles, indigniores: quod si postea respiciatur vlterior finis, id est vsus operis, ille dignior erit opera, vt antea dicebamus de inhabitatione domus, cum ad ædificium refertur. Et ratio est, quoniam tunc inhabitatio est finis Cuius causa, domus autem finis Cui.
units.tr: Further, it is asked: since we have given the reason why the work is more excellent than the making by which it is effected, because it is ordered to the work, is it true in general that whatever is directed to another thing as its end is thereby less noble? This does not seem to be granted. For the end of the shepherd is to care for his sheep so that they are well, and he strives to achieve this by his art, and yet he is far superior to the sheep. For who would doubt that man is to be preferred to cattle? Indeed the angels, as it is said to the Hebrews, are ministering spirits sent to serve those who are to inherit salvation, and yet their dignity and nature surpass men. And finally Aristotle, in On Generation and Corruption, said that the end of the heavenly bodies is that men may be generated, and yet no Peripatetic doubts that the heavens are more worthy than men. Some thought they had escaped the difficulty by saying that it is only recorded that these are the ends of actions, not of those who effect them, namely the heavens, the angels and the shepherd. But this does not help, for efficient causes attain their ends only through actions, and therefore the same end must be assigned to the efficient cause and to its work. But it must be understood that, as is found in the second book of On the Soul, at 35 and 37, there is a twofold end: one is called that for the sake of which (cuius gratia), the other that to which (cui), the Greek hou [ἕ] and hō [ᾧ]. The generating animal has an end for the sake of which, namely that eternal and divine thing, that is perpetuity, which it wishes to attain; since it cannot have it absolutely, it claims it for itself at least by generating. The end to which is the thing that is generated; and in plants the end of nature is that they produce fruit or flowers, and this is the end cuius, but the use of men is the end cui. Then it may well happen that the end to which is less noble, and so is referred to that which is the end for the sake of which; for the end for the sake of which is more worthy, as matter that is directed to form, and no one is ignorant that form is more excellent than matter. But conversely it happens when something is directed to that which is an end to which, not so that it may be perfected by it but so that it may perfect it; then the end to which is less worthy, because it is for such an end. So it is with the angels and the heaven: the end for the sake of which the heaven exists is to be made like God and to perfect other things, which is better, for the heaven is more worthy when it does these things than if it did not do them. Similarly the end of the angels is to obey God and to keep us, which by doing they are more worthy than themselves would be if they did not do it. And the shepherd has as his end for the sake of which his own abundance and fertility, with which he is better than if he were deprived of them, and the abundance of his household and city. But the end to which are the sheep themselves, for which he is ordained to perfect them. And an example of this, that something is ordered to another so as to perfect it and be more worthy by it, is found when kings and monarchies appoint certain prefects or vicars and direct them to the people to rule and care for it; they are not referred to that end as less noble than the common people, but as those who are observed by it, and are honoured; but in these the end is cui. Yet if we look at the end for the sake of which this is done, we shall always acknowledge that the end is more excellent. By this distinction the instances already brought forward concerning the heavenly bodies, the angels and the shepherd are resolved: for although these are more worthy than the end to which, they are not more worthy than the end for the sake of which. For the shepherd is more excellent than the sheep, but not than himself or his master if he is a hired man, or his household, or the city; for he cares for the sheep either for his own sake, or for the sake of his master, or of his household or city. Likewise the angels and the heavenly bodies minister to us, not for their own sake at all, but partly that they may satisfy God and partly that they may exercise their own perfection. But when the work is referred to the preceding actions and looks no further, it is the end for the sake of which; hence the preceding actions are less worthy than it, as Aristotle says. But if a further end is afterwards regarded, namely the use of the work, that will be more worthy than the work, as we said before about the habitation of a house, when it is referred to the building. And the reason is that then the habitation is the end for the sake of which, and the house the end to which.

units.la: De definitione finis iam allata dubitatur an sit extremæ finis, vel vniuersalis ad omnes fines. Respondemus posse esse generalem & particulare. Particularis est finis extremi, si addas extremam partem, καὶ αὐτὸ [illegible, ~10 letters] ἕτερον ἐνὸς καὶ αὐτὸ: ista particulæ coniunctæ prioribus definiunt extremam finem. Sed si adimantur et tantum relinquantur priores partes, tunc definitio est generalis, quod finis sit propter quem alia, aut finis est Cuius causa alia.
units.tr: It is disputed whether the definition of the ultimate end already given is meant only of the ultimate end, or is universal to all ends. We reply that it can be both general and particular. It is particular of the ultimate end if you add the final clause, "and itself [illegible] other of one and itself" [καὶ αὐτὸ ... ἕτερον ἐνὸς καὶ αὐτὸ]. These words added to the earlier ones define the ultimate end. But if they are removed and only the earlier parts are kept, the definition is general: an end is that for the sake of which other things are, or an end is that for whose sake (the final cause) other things exist.

units.la: Ad hæc ambigitur, cum Aristoteles inquit, Quoniam multæ sunt artes actiones & scientiæ, complures etiam sunt fines, An retrò commeet pro-positio & conuertatur, nimirum quod vbicunq; fuerint plures fines, plures etiam sint res ad illas fines relatæ. Ad quæstionem respondemus, hoc non esse necessarium: quandoquidem natura sæpius unius & eiusdem rei plures fines instituit: verbi gratia, Lingua non tantum dirigitur ad loquendum, sed sed ad sapores gustandos: item dentes cibum scindunt & commoliunt, atq; iuvant sermonem: & facultate Dialectica non tantum vera confirmamus, verum etiam falsa refellimus. Quamobrem cum multæ sint facultates et artes, multas esse fines dabimus, ex numero finium rerum numerus non colligetur.
units.tr: There is also a question about Aristotle's statement, "Since there are many arts, actions and sciences, there are also many ends." Does the proposition run backwards and convert, so that wherever there are several ends there are also several things related to those ends? To this question we reply that this does not follow, since nature has often set several ends for one and the same thing. For example, the tongue is directed not only to speaking but also to tasting flavours; the teeth both cut and grind food and help speech; and by the art of dialectic we not only confirm truths but also refute falsehoods. Therefore, since there are many faculties and arts, we shall grant that they have many ends. The number of arts is not inferred from the number of ends.

units.la: Dubitamus etiam quoniam Aristoteles dicit medicæ facultatis finem esse sanitatem, militaris victoriam, &c. contra quam sententiam scribit ipsemet in Topicis libro 1. capite 2. & Quintilianus libro 2. capite 12. Quam doquidem medicinæ finis est non sanitas, verum adhibere omnia & nihil omittere eorum quæ valeant ad sanandum: quod si ægrotus vel propter intemperantiam victus, vel ex nimia debilitate naturæ, vel ex indomita & insuperabili violentia morbi non sanetur, medicus non excidit a fine artis: idem est dicendum de oratore, cuius finis est omnia dicere quæ faciant ad suadendum & nihil omittere quod eo pertineat, unde licet non persuaserit, minime tamen a fine suo aberrat si hoc observaverit. Eademq; dicere possumus de Oeconomo & Imperatore. Sed in hac dissoluenda quæstione multum non est laborandum, quoniam Aristoteles in exemplis afferendis pinguiori Minerva rem offendit, neq; sollicitus est ut exempla semper ad amussim congruant, verum ea proserit ut vulgo iactantur: deinde licet sanare, persuadere, ac vincere, non semper consequantur actiones medicorum, rhetorum & militum, attamen a nullo potest negari quin ad ista respiciant hæ facultates, & pro viribus nitantur ea consequi.
units.tr: We also question why Aristotle says that the end of the medical art is health, and that of the military art is victory, and so on. He himself writes against this view in the first book of the Topics, chapter 2, and Quintilian in the second book, chapter 12. For the end of medicine is not health itself, but to apply all the means that serve to heal and to omit none of them. If the patient is not healed, whether because he is overcome by intemperance, or by excessive weakness of nature, or by the untamed and unconquerable violence of the disease, the physician has not fallen away from the end of his art. The same must be said of the orator, whose end is to say everything that tends to persuade and to omit nothing that pertains to this. So, although he fails to persuade, he does not wander at all from his end, provided he has observed this. We may say the same of the household manager and the commander. But we need not labour much over resolving this question, since Aristotle, in bringing forward his examples, has rather crude wit, and he is not concerned that the examples always fit exactly; he sets them forth as they are commonly bandied about. Moreover, although healing, persuading and conquering do not always follow the actions of physicians, orators and soldiers, yet no one can deny that these arts aim at these things and strive, as far as their powers allow, to attain them.

units.la: Postremo quia de finibus agitur, dubium est, quomodo dicatur aliquod opus finis esse vel actionis vel artis: nam si res consideretur quæ facta est ab artifice, illa est effectum, non igitur causa: nam causam oportet priorem esse effectu esse, & nihil seipso prius esse potest. Hic respondent aliqui, rem factam esse finem, non quatenus extat & iam perfecta est, sed qua prius a mente artificis comprehendebatur: & res potest esse prior seipsa diversa ratione, quoniam prius in mente versatur artificis quam actu fiat. Huic ego responsioni minime acquiesco: quoniam forma illa cognita quæ in animo versatur artificis, rationem habet efficientis: nam ut obiectum movet illius mentem. Accedit ad hoc quod artifex non desiderat talem habere formam qualem habet in animo, sed in re vult expressam, atq; illo tanquam in finem tendit. Proinde res ipsa exterior causa finalis est, non qua extat vel efficitur, sed qua rationem boni habet, & ea perficitur vel efficiens vel eius actio: atque fateor hæc oportere prius intelligi & cognosci ab efficiente, sed nego ista finis rationem rationem habere vt formae sunt & species in mente, sed pro his quae significant & referunt intelligentia artificis.
units.tr: Finally, since we are discussing ends, it is doubtful how a work can be called the end of an action or of an art. For if we consider the thing made by the craftsman, that thing is an effect, and so not a cause, since a cause must be prior in being to its effect, and nothing can be prior to itself. Some reply here that the thing made is the end, not insofar as it exists and is already finished, but insofar as it was first grasped by the mind of the craftsman. And a thing can be prior to itself in a different respect, since it exists in the mind of the craftsman before it is actually made. I do not at all accept this reply. For that form which is known and dwells in the craftsman's mind has the character of an efficient cause, since as an object it moves his mind. Moreover, the craftsman does not desire to have the form only as he has it in his mind, but wants it expressed in the thing, and he strives towards that as his end. Therefore the external thing itself is the final cause, not insofar as it exists or is produced, but insofar as it has the character of a good, and by it the efficient or its action is completed. I grant that these things must be understood and known first by the efficient, but I deny that these ideas in the mind have the character of end. Rather, they have it insofar as they signify and refer to the understanding of the craftsman.

units.la: Quotquot autem sunt huiusmodi, uni alicui facultati subiiciuntur: veluti rei equestri, frenorum effectrix: aliaeque omnes quae equestria instrumenta conficiunt: atque haec, omnisque demum actio bellica sub militarem, atque eodem modo sub alias, aliae. Atque in iis omnibus, fines earum quae architectonicae habentur, magis quam reliqui omnes aliarum quae subiacent, expetendi sunt: nam illos quoque horum causa sectamur.
units.tr: All such arts are subordinated to some one art. For example, the art of making bridles belongs to horsemanship, and all the other arts that make equestrian equipment are likewise subordinate to it. And this art, together with all military action, is subordinated to the military art, and in the same way the others are subordinated to other arts. In all these cases, the ends of those arts that are regarded as architectonic are to be sought more than the ends of all the rest that are subordinate to them, for we also pursue the latter for the sake of the former.

units.la: Sensus est, Cum multae sint artes atq; scientiae, illae inter se ordinem habent, ita ut summa & praecipua omnium sit civilis, quae prae cateris est ἀρχι-τονικὴ[?]: unde finis eius maxime ob oculos habendus est ceu perfectissimus. Propterea multae artes copulantur ad unam, & multae item fines ad unam quandam, ut ad eam perveniatur propter quam homo est. Et sciendum, quod ut facultates praestatiores sunt inter se, ita & illarum fines. Aristotelis exempla sunt artis eius quae frena conficit, & caeterarum quae sunt effectrices ephippiorum, quas omnes sub equestri facultate contineri affirmat. Item ipsius equestris & omnium actionum bellicarum, sicut est equitare, sagittare, iaculari, uti scutis, est una ars architectonica, unde ait sub re militari istas omnes artes comprehendi. Et sciendum, artem illam seu facultatem architectonicam, inferioribus quas habet sub se praescribere ac imperare, & illius finem moderari finibus istarum.
units.tr: The sense is this: since there are many arts and sciences, they stand in an order among themselves, so that the highest and chief of all is the civil art, which is architectonic above the rest. Hence its end is especially to be kept before our eyes as the most perfect. Therefore many arts are joined to one, and many ends likewise to one particular end, so that we may attain that for which man exists. And it should be noted that just as the faculties are superior to one another, so are their ends. Aristotle's examples are of the art that makes bridles and the other arts that produce saddles, all of which he says are contained under horsemanship. Likewise, horsemanship and all military actions, such as riding, shooting with the bow, throwing the javelin and using shields, are under one architectonic art, and so he says that all these arts are comprehended under the military art. And it should be noted that this architectonic art or faculty prescribes and commands the inferior arts under it, and regulates its own end by the ends of these.
