units.la: Appellat hic Aristoteles Artem δύναμιν, respiciens (ut inquit Eustratius) materiem, ut enim materia est potentia, & per potentiam cognoscitur, ita & artes in potentia sunt ad consequendum & non consequendum suam finem. Medicus quandoque sanat, interdum frustratur: orator nonnunquam persuadet, & quandoque id non efficit. In potentia etiam sunt ad diversa, ut medicus & sanare potest & sanitatem corrumpere, orator suadere atq; dissuadere, Dialecticus probare & confutare. Quamuis textus legant ἀρε[?]τῶν, quod tamen in idem recidit, quoniam ἀρετὴ non tantum habitum significat, verum etiam δύναμιν. Atque nihil interest siue actiones fuerint fines actuum, uel praeter ipsas quippiam aliud, ut in scientiis iam commemoratis apparet.
units.tr: Here Aristotle calls art a [δύναμιν] "power" or "capacity", looking (as Eustratius says) to the matter. For as matter is potential, and is known through potency, so the arts are potential with respect to attaining or failing to attain their end. The physician sometimes heals and sometimes fails; the orator sometimes persuades and sometimes does not succeed. They are also potential towards opposite things: the physician can both heal and corrupt health, the orator can both persuade and dissuade, the dialectician can both prove and refute. Although some texts read [ἀρετῶν] "of the virtues", this comes to the same thing, since ἀρετή signifies not only a habit but also a [δύναμιν] power. Nor does it matter whether the ends are actions of the acts themselves, or something apart from them, as appears in the sciences already mentioned.

units.la: Quoniam in genere finium differentiam assignauerat, quod aliqua illarum essent actiones, alia vero opera, & praeceptionem vniuersalem intulerat, quòd vbi finis esset opus, id haberetur praestantius omni actu quo fuisset confectum: ideò nunc, vt non arbitremur illas facultates meliores quae opus habuerint pro fine aliis quae tantummodo in actiones definiát, ista subiicere voluit, quibus affirmat nihil interesse quoad dignitatem facultatum, siue opus finem habeant siue actionem. Nam si facultas eo nomine censeretur nobilior, quòd post actum relinqueret opus, tunc ars fabrilis melior esset ciuili, cùm finis ciuilis constituatur felicitas, quae non est opus sed actio: quod absurdissimum esset, cùm felicitate nihil melius aut felicius possit inueniri: atq; istud etiam superius praemonuimus. In summa statuit iam adductâ sententiam, qua dixerat, illarum facultatum fines esse meliores quàm alias sub se continent quibus imperant & praescribunt, nec debilitari hanc doctrinam illa superiori distinctione de finibus, quòd alia interdum sint actiones, alia vero nonnunquam opera.
units.tr: Having set out in general a distinction among ends, namely that some of them are actions and others works, and having stated the general rule that where the end is a work, it is more excellent than any action by which it was accomplished, Aristotle now wishes to add the following, lest we think that those faculties are better which have a work as their end, rather than those which terminate only in actions. He affirms that, as regards the dignity of the faculties, it makes no difference whether their end is a work or an action. For if a faculty were judged more noble on the ground that it leaves a work after the act, then the art of the smith would be better than the civil art, since the civil end is set as happiness, which is not a work but an action. This would be most absurd, since nothing better or happier can be found than happiness; and we have already forewarned of this above. In sum, he confirms the view stated already, namely that the ends of those faculties which govern and prescribe the faculties subordinate to them are better than those others, and that this doctrine is not weakened by the earlier distinction about ends, that some are sometimes actions and others sometimes works.

units.la: Sed hic dubium est, quando Aristoteles colligit dignitatem cuiusq; finis ex nobilitate facultatis, quodnam sit hoc genus demonstrationis: & respon-demus esse ab effectis, vel vt vulgò dicunt à posteriore, quoniam reuera facultates nobilitatem suam & dignitatem ex finibus trahunt: quare cùm ab illis nobilitentur, ex earum dignitate conficere praestantiam finium, est ab effectis ad causas progredi, quamuis propositio ista retrò commeet siue conuertatur: vt enim dicimus finem melioris facultatis esse praestantiorem, sic etiam dicere possumus nobiliorem esse facultatem quae digniorem finem habuerit.
units.tr: But here a question arises: when Aristotle infers the dignity of each end from the nobility of the faculty, what kind of demonstration is this? We reply that it proceeds from effects, or, as they commonly say, from the posterior. For in truth the faculties derive their nobility and dignity from their ends. Therefore, since they are ennobled by these ends, to infer the excellence of the ends from the dignity of the faculties is to proceed from effects to causes, although this proposition runs backwards, or converts. For just as we say that the end of the better faculty is more excellent, so we may also say that the faculty which has the more worthy end is more noble.

units.la: Cùm sic res habeat, videndum est quomodo haec respondeant sacris li-teris. Primùm dabimus Christiani hominis in agendo multiplices esse fines, nam quandoque spectat eò vt Deum ipsum innocet nomë eius celebret, gratiâs agat, & consimilia, vbi Deum absque vllo medio spectat. Interdum vero contendit vt seipsum instauret, atq; virtutibus & actionibus pulcher-rimis recuperet imaginem Dei, ad quam est conditus. Est etiam aliquando, imò frequentissimè in aliis hominibus iuuandis, vel opibus, vel doctrina, vel consilio: quare manifestum est & Christianae vitae multos esse fines, qui tamen fines vt dicimus gradus inter se atque ordinem habent. Verùm[?] quod Aristoteles ait, vbi opus relinquitur post actū, ipsum opus me-lius esse præcedenti confectione, minimè videtur locum habere in nostris fi-nibus, si vniuersaliter loquamur: nam cùm aliquis charitate adductus pau-perem vestierit, aluerit, sanauerit, aut docuerit, certum est, quod post actū relinquit opus, nempe sanitatem, alimentum vel vestitum, seu doctrinam in pauperem: quo genere operum actio quæ præcedit, nempe obedientia erga De-um & usus charitatis, longè magis placent Deo & sunt pluris æstimanda quam opus post actū remanens, cùm id sit caducum & periturum. Quo-modo autem in Christiano instituto fines quæ multa sunt (ut diximus) in-ter se ordinem habeant, videre licet in Fide, Spe & Charitate: nam prout est Fides maior, & magis per illam Deus agnoscitur, eò Charitas magis cir-ca finem suam inflammatur, ita ut finis & (ut dicunt) obiectum fidei præ-scribat charitati, & quanta est fiducia erga Deum tantus amor in proxi-mum. Finis igitur Charitatis, qui est bonum proximi, ita continetur sub fi-ne Fidei: sic etiam facit ut Fidei facultas quoad hoc, emineat & præstet fa-cultati Charitatis: atque tertiò, ut Fides est firma atque Charitas actuosa, Spes habetur constantior, & patientia seu fortitudine robustiore expecta-mus ut perficiantur divina promissa, quo illa maiore fide apprehendimus atque per charitatem nos fructuosius exercuimus. Satis itaq; ad id quoduo-lumus ostendere essent hæ tres facultates, nimirum fides, spes et charitas. Ve-rum quando se offert ordo tabularum decalogi, possumus aperte hoc idem in illis declarare: nam prima tabula est quæ circa Deum absq; ullo medio ver-satur, altera verò ad proximum dirigitur: & sentiendum est prioris tabulæ, quoniam alteram continet & sub se habet ceu ἀρχιτεκτονικὴ, maiorem esse dignitatem atq; finem eius nobiliorem, quoniam posterioris tabulæ finis re-gitur & gubernatur à priori: unde Lutherus in suo cathechismo finem pri-oris tabulæ prudentissimè repetebat in singulo quoq; præcepto posterioris. Verbi gratia, Quoniam Deus toto corde & tota anima est diligendus, ideò tu non occides: item, quoniam Deus toto corde & tota anima est di-ligendus, adulterium ne committas. Ab his non differt Aristoteles, qui statuit ex eo quòd hoc vel illo modo est equitandum, artem quæ frena conficit & ephippia equorum debere talia vela-lia sua opera facere: proinde quoad hac, non malè consentiunt.
units.tr: Since this is so, we must consider how these points agree with the Holy Scriptures. First, we grant that a Christian man's actions have many ends. Sometimes he aims at honouring God himself, that is, at blessing his name, praising him, giving thanks and similar acts, where he looks to God without any intermediary. At other times he strives to renew himself and to recover, through virtues and most excellent actions, the image of God in which he was created. And sometimes, indeed very often, his aim is to help other people, whether with wealth, teaching or counsel. So it is clear that the Christian life has many ends, and yet, as we say, these ends have degrees and an order among themselves. But what Aristotle says, that where a work remains after the action, the work itself is better than the preceding action that produced it, does not seem to hold in our ends if we speak in general terms. For when someone, moved by charity, clothes, feeds, heals or teaches a poor man, it is certain that what remains after the action is health, food or clothing, or instruction given to the poor man. In this kind of work, the action that comes first, namely obedience towards God and the exercise of charity, pleases God far more, and is to be valued more highly, than the work that remains after the action, since that is perishable and will pass away. Now that the many ends of the Christian way of life (as we have said) have an order among themselves can be seen in faith, hope and charity. For as faith is greater, and God is recognised more through it, charity is inflamed all the more around its own end, so that the end, or (as they say) the object, of faith prescribes to charity, and as great as our trust in God is, so great is our love for our neighbour. Thus the end of charity, which is the good of our neighbour, is contained under the end of faith; and in this way the faculty of faith, in this respect, stands out and surpasses the faculty of charity. And thirdly, as faith is firm and charity active, hope is held to be steadier, and we await with a more robust patience or fortitude the fulfilment of the divine promises, in proportion as we lay hold of them with greater faith and exercise ourselves more fruitfully through charity. Therefore it is enough, for the purpose we have in view, to have shown that these three faculties exist, namely faith, hope and charity. But when the order of the tables of the Decalogue is brought forward, we can openly declare the same thing from them. For the first table is that which concerns God without any intermediary, while the second is directed to our neighbour. And it must be understood that the first table, since it contains the second and holds it under itself as the [architectonic] art, has the greater dignity and its end is the nobler, because the end of the second table is governed and directed by the first. Hence Luther in his catechism most wisely repeated the end of the first table in each single precept of the second. For example: since God is to be loved with the whole heart and the whole soul, therefore you shall not kill; and again: since God is to be loved with the whole heart and the whole soul, do not commit adultery. Aristotle does not differ from these, for he holds that the art which makes bridles and saddles for horses ought to make such things as its works, from the fact that a horse must be ridden in this or that manner; therefore in these respects they agree well.
CHAPTER II.

units.la: Itaque si quis est finis rerum agendarum quem per seipsum velimus & propter ipsum cætera, nec omnia propter aliud eligimus, nam sic processus esset in infinitum, unde noster appetitus esset inanis & vanus, perspicuum est talem finem bonum & optimum esse.
units.tr: So if there is some end of our actions which we want for its own sake, and for the sake of which we want everything else, and if we do not choose everything for the sake of something else (for otherwise the process would go on to infinity, and our appetite would be empty and vain), it is clear that such an end is good and best.

units.la: IN isto capite secundo duo præcipuè tractantur: nam primo loco demonstratur ex finibus aliquem oportere cōstituì extremum & optimum, deinde traditur ad quam scientiam seu facultatem consideratio eius pertineat: sed inter primum & alterum interponuntur de utilitate notitiæ finis extrema. Primæ partis est sensus: In rebus humanis finis est quidam supremus omnium, nisi velimus in immen-sum progredi & appetitum nostrum facere prorsus inanem. Censet Eustratius probationem adductæ propositionis eius esse generis quæ ad absurdum adducunt, quia si non esset aliqua extrema finis, desideria nostra in infinitū abirent, & vanus efficeretur humanus appetitus. Sed nostra desideria in infinitum non abeunt, & appetitus noster non est inanis, ergo est aliqua ex-trema finis: eversione consequentis ad eversionem antecedentis. Verùm hoc videndum est quomodo infinitus progressus vanum efficiat appetitum: de-inde quare tam sit absurdum, si poneretur vanum esse humanum studium. Primum declaratur, quoniam infinitum est quod non potest pertransiri, ut habetur de auditu physico in 4. & in 2. eiusdem operis, vanum scribitur es-se quod ad finem minimè pertingit. Vnde manifestum est appetitum nostrum cum non possit infinitum pertransire, fine suo esse frustrandum, nisi terminus detur & aliquod extremum bonum constituatur. Sed alterum idcirco verum est, nimirum pro absurdissimo habendum, si vanus hominum appetitus esset, nam tunc natura illum frustra dedisset: vulgatissima autem et re-cepta est sententia, Deum & naturam nihil frustra efficere.
units.tr: In this second chapter two main matters are treated. First, it is shown that some supreme and best end must be set up among ends; then it is taught to which science or faculty the consideration of this end belongs. Between the first and the second, Aristotle inserts a point about the usefulness of knowing the final end. The sense of the first part is this: in human affairs there is some supreme end of all, unless we wish to proceed into the immense and make our appetite wholly empty. Eustratius holds that the proof of the proposition is of the kind that leads to an absurdity: if there were no ultimate end, our desires would go on to infinity and human appetite would become vain. But our desires do not go on to infinity, and our appetite is not vain; therefore there is some ultimate end. This is a reasoning by the denial of the consequent to the denial of the antecedent. But we must see how an infinite progress makes appetite vain, and then why it would be so absurd to suppose that human striving is vain. The first point is explained as follows: the infinite is what cannot be traversed, as is stated in the Physics, book 4 and book 2 of the same work, and what does not reach its end at all is rightly said to be vain. Hence it is clear that since our appetite cannot traverse the infinite, it must be frustrated of its end, unless a limit is given and some ultimate good is set up. But the other point is true as well, namely that it must be held most absurd if human appetite were vain, for then nature would have given it in vain; and the most widely received opinion is that God and nature do nothing in vain.

units.la: In verbis textus duo annotabimus, unum quid proprie sit πρακτὰ[?]: si credamus Eustratio, ea sunt quæ nobis aliquid agentibus accedunt, quæ scilicet quisq; actu suo facit, & liquet ista non posse ultimos esse fines, ideo Aristoteles inquit, si talium est aliqua finis quam propter seipsam velimus, &c. nā si agensi agẽda sunt aut faciẽda, propter aliquid aliud fiunt, nemo enim vel frustra vel sine causa quicquam aggreditur. Non errant qui vocem illam converterunt Agenda, nam sic etiam Cicero videtur loqui. Alterum est, quòd rur-sus hic τ᾽ ἀγαθόν [?] nonnulli dixerunt summum bonum, quasi articulus ille appositus id exprimat. Verum nos idem hic sentiendum putamus quod superius ostendimus, ut significetur ipsum bonum, & sensus erit, Eiusmodi finé rerum agendarum qui fuerit extremus, non tantum bonum esse, quòd & aliis finibus est commune, sed optimum: alioqui dicere summum bonum & optimum, esset idem repetere.
units.tr: In the words of the text we shall note two things. The first is what exactly the practical things [πρακτὰ] are. If we believe Eustratius, they are those things which come about through our acting, which each person does by his own action; and it is plain that such things cannot be ultimate ends. Therefore Aristotle says: "if there is some end of such things which we want for its own sake," etc. For if things to be done or made are done for the sake of something else, since no one undertakes anything either in vain or without a cause. Those who translated that word as "things to be done" were not wrong, for Cicero also seems to speak this way. The second point is that some have rendered τἀγαθόν [the good] here as "the highest good," as if the article added there expressed that. But we think the same should be understood here as we showed above, that the good itself is meant. The sense will be: an end of human actions which is the ultimate is not only good, which it shares with other ends, but best. Otherwise, to say "the highest good and best" would be to repeat the same thing.

units.la: Aduersus ea quæ dicta sunt, id facere videtur, quòd appetitus interdum vanus est, nec suam potest finem consequi. Quod primùm apparet quoad illa quæ carent anima: lapides enim cum sint graues, propensionem habent ut deorsum cadant, & nihilominus in ædificijs detinentur sursum, neque suam finem assequuntur. In brutis idem videmus: quoniam talpæ foueam & canum oculorum habent, quin & ipsos oculos, verum occlusos palpebris, quibus nunquam possunt uti, unde natura videtur in eis hæc produxisse frustra: mulæ quoq; uterum habent, cum tamen parere non possint: unde in eis frustra pars illa corporis habetur: quin et in ipsis hominibus idem cernimus, quandoquidem permulti sunt, qui nonnunquam ea cupiunt, quæ nullo modo fieri possunt: unde Aristoteles dixit in his libris, voluntatem esse quandoq; eorum quæ fieri nequeunt, quamobrem non erit firmum quod statue-batur, appetitum non frustrari fine, ac naturam nihil frustra facere. Verùm ad hæc respondemus, tuendo quod est positum, atque incipiemus à carentibus anima, in quibus cum appetitus sit, qui non interiori notitia regitur, sed externa, quippe regis naturæ qui omnia sua prouidentia dirigit, unde fit ut cum eius consilium frustrari non possit, ista quoq; possint omnino suas fines assequi. Unde videas omnia grauia, ut sunt lapides & metalla, deorsum tendere ac iacere in ima parte orbis: quòd si aliquando secus fiat, per accidens euenit: nam industria hominum impediuntur, vel aliquo alio casu, unde submoto impedimento fine potiuntur, à quo si prohibentur, id raro accidit & quoad pauciora. Bruta verò licet sensu prædita sint, praxi tamen & electione carent, ut in sexto libro videbimus: unde etiam diriguntur naturæ intelligentia, quæ cum firma sit & constans, sine sua non frustratur, nisi, ut diximus, per accidens & quoad pauciora.
units.tr: It seems that something is done against what has been said, namely that appetite is sometimes vain and cannot attain its end. This appears first in things that lack soul. For stones, though heavy, have a tendency to fall downwards, and yet they are held up in buildings and do not reach their end. We see the same in brute animals: moles have burrows and dogs have eyes, indeed the eyes themselves, though closed under the eyelids and never usable, so that nature seems to have produced these things in vain. Mules also have a womb, yet they cannot bear young, so that this part of the body is held to be in them in vain. Indeed we see the same in men themselves, since there are very many who sometimes desire things that can in no way come about. Hence Aristotle said in these books that the will is sometimes of things that cannot be done. Therefore what was laid down, that appetite is not frustrated of its end and that nature does nothing in vain, will not be firm. But to these objections we reply by defending what has been stated, and we begin with things without soul. In these there is an appetite which is not governed by inner knowledge but by an external one, since they are ruled by nature, which directs all its things by its providence. So it comes about that, since its purpose cannot be frustrated, these things too can altogether attain their ends. Thus you may see that all heavy things, such as stones and metals, tend downwards and lie at the lowest part of the world. If at any time this happens otherwise, it happens by accident: they are impeded by human industry or by some other chance, and when the impediment is removed they obtain their end; and if they are prevented, this happens rarely and in few cases. Brute animals, though endowed with sense, lack practical reason and choice, as we shall see in the sixth book; hence they too are directed by the understanding of nature, which, since it is firm and constant, is not frustrated of its end, except, as we said, by accident and in few cases.

units.la: Ad ea quæ obiciuntur de talpis & mulis, Galenus de usu partium li-bro 14. scribit de talpis, quòd natura conata quidem est perfectas illas effi-cere, ideoq; delineauit oculos in earum formatione, atq; intra palpebras illos claulos clausit semiperfectos, debilitate vero temperamenti & spiritus impedita est ne posset ipsos propellere in apertum, unde sic remanserunt. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, aliqua interdum esse impedimenta finis consequenda per occasionem materiae, quod nos antea dicebamus esse per accidens. Acidem [?] in lib. 2. de semine. Impedimentum itaq; non est per se, atq; contingit quoad pauciora, id est duntaxat in una talparum specie. Neq; tamen hic natura sua fine frustratur: quoniam talpis ut huiusmodi habeant oculos conducit, nam victurae sunt in terra quam perpetuo fodiunt, ubi oculorum nullus esset usus ob perpetuas tenebras: quin & laederentur aperti pulvere, in quo perpetuo genus hoc animatis versatur. Debilitatem itaque materiae intercedere non nego, ut in canibus videmus, qui ante octavum diem propter ipsorum imperfectionem oculos aperire non possunt, sed in his imperfectio materiae tolli potest, ideo tandem post octo dies canes vident: sed quia in talpis est tanta materiae debilitas, ut oculi exterius protrudi nequeat, ideo Deus naturae autor in hanc finem direxit istud impedimentū oculorum, ut commodius agerent sub terra. Unde in simili casu scribit Galenus locis iam adductis, quod natura in foeminis genitalia delineauit ut in maribus, verum debilitate spiritus & materiae impedita est ne illa exterius, ut sunt in maioribus, extrude-ret, ideo sic manserunt inversa: sed hoc demum in hanc finem & utilitatem ordinatum est, ut sic valeant in seipsis gignere et foetum concipere. Haec Dei est summa prudentia ut materiae infirmitate ad optimas & necessarias fines abutatur, propter quas concedendum est illam debilitatem non esse frustra. De mulis autem dicendum est quoad mares quod procreant, ut vult Aristoteles de historia animalium libro 6. & De generatione animalium libro 2. foeminae vero interdum concipiunt, raro pariunt, & utrunq; habetur pro ostetio si quando contigerit, sed cum fortasse peperit, educare non potest, quandoquidem lacte prorsus caret. Impedimentum ad concipiendum & pariendum est penuria materiae: desunt enim menstrua. Et hoc habet ista species a suis principiis, nimirum asino & equo: nam haec duae naturae promisi-mae [?] sunt ad sterilitatem, partim propter frigiditatem ut asinus, partim ob defectum menstrui ut equa, sicut narrat Aristoteles iam adducto loco. Unde apparet fieri per accidens ut mularum uterus non possit finem assequi. Hoc autem defectu materiae ad quam utilitatem natura providentia vtatur, demonstrari potest: quoniam sic reddunter [?] fortiores, & onera gestando praeponuntur equis: quamuis in Syria mulae sint quae pariant & prolem alant, quas tamen Aristoteles diversas esse putat a communi specie mularum.
units.tr: As for the objections about moles and mules: Galen, in book 14 of On the Use of the Parts, writes of moles that nature indeed tried to make them perfect, and therefore it sketched their eyes in their formation and enclosed those eyes, half-formed, within the eyelids; but, impeded by the weakness of their temperament and spirit, it could not push them out into the open, and so they remained thus. From these words it is gathered that sometimes there are impediments to attaining an end, arising from the occasion of matter, which we said before are by accident. Idem, in book 2 On the Seed. So the impediment is not per se, and it happens in few cases, that is, only in one species of moles. Nor does nature here fail of its end, since it is advantageous for moles, as such, to have eyes that are of little use: for they are going to live in the earth, which they dig continually, where there would be no use of eyes because of the perpetual darkness; indeed they would be harmed if open, by the dust in which this kind of animal constantly lives. I do not deny, therefore, that weakness of matter intervenes, as we see in dogs, which cannot open their eyes before the eighth day because of their imperfection; but in these the imperfection of matter can be removed, so that at last after eight days dogs see. But because in moles the weakness of matter is so great that the eyes cannot be pushed outwards, God, the author of nature, has directed this impediment of the eyes to this end, so that they may act more conveniently under the earth. Hence in a similar case Galen, in the places already cited, writes that nature sketched the genital parts in females as in males, but, impeded by the weakness of spirit and matter, it could not thrust them outwards as they are in males, and so they remained inverted; yet this too has in the end been ordered to this purpose and use, that they may thus be able to generate and conceive offspring within themselves. This is the supreme prudence of God, that by the weakness of matter he makes use of the best and necessary ends, for the sake of which that weakness must be granted not to be in vain. As for mules, it must be said, as regards the males, that they do beget, as Aristotle holds in the History of Animals, book 6, and in On the Generation of Animals, book 2. The females sometimes conceive, rarely bear young, and both are regarded as a portent if it ever happens; but when perhaps she has given birth, she cannot rear the offspring, since she altogether lacks milk. The impediment to conceiving and bearing is a lack of matter: for the menstrual fluid is absent. This species has this from its sources, namely from the ass and the horse; for these two natures are both prone to sterility, partly through coldness, as in the ass, and partly through a defect of menstruation, as in the mare, as Aristotle relates in the passage already cited. Hence it appears that it happens by accident that the mule's womb cannot attain its end. Moreover, it can be shown what useful purpose nature, by its providence, makes of this defect of matter: for in this way mules become stronger, and they are preferred to horses for carrying burdens; although in Syria there are mules that bear young and nourish their offspring, which Aristotle nevertheless thinks are different from the common species of mules.

units.la: Sed his omissis, ad homines veniamus, quorum appetitus est distinguen-dus. Alius enim vagus est, subitus & imperfectus, atque destituitur electi-one: & iste est qui fertur interdum ad ea quae fieri non possunt, et cum sit imperfectus, frustrari potest: verum qui absolutus fuerit & cum electione iu-gitur, is potest sine potiri. Quare Aristoteles in magnis moralibus scribit tres esse appetitus, nimirum ἐπιθυμίαν, θυμόν[?] & βούλησιν, hoc est cupidi-tatem, iram & voluntatem: & cum voluntas sit quae desiderat quippiam cum ratione, ipsa non frustratur, quia nemo cum ratione quae fieri non possunt diligit: cupiditas vero & ira, cum adversus rationem vehementius incitantur, libidines potius dicendae sunt, cumq; ad stultitiam accedant, non mirum si fraudentur finibus. In summa videas in omnibus aut esse per accidens aut imperfectionem. Sed Aristoteles ut artifex considerat quod est per se, non per accidens, & quae in pluribus, non in paucioribus. Deinde agit de re perfecta, scilicet humano appetitu iuncto cum ratione: adhaec in illis datur compensatio maioris boni, quod hic fieri non potest, quoniam extrema fine, id est felicitate nihil est melius.
units.tr: But setting these aside, let us come to human beings, whose appetite must be distinguished. For one kind of appetite is wandering, sudden and imperfect, and lacks choice; this is the kind that is sometimes carried toward things that cannot be done, and since it is imperfect it can be frustrated. But the appetite that is complete and joined continually with choice can attain its goal without fail. Hence Aristotle, in the Magna Moralia, writes that there are three appetites, namely desire [ἐπιθυμίαν], spirit [θυμόν] and will [βούλησιν], that is, cupidity, anger and will. Since will is the appetite that desires something with reason, it is not frustrated, because no one with reason loves what cannot be done. Cupidity and anger, however, when they are stirred up more violently against reason, are rather to be called lusts, and since they go together with folly, it is no wonder if they miss their ends. In sum, you will see that in all these things there is either chance or imperfection. But Aristotle, as an artist, considers what is per se and not per accident, and what holds in most cases rather than in few. Next he treats of the perfect thing, namely human appetite joined with reason; besides, in those cases there is compensation by a greater good, which cannot happen here, since nothing is better than the final end, that is, happiness.

units.la: Sacra literae bene his consentiunt: nam finem extremum hominum statuunt & praescribunt. Unde Salamon ad finem Ecclesiastis, cum multa de finibus iuxta vulgares opiniones prius tractasset, de timore Dei loquitur, qui Hebraica phrasi veram & solidam pietatem significat, adiecit, Et hoc est omnis homo: quia sunt ad hoc instituti & conditi homines, ut Deum colant & revereantur. Et Dauid, Unum petij a Domino, & hoc requiram, ut habitem in domo Dei. Et Christus, Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te solum verum & quem misisti Iesum Christum. Sed obstare videtur quod Solomon dixit, Vanitas vanitatum, & omnia vanitas. At id non est ex eo quod sit finis constitutus, sed quod homines illam vel ignorant aut respuunt, & summum bonum alibi quaerunt: unde in immensum eorum desideria circuitu extenduntur, necunquam quiescunt: In circuitu impij ambulant, Psalm. 12. Et hoc interest inter nos & Philosophos, quod illi suam finem extremam ut propriis viribus atque studio comparandam proponunt: nos vero statuimus ex divinis literis, praecipuum bonum obtineri non posse, nisi spiritu & gratia Christi fuerimus adiuti.
units.tr: The holy letters agree well with these things, for they set out and prescribe the final end of human beings. Hence Solomon, at the end of Ecclesiastes, after he had first treated of many ends according to common opinions, speaks of the fear of God, which in Hebrew idiom signifies true and solid piety, and added: "This is the whole duty of man," because human beings have been appointed and created for this, to worship and revere God. And David: "One thing I have asked of the Lord, and this I will seek, that I may dwell in the house of God." And Christ: "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." But what Solomon said, "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity," seems to stand in the way. Yet this is not because the end has not been appointed, but because men either are ignorant of it or reject it, and seek the highest good elsewhere; hence their desires are stretched out in endless circuits and never rest: "The wicked walk on every side," Psalm 12. And this is the difference between us and the philosophers: they propose that the final end is to be attained by their own strength and effort, but we hold, from the divine letters, that the chief good cannot be obtained unless we have been helped by the Spirit and the grace of Christ.

units.la: Igitur & ad vitam notitia eius magnum momentum habet, & ceu sagittarij scopum habetes facilius assequemur decorum: cumq; ita fit, adnitendum est forma quadam seu figura quidnam ipsum sit comprehendere, & cuiusnam scientiae aut facultatis sit.
units.tr: Therefore the knowledge of this end is of great importance for life too, and, like archers having a mark before them, we shall more easily attain what is fitting. Since this is so, we must strive to grasp in some outline or figure what this end itself is, and to which science or faculty it belongs.

units.la: Quia iam constituit extremam quandam esse finem hominibus praescriptam, nunc adhortatur nos ad eius notitiam capessendam, deinde in eius perscrutatione duo pronunciat se velle facere, id est, ut exponat quidnam sit, deinde ad quam scientiam vel facultatē pertineat. Quoad illud prius, hac propositio esto: Summi finis notitia est inquirenda. Rationem adfert ab utili, Quod vitae conducit est sectandum. Notitia finis huius magnum momen-tum habet ad vitam. Igitur debemus illam comparare. Minor probatur similitudine sagittantium. Procedit Aristoteles magno artificio: quia si eiusmodi finis non esset, quis laboraret in eius perceptione? deinde si esset, nec afferret nobis utilitatem, notitia eius esset inutilis: postremo si prodesset quidem, at non multum, studium remitteremus cognitionis eius. Nunc vero cum sit, & prosit, & maximum momentum habeat ad totam vitam, incitamur vehementissime ad illius inquisitionem.
units.tr: Since he has now established that there is a certain final end prescribed for human beings, he now urges us to take up the knowledge of it. Then in investigating it he declares that he wishes to do two things: to explain what it is, and then to which science or faculty it pertains. As to the first, let this be the proposition: the knowledge of the highest end is to be sought. He brings an argument from usefulness: what is conducive to life is to be pursued. The knowledge of this end is of great importance for life. Therefore we ought to acquire it. The minor premise is proved by the comparison with archers. Aristotle proceeds with great skill: for if there were no such end, who would labour to perceive it? Then, if there were one but it brought us no benefit, its knowledge would be useless; lastly, if it did benefit us but not much, we would relax our zeal for knowing it. But now, since it both exists and benefits us, and has the greatest importance for the whole of life, we are most strongly driven to inquire into it.

units.la: Vox illa ῥοπὴ metaphoram subindicat, ceu monuit Eustratius, desum-ptam à lancibus quae iugum habent in iugo ligulam, quae semper inclinat ad ea quae magis ponderosa fuerint, ut praferantur cæteris: ita notitia ista multum conducit ad vitam, & pondus habet quo inclinet ad se nostra studia. Exemplum sagittariorum eo spectat, ut sicut illi, si propositum non habeant signum, in casum feriunt, sed eo proposito, cum fructu & artificiose: ita & nos extremo bono proposito non agemus casu, sed cum ratione: et certe in itineribus non recte ambulat qui viae terminum ignoraverit.
units.tr: That word rhope [ῥοπὴ] hints at a metaphor, as Eustratius has warned, taken from scales which have at the beam a tongue that always leans toward whatever is heavier, so that it is preferred to the rest. So that knowledge contributes much to life and has a weight by which it inclines our studies toward itself. The example of the archers aims at this: just as they, if they have no mark set before them, strike at random, but with a set mark strike fruitfully and skilfully, so we too shall not act by chance toward the highest good when it is set before us, but with reason. And surely one who does not know the end of the road does not walk rightly on his journey.

units.la: Neq; ab hac sententia divinae literae abhorrent, utilem esse finis extremi notitiam. Christus enim cur tam diu docuit in terris, cur Apostolos misit in mundum praedicatum, quid iubebat ut se sequerentur homines, nisi ut extremam finem tandem cognoscerent, propter cuius ignorationem querebatur populum errare instar ovium absq; pastore?
units.tr: Nor do the divine letters dissent from this opinion, that knowledge of the final end is useful. For why did Christ teach on earth so long, why did he send the Apostles into the world to preach, what did he command when he bade men follow him, except that they might at last come to know the final end, on account of whose ignorance he complained that the people were wandering like sheep without a shepherd?

units.la: Hac propositione confirmata, ut vidimus, duo infert. Primum de hoc supremo fine statuendum quidnam sit, verum pingui, ut aiunt, Minerva: Postea inquirendum ad quam facultatem vel scientiam pertineat. Hoc sane ordine ista duo proponit, sed illum invertit, dum exequitur, quoniam prius de illius facultate seu scientia tractat, & postea definitione aggreditur. Idcirco aut arbitror ordine huius tractationis invertit, quoniam si prius Aristoteles finem hanc extremam definiisset, dicere quis poterat, Cur tu nunc istud agis, cum ad istam facultatem quam pro manibus habes ea definitio non pertineat? Hoc sibi ne iure obiciatur, anteuertit, explicatq; cuiusnam facultatis fit de summo fine agere. Inter scientias & facultates multum interest: nam scientia constat propositionibus necessarijs per se atq; immediatis proprijs, unde necessariæ conclusiones inferuntur, aut in pluribus, aut in his quæ ita demonstrata fuerint. Deinde scientia est ad unum, non versatur inter contraria, nec interrogat, sed accipit. At facultates modo unum, modo aliud concludunt, unde propter materiam dicuntur potentiæ, ut rhetorica, dialectica. Sic illæ artes quæ sunt coniecturales, ut gubernans naues & medica tendentes ad salutem, sæpe cadunt in exitium, & qui sunt periti quandoq; ad salutem illis utuntur, quandoq; ad perniciem.
units.tr: This proposition having been confirmed, as we have seen, he infers two things. First, it must be settled what this supreme end is, truly, as they say, with plain Minerva [that is, with plain common sense]. Afterwards it must be inquired to which faculty or science it belongs. He certainly sets out these two things in this order, but he reverses it in carrying it out, since he first treats of the faculty or science of it and afterwards approaches the definition. I therefore think that he reverses the order of this treatment, because if Aristotle had first defined this final end, someone could say: "Why are you now doing this, since that definition does not belong to the faculty you have in hand?" Lest this be rightly objected to him, he anticipates it and explains to which faculty it belongs to treat of the highest end. There is a great difference between sciences and faculties: for a science consists of propositions that are necessary, known through themselves and immediate and proper to it, from which necessary conclusions are drawn, either in most cases or in those things that have been so demonstrated. Further, a science is directed to one thing; it does not move between contraries, nor does it question, but receives. But faculties conclude now one thing, now another, and for this reason, on account of their matter, they are called potential, as rhetoric and dialectic are. So those arts which are conjectural, such as the steering of ships and medicine aiming at health, often fall into ruin, and those who are skilled sometimes use them for salvation, sometimes for destruction.

units.la: Primo ait hoc negotij ciuilis esse scientia, cum ea sit quæ imperet cæteris artibus, illasq; sibi subiectas habeat et ipsis utatur. Hæc omnia suis locis mo-strabuntur in hoc capite. Propositio erit, Ad ciuilem facultatem pertinet de vltimo fine agere. Componitur autem ratio in hanc formam,
units.tr: First he says that this business belongs to the science of civil life, since it is the science that commands the other arts and has them subject to itself and makes use of them. All these things will be shown in their places in this chapter. The proposition will be: "To the civil faculty it belongs to treat of the final end." The argument is put together in this form:

units.la: Ad illam scientiam hæc res attinet, quæ maxime est architectonica.
units.tr: To that science belongs this thing, which is most of all architectonic.
Civil science is of this kind.

units.la: Quare illius est de fine extremo tractare.
units.tr: Therefore it is its task to treat of the final end.

units.la: Maior propositio declarata est antea, cum diceretur melioris facultatis esse meliorem finem. Minor probatur, nimirum ciuilem esse facultatem supremam & maxime architectonicam, quoniam dicitur in textu,
units.tr: The major premise was explained earlier, when it was said that the better faculty has the better end. The minor is proved, namely that civil science is the supreme faculty and most of all architectonic, since it is said in the text:

units.la: Videbitur autem eius esse quæ maxime nominatur præ cæteris architectonica, & talis apparet ciuilis: etenim quas oportet scientias in ciuitatibus esse, quales item quisque addiscere, nec non quous-que, ipsa præcipit.
units.tr: It will seem to belong to that science which is most of all called architectonic before the others, and such civil science appears to be: for it prescribes which sciences ought to be in cities, and which each person should learn, and up to what point.

units.la: Hæ sane conditiones & propria sunt scientiæ principis: quare videtur ar-gumentari ab eius descriptione, quæ constet tribus partibus, quarum prima est, Ad principem scientiam attinere ut statuat quænam scientiæ atq; artes in ciuitate sint retinendæ: non enim patitur ciuilis ratio, ut sinantur in ciuitatibus inanes & superuacaneæ artes, nam cives illis occupati ab vtilibus revocantur: nec minus tolerat, ut artes malefica, quæ vergunt ad corruptionem animi seu corporis aut fortunarum, admittantur, atq; istud facere ciuilem scientiam videmus apud Aristotelem 7. & 8. Politicorum. Plato item de Republica & de Legibus poetas summouit è republica, & alias quoque artes quæ ad homines effœminandos & corrumpendos faciunt.
units.tr: These conditions are indeed proper to the science of the prince; so it seems that he argues from its description, which consists of three parts. The first is that it belongs to the principal science to determine which sciences and arts are to be retained in the city. For civil reason does not allow empty and superfluous arts to be tolerated in cities, since citizens occupied with them are called back from useful things; nor does it tolerate less that harmful arts, which tend toward the corruption of the mind or body or fortunes, be admitted; and we see civil science doing this in Aristotle, Politics 7 and 8. Plato likewise in the Republic and the Laws removed poets from the commonwealth, and other arts too which work to make men effeminate and corrupt.

units.la: Præterea quia omnes minimè apti sunt ad quancunq; artem, ideò addi-tur, Et quales quisq; debeat addiscere.) Qui enim militiæ apti sunt, ad fabricas relegari non debent: & qui habent literis accommodata ingenia, hi non debent agricolæ fieri. Est enim vulgò tritum, Nihil inuita disces faciésue Minerua: & Inuitis canibus non bene venamur. Facilitas verò inge-niorum ad has vel illas facultates, à temperamento corporis prouenit, per-tinentq; inclinationes & propensiones istæ animi vel ingenij, ad prædica-mentum qualitatis, & ad secundum eius genus, hoc est naturalem potenti-am: natura enim cuiq; inseruntur, non accersuntur studio vel industria. Of-ficium verò est artificum & præceptorum, iuuenis commissi fidei suæ inge-nium & propensionem ab initio explorare: qui si persentiscat ad illa studia vel artes eum non esse idoneum, ne respublica detrimentum capiat in suis ciuibus, rem curatoribus adolescentis patefacere, quo possit ad ea discenda transmitti quorum natura capax fuerit, magnaq; debet in educanda pueri-tia cum publicè tum priuatim diligentia præstari.
units.tr: Moreover, since not everyone is suited to every art, it is added: "and what sort of person each should learn." For those who are suited to military service should not be assigned to crafts, and those whose minds are fitted to letters should not become farmers. It is a commonly repeated saying: "You will learn nothing against the will of Minerva," and "We do not hunt well with unwilling dogs." The ease with which minds take to these or those skills arises from the temperament of the body, and these inclinations and propensities of mind or talent belong to the category of quality, and to its second species, namely natural power. For they are implanted in each person by nature; they are not acquired by zeal or industry. But it is the duty of teachers and instructors, to whom a young person has been entrusted, to test the young person's talent and inclination from the beginning. If they perceive that he is not fit for those studies or arts, they should disclose this to the young person's guardians, so that he may be transferred to learn those things for which his nature is capable, lest the commonwealth suffer harm through its citizens. Great diligence must be shown in the upbringing of boys, both publicly and privately.

units.la: Additur præterea, Et usque quo.) Cuius particulæ sensus multiplex esse potest. Primus, ut referatur ad ætatem discentium, et annos aut tempus impendendum artibus: non enim decet, ut aliqui per bonam aut maiorem partem vitæ nihil aliud agant quàm Grammaticam discere, vel Rhetoricam vel Dialecticam: distribuendæ sunt partes ætatis, ut cum fructu reipublicæ possint ciues à facultatibus minoribus ad potiorum studia reuoca-ri. Alter sensus est, ut Quousque referatur ad terminos artificiorum: debet enim ciuilis magistratus prospicere, ne artes progrediantur ad inuti-lia, quæ solum voluptates afferunt superuacaneas, & leues curiosasque oblectationes, ut in ædificijs quandoque agitur. Potest enim domus com-modè habitari, licet non habeat lapides magnis impensis expolitos, & sculpturas admirabiles & sumptuosissimi artificij. Sutores item modum quendam retineant in vestibus parandis, neque eis liceat quamuis formam aut figuram vestibus aptare. Musicis quoque imponetur modus & & poetis, neque quicquam lasciuum aut molle fingant aut canant: & quod est de his artibus aliud, de aliis intelligi debet, nempe ut ciuilis cuique illarum terminos definiat. Tertiò præscribitur ab eadem facultate, quousque inferiores artes debeant obsequi superioribus, ut qui facit frena pro equestri arte, ad certum numerum conficiat, & qui naues compingunt quo instruatur classis & navigatio, ad arbitrium ciuilis magnitudinem faciant. Conspicimus autem nobilissimas quasque facul-tates sub ista esse, ut militarem, domesticam, oratoriam, &c.
units.tr: It is further added: "and how far." The sense of this particle can be manifold. The first is that it refers to the age of the learners, and to the years or time to be spent on the arts. For it is not fitting that some people should spend the greater or better part of their lives doing nothing but learning grammar, or rhetoric, or dialectic. The stages of life should be divided, so that citizens may be recalled from lesser skills to the pursuit of more important ones, to the benefit of the commonwealth. The other sense is that "how far" refers to the limits of the crafts. For the civil magistrate ought to see to it that the arts do not advance to useless things, which afford only superfluous pleasures and light and idle delights, as sometimes happens in buildings. For a house can be lived in comfortably even if it has no stones polished at great expense, and no wonderful sculptures of the most costly workmanship. Likewise, let cobblers keep a certain measure in preparing clothes, and let them not be permitted to fit any shape or figure to garments. Limits should also be imposed on musicians and poets, and they should not invent or sing anything wanton or soft. What is said of these arts should be understood of others as well: the civil power should define the limits of each. Thirdly, this same faculty prescribes how far the lesser arts ought to obey the higher. For example, the maker of bridles, for the art of horsemanship, should make a fixed number, and those who build ships should make them in a size according to the decision of the civil authority, so that the fleet and navigation may be equipped. We observe, moreover, that all the most noble faculties are placed under it, such as military, domestic, oratorical, and so on.

units.la: Confirmat his verbis probationem iam allatam, & est ac si diceret, Imperat quidem ciuilis artibus & facultatibus, at non quibusuis sed praestantissimis, ut illae sunt quae hic recensentur. Nam si de his loquamur quae in republica sunt honestissimae, non possumus inuenire praestantiores militari facultate atq; oratoria, quibus ciuilis ita praest, ut Imperatore eligat, genus expeditionis assignet, fines quousq; progrediendum sit circumscribat, & consimilia. Imperat etiam saepius oratoribus quando sententiam dicunt in senatu vel apud populum, nec non cum accusant aut defendunt, ut affectus non moueant, nihil extra causam dicant, sed narrent simpliciter, & argumentis fidem faciant. Est etiam res domestica in ciuitatibus momenti non vulgaris, cui tractandae & gubernandae ciuilis multa praescribit & mandat, nimirum ut sit modus aliquis agrorum, famulorum, temporum vendendi atq; emendi, & cetera huius ordinis.
units.tr: He confirms with these words the proof already given, and it is as if he said: the civil power indeed commands the arts and faculties, but not just any, only the most excellent, such as those listed here. For if we speak of those things in the commonwealth that are most honourable, we cannot find any more excellent than the military and the oratorical faculties. Over these the civil power so presides that it chooses the commander, assigns the kind of expedition, and marks out how far it is to advance, and similar matters. It also often commands orators when they deliver an opinion in the senate or before the people, and likewise when they accuse or defend, so that they do not stir the emotions, say nothing beyond the case, but narrate plainly and win belief by their arguments. There is also the domestic matter, which is of no small importance in cities. In handling and managing it, the civil power prescribes and enjoins much, namely that there be some measure in the selling and buying of fields, servants, and times, and other things of this kind.

units.la: Cum itaque scientiis aliis practicis utatur, & legibus decernit quid agere oporteat & a quibus temperare, finis profecto ipsius aliarum fines comprehendet, ita ut ipse humanum bonum sit.
units.tr: Since, therefore, it makes use of the other practical sciences, and by its laws decides what ought to be done and from what things one should abstain, surely its end will comprehend the ends of the others, so that it itself is the human good.

units.la: Addit etiam ciuilis facultatis quandam eximiam facultatem, nempe ut caeteris omnibus tanquam administris utatur: quod non est leue. Nam quandoque fit, ut quippiam sub se habeat nonnulla quibus praescribat & praesit, non tamen eis utatur: quemadmodum Geometria sub se comprehendit Astronomiam, eiq; praescribit quoad principia et materiam, hoc est orbes & figuras, non tamen ea scientia utitur ceu administra: quod idem Arithmeticae accidit circa Musicam. Quare cum ita res habeat, robustè demonstratum est, ciuilis esse facultatis de extrema hominis fine agere.
units.tr: This civil faculty also has a certain outstanding quality, namely that it uses all the others as its servants, which is no small matter. For it sometimes happens that a science has under it certain others, which it prescribes for and presides over, yet does not use them. Thus geometry comprehends astronomy under it and prescribes to it as regards its principles and matter, that is, orbs and figures, yet that science does not use astronomy as a servant. The same thing happens with arithmetic in relation to music. Since matters stand thus, it has been firmly demonstrated that it belongs to the civil faculty to treat of the ultimate end of man.

units.la: Etenim si est idem bonum uni & ciuitati, maius utique ac diuinius esse videtur ciuitatis suscipere & conseruare: amabile quidem enim quod uni soli, pulchrius vero & diuinius quod genti & ciuitati-bus. Haec igitur doctrina, cum sit quaedam ciuilis, i-sta appetit, &c.
units.tr: For if the good of one and the good of a city are the same, then surely it seems greater and more divine to undertake and preserve the good of a city. For what is good for one alone is lovable, but what is good for a nation and for cities is more beautiful and more divine. This teaching, therefore, since it is a kind of civil doctrine, seeks that, and so on.

units.la: Mihi sanè videntur hæc dici per occupationem: nam antea constituerat ciuilis esse facultatis de optima fine hominis & summa considerare: quod item cum ipse velit nunc facere, facile quispiam obiceret, Quid tu hoc ag-grederis, quasi tua scientia & ciuilis sit eadē, quasi finis Ethices, de qua modo agis, et finis Politicæ sint idem. Ad hæc respondet, et primū de fine quod ipsa eadem est quæ ad unū hominem spectat et quæ ad gentem seu ciuitates: nō differt finis unius hominis et reipublicæ nisi ratione, nepe quod gētis aut ciuitatis finis ad plures extenditur, moralis autem ad unum: materia ita-que acres est eadē, & à seipsa differt ut magis vel minus ampliatur. Quid enim tanquam finis quæritur in Ethicis, nisi ut quisq; singillatim viuat ex virtute, quod idem studet politica facultas in republica, nimirum ut cives omnes ex virtute agant: & fatetur Aristoteles bonum illud & finem publicum melius esse ac optabilius cum sit latius, quemadmodum diceremus lucem præstantiorem & clariorem quæ latissimum tractum illustrat, quàm sit ea quæ vel cubiculum vel aliud aliquis locus paruus illuminatur, non sane quod materia variet, sed quia extensio non est eadem. Accedit præterea bonum illud amplius ideo magis expetendum esse, quia in communi etiam particularia comprehenduntur, at non e diuerso. Appellat illud quoq; diui-nius, quoniam Dei munera ut videmus in natura diffunduntur, ita ut res quælibet eius bonitatem vtcunque participet. Atque cum dicitur Vni soli, potest id ad seipsum referri, vel ad quempiam alterum particularem: namis qui plures iuuat longè præfertur ei qui tantum sibi ipsi vel vni cui-piam alteri prodest.
units.tr: It seems to me that these things are said by way of anticipation. For he had earlier established that it belongs to the civil faculty to consider the best end of man and the highest good, and since he now wishes to do the same, someone might easily object: "Why do you take this up, as if your science and the civil science were the same, as if the end of Ethics, of which you are now treating, and the end of Politics were identical?" To this he replies, and first about the end, that it is indeed the same, since it concerns both the single man and the nation or cities. The end of one man and of the commonwealth differs only in its scope: the end of a nation or city extends to more people, while the moral end extends to one. Thus the matter is the same in both, and it differs from itself only as it is enlarged more or less. For what is sought as the end in Ethics, if not that each individual should live in virtue? The civil faculty in the commonwealth pursues the same thing, namely that all citizens should act virtuously. And Aristotle admits that this public good and end is better and more desirable because it is wider, just as we would say that a light which illumines a very broad region is more excellent and clearer than one which lights a small room or some other small place. This is not because the matter varies, but because the extent is not the same. Moreover, that greater good is more to be desired for this reason too, that in the common good the particular goods are also included, but not the reverse. He calls it also more divine, since, as we see, God's gifts are spread through nature, so that every thing in some way partakes of his goodness. And when it is said "for one alone," this can be referred to himself or to some other particular person. For one who helps many is far preferred to one who benefits only himself or some single other person.

units.la: Sicitaq; declaratum est, fines Politices vel Ethices non re, sed tantùm ratione differre, quare si de illo tractatur, tam hic quàm ibi nihil absurdi committitur, quod adhuc vt magis declaret, adjcit hanc doctrinam, quam videlicet habemus præ manibus, ciuilem quandam esse, vnde consequitur, cùm ita conueniant, in fine non dissentire. Quid enim moralis facultas tractat nisi elementa ciuilis, nam partes ex quibus componitur ciuitas sunt bo-ni ciues: & hoc vt melius intelligatur, sciendum est ciuem dici bonum virum qui prudentibus auscultans virtutem exercet. Ciuilis autem vir est, qui iu-[?][?]ta & honesta habet ex seipso præcepta, eaq; in ciuitatibus præscribit & do-cet, atq; perfectionem publicam, qua multorum sit, studiosè promouet. Qua re cùm in Ethicis rationes virtutum tradantur, quæ sunt ciuilis facultatis principia, recte dicitur ipse liber ciuilis esse facultatis, verùm nō absolutè, sed quædam, quod ab aliquibus ita intelligitur, quasi ciuilis nomen, ac na-tura sit communis quæ postea in tria membra deducatur, moralem inquam OecoOeconomicam & ciuilem propriam, sed mihi magis arridet prior sensus, ut hæc idcirco dicatur ciuilis quadã, quod elementa et principia politicis tradat: et finis humanus ad ista quoq; pertinet, at non simpliciter, sed quauis est.
units.tr: Thus it has been made clear that the ends of Politics and of Ethics differ not in reality but only in the way they are conceived. Therefore, when one treats of the one, nothing absurd is committed in treating the other as well. To make this clearer still, he adds that this teaching which we have before us is a kind of civil doctrine, from which it follows that, since they agree in this way, they do not differ in their end. For what does moral science treat of, except the elements of civil science? The parts of which a city is composed are good citizens. And so that this may be better understood, it should be known that a citizen is called a good man who, listening to the prudent, practises virtue. A civil man, moreover, is one who has from himself rules of what is just and honourable, and who prescribes and teaches these in cities, and zealously promotes the public perfection, which belongs to many. Therefore, since in Ethics the reasons for the virtues are set out, which are the principles of the civil faculty, it is rightly said that this very book belongs to the civil faculty, yet not absolutely, but in a certain sense. Some understand it in this way, as if the name and nature of "civil" were common, and later divided into three parts: the moral, I mean, the economic, and the civil proper. But I prefer the former sense: this is called civil in a certain way because it hands down the elements and principles of politics, and the human end pertains to these also, not simply, but in some measure.

units.la: Duo nunc excutienda sunt dubia. Primum, quod superius ait ciuilem v-ti reliquis practicis scientijs, qui factu est ut contemplantes tacuerit? Respon-detur, quoniam illis nō proprie utitur, sed tantum imperat ut in ciuitate habeã-tur, & inter eas discrimen ponit decernens quæ magis & quæ minus sint ne-cessariæ: necetiā proprie dicitur uti eis, quoniam postquā ciuitas & bonis mo-ribus instituta fuerit, & rebus ad victū necessarijs instructa, ut perfectio quadã extrema & summa ornamenta contemplantes admittit scientias, unde Romæ primus erat quodammodo perfecta respub. quā ibi philosophi aut uisi aut auditi essent. Non aut utimur fine, sed his potius quæ sunt ad finem, uerum contemplari diuina & naturalia, finis est post uirtutes, ut videbitur in de-cimo prudenter itaque cum ageretur de usu, contemplantes facultates re-ticuit. Quæritur prætera, cur dicat hanc doctrinam ista desiderare, loqué-do plurali numero, cū de una & summa fine hominū agatur? Ad hoc respō-det Eustratius, quoniā perfectissimus est hic finis, ideo sub se multos alios habet qui ad ipsum referuntur: et oportet quelibet ad illū tedere iuxta suā có-ditionē, ita ut eo dirigat quæ habet ad illū pertinetia. Vel, ait, dicendū est, quod licet hæc moralis facultas bonum tradat unius hominis, attamen quia non ignorat se ministram esse ciuilis, & homines quos instruit parari ut re-rum publicarum & ciuitatum possint esse boni ciues, ideo cum sua fine pu-blicam etiam desiderat.
units.tr: Two doubts must now be examined. First, he said above that civil science uses the other practical sciences. How is it that he has been silent about the contemplative ones? The answer is that civil science does not properly use them. It only commands that they be kept within the state, and it distinguishes among them, deciding which are more and which less necessary. It is even said to use them properly, since once the state has been founded on good morals and furnished with what is needed for life, it admits the contemplative sciences as a kind of final perfection and highest ornament. That is why at Rome the republic was in a sense already perfect when philosophers were seen or heard there. Moreover, we do not use the end; we use the things that are toward the end. But to contemplate divine and natural things is the end, after the virtues, as will be seen in the tenth book. Therefore, since the discussion concerned use, he was silent about the contemplative faculties. Further, it is asked why he says this doctrine requires these things, using the plural, when the subject is the one and highest end of humans. To this Eustratius answers that since this end is most perfect, it has many others under it that are referred to it, and each must strive toward it according to its own condition, so that it directs to it whatever it has that pertains to it. Or, he says, it must be said that although this moral faculty teaches the good of one man, nevertheless, because it knows that it serves civil science, and that the men it instructs are prepared to be good citizens of commonwealths and states, therefore it also desires the public good along with its own end.

units.la: Modo videndum, quomodo sacris literis quæ dicta sunt, bene congruāt: ubi primū illud occurrit, proprietate illā principis facultatis: vel, ut ipse lo-quitur, [?]ἀρχιτεκτονικὴ[?], facultati diuinarum literarū debere assignari nā ibi habetur summa & princeps notitia perfectissimi boni, quare Deus aiebat Israelitis eā fore illorū sapientiā quā omnib. gentibus tandem essent admi-rationi. Quod si iū verū fuit, quādo legem duntaxat acceperūt, quid postea censemus adiectis prophetarū scriptis, & noui testamenti uoluminibus? Cer-tè hic ea est ars & facultas quæ omnibus aliis imperat, eximias quasq; sub se habet, & omnib. ad suā fine vtitur. Quod enim de ciuili dicebatur, quod statuat quas artes & scientias debeat admittere respublica, & quas debeat repudiare, hoc animaduertimus in sacris libris exquisitè fieri: approbant e-nim magistratus, volunt esse pastores, episcopos, doctores, artificia quoq; me-chanica, ut pauperes laboret ac sua industria necessaria pareat, non modo si-bi, nerū et alijs quos interdū oportet iuuare, ac è diuerso excludit magos, py-thonicos thonicos, ariolos, meretricia et lenonia arte. Utq; illa civilis phibebatur de--finire quales artes quisq; oporteret addiscere, quod non oes ad omnia sunt a-pti, sicubet sacra litera, ut non confundamus vocationes, utq; nullus in alie-nam irrupat: maneat quisq; inquit Apostolus, in eo quod est vocatus; nam si fueris in coiugio, re œconomica, uxoris, inquã, liberorũ & familiæ curãne abijcito, ut præposterè cœlibatũ velis tibi vendicare: quòd si e diverso in cœli-batu es, ac in eo magis promoues gloriã Dei, nec d:sunt vires à spiritu sancto collatæ, ibi maneas. Ite cũ nõ possint oes esse doctores, prophetæ aut pasto-ees[?], quisq; sit charismate suo cotentus & illo quã diligetissimè utatur. Præ-scribunt etiã sacra litera, quousq; in facultatib. et functionib. progrediendũ sit. ceremonijs neterib. ut veteretur Christiani concessit quidè primitiua eccle-sia, sed aliquatisper: obedietiã quoq; commendat erga magistratus, sed usq; ad aras: vult ut Propheta insituat populũ, sed tantisper dum alteri non revela-tur, quòd cũ factum fuerit: inquit Paulus, prior taceat: libertate Christi-anam & piam in cibis & rebus externis ac civilibus laudat ac probat, sed coufq; ut caveatur offensa infirmorum: moderationem quoq; prædicat, qua nos admittamus ad simplicitatis infirmitates, sed coufq; ut nostra simulatione nõ confirmemus abusus. Etiam numerũ præscribit, ut Politia, & ordinem, nam Paulus duos aut tres voluit esse prophetas, qui per vices loquerentur, & constituit ut donum linguarum cederet utilioribus facultatibus. Habet etiã divina scriptura sub se nobilissimas functiones, præcipit enim regibus, magistratibus, œconomis, & oratoribus. nulla est enim harum facultatum quæ in divinis literis non habeat sibi descripta singularia præcepta, & istis omnibus utitur, magistratibus & principibus ad pietatem & veritate divini cultus defendendam: eloquentia, ut utilia & pia suadeat: œconomia, ut nova soboles semper Christo succrescat, & deniq; omnibus artibus tum ad gloriam Christi tum ad proximorum utilitatem.
units.tr: Now we must see how the things said agree well with the sacred letters. Here first occurs the point that the principal faculty, as he calls it, the architectonic, ought to be assigned to the faculty of the divine letters. For there is found the highest and chief knowledge of the most perfect good. Hence God said to Israel that their wisdom would be such that at last they would be admired by all nations. If this was true when they had received only the law, what shall we judge afterwards, with the writings of the prophets added and the volumes of the New Testament? Surely here is that art and faculty which commands all the others, has the choicest of them under it, and uses all of them for its end. For what was said of civil science, that it determines which arts and sciences the commonwealth should admit and which it should reject, we observe is done exquisitely in the sacred books. They approve magistrates; they want there to be ministers, bishops, teachers, and also mechanical arts, so that the poor labour and by their industry earn what is necessary, not only for themselves but also for others whom it is sometimes right to help. Conversely, they exclude magicians, pythonists, soothsayers, and the arts of harlots and pimps. And as civil science was said to define which arts each person ought to learn, since not all are fit for all things, so the sacred letters do likewise, so that we do not confuse callings and no one intrudes into another's. Let each remain, says the Apostle, in that in which he was called. For if you are married, do not cast off the economic care of wife, children and household, as if you could foolishly claim celibacy for yourself. But if on the contrary you are unmarried, and in that state you promote the glory of God more, and the powers conferred by the Holy Spirit are not lacking, remain there. Again, since not all can be teachers, prophets or pastors, let each be content with his own gift and use it most diligently. The sacred letters also prescribe how far one should advance in faculties and functions. The primitive Church indeed allowed Christians to use indifferent ceremonies, but only for a while. It also commends obedience toward magistrates, but only up to the altars. It wills that the prophet instruct the people, but only so long as it is not revealed to another; when that happens, says Paul, let the first keep silent. They praise and approve Christian and pious liberty in foods and external and civil matters, but only so far as the offence of the weak is avoided. They also preach moderation, by which we admit the weaknesses of simplicity, but only so far that we do not by our pretence confirm abuses. It also prescribes number and order, as a polity does. For Paul wanted two or three prophets to speak in turn, and ordained that the gift of tongues give way to the more useful faculties. Divine Scripture also has the most noble functions under it, for it instructs kings, magistrates, economists and orators. There is none of these faculties for which the divine letters do not have particular precepts described, and it uses all of them: magistrates and princes to defend piety and the truth of divine worship; eloquence, so that it persuades what is useful and pious; economy, so that a new offspring always grows up to Christ; and finally all the arts, both for the glory of Christ and for the usefulness of neighbours.

units.la: Etiam ut opinor, hinc potest liquere, quomodo ministri ecclesiarum, qui has[?] divinas literas profitentur, se habeant erga magistratus, et magistratus erga eos. Illi ex divinis literis depromunt functionis principalis præcepta et regulas, eas audire debet magistratus: quas etiam si nonnunquã transgrediatur, pati debet monitores, nec indignari si modeste ac justa reverētia corrigatur: è diverso cũ ministri vel negligenter in suo munere vel contra præscripta divina se gesserint, à magistratu contineri possunt in officio & si non emendarint vitia, poterunt loco moveri. Sic itaq; ministerium ecclesiæ juvat civilem facultatem, atq; vicissim ea ministerium curat, ut purum sit et Christiana respublica utile. Ex eo verò quòd summam facultatem attribuimus illi sapientiæ quam habemus in diuinis literis, nihil detractum vel diminutum censeri debet administrationi politicæ: manet enim sua authoritas principibus & magistratibus, sed tantùm voluimus ostendere, vnde nam ipsi regulas & principia suæ facultatis debeant sumere, ne sic admirentur Philosophorum doctrinas & hominum leges, vt à purissimis fontibus iustitiæ et honestatis, qui scatent in sacris literis, aberrent: poterunt autem notitiam huiusmodi sibi com-parare, vel sacras literas per seipsos sedulo euoluendo, quod præcepit Deus regibus vt facerent, vel poterunt per Ecclesiæ ministros instrui. Cumq; dici-tur ciuilis esse, vt imperet quæ retinenda sint in ciuitate studia, quæq; inde sint explodenda, intelligant principes & magistratus rationem diuini cul-tus ad se spectare, nempe vt legitimum conseruent, promoueant et tueatur: impurum verò & interdictum prohibeant ac funditus extirpent.
units.tr: Also, as I think, it can be made clear from this how the ministers of the churches, who profess these divine letters, stand toward the magistrates, and the magistrates toward them. The former draw from the divine letters the precepts and rules of their principal function, and the magistrate ought to hear these. Even if he sometimes transgresses them, he ought to bear with those who admonish him, and not be indignant if he is corrected modestly and with due reverence. Conversely, when ministers have behaved negligently in their office, or contrary to the divine precepts, they can be restrained in their duty by the magistrate, and if they do not amend their faults, they can be removed from their place. Thus the ministry of the Church helps the civil faculty, and in turn the civil faculty takes care of the ministry, so that the Christian commonwealth may be pure and useful. Yet from the fact that we attribute the highest faculty to that wisdom which we have in the divine letters, nothing should be thought to be taken away or diminished from political administration. For authority remains to princes and magistrates. We have only wished to show whence they ought to take the rules and principles of their own faculty, so that they do not so admire the doctrines of philosophers and the laws of men as to stray from the purest fountains of justice and honesty, which overflow in the sacred letters. They will be able to acquire this knowledge for themselves, by diligently reading the sacred letters, as God commanded kings to do, or they may be instructed through the ministers of the Church. And since it is called civil in that it commands which studies are to be retained in the state, and which are to be cast out from it, let princes and magistrates understand that the regulation of divine worship belongs to them: namely, that they preserve, promote and protect what is lawful, and that they forbid and utterly root out what is impure and prohibited.
CHAPTER III.

units.la: DIcetur autem satis, si iuxta subiectam materiam explanabitur. Non enim in omnibus disputa-tionibus similiter exquisitum & subtile genus requi-ritur, veluti nec in ijs quæ arte fabricantur.
units.tr: It will be said enough if it is explained according to its subject matter. For not every kind of discussion requires the same exact and subtle method, just as it does not in the case of things made by craft.

units.la: EVstratius arbitratur hic alterum haberi ab Aristotele proœmi-um: ego verò non nisi vnum esse statuo, in quo cum prius docu-erit rerum humanarum aliquem esse finem, postea q; ostenderit varios & multiplices ibi deprehendi fines, & adhæc inter mul-tos vnum esse summum atq; præcipuum, cuius notitia sit apprime vtilis, e-iusq; tractationem ad ciuilem pertinere: nunc exponit quo genere doctrinæ sit agendum, & hoc tertio capite non tantùm id facit, sed etiam ostendit duo quæ ad auditorè pertinent, vnû vt eo sit contentus [?], quod res quæ tractatur po-test pati: alterum ne impediatur eius iudicium perturbationibus & pra-uis affectibus. Hæ sunt præcipuæ tres partes huius capitis, quarũ termini et initia suis locis indicabuntur.
units.tr: Eustratius thinks that Aristotle here has a second proem. I hold that there is only one. In it, he first teaches that there is some end of human affairs, then shows that various and manifold ends are found there, and that among many there is one supreme and chief end, whose knowledge is especially useful and whose treatment belongs to civil science. Now he explains what kind of teaching the matter requires. In this third chapter he does not only do this, but also shows two things that concern the hearer: first, that he be content with what the subject under discussion can bear; second, that his judgement not be disturbed by passions and depraved affections. These are the three chief parts of this chapter, whose limits and beginnings will be indicated in their places.

units.la: Primùm agit de forma & conditione doctrinæ, atq; id merito, nam si coepisset de summafine hominis rationibus agere pinguiorib. ac verisimilibus, potuisset accusari negligetia, ideo anteuertit, monetq; rerum naturam quæ hic tradendæ sunt non posse aliter tradi, quod non multum habeant certitudinis & parum admodum constantiæ, quæ in re non multum videtur ab Academicis, inter quos edoctus fuerat, discedere: est ac si diceret, Talis de debet esse doctrina quales res fuerint de quibus agitur. Hoc fundamentum in-de potest illustrari, quod res & sermones quibus hæ explicantur, dum con-feruntur inter se, unum eorum mensuræ habet rationem, alterum vero e-ius quod metimur: inter quæ omnes intelligunt æqualitatem seu proportio-nem esse debere. Et Plato dicebat in Timæo, inter orationes & res quæ dicu-tur, germanam quandam cognationem oportere intercedere, ut si de re fir-ma & stabili disputetur, oratio eiusdem generis adhibeatur: quod si occur-rant mobilia & incerta dicenda, verisimili utamur oratione. Argumenti Aristotelis hæc est forma:
units.tr: First he treats of the form and condition of the teaching, and rightly so. For if he had begun to speak of the final end of man with rich and merely plausible arguments, he could have been accused of negligence. So he anticipates the charge and warns that the things to be taught here cannot be taught otherwise, since they have little certainty and very little stability, and in this matter he seems to depart little from the Academics, among whom he had been educated. It is as if he said: the teaching must be of the same kind as the things it deals with. This principle can be made clearer as follows: when things and the words by which they are explained are compared with each other, one of them stands as a measure, the other as the thing measured; and everyone understands that between these there ought to be equality or proportion. Plato also said in the Timaeus that there ought to be a kind of genuine kinship between the speeches and the things spoken of, so that if the discussion concerns something firm and stable, the speech used is of the same kind; but if things mobile and uncertain are to be spoken of, we use probable speech. The form of Aristotle's argument is this:

units.la: Quæcunq; facultas de rebus parum certis & variis agit, illa non potest uti exactis & absolutis demonstrationibus:
units.tr: Whatever faculty deals with matters that are little certain and variable cannot use exact and absolute demonstrations.
Ethics and Politics are concerned with such matters.

units.la: Itaq; oratione probabili docent, neq; perfectissimas & exquisitas demon-strationes adducent.
units.tr: Therefore they teach by probable discourse, and they will not bring forward the most perfect and exquisite demonstrations.

units.la: Maiorem probat, quia non in omni genere similiter exactum requiritur, quod patet in artibus. Minorem postea exponit de honesto, iusto & bono. Per subiectam materiam intelligit Aristoteles ipsas res circa quas versa-tur facultas, & vulgo appellatur scientiæ aut doctrinæ subiectum, unde sci-endum est, doctrinas & scientias esse qualitates primæ speciei, atq; ob id ma-teriam non habere ex qua fiant, cum ea sit duntaxat compositorum in gene-re substantiæ, sed conceditur eis duplex aliud genus materiæ, unum in quo nempe sunt, & ita facultatum, scientiarum & artium materia est animus, quia in eo sunt & illi tanquam subiecto innituntur, quod est omnibus accidentibus commune: alterum genus materiæ habent quod tractant, circa quod versantur & se exercent, atque de hac materia in præsentia loquitur Aristoteles, & ea in Ethicis & Politicis est, agenda in rebus humanis u-nà cum ipsis actionibus: differentiæ vero adhibentur, quod hic sub ratione unius ista traduntur, in Politicis vero ut ad plures diffunduntur.
units.tr: He proves the major premise, because a similarly exact standard is not required in every kind of thing, as is evident in the arts. He then sets out the minor premise concerning the honourable, the just and the good. By "subject matter" Aristotle means the very things with which a faculty is concerned, which is commonly called the subject of a science or doctrine. Hence it must be known that doctrines and sciences are qualities of the first species, and for that reason do not have a matter out of which they are made, since that belongs only to composite things in the genus of substance. But they are granted a twofold other kind of matter. One is that in which they exist: thus the matter of faculties, sciences and arts is the mind, because they are in it and rest upon it as their subject, which is common to all accidents.
