The other kind of matter is what they handle, what they are concerned with and exercise themselves upon. It is of this matter that Aristotle speaks at present, and in the Ethics and Politics it is to be treated in human affairs together with the actions themselves. The differences are that here these things are taught under the aspect of one unity, whereas in the Politics they are spread out over more.

units.la: Hinc tamen quod ista non tam exquisitè ac tanta certitudine tradi pos-sunt, quanta multæ aliæ scientiæ docentur, non debet adduci quispiam, ut stu-dium remittat, vel hoc genus facultatis abiiciat, nisi eadem ratione velit & nobilissimas alias doctrinas explodere, ut est medica, rhetorica & aliæ consimiles. Ratio quam adducit Aristoteles ita ponitur. Exquisitum, subtile atq; accuratum genus docendi non est in quouis genere simili ratione quære[?]-dum: quod probat, quia non requiritur à quolibet artifice perfectum et exactum opus, nam ratio habetur materiae circa quam versatur. Atq; hoc Eustratius pulchrè declarauit. Circa imaginē, inquit, hominis effingendam multi artifices laborant, pictura & statuaria: atq; statuaria multiplex est, nam quandoq; per eam cera formatur, aut lutum, celantur metalla, exsculpuntur ligna & lapides, & inter has artes maioris negocij est pictura, quoniam ab illa subtilius opus & perfectius exigitur, plus deinde postulant artificij in cera, quam in ligno aut lapide, quod facilius manibus cedat artificis: quòd si hoc in artib. accidit, in his etiam concedendum est doctrinis et facultatibus.
units.tr: From the fact that these things cannot be taught with such exactness and such great certainty as many other sciences are, no one should be led to relax his study or reject this kind of faculty. Otherwise, by the same reasoning, he would also have to reject the most noble disciplines, such as medicine, rhetoric and others like them. The reason Aristotle gives is put thus: an exact, subtle and accurate method of teaching is not to be sought in every kind of subject alike. He proves this because a perfect and exact work is not required of every craftsman, since regard is had to the matter with which he works. Eustratius has explained this well: "In fashioning the likeness of a man," he says, "many craftsmen labour: painters and sculptors. Sculpture is of many kinds, for sometimes wax or clay is shaped by it, metals are chased, wood and stone are carved. Among these arts painting is of greater labour, since a more subtle and perfect work is demanded from it. Then more skill is needed in wax than in wood or stone, which yields more easily to the craftsman's hand." But if this happens in the arts, it must be conceded also in these doctrines and faculties.

units.la: Artes Δημιουργικαὶ[?] sunt ποιητικοὶ[?] & δημιουργούμενα sunt opera quæ remanent. Tria igitur genera sunt facultatum, θεωρητικὸν πρακτικὸν, ποιη-τικὸν, sed posteriora duo membra sub uno comprehenduntur, quando philosophia distinguitur in contemplantem & agentem. Ideò autem probatio nunc inducitur quo ad artes quæ sunt ποιητικαὶ: quoniam ibi & opera & actiones vel sensibus manifesta sunt. Nec mirum est quod Aristoteles hic subiectum artium & facultatum appellet genus: nam id alibi quoq; facit, ut cùm dicit in Analyticis posterioribus, Non oportet demonstrantem ex uno genere ad aliud transfire: huius appellationis ratio assignatur, quia materia cum genere magnam habet affinitatem, materia enim ut genus, confusa est et rudis, utq; genus per differentias deducitur ad species, ita materia dirigitur & ornatur formis: & deniq; ut genus in potentia est ad species, ita materia est in potentia ad formas, & ex illarum privatione deducitur in actum.
units.tr: The arts [Δημιουργικαὶ] are productive [ποιητικοὶ], and the things made [δημιουργούμενα] are the works which remain. There are therefore three kinds of faculties: [θεωρητικὸν, πρακτικὸν, ποιητικὸν] (theoretical, practical, productive), but the last two members are comprehended under one when philosophy is divided into the contemplative and the active. The proof is now introduced with regard to the arts which are productive, since there both the works and the actions are manifest to the senses. Nor is it strange that Aristotle here calls the subject of the arts and faculties a genus. He does this elsewhere too, as when he says in the Posterior Analytics that one ought not to pass from one genus to another in demonstrating. The reason for this name is given: matter has a great affinity with genus. For matter, like genus, is confused and rough, and just as genus is brought down by differences to species, so matter is directed and adorned by forms. And finally, just as genus is in potency to species, so matter is in potency to forms, and is brought into act by the removal of those privations.

units.la: Honesta autem & justa, de quibus civilis cōside-rat, tantam differentiam & errorem habent, ut videantur lege tantum, non natura constare: atq; eūdem habent errorem bona ipsa, quod multis damna ex illis accidant, quippe nonnulli propter divitias perierunt, & alij propter fortitudinem.
units.tr: The honourable and just things, with which civil science is concerned, have such great difference and error that they seem to rest only on law, not on nature. Goods themselves have the same error, since many suffer harm from them: some have perished on account of riches, and others on account of courage.

units.la: Minor hic probatur, quæ fuit, morale & politicam circa res versari dubias & parum certas: quia honesta & justa & bona his conditionibus subiacent: & primum id exponet de honestis & justis quæ tractantur hic in cæteris libris post primum, nec non in politicis: adiecit & bona, quia de hac re statim aget felicitatem describendo.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved here, which was that moral and political science is concerned with matters that are doubtful and little certain, because the honourable, the just and the good are subject to these conditions. He will first explain this of honourable and just things, which are treated here in the books after the first, and also in the Politics. He added goods because he will treat of this matter straightaway, in describing happiness.

units.la: Honesta & justa differentiam habere dicit & errorem: quoniam pro rerum conditione, locorum & temporum diversitate, honestum et justum immu-tatur. Ideoq; dicitur videri potius ista constare lege quadam, hoc est hominum decreto & voluntate seu consuetudine quàm natura, vt Pyrrhonis fuit sententia, nihil suapte natura vel bonum vel malum esse, potius tales res haberi legibus vel consuetudine hominum: quod salsissimum est. Nam licet in hominibus multae sint tenebrae, illis non fit vt nihil sit constans aut firmum in his rebus. Neq; Aristoteles dixit ita esse, imo adiecit videri. Et quod scribit non natura, idcirco dicit, quoniam quae sunt natura, quoad omnes & semper talia sunt, neq; mutantur vt modo hoc, modo illud fiant: verum è diuerso accidit in his quae lege tantum & humanis iudicijs cõsistunt.
units.tr: He says that the honourable and the just have difference and error, because the honourable and the just change according to the condition of things and the diversity of places and times. Hence he is said to seem to rest these things on a certain law, that is, on the decree, will or custom of men, rather than on nature. This was the opinion of Pyrrho, that nothing is good or bad by its own nature, but such things are held to be so by the laws or customs of men, which is most absurd. For although there is much darkness in men, it does not follow that nothing in these matters is constant or firm. Nor did Aristotle say that it is so; rather he added "seem". And when he writes "not by nature", he says this because things that are by nature are such for all and always, and do not change so that now this, now that, comes about. On the contrary, it happens in those things which consist only in law and human judgements.

units.la: Quod ex eo patet, quia olim piraticam exercere non erat infame aut probrosum, quemadmodum postea fuit, sed viri qui habiti sunt præclari & insignes illam exercuerunt: quin apud Lacedemonios furari non dabatur vitio, sed furem deprehendi habebat probrum. Sybaritis præcipuum erat bonum luxuria & incontinentia. His adde iusta & honesta varietatem subire ex modis & formis magistratus, multa enim licent in ἀριστοκρατεία[?], quae in regno aut republica neque iusta essent neq; honesta. Quis etiam non videat aliter sub tyrannis in oligarchijs & popularibus ciuitatibus de iustis & honestis constitui?
units.tr: This is clear from the fact that formerly piracy was not infamous or shameful, as it later became; men who were regarded as distinguished and eminent practised it. Indeed, among the Lacedaemonians stealing was not counted a vice, but being caught as a thief was a disgrace. For the Sybarites the chief good was luxury and self-indulgence. To these add that the just and the honourable undergo change according to the forms and modes of government. For many things are permitted in aristocracy [ἀριστοκρατεία] which would be neither just nor honourable in a kingdom or a commonwealth. Who does not see that under tyrants, in oligarchies and in popular states, the just and the honourable are determined otherwise?

units.la: De bonis item non posse facile definiri, propterea inquit, quod multis fuerunt sæpius damnosa: quod ille duobus probat, nempe diuitijs & fortitudine, quibus nos permulta possemus addere. Cibi existimantur boni, & sæpe in morbos coniciunt: domus expetuntur, quæ sua ruina interdum conficiunt habitantes: emuntur gladij quibus postea interficiuntur emptores: elementa ipsa, Sol, Luna & sidera frequenter nocent. Lucretia castitas ei fuit exitio, Virginiæ forma, Decijs amor patriæ, Regulo fides, Tullio eloquentia, Socrati & Aristidi virtus & innocentia: unde ratione Epicurus captauit, qua probaret virtutem non esse summum bonum, quod multis fuerit causa interitus. Sed redeamus ad Aristotelem, qui multos dicit periisse ob diuitias: quod potest duplici ratione fieri. Vel quod non raro diuitibus tenduntur insidiae ac calumniae vt pereant, exemplo sunt in poetis Sichæus & Polydorus, in historijs multi proscripti Syllanis temporibus, in sacris literis Naboth Izreelites qui propter vineam fuit interemptus. Accidit hoc idem exitiu his qui nimio studio parare satagunt diuitias, ut quotidie faciunt mercatores, qui pericula subeunt incredibilia illarum causa: & Crassus ut magis ditesceret, bellu mouit in Parthos, à quib. misere vna cu filio est occisus.
units.tr: Likewise, that good things cannot easily be defined is shown, he says, by the fact that they have often proved harmful to many people. He proves this with two examples, riches and strength, to which we could add a great many more. Foods are thought good and often bring on diseases. Houses are sought after, yet sometimes their occupants are destroyed by their collapse. Swords are bought, with which the buyers are afterwards killed. The elements themselves, the sun, the moon and the stars, often do harm. Lucretia's chastity was her ruin, Virginia's beauty, the love of country of the Decii, the good faith of Regulus, the eloquence of Cicero, the virtue and innocence of Socrates and Aristides. Hence Epicurus reasoned rightly in arguing that virtue is not the highest good, since it has been the cause of destruction for many. But let us return to Aristotle, who says that many have perished because of their riches. This can happen in two ways. Either the rich are often beset by plots and false accusations so that they perish; examples of this are Sychaeus and Polydorus in the poets, many proscribed men in the times of Sulla in histories, and in Sacred Scripture Naboth the Jezreelite, who was killed on account of his vineyard. The same ruin befalls those who labour with excessive eagerness to acquire riches, as merchants do every day, who undergo incredible dangers for their sake. And Crassus, in order to grow richer, made war on the Parthians, by whom he was wretchedly killed together with his son.

units.la: Hoc deinde probat Aristoteles ob fortitudine, quæ multis fuit exitio. Dubitat Eustratius an hic ἀνδρεία[?] sumatur pro fortitudine, quæ una censetur ex præcipuis virtutib. an p robore corporis, quod alio nomine dicitur ἰχύς[?]: quod videtur admodum verisimile. Crotoniata quippe Milo, dum nimium sideret lacertis, arborem tentauit fissam ut aperire atq; scindere, sed cum eius robore superaretur, interceptus ipse est ac attritus, ita ut ex eo moreretur: multiq; gladiatores & consimiles, elati & freti plus quam oportebat viribus corporis, infelicissime perierunt. Sed si hoc modo Aristotelem intelligamus, non videbitur expendere significationem vocis: quandoquidem ἀν-δρεία potius animi virtutem referat, quæ mediocritas est inter audaciam et timorem, quàm significet robur corporis. Ad hoc respondet Eustratius, & ait, quatuor esse vires & præstantias corporis, quæ pulchrè quatuor animi præcipuis virtutibus respondent. Sanitas, firma inquam valetudo, quæ sita est in quadam humorum æquali & temperata ratione, iustitiæ componitur, quæ itè captat semper æqualitatem in rebus quæ tractantur. Sensuū perspicacia & acumen prudentiæ, quæ ubiq; media conspicatur. Pulchritudo, quæ in mensura & proportione iusta membrorum & colorum, temperantiæ. Robur corporis fortitudini: quare, inquit, ἴσως[?] cùm respondeat ἀνδρείᾳ, non ab ea est alienum, ideoq; potestid significari per ἀνδρείαν. Atq; si per ἀνδρείαν intelligamus robur corporis, cognata erunt quæ hic recensentur. Nam tam diuitiæ quàm vires instrumenta sunt, quorum cum bonus tum malus usus esse possit: ut interdum prosunt, ita sæpe nocent, prout illi sunt qui utuntur. Istos ad hæc qui præ cæteris in prælio sunt robusti, & magis in pugna strenuè se gerunt, maiori vi hostes aggrediuntur. Et sæpe fit, ut qui a singulis vinci non possunt, ab hostium numerosa manu vehementius opprimantur. Quodq; vi aperta interdum perfici non potest, occultis insidiis peragitur. Quamobrem quod modò inquit Aristoteles, non est dubium, nonnullos & quidem non obscuros propter fortitudinem, hoc est, corporis vires interiisse. Quid vero dicemus de fortitudine quæ animi virtus est? an ne erit exitio fortibus? Quid ni? Et Aristotelem de ea loqui non est vero dissimile: quia de his agit quæ in Ethicis tractantur. Omnes autem intelligunt hic non solum de bonis externis agi, ut sunt diuitiæ, sed et de interioribus animi virtutibus, de quibus cum non facile iudicetur an semper homini conducant, de bonis humanis diuisione perfecta demonstratum erit in universum, quàm multiplex ibi error lateat, cùm ea quæ sunt damnosa expetuntur. Si fortitudo etiam quæ inter animi virtutes præclara semper habita est, exitium interdum affert, in nostris propriis bonis hærebimus, non in his tantum quæ vel ad corpus vel ad fortunam attinent. Contra fortes nō semel invidia est excitata: insidiæ plerunq; his tenduntur, & periculis propulsandis & iustis causis defendendis fortes viros plerùq; videmus occumbere. Neq; sumus nescij proverbium verbium vulgo jactari, Timidos tantum extra periculum esse, neq; matri-bus luctum apportare. Sic ut fit de vera fortitudine locus iste commodissi-mè possit intelligi.
units.tr: Aristotle next proves this from strength, which has been the ruin of many. Eustratius doubts whether courage [ἀνδρεία] is here taken for fortitude, which is counted one of the chief virtues, or for bodily strength, which is called by another name, might [ἰσχύς]. This seems very probable. Milo of Croton, because he trusted too much in his arms, tried to split and tear open a tree that had been cleft, but being overcome by its strength, he was caught and crushed, so that he died of it. And many gladiators and such men, puffed up and relying more than was fitting on the strength of their bodies, perished most unhappily. But if we understand Aristotle in this way, he will not seem to weigh the meaning of the word carefully, since courage [ἀνδρεία] refers rather to a virtue of the soul, which is a mean between boldness and fear, than signifies bodily strength. To this Eustratius replies, saying that there are four powers and excellences of the body, which correspond finely to the four chief virtues of the soul. Health, that is, firm well-being, which consists in a certain equal and temperate proportion of the humours, corresponds to justice, which always seeks equality in the matters it deals with. Keenness and acuteness of the senses corresponds to prudence, which everywhere perceives the mean. Beauty, which consists in the due measure and proportion of the limbs and colours, corresponds to temperance. Bodily strength corresponds to fortitude. Therefore, he says, since perhaps [ἴσως] corresponds to courage, it is not foreign to it, and so it can be signified by courage. And if by courage we understand bodily strength, the things listed here will be related. For riches and strength are both instruments, which can have either a good or a bad use. As they sometimes benefit, so they often harm, according to the people who use them. Those who are the most robust of all in battle, and who conduct themselves most vigorously in fighting, attack the enemy with greater force. And often it happens that those who cannot be conquered one by one are more fiercely overwhelmed by the numerous band of enemies. And what cannot sometimes be accomplished by open force is carried out by hidden ambushes. Therefore, what Aristotle has just said is beyond doubt: some, and indeed notable men, have perished on account of their strength, that is, the powers of the body. But what shall we say of fortitude, which is a virtue of the soul? Will it not be ruinous to the brave? Why not? And it is not far from the truth that Aristotle is speaking of it, since he deals with those things which are treated in the Ethics. Yet everyone understands that he is speaking here not only of external goods, such as riches, but also of the inner virtues of the soul. Since it is not easily judged whether these always profit a man, the full division of human goods will show in general how much error lies hidden there, when things that are harmful are sought. If fortitude too, which has always been held to be an outstanding virtue among the virtues of the soul, sometimes brings destruction, we shall be stuck in our own proper goods, not only in those which pertain to the body or to fortune. On the other hand, the brave have not once been the object of envy; plots are usually laid against them, and we often see brave men fall while repelling dangers and defending just causes. Nor are we unaware of the proverb commonly tossed about, that only the timid are out of danger, and they bring no grief to their mothers. Thus, as is the case with true fortitude, this passage can be understood most suitably.

units.la: Verum duo tamen se offerunt non dissimulanda, quae cum dubia sint, expla-natione indigent. Justa & honesta dabimus, ut hic videtur dici, lege nō au-tem natura constare. Atq; si natura etiam constant, ab utro istorum magis pendent? Ut de hoc prius dicam, Fateor Platonicorum sententiam esse, virtutes hominibus natura ingenerari, quae postea exercitio, consuetudine ac moribus excolantur. Verum Aristoteles huic opinioni non assentitur, ut postea suo loco videbimus: & ut non aliud afferretur argumentum, cum natura virtutis id videtur pugnare, quae ut demonstrabitur est habitus, & is hoc maxime differt a naturalibus facultatib. quod a crebris actionibus oritur, & nostris animis sedulitate agendi comparatur. Ubi quod natura concedi-tur, nulla nostra industria insitum habemus. Dandum tamen censeo prin-cipia virtutum à natura esse. Ex natura quippe nobis provenit, ut eligamus quae agenda sunt, & ingenij acumine de illis judicamus. Viribus item agimus, quae nobis attributa sunt à natura. Neq; corporis temperamentum ad hoc parum vel conducit vel obest, cum aliqui naturae impulsu magis aliis ad justa & recta sint propensi: ex quibus omnibus virtutum habitus adipiscimur. Qui fit ut cum ista sint naturalia cuiq; nostrum, virtutum principia dicemus a natura esse petenda. Non tamen propterea statuetur virtutes hominibus innasci. Quoniam si studium, legum, morum, & educationis disciplina non accesserit, animos virtutibus non excolimus. Et hac de justitia et rectitudine, quae natura sunt virtutes, dicta sunto. Verum de ipsis rebus ho-nestis & justis, an ex natura id habeant ut justa sint, & honesta, an ex legi-bus & decretis sapientum legislatorum hoc sibi vendicent, non multo secus quàm dictum jam sit, oportet definiri. Rerum quippe justitia & honestas ab ipsis primum ut in natura sunt, non à legibus & doctrinis ortum habent. Quia nisi res à principio ita se considerandae obtulissent mentibus legislato-rum, quibus moverunt animum & intelligentiam, non ita potuissent de illis pronuntiare. Nam prius in officijs vitae senserunt esse decentiam, æquabili-tatem, & rectitudinem, quam de illis ferrent suas leges. Neque in potestate nostra situm est, sed in natura quo pacto his rebus remoueamur quas intel-ligimus. Quamobrem honesti et justi à natura existimo esse initium, ad quae postea indicanda populis cum non omnes exquisita perspicacia sint praediti, bonas leges multum facere non diffiteor. Quandoquidem illis non tantum justa & honesta defenduntur & retinentur in repub. sed etiam ignaris & rudiorudioribus indicantur. Atq; ista de legibus quæ latæ sunt & conscriptæ volo accipi. Nam si debinc interrogarer, unde nam res ipsa habeat, ut honesta, iusta, commodaq; videantur nostro generi cum à legislatoribus consyderantur: Nil habeo quod respondeam, nisi legem Dei quandam ex æterno sic re-bus prospicientem, quæ si aliter decreuisset, res ipsa omnino aliter essent et ui-derentur. Sed si quis altius rem exquirat, ex ipsa huiusmodi lege totam na-turam pendere intelliget. Attamen quia nunc philosophum ago, idcirco de illa Dei lege nil dico. Sed quod iam dixi confirmo, rerum honestatem atq; iu-stitiam à natura incipere quidem, perfici tamen à legibus.
units.tr: Yet two points present themselves which must not be passed over, and which, since they are doubtful, need explanation. Here it seems to be said that just and honourable things exist by law and not by nature. And if they also exist by nature, on which of the two do they depend more? To deal with this first: I admit that it is the opinion of the Platonists that virtues are implanted in men by nature and afterwards cultivated by practice, habit and custom. But Aristotle does not assent to this opinion, as we shall see later in its place. And even if no other argument were brought forward, the nature of virtue seems to oppose it, since, as will be demonstrated, virtue is a habit, and this differs most from natural faculties in that it arises from frequent actions and is acquired in our souls by diligence in acting. Where something is granted to be natural, we have it implanted without any effort of ours. Nevertheless, I think it must be conceded that the principles of the virtues come from nature. For it is from nature that we have the ability to choose what is to be done, and by the keenness of our wit we judge about those things. We also act by powers which have been assigned to us by nature. Nor does the temperament of the body contribute or hinder much in this, since by a natural impulse some are more inclined than others to what is just and right. From all these things we acquire the habits of the virtues. Hence, since these dispositions are natural to each of us, we shall say that the principles of the virtues are to be sought from nature. Yet it is not on that account to be affirmed that virtues are innate in men. For if the study of laws, of morals and the discipline of education do not come in, we do not cultivate our souls in virtue. And let this be said about justice and uprightness, which are virtues by nature. But concerning the honourable and just things themselves, whether they have their justice and honour from nature, or claim this for themselves from laws and decrees of wise legislators, must be settled in much the same way as has already been said. For the justice and honour of things arise first from the things themselves, as they are in nature, not from laws and teachings. For unless the matters had first presented themselves to the minds of the legislators in such a way that they should be considered, they would not have been able to pronounce about them as they did; the minds and understanding of the legislators were moved by them. For first they perceived in the duties of life that there was propriety, equality and rectitude, before they passed their laws about them. Nor does it lie in our power, but in nature, how we are moved by those things which we understand. Wherefore I hold that the honourable and the just take their beginning from nature. Yet, since not all men are endowed with exquisite perceptiveness, to make these known to peoples, I do not deny that good laws do much. For by them the just and honourable are not only defended and maintained in the commonwealth, but are also pointed out to the ignorant and the less rudioribus indicantur. And I want these words about laws to be taken as referring to those that have been enacted and written down. For if I were then asked whence the thing itself has that it appears honourable, just and advantageous to our kind when it is considered by legislators, I have nothing to answer except a certain law of God, which from eternity thus foresees things, and if it had decreed otherwise, the things themselves would be entirely otherwise and would appear so. But if anyone investigates the matter more deeply, he will understand that all nature depends on this very law. Nevertheless, because I am now engaged as a philosopher, I say nothing about that law of God. But I affirm what I have already said: the honourableness and justice of things begin indeed from nature, yet are perfected by laws.

units.la: Est secundo loco dubium, quomodo Aristoteles incertas dicat esse cum uirtutes, tum diuitias, cum inter bona ille ipse hæc habeat, neq; de diuitijs cum Stoicis faciat, qui illas ex bonorum albo expunxerunt. Bona sane illas esse quamuis non primi ordinis arbitratur. Virtutes vero non modo is, at nobi-liores quiq;[?] Philosophi nunquam non habuerunt pro bonis præstantissimis. Ad hæc respondemus, bona quidem esse per se, verum per accidens interdum nocere. Et Aristoteles cum suam dicit sententiam de his, ut philosophus egregius qui res optime distinguit, reiectis accidentibus, id quod est per se amplectitur. Hic vero in proœmio res istas & dubias esse & errorem habere coniunctum secum affirmat: quia de hominum vulgo agit, quorum perpauci sunt, qui quod est per se, ab eo quod est per accidens, acutè internoscât. Qua de re fuit Epicurus vehementer hallucinatus, qui virtutem ideò putauit summi boni rationem habere non posse, quòd Aristidi, Socrati, & consimilibus exitio fuerit: cum hoc virtuti per accidens, non autem per se ad-iungatur.
units.tr: A second difficulty arises: how Aristotle can call both virtues and riches uncertain, since he counts them among the goods, and does not side with the Stoics, who struck riches from the roll of goods. He does think riches are goods, though not of the first rank. Virtues, moreover, were regarded as the most excellent goods not only by him but by the nobler philosophers generally. To this we reply that these things are good in themselves, but sometimes do harm by accident. When Aristotle states his view on these matters, he does so as an eminent philosopher who distinguishes things well: he sets aside accidents and keeps to what is per se. Here, in the proem, he says that these matters are doubtful and carry error with them, because he is speaking to the common run of men, very few of whom can sharply tell what is per se from what is per accidens. It was on this point that Epicurus went badly astray. He thought virtue could not hold the place of the highest good because it had proved fatal to Aristides, to Socrates and to others like them; but this harm attaches to virtue by accident, not per se.

units.la: Expetendum igitur est his qui de talibus & ex talibus dicunt, crassè ac forma uerum ostendere: & cū de his quæ plærunq; fiunt, & ex talibus dicunt, etiā quæ talia sint concludere.
units.tr: Those who speak about such matters, and from such premises, must therefore aim to show the truth roughly and in outline, and when they speak from things that generally happen, they must also reach conclusions about things of that kind.

units.la: Quamuis ista sint ambigua, neq; de iustis, honestis & bonis omnes consentiant, & crassior harum rerum instituatur tractatio, sic tamen oportet nos esse contentos, quandoquidem talis est harum rerum natura. Et cùm ista non sint necessaria, neq; similiter perpetuò se habeant, quid mirum si concludantur ex talibus, cùm inter conclusiones et argumenta cognatione oporteat intercedere. Sunt illa plane de quibus agimus, ut vocant, contingentia, quorum conditio inde oritur, quia cum sunt, & fiunt, nec esse neque fieri est necesse, sed impediri possunt. Vnde principia contingentiæ faciunt physici materiâ, ciuiles autem nostram voluntatem siue delectum. Materia enim cum hac vel illa forma deberet ornari, quandoq; impeditur, vel quòd efficiendi cau-sa defit, uel quòd aliquo casu debilitata fuerit eius vis. Quod item in nostris electionibus apparet. Quis ignoret patrem iure debere liberos suos maxima charitate prosequi? Sed hoc interdum ne velit, uxoris quam nouercam fi-lijs induxit opera incidit: ibi enim mulierculæ illius nimio amore captus impeditur ne honesta eligat. Item à viro bono sanum consilium esset expectan-dum, sed impeditur aliquando temporis angustia, ne rem quanta deberet diligentia expendat, vel alijs curis aut corporis debilitate auertitur, neque fidelem operam potest nauare. Vnde liquet satis, ea quæ hic tractantur, non semper, sed sæpius cuenire. Tres vero partes contingenti omnes assignant, vt quaedam dicant fieri frequenter, alia ex æquo, nonnulla deniq; raro. Circa necessaria, quæ se aliter habere non possunt, uersantur scientiæ: in his quæ frequentius, artes: rationis autem sunt & electionis, ea quæ ex æquo contin-gunt: nam istæ sunt vires iudicandi, ideoq; librant vtrinq; partes contradi-ctionis. At illa quæ raro accidunt, cum de ipsis ratio nulla reddi possit, & ar-te tractari nequeant, casui & fortunæ relinquuntur. Quæ sic inter se dif-ferunt, vt casus ad ea quæ in natura fiunt raro pertineant, fortuna vero in in rebus humanis ponitur quando sic fiunt.
units.tr: Although these matters are ambiguous, and not all agree about the just, the honourable and the good, and although the treatment of them is rougher, we ought nonetheless to be content with it, since such is the nature of these things. And since they are not necessary, and do not always stand in the same way, why should it surprise us if conclusions are drawn from such premises? Conclusions and arguments ought to have a kinship with each other. The things we are dealing with are, as they say, contingent. Their condition arises from this: when they exist and come about, it is not necessary that they exist or come about, but they can be hindered. Hence natural philosophers make matter the source of contingency, and civil philosophers make our will or choice the source. Matter, when it ought to be furnished with this or that form, is sometimes hindered, either because the efficient cause is lacking or because its power has been weakened by some accident. The same appears in our choices. Who does not know that a father ought by right to love his children with the greatest affection? Yet sometimes he fails to do so, because he has fallen under the influence of a wife whom he has brought in as a stepmother to his sons; captivated by the excessive love of that little woman, he is prevented from choosing what is honourable. Likewise a good man ought to wait for sound counsel, but sometimes he is prevented by lack of time from weighing the matter with the care it deserves, or is turned aside by other cares or by weakness of body, and cannot perform faithful service. From this it is clear enough that the things treated here do not always, but more often, come about. Moreover, all the authorities assign three parts to the contingent: some things happen frequently, others equally often and not often, and some rarely. Sciences deal with necessary things, which cannot be otherwise; arts deal with those that happen more frequently; reason and choice deal with those that happen equally on either side, for these are the powers of judgement, and therefore they weigh both parts of the contradiction. But things that happen rarely, since no reason can be given for them and they cannot be handled by any art, are left to chance and fortune. These differ in this way: chance pertains to rare events in nature, while fortune is placed among human affairs when things turn out thus.

units.la: Et cum itares habeat, quia de his dicitur, ex his quoq; docendum est: & quando ex his progredimur, de talibus oportet conclusiones inferri. atq; id sibi vult quod modo Aristoteles habet πρὶ τύτωυ καὶ ἐν τύτῳ. Primum significat problemata & quæstiones aut conclusiones: alterum propositiones & argumenta. Cumq; ea sit huius nostræ materiæ conditio, si quis de his rebus pronuntians aliquando sit falsus & mentiatur, vitio illi non est vertendum quia talis est rei natura quam tractat. Quodq; dicit Aristo-teles ψαχνῶς, πρὸς τὸ λεπτομερὲς opponitur. vt τυπῶς, πρὸς τὸ φανερῶς. & φλεγνυσι, πρὸς τὸ ἀπολέγνυσι. & ὡς τὸ πολύ, πρὸς τὸ ἀναγκαῖον. Subtilis & exquisita demonstratio ea est, quæ resoluit usq; ad immediata principia.
units.tr: And since this science has an [ethical] character, because it is about these things, we must teach from these things too; and when we proceed from these, conclusions about such things ought to be drawn. And this is what Aristotle means by the words pri toutōn kai en toutō [πρὶ τύτωυ καὶ ἐν τύτῳ]. The first phrase signifies problems and questions or conclusions; the second, propositions and arguments. Since this is the condition of our subject, if anyone who pronounces on these matters is sometimes wrong and speaks falsely, the fault should not be imputed to him, because such is the nature of the thing he treats. And what Aristotle says, psachnōs [ψαχνῶς], is set against to leptomeres [πρὸς τὸ λεπτομερὲς], as typōs [τυπῶς] is set against phanerōs [φανερῶς], and phlegnysi [φλεγνυσι] against apolegnysi [ἀπολέγνυσι], and hōs to polu [ὡς τὸ πολύ] against to anankaion [τὸ ἀναγκαῖον]. A subtle and exact demonstration is one that resolves matters all the way down to the immediate principles.

units.la: Eodemq; modo oportet accipere quæ dicuntur. Eruditi quidem est exquisitum in unoquoque genere tantisper quærere, quam diu ipsum rei natura patitur. Nam propemodum idem uidetur admittere mathematicum suadentem, & ab oratore demonstrationes postulare. Hac secunda parte huius capitis transiit ad auditorem, ac tradit quonam modo affectus esse debeat erga doctrinam. Forma rationis.
units.tr: The same must be understood of what is said here. It is a mark of the educated person to seek, in each kind of subject, only as far as the nature of the thing allows. For he seems to admit almost the same thing from a mathematician when he urges him, and to demand demonstrations from an orator. In this second part of the chapter he passes to the hearer, and sets out how the hearer ought to be disposed towards this teaching. The form of the argument:

units.la: Eruditi est non plus requirere quàm natura & genus subiectum patiatur à docente.
units.tr: It is the mark of the educated not to ask more than the nature and kind of subject allows the teacher to give.

units.la: Auditorem huius scientiæ non rudem, sed eruditum esse oportet.
units.tr: The hearer of this science ought not to be untrained, but educated.
Therefore, etc.

units.la: Atq; dum inquit eruditi esse huic generi doctrinæ in talibus acquiescere, tacitè innuit è diverso ineruditi esse aliter se gerere. Mathematicum debere alienum à suasione in sua facultate agere patet, quia materia illius ha-bet proprietates necessariò sibi inhærentes: & nulla impedimenta, quæ contingentiæ sunt initia, possunt ibi locum habere, quandoquidem à materia quæ sentiatur recedit, neq; causam efficiendi considerat[?], nosq; antea probauimus hinc quo ad naturam principium esse contingentia: atq; simul ex altero capite, nimirum electionis humanæ, quæ in mathematicis prorsus est superuacanea, contingentia esse non potest. Orator ἀπόδειξιν[?] non habet, sed cùm tractat incerta, ut illa suadeat, verisimilibus duntaxat utitur, vel his quæ verisimilia visa fuerint.
units.tr: And when he says that it belongs to an educated person to be satisfied with such things, in the nature of this kind of teaching, he tacitly suggests that the uneducated person behaves otherwise. It is clear that the mathematician ought to act in his own field without being open to persuasion, because his subject has properties which necessarily inhere in it, and no hindrances, which are the beginnings of contingency, can have a place there, since it withdraws from matter that can be perceived, and does not consider an efficient cause. We have already shown that contingency is, as far as nature goes, the principle here; and at the same time, from the other side, namely human choice, which is wholly superfluous in mathematics, contingency cannot exist. The orator has no apodeixin [ἀπόδειξιν], but when he deals with uncertain matters, in order to persuade about them, he uses only probable arguments, or those which seem probable.

units.la: Oratores verò hic Aristoteles eos appellat qui ad populum in senatu vel ad tribunalia dicunt. Quorum res ut ambiguæ sint, ex his differentijs temporum quibus utuntur possumus colligere. Præteritum ad iudiciale tempus attinet, futurum ad deliberatiuum, præsens ad demonstratiuum. In coniecturis de præterito quot ambiguitates lateant, non est qui non videat. In coiecturis de futuro miserè hallucinamur. Quæ verò in rebus præsentibus laude aut vituperio digna sint, nemo non videt quantum sit incertitudinis.
units.tr: Aristotle here calls orators those who speak to the people in the senate or at the tribunals. That their subject-matter is uncertain we can gather from the differences of tense they use: the past pertains to the judicial time, the future to the deliberative, the present to the demonstrative. In conjectures about the past, who does not see how many ambiguities lie hidden? In conjectures about the future we go badly astray. As for what deserves praise or blame in present affairs, everyone sees how great the uncertainty is.

units.la: Quod verò Tullius interdum & nonnunquam Demosthenes utantur ne-cessarijs argumentis, sententia ab Aristotele posita non officit, nam id spectat quod oratoribus frequentiori est usui. Discrimen hic ferme oës annotarunt non contemnendum inter mathematicum & Oratorem: Quòd ille cogat etiam nolentes, ille verò in suam sententiam non ducit nisi persuasos & assentientes.
units.tr: That Cicero sometimes, and Demosthenes now and then, use necessary arguments does not count against the opinion laid down by Aristotle, for he has in view what is more often in use among orators. Almost all have noted the not inconsiderable difference between the mathematician and the orator: the former compels even the unwilling, while the latter does not lead to his own opinion except those who are persuaded and assent.

units.la: Quamobrem Aristoteles materiam artis & facultatis genus appellet, an tea[?] exposuimus. Nunc videndum superest, quid hæc iam allata cum religione consentiant, aut pugnent. Primum id occurrit, ea quæ ad mores pertinent in sacris literis cum traduntur, constantia & certissima esse, non enim variant, sed apud omnes nationes, modò Christum credant, sunt eadem: cùm in ecclesia catholica iudicium de honestis iustis & bonis non faciamus ex hominum opinionibus, sed potius ex uno Dei verbo, quod ut certissima est reest regula, ita nobis omnibus est summum κριτήριον[?]. Est attamen expendendum diligenter, huic nostro consensui de honestis, iustis & bonis, ut sacras literas voluntatem Dei respiciunt, & ad vitam aeternam spectant non adversari civilium seu municipalium legum diversitates, quae in variis Christianorum & generibus rerum publicarum habentur: quae nos fatemur (ut dicit Aristoteles) varietatem inter homines habere, omnia tamen huius generis discrimina sub una regula divinarum literarum comprehenduntur. Magistratibus esse parendum quo ad non praecipiant quicquam divinis institutionibus contrarium.
units.tr: Therefore Aristotle calls the matter of an art and faculty its genus; I have explained this earlier. It remains now to see how these things just brought forward agree with religion or conflict with it. First, this occurs: the matters that pertain to morals, when they are delivered in the sacred letters, are constant and most certain, for they do not vary, but are the same among all nations, provided they believe in Christ. For in the catholic Church we do not form our judgement of the honourable, the just and the good from the opinions of men, but rather from the one Word of God, which is both the most certain rule and for all of us the highest criterion. Yet we must carefully consider that our agreement about the honourable, the just and the good, insofar as the sacred letters regard the will of God and look to eternal life, is not opposed by the diversities of civil and municipal laws, which are found among the various kinds of Christian commonwealths. We admit, as Aristotle says, that there is variety among men; yet all differences of this kind are contained under the one rule of the divine letters. The magistrates are to be obeyed, provided they do not command anything contrary to the divine institutions.

units.la: Sed ut rem magis aperiam, ita respondendum arbitror. Cum id quaesierit quispiam, An iustum & rectum mutatum sit unquam in divinis literis: annuamus quo ad Ceremonialia et civilia. Alia quippe Ceremonia post Christum substitutae fuerunt veteribus, ac deleta Republica Israelitica. Civiles eius leges inter alias nationes, quamvis religiosae sint & Christum receperint, vim non amplius habent. Sed quo ad moralia, aeterna illa sunt, neque possunt extingui. Quare iustum & honestum quod ibi continetur est perpetuum.
units.tr: But to make the matter clearer, I think the answer should be this. When someone asks whether what is just and right has ever been changed in the divine writings, we agree for the ceremonial and civil laws. Other ceremonies were substituted for the old ones after Christ, and the Israelite commonwealth was abolished. Its civil laws no longer have force among other nations, even though they are religious and have received Christ. But the moral laws are eternal and cannot be abolished. Therefore the just and honourable that is contained in them is perpetual.

units.la: At sunt nonnulli, & hi quidem non admodum indocti, qui de diuortio quamvis ex causa concesso populo Hebraeo & de πολυγαμίας[?] veterum dubitant: quae cum ad mores pertineant, sublata modo sunt, & quae licuerunt veteri populo, nunc sunt interdicta. His dicimus, vel concessiones illas ad civilia decreta illius aetatis esse referenda, & ideo mutari potuisse: Vel si moralia contenderis esse, quod improbari queant rationibus certis, quae ducantur ex moralibus praeceptis, ut πολυγαμία[?] propter charitatem exploditur, quae non potest aequabilis retineri inter plures uxores: Et diortium ex quamvis causa factum, quod temere coniunctio ea rescindatur, quam Deus instituerat ut esset arctissima. Respondebimus: Fuisse quidem haec natura sua in veteri lege nonnihil diversa a recto & honesto, sed tamen ex Dei concessione legitima. Nam in diuortio habuit rationem durissimae pertinaciae Iudaeorum, & in uxoribus multiplicibus quas concessit, augeri volebat iuxta promissiones Abrahamo factas, quoad illius populi numerum. Unde privilegia non sunt nobis in exemplum trahenda, sed retinere debemus illud primum rectum & honestum, quod sacrae literae statuunt, praesertim cum ad id Christus & eius Apostoli nos revocarint. Atque haec de iusti & honesti constantia quoad religionem. In altero vero cum philosophis nostra con- sentiunt, quando & sacrae literae non vtuntur argumentis exquisitis & subtilibus: & raro perfectissimas illas demonstrationes adhibent, quia Deo visum est ad infirmorum captum doctrinam accommodari. Quamobrem pa-rabolis, historiis atq; similibus, bonam partem suae doctrinae complexus est. Interest nihilominus hoc facere, quia rerū natura aliter non patiatur, quod Philosophis accidit, et quia noluerit rem aliter instituere, quod Deus fecit, qui sane potuisset accuratissimis uti rationibus, quas euitauit, partim ut simplicioribus consuleret, partim ut vim crucis Christi non extenuaret, partim ut obedientia fidei & humanae[?] rationis captiuitas, cum nobis esset utilior, tum nomini eius ad maiorem gloriam cederet. Atq; nos ea forma doctrinae contentos esse oportet, nisi velimus aeternam vitam repudiare.
units.tr: But there are some, and not very unlearned ones either, who doubt about divorce, though it was granted to the Hebrew people for a cause, and about the polygamy [πολυγαμίας] of the ancients. Since these matters pertain to customs, what was once permitted to the ancient people has now simply been taken away and forbidden. To these we say: either those concessions must be referred to the civil decrees of that age, and so could be changed; or, if you insist that they are moral matters, which can be disapproved on certain grounds drawn from the moral precepts, then polygamy [πολυγαμία] is rejected on account of charity, since equal love cannot be kept among several wives, and divorce for any cause is rejected because by rash dissolution that union is torn apart which God instituted to be most close. We reply: these things were, in their nature, somewhat different from what is right and honourable, yet in the old law they were lawful by God's concession. For in the case of divorce he took account of the extreme obstinacy of the Jews, and in the several wives he permitted, he wished to increase them, according to the promises made to Abraham, as to the number of that people. Hence such privileges are not to be drawn into an example for us. Rather we ought to retain that first thing which is right and honourable, which the sacred letters lay down, especially since Christ and his Apostles have recalled us to it. These points concern the constancy of the just and honourable as regards religion. In the other respect, however, our teaching agrees with the philosophers, since the sacred letters also do not use exquisite and subtle arguments, and rarely employ those most perfect demonstrations, because it has pleased God to accommodate the teaching to the capacity of the weak. Therefore he has embraced a good part of his doctrine in parables, histories and the like. It is nevertheless right to do this, because the nature of things does not allow otherwise, as happens to the philosophers, and because God was unwilling to arrange the matter otherwise. He could certainly have used the most exact reasons, which he avoided: partly to provide for the simpler folk, partly so as not to weaken the power of Christ's cross, and partly so that the captivity of reason to the obedience of faith, which was more useful to us, might also redound to his name's greater glory. And we ought to be content with that form of teaching, unless we wish to reject eternal life.

units.la: Quisq; autem rectè iudicat quæ agnoscit, atq; ho-rum est bonus iudex. quamlibet itaque rem erudi-tus, absolutè uero eruditus de omnibus.
units.tr: Whoever judges rightly recognises what he knows, and of these things he is a good judge. So a person may be learned in any particular subject, but is learned in the unqualified sense only if he knows about all things.

units.la: Propositum in hoc loco est, ubi tertia pars huius capitis exponitur, neq; iuvenes neq; incontinentes huius facultatis idoneos esse auditores: & ratio est quo ad iuvenes, quod istarum rerum ullam habeant experientiam, & idcirco de illis iudicare non possint, & propterea non facile recipere. Hoc sa-nè utitur argumento.
units.tr: The point in this place, where the third part of this chapter is set out, is that neither young men nor the incontinent are fit hearers of this discipline. The reason, as regards young men, is that they have no experience of these matters, and so cannot judge them and therefore do not readily accept them. The philosopher uses this argument.

units.la: Qui rerum istarum notitiam habet & experientiam, hic est auditor i-doneus,
units.tr: Whoever has knowledge and experience of these things is a fit hearer.

units.la: Iuvenes per aetatem ista non norunt, neque habere possunt illorum expe-rientiam,
units.tr: Young men, by their age, do not know these things, nor can they have experience of them.
Therefore they are not fit hearers.

units.la: Minor propositio patet ac per se satis est euidens. Maior probatur ab antecedentibus, quia notitia semper exquiritur ante iudicium, neque de ignotis potest quisquam iudicare, & quae non recte iudicata fuerint, non possunt recte vel admitti vel explodi. Rei porro cognitio & experientia, regulam quandam parit in animis hominum, qua metiuntur quae in humanis actionibus, electionibus & affectibus occurrerint, & inde considerant, quomodo a regula dissentiant, seu cum ea pugnent, ex qua collatione iudicium oritur, & destitutos huiusmodi regula necesse est non posse fieri bonos iudices. Non satis erat philosopho dixisse, quemlibet recte iudicare quae nosset: sed ut rem maiori significantia exponeret, adiecit, Et quo ad singula hoc esse verum, hoc est, ut exemplis agamus & descendamus ad minima, bonum iudicem Musices esse, qui de sonis aliquam habuerit experientiam: et picturae, qui colores, mensuras, lineas, & umbras vtcunq; noverit. Itaq; qui cognitionibus hisce singularibus praediti sunt, eruditi dicuntur, non quidem absolute, verum in hoc vel illo genere. Simpliciter vero ac perfecte censetur eruditus, qui de omnibus aliquam habeat experientiam. Mitto quaerere an aliquis huiusmodi possit reperiri: quia sive sit, sive non sit, ad id quod agimus nihil refert: nam ex illis particularibus eruditionibus datis, recte consequitur, eum, si esset qui de omnibus aliquam haberet experientiam, posse de omnibus recte iudicare. Atque hanc distinctionem ideo inductam arbitror, ut ostendat non solum ad bene iudicandum experientia opus esse, verum etiam ut doceat se non requirere ad hanc facultatem summam eruditionem, sed eam tantum quae ad hoc negotium spectet. Et hoc loco diligenter considerandum, non appellare Aristotelem [?], scientem & [?]. Qui enim sunt huiusmodi, non opus habent praeceptoribus, neque auditores censentur. Sed eruditum illum dicit, qui experientia usu quodam fuerit consecutus. Quosdam enim videas qui nunquam pinxerunt, neque si velint, possint, & hi tamen ita sunt exercitati in signis & picturis contemplandis, ut de his facile iudicent. Quod etiam de carminibus accidit: nam quidam cum poetae non sint, usu tamen et electione ita profecerunt, ut experientia & usu de poesi oblata no male iudicent, et voce [?] Aristoteles in hac significatione utitur.
units.tr: The minor premise is plain and is evident enough in itself. The major is proved from what has gone before: knowledge is always sought before judgement, and no one can judge of things unknown, and things not rightly judged can be neither rightly admitted nor rightly rejected. Moreover, knowledge and experience produce a certain rule in men's minds, by which they measure what occurs in human actions, choices and affections, and from this they consider how such things differ from the rule or clash with it. From this comparison judgement arises, and those deprived of such a rule necessarily cannot become good judges. It was not enough for the philosopher to have said that anyone judges rightly what he knows; to set the matter out with greater force he added that this holds for each particular, that is, that we should proceed by examples and descend to the smallest things: a good judge of music is one who has had some experience of sounds, and a good judge of painting is one who knows colours, measures, lines and shadows in some way. Thus those endowed with these particular knowledges are called learned, not absolutely, but in this or that kind. Simply and perfectly, however, one is reckoned learned who has some experience of all things. I pass over asking whether anyone of this kind can be found, for whether he exists or not makes no difference to what we are doing: for from those particular learnings it rightly follows that, if there were someone with experience of all things, he could judge all things rightly. I think this distinction was introduced to show that experience is needed not only for judging well, but also to teach that for this faculty one does not require supreme learning, only that which pertains to this business. And here it must be carefully noted that Aristotle does not call such a man "knowing" [?] and "skilled" [?]. Those of that kind have no need of teachers, nor are they counted as hearers. He calls learned the one who has attained a certain practice through experience. For you may see some who have never painted, nor could if they wished, and yet they are so practised in examining signs and pictures that they judge them easily. The same happens with poems: some, though they are not poets, have nonetheless advanced by practice and choice so far that they judge poetry set before them by experience and practice not badly, and in this sense Aristotle uses the word [?].

units.la: Propterea ciuilis facultatis iuuenis non est aptus auditor: actionum quippe uitae non habet experientiam. Hi uero sermones & ex his & de eis agunt.
units.tr: Therefore a young man is not a fit hearer of civil science, for he lacks experience of the actions of life. Yet these discourses both arise from such things and deal with them.

units.la: Minor est in his verbis propositio, quod iuuenis careat experientia, praesertim actionum humanarum, cum in eis parvo admodum tempore sit versatus.
units.tr: In these words the minor premise is that a young man lacks experience, especially of human actions, since he has spent very little time in them.

units.la: Praeterea quod affectibus sit obnoxius, frustra & inutiliter audit: quandoquidem finis est non quidem notitia, sed actio.
units.tr: Moreover, since he is subject to the passions, he hears in vain and to no purpose, since the end is not knowledge but action.

units.la: Alia ratione iuuenes excludit quod perturbationibus subiaceant, & sint incontinentes, cosque non esse ad ista idoneos praedicat, & ex fine concludit,
units.tr: By another argument he excludes the young, because they are subject to disturbances and are incontinent. He declares them unfit for these things and concludes from the end,

units.la: Qui non potest facere quae hic docentur, frustra & inutiliter ea audiet, Iuuenes qui suis ducuntur affectibus, facere non queunt huius doctrinae praecepta.
units.tr: He who cannot do what is taught here will hear it in vain and to no purpose. Young people who are led by their passions cannot perform the precepts of this teaching.
They would therefore hear those things in vain and without profit.

units.la: Minor est euidens. Maior probatur: quia doctrinae huius finis est actio, non perceptio & contemplatio. Locus iste omnino illos confutat qui arbitrantur de rebus ethicis contemplantem scientiam duntaxat haberi posse: cum Aristotcles his verbis longe secus esse testetur, neq; sit cuiquam dubium ex fine scientiae vel σωφρονικὰς vel ἀκρατικὰς appellari.
units.tr: The minor is evident. The major is proved: because the end of this teaching is action, not perception and contemplation. That passage utterly refutes those who think that only contemplative science can be had in ethical matters, since Aristotle testifies in these words that it is far otherwise; and there is no doubt that from the end of the science they are called either sophronikas [σωφρονικὰς] or akratikas [ἀκρατικὰς].

units.la: Nil autem interest an ætate sit iuuenis, an iuuenilibus moribus: nō.n.penes tēpus defectus est, sed qp ex perturbationibus uiuat & omnia persequatur, talibus enim inutilis redditur notitia ceu incontinentibus. His uero qui iuxta rationem appetitus moderantur & regunt, utilissimum erit de his cognoscere. Et de auditore quidē, & quomodo hęc sint recipienda, quid'ue sit quod proponitur, tot in proœmio dicta sunt.
units.tr: It makes no difference whether a man is young in age or in youthful character. The deficiency lies not in time but in the fact that he lives by his perturbations and pursues everything; for knowledge becomes useless to such people, as it does to the incontinent. But for those who moderate and govern their appetites by reason, it will be most useful to know these things. Concerning the hearer, and how these things are to be received, and what is proposed, enough has been said in the proem.

units.la: Duplex ratio iuueni obstat ne magno cū fructu hæc audiat. Prima, quòd experientia destituatur, altera, quòd cupiditatibus & affectibus viuat obnoxius. Nunc alteram illam causam ad maiores natu extendit, quos saepe fieri posse, quod sæpius nimium videmus quàm velimus, vt iunioribus nihil sint meliores. Vnde liquido apparet, ætatem non esse tempus definitum perturbationibus, vt spacia annorum solum in hominibus vigeant. Incontinēs quoque vt dicitur, absq; fructu audiet: in eo quippe licet ratio sit recta, vincitur attamen affectibus & ita vincitur, vt quae viderit esse iusta, nequeat facere. Itaque vt superatur eius ratio, sic doctrina haec si ab eo percepta sit vincitur, & cum illam in actum non valeat educere, frustra laborabit audiendo. Hinc argumento à contrarijs efficitur, illos ista facultate si eam audiuerint vehementer adiuuari, qui suos affectus rationi gubernandos permiserint.
units.tr: There are two reasons why a young man cannot hear these things with great profit. The first is that he lacks experience; the second is that he lives subject to desires and passions. Now he extends this second cause to older men, for we often see, more often than we would like, that some elders are no better than the young. Hence it is clear that age is not a fixed time for the perturbations, as if only the span of years made men flourish in them. The incontinent, as is said, will also hear without profit. For although his reason is sound, he is overcome by the passions, and so thoroughly overcome that he cannot do what he has seen to be just. Therefore, as his reason is overcome, so if this teaching is grasped by him, it too is overcome; and since it cannot be brought into action, he will labour in vain in hearing it. Hence it follows by argument from the contraries that those who have allowed their passions to be governed by reason are greatly helped by this discipline when they hear it.

units.la: Sed videretur iure id reprehendi posse quod hic statuitur. Quoniā perfectorum est animi perturbationes rationi subiecisse, at qui iā absoluti sunt, doctrina non indigent. Et qui emendatione quam maximè opus habent, iuuenes & incontinentes, idonei ad ista non iudicantur: quod si de auditorum numero detrahantur, nullum sanè genus hominum reliquum erit, cui hæc vllam utilitatem afferant: unde non evadet facile, quin superuacanea sit futura. Respondet Eustratius, esse quosdam, & eos non paucos, qui tantum consuetudine adducantur ut boni sint, sed ratione & via procedere nequeant, cùm regulis certis destituantur, quas postea cùm sibi ex hac doctrina comparauerint, in actionibus justis & honestis maximè confirmantur, adducti jam non consuetudine, sed πληροφορίᾳ[?] vehementissimè persuasi. Nec desunt qui statim naturali quodam impulsu à prauis abhorrent, & appetant bona: sed quomodo illa inter se differant, quæue ratione possint ex bonis, quæ sanè multiplicia sunt, meliora sectari, per seipsos ignorant: nec dubium est ita factos, hinc magna posse nancisci adiumenta. Neq; propterea quæ ab Aristotele audiuimus putandum est, incontinentes & perturbationibus obnoxios hæc absque vllo fructu esse audituros. nisi enim sensu omnino sint destituti, cùm illis hæc proposita fuerint, saltem quónam à cupiditatibus abducti sint cognoscent, & ut à recto jam diffent animaduertent, & fieri non poterit quin ad meliora quoquo modo extimulentur. Unde paulatim & sanari & proficere poterunt, ut Athenis Polemoni adolescenti perditissimo accidisse legimus, cùm Xenocratem multa de temperantia disputantem audiuisset. Proinde quæ hæc de re nunc dicuntur, non sunt citra exceptionem intelligenda: sunt enim aliquando juvenes natura sic facti, disciplina & educatione tantum emendati, ut ex hoc doctrinæ genere multum queant proficere, quo ad externam justitiam & civilem conversationem, quod illis euenire maximè arbitror qui Christiana fide à teneris imbuti pietatem ex animo colunt: quod exemplo illustrissimo testatus est Eduardus V I. Anglia Rex, adolescés profecto ad omnem virtutem exercendam prima sua ætate paratissimus.
units.tr: But what is laid down here might seem rightly open to objection. For it belongs to the perfect to have subjected the perturbations of the mind to reason, and those who are already complete have no need of teaching. Yet those who most need correction, young men and the incontinent, are judged unfit for these things; and if they are removed from the number of hearers, no kind of men will remain to whom these things bring any benefit, and so it will not easily be avoided that the teaching becomes superfluous. Eustratius replies that there are some, and not a few, who are led by habit merely to be good, but cannot proceed by reason and method, since they lack fixed rules. When they have afterwards acquired such rules from this teaching, they are most strongly confirmed in just and honourable actions, now moved not by habit but by full conviction [πληροφορίᾳ], most vehemently persuaded. Nor are there lacking those who by a natural impulse shrink at once from wicked things and desire good things, but who do not know by themselves how the goods differ from one another, or by what reason they might pursue the better among the goods, which are indeed many. There is no doubt that such people, being so disposed, can gain great help from this teaching. Nor, because of what we have heard from Aristotle, should we think that the incontinent and those subject to the perturbations will hear these things without any fruit. For unless they are wholly deprived of sense, when these things have been set before them they will at least recognise by what desires they have been led away, and will notice that they already depart from the right; and it will not be possible that they are not somehow stirred up towards better things. Hence they will be able gradually both to be healed and to make progress, as we read happened at Athens to the most dissolute young man Polemo, when he heard Xenocrates disputing at length about temperance. Therefore what is now said on this matter is not to be understood without exception. For there are sometimes young men who are by nature so made, and are improved only by training and education, that they can make great progress from this kind of teaching as regards external justice and civil conduct. I think this happens above all to those who, imbued with the Christian faith from tender years, cultivate piety from the heart. The most illustrious example of this was Edward VI, King of England, a young man assuredly most ready in his early age to exercise every virtue.

units.la: Quod idem et vobis usu veniet, si doctrinam Evangelij eo studio quo cœpi-stis, persequamini. Non itaque voluit Aristoteles omnes juvenes in universum excludere, sed in hoc proœmio id quàm maximè curauit, ut depelleret obiectiones quæ dignitati ac existimationi facultatis huius possent officere: atque hoc agit, ne si videris juniores in doctrina versatos aliquando nihilo fieri meliores, id ei vitio vertas, quasi minimi pretij sit & ignaua, reijcit igitur culpam in defectum ætatis, quòd experientia destituatur & animi perturbationibus versetur. Hæc inquit esse impedimenta, propter quæ progressus doctrinæ atque fructus ex ea spectati non succedant. Neque tantum hoc sentit Aristoteles, verùm illi Pindarus etiam subscribit, dicens, ἄν ποτέρᾳ[?] γὰρ ἀ-[?] πειράτων φρένες[?]. & Homerus, ἀεὶ γάρ τε νεώτεροι[?] ἀφραδέστεροι[?]. Horatius ad hæc, cereus in vitium flecti, monitoribus asper, de juvene pronuntiat. Utq; plerunq; sint petulantes & affectibus æstuent, Comœdiam testem habemus luculentissimam: demonstrant etiam Historiæ, vt Cicero fuerit deceptus in Octauio, & quàm ipse Aristoteles, quo ad mores formandos in suo Alexādro Macedone parum efficere potuerit, cum maxima flagraret semper ambitione, secundam fortunam insolentissimè tulerit, deitatem stultissimè affectarit, & sic vino indulserit, vt ebrius amicissimos interficeret, ac Persipolim regiam vrbem nobiliss. frequentiss. & ampliss. ad nutum meretriculæ incen-derit, ita vt prorsus deleta sit. Plato in Gorgia consentanea loquitur, cum duo constituit foramina per quæ studia honesta ex animis effluant, nimirum obliuionem & incredulitatem: nam obliuione peritia tollitur, & ἀπιστία[?] quæ memoria colliguntur: per alterum verò, id est, incredulitatem, fit, ne mo-nitoribus credamus. Iuuenes autem quæ semel aut iterum viderunt & experti sunt facilè obliuiscuntur: vnde sententias & regulas vniuersa-les difficilè sibi parant, non enim illa possumus adipisci, nisi ex longa & diuturna obseruatione, quàm breui spatio vitæ iuuenes colligere non po-tuerunt, neque credunt libenter monentibus, quòd cæco affectuum impetu ducantur.
units.tr: The same will happen to you too, if you pursue the teaching of the Gospel with the zeal with which you have begun. Aristotle therefore did not wish to exclude all young men in general, but in this proem he took the greatest care to drive away objections that could harm the dignity and reputation of this discipline. He does this so that, if you see younger men who have been occupied with learning sometimes become no better, you do not blame the discipline for it, as if it were of little worth and idle. He therefore puts the blame on the defect of age, that it lacks experience and is busied with the perturbations of the mind. These, he says, are the impediments on account of which the progress of learning and the fruit expected from it do not follow. Nor does Aristotle alone hold this; Pindar also agrees, saying, "for the minds of the inexperienced [ἄν ποτέρᾳ γὰρ ἀ-πειράτων φρένες]," and Homer, "for the younger are always more witless [ἀεὶ γάρ τε νεώτεροι ἀφραδέστεροι]." Horace, to the same effect, describes the young man as pliant to vice and hard to advisers. That young men are commonly wanton and seethe with passions, we have a most brilliant witness in comedy; histories also demonstrate it. Cicero was deceived about Octavius, and Aristotle himself could accomplish little in forming the morals of his Alexander of Macedon, who always blazed with the greatest ambition, bore good fortune most insolently, aspired most foolishly to divinity, and indulged in wine so much that, drunk, he killed his dearest friends; and at the nod of a little harlot he burned the royal city of Persepolis, most noble, most crowded and most splendid, so that it was utterly destroyed. Plato in the Gorgias speaks to the same effect, when he posits two holes through which honourable studies flow out of minds, namely forgetfulness and incredulity: for by forgetfulness skill is lost, and by unbelief [ἀπιστία] what is gathered by memory is lost. Through the other, that is incredulity, it happens that we do not believe those who advise us. Young men easily forget what they have seen and experienced once or twice; hence they find it hard to acquire general maxims and rules for themselves, for these cannot be attained except from long and lasting observation, which young men, in so short a span of life, have not been able to gather. Nor do they willingly believe those who warn them, because they are driven on by the blind impulse of their passions.

units.la: Neq; mihi dixeris iuuenes personare, ac in ore habere, memoriter quæ te-nere præclaras & honestas philosophiæ sententias: quia licet speciosè multa dicant, non ita vt loquuntur sentiunt, & paulò magis interdum gustant & afficiuntur his quæ proferunt, atq; psytaci hominum verba intelligunt, quæ solent effutire. Quin ebrij etiam atq; intemperati multa sæpius aut cantil-lant, aut præclarè narrant, cum tamen vel contra ea sentiant: aut quid loquantur ignorent, & in summa oratio non est menti eorum συμφωνὸς[?], sed aliud in lingua & aliud in corde habent: quod tum maximè perspicitur, quā-do libertatem nancisc untur & solutam eligendi optionem habent. Ibi quā-nuis prius modesti & casti fuerint, sensum interius latitantem, & abscondi-tum ingenium produnt. Quis laudatior princeps fuerit ipso Nerone primis annis, quibus adhuc Senecæ arbitratu regebatur? De quo maior spes fuit, quàm de Commodo, qui vt fuit ab adolescentia præclarissimæ indolis, ita postea euasit in portentosam beluam. Et in sacra Historia nonne commemo-ratur Ioas qui principatus initio se gessit integerrimè quàm diu Ioiadæ Pon-tificis incorrupti consilijs res gerebat, cuius deinde autoritatem cum spreuisset, statim est depravatus, & ex libertate quam sibi vindicauerat, animi sui turpissimos affectus patefecit.
units.tr: Nor can you say to me that young men repeat and have on their lips, by heart, the fine and honourable maxims of philosophy. For although they speak many things splendidly, they do not feel as they speak; sometimes they are moved a little more by what they utter, and, like parrots, they understand the words of men which they are accustomed to chatter. Indeed drunkards and the intemperate too often either sing or relate many things excellently, though they think otherwise, or they do not know what they are saying; in short, their speech is not in harmony [συμφωνὸς] with their mind, but they have one thing on the tongue and another in the heart. This is most clearly seen when they obtain liberty and a free choice of option. There, although they were previously modest and chaste, they reveal the sense that lay hidden within and their concealed nature. What prince was more praiseworthy than Nero himself in his first years, while he was still governed by the counsel of Seneca? Of him greater hope was held than of Commodus, who, as he was of most brilliant disposition from youth, afterwards turned into a monstrous beast. And in sacred history, is it not recorded of Joash, who conducted himself most uprightly at the beginning of his reign as long as he managed affairs by the counsels of the incorrupt high priest Jehoiada; but afterwards, when he had scorned that authority, he was at once corrupted, and from the liberty he had claimed for himself he revealed the most shameful affections of his mind.

units.la: Attamen propter has rationes nunquam sunt maiores nostri illuc addu-cti, neq. hodie prudentes viri adducuntur, quin suos liberos, quum ex ephebis exbis excesserint, adducant ad Philosophos, ut eorum doctrina & sapientia erudiantur: mittunt etiam eosdem ad Iurisperitos, ut ab eis quae iusta sint & honesta percipiant. Atq; hoc totum ex Axiocho Platonis & Philosophorum vitis intelligimus, tum animaduertimus nostrorum temporum consuetudinem. Quod ideo factum est antiquitus & hodie quoq; facilitatur, quia illa quae Aristoteles modo scribit, non eum sensum habent, quasi Iuvenes ex ista philosophia nullam percepturi sint utilitatem, sed quod non eo usq; proficere queant ut animo sentiant quae hic docentur, & ex virtute statim agant, sibiq; bonos & rectos habitus acquirant. Quandoquidem ista exigunt animum plane persuasum & vere assentientem. In aliys autem facultatib.per-cipiendis satis est ut ingenium adhibeatur, quod quicunq; habuerint obtu-sum & hebes, non euadent periti: verum in hac nostra duo praestanda sunt, unum ut praecepta intelligantur, deinde ut fiant. Illud prius nihil obstat quin Iuvenes & intemperati qui dissolute vivunt consequantur. Si enim paulo acuti sint & ingeniosi, quae traduntur nullo negotio intelligent, sed ut praecepta huius facultatis vita exprimant non adducentur, partim quod experientia careant, ut dicit Aristoteles, partim quod affectibus prauis rapiantur. Queres fortasis cuiusmodi experientiam exigamus ab idoneis auditoribus: exemplis demonstrabo, nempe cupiditates abstinentia superare: ex actionibus fortibus & temperatis, si crebrae fuerint, homines euadere tandem fortes & temperatos, ita ut absq; ulla molestia, sed potius summa cum voluptate in harum virtutum officijs se ipsos exerceat. Et ut semel finiam, scire vos oportet, duplice esse fine huius artis, unā ut intelligamus quae docentur, alteram & eam quidem summam atq; praecipuam, ut quae didicimus, faciamus, a qua extrema fine cum viderit Aristoteles cum iuvenes tum incontinentes deficere, ideo genus hoc auditorum minus idoneum pronun-tiauit, si cum alijs conferatur qui iam suos affectus atq; animi perturbationes rationi praeceptrici subiecerunt, quandoquidem hi non tantum intelligere possunt quae dicuntur, at de illis etiam valent recte iudicare, quod ut perspicuum est, maxime spectauit Philosophus, cum tota eius ratio fundamento innitatur, quod Iuvenes et incontinentes de his recte iudicare non possint.
units.tr: Yet for these reasons our forefathers were never led to this study, nor are prudent men today led to it, but they send their sons, once they have left boyhood, to the philosophers, that they may be trained in their teaching and wisdom; they also send them to the jurists, that they may learn from them what is just and honourable. We understand all this from the Axiochus of Plato and from the lives of the philosophers, and we also observe the custom of our own times. This was done in antiquity and is still made easier today, because the things Aristotle now writes do not have the sense that young men will gain no benefit from this philosophy, but rather that they cannot advance so far as to perceive in their minds what is taught here, and to act at once from virtue and acquire for themselves good and upright habits. For these things demand a mind fully persuaded and truly assenting. In other faculties, however, it is enough to bring a good mind to the task; whoever has a dull and sluggish mind will not become skilled in them. But in this study of ours two things must be achieved: first, that the precepts be understood, and then that they be carried out. As for the first, nothing prevents young men and the intemperate, who live dissolutely, from grasping it. For if they are somewhat sharp and clever, they will understand what is taught without any difficulty; but they will not be brought to express the precepts of this discipline in their lives, partly because they lack experience, as Aristotle says, and partly because they are carried away by depraved passions. Perhaps you will ask what kind of experience we require of suitable hearers. I will show by examples: namely, to overcome desires by self-restraint, and that from brave and temperate actions, if they are frequent, men at last become brave and temperate, so that they exercise themselves in the duties of these virtues without any trouble, but rather with the greatest pleasure. And to end at once: you must know that this art has a twofold end, one that we understand what is taught, and the other, which is the highest and chief, that we do what we have learned. Since Aristotle saw that young men and the incontinent fall short of this final end, he therefore pronounced this kind of hearer less suitable, when compared with others who have already subjected their desires and disturbances of mind to guiding reason; for these can not only understand what is said, but are also able to judge rightly about these things. As this is plain, the Philosopher chiefly had this in view, since his whole argument rests on the foundation that young men and the incontinent cannot judge these things rightly.

units.la: Distinguemus etiam genus hominū, quòd alij sani sint, alij prorsus incu-rabiles, alij vero medij: & sanos his doctrinis opus habere non censemus, cū absoluti sint & perfecte vivant. Incurabiles & intemperati & qui se prorsus turpissimis voluptatib.adiecerunt, quo ad hunc animum nō deposuerint, minimè iuvabuntur: q; vero sunt medij, hinc uberrimū fructū capiēt. Placet sane ista distinctio, si tamen ei addatur de illis qui sunt desperatæ salutis, nūquam ita desperandum, quin possint illis aliquando meliora consilia & salutaria monita prodesse. Nam ut medicinæ vis est non tantum sanitatē partam tueri, & inchoatam perficere, sed etiam illa destitutos curare: Sic admonitiones & bonæ doctrinæ quæ sunt animi pharmaca vim habent ut non solum bonos retineant habitus & inchoatas virtutes absoluant, sed etiam ut ad animi sanitatem reuocent qui iam illam funditus amiserunt. Præsertim si fines ciuilis iustitiæ atque conuersationis externæ non egrediamur.
units.tr: We will also distinguish kinds of men: some are sound, others altogether incurable, and others in between. We do not think the sound need these teachings, since they are complete and live perfectly. The incurable, and the intemperate who have given themselves wholly to the most shameful pleasures and have not laid aside this disposition of soul, will receive no help; but those who are in between will gain great fruit from them. This distinction certainly pleases, provided that this be added: that those who are of desperate health should never be despaired of so completely that better counsels and salutary warnings may not at some time profit them. For as the power of medicine is not only to preserve health already gained and to perfect what has been begun, but also to cure those who have been abandoned by it, so admonitions and good teaching, which are the medicines of the soul, have the power not only to keep good habits, to complete virtues that have been begun, but also to recall to the health of the soul those who have utterly lost it. Especially if we do not go beyond the limits of civil justice and outward conduct.

units.la: Sed mirum est cur Aristoteles rationem hanc posteriorem à Iuvenibus ad maiores natu transtulerit, quod & illi sint persæpe affectibus addicti, & ad eosdem non deriuarit priorem rationem, nimirum priuationem experientiæ, quam iuvenibus attribuit. Respondetur, quoniam illud frequenter accidit, ut adulti, etiā in virili ætate constituti, corrupti sint et depravati affectibus, cùm tamen iisdem[?] raro eueniat ut rerum experientia destituantur, quæ semper cum ætate copulata est, ut ab ea vix abstrahi & diuelli possit. Quia igitur spectauit Philosophus quod sæpe fieri videmus, idcò id non attigit, quod aut nunquam aut quàm rarissimè contingit.
units.tr: But it is strange why Aristotle transferred this latter reason from young men to older men, since they too are very often given over to the passions, and did not derive from it the former reason, namely the lack of experience, which he attributed to young men. The answer is that it frequently happens that adults, even those established in manly age, are corrupted and depraved by the passions, whereas it rarely happens that they are destitute of experience of things, which is always joined with age, so that it can scarcely be separated and torn away from it. Therefore, since the Philosopher looked to what we often see happen, he did not touch upon what happens never or very rarely.
