units.la: In verbis Aristotelis id considerandum occurrit, in epilogo proœmij postremo loco recenseri, quod ante omnia fuit propositum, quid nimirum sit tractandum, τι προτιθέμεθα[?], quod sanè haud temerè factum est: coniugi quippè apte voluit quæ statim dicentur proœmio: De fine autem è vestigio tractabitur, propterea licet prius de illa sit locutus, nunc postremò repetit, ut his quæ sequuntur melius cohæreat.
units.tr: In the words of Aristotle it is to be considered that, in the epilogue of the proem, he lists last what was proposed first of all, namely what is to be treated, τι προτιθέμεθα, which was certainly not done rashly: he wished to link aptly what is said immediately after the proem. The end, however, will be treated at once, so although he spoke of it earlier, he now repeats it at the end, so that it coheres better with what follows.

units.la: Nunc superest ut disputationē pernecessariam nō prætereamus, ea est, Quî fiat ut cùm Aristoteles parùm idoneos auditores dixerit adolescentes et incontinentes, non item illos adnumerauerit, qui sunt ea constitutione, temperamento seu natura præditi, ut meliores effici non possint, et ad virtutes capessendas omninò sint inepti. Et aliquos ita esse nō uno in loco Galenus docuit, & præsertim in libro de animi morum et corporei temperamenti mutua consequutione: ubi ait, eos qui oes ad virtutes accommodatum habere animum arbitrantur, vel è diverso nullos, nostrum genus ex dimidio æstimare, neq; illud totum habere cognitum atq; perceptum. Non enim inquit omnes ex temperamento corporis nascuntur hostes virtutis, neq; omnes illius cupidi sunt atq; amantes vi & natura sua. Deinde suâ hanc sententiam seu definitione quadam obiectione depellit, Quod videamus aliquos egregiè probari atq; laudari ob insignes eorum virtutes, aliosq; vicissim damnari ac vituperari, quòd ri, quod vitijs corrupti & deprauati sint. Neq par est ut propter illa quae in nobis naturaliter insunt, aut commendemur aut vituperemur. Quin & illi vbi respub. bene instituta est, puniuntur, isti vero praemijs ornantur. Ad hoc ille ait, istud esse naturale hominum iudicium, ut illa probent, foveant, iuvent, laudet, quae bona sunt, utilia & decora, undecunq; prouenient, si-ue à natura, siue ab industria & quae mala sint, dānosa & dedecoris plena, vituperent, coerceant, & pro viribus tollant, nil cogitantes à qua causa sint profecta. Quod exemplis conatur perspicuè docere. Phalangas occidimus, aspides & colubros, neq; prius apud nos deliberamus an venenum in eis natura sit insitum, an studio & voluntate ipsum accersiuerint. Et Deum amamus & colimus, nobiscum haud reputantes an suam bonitatem industria & propria voluntate acquisiuerit, an illam sibi natura insitam ab aeterno tempore habuerit. Possemusq; nos addere speciosa corpora omnibus admirationi esse, & praeclaris encomijs laudari, licet natura forma ea contigerit: & dona gratis data, ut theologi dicunt[?], laudari debent. Atq; id in summa videtur affirmare, damnari & vituperari malos, uicissimq; bonos probari & laudari, licet non habeatur compertum utrum industria vel natura vel alia quapiam ratione, seu malitia seu bonitas illos peruaserit. Atq; Sto-icos hoc nomine reprehendit: quod omnes existimarent homines ad virtutem natura factos & idoneos, ad quam licet ingenio & vi sua sint propensi, nihilominus ab ea revocantur aliorum pravo exemplo, perversis opinionibus, colloquijs & conversatione hominum corruptorum. Quod si daretur eis, quid obsecro possent afferre de primis hominibus? quos interdum et saepius in mundo fuisse non possunt inficiari, quando per multas vices & statis quibusdam temporibus, mundum opinantur aut inundatione aquarū, aut conflagratione universorum cum perire tum denuo instaurari? Quos inquam ponent illos primos homines, denuo in lucem editos, aut pravis exemplis, aut prava doctrina, vel repertis voluptatibus, aut vitiosis inventis depravasse? Valet ista quidem ratio contra Stoicos. At adversum Peripateticos & alios qui mundum nunquam incepisse arbitrantur, alio sane argumenti genere utuntur. Quod est: Aliquot fratres constituantur eisdem sati parentibus, qui cibis eisdem utantur, sub eodem paedagogo degant, non habeant cum alienis commercium, quis profecto dabitur author quo alij sint moribus corruptis & pravis, alij vero indolem castam & ingenuam perpetuo praeferant? Atq; si volumus quod plerunq; accidit, fateri, statuemus pau-cos admodum, imo propemodum nullos pueros natura propensum habere ingenium ad virtutem, ut qui ad eam minis, castigationibus & monitu perpetuo praeceptorum sint incitandi. Statim enim à prima aetate sunt vel nimis timidi vel plus æquo audaces, inexplebiles, ignaui, petulantes, iracundi et inuidi. Quare mirum est unde Stoici suum illud placitum queant defendere, Omnes natura esse ad virtutem capessendam idoneos. Nec minus ut putant illi verisimilia dicunt, qui statuerunt nostrum genus à voluptate sibi oborta distorqueri, quo cursu ad virtutem contentissimo non pergant, nam eos qui sic dicunt, Posidonius, ut refert, egregie reprehendit, qui nos affirmat ab ipsa prima generatione igniculos habere in animis ad vitia incitates: qui fit ut non possimus nobis cauere, quin simus intus vitiosi, cum tamen liceat prouidere ne mala huiusmodi semina & vitiosæ scintillæ erumpant in scelera, & eo augeantur, ut amplius coerceri non possint. Et istorum deinde hominum iudicio longè maius est & grauius malum quod intus nobiscum gestamus, quàm id quod externo contagio affricatur. Concedunt sane consuetudinem prauam, cum accesserit, nos prauos reddere, atq; id longe maius quàm prius natura fuerimus. De facultate verò qua intelligimus, haec docent, primum à praeceptoribus vel sapientibus vel indoctis fieri posse ut veras aut falsas opiniones percipiamus. Ingenij tamen acumen, stultitiam seu stupiditatem, & huiusmodi, quae intelligentiam spectant, ex temperamenti qualitate nanciscimur, quam in utero contrahimus è rerum procreatium materia: cui postea multae ac mirabiles fiunt accessiones, cum ex cibis qui bonum aut malum succum pariunt, tum ex aeris affectibus et variis rerum incidentium casibus. Citatq; ibi Aristotelem, qui de partibus animalium, uiros etiam docet materni sanguinis temperiem sequi. Et primo de historia animalium, statuit, configurationem partium instrumentariarum siue membrorum ad animi mores accommodari, atque idcirco illis inspectis multa posse à peritis physiognomicae artis de moribus & affectibus interioribus pronuntiari. Haec sunt argumenta, propter quae possit videri Aristoteles hoc loco minus prudenter egisse: qui δυσκρασίαν[?], hoc est, prava temperatura corporis natura procreatos, non dixerit huius doctrinae parum fore idoneos auditores. Sed illum hac ratione tuebimur, quod licet hominum bona pars, imò propemodum omnes in lucem edamur igniculis vitiorum & libidinum infecti, propensi ad turpitudines & flagitia, tamen ista non esse adeò robusta & firma, quin vel prorsus queant superari vel saltem placari & leniri, quo vel egregiè euadant homines quod ad morales virtutes & externam conuersationem, vel saltem minus prauis affectibus vexentur. Et quia dum experientia rerum animi deflituuntur, vt iuuenibus accidit, dumque perturbationum impetu aliqui rapiuntur & incontinentiae sunt obnoxij, non potest fieri ut virtutibus ornentur, & re praestent quæ in hac facultate audi-uerunt, ideo illos, juvenes inquam & incontinentes pronuntiavit minus i-doneos fore auditores. Verū quia fieri potest ut multū proficiant homines, li-cet impetu mali temperamenti & natura incitentur ad vitia, ideò eos nō re-movit philosophus ab auditorum numero. Etenim quod natura deest indu-stria & studio possumus resarcire, ita ut impulsus & incitationes malæ coer-ceantur & reprimantur: neq; ad virtutes capessendas requiritur, ut illas insitas pranitates omnino exuamus. requiritur tantum ut illis debilitandis quantum datur studeamus. Quod si præstitum fuerit industria & exercita-tione, virtutum possessio minime impedietur, quam quia nunquam vendi-care poterimus nisi rerum experientia quæ necessaria est accesserit, & nisi rationis mollitia emendetur quæ laborant incontinētes, ideo illos auditores Aristot. quodammodo reiicit & istorum non duxit mentionem faciendam. Et ipse ad id quod obiiciebat Galenus, paulo aliter responderet de laude ac vituperio. Diceret enim ideo laudari amantes virtutū, nō quod ad eam na-turæ impetu ducantur, sed quia contenderint aduersus eius prauam incli-ī-nationem, atq; in ea pugna pulcherrimè vicerint. Ac è diuerso improbos vituperari quod victi ac debilitati naturalis impetus vi, ea se trahi ad tur-pia sint passi. Neq; Galenus, licet prima fronte reluctari videatur, ab hac sen-tentia est diuersus:nam in libello de cognoscendis & curandis animi affecti-bus, testatur, neminem debere à studio seipsum faciendi meliorem deterreri, quamuis ætate fuerit sexagenarius. Et ad hæc inquit, si cui esset id comper-tissimum quod animum sapientis consequi non possit, saltem eò deberet ad-niti ne illum prorsus haberet deformem, ut corpus Thersitis curandum su-it quamuis alioqui esset ineptum. Atq; si contingat ut cum optimis & sapi-entissimis viris non possimus primas occupare sedes, id attamen debemus conari ut in secundis, tertijs aut quartis recipiamur. Quibus autem medijs quaue ratione hoc fieri possit admonet, ratione dicens ac improbo exercitio consequi potest quicunq; voluerit. Vtq; animos addat, ut grammaticus fias, inquit, multum laboras, & quo absolutus euadas musicus, nihil recusas to-lerare. Quid ergo non feras ut vir bonus efficiare? Tum in eodem libro hanc diligentiam consectandi vitæ integritatem, componit cum industria quam coloni circa plantas adhibent. Fateor, inquit, non posse labore suo & studio agricolam rubum mutare ac eius naturam tollere, seu fructiferam reddere. Sed tamen vites quæ natura sua paratæ sunt ad fructus ferendos, si negligatur, cōmittantur fertilitati soli dūtaxat gubernandæ, aut deterio-rem fructū aut propemodū nullū feret. Ita sunt bonæ indoles alioqui bonorū morum capaces, si deserantur cultura, facile reddentur aut vitiosæ aut ignauæ. At licet à prima ætate in adolescentibus cultura hæc videatur difficilis moderandorum affectuum, nihilominus processu temporis labor imminuetur. Nam ratio in his laudabilibus exercitijs corroboratur & effecta fortior, maiorem obedientiam quo ad vires animi inferiores consequetur.
units.tr: Now there remains a most necessary question that we must not pass over: how is it that when Aristotle called the young and the incontinent unsuitable hearers, he did not likewise count those who are endowed with such a constitution, temperament or nature that they cannot be made better and are altogether unfit for taking up the virtues? That some people are like this Galen has taught in more than one place, especially in his book on the mutual consequence of the temperament of the soul and that of the body, where he says that those who think everyone has a mind adapted to all the virtues, or conversely that no one has, judge our kind by half and do not have the whole of it known and understood. For, he says, not all are born from bodily temperament as enemies of virtue, nor are all eager for it and lovers of it by their own power and nature. Then he meets this view of his with a certain objection: we see some men excellently approved and praised for their outstanding virtues, and others in turn condemned and blamed because they are corrupted and depraved by vices. Yet it is not right that we should be commended or blamed for what is naturally in us. Indeed, where the commonwealth is well ordered, the latter are punished and the former are rewarded. To this he replies that it is the natural judgment of men to approve, foster, help and praise those things that are good, useful and fitting, from whatever source they come, whether from nature or from effort, and to censure, restrain and, as far as they can, remove those that are bad, harmful and full of disgrace, without considering from what cause they have arisen. He tries to show this clearly by examples. We kill phalanges, asps and snakes, and we do not first consider whether the poison is implanted in them by nature or whether they have acquired it by their own study and will. We love and worship God, without asking whether he acquired his goodness by his own effort and will, or whether he has had it implanted in him by nature from eternity. We could add that beautiful bodies are an object of admiration to all and are praised with notable eulogies, although that form has fallen to them by nature, and that the gifts freely given, as the theologians say, ought to be praised. In sum, he seems to affirm that the bad are condemned and blamed, and the good in turn approved and praised, even though it is not known whether they were moved by effort or by nature or by some other cause, whether by malice or by goodness. And he rebukes the Stoics on this account: because they all supposed that men are made by nature fit and suited to virtue, and although they are inclined to it by their own talent and power, they are nonetheless called back from it by the bad example of others, perverse opinions, conversations and the company of corrupt people. But if they were asked, I beg you, what they could say about the first men, whom they cannot deny to have existed at times and often in the world, since over many cycles and at certain fixed times they think the world perishes either by a flood of waters or by a conflagration of all things and is then renewed again: what, I ask, will they say those first men, brought again into the light, were corrupted by, whether by bad examples, bad teaching, pleasures discovered, or vicious inventions? This argument certainly holds against the Stoics. But against the Peripatetics and others who think the world never began, they use a different kind of argument. It runs thus: suppose several brothers are born of the same parents, eat the same food, live under the same tutor, and have no dealings with outsiders; who will surely be the author of why some have corrupt and depraved characters, while others always show a chaste and noble disposition? And if we want to admit what most often happens, we shall declare that very few boys, indeed almost none, have a mind by nature inclined to virtue, so that they must be spurred to it by threats, punishments and constant admonition of precepts. For from the earliest age they are either too timid or more bold than is right, insatiable, lazy, wanton, irascible and envious. Hence it is a wonder how the Stoics can defend their opinion that all men are by nature fit to take up virtue. Nor, as they think, do those say anything less probable who have held that our kind is turned aside from its course by pleasure arising within it, so that it does not proceed with the most intense effort toward virtue. Posidonius, as he reports, rebukes excellently those who say this, since he affirms that we have from our very first generation little sparks in our souls that incite us to vices; so it happens that we cannot guard ourselves against being inwardly vicious, although it is possible to take care that evil seeds of this kind and vicious sparks do not break out into crimes and grow to such a degree that they can no longer be restrained. And in the judgment of these men the evil we carry within us is far greater and more grievous than that which is contracted by external contagion. They concede indeed that a bad habit, once it has taken hold, makes us bad, and that this is far greater than what we were by nature before. But concerning the faculty by which we understand, these men teach the following: first, that by teachers, whether wise or unlearned, it can happen that we perceive opinions true or false. Yet the keenness of wit, dullness or stupidity, and such things as concern understanding, we obtain from the quality of temperament, which we contract in the womb from the matter of the things that generate us; to this many wonderful additions are later made, both from foods that produce good or bad juice and from the conditions of the air and the various chances of things that befall us. And he cites there Aristotle, who in his work on the parts of animals also teaches that men follow the temperament of their mother's blood. And in the first book of his History of Animals he holds that the configuration of the instrumental parts, or limbs, is adapted to the character of the soul, and therefore, when these have been inspected, many things about character and inner affections can be pronounced by those skilled in the art of physiognomy. These are the arguments on account of which Aristotle may seem to have acted less prudently in this place: he did not say that those born of a bad temperament of body, dyskrasia, that is, a depraved constitution of the body, would be unsuitable hearers of this teaching. But we shall defend him on this ground: although a good part of mankind, indeed almost all of us, are brought into the light infected with the sparks of vices and lusts, inclined to base and shameful deeds, yet these are not so strong and firm that they cannot be wholly overcome, or at least calmed and softened, so that men may either excel in moral virtues and outward conduct, or at least be less troubled by depraved affections. And because, while they lack experience of things, as young people do, and while some are carried away by the impulse of disturbances and are subject to incontinence, they cannot be adorned with virtues or achieve what they have heard in this discipline, therefore he pronounced that they, the young and the incontinent, would be unsuitable hearers. But since men can make great progress, even when they are driven to vices by the impulse of a bad temperament and nature, the philosopher did not remove them from the number of hearers. For what nature lacks we can make up by effort and study, so that bad impulses and incitements are restrained and repressed; nor is it required for taking up the virtues that we strip ourselves entirely of those innate depravities; it is only required that we strive to weaken them as far as is granted to us. If this has been achieved by effort and practice, possession of the virtues will not be impeded in the least; but because we can never make it our own unless experience of things, which is necessary, is added, and unless the softness of reason, under which the incontinent labour, is corrected, therefore Aristotle in some measure rejects those hearers and did not think they should be mentioned. And in reply to what Galen objected, he would answer somewhat differently about praise and blame. He would say that those who love the virtues are praised not because they are carried toward it by natural impulse, but because they have striven against its depraved inclination and conquered most splendidly in that struggle. And conversely the wicked are blamed because, having been defeated and weakened by the force of natural impulse, they have allowed themselves to be drawn to base things. Nor does Galen, although at first sight he seems to resist, differ from this opinion: for in his little book on recognising and curing the affections of the soul he testifies that no one ought to be deterred from the effort of making himself better, even if he is a man of sixty. And he adds that if anyone knew for certain that he could not attain the soul of the wise man, he should at least strive not to have it wholly deformed, just as the body of Thersites was to be cared for although otherwise it was unfit. And if it happens that we cannot occupy the first seats with the best and wisest men, we ought nonetheless to try to be received in the second, third or fourth. He also advises by what means and in what way this can be done, saying that whoever wishes can attain it by reasoning and by diligent exercise. And to encourage the mind he says: you labour much so that you may become a grammarian, and you refuse to endure nothing so that you may come out a finished musician. Why then would you not bear things so that you may become a good man? Then in the same book he compares this diligence in pursuing integrity of life with the effort that farmers apply to plants. I admit, he says, that by his labour and study a farmer cannot change a bramble and take away its nature, or make it fruitful. But vines, which by their nature are fit to bear fruit, if they are neglected and left only to the fertility of the soil to govern, will bear either poorer fruit or almost none. So too good natural dispositions, otherwise capable of good morals, if they are abandoned by cultivation, will easily become either vicious or lazy. But although in young people at the earliest age this cultivation seems difficult, in the moderation of the affections, nevertheless with the passage of time the labour will be lessened. For reason is strengthened and made stronger by these praiseworthy exercises, and will gain greater obedience from the lower powers of the soul.

units.la: Neq; ab his dissentit Plutarchus qui de profectu morum & ipse confitetur infinitam quandam et inexplicabilem malitiam in animis nostris residere, quæ tamen accessione possit augeri, & defectione aliqua imminui. Idemq; de libris educandis tria esse constituit, quæ ad hominem absoluendum exigantur, naturam, disciplinam, & exercitationem. Quid per naturam intelligatiam [?] est dictum, corporis inquam temperamentum, & inclinationem natiuam: neq; opus labore ut explicemus quid sit exercitiu, solum videtur esse dubium de disciplina. Propterea illam esse dicimus facultatem quandam, quæ hominum actiones & electiones accommodet ad rationem, idq; doctrina, correctionibus monitionibus & pœnis efficit cum opus fuerit. Et quicquid istorum desit cuipiam, is non potest quo ad mores ciuiles & virtutes perfici. Confert huic sua doctrina agriculturam, quæ ut succeßus optatos habeat, solum requirit fertile, deinde cultura operosam & decentem, postremò bona & utilia semina. Et si quid horum trium defuerit, fructibus expectatis destituimur. Solum naturæ respondet, cultus disciplinæ, semina vero exercitationi. Quod si gutta pluuiæ lapides excauant assiduo casu, ferrum & æs licet durißima sint usu atterüntur, corpora desidia & ignauia debilitantur, debilia vero commodo victu & iusta exercitatione ad incredibile robur prouehuntur. Sterilis ager bene cultus non est penitus absque fructu, & fertilis neglectus squallet, ac tantum fert spinas & herbas cum noxias tum inutiles. Et feræ crudelissimæ humano labore atq; industria curantur: quæ vero iumenta sua natura mitia essent & tractabilia, si sic sinantur, efferarari consueuerunt, vt in equis & tauris fieri videmus. Sed quid plura? Nonne duo catuli ex eisdem canibus orti quos Lycurgus produxit in concione Lacedemoniorum, suo cursu ad diuersissima, declararunt quid possit varietas educationis?
units.tr: Plutarch does not disagree with these points either. In his work on the progress of character he admits that an infinite and inexplicable malice dwells in our minds, which can nevertheless be increased by addition and diminished by some subtraction. He likewise laid down that three things are required to bring a person to completion in education: nature, discipline, and exercise. What is meant by nature has already been said: I mean the temperament of the body and natural inclination. There is no need to labour to explain what exercise is; only the matter of discipline seems doubtful. So we say that discipline is a certain faculty that adjusts people's actions and choices to reason, and it achieves this by teaching, correction, admonition, and punishment when necessary. Whoever lacks any of these cannot be perfected in civic morals and virtues. His doctrine compares this to agriculture, which, to have the hoped-for success, requires first a fertile field, then careful and fitting cultivation, and finally good and useful seed. If any of these three is lacking, we are deprived of the expected fruits. Nature corresponds to the soil, cultivation to discipline, and seed to exercise. If drops of rain hollow out stones by constant falling, and iron and bronze, however hard, are worn down by use, and if bodies are weakened by idleness and sloth while weak bodies are brought to incredible strength by proper diet and right exercise, then the same holds here. A barren field that is well tilled is not wholly without fruit, while a fertile field that is neglected grows foul and bears only thorns and weeds, both harmful and useless. The fiercest wild beasts are tamed by human labour and industry, and beasts of burden that would by nature be gentle and tractable, if left alone, tend to become wild, as we see with horses and bulls. But why say more? Did not two puppies, born of the same dogs and brought forward by Lycurgus in an assembly of the Lacedaemonians, show by their very different courses what variety of upbringing can do?

units.la: Verum quid ad Platonem dicemus in Protagora? Qui videtur ibi statuere virtutes non posse doceri, Quoniam, inquit, Pericles & alij viri eximij, licet suos liberos instrui curauerint literis, musica, & consimilibus bonis artibus, in quibus eorum liberi multum profecerunt, non tamen ornatos virtutibus reddiderunt, quod sane credendum est illos maximè optasse, si doctrina & industria id potuissent assequi. Unde videtur confici, quosdam esse natura sic à virtutibus abhorrentes, vt eas comparare sibi nequeant, & alios incassum esse laboraturos cum eos ad ipsas conati fuerint flectere. Verum hoc quoq; nihil ea quæ constituimus labefactat: quia vel ipsorum parentes illis educandis non studuerunt quantū par erat, aut si diligentiæ quantum satis erat adiunxerunt & liberorum natura propter corporis temperamentum aliena erat à virtutibus, non prorsus nihil suo labore atq; industria sunt assecuti. nam licet si collati essent summis, perfectis, & absolutissimis ciuibus, virtus eis penitus videretur detracta, nihilominus agrestibus et efferatis hominibus collati, qui omnino absq; disciplina sunt educati, habiti esset ciuiles, urbani et aliqua specie virtutū ornati. Concluditur itaq; non esse industriam, disciplinam, & studium, prorsus inania, etiam quo ad eos qui naturali propensione virtutes auersantur.
units.tr: But what shall we say to Plato in the Protagoras? There he seems to hold that virtues cannot be taught, since, he says, Pericles and other outstanding men, although they took care to have their sons instructed in letters, music, and similar good arts, in which their sons made much progress, nevertheless did not render them adorned with virtues. We must surely believe they would have most wished for this, had teaching and effort been able to achieve it. From this it seems to follow that some people are by nature so averse to virtue that they cannot acquire it, and that others will labour in vain when they try to bend them towards it. But this also does not overturn what we have laid down. Either the parents themselves did not devote as much attention to their children's upbringing as was fitting, or, if they applied as much diligence as was enough, the children's nature, owing to their bodily temperament, was foreign to virtue, and yet they did not achieve nothing by their labour and industry. For although, if compared with the highest, most perfect, and most accomplished citizens, they would seem to have been stripped of virtue entirely, nevertheless, compared with rustic and savage men who had been brought up without any discipline at all, they would have been considered civil, urbane, and adorned with some kind of virtue. It follows, therefore, that industry, discipline, and study are not altogether vain, even with regard to those who, by natural propensity, shun the virtues.

units.la: Quæ Aristoteles iam protulit, ut cum sacris literis vel congruant vel discrepent, iam de more suscepto aperiendum est. Iuuenes & incontinentes ibi non excipiuntur, nec ab audiedo verbo Dei Ulli remouentur, ob eam cau-sam, quòd animi perturbationibus adhuc concitentur & vincantur, neque illo nomine quod experientia & Usu rerum sint destituti. Videas enim publicanos, meretrices, nec non latrones à Christo in suam disciplinam admissos, nec tantum iuuenes imò paruulos ipsos accersitos. Et ex historiis possemus excitare quamplures, qui prius turpiter ac flagitiosissimè vixerunt, statim doctrina Christi sic emendatos & correctos, ut postea non tantum summam vitæ innocentiâ sint assecuti, sed etiam incredibili fortitudine se magnis cruciatibus necari pertulerint, ne decreta nostræ fidei & pietatem, quam erant adepti, violarent, cùm ipsis & liberatio & maxima præmia si ab instituto discessissent proponerentur. Neque solos viros in certamina huius generis descendisse videmus, sed mulieres alioquin imbecilles, pueros & puellas hæc eadem fortiter pertulisse non ignoramus.
units.tr: Now that Aristotle has put forward these points, it must be shown, as is our custom, whether they agree or disagree with Holy Scripture. Young people and the incontinent are not excluded there, nor is anyone removed from hearing the word of God, on the ground that their minds are still stirred and overcome by the disturbances of the passions, or that they lack experience and practical knowledge of affairs. For you see tax collectors, prostitutes, and robbers admitted by Christ to his teaching, and not only youths but even little children summoned to him. From histories we could cite very many who had previously lived shamefully and most disgracefully, yet who, at once, by the teaching of Christ were so amended and corrected that afterwards they attained not only the highest innocence of life but also, with incredible fortitude, endured being put to death with great torments, so as not to violate the decrees of our faith and the piety they had acquired, though both deliverance and very great rewards were offered to them if they abandoned their profession. Nor do we see only men entering contests of this kind; we know that women, otherwise weak, and boys and girls have endured the same things bravely.

units.la: Neq; id dixerit quispiam, illos qui peccant in Spiritum S. sermonibus diuinis quicquam non proficere, ideoq; videri ab eorum auditu arcendos. Fatemur sanè qui sic peccant, frustra verbum Dei audire, sed cùm à nobis visitata ratione internosci non queant, minimè excluduntur. Deus bene novit qui hoc peccati genere sint implicati: at homines cùm ignorent qui natura in tantum sceleus prolapsi sint, eos non possunt à sacra doctrina remouere. Oportet sanè peccantes in spiritum sanctum neq; ignoratione, neq; infirmitate succumbere, sed tantum veritatis odio ad eam oppugnandam indu-ci, ita ut volentes & scientes, vero, quod probè noverint, se opponant, resistant, & cursum eius pro viribus impediant. Hoc qui homines possent intelligere? cùm ad mētis [?] & voluntatis arcana cuiusquā non pertingant? Unde qui tam praue affecti sunt, verbum Dei audiunt absq; fructu, licet ab auditorio non excludantur, ob id sane, quòd nequeant deprehendi, sed illis quod audiunt grauiorem auget condemnationem: ea quippe vis est diuini sermonis, ut vel seruet audientes, vel eis fiat exitiosus. Adeoq; cauet Ecclesia ne quos explodat à sermonibus diuinis, ut excommunicatos etiam & nondum credentes ad illos admittat, quos alioqui tum à sacramentis, tum à publicis precibus arcet. Queras forsitan unde hoc discrimen inter verbum Dei, & philosophorum doctrinas? Ex eo profecto, quod humani sermones quantumuis eximij atq; laudabiles, non ea praediti sunt vi atq; potentia, ut ineptos & corruptos animos immutare, seu corrigere valeant: at verborum Dei potentia & vis incredibilis est, reuocandi homines ad Deum. Nō quasi etiam illa vera quae philosophi seu docuerunt, seu literis mandarunt, sua vi careant. Non enim inficiamur sententiam illam vetustate tritissimam, quà dicitur, à spiritu sancto proficisci quicquid veri ab authore cuiusq; modi prolatum fuerit: quæ verò diuini spiritus impulsu dicuntur, non possunt esse omnino vacua efficacia, quamuis longè minor ea sit, atq; vehementia quàm sacræ literæ sint instructæ. Quis negauerit vulgares lapides robore suo & propria facultate eaq; non inutili nostræ vitæ ornatos, licet conferri nequeant cum viribus gemmarum?
units.tr: Nor should anyone say that those who sin against the Holy Spirit gain nothing from divine words, and therefore seem to be kept away from hearing them. We admit that those who sin in this way hear the word of God in vain, but since they cannot be recognised by any method available to us, they are by no means excluded. God knows well who are entangled in this kind of sin; but since men do not know who has fallen into such great wickedness by nature, they cannot remove them from sacred teaching. Indeed, those who sin against the Holy Spirit ought not to succumb through ignorance or through weakness, but only be driven by hatred of the truth to attack it, so that, willingly and knowingly, they set themselves against the truth they know well, resist it, and impede its course as far as they can. How could men understand this, since they cannot reach the hidden places of anyone's mind and will? Hence those who are so depraved hear the word of God without fruit, although they are not excluded from the hearers, certainly because they cannot be detected; but what they hear increases their heavier condemnation. Such is the power of divine speech that it either preserves the hearers or becomes deadly to them. So the Church takes care not to cast anyone out of divine sermons, and therefore admits to them even the excommunicated and those not yet believing, whom otherwise it keeps away both from the sacraments and from public prayers. You may perhaps ask whence this difference between the word of God and the doctrines of the philosophers arises. Surely from this: human discourses, however outstanding and praiseworthy, do not possess such force and power as to change or correct unfit and corrupt minds, whereas the power of the words of God is incredible in calling men back to God. Not that those true things which the philosophers either taught or committed to writing lack their own force. For we do not deny that old and well-worn saying, by which it is said that whatever truth has been uttered by any author of whatever kind proceeds from the Holy Spirit; and those things which are said to come from the impulse of the divine Spirit cannot be wholly without efficacy, although it is far less, and less vehement, than what Holy Scripture is furnished with. Who would deny that common stones are endowed with their own strength and natural property, and that this is not useless to our life, although they cannot be compared with the powers of gems?

units.la: Scd ad rem redeo. Vnum tantummodo genus hominum reperio, quibus doctrina sacra non sit impartienda, & hi sunt qui rident & proscindunt publicè Christi doctrinam: nam ipse mandauit Apostolis ne canibus & porcis doctrinam cœlestem crederent. quod porrò accipiendum est de conceptione, ac risu externo, id est, quando maledictis & contumeliis veram pietatem insectantur: quod si faciant ipsi secum, modò audire velint quieti, & patiantur se moneri, & doceri, non sunt arcendi. Neq; tamen propter illos qui palàm sunt petulantes, maledici & contumeliosi à concione publica desistendum est, quando ipsi arceri non possunt, quod fortasse sint praepotentes, ne propter unum aut alterum, plebs universa animi pabulo fraudetur. Videtis itaq; solum istos à sacra doctrina remoueri, à qua cæteri homines cuiusq; modi prohibendi non sunt, imò potius cohortandi, ut non parum sæpè accedant.
units.tr: But I return to the matter. I find only one class of people to whom sacred doctrine should not be imparted, namely those who openly mock and tear apart the teaching of Christ in public; for he himself commanded the Apostles not to give heavenly doctrine to dogs and swine. This, moreover, must be understood of contempt and outward ridicule, that is, when they assail true piety with curses and insults. But if they keep such things to themselves, provided they are willing to listen quietly and allow themselves to be admonished and taught, they are not to be excluded. Nor, on account of those who are openly wanton, abusive, and insulting, must the public sermon be abandoned, since those men cannot themselves be excluded, perhaps because they are very powerful; lest, on account of one or two, the whole common people be defrauded of spiritual food. You see, then, that only these are removed from sacred teaching, while other men of whatever kind are not to be forbidden, but rather encouraged to come quite often.

units.la: Quæ dixi, ad usitatum morem & receptum institutum Ecclesiæ pertinent, cum sciam spiritum nonnunquam prohibuisse Apostolos, & aliquos modò posse comprimere, ne alicubi loquantur, quibus alioqui prædicare destinauerant: quod quia Dei opus est, non ho-minum, ideò huc non facit.
units.tr: What I have said pertains to the usual practice and accepted order of the Church, since I know that the Spirit has sometimes forbidden the Apostles, and can now restrain some, from speaking in certain places where otherwise they had intended to preach. Since this is God's work and not men's, it does not bear on the present question.
CHAPTER 4.

units.la: ATrepetētes dicamus, cum omnis notitia & delectus bonum quoddam appetat, quid illud est quod ciuilem facultatem appetere dicimus: & quid sit extremum omnium bonorum agendorum. De nomine quidem fere inter plurimos conuenit. Felicitatem enim & uulgus & elegantes dicunt: & bene uiuere & bene agere eadem significatione accipiunt qua felicem esse. De Felicitate autem quae sit ambigunt.
units.tr: Let us go back and say: since all knowledge and choice seeks some good, what is that which we say the civil art seeks, and what is the highest of all the goods to be done? About the name, almost everyone agrees. Both the common people and the refined call it happiness, and they take "living well" and "acting well" in the same sense as "being happy." But what happiness is, they dispute.

units.la: Conclusò & perfecto proœmio, quo tradiderat rerum huma-narum aliquam esse summam & extremam finem: nunc se confert ad explicandum quae sit eius ratio & natura: proinde refert suum conatum ad eius definitionem absolutè docenda, qua probè cognita, ad agendum fusè lateq; de virtutibus aditus patefiet. Tota vero hac tractatio in quinq; partes distribuitur. Primum sanè de bono extremo aliorum opiniones recitat, deinde allatas refellit, Tertiò praecipuè inter illas eam quae Platonis est nititur conuellere. praeterea suam definitionem prodit, qua Felicitatem putat explicari. Quinto deniq; ac postremo loco demonstrat opiniones iam recitatas aliorum cum sua facilè posse congruere. Prima parte cum recensent aliorum sententias, adjicit modum seu formam qua procedendum arbitratur ad summum bonum definiendum, inq; duo istud quartum caput dissecatur[?].
units.tr: Having concluded and completed the proem, in which he taught that there is some highest and ultimate end of human affairs, he now turns to explain its nature and character. He therefore directs his effort to defining it absolutely, so that once this is well understood, the way will be open to a full and broad treatment of the virtues in action. The whole treatment is divided into five parts. First he recounts the opinions of others about the ultimate good; then he refutes those brought forward; thirdly he chiefly sets out to overthrow among them the one that belongs to Plato. Besides this, he sets forth his own definition, by which he thinks happiness is explained. Fifthly and lastly, he shows that the opinions already recited from others can easily agree with his own. In the first part, when they review the opinions of others, he adds the method or form by which he thinks one should proceed in defining the highest good; and this fourth chapter is divided into two.

units.la: Propositio huius loci est, de nomine felicitatis omnes propemodum con-sentire, cum de re in qua sita sit, magnopere dissideat. Prior pars ex eo pro-batur, quod omnes cum vulgares tum eruditi consentiunt idem esse rectè viuere, bene agere, ac felicem esse: ratio ab etymologia nominis est deducta. Altera verò pars propositionis confirmatur, quia nonnulli firmam valetudinem, alij voluptatem, alij diuitias, alij honores, alij scientiam, alij quiddā per se ac natura sua bonum, quod à rebus vniuersis secretum sit, felicitatem existimant, & à materia sumitur haec probatio, quandoquidem varia subiecta felicitatis diuersi homines adinuenerunt. Tota haec tractatio con-futatione, cōfirmationeq; perficitur: nam veterū opiniones refellit, & suam communit ac defendit. Ordinem hunc sequitur, vt prius aliena confutet quàm propria stabiliat: quem morem in aliis etiam locis fere semper retinu it. In physicis disputat ab initio contra Parmenidem et Melissum. De animo, totum fere primum librum in opinionibus veterum recensendis & consu tandis absoluit. Quod sanè licet ab eo alia de causa fieri potuerit, attamen inde hunc aperte videmus fructum haberi, quòd ex falsi depulsione, facili or redditur veri adeptio: nam errore patefacto, cognoscimus qua via & ra tione possimus ab eo cauere.
units.tr: The proposition of this place is that almost everyone agrees on the name of happiness, though they differ greatly about the thing in which it lies. The first part is proved by the fact that all, both the common people and the learned, agree that living well, acting well, and being happy are the same; the argument is drawn from the etymology of the name. The second part of the proposition is confirmed because some think happiness is firm health, others pleasure, others riches, others honours, others knowledge, and others something good in itself and by its own nature, separate from all things. This proof is taken from the subject matter, since different people have devised various subjects of happiness. This whole treatment is accomplished by refutation and confirmation: for he refutes the opinions of the ancients and establishes and defends his own. He follows this order, so that he first refutes others' views before establishing his own: a method he has kept almost always in other places as well. In physics he disputes from the beginning against Parmenides and Melissus. In the book On the Soul he completes almost the whole first book by reviewing and examining the opinions of the ancients. Although he may have done this for another reason, we clearly see this benefit from it: by driving out falsehood, the attainment of truth is made easy, for once the error is exposed we learn by what way and method we can guard against it.

units.la: Repetit quòd iam inde ab initio proœmij scripserat, omnem notitiam & electionem bonum aliquod expetere, vt facilem transitum patefaciat ad inquirendum quid sit extremum bonum. Communi vocabulo notitiæ comprehendit hoc loco scientiam & artem: & quod additur, extremum omnium bonorum agendorum, subiectum est per expositionem: etenim ea sententia bonum explicatur, quod ciuilis facultas expetit. Inquit omnes propemodum consentire de nomine: & qualis ista conspiratio sit, demonstra tur non absq; fructu: valet enim ad intelligendum quæ vis huic voci felici tatis subiiciatur.
units.tr: He repeats what he had written from the beginning of the proem, that all knowledge and choice seeks some good, so as to open an easy transition to inquiring what the highest good is. By the common word "knowledge" he here includes science and art. What is added, "the highest of all the goods to be done," is set out as the subject by way of explanation, for that sentence explains the good which the civil art seeks. He says that almost everyone agrees about the name, and what kind of agreement this is, is shown not without profit, for it helps us understand what force is placed under this word happiness.

units.la: Nominis porrò expositio, quid aliud est quàm definitio quædam non lata & ampla, sed contracta, quæ postea fusius & latius explicatur, cùm defini tur ipsa rei substantia. Dicit forte, quia nonnullos reperias interdum adeò rudes inerudites & indoctos, qui vel etiam nomen felicitatis ignorent. Aut forte particulam illam inseruit vt eos notaret, qui nullos existimarūt felices dum hic vixerint, sed expectandam extremam horam, vt Solon docuit. A nominis explicatione sumpsit initium, tanquam à re notiore, iuxta regulam quam ipse in multis locis repetit, à magis perspicuis & manifestis in omni doctrina esse ordiendum. De nomine inquit omnes conuenire, atq; multitudinem hominum distribuit in vulgares, & elegantes, id est χαρίεν-τας [?], elegantes verò sunt participes eruditionis, quorum longè minor est nu merus quàm vulgarium: etenim permultos reperias, qui bonos egregiosq; habitus virtutum consuetudine quadam sibi comparent, cùm alioqui eru ditione atq; doctrina minimè sint exculti.
units.tr: Moreover, what is an explanation of a name but a definition that is not broad and ample but contracted, which is later explained more fully and widely when the very substance of the thing is defined. He says perhaps, because you may sometimes find some so rude, unlearned and untaught that they do not even know the name of happiness. Or perhaps he inserted that particle to mark those who thought no one was happy while he lived, but that the last hour must be awaited, as Solon taught. He began with the explanation of the name, as from a more known thing, following the rule he repeats in many places: in all teaching one must begin from what is clearer and more manifest. He says all agree about the name, and he divides the multitude of men into the common people and the refined, that is, [χαρίεντας]. The refined are those who share in learning, and their number is far smaller than that of the common people. For you will find very many who, by a certain habit, acquire for themselves good and excellent dispositions of the virtues, although otherwise they are not at all cultivated by learning and teaching.

units.la: De felicitate autem quæ sit ambigunt.) Eustratius discrimen po nit vt aliud sit dicere τίς ἐστιν [?] ... τί ἐστι [?], ita vt primum de subiecto quæratin quo felicitas collocanda sit, alterum verò de illius absoluta & perfecta de finitione. Aggreditur proinde philosophus explicationem subiecti, & quæ nam ea sit quærit, sed circa finem tractationis huius quid sit, & defini tionem eius tradit. Et ad ordinem non parum facit quod suam disputationem continuo à materia exorsus est, ita etiam fecit in Physicis, nam cùm ibi de motu seu mutationibus esset acturus, primum omnium subiecti seu materiae naturam inuestigauit: atque in Dialecticis priusquam ad Syllogismos accederet & ἀποδείξεις[?], de propositionibus egit & Topicis, quae materiam suppeditat argumentationibus. Materia quamuis per se ipsam sit rudis et inculta, nihilominus fundamentum est, quod postea formis & definitionibus terminatur ac perficitur. Quis enim felicitatem recte poterit genere suo & differentijs comprehendere, qui prius non cognouerit quod & subiectum & materiam habeat?
units.tr: But what happiness is, they dispute.) Eustratius makes a distinction, so that it is one thing to say [tis estin] and another [ti estin]: the first asks about the subject in which happiness is to be placed, the second about its complete and perfect definition. The philosopher therefore sets about explaining the subject and asks what it is, but near the end of this treatment he says what it is and gives its definition. It contributes not a little to the order that he begins his discussion straight from the matter. He did the same in the Physics: when he was about to treat motion or change, he first of all investigated the nature of the subject or matter. And in the Dialectics, before he came to syllogisms and demonstrations [ἀποδείξεις], he treated propositions and the Topics, which supply the matter for arguments. Matter, although in itself rude and uncultivated, is nevertheless the foundation, which is afterwards bounded and perfected by forms and definitions. For who could rightly comprehend happiness by its genus and differences, if he had not first known that it has both a subject and matter?

units.la: Et non similiter uulgus ac sapientes hoc tradunt: quidam enim quippiam eorum quae clara manifestaque sint, ueluti uoluptatem, aut diuitias, aut honores: alij uero aliud: plerunque etiam idem aliud atque aliud. Quando enim quis aegrotat, sanitatem: uel cum egestate laborat, diuitias: qui uero sibi conscij sunt ignorationis, eos qui dicunt grandia, quaeque captum suum excedunt, mirantur. Quidam uero putarunt praeter haec multa bona, aliud quoddam per seipsum, quod his omnibus quoque causa fit, cur bona sint. Omnes autem scrutari opiniones, uanius fortasis est: sufficiat eminentes maxime, quaeque aliquam rationem habere uideantur, exquirere.
units.tr: The common people and the wise do not hand this down in the same way. Some name one of those things that are clear and manifest, such as pleasure, riches, or honours; others another; and often the same person names one thing and then another. For when someone is sick he names health, or when he labours in want, riches. But those who are conscious of their own ignorance marvel at those who speak of grand things that exceed their grasp. Some, however, thought that besides these many goods there is something else, which is good through itself and is also the cause of all these goods being good. But to examine all opinions would perhaps be too much; it is enough to inquire into the most eminent ones, which seem to have some reason behind them.

units.la: Confirmat his verbis de re felicitatis magnam esse dissensionem: nam vulgares à sapientibus differunt, imò si pressius rem considerueris, nō o-mnes vulgares congruunt secum, & sapientes cum sapientibus non parum discrepant. Sententiae philosophorum ita distingui possunt, vt aliquas earum fuisse dicamus illustres, quae celebres habuerunt patronos: alias verò ignobiles & obscuras, quod viliorum hominum fuerint, neq; firmis perspicuisq; rationibus sint confirmatae. atq; huius generis sunt, firma valetudo, diuitiae, & consimilia, quorum propugnatores non fuerunt insignes. Ad alterum genus pertinent voluptas, honestum, virtus, viuere congruè cum primis naturae datis, scientia. Haec sanè fines numerantur simplices: aliquae verò coniuncta, quandoquidem nonnulli ad virtutem voluptatem adiungunt: alij ad honestum nestum vacuitatem doloris:nonnulli coniungunt cum virtute perfecta vitae absolutionem. Augustinus appellat contra Iulianum Scyllaeum bonum quod cum voluptate componitur. Quod enim ibi ponitur honestas, humanam faciem refert: voluptas, quae admiscetur, est res belluina. Sed qui plenius de his vult cognoscere, Ciceronem cum in 2. libro de finibus legat, tum in Tusc. Videas etiam quandoq; secum aliquos discrepare, quoda[?] prius censebant extremum bonum, mox repudiant. Qui enim dum valerent sanitate visi sunt parui ducere, cum postea fuerint ea destituti, ponunt in summo bono. Quod item illis accidit qui premuntur egestate: nam hi divitias, non tantum pluris faciunt, sed unice persequuntur. Et hi quos enumerauimus aliquid constituunt evidens & manifestum. Quoniam haec, voluptas, divitiae, honores, sunt adeo perspicua & clara, ut vel ipsos sensus incurrant. Imo Epicurus ideo se voluptatem aiebat summum bonum existimare, quod esset & notissimum & apertissimum bonum: nec minus aiebat cognosci manifeste voluptate esse praecipuum bonu, qua niuem esse albam vel ignem calere.
units.tr: By these words he confirms that there is great dispute about the matter of happiness. For the common people differ from the wise; indeed, if you consider the matter more closely, not all the common people agree among themselves, and the wise do not differ little from the wise. The opinions of the philosophers can be distinguished, so that we may say some of them were illustrious and had famous defenders, while others were obscure and unknown, because they belonged to baser men and were not confirmed by firm and clear reasons. Of this kind are firm health, riches, and the like, whose champions were not distinguished. To the other kind belong pleasure, the honourable, virtue, living in agreement with the first gifts of nature, and knowledge. These are counted as simple ends, but some are joined together: some add pleasure to virtue, others add to the honourable the absence of pain, and some join to perfect virtue the completeness of life. Augustine, in his work against Julian, calls the good that is combined with pleasure a monstrous thing. For what is there called honesty presents a human face, while the pleasure that is mixed in is a beastly thing. But whoever wishes to know more fully about these should read Cicero, first in the second book On Ends and then in the Tusculans. You may also see that some sometimes disagree with themselves, when they first judged something to be the highest good and soon reject it. Those who, while they were well, seemed to think little of health, afterwards, when they were deprived of it, place it in the highest good. The same happens to those oppressed by want: these not only value riches more, but pursue them alone. Those we have enumerated set up something evident and manifest, for pleasure, riches and honours are so plain and clear that they strike even the senses. Indeed, Epicurus said that he judged pleasure the highest good because it was both the best known and the most obvious good; and he said that pleasure is manifestly known to be the chief good no less clearly than snow is known to be white or fire to be hot.

units.la: Quod memorat Aristoteles de sanitate atq; diuitiis, non absolute simpli-citerq; dicit, sed priuationem adiunxit, quando quis aegrotat vel egestate laborat. Auiditas enim quam ferimur in summum bonum, duplici ex parte oritur, cum ex cognito bono quod amamus, & notitia quam sentimus nos eo destitutos. Unde Plato in Symposio recte censuit amorem ἐκ τῆς πόρου καὶ τῆς πενίας[?] esse natum. Atq; modo Aristoteles quoq; docet, eos qui vident se morbo cruciari, aut premi egestate, incendi tanto studio sanitatis & pecuniae, ut ista putent summa bona. Quibus verbis agnoscimus priuationem seu paupertatem initium esse huius opinionis, quod non minus apparet ex eo quod addit, Illos qui sibi conscij sunt ignorationis, eos vehementer mirari qui dicunt grandia & quae suum ipsorum captum excedunt: in his oppido admirantur duo, cum sapientiam tum eloquentiam.
units.tr: What Aristotle says about health and wealth he does not state absolutely or without qualification. He adds a privation: when someone is sick or suffers from want. The eagerness with which we are drawn toward the highest good arises from two sources: the knowledge of a good that we love, and the awareness that we lack it. So Plato in the Symposium rightly judged that love was born from Poros and Penia [ἐκ τῆς πόρου καὶ τῆς πενίας]. Aristotle also teaches that those who see themselves racked by sickness or pressed by poverty burn with such zeal for health and money that they think these are the highest goods. By these words we recognise that privation or poverty is the origin of this opinion. This appears no less from what he adds: that those who are conscious of their own ignorance greatly admire those who speak grandly and beyond their own grasp. In these people, he says, two things are especially admired: wisdom and eloquence.

units.la: Alij putarunt praeter haec multa bona unum per seipsum.) Plato citatur hoc loco, qui Deum ipsum a creaturis quae corrumpuntur secretum bonum posuit, id est, per seipsum: nam dixit eum omnibus causam esse cur bona essent, ipsum vero non aliunde quam ex seipso bonitatem suam habere: ibi posuit ideam boni, ad cuius exemplum & formam omnia sint bona. Verum cum haec in variis locis traderet, de summo bono simpliciter dicebat, non autem de summo hominis bono loquebatur, idcirco videtur extra propositum nunc adduci, ubi de ipsa hominis felicitate controuersia explicatur: quandoquidem non sunt homines felices illa communi idea boni, de qua saepius egit Plato, sed ea felicitate quae ipsis inhaereat. Quemadmodum viride aliquid appellamus quod in seipso viriditatem habet: ita & nunc de felici homine loquimur, vt in eo felicitas inest. Sed nescio quo consilio vel impetu quandoque Aristoteles in Platonem concitetur. Quod scio aliquos dicere non ab eo factum vt ipsum carperet, sed vt verba eius & loquutiones castigaret, quæ iam suo tempore praue à nonnullis intelligebantur, & aliis tradebantur. At si voluisset ita facere, debuit illum excusare candidè, & postea pro arbitrio malorum eius interpretum calumnias traducere: quod quando multum abest vt faciat, excusari ne vix quidem potest, quin aduersus illum contendendi occasionem captet.
units.tr: Others have thought that, besides these many goods, there is one good that is good through itself. Plato is cited at this point, who posited a separate good, that is, a good through itself, distinct from the corruptible creatures. For he said that God is the cause of all things being good, while God himself has his goodness from no other source than himself. There he posited the idea of the good, by whose example and form all things are good. But since Plato taught this in various places, he spoke of the highest good absolutely and not of the highest good of man. Therefore it seems to be brought in here beside the point, where the controversy concerns human happiness itself. For men are not made happy by that common idea of the good, which Plato discussed quite often, but by the happiness that inheres in them. Just as we call something green that has greenness in itself, so also now we speak of a happy man, in whom happiness is present. But I do not know by what plan or impulse Aristotle is sometimes stirred against Plato. I know that some say he did not do this in order to attack him, but to correct his words and expressions, which in his own time were being wrongly understood by some and passed on to others. But if he had wished to do so, he ought to have excused Plato candidly, and afterwards to turn the slanders of Plato's bad interpreters back on them as he saw fit. Since he is far from doing this, he can scarcely be excused from the charge of seizing an occasion to contend against him.

units.la: Omnes autem scrutari opiniones uanius fortasis est.) Solum in-quit se velle disputare de opinionibus eminentioribus, quæque aliquam rationem habeant: nam omnes velle examinare, vanius esset, non enim succederet, quum propemodum sint infinitæ, atque illarum bene magnus numerus longè abest à ratione. Illas tractare operæpretium est quæ ad verum quam proxime accedunt, & in quibus homines facilè possunt ex veri similitudine hallucinari. Magnum fuisse hac de re numerum opinionum docuit Varro, sicut tradit Augustinus de ciuitate Dei. nam inquit, sententias de felicitate potuisse ducentas octuaginta & octo numerari. Quare quum tot numero sint aut esse possint, omnes recensere, nedum examinare, admodum laboriosum esset. Ne itaque res tentetur superuacanea, illæ in hac tractatione sunt deligendæ, quæ nos facilè deciperent, cum magna veri assimulatio in eis conspiciatur. Quod Eustratius doctissimo quodam simili demonstrauit, Si palumbem, inquit, quis videat, columbam facilè putabit se cernere, quod non ei usu veniet, quando aquilam conspexerit, cum valdè sit columbæ absimilis: ita quasdam existimemus esse opiniones de beatitudine adeo à vero semotas, vt pauci admodum seu potius nulli hallucinentur ipsis. alias verò sic veritatem propemodum attingentes, vt non sit omnium eas à se inuicem discernere, vel internoscere. Unde quæ sunt huius generis, non præteriri, sed examinari quam accuratissimè debent.
units.tr: Yet to examine all opinions is perhaps more than is useful. He says that he wishes to dispute only the more prominent opinions, those that have some reasonable basis. For to examine them all would be vainer still, since it would not succeed: they are nearly infinite, and a very large number of them are far from reason. It is worth treating those that come closest to the truth and in which men can easily be led astray by a semblance of truth. Varro, as Augustine reports in the City of God, taught that there were a great many opinions on this matter: he says that opinions about happiness could be counted as two hundred and eighty-eight. Since there are, or could be, so many, to list them all, let alone examine them, would be exceedingly laborious. So that the effort is not spent in vain, those opinions must be chosen for this treatment which would most easily deceive us, since in them a close resemblance to the truth is seen. Eustratius illustrated this with a very apt comparison: If someone sees a wood pigeon, he says, he will easily think he is looking at a dove. That will not happen to him when he has seen an eagle, since it is very unlike a dove. So we should consider that some opinions about blessedness are so far removed from the truth that very few, or rather no one, is deceived by them. But others come so close to the truth that it is not for everyone to distinguish them from one another or tell them apart. Therefore those of this kind should not be passed over, but examined as carefully as possible.

units.la: In hoc Aristot. contextu tria occurrunt dubia. Primum est, Quonam pacto in nomine felicitatis consentiant, cum adeo inter se mortales discrepent lingua. Quod enim nos dicimus felicitatem seu beatitudinem, Græci Εὐδαιμονίαν[?], & Hebræi אשרי nominant, multitudinis numero: quod quare fecerint non est obscurum: natura quippe nostra non ea est quæ vna duntaxat professione possit absolui, ideoq; cum multa requirantur, vt plenè quiescamus, ideò Hebræi sapientissimi numerum multitudinis huc asciuerunt. Sed ad quæstionem respondemus. Licet non conueniant omnes mortales inter se idiomate, nihilominus hoc satis est Aristoteli, quod quicunq; sunt eiusdem linguæ, hi omnes de nomine felicitatis non altercantur, sed de re ipsa, et præsertim in quo vel subiecto vel materia sit ponenda: quod fieri manifestum est inter Latinos, Græcos & Hebræos. Nulli enim eorum ut videmus inter se de nomine rixantur.
units.tr: In this passage of Aristotle three doubts arise. The first is: how do they agree on the name of happiness, when mortals differ so much in language? For what we call felicitas or beatitudo, the Greeks call eudaimonia [Εὐδαιμονίαν], and the Hebrews call ashrei [אשרי], in the plural. Why they did this is not obscure: our nature is not one that can be satisfied by a single profession, and therefore, since many things are required for us to rest fully, the wisest of the Hebrews adopted the plural form here. But we answer the question thus. Although all mortals do not agree with one another in language, this is enough for Aristotle: that all who speak the same language do not dispute about the name of happiness, but about the thing itself, and especially about what should be posited as its subject or matter. That this is so is plain among Latins, Greeks and Hebrews. For, as we see, none of them quarrels with another about the name.

units.la: Dicitur prætereà in textu, Benè agere, bene viuere, & felicem esse pro e-odē haberi. In quibus sanè verbis, quæsieris fortasse quid viuere proprie significet. Ad quod respondeo, vitam accipi bifariam, nam interdum viuere nihil aliud significat nisi esse, quod vniuersa quæ animam sortiuntur, ex ipsius coniunctione cum corpore statim habent. Philosophi appellarunt actum primum. Deinde viuere idem est quod operari, & id Philosophi secundum actum dixerunt: atq; istaposteriori significatione modo accipiendum est rectè viuere.
units.tr: Furthermore, the text says that to act well, to live well and to be happy are regarded as the same thing. Perhaps you will ask what living properly means in these words. To this I reply that life is taken in two ways. Sometimes to live means nothing other than to exist, which all living things have at once from the union of the soul with the body. The philosophers called this first actuality. Then to live is the same as to act, and the philosophers called this second actuality. It is in this latter sense that living well must be understood.

units.la: Occurrit postremò ut quæratur, cur tot atq; tam variæ de felicitate opiniones prodierint. Quod ideò factum dicimus, quòd homines hac de re cum meliore animi parte non deliberarint, sed potius affectus ipsos consultores adhibuerint, qui ut varij sunt, varieq; motus incitant, hominum metes[?] ad fines tam multiplices atq; diuersas inclinarunt. Adolescentes videas qui multis modis calent in amando, se beatos putare: aliorum Deus venter est: honori nonnulli mancipiorum instar sese dediderunt[?], sunt etiam & hi qui diuitijs nil anteponendum censeant, & Diogeni tandem eiusq; similibus cynica libertas summopere arrisit. Quod si ratio ipsa præ sensibus & affectibus in hac quæstione fuisset consulta, non tot proculdubio tamq; pugnantes habuissemus opiniones.
units.tr: Finally it occurs to ask why so many and such varied opinions about happiness have arisen. We say this happened because men did not deliberate on this matter with the better part of their minds, but rather called upon their passions as advisers. These, being various, stir up various movements, and so they have turned men's minds toward ends that are as manifold and diverse as themselves. You may see young men who, burning in many ways with love, think themselves blessed. For others the belly is god. Some have given themselves over like slaves to honours, and there are also those who think nothing should be preferred to riches, while the cynical freedom of Diogenes and others like him has greatly pleased them. But if reason itself had been consulted in this question, rather than the senses and passions, we would undoubtedly not have had so many and such conflicting opinions.

units.la: Sacræ porrò literæ hoc sunt philosophia præstabiliores, quòd illæ finē du-plicem constituunt hominum, quorum alter dum hic viuimus potest obti-neri, alter verò expectatur deniq; cum hinc soluerimus, quem quia perfectior est, priori loco aperiemus. Is autem est, ut Deum præsentem videamus & eius conspectu plenè ac perfectissimè fruamur. Quod Paulus ut assequeretur vehementer optabat, quum ad Philippenses scriberet, Cupio hinc soluere ac esse cum Christo. Idemq; aiebat, Nunc per speculum videmus & in ænigmate, tunc autem facie ad faciem. Item, nunc ex parte cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus, cùm autem venerit quod perfectum est, euacuabitur quod ex parte est. Et hanc Euangelia nobis proponunt eximiam mercedem, quam in cælis post multos labores ac huius vitæ ærumnas propositam habe-amus. amus. Huius autem vitæ summa finis & extremum bonum est, ut per Christum iustificemur, in gratiam recipiamur ab æterno patre, cuius iræ nasci-mur obnoxij. Quare Dauid merito aiebat, Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, quorum tecta sunt peccata. Beatus vir, cui non imputauit Dominus peccatum. Quem locum haud iniuria Paulus ad Romanos tam accurate citauit. Et hi tandem hic beati sunt, qui Iehouam pro Deo habent, illiq; toto pectore fidunt & credunt: ac tales non frustra Dauid appellat beatos. Neq; vitæ huius beatitudo prorsus disiuncta[?] est à fine ac extremo bono, quod in altera vita à fide constanti & spe indefessa expectamus. Huius quippe vitæ summum bonum nil est aliud, nisi illud ipsum quod postremo sumus habituri, graduum tantùm & perfectionis discrimen intercedit.
units.tr: Holy Letters, moreover, are superior to philosophy in this, that they establish a twofold end for men. One of these can be attained while we live here; the other is expected at last when we have departed from this life. Since the latter is more perfect, I shall set it out first. It is this: that we see God present and enjoy him fully and most perfectly in his sight. Paul earnestly desired to attain this when he wrote to the Philippians: I desire to depart and be with Christ. And he also said: Now we see through a glass, in a riddle, but then face to face. Likewise: now we know in part and prophesy in part, but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away. The Gospels set before us this excellent reward, which is laid up for us in heaven after many labours and the hardships of this life. But the chief end and highest good of this life is that through Christ we are justified and received into favour by the eternal Father, to whose wrath we are born subject. Therefore David rightly said: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin. Paul cited this passage in Romans most carefully, and not without reason. And finally those are blessed here who hold Jehovah to be God and trust and believe in him with their whole heart. David did not call such people blessed in vain. Nor is the blessedness of this life altogether separate from the end and highest good, which we await in the other life with steadfast faith and tireless hope. For the highest good of this life is nothing other than that very thing which we shall finally possess; only a difference of degrees and perfection lies between them.

units.la: Non autem nos lateat, interesse rationes quæ à principiis, & quæ ad principia. Rectè enim & Plato de hoc ambigebat, quærebatq;, utrum à principiis, an ad principia proficiscendum esset: veluti in stadio ab iis qui præmia decernunt ad metas, an è con-verso.
units.tr: But we should not overlook that there is a difference between arguments that proceed from principles and those that proceed toward principles. Plato too was rightly uncertain about this, and asked whether one ought to proceed from the principles or toward them, as in a race-course, whether from the starting-point, where the judges who award the prizes stand, to the turning-posts, or conversely.

units.la: Posteriori parte huius capitis ea tractat, quæ pertinent ad Demonstrati-onum genus, quæ in hac investigatione possunt usui esse. Propositio est, Ab effectibus ad causas in hoc negotio est procedendum. Quod eo maximè con-firmatur, quia semper est à notioribus inchoandum: hic verò effecta initiis ipsis multò sunt notiora, igitur inde auspicandum. Quod assumpsimus effecta in hac tractatione magis esse perspicua, post suo loco declarabitur. Prius itaq; Aristoteles ponit utroq; modo licere argumentari. Secundò rationem adducit usus, declarando cur hac vel illa via sit procedendum, & denique tradit, quæ capacitas necessariò in auditore requiratur. Primum id statua-mus, quatuor, ut ubiq; docet Aristoteles, esse causas, materiam, formam, efficiens & finem, ex quibus nos in præsentia unam duntaxat iniquiri-mus, nimirùm finem. De felicitate quippe quæ nam sit disputatur, cuius comprehen-sionem cùm non liceret nisi ex effectis consequi, de eo voluit Aristoteles monitos auditores, ne hoc processus genere offendantur, quandoquidem alterius generis argumenta hic non possunt haberi.
units.tr: The latter part of this chapter deals with the kind of demonstration that can be useful in this inquiry. The proposition is: in this business one must proceed from effects to causes. This is confirmed above all by the principle that one must always begin from what is better known, and here effects are far better known to us than the beginnings themselves; therefore we should start from them. That we have assumed effects to be clearer in this treatise will be explained in its proper place. First, then, Aristotle states that one may argue in either way. Second, he gives the reason of practice, explaining why this or that way should be followed. Finally, he sets out what capacity is necessarily required in the hearer. As for the first point, we should note that there are four causes, as Aristotle teaches throughout: matter, form, efficient cause and final cause. Of these, for the present we inquire into only one, namely the final cause. For since it is disputed what happiness is, and its grasp could be reached only from its effects, Aristotle wished his hearers to be forewarned, lest they be put off by this method of procedure, since arguments of another kind cannot be had here.

units.la: Dicit itaq; duplex argumentorum esse genus, id est, vel à principiis vel ad principia. Et sanè cum ab initiis ad effecta proficiscimur, à naturæ ordine non discedimus, quoniam & illa sic res instituit & producit. At cum ab effectis ad ipsa principia regredimur, id est, ex accommodatione ad nostrum captum. Ita enim geniti sumus & conformati, ut semper ordiamur scientias & notitias à magis cognitis, sive ea causæ fuerint sive effectus. Neque tantum ad hoc confirmandum adducitur Platonis testimonium, sed etiam facilis & apposita similitudo. Ut enim, inquit, in stadio procedunt currentes, tum à carceribus ubi sunt iudices & qui præmia decernunt victoribus, ad metas quæ curriculum ipsum terminant, tum à termino seu meta vicissim ad carceres. Plato sane in Philebo & in Phædro, quædam scribit quæ cum his quæ modo traduntur non habent dissimilitudinem, sed tamen hanc translationem cursorum ibi non legimus, unde suspicari licet, ab Aristotele fuisse inductam. Duplex forma cursus quæ commemoratur, diversum oppido continet ordinem, quamuis spacium & via per quam currentes feruntur sit eadem. Quod idem in scalis videas, in quibus ut gradus idem manent, motus ascendendi & descendendi sunt diversi. Ad rem quam tractamus, propositum simile ita debet accommodari, ut carceribus ubi ἀθλωθέτα[?] manent, subiicias rerum causas & initia, calci vero stadii seu metæ quæ ducuntur ex causis, atque suum ortum inde habent. Et ne quid prætermittatur, id etiam monuisse non pigeat, stadium apud veteres centum viginti quinq; passus habuisse. Quocirca octo stadia Romanum miliare, quale hodie Italicum est, absoluebant. Quemadmodum itaque in cursu, qui affertur in hoc simili, via est eadem, sed figura currentium prorsus diversa: Ita eandem constituere oportet distantiam inter principia & effecta, quamuis genus demonstrationis quod inter ista cadit, sit duplex & vehementer dissimile. Materia quidem argumenti consentit, sed modus & forma rationum pugnat. Et genus illud conclusionis quod ex effectis ducitur, Demonstratio appellatur, ut vulgò dicunt, secundum quid: at aliud quod à causis ad effecta proficiscitur, usitato in scholis nomine, Demonstratio simpliciter nominatur. Atque ipse idem Aristoteles de auditu physico eadem fermè dixit, quamuis aliud agens: docebat enim tunc inter eosdem terminos contrarios motus posse contingere. Quia inquit Athenis Thebas & Thebis Athenas eadem est via.
units.tr: He says, therefore, that there are two kinds of argument, that is, those that proceed from principles and those that proceed toward principles. Indeed, when we proceed from beginnings to effects, we do not depart from the order of nature, since nature itself so arranges and produces things. But when we go back from effects to the principles themselves, we follow the order of our own understanding. For we are so born and so formed that we always begin our sciences and our knowledge from what is more known to us, whether these be causes or effects. And to confirm this, Plato's testimony is brought in, and also an easy and fitting comparison. For, he says, as in a race-course the runners set out from the starting-gates, where the umpires [ἀθλοθέται] and those who award the prizes to the victors are, toward the turning-posts which mark the end of the course, and then in turn from the goal back to the gates. Plato indeed, in the Philebus and the Phaedrus, writes some things that are not unlike what has just been said, but we do not read this comparison of the runners there, so one may suspect that Aristotle introduced it himself. The two forms of running that are mentioned contain a quite different order, although the space and the track along which the runners are carried are the same. You may see the same in stairs, where the steps remain the same but the movements of ascending and descending are different. To the matter we are treating, the comparison should be applied in such a way that you place beneath the starting-gates, where the umpires remain, the causes and beginnings of things, and at the goal of the stadium or turning-post, the things that are derived from causes and have their origin from them. And lest anything be left out, I will not hesitate to remark that among the ancients the stadium measured one hundred and twenty-five paces; hence eight stadia made up a Roman mile, such as the Italian mile is today. Therefore, just as in the race which is brought in as this comparison, the track is the same but the course of the runners is quite different, so we must posit the same distance between principles and effects, although the kind of demonstration that falls between them is twofold and very dissimilar. The subject matter of the argument indeed agrees, but the mode and form of the reasonings clash. That kind of conclusion which is drawn from effects is called demonstration, as they commonly say, "according to what is" (secundum quid); but the other, which proceeds from causes to effects, is called, in the usual term of the schools, demonstration simply (simpliciter). Aristotle himself said much the same thing about physical hearing, although he was dealing with another subject: for he then taught that contrary motions could occur between the same termini. "Because," he says, "the road from Athens to Thebes is the same as the road from Thebes to Athens."

units.la: In eo de quo nunc agimus, ita res habet. Actiones iustæ, fortes, moderatæ, prudentes, liberales, à virtutibus fiunt, virtutes ipsæ ut à fine pendent ex felicitate: nam in eam omnes ut in supremum bonum feruntur. Ex quo fit, ut cum Aristoteles ordiatur ab ipsis probis & rectis actionibus, & inde ascendat ad virtutes, atque postremò ad felicitatis notitiam pervenit, ex consesequentibus & posterioribus rationes conquirat. E diuerso faciundum erat, si ex causis & prioribus, in animo fuisset ad posteriora & effecta tendere. Felicitatem porrò tradere oportuit ante omnia quae nam esset. Deinde virtutum naturam expedire, ac tandem bonorum & laudabilium actionum formam & modum explicare. Qui ordo quoniam est naturalis, ab Aristotele non est neglectus, sed in digerendis & componendis his libris accuratissimè conseruatus. In primo sanè libro, ut ab initio monui, de felicitate docet. Postea in aliis de virtutibus praeclarè scribit. Proximè actiones humanas explicat. Et denique ceu delatus circulo in calce huius tractationis de felicitate perfectissimè quae tradi poterant est persequutus. Quae igitur nunc dicuntur seriem librorum ordinemque tractationum minimè respiciunt, sed id tantum spectant, ut intelligamus quibus argumentis ad virtutum & felicitatis notiones quaeamus[?] peruenire. Quod sanè dicit concedendum, si à notioribus nobis coeperimus, quae (ut iam dixi) & res ipsa demonstrabit, sunt recta atq; praeclarae actiones.
units.tr: In the matter we are now discussing, the case is as follows. Just, brave, temperate, prudent and liberal actions are done from the virtues, and the virtues themselves depend on happiness as on their end, for all people are carried toward it as toward the highest good. From this it follows that, since Aristotle begins from the good and upright actions themselves, and from them ascends to the virtues, and at last arrives at the knowledge of happiness, he seeks his reasons from what is consequent and posterior. On the other hand, he would have had to do the opposite if he had intended to proceed from causes and prior things to what is posterior and to effects. Moreover, it was necessary first of all to explain what happiness is; then to set out the nature of the virtues; and at last to explain the form and manner of good and praiseworthy actions.
