Since this order is natural, Aristotle has not neglected it, but has observed it most carefully in arranging and composing these books. In the first book, as I warned at the beginning, he teaches about happiness. Afterwards, in the others, he writes admirably about the virtues. Next he explains human actions. And finally, as if carried round in a circle, he has pursued at the end of this treatise, most perfectly, what could be taught about happiness. What is now being said, therefore, does not regard the sequence of the books or the order of the treatises at all, but only aims to make us understand by what arguments we may come to the notions of the virtues and of happiness. This, he says, must be conceded, if we begin from what is better known to us; and, as I have already said, the thing itself will show that these are upright and excellent actions.

units.la: Necprofecto debetis mirari cùm in hoc ordine Aristotelico formâ quandam circuli conspicitis: quoniam in agendo animus noster haud secus mo-veatur[?]. Semper enim id de quo primum statuimus est finis. Deinde quae nam idonea sint cogitamus, ut ad finem assequendam proficiant, tum illam persequimur, tum finem quem optaueramus adipiscimur. Videas itaque hinc perspicuè, nostram actionem ibi terminari, unde sua initia primum sumpserat.
units.tr: Indeed, you ought not to be surprised when you see in this Aristotelian order a certain form of a circle, since our mind is moved in acting in no other way. For what we first determine is always the end. Then we think about what means are suitable to help us attain the end; then we pursue those means, and at last we obtain the end we had desired. You may therefore see clearly here that our action ends where it had first taken its beginnings.

units.la: Possem hic obiter monstrare cur coelorum orbes circuli ambitu circa nostrum hunc mundum torqueantur, & ratione concludere talem mutationis formam inter cateras esse perfectissimam. Sed quia non est animus à proposito longius abire, non interim in hanc disputationem ingrediar: Sed tantum duo quaeram, primum quid fiat ut felicitas, quae finis est, principium etiam dicatur? cùm principij ratio multum cum termino seu fine discrepet? Respondeo, ut ista inter se pugnent si absolutè sumantur, cum diuersa ratio & respectus adhibetur, recte pulchreq; consentiunt. Nam quo ad consilium propositum & dispositionem efficientis, id quod primum expetitur est bonum, & id maximè quod inter bona extremum fuerit. Quod si postea in persequendo quod optamus extremo loco adipiscimur, iam de exequutione agitur, non de proposito seu consilio. Nam in architectanda domo primum quod quaerimus est ut septi et muniti simus ab iniurijs coeli: quod ut obtineamus, de tecto cogitamus, de parietibus, & deniq; de fundamentis. Videsitaq; ut in hac serie bonum ipsum, ut nos tueamur ab aeris inclementia primum esse. At postea si respectu et ratione mutes, molieris, desyderatu adipisci, primum erit, fundamenta jacere, parietes erigere, tandemq; tectum superponere, quibus perfectis tuto poteris habitare. Ex quo fit ut quod in altero ordine fuit initium, modo convertatur in extremum. Potest itidem exponi, ut bonum quod appetimus principium dicatur, quia mouet animum efficientis & impellit ad agendum. Quamobrem motus inde sua initia consequitur.
units.tr: I could here digress and show why the spheres of the heavens are turned in circular motion around this our world, and by reasoning conclude that this form of motion is the most perfect of all. But since I do not want to stray too far from my purpose, I will not enter into that discussion now. I will ask only two things: first, how it happens that happiness, which is the end, is also called a beginning, since the notion of a beginning differs greatly from that of a terminus or end? I answer that these things, if taken absolutely, clash with each other, but when a different account and point of view is applied, they agree well and rightly. For in respect of the intended purpose and the disposition of the efficient cause, what is first sought is the good, and especially that which is the last among goods. But if afterwards, in pursuing what we desire, we attain it at the last place, then we are dealing with execution, not with the purpose or plan. For in building a house, the first thing we seek is to be sheltered and protected from the injuries of the sky; to obtain this we think about the roof, the walls, and finally the foundations. So you see that in this sequence the good itself, that we be protected from the inclemency of the air, comes first. But afterwards, if you change the point of view and the reasoning, and set out to obtain what you desire, the first thing will be to lay the foundations, to raise the walls, and at last to put the roof on top, after which, once these are finished, you can live there safely. From this it follows that what was the beginning in the one order is turned into the end. It can also be explained that the good we desire is called a principle because it moves the mind of the efficient cause and impels it to act. Therefore motion takes its beginnings from it.

units.la: Altera quæstio est, An quæ hic Aristoteles tradit in 4. capite, cum illis eadem sint quæ superius docuit, cum de forma doctrinæ huius Philosophiæ scriberet. Minimè. Quia ibi generaliter dixit, non hic illud exquisitum docendi genus se spectasse quod in alijs scietijs & præsertim mathematicis adhibetur, cum potius hic locum habeant persuasiones, exempla, similitudines, inductiones, omniaq; latius tractentur & pinguiori minerva, ut res de quibus dicitur ferre queunt. Ast hic priuatim agitur de genere demonstrationis, quod usurpandum est in captanda felicitatis definitione, ac virtutum natura explicanda.
units.tr: Our second question is whether the things Aristotle teaches here in chapter 4 are the same as those he taught earlier, when he wrote about the form of this philosophical teaching. By no means. For there he spoke in general terms, and he was not here looking to that exact method of teaching which is used in the other sciences, and especially in mathematics, since here persuasions, examples, comparisons and inductions have their place, and all these things are treated more broadly and with a fuller, more earthy wisdom, as the subject matter allows. But here the discussion is specifically about the kind of demonstration that must be used in grasping the definition of happiness and in explaining the nature of the virtues.

units.la: Auspicandum igitur à notis: hæc autem sunt duplicia: alia quidem nobis, alia uero absolutè. Ac forte ab iis quæ nobis notiora sunt auspicandum est.
units.tr: We must therefore begin from what is known; and these things are twofold: some are known to us, others known absolutely. Perhaps we ought to begin from those things which are better known to us.

units.la: Cum iam perspicuum sit, licere interdum à principijs, interdum ab effectis argumenta inducere. Nunc aperit quando vel isto vel illo modo sit argumentandum. Videndum, inquit, utrum vel principia vel effecta sint nobis manifestiora. Quod ut fiat euidentius, distinctionem profert, alia nobis, alia vero absolutè reperiri notiora. Neq; hic solum hac usus est partitione, sed illam in Analyticis posterioribus & in primo physicorum attigit. Verùm dixeris, Ita ne opponuntur notiora nobis & absolutè, ut nulla inveniantur quæ cum nobis tum per seipsa & absolutè sint nota? Potest sanè contingere, ut quandoq; ista simul coniungantur. Quod tantum usu venisse in mathematicis videmus, ubi causæ seu principia, tam nobis ipsis quàm sua natura & vi sunt nota, id est absolutè, ut modo loquitur Aristoteles, verùm quod nobis nota sint, non sua natura consequuntur, sed quia principia ipsa & causæ in tabella seu in pulvere describuntur, & cùm in sensum incurrant, ita nobis fiunt notiora. Neq; dicuntur causæ, initia principiaq; rerum notiora natura, quasi ea natura intelligat, sed quia natura sua, vi, sponte, ac per seipsa notiora esse debuerant, nisi nostræ mentis imbecillitas obstaret, unde hic A-riftoristoteles quod alibi dixit natura notiora, dicit absolutè seu simpliciter nota, quod non est aliud nisi ratione infirmitatis nostræ seposita. Quamuis non sim nescius nonnullos exposuisse nota naturæ, quòd si natura cognosceret, inde suam notitiam auspicaretur, cuius sententia fuit Auerroes. Sed pulchrius eo Græci rem intellexerunt, nota naturæ nil aliud esse atq; naturæ illa prius constare, cùm inde rei productio hauriat sua initia: dum enim quidq; oritur, eius initia & causæ prius eduntur.
units.tr: Since it is now clear that it is sometimes permissible to draw arguments from principles and sometimes from effects, he now shows when we should argue in one way or the other. We must see, he says, whether principles or effects are more manifest to us. To make this clearer, he offers a distinction: some things are better known to us, others absolutely. He does not use this division only here; he touched on it in the Posterior Analytics and in the first book of the Physics. But you may ask: are things better known to us and things known absolutely opposed in such a way that none are known both to us and in themselves, absolutely? Certainly it can happen that these are sometimes conjoined. We see this happen in mathematics, where causes or principles are known both to us and by their own nature and power, that is, absolutely, as Aristotle now puts it. But that they are known to us does not follow from their nature. Rather, the principles and causes are drawn on a tablet or in the dust, and since they fall under the senses, they thus become better known to us. Nor are the causes, beginnings and principles of things said to be better known by nature as if nature understood them. Rather, they ought by their own nature and power, of their own accord and in themselves, to be better known, were it not for the weakness of our mind standing in the way. Hence Aristotle, who elsewhere said "known by nature," here says "known absolutely or simply," which is nothing other than what is set aside on account of our weakness. Although I am not unaware that some have explained "known by nature" to mean that, if nature knew, knowledge would begin from it, and that Averroes held this opinion, the Greeks understood the matter more finely: the things known by nature are nothing else than those which are prior in nature, since the production of a thing draws its beginnings from there. For when anything comes into being, its beginnings and causes are brought forth first.

units.la: Exempla quibus patefacere possumus causas per effecta demonstrari, complura se offerunt. Primum, ex defectu Lunæ probamus terræ interpositionem inter ipsam & Solem. Deinde quoniam tota non obscuratur, concludimus terram esse illa maiorem. E diuerso autem quia Sol dum Luna ei subiicitur lumen totum non amittit, demonstramus illâ magnitudine præstare orbi lunari. Tum etiam cùm Luna sic accessiones & imminutiones lunares variet, ut subinde cornuta rotundaq; appareat, eam concludimus figuram habere sphæricam. Nec non animalia quæ non spirant, carere statuimus pulmonibus & arteria, quæ omnia, ut perspicuum est, ex effectis demonstrant causas. Utq; ad rem redeam, sic nunc ex actionibus iustis, rectis & laudabilibus ad notitiam virtutum inducimur, & deniq; subleuamur ex virtutibus cognitis ad ipsius felicitatis intelligentiam. Et rem si quis pressius expendat, cernet facile non posse in hac facultate de beatitudine tradi scientiam ex principiis & causis, quia cum ipsa in accidentibus numeretur, non potest agnosci nisi subiecti quo innititur haberetur perfecta notitia. Quare si per causas docendi essemus, animi nostri & sane quo ad vim intelligentem prius notitia esset habenda, neq; id satis esset, cùm humanæ mentis natura ex ipso Deo pendeat. Unde liquet, felicitatis demonstrationem per causas adduci non posse, nisi mentis & Dei natura sit perspecta, quæ cùm ardua sint, neq; dum hic viuimus perfectè concedantur, ad effecta se conuertere necesse fuit, ex quibus definitionem felicitatis & virtutum notitiam consequeremur. Cur autem aduerbium, forte, adiecerit, ideò factum puto, quia interdum repertis causis ab iis ipsis redijt ad effecta demonstranda. Et quandoq; non [?]ἀποδείξει utetur, sed leui & verisimili probatione.
units.tr: Many examples offer themselves by which we can show that causes are demonstrated through effects. First, from an eclipse of the Moon we prove that the earth is interposed between it and the Sun. Next, since the whole Moon is not darkened, we conclude that the earth is larger than it. On the other hand, since the Sun does not lose all its light when the Moon is placed under it, we demonstrate that the Sun surpasses the lunar sphere in magnitude. Again, since the Moon varies its waxing and waning so that at times it appears horned and at times round, we conclude that it has a spherical shape. Likewise, we judge that animals which do not breathe lack lungs and windpipe; all of these, as is clear, demonstrate causes from effects. And to return to our matter: in the same way, from just, right and praiseworthy actions we are led to knowledge of the virtues, and finally, from the known virtues we are raised to an understanding of happiness itself. If someone weighs the matter more closely, he will easily see that in this discipline no science of blessedness can be delivered from principles and causes. Since happiness is numbered among the accidents, it cannot be recognised unless a perfect knowledge of the subject on which it rests is first had. So if we were to be taught through causes, we would have to have prior knowledge of our soul, and certainly of its power of understanding, and that would not be enough, since the nature of the human mind depends on God himself. Hence it is clear that the demonstration of happiness cannot be brought about through causes unless the nature of the mind and of God is thoroughly known. Since these things are difficult and are not perfectly granted while we live here, it was necessary to turn to effects, from which we might obtain the definition of happiness and the knowledge of the virtues. As for why he added the adverb "perhaps," I think it was done because at times, having found the causes, he returned from them to demonstrate effects. And at times he will use not demonstration [ἀποδείξει] but a light and probable proof.

units.la: Propterea necesse est pulchrè moribus institutum esse qui futurus est idoneus auditor, de honestis & iustis, deq; omnibus ciuilibus. Est enim principium, quod sit, Idq; si satis patuerit, non opus erit cur sit dicere. Sic autem institutus, aut principia tenebit, aut ea facilè percipiet. Qui uero neutrum istorum habet, hæc Hesiodi audiat:
units.tr: Therefore it is necessary that the one who will be a suitable hearer be well instructed in morals, in matters of honour and justice, and in all civic matters. For the principle is that it is so; and if this has been sufficiently made clear, there will be no need to ask why it is so. A person so instructed will either hold the principles or will easily grasp them. But whoever has neither of these, let him listen to these words of Hesiod:

units.la: Tertio loco nunc patefacit, quid inquiratur in auditore qui sit futurus idoneus, quíq;[?] ista cum fructu velit percipere, nempe ut liberalibus & honestis moribus sit præditus. Propositio esto. Idoneus auditor harum rerum debet esse bene moratus. Confirmatur, In qualibet facultate principiis inuestigationis oportet assentiri, ac ea concedere, alioqui pergere non possumus ad concludendum. Principia nostræ inuestigationis habemus actiones probas & rectas. Igitur auditorem seu addiscentem, hæc oportet admittere. At qui non est bene moratus id non faciet, nam ea quæ nos ut iusta & honesta laudibus efferemus, illi displicebunt, etenim improbis non probantur nisi prava & corrupta. Proinde talis haberi non poterit nisi vir inutilis. Quod item Hesiodi testimonio magis corroborat.
units.tr: In the third place he now sets out what is required in a hearer who will be suitable, and who wishes to grasp these things with profit, namely that he be endowed with liberal and honourable morals. Let the proposition be: a suitable hearer of these matters must be well mannered. It is confirmed thus: in every discipline one must assent to the principles of inquiry and grant them, otherwise we cannot proceed to a conclusion. The principles of our inquiry are good and right actions. Therefore the hearer or learner must admit these. But one who is not well mannered will not do so, for those things which we will extol as just and honourable will displease him, since the wicked approve only what is base and corrupt. Therefore such a man cannot be held to be anything but a useless person. Hesiod's testimony confirms this even more.

units.la: Vim rationis attingit his verbis:Est enim principium ὅτι, id est cum res esse dicitur. Hoc autem principium minime dabit nobis qui non sit imbutus bonis moribus, imo vitiosè fucrit educatus. Vnde quando id quod quærimus, id est felicitas, obscurum sit & inuestigandum accuratius, qui poterimus id facere, si nobis non concedatur, probas actiones iustas & honestas esse? non poterimus profecto ex illis conficere felicitatem esse, ideoq; carebimus notitia eius duplici & ὅτι & διότι, cum non possimus illam cognoscere διότι: est enim primum inter humana bona, neq; sic habet quicquam prius nisi ad Deum rem velimus transferre: negatis probis & honestis actionibus, neq; de ipsa ὅτι scire poterimus. Neque mihi id dixeris, Qui prauis moribus est institutus, potest quæ recta sunt & honesta cognoscere, quæ licet non probet, fortasse concedet: quare via huius inuestigationis non intercludetur. Hoc inquam non licet ponere, quia hic non quæuis notitia exigitur, sed ea in qua facilè ac liberter acquiescamus. quippe (ut monuimus prius) ἀρχιτεκτονική[?] est hæc facultas, non tantum intuens, nudeq; propositá contemplans. Et huc accedit, neminem ut recta iustaq; habere quæ cum suo iudicio discrepant, qui fit ut prauis moribus corruptus & honestis non assuetus, harum rerum sit futurus prauus iudex & æstimator.
units.tr: He touches on the force of reason in these words: For the principle is that [ὅτι], that is, when a thing is said to be. But this principle will by no means be given to us by one who has not been imbued with good morals; indeed, if he has been badly brought up, he will not give it. Hence, since what we seek, that is happiness, is obscure and must be investigated more carefully, how will we be able to do it, if it is not granted to us that just and honourable actions are good? Certainly we will not be able to conclude from them that happiness is such; and therefore we will lack a knowledge of it both as to the that [ὅτι] and as to the why [διότι], since we cannot know it by the why [διότι]. For it is first among human goods, and nothing is prior to it, unless we wish to transfer the matter to God. If good and honourable actions are denied, we will not be able to know even the that [ὅτι]. Nor may you say to me: one who has been brought up in bad morals can know what is right and honourable, and though he does not approve it, perhaps he will concede it; so the way of this inquiry will not be blocked. This, I say, may not be assumed, because here what is demanded is not any knowledge at all, but that knowledge in which we rest easily and gladly. For (as we said before) this discipline is architectonic [ἀρχιτεκτονική], not merely looking on and contemplating bare propositions. And to this is added that no one has a right and just view which disagrees with his own judgement; so it comes about that one corrupted by bad morals and not accustomed to honourable things will be a depraved judge and estimator of these matters.

units.la: Aristoteles cum dixisset de honestis & iustis, De omnibus ciuilibus etiam addidit, Quod porrò licet duobus modis explicare, Primum ut intel-ligat, ligat, alia permulta de quibus in libris de repub. est agendum: quæ item cū sint fines, hac eadem ratione oportebit peruestigare. Deinde cæteras fortas-se virtutes respexit, ut fortitudinem, moderationem, liberalitatem, &c. quarum naturam isto eodemq; modo inquiret.
units.tr: Aristotle, having spoken of honourable and just things, also added "all civic matters." This may be explained in two ways. First, so that he understands the many other matters which must be treated in the books on the republic; these, since they are also ends, must be investigated in the same way. Second, perhaps he had in view the other virtues, such as courage, moderation, liberality, etc., whose nature he will inquire into in this same way.

units.la: Idq; si satis patuerit, non opus erit cur sit dicere.) Sensus est. Si per probas actiones & honestas de felicitate nouerimus quod sit, laborare cur sit non erit necessarium, quoniam ex horum principiorum notitia illa quoque satis erit cognita. Principium autem ὅτι dicitur id per quod notitia de eo quod concludere volumus paritur, quod sit: principium διότι hoc appel-latur quo non esse, verum qua de causa curue sit intelligimus id quod quæritur. Vnde apparet ea quæ modo in ista inuestigatione dicuntur principia, non esse rei quæsitæ causas & initia, sed tantum notitiæ nostræ, nam capen-det ex his ceu a suo fonte & origine.
units.tr: That is, if it has been made clear enough through good and honourable actions what happiness is, there will be no need to labour over why it is so, since knowledge of these first principles will also be sufficiently known from them. A principle is called hoti [ὅτι] when it gives us knowledge that something is the case, and dioti [διότι] when it gives the reason why it is so and what its cause is. Hence it is clear that the things just now called principles in this inquiry are not the causes and origins of the thing sought, but only of our knowledge, for we derive our understanding from them as from their source and origin.

units.la: Sic autem institutus aut principia tenebit, aut ea facile percipi-et.) Modo, inquit, si bene moratus fuerit auditor, ista principia huius notitiæ, non rei quam peruestigamus, aut tenebit per se, quia videbit sponte sua honesta, iusta & expetenda esse. Aut si forte non adhuc tantum profecerit, illis non difficulter assentietur, a præceptore monitus. nam per bonam institutionem & rectos mores quos iam imbibit, paratus erit & promptus ad se inclinandum ad ista, quæ pro initijs debemus assumere. At si e diuerso fuerit comparatus, aut in his hærebit subinde, aut illis impudenter refragabitur. Hæc sanè illa eadem sunt quæ prius dixerat in proœmio, remouendos auditores qui vel experientia & vsu rerum moralium essent destituti, vel perturbationibus & cupiditatibus ac prauis affectibus corrupti. Quæ si nunc repetit, repetit ea causa quod ista principia quæ vult sumere in beatitudine indaganda indicet non tam esse perspicua, vt quibusuis hominibus possint esse nota. De vniuersa doctrina prius id propositum, nunc vero pro isto demonstrationis genere peculiariter adducit, Vt in mathematicis opus est auditores quædam a seipsis afferre, quædam vero a præceptoribus accipere, ita in hac nostra facultate usu venit. Nemo enim mathematicos professores accedit, quem lateat ipsum totum sua parte maius esse, ac de quolibet enuntiato fatendum aut verum aut falsum esse: accipit autem a docentibus lineæ definitionem, anguli & consimilium. Sic qui futurus est idoneus harum rerum auditor, non sit nescius & expers elegantium morum et ingenuarum actionum, sit aliquantū expertus robore mentis vinci cupiditates, & crebris actionibus quenq;[?] sibi vendicare habitus & agendi facilitate. in quiquibus si non ad extremum summamq; rationem profecerit, à monitoribus & doctoribus iuuabitur, modò illis velit auscultare. Dices tu, eos qui iam bene sunt instituti atq; morati quid attinet ista discere: videntur porrò consequuti quod hac scientia quaeritur. Sed qui hæc dicunt nobiscum cogitent, solum hic requiri bonam liberalemq; educationem, & nonnullam experientiam proborum morum, non autem de his absolutam notitiam, perfectaque adeptionem. Qui enim haud male sunt instituti, & aliquem honestorum iustorumq; gustum ceperunt, hi possunt ex his quae dicentur, vendicare sibi plenam doctrinam eorum, quae hactenus tantum confusè atq; usu aliquo nouerunt, & adepta scientia poterunt ad absolutissimam vitam, & felicitatem consequendam multum proficere.
units.tr: He says that the student, if he has been so trained, will either hold these principles, which are principles of our knowledge and not of the thing we are investigating, or will readily grasp them. That is, if the hearer has been well brought up, he will hold these principles of himself, because he will see of his own accord that honourable, just and desirable things are to be pursued. Or, if he has not yet advanced so far, he will not find it difficult to assent to them when instructed by his teacher, for through good upbringing and the sound morals he has already imbibed, he will be ready and prompt to incline to those things which we must take up as starting points. But if, on the contrary, he has been formed otherwise, he will either keep hesitating over them or shamelessly reject them. These are the same points he made earlier in the preface, that hearers who lack experience and practice in moral matters, or who are corrupted by passions, desires and wicked affections, must be set aside. If he now repeats this, he does so because he indicates that the principles he wishes to take up in inquiring into happiness are not so evident that they can be known to any sort of person. Earlier he proposed this about the whole discipline; now he adds it specifically for this kind of demonstration. As in mathematics, the students must bring some things with them and receive others from their teachers, so it is in our discipline. For no one comes to the professors of mathematics without knowing that the whole is greater than its part, and that every statement must be admitted to be either true or false; but he receives from the teachers the definition of a line, of an angle, and of similar things. So he who is to be a fit hearer of these matters should not be ignorant of, or without experience of, refined manners and noble actions; he should have some experience of the strength of mind that overcomes desires, and by frequent actions he should have acquired habits and ease in acting. If in these things he has not advanced to the final and highest reason, he will be helped by his advisers and teachers, provided he is willing to listen to them. You may say: what is the point of those who are already well brought up and morally formed learning these things, since they seem already to have attained what this science seeks? But let those who say this consider with us that what is required here is only a good and liberal education and some experience of upright morals, not a complete knowledge and perfect acquisition of these things. For those who have been reasonably well brought up, and have tasted something of what is honourable and just, can from what will be said claim for themselves the full teaching of those things which until now they have known only confusedly and by some practice; and once they have gained this knowledge they will be able to advance greatly toward the most perfect life and the attainment of happiness.

units.la: Auditores itaq; horum principiorum non oportet omnino esse rudes & imperitos, educatione ac exercitio, quae nobis principia futura sunt, veliam teneant, vel si quid deest, à docentibus & se monentibus percipiant. Quo-rum neutrum habentes, Hesiodum audiant: ipsi enim qui sint non aude-mus dicere, dicet autem pro nobis poeta:
units.tr: Hearers of these principles, therefore, ought not to be wholly raw and inexperienced, so that the training and practice which are to be our principles either hold them, or, if something is lacking, they receive it from teachers who advise them. Lacking both of these, let them listen to Hesiod; for we do not dare to say what such people are, but the poet will say it for us:

units.la: Is est optimus qui omnia intelligendo norit, quę postea in finem sint meliora.
units.tr: He is the best who knows all things by understanding, which are better afterwards for the end.

units.la: Sensus est, Primas ille habet qui per seipsum nouit omnia. Quod absolutè non debemus accipere: nulli enim eo peruenient, ut omnium sint periti. Sed ea intelligit quae ad finem propositum consequendum meliora sint & magis conducant, omnesq; nouimus hanc prudentissimorum virorum esse functionem, ut nihil eos lateat quod ad finem assequendum pertineat, & inter ista selectione utuntur, ut meliora & potiora decernant.
units.tr: The meaning is that he is first who knows all things by himself. We must not take this absolutely, for no one attains to knowing everything. Rather, he understands those things which are better and more useful for attaining the proposed end; and we all know that it is the task of the wisest men that nothing escapes them which pertains to reaching the end, and in making this choice they use discernment to decide what is better and more important.

units.la: Bonus & is rursus est qui pareat recta monenti: qui vero neque alium audiendo in animo infigit, is rursus est inutilis.
units.tr: Good too, in turn, is he who obeys one who advises rightly; but he who neither grasps things himself nor takes them into his mind by hearing another, he in turn is useless.

units.la: Hoc porro loco Titus quoq; Liuius usus est Decad. 3. lib. 2. Vbi Minutiū loquentem induxit de bello Punico, in hac verba: Saepe ego audiui milites eum primum esse virum, qui ipse consulit quid in re sit, secundum eum qui bene monenti pareat, qui nec ipse cōsulere nec alteri parere scit, eū extremi ingenij esse. Item Cicero pro Cluentio, Sapientissimum dicunt esse eum cui quod opus sit ipsi veniat in mentem: proximi accedere illum qui alterius bene inuentis obtemperat. Neq; soli scriptores historiarum, oratoresq; vsurpa runt[?] interdum testimonia Poetarum, sed etiam philosophi, vt hic deprehendimus Aristotelem fecisse, is non modo hic, verum in philosophia naturali subinde atq; in Metaphysicis versus Poetarum citauit. Quod idem Plato factitauit: estq; vulgo tritum, apud Poetas philosophiae, bonarumq; artium semina passim reperiri. Quin etiam Paulus noster ab illorum sententijs non se aliquando abstinuit.
units.tr: Here Titus Livy also used this in the third Decade, book two, where he introduces Minucius speaking about the Punic war, in these words: "I have often heard soldiers say that the first man is he who himself considers what is needed in a matter; second is he who obeys one who advises well; but he who knows neither how to consider for himself nor to obey another is of the lowest ability." Likewise Cicero, in the Pro Cluentio: "They say that the wisest is he to whom what is needful comes to mind himself; those who come next are those who comply with the good discoveries of another." Nor do writers of histories and orators alone sometimes make use of the testimonies of poets, but also philosophers, as we find Aristotle has done here; and he has quoted verses of the poets not only here but also in natural philosophy and repeatedly in the Metaphysics. Plato did the same, and it is commonly observed that seeds of philosophy and of the good arts are found scattered among the poets. Indeed our Paul too did not refrain from their sayings at times.

units.la: Fuit autem Hesiodus poeta γνωμολόγος egregius: ea enim luculenter scripsit, quae ad mores & bene beateq; viuendum non parum proficerent. Sacerdos erat Musarum in monte Helicone Baeotica, vixitq; ad eiusdem montis radices in ciuitate quae Ascra dicta est, adeoq; suauiter scripsit, vt veteres fabulati sint, Musas illi donasse calamos, ad quos suos versus cecinerit. Et Pausanias tradit vsque ad sua tempora in Helicone fuisse conseruata monimenta, id est, tabulas plumbeas, in quibus ad verbum poema eius totum cernebatur descriptum. Cumq; non liquido constet qua aetate vixerit, attamen si dicendum sit quod apparet cum varietate magis congruum atq; consentiens, centum annis post Homerum vixit. Carmina eius tanto consensu approbata sunt, vt Columella sit testatus, voluisse antiquos ea memoriae a pueris mandari, prima eorum aetate, quo viuerent illorum semper bene memores.
units.tr: Now Hesiod was an outstanding poet and writer of maxims: for he wrote brilliantly those things which contribute not a little to morals and to living well and happily. He was a priest of the Muses on Mount Helicon in Boeotia, and he lived at the foot of that same mountain, in the town called Ascra; and he wrote so sweetly that the ancients fabled that the Muses gave him a reed with which he sang his verses. And Pausanias reports that down to his own time there were preserved on Helicon memorials, that is, leaden tablets, on which his whole poem could be seen written out word for word. Since it is not clearly established in what age he lived, yet if one must say what appears more consistent and agreed upon with variation, he lived a hundred years after Homer. His songs were so widely approved that Columella testifies that the ancients wished them to be committed to memory by boys in their earliest age, so that they might always remember them well while they lived.

units.la: Qui tamen vt talis ac tantus fuerit, omnibus partibus non potuit omnibus satisfacere. Nam Zeno Stoicorum princeps, vt refert Diogenes lib.7. per Antistrephonta carmina ista correxit, Κεῖν᾽[?] μὲν[?] ϝωνάρις[?] ὃς ἂν εἰ-πόντι τιθῆντας[?] Ἔσλός[?] δ᾽ ἂν κακεῖν᾽[?] ὃς αὐτὸς ταῦτα νοῆσῃ[?]. His ita inuersis Zeno voluit primas illi iure deberi, qui tametsi nondum teneat, sitq; assequutus quae ad probitatem conducunt, iustitiae tamen tanto flagrat desyderio, vt non recuset facere, quae audit a prudentioribus proficere ad illam obtinendam. Posterior vero locus ei datur, qui per seipsum intelligit, quod eo cō ducit: quoniam cuiq; facilius est suo iudicio stare, quam alienum sequi. Vnde cum is qui per se videt utilia, sua ipsius ducatur sententia, non ita visus est laudabilis vt prior, qui proprio sensu posthabito, statuit potius cedere sanis monitoribus quam persequi consilij proprij blanditias et illecebras.
units.tr: Yet, great and renowned as he was, he could not satisfy everyone in every respect. For Zeno, the prince of the Stoics, as Diogenes reports in book seven, corrected these verses in the Antistrephonta: "That one is a man of speech who obeys one who speaks well; but good too is he who himself understands these things." With the order reversed in this way, Zeno wanted the first place to be owed by right to him who, although he does not yet possess these things, and has not attained what contributes to uprightness, nevertheless burns with such a desire for justice that he does not refuse to do what he hears from the wiser to attain it. The second place is given to him who understands for himself what leads to it, since it is easier for each person to stand by his own judgment than to follow another's. Hence, since one who sees for himself what is useful is guided by his own opinion, he did not seem as praiseworthy as the first, who, setting aside his own sense, resolves rather to yield to sound advisers than to pursue the flatteries and allurements of his own counsel.

units.la: Quod idem nos etiam in religione Christiana minoribus laudibus efferimus. Et sui ipsius abnegationem appellamus, quando quis repulsis ac reiectis quae magis visa fuerint verisimilia, illis assentitur quae Deus diuinis literis reuelauit, vt sint minus naturaliter cognita, et rationi per absurda interdum videantur. Et sancti viri eo nomine plurimi æstimatur, quod quæ intelligentia naturali ducunt fieri non posse, eadem cùm Deus illa promiserit, firmè atque constanter fore sperant. Attamen sententia hæc Stoici quæ sensum habet minimè reijciendum, illa quæ dixit Hesiodus, & modo Aristoteles docet, non euertit. Quandoquidem & ipsa si æstimentur iusta ratione, sunt verissima. Quis enim magis acrem vigentemq; animo seu intelligentia eum negauerit, qui per seipsum norit quæ facilia sint & expedita ad propositam finem consequendam? Esto ille qui paret rectè monentibus, cùm per sese non intelligat, moderatior, & probior, acumini tamen & ingenio alterius cedat oportet. Neq; in religione quam profitemur, non iudicabimus beatiorem esse illorum sortem, qui ea vident coram, & apertè vt sunt intuentur, quæ nos, dum hic viuimus, tenebris corporis circumfusi, debemus credere, sumusq; credendis his multò laudabiliores, quàm si nostrum hebes iudicium vellemus consectari: cùm tamen nos agnoscamus non æquè felices, atq; tum futuri simus, quando liquida et patefacta nobis erunt, quæ nunc operta & inuoluta, Dei authoritate adducti credimus. Proinde (vt ait Aristoteles & Hesiodus testatur) qui nec exercitatione neque mentis acumine tenuerit principia, quiq; ab alijs quod sibi defuerit accipere non est paratus, verum tardus & inuitus ad recte agendum adducitur, is est prorsus inutilis.
units.tr: We also praise this same thing in the Christian religion, though with lesser commendation. We call it self-denial when someone, rejecting and setting aside what seemed more likely, assents to what God has revealed in the divine writings, even though it is less known by nature and sometimes seems absurd to reason. Holy men are esteemed very highly for this reason: what natural understanding judges cannot come to pass, they nevertheless hope firmly and constantly will happen, because God has promised it. Yet this saying of the Stoics, which contains a sense not to be rejected, does not overturn what Hesiod said and Aristotle now teaches. For these also, if they are rightly weighed, are most true. For who would deny that he is keener and more vigorous in mind or intellect, who knows by himself what is easy and convenient for reaching the proposed end? Let him who obeys those who advise rightly, though he does not understand by himself, be more moderate and upright; yet he must yield to the sharpness and talent of another. Nor, in the religion we profess, shall we judge that the lot of those is happier who see openly, face to face, and look upon things as they are, whereas we, while we live here surrounded by the shadows of the body, must believe what we ought to believe. We are far more praiseworthy for believing these things than if we wished to pursue our dull judgment; yet we acknowledge that we are not as happy as we shall be when the things now hidden and wrapped up, which we believe on the authority of God, are made clear and laid open to us. Therefore (as Aristotle says, and Hesiod testifies) the man who has grasped the principles neither by practice nor by keenness of mind, and who is not ready to take from others what he lacks, but is slow and reluctant to act rightly, is altogether useless.

units.la: Animum dixit Hesiodus θυμὸν, quod Eustratius demonstrat ideò fieri, quod triū partiū sit animus, λογιστικὸς θυμὸς, & ἐπιθυμία, id est, rationalis, irascens, & cupiditas. Cùm inter duas partes θυμὸς media sit, ex ea sic totus animus nominatur. Vel sic nominatum putabimus animum, quòd sit αὐτοκινητικὸν, ac se ipsum moueat, nec aliud est Græcis θυμὸς quàm ὁρμὴ, impetum facere & ciere motum. Corpus oppidò ab animo mouetur: ast animus, quia seipsum mouet, θυμὸς iure dicitur.
units.tr: Hesiod said thymos [θυμὸν] for the soul, which Eustratius shows is so called because the soul has three parts: the reasoning part [λογιστικὸς], the spirited part [θυμὸς] and the appetitive part [ἐπιθυμία], that is, the rational, the irascible and the desiring. Since the spirited part lies in the middle between the other two, the whole soul is named from it. Or we may think the soul is so named because it is self-moving [αὐτοκινητικὸν] and moves itself; for to the Greeks thymos is nothing other than impulse [ὁρμὴ], making an onset and stirring motion. The body is moved by the soul, but the soul, because it moves itself, is rightly called thymos.

units.la: NVNC vero quando iam ad huius capitis calcem delati sumus, omnibus quantum satis erat expositis, quædam superest & quidem gravissima quæ-stio. Dixit enim Philosophus, quædam esse nota nobis, & alia absolutè: ideoque videndum, quæ nobis dicantur nota. nam hac de re nequidem omnes Peripatetici secum plane consentiunt, sed eis intercesserunt sæpius magna dissidia circa illud quod in scholis primum cognitum vulgò appellant. Nos verò circumscriptis reiectis, quæ ab altercantibus vtrò citròq; afferuntur, distinctiones quasdam faciles & expeditas faciemus, & ad singulas earum partes certas quasdam propositiones aut sententias sic accommodabimus, vt res tota paucis plana, perspicua & aperta nobis fiat. Quàdo à nobis ali-
units.tr: Now that we have come to the end of this chapter, and have explained everything sufficiently, one question remains, and indeed a very weighty one. The Philosopher said that some things are known to us, and others absolutely; so we must see which things are said to be known to us. On this matter not all the Peripatetics agree fully among themselves, and among them there have often been great disagreements about what in the schools they commonly call the first known. We, however, setting aside what is brought forward by the disputants on each side, will make certain easy and convenient distinctions, and to each of their parts we will fit certain propositions or opinions, so that the whole matter may become plain, clear and open to us in a few words. When

units.la: quid vel cognoscitur vel intelligitur, hoc interdum fit ordine seruato, quo à notis ad occulta scrutanda pergimus: nonnunquam vero prout casu ac te mere se aliquid offert, aut id ex proposito destinatoque consilio suscipimus cognoscendum. Ac tum cum voluntate seu fortuito mouemur ad quippiam nobiscum rimandum & putandum, lex nulla sanciri potest: occurrunt enim vt fors tulerit nostrae menti quandoque magis fusa & ampliora, aliquando magis contracta, interdum causae, interdum effecta, quae seipsa ultro suggerunt vt spectentur. Et non raro fit, vt quisque industria & data opera sibi certa quaedam seligat, apud se contemplanda & excutienda, nulla ratione à principio adhibita, sint ne illa magis minusue communia, causae an effectus, quamuis & hoc illi postea in ipsa eorum contemplatione innotescat. Verum quum ordine agimus & à perspicuis magis operta volumus discere, secus accidit. Enimuero non à quibusuis, sed à certis quibusdam auspicamur, quae apertiora fuerint, & ea cuiusmodi sint, nunc inuestigamus.
units.tr: something is known or understood by us, this sometimes happens in the order in which we proceed from what is known to search out what is hidden; but sometimes it happens as chance and accident offer something to us, or we take it up to be known by a deliberate and settled plan. And when we are moved by will or by chance to consider and think something through with ourselves, no rule can be laid down: things come to our mind as fortune brings them, sometimes broader and more extended, sometimes narrower, sometimes causes, sometimes effects, which of themselves offer themselves to be viewed. And it often happens that each person, by diligence and deliberate effort, selects for himself certain things to contemplate and examine, without any principle being applied at the start, whether they are more or less common, causes or effects, although this too becomes known to him afterwards in the very contemplation of them. But when we proceed in order and wish to learn what is hidden from what is plainer, it happens otherwise. Indeed we begin not from just any things, but from certain ones, those which are more evident, and we now investigate what kind they are.

units.la: Et ad inueniendu quod quaerimus non mediocriter proficiet, si rursus aliquas interposuerim diuisiones, quarum prima est. In hoc ordine quo à notis ad ignota contendimus, aut naturaliter aut artificiose res agitur. Secunda cum arte vtimur, vel definimus & diuidimus: idque bifariam, id est notitia distincta seu confusa. Vel quod propositum fuerit argumentis, quae demonstrationes appellantur, confirmamus. Tertia, Cum demonstrationibus vtimur fieri potest vt rem perucstigemus[?], seu iam compertam alterum doceamus. His ita positis, quando naturalem ordinem sequimur, ante omnia sin-gularia haec & individua cognoscimus, quae in sensum incurrunt: nam ex illis intelligentia formas colligimus, & notiones quas vsitato nomine vocant vniuersalia, semperque ea ratio retinetur, vt à contractioribus ascendamus ad magis communia: quoniam vis intelligendi, à formis quae individuis fuerint viciniores, notiones parit latius patentes & ampliores donec in supremas quae omnium latissimae sunt desinant. In hac itidem ratione ac via naturali, constans firmumque id habetur, ea singularia seu individua quae subiiciuntur sensibus, prius cognosci, quae sensus ipsos vehementius percellunt & mouent. Et in hac sententiam, quam expositimus[?], loquitur Aristoteles primo posteriorum Analyticorum, vbi affirmauit ea nobis esse notiora, quae propiora sensibus fuerint: nam verè & absolutè illa esse manifesta, quae longius à sensibus distent, ceu sunt quae magis vniuersalia dicimus. Sed nos hic ne id quidem lateat, ea esse facultatis cognoscentis imbecillitate, vt ipsa quoque individua, et quae sub sensum cadunt, primo occurrunt imperrecte[?] admodum intelligat, hoc est, confusè parumq; distinctè, qui fit, ut pueri soleant viros quotquot viderint, patres vocitare: ut primo Physicorum dicitur. Quare ipsis etiam singularibus cognoscendis, imperfecta, & consu-sa notitia, distinctam, propriam & exquisitam multò antecedit. Nunc de artificioso dicendum est ordine, quando quod satis judicauimus de naturali sumus loquuti. Si definiendum quippiam fuerit, ipsa forma & natura quâ definiendam suscipimus priori loco semper cognoscitur, & saltem illius nomen tenemus. Quin ad istam notitiam vel maximè conuenit, ut prius definitionem, quam vocant quid nominis habeamus, quàm ad illam quæ rem ipsam explicet perueniamus. At que hoc argumento concluditur hæc nostra sententia, quod totum est semper suis partibus manifestius: nam ut paulò ante dicebam, imperfecta, confusa et indistincta notitia, propriam et distinctam perpetuò antecedit. At certius eo nihil est, facilius totum quoquo modo posse cognosci quàm in omnes partes ex quibus constat dissolui. (umq;[?] sic de ipsis definitionibus existimemus, ut ita etiam sentiamus in diuidendo necesse est: siquidem prius totum ipsum occurrit quod partiri debemus, quas partes illas in quas tribuitur videamus. Quodq; hactenus de diuisionibus & definitionibus tradidi, intelligatis oportet de prima notitia, confusa, indistincta, unde vel definire vel diuidere incepimus ab initio. Nā in genere notitiæ distinctæ, propriæ atq; perfectæ, cum definiendo tum diuidendo, à communissimis est inchoandum, nam ea sunt nobis magis nota, cum tota sint, et quidem amplissima: quæ sanè omnia quæ sub se habent, potentia continent.
units.tr: And for finding what we seek it will contribute no little if I again interpose some divisions, of which the first is this. In this order, by which we proceed from the known to the unknown, the matter is handled either naturally or artfully. Second, when we use art, we either define and divide, and this in two ways, namely by distinct or by confused knowledge; or we confirm what has been proposed by arguments, which are called demonstrations. Third, when we use demonstrations, it can happen that we investigate a thing, or teach another what has already been discovered. These things being laid down, when we follow the natural order, first of all we know these singulars and individuals which fall under the senses; for from them the understanding gathers forms, and notions which they call universals by the common term. This rule is always kept: that we ascend from the more contracted to the more common, since the power of understanding, from forms nearer to individuals, produces notions more widely spread and broader, until they end in the highest, which are the broadest of all. In this same reason and natural way it is held as settled and firm that those singulars or individuals which are subject to the senses are known first, since they strike and move the senses more vehemently. In this sense, which we have set out, Aristotle speaks in the first book of the Posterior Analytics, where he affirmed that those things are more known to us which are nearer to the senses; for those things are truly and absolutely manifest which are further from the senses, such as what we call more universal. But let this not be hidden from us here either: owing to the weakness of the cognitive faculty, it understands even the individuals, and those which fall under the sense, which first meet it, very imperfectly, that is, confusedly and rather indistinctly. Hence it is that children are wont to call all the men they see "fathers," as is said in the first book of the Physics. Therefore, even in knowing singulars themselves, imperfect and confused knowledge greatly precedes distinct, proper and exact knowledge. Now we must speak of the artful order, since we have spoken sufficiently of the natural. If anything is to be defined, the form and nature by which we undertake to define it is always known first, and at least we hold its name. Indeed, for this knowledge it is most fitting that we first have what they call the definition of the name, before we arrive at that which explains the thing itself. And by this argument our opinion is concluded, that the whole is always more manifest than its parts; for, as I said a little before, imperfect, confused and indistinct knowledge always precedes proper and distinct knowledge. But nothing is more certain than this, that the whole can be known in some way more easily than it can be dissolved into all the parts of which it consists. Whenever we think this way about the definitions themselves, we must also think so in dividing; for the whole itself, which we ought to divide, comes first, and then we see what the parts are into which it is distributed. And what I have hitherto taught about divisions and definitions must be understood of the first knowledge, confused and indistinct, whence we began to define or divide from the start. For in the genus of distinct, proper and perfect knowledge, both in defining and in dividing, one must begin from the most common, since these are better known to us, being wholes and indeed the most extensive; and these, certainly, all contain potentially whatever they have under them.

units.la: Superest jam ut doctrinam exponamus hanc quo ad argumenta quæ Demonstrationes appellantur. Dum ipsis ad rem quæ nos latet inueniendâ utimur, effecta priorem notitiæ ac certitudinis locum sibi vendicant: quandoquidem propemodum semper euidetius[?] patent. Semper idcirco non dixi, verùm adieci Propemodum, ut mathematicas scientias exciperem, in quibus (ut dixi) accidit causas esse notiores effectis, quòd cùm in pulvere seu tabella pingantur, queant in sensus incurrere.
units.tr: It remains now to set out this doctrine as it applies to the arguments called demonstrations. When we use them to discover what is hidden from us, they claim the first place in knowledge and certainty, since they are almost always more evident. I said "almost always" rather than "always" so as to except the mathematical sciences, in which, as I said, it happens that causes are better known than effects, because they are drawn in dust or on a tablet and so can fall under the senses.

units.la: At que hoc illud est quod modo Aristotelem audiuimus affirmare, ordiendam beatitudinis doctrinam ex effectis. Et ut dicam in universum, hoc argumentorum genus ab illis effectis proficiscitur, quæ sensui magis vicina sunt, & in singularib. quæ subeunt sensum enumerantur, distantq; longius ab his communioribus quæ universalia dicimus. At cū deniq; volucrimus quæ aperta sunt, docere, librosq; methodo ac ratione conscribere, semper communiora et quæ latius pateant, omnibus aliis anteponimus. Atq; hoc est quod Aristoteles inquit in primo Physicorum, dum ostenderet quam ob causam, de communissimis rerum naturalium ralium principiȳs ante omnia sibi esset tractandum. Videtis itaq; totam hanc rem inuolutam satis & opertam, breuibus explicatam, atque cum hac mea expositione non tantum rationes verum etiam quae alibi Aristoteles dicit consentire. Vnum tamen adhuc addam, quia natura longe prius extat quam ars, & ars in eo tota est vt illa imitetur, & ex ea perpetuo sua initia promit, ideo si absolutè quaerat, quod nam sit nobis prius notum, respondendum est individua & singularia, nam illa sunt quae sensibus comprehenduntur, et sensus notitia prior omnib. in nobis oritur, & oes alias antecedit. Notiora vero absolutè seu natura quae sint, ex his quae iam attulimus facilè potest intelligi, quia notioribus nobis opponuntur, & vt in schola peripateticorum vulgarium est. Eadem est oppositorum doctrina: Quae magis contracta sunt latioribus & communioribus opponuntur, nec non effecta causis. Vnde in vnaquaque sententia, ex his quae iam attulimus, videte quid opponatur notioribus nobis, illud q; in eo ordine constituite primum absolutè atq; natura sua notum.
units.tr: This is what we have just heard Aristotle affirm: that the doctrine of happiness should be begun from effects. And to speak generally, this kind of argument proceeds from those effects which are closer to sense, and which are enumerated in particulars that come under the senses, and they stand further from those more common things we call universals. But when at last we wish to teach what is open, and to write books by method and reason, we always put the more common things, which extend more widely, before all others. And this is what Aristotle says in the first book of the Physics, when he shows why one must treat of the most common principles of natural things before all. You see, then, that this whole matter is sufficiently involved and hidden, and has been briefly explained, and that not only the reasons but also what Aristotle says elsewhere agree with my exposition. I will add one thing more. Since nature is far prior to art, and art is wholly in this, that it imitates nature and continually draws its beginnings from it, therefore if one asks absolutely what is first known to us, the answer must be individuals and singulars, for these are what the senses apprehend, and knowledge by sense arises first in us and precedes all others. What is more known absolutely or by nature can easily be understood from what we have already said, since those things are opposed to the things more known to us, as is taught in the school of the common Peripatetics. The doctrine of opposites is the same: what is more contracted is opposed to what is broader and more common, and likewise effects to causes. Hence in every opinion, from what we have already said, see what is opposed to the things more known to us, and place that first in the order as what is absolutely and by nature known.

units.la: His itaq; perfectis & conclusis quae salebrosa & perobscura multis visa sunt, speculemus nunc, quid ista quae Aristoteles docuit de forma rationum velargumentorum quibus vti constituit, & de auditoris institutione, cum diuinis literis congruant. Porrò Deus in ipsius literis frequentissimè se declarauit nostrum Deum, nostram beatitudinem atq; felicitatem, ex praeclaris & mirabilibus effectis, quae de suis conseruandis edidit. Primum ab homi-nibus nosci voluit, ex rerum vniuersarum mole quam condidit in eorum vsum & commoditatem. Deinde Abrahamo dixit, se copiosam amplamq; mercedem eius esse, quod vel eo maxime confirmauit, quod semen ei daturus esset amplissimum, quod auctum & maximè numerosum non tantum foret eripiendum ab Aegyptiaca oppressione, atq; dominum possessoremq; constituendum regnorum Chanaan, vbi tum temporis haec Deus reuelabat, sed eo processurum hoc eius semen, ut ex eo incolae totius orbis, percepturi essent solidam felicitatem. Et cum innumera possem in hac sententia dicere, tantum illud vnum memorabo quod Paulus habet ad Romanos, Qui proprio filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, quomodo non omnia simul donauit? Quis accusabit aduersus electos Dei, &c. Hoc porrò sermone beatitudinis assequendae cuiq; nostrum ex eo fidem facit, quod filium vnigenitum ob eam causam tradiderit. Quare felicitas huius vitae, quae in eo sita est vt iustificemur, condonetur peccata, recipiamur in gratia, certa redditur, nec ea minus quam expectamus cum hinc soluerimus: nam, vt in eadem epistola scribitur, Quos vocauit, hos & iustificauit, quos iustificauit & glorificauit. Proinde satis argumenti habemus, quamobrem si-mus in cœlis beandi, quod hic iam nos animaduertimus cum vocatos tum iustificatos. Ut igitur Aristoteles vult uti demonstrationibus ex postero et eo quod consequens est, ita & nos ex istis effectis, quae commemorauimus, con-cludamus partam nobis felicitatem æternam, condonata item nobis esse pec-cata & iustificatione adeptam ex illo præclaro effecto colligamus, quod Pau-lus recenset, nempe in cordibus suis pacem & tranquillitatem habere qui iustificati fuerint, quod qui non sint consequuti animum et conscientiam ha-bere mirum in modum turbulentam.
units.tr: Having now completed and concluded these matters, which many have found rough and very obscure, let us consider how what Aristotle taught about the form of reasons or arguments that he sets up for use, and about the training of the hearer, agrees with the divine letters. God, in his own writings, has very often declared himself to be our God, and our blessedness and happiness, by the excellent and wonderful effects which he has produced for the preservation of his own. First he wished to be known by men from the vast mass of all things which he created for their use and convenience. Then he said to Abraham that he was his copious and ample reward; and he confirmed this especially in that he would give him a seed most ample, which, having grown and become most numerous, would not only be rescued from Egyptian oppression and established as lord and possessor of the kingdoms of Canaan, where God was then revealing these things, but that this seed of his would advance so far that from it the inhabitants of the whole world would receive solid happiness. And although I could say innumerable things on this point, I will mention only that one thing which Paul has in the letter to the Romans: "He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not also with him freely give us all things? Who shall bring an accusation against the elect of God?" etc. Now this discourse makes certain for each of us the attaining of blessedness, because he gave up his only-begotten Son for this very cause. Therefore the happiness of this life, which lies in this, that we are justified, have our sins forgiven, and are received into grace, is rendered certain, and it will be no less than we expect when we depart hence; for, as is written in the same epistle: "Whom he called, these he also justified; whom he justified, these he also glorified." Accordingly we have sufficient ground why we shall be blessed in heaven, since here already we perceive ourselves both called and justified. Therefore, as Aristotle wishes to use demonstrations from what follows and from what is consequent, so we too, from those effects which we have recalled, conclude that eternal happiness is obtained for us, and gather that sins are forgiven us and that justification is attained, from that excellent effect which Paul recounts, namely that those who have been justified have peace and tranquillity in their hearts, while those who have not attained it have a mind and conscience wonderfully troubled.

units.la: Quo vero ad auditoris institutionem, ut prius demonstrauimus, tot et talia Deus non moratur, ut qui ad suam doctrinam audiendam quosuis accersat. Nec quisquam est mortalium, qui ad diuina percipienda, ad credēdum, & perficienda quae audierit & crediderit, suapte natura sit idoneus. Vnius Spiritus sancti munus est, ut quemq; nostrum hac doceat, qui tamen de ipsis persuadendis, usitata via & ratione uti ministrorum ecclesiæ opera, cùm tamen per seipsum absque humani laboris adminiculo, id & facere possit & interdum præstiterit. Id tamen hic non omittendum censeo, cos qui suaden-te spiritu interius non destituuntur, si pergant audire uerbum Dei externū, eiq; studio egregio & diligentia exquisita pareant, incredibiles progressus esse facturos: cùm vicissim illi qui familiarem sibi atque intimum spiritum Dei iactent, quando in ecclesia sermonem externum Dei aspernentur, eiq; vel remisse vel nullo modo obtemperent, prorsus euasuri sint inutiles, ut modo Aristoteles de his pronuntiat, qui neq; per seipsos norunt, neq; ex aliis parati sunt addiscere.
units.tr: As for the training of the hearer, as we demonstrated earlier, God does not delay so many and such great means in order to summon to hear his doctrine whomever he chooses. Nor is there any mortal who is by his own nature fit to perceive divine things, to believe, and to carry out what he has heard and believed. It is the work of the Holy Spirit alone to teach each of us these things; yet in persuading them he uses the usual way and method, namely the labour of the ministers of the Church, although he himself, without the aid of human labour, both can do this and has sometimes done it. Yet I think it should not be omitted here that those who are not deprived of the inward persuasion of the Spirit, if they continue to hear the external Word of God and obey it with an excellent zeal and exact diligence, will make incredible progress. Conversely, those who boast of a familiar and intimate Spirit of God, when they despise the external preaching of God in the Church and obey it either carelessly or not at all, will certainly turn out useless, as Aristotle now pronounces of those who neither know by themselves nor are ready to learn from others.
CHAPTER V.

units.la: SEd de his iam dicamus à quibus digressi sumus. Siquidem bonum & felicitatem non absque ratione arbitrantur ex uitæ generibus suscipi. Multitudo quidem molesta & intolerabilis, uoluptatem. Tria enim sunt maximè excellentia: hoc, quod modo dictum est, & ciuile, & tertium contemplans.
units.tr: But let us now return to those from whom we have digressed. They think that good and happiness are not without reason taken from the kinds of life. The crowd, indeed, is troublesome and intolerable, and chooses pleasure. For there are three most excellent kinds: the one just mentioned, the civic, and the third, the contemplative.

units.la: DOCTRINAM felicitatis inuestigāda instituerat, inde nonni-hil digressus genus demonstrationum ostendit, quod ad rem propositam concludendam maximè proficeret, nunc verò ad inchoatam dispositionem regreditur, universumq; istud quintū caput in quinq; partes distribuitur. In quarum prima declarat homines de bonis extremis accommodasse opiniones, ad ea uitæ genera, quæ consectari decreuissent, quæ oppidò tria numerantur, uoluptarium, ciuile, atq; contemplans. Secundo loco eos refellit, qui uoluptatibus hoc detulerunt, ut summum in bonis locum obtinerent. Illorum tertio sententia confutatur, qui honores ut extremam finem amplectuntur. Quarto de uirtute decernit, cui etiam consulit inter fines primas non deberi. Et denique in eos dicit, qui diuitias in summa bonorum sede collocarunt. Hæc præcipua sunt quinti cap. membra, inter quas, ut suis locis uidebimus, nonnulla interiecta sunt quæ ad rē tractandam non parum conducunt.
units.tr: Having begun to investigate the doctrine of happiness, he digressed a little to show a kind of demonstration that would be most useful for concluding the matter in hand. Now, however, he returns to the arrangement he began, and this whole fifth chapter is divided into five parts. In the first he shows that men have fitted their opinions about the highest goods to the kinds of life they had decided to pursue, which are clearly numbered as three: the life of pleasure, the civic life, and the contemplative life. Second, he refutes those who have assigned the highest place among goods to pleasures. Third, the opinion of those is refuted who embrace honours as the final end. Fourth, he decides about virtue, and argues that it too should not be counted among the first ends. Finally, he speaks against those who have placed riches in the seat of the highest goods. These are the chief members of the fifth chapter; among them, as we shall see in their places, some things have been inserted that contribute not a little to handling the subject.

units.la: Propositio prioris partis est, Inter hominum fines iure varietates reperiri. Cuius sententiæ inde satis habemus argumenti, quod quisq; ut genus vitæ instituit, finem quoque sibi expetit. Atqui varia, multiplicia, & ut minimum tria sunt vitæ genera. Sunt itaq; iure inter homines multiplices fines, atq; tres ut minimum. Verbis Aristotelis utraq; huius rationis propositio est expressa, id est quemque sibi finem adscisc[?]ere pro vitæ genere, ac vitæ genera multiplicia esse. Rationis huius vis in eo sita est, quòd finis ab eo non debet dissidere cuius est finis atq; perfectio, imò requiritur ut cum eo cōsentiat: & eo commutato quo perficiendum est, finem quoq; mutari est necesse: quandoquidem in his quæ ad aliud referuntur, si fundamentū diuersum feceris & collationis seu relationis terminus non poterit idem permanere. Finis proculdubio ad vitam refertur quam perficit, ita ut in huius relationis genere, vita ut fundamentum habeatur, finis ut terminus.
units.tr: The proposition of the first part is: among the ends of men there are rightly found varieties. We have enough argument for this opinion from the fact that whoever adopts a way of life also seeks an end for himself. But there are various, manifold, and at least three ways of life. Therefore there are rightly many ends among men, and at least three. Aristotle's words express both parts of this reasoning, namely that each man assigns himself an end according to his way of life, and that the ways of life are manifold. The force of this argument lies in this: that the end must not disagree with that of which it is the end and perfection; indeed it is required that it agree with it. And if the thing by which something is to be perfected is changed, the end too must necessarily change, since in things that are referred to something else, if you make the foundation different, the term of the comparison or relation cannot remain the same. Doubtless the end is referred to the life which it perfects, so that in this kind of relation life is taken as the foundation and the end as the term.

units.la: Quod Aristoteles inquit, ἀλόγως[?], Non absq; ratione, non ita debet accipi: quasi ratio probetur uniuscuiusq; vitæ, atq; voluptarij rationem sequantur cum voluptati concedunt in bonis præcipuam & summam sedem. Et nihilomagis iuxta rationem opinantur, qui honori primas deferunt: demonstrabitur enim haud obscurè quàm in iis sententijs à iusta ratione discedatur.
units.tr: As for what Aristotle says, not without reason [οὐκ ἀλόγως], this should not be understood as if reason were being approved for each way of life, or as if those who follow pleasure grant pleasure the chief and highest place among goods. Nor do those who give the first place to honour think any more in accordance with reason; for it will be shown, quite clearly, how far these opinions depart from sound reason.

units.la: Proinde, Non sine ratione, referendum ad consequentia necessitatem, quam homines acutè sapienterque viderunt, ut posita & approbata distinctione triplicis vitæ, concludatur inde multiplices ac varios esse fines, quum ijdem omnibus vitæ generibus præscribi nequeant.
units.tr: Therefore, "not without reason" is to be referred to the necessity of consequence, which men have seen keenly and wisely: once the distinction of a threefold life has been posited and approved, it follows that the ends are many and various, since the same ends cannot be prescribed for all ways of life.

units.la: Et ea est huius vis rationis, vt retro commeet. Vt enim sequitur, Diuersa sunt genera uitæ, igitur plures constituendi fines: ita è diuerso fit, vt si omnes vnam vitæ rationem consectarentur, vnus esset necessario deniq; omnium finis. Et vt istarum vitarum causa quædam reperiatur et sint, non tamen oes iustæ sunt aut laudabiles. Quòd si causas requiras, cur ille ad hoc genus vi-ta, ille ad aliud deflexerit, variæ possunt reddi: multi enim gerendis rebus, & instituendis actionibus temperamentum corporis sequuntur, quo si proni fuerint ad crapulam, ad ebrietatem, ad Venerem, ad elegantes & bonas artes, ad iniurias vlciscendas, tum se beatos oppido arbitrantur, cùm ea obtinuerint, ad quæ naturali quodam impetu concitantur. Alij adducuntur educatione, vt hoc aut illud maximopere cupiant assequi: neq; parum sæpè fit, vt eorum similes homines euadant cum quibus versantur & amicitia sunt coniuncti. Alijs autem & his quidem non paucis neq; semper malis, satis est argumenti & causæ ad aliquid persequendum, quod spectent illorum authoritatem qui vel reipub. vel ecclesiæ, vel scholis, vel militiæ præsunt. Etenim quod sibi deliguntur finem ac expetendum maximè principes, viri graues & sapientes, quorumq; authoritas valet plurimum, id bona hominum pars & suscipit atq; optat. Sunt sanè istæ causæ, at iustæ non sunt, quia non authoritas, non exemplis moueri debemus, neq; impetu corporei temperamenti, sed rationis ac mentis dictatu, rerumq; ipsarum pondere. Rationes itaq; seu argumenta iam allata, imbecilla iuni[?] & perinfirma, ideoq; cauendum ne illis temere cedamus.
units.tr: And this is the force of the argument, that it runs back again. For as it follows, "there are different ways of life, therefore several ends must be set up," so conversely, if all pursued one way of life, there would necessarily be one end for all. And although there are certain causes for these ways of life, they are not all just or praiseworthy. But if you ask why this man has turned to this kind of life and that man to another, various reasons can be given. For many, in conducting affairs and directing their actions, follow the temperament of the body; if they are prone to gluttony, drunkenness, lust, elegant and fine arts, or to avenging injuries, then they think themselves very happy when they obtain those things to which they are driven by a certain natural impulse. Others are led by upbringing to desire very much to attain this or that; and it often happens, not rarely, that men become like those with whom they live and with whom they are joined in friendship. For others, and these not few nor always bad, there is sufficient argument and cause for pursuing something in the fact that they look to the authority of those who preside over the commonwealth, the Church, the schools, or the army. For what the chief men, grave and wise, whose authority counts for most, have chosen as an end to be sought, that a good part of mankind takes up and desires. These are indeed causes, but they are not just, because we ought to be moved neither by authority nor by examples, nor by the impulse of bodily temperament, but by the dictate of reason and mind and the weight of the things themselves. Therefore the reasons or arguments already brought forward are weak and very feeble, and so we must take care not to yield to them rashly.

units.la: Multitudo quidem molesta & intolerabilis. ) Hæc interiecta sunt & parenthesi quadam inferuntur. Nam cùm dixisset, quòd non absq; ratione arbitrantur bonum suscipi ex vitæ generibus, statim & absq; intercapedine videbatur subjiciendum, quot nam essent vitæ genera. At ipse id non fecit: verùm interiecit nonnihil de his qui voluptarium genus vitæ delege-runt. οἱ πολλοὶ[?] vulgum appellat, & multitudinem, si maiore eius parte sæpe claris. Quod idcirco dixerim, quia interdum in ipsa plebe aliqui reperiuntur, qui præ auaritia vel minimarum voluptatum existimantur inimici, at hi non usquè adeò multi sunt. Et quòd natura in voluptates sint proni, ex eo apertum est, quoniam si non sint sumptuosæ atq; illis gratuito offerantur, se plerunq; ipsis ingurgitant. Deinde tales ad illorum ordinem sunt referendi qui diuitias pro summo bono habeant. Nec desunt in ipsa multitudine, qui propter res angustas & curtam substantiam non possunt voluptatibus indulgere, qui non ex eo quod agunt iudicandi sunt, sed ex effectu, ac voluptate[?], videndumq; est quid facerent aut qd faciât cum se opportunitas offert. Alioqui sunt & in populo nonnulli bonis instituti moribus, qui tamè pauci sunt, & hi etiam fortasse his accensendi sunt, qui virtutem pro summo bono habent. φορτικώτατοι appellantur, id est molestissimi & intolerabiles. Ociari volunt, nullisq; prodesse, verum pro viribus labores effugere, Et terrae pondus fruges consumere natum, Horatius. Vitam amant ἀπολαυστικόν[?], frui semper vellent delitiis: molles itaque sunt & delicati, atque omnino affectibus & perturbationibus agantur.
units.tr: The crowd, indeed, is troublesome and intolerable. These things are inserted by way of a parenthesis. For when he had said that good is not without reason taken from the kinds of life, it seemed that he should at once and without interruption add how many kinds of life there are. But he did not do this; rather he inserted something about those who have chosen the life of pleasure. He calls the many [οἱ πολλοί] the common people, and the multitude, at least the greater part of it, often being distinguished men. I say this because sometimes among the common people themselves some are found who, out of avarice, are thought to be enemies even of the smallest pleasures; but these are not very many. And that by nature men are prone to pleasures is evident, since, if pleasures are not costly and are offered to them free of charge, they mostly gorge themselves on them. Next, such men are to be counted in the order of those who hold riches to be the highest good. Nor are there lacking in the multitude those who, on account of narrow means and a small estate, cannot indulge in pleasures; they are not to be judged by what they do, but by the outcome and the pleasure, and one must see what they would do, or what they would do, when opportunity presents itself. Otherwise, there are also among the people some well brought up in good morals, though these are few; and perhaps these too should be reckoned among those who hold virtue to be the highest good. They are called coarsest [φορτικώτατοι], that is, most troublesome and intolerable. They wish to be idle, to be useful to nobody, but to escape labours as far as their strength allows, and "to consume the fruits of the earth, born as a weight upon the ground," says Horace. They love the life of enjoyment [ἀπολαυστικόν], and would always wish to enjoy delights; therefore they are soft and delicate, and are wholly driven by affections and perturbations.

units.la: Ciuiles autem, quorum est alterum vitae genus, vtique affectibus non carent, verùm millis[?] moderationibus vtuntur. Sed contemplantem affirmat Eustratius non moueri affectibus. Quod ego dum in hac vita sumus, nemini concesserim: unde si fortasse intellexit, quoddam esse hominum genus, quod minus longè, quàm alij, vincatur perturbationibus, annuere possumus, sed qui vllis non incitetur fieri non potest. Deinde θεωρητικὸς non distinguitur à reliquis vitae generibus, propter affectuum maiorem aut minorem vehementiam. Sed quia rebus agendis non immoratur, solum spectat & contemplatur vel naturalia, vel mathematica, vel diuina. Hoc quidem verum est illum non posse id agere si rapiatur vehementer perturbationibus. Oportet enim contemplantem sedatum habere animum, non tamen est necesse vt sit affectibus prorsus vacuus. Alia duo genera vitae sic se habent, vt vnum in moderandis affectibus versetur, id est ciuile: alterum vero prorsus ijs vexetur & regatur: Tertium vero quod est contemplans, omnino aliud opus habet, neque circa affectus versatur. non enim est is eius scopus vt passiones frenet, vt luctetur cum affectibus, neque vt virtutes exerceat, sed tantum vt contempletur. Et ita haec vitae genera dispositia sunt & ordinata, vt primum sit vilissimum, alterum nobilius, tertium vero caeteris praestet.
units.tr: Civic men, whose is the other kind of life, certainly are not free from affections, but they use moderations for them. But Eustratius affirms that the contemplative man is not moved by affections. As long as we are in this life, I would never grant this to anyone; hence, if perhaps he meant that there is a kind of men who are far less overcome by perturbations than others, we may assent; but that someone should not be stirred by any affections cannot happen. Further, the theoretical man [θεωρητικὸς] is not distinguished from the other kinds of life by a greater or lesser vehemence of affections, but because he does not dwell on things to be done, and looks only at and contemplates natural things, or mathematical, or divine ones. This is indeed true: he cannot do this if he is violently seized by perturbations. For the contemplative man must have a calm mind, yet it is not necessary that he be utterly free from affections. The other two kinds of life are such that one is occupied in moderating the affections, namely the civic; the other is wholly vexed and ruled by them. The third, the contemplative, has an altogether different task and is not concerned with the affections. For its aim is not to bridle the passions, nor to struggle with the affections, nor to exercise the virtues, but only to contemplate. And so these kinds of life are arranged and ordered so that the first is the lowest, the second is nobler, and the third surpasses the others.

units.la: Ac multitudo quidem omnino mancipiorum instar est, pecudum vitam deligens. Hac autem ratione adducuntur, propterea quod multi potestate insignes non secus atque Sardanapalus sint affecti.
units.tr: And the multitude, indeed, are altogether like slaves, choosing the life of cattle. They are drawn to this because many who are distinguished by power are affected no differently from Sardanapalus.

units.la: Propositio est, non esse Voluptatem summum bonum: in qua profecto af-ferenda non est solus Aristoteles, verum habet socios, Platonem, Stoicos, & omnes fermè qui sunt paulo elegantiores. Ratio affertur, Quoniam istud bonum est commune brutis: atque hoc pacto bruta possent esse felicia. & certè iuxta hanc rationem bruta essent hominibus feliciora: quandoquidem voluptatibus his crassioribus laxius & copiosius quàm homines fruantur. Ratio ista communitur, quòd felicitatem & summum bonum cuiusq; naturae illi oportet esse proprium: quod in voluptate non potest reperiri, cùm & bruta sint eius participia. Atq; vt euidens est, loquitur hic Aristoteles de his crassis voluptatibus, quae gustu & tactu percipiuntur: quandoquidem illae duntaxat brutis sunt communes ac eis ducuntur. voluptatibus enim odoratus, visus, aut auditus bellua non mouentur. Quod igitur bonum modò tractat, belluinum est, & ad ventrem libidinesq; maxime attinet. Ea porrò debet hominis beatitudo constitui quae illum ad diuina subleuet, non quae ad bestias deprimat, alioqui felicitate non perficeretur, sed potius corrumperetur nostrum genus. Neq; tantum dicit Aristoteles quòd eligant pecudum vitam, sed ait, esse mancipia. Instar sanè pecudum sunt atq; mancipiorum, qui ducuntur trahunturq; non proprio, sed alieno duce. Proprius hominum dux ratio esse debet, non sensus, aut cupiditas quae sensuum comprehensionem sequitur. Alieni dicuntur isti duces, quoniam non hominibus, verùm pecudibus sunt destinati.
units.tr: The proposition is that pleasure is not the highest good.
