In this Aristotle is not the only one to be cited; he has companions: Plato, the Stoics, and nearly all who are somewhat more refined. The reason given is that this good is common to brutes, and so brutes could be happy in this way. Indeed, by this reasoning, brutes would be happier than men, since they enjoy these grosser pleasures more freely and abundantly than men do. The argument is further supported by the point that happiness and the highest good must be proper to the nature of each thing, which cannot be found in pleasure, since brutes also partake of it. And as is clear, Aristotle here speaks of these gross pleasures that are perceived by taste and touch, since these alone are common to brutes and lead them on. For a beast is not moved by the pleasures of smell, sight, or hearing. So the good he is now treating is bestial and pertains chiefly to the belly and the lusts. Human blessedness ought to be set in that which lifts us up to divine things, not in that which drags us down to beasts; otherwise our race would not be perfected by happiness but rather corrupted. Nor does Aristotle merely say that they choose the life of cattle; he calls them slaves. Indeed they are like cattle and slaves, who are led and dragged not by their own leader but by another's. The proper leader of men ought to be reason, not sense or desire, which follows the apprehension of the senses. Those leaders are called "alien" because they are destined not for men but for beasts.

units.la: Hac ratione adducuntur, propterea quod multi potestate insignes non secus atq; Sardanapalus sint affecti.) A ratione qua vsus est Epicurus hi non multum videntur abesse. Is enim volens confirmare, Voluptatem hominum esse finem extremam, vel, vt rectius dicam, bonorum summum, à paruis pueris ducebat argumentum, quòd in his natura doceret homines: hi enim cùm adhuc educatione peruersa non sunt depravati, neq; falsis opinionibus imbuti, sed integrè atq; incorruptè iudicant, Voluptatem persequuntur, atq; dolorem vt rem exitiosam fugiunt: quare vox naturae audienda est, & in his qui eius quodammodo speculam quandam sunt, est contemplandum, quae natura sit humanae felicitatis.nam si natura homines ad alia essent destinati, primo ab ortu in ea essent propensi. Ita isti vulgares, cùm principes vident summa praeditos potestate omnibus modis ac partibus crassiores has voluptates persequi, existimant illas extremum esse bonum, quod homines possint sibi vendicare. Etenim cùm principes legibus, vt caeteri, non coerceantur, neq; plurimi faciant de se quid vulgus opinetur, neq; ad eas dignitates putentur absq; numine, atq; illorum praeclara sapientia euecti: quod ipsis vt praecipuum bonum est gratum, & caeteris anteponitur. Quodq; suis vt praemium proponunt, id à caeteris vt felicitas & bonum extremum constituitur.
units.tr: They are drawn by this reasoning, because many who are distinguished by power are affected no differently from Sardanapalus.) The reasoning used by Epicurus does not seem far from this. He, wishing to confirm that pleasure is the final end of men, or, to speak more correctly, the highest good, drew his argument from small children, in whom nature, he said, teaches men. For these, not yet corrupted by a perverse upbringing nor imbued with false opinions, judge wholly and uncorruptedly: they pursue pleasure and flee pain as a harmful thing. Therefore the voice of nature should be heard, and in those who are in some way its watchtower one should consider what nature human happiness is. For if nature had destined men for other things, they would be inclined to them from the beginning. Thus the common people, when they see princes endowed with supreme power pursuing these grosser pleasures in every way and in every part, think those pleasures are the highest good that men can claim for themselves. For since princes are not restrained by laws as others are, and do not greatly care what the common people think of them, and are thought to have been raised to those dignities not without the divine will and by their own remarkable wisdom, what is pleasing to them as their chief good is set above all others by them. And what they propose to their own people as a reward, that is established by others as happiness and the final good.

units.la: Et haec sanè Platonis & aliorum sapientum semper fuit laudata sententia, Tales esse populos cuiusmodi reges eius & principes fuerint. Cum An-glia sanctum habuit & bonarum literarum studiosum Eduardum, iuuentus vniuersa conabatur studia eius imitari. Atq; vt à simili Aristotelis non longius abeamus, in eo maxime vulgus & mancipia & pecudes refert. Nam is omnium mos videtur, vt si aries, aut quae in grege primum obtinet locum, in vnam partem discedant, sequuntur omnes. Item sine iudicio vel vllo delectu mancipia suos dominos consectantur.
units.tr: Indeed this has always been the praised opinion of Plato and of other wise men: that peoples are such as their kings and princes have been. When England had the holy Edward, a lover of good letters, the whole youth strove to imitate his studies. And so that we may not stray far from a similar passage of Aristotle, in this respect he compares the common people to slaves and cattle. For this seems to be the custom of all: if a ram, or whichever one holds first place in the flock, turns off in one direction, all follow. Likewise slaves, without judgment or any choice, follow their masters.

units.la: De Sardanapalo multa dicerem, nisi quae Iustinus habet omnibus essent in promptu. Id tantum dicam, quod semper ferunt ei fuisse in ore, Ede, bibe, lude. Sed Horatius illa redarguit, in suis Epistolis:
units.tr: I would say much about Sardanapalus, but what Justin records is at hand for everyone. I will say only this, which they report he always had on his lips: "Eat, drink, play." But Horace refutes those words in his Epistles:

units.la: Lusisti satis, edisti satis atq; bibisti, Tempus abire tibi est.
units.tr: "You have played enough, eaten enough and drunk enough; it is time for you to depart."

units.la: In quinta Tusculana Cicero inquit eum suo busto voluisse inscribi, Hac habeo quae edi quaeq; exaturata libido Hausit, at illa iacent multa & praeclara relicta.
units.tr: In the fifth Tusculan Disputation, Cicero says that he wished to have this inscribed on his tomb: "These things I have, which I ate, and which insatiable lust swallowed; but those many splendid things are left behind."

units.la: Addit Cicero Aristotelem dicere, Quid aliud in bouis, non regis sepulchro inscriberes? Ista quae commemorat Cicero, nusquam in Aristotelis voluminibus leguntur. Unde satis apparet, quemadmodum viri doctissimi obseruarunt, permulta istius viri monimenta perijsse [?]: qua de re alibi fortasse latius. Verum quid de Sardanapalo tantum conquerimur, quasi Ti-berius Romanorum princeps, non adeo fuerit deditus his illecebris & blandimentis, vt sibi munus constituerit à voluptatibus. Vt enim sunt qui regi-bus & magistratibus sunt à libellis, ab epistolis, ab equis, ita ille voluit ali-quos habere à voluptatibus. Item Heliogabalus, quem nescio an Imperato-rem an portentum dicere debeam, praemia constituit inuentoribus nouorum condimentorum, quo gulam & palatum magis irritaret. Neq; soli peccarunt hac in parte Romanorum αὐτοκράτορες [?], sed etiam Persarum Rex magnus, ille inquam Xerxes, praemia & quidem non vulgaria constituit inuentoribus nouarum voluptatum.
units.tr: Cicero adds that Aristotle said: "What else would you inscribe on the tomb of an ox rather than of a king?" The things Cicero records are nowhere read in Aristotle's writings. Whence it is sufficiently clear, as very learned men have observed, that many of that man's monuments have perished [?]; on which matter perhaps elsewhere more fully. But why do we complain only about Sardanapalus, as if Tiberius, prince of the Romans, had not been so given to these allurements and flatteries that he appointed for himself an office drawn from pleasures? For as there are those who, for kings and magistrates, are secretaries of petitions, of letters, of horses, so he wished to have some from pleasures. Likewise Heliogabalus, whom I do not know whether I should call emperor or monster, established rewards for the inventors of new seasonings, to stimulate the gullet and palate the more. Nor did the Roman emperors alone sin in this respect, but also the great king of the Persians, that Xerxes I mean, established rewards, and not ordinary ones, for the inventors of new pleasures.

units.la: Hic deniq; dubia occurrunt nonnulla, cur Aristoteles ab hac praesertim opinione sit auspicatus censum sententiarum de summo bono. Id factum dicunt interpretes, quod maiorem vulgi consensum habeat, sitq; facilior. Ite quia naturae ordinem sequitur: & cum vita huiusmodi animalis dici possit, & id genus vitae prius in homine sit quam sese exerat ratio, ideo confutatur priori loco.
units.tr: Here at last several doubts arise: why Aristotle chose to begin his survey of opinions on the highest good especially with this opinion. The interpreters say this was done because it has the greater agreement of the common people and is easier. Or because it follows the order of nature: and since a life of this kind can be called that of an animal, and this kind of life comes first in man before reason displays itself, therefore it is refuted first.

units.la: Est praeterea mirum, cur multitudini tribuatur ista opinio et plebeis hominibus, cum habuerit Epicurus satis celebre patronum. Cur illum nominatim in quem diceret non appellavit ? Quia cùm Aristoteles iam senex esset, & mortuo Alexandro Macedone Athenis discessisset, & degeret in Chalcide, ne peccandi bis in philosophiam Atheniensibus daret occasionem, hos libros conscripsit: quo tempore coeperat Epicurus animum ad literas applicare, necdum fama clarus aut cognitus erat. Ideo est opinio haec in vulgus reiecta, quoniam usque ad ea tempora nullum insignem defensorem habuerat.
units.tr: Moreover, it is strange why this opinion is attributed to the multitude and to plebeian men, since Epicurus had a rather famous advocate. Why did he not name expressly the one against whom he would speak? Because when Aristotle was already old, and after Alexander of Macedon had died, he had left Athens and was living at Chalcis, so as not to give the Athenians a second occasion to sin against philosophy, he wrote these books. At that time Epicurus had only begun to apply his mind to letters and was not yet famous or known. Therefore this opinion was thrown back upon the common people, because up to that time it had no notable defender.

units.la: Qui haec dicunt, ignorare videntur Aristippum, qui vixit Platonis tempore, auditorq; fuit Socratis, & à patria Cyrenaicus est appellatus, isq; huius opinionis acerrimus fuit propugnator. Unde si Epicurum tacuit, ut se posteriorem, mirum quomodo Aristippum praeteriit, hominem satis clarum, quiq; cum regibus, & praesertim Dionysio, familiarissime vixit. Potuerat Epicurus profecto minori periculo praeteriri: quoniam is hac de re dubie admodum, ni velimus inconstanter dicere, loquutus est. nam ut aliquando voluptates sensuum mirifice praedicare, tamen inde nonnunquam se colligit, & vacuitatem doloris ponere videtur eam esse voluptatem quam tantopere consectandam putet. Qua de re Cicero praeclare scripsit primo & secundo de finibus. Mitto Senecam, qui hominem mirifice praedicat, & sententias eius magno plausu amplectitur, & frugalitatem eximie commendat. Quem nihilominus aetate post Aristotelem fuisse non ambigo. Sed hoc afferre volui quod etiam si aequales fuissent, non absq; ratione poterat nomen eius taceri. Cur vero mentio Aristippi facta non fuerit, hanc arbitror causam, quod licet ipse ob ingenium versatile quod ad omnia posset accommodari: nam dicebat Plato Aristippo sibi datum, ut chlamyde uti posset & panno: Horatiusq; de illo eleganter scripsit: Omnis Aristippi decet status & color & res. Licet inquam ob hanc causam esset celebris, & quia regibus & summis tyrannis esset gratus: attamen quo ad finis constitutionem extremi, quoniam à vulgaribus non dissidebat, propterea non fuit committendum, ut tanquā propria ei assignaretur ea sententia, quae totius propemodū vulgi erat.
units.tr: Those who say these things seem to be ignorant of Aristippus, who lived in the time of Plato, was a hearer of Socrates, and was called Cyrenaic from his homeland, and he was the fiercest champion of this opinion. Whence, if he kept silent about Epicurus as being later, it is strange how he passed over Aristippus, a man quite famous, who lived most intimately with kings, and especially with Dionysius. Epicurus could certainly have been passed over with less risk, since he spoke on this matter quite doubtfully, unless we wish to say inconsistently. For although at times he extols the pleasures of the senses wonderfully, yet sometimes he gathers himself back from that and seems to posit the absence of pain as the pleasure which he thinks is to be pursued so eagerly. On this matter Cicero wrote admirably in the first and second books On Ends. I pass over Seneca, who praises the man marvellously, embraces his maxims with great applause, and commends frugality remarkably; yet I do not doubt he came after Aristotle in time. But I wished to bring this forward: that even if they had been contemporaries, his name could not have been passed over without reason. Why no mention of Aristippus was made, I think this is the cause: although he, on account of his versatile disposition, which could adapt itself to anything (for Plato said that Aristippus had the gift of being able to use both a cloak and a rag), and Horace wrote elegantly about him: "Every condition, colour and circumstance suits Aristippus." Although, I say, he was famous for this reason, and because he was pleasing to kings and supreme tyrants, yet as to the establishing of the final end, since he did not differ from the common people, it was therefore not to be entrusted that that opinion, which was almost the whole common people's, should be assigned to him as his own.

units.la: Vnum praeterea reliquum est quod percunctemur, cum hoc voluptariū viuendi genus abiectum sit & contemptum, qui fiat, ut eminere dicatur, an ullo modo excelluit? Non profecto, si homines ad belluas detrudit. Verum sciendum est, etiam quandoq; vitia eminere, quando sunt in propatulo & maximè conspicua. Non itaq; genus hoc vitae aliis praestat dignitate, sed voluptariorum hominum numero qui hanc vitae rationem consectantur. Neq; praedicatur ob felicitatem quam nobis tribuat, sed quam afferre male sanis videtur, et quia illi (ut dictum est) hi[?] sunt prae caeteris addicti, qui magistratibus funguntur & summa potentia in Rebuspublicis pollent.
units.tr: One thing remains to be asked: since this pleasure-seeking way of life is rejected and despised, how does it come about that it is said to stand out, or has it excelled in any way? Certainly not, if it drags men down to the level of beasts. But it must be understood that vices too sometimes stand out, when they are in the open and most conspicuous. So this way of life does not surpass others in dignity, but only in the number of pleasure-loving men who pursue it. Nor is it praised for the happiness it bestows on us, but for the happiness it seems to offer to the ill-disposed. And those who hold office and wield the greatest power in commonwealths, as has been said, are more addicted to it than others.

units.la: IAM eò vocamur, vt nonnulla de voluptate disseramus, quod à nobis restrictè admodum & parcè fiet: quoniam in 7. huius operis lib. & in 4. fusè copiosè, hac de re agetur. Aliqua tamen vt dicamus necesse est, vt non putemus omne voluptatis genus à summo bono seu felicitate secludi: nam reuera felicitas nostra seu naturalem spectas seu theologicam, aut voluptas est, aut cum illa copulata, vt à se mutuò diuelli nequeant. Primum quæ ex Platonis doctrina hinc inde collegerim proferam, Deinceps comprehendā summatim quid in Aristotele habeatur.
units.tr: NOW we are called to discuss some points about pleasure, and we shall do so rather briefly and sparingly, since the subject is treated fully and at length in book 7 of this work and in book 4. Still, something must be said, so that we do not think every kind of pleasure is excluded from the highest good or happiness. For in truth our happiness, whether natural or theological, either is pleasure or is so joined with it that the two cannot be torn apart. First I shall set out what I have gathered here and there from Plato's teaching; then I shall summarise what is found in Aristotle.

units.la: Plato non semel nostrum animum in duas minimùm partes diduxit, me-tem, inquam, & sensus: harum partium vt vna sublimis est & præstantissima, quaq; ad Deum quàm proximè accedimus: ita crassa & penè bruta est altera, eaq; cum pecudibus communicamus. Hac animi distinctione posita & confirmata, tribuit menti lætitiam & gaudium, sensui autem voluptatem. Quid autem interfit inter gaudium & lætitiam, ex eius opinione, vt mihi videor deprehendere, patefaciam. Lætitiam vult interdum bonam atque laudabilem, nonnunquam verò, si limites fuerit prætergressa, vitium affirmat & vituperandam. Quod magis perspicuè apparebit si definiatur, Est enim quædam animi elatio ex alicuius boni præsentia. Nemo autem non videt, rectam esse lætitiam, si pro ratione præsentis boni efferamur, id est non minus neque magis atque ipsum mereatur. Sunt itaque inepti qui efferuntur ob falsa bona, vel nimium subleuantur adeptione vilium & minutorū bonorum. Sed illi detestabiles, qui exultant ob admissa scelera, quæ animis illorum per iudicij corruptionem bona videantur. Sed vicissim tum laudatur & commendatur lætitia, cùm animus non plus exhilaratur & effertur, quàm adepto bono conuenit. Et Cicero 2. de finibus lætitiam vitiosam his verbis complexus est, vt à Stoicis accepit, Illam dicens sublationem animi sine ratione opinantis se magno bono frui. Sed ad Platonem redeo, qui gau-dium etiam menti ascribit, sed ita vt ei vitium non possit hærere, quòd illud definiat iucunditatem, quæ vel à contemplatione sapientis, aut virtutum actionibus fluat. Hæc iucunditas vitiosum excessum pati non potest: nam quæ iusta, recta & decentia sunt, non queunt cupiam [?] nimis placere. Gaudiumq; ita commendauit, vt in libro de pulcro, cùm de vita cœlesti & verè beata loqueretur, eo affirmauit animos felicium ali. Atq; vult poetas hoc genus cibi artificiosè appellasse ambrosiam & nectar. Voluptas autem quæ sensus, vt putat, solum perfunduntur, suauis est motio quæ sensus titillat. A qua sententia nil Cicero dissentit, qui secundo de finibus ait, Voluptatem hanc esse sentiunt omnes, quam sensus accipiens monetur, & iucunditate quadam perfunditur. Et paucis interiectis idem non piguit illum sic repetere, Oes iucundu motu quo sensus hilaretur, Graecè ἡ ἡδονή[?], Latinè voluptatem vocant. Ex his quae nunc trado vos oportet id observare, tā Platonem, quàm Stoicos, caterosq; veteres, voluptatem censere motū seu actione esse: nā postea visuri sumus quid hoc in se veritatis habeat. Arbitratur Plato hanc sensuum voluptatem ab indigentia naturae oriri: nā ea si fuerit exhausta, incipit appetere illa quib. resarciri & instaurari se posse censet: dumq; naturali indigentia satisfaciamus, sensus & titillantur & perfunduntur iucunditate. Ac è diverso, dū natura quibus eget non potest assequi, & deficit, & ex defectu mirificè dolet. Unde idem author in Philebo, voluptates dixit esse dolorum effugia: et inde concludit, aegrotantium maiores vehementioresq; voluptates esse quàm bene valentium: quia cū doloribus admodū cruciētur, cupiditate medicamentorum, voluptatū inquā flagrant maximè omnium, ideoq; cum eas assequuntur, illis impensissimè delectantur, ut in his videre licet, qui acutissimis febribus laborant, & siti propemodum intolerabili conficiuntur, quibus dum conceditur à medico, ut frigida vel alio genere potus satisfaciant, dici non potest quanta perfundantur voluptate. His addit in eodem loco, voluptates istas crassiores, quae ad sensus pertinet, minimè simplices esse, sed mixtas: nam semper aliquid doloris coniunctum habent: siquidem naturae indigentia (ut diximus) dolores parit. Neq; voluptates huius generis ulterius proferuntur cum indigentia naturalis expleta fuerit. Saturis enim & repletis abundè, non placet cibus: neq; potus est gratus his qui affatim sunt irrigati. Quod si quandoque secus accidat, ut in ebriosis & sagonibus interdum fieri videmus, alia causa est eius voluptatis, quàm naturae indigentia, nimirum peruersus habitus, vel aliquid aliud, quod modo exponere non est, opportunum, quum de naturalibus voluptatibus agatur.
units.tr: Plato more than once divided our soul into two parts, mind, I mean, and sense. Of these, one is lofty and most excellent, and by it we draw closest to God. The other is gross and almost brutish, and we share it with the beasts. Having posited and confirmed this division of the soul, he assigned gladness and joy to the mind, but pleasure to the senses. What difference there is between joy and gladness, in his view, as I seem to make out, I shall explain. He holds that gladness is sometimes good and praiseworthy, but sometimes, when it has overstepped its limits, he declares it a vice and worthy of blame. This will appear more clearly if it is defined: gladness is a certain elation of the soul from the presence of some good. Now no one fails to see that gladness is right if we are lifted up in proportion to the present good, that is, neither more nor less than it deserves. Thus those are foolish who are elated by false goods, or who are excessively raised up by winning trifling and petty goods. But those are detestable who exult in crimes committed, which through a corruption of judgement seem good to their minds. Conversely, gladness is praised and commended when the soul is not cheered and elated more than is fitting for the good obtained. Cicero, in book 2 of On Ends, comprehended vicious gladness in these words, as he took them from the Stoics: calling it an uplifting of the soul, without reason, of one who thinks he enjoys a great good. But to return to Plato, who also ascribes joy to the mind, yet in such a way that vice cannot cling to it, since he defines it as delight which flows either from the contemplation of the wise or from the actions of the virtues. This delight cannot suffer vicious excess, for things that are just, right and fitting cannot please too much. He commended joy so highly that in the book On the Beautiful, when speaking of the heavenly and truly blessed life, he affirmed that the souls of the blessed are nourished by it. He also wants the poets to have artfully called this kind of food ambrosia and nectar. But pleasure, which he thinks bathes the senses alone, is a sweet motion that tickles the senses. Cicero does not dissent from this view. In book 2 of On Ends he says: all men feel this pleasure, which the sense receives and is warned by, and is bathed in a certain delight. And after a few words he was not ashamed to repeat it thus: every delightful motion by which the sense is cheered, which in Greek is called hē hēdonē [ἡ ἡδονή], and in Latin voluptas. From what I now deliver, you should observe this: Plato, the Stoics and the other ancients all judged pleasure to be a motion or action. For afterwards we shall see what truth this has in it. Plato holds that this sensual pleasure arises from the want of nature. For when nature is exhausted, it begins to desire those things by which it thinks it can be restored and renewed; and while we satisfy natural need, the senses are both tickled and bathed in delight. Conversely, while nature cannot attain what it lacks, it fails and grieves greatly from the lack. Hence the same author, in the Philebus, said that pleasures are escapes from pains; and from this he concludes that the sick have greater and more vehement pleasures than the healthy. For since they are cruelly tormented by pains, they burn above all with desire for remedies, that is, for pleasures; so when they obtain them, they delight in them most intensely. This can be seen in those who suffer from the most acute fevers and are worn down by an almost intolerable thirst, to whom, when the physician allows them to slake it with cold drink or some other kind of drink, it cannot be said how greatly they are bathed in pleasure. He adds in the same place that these pleasures, the grosser ones which belong to the senses, are by no means simple but mixed, for they always have some pain joined to them; since need of nature, as we said, produces pains. Nor do pleasures of this kind go on once the natural need has been filled. For to the sated and the full, food no longer pleases, nor is drink agreeable to those who are drenched to the full. But if at times it happens otherwise, as we see sometimes happen in drunkards and in those with a diseased appetite, the cause of that pleasure is other than the need of nature, namely a perverse habit or something else, which it is not now the place to explain, since we are treating natural pleasures.

units.la: Aristoteles verò nō hæc posuit vocum discrimina, sed illas delectationes, tam quae ad mentem seu rationem pertinent, quàm quae sunt sensuum, Voluptates, id est ἡδονὰς appellauit. Quin in 7.cap.11. μακαρίσι[?], dici vult ἀπὸ τοῦ[?] χαίρειν, quod est gaudere, atq; ibi de voluptate loquitur, quã cũ beatitudini coniungat, certū est non de hac loqui, quā sensus et animi crassior pars perfunditur. Ea enim tantum cum felicitate copulatur, quae animi fuerit, quae, ut dixi, promiscua voce nominatur voluptas. & forte noluit Aristoteles nomina variare, quod sibi loquendum ut plures existimarit, quamuis de rei discrimine cum Platone consentiret.
units.tr: Aristotle, however, did not make these distinctions of words. He called both those delights which pertain to the mind or reason and those which belong to the senses pleasures, that is, hēdonai [ἡδοναί]. Indeed, in book 7, chapter 11, he wants the word for blessedness, makarisi [μακαρίσι], to be derived from chairein [χαίρειν], which means to rejoice, and there he speaks of pleasure. Since he joins it with blessedness, it is certain that he is not speaking of that by which the coarser part of the sense and soul is bathed. For only that which belongs to the soul is joined with happiness, and this, as I said, is named by the common word pleasure. Perhaps Aristotle did not want to vary the names, because he thought he should speak as most people do, although he agreed with Plato about the difference of the thing itself.

units.la: Hoc tamen inter se differunt, quòd Aristoteles, ut Plato & prisci philo-sophi sophi, non arbitratur voluptatem esse motum vel actione, sed potius est af-sectus motui seu operationi adhaerescens. Unde ista ratione differunt, licet subiecto conveniant: & si quando ipse Aristoteles aut ullus Peripateticus Voluptatem dixerit motum, ea praedicatio illis est accensenda, quam vulgo in scholis identicam vocant: nam ut est dictum, & affectus & motus vel actio idem subiecto sunt. Genus itaq; illius est praedicamentum qualitatis, & ad eius tertiam speciem attinet Voluptas, eaq; nuncupatur passio & passibilis qualitas. [illegible, ~4 letters] dicitur, qua suauiter afficimur ex alicuius boni congruenti cum natura nostra praesentia. Vtq; pulchritudo qualitas est quae resultat ex iusto rectoq; temperamento corporis, congrua figura, & colore decenti, sic voluptas ex motu & actione congrua oritur. Quam ob rem sic ea licebit definire. Voluptas est affectus, quo suauiter afficimur propter actionem quae à natura proficiscatur bene constituta, vel habitu secundum naturam absq; impedimento. Actiones quippe tum edendi tum bibendi & procreandi cum à natura oriuntur, recte habenti semper voluptatem afferunt, nam per morbum aut debilitatem non impediuntur, neq; per saturitatem & repletionem. Ita contemplationes & virtutum actiones, quandoquidem ab habitu nascuntur, prompta sunt & faciles, suntq; bonum praesens, quod cum natura congruit hominis: ideo semper annexam habent voluptatem. Probat Aristoteles voluptatem non esse motum, in decimo: quoniam tota est simul, ut visio: & voluptas non habet successionem nisi per accidens. Si enim consequatur actiones quae successum habeant, illa itidem extenditur, ut fit in edendo & bibendo, sed si actio momentanea sit, ut visio, auditus, intelligentia, tum voluptas illico habetur tota. Vt visio tota est simul, si vis & facultas videndi sit integra, si visibile totum simul proponatur, si medium non sit obfuscatum & distantia congrua interponatur. Motus non est perfectus in suis partibus, voluptas tota simul est: igitur non est motus: Isq; in momento seu instanti esse non potest, at voluptas potest. Proprietates motus sunt velocitas & tarditas, & haec voluptati non conveniunt, dum enim quis laetatur, neq; velocius neq; tardius gaudet: Si enim voluptas per horam duret, in omni parte horae tota est simul.
units.tr: Yet they differ in this: Aristotle, like Plato and the ancient philosophers, does not hold that pleasure is a motion or action, but rather an affect adhering to a motion or operation. Hence they differ in this respect, although they agree in subject. And if ever Aristotle himself or any Peripatetic says that pleasure is a motion, that statement is to be counted among those which in the schools they call identical predication, for, as has been said, affect and motion or action are the same in subject. Its genus, therefore, is the category of quality, and pleasure belongs to its third species, and is called a passion and a passible quality. (The next words are illegible in the scan.) It is said to be that by which we are sweetly affected from the presence of some good agreeing with our nature. Just as beauty is a quality that results from the right and proper temperament of the body, a fitting figure and a decent colour, so pleasure arises from a fitting motion and action. Wherefore it may be defined thus: pleasure is an affect by which we are sweetly affected on account of an action proceeding from a well-constituted nature, or from a habit according to nature without impediment. For the actions of eating, drinking and procreating, when they arise from nature, always bring pleasure to one who is well disposed, for they are not hindered by sickness or weakness, nor by satiety or repletion. So too the contemplations and actions of the virtues, since they arise from a habit, are ready and easy, and are a present good that agrees with the nature of man; therefore they always have pleasure attached to them. Aristotle proves in book 10 that pleasure is not a motion, since it is wholly simultaneous, like seeing, and pleasure has no succession except per accidens. For if it follows actions that have succession, it is extended in the same way, as happens in eating and drinking. But if the action is momentary, like seeing, hearing or understanding, then pleasure is had at once, in its entirety. Seeing is wholly simultaneous if the power and faculty of sight is whole, if the whole visible object is presented at once, if the medium is not obscured and a suitable distance is interposed. Motion is not perfect in its parts; pleasure is wholly simultaneous; therefore it is not motion. Motion also cannot exist in a moment or instant, but pleasure can. The properties of motion are swiftness and slowness, and these do not belong to pleasure. For while someone rejoices, he does not rejoice more quickly or more slowly; if pleasure lasts for an hour, it is wholly simultaneous in every part of the hour.

units.la: Ex definitione iam adducta, cum habeamus oportere vim esse integram & habitum firmum, ut actio sit absq; impedimento, & obiectum sit egregium atque praestantissimum, colligitur quam diu possit voluptas durare. Tantisper manet quoad obiectum & facultas seu vis agendi manent integra: nam si obiectum a sua praestantia cadat, vel facultas non sit acris & attenta, non sequitur delectatio. Hinc fit, ut cum homines operando fatigentur, sæpe imminuantur voluptates: quod idem fit cùm aliquid ab obiecto de sua excellentia detrahitur. Apparet etiam quare tantopere nouæ res placeant, quoniam mens cum primum quippiam nobile ac præstans offert se contemplandum, acriter & attentè ipsum intuetur, quo cognito de studio remittit, ideò voluptas desinit: verum si priori obiecto aliquid aliud recens supponatur, denuò intelligentia contendit studium eo contemplando, & voluptas redit, atque hoc pacto semper rebus nouis nos oblectamus. Ostenditur præterea hinc, actiones quæ fiunt, priusquam habitu adipiscamur, voluptatem non parere, quoniam non sunt faciles & expeditæ, verùm cum aliqua difficultate ac labore fiunt. Hæc ex illa definitione patefiunt.
units.tr: From the definition just given, since we have said that the power must be whole and the habit firm, so that the action is unhindered, and that the object must be excellent and most outstanding, it follows how long pleasure can last. It remains for as long as the object and the faculty, or power of acting, remain whole. For if the object falls from its excellence, or the faculty is not keen and attentive, delight does not follow. Hence it happens that pleasures are often diminished when people are worn out by working, and the same happens when something is taken away from the object's excellence. It also appears why new things please so much: when something noble and outstanding first presents itself for contemplation, the mind looks at it keenly and attentively, and once it is known, the zeal slackens and so the pleasure ceases. But if something else fresh is placed beside the first object, the understanding again strains its zeal to contemplate it, and the pleasure returns; in this way we always delight ourselves with new things. It is further shown from this that actions performed before we have gained the habit do not produce pleasure, because they are not easy and ready, but are done with some difficulty and labour. These things are made plain from that definition.

units.la: Nunc per suas formas ac species est voluptas diducenda. Neque dubium est quin specie distinguantur inter se voluptates, cùm actiones discrepent: voluptas verò (ut scimus) actionis est perfectio, mutatáq; re perficienda, eius quoq; perfectio mutatur: sunt enim hæc ex his quæ inter se conferuntur: neq; vllus ignorat, aliam esse perfectionem arcæ, aliam domus, aliam stirpis, aliam hominis. Quare cùm actiones inter se diuisæ sint, ita voluptates different à quibus perficiuntur. Præterea inter se pugnant & vna extinguit seu impedit alteram, vnde fit vt distinguantur. Quæ fuerit ex musica, illam tollet quæ fluit ex sermonibus: quæq; sunt crassiores, aduersantur & impediunt intelligentiæ ac rationis delectationes. Deinde Actionum aliæ prauæ sunt, aliæ rectæ, aliæ mediæ. Vnde efficitur, vt voluptates, quæ sequuntur eas, varietatem & distinctionem habeant. Quod etiam ex eo fit, quia cupiditates actionum variæ sunt: nam si cupiditates variantur, multò magis voluptates, quæ plus coniunctæ sunt cum actionibus quàm desideria: nam desideria sæpe ab opere diuelluntur, cum voluptates à suis actionibus non queant separari. Certè aliæ sunt voluptates equorum, aliæ leonum, aliæ vrsorum, ergo & aliæ sunt hominum, neque solum eas habent diuersas ab alijs animatibus, verùm etiam inter se homines ipsi non habet eadem: nā quæ prauæ sunt, prauis placent: & quæ honestæ, probis arrident.
units.tr: Now pleasure must be unfolded through its forms and kinds. There is no doubt that pleasures differ from one another in kind, since the actions differ; and pleasure (as we know) is the perfection of an action, and when the thing to be perfected is changed, its perfection is changed too. For these are things that are compared with one another, and no one is unaware that the perfection of a chest is one thing, that of a house another, that of a plant another, and that of a man another. Therefore, since the actions are divided from one another, the pleasures that perfect them differ too. Moreover, they contend with one another, and one extinguishes or impedes the other, which is another reason they are distinguished. The pleasure that arises from music will drive out the one that flows from conversation; and the cruder pleasures oppose and hinder the delights of understanding and reason. Next, some actions are wicked, some right, and some indifferent. Hence it follows that the pleasures which follow them have variety and distinction. This also happens because the desires for actions are various; for if desires vary, much more do pleasures, which are more closely joined with the actions than desires are. For desires are often torn away from the work, whereas pleasures cannot be separated from their own actions. Certainly the pleasures of horses are one thing, those of lions another, those of bears another; therefore men also have their own, and not only do they have them different from those of other animals, but men themselves do not have the same pleasures among themselves: for what is wicked pleases the wicked, and what is honourable delights the upright.

units.la: Proinde iam satis (ut arbitror) confirmatum est, voluptates esse distinguendas. Quare prima esto hæc distinctio. Voluptatum quædam sunt puræ, quædam verò impuræ. Sumiturq; diuisio hæc ab operib, & actionibus, vt eorum aliquæ sunt circa obiecta magis à materia secreta, vel magis cum ea coniunctæ. Quod vt sit verum, à Galeno pulcherrimè declaratur in lib.2. de causis symptomatum. Inueniuntur, inquit, dolores & voluptates in omnib. sensibus. Dolores (vt dicit) ex eo fiunt, quòd sensus à sua constitutione ac natura-li statu li statu dimouentur, voluptates autem cum ad illam redeunt. Id vero ut li-quido magis pateat, per singulos ita excurrit sensus. Tactus dimouetur à (uo statu, si nimiÿ calores aut nimia frigora incidant, vel si ea incurrat quæ contundunt, arrodunt, rumpunt, &c. hinc illi dolores oriuntur. Gustus his iisdem dolet, qua cum tactu comunicat: ut vero gustus est, saporibus nimis acidis, acerbis, acribus & amaris dolet: nam his naturalis eius constitutio turbatur, & soluitur continuum. Olfactus turbatur ex dissolutione vaporum nimis acriū: nam illis continuum soluitur. Et auditus deiicitur à suo statu, voce aspera, graui, maxima & celerrima, nec non quouis strepitu violento. Visus deniq; cum incurrit in splendidissima lumina & colores: nam ista vim eius disgregant & dispergunt. Iis omnibus sensus dolent, quod per illa di-scedunt ab æquabili & quieto suo statu. Vicissim delectantur & voluptate capiunt, quando ad suum proprium naturalemq; statum reducutur. Quod visus experitur, quando se convertit ad fuscum colorem, quo vis eius con-gregatur in unumq; magis cogitur, vel cum intuetur blandos colores, ut vi-ridem, aureum & ceruleum seu cœlestem. Auditus leni & tarda voce. Ol-factus cum vapores hi resoluuntur, qui suavitate quadam roborant & con-firmant organa olfaciendi. Gustui sunt voluptati pingues & dulces sapo-res: oblectatur, etiamsi nonnihil ægrotemus, subacidis, & aliquantisper a-cerbis. Tactum iuvant qualitates temperatæ, lenes, tepidæ. Sic delectantur sensus & voluptate capiunt, cum reducuntur ad naturalem propriamq; co-stitutionem. Sed sciendū illos etiā voluptatem capere, licet offensi prius nō fuerint, aut remoti à naturali statu. Nam si offerat se blandus color aut iu-cunda vox, delectatur visus & auditus, licet prius à sua constitutione di-motus non fuerit. Pergit Galenus in his quæ dixit, atq; ostendit gradus esse maioris aut minoris puritatis in his actionibus sensuum & voluptatibus, e-amq; penes media quibus utuntur sensus, explicat. Lumen est per quod visus agit, auditus per aerem, olfactus per saporem. Subtilia ista sunt, et mi-nus habent crassioris & feculentæ materiæ. Infimum locum tenent ea circa quæ versatur tactus, crassa ea sunt & terrestria. Ascenditur ad gustum, is quoq; circa humores aqueos versatur, satis crassos. Olfactus elevatur ad vapores, aqua longe subtiliores. Auditui proprius est aer & quidem pu-rus. Venitur postremo ad lumen quod inter ea quæ sentiuntur est subtilissi-mum, ac multum habet puritatis: sed non ibi sistendum est, verum post ista occurrunt imaginatio, cogitatio, memoria, intelligentia, quæ versantur cir-ca similitudines & imagines rerū longe priores. Proinde apparet ex his pri-ma illa distinctio voluptatū, quod alia est purior, & alia crassior, & ex Galeno diuisionis fundamentum explicuimus.
units.tr: Therefore it is now, I think, sufficiently established that pleasures must be distinguished. So let this be the first distinction: some pleasures are pure, others impure. This division is taken from the works and actions, in that some of them are concerned with objects more removed from matter, or more joined with it. That this is true is most finely explained by Galen in the second book On the Causes of Symptoms. Pains and pleasures, he says, are found in all the senses. Pains (as he says) arise because the sense is moved from its constitution and natural state, but pleasures come when it returns to that. To make this clearer, he runs through the senses one by one. Touch is moved from its state if excessive heat or excessive cold falls upon it, or if things that bruise, gnaw, tear and so on touch it; hence those pains arise. Taste suffers from the same things with which it is in contact with touch; but as far as taste is concerned, it is pained by flavours that are too sour, bitter, sharp and bitter-tasting, for by these its natural constitution is disturbed and its continuity dissolved. Smell is disturbed by the dissolution of vapours that are too sharp, for by these its continuity is broken. Hearing is thrown from its state by a voice that is harsh, deep, very loud and very quick, and also by any violent noise. Lastly, sight is hurt when it meets with the most brilliant lights and colours, for these scatter and disperse its power. The senses suffer in all these cases, because through them they depart from their even and quiet state. Conversely, they are delighted and take pleasure when they are brought back to their proper and natural state. Sight experiences this when it turns to a dark colour, by which its power is gathered and forced more into one, or when it looks at pleasing colours, such as green, golden and sky-blue. Hearing (is delighted) by a soft and slow voice. Smell, when those vapours are released which strengthen and confirm the organs of smelling by a certain sweetness. Taste is pleased by rich and sweet flavours; it is delighted, even when we are somewhat unwell, by slightly sour and somewhat bitter things. Touch is pleased by temperate, gentle, lukewarm qualities. Thus the senses are delighted and take pleasure when they are restored to their natural and proper constitution. But it must be understood that they also take pleasure even if they were not offended beforehand or removed from their natural state. For if a pleasing colour or a delightful voice presents itself, sight and hearing are delighted, even though they had not been moved from their constitution before. Galen goes on in what he has said, and shows that there are degrees of greater or lesser purity in these sensations and pleasures, and he explains them according to the media which the senses use. Light is that by which sight acts, hearing acts through air, smell through vapour. These are subtle things and have less of the cruder and muddier matter. The lowest place is held by the things with which touch is concerned; these are gross and earthy. We rise to taste, which also deals with watery humours, fairly gross. Smell is raised to vapours, far more subtle than water. Hearing has air as its proper object, and indeed pure air. Finally we come to light, which is the most subtle of the things that are perceived and has much purity; but we should not stop there, for after these come imagination, thought, memory and understanding, which are concerned with likenesses and images of things, far more remote. Thus it appears from these things that the first distinction of pleasures is this: that one is purer and another cruder; and from Galen we have explained the ground of this division.

units.la: Ad hanc deinceps distinctionem sequitur alia, quod nonnulla voluptates corporeae sunt et aliae incorporeae. De corporeis in genere hoc affirmamus, quod neq; bonae sunt neq; malae, ut actiones etiam se habent circa potum, cibum & venerea. Quo vero ad species & partes, dicendum est, quod si modum excedunt, pravae sunt: sin vero continent se iustis ac debitis terminis, mediae sunt, quandoquidem illis homines & rectè possunt uti, hoc est, ex virtute atq; ad bonas & laudabiles fines. Illis etiam nonnunquam abutuntur, nempe malo consilio & ex vitio, ut Catilina, cum à deliciis & voluptatib. temperabat, nimirum ut patriam perderet. Natura tamen sua si æstimen-tur, potius bonae sunt civili bonitate quam malae.
units.tr: Next to this distinction follows another: some pleasures are bodily and others incorporeal. Of bodily pleasures we affirm this in general: that they are neither good nor bad, just as the actions concerned with drink, food and sexual pleasure are not. As to their kinds and parts, it must be said that if they exceed the measure they are wicked, but if they keep within just and due limits they are indifferent, since people can use them rightly, that is, from virtue and towards good and praiseworthy ends. Men also sometimes abuse them, namely from a bad purpose and from vice, as Catiline did when he abstained from delights and pleasures, clearly so that he might destroy his country. Yet if they are judged by their own nature, they are rather good with a civil goodness than bad.

units.la: Tertia jam occurrit voluptatum distinctio. Aliquæ sunt in quib.locū habet excessus, in aliis verò esse non potest, ut etiam evenit in actionibus. Quis enim unquam rectè aut iuste plus quam par sit fecit? ita & contemplationib. veritatis vel in physicis, vel in mathematicis, vel in divinis nemo potest plus quam par sit lætari, ac de ipsis voluptate capere: nec itidem de rectè fa-ctis & iustitiæ operib. Excedere autem possumus, irascendo, ambiendo, dan-do, audendo, non minus quam edendo, bibendo & procreando.
units.tr: Now the third distinction presents itself. There are some pleasures in which excess has a place, while in others it cannot be, as also happens in actions. For who has ever done what is right or just more than is fitting? So also in the contemplation of truth, whether in natural philosophy, in mathematics, or in divine things, no one can rejoice or take pleasure in them more than is fitting; nor likewise in right deeds and works of justice. But we can exceed in being angry, in ambition, in giving, in daring, no less than in eating, drinking and procreating.

units.la: Quarta deniq; distinctio est, quod voluptatum nonnullæ dicuntur, sim-pliciter & per se, quod non habeant dolores admixtos, neq; sunt dulces ex eo quod expleant & instaurent naturam exhaustam & deficientem: neque sunt uno tempore iucundæ, alio insuaves, at semper expetendæ atque desi-derabiles natura sua, & hæ potissimum sunt quæ mente percipiuntur. Aliæ verò mixtæ sunt, nempe cum doloribus, & ob id iucundæ sunt, quod naturam satisficentem reficiant & instaurent, ideoq; non semper omniq; tempore sunt optabiles.
units.tr: Lastly, there is a fourth distinction: some pleasures are called simple and absolute, because they have no pains mixed in with them, and they are not sweet because they fill up and restore a nature that is drained and failing. They are not pleasant at one time and unpleasant at another, but are always desirable and worth wanting by their very nature. These are chiefly the pleasures that are perceived by the mind. Other pleasures are mixed, namely those that come with pains. They are pleasant because they refresh and restore a nature that is being satisfied, and so they are not always and at every time to be desired.

units.la: His ita constitutis sumamus voluptates impuras, corporeas, quæ habent excessum, quæq; sunt mixtæ. Atq; de illis hæc prior esto propositio, Si modum excedant, omnino sunt fugiendæ: nam tales aut à prava natura oriuntur. Sunt enim proprietate naturæ quidam immanes, efferati & crudeles: alii vero immundi & omnibus modis intemperantes. Aut proveniunt hæ pravæ actiones & voluptates à vitioso habitu improba consuetudine in-ducto, ut in ebriosis, fagonibus, & libidinosis videmus. At turpibus itaq; ac improbis huiusmodi causis nil evenire potest, quod (ut diximus) non sit fugiendum. Ad hæc cum voluptates huius generis, quemadmodum jam est pa-situm, adinventæ sunt ut nobis instar medicinarum sint, cum sinimus eas modum egredi, tantum absunt ut medicinæ sint, ut vehementer nos lædat, & et quidem in omni bonorum genere, primumq; fortuna. Etenim quot sunt asoti, qui suis patrimoniis quamvis amplis & magnis absumptis coguntur infeliciter egere? Nil dico de bonis corporis, cum gula & venus longe plures interficiat quam gladius vel ordinarius aliquis natura morbus aut defectus.
units.tr: With these distinctions made, let us take up impure, bodily pleasures, which have excess and are mixed. Concerning these, let this be the first proposition: if they exceed the measure, they must altogether be avoided. For such pleasures arise either from a depraved nature or from a vicious habit induced by bad custom, as we see in drunkards, gluttons and lechers. Now nothing can come from such base and wicked causes that is not, as we have said, to be avoided. Moreover, although pleasures of this kind have been devised, as has already been laid down, to serve us in the manner of medicines, when we allow them to go beyond the measure they are so far from being medicines that they gravely harm us, and that in every kind of good, and first of all in our fortune. For how many spendthrifts are there who, once their patrimonies, however ample and great, have been used up, are forced to live in misery? I say nothing of the goods of the body, since gluttony and lust destroy far more people than the sword or any ordinary natural disease or defect.

units.la: Quin Galenus de semine lib. 2. scripsit, voluptas nonnunquam est per seipsam causa dissoluendi vitalem vigorem, & firmitudinem. Ac reperti sunt nonnulli, qui animam exhalarunt ob nimiam voluptatem. Quod si omnis rerum abusus est euitandus, immoderatae voluptates huius generis prorsus fugiendae, sunt, cum iam hoc modo non medeantur corpori, sed illud vehementissime destruant. Taceo de bonis animi, cum nil magis noceat prudentia, nilq; plus labefactet iudicium rectum agendarum rerum, quam hae immodicae voluptates. Ratio quam adduxi, quod his crassis & immoderatis voluptatibus omnia genera bonorum hominis labefactentur, a Cicerone scripta est in suo Hortensio, qui liber desideratur. Eius tamen verba referam ut ab Augustino recitantur, lib. 4. contra Iulianum, cap. 14. An vero voluptates corporis expetendae, quae vere & graviter a Platone dicta sunt illecebrae esse atq; esca malorum? Quae enim confectio inquit valetudinis, quae deformatio coloris & corporis, quod turpe damnum, quod dedecus, quod non euenit, atq; eliciatur voluptate? Cuius motus ut quisq; est maximus, ita est inimicissimus philosophiae. Congruere enim cum cogitatione magna voluptas corporis non potest. Quis enim cum utatur voluptate ea, qua nulla possit maior esse, attendere animo, inire rationem, cogitare omnino quicquam potest? Quis autem tantus est gurges, qui dies ac noctes, sine ulla minimi temporis intermissione, velit ita moueri suos sensus, ut moventur in summis voluptatibus? Quis autem bona mente praeditus, non mallet nullas omnino nobis a natura voluptates datas? Haec ille. Qua eius sententia comprehenduntur damna, quae ab his voluptatibus corporis modum excedentibus inferri soleant.
units.tr: Indeed Galen, in the second book of his work On Semen, wrote that pleasure is sometimes in itself a cause of dissolving vital vigour and firmness. And some have been found who breathed out their souls from excessive pleasure. If every abuse of things is to be avoided, then immoderate pleasures of this kind are altogether to be shunned, since they no longer heal the body but very violently destroy it. I say nothing of the goods of the mind, since nothing harms prudence more, and nothing weakens the right judgement about what is to be done, than these immoderate pleasures. The reason I have adduced, that by these gross and immoderate pleasures every kind of human good is weakened, was written by Cicero in his Hortensius, a book that has been lost. Yet I shall give his words as Augustine recites them, in the fourth book against Julian, chapter 14: "Are bodily pleasures really to be desired, which Plato has rightly and gravely called the enticements and bait of evils? For what wasting of health, what disfiguring of colour and body, what shameful loss, what disgrace does not arise from pleasure? And the greater its movement, the more hostile it is to philosophy. For great bodily pleasure cannot agree with serious thought. Who, while enjoying that pleasure than which none can be greater, can attend to the mind, reckon, or think of anything at all? Who is so great a whirlpool that, day and night, without any interruption even for a moment, would wish his senses to be stirred as they are in the greatest pleasures? Who, endowed with a good mind, would not rather that no pleasures at all had been given us by nature?" So he. By his opinion are comprehended the harms that are usually brought by those bodily pleasures that exceed their measure.

units.la: Sed dixeris, Ista ratio si valeat, damnabit voluptates quae oriuntur ex contemplatione, nec non illam quae nascitur ex iustis actionibus, quoniam & corpus laeditur nimio studio & contemplatione, atq; ob sua probitate Socrates periit, nec non & Aristides. Respondetur, hoc esse per accidens: quoniam in malos viros incurrebat Socrates. Et spiritus capitis, qui cogitationi seruiunt, aliquando nimis consumi.
units.tr: But you may say: if this argument holds, it will condemn the pleasures that arise from contemplation, and also those that arise from just actions, since the body too is harmed by excessive study and contemplation, and Socrates perished because of his uprightness, and Aristides too. The answer is that this is so only by accident, since Socrates fell in with wicked men; and the spirits of the head, which serve thought, are sometimes used up too much.

units.la: Sed repetet argutus quispiam, istud item esse per accidens quo ad corporis voluptates, quae scilicet ex his actionibus nascuntur, quae corpus labefactant & nostra bona, quod ipsae per seipsas non facerent.
units.tr: But some clever person will return and say that this too is only by accident with regard to bodily pleasures, namely those that arise from these actions, which weaken the body and our goods, although the actions themselves do not do so in themselves.

units.la: Verum ad hoc respondetur, non semper fieri ut ob iustitiam quis pereat neq; semper contemplationem ledere. At hæ voluptates crassæ ac mixtæ quoties modum excedant, fieri non potest quin dent damnum: itaq; non utrinq; par habetur similitudinis lasio[?].
units.tr: To this the answer is that it does not always happen that someone perishes on account of justice, nor that contemplation always harms. But these gross and mixed pleasures, whenever they exceed the measure, cannot fail to do harm. Therefore the comparison is not equal on both sides.

units.la: Sed hoc nonnullis videtur difficile, quòd sint hæ voluptates fugiendæ, cùm voluptas per seipsam bona sit & optabilis. Quare ut hoc effugiant, dicere solent reuera non esse voluptates, sed tantum videri, & licet apparent, non tamen à prudentibus voluptates debere existimari. Quemadmodum alba non dicuntur quæ talia lippis apparent, neque dulcia vel amara quæ sic esse pronuntiant ægroti. Mihi nihilominus non videtur ita respondendum, quoniam & Plato & Aristoteles illas voluptates appellant, eisq; definitio superius allata reuera conuenit. Ideò potius ad argumentum dicerem, voluptatem quidem natur a sua bonam & expetendam, at non ex omnibus rebus, ut famem cupimus explere, at non ex quouis cibo. Ditari quoq; vellent iusti homines, at non ex quouis lucri genere. Sanitatem quoq; desyderamus, verùm non ex quouis medicamenti genere: Ita & voluptates volumus, at non eas quæ oriantur ex inhonestis, turpibus, & corpus omniaq; nostra bona ledentibus actionibus.
units.tr: But this seems difficult to some, that these pleasures are to be avoided, since pleasure in itself is good and desirable. Therefore, to escape this, they are accustomed to say that these are in truth not pleasures but only seem to be, and that, although they appear so, the wise ought not to judge them to be pleasures. Just as things are not called white which look white to people with bleary eyes, nor sweet or bitter things which sick people pronounce to be so. Nevertheless I do not think we should answer in this way, since both Plato and Aristotle call those things pleasures, and the definition given above truly applies to them. Rather, I would reply to the argument that pleasure is indeed good and desirable by its nature, but not from all things, just as we desire to satisfy hunger, but not with any food. Righteous men also wish to be made rich, but not by any kind of gain. We likewise desire health, but not from any kind of medicine. So we also want pleasures, but not those that arise from dishonourable, shameful actions that harm the body and all our goods.

units.la: At cùm hoc voluptatum genus & damnosum sit et fugiendum, qui fit ut à tam multis expetatur? Quia voluptas sua natura quid habet in se diuinum, & ab omnibus expetitur. Verùm usu venit, ut cùm multis natura nō sit adhuc absoluta & confirmata, ut in pueris, vel cùm malis & pravis habitibus sint prediti, ut ebriosi & libidinosi, fallantur, & voluptates quaerant ubi non deberent. Quare mirandum est Epicurus, qui à pueris argumentum sumit, qui naturæ adhuc sunt imperfectæ atq; nulla virtute præditi, ideoq; facile possunt decipi. Deinde cogitandum est, homines perpetuò laborare atq; diversis exercitijs fatigari, ideoq; ut reficiantur ac recreentur, ad voluptates se converterunt, cumq; honestas, puras & simplices habere non possint, his crassioribus & damnosis voluptatibus expleri. Et homines compositi naturam habent, neq; unam & simplicem, ideo fit, ut varia genera voluptatum amplectantur: illas quandoq; capiant quæ ad animum pertinent, interdum illas quæ sunt corporis, quandoquidem tam ex animo quàm corpore constant. Quinipsum corpus quia plures habet humores, variisq; sensibus est præditum, idcirco modo ad has voluptates modo ad illas impellimur, ut humores incitant, vel ut varia obiecta in sensus incurrunt. Deus verò cùm sit unus & simplicissimus, una eademq; simplici & æterna voluptate fruitur. Ad has verò corporis maximè propensi sunt iuuenes & melancho-lici[?]: illi, quoniam dum augetur natura eorum, perturbantur humores, & natura fatigatur atq; conuellitur: ideoq; tanquam ad medicinam quādam & recreationem confugiunt ad voluptates. Melancholicos identidem atra bilis diuexat, mordicat, & non sinit quiescere: ideò fatigati, ad voluptates, quibus sese nonnihil instaurent & exhilarent, conuertuntur. Unde ap-paret naturam & Deum ipsum non inutiliter has voluptates, ut earum immoderatus vsus sit euitandus, nostro generi dedisse. Nam vita per illas ducitur commodius, & opera vitæ necessaria & conseruationem generis libentius obimus, medicamurq; promptius nostris quotidianis defectibus. Quin iuuenes honestis & moderatis quibusdam voluptatibus ad honesta officia & præclaras virtutes incitantur, doloribus vero à vitijs & sceleribus absterrentur. Et Augustinus addit, has infimas voluptates Dei quosdam esse vestigia, et naturæ felicitatis ac summi boni tenuem umbram, qua possumus incitari ad illius vehemens desyderium. Valent itaque ad nos expergefaciundos, in quibus tamen insistendum non est, verū ad meliora potius assurgendum. Utq; in his non maneamus, Deus adeò bonus est ut amara permulta his voluptatum generibus asperserit.
units.tr: But since this kind of pleasure is harmful and to be avoided, how is it that it is desired by so many? Because pleasure, by its nature, has something divine in it, and it is desired by all. But it comes about through use that, since in many people nature is not yet complete and confirmed, as in children, or because they are endowed with bad and wicked habits, as drunkards and lechers are, they are deceived and seek pleasures where they ought not. Hence Epicurus is to be wondered at, who draws his argument from children, whose natures are still imperfect and endowed with no virtue, and who therefore can easily be deceived. Next we must consider that men labour continually and are worn out by various exercises, and therefore, so that they may be refreshed and recreated, they turn to pleasures; and since they cannot have honest, pure and simple pleasures, they are filled with these grosser and harmful pleasures. Also, man has a composite nature, not a single and simple one, and so it happens that he embraces various kinds of pleasures: at times he takes those that pertain to the mind, at other times those that belong to the body, since he consists of both mind and body. Moreover, because the body itself has many humours and is endowed with various senses, we are driven now to these pleasures and now to those, as the humours stir us or as various objects fall upon the senses. But God, since he is one and most simple, enjoys one and the same simple and eternal pleasure. Young people and melancholics are most inclined to these bodily pleasures: the young, because while their nature is growing, their humours are disturbed and their nature is worn out and racked; therefore, as if to some remedy and recreation, they flee to pleasures. Melancholics are repeatedly troubled and gnawed by black bile, which does not let them rest; so, being worn out, they turn to pleasures by which they may somewhat restore and cheer themselves. Hence it appears that nature and God himself have given these pleasures to our kind, not uselessly, though their immoderate use is to be avoided. For life is led more comfortably through them, and we undertake the necessary works of life and the preservation of the species more willingly, and we are more readily restored from our daily failings. Indeed, young people are spurred by certain honest and moderate pleasures to honourable duties and excellent virtues, while they are turned away from vices and crimes by pains. Augustine also adds that these lowest pleasures are certain traces of God, and a faint shadow of nature's happiness and of the highest good, by which we can be stirred to a vehement desire for that good. So they are of value for waking us up, yet we ought not to remain in them, but rather to rise to better things. And so that we should not remain in them, God is so good that he has mingled many bitter things with these kinds of pleasure.

units.la: De illis voluptatibus puris, simplicibus, incorporeis, quaeq; non habent excessum, hæc esto propositio. Repudiari non debent, sed cum sint præstantiores, ad summi boni naturam non parum accedunt: nam per se ipsa non per aliud expetuntur. Dixi accedere propemodum ad summi boni rationem, quia revera in voluptate etiam huius generis non est summum bonum. id enim (ut ostendemus) in actione perfectissima situm est, ad illam autem perpetua comes adiungitur voluptas. Unde à summo bono diuelli non potest, ut non comprehendatur in eius ratione. Concedimus plane illam ab omnibus expeti, quando nullus est qui non appetat & viuere, & bene viuere. Utq; viue-re est operari, sic bene viuere est in optima uersari actione, ad quam cum ad iuncta sit voluptas præstantissima omnes illa expetunt, quando id optant cuius est perpetua comes. Optima vero actio esse non potest, nisi circa nobilissimum versetur obiectum, à quo nostra perfectio ut à fonte pendet. Quod ut perspicue videatur, sciendum est, obiecto præstantissimo nos perfici, ut ab efficienti causa, qua nostra mens et voluntas impellitur, seu ad ipsum alliciTUR: ut ipsius voluptate perficimur, quæ affectus est & qualitas qua noster animus perfunditur. At in dubium nonnulli reuocant, An voluptas propter vi-tam seu vita propter voluptatem sit expetenda. Et ut quæ dicantur ex altera parte omittam, quod mihi videtur sic expono. Voluptas propter vi-tam expetitur, non è diuerso. quoniam voluptas oritur ex eo, quod actio cum natura congruit, & id sentimus atq; cognoscimus: quare id ante omnia expetedum est, ut actio habeatur perfectissima. Nec ignorat quisquam perfectionem institutam propter id quod perficit, praesertim cum sua natura nullam constantiam habeat. Et omnes vident cibum ipsum praestabiliorem esse suo condimento. At de voluptate tot atq; huiusmodi sint dicta.
units.tr: Here is the proposition about those pleasures that are pure, simple and incorporeal, and that have no excess. They should not be rejected; and since they are more excellent, they come not a little near to the nature of the chief good, for they are sought for their own sake and not for the sake of something else. I said that they come almost near to the account of the chief good, because in truth even pleasure of this kind is not the chief good. For the chief good (as we will show) lies in the most perfect activity, and a lasting pleasure is joined to that activity as its companion. Hence pleasure cannot be separated from the chief good, so that it is not included in its account. We plainly concede that pleasure is desired by all, since no one fails to desire both to live and to live well. And as to live is to act, so to live well is to be engaged in the best activity, to which the most excellent pleasure is joined. Since all desire that to which pleasure is a lasting companion, they all desire pleasure. But the best activity cannot exist unless it is concerned with the most noble object, on which our perfection depends as on its source. So that this may be seen clearly, it must be understood that we are perfected by the most excellent object as by an efficient cause, by which our mind and will are moved, or by which they are drawn to it; so that we are perfected by its pleasure, which is the affection and quality with which our soul is filled. But some call in doubt whether pleasure is to be sought for the sake of life, or life for the sake of pleasure. To pass over what may be said on the other side, this is how I explain it to myself. Pleasure is sought for the sake of life, and not the reverse; since pleasure arises from the fact that an activity agrees with nature, and we perceive and recognise this. Therefore that must above all be sought, so that the activity may be most perfect. Nor does anyone fail to recognise that a thing established exists for the sake of what it perfects, especially since in its own nature it has no constancy. And everyone sees that the food itself is more valuable than its seasoning. But enough has been said of pleasure.

units.la: Quomodo vero, quae affert Aristoteles cum sacris conveniant, facile est videre. Inquit primo huiusmodi opinionem de crassioribus voluptatibus plurium esse, ac vulgarium hominum, quod idem Christus docuit, affirmās viam perditionis latam esse, ac multos per eam ire. Addit praeterea sic opinantes esse φορτικοτάτους[?]. Et in Isaia scimus ad Achazum impium regem dictum, An parum est vobis molestos esse hominibus, quòd molesti estis & Deo meo? Sunt, ait Aristoteles, mancipia. Et Dominus, Qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati. Necnon Petrus, Quisq; servus eius efficietur à quo est victus. Beluinam vitam inquit illos deligere. Atque in sacris Psalmis habetur, Homo quum in honore esset, comparatus est iumentis insipientibus, & similis factus est illis. Hieremias quoque, Hinniebat quisque ad uxorem proximi sui. Et rursus in Psalmo, Nolite fieri sicut equus & mulus quibus non est intellectus. Qui sic putant, scribit Philosophus, tuentur se authoritate principum, qui viuunt more Sardanapali. Neq; à diuinis literis hoc discrepat, in quibus legimus fere semper talem fuisse populum, quales habuissent reges. Et in Osea dicitur, Qualis populus talis sacerdos. In proverbijs cap.29. Cum regnauerit impius, multiplicatur transgressio. Atq; in Euangelijs de Herode, cum Magi venissent Hierosolymam, habemus non tantum illum fuisse turbatum, sed cum eo universam urbem. Postremò concluditur in his crassioribus voluptatibus non posse reponi summum bonum: quod & Apostolus confirmat ad Corinth. Esca ventri & venter escis, hunc & has destruet Deus. Ipse vero Christus de voluptate procreandi, In regeneratione non nubent neq; ducent, verum sicut angeli Dei erunt.
units.tr: How the things that Aristotle brings forward agree with the sacred writings is easy to see. He says first that this opinion about the cruder pleasures belongs to most people and to the common sort, which Christ himself taught, when he affirmed that the way to destruction is broad and that many go by it. He adds further that those who think so are most vulgar [φορτικωτάτους]. And we know from Isaiah that it was said to Ahaz the impious king: "Is it a small thing for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?" They are, says Aristotle, slaves. And the Lord says: "Whoever commits sin is the servant of sin." Peter too: "Whoever is overcome by someone, to him he will become a slave." Aristotle says that such men choose a brutish life. And in the sacred Psalms it is written: "Man, when he was in honour, was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them." Jeremiah also: "Each neighed after his neighbour's wife." And again in a Psalm: "Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding." Those who think so, the Philosopher writes, shelter themselves under the authority of princes, who live after the manner of Sardanapalus. Nor does this differ from the divine letters, in which we read that the people were almost always such as their kings were. And in Hosea it is said: "Such as the people, such the priest." In Proverbs 29: "When the wicked rule, transgression increases." And in the Gospels, concerning Herod, when the Magi had come to Jerusalem, we read that not only he was troubled but the whole city with him. Lastly, it follows that the chief good cannot be placed in these cruder pleasures; which the Apostle also confirms in 1 Corinthians: "Food for the belly and the belly for food; God will destroy both this and these." And Christ himself, speaking of the pleasure of procreation: "In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God."

units.la: Elegantes vero & agentes honorem, ciuilis quippe vitae fere is est finis.
units.tr: Men of distinction who seek honour; for the end of civic life is almost this.

units.la: De voluptatibus prius egit, nunc de honoribus. Ac merito ista coniungū-tur: cum utrunq; illorum comitetur actiones, licet diversa ratione. Cū enim actio cū natura congruit, idq; animadvertimus voluptateq; exhilaramur, & ad easdem, cum probae fuerint & iustae ac honestae adiungitur honor. Primum suo more proponit sententiam, deinde confutat & quidem ratione geminā, quae suis locis demonstrabuntur.
units.tr: He treated the pleasures first; now he treats honours. And rightly these are joined, since both accompany actions, though in different ways. For when an action agrees with nature, and we notice this and are cheered by the pleasure, honour is joined to these same actions, when they are upright, just and honourable. He first sets out the opinion in his usual way, then refutes it, and indeed with a twofold reason, which will be demonstrated in their places.

units.la: Sectatores huius opinionis dicitesse χαρίεντας nō vulgares & belluinos, ut priores, sed gratiosos, quod ex bene administrata repub. & commodis publicis aut comparatis aut seruatis gratiam sibi conciliarint. Ita enim fit ut ciuiles ob suos publicos labores quos ob rem communem suscipiunt, ineant populorum gratiam, unde gratiosi & elegantes dicuntur, emergunt-que à communi hominum sorte. Vtq; dicit Eustratius, ἀχαρις is est & dicitur, qui nihil aliorum causa facit, sed tantum sibi viuit: è diuerso autem χαρίεντες, qui sunt efficientes illustrium & praeclarorum facinorum: quare iure meritoq; dicuntur ἰδεμ πραξ[?]
units.tr: The followers of this opinion are said to be graceful men [χαρίεντας], not common and brutish like the former, but agreeable, because by the well-ordered government of the commonwealth and by the public advantages either gained or preserved they have won favour for themselves. For it happens that citizens, on account of their public labours which they undertake for the common good, win the favour of the peoples; whence they are called agreeable and elegant, and rise above the common lot of men. And as Eustratius says, a man is ungracious [ἀχαρις] who does nothing for the sake of others but lives only for himself; on the other hand, those are graceful [χαρίεντες] who bring about illustrious and distinguished deeds. Wherefore they are rightly and deservedly called ... [the Greek here is corrupt in the scan].

units.la: Huius vitæ finis feré videtur esse honor. Athenis honoris ergò nonnulli ædificabant muros, alij naues instruebant, & aliqui alebant suis stipendijs milites: cumq; tantum spectarent fructum honoris, ciuilis vitæ is feré videbatur finis. Feré dicitur, quia non esse debet, nec est quo ad omnes: nā sunt aliqui ciuiles qui suas actiones non ad honorem dirigunt, sed potius ad honestatem. Exempla vtriusq; affert Eustratius. Achilles potius breuem delegit sibi vitam apud Homerum cum gloria, quàm longam & obscuram. Vitæ itaq; præposuit gloriam seu honorem. Socrates è diuerso paratam habuit furtiuam vitam cùm esset in carcere: nam potuit fugere si voluisset, quod recusauit cùm honestati atq; iustitiæ aduersaretur. Quare propter honestatem & virtutis ergò delegit præsentem mortem. Dixit tamen iure Aristoteles feré, quoniam plerunq; itafit: & multi, licet non rectè, honorem appellarunt præmium virtutis.
units.tr: The end of this life seems to be almost honour. At Athens some built walls for the sake of honour, others fitted out ships, and some supported soldiers at their own expense; and since they looked only to the fruit of honour, this seemed to be almost the end of civic life. It is said "almost", because it ought not to be so, and it is not so for everyone; for there are some citizens who do not direct their actions to honour but rather to honesty. Eustratius brings forward examples of both. Achilles, in Homer, chose for himself a short life with glory rather than a long and obscure one; so he put glory or honour before life. Socrates, on the other hand, had a secret escape ready while he was in prison; for he could have fled if he had wished, but he refused, since it was opposed to honesty and justice. Therefore, for the sake of honesty and virtue, he chose present death. Nevertheless Aristotle spoke rightly, "almost", since it usually happens so; and many, though not rightly, have called honour the reward of virtue.

units.la: Sed cùm tam ex honore consequuto quàm ex aliis actionibus vitæ congruis voluptas capiatur, quomodo hæc opinio à superiori diuulsa est, & non simul tractatur? Dicemus, quoniam si loquutus esset prius de voluptate in vniuersum, ratio esset efficax. At solum de illa impura corporea & mixta egit: ad cuius actiones, quibus nimirum innititur, non sequitur honor. Ideò seorsim hæc tractantur, cùm ad diuersa genera actionum adiungantur.
units.tr: But since pleasure is taken both from honour obtained and from other actions fitting to life, how is this opinion separated from the previous one and not treated together with it? We reply: if he had spoken first of pleasure in general, the reasoning would have been effective. But he treated only of that impure, bodily and mixed pleasure; and honour does not follow from the actions on which it rests. Therefore these are treated separately, since they are joined to different kinds of actions.

units.la: Sed uidetur leuius esse bono eo quod quærimus. Nam in his potius qui honore afficiunt, quàm in eo qui honore afficitur, esse uidetur. Summum autem bonum proprium quid talecq; esse uaticinamur, ut auferri facilè nequeat.
units.tr: But it seems to be lighter than the good we are seeking. For it seems to lie more in those who bestow honour than in the one who is honoured. Yet we conjecture that the proper chief good is something such that it cannot easily be taken away.

units.la: Hic iam incipit confutatio. Quod ego dixi leuius, Græce ἐπιπολαιότερον. Et nonnulli verterunt, remotius aut distantius. sed reuera id significatur quòd natat, in summo fluctuat, & apparet in superficie, idcirco dixit le-vius. In summa id est, quod altius non hæret, profundius nõ egit radices: unde neq; solidum neq; firmum neq; stabile potest haberi. Qui autem ita fuerint, in nobis leviter inhærent, & quia malè cohærent, ideò facilè adimuntur. Propterea de priori Aristoteles dicit, quòd nobis non hæreat sed potius actio sit honorantis, non eius qui recipit honorem: non enim actio eius à no-bis ipsis proficiscitur, sed ab honorante: & in manu eius positum est, non autem in potestate illius qui honore afficitur. Verba Aristotelis hæc sunt: Nā in his potius qui nos honore afficiunt quàm in eo qui honore recipit esse videtur.) Verum id porrò est, quemque nostrum in seipso habere, cum recti & iusti sumus, causas quæ allicere possunt & provocare alios, ut nos in honore habeant, sed illæ causæ non sunt necessariæ, atq; potest fieri ut ex ipsis non prodeat effectus. Laborant enim interdum homines invidia: quandoq; arbitrantur honorem collatum in alios existimationem suam ledere: nonnunquam verò ignorant, neq; satis intelligunt, quæ actiones merentur honores: & fit interdum, ut satietate quadam bonos fastidiant, ut egregij sint & præclari, atq; sese convertunt ad novos alios qui nuper emerserint ornandos. Proinde cum honor in nostra potestate non sit, facilè auferitur. Quod proculdubio longè alienissimum est à summi boni natura. Unde subditur a Philosopho. Summum autem bonum proprium quid, talecq; esse vaticinamur, ut auferri facile nequeat.) Non dicit absolutè ἀφαιρέτον[?], sed δυσαφαίρετον[?]. Hanc sententiam non video quomodo Peripatetici queant ad suum extremum bonum accommodare, cùm illi bona fortuna atq; corporis admisceant. Et certè dum vivimus, facilè possumus in alteram partem commutari. Vnde sanè dictum illud sapientis extat: Felix ante obitum nemo. Auguramur, inquit, μαντευόμεθα[?].) Ideò sic loquitur quia nondum hac de re definierat, & nunc sub his initijs quodammodo ait se ita coniecturam facere. Quam inde ortam puto coniecturam quòd sic audiebat passim alios de summo bono loqui. Sed quicquid sit, id manifestum est, philosophorum felicitati hanc sententiam non convenire. Quæ enim dum hic vivimus haberi potest beatitudo, potest, proculdubio morte finiri. Vt autem in proclivi sit omnibus mori, neminem arbitror ignorare. Deinde si propria debet esse felicitas & ἀυσαφαίρετος[?], ut inquit Aristoteles, Papistæ quomodo iubent nos perpetuò incertos esse ac dubitare an recepti simus in gratiam, & condonata sint nobis peccata, cùm ista sit Christianorum felicitas quam hic habere possunt, ut dicit Dauid & Paulus, Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, & quorum tecta sunt peccata?
units.tr: Here the refutation now begins. What I have called "lighter" is in Greek [ἐπιπολαιότερον]. Some have translated it "more remote" or "more distant", but what is really meant is that which floats, plays on the surface, and appears on the top; that is why he said "lighter". In short, that is what does not cling deeply, does not strike its roots more deeply; whence it can be held neither solid nor firm nor stable.
