Those things, however, which are such, cling to us lightly, and because they hold on poorly, they are easily taken away. Therefore Aristotle says of the first that it does not cling to us, but rather that it is the action of the one who honours, not of the one who receives the honour; for its action does not proceed from ourselves but from the one who honours, and it is placed in his hand, not in the power of the one who is honoured. The words of Aristotle are these: "For it seems to lie rather in those who bestow honour on us than in the one who receives honour." It is true, however, that each of us has in himself, when we are upright and just, the causes that can attract and provoke others to hold us in honour; but those causes are not necessary, and it can happen that no effect comes from them. For men sometimes labour under envy; sometimes they think that honour bestowed on others diminishes their own esteem; and sometimes they do not know, and do not sufficiently understand, which actions deserve honours; and it sometimes happens, through a certain satiety, that they grow weary of good men, even of the excellent and distinguished, and turn to new men who have lately emerged to be honoured. Therefore, since honour is not in our power, it is easily taken away. This is undoubtedly very far removed from the nature of the chief good. Hence the Philosopher adds: "We conjecture that the proper chief good is something such that it cannot easily be taken away." He does not say absolutely [ἀφαιρέτον], but [δυσαφαίρετον], hard to take away. I do not see how the Peripatetics can apply this opinion to their ultimate good, since they mix in goods of fortune and of the body. And certainly while we live we can easily be changed into the other state. Whence that saying of the wise man stands: "No one is happy before his death." "We divine," he says [μαντευόμεθα]. He speaks thus because he had not yet defined the matter, and now at this beginning he says that he is making a conjecture in this way. I think the conjecture arose from his hearing others speak everywhere of the chief good in this manner. But whatever the case, this is clear: this opinion does not agree with the happiness of the philosophers. For the blessedness that can be had while we live here can undoubtedly be ended by death. And that it is easy for all to die, I think no one is ignorant. Next, if happiness ought to be one's own and not [ἀναφαίρετος], as Aristotle says, how do the Papists order us to remain forever uncertain and in doubt whether we have been received into grace and whether our sins have been forgiven, since that is the happiness of Christians which they can have here, as David and Paul say: "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered"?

units.la: Forma Syllogismi sic potest componi: Quicquid non inhaeret in nobis neque proprium est, sed facile potest adimi, non est summum bonum. Honor est huius generis, Quare illi non hoc tribuendum ut fit summum hominis bonum. Est sane obseruandum in his absurdarum opinionum confutationibus, Ariftotelem consueuisse proprietates rerum dicendarum colligere, quibus postea uti possit in rei expositione. Colligebat itaq; prius, cum ageretur de voluptate, summum bonum esse non posse nobis commune cum belluis. Nunc vero vult esse proprium quod reipfa nobis inhaereat, & difficulter adimi possit.
units.tr: The form of the syllogism can be put together thus: whatever does not inhere in us and is not our own, but can easily be taken away, is not the highest good. Honour is of this kind. Therefore it is not to be attributed to man as his highest good. In these refutations of absurd opinions it must indeed be observed that Aristotle was accustomed to gather the properties of the things to be discussed, which he could then use in explaining the matter. Earlier, when pleasure was under discussion, he gathered that the highest good cannot be common to us and the beasts. Now, however, he wants the good to be what really inheres in us and can hardly be taken away.

units.la: Praeterea honores persequi uidentur, ut aliis fi-dem faciant se bonos esse.
units.tr: Moreover, they seem to pursue honours so that they may make others believe they are good.

units.la: Hic aliam texit rationem, Illud nimirum esse summum bonum quod in aliud non dirigitur. at inquit, hi ciuiles dum honores expetunt, aliud prose-cto spectant, nimirum ut boni habeantur & virtute praediti. Quare opor-tet eos plus virtutibus & probitati deferre quam honori, quandoquidem ipsum huc dirigunt. Ex qua Philosophi confirmatione aliam profecto sum-mi boni proprietatem elicimus, nempe ut sit extremum, neq; aliud se melius habeat. Et apparet honorem offerri bene ac recte viuentibus ut virtutis & iustitiae testimonium.
units.tr: Here he weaves in another argument: that is surely the highest good which is not directed towards something else. But he says that these civic men, while they seek honours, certainly aim at something further, namely to be held good and endowed with virtue. Therefore they must defer more to virtues and uprightness than to honour, since they direct honour towards these. From this confirmation of the Philosopher we surely draw out another property of the highest good, namely that it is the final end, and that nothing else is better than it. And it appears that honour is offered to those who live well and rightly as a testimony of virtue and justice.

units.la: Quapropter à prudentibus & his qui se noscant, atq; ob uirtutem, petunt honores.
units.tr: Wherefore honours are sought from prudent men, and from those who know themselves, and on account of virtue.

units.la: Vt honor sit solidus, praestari debet à prudentibus qui sciant quid nam inter homines honore sit dignum: idcirco à stultis vel à prauis hominibus laudibus ornari, non solet esse gratum. Requiritur deinde ut simus noti his à quibus honore afficimur. Nam licet aliqui norint, quae illorum prudentia sit, probos iustos & bonos tantum honorandos, oportet ut bene norint nos eiusmodi. Quare ab exteris & ignotis, quiq; de nobis nihil norunt, honor parui penditur. Additur postremo virtutis ergo desyderari honorem, quo-niam illa ex electione videtur esse, ideoque propria, deinde stabilis, quaeque differamus à caeteris, & qua praediti multum aliis queamus prodesse.
units.tr: That honour may be solid, it ought to be bestowed by prudent people who know what is worthy of honour among men; so praise from foolish or wicked people is not usually welcome. It is required next that we be known to those by whom we are honoured. For although some know what prudence is, that only the upright, just and good are to be honoured, it is necessary that they know us to be such. Therefore honour from strangers and unknown persons, who know nothing of us, is held in little esteem. Lastly it is added that honour is desired for the sake of virtue, since virtue seems to come from our own choice and so is our own, and then stable, and by it we differ from others, and being endowed with it we can greatly benefit others.

units.la: Forma rationis in secunda figura potest componi hoc modo:
units.tr: The form of the argument in the second figure may be framed in this way:

units.la: Summum bonum in aliam finem non potest dirigi, Honor dirigitur in aliam finem, Igitur honos non est summum bonum.
units.tr: The highest good cannot be directed to another end. Honour is directed to another end. Therefore honour is not the highest good.

units.la: Manifestum igitur ex horum sententia virtutem esse meliorem.) Hac porro sententia concludit, honorem, non ponendum extremum hominis bonum, cum aliquid eo sit praestabilius, nempe virtus, cuius dignitati concedat oportet, nisi patroni eius vehementer sint pertinaces. At in Aristotelis verbis quaedam videtur vel pugna vel inconstantia: prius enim statuit civiles de quibus loquitur, finem sibi extremum honores praescribere, cuius eorum propositi nescio an postea oblitus, an de ipso non cogitans, illos ait honores persequi ut aliis fidem faciant se bonos esse, ideoque a prudentibus & his quibus cogniti sint, virtutis ergo laudari cupiunt. Haec procul dubio secum dissentiunt, honorem habere pro summo bono, deinde ipsum propter virtutem cupere. Huic scrupulo sic occurrendum censeo, ut cogitemus hoc praesertim nomine sententiam istam civilium oppugnare, quod a seipsis discordent. Quod ut absurdum est, ita omni studio evitari a sapientibus oportet, quamobrem & illa thesis est deserenda, quam sit necesse tale absurdum parere ut nobiscum discordemus. Honorem summum esse bonum illorum thesis erat. Et ne arbitremur illos ob probitatem aut virtutem honores expetere, testimonium ab ipsis extorquet, qui passim fatentur se a mal-is commendari nolle, sed tantum a prudentibus & causa virtutis ac rerum bene gestarum. Proinde hoc argumento ἐλεγχῶ manifesta habetur, nec ei ullo pacto resisti potest.
units.tr: Clearly, then, from the opinion of these men, virtue is better. (By this opinion he concludes that honour is not to be put as the highest good of man, since something is more excellent than it, namely virtue, to whose dignity honour must yield, unless its defenders are very obstinate.) But in Aristotle's words there seems to be some conflict or inconsistency. For first he states that the civic men he is speaking of set honours before themselves as their ultimate end; then, whether he forgot this afterwards, or was not thinking of it, I do not know, he says that they pursue honours so that they may win credit with others that they are good, and therefore desire to be praised by wise men and those who know them, for the sake of virtue. These things plainly disagree with each other: to hold honour as the highest good, and then to desire it on account of virtue. I think this difficulty should be met as follows: we should consider that this doctrine of the civic men is attacked chiefly on this ground, that they contradict themselves. As this is absurd, so wise men must take great care to avoid it; for this reason also that thesis must be abandoned, since it necessarily produces such an absurdity that they disagree with us. Honour being the highest good was the thesis of those men. And lest we think they seek honours for the sake of uprightness or virtue, Aristotle extracts a testimony from them, since they everywhere confess that they do not wish to be commended by bad men, but only by wise men and for the sake of virtue and well-done deeds. Therefore by this argument the elenchus [ἔλεγχος] is plainly established, and it cannot in any way be resisted. ## On honour.

units.la: SED ut quod tractatur liquidius patefiat, de natura honoris & quae ad ipsum attinent, nonnulla dicam. Ante omnia eius explicetur definitio. Aristoteles primo Rhetoricorum vult significationem esse opinionis quae de probitate alicuius habeatur, & ea signis externis constat. Huic definitioni, quo perfecta sit, addendam censeo causam finis, quam cum ex philosophis haurire nequeam, ex nostra theologia mutuabor. Ideo testamur signis apertis ut bene de probis viris sentiamus, ut in ipsis Deus honoretur, omnis iustitia ac probitatis author. Deinde quo illorum authoritas & exemplum aliis prosit. Iam omnes honoris causas complectimur: forma est significatio, declaratio testimonium, nostri sensus de bonis viris. Efficiens attingitur cum probitatem cuiuspiam adiecimus: etenim illa incitantur homines ad bene sentiendum. Materia vero, in his omnibus erit signis, quibus iustis & bonis viris testimonium damus. Atque ista cum sint multiplicia, loco iam adducto Rhetoricorum non tacentur, monimenta, imagines, praesidentia, carmina, sepulchra, victus ex publico, dona: nos vero addamus aperire caput, loco cedere, assurgere, &c. Utq; ista omnia multa numero sunt, honoris partes, forma aut species totidem constituentur, eritq; distinctio penes materiam. Fines utique nos adiecimus, ut in deum redundet hoc nostrum testimonium, & ut bona exempla iustorum reddamus honoribus nostris magis illustria, quoue his qui bene se gerunt addatur authoritas, & illa complures alij iuuentur. A sensu definitionis huius non longe discessit Augustinus, qui ait, Gloriam esse iudicium hominum bene de hominibus opinantium. His addidimus iudicij huius externa testimonia, & quibus hominibus ea danda sint expressimus, probis inquam & recte se gerentibus. Desyderatur autem ut in Aristotele, ita etiam in Augustino, qui debeant esse hi opinantes, qui suam opinionem significent. Eos certe decet ut ex hoc loco Ethicorum deprehendimus, prudentes & qui nos bene cognorint. Quintilianus adhuc breuius & compendio quodam sic rem explicuit, Gloria, inquit, est consentiens laus bonorum: ubi ea vox bonorum tam laudatis quàm laudantibus coniungi potest, nam utrofq; bonos esse oportet. Quod ut magis perspicuum fiat, honores ita secabimus, ut eorum quosdam leues & adumbratos faciamus, qui populari duntaxat rumore conflantur, & hi cum à sano iudicio no proueniant, neq; firmi sunt neq; illis habentur, quibus praestandi essent. Alij vero (ut aiebat Quintilianus) ex bonorum consensu prodeunt, quare solidi sunt, & illis probi duntaxat honestantur. Priores autem illos adeo leues & inconstantes experimur, ut eodem propemodum die nonnullos & probari et condenari a populo videas. Quare id genus boni qui vitreu appellauit, quod caducu admodum sit & fragile, non multum a vero aberrauit.
units.tr: But so that what is being treated may be made clearer, I shall say some things about the nature of honour and what pertains to it. First of all its definition should be explained. Aristotle, in the first book of the Rhetoric, holds that it is the expression of an opinion held about someone's uprightness, and that it consists of external signs. To this definition, to make it complete, I think the cause of the end should be added, which, since I cannot draw it from the philosophers, I shall borrow from our theology. We bear witness by open signs so that we may think well of upright men, so that God, the author of all justice and uprightness, may be honoured in them. Then, so that their authority and example may benefit others. Now we embrace all the causes of honour: the form is the signification, the declaration, the testimony of our feeling about good men. The efficient cause is touched upon when we add the uprightness of someone: for men are roused by it to think well. The matter, however, will be in all these signs by which we give testimony to just and good men. And since these are many, they are not passed over in the Rhetoric passage just cited: monuments, images, presidencies, poems, tombs, maintenance at public expense, gifts; and we may add to these uncovering the head, giving way, rising, etc. Since all these are many in number, they will constitute as many parts or forms of honour, and the distinction will rest on the matter. We have added the ends so that this our testimony may redound to God, and so that the good examples of the just may be made more illustrious by our honours, and so that authority may be added to those who conduct themselves well, and many others may be helped by it. Augustine did not depart far from the sense of this definition, when he says that glory is the judgement of men who think well of men. To this we have added the external testimonies of this judgement, and we have expressed to whom they are to be given: to the upright, I mean, and those who conduct themselves rightly. But, as in Aristotle, so also in Augustine, it is wanting who these thinkers must be who express their opinion. Certainly they ought to be, as we gather from this place of the Ethics, wise men and those who know us well. Quintilian explained the matter still more briefly and in a kind of summary: glory, he says, is the agreeing praise of good men; where that word "good" can be joined both to those who are praised and to those who praise, for both ought to be good. To make this clearer, we shall divide honours thus, so that we make some of them light and shadowy, which are formed merely by popular rumour; and these, since they do not come from sound judgement, are neither firm nor held by those to whom they should be given. Others, however (as Quintilian said), arise from the agreement of good men, and therefore are solid, and only the upright are honoured by them. We find the former so light and inconstant that you may see some men both approved and condemned by the people on almost the same day. Therefore he who called this kind of good "glassy", because it is very fleeting and fragile, did not stray far from the truth.

units.la: Verùm quæstio se nunc offert an honos ut de illo syncero & constanti loquamur, bonum sit honorantis vel eius cui adhibetur? Hoc Seneca tractauit ad Lucillum Epistola 103. Vtriusque bonum esse affirmo. Est sane laudatis, cum eius iusta & recta sit actio. Nec dubium arbitror, omnem actionem probam eius esse bonum, cuius fuerit actio. Deinde quoniam is qui honore afficitur, in seipso probitatem habet, iustitiam & rectitudinem, quibus & boni & prudentes alliciuntur & prouocantur ad eum commendandum, ideo eius quoque bonum dicitur honos, nam eius initium & causam in se habet. Praeterea illius honoris ipse fructum percipit, quando authoritas eius crescit, fitq; validior, ad suadendum alijs quae decent, & illos in officio continendos. Tertiò quoque ob id illius bonum est, quoniam dum bonos, rectos & gratos iudices animaduertit, de rebus a se præclare gestis iu-ste sentire, vehementer laetatur. Rationem itaque attuli cur tam laudati quàm laudantis bonum esse honorem iudicem. Neque propterea pugno cum Aristotele, qui eum ait in illo esse qui honore afficit, non in eo qui honorem recipit. Quoniam ipse (ut in definitione iam allatum est) honorem dicit significationem opinionis & sensus, ideoq; recte indicat, cum tam opinio quam significatio eius ab honorante proficiscantur, & illo ut fundamento quodam & subiecto nitantur. Ego vero principium, quo cietur haec opinio, & is excitatur sensus in animis prudentium, spectato, & ad haec opinionis istius fructus, & eain homine laudato esse video, maior inquam authoritas & laetitia. Neq; mea haec definitio tantum in honoribus locum habet, verum non aliter de probato iudicio praetoris, & justa sententia quando jus dicit existimandum est: nam haec propria sunt illius bona, quae simul ei bono sunt secundum quem judicatur: & de justitia non secus dicere debemus, ea sane bonum est eius qui fit justus, at etiam illi bono est, cui ex ipsa justitia redditur & soluitur quantum debetur. His exemplis liquido apparet quomodo fit honor bonum quoddam tam ad eum qui habetur in precio quam ad illum qui ipsum tribuit attinens.
units.tr: But now the question presents itself: whether honour, when we speak of that sincere and constant kind, is a good of the one who honours or of the one to whom it is paid. Seneca treated this in Letter 103 to Lucilius. I affirm that it is a good of both. It is certainly a good of the one who is praised, since his action is just and right. Nor do I think it doubtful that every upright action is a good to the one whose action it is. Then, since he who is honoured has in himself uprightness, justice and rectitude, by which both good and wise men are attracted and stirred to commend him, therefore honour is also called his good, for it has its beginning and cause in him. Moreover, he himself receives the fruit of that honour, when his authority grows and becomes stronger, to persuade others to what is fitting and to keep them in their duty. Thirdly, it is also a good for him for this reason: while he perceives that the judges are good, upright and grateful, and judge rightly about the deeds he has done well, he rejoices greatly. I have therefore given the reason why honour is judged to be a good both of the one who is praised and of the one who praises. Nor on that account do I quarrel with Aristotle, who says that it is in him who bestows honour, not in him who receives it. For he himself (as has already been stated in the definition) says that honour is the signification of opinion and feeling, and therefore he rightly indicates that both the opinion and its signification proceed from the one who honours, and rest upon him as a kind of foundation and subject. But I, looking at the principle by which this opinion is stirred, and by which that feeling is aroused in the minds of wise men, and at the fruits of this opinion which I see to be in the man who is praised, namely greater authority and joy, say the same. Nor does my definition hold good only for honours; rather, the same must be judged of the approved judgement of a magistrate, and of a just sentence when he pronounces law: for these are the proper goods of that man, which are at the same time a good to him in accordance with whom judgement is given. And we must speak no differently of justice: it is certainly a good of the one who becomes just, but it is also a good to that person to whom, from justice itself, what is owed is rendered and paid. From these examples it is clear how honour is, in the same way, a certain good pertaining both to the one who is held in esteem and to the one who bestows it.

units.la: Dubitant identidem an ad verum solidumq; honorem sufficiat, vnius probi & prudentis viri testimonium, an potius complurium significatio exigatur. Dicendum arbitror, juxta naturam honoris veri atq; synceri, vnius prudentis & probi viri, quiq; nos recte norit, testimonium esse satis, quoniam in vno qui sit huiusmodi, omnes alios similes eius habemus. Vna enim est vox, & vnum judicium omnium prudentium, & proborum virorum. At ad id ut illustretur exemplum, utque authoritas crescat & confirmetur laudati, vnius testimonium minime valet, quoniam ad hoc plurimum fama & nomen proficit, quae multorum testimonia requirunt.
units.tr: They sometimes ask whether the testimony of one upright and prudent man is enough for true and solid honour, or whether the agreement of many is required. I think that, according to the nature of true and genuine honour, the testimony of one prudent and upright man, who knows us rightly, is sufficient, since in one such man we have all others like him. For there is one voice and one judgement of all prudent and upright men. But to make an example more widely known, and to increase and confirm the praise, the testimony of one man is by no means enough, since fame and reputation, which require the testimony of many, contribute most to this.

units.la: Id modo videndum est, an unquam a virtutibus & rectè factis disiungatur honos? aliqui affirmant & aliqui negant. Certè vulgatissima est inter doctos sententia, honorem sequi virtutem, ut umbram corpus. Quod simile judicio meo quaestionem explicat. Umbra quidem corpus comitatur: at non semper eodem modo, nonnunquam antecedit, aliquando jungitur a latere, atq; incedit unà, interdum vero pone sequitur. Ita quorundam virtus sub ipsis eius initijs habetur in honore, aliorum non suspicitur nisi cum aucta est & perfecta. Deniq; videas aliquos non prius honoratos quam esse desierint: nam tunc sentire homines aliquando consueuerunt licet sero, quantum bonum amiserint. Quod antiquitus prophetis & Apostolis, nostris quoque temporibus multis justissimis principibus, bonis pastoribus, & pijs concionatoribus euenisse scimus: dum eorum fuit copia contemnebantur: cum vero sublati iam essent, tum incredibile sui desyderium excitarunt. runt. Comitatur itaq; honos virtutem, at non semper eodem gradu: interdum ante, nonnunquam simul, & saepius ponè. Et ad hac testimonium & significatio prudentium verae virtuti & iustis actionibus nunquam deest, nisi cum prudentes & qui ista viderint & novthings erint esse desierint.
units.tr: The only question to consider is whether honour is ever separated from virtue and right deeds. Some affirm it and some deny it. Certainly the most widely held opinion among the learned is that honour follows virtue as a shadow follows a body. This comparison explains the question in my judgement. The shadow indeed accompanies the body, but not always in the same way: sometimes it goes before, sometimes it walks alongside and proceeds together with it, and at other times it follows behind. So the virtue of some is held in honour from its very beginnings, while the virtue of others is not esteemed until it has grown and been perfected. Finally, you may see some who are not honoured until they have ceased to be, for then men have sometimes been accustomed to perceive, though late, how great a good they have lost. We know that this happened of old to the prophets and Apostles, and in our own times to many most righteous princes, good ministers and godly preachers: while there was plenty of them they were despised, but when they had now been taken away, they aroused an incredible longing for themselves. So honour accompanies virtue, but not always at the same pace: sometimes before, sometimes together, and more often behind. Moreover, the testimony and approval of prudent men is never lacking to true virtue and just actions, except when the prudent, and those who have seen these things and know them, have ceased to be.

units.la: Nunc tandem ad rem propius accedamus, & mecum unà cogitate, An desyderium honoris in bonis an in malis ponendum sit? Nonne commendabimus ipsum, cum à Deo & à natura sit insitum? cum Deus ipsum promittat suis, & quidem non parum saepe, Glorificantes me, glorificabo, inquit. Et presbyteri à Paulo duplici honore digni pronuntiantur. Et ideo videtur Deus in animis nostris hunc appetitum infevisse, ut ad bene rectèque viuendum magis ac magis incitemur. Nec temerè abijciendum est vulgatum proverbium, Honos alit artes, & virtus laudata crescit. Deinde nullus, qui vel micam pietatis habet, inficiari potest, omnia nostra opera sic esse institu-enda, ut cum Deo tum hominibus probari possint, nempe ut homines, illis visis, Deum (quemadmodum par est) glorificent. Quare cum honos ob res bene gestas in nobis non resideat, sed in ipsum Deum redundet, quotquot eius gloriae cupidi sunt, ut omnes esse debemus, hoc saltem nomine honorem possumus expetere.
units.tr: Now let us come closer to the matter and consider together: should the desire for honour be placed among the good or among the bad things? Shall we not commend it, since it is implanted in us by God and by nature? Since God promises it to his own, and indeed quite often: "Those who glorify me, I will glorify," he says. And elders are declared by Paul worthy of double honour. Therefore God seems to have implanted this appetite in our minds, so that we may be incited more and more to live well and rightly. Nor should the common proverb be rashly cast aside: "Honour nourishes the arts, and praised virtue grows." Next, no one who has even a grain of piety can deny that all our works must be so ordered that they can be approved both before God and before men, namely so that men, seeing them, may glorify God, as is fitting. Therefore, since honour arising from good deeds does not remain in us but returns to God himself, all who desire his glory, as all of us ought to, may seek honour on this ground at least.

units.la: Praeterea quis non debeat cupere, ut omnes fratres in suo fungendo munere atque officio non desint? Deus verò id omnibus praecepit ut honore prosequantur parentes, ac eadem causa magistratus, mandatq; per Paulum, Honore vos inuicem praevenientes. item 1. Timoth. 5. Honora viduas, quae verè viduae sunt. 1. Pet. 2. Omnes honorate, fraternitatem diligite. ac de Epaphrodito ad Philipp. 1. cap. 2. Et qui huiusmodi sunt in honore habetote. Possum adducere loca similia non pauca, sed cum ista sint satis, patet cum honore afficitur quispiam eo dignus, diuinis mandatis obtemperari: quod ut fiat, qui probi sunt & bene se gerunt nonne debent commendare, ac ea re laetari, nec non optare ut fiat? Cur, Fiat voluntas tua sicut in coelo & in terra, oramus? His adde homines honore prosequendo bo-nos praemia & bona consequi, Vt fis, inquit Deus, longaevus super terram: & vicissim contemnendo, malam sibi rem accersunt, ut pueri qui derise-runt prophetam Helisaeum ab ursis discerpti sunt. Quod cum ita sit, proximum non diligit, qui non cupiat illum has vitare poenas, & ista commoda & praemia consequi. Vt itaque dilectione Dei optare possumus debitos honores, ita impellimur ad istud idem ea charitate qua proximum debemus complecti. Quod id vel maximè confirmat Dauid Psal. 15. cùm de illo ageret, qui locum in domo Dei ac aeterno habitaculo esset habiturus, inter ca-teras eius virtutes id commemorat, In cuius oculis despicitur reprobus & timentimentes Dei glorificat. Proinde cum vita æterna citra controversiam proximis sit optanda, id expetendum est ardentissimis votis, ut pii, quique Deum reverentur, habeantur in honore, quod est hoc honoris genus, illos in precio habere, illorum commertio delectari, existimationem ipsorum tueri, & illorum necessitatibus alacriter succurrere. Quæ omnia cum hodie à tam multis frigide fiant, qui pii sunt non possunt non vehementer dolere, atque optare ut tandem quemadmodum iussit Deus efficiatur. Augustinus in Soliloquijs libro primo, capite undecimo sentit, Authoritas cum ex honoribus crescat, eaque multum faciat, ad persuadenda honesta, & pellicien-dos homines cum ad vera dogmata, tum ad vitæ sanctitatem, sunt optandi. Quin & propter illos quos debemus nostro ministerio iuuare, si videri-mus nostram authoritatem vilescere, illam iustis honestisque rationibus debemus tueri, ne scilicet reddatur inutilis. Hucillud [?] spectat quod Paulus ad Timotheum scribebat, Iuuentutem tuam nemo contemnat. Nec parum proficit ad nos confirmandos cum recte agimus, commendatio proborum si accesserit. Ut enim philautia laboramus plerique omnes, in rebus & actionibus facile decipimur, & quæ minus laudabilia facimus, plurimi æstimamus. Idque quia non raro accidit, in agendo rudiores magis dubios & ambiguos reddit. Quibus iisdem, honos, laus & approbatio, si externis signis exhibita fuerit, vehementer prodest. Etenim his rebus eorum stabilitur animus & iudicium. Qui vero dubii non sunt, imo quæ agunt, recta esse compertum habent, cum ornantur iusto genere honoris à prudentibus & bonis viris, non possunt non mirifice gaudere ac sibi gratulari, quòd tam bonos & rectos iudices nacti fuerint. Quamobrem his quoque honores prosunt. Nec ab Aristotelis sententia nostra hæc discrepant: etenim quanquam is honorem summum bonum esse negat, non tamen ipsum à bo-{o}norum censu excludit. Et his quæ diximus de firmo & solido honore nihil est tam consentaneum, quàm illum fore summum, quem fideles extremo iudicij tempore à Christo sunt habituri, cum ipsis dicet, Venite benedicti patris mei, &c. Nam ea laus à iudice sapientissimo proficiscetur, cui omnis iustitia est notissima: neque nostra ulla ex parte queunt ipsum latere.
units.tr: Moreover, who ought not to desire that all brethren should not be lacking in performing their office and duty? God indeed commands all people to honour parents, and for the same reason magistrates, and through Paul he commands: "Going before one another in honour" (Rom. 12.10). Likewise 1 Tim. 5: "Honour widows who are truly widows." 1 Pet. 2: "Honour all men, love the brotherhood." And concerning Epaphroditus, Phil. 2: "Hold such men in honour." I could bring forward not a few similar passages, but these are enough. It is clear that when someone worthy is honoured, the divine commands are obeyed. Should not the upright, who behave well, commend this, rejoice in it, and wish that it may happen? Why do we pray, "Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven"? To these add that by honouring good men people obtain rewards and blessings, as God says: "That you may be long-lived upon the earth" (Exod. 20.12); and conversely, by despising them they bring evil upon themselves, as the boys who mocked the prophet Elisha were torn apart by bears. Since this is so, whoever does not wish that his neighbour avoid these punishments and obtain these advantages and rewards does not love him. Therefore, just as by the love of God we can desire the honours that are due, so we are driven to the same thing by the charity with which we ought to embrace our neighbour. David confirms this most of all in Psalm 15, when he speaks of the man who shall dwell in the house of God and in the eternal tabernacle; among his other virtues he records this: "In whose eyes the reprobate is despised, but he glorifies those who fear the Lord." Accordingly, since eternal life is beyond dispute to be desired for our neighbours, this must be sought with the most ardent prayers, that the godly, who revere God, be held in honour. This kind of honour consists in holding them in esteem, delighting in their company, protecting their reputation, and readily coming to the aid of their needs. Since all these things are now coldly done by so many, those who are godly cannot but grieve greatly and wish that at last it may come about as God has commanded. Augustine, in the first book of the Soliloquies, chapter eleven, holds that authority grows from honours, and that it counts for much in persuading what is honourable and in drawing men both to true doctrines and to holiness of life, and so authority is to be desired. Indeed, on account of those whom we ought to help by our ministry, if we see our authority becoming cheap, we ought to defend it by just and honourable means, so that it may not be rendered useless. To this belongs what Paul wrote to Timothy: "Let no one despise your youth" (1 Tim. 4.12). The commendation of upright men also contributes not a little to strengthen us when we act rightly. For most of us, through self-love, are easily deceived in our deeds, and we value highly what we do that is less praiseworthy. And since this often happens, it makes the more inexperienced doubtful and uncertain in acting. For such people honour, praise and approval, if shown by outward signs, are of great benefit, since by these things their mind and judgement are steadied. Those who are not doubtful, but know for certain that what they do is right, when they are adorned with the proper kind of honour by prudent and good men, cannot but rejoice greatly and congratulate themselves that they have found such good and upright judges. Therefore honours help these people too. Nor do these remarks differ from the opinion of Aristotle: for although he denies that honour is the highest good, he does not exclude it from the number of goods. And nothing agrees so well with what we have said about firm and solid honour as that the highest honour will be that which the faithful shall receive from Christ at the last day of judgement, when he will say to them, "Come, blessed of my Father," etc. For that praise will proceed from the most wise judge, to whom all righteousness is most well known, and nothing of ours in any way can be hidden from him.

units.la: Proinde his iam conclusum & demonstratum satis puto, moderatum honorum appetitum non esse vitio vertendum: quia tamen facile in hoc à multis erratur, & locus est lubricus, idcirco nonnulla sunt explicanda quæ oportet cauere, ne dum virtutem sectamur in vitia turpiter incidamus. Idin-primis videndum est, quod Aristoteles Ethnicus vidit, ne honorem propter seipsum scipsum[?] expetamus: hoc enim esset ex medio bono extremum facere, atque his frui quibus debemus uti. Tendat itaq; is appetitus tum ad gloriam Dei, tum ad fratrum aedificationem. Proxime caueamus, ne anxia cura sollicite-mur honoris causa, quia facile perturbaretur animus. Quod multi, qui ci-viles habiti sunt, cum non vitarint, præ laudum cupiditate quodam modo insanierunt. Scimus quo furore Alexander Macedo per universum orbè fere actus fuerit, absq; modo & ratione gloriam quærens, qui tandem eò est adductus ut alios mundos præter hunc expugnandos existimaret. Unus Pelleo iuvenì non sufficit orbis. Quo eodem morbo laborans Iulius Cæsar, manus iniecit patriæ, ac eius iura & libertatem temerè violauit. Sit igitur moderatum hoc desyderium, & certis iustisq; terminis finiatur. Et honoribus percipiendis Augustini sequamur consilium, Neq; totum accipias, inquit, quod offertur, nec totum respuas: nam qui reijcit quicquid honoris defera-tur pro rebus à se rectè ac præclarè gestis, dona Dei videtur quasi deprimere ac nolle agnosci, quod sanè à vera pietate alienum est. Et vicissim qui am-plectitur, quantum oblatum fuerit, non parum sæpe limites modestiæ trans-gredietur. Est præterea spectandum, ne delatum honoris genus maius sit quàm hominum dignitas queat ferre. Quod ubi accidit, non est toleran-dum: ibi enim Deus irascitur, seuereq; vindicat suos honores ab hominibus usurpatos. Herodes est grauissimè punitus, cum populus ei voces non homi-ne dignas acclamasset, sed quæ Deo conuenirent. Eademq; culpa merito dä[?]-nantur Domitianus, Nero, & plerique alij Cæsares insolentissimi, qui iam nō ut principes, sed instar Dei se voluerunt coli. Quæ sunt Dei reddatur Deo, & honores humanos rectè ac moderatè boni viri cum offeruntur percipiant. Seruetur etiam iustus & rectus modus in honoribus asseq̃uendis. tantum una commendatur via & ratio, eaq; est bonis effectionibus, quas Græci dicunt κατορθώματα[?]. Quæ hypocritæ assimulant, dumq; se pios & san-ctos conantur declarare signis externis, à populo habentur in pretio. Verum de illis Christus dixit, Receperunt mercedem suam. Alij verò feruntur eò usque, ut emant honores: quod sanè vitium omnibus legibus iustis damna-tur: & à Latinis dicitur ambitus: est enim turpissimum largitione corro-gare populi suffragia. Hac de re in ff. extant multa ad legem Iuliam de ambitu. Conuicti damnabantur infamia & multa etiam pecuniaria. Suntque pœnæ huius vitij nonnunquam in Romana Republica auctæ: quoniam vitium sine modo grassabatur. Quin & Ecclesiastici Canones le-ges Romanos imitati sunt: et quia iste vitium in ecclesia inoleuit plurimū, & hodie passim regnat, multa fuerunt sancita quæ habentur prima, q.1.per totam quæstionem, & lib. 5. decretalium, de Simonia, & in alio titulo, ne prælati vices suas vel ecclesiæ sub annuo censu concedant. Qui dignitates ecclesiasticas vendunt, Ghiezi puerum Helizæi sectantur, & qui emunt, Simonem magnum referunt. Neq; precium est solum pecunia, sed verba & cuiusuis generis obsequia, si præstentur in eum finem, vt Ecclesiastici honores obtineantur. Adeoq; patres hoc vitium sunt persequuti, vt contra Simoniacos admiserint accusatores quosuis, etiam infames, turpes, meretrices, & alios id genus homines, quod in aliis criminibus deferendis minimè toleratur. Est postremò confyderàdum, vt honoribus adeptis bene vtamur: quod idcirco dixerim, quia passim aliquos videre licet, qui eis abutuntur ad potentiâ obtinendam, ad opes comparandas, aut voluptates consequendas, ad quæ omnia viam sibi per dignitates, & honores tam ciuiles quàm ecclesiasticos patefaciunt.
units.tr: Therefore I think enough has now been concluded and shown that a moderate desire for honours is not to be blamed. But because many go wrong here easily, and the ground is slippery, some things must be explained that we ought to guard against, lest while we pursue virtue we fall shamefully into vice. First of all we must take care, as the pagan Aristotle also saw, that we do not seek honour for its own sake: for this would make an intermediate good into an ultimate end, and would enjoy things we ought only to use. So let that desire be directed both to the glory of God and to the edification of our brothers. Next, let us take care not to be anxiously troubled by cares about honour, since the mind would easily be disturbed. Many who were considered civil men, when they did not avoid this, went in a way mad through a desire for praise. We know with what frenzy Alexander the Macedonian was driven across almost the whole world, seeking glory without measure or reason, until at last he was brought to think that other worlds besides this one had to be conquered. For the Pellaean youth one world was not enough. Julius Caesar, labouring under the same disease, laid hands on his country and rashly violated its laws and liberty. Let this desire therefore be moderate, and bounded by certain just limits. In receiving honours, let us follow the counsel of Augustine: "Do not accept everything that is offered, nor reject all of it." For he who rejects whatever honour is conferred on him for things he has done rightly and well seems, as it were, to depress the gifts of God and refuse to acknowledge them, which is certainly foreign to true piety. And conversely, he who embraces as much as is offered will often overstep the limits of modesty. Moreover, one must watch that the kind of honour conferred is not greater than the dignity of the man can bear. When this happens it is not to be tolerated, for then God is angry and severely avenges his honours usurped by men. Herod was most severely punished when the people acclaimed him with words not fit for a man but fit for God. For the same fault Domitian, Nero and many other most insolent Caesars are rightly condemned, who wanted to be worshipped not as princes but as gods. "Render to God what is God's," and let good men receive human honours rightly and moderately when they are offered. A just and right measure must also be kept in seeking honours. Only one way and method is commended, namely good deeds, which the Greeks call right deeds [κατορθώματα]. Hypocrites imitate these, and while they try to show themselves pious and holy by external signs, they are held in esteem by the people. But of such people Christ said, "They have received their reward." Others go so far as to buy honours. This vice is condemned by all just laws, and the Latins call it ambitus, for it is most shameful to win the votes of the people by bribery. Much on this matter is found in the Digest under the Julian law on ambitus. The convicted were condemned to infamy and also to fines. The penalties for this vice were sometimes increased in the Roman republic, since the vice ran rampant without measure. Indeed the ecclesiastical canons also imitated the Roman laws. Since this vice has grown very strong in the Church and today reigns everywhere, many things have been enacted, which are found in the first part, distinction 1, throughout the whole question, and in book 5 of the Decretals, under simony, and in another title, that prelates should not grant their offices or the revenues of the Church for an annual rent. Those who sell ecclesiastical dignities follow Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, and those who buy them resemble Simon the Magician. Nor is the price only money, but also words and services of every kind, if they are rendered for the purpose of obtaining ecclesiastical honours. So greatly did the Fathers pursue this vice that against simoniacs they admitted any accusers at all, even infamous and shameful persons, prostitutes and others of that sort, which in bringing charges for other crimes is by no means tolerated. Lastly, one must consider that, once honours are obtained, we should use them well. I say this because one can see many everywhere who abuse them to gain power, to acquire wealth, or to obtain pleasures, for to all these ends dignities and honours, both civil and ecclesiastical, open the way.

units.la: Hæc visa sunt recensenda, quo ad eos qui honores percipiunt. Nunc paucis de his est dicendum, quorum interest alios honore afficere: nam hi quoq; monendi sunt, quandoquidem varie ac multipliciter in hoc peccari potest.
units.tr: These things seemed worth reviewing as regards those who receive honours. Now a few words must be said about those whose business it is to confer honour on others, for these too must be admonished, since one can sin in this in various and manifold ways.

units.la: Nullos arbitror ambigere, vt hi grauiter errent, qui iustos & conuenientes honores probè ac rectè se gerentibus denegant: quos tamen complures esse videmus. hisq; illi sunt multò deteriores, qui honoris loco inuidia illos prosequuntur, detrahunt etiam meritis, torquentur & dolet si eis bene procedere quicquam viderint. Hi sanè iniusti, & ingratissimi habendi sunt.
units.tr: I think no one doubts that those err gravely who deny just and fitting honours to those who conduct themselves well and uprightly, and we see that there are many such people. Yet those are much worse who, instead of honour, pursue such people with envy, detract from their merits, and are tormented and grieved if they see anything going well for them. These are certainly to be regarded as unjust and most ungrateful.

units.la: Nonnulli vero satis liberaliter honore bonos viros afficiunt, sed id agunt ab eis quærentes vicissim aliquod beneficium, fauorem, aut auxilium. Et hi proborum virorum benefacta non multùm curant, sed tantum illorum bona quærunt. Vnde suum honorem potius vendunt quàm pro virtutibus rependant. Et alios nouimus, qui honores probis exhibere satis parati sunt, sed peruerso iudicio id faciendo vtuntur: nam bona illa quæ suspicere debèrent, negligunt, & quæ minoris momenti sunt, admirantur. Si quis bene curet ecclesiam, sanam doctrinam afferat, sanctè viuat, & bona passim edat exempla, hoc nomine parui faciunt: sed idem si callidum aut prudens consilium det ad rem augendam, vel quippiam ignotum monstret in agricultura vel in re medica, ibi eum mirantur, & laudibus in cœlum euehunt. Sunt etiam qui adulentur, & quidem turpissima vitia nominibus virtutum ornantes. Neq; desunt, qui dandis honoribus modū non seruant, sed illos vel maligne deferunt, vel maiores quàm oporteat.
units.tr: Some indeed honour good men quite generously, but they do so seeking in return some benefit, favour or help from them. These care little for the good deeds of upright men and seek only their goods. Hence they sell their honour rather than repay virtues with it. And we know others who are quite ready to show honour to the upright, but use it with a perverse judgment, for they neglect the good qualities they ought to esteem and admire what is of lesser importance. If someone cares well for the Church, teaches sound doctrine, lives holily and gives good examples everywhere, they make little of this. But if the same man gives a shrewd or prudent counsel for increasing wealth, or shows something unknown in agriculture or medicine, there they marvel at him and raise him to heaven with praises. There are also those who flatter, and indeed adorn the most shameful vices with the names of virtues. Nor are there lacking those who do not keep a measure in conferring honours, but bestow them either spitefully or more than is fitting.

units.la: Hæc omnia quæ recensui sunt diligenter cauenda: quæ cum fusè satis recensuerim, nunc superèst vt ostendam quomodo Aristotelis doctrina literis diuinis consentiat, vel ab ipsis discrepet. Principio quidem cum honos dici-tur non esse summum bonum, cum sacris literis nullum est dissidium: quia summum bonum plus æquo non potest appeti: at in honoribus expetendis moderandum est appetitui. Nolite, inquit, Dominus Apostolis, vocari rab-bi, aut magistri, aut patres, verum id potius curate ut alij inserviatis, idq; submisso & moderato animo. Deinde Servator noster nō paterētur suos fran-dari summo bono, cum ad id venerit ut nos felices faciat. Sed nos quodam-modo opprobrijs exponit, & suos prædixit fore cotumelijs afficiendos: quos exemplo suo consolatur, qui semetipsum exinaniuerit, & forma serui assumpta factus fuerit obediens usq; ad mortem crucis. Quodq; statuitur no-strum summum bonum debere firmum esse, proprium, et non facile mobile, cum eo facit quod Paulus inquit, ideo salutem nostram & iustificationem constare gratia & fide, non autem operibus, ut firma sit promissio. Honores vero facile auferri, testantur divina litera: nam Christus dixit, Nullū pro-phetam cum honore in patria sua esse. Videmusq; sanctos nonnunquam honore affectos, à populo mox ad supplicium postulatos & raptos. Demūq; ho-norem ex illorum bonorum esse genere qui alio referantur, divina oracula tradunt: quoniam, dicebat Dominus, bona opera vestra videant alij & glorificent patrem vestrum. Ubi videmus gloriam & honorem non tantum in nobis debere quiescere, sed in divinos honores & laudes referri.
units.tr: All these things I have listed must be carefully guarded against. Having listed them at sufficient length, it now remains for me to show how Aristotle's teaching agrees with the divine writings, or differs from them. First, that honour is not the chief good: there is no disagreement with Holy Scripture on this, since the chief good cannot be desired beyond measure, whereas in seeking honours our desire must be moderated. "Do not," says the Lord to the apostles, "be called rabbi, or teachers, or fathers; rather take care to serve others, and to do so with a humble and moderate mind." Then, our Saviour would not allow his people to be defrauded of the chief good when he came to make us happy. Rather, he exposes us in a way to reproaches, and foretold that his own would be subjected to insults. He comforts them by his example, for he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. As for the teaching that our chief good must be firm, our own, and not easily moved, it agrees with what Paul says: that our salvation and justification rest on grace and faith, not on works, so that the promise may be firm. But that honours are easily taken away the divine writings testify, for Christ said, "A prophet has no honour in his own country." And we see that holy men, when at times they have been honoured, were soon demanded by the people for punishment and seized. Finally, the divine oracles teach that honour belongs to the class of good things that are referred to another, since the Lord said, "Let others see your good works and glorify your Father." Here we see that glory and honour must not rest only in us, but must be referred to divine honours and praises.

units.la: Constat igitur horum sententia honore præsta-biliorem esse virtutem. Et forsitan eam civilis vitae quispiam existimaret potius esse finem, verum & ip-sa minus perfecta est. Videtur enim fieri posse, ut is qui virtute præditus sit, aut dormiat, aut in vita nihil agat: præterea malis aut infortunijs gravibus ia-ctetur: eum autem qui ita vivat, felicem appellaverit nemo, nisi qui sibi thesim aliquam defendendã pro-posuerit. Ac de his quidem satis. Abundè enim de his Encyclijs est dictum.
units.tr: Therefore, by their judgement, virtue is more to be preferred than honour. Someone might think that civil life is rather the end, but even this is less perfect. For it seems possible that a man endowed with virtue may either sleep or do nothing in his life, and he may also be battered by evils or grievous misfortunes. Yet no one would call a man who lives like that happy, unless he had proposed some thesis to defend. But enough of these things, for enough has been said about them in the encyclical studies.

units.la: Concludit ea quae de honore dixerat, & de virtute incipit agere, an ipsa sit extrema finis. Propositio est, Virtutem non esse summum bonum. Proba-tur hac ratione,
units.tr: He concludes what he had said about honour and begins to treat of virtue, whether it is itself the ultimate end. The proposition is that virtue is not the highest good. It is proved by this reasoning:
The highest good must be perfect.
Virtue is not perfect.
Therefore virtue is not to be called the highest good.

units.la: Maior propositio liquet: nam si perfectum non sit extremum bonum, in eo non acquiescet noster appetitus, sed aliud aliquod bonum ulterius desyderabit. Minor propositio, nimirum, virtutem esse minus perfectam, probatur, quia est habitus, hoc est potentia non actu, & sæpius in subiecto esse potest, absque actione, ut quæ multis modis possit impediri, somno, & occasione sublata si materia desit, & cum afflictiones morbi & infortunia nos diuexant.
units.tr: The major premise is clear: for if what is perfect is not the ultimate good, our appetite does not rest in it but desires some further good. The minor premise, namely that virtue is less perfect, is proved because it is a habit, that is, a potency and not an act, and it can often be in its subject without action, since it can be impeded in many ways: by sleep, by the removal of the occasion when the matter is lacking, and when the afflictions of disease and misfortunes vex us.

units.la: Verum singula hæc impedimenta spectemus. Horum primum est somnus, cuius naturam Aristoteles explicat lib. 1. de somno & vigilia, statuitq; somnum esse vigiliæ privationem, & usu sensuum vigilam[?] finit, quoniam eum vigilare dicimus qui sentiat motus externos. Est ita somnus affectio sentientis partis, qua vincitur & immobilis redditur, à quo vinculo seu nexu cum exoluitur animans, dicitur vigilare. Unde vero affectio hæc oriatur, idem explicat, Quod vapores ad caput per calorem natiuum attollantur, ipsumq; grauent, & ibi refrigerati propter loci distantiam à sede caloris, deorsum rursus fluat, & reciprocent instar Euripi. Ac descensu eorum, cum iam frigidi sint, calor depellitur ad interiora, & animans iacet sepultu[?] & dormit. Quare nunc vere dicitur per somnum impediri virtutem ne in actum erumpat, cum in sopore neq; sentiri neq; moueri possimus.
units.tr: Let us consider each of these impediments. The first is sleep, whose nature Aristotle explains in the book On Sleep and Waking. He defines sleep as the privation of waking, and says that it is being awake through the use of the senses, since we say a man is awake when he perceives external motions. Sleep is thus an affection of the sentient part by which it is overcome and rendered immobile; when the animal is released from this bond or tie, it is said to be awake. The same author explains where this affection arises: vapours are raised to the head by natural heat, weigh upon it, and there, being cooled because of their distance from the seat of heat, flow down again and ebb back like the Euripus. With their descent, now cold, the heat is driven back to the interior, and the animal lies buried and sleeps. Hence it is rightly said that by sleep virtue is hindered from breaking out into act, since in slumber we can neither perceive nor move.

units.la: Obstat etiam virtuti ne agat, opportunitas cum adempta fuerit. Sunt e-nim aliqui iustitia præditi, alij quoq; fortitudine. Sed euenire potest, ut illi nunquam mandetur ullus magistratus quo se in iure dicēdo exerceat, utq; optat unicuiq; reddat sua, quod est iustitiæ proprium, et alter fortasse vinet his temporibus quib. respublica est pacatissima, nulla geruntur bella, nec ipsi da-tur ansa, ut pro suis, pro patria vel ob honestas causas tuendas ulla subeat & fortiter pericula toleret. Fingito quoq; reperiri aliquem, ad liberalitatē propensissimum, nec non ea virtute præditum quam vocamus magnificen-tiam: qui si pauper fuerit, nec habebit, unde possit indigentibus dare, vel res magnas, amplas, excelsas, splendide faciat.
units.tr: Opportunity, when it has been taken away, also hinders virtue from acting. For some are endowed with justice, others with courage. But it can happen that the first is never entrusted with any magistracy in which he may exercise himself in judging and render to each his own, as he wishes, which is the property of justice; and another perhaps lives in times when the commonwealth is most peaceful, no wars are waged, and he is given no occasion to undertake dangers for his own people or his country, or to defend honourable causes, and to endure them bravely. Suppose too that someone is found very inclined to liberality and also endowed with that virtue we call magnificence; if he is poor, he will have nothing from which he can give to the needy, or make great, ample and lofty things splendidly.

units.la: Aerumnæ adhæc morbi, cruciatus, dolores corporis, adeò uehementes nunquam interueniunt, ut qui in eos incurrant, mente alienentur, & ita extra se ponantur quamuis prudentia & sapientia ornatum animum habeant, illis tamen dum sic afflictantur uti nequeant. Hæc ferme sunt impedimenta quorum nunc Aristoteles meminit: quæ idcirco nunc obiicit, quia si accidant, ut virtutes non desint, earum nihilominus actio intercipitur, & hi quibus virtutes adsunt, occasiones, materiamq; illarum, & prospe-ram varam valetudinem, atq; instrumenta expedita ad recte agendum optabunt, quasi ea desint, quibus eorum felicitas compleri possit, id vere à summi boni natura est alienum, vt quis in eo non omnino quiescat.
units.tr: Moreover, the distresses of disease, torments and pains of the body never come on so violently that those who fall into them are driven out of their minds and placed outside themselves, so that, although their soul is adorned with prudence and wisdom, they cannot use these while they are so afflicted. These are about the chief impediments of which Aristotle now speaks, and he objects to them because, even if the virtues are not lacking, when these things happen their action is nevertheless cut off. Those who have the virtues will wish for occasions and matter for them, a prosperous and healthy condition, and tools ready for acting rightly, as if things were lacking by which their happiness could be completed. This is truly foreign to the nature of the highest good, so that one would not wholly rest in it.

units.la: Huc praeterea illud accedit, eum qui grauib. iactetur infortunijs, magnis calamitatibus obruatur, horrendisq; diuexetur cruciatibus, felicem appellare, nil aliud esse quàm à communi sensu longissimè discedere.
units.tr: Besides this, to call happy one who is tossed about by grievous misfortunes, overwhelmed by great calamities and vexed with dreadful torments is nothing other than to depart very far from common sense.

units.la: Quod sane nulli faciunt nisi qui sibi thesim aliquam defendendam uel peruicaciae uel exercitij causa proposuerit. ) Per thesim hoc loco intelligit, sententiam vel dogma ἀντιδόξου[?] aduersus ea quae in Physica, et communi hominum sensu atq; opinione sunt percepta, vt Heraclitus dicebat contraria vnum ac idem esse: & Parmenides qui asserebat omnia quae sunt, vnum esse: & Zeno qui motum funditus tollebat. Haec porrò mirabilia sunt, & contra sensum opinionemq; omnium affirmantur, & defenduntur. Similiter iudicat Aristoteles nihilo minus paradoxon, statuere aut nihil agentem, aut infortunatissimè agentem felicem. Hoc inquam nullus diceret ac tueretur, nisi qui thesim aut propositum aliquod susceperit defendendum. Existimo autem vos non latere quid inter illas sententias quae thesis dicuntur & quae hypotheses interfit. Cicero in Topicis inquit, quod Graeci thesim dicunt, nos propositum possumus nominare. Propositum vero est quaestio nulla persona certa, nullo tempore loco aut negotio comprehensa, vt, Sit ne sapientis ad rempub. accedere. Huius generis potest esse thesis, cuius nunc Aristoteles mentionem facit, Sit ne sapiens beatus in tormentis. Sed hypothesis (vt idem in eodem loco tradit) quaestio est definita, qua nos causam dicimus. nam comprehenditur certa persona, loco, tempore, certoq; negotio. Sed quod magis ad rem praesentem facit, vt per thesim intelligamus propositum προσκατάλογον[?], idem Cicero in paradoxis habet, dicens: Degustabis genus hoc exercitationum mearum, quibus vti consueui, cùm ea quae dicantur in scholis θέσεις ad nostrum hoc oratorium dicendi genus transfero. Vbi nil tam perspicuum est quàm eum velle παράδοξα esse ἐν τοῖς θέσεις[?].
units.tr: Which indeed nobody does, except one who has proposed some thesis to defend, either out of obstinacy or for practice. By "thesis" here he means an opinion or dogma contrary to received opinion [ἀντιδόξου], against those things perceived in physics and in the common sense and opinion of men: as Heraclitus said that contraries are one and the same; Parmenides asserted that all things that are, are one; and Zeno utterly removed motion. These are indeed marvels, and they are affirmed and defended against the sense and opinion of all. Aristotle likewise judges that it is no less a paradox to hold that a man who does nothing, or who acts most unfortunately, is happy. Nobody would say or defend this, I say, unless he had taken up some thesis or proposition to defend. I think you are not unaware of the difference between those statements which are called theses and those which are hypotheses. Cicero in the Topics says: what the Greeks call a thesis we may call a proposition (propositum). A proposition is a question with no fixed person, and comprehended in no time, place or business, such as: whether the wise man should enter public affairs. Of this kind may be the thesis Aristotle now mentions: whether the wise man is happy on the rack. But a hypothesis (as the same author teaches in the same place) is a definite question, which we call a case, for a certain person, place, time and definite business are comprehended in it. But, to bring out what bears more on the present matter, that we understand by thesis a proposition [προσκατάλογον], the same Cicero says in the Paradoxes: you will taste this kind of my exercises, which I was accustomed to use, when I transfer those things that are said in the schools as theses [θέσεις] to this oratorical manner of speaking of ours. Where nothing is so clear as that he wishes paradoxes [παράδοξα] to be among theses [ἐν τοῖς θέσεις].

units.la: NVNC vero quando iam verba explicuimus, demonstrauimus propositionem, & firmamenta eius ostendimus: Deinceps nonnulla de re ipsa videnda sunt. Haec opinio quae summum bonum in ipsa virtute collocat, omnibus quas hactenus recensuimus est vero proximior, ideoq; magnos grauesq; habuit patronos. Quomodo vero propius ad veritatem accesserit, hinc facile colligimus: quod nulla est certior firmiorq; ad felicitatem praeparatio quàm Virtus: nam ex virtutis habitu proficiscitur ea actio, quae ipsa statuitur ab Aristotele felicitas. Proinde virtus erit proxima & vicinissima potentia seu facultas ad felicitatem.
units.tr: Now that we have explained the words, demonstrated the proposition and shown its supports, some things about the matter itself must be considered next. This opinion, which places the highest good in virtue itself, is closer to the truth than all those we have so far reviewed, and therefore has had great and weighty defenders. How it came nearer to the truth we easily gather from this: that there is no surer or firmer preparation for happiness than virtue; for from the habit of virtue there proceeds that action which Aristotle himself lays down as happiness. Therefore virtue will be the nearest and most neighbouring power or faculty for happiness.

units.la: Cur autem ipsa extremum bonum & felicitas esse non possit, satis causæ inde est, quod ad ulteriorem finem refertur. Quorsum enim comparamus nobis virtutum habitus, nisi quo facilius expeditiusque recte agamus? Quare cum virtus ad actionem dirigatur, actio erit ea potior, & magis expetibilis.
units.tr: Why virtue itself cannot be the ultimate good and happiness is clear enough from the fact that it is referred to a further end. For why do we acquire habits of virtue, except that we may act rightly more easily and readily? Therefore, since virtue is directed to action, action will be the more excellent and the more to be desired.

units.la: Non me latet eos qui stare solent à Stoicis, consuevisse Peripateticis occurrere, dicendo, se non accipere virtutem, dum illam summum bonum ponunt, ut est in potentia, & sine actu iacet, sed eam sumere quæ cum actione sua coiungitur, & ita rident Aristotelem, qui sibi non obiecerit virtutem nisi otiosam & ab actione recta disiunctam. Videtur primo aspectu nonnullis responsio hæc iusta & verisimilis: at si pressius res cogitetur, & accuratius in eam introspexerimus, potius latebra est, quam vera dissolutio argumenti, quia velint nolint, actio & virtus à qua proficiscitur distinguuntur: diversis enim continentur prædicamentis, & à se invicem nonnunquam seiunguntur. Nam virtus, cùm sit habitus, ad qualitatem spectat, actus verò quem efficit, sub actionis prædicamento comprehenditur. Ut verò à se mutuo separentur, neminem puto, qui rem expendat attentè, nescium, siquidem scientia vel sapientia præditus, neq; contemplatur perpetuò, neq; circa illa quæ scit, semper versatur. Unde fit ut qui duo pro uno complectantur, neq; distinguant, facilè à scopo ad quem collimandum est aberrent, & pro absoluta exquisitaq; doctrina, confusam & parum explicatam sectentur. Aristoteles dum hæc intelligit, à se mutuo distinguit & seponit, & eorum cùm alterum videt in alterum referri, id quod in alteram finem tendit, summâ negat esse posse: qua sententia illius ratio tam est evidens ut nil ea magis perspicuum existimem. Verùm qui eam convellere nequeunt, argumentum in ipsum Aristotelem retorquent, qui negat idcirco felicitatem in virtute poni tam, quòd virtus facile ac multis modis impediatur.
units.tr: I am aware that those who usually side with the Stoics are wont to object to the Peripatetics, saying that they do not take virtue when they place it as the highest good, as it is in potency and lies without act, but take it as joined with its action; and so they mock Aristotle, who, they say, objected to himself only a virtue idle and separated from right action. At first sight this reply seems just and plausible to some; but if the matter is considered more closely and we look into it more carefully, it is a hiding place rather than a true solution of the argument. For whether they will or not, action and the virtue from which it proceeds are distinguished: they are contained under different categories and are sometimes separated from each other. For virtue, since it is a habit, belongs to quality, but the act it produces is comprised under the category of action. That they are separated from each other I think no one who weighs the matter carefully is ignorant, since a man endowed with knowledge or wisdom neither contemplates continually nor is always occupied with the things he knows. Hence it happens that those who grasp two things as one, and do not distinguish them, easily wander from the goal at which they should aim, and pursue a confused and little explained doctrine instead of a complete and exact one. Aristotle, while he understands these things, distinguishes and separates them from each other, and when he sees one of them referred to the other, he denies that what tends toward another end can be the highest. His reasoning here is so evident that I think nothing is clearer. But those who cannot overturn it turn the argument back upon Aristotle himself, who denies that happiness is placed in virtue for the reason that virtue is easily and in many ways impeded.

units.la: Si tibi hoc, inquiunt, tantopere placet, nec actionem sane perfectissimam poteris tueri summum bonum esse, quandoquidem illa etiam totidem impedimentis est obnoxia, quot virtuti obieceras. Nam qui dormit, non contemplatur, nec idè facere potest qui cruciatib. gravissimis torquetur, & periculla[?] obire non potest, qui degit in tranquillis & pacatis rebus publicis: Proinde qui dicis virtutem his de causis non esse bonum extremum, idem dices actionem perfectissimam pro felicitate non habendam. Veri porrò speciem habet quod objcitur, sed nihil efficit, quia facilè Peripatetici annuet, actioni-onem onem illam absolutissimam, quam felicitatem prædicant, nō esse continen-tem ita vt interrumpi nequeat, sed id nō concederent quando est, felicitate non esse, & multò minus dabūt eam in finem præstabiliorem referri. Quo-rum vtrunq; de habitu quæ est virtus dici non potest: nam is vt in homine dormiente sit, aut diuexato atrocissimis doloribus, nec felicitas dici potest, nec illum beare in cuius animo inest, etenim habitus actione detracta mane re potest, verum actio impedita ne erumpat, nec est neq; manet. Et adhæc habitus dum impeditus manet, quis non videat, in actionem adhuc referri, cùm ad eam inclinat animum et appetitionem? Prætera, nostra felicitas ea debet statui quæ ad diuinam quàm maximè accedat. Deus verò cùm non tantum sit perfectus verum ipsa perfectio, actu non potentia, reipsa non in habitu felicitatem habet, ideò & nostra felicitas erit actio, quæ tamen par est vt minor sit Dei beatitudine, quod ex eo eucnit quia eius actus deficere non potest, at noster[?] non parum sæpe interrumpitur. Et quod Aristoteles modo scribit de Virtute, nempe eam non esse felicitatem, idem Ethicorum 10. tenet.
units.tr: "If you are so set on this," they say, "you cannot defend the most perfect activity as the highest good either, since that activity is subject to just as many hindrances as you have objected to virtue. For a man who is asleep does not contemplate, and one who is racked by the most severe pains cannot act, and a man who lives in peaceful and quiet commonwealths cannot undertake dangers. So if you say that virtue is not the final good for these reasons, you will also have to say that the most perfect activity should not be counted as happiness." The objection has a look of truth, but it achieves nothing. The Peripatetics will readily agree that this most absolute activity, which they declare to be happiness, is not so continuous that it can never be interrupted. But they would not concede that it is no longer happiness when it is interrupted, and still less will they grant that it is referred to some more excellent end. Neither of these can be said of the habit that is virtue. For whether the habit is present in a sleeping man or in one tormented by the most dreadful pains, it neither is happiness nor makes the person in whose mind it resides blessed. The habit can remain when the activity is taken away, but when the activity is impeded it does not break out, and so it neither exists nor remains. Moreover, while the habit remains impeded, who does not see that it is still directed to action, since the mind and its appetite incline towards it? Furthermore, our happiness ought to be set in that which comes as near as possible to the divine. But God, since he is not only perfect but perfection itself, is actual and not potential, and possesses happiness in fact and not in a habit. Therefore our happiness too will be an activity. Yet it must be less than the blessedness of God, and this comes about because his act cannot fail, whereas ours is not seldom interrupted. And what Aristotle has just written about virtue, namely that it is not happiness, he also holds in the tenth book of the Ethics.

units.la: Post ea quæ iam diximus etiam illorum cauillus refellendus est, qui ridet argumentum adductum de impedimentis, quibus actio virtutum reprimi-tur ne sit in effectu. Fingitis, inquiunt, virtutum opus pertinere ad corpus: at non ita est, quia in anima tota est actio virtutis, & in eo plena & perfecta consistit: nil ad eam vel corporis bona vel fortunæ instrumenta. Et sanè pauper liberalis esse potest optando illis dare quibus largiendum censet: nec non in mediis cruciatibus atq; in ipsis flammis metus magis resplendet et e-uadit multò gloriosior. In quam sententiam Seneca ad Lucillum Epistola 79. multa scribit, & ait inter cætera: In lecto quoq; virtus habet locum: vincas morbum forti animo, quoniam si alij qui adsunt excelsum, magnum & erectum in cruciatibus viderint, mirabuntur nitorem virtutis, tuq; dum sic diuexaris, eos recte instituës, ac non solum te ipsum uirtute sed illos quoq; plurimum iuuabis.
units.tr: After what we have already said, we must also refute the quibbling of those who mock the argument from the hindrances by which the activity of the virtues is restrained so that it does not come into effect. "You imagine," they say, "that the work of the virtues pertains to the body. But that is not so, because the whole activity of virtue is in the soul, and in the soul it consists fully and perfectly. Neither the goods of the body nor the instruments of fortune have anything to do with it. Indeed a poor man can be liberal by wishing to give to those to whom he thinks gifts should be made. And in the midst of torments, and even in the flames, courage shines forth more brightly and comes out much more glorious." Seneca writes much to this effect in Epistle 79 to Lucilius, and among other things says: "Virtue has a place even in bed. Overcome your sickness with a brave mind, for if others who are present see you lofty, great and upright in your sufferings, they will marvel at the brilliance of virtue, and while you are so tormented you will rightly instruct them and help not only yourself but them very greatly by your virtue."

units.la: Qualia hæc sint iam propius contemplemur, Petunt, actionem virtutis in animo totam plenam & perfectam esse: id nos pernegamus, quia si explicetur habitus natura, ea nil est aliud quam inducta qualitas exercitatione diuturna, cuius beneficio animi & corporis facultates ad agendum reddun-tur magis expedita atq; idonea. Neq; virtus in animo duntaxat suam explicat actionem. Qui dicunt potui, cibo, Veneri, & horum similibus virtute moderari, ijdem dicent actionem eius virtutis, in corpore quoque non solum in animo explicari. De fortitudine, liberalitate atq; permultis aliis virtuti-bus libus licet idem proferre, ut ostendatur corpus & bona fortunæ non fuisse à Deo generi nostro concessa. Verum isti fortasse persuasum habent hominis naturam solum in animo compleri & perfectam esse: quod ut sit à vero alie-num, uosipsi me tacente intelligitis. Pauper, inquiunt, liberalis esse potest, dum largiri optat quibus dandum iudicauerit. Sed de Stoicis istis velim au-dire, an uirtute prediti cum impediuntur & ex illa optat agere, cur id ex-petant, nonne causa beatitudinis? Hoc si negarint, indicabunt se parum pru-dentes, qui ea cupiant quæ in bonum extremum non referant. Sin annuerint fe-licitatis opera illa optare, licebit dicere, felicitatem non in virtute sed in a-ctione perfecte haberi. In medijs flammis & atrocissimis cruciatibus virtute splendere ac magis gloriosam esse facile dabo, et illum, qui forti animo ista fe-rat, laudibus una cum viris bonis et prudentibus efferam, sed ita ut negem interea solida perfectaq; frui felicitate. Suo exemplo recte alios instituet & do-cebit, non tamen perfecte ac omnib. modis erit beatus. Hac adeo vera sunt,ut & hi, qui Stoicam disciplinam sunt professi, tandem velint nolint in hac sententia pedibus eant. Nam Cicero Tusculana. 5. ab initio inquit, Si virtus tantarum virium non est ut seipsam tueatur, uereor ne non tam virtutis fiducia nitendum nobis ad spe beatè uiuendi, qua vota facienda videatur. Equidem eos casus in quibus me fortuna vehementer exercuit, mecum ipse consyderans huic incipio sententiæ diffidere, interdum etiam humani ge-neris imbecillitate fragilitatemq; extimescere. Vereor enim ne natura cũ cor-pora nobis infirma dedisset, ijsq; & morbos insanabiles, & dolores intolera-biles adiunxisset, animos quoq; dederit corporũ dolorib. congruentes & se-paratim suis angoribus & molestijs implicatos. Sed in hoc me ipse castigo, quòd ex aliorũ & ex nostra fortasse mollitie, non ex ipsa virtute, de virtutis robore existimo, &c. Ut dubitet & propemodum in hanc sententiam disce-dat, his verbis luculenter expressit, nec refert quod subdat correctionem se adhibere, quoniam ea incerta est, &, Fortasse, additur, quæ dubitationis est nota. Deinde quid tam certum est, quàm ipsum Ciceronem. 4. de finibus contra Catonem disseruisse, qui prius in 3. sententiam Zenonis & Stoicorumlaudibus in cælum extulerat. Quin & Stoici ut una virtute se beatos fieri prædicarint, in ea tamen una non acquiescebant, verũ corporis vires, inte-gritate sensuũ, dignitates, opes, & horũ similia ωγονγμία[?] dixerunt, quæ Cicero producta, promota, seu præcipua & præposita vocat, ex quarum vo-cum significatione si velimus urgere Stoicos, eos dicemus plus huic generi rerum tribuere quàm Peripateticos, ut qui ea præcipua & præposita nomi-nent, cùm Peripatetici ea quidem appellent bona, gradus nihilominus infi-mi[?], & mi, & quæ non sint plurimi, cum rectis & honestis collata, ideoq; in tempore contenenda, nec expetenda magnopere. Scio quidè Stoicos ista præcipua & præpositta vocare, dum suis comparantur contrariis, non quando cum virtutibus comparantur, sed tamen suis nouis & factis vocibus, huic rerum ordini plurimum dant, cùm ista commoda præpositia præcipua dicant, & eorum opposita Græcè ἀποπροηγμένα[?], quæ dixeris Incommoda Latinè ac Reiecta. Quamobrem ut Stoici velint cum Peripateticis oratione pugnare, attamen cum illis ratione ac re ipsa consentiunt. Magnifico sermonis genere Stoici gaudent, & verbis duntaxat ἀπαθείαν[?] inducunt, quam cum deinceps ad rem veniunt, omnes experiuntur à sensibus & probatis moribus alienam, nec non à viribus humanis valde longinquam. Neque arbitror pertransfeun-da leuiter quæ paulo ante citabam ex 5. Tusc. Si, inquit Cicero, virtus in se non habuerit satis præsidij, iam vota esse facienda. Quid audimus? An si uir tus sibi ipsi fuerit satis, nil iam optandum vel à Deo petendum, quasi totum in nobis situm habeamus? Siccine pluris faciendo virtutem quam par sit, virtutum optimam pietatem invocatione Dei sublata tollet? Certè sic Stoici denique senserunt. Seneca enim scribit Jouem non plus posse quam virum bonum. Proinde non tam magnifica oratione Stoici usi sunt, quam dogmate omnino à religione alieno. Quod non idcirco dico, quasi studeam opinionem Aristotelis, de quapostea suo loco agetur, piam & religiosam prædicare, sed ut moneam Stoicos non ita suspiciendos, quasi suam laudando virtutem, quàm proximè ut nonnulli putant, ad dogma Christianum accesserint.
units.tr: Let us examine more closely what such claims amount to. They say that the activity of virtue is whole, full and perfect in the soul. We deny this, because if the nature of a habit is explained, it is nothing other than a quality induced by long practice, by whose benefit the faculties of mind and body are made more ready and fit for acting. Nor does virtue unfold its activity in the soul alone. Those who say that virtue governs drink, food, sex and similar things will also say that the activity of that virtue is unfolded in the body and not only in the soul. The same can be said of courage, liberality and very many other virtues, so that it may be shown that the body and the goods of fortune were not granted to our race by God. But perhaps these men are persuaded that human nature is completed and made perfect in the soul alone. That this is far from the truth, you yourselves understand without my saying so. "A poor man," they say, "can be liberal, while he wishes to give to those to whom he judges a gift should be made." But I would like to hear from these Stoics whether, when men endowed with virtue are hindered and wish to act from it, they desire these things for their own sake. Is it not for the sake of blessedness? If they deny this, they will show themselves to be rather unwise, since they desire things that they do not refer to the highest good. But if they agree that they wish for those works for the sake of happiness, we may say that happiness is not had in virtue but in activity perfectly possessed. I will readily grant that in the midst of flames and most dreadful torments virtue shines and is more glorious, and I will praise the man who bears these things with a brave mind, together with good and prudent men. But I deny that he meanwhile enjoys solid and perfect happiness. By his example he will rightly instruct and teach others, yet he will not be blessed perfectly and in every way. So true are these things that even those who have professed the Stoic discipline are compelled, whether they wish it or not, to go over to this opinion. For Cicero, at the beginning of the fifth Tusculan Disputation, says: "If virtue does not have such strength that it can defend itself, I fear that we must not rest our hope of living happily on the confidence of virtue, but must make vows for it.
