Indeed, considering with myself the misfortunes by which fortune has greatly troubled me, I distrust this beginning of my opinion, and sometimes even fear the weakness and frailty of the human race. For I fear that nature, when it gave us weak bodies and joined to them incurable diseases and intolerable pains, has also given minds that correspond to the sufferings of the body, and are entangled in their own distresses and troubles separately. But I rebuke myself for this, because I judge the strength of virtue from the softness of others and perhaps of ourselves, not from virtue itself," and so on. That he doubts, and almost departs into this opinion, he has expressed brilliantly in these words. Nor does it matter that he adds that he applies a correction to himself, since that correction is uncertain; and the word "perhaps" that is added is a mark of doubt. Next, what is so certain as that Cicero himself, in the fourth book of the De finibus, argued against Cato, who had earlier praised to the skies the opinion of Zeno and the Stoics in the third book? Moreover, although the Stoics declared that they became blessed by virtue alone, they did not rest in that one thing alone. Instead they called the strength of the body, the integrity of the senses, honours, wealth and similar things preferred things [προηγμένα], which Cicero calls producta, promota, or praecipua and praeposita. If we wish to press the Stoics with the meaning of these words, we will say that they attribute more to this class of things than the Peripatetics do. For they name these things praecipua and praeposita, whereas the Peripatetics indeed call them goods, but of the lowest degree and of little value, and when compared with the right and the honourable they are to be set aside in time and not greatly sought. I know that the Stoics call these things praecipua and praeposita while they are compared with their opposites, not when they are compared with the virtues. Nevertheless, by their new and invented words they give very much to this order of things, when they call these advantages praepositia and praecipua, and their opposites, in Greek apoproēgmena [ἀποπροηγμένα], which you could call in Latin incommoda or reiecta. Therefore, although the Stoics want to fight with the Peripatetics in words, they nevertheless agree with them in reason and in fact. The Stoics rejoice in a magnificent style of speech, and they introduce apatheia [ἀπάθειαν] in words alone. But when they come to the matter itself, all experience that it is foreign to the senses and to approved morals, and also very far from human strength. Nor do I think that what I cited a little earlier from the fifth Tusculan Disputation should be passed over lightly. "If virtue," says Cicero, "does not have enough protection in itself, then vows must be made." What are we hearing? Or if virtue is sufficient for itself, is nothing now to be wished for or asked of God, as if we held everything placed in ourselves? Will the Stoics, by valuing virtue more than is fitting, remove the best of the virtues, piety, by taking away the invocation of God? Certainly the Stoics finally thought so. For Seneca writes that Jupiter can do no more than a good man. Therefore the Stoics used not so much a magnificent style of speech as a doctrine altogether alien to religion. I do not say this as though I were eager to proclaim Aristotle's opinion, which will be discussed in its place later, to be pious and religious, but to warn that the Stoics should not be so admired, as if by praising their own virtue they had come, as some think, very near to the Christian doctrine.

units.la: Stoicis nihilominus hac in parte plus concedam quàm Epicureis, quòd suæ sententiæ dicant propemodum semper cosentanea, cùm Epicurei ea no-nunquam affirment, quæ suis thesibus non sunt consequentia. Quoniam Epicurus dolorem habeat in summo malo, & voluptatem etiam corporis, aut vacuitatē doloris in summo bono ponat. Si torqueatur uel descendat in Phalaridis taurum, & dicat ut hoc est suaue, quemadmodum iactat suum sapientem dicturum, inconstantissimè proculdubio loquetur, & quæ inter se nullo modo congruant. Hæ voces tam gloriosæ ac memorandæ reliquantur Stoicis, qui suas virtutes adeò prædicent, ut sapientem illis præditum nunquam beatitudine censeant destituendum. Neque possunt in animum inducere ut cùm felicitas perpetuò comitetur virtutes, illas tum deseret, & ipsis ingredientibus carcerem in eius limine restituet, quasi ei non liceat ingredi tristem locum, neq; ut aiebat Theophrastus in equuleum vel rotam ascen-dere. Certe fuit Theophrastus longe prudentior Epicuro: qui enim vidit ex Peripateticorum doctrina requiri ad ciuilem felicitatem, de qua modo agimus, & corporis & externa bona, idem intellexit non posse fieri vt vel sapientissimus in cruciatu et ærumna sit beatus. At Epicurus cui placuit summum bonum quale iam exposuimus, neq; consentanea neq; consequentia suo proposito dicet, dum tam magnifice loquitur adeoq; splendida sententia vtitur. Non tamen hoc mirum, quia Dialecticam quæ est recta disputandi ratio, contempsit. Sed hac de re satis multa.
units.tr: I will concede more to the Stoics on this point than to the Epicureans, because the Stoics nearly always say things consistent with their own opinion, whereas the Epicureans sometimes affirm things that do not follow from their theses. For Epicurus places pain in the greatest evil, and places bodily pleasure, or freedom from pain, in the greatest good. If he were tortured, or were put into the bull of Phalaris, and said, as he boasts his wise man would say, "how sweet this is," he would undoubtedly be speaking most inconsistently, and saying things that in no way agree with one another. Those glorious and memorable words are left to the Stoics, who so extol their virtues that they think the wise man endowed with them can never be deprived of blessedness. Nor can they bring themselves to believe that happiness, which always accompanies the virtues, would then desert them, and at the very moment they entered the prison would stand aside at its threshold, as if it were not allowed to enter a sad place, or, as Theophrastus said, to climb onto the rack or the wheel. Certainly Theophrastus was far more prudent than Epicurus. For he saw that, according to the doctrine of the Peripatetics, both bodily and external goods are required for the civil happiness we are now discussing, and he understood that even the wisest man cannot be blessed in torment and distress. But Epicurus, who held the supreme good as we have now set it out, will say things neither consistent nor consequent with his position, while he speaks so magnificently and uses such splendid language. This is not surprising, however, because he despised dialectic, which is the right method of reasoning. But enough on this matter.

units.la: Quid vero ad hæc diuinæ literæ? Virtutum sane mentionem non faciunt, cum hominis felicitatem offendunt. In Psalmo quo commemoratur opinio vulgi existimantis felicem illum qui sit copiosus, & infinita bonorum huius mundi abundantia sit refertus, voce Dei secus monemur: etenim subditur, Beata gens cuius est Dominus Deus eius. Hic actus non potentia prædicatur. Beatus vir qui timet Dominum, beatus vir in lege Domini. Bonos adhæc habitus posse interdum ociari ac esse inutiles, inde perspicuum est, quod Paulus monet vt gratiam videamus ne frustra receperimus. Et Timotheum admonet Paulus, vt dona quæ in se iam habebat per impositionem manuum presbyteri excitaret. Cum itaq; dona Spiritus, quæ præstabiliora sunt moralibus virtutibus, referuntur ad actionem, vt alij inuentur & instruantur, aliequin ob ipsa meliores no euadimus, id multo verius ac certius de humanis virtutibus est sentiendum. Deinceps cum dicitur ab Aristotele, calamitates & ærunas impedire quo minus homines habendi sint felices, id si cogitetur perse vt dicitur absq; vlla distinctione, diuinis literis non consentit: quoniam qui pro Christo patiuntur in summa penuria sunt, & grauissimis pœnis afficiuntur, ea tamen beatitudine fruuntur quam dum hic viui mus habere licet, quia illis peccata non imputantur, & ad æternam vitam eorum animus & corpus tum maxime instaurantur. Sed quoniam hæc felicitas vitæ huius non plena est sed inchoata, ideo concedemus sanctos qui sic afflictantur, in beatitudine perfecta & absoluta non esse, cum eam iam iam expectent, in qua nil huiusmodi angustiarum sentient. Diuina quippe oracula dicunt, Abstergetque Deus omnem lachrymam ab oculis sanctorum, nec erit amplius luctus neq; clamor: nam hæc priora transierunt. Quare dicemus cum Aristotele inter perfectam & plenam felicitatem & ærumnas atq; calamitates minime congruere, quæ tamen felicitati, quam hic habemus inchoatam, minime aduersantur. Et Paulus adeo vidit huius vitæ incommoda repugnare perfectæ beatitudini, & se non passimul, vt dixerit ad Corinthios: Mortui si non resurgunt, sumus omnibus hominibus infeliciores. Quod si Christus beatos prædicauit lugentes & qui persequutione paterentur ob ipsius nomen, id non sic intelligedum, quasi beati simus quia ploramus vel gemimus & persequutionem patimur, sed quia post hæc expectamus meliora, & spe seruati sumus. Neq; diffiteor in medijs angustijs carnis Deum suis admirabiles adhibere consolationes, quas mihi persuadeo vincere omnes iucunditates ciuilis felicitatis: non tamen ex eo fit, cum illis calamitatibus perfectam esse felicitatem. Paulus ita Christi athletas consolabatur, Non, inquit, ea quæ hoc tempore patimur, sunt paria & eiusdem æstimationis cum his quæ in nobis tandem patefient quando cum Christo vna regnabimus. Aristoteles autem, vt dicit, sentire coactus est, quia futuram ignorauit beatitudinem, & cernebat quam tractabat ciuilem, ab aduersis casibus in afflictis rebus obscurari & imminui. Neq; illi cognitæ fuerunt illæ cœlestes consolationes, quas Deus supra naturæ vires confessoribus veritatis in ipsis cruciatibus affert. Unde si quo ad hoc Stoici videntur nonnihil à nobis non discedere, id temere fecerunt, cum ipsi quoq; de futura vita nihil sciuerint, neq; Dei consolationes in medijs ærumnis & morte vnquam fuerint experti. Sed his omissis ad verba philosophi nos denuo recipiamus.
units.tr: What, then, do the divine letters say to these things? They certainly make no mention of virtues when they touch on human happiness. In the Psalm which records the opinion of the crowd, who think that he is happy who is wealthy and filled with the endless abundance of this world's goods, we are warned otherwise by the voice of God. For it is added, "Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord." Here it is the act, not the power, that is praised. "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; blessed is the man in the law of the Lord." That good habits can sometimes lie idle and be useless is clear from Paul's warning that we should see that we have not received grace in vain. And Paul admonishes Timothy to stir up the gifts he already had through the laying on of the hands of the elders. Since, therefore, the gifts of the Spirit, which are more excellent than the moral virtues, are referred to action, so that others may be found and instructed, and otherwise we do not become better through them, this must be felt much more truly and certainly of human virtues. Next, when Aristotle says that calamities and hardships prevent men from being called happy, if this is taken per se, as it is said, without any distinction, it does not agree with the divine letters. For those who suffer for Christ are in great want and are afflicted with the most grievous punishments, yet they enjoy that blessedness which we are able to have while we live here, because their sins are not imputed to them, and their soul and body are then especially restored for eternal life. But since this happiness of the present life is not full but only begun, we will concede that the saints who are so afflicted are not in perfect and complete blessedness, since they are now waiting for it, and in it they will feel nothing of such distress. For the divine oracles say: "God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and there will be no more mourning or crying, for the former things have passed away." Therefore we will say with Aristotle that perfect and full happiness does not agree with hardships and calamities, which nevertheless do not greatly oppose the happiness we have here in its beginning. And Paul saw so clearly that the discomforts of this life are incompatible with perfect blessedness, and that we do not possess both at once, that he wrote to the Corinthians: "If the dead do not rise, we are more wretched than all men." But if Christ pronounced blessed those who mourn, and those who suffer persecution for his name, this is not to be understood as if we are blessed because we weep, groan and suffer persecution, but because after these things we expect better things, and we are saved by hope. Nor do I deny that in the midst of the afflictions of the flesh God gives his people wonderful consolations, which I am persuaded surpass all the delights of civil happiness. Yet it does not follow from this that perfect happiness exists together with those calamities. Paul thus comforted the athletes of Christ: "The sufferings of this present time," he says, "are not equal to, nor of the same worth as, the glory which will at last be revealed in us when we reign together with Christ." But Aristotle, as he says, was compelled to think otherwise, because he did not know the future blessedness, and he saw that the civil happiness he was treating is obscured and diminished by adverse events in afflicted circumstances. Nor were those heavenly consolations known to him, which God, beyond the powers of nature, brings to the confessors of the truth even in their torments. Hence, if the Stoics seem in some respect not to depart from us here, they did so rashly, since they too knew nothing of the future life and had never experienced God's consolations in the midst of distress and death. But setting these aside, let us return once more to the words of the philosopher.

units.la: Abunde enim de his in encyclijs est dictum. ) De his encyclijs, vt in re dubia fieri solet, multi varia sunt commenti. Visum est aliquibus & his quidem non indoctis, nam inter eos est Eustratius, carmina quædam ab Aristotele fuisse conscripta, quæ terminabantur illo elemento, à quo initium ceperant. Et alij crediderunt gymnasticas designari congressiones: nam philosophi nonnunquam magna auditorum corona disputabant. Et quòd Romani dixerunt coronam, Græci appellarunt aliquando κύκλον[?]. nec desunt qui scripta hæc ad encyclopædiam fecisse opinentur, hoc est ad disciplinarum liberalium orbem. Nam fuit antiquitus & hodie deberet esse ductus quidam scientiæ ex multis disciplinis. Verum hac de re quicquid sit, id citra controuersiam est, Diogenem Laertium scribere, Aristotelem duos libros encyclicorum scripsisse, qui vna cum plerisque philosophi huius lucubrationibus perierint. Cur autem sic eos inscripserit, nosse haud magni refert. Exigit attamen loci huius oratio vt cogitemus in eis de felicitate complura fuisse præcepta, nec non de natura virtutis, possitne interdum esse otiosa, & an in tormentis atq; grauissimis doloribus hominem beatum redderet vel ipsum à miseria & infelicitate vendicaret.
units.tr: For enough has been said about these in the encyclica. Concerning these encyclica, as usually happens in an uncertain matter, many have invented various accounts. Some, and these not unlearned men (among them Eustratius), have thought that certain poems were written by Aristotle, which ended with the element from which they had begun. Others believed that gymnastic gatherings are meant, for philosophers sometimes disputed before a large crowd of listeners; and since the Romans called such a gathering a "corona," the Greeks sometimes called it "kyklos" [κύκλον]. Nor are there lacking those who think these writings were made for an encyclopaedia, that is, the circle of the liberal disciplines; for there was from antiquity, and there ought to be today, a certain outline of knowledge drawn from many disciplines. But whatever the truth of this matter, it is beyond controversy that Diogenes Laertius writes that Aristotle wrote two books of encyclica, which have perished along with most of this philosopher's writings. Why he entitled them thus, it is not greatly important to know. The argument of this passage nevertheless requires us to think that in them there were many precepts about happiness, and also about the nature of virtue: whether it can sometimes be idle, and whether it would make a man blessed in torments and the most grievous pains, or would rescue him from misery and unhappiness.

units.la: Tertium vitæ genus est contemplans, de quo in his quæ sequuntur agemus.
units.tr: The third kind of life is the contemplative life, which we shall discuss in what follows.

units.la: Tria vitae genera, quae Aristoteles ab initio proposuerat, haec sane fuerunt, Voluptuarium, Ciuile, atq; Contemplans. Ac de voluptuario iam est dictum, nec non de Ciuili. Restaret itaq; θεωρητικὸν[?] tractandum, quod in sequentia differt, quoniam hic illas duntaxat opiniones recenset quae sunt refellendae, quo illis explosis, facilius ei sit exponere suam sententiam, contemplandi vero munus à felicitate humana reiici non potest: ideo postea inquit eius habebitur accurata consyderatio. Atq; in 10. libro, quod modo pollicetur[?] praestitit. Accedit huc, genus illud felicitatis quod est in contemplatione, alterum genus prius exigere, illud nimirum quod in agedo situm est, ideo prius de felici actione hominum scribet, deinde beatam eorundem pa-tefaciet contemplationem. In his generibus vitae disponendis ordinem eiusmodi conseruauit, vt minus digna & imperfectiora prius recensuerit, & deinceps ascenderit ad praestantiora. De voluptate ante omnia egit, quod haec opinio crassior ceteris fuerit. Deinde ad ciuiles orationem transtulit, qui partim honores, partim virtutem pro bono extremo habent. Nunc vero ad summum ac perfectissimum gradum assurgeret pertractandum, quod fieri non potest, nisi antea de omnibus virtutibus singillatim dicatur. Vitam intelligit modum conuersandi in corpore iuxta humanum delectum. Etenim quia conuersandi rationem & agendi alij aliam sibi delegerunt, diuersa vitae genera ortum habuerunt.
units.tr: The three kinds of life that Aristotle set out at the beginning were these: the life of pleasure, the civic life, and the contemplative life. We have already spoken of the life of pleasure and of the civic life. What remains is the theoretical life [θεωρητικόν], which he defers to what follows. Here he reviews only those opinions that must be refuted, so that once they are overthrown it will be easier for him to set out his own view. The office of contemplation, however, cannot be excluded from human happiness, so he says that a careful consideration of it will come later. He does this, as he now promises, in the tenth book. Moreover, the happiness that lies in contemplation requires the other kind to come first, namely the happiness that lies in action. For this reason he will first write about the happy action of human beings and then set forth their blessed contemplation. In arranging these kinds of life he kept to an order by which he first reviewed the less worthy and more imperfect, and then rose to the more excellent. He dealt first with pleasure, because this opinion is cruder than the others. Then he turned to the civic life, which holds either honours or virtue to be the highest good. Now he rises to the highest and most perfect level to be treated, which cannot be done unless all the virtues have first been discussed one by one. By "life" he means the manner of living in the body according to human choice. Since different people have chosen different ways of conducting themselves and acting, different kinds of life have arisen.

units.la: Quaestuosa autem violenta quaedam est vita. Atque diuitiae non sunt quod quaerimus bonum: utiles enim & propter aliud.
units.tr: The pursuit of wealth is a certain violent kind of life. Riches are not the good we seek, for they are useful and exist for the sake of something else.

units.la: Vitae genera (vt vidimus) tria numerauit, & opiniones recessuit quae prae ceteris eminebant, nec tamen diuitiarum mentionem fecerat: ne igitur illas praetereat, cum eas permulti homines, & quidem non vulgares, vt summum bonum admirentur, nunc ipsarum mentionem fecit, & à felicitate duplici ratione remouet. Prima quod ad violentiam pertineant: non enim quod violentum est, habet felicitatis rationem. Diuitiarum vero possessionem, & adeptionem rem violentam esse, non quidem probat, sed usus & experientia nos docet. Summas enim & amplissimas diuitias nullus vel acquirere vel retinere diu potest, nisi vis & quidem non leuis adhibeatur. Ratio altera est, quod sunt utiles & in aliud referuntur: quare illarum conditio est seruilis. Etenim ad hoc illas habemus vt alia subministrent, quae cupimus: nec illas quisquam vel pili faceret, nisi utiles ad quæ vellet esse intelligeret. Hoc autem ut alienum sit a ratione summi boni, omnes hi non ignorant, qui illud per se ipsum intelligunt persequendum. Attingit obiter Eustrathius defensionem quandam Philosophiæ, occasionem arripiens ex hoc Aristotelis posteriori argumento. Ideo enim dixit diuitias non esse felicitatem, quod sint utiles. Hinc inquit apparet quam misere hallucinentur, qui Philosophiam spernunt, eo nomine quod sit inutilis, neque intelligunt hanc esse boni supremi rationem, ut in nullum aliud bonum referatur. Hac summa est Philosophiæ laus, quæ præ cæteris institutis id habeat, ut a nulla quapiam re alia pendeat, sed se ipsa contenta, cætera omnia quæ bona sunt & existimantur, dirigat & gubernet. Unde si quis bonus fuerit æstimator & iudex, facile intelligit viros ciuiles qui rempub. administrant, ei cum primis inseruire: nam omnes in hunc finem ciuitatibus quæ ad viuendum sufficiant ocium & pacem comparant, ut ciuibus vacet ex virtute viuere, & diuinis ac naturalibus contemplationibus se oblectare, quæ maximè ad philosophiam pertinent. Plurimum igitur falluntur qui diuitias in summo habent honore, quòd ad omnia sint utiles. Id si Midas ob oculos habuisset, non sic studio congerendarum diuitiarum se addixisset, ut merito χρυσομα-νὴς[?] dictus fuerit.
units.tr: Having named three kinds of life, and having reviewed the opinions that stood out above the rest, he had not yet mentioned riches. So that he does not pass them by, since very many people, and not ordinary ones either, admire them as the highest good, he now mentions them and removes them from happiness on a twofold ground. The first is that they belong to violence: what is violent has no claim to happiness. That the possession and acquisition of wealth is a violent matter he does not so much prove as show us through use and experience. For no one can acquire or keep very great and ample riches for long unless force, and no slight force, is applied. The second ground is that riches are useful and refer to something else, so their condition is servile. For we have them in order that they may supply other things we desire, and no one would value them at a hair's breadth unless they understood them to be useful for whatever they wished. That this is foreign to the nature of the highest good, all those know who understand that the highest good is to be pursued for its own sake. Eustratius touches in passing on a certain defence of philosophy, seizing the occasion from this second argument of Aristotle. He said that riches are not happiness because they are useful. From this, he says, it appears how wretchedly they are deceived who scorn philosophy on the ground that it is useless, not understanding that this is the very mark of the highest good: that it refers to no other good. This is the chief praise of philosophy, that among all pursuits it depends on nothing else but is content in itself, while it directs and governs all the other things that are or are thought to be good. Hence, if someone is a good judge and assessor, he readily understands that statesmen who administer the commonwealth serve philosophy above all: for all of them, to this end, provide cities with leisure and peace sufficient for living, so that citizens may have time to live from virtue and to delight in divine and natural contemplations, which pertain most of all to philosophy. Those therefore are greatly mistaken who hold riches in the highest honour because they are useful for everything. If Midas had kept this in view, he would not have devoted himself so eagerly to heaping up riches, and he would not rightly have been called chrysomanes [χρυσομανής], the gold-mad.

units.la: Neque inter principes ac reges ille unus est taxandus, cum maxima iam eorum pars hoc vitio laboret: qui tamen potuissent non solum his duabus Aristotelis rationibus admoneri, sed multis aliis, ut aliquem modum suæ cupiditati ponerent. Nam absq; ratione boni genus tanti fit quod externum est, & nil propemodum ad animum pertinet, sed tantum instrumentis accensetur, quibus homines juventur ad agenda quæ proposita erint. Dementat ite homines hoc boni genus, si accesserit imprudentes, laborant de acquirendis diuitijs plurimum, non aut de filijs quib. eas sunt reliqui- turi, neq; de seipsis qui sunt usuri. Sut[?] ut ille, qui multos calceos habere volu-it, & interea loci negligebat pedes. Præterea earum ingenium est anceps, ut nō minus prauis cupiditatibus & scelerib. perpetrandis inseruiat, quàm honestis & rectis officijs. Deinde si virtus ideò summum bonum non est, quòd & dormientib. & calamitosis adesse queat, quos nullus prudenter iudicas felices diceret, quomodo felicitas opibus attribuetur, cum possideantur non raro à miserrimis hominibus, imò potius à mostris[?] & prodigijs quib. odio sunt oes honestæ artes & omnes virtutes? Honori, & quidem iure, negatu[?] est ne ut beatitudo habeatur, quod non sit in eorum potestate, qui honore afficiuntur.
units.tr: Nor should that one man alone be censured among princes and kings, since the greater part of them already suffer from this vice. Yet they could have been admonished not only by these two reasons of Aristotle but by many others, to set some limit to their greed. For apart from the reason of the good, this kind of good, which is external and hardly pertains to the soul at all, is valued so highly, and is counted only among the instruments by which people are helped to do what has been proposed. Men lose their wits over this kind of good when, being unwise, they labour greatly to acquire riches, caring neither for the sons to whom they will leave them nor for themselves, who are going to use them. They are like the man who wished to have many shoes and meanwhile neglected his feet. Besides, the nature of riches is double-edged: they serve the commission of wicked desires and crimes no less than honourable and upright duties. Next, if virtue is not the highest good because it can be present even to sleepers and to the wretched, whom no prudent judge would call happy, how is happiness attributed to wealth, when it is often possessed by the most miserable men, or rather by monsters and prodigies, to whom all honest arts and all virtues are hateful? Honour, too, and rightly so, has been denied the status of blessedness, because it is not in the power of those who are honoured.

units.la: Quod si dicimus, de diuitijs proculdubio idè constituemus, cum periculis infinitis obnoxia sit earum possessio, eodem fere momento eripiuntur & acquiruntur. Iactabat quidam ingentes diuitias quas ipsi naues eius aduecherant, alter illum audiens respondebat, se non morari bona quæ à rudentibus & ventis penderent. Utq; non sint revera summum bonum illi videntur præclare intellexisse, qui diuitias bracteatam felicitatem dixerunt. Nec sane inficiamur diuitias bonas, at quod summum bonum sint nunc refellitur. Verum de hoc argumento non multa dicam: quandoquidem omnes præditi mediocri vel pietate vel prudentia per seipsos apprime sentiunt, non esse hic ultimam hominis finem, sed alia bona complura his præferenda. Ideoq; subiecit Aristoteles,
units.tr: But if we say that riches should certainly be set down as the good, since their possession is subject to infinite dangers, and they are taken away and acquired in almost the same moment. A certain man was boasting of the great riches that his ships had brought him, and another, hearing him, replied that he did not rely on goods that depended on ropes and winds. And since they are not truly the highest good, those who called riches gilded happiness seem to have understood this admirably. Nor indeed do we deny that riches are good, but it is now being refuted that they are the highest good. I shall not say much more on this argument, since all who have even moderate piety or prudence feel for themselves at once that this is not man's final end, but that many other goods are to be preferred to it. Therefore Aristotle added,

units.la: Propterea quæ iam dicta sunt potius quispiam existimauerit fines esse, nam per seipsa desyderatur: at ea non videntur, licet de ipsis multæ rationes iactatæ fuerint. Hæc igitur missa faciamus.
units.tr: For this reason, someone might rather think that the things already mentioned are ends, since they are desired for their own sake. But the other things do not seem to be ends, although many arguments have been advanced about them. Let us set these aside for now.

units.la: Confutat adhuc propositam sententiam ratione à comparatis, quæ illi regulæ innituntur peruulgatæ, si quod magis videtur inesse non inerit, multo minus concedetur, quod non videbatur inesse. At bona quæ iam recensuimus, habuerunt magis rationem finis quàm diuitiæ, & non sunt nec videntur finis: igitur diuitiæ multò minus erunt. Quod illa visa sint fines, ex eo probatur, quòd per seipsa expetebantur. Quomodo verò ibi non sit collocandum summum bonum, est antea demonstratum.
units.tr: He still refutes the proposed opinion by an argument from comparatives, which rests on the very common rule: if what seems more likely to belong to a thing does not belong to it, then what did not seem to belong to it will much less be granted. But the goods we have just listed have had more the character of an end than riches do, and they are not, nor do they seem to be, ends; therefore riches will be much less so. That those things seemed to be ends is proved from the fact that they were sought for their own sake. How the highest good should not be placed there has been demonstrated before.

units.la: Quod inquit, de illis multas rationes & sermones habitos, licet intelligere, quia philosophi permulti fuerunt qui voluptatem defenderint summum esse bonum. Aristippus enim æqualis Platoni eam sententiam defendit, deinde successit Epicurus, Metrodorus, & consimiles. De honore identidem accidit. Quin à Socrate non parum sæpe ciuiles homines referente Platone reprehensi sunt, quod nimis effrenatè honorum cupidi fuerint. Plures itaq; de his habebantur passim sermones dum illi defendunt, isti vero confutant propositam opinionem. Ubi vero inquit Aristoteles, Quæ tamen non vi-dentur.) de voluptate solum, honore & virtute intelligenda sunt, non de contemplatione: quia non inficiatur ibi summum esse nostrum bonum.
units.tr: That he says many arguments and discussions have been held about them can be understood, because there were very many philosophers who defended pleasure as the highest good. For Aristippus, a contemporary of Plato, defended that opinion, and then Epicurus succeeded him, and Metrodorus and others like them. Something similar has happened with honour. Indeed, civic men were not infrequently rebuked by Socrates, as Plato reports, for being excessively greedy for honours. So there were many discussions on these matters everywhere, while some defended and others refuted the proposed opinion. But where Aristotle says "which yet do not seem," this must be understood only of pleasure, honour and virtue, not of contemplation, because there he does not deny that contemplation is our highest good.

units.la: Quod violentæ & in aliud referendæ sint diuitiæ, uno verbo testantur sacræ literæ: Facite vobis amicos de mammona iniquitatis. Quod imprudentes lædant: Radix omnium malorum est cupiditas. Qui volunt ditari incident in laqueum, in tentationem, &c. De inconstantia, præcipe ut non spesperent in incertis divitiis. Hac nocte tollent a te animam tuam. Denique impediunt: Et adolescens cum esset dives, tristis abijt. Bona itaq; sunt, sed in suo ordine.
units.tr: That riches are to be used for force and referred to something else, the sacred letters testify in a single word: "Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness" (Luc. 16.). That they harm the imprudent: "The love of money is the root of all evils" (1 Tim. 6.). "They that will be made rich fall into temptation and a snare" (1 Tim. 6.). Concerning their inconstancy: "Charge them not to trust in uncertain riches" (1 Tim. 6.). "This night they will require your soul of you" (Luc. 12.). Finally, they hinder: "And the young man, when he had great possessions, went away sorrowful" (Matth. 19.). Riches are therefore good, but in their own order.
CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Præstat forsitan de uniuersali consyderare, ac dubitare quonam modo dicatur.
units.tr: Perhaps it is best first to consider the universal and to ask in what sense it is said.

units.la: Initium[?] hoc est sexti capitis, ubi opinio de ideis confutatur: atque consilium Aristotelis est, demonstrare summum bonum hominis non esse in idea situm, quod Platonici videbantur affirmare. Quatuor vero sunt huius capitis praecipuae & summae partes. In prima Quaestionem proponit, & quadam modestia & excusatione utitur. Deinde variis rationibus sententiam hanc de ideis confutat. Ad haec tertio loco dubitationem cum eius declaratione interposuit. At denique adiicit ut essent ideae, quemadmodum isti volunt, ad rem praesentem non faciunt, neque ad summum bonum hominis queunt pertinere. Haec praecipua loca sexti capitis, mox, ut ad illa venerimus, diligentius ac subtilius dividemus. Opinionem istam postremo loco posuit: quia caeteris videtur sublimior. Et Plato de idea est loquutus, cum de primo bono ageret: & certe visus est afferre non humilia, sed quae possent, ut putabatur, animos, ad altissimas haec de re cogitationes attollere.
units.tr: This is the beginning of the sixth chapter, where the opinion about ideas is refuted. Aristotle's purpose is to show that the highest good of man does not lie in an idea, which the Platonists seemed to affirm. There are four principal and chief parts of this chapter. In the first he proposes the question and uses a certain modesty and apology. Then by various arguments he refutes this opinion about ideas. In the third place he interposes a doubt with its explanation. Finally he adds that even if there were ideas, as those men want, they are irrelevant to the present matter and cannot pertain to the highest good of man. We shall divide these chief passages of the sixth chapter more carefully and subtly when we come to them. He put this opinion last because it seems to the others more lofty. Plato spoke of the idea when treating of the primary good, and he certainly seemed to bring forward not humble things, but things which could, as was thought, lift minds to the most lofty thoughts on this subject.

units.la: Licet quaestio haec molesta sit, quo'd amici sint qui formas induxerunt. Sed praestare forsitan & opus esse videtur veritatis defendendae causa sua quoque propria refutare, praesertim Philosophos. Nam cum ambo sint amici, sanctum est praeferre veritatem.
units.tr: Although this question is troublesome because those who introduced the forms were friends, yet it seems fitting, and perhaps necessary, for the sake of defending the truth, to refute even one's own views, especially as Philosophers. For since both are friends, it is holy to put truth first.

units.la: Multis in locis Aristoteles aduersus Platonis Ideas est loquutus, ut in metaphysicis, in libris de Anima, & in Analyticis, atq; alibi, & nusquam praeterquam hic est usus praefatione: Quasi vel difficilis vel iniucunda fuerit ipsi quaestio. At nunc ob eam causam excusat, quoniam de moribus agit, & nonnihil videtur ab officio discedere, qui amicum aduersatur, aut suos praeceptores traducit.familiares vero inter se fuisse Platonem & Aristotelem, est certissimum, atque ipsum cum Socratis tum Platonis fuisse discipulum nemo ambigit. Et huc etiam nempe ad hanc moderationem id pertinet quod quaestionem movendo inquit,
units.tr: In many places Aristotle spoke against Plato's Ideas, as in the Metaphysics, in the books On the Soul, in the Analytics, and elsewhere, and nowhere except here does he use a preface, as if the question were either difficult or unpleasant for him. But now he makes an excuse for this reason: since he is treating of morals, and it seems somewhat to depart from duty to oppose a friend or disparage one's teachers. That Plato and Aristotle were intimate friends is most certain, and no one doubts that he was a disciple both of Socrates and of Plato. And to this moderation there pertains also what he says when raising the question,

units.la: Praestat forsitan.) Sic loquitur quasi res ipsa & veritas potius huius quaestionis tractationem exigant, quam ipse sponte aut volens eam induxit. Et Eustrathius addit quae dicantur non dici contra Platonem, sed potius aduersus eos qui sententiam eius accipiebant longe aliter & minus cō-modè quàm ipse dixisset. Quare molesta sit quaestio, rationem affert, quoni-am oppugnandi sunt amici. Sed excusat, quod veritas sit defendenda, pra-sertim à Philosophis: & ratio est, quoniam hi sunt amatores sapientia. Sapi-entia vero citra controuersiam est veritas: quare si non tuerentur verita-tem non essent Philosophi.
units.tr: "Perhaps it is best." He speaks as if the matter itself and the truth demanded the treatment of this question, rather than that he introduced it of his own accord or willingly. Eustratius adds that what is said is not said against Plato, but rather against those who received his opinion much differently and less fairly than he himself had stated it. He gives the reason why the question is troublesome: because friends must be opposed. But he excuses it, because the truth must be defended, especially by Philosophers; and the reason is that they are lovers of wisdom. Now wisdom, beyond controversy, is truth; therefore, if they did not defend the truth, they would not be Philosophers.

units.la: Cumq; duo sint amici oportet veritatem praeferre.) Atque cum simus Philosophi, decet ut vel natura ipsorum propter veritatem dogmata tollamus. Si natura ipsorum, cur non & aliena? Hanc utinam sententia illi recinerent, qui saepe in ecclesia ut sua ipsorum tueantur dogmata, non verentur quoduis absurdum proferre. Deinde monemur ut propter verbum Dei, quod summa est veritas, nullius personae respectum habeamus.
units.tr: "And since both are friends, it is right to put truth first." And since we are Philosophers, it becomes us to set aside even our own doctrines for the sake of truth. If we should do so for their doctrines, why not also for those of others? Would that those men would sing this tune who often in the Church, to defend their own dogmas, do not hesitate to put forward any absurdity whatever. Then we are admonished that for the sake of the Word of God, which is the highest truth, we should have regard to no person whatever.

units.la: Haec est huius prioris partis sexti capitis sententia. Nunc rationes oporteret audire, sed prius operae pretium est de ideis nonnulla praefari, quo Platonis percipiatur opinio, contra quam pugnat Aristoteles. Plato de Deo utique praeclarissima cognovit. Et primum quidem illum esse unum & ineffabile. Unum, ne in immensum progrediamur, in causis, namque primam esse verum est, Ineffabilem, quoniam ex communibus vocabulis humanis non habentur vocabula quae Dei proprietates exprimant. Ut si homo subiret aliquando naturam equinam, vocem non haberet inter caeteros equos nisi hinnitum, & eo certe nonposset qua mente humana teneret aliis equis exponere. Ita Philosophi & magni viri, cum de Deo sublimia cognouerint, voces non habuerunt humanas quibus ipsa expedirent. Nouit adhac Plato Deum in se omnia complectii, sed ita ut omnia identidem excederet, neque est in mundo ullum tam parvum bonum, quin sit in Deo, neq; tam magnum quin ab illo superetur, ac infinitis partibus vincatur. Omnia penetrat Deus & seipsum nunquam egreditur. Quod infinitus sit, & ubicunq; fuerit sit in seipso. Pro-duxit omnia, non alia sane causa impulsus quam sua ipsius bonitate: nil e-nim nim inveniri potest ea praestantius quod expetierit Deus in universi orbis productione. Bonus est & ex bonitate sua omnia edidit quae fecit. Bonitate vero non habet acquisitam vel studio vel industria amore hominum, sed illi natiua est, & suopte ingenio naturaliter insita. Quare optione aut delectu ullo ipsam non sibi asciuit. Quemadmodum Sol illustrat omnia sua luce, quam tamen lucem non habet adscititiam, sed genuinam & innatam. Nec solum omnia creauit Deus, verum in ipsum omnia tendunt ut in extremam finem. Nec mirum si ad eum omnia referantur, cum ab ipso pendeat omnium perfectio. Haec quae recensui & alia complura de Deo praeclarissime sensit & scripsit. Quae partim in divinis literis habentur expressa, partim vero sunt usurpata ab ecclesiasticis scriptoribus, & quidem vetustis. De his habet permulta Dionysius ille, quem Areopagitam vocant, vetustus sane scriptor, licet non putem illum esse qui perhibetur S. Apostolorum discipulus. Quod probari potest primum ex argumento, & scribendi genere. Platonice siquidem permulta philosophatur, neque scripta eius apostolicam spirant doctrinam. Deinde librorum eius neque Iustinus martyr, neque Irenaeus, neque Tertullianus, neque Cyprianus, neque Eusebius Caesariensis meminit, qui nullum propemodum tacuit illustrem scriptorem qui antiquitus floruerit. Hieronymus etiam in lib. de Scriptoribus illustribus eum tacuit. Tantum postremo tempore Gregorius Romanus eius meminit. Tertio mentionem fecit monachorum in ecclesiastica Hierarchia qui medium gradum seu locum & dignitate habuerint inter plebe & clericos: quod temporib. Apostolorum inauditum fuit. Sed quicquid sit, antiquus fuit Scriptor, & is uti dixi usurpat haec & alia fere pleraque Platonis, nec non rationem videtur idearum attingere: quare non est ea sententia ab omnibus ex partibus absurda.
units.tr: This is the sense of this first part of the sixth chapter. Now it would be worth hearing the arguments, but first it is worth saying something about ideas beforehand, so that the opinion of Plato, against which Aristotle fights, may be understood. Plato indeed knew most excellent things about God. And first, that He is one and ineffable. One, so that we do not go on to infinity, since it is true that the first is in causes; ineffable, because from common human words there are no words which express the properties of God. As if a man were at some time to take on the nature of a horse, he would have no voice among other horses except a neigh, and he could certainly not explain with a human mind to other horses what he understood. So philosophers and great men, when they have known sublime things about God, have not had human words with which to express them. Plato also knew that God embraces all things in Himself, yet in such a way that He at the same time exceeds all things; nor is there any good in the world so small that it is not in God, nor so great that it is not surpassed by Him and overcome by infinite parts. God penetrates all things and never goes out of Himself; because He is infinite, He is wherever He is, in Himself. He produced all things, moved by no other cause than His own goodness; for nothing more excellent can be found than what God aimed at in producing the whole world. He is good, and out of His goodness He brought forth all that He made. But He does not have goodness acquired by study or industry or by the love of men; it is native to Him and naturally implanted by His own nature. Therefore He did not assume it for Himself by any choice or selection. As the sun illumines all things with its light, which light it does not have as an addition, but as its own and innate. Nor did God only create all things; all things also tend toward Him as their ultimate end. Nor is it surprising that all things are referred to Him, since the perfection of all depends on Him. These things I have recounted, and many others besides, Plato thought and wrote most excellently about God. Some of these are expressed in the divine writings, but some were borrowed by ecclesiastical writers, and indeed the ancient ones. Much about these is found in that Dionysius whom they call the Areopagite, an ancient writer certainly, although I do not think he is the one who is said to have been a disciple of the holy Apostles. This can be proved first from the subject matter and the manner of writing: for he philosophises very much in the Platonic manner, and his writings do not breathe the apostolic doctrine. Next, neither Justin Martyr, nor Irenaeus, nor Tertullian, nor Cyprian, nor Eusebius of Caesarea mentions his books, although Eusebius passed over almost no illustrious writer who flourished in antiquity. Jerome also passed him over in his book On Illustrious Writers. Only in more recent times does Gregory of Rome mention him. Thirdly, he mentions monks in the ecclesiastical Hierarchy as holding a middle rank or position and dignity between the laity and the clergy, which was unheard of in the times of the Apostles. But whatever the case, he was an ancient writer, and, as I said, he borrows these and nearly all the other things of Plato, and also seems to touch on the doctrine of ideas; therefore that opinion is not absurd in every respect.

units.la: Idea dicunt quid universum, ut nunc manifeste dicit Aristoteles in textu, quando scribit, Praestat itaque forsan de universo consyderare.) Non autem hic accipitur universum, ut in Dialecticis: nam illud est quod ex multis singularibus colligimus, animadversa forma, natura seu conditione, in qua conveniunt, eamq; concipimus in animo: ut quicquid postea viderimus consimile, illa forma seu specie iam concepta intelligamus quid sit. Atq; ut de nomine prius agatur, ἀ εἶδη, seu ἰδέα ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδέων, seu ἰδεῖν dicitur, quod est cognoscere ac intelligere. Contingit autem rem cognoscere aut priusquam fiat, aut postquam est producta. Si agnoscatur priusquam fiat, & praesertim ab eius efficienti, dicitur idea, eamque idcirco dixeruntante multa & post genita, quoniam antecedit singularia quae sunt multa, eaq; producuntur, & non possent produci nisi praecessisset hoc genus formae ac universi in mente artificis, nisi indicaretur agere quod nesciat. Quare iure meritoq; dicuntur hæc ante genita. Et quicquid fit, ad suum respicit universum, ad cuius exemplum & imaginem est factum. Suntq; huiusmodi ideæ à multis separatæ naturæ diuinæ, quæ nec intereunt nec generantur. Dici possunt formæ, species, exempla, universa. Vbi autem sint, Platonici nō consentiunt, alij in Deo, nonnulli in alia mente à Deo producta. Vnde Varro quemadmodum commemorat Augustinus de Civitate Dei, dixit, Iouem ef-se cælum, Iunonem referre terram, Mineruam autem ideas & rationes re-rum quæ fiunt, illam q; constituerunt è capite Iouis natam, quasi sit mens à Deo producta, in qua ideæ & rationes producendarum rerum inessent. Mitto astrologos, qui in suprema Sphæra orbis collocarunt. Verum de hoc po-stea, satis est nunc videre talia universa, formas et species poni ut Deus per illa noverit quæ facturus erat & quæ facit.
units.tr: The Ideas are said to be the universal, as Aristotle now plainly says in the text, when he writes: "Perhaps it is best to consider the universal." But the universal is not taken here as in the Dialectics. For that is what we gather from many singulars, when we have noticed a form, nature, or condition in which they agree, and conceive it in the mind, so that whatever similar thing we afterwards see, we understand what it is by that already conceived form or species. And to speak first of the name: ἰδέα (idea), or εἶδος, is so called from εἰδέναι or ἰδεῖν, which means to know and understand. Now a thing may be known either before it is made or after it has been produced. If it is recognised before it is made, and especially by its efficient cause, it is called an idea; and they have called it so because it precedes the many singulars which are made and brought forth, and these could not be produced unless this kind of form and universal had first been in the mind of the craftsman, unless he were thought to act without knowing what he does. Therefore these things are rightly and deservedly said to be before things were made. And whatever is made looks to its own universal, after whose pattern and image it was made. Such ideas are by many taken to be separate natures of the divine, which neither perish nor come into being. They may be called forms, species, patterns, universals. Where they are, the Platonists do not agree: some place them in God, some in another mind produced by God. Hence Varro, as Augustine recalls in The City of God, said that Jupiter is heaven, Juno the earth, and Minerva the ideas and reasons of the things that are made, and that she was born from the head of Jupiter, as if she were a mind produced by God, in which the ideas and reasons of the things to be produced were present. I pass over the astrologers, who placed them in the highest sphere of the world. But of this later; it is enough now to see that such universals, forms, and species are posited so that God by them knew what He was going to make and what He makes.

units.la: Secunda rerum notitia est, cum iam producta sint, ibi mens hominum tandem (ut prius dicebamus) colligit formas quæ ad plura possunt accommodari, & appellantur universalia, quasi tota quædam respectu singularium: nam illa comprehendunt in se, ut nullum eorum inueniatur, quin universale iam conceptum de ipso queat dici. Vtq; res adhuc intelligatur apertius, quia universum totum est, triplex totum esse dixerunt: Vnum ante partes, alterum ex partibus, tertium verò in partibus. Ante partes est exemplar, notitia ante multa, quia ante genita, nam omnia illa quæ fiunt ad talium universorum simulacrum, dicuntur eorum partes. Ex partibus totum sunt ipsa composita quæ in natura existunt, & constat partibus aliquā do homogeneis, interdum heterogeneis. Terra diuiditur in partes, quæ & terra dicuntur, & terra definitionem habent: ista sunt homogenea. Homo verò in membra diuiditur, quorum nullum homo dicitur, neq; hominis habet definitionem: & hæc sunt heterogenea. Totum in multis est ipsa forma quæ ab humana mente concipitur, & ex singulis rebus, ut antea bis præmonuimus, colligitur. Hinc soluitur quæstio illa quæ in scholis agitatur de naturalibus, an sint in rebus an à rebus existant separata. Si totum accipitur ut exemplar, à rebus est separatum, quoniam antecedit, & priusquam res fiant habetur saltem in mente artificis. Sin verò pro toto composito naturali, id nunquam extra res inueniri poterit. At si de tertio, id est, de toto in partibus loquamur, id est Dialecticum, & solum in mente humana locum habet, ideoque dicitur in partibus quoniam in ipsis est per accommodationem quandam & prædicationem. De hoc Aristoteles dixit in Analyticis posterioribus. Animal, hoc est naturale, aut nihil est aut posterius est. Nam si loquamur de rebus actu ac reipsa existentibus nihil est: at si consideretur ut mente ac ratione collectum in animis habetur, posterius est, quàm res existant, quoniam ex ipsis est collectum. Est itaq; idea & universum de quo loquimur principium notitiæ, at non cuiusuis, sed tantum facientis, hoc est, illius quam appellat [illegible, ~8 letters]. Et ideo sunt ista simulachra & formæ non quidem adscititiæ, sed natiuæ. Neq; ibi sunt otiosæ, imò efficaces: quod non accidit in artificum intelligentia, qui ut multa habeant archetypa, illa non faciunt: at Deus rationes suas impressit & quotidie imprimit. Est etiam natura forma quædam, sed in rebus ipsis inclusa, quæ dum in eis movet, efficit ut sic erumpant res multiplices & diuersæ: at formæ de quibus agimus ab ipsis rebus separatæ sunt, subsistunt et omnia corpora et naturas excedunt.
units.tr: The second knowledge of things comes when they have already been produced. Then the human mind at last (as we said before) gathers forms that can be applied to many things, and these are called universals, as if they were a kind of whole in relation to the singulars. For they contain them all, so that none of the singulars can be found of which the universal, once conceived, cannot be predicated. To make the matter clearer: since the universal is a whole, they have said that a whole is threefold: one before its parts, another made up of its parts, and a third existing in its parts. The whole before its parts is the exemplar, a knowledge prior to many things because it is prior to what is produced; for all the things that are made after the likeness of such a universal are called its parts. The whole made of its parts is the composite things themselves that exist in nature, and it consists of parts that are sometimes homogeneous and sometimes heterogeneous. Earth is divided into parts which are also called earth and have the definition of earth: these are homogeneous. But a man is divided into limbs, none of which is called a man or has the definition of a man: these are heterogeneous. The whole in its many parts is the form conceived by the human mind, gathered from the individual things, as we have twice noted before. Hence is resolved the question debated in the schools about natural universals: whether they exist in things or exist separately from things. If the whole is taken as the exemplar, it is separate from things, since it comes before them, and before things are made it is held at least in the mind of the craftsman. But if we speak of the whole natural composite, this can never be found outside the things. And if we speak of the third kind, that is, the whole in its parts, this belongs to dialectic and has a place only in the human mind; it is therefore said to be "in its parts" because it is in them by a certain application and predication. Aristotle spoke of this in the Posterior Analytics: "Animal, that is, the natural, either is nothing or is posterior." For if we speak of things actually and really existing, there is nothing; but if it is considered as gathered by the mind and reason, and held in the spirits, it is posterior to the things, since it has been gathered from them. The idea, then, and the universal of which we speak, is the principle of knowledge, but not of any knowledge, only of the maker, that is, of that which he calls [illegible]. And so these likenesses and forms are not borrowed but native. Nor are they idle there, but indeed effective; this does not happen in the understanding of craftsmen, who, though they have many archetypes, do not make things by them. But God has impressed his reasons and impresses them daily. There is also a form of nature, but enclosed in the things themselves, which, while it moves within them, causes the manifold and diverse things to come forth in this way. But the forms we are discussing are separate from the things themselves; they subsist and exceed all bodies and natures.

units.la: Plato ideo adductus est ut poneret ideas: quoniam Deum nouerat efficientem omnium rerum causam, non quidem temerariam aut fortuitam. Qua re oportuit ut in se coclusas haberet ideas & rationes rerum faciendarum.
units.tr: Plato was led to posit ideas because he knew God to be the efficient cause of all things, not a rash or chance cause. Hence it was necessary that he should hold within himself the ideas and reasons of the things to be made.

units.la: Quod item Boetius vidit, cùm ita caneret:
units.tr: Boethius also saw this when he sang:

units.la: Qui cuncta superno Ducit ab exemplo pulchrum, pulcherrimus ipse, Mundum mente gerens, simili in imagine formans.
units.tr: He who leads all things from the supreme exemplar, beautiful and most beautiful himself, bearing the world in his mind and forming it in a likeness to himself.

units.la: Nec in deo possunt hæ formæ ut accidentia poni, quia nil à Deo potest adimi: & accidens est quod adesse potest & abesse præter subiecti interitu. Neq; si Deus admitteret accidentia, compositionem effugeret. Adhæc res in ipso Deo poni nequeunt, cum materia & defectibus, ut quæ nunc in rerum natura existunt. Quare in ipso tantum rationes earum collocantur, qui factu est, ut ideæ, cum pronomine αὐτὸ efferuntur, αὐτάνθρωπος[?], αὐταγαθόν, αὐταλήθεια, hoc est, ipse homo, ipsum bonum, ipsa veritas. Distinguuntur autem hæ ideæ non re ipsa in Deo, sed ratione. Ut spacium à radice montis ad verticem re ipsa unum est, at dicitur ascensus & descensus pro diversa illius ratione. Et via Thebis Athenas est eadem re, sed ratione distinguitur. Ex artificib. quos hic inter nos videmus, ratio idearum est inducta: nam faber sine archetypo nil ædificat: neq; pictor aut statuarius ullum edit signum quòd prius mente non conceperit. Sed hoc interest, quod illi species industria & labore quodam sibi in animo finxerunt, Deus verò tales ideas in se naturaliter habet insitas. Deinde in mente artificum distinguuntur à se ipsis ideæ re, at in Deo solum ratione. Quod ad propositum facit, ut videmus, in mundo plurima & distincta sunt bona, quæ omnia cum ad Deo sint, ad unam communem ideam sunt referenda, & tantisper bona sunt quo ad illam unã for mam seu speciem boni participant & referunt. Quare nonnullis visi sunt homines beati esse non posse, nisi illius ideae facti fuerint participes, et in ea propter suos[?] acquieuerint: ideo Aristoteles de hac opinione in praesentia scribit. Quamuis reuera talis felicitas ad hoc institutum, si esset, non multum faceret, ut audiemus ad calcem huius capitis, cum hic tractatio sit de illo boni genere, quod in nobis inhæret, quale non potest idea boni esse.
units.tr: Nor can these forms be posited in God as accidents, because nothing can be taken away from God; and an accident is that which can be present or absent without the destruction of its subject. Nor, if God admitted accidents, would he escape composition. Moreover, these things cannot be placed in God himself with matter and defects, as those things which now exist in the nature of things. Therefore only their reasons are located in him. This is why they are expressed, as ideas, with the pronoun αὐτὸ: αὐτάνθρωπος [autanthropos], αὐταγαθόν [autagathon], αὐταλήθεια [autaletheia], that is, man himself, the good itself, truth itself. These ideas are distinguished in God not in reality but in reasoning. Thus the ascent and descent of a mountain from its root to its peak is one in fact, yet it is called ascent or descent according to its different aspect. And the road from Thebes to Athens is the same in fact, but is distinguished by reason. From the craftsmen whom we see here among us, the notion of ideas has been drawn: for a builder makes nothing without an archetype, nor does a painter or sculptor produce any image that he has not first conceived in his mind. But this differs, that those craftsmen have fashioned their forms in their minds by industry and a certain labour, whereas God has such ideas naturally implanted in himself. Further, in the minds of craftsmen the ideas are distinguished from themselves in reality, but in God only in reason. What is pertinent to our purpose is this: as we see, in the world there are many distinct goods, all of which, since they are from God, must be referred to one common idea, and they are good only so far as they share in and refer to that one common form or species of the good. Therefore some men have seemed unable to be blessed unless they became partakers of that idea and found rest in it; for this reason Aristotle writes about this opinion at present. Yet in truth such a happiness, if it existed, would not greatly serve this undertaking, as we shall hear at the end of this chapter, since the present treatment concerns that kind of good which inheres in us, and such a good cannot be the idea of the good.

units.la: Augustinus in 83. quaestionib. quaestione 46. pulcherrime de ideis scribit. Primum, inquit, ut nominatae sic fuerint a Platone, haud tamen ab illo reperta esse: nam ante illum si sic non dicebantur, alio fortasse nomine appellabantur. Quod autem prius fuerint, inde probat, quod ante Platonem permulti alii fuerint sapientes. Nemo autem sapiens aut dici aut esse potest, qui ad idearum notitiam non peruenerit. Nec solum in Graecia fuerunt sapientes ante Platonem, verum etiam in aliis orbis partibus, quos ut viseret & audiret Plato, idem varias, ut legimus, peregrinationes suscepit. Ideas, inquit, interpretari possumus formas & species. A nonnullis dictae sunt λόγοι.
units.tr: Augustine, in his eighty-three Questions, question 46, writes most beautifully about ideas. First, he says, that they were so named by Plato, yet were not discovered by him; for if they were not called this before him, they were perhaps called by some other name. He proves that they existed earlier from the fact that many other wise men existed before Plato. But no one can be called or be wise who has not attained knowledge of the ideas. Wise men existed before Plato not only in Greece but also in other parts of the world, and Plato, in order to see and hear them, undertook, as we read, various journeys. The ideas, he says, we may interpret as forms and species. By some they have been called λόγοι [logoi].

units.la: Quamuis ista vox proprie sermones et rationes significet, dat nihilominus ita ut cunq; posse nominari. Accedit praeterea ad definitionem: & ideas, inquit, esse formas seu rationes stabiles & incommutabiles, non formatas, sed quae semper eodem modo se habeant, & in divina intelligentia comprehendantur. Et quamuis ipsae nec oriantur, nec intereant, nil tamen quod oriatur aut intereat formatur, nisi ad illarum exemplum. Cognoscantur (ut vult) sed ab anima tantum & ea rationali, nec per quamuis eius partem, sed solum per supremam, nempe mentem quasi quodam eius interno vultu & oculo. Quem oculum adhuc, inquit, requiri, ut sit repurgatus & purus: alioquin ad idearum notitiam minime pertingit. Quis itaq;, addit, religiosus, aut vera praeditus religione, tales ideas negabit, aut illas non profitebitur? Certe nullus, nisi dicere velit, quae sunt, a Deo ipso non habere ut sint, aut ab illo non regi neq; gubernari. Aut si hoc dederit, affirmare velit, id sine cognitione ac ratione fieri: quod esset velle Deum agere quae agit temere, quae omnia cum sint absurdissima, necesse est ut ideas ponamus, easq; distinctas: quaedoquidem alia ratione formetur homo & alia equus. Atq; haec quia danda sunt, ubi nam collocari poterunt, nisi diuinain[?] mente, quoniam Deus extra se nihil habet quod respiciat, ad cuius exemplum fingat quae producit. Nil autem in Deo poni vel affirmari potest quod non sit aeternum atq; verissimum. Ex quo dicendum est ideas & verissimas & aeternas esse oportere. Omnia vero tantisper sunt & durant quoad sua idea fuerint participia. Cumq; inter caetera humanus animus sit nobilissimus, ad illarum notitiam potest ascendere, qua tandem beatus est & felix. Hæc omnia loco iam adducto Augustinus refert. Unde apparet duplici de causa ideas inventas. Prima est ut sint principium producendi res, & easdem cognoscendi perfectè atq; absolutè: nam per singularia parùm & minus verè cognoscuntur. Quod si fuerit, in mente Dei eas esse oportet: nam vis & principium producendi collocatur in efficienti causa, & (similiter cognoscendi principium in cognoscente. In Deo itaq; sunt, non ut quid illius essentiæ ac naturæ adiunctum: est enim Deus simplicissimus neq; ullam admittit compositionem. Neque etiam in eo ponuntur quasi dirigente opus habeat Deus aliquo alio à seipso: nam cognitione suæ ipsius essentiæ sapientissimus est, neq; regulam extra se ullam intuetur. Et hoc fortasse spectarunt Peripatetici, ac inter illos præcipue Auerroes celeberrimus, qui dixit in metaphysicis, omnes formas in materia esse in potentia, & in primo efficiente, ut in vi agente. Utq; res pateat facilius, est intelligendum omne agens aut esse naturale, aut ex arte producere, quæ facit, si naturaliter agat, tum habet formam eiusdem speciei sui naturæ cum reproducta: ut homo generat hominem, & ignis ignem. aut si eam non habet ὁμωνύμως [?], habet saltem vi & efficacia, quod propter cælum dixerim & intelligentias, quæ formaliter, ut loquuntur, non sunt vel plantæ vel animalia, cum tamen per illa hæc fiant. Quod verò per artem operatur, non quidem est eiusdem formæ aut naturæ cum eo quod agit: nam architectus non est domus, neq; faber est arca, sed ista in mente habent concepta, et ad eiusmodi archetypa respicientes, fabricantur quæ producunt.
units.tr: Although that word properly signifies discourses and reasons, it nonetheless allows them to be named in whatever way. Moreover, he comes to a definition: the ideas, he says, are forms or reasons that are stable and unchangeable, not formed, but which always remain in the same way, and are comprehended in the divine intelligence. And although they themselves neither arise nor perish, yet nothing that arises or perishes is formed except after their example. They are known (as he wishes) only by the soul, and that the rational soul, not through any part of it, but only through its highest part, namely the mind, as it were through its inner countenance and eye. This eye, he says, still needs to be cleansed and made pure; otherwise it does not at all reach the knowledge of the ideas. Who, then, he adds, being religious or endowed with true religion, will deny such ideas, or will not profess them? Certainly no one, unless he wished to say that the things which exist do not have their being from God himself, or are not ruled and governed by him. Or if he grants this, but wishes to affirm that it happens without knowledge and reason, that would be to say that God acts rashly in what he does; since all these things are most absurd, we must necessarily posit ideas, and distinct ones, since man is formed by one reason and the horse by another. And since these must be granted, where could they be located, if not in the divine mind, since God has nothing outside himself to look upon, after whose example he might fashion what he produces? Nothing, however, can be posited or affirmed of God that is not eternal and most true. From this it must be said that the ideas must be both most true and eternal. But all things are and endure only so far as they participate in their idea. And since among other things the human spirit is most noble, it can ascend to knowledge of them, by which at last it is blessed and happy. Augustine reports all these things in the passage already cited. From this it appears that ideas were discovered for two reasons. The first is that they are the principle of producing things and of knowing them perfectly and absolutely; for through singulars they are known little and less truly. If this is so, they must be in the mind of God; for the power and principle of producing is located in the efficient cause, and likewise the principle of knowing in the knower. They are therefore in God, not as something added to his essence and nature, for God is most simple and admits no composition. Nor are they posited in him as though God needed some guide other than himself for his work; for he is most wise in the knowledge of his own essence, and looks to no rule outside himself. Perhaps the Peripatetics had this in view, and among them especially the most celebrated Averroes, who said in the Metaphysics that all forms are in matter in potency, and in the first efficient cause as in an agent power. To make the matter clearer, we must understand that every agent either acts naturally or produces by art what it makes. If it acts naturally, it has a form of the same species as its nature with the thing produced: as a man generates a man, and fire generates fire. Or if it does not have that form univocally, it has at least the power and efficacy of it; this I would say of the heavens and the intelligences, which, as they say, formally are neither plants nor animals, though through them these things are made. But what works through art is not indeed of the same form or nature as that which it makes: for the architect is not a house, nor is the carpenter a chest; rather they hold these things conceived in the mind, and looking to such archetypes, they fabricate what they produce.

units.la: Sed illud nonnullis videtur difficile, quomodo id quod unum sit & simplicissimum, tam multiplex esse ac dici possit, ut necessarium est ideas consistere, si forma sint omnium specierum, quas hic in mundo inferiori habemus. Verum quo ad hoc, id sciendum est, vis esse intellectus, ut quæ in aliquo sunt coniuncta queat seorsim ac diuisim considerari. Ut causa exempli de numero quaternario possum dicere, hunc numerum ut sit unus, à mente tamen cogitari potest, ut binarius & ut ternarius, quoniam ista in seipso comprehendit. Neq; ambigendum [?] est iuxta Philosophi sententiam, species & naturas rerum instar numerorum esse: ut enim in his una superaddita unitate mutatur numerus, ita in formis & naturis rerum si unam aliquam vel addas vel demas differentiam, species mutatur. Fatemur itaq; naturam diuinam simplicem & unam esse, at perfectissimam, cumq; illam creaturæ imitentur, non omnes totam neq; omnes eodem modo & gradu. Quare ut referatur essentia Dei tanquam exemplar ad species diuersas, ita in ea diuersi gradus perfectionis possunt notari et distingui, non quidem re sed ratione. Deus itaq; seipsum dū intelligit, ut imitandum & exprimendum à rebus quas condit, secundum diuersos gradus pro illarum rerum modo, dicitur intueri suas ideas, quæ cum alioquin sint nobis occultæ: reddūtur[?] per conditas res manifestæ. Unde ad Hebræos dicitur, Fide credimus aptata secula, ut spectacula fierent earum rerum quæ non apparebant. Et ad Romanos ita dicitur, à creatura mundi & per ea quæ facta sunt inuisibilia Dei esse patefacta philosophis.
units.tr: But to some this seems difficult: how can that which is one and most simple be so manifold, and be called so, that ideas must exist if they are the forms of all the species we have in this lower world? On this point, however, we must understand that the intellect has the power to consider things that are joined together in one thing separately and apart. For example, of the number four I can say that, while it is one number, the mind can still think of it as two and as three, since it contains these within itself. Nor, following the Philosopher's opinion, should we doubt that species and natures of things are like numbers: just as a number changes when one unit is added or removed, so the species of a thing changes when we add or remove one difference in its forms and natures. We confess, then, that the divine nature is simple and one, yet most perfect, and since creatures imitate it, not all of them imitate the whole of it, nor all in the same way and degree. Therefore, when the essence of God is referred to as the exemplar of the diverse species, diverse degrees of perfection can be noted and distinguished in it, not indeed in reality but in our reasoning. So God, when he understands himself as the thing to be imitated and expressed by the things he creates, according to the diverse degrees suited to the nature of each thing, is said to behold his ideas. These, although otherwise hidden from us, are made manifest through the created things. Hence it is said to the Hebrews: "By faith we understand that the worlds were framed, so that what is seen was not made of things that appear" (Heb. 11.). And to the Romans it is said thus: "From the creation of the world the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made" (Rom. 1.), and so were made known to the philosophers.

units.la: Potest itaq; idea tribus modis a nobis cogitari, primò ut res est in seipsa, & ita una est & simplex Dei essentia: vel ut diuini intellectus est obiectum practicum, atq; hoc item modo una est, nam Deus uno actu seipsum intuendo videt & cognoscit omnia: tertiò ut forma est & exemplar, & tunc permultæ ideæ sunt condendæ, quia multarum rerum specie differentium, complura & distincta sunt exemplaria. Utq; videamus dilucidè quomodo tam multæ res quæ natura sunt distinctæ ac diuersa magna distantia, in essentia Dei poni possent quàm coniunctissimè, simul afferam de circulo, lineis & centro. Certè si lineæ cogitentur, ut circumferentiæ sunt proximæ, sunt à se inuicem quàm maximè distinctæ atque distantes: at vicissim eadem ut in centro coeunt, sunt coniunctissimæ, & idem cum puncto centri, qui est simplicissimus. Ita res ut eas in materia videmus, utquè à Deo fluxerunt ad nos, & distantiam & diuersitatem maximam habent: ut verò ad suas ideas referuntur & ad diuinam formam & naturam, sunt simul coniunctissimæ.
units.tr: An idea, therefore, can be thought of by us in three ways. First, as the thing is in itself, and so the essence of God is one and simple. Second, as it is the practical object of the divine intellect, and in this way too it is one, for God, by one act of seeing himself, sees and knows all things. Third, as it is a form and exemplar, and then very many ideas must be posited, since there are many distinct exemplars of many things differing in species. And so that we may see clearly how so many things, which are distinct in nature and very far apart, can be placed in the essence of God as most closely joined, I will at the same time bring in the comparison of a circle, its lines and its centre. Certainly, if the lines are thought of as they are near the circumference, they are as distinct and distant from one another as possible. But on the other hand, the same lines, as they meet in the centre, are most closely joined, and they are one with the point of the centre, which is most simple. So things, as we see them in matter, and as they have flowed from God to us, have the greatest distance and diversity; but as they are referred to their ideas, and to the divine form and nature, they are at the same time most closely joined.

units.la: Ut res magis adhuc fiat perspicua, nobiscum reputemus, quacunq; sunt, variis & multiplicibus modis existere. Jam primùm omnium in materia, quæ magna est omnium mater, sunt: nam elicuntur inde, cum proueniunt: prius itaq; ibi erant, ut philosophi loquuntur, potentia. In effectrice quoq; causa, priusquam fierent, vi, energia seu efficacia quadam erant. Postea cum sunt, reipsa in materia seu composito existunt. Atque adeò cum intelligun tur, quodammodo plane ea esse non ambigimus: etenim in nostra sunt intelligentia, deinde in mentibus æthereis, & quidem longè nobilius quàm nostro intellectu comprehenduntur, sed tandem præstantissimè in summa Dei sapientia eminent, ubi ab omni materia seu corporum contagione libera iam inde à seculorum æternitate manent. Cumq; variis modis (ut exposuimus) esse possent, solum hoc postremo ideæ possunt appellari.
units.tr: To make the matter still clearer, let us consider that, whatever things are, they exist in various and manifold ways. First of all, they are in matter, which is the great mother of all things, for they are drawn out from it when they come forth. Therefore, as the philosophers say, they were there before in potency. Also, before they were made, they were in the effecting cause, in a certain power, energy or efficacy. Afterwards, when they are, they actually exist in matter or in the composite. And so, when they are understood, we do not doubt that in a certain way they are then truly what they are: for they are in our understanding, then in the ethereal minds, and indeed they are grasped far more nobly than by our intellect; but at last they stand out most excellently in the supreme wisdom of God, where, free from all matter and contagion of bodies, they remain from the eternity of the ages. And since they could be in various ways (as we have explained), only this last mode can be called ideas.

units.la: Nec pauca, qui hæc sapienter tractant, ad naturam idearum aiunt concurrere. Primùm (ut volunt) quàdam oportet inter eruenire similitudinem, qua cum his conueniant ideæ quæ ipsas imitantur. Deinceps ut seiuncta sint ab his fragilibus atq; mortalibus, quorum sunt exemplaria. Est ad hæc necesse, ut mente diuina sint comprehensa, à qua intelligantur non contemplatione tione simplici ac nuda, sed ea notitia, quæ faciendi voluntatem coniunctam secum habeat, eamq; Græci vulgò Practicen appellant. Præterea non sunt ideæ nisi tempore anteuertant ea, quarum sunt æternæ imagines. Accedit & illud eas naturam intellectus diuini subire in quo clauduntur, & æque ac illæ sunt immortales, perpetuæ, æternæ, simplices atq; syncerę. Vtq; tandem si niam, omnium quæ ad eorum imitationem in mundo procreantur sunt causæ. Hæc perfectè recensentur vt propria, & quæ ab idearum natura diuelli nequeant. Res autem à Deo conditæ tantisper veræ haberi debent, vsque dum suis idæis æquantur, & eas, quemadmodum par est, exprimunt. Etenim si eas referre desinant, de numero eorū quæ sunt extemplo decidūt. Et profecto discrimen hoc illud est, quod inter veritatem rerum, ac humanæ mentis deprehenditur ac orationis. Oratio tū habetur vera, cū à mentis intelligentia non discrepat: at ratio seu animus verus est vbi à rerum natura intelligendo non recedit, sed vt est cōcipit ac æstimat. Res deniq; verè quod sunt esse dicuntur, quando idearum exemplis rectè consentiunt.
units.tr: Those who treat these matters wisely say that not a few things contribute to the nature of ideas. First, as they hold, there must be some likeness among them, by which the ideas that imitate those things agree with them. Next, they must be separated from these frail and mortal things, of which they are the exemplars. In addition, it is necessary that they be comprehended in the divine mind, by which they are understood not by simple and bare contemplation, but by that knowledge which has the will to act joined with it, and which the Greeks commonly call practical knowledge. Moreover, ideas exist only insofar as they precede those things of which they are the eternal images. It is also added that they take on the nature of the divine intellect in which they are contained, and, just as they are immortal, so they are perpetual, eternal, simple and pure. And finally, since they are the causes of all the things that are produced in the world in their imitation, these are fully counted as proper to them and cannot be separated from the nature of ideas. Things created by God, however, ought to be held true only so long as they match their ideas and express them as is fitting. For if they cease to refer to them, they immediately fall from the number of things that are. And indeed this is the difference found between the truth of things and that of the human mind and of speech. Speech is held true when it does not differ from the understanding of the mind; but reason or the mind is true when it does not depart from the nature of things in understanding, but conceives and judges them as they are. Finally, things are rightly said to be truly what they are when they agree rightly with the patterns of their ideas.
