units.la: Cum idearum porrò natura, quam modò tractamus & prouidentia & prædestinatio magnam habent affinitatem, de quibus locum in præsentia non esse quia video, idcirco sermones de ipsis prætereo, ac de Platone, quem modò reprehendit Aristoteles, hoc dico, Si nil aliud sensit ideas esse quā Dei naturam seu essentiam, ab ipso Deo cognitam, qua illum res creatæ imitentur, vt etiam ⌣Augustinus explicauit, erroris accusari non potest. Sin verò putauit ideas esse naturas rerum quas Deus ab æternitate seculorum nouerit, & ad quarum exempla mundum condiderit, non vanæ contra illum sunt Aristotelis rationes. nam ponere quædam sic à materia libera, & à coniunctione creatarum rerum secreta, quæ non sint ipse Deus, sed à Deo solū cognoscantur vt faciundorum exempla, est à vero longius abesse. Horum verò Plato vtrum dixerit, incertum est, & vt quod est dicam densis circumfusum tenebris. Qua tamen de re fortasse nonnihil cognoscere poterimus, vbi de Platonis, atque Platonicorum sententia nonnulla in medium prolata fuerint.
units.tr: Since the nature of ideas, which we are now treating, has a great affinity with both providence and predestination, about which, as I see, there is no room for discussion at present, I pass over discourse on them. As for Plato, whom Aristotle now criticizes, I say this: if he meant nothing else by ideas than the nature or essence of God, known by God himself, by which created things imitate him, as Augustine also explained, he cannot be accused of error. But if he thought that ideas are the natures of things which God knew from the eternity of the ages, and according to whose patterns he made the world, then Aristotle's arguments against him are not vain. For to posit certain things thus free from matter and separated from the conjunction of created things, which are not God himself but are known by God alone as the exemplars of things to be made, is far from the truth. Whether Plato said this, however, is uncertain, and, to say what is the case, it is surrounded by thick darkness. Yet perhaps we may learn something about this matter when some points about the opinion of Plato and the Platonists have been brought forward.

units.la: Attigi iam duplici de causa Platonem ideas induxisse. Vna fuit, ob rerum procreationem, altera ob notitiam seu scientiam afferendam. Verum enimuero ista solùm dixi, non autem vt intelligeretur, exposui. Proinde quo ad generationem, sic ille putauit: Quicquid procreatur, à simili sui fieri, ne causa re à se producta indignior deprehenderetur. Cū enim femina expectamus, illa plane longè sunt ignobiliora viuentib. ac animantibus, quæ ex illis oriūtur, vt vel sensus ipse testari potest. Nec mihi quispiam dixerit, ut ani tis unde semen est, elicitus fœtus & plantæ producantur, quoniam vis illa, ut ut sit nobilis, accidens omnino est, nullum vero accidens haberi debet substantia dignius. Quare sive semen seu vim animantis, cuius est, illi adhuc etiam spectaueris, nil simile reperire poteris eius quod generatur. Mitto commemorare permulta gigni, non utique feminæ, sed putri corruptaq; materia, ut mures, ranæ, atq; nonnullæ plantæ vel herbæ quarum dignitati quis obsecro æquauerit unquam putrem corruptamq; materiam e qua proficiscuntur? Iudicauit igitur Plato naturas quasdam poni oportere communes, formas inquam certas seu species ad quarum exemplū producerentur quæ fierent, cum effectrices causæ quas videmus, ad illarum procreationem minime sufficiant.
units.tr: I have already touched on the two reasons for which Plato introduced ideas: one was for the production of things, the other for providing knowledge or science. But I have only mentioned these, not explained them so that they might be understood. Accordingly, as to generation, he thought thus: whatever is produced is made from something like itself, lest the cause be found to be less noble than the thing it has produced. For when we look at seeds, the things that spring from them are plainly far nobler than the living beings and animals that arise from them, as sense itself can testify. Nor let anyone say to me that the offspring and plants are drawn forth from the power of the animal from which the seed comes, since that power, however noble it may be, is altogether an accident, and no accident should be regarded as worthier than substance. Therefore, whether you look at the seed or at the power of the animal to which it belongs, you will find nothing like what is generated. I pass over the many things that are born not from seed but from putrid and corrupt matter, such as mice, frogs and some plants or herbs; and who, I ask you, would ever equal the dignity of those things to the putrid and corrupt matter from which they come? Plato therefore judged that certain common natures must be posited, namely fixed forms or species, after whose example the things that come into being would be produced, since the efficient causes we see are by no means sufficient for their production.

units.la: Impulit ad hæc Platonem ut ita sentiret, scientiarum defensio: cum enim Heraclitus & qui cum eo faciebant, omnia quæ hic apud nos cernuntur perpetuo motu ac agitatione turbari dicerent, ita ut nunquā eadem permanerent, veriti non sunt, scientiam penitus auferre, quam omnium consensu oportet, si esset, firmitatem, constantiam, & certitudinem habere, quod fieri non posse arbitrabantur, cum omnia quæ sunt nullam haberent stabilitatem. His profecto voluit occurrere Plato, & scientiam, inquit, idcirco relinquendam hominibus, quòd non hæc singula quæ videmus oriri & interire sciantur, sed universæ quædam simplices & incorruptæ naturæ: ad hæc, inquit, illi respiciunt, qui scientia quicquam comprehendunt. Ex eo vero argumentabatur, quod quæ de homine scimus, nō de Callia, Xenophonte, Demosthene, aut alijs priuatis cognoscimus, verum de ipsa hominis natura, quod si detur, ut dandum videtur, addebat, nil posse sciri nisi fuerit: enimuero quod non est, nullo modo sciri utique potest. Quare conclusum putabat universalia hæc sciuncta esse à singularibus & per scientiam cum esse tum conseruari.
units.tr: The defence of knowledge drove Plato to this view. When Heraclitus and those who agreed with him said that everything we see here among us is disturbed by perpetual motion and agitation, so that nothing ever remains the same, they feared that this would take away knowledge altogether. Knowledge, if it existed, ought by general agreement to have firmness, constancy and certainty, and they judged this impossible, since all things that exist had no stability. Plato certainly wanted to meet this objection. Knowledge, he said, must be left to humans for this reason: not that these individual things we see arising and perishing are known, but certain universal, simple and incorruptible natures. To these, he said, those look who grasp anything by knowledge. From this he argued that what we know about a human, we know not about Callias, Xenophon, Demosthenes or other private persons, but about the very nature of man. If this is granted, as it seems it must be, he added, nothing can be known unless it is, for what is not cannot in any way be known. Hence he thought it concluded that these universals are separate from singulars, and that both they exist and are preserved through knowledge.

units.la: Videbatur etiam sibi hoc inde ostendere, quòd universa hæc, formæ inquam & species communes intelligerentur absq; singularibus, dum inquā jam non essent, ut rosæ natura & violarū vel in media hyeme cum non sunt agnoscantur, quod argumento esse credidit, formas illarum rerum extare quando singularia earum non reperiebantur, quoniam uti dixi hoc statuendum cesuit[?], nil intelligi posse, quod non esset. Dicebat etiam omnia hæc sin-gularia quæ cernimus id quod sint participatione quadam esse. Alcibiades enim, Aristoteles & Alexander homines idcirco sunt & dicuntur, quòd sint humanitatis participes: illa enim inter se congruunt. Quare dari oportere concludebat humanitatem per se, cuius communione tam multi possint homines esse.
units.tr: This also seemed to him to show that these universals, I mean the common forms and species, are understood apart from singulars. When the singulars are not present, as the nature of the rose and of the violet is still recognised in the middle of winter when they are absent, he believed this was an argument that the forms of those things exist when their singulars are not found. For, as I said, it was granted that this must be laid down: nothing can be understood that does not exist. He also said that all these singulars we see are what they are by a certain participation. For Alcibiades, Aristotle and Alexander are and are called men because they participate in humanity, since those things agree with one another. Hence he concluded that humanity must exist in itself, by whose communion so many men can be men.

units.la: Hæc autem quando ita sunt, non possum non vehementer mirari Themistium, qui libro de anima primo cap. 23. dixerit non omnium ideas Platonem posuisse, non inquam fortuitorum, non vilium & abiectorum, neq; eorum quæ producantur ex fecibus & materia corrupta, cum præsertim ab istis sic procreatis, vt iam demonstrauimus, ideas inuenerit Plato. Nec in dubiũ reuocandum est de his an habeatur scientia, cum multa de his demonstrentur & sciantur quo ad illorum ortum & actiones. Credidit etiam vt idem refert, generum seu subalternorum seu generalissimorum non esse ideas, quoniam atomæ naturæ, seu species quas vocant specialissimas, quum ideæ sint, liberæ à materia, nil debet illis poni syncerius aut separatius. Quare si quis velit ab idea ideam aliam secernere, id plane fieri non potest, nisi dixeris, illam ideam hominis aut equi, à qua rursus coneris elicere, animalis ideam habere certam aliquam materiam, à qua eam velis removere. Nec si Plato seu Platonici sic dixerint, illos arbitror confentienter suis principijs esse loquutos. Nam si repererunt ideas, vti dixi, ob conseruandam et tuendam scientiam, oppido generum quoq; illas concedere oportet, quoniam & de generibus habentur scientiæ, quod qui nesciunt, libros de physico auditu non euoluerunt, vbi de motu in genere, ac de materia, priuatione[?] atq; consimilibus non speciatim agitur. Neq; abstractio seu remotio, ceu existimant, fit à specie separata, cum genus formatur: tam enim gradus speciei quàm generum ab indiuiduis eliciuntur. Idem enim Petrus dum cogitatur vt rationalis, dat speciem: si vt sentit, animal quod est genus prodit, vbi verò qua viuit, tum aliud genus habetur, nempe corpus animatum: & de his habentur singillatim scientiæ nec sciri potest nisi quod est. Quare illorum ideæ generum ab illis debuissent poni, si manere in sententia volebant.
units.tr: But since these things stand as they do, I cannot help being greatly surprised at Themistius, who in the first book On the Soul, chapter 23, said that Plato did not posit ideas of all things. I mean, not of chance things, nor of base and abject things, nor of those produced from dregs and corrupt matter, especially since Plato discovered ideas of things so produced, as we have already shown. Nor should it be called in doubt whether there is knowledge of these, since many things about their origin and their actions are demonstrated and known. He also believed, as the same author reports, that there are no ideas of genera, whether subaltern or most general, since the lowest natures, or the species they call most specific, are ideas, free from matter, and nothing can be posited purer or more separate than them. Hence if anyone wishes to separate one idea from another, this simply cannot be done, unless you say that the idea of man or horse, from which you then try to derive the idea of animal, has some definite matter from which you wish to remove it. Nor, if Plato or the Platonists said this, do I think they spoke consistently with their principles. For if they found ideas, as I said, for the sake of preserving and defending knowledge, they must very much grant ideas of genera too, since there is knowledge of genera also. Those who do not know this have not read the books on physical hearing, where motion in general, and matter, privation and the like, are discussed not specifically. Nor is abstraction or removal, as they think, made from a separated species when the genus is formed. For both the degrees of species and of genera are drawn from individuals. Peter, when thought of as rational, gives the species; if as sentient, the genus animal results; where he is considered as living, another genus is had, namely animate body. Knowledge of these is had severally, and nothing can be known except what is. Hence they ought to have posited ideas of genera, if they wished to remain in their opinion.

units.la: Sed magis est mirum quòd de numeris inquit. Nam eorum quoq; refert (vt mox etiam dicet Aristoteles) Platonem ideam non dedisse, nimirum quòd sic ordinati sint vt se copleCtantur, ideæ verò de his poni debeāt, quæ inter se nõ sunt coniuncta. Quomodo si res hoc pacto se haberet, scientiā numerorum defendissent Platonici, arithmeticā sanè qui tanti faciūt? nisi numerorum essent pro illorum sententia ideæ, nil de numeris potuisset sciri. Quamobrem arbitror, si rectè loqui velint, & consentienter his quæ loco fundamenti posuerunt, omnium illos debere concedere ideas quæ vel producì vel cognosci possunt. Ad hæc nonnulli ambigunt quales istas ideas illi crediderint. Respondetur, impartibiles, non enim sic diuiduntur vt vnum aliquod singularium partem accipiant, et aliam aliud sibi vendicet, neq; si de loco agatur, dici debent abiunctæ prorsus à singularibus, cum ab illis participentur. Illis adsunt, vt similitudo similibus: Non tamen loco comprehenduntur, cum sint incorporeæ. Atq; illorum nonnulli similitudinem lucis afferunt quæ adest illuminatis, quamuis loco eorum non claudatur, vt pote quæ sit qualitas admodũ tenuis, & ceu dicunt, spiritualis. Si præterea quæras, quo nam pacto indiuidua sint idearum principia, respondent, quod vulgò dicitur de animo hominum, quam libet earum esse totam in toto, & totam item in qualibet parte.
units.tr: But it is more remarkable that he says this about numbers. For he also reports (as Aristotle will say shortly) that Plato did not give an idea of numbers, doubtless because they are so ordered that they embrace one another, whereas ideas ought to be posited of things that are not joined together. If the matter stood in this way, would the Platonists, who value arithmetic so highly, have defended the knowledge of numbers? Unless, in their view, numbers were ideas, nothing about numbers could be known. Wherefore I think that, if they wish to speak rightly and consistently with what they laid as a foundation, they must concede ideas of all things that can either be produced or known. Here some are in doubt what kind of ideas they believed these to be. The answer is: indivisible ones. For they are not divided so that one of the singulars takes one part and another claims a different part for itself. Nor, if we speak of place, should they be said to be wholly separated from singulars, since they are shared by them. They are present to them as likeness is to like things, yet they are not contained in place, since they are incorporeal. Some of them bring forward the likeness of light, which is present to the illuminated, though it is not enclosed in a place, since it is a very thin quality and, as they say, spiritual. If you ask further in what way individuals are principles of ideas, they answer, as is commonly said of the human soul, that each idea is whole in the whole, and likewise whole in every part.

units.la: Cum ex Platone tum ex Platonicis hæc de ideis eliciuntur. Nunc proponamus quæ Aristoteles contra opponat. Producũtur, inquit, & accidentia, & illorum est scientia: quare ideam quoq; illorum propriam habebit. Erit itaq; accidens à subiecto seiunctum. At id rationi proprie accidentium aduersatur, cuius natura & essentia est vt inhæreat. Hanc rationem si hoc tempore transsubstantiatoribus obiceret Aristoteles, illum riderent, cum ipsis facillimum sit in Eucharistia statuere accidentia, quum substantiam subtraxerint. Deinceps oppugnat illos, quoniam iuxta illorum sententiam idea aliqua esset idea: quadoquidem singularia (vt ipsi fatetur) cum idea conueniunt: ab his autem quæ similia sunt & communicant, aliqua species aut forma communis potest elici: quare tam ideæ quam suorum singularium, aliqua forma communis abstrahitur, et ita fiet, vt testati sumus, ideam esse ideæ. Non assequuntur isti præterea quod volunt quo ad generationem: ideo enim dicunt esse ideas, vt quæ producuntur à simili gignantur. At idea illorum libera est à materia, æterna & perpetua, quæ vero procreantur sunt materiæ coniunctæ, mortalia & caduca. Differunt itaque à se inuicem plusquam genere, quæ autem ita distant, similia non sunt. Quare dum similitudinem quærunt ab illa quã longissimè discedunt. Neq; videntur ideæ sic positæ notitiæ aut scientiis tuendis quicquam adiumento esse, nam quisque sua forma solet cognosci. Vnde cum ideæ Platonis nullius singulæ rei quæat esse formæ, nullarum omnino rerum de quibus disputatur scientiam suppeditabunt. Statuit proinde Aristoteles naturas vniuersas quæ vi nostræ intelligentiæ collectæ sunt ex individuis, nosci atque sciri, quum singulæ res ac priuatæ ob illarum motum & interitum scientia comprehendi non possint, & quod ad generationem attinet, rem quamque compositam aut mixtam, vt omnia sunt quæ procreantur, à mixtis item atque compositis fieri affirmat, adiuuantibus ad id vi naturæ, stellis atque Sole. Quæ omnia quum ad hoc munus obeundum sint satis, ideas ob hanc causam non esse induinducendas tradit. Quare inter Platonem & eos cum quibus Plato conten-debat, media quadam via incedit, cum illis fatetur, quæcunque sunt singula esse ac motu perpetuo verti, quarum formas ab ipsis auelli posse, aut rei-psa vel à materia vel corporibus negat solutas degere. Verum in eo cum Pla-tone facit, dum species aut formas rerum, quæ corruptioni sunt obnoxia, in-quit à singulis & priuatis rebus tantum secerni mente, ratione atque in-telligentia, de quibus ita solutis & liberatis à materia scientia haberi pos-sint.
units.tr: From Plato and from the Platonists these things about ideas are drawn out. Now let us set out what Aristotle opposes to them. Accidents too, he says, are produced, and there is knowledge of them; therefore they will also have their own idea. So an accident will be separated from its subject. But this is contrary to the very reason of accidents, whose nature and essence is to inhere. If Aristotle were to object this argument to the transubstantiators today, they would laugh at him, since it is very easy for them to posit accidents in the Eucharist once they have removed the substance. Next he attacks them: according to their opinion there would be some idea of an idea, since singulars (as they themselves confess) agree with the idea, and from things that are similar and share in something a common species or form can be drawn. Therefore a common form is abstracted both from the idea and from its singulars, and so it will come about, as we have shown, that there is an idea of an idea. Moreover, these men do not attain what they want as regards generation. For they say there are ideas so that things produced may be begotten by something like them, but their idea is free from matter, eternal and perpetual, whereas things that are produced are joined to matter, mortal and fragile. They therefore differ from one another more than in kind, and things so far apart are not similar. Hence, while they seek likeness, they seek it from that from which they depart most widely. Nor do ideas so posited seem to be of any help in preserving notions or sciences, for each thing is usually known by its own form. Hence, since Plato's ideas cannot be the form of any single thing, they will supply knowledge of none of the things about which disputation is held. Aristotle therefore holds that universal natures, which by the power of our understanding are gathered from individuals, are known and understood, since single and private things cannot be grasped by science because of their motion and perishing. As regards generation, he affirms that each composite or mixed thing, as all things are that are produced, is made from mixed and composite things, with the aid of the power of nature, the stars and the Sun. Since all these are sufficient to perform this office, he teaches that ideas should not be introduced for this cause. Therefore he walks a middle way between Plato and those with whom Plato contended. With them he confesses that whatever things are singular are subject to perpetual motion, and he denies that their forms can be drawn off from them, or that they live separated in reality from matter or from bodies. But in this he agrees with Plato: he says that the species or forms of things, which are liable to corruption, are separated from singular and private things only in the mind, by reason and understanding, and that of these, freed and liberated from matter, knowledge can be had.

units.la: At de formarum auulsione vel secretione à materia ne quid erremus, ex Peripateticorum sententia, distinctione huiusmodi censemus vtedum. Quæ-dam sunt corpora, quæ vt in sua natura & certa specie à propriis formis con-tinentur, ita vicissim formæ illorum ab ipsis pendent, & de his pronunciandum est, illas è sua materia quam formant, nunquam saluas & integras au-elli, ita est canis, equi, & plantarum, lapidum, & similium forma. Alia ve-rò dantur corpora, quæ vt sua forma, in natura & propria specie cohæreat & constent, vicissim tamen ipsorum forma nequaquam ab illis pendet, at-que in his dicetur formam reipsa liberam à materia, & ab ea non ratione modo, sed reipsa secerni & auelli. Huius ordine ponuntur hominum animi ex illorum sententia qui eos immortales opinantur, ac singulares intelligen-tiae, quibus cœlestes globi perpetuo versantur. Ex iis iam liquere arbitror,cuius erroris Plato in hac causa cum ab Aristotele tum à Peripateticis accu-setur, nempe quod rerum formas quamuis mortalium ab ipsis auulsas con-stituerit, quas appellauerit ideas. Eas verò si naturam aut essentiam Dei di-xisset, iure reprehendi non posset, sed eo tantum traducitur, quod eas distinctas à rebus affirmarit, nec plane disseruerit, vt Christiani patres explicu-erunt, eas idem atq; naturam & essentiam Dei esse.
units.tr: But lest we go wrong about the separation or detachment of forms from matter, let us use the following distinction, in keeping with the opinion of the Peripatetics. Some bodies are such that, just as they are contained in their own nature and fixed species by their proper forms, so conversely their forms depend on them. Of these it must be said that their forms can never be removed from the matter they shape whole and intact. Such are the forms of a dog, a horse, plants, stones and the like. But there are other bodies which subsist and cohere in their own nature and proper species by their form, yet conversely their form in no way depends on them. Of these it is said that the form is really free from matter, and is separated and detached from it not only in reason but in reality. In this order, according to their opinion, are placed the souls of men, which they think immortal, and the singular intelligences by which the heavenly spheres are perpetually moved. From these things I think it is now clear what error Plato is accused of in this matter, both by Aristotle and by the Peripatetics: namely, that he posited the forms of things, even of mortal things, as detached from them, and called them ideas. But if he had said that they are the nature or essence of God, he could not rightly be blamed. He is charged only with this, that he affirmed them to be distinct from things, and did not plainly explain, as the Christian fathers have expounded, that they are the same as the nature and essence of God.

units.la: Albertus, qui vt barbarus lingua fuerit, Magnus tamen, ob multipli-cem summamq; rerum scientiam, est appellatus, in suis metaphysicis, has pu-tat ideas& formas rerum impressas in orbe summo stellarum inerrantium: idcoq; illic non tantum vires producendi res quæ hic apud nos oriuntur & intereunt contineri, sed etiam exemplaria, quæ res procreatæ quam diu sunt imitantur. Et Hermetem adducit illum τρὶς μέγιστον[?], qui ait nec lapillum quidem in hac nostra infima regione inueniri, cuius non extet in cœlo propria vis & exemplum, vnde fit productus, & dum est, conseruetur & augetur. Quin & animos hominum, cum ad corpora devoluuntur, ac per illos cœlorum globos transeunt, non inanes inde abire, Plato & sui studiosi putarunt. Nam cum sint natura faciles ad impressiones accipiendas, illis confi[?] gnari volunt præclarissimis ideis ac formis cœlestibus, ac secum exemplaria rerum omnium ad corpora deferre, à quorum nihilominus prima ætate impediantur contemplatione, ceu mersi & præfocati aliquo pacto, mole ac humore copioso & redundanti corporis, quod recens induerunt, sed ætatis deinde processu, ab his quæ in mundo vident & sentiunt, vel à præceptorum doctis interrogationibus & monitis, ad illa diuina simulachra intuenda et contemplanda excitari. Quare Plato non semel scire aut discere, nil aliud esse testabatur quam reminisci, ut licet ex Menone & Theæteto ipsius cognoscere. Idem quoq; de Repub. lib. 7. cum specum finxisset, in quo collocauit homines compedibus vinctos, qui tantum umbras in adverso pariete cernerent, eos inquit, si forte soluerentur, & ad vera corpora se converterent intuenda, quorum prius tantum vidissent umbras, tum demum scientiæ fieri compotes: ut inquam hæc dixit, & aptissima exposuit similitudine, tum intulit eos qui docent aut erudiunt homines, quod nil plane aliud censuit, quàm vincula ignorationis ac tenebrarum soluere, tantum illos convertere ad veras ideas & formas, quas in animo habeant spectandas, non tamen illis novam doctrinam vel notitiam ullam quam prius non habuerint, cum nascerentur, afferre. Neq; reticuit Aristoteles hanc Platonis opinionem de scientia, quæ nova nunquam accederet, sed potius excitaretur, in Analyticis posterioribus, & in libris de Anima, nec no in aliis quibusdam locis. Hæc quæ partim memorauit Albertus, partimq; in libris Platonis & studiosorum eius reperiuntur, dubios de sententia eius nos reddunt, ideas ne voluerit es-sentiam & naturam Dei esse, an extra eam illas collocarit.
units.tr: Albert, who, though a barbarian in language, was nevertheless called Great on account of his manifold and supreme knowledge, thinks in his Metaphysics that these ideas and forms of things are impressed on the highest sphere of the fixed stars. Hence there are contained there not only the powers of producing the things that arise and perish here among us, but also the exemplars which created things imitate for as long as they exist. He cites Hermes Trismegistus [τρὶς μέγιστον], who says that not even a little stone is found in this lowest region of ours of which the proper power and exemplar does not exist in heaven, whence it is produced and, while it exists, is preserved and increased. Moreover, Plato and his followers thought that the souls of men, when they are sent down into bodies and pass through those heavenly spheres, do not depart thence empty. For since they are by nature easily receptive of impressions, they want them to be stamped with those most excellent ideas and heavenly forms, and to carry the exemplars of all things with them into bodies. Yet in early life they are hindered from contemplating these, as if drowned and suffocated in some way by the mass and abundant moisture of the body which they have newly put on. Then, as age advances, they are roused to look upon and contemplate those divine images, either from what they see and perceive in the world or by the learned questions and admonitions of teachers. Hence Plato more than once declared that to know or to learn is nothing other than to recollect, as may be gathered from his Meno and Theaetetus. Likewise in the seventh book of the Republic, when he had imagined a cave in which he placed men bound in chains, who saw only shadows on the wall opposite them, he said that if they were perchance loosed and turned to look at the true bodies, of which they had seen only the shadows, then at last they would become possessed of knowledge. When he had said this and set it out in a most apt likeness, he added that those who teach or educate men do nothing else, as he thought, than loose the chains of ignorance and darkness and turn them towards the true ideas and forms, which they have in their minds to be looked upon. Yet they do not bring to them any new doctrine or knowledge which they did not have when they were born. Nor did Aristotle keep silent about this opinion of Plato, that knowledge never comes in anew but is rather roused, in the Posterior Analytics, in the books On the Soul, and in some other places. These things, partly recalled by Albert and partly found in the books of Plato and his followers, leave us in doubt about his opinion: whether he wished the ideas to be the essence and nature of God, or placed them outside it.

units.la: Nec defuerunt ex ipsa eius familia, qui crediderint ideas rerum prius locum habuisse in mente quadam, à primo illo summoq; omnium parente Deo procreata. Alij quoq; posuerunt eas primum omnium in anima mundi, cuius unius opera cuncta fieri & moueri censuerunt. Quæ res cum adeo varia sit & incerta, relinquitur à nobis in medio, atq; hoc tantum dicam, Ideas nunc ab Aristotele oppugnari, quasi ponantur seiuncta à rebus, & ipsa per se constent, ut omnium quæ fiunt causæ & exemplaria. Simplicius non parum Platoni addictus, in multis locis ait, non sensum Platonis, verum Xenocratis aut quorundam sectatorum eius interpretationem ab Aristotele reprehendi. Atq; idem plane vult Ammonius interpretando librum περὶ ἰδεῶν[?]. Cæterum cum hac de re iam satis multa, & plura fortasse quàm oporteat sim præfatus, ad Aristotelis verba me recipiam.
units.tr: Nor were there lacking, from his own school, those who believed that the ideas of things first had a place in a certain mind, created by that first and highest parent of all, God. Others also placed them first of all in the soul of the world, by whose work alone they thought all things were made and moved. Since this matter is so varied and uncertain, we leave it aside, and will say only this: the ideas are now assailed by Aristotle, as if they were posited separate from things and subsisted of themselves, as the causes and exemplars of all things that come to be. Simplicius, who was not a little devoted to Plato, says in many places that it is not Plato's meaning but the interpretation of Xenocrates or of some of his followers that Aristotle reprehends. Ammonius, in interpreting the book On Ideas [περὶ ἰδεῶν], plainly means the same. However, since I have already said a great deal on this matter, perhaps more than is fitting, I will turn to Aristotle's words.

units.la: Qui igitur hanc attulerunt opinionem, in his non faciebant ideas, in quibus prius & posterius aliquid dixerunt. Idcirco neque numerorum ideam consti-tuebant.
units.tr: Those, therefore, who brought forward this opinion were not positing ideas in which something is said to be prior and posterior. For this reason they did not even posit an idea of numbers.

units.la: Quatuor, uti jam ab initio dixi, rationes Aristoteles adversus Platone inducit: a prima jam incipimus. Quæstio sic proponenda est, Communis an danda sit idea bonorum omnium: Ea si de unius Dei natura seu essentia intelligeretur, danda effet citra contentionem. Sin vero idea sumatur ut communis natura suorum individuorum, ut Plato de illa sapius est loquutus, neq; Scotus ex recentioribus longius a tali cogitatione abfuit, negatur. Prima ratio huius confutationis, hoc modo producitur.
units.tr: As I said at the beginning, Aristotle brings four arguments against Plato; let us begin with the first. The question must be put thus: whether a common idea of all good things is to be granted. If this were understood of the nature or essence of the one God, it would be granted without dispute. But if the idea is taken as the common nature of its individuals, as Plato has often spoken of it, and Scotus among the more recent writers was not far removed from such a thought, it is denied. The first argument of this refutation is set out in this way.

units.la: In quibuscunque ordo prioris & posterioris fuerit, in eis communis alia idea non ponitur.
units.tr: In whatever things there is an order of prior and posterior, no other common idea is posited among them.

units.la: Bona quæ hic habentur, sic instituta sunt, ut quædam eorum sint priora & quædam posteriora.
units.tr: The goods that are here are so arranged that some of them are prior and some posterior.
Therefore they cannot have a common idea.

units.la: Maior propositio ceu confessa & evidens in Schola Platonis assumitur, & in ea sic eos fuisse concordes, quos arguit, demonstrat.
units.tr: The major premise is assumed as conceded and evident in Plato's school, and in it those whom he argues against are shown to have been agreed.

units.la: Idcirco neq numerorum ideas constituebant.) Numeros ita com- paratos ut unus eorum prior sit altero neminem fugere arbitror. Themi-stius, ut vobis antea dixi, 23.cap.primi libri de Anima hoc docuit, ideas a Platone numeris non fuisse præpositas. Quod aiebam, & modo repeto, non videri, quomodo fundamentis & principiis Platonis consentiat. Quia si po-suit[?] ideas ob tuendas scientias, & numerorum haberi scientiam omnes confitentur, eorum quoq; danda erat idea, cum numeri singulis rebus inhærentes, una cum illis & pereant & mutentur.
units.tr: I think no one doubts that numbers are so constituted that one of them is prior to another; therefore they did not posit ideas of numbers. Themistius, as I told you before, taught in the twenty-third chapter of the first book On the Soul that Plato did not set ideas above numbers. What I was saying, and repeat now, is that it does not appear how this agrees with Plato's foundations and principles. For if he posited ideas in order to preserve the sciences, and everyone admits there is a science of numbers, then an idea of numbers too had to be granted, since numbers, inhering in individual things, both perish and change together with them.

units.la: Quid vero impulerit illos ut a numeris ideas amouerint, Eustrathius refert, Sunt, inquit, Platonis idea uti species & genera; ista vero sic habet, ut ex æquo de his dicantur, quæ ipsis subiunguntur: nam animalis nomen & definitio leoni, equo, bouì ac homini æque tribuitur, nec istorum quicquam illa prius altero sibi vendicat, ita ut causa sit propter quam alia & sint & di-cantur animalia. Aristoteles in his quæ præfatus est ante Categorias, hæc ὁμώνυμα vocauit, nostri vero, ut eorum more loquar, appellarunt univoca, utpote quæ nomé & definitioné omnib. modis communem habent. συνώνυμα vero, quæ nostri dixerunt æquivoca, dici statuit, quæ utut nomé aut vocabulû sortiantur commune, eadé tamé definitione nominari non possunt: nā voce canis & ad sydus, & ad quadrupedē, & ad marinū piscē accōmodamus, quæ diversissimam definitionem habent. Ponitur inter ista duo quid medium, idq; vulgò in scholis appellatur ἀναλογον, tumq; locum habet vbi multis idem est inditum nomen, & ratio eis conuenit eadem, sed per unum communicatur alij. Nec omnia quæ pari nomine appellantur, extemplo sunt definitionis participia, sed natura quæ per definitionem significatur, unius eorum est propria, & per ipsum delabitur & meat ad alia. Ut sanitas in corporibus animantium primum omnium inest, dicitur inde in pharmacis, in urinis: ista etiam consueuimus nominare sana, at prius omnibus animans est & dicitur sanū, & urina, vt indicium eius, ita vocatur. Pharmacum vero, quòd illam efficiat. ἀναλογα hæc dicuntur vt in quibus & prius & posterius deprehendas.
units.tr: What moved them to remove ideas from numbers, Eustathius reports: "Plato's ideas are like species and genera, but these are such that they are predicated equally of those things which fall under them. For the name and definition of animal is given equally to the lion, the horse, the ox and the man, and none of these claims it before another, so that there is no cause why the others both are and are called animals. Aristotle, in what he prefaced before the Categories, called these homonyms [ὁμώνυμα]; our writers, to speak in their manner, called them univocals, as those which have a common name and definition in every respect. He decided that those are called synonyms [συνώνυμα], which our writers called equivocals, which, though they receive a common name or word, cannot be named by the same definition: for we apply the word 'dog' both to a constellation, and to a quadruped, and to a sea fish, which have very different definitions. Between these two there is something intermediate, which in the schools is commonly called analogous [ἀναλογον]. It occurs where many things have the same name given to them and the same account belongs to them, but it is communicated through one to the others. Nor are all things called by the same name immediately participants in the definition; rather, the nature signified through the definition belongs properly to one of them, and flows and passes through it to the others. Thus health is first of all in the bodies of living creatures; it is then said of medicines and of urines. We are accustomed to call these healthy too, but it is first in every living thing and is called healthy; urine is so called as a sign of it, and a medicine because it produces it. These are called analogous, in which you find both prior and posterior."

units.la: Hocidem numeris usvenit: etenim binarius, ternarius, quaternarius, ternarius, quinarius & sic deinceps, numerus & dicitur & est, attamen hi omnes ex æquo non sunt numeri: quia natura numeri per binarium tendit in ternarium, & ex ternario in quaternarium transfunditur. Atq; hoc est quod modò inquit Aristoteles, prius & posterius in eis esse, quia varij numeri analogi sint inter se ac non reuera univoci.
units.tr: The same happens with numbers. Two, three, four, three, five, and so on, are all called numbers and are numbers, yet they are not all numbers in the same way, because the nature of number tends from two to three and passes from three to four. This is what Aristotle means when he says that there is prior and posterior among them: the various numbers are analogous to one another and not truly univocal.

units.la: Neq; sua vi seu ironia carent Aristotelis illa verba, ἔνιοι γὰρ & κατασκευάζα ἔου[?] quod est faciebant & constituebant ideas. nam sic dicendo, ideas per se ac natura sua nihil esse innuit, ut quæ solum ab ipsis fuerint reperta ac ficta. Non reticendum est, prius & posterius quocunq; modo accipiatur, nō auferre à rebus veram formæ seu generis rationem, alioqui nullæ in mundo esse possent species aut genera. Enimuerò si attentius rerum naturæ spectentur, vt vere alibi dixit Aristoteles, instar numerorum se habent, & vna dignitate alteram antecedit, idq; ordine summo & coniunctissimo: quare in eis fieri nequit quin & prius & posterius habeatur, sed tum analogia nascitur à priori & posteriori, vbi quod prius posteriori communicat totum id in quo simul congruunt. Familiari vtar simili, Duo fratres in eadē stirpe seu familia iunguntur, & vnus est prior altero, qui enim ante alium nascitur, eo prior est, non tamē qui maior natu fuerit, dat fratri vt eiusdem stirpis atq; familiæ sit secum. Minor vero sic ponitur.
units.tr: Nor are Aristotle's words without force or irony: "for some [ἔνιοι γὰρ] ... made and set up ideas." By saying this he implies that ideas have nothing of their own, in their own nature, but are only things discovered and fashioned by those who posited them. It must not be overlooked that prior and posterior, however they are understood, do not take away from things the true reason of form or kind; otherwise there could be no species or genera in the world. Indeed, if the natures of things are examined more closely, they stand, as Aristotle truly said elsewhere, like numbers, one surpassing another in dignity, and this in the highest and most closely joined order. Hence in them it cannot fail that there is both prior and posterior. Analogy arises from prior and posterior when what the prior shares with the posterior is the whole in which they agree. I will use a familiar comparison. Two brothers are joined in the same stock or family, and one is prior to the other: he who is born before the other is prior to him, yet the one who is older by birth does not give his brother the fact that he belongs to the same stock and family with him. The younger is put in this way.

units.la: At bonum in substantia dicitur & in quali & in eo quod est ad aliquid. Atq; id quod est per se substantiaue, prius est eo natura quod est ad aliquid. Hoc enim simile est rei adnascētis, & ei quod est accidentis. In his igitur nō potest esse communis idea.
units.tr: But the good is said of substance, of quality, and of that which is relative to something. And that which is substance in itself is prior by nature to that which is relative. For this is like a thing that grows onto another, and like that which is an accident. In these, therefore, a common idea cannot exist.

units.la: Ex his primùm constituas bona esse multa, quoniam in varijs multisq; locantur prædicamentis. Cogites præterea categorias non temerè poni, sed inter se iustum pulcherrimumq; ordinem habere, quoniam aliqua communi natura qua continentur ex æquo omnia inter se non congruunt. Siquidem id quod est & vulgò appellatur ens, de illis non dicitur ex æquo, sed ratione quadam, unde collatum ad ea dicitur analogum: nam substantia prima omnium est, in ea cætera categoriæ insunt atq; illi nituntur. Quo verò inter hæc prædicamenta discrimen prioris & posterioris intelligamus, quæ sunt euidentiora, & quodammodo tanguntur, substantias inquam & Qualitatem, cum relatione confert, cuius natura vel essentia tenuis adeò est, ut non nisi ab eruditis hominibus cognoscatur, cùm substantia & Qualitas maximè omnium sint nota. Quod præterea mirabimur, si bonum per diuersas Categorias inueniatur sparsum, cùm bonum pateat non minus latè atq; id quod est? Ut enim passim dicitur, Ens & bonum retrò commeant: nil enim esse videas quod idem non sit bonum. Quid itaq; dices, bonum ab eo quod est differt? affectu inquam seu relatione, nam essentiæ rei addit collationem ad appetitum: natura bonum enim idem est quod expetendum. Verum quoq; tam latè atq; id quod est patet, & relationem æqualitatis adiungit essentiæ ad intelligentiam seu mentem. Vnum etiam fusissimè per omnes categorias meat, & duos ei quod est affectus adjcit[?], primum ut à seipso sit indiuiduum, nec à seipso distrahatur. Alterum, ut à diuersis disiunctum sit. Verùm de his obiter diximus, ut declararetur non tantum ipsum bonum æquè ac ens patere, sed alia similiter inueniri, quæ identidem per omnes categorias miscerentur. Sed ad rem redeo.
units.tr: From these points you may first establish that goods are many, since they are placed in various and many categories. Consider further that the categories are not laid down carelessly but have a just and most beautiful order among themselves, since some common nature by which all are contained does not apply equally to them. For what is, and is commonly called being, is not said of them equally, but in a certain sense, and so, compared with them, it is called analogous. For substance is first of all; the other categories inhere in it and lean upon it. But to understand the difference of prior and posterior among these predicaments, let us take those that are more evident and somehow touched upon, namely substance and quality, and compare them with relation, whose nature or essence is so subtle that only learned men know it, whereas substance and quality are most widely known of all. Moreover, we should not be surprised if good is found scattered through the different categories, since good extends no less widely than being itself. For, as is commonly said, being and good are interchangeable: you will see nothing that is not also good. What then will you say? Does good differ from what is? In affect, I say, or in relation: for it adds to the essence of a thing a relation to appetite, since by nature good is the same as what is to be desired. Truly it also extends as widely as being, and it adds to essence the relation of agreement to the understanding or mind. Good also runs through all the categories and adds two affections to what is: first, that it is undivided from itself and not drawn apart from itself; second, that it is disjoined from different things. But we have said these things in passing, so that it might be shown that not only good extends as widely as being, but that other things are similarly found, which are mixed through all the categories in turn. But I return to the matter.

units.la: Aristoteles per id quod ait τι, substantiam intelligit, quoniam ea per sese constat, & alia cùm nituntur ei, non habent nec patiuntur interrogationem per τι, nisi prout substantiæ modum quod ad notionem imitantur. Cùm enim petimus quid sit dulce, quidue amarum, de his non vt adiacentibus, sed vt de substantijs cogitamus: nam ita possumus aliquas eis definitiones attribuere.
units.tr: By the word τι [what], Aristotle means substance, since it stands through itself, while other things, when they lean on it, neither have nor admit the question "what," except insofar as they imitate the mode of substance in their notion. For when we ask what is sweet or what is bitter, we think of these not as adjuncts but as substances, since in this way we can assign definitions to them.

units.la: Sed quam ob causam in isto censu prætereatur quantitas, non vna ratio nobis occurrit. Dicere quippè licet, hoc ideò factum, quod in animo Aristoteli non fuerit omnes numerare categorias, ideò si vnam prætermiserit, nõ esse mirandum. Præterea quantitas ideò fortasse tacita est quòd nonnulli à materia, quæ initium est substantiæ, vix illam discernunt. Reuocet etiam forte aliquis in dubium, Cur ex posterioribus relationem duntaxat vume-ret[?]. Quibus quod respondeatur in promptu est, nempe omnes alias quæ sesequuntur Categorias aut affectus ac relationes esse, aut saltem non posse absque illis vel intelligi vel esse. Quare numerando relationes, illas quoque recensuisse videtur. Haec primo aspectu dicerentur commodissime, verum aliud est quod verius potest responderi, alias nimirum categorias, quae hic non sunt nominatae, in alia ratione quae mox adducetur, nominatum iri, saltem quo ad eorum maximam partem.
units.tr: But for what reason quantity is passed over in this list, more than one explanation occurs to us. It may be said that this was done because Aristotle did not intend to enumerate all the categories, so it is no wonder if he left one out. Besides, quantity is perhaps passed over in silence because some scarcely distinguish it from matter, which is the beginning of substance. Perhaps someone may also raise the question: why did he take only relation from the later categories? The answer is ready: all the other categories that follow are either affections and relations, or at least cannot be understood or exist without them. So by enumerating relations he seems to have listed those too. This might be said most conveniently at first sight, but there is another answer that is more true: other categories, not named here, will be named for another reason which will be brought forward shortly, at least for the greater part of them.

units.la: Dum inquit καθ’ αὑτὸ [?], Quod est per se, ut retur Eustrathius, non substantiam sed qualitatem significat: etenim qualitas etiam natura libera, non affectus, non relatio neque collatio. Novi quidem qualitatem non esse relationem, sed tamen Aristotelem non arbitror, per καθ’ αὑτὸ [?], intelligere qualitatem, sed tantum eam natura quae per seipsam constat atque cohaeret. Quodq; prius dixerat, illico voce proxima exprimit apertius. At quare non opponit relationi qualitatem una cum substantia, sicut eam ab initio commemorauit cum substantia, dum hanc rationem induceret? Quia vidit fortasse nonnullos, imo permultos, qui qualitates a substantiae formis non discernerent. Vel quod magis opinor, ut rationem magis perspicuam redderet, id quod fuit evidentius assumpsit, nempe substantiam, quam nulli ambigunt, priorem natura esse relationibus. Nam ut ex Dialecticis & metaphysicis cognosci potest, omnia ea quae cum aliis conferuntur & vocantur relata, ex tribus primis generibus oriuntur, substantia, inquam, quantitate, ac qualitate. Substantiae innituntur pater & filius: Quantitati aequale ac inaequale: tardem qualitati simile atque dissimile. Idq; demonstratur admodum eleganter his verbis, Hoc enim simile est rei adnascentis, & ei quod est accidentis.) Ratione hac ostenditur plane, quomodo, quae cum aliquo conferuntur, sint posteriora substantia, quod illi ut propago quaedam adnascantur, eiq; omnino accidant.
units.tr: When he says καθ’ αὑτό [what is per se], as Eustathius explains, it signifies not substance but quality. For quality too is a free nature, not an affection, not a relation or comparison. I know indeed that quality is not relation, but I do not think Aristotle means by καθ’ αὑτό [per se] quality, but only that nature which stands and coheres through itself. What he had said before, he immediately expresses more plainly in the next word. But why does he not set quality against relation together with substance, as he mentioned it at the beginning along with substance when he was introducing this reasoning? Perhaps because he saw some, indeed very many, who did not distinguish qualities from the forms of substances. Or, what I think more likely, in order to make the reasoning clearer he took up what was more evident, namely substance, which no one disputes is prior by nature to relations. For, as can be known from the dialecticians and metaphysicians, all those things that are compared with others and called relatives arise from three first genera: substance, I say, quantity, and quality. Father and son lean on substance; equal and unequal on quantity; finally, like and unlike on quality. This is demonstrated very elegantly in these words: "for this is like a thing that grows onto another, and like that which is an accident." By this reasoning it is plainly shown how those things which are compared with something are posterior to substance, since they grow onto it like a kind of offspring and happen to it altogether.

units.la: In his igitur non potest esse communis idea. Conclusio haec est dilucida rationis [?] ... lata, quia tota ex eo pendet quod in prioribus & posterioribus idea communis minime ponitur: nam in numeris eam non dederunt. Nec a vero prius & posterius habere demonstrat, quod sint non solum in his quae liberae sunt, verum & in illis quae cum aliquibus conferuntur. Et relata posteriora esse liberis, ut sit evidens, ex eo tamen docet, quod illis adnascatur instar propaginis, et accidentis. Causa igitur non est ob quam bonorum licet communem ideam penere. Eustrathius quo magis aperiat, in prioribus atque posterioribus idea communis statui non posse ait. Id quod est posterius oportere longinquius esse ab idea priori, atque adeo illius minus esse particeps. Verum cuius maior aut minor est communicatio, inter accidentia censetur, quae alba sunt, sunt, calida, vel dulcia, vt liquet, harum qualitatum non eodem modo sūt participia, sed alia magis, alia vero minus his accidentibus afficiuntur. Indefit vt si priora & posteriora sic idem respiciant, vt eam ista magis, illa vero minus participent, iam idea sit accidens omnibus his quibus plus aut minus sese impertit. Quam vero id alienum sit, vt ideas dicant accidentia singularum rerum, cum quibus naturam suam communicant, omnes vident. Quandoquidem tunc indiuidua essent illarum substantia quibus accidêrent, atq; ob eam causam ipsis longe firmiora atq; constantiora. Nec quisquam qui vel mediocriter sit eruditus ignorat, subiectum accidenti suo multo prius esse atq; nobilius. Quare idea in prioribus & posterioribus posita, non modo illis accideret, verum ipsis & posterior esset & ignobilior. Quo sane dicto quid absurdius Platonicis obici posset? Præsertim cum illi statuant ideas in hanc finem, vt singularum rerum quæ fiunt, & indiuiduorum quæ passim intereunt, firma sint exemplaria & immortalia vt ipsi dicunt, ἐκτυπα[?] seu imagines? Vnde quæ ita esse volunt, iudicari & pronunciari non possunt vel ignobiliora, vel posteriora illis qui ea participant. Sed age secundam rationem Aristotelis explicemus.
units.tr: In these, therefore, a common idea cannot exist. This conclusion is clear, its reasoning ... broad, because the whole depends on this, that a common idea is by no means posited in prior and posterior, for they did not give one in numbers. Nor does he show that prior and posterior hold, since they are not only in things that are free but also in those that are compared with others. That relatives are posterior to free things is evident from the fact that he teaches they grow onto them like an offspring and an accident. Therefore there is no reason why one should hold a common idea of goods. To make this clearer, Eustathius says that a common idea cannot be established in prior and posterior. That which is posterior must be further from the prior idea and so less a participant in it. But whatever communication is greater or less is counted among accidents, as is clear: white, hot, or sweet things do not participate in these qualities in the same way, but some are more affected by these accidents, others less. It follows that if prior and posterior so regard the same thing that one participates in it more and the other less, then the idea will be an accident to all those to whom it imparts itself more or less. How alien it is to say that ideas are accidents of individual things with which they share their nature, everyone sees. For then they would be the substances of those things to which they happen, and for that reason far firmer and more constant than they. Nor does anyone who is even moderately learned fail to know that the subject is much prior and nobler than its accident. Therefore an idea placed among prior and posterior would not only be an accident to them but would also be posterior and less noble than they. What more absurd objection could be brought against the Platonists? Especially since they hold that ideas exist for this purpose, that they are firm and immortal patterns, which they call copies or images, of the individual things that come to be and of the individuals that perish everywhere. Those who want them to be so cannot judge or pronounce them less noble or posterior than those who participate in them. But come, let us explain Aristotle's second reason.

units.la: Præterea cum bonum tot dicatur modis quotid[?] quod est, (Etenim dicitur in substantia, ut Deus & mens: & in qualitate uirtutes: in quantitate mediocritas: in his quæ sunt ad aliud, utile: in tempore, opportunitas: in loco, uictus salubritatisq; ratio seu conuersatio, & quæ sunt huiusmodi:) perspicuum est, nō esse bonum commune generaliter, & unum: nec enim in omnibus categoriis, sed tantum in una diceretur.
units.tr: Moreover, since the good is said in as many ways as there are kinds of being (it is said of substance, as God and mind; of quality, as the virtues; of quantity, as the mean; of relation, as the useful; of time, as opportunity; of place, as a healthy dwelling or way of life, and things of that sort), it is plain that the good is not a single common thing in general. For it would then be predicated in all the categories, not in only one.
Thus this argument is set out.

units.la: Quæ sunt in diuersis Categoriis communem ideam non habent.
units.tr: Things that belong to different categories do not have a common idea.
Goods are placed in different categories.

units.la: Quare fatendum est ea communem ideam non habere.
units.tr: Therefore it must be admitted that they do not have a common idea.

units.la: De priori propositione dubium nullum est, cum decem Categoriae communem aliquam definitionem non habeant, licet eodem nomine associentur. Id enim quod est, & jam vulgò tam in Dialecticis quàm metaphysicis ens vocatur, de his omnibus decem generibus dicitur, cuius tamen assignari no potest una definitio, quam omnes categoriæ ex æquo participent. Alteram propositionem quam Minorem vocat, inductione Aristoteles confirmat, initium faciendo à substantia: in quo sanè genere ut bona egregia numerat, Mentem atq; Deum, quæ utut pro exemplis adducantur & ab exemplis argumenta firma deduci nequeant, consyderasse tamen inutile non erit. Mentem hic non facultatem animi, quæ collocari solet in secunda specie qualitatis, diciturq; naturalis vis aut potentia, intelligit, sed pro substantia seu forma substantiæ, animumq; significat rationis atq; intelligentiæ participē, complectiturq; tum hominum formam, tum substantias illas intelligentes quæ motus cœlestium orbium cient.
units.tr: There is no doubt about the first proposition, since the ten categories have no common definition, although they are joined under the same name. For that which is, and which is now commonly called being, both in the dialectical and in the metaphysical writings, is predicated of all these ten genera, yet no single definition can be assigned which all the categories share equally. Aristotle confirms the second proposition, which he calls the minor, by induction, beginning with substance. In this genus he counts as outstanding goods mind and God. Although these are offered as examples, and firm arguments cannot be drawn from examples, it will not be useless to consider them. By "mind" he here understands not the faculty of the soul, which is usually placed in the second species of quality and is called a natural power or potency, but substance, or the form of substance; he means a soul that partakes of reason and understanding. He comprehends both the form of man and those intelligent substances which move the orbs of the heavens.

units.la: Propterea Deum ipsum cum mente statim coniungit. Miranturq; plu-rimi quomodo in categoria Deum Aristoteles ausus sit collocare, cùm omnes formæ Categoriarum definiendo possint aperiri, nullaq; definitio sit quæ genere differentiisq; suis non constet: quæ omnia Deo minimè omnium possunt attribui, ut qui sit quàm simplicissimus, & simplicitati compositio generis ac differentiarum minimè conveniat. Et nil est in ulla categoria quod sua definitione comprehendi non possit. Qui vero termini erunt, quibus Dei naturam queamus concludere? Proinde fuerunt inter Scholasticos theologos sapientissimi & quidem non pauci, qui Deum nullo pacto Aristotelicis Ca-tegoriis voluerunt includi. Cum quibus & ille facere visus est Dionysius, quem Areopagitam finxerunt. Is enim dixit Deum & omnia esse & nihil esse. Omnia est, ait, quoniam quicquid est illum participat: Nil vero est, non quidem defectu, quasi substantia, vel ut ita dicam essentia illum deficiat, sed quoniam omnia quæ sunt excedit. Alij vero ut Aristotelem tueantur, qui Deum hic inter formas recenseт primæ Categoriæ, inquiunt, si re ipsa & naturaliter agendum esset, Deum citra controversiam nullo genere nullaq; forma categoriarum concludi posse. At si Dialecticè spectetur, nihil obstare quin illi citra jacturam suæ simplicitatis, & infinitæ naturæ ac virium, possit aliquod genus, & aliquot differentiæ affingi. Nec dubitant rationes quas Aristoteles modo producit, esse dialecticas. Hæc ego notasse volui, quandoquidem locus iste sæpissime in scholis citatur.
units.tr: Therefore he immediately joins God with mind. Many wonder how Aristotle dared to place God in a category, since all the forms of the categories can be opened up by definition, and every definition consists of genus and differences. None of these can be attributed to God, least of all, since he is most simple, and composition of genus and differences does not at all agree with simplicity. Nothing in any category cannot be comprehended by its definition. What terms, then, will we have by which we may conclude the nature of God? Accordingly there were among the scholastic theologians some very wise men, and indeed not a few, who wished God in no way to be included in the Aristotelian categories. Dionysius, whom they feigned to be the Areopagite, seems also to have agreed with them. For he said that God both is all things and is nothing. He is all, he says, since whatever is partakes of him; but he is nothing, not through deficiency, as if he lacked substance, or, so to speak, essence, but because he exceeds all things that are. Others, however, to defend Aristotle, who here lists God among the forms of the first category, say that if the matter were to be treated really and naturally, there is no doubt that God could not be concluded under any genus or form of the categories. But if it is viewed dialectically, nothing prevents some genus and several differences from being ascribed to him without loss of his simplicity and infinite nature and powers. Nor do they doubt that the arguments Aristotle now produces are dialectical. I have wished to note these things, since this passage is very often cited in the schools.

units.la: In qualitate ut bona recensuit Virtutes, quæ, ut omnes norunt, ad primam qualitatis formam pertinent, quæ habitus & dispositio nominatur: sunt enim virtutes, ut suo loco tradetur, habitus animi crebris actionibus partæ, sive fuerint circa mores sive circa rerum notitias: in quantitate verò bonum bonum esse scribit mesuram, (quod solet ab omnibus commendari mediu) seu mediocritatem. Quod si dixeris videri etiam esse qualitatem: nam affectus dicuntur mediocres fieri, & humores sive qualitates eorum, ut calor, frigus, siccitas & humidum, in quibus mediocritas est sanitatis animantium effectrix. Respondeo, Mediocritatem quidem in his rebus esse, at non si vere proprie loqui velimus: mediocritas enim quantitatis est. Verum in qualitates transfertur, quando illas ceu extensas & magnitudinem seu latitudinem quandam habentes intelligimus. Dum enim cogitamus varios esse gradus frigoris, caloris, candoris, aut dulcedinis, aut affectuum, quia iuxta eos qualitates has vel maiores dicimus, vel minores, ideo rationem quantitatis, dum sic accipiuntur, subeunt, & ideo mirum non est, si etiam mediocritatis sint participes: illam enim a quantitate trahunt.
units.tr: Among the goods in quality he listed the virtues, which, as everyone knows, belong to the first form of quality, called habit or disposition. For virtues, as will be explained in its place, are habits of the mind acquired by frequent actions, whether they concern morals or knowledge of things. In quantity, however, he writes that the good is the measure (which is commonly commended by all as the mean), or mediocrity. But if you should say that it seems also to be a quality, since affections are said to become moderate, and humours, or their qualities, such as heat, cold, dryness and moisture, in which mediocrity is the cause of the health of living things: I reply that mediocrity is indeed in these things, but not if we wish to speak truly and properly, for mediocrity belongs to quantity. Yet it is transferred to qualities when we understand them as extended and having a certain magnitude or breadth. For when we think of various degrees of cold, heat, whiteness, or sweetness, or of affections, and call these qualities greater or lesser according to them, they take on the character of quantity when so understood. So it is no wonder if they also share in mediocrity, for they draw it from quantity.

units.la: Et in iis quæ cum aliquo conferuntur, utile: & in tempore, opportunitas: & in loco id est loci salubris inhabitatio, & quæ sunt generis eiusdem.) Utile referri ad aliud nō dubitatur: nam quicquid est utile in aliud dirigitur quod effectum volumus. Et prodest bifariam: vel ut conficiatur quouis modo, vel ut facile absoluatur. Occasio pertinet ad tem-pus: nam pars illius est, & merito censetur inter bona, cum in rebus faciendis quisq; laudatus & prudens artifex occasione captet, ut nō multò postea dicemus. Per diætam intelligit locum & quidem salubrem: nam talem medici præscribunt. His potuisset addere Categoria de actione exempla, nempe felicitatem, victoriam, reipub. iustam administrationem & cætera huius ordinis. De habitu, apte, decenter, & commodè vestiri. De situ, rectè stare, seu appositè iacere. Verum his omissis satis exemplorum per ea quæ commemorauit, adductum esse arbitratur, ideoque rem ad hunc modum concludit:
units.tr: And among things that are referred to something, the useful; and in time, opportunity; and in place, that is, a dwelling in a healthy place, and things of the same kind. That the useful is referred to another is not doubted: for whatever is useful is directed to some end that we want to bring about. And it is useful in two ways: either so that a thing may be accomplished in any manner, or so that it may be easily finished. Occasion pertains to time, for it is a part of time, and it is rightly counted among goods, since in doing things every praised and prudent craftsman seizes the occasion, as we shall say not much later. By "diet" he understands a place, and indeed a healthy one, for physicians prescribe such. To these he could have added examples from the category of action, namely happiness, victory, the just administration of the commonwealth, and the others of this order; from the category of habit, to be dressed aptly, decently and suitably; from position, to stand upright or to lie properly. But these being omitted, he judges that enough examples have been adduced through those he has mentioned, and so he concludes the matter in this way:

units.la: Perspicuū est, nō esse bonum commune generaliter, & unum: nec enim in omnibus categoriis, sed tantum in una diceretur.) Etenim ratio hæc est illarum rerum quæ existunt, quæq; unam communem habant rationem.
units.tr: It is plain that the good is not a single common thing in general; for it would then be predicated in all the categories, not in only one. For this is the reasoning about those things which exist and which have one common account.

units.la: Eustrathius Platonem tuendo putat Aristotelis argumentum convincere, si de bono loqueremur communi atq; universo, quod diceretur de omnibus bonis, & post singula bona esset. At inquit, Plato per ideam boni hoc non intellexit. Sed primum & summum illud, quod est Deus, à cuius bonitate cūcta quæ bona sunt derivantur. De bono itaq; agit, quod aliorum bonorum est causa, & commune ideo illud appellat, quod ipsum omnia sibi expetant, quod & Aristoteles in initio libri huius confitebatur. Verum si hæc Platonis erat erat sententia, tu de causa efficiente, nō de idea seu forma loquutus esset. Neque verum est Aristotelem à libri huius initio docuisse omnia Deum appetere. Omnia quidem ait bonum appetere, at non idem, sed quodq; bonū suae naturae aptum: Dei verò nullam facit mentionem. Deinde cur scientiam bonorum ex notitia huius ideae habere statuit, cùm Deus menti nostrae sit ignotissimus, & id per quod cetera sciuntur, oporteat esse notum ante omnia & multò clarius perceptum. Ratio verò Aristotelis ex eo vim habet, quòd hi statuerint ideam boni, cùm id facere minimè potuerint: est enim bonum, uti demonstratum est, multiplex & varium, nec una ratione seu propria definitione comprehendi potest. Neq; Deum ita collocari decet supra decem categorias, ita ut de illis omnibus dicatur. Superat quidem illas omnes, quoniam earum causa efficiens est: sed nos, uti dixi, non de efficiente, sed forma communi loquimur.
units.tr: Eustathius, defending Plato, thinks that he refutes Aristotle's argument if we speak of a common and universal good, which would be predicated of all goods and would stand prior to each single good. But, he says, Plato did not understand the idea of the good in this way; rather he meant that first and highest good, which is God, from whose goodness all good things are derived. So he treats of the good which is the cause of other goods, and calls it common because all things desire it, which Aristotle also acknowledged at the beginning of this book. But if this was Plato's opinion, you would be speaking of an efficient cause, not of an idea or form. Nor is it true that Aristotle taught at the beginning of this book that all things desire God. He says indeed that all things desire the good, but not the same good; rather each thing desires the good suited to its own nature. Of God he makes no mention. Next, why does he hold that the knowledge of goods comes from the knowledge of this idea, when God is most unknown to our mind, and that by which other things are known must be known before all else and perceived far more clearly? Aristotle's argument has its force because these men held that there is an idea of the good, though they could by no means have done so. For the good, as has been shown, is manifold and various, and cannot be comprehended by one account or proper definition. Nor is it fitting that God should be placed above the ten categories in such a way that he is predicated of all of them. He indeed surpasses them all, since he is their efficient cause; but we, as I said, speak not of the efficient cause but of the common form.

units.la: Atque cùm una sit scientia earum rerum quae una specie continentur, omnium quoq; bonorum esset unica scientia: nunc autem multae sunt, & quidem earum rerum quae in unam categoriam concludun-tur: ut occasionis, in bello quidem, ars militaris: in morbo verò, medica facultas: & mediocritatis, in victu medicina: in laboribus gymnastice.
units.tr: Since there is one science of the things contained under one species, there would also be a single science of all goods. But there are in fact many sciences, and these concern things that fall under one category: for example, of opportunity, the military art in war, and the medical art in sickness; and of the mean, medicine in diet and gymnastics in exercises.

units.la: Hac Aristotelis ratio ad secundum syllogismorum ordinem spectat.
units.tr: This argument of Aristotle belongs to the second order of syllogisms.

units.la: Omnium quae habent unam ideam, est etiam una scientia.
units.tr: Of all things that have one idea, there is also one science.
But there is not one science of goods.

units.la: Quare omnium bonorum non erit una idea.
units.tr: Therefore there will not be one idea of all goods.

units.la: Propositio maior est evidens, quoniam scientia & idea ad se mutuò referuntur, & sic affectorum inter se natura est, ut unum comutari non possit, quin alterum varietur. Minor probatur & quidem inductione, qua ostenditur boni eiusdem categoriae multas esse scientias, ut demonstrabit, quo ad occasionem & mediocritatem. Rationis firmamentum est à coparatis, utq; vulgò dicitur à maiore, quia magis videtur una esse scientia boni, quod pertineat ad unam categoriam, quàm bonorum quae à diuersis categoris comprehendantur. At non una scientia est, sed multae, cum occasionis quae concluditur in categoriam temporis, tum mediocritatis, quae collocatur in categoria magnitudinis. Atq; hæc sic declarantur, prius definitionem aperiendo, quid sit Occasio. Ea est pars ac momentum temporis, quod ad rem faciendam, seu facile & expedite producendam ad finem, magnam præbet commoditatem. Ea vt diuersarum rerum est, sic ad scientias varias attinet. Primùm, vti dicit Aristoteles, Artis est militaris in bello, vbi plus adiuuare solet occasio, quā virtus. Quæ aut versatur in morbo, medicæ facultatis est. Quamobrem Hippocrates scripsit, occasione præcipitē, vnde voluit ostendere medicinæ difficultatem. Et certè verū est, quod vulgò dicitur, occasione vbiq; rapiendam, quam si quis effugere ac elabi sinat, non valebit postea ipsam recuperare. Idem confirmat de Mediocritate. Ea est categoria quantitatis, cùm tamen ipsius non vna, sed multa habeantur scientiæ. Etenim à medico traditur ac docetur, qui vult plus aut minus adhiberi alimenti ægrotantibus iuxta morbi rationem, & pharmaca temperat vt mediocritate correctâ non lædant.
units.tr: The major premise is evident, since science and idea refer to each other mutually, and such affections are so bound together in nature that one cannot be changed without the other being altered. The minor premise is proved by induction, which shows that there are many sciences of goods within the same category, as he will demonstrate with regard to opportunity and the mean. The argument rests on things compared, and, as is commonly said, on the greater: it seems more likely that there is one science of a good that belongs to one category than of goods comprehended under different categories. But there is not one science, but many, both of opportunity, which falls under the category of time, and of the mean, which is placed in the category of quantity. These points are explained by first setting out the definition of opportunity. It is the part and moment of time which offers great convenience for doing a thing, or for bringing it easily and promptly to its end. As it belongs to various things, so it pertains to various sciences. First, as Aristotle says, it belongs to the art of war, where opportunity usually helps more than courage. Where it occurs in sickness, it belongs to the medical art. For this reason Hippocrates wrote that opportunity is fleeting, wishing thereby to show the difficulty of medicine. And it is certainly true, as is commonly said, that opportunity must be seized wherever it is offered; if someone lets it slip away, he will not afterwards be able to recover it. The same holds for the mean. It belongs to the category of quantity, yet there is not one science of it but many. For it is taught and explained by the physician, who decides how much more or less food is to be given to the sick according to the nature of the disease, and who tempers the medicines so that, with the mean preserved, they do no harm.

units.la: Eandem mediocritatem gymnastica facultas obseruat, hoc est, ars illa, quæ rationem tradit exercendorum corporum, & ea semper cauetur, ne quid nimis, ne quid parum. Est autem mediocritas certus & iustus modus inter nimium & parum. Proinde patet eorum bonorum quæ sunt vnius prædicamenti, non esse scientiam vnam, nedum vna sit eorum quæ per diuersas categorias sunt dispersa. Quare si bonorum non possit vna esse scientia, eorundem statui non poterit vnaidea.
units.tr: Gymnastics, that is, the art which gives the rule for training bodies, observes the same mean, and always takes care that there be neither too much nor too little. The mean is a certain and just measure between excess and deficiency. Accordingly it is clear that there is no single science of goods belonging to one category, much less of those scattered among different categories. So if there cannot be one science of goods, there cannot be one idea of them either.

units.la: Ambigat autem quispiam, quid nam dicere ue-lint de singulo quoq; ipsum, siquidem & ipsius hominis & hominis una & eadē ratio est & definitio, nempe hominis qua homo est, nihil à se inuicem dif-ferent: quod si ita est neque qua bonum.
units.tr: But someone may ask what they mean about each thing taken singly, since the being and definition of man and of a man are one and the same, namely of man as man; they do not differ from one another. If that is so, neither do they differ as good.

units.la: Ratio hæc quarta iam non contra bonum ipsum tantū inducitur, sed ad-uersus omnia vniuersa Platonicorum, vt demonstrentur superuacanea, & prorsus inutilia, & innititur argumento vulgatæ sententiæ, qua dicitur, illa esse inter se eadem, neq; differre quæ definitionem eandem habuerint. Quamobrem cùm homo ille vniuersus, qui ponitur vt idea hominum, eandem habeat definitionem quam habeat homo qui existit, nullum discrimen inter ea relinquitur, neq; quicquam supererit, quod tribuatur ideæ, ac id e non sit hominum quos videmus: & quod pronunciatur de homine ac eius idea, similiter accommodatur ad bona & bonorum ideam: nam illa etiā definitionem eandē habet. Quare cocludit hac ratione, ideas non ponendas vt inutiles ac superfluas. fluas. Ut autem Aristotelis verba intelligantur facilius, sciendum est, Plato-nem in plerisq; locis, & in libro praesertim de Repub. 6. cum vult ideas significare, nomini rei addit pronomen αὐτὸ, & inquit αὐτὸ ἀγαθόν, αὐτὸ καλόν hoc est, ipsum bonum & ipsum honestum. Et hoc est quod nunc dicitur ipse homo αὐτοάνθρωπος. Verum Aristoteles se nũcopponit Eustratius, et negat assumptum, nimirum boni, acideæ boni eadem esse rationem: quoniam fieri non potest, ut arbitratur, ut res quæ materia careat, & quæ illa secum habeat coniunctam, ut imago & exemplar, ut simplex & compositum, ut quod participat quæ habet, & quod per seipsum id quod est fuerit, eadem habeant rationem: at in eo hallucinatur, quod existimat per ideam Platonem intellexisse Deum, quod Aristoteles non confitetur. Verum hæc de re superius fusè ac ampliter est dictum: unde nunc satis fuerit monuisse.
units.tr: This fourth argument is directed not only against the good itself, but against all the universals of the Platonists, to show that they are superfluous and wholly useless. It rests on the argument of the common opinion, which holds that things having the same definition are themselves the same and do not differ. Therefore, since that universal man, which is posited as the idea of men, has the same definition as the man who exists, no difference remains between them, and nothing is left to be attributed to the idea that is not of the men we see. What is said of man and his idea is similarly applied to goods and the idea of good, for the idea also has the same definition. Hence he concludes by this reasoning that ideas are not to be posited, as useless and superfluous. So that Aristotle's words may be understood more easily, it must be noted that Plato, in many places, and especially in book 6 of the Republic, when he wishes to signify ideas, adds the pronoun to the name of the thing and says "itself the good [αὐτὸ ἀγαθόν], itself the honourable [αὐτὸ καλόν]", that is, the good itself and the honourable itself. And this is what is now called "man himself" [αὐτοάνθρωπος]. But Aristotle now sets himself against Eustratius, and denies the assumption, namely that the reason of good and the idea of good are the same. For, as he judges, it cannot be that things which lack matter, and which have that other thing conjoined with them, as image and exemplar, as simple and compound, as what participates and what is what it is through itself, should have the same reason. But Eustratius goes astray in thinking that Plato by "idea" meant God, which Aristotle does not grant. These matters have been discussed at length above, so it is enough now to have made this remark.

units.la: Neque vero, quia perpetuum est, magis erit bonum, siquidem neque id quod ad longum tempus fuerit candidum, eo candidius est quod uno die fuerit candidum.
units.tr: Nor, because a thing is perpetual, will it be more good; for what has been white for a long time is no whiter than what has been white for one day.

units.la: Per occupationem ista dicuntur, ceu quis obiecerit Aristoteli, quomodo hæc dicere audes nihil à se invicem distare, cum idea sit incorruptibilis & sempiterna: quæ vero cernimus, & fiant & intereant. Respondet Aristoteles, Longinquitatem temporis aut brevitatem non constituere in ratione vel essentia rerum discrimen. Ut q; magis perspicuum sit quod dicit, re transfert ad ea quæ sunt alba, & quod attinet ad candorem nihil interesse dicit, sive diu sive parvo tempore illo colore afficiantur, quoniam tantummodo hic agitur de ratione seu definitione quæ à se temporis circumstantia segregat.
