Et quod Aristoteles dixit de his quæ alba sunt, nos in hominibus possumus considerare. Vixit diutissimè (ut sacræ litteræ tradunt) Matusalé, Abrahamus non tam diu, & tamen definitionis hominis non magis unus quam alter eorum fuit particeps. Verum & hanc rationem seu responsionem labefactare voluit Eustratius, & ait, posse quidem diuturniora & minus diuturna communè habere rationem, sed æterna & mortalia non posse: Sed is non intelligit Aristotelis rationem ex eo duci, quod fateretur, posse quidem inter eos qui definitionis humanæ sunt participes evenire, ut unus altero esset longævior, & tamen utrique definitionis humanæ participes essent ex æquo. Sed hominem aliquem æternum et immortale haud quaquam concederet. Nam Nam aeterna oportet ut materia careant et contrarijs, quod in naturam humanam minime conuenit. Ideoq; cum illi suam ideam hominis & homine appellent & vere hominem esse velint, eam perpetuam & immortalem statuere nequeunt. Atq; hinc est quod Aristoteles collationem fecit inter magis et minus diuturna, non autem inter aeterna & caduca: quod sane ab eo non vulgari artificio factum intelligo.
units.tr: These things are said in objection, as if someone had objected to Aristotle: how dare you say that these do not differ from one another, since the idea is incorruptible and everlasting, but the things we perceive both come into being and perish? Aristotle replies that length or brevity of time does not establish a difference in the reason or essence of things. And so that what he says may be more clear, he transfers the point to things that are white, and says that as regards whiteness it makes no difference whether they are affected by that colour for a long or a short time, since here we are dealing only with the reason or definition, which sets aside the circumstance of time. What Aristotle said of white things we can consider in men. Methuselah lived for a very long time (as the sacred letters report), Abraham not so long; yet neither was more a partaker of the definition of man than the other. Eustratius wished to weaken this reasoning or answer, and says that things that last longer and things that last less long can have a common reason, but eternal and mortal things cannot. But he does not understand that Aristotle's reasoning is drawn from this: he would grant that among those who partake of the human definition it may happen that one lives longer than another, and yet both equally partake of the human definition; but he would by no means grant any man to be eternal and immortal. For things that are eternal must lack matter and contraries, which does not agree at all with human nature. Therefore, since they call their idea of man "man" and wish it to be truly man, they cannot posit it as perpetual and immortal. And hence it is that Aristotle made the comparison between things that last longer and things that last less long, and not between eternal and perishable things; which I understand he did with no ordinary skill.

units.la: Videntur autem Pythagorei probabilius de ipso dicere, qui ponunt in cosortio bonorum ipsum unum, quos & Speusippus uidetur secutus. Verum de his alius erit sermo.
units.tr: The Pythagoreans seem to speak more probably about it, since they place the One itself among the company of goods, and Speusippus also seems to have followed them. But that will be a different discussion.

units.la: Pythagorei duos ordines rerum constituerunt, collocantes ex una parte finem, impar, vnum, dextrum, masculum, rectum, lumen, quadratum, quiescens, & bonum. Ex altera vero infinitum, par, multitudinem, sinistrum, foeminam, obliquum, tenebras, quod est altera parte longius, quod movetur, & malum. Atq; hos ordines appellarunt συστοιχίας. Sunt enim consortia aut societates rerum, quae sibi mutuo sunt oppositae: Etenim finis infinito aduersatur, & impar pari, atq; ita deinceps. Et in his ponendis ostendere voluerunt Pythagorei, principia rerum esse contraria: inter contraria vero id vsu venit, vt alterum altero sit praestantius. Quis n. non videat lucem praeponi tenebris, dextrum sinistro, marem foeminae? Atq; hoc pacto in caeteris possumus deprehendere. Ob id aut Aristoteles Pythagoreos commendat, & quidem prae Platone, quod bonum minime retulerint ad ideam, vel ad aliquid vniuersale, quod per se cohaereat & constet, quemadmodum fecit Plato: sed ad vnum, quandoquidem vnitati probabilius rerum conseruatio videatur posse attribui. Nam quicquid est, dum manserit vnum et coniunctum secum, durat ac seruatur: cum vero deiicitur ac disciperitur a seipso, necesse est vt pereat. Possunt haec exemplis confirmari. Dum animus cum corpore coniunctus est, tunc ex illis fit vnum, quod est homo: dumq; congregantur elementa, compositum habetur, & est vnum, vt esse videmus lignum & lapidem. Et quando plures voces certa ratione copulantur, fit vnus concentus & suauis harmonia: quare vnum rei cuilibet perfectionem & rei salutem affert. Cum e diuerso pluralitas & diuisio interitu concilient. Etenim quando corpus disgregatur in elementa, destruitur: Et cum animus a corpore diuellitur, animantes intercidunt. Et sic deinceps. Proinde in hac ratione Aristoteles vnū cōfert cum idea, seu cum vniuersali, & ait, Res potius videri ad vnitatē referen-das, das, quàm ad ideas per Platonicos fictas. Non tamen commédat simpliciter & absolutè Pythagoreorum sententiam, quasi prorsus veritate attigerint, sed anteponit Platonicis: quod illæ voces demonstrant quibus utitur. Nam inquit, ἔοικασιν [?] & πιθανώτερον, hoc est, videntur & probabilius. Vtq; con-firmet illorum sententiam meliore Platonica, subiicit, Speusippum deserto Pla-tone scripsisse Pythagoricis, qui tamen Academicæ disciplinæ, hoc est schola post Platonem præfuit, et fuerat nepos illius ex sorore. Id etiam nunc memorat, quo demonstret se non iniuste facere discedendo à Platone præceptore suo, cùm ab eodem desciuerit Speusippus, non tantum philosophus nobilis, verùm successor Platonis, & cum eo sanguine coniunctus. Facit hoc & quidè non parum ad Aristotelem excusandum. Argumenti proinde summa est. Pythagoreos idcirco laudari, quòd omnia bona reuocauerint ad vnum, repertum inter nos, & coniunctum cum rebus, non autem ad aliquod auul-sum, & disiunctum à singulis, quod videri non potest, sed ad fictionem potius accedit, quemadmodum fecerunt Platonici. De sententia nihilominus Pythagoreorum noluit hic prolixius agere, sed illud in aliud tempus distu-lit, nempe cum diuina seu metaphysica esset conscripturus.
units.tr: The Pythagoreans set up two orders of things. On one side they placed limit, odd, one, right, male, straight, light, square, at rest, and good. On the other side they placed the unlimited, even, multitude, left, female, oblique, darkness, what is longer on the other side, what moves, and bad. They called these orders systoichiai [συστοιχίας], for they are series or societies of things that are mutually opposed: limit is opposed to the unlimited, odd to even, and so on. In setting these out, the Pythagoreans wished to show that the principles of things are contraries, and that among contraries it happens that one is more excellent than the other. For who does not see that light is preferred to darkness, right to left, male to female? In this way we can perceive it in the rest. For this reason Aristotle commends the Pythagoreans, and indeed in preference to Plato: they did not refer the good to an idea, or to some universal that coheres and stands by itself, as Plato did, but to the one. For the preservation of things seems more probably attributable to unity. Whatever exists, as long as it remains one and joined with itself, endures and is preserved; but when it is dissolved and torn away from itself, it must perish. These things can be confirmed by examples. While the soul is joined to the body, they make one thing, which is man. While the elements are gathered together, there is a compound, and it is one, as we see in wood and stone. When several voices are joined by a certain rule, there arises one concord and a sweet harmony. So unity brings perfection and the safety of any thing whatever, whereas plurality and division bring about destruction. When a body is broken up into its elements, it is destroyed; when the soul is torn from the body, living things perish. And so on. Therefore in this argument Aristotle compares the one with the idea, or with the universal, and says that things are rather to be referred to unity than to the ideas invented by the Platonists. Yet he does not simply and absolutely commend the opinion of the Pythagoreans, as if they had entirely grasped the truth; he places them before the Platonists, as the words he uses show. For he says they seem [ἔοικασιν] and more probably [πιθανώτερον], that is, they seem and are more probable. And to confirm their opinion with something better than the Platonic one, he adds that Speusippus, deserting Plato, wrote along Pythagorean lines; yet Speusippus presided over the Academic school after Plato, and had been his nephew through his sister. He mentions this now to show that he does not act unjustly in departing from Plato, his teacher, since Speusippus had revolted from him too, though he was not only a noble philosopher but also Plato's successor and joined to him by blood. This also does not a little to excuse Aristotle. The sum of the argument, then, is this: the Pythagoreans are praised for referring all goods to the one, which is found among us and joined with things, and not to something torn away and separated from single things, which cannot be seen and comes close to fiction, as the Platonists did. Nevertheless, Aristotle was unwilling to treat the opinion of the Pythagoreans at greater length here, but deferred it to another time, namely when he should write his divine or metaphysical work.

units.la: In iis autem quæ dicta sunt, dubium quoddam apparet, propterea quòd non dictæ sunt rationes omnes de bono, cùm unius formæ illa sint, quæ per seipsa diliguntur, & expetuntur, alterius vero quæ propter hæc dicuntur & alio modo, ut efficientia bonorum, vel conseruantia, vel quæ prohibent eorum contraria.
units.tr: In what has been said, however, a certain doubt arises, because not all the accounts of the good have been given. For some goods are of one form: they are loved and sought for their own sake. Others are said to be for the sake of these, in another way, as efficient causes of goods, or their preservers, or things that ward off their contraries.

units.la: Hæc dicit Aristoteles quasi modo velit de bonis accuratius loqui, distinguendo ea per sua genera. Nam prius visus est confusè de ipsis loqui. Et sanè distribuuntur bona omnia in duo genera. Nam alia propter se dicuntur, quod per seipsa expetantur: alia vero bona dicuntur, non sua vt ac natura propria, sed propter illa priora quorum gratia diliguntur, vt quæ illa efficiant aut conseruent, aut eorum contraria propulsent. Prioris membri exempla possunt adduci, nimirum, sanitas & virtus. Sanitas bonum est corporis, & ab omnibus animantibus præstantia & dignitate sua expetitur. Et virtus est animi perfectio, quam omnes qui sapiunt vehementer exoptant: atque priora ista bona perficiunt mirificè in quibus inhærent, posteriora verò id non non habent, nec præstant, sed ad illa priora vel addenda vel retinenda plu-rimum conferunt. Concludit illatam distinctionem his verbis:
units.tr: Aristotle says this as if he now wished to speak of goods more accurately, distinguishing them by their kinds, for earlier he seemed to speak of them in a confused way. Indeed all goods are divided into two kinds. Some are called good for their own sake, because they are sought through themselves; others are called good not in their own proper nature, but for the sake of those former goods for whose sake they are loved, as things that produce or preserve them, or drive off their contraries. Examples of the first kind can be given, namely health and virtue. Health is a good of the body, and all living things seek it for its own excellence and dignity. Virtue is the perfection of the soul, which all who are wise earnestly desire. Those first goods wonderfully perfect the things in which they inhere, whereas the latter do not have this quality and do not confer it, but contribute greatly either to adding those former goods or to retaining them. He concludes the distinction he has introduced in these words:

units.la: Manifestum igitur, bona dici bifariam, & alia quidem per seipsa, alia vero propter ista. Segregantes ergo ab utilibus ea quæ per seipsa sunt, consideremus an secundum unam ideam dicantur.
units.tr: It is clear, then, that goods are spoken of in two ways: some for their own sake, others for the sake of these. Setting apart, therefore, those things that are good in themselves from the useful ones, let us consider whether they are called good according to one idea.

units.la: Dicuntur hæc, ut videtur, in eum finem, ut innuat ea quæ non sunt per se bona posse ad unam aliquam speciem vel ideam (ut loquebatur Platonici) referri: Quemadmodum possunt ea quæ bona sunt per seipsa. Merito itaque illa segregauit à se inuicè. Atque utriusque horum generum definitiones nunc seorsim & perspicuè adducit, cum inquit:
units.tr: These things are said, it seems, with the aim of hinting that those things which are not good in themselves can be referred to one species or idea (as the Platonists spoke), just as those things which are good in themselves can. Rightly, therefore, he has separated them from each other in turn. He now sets out the definitions of each of these two kinds separately and clearly, when he says:

units.la: Qualia nam vero statuat aliquis per se bona, eane[?] quæ etiam si sola fuerint, expetuntur, ut sapere, videre, nonnullæ voluptates atq; honores. Hæc enim quavis & propter aliud sequimur, tamen in iis quæ per se bona sunt aliquis ea ponat.
units.tr: What sorts of things, then, would anyone set down as good in themselves? Those which are sought even if they are alone, such as to know, to see, and some pleasures and honours. For we pursue these even for the sake of something else; yet among the things that are good in themselves, one should place them.

units.la: Definitio per se bonorum est, quòd sint expetenda, quamuis nullis aliis comitata fuerint bonis. Ea dum per se sola offeruntur, expetimus & amamus. Et interponit exempla. ut sapere, videre, &c. Et sciendum quidem est, ea quæ hic recensentur, habere coniunctam secum aliquam utilitatem. Nam cernere, præter id quod sua natura suaue ac iucundum est, ac ab omnibus expetitur, multùm prodest ad id, ut utilia persequamur, & noxia euitemus. Sapere quoq; magnam habet secum oblectationem coniunctam. Deinde conducit ad vitam propriam & aliorum commodè & rectè instituendam. Unde quidam conati sunt bona omnia sic partiri, ut aliqua sic per se-ipsa expetantur ut ad alia detorqueri nequeant. Ut est felicitas ipsa Deus. Alterum ordinem faciūt eorum, ut quæ per seipsa expetantur: attamen in alia etiam possunt dirigi, ut sanitas & virtus. Hæc enim sunt natura sua bona, sed aliis quoque rebus multum prosunt. Postremum genus statuunt illorum bonorum, quæ nullo modo per seipsa diligerenter, nisi commoda essent ad alia percipienda, & in hoc ordine collocantur pharmaca, incisiones, adustiones & catera molestia, quas nonnulli subeunt, ut propositas vires consequantur. Potest quidem haec distinctio ad perspicuitatem facere, sed eam adducere non est necesse: quia secundum genus bonorum ad primum facile accommodatur. Nam ea etsi commoditates aliquas afferant, per seipsa tamen, absque illis expetenda essent.
units.tr: The definition of goods in themselves is that they are to be desired even when they are accompanied by no other goods. When these are offered alone, we desire and love them. He interposes examples: such as to know, to see, and so on. It should indeed be noted that the things recounted here have some usefulness joined with them. For seeing, besides being pleasant by its nature and sought by all, greatly helps us to pursue what is useful and avoid what is harmful. Knowing also has a great pleasure joined with it, and it conduces to ordering one's own life and that of others rightly and well. Whence some have tried to divide all goods in this way: some are sought for themselves in such a way that they cannot be turned toward other things, as happiness itself, which is God. They make another order of those that are sought for themselves, yet can also be directed to other things, such as health and virtue. For these are good by their nature, but they also greatly benefit other things. They set down a last kind of goods which are in no way loved for themselves unless they are useful for attaining other things; in this order are placed medicines, incisions, cauterizings and the other discomforts which some undergo in order to obtain the strength they propose. This distinction can indeed make for clarity, but it is not necessary to bring it forward, because the second kind of goods is easily fitted to the first. For although these bring some advantages, they would nevertheless be desired in themselves, apart from those advantages.

units.la: Annotandum vero est, Aristotelem non dixisse, aut sapientiā, aut visum, sed sapere ac videre: nam priora sunt habitus, qui non expeterentur absque opere. Actiones igitur posuit, quae natura sua bona sunt atque expetenda. De honoribus autem, ac voluptatibus, non citra delectum est loquutus, cum inquit, Certos, vel aliquos. Contemplatio quippe veri & affectuum moderatio, quae honestissimae sunt voluptates ab omnibus per se expetendae iudicantur, quod sane de illis non potest affirmari quas intemperantes vani homines consectantur. Honores quoque non omnes sunt expetendi, sed tantum qui deferuntur a sapientibus. Quos vero adulatores vel imperita multitudo elargitur, sunt aspernandi. Cum acceperit esse quaedam bona per seipsa, idque cum exemplis tum definitione monstrauerit, Ideas excludit, ut superuacaneas & prorsum inutiles. Verba eius haec sunt:
units.tr: It must be noted that Aristotle did not say wisdom or sight, but to be wise and to see; for the former are habits, which would not be desired without the act. He therefore set down actions, which by their nature are good and to be desired. Concerning honours and pleasures, however, he did not speak without selection, when he said certain, or some. For the contemplation of truth and the moderation of the affections, which are the most honourable pleasures, are judged by all to be sought for their own sake; this can certainly not be affirmed of those pleasures which foolish and intemperate men pursue. Honours too are not all to be sought, but only those conferred by the wise; those which flatterers or the ignorant crowd bestow are to be spurned. Having said that some things are good in themselves, and having shown this both by examples and by definition, he excludes the Ideas as superfluous and wholly useless. His words are these:

units.la: An vero propter ideam nullum aliud ponit esse bonum: Itaque vana species erit & inanis.
units.tr: Or does he say that there is no other good apart from the idea? Then the form will be empty and vain.

units.la: Ideas iam sic refellit, quod in illis viderentur Platonici quaerere bonum per se, verum per se, atque homine per se, & ita de singulis. Frustra inquit Aristoteles id fieri, quoniam hic bona per se habemus, quae videantur & sentiantur: quamobrem illa non debemus persequi aulsa ac separata. Et certe ratione superiori ostendit, ideas ideo vanas & inutiles, quod easdem [?] haberet definitiones cum singulis rebus, & propterea redundarent: idem nunc monstrat, cum inquit bona per se apud nos reperiri, quae sunt euidetia. Quamobrem illa debemus relinquere quae ignota sunt & ab iis confinguntur. Si non haberemus hic per se bona, fortasse necessaria esset idea. Verum cum ea hic habeamus, absque ideis habere possumus, quod isti aiunt se quaerere. Occurrit huic Aristotelicae rationi Eustratius & ait, Quae commemorata sint esse bona, ut videre, sapere, voluptates quaedam & honores, per se quidem bona esse fatebimur, quod expetantur natura sua: & si absque commodo alio nobis offerrentur: non tamen ita sunt per se bona, quasi sint ex seipsis, neque pendeant ab aliis, neque in aliis inhaereant, neque ab aliis producantur, nec etiam talia confiteremur, ut aliorum sint exemplaria quae omnia dicimus de ideis: ita ut putet Eustratius, Aristotelem admittere paralogismum Homonymias, quod aliter acceperit per se, quam Plato cum loquitur de ideis. Verum instantia hæc dissoluitur ex eo, quod ille modus per se, quem tribuunt ideis, sit absurdus, nempe ut non sint in alio, verùm cohæreant & consistent in seipsis. Nam id proprium est tantum singulis rebus, quas primas substantias appellant.
units.tr: Aristotle refutes the Ideas in this way: the Platonists seemed to seek the good in itself, the true in itself, and man in itself, and so for each thing. Aristotle says this is done in vain, since we have here goods in themselves which are seen and perceived. For this reason we ought not to pursue those things which are abstracted and separated. Indeed, by the earlier argument he showed that the Ideas are vain and useless, because they would have the same definitions as the individual things and so would be superfluous. Now he shows the same thing when he says that goods in themselves are found among us, and these are evident. Therefore we ought to leave aside those things which are unknown and are feigned by the Platonists. If we did not have goods in themselves here, perhaps an Idea would be necessary. But since we have them here, we can do without the Ideas which they claim to seek. Eustratius meets this argument of Aristotle and says: we will confess that those things mentioned as goods, such as seeing, knowing, certain pleasures and honours, are good in themselves, since they are desired by their nature, even if they were offered to us without any other advantage. Yet they are not good in themselves in the sense that they exist of themselves, or do not depend on others, or do not inhere in others, or are not produced by others. Nor would we confess that they are such that they are exemplars of others, which is what we say of the Ideas. So Eustratius thinks that Aristotle admits the paralogism of homonymy, because he took "in itself" differently from Plato when he speaks of Ideas. But this objection is resolved by the fact that the mode of "in itself" which they attribute to the Ideas is absurd, namely that they are not in another but cohere and subsist in themselves. For this is proper only to individual things, which they call primary substances.

units.la: Si autem & ista inter ea quæ sunt per se ponuntur, oportebit eandem rationem boni in his omnibus declarari, quemadmodum in niue & cerusa eadem ratio candoris: honoris autem, prudentiæ & voluptatis, alię atque differentes sunt rationes, quatenus bona. Quamobrem bonum non erit quippiam uniuersum, secundum unam ideam.
units.tr: If, however, these too are placed among the things that are in themselves, it will be necessary that the same account of good be declared in all of them, just as in snow and white lead there is the same account of whiteness. But the accounts of honour, prudence and pleasure are different from one another, insofar as they are good. Therefore good will not be something universal according to one Idea.

units.la: Ostendit prius Aristoteles ideam boni redundare, cùm hic habeamus inter nos per se bona. Nunc verò quoniam ei dici posset, Hæc quæ tu affirmas nos hic habere per se bona, nihil obstat, quin ad vnam aliquam ideam pertineant, quam omnia participent, & propter quam dicantur & sint per se bona. Hoc in præsentia negat fieri posse. Nam illa quæ sub vna idea comprehenduntur, oportet vt in quadam communi definitione consentiant. Ideoq; si statuerint multa hæc per se bona, quæ cernimus & negari nequeunt, ad vnam eandemq; ideam pertinere omnia ea oportebit, vna propria & communi definitione comprehendi: at hoc fieri non potest. Nam ista quæ recen-suimus, vt bona per seipsa nequeunt ad vnam eandem rationem reuocari. Ad probandum autem assumptum, nimirum debere consentire definitione communi quæ sunt vnius ideæ, simile profert niuis & cerusa, quæ cum specie seu qualitate candoris inter se communicent, eius etiam definitionis sunt participes. Quæ eadem ratione, sapere, videre, certi honores, & aliquæ voluptates, quæ diximus esse per se bona, necesse foret eandem habere definitionem: quod tamen haud quaquam potest dari. Nam prudentia perficit mentem, & est in eius potestate cuius est prudentia: honores autem illum nō perficiunt, cui exhibentur, neque reddunt propterea meliorem, ac omnino sunt in alterius potestate, illius nimirum, qui exhibet. Artificium verò Aristotelis ex eo demonstratur, quod ratione priori declarauit, redundare ideam si ponatur, cùm hic habeamus per se bona. Sed nunc demonstrauit etiam fieri nō posse, vt hæc ad vnam contrahätur ideam, cùm nequeant definitionem eandem participare.
units.tr: Aristotle first showed that the Idea of good would be superfluous, since we have goods in themselves among us. But now, since it could be said to him, "These things which you affirm we have here as goods in themselves do not prevent them from belonging to some one Idea, in which all of them participate and on account of which they are called and are good in themselves," he denies that this can happen. For those things which are comprehended under one Idea must agree in some common definition. Therefore, if they have established that many of these are good in themselves, which we see and cannot deny, all of them must belong to one and the same Idea and be comprehended by one proper and common definition. But this cannot happen. For those things which we have listed as good in themselves cannot be reduced to one and the same account. To prove the assumption, namely that things belonging to one Idea must agree in a common definition, he brings a similar case of snow and white lead, which, since they share the species or quality of whiteness, also participate in that definition. In the same way, prudence, seeing, certain honours and some pleasures, which we have said are good in themselves, would need to have the same definition. Yet this cannot in any way be granted. For prudence perfects the mind and is in the power of the one whose prudence it is; but honours do not perfect the one to whom they are shown, nor make him better for it, and in general they are in the power of another, namely of the one who bestows them. Aristotle's artifice is demonstrated from this: by the earlier argument he showed that the Idea would be superfluous if posited, since we have goods in themselves here. But now he has also shown that these cannot be brought under one Idea, since they cannot share the same definition.

units.la: At Eustratius inquit, Argumenti huius dissolutionem ex verbis eiusdem Aristotelis facilè haberi. Quandoquidem ipsemet definitionem prius attulit bonorum per se, & ea esse pronunciauit quæ persequimur & amamus, quamuis fuerint sola. Hæc inquit definitio ea est, quam omnia per se bona participant. Nec exigitur ut prudentia, honores & voluptates eandem habeant definitionem, nisi qua bona sunt, & ad hæc illa quæ in una ratione consentiunt, fit sæpenumero, ut non eodem modo illam participent, quemadmodum alba, non omnia pari gradu ac perfectione albescunt. Sic inquit, Bonum unum est per se, quod bona singula non eodem modo percipiunt, sed magis aut minus, prout sunt eius capacia, & aliter illud in seipso est, & aliter in illis habetur. Habent sanè responsiones huius viri speciem aliquam: nihilominus cum penitus considerantur, minimè satisfaciunt, quoniam ista quæ memorauimus per se bona, eandem rationem qua bona sunt minimè habere possunt: quod ut intelligatur, simile quod adducit Aristoteles, Cerusam & niuem alba esse fatemur, & cum rationem quæsieris, quare sint alba, non poteris aliam afferre, nisi quia disgregant & dispergunt visum: at si causam sis dicturus, cur prudentia, voluptates & honores per se bona sint, non unam rationem, sed longè diuersas adduces. Et de prudentia respondebis, quia virtus est, de honore, quod sit testis, aut præmium virtutis: de voluptate, quia commotionem suauitatis iucundam habeat. Hæc plana sunt rationes, & quidem varia, cur ista bona per se ipsa licet sola expetantur. Proinde recte dixit Aristoteles, ea non habere communem unam rationem, & quamuis definitio quam attulit una videatur, non verè una esse[?], sed multiplex. Et quod sit genus multiplicis, multa enim sunt eiusmodi, statim explicabitur.
units.tr: But Eustratius says that a solution of this argument is easily had from the words of Aristotle himself. For Aristotle first gave the definition of goods in themselves, and pronounced them to be those which we pursue and love, even if they are alone. This definition, he says, is that in which all goods in themselves participate. Nor is it required that prudence, honours and pleasures have the same definition, except insofar as they are good. And to these things which agree in one account, it often happens that they do not participate in it in the same way, just as white things are not all white with the same degree and perfection. Thus he says: the good is one in itself, which individual goods do not receive in the same way, but more or less according as they are capable of it; and it is one way in itself and another way as it is found in them. These replies of this man certainly have some appearance. Nevertheless, when they are considered thoroughly, they hardly satisfy, since those things we have mentioned as goods in themselves cannot possibly have the same account by which they are good. To make this understood, take the similar case that Aristotle adduces. We grant that white lead and snow are white, and when you ask why they are white, you can give no other reason than that they scatter and disperse sight. But if you are going to state the cause why prudence, pleasures and honours are good in themselves, you will adduce not one reason but quite different ones. About prudence you will reply that it is a virtue; about honour, that it is a witness to virtue or its reward; about pleasure, that it has an agreeable motion of sweetness. These are plain and varied reasons why these goods, although they are desired alone in themselves, are such. Therefore Aristotle rightly said that they do not have one common account, and although the definition which he gave seems to be one, it is not truly one but manifold. And that it is a genus of the manifold, for many things are of this kind, will be explained at once.

units.la: Sed quomodo dicuntur, non enim quemadmodum illa, quæ Homonyma sunt fortuito.
units.tr: But in what sense are they said? For they are not like those that are homonyms by chance.

units.la: Cum nomen habeant commune, videndum est, quomodo illud de eis dicatur. Neq; sunt hæc statuenda, ex illorum censu esse quæ nomen tantum communé habeant, neque definitione ulla inter se congruunt, alioquin essent prorsum homonyma, quæ vulgò appellant æquiuoca, & nunc ab {*}Aristotele dicuntur ex fortuna seu fortuita, et sic dicta sunt, quia non est consilium, aut ratio propter quam nomen commune habeant, ut cum in Aegypto puer nascitur, illi nomen inditur Alexander, idem si Roma tunc eueniat, ut pater filium suum Alexandrum appellet, erunt quidem pueri cognomines, sed ratio aut consilium afferri non poterit istius communionis: quoniam illi & parentes eorum, nec quidem se noverunt invicem. Certum quidem est bona, non tantum nomine consentire, verum etiam communem aliquo modo rationem habere. Merito igitur Aristoteles, abiectis homonymis quae sunt à fortuna, alios profert modos, quibus definitio potest esse communis. Licet non absolute seu perfecte, quemadmodum in Synonymis esse debet.
units.tr: Since they have a common name, we must consider how that name is applied to them. Nor should it be held that things which merely share a name belong to the class of those that have no agreement in definition at all; otherwise they would be altogether homonyms, which are commonly called equivocals. Aristotle says these are named from chance or accident, and they are so called because there is no plan or reason why they share a name. For example, if a boy is born in Egypt and is given the name Alexander, and at the same time at Rome a father names his son Alexander, the boys will indeed be namesakes, but no reason or plan can be given for this sharing, since they and their parents do not know one another. It is certain that good things agree not only in name but also have some common reason in some way. Rightly, therefore, Aristotle, setting aside the homonyms that arise from chance, sets forth other modes by which a definition can be common, though not absolutely or perfectly, as it must be in synonyms.

units.la: Sed nunquid eo quod ab uno sunt? an quod ad unum omnia conferunt? an magis secundum proportionem? Quemadmodum in corpore visus, ita in animo mens, & aliud in alio.
units.tr: But is it because they derive from one thing? Or because they all refer to one thing? Or rather according to proportion? As sight is in the body, so mind is in the soul, and one thing is in another.

units.la: Tres istæ formæ sunt analogæ, prima tum habetur, cum multa quæ sunt eiusdem nominis, participant etiam eandem rationem, at non simpliciter ac natura sua, verum quo ab uno aliquo communi principio proficiscuntur, ut pharmaca, chirurgorum instrumenta, libri, & consimilia, quæ omnia possunt dici medica, non alia sane causa, nisi quia inventa sunt & orta & composita ab arte seu facultate medicinæ. Altera forma est, quando plura cum ad unam eandemq; finem tendant, inde sibi nomen & rationem vendicant, ut exercitia, missio sanguinis, dieta, & alia huius generis dicuntur sana, cum omnia simul eò spectent, ut sanitas vel acquiratur vel conserue-tur. Et possent fortassis hæ duæ rationes coniungi, ut cum res ab uno principio seu causa prodeunt, & ad eundem finem tendunt, primam speciem seu formam huius homonymiæ constituant: & sic videtur interpretari Eustra-tius. Sed tamen Aristoteles hæc ut disiuncta non tanquam eadem protulit. Tertia forma est Analogia, quæ satis perspicua est exemplo in textu alla to de mente atq; oculo, ubi primum de analogia seu proportione constituendum est, ut sicut se habet oculus ad corpus, ita mens ad animum. Deinde videndum an unum sit bonum eius in quo est, & cuiusmodi bonum an propter se an propter aliud, ut dicamus, Quod oculus corpori, est animo mens: at oculus est corpori bonum: igitur & mens tale erit animi bonum. Ista igi-tur demonstrantur hoc modo non solùm conuenire nomine, sed ratione, sed tantum ex analogia. Quod verò habetur in verbis Aristotelis (Et aliud in alio) ita censeo intelligendum, ut si quid aliud in alio sit eodem modo ut oculus in corpore vel mens in animo, de illo vtique idem pro-nuntiabitur.
units.tr: These three forms are analogous. The first is found when many things that have the same name also share the same reason, not simply by their own nature, but because they proceed from some one common principle. Examples are medicines, surgical instruments, books and the like, all of which can be called medical, for no other cause than that they have been discovered, produced and composed by the art or faculty of medicine. The second form is when several things tend to one and the same end, and from this they claim their name and reason: thus exercises, bloodletting, diet and other things of this kind are called healthful, since all of them look to this, that health may either be acquired or preserved. Perhaps these two reasons could be joined, so that when things proceed from one principle or cause and tend to the same end, they constitute the first species or form of this homonymy; and this seems to be how Eustratius interprets it. But Aristotle did not present these as separate, nor as the same. The third form is analogy, which is clear enough from the example given in the text concerning mind and eye, where it must first be established what the analogy or proportion is: as the eye is to the body, so the mind is to the soul. Then one must see whether the good belongs to that in which it is, and of what kind the good is, whether for its own sake or for the sake of another. Thus we say: as the eye is to the body, so the mind is to the soul; but the eye is a good to the body; therefore the mind will be such a good to the soul. These things are demonstrated in this way, so that they agree not only in name but in reason, yet only by analogy. As for what is found in Aristotle's words (and one thing in another), I think it should be understood thus: if anything is in another in the same way as the eye is in the body or the mind in the soul, then of that thing the same will be affirmed.

units.la: Sed hæc forte in præsentia sunt omittenda: de illis enim exquisitè tractare, alìj philosophiæ magis proprium. Similiter autem & de idea.
units.tr: But perhaps these matters should be passed over for the present. To treat them exactly belongs more to philosophy proper. Similarly also concerning the idea.

units.la: Hæc est quarta & ultima pars huius capitis, ubi Aristoteles tractationem de ideis hinc semouet, ut quæ huic loco minimè sit propria. De ratione multiplici, quam modo ad bona accommodauerat, inquit alibi esse tractandum, nempe in Metaphysicis: ibi enim lib. 4. explicatur diligenter, quot modis aliquid multipliciter dicatur. Similiter autem & de idea.) Iste etiam non est locus ubi subtiliter de Ideis agatur, nam hoc quoq; ad Metaphysicam pertinet. Et certe in 2.[?] in 12. & 13. metaphysica de Ideis plurima dicuntur, ubi eas Aristoteles identidem insectatur. Atq; si quæsieris cur hæc duo ad illam facultatem pertinuerint, Id respondemus ideò esse, quoniam metaphysici proprium est, & definitiones & formas rerum contemplari.
units.tr: This is the fourth and last part of this chapter, where Aristotle sets aside the discussion of ideas from this place, since it is not properly suited to it. Concerning the manifold reason which he had just applied to goods, he says it must be treated elsewhere, namely in the Metaphysics, for there in Book 4 it is explained carefully in how many ways a thing is said in many senses. "Similarly also concerning the idea": this is not the place to treat ideas subtly, for this too belongs to Metaphysics. Indeed in the second, twelfth and thirteenth books of the Metaphysics a great deal is said about ideas, where Aristotle repeatedly attacks them. And if you ask why these two matters pertain to that faculty, we answer that this is because it is proper to the metaphysician to contemplate the definitions and forms of things.

units.la: Etenim si bonum quiddam unum est, quod communiter dicitur, aut separari potest per seipsum, manifestum est id non esse in rebus agendis, neque ab homine comparari posse. At nunc tale quiddam quæritur.
units.tr: For if the good is some one thing that is named in common, or can be separated by itself, it is manifest that it is not among things to be done, nor can it be acquired by man. But now such a thing is being sought.

units.la: Propositum Aristotelis est, demonstrare, hoc loco superuacaneam fore inquisitionem boni per se. Nam siue fuerit conceptus universa natura, ac nomen quod in multis dicatur, siue ut Platonici voluerunt forma separata, notitia eius ad hanc tractationem minimè pertinet. Ratio est, quoniam talia non possunt actione vel industria humana comparari & possideri. Nam si consyderemus ideam, ut genus, & quiddam universum, seu quasi speciem separatam, sunt potius hæc contemplationis non actionis, & alterum eorum ad Dialecticam reuocabitur, alterum verò ad Metaphysicam: nos verò in præsentia bonum illud quærimus, quod nobis queamus agendo vendicare. Neq; refert an Ideæ constituantur separatæ, ita ut constent & cohæreant per seipsas, an in mente Dei collocentur, quoniam à nobis neutro modo possunt comparari. Aristotelis itaq; ratio sic potest explicari.
units.tr: Aristotle's purpose is to show that an inquiry into the good in itself is superfluous in this place. For whether it is taken as a universal concept and a name predicated of many things, or, as the Platonists wished, as a separate form, knowledge of it does not belong at all to this treatment. The reason is that such things cannot be acquired and possessed by human action or effort. For if we consider the idea as a genus, and as a universal thing, or as a kind of separate species, these belong rather to contemplation than to action, and the one will be referred to dialectic, the other to metaphysics. But we, for the present, are seeking that good which we can claim for ourselves by acting. Nor does it matter whether the ideas are posited as separate, so that they subsist and cohere through themselves, or whether they are placed in the mind of God, since by us they can be acquired in neither way. So Aristotle's argument can be explained thus.

units.la: Notitia eius boni quod ab homine acquiri ac possideri non potest ad moralem philosophiam minimè pertinet. Idearum vero cognitio ita se habet.
units.tr: The knowledge of that good which cannot be acquired and possessed by man does not belong at all to moral philosophy. The knowledge of the ideas is related in this way.
Therefore it must be driven out of this philosophy.

units.la: Caeterum hic dubitarit quispiam, si acceperimus ideam ut conceptus est animi alicuius naturæ universæ, nonne fit & producitur à nostra intelligentia? quod si est, ut experimur esse, cur negabitur ab homine fieri vel acquiri? Ad hoc respondetur, fieri quidem in animis nostris huiusmodi species ac formas, cum singula incurrant in sensus & fiunt naturæ, non autem electione, & ideo noticiam quam appellant πρακτικὴν[?] non constituunt, & de ea solum in præsentia tractatur.
units.tr: Moreover, someone might here raise a doubt: if we take the idea as a concept of the mind of some universal nature, is it not made and produced by our understanding? And if it is so, as we experience it to be, why should it be denied that it is made or acquired by man? To this it is answered that such species and forms indeed come about in our minds, since individual things fall under the senses and become part of our nature, but not by choice; and therefore they do not constitute that knowledge which they call practical [πρακτικὴν], and it is only this that is treated at present.

units.la: Fortasis autem cuipiam videatur utilius esse noscere ipsum propter ea bona quæ aguntur & possidentur, nam ipsi habentes ceu exempla agnoscemus etiam nostra bona, & ea si cognoverimus assequemur.
units.tr: Perhaps someone may think it more useful to know the good itself for the sake of the goods that are done and possessed. For by having them, as if they were examples, we shall recognise our own goods too, and if we have recognised them we shall attain them.

units.la: Sibi ipsi[?] opponit, & ait, Ut ut idea vel bonum per se neq; fieri neq; possideri queat a nobis, eius tamen notitia utilis esse poterit ad nostra propria bona adipiscenda. Nam inde consequemur illorum notitiam, siquidem habentes commune illud bonum, tanquam formam conferendo ista cum illo, ea cognoscemus qualia sint, quemadmodum accidit de imaginibus, quas tu probe noscimus, cum illas ad archetypa sua referimus, quifit ut si bona hæc quæ nobis propria sunt, agnoscantur, futura sint comparatu faciliora. Nam si quem lateant, is facile illa inquirendo aberrabit, & in eam si fortasse inciderit, aliud se putabit nactum, & vicissim alia consequutus id quod quærebat existimabit acquisivisse. Nec videtur esse dubium, quin exemplari cognito facilius & commodius efficiamus quæ ab ipso pendent. Quemadmodum sagittantes se certius exercent cum propositum habuerint signum. Et iis Plato de repub. 6. adiecit, ideam secum afferre duplicem utilitatem, quarum una est, ut res per ipsam veritatem habeant, altera vero, per quam intelligentes vim habent cognoscendi. Scio quidem hæc ab eo dicta, sed non probata: sentiunt alioquin Peripatetici res ipsas quæ sunt veras esse. Atque nos absque opera ideæ in animis nostris naturæ beneficio vim facultatemque cognoscendi habere, nec non lumen, quo cognita discernamus. Et iuuari homines in inquirendo præcedenti notitia quæsitorum fatebimur: sed species & formas eius generis in animis nostris constituimus, non quæ conconstent & cohareant per se se aut in mente diuina resideant. Nam utrisq; his, etiamsi fuerint in nostris actionibus, non tuuamur. Unde cùm Cicero de oratore ideam proposuit & quidem perfectissimam rhetoris, non quidé eius qui aliquando fuerit vel talis sit futurus: non lusit operam, quia exemplum finxit in quod nostri conatus debeant quàm maximè intendere. Sed talem notitiam non ille quaesiuit ex mente diuina, neque à seperatis formis, s[?] dà singulis perfectionibus quas obseruauit in oratoribus nobilioribus. Vidit eas dispersas, quia nũquam vnus fuit omnibus praeditus, illas industria sua collegit, & ex ipsis vnam formam perfecti oratoris in animo suo constituit. Sed vt redeamus ad rem, aduersariorum instantia sic explicabitur.
units.tr: Aristotle raises an objection against himself and says: although the idea, or the good in itself, cannot be made or possessed by us, its knowledge can still be useful for obtaining our own goods. For from it we shall grasp the knowledge of those goods, since, having that common good, we shall know them by comparing them with it as with a form, just as with images, which we recognise well when we refer them to their archetypes. So if these goods that are our own are recognised, they will be easier to obtain. For if they are hidden from someone, he will go astray in seeking them, and if he happens to fall upon one, he will think he has grasped another; and conversely, having obtained one thing, he will think he has acquired what he was seeking. Nor does it seem doubtful that, once the exemplar is known, we shall accomplish more easily and conveniently the things that depend on it, just as archers practise more accurately when they have a target set before them. Plato too, in Republic 6, added that the idea brings a twofold usefulness: one, that things have their truth through it; the other, that through it those who understand have the power of knowing. I know these things were said by him, but not proved; otherwise the Peripatetics hold that the things themselves are true. We, however, without any work of an idea, have by nature's gift the power and faculty of knowing, and also the light by which we distinguish what is known. And we shall grant that men are helped in inquiry by a prior knowledge of what is sought; but we posit species and forms of that kind in our minds, not forms that subsist and cohere in themselves or reside in the divine mind. For we are helped by neither of these, even if they were present in our actions. Hence, when Cicero in De oratore proposed an idea, indeed the most perfect idea of the orator, not of one who has been or will be such, he did not labour in vain, because he fashioned an example at which our endeavours ought to aim as high as possible. But he did not seek such knowledge from the divine mind, nor from separate forms, but from the individual perfections which he observed in the more noble orators. He saw them scattered, because never was one man endowed with all of them; by his diligence he gathered them together, and from them he formed in his mind one form of the perfect orator. But to return to the matter, the opponents' objection will be explained thus.

units.la: Ea notitia pertinet ad moralem philosophiam quae ad id conducit vt bona quae nobis propria sunt agnoscantur.
units.tr: That knowledge pertains to moral philosophy which conduces to recognising the goods that are our own.
Such is the knowledge of ideas.

units.la: Proinde ab hac philosophia non est aliena.
units.tr: Therefore it is not foreign to this philosophy.

units.la: Huius obiectionis Aristoteles minorem propositionem inficiatur ratione quae statim subiicitur:
units.tr: Aristotle denies the minor premise of this objection, by the reasoning that immediately follows:

units.la: Probabilitatem igitur quandam ratio habet, uidetur autem dissentire à scientiis. Omnes enim aliquod bonum expetunt, & quòd sibi opus est inquirunt. Huius uero boni praetermittunt notitiam, cùm tamen uerisimile non sit omnes artifices tantum adiumentum ignorare, nec inquirere.
units.tr: Reason therefore has a certain probability, but it seems to disagree with the sciences. For all men seek some good, and they inquire into what they need; yet they neglect the knowledge of this good, although it is not likely that all craftsmen are ignorant of so great an aid, or fail to inquire into it.

units.la: Primis illico verbis debilitat aduersariorum argumentum, non veritatem, sed probabilitatem ei tribuendo. Nemo autem ignorat multa probabilia esse falsa, quemadmodum vicissim permulta reperiri vera, quae tamen verisimilia non sunt. Deinde vt magis adhuc debilitet quod obiiciunt, probabilitatem ei non simpliciter & absolutè attribuit, sed quandam, hoc est, aliqua ex parte, non modis omnibus. Confutat praeterea quod aiunt, à scientiis & artibus: & obseruandum est ipsum hoc loco voce illa, scientiis, intelligere artes: quod ex eo confirmatur, quia è vestigio subiicit, non esse consentaneum omnes artifices praetermissuros tantum commodum. Rationis autem eius robur in consitum est, quod artes proprium suum bonû quaerunt. Vnde notitiam illam non praeterirent, si eam experirentur sibi commodam. dam. Deinde illa curant & student consequi, quibus indigent, propterea non contemnerent idearum notitiam, si ea opus haberent ad bonum proprium acquirendum. Ratio Aristotelis ita constat:
units.tr: In the very first words he weakens the opponents' argument, not by denying its truth but by granting it only probability. No one is unaware that many probable things are false, just as conversely many true things are found which are nevertheless not likely. Next, to weaken further what they object, he does not attribute probability to it simply and absolutely, but a certain probability, that is, in some respect, not in every way. Moreover, he refutes what they say about the sciences and arts; and it must be observed that here, by the word "sciences," he means the arts. This is confirmed by his immediately adding that it is not consistent for all craftsmen to neglect so great an advantage. The strength of his reasoning lies in this: the arts seek their own good. Hence they would not pass over that knowledge if they found it suitable for them. Again, they take care and strive to obtain what they lack; therefore they would not despise the knowledge of ideas if they needed it to acquire their own good. Aristotle's argument stands thus:

units.la: Notitia ea quam artes propemodum omnes prætereunt vtilis non est ad agnoscenda bona quæ homines possunt sibi vendicare.
units.tr: The knowledge which almost all the arts pass over is not useful for recognising the goods that men can claim for themselves.
All craftsmen neglect the knowledge of ideas.

units.la: Quare non est vtilis ad nostra bona dignoscenda.
units.tr: Therefore it is not useful for discerning our goods.

units.la: Ac dubium est quid adiuuandi sint textor aut faber in arte sua, si ipsum nouerint bonum, aut quomodo peritior medicus aut præstantior dux militaris sit futurus is, qui ideam ipsam fuerit contemplatus: non enim sic valetudinem medicus uidetur spectare, sed hominis ac potius fortasis unius alicuius: etenim singulis medetur. Sed his de rebus hactenus.
units.tr: And it is doubtful how a weaver or a smith would be helped in his craft if they knew the good itself, or how a physician would become more skilled, or a military commander more excellent, if he had contemplated the idea. For the physician does not seem to look to health in general, but to man, or rather perhaps to one particular man, since he heals individuals. But so much on these matters.

units.la: Duas hæc Aristotelis verba rationes comprehendunt, quarum prima ex eo deducitur, quod artifices si noscerent ideam, nihilo essent meliores: neque iuuarentur, quo ad suas artes ea contemplatione. Argumentum ita potest contexi.
units.tr: These words of Aristotle contain two arguments. The first is drawn from this: that craftsmen, even if they knew the idea, would be no better, nor would they be helped in their arts by that contemplation. The argument can be framed thus:

units.la: Notitia eius rei qua nihil iuuantur artifices, aliena est à nostro proposito.
units.tr: The knowledge of that thing by which craftsmen are not helped is foreign to our purpose.
Such is the knowledge of the idea.

units.la: Quamobrem ad hanc philosophiæ tractationem haud spectat.
units.tr: Wherefore it does not pertain to this treatment of philosophy.

units.la: Altera deinde ratio sumpta est à materia subiectisq. artium, nec non ab actionibus quæ inde oriuntur: etenim medicus nequaquam contemplatur sanitatem communem, sed hominis. Et cum ad sanandum se confert, eius certi hominis quem curat valetudinem tractat & promouet. Etenim eius actiones circa indiuiduum & singulum hominem versantur, neque solicitus est de idea, nil etenim circa illam est acturus. Cautè nihilominus loquitur Aristoteles: nam inquit, ἴσως γὰρ μᾶλλον [?]. Quia reuera medicus non in vniuersum abstinet à communium rerum consideratione: arte quippe suam addiscens & mente concipiens, rationes quasdam & canones habet communes, quæ late patent: at cum ad agendū se confert, & curationes vult exercere, circa singula totus versatur. Et hac distinctione conciliare possumus quæ in Aristotele videntur pugnantia: nam alibi scribit, scien
units.tr: The second reason is taken from the matter and subject of the arts, and also from the actions that arise from them. For the physician by no means contemplates common health, but that of man; and when he sets himself to heal, he handles and promotes the health of that particular man whom he treats. For his actions are concerned with the individual and single man, and he is not concerned with the idea, since he will do nothing at all in relation to it. Aristotle nevertheless speaks cautiously, for he says, "perhaps rather" [ἴσως γὰρ μᾶλλον]. For in truth the physician does not altogether abstain from consideration of common things: learning his art and conceiving it in his mind, he has certain common rules and canons that extend widely. But when he sets himself to act and wishes to exercise cures, he is wholly occupied with particulars. By this distinction we can reconcile what seem to be contradictions in Aristotle, for elsewhere he writes that science

units.la: Analysis. tiam esse vniuersalium. & in Rhetoricis ponit, ac scribit in hunc modum, ἐπιστήμια[?] δὲ τέχνη σκοπεῖ[?] καθόλου[?], οἷον ἰατρικὴ τί ὑγιεινὸν ἢ σωτηρίας ἢ κα[?]λλία[?]. Quoniam in his locis de facultatibus his loquitur, vt mente compre-henduntur, hic vero de actionibus artificum, & materijs circa quas actio-nes illae exercentur. Atq; si dixeris, hoc id est, quod Platonici quaerebant, scientias & artes non haberi neq; ab animis nostris percipi, nisi mente ad vniuersa ipsa respiciamus. Hoc illi nequeunt obijcere nobis, quia ideas ex-tra nostrum animum esse confinxerunt, & illae profecto sunt quas Aristote-les affirmat nihil artificibus prodesse. Addam praeterea ex patribus nostris religionis qui iudicarunt ideas concedendas, vt fecit Augustinus, illas non induxisse, vt artifices ad ipsas conuersi docerentur, quomodo sua opificia ef-sent facturi, sed ad quas Deus ipse respiciens condiderit rerum diuersarum naturas. Posterior vero haec ratio Aristotelis sic ordinabitur:
units.tr: is of universals. And in the Rhetoric he puts it and writes in this manner: "Science [ἐπιστήμη] and art regard the universal, as medicine regards what is healthy, or what is salutary, or..." Since in those passages he speaks of these faculties as they are grasped by the mind, but here of the actions of craftsmen and the matters about which those actions are exercised. And if you say that this is what the Platonists sought, namely that sciences and arts are neither held nor perceived by our minds unless we look to the universals themselves, they cannot object this to us, because they feigned ideas to exist outside our mind, and those are surely what Aristotle affirms to be of no benefit to craftsmen. I will add besides, from our religious fathers, that those who judged that ideas should be conceded, as Augustine did, did not hold that they were introduced so that craftsmen, turning to them, might be taught how to make their works; rather, God himself, looking to them, established the natures of diverse things. The latter argument of Aristotle will be ordered thus:

units.la: Bonum illud circa quod artifices non versantur & quod actionibus eorum non subiicitur, alienum à nostro est instituto.
units.tr: That good with which craftsmen are not concerned, and which is not subject to their actions, is foreign to our undertaking.

units.la: Idea licet esset, & bonum esset, neq; materia illorum artificum, neq; sub-iectum artificiosarum actionum statui potest.
units.tr: Even if there were an idea, and it were a good, it could be established neither as the matter of those craftsmen nor as the subject of their artful actions.

units.la: Igitur praetereunda est eius notitia in ista philosophiae parte.
units.tr: Therefore its knowledge must be passed over in this part of philosophy.
CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Rursus ad id quod inquiritur bonum reuertamur, & quid nam sit uideamus. Aliud quidem in alia actione & arte uidetur: aliud enim in arte medica, aliud in re militari, & item in reliquis.
units.tr: Let us return once more to the good, which is what we are seeking, and see what it is. Indeed it appears to be one thing in one action or art, and another in another: for the good is one thing in the medical art, another in the military art, and likewise in the rest.

units.la: Tres habet istud caput partes potiores. Primo enim traduntur felicitatis quaedam praecipuae proprietates, vtpote quod vna sit & summa, deinde quod perfectissima, & postremo loco demonstratur sibi ipsis sufficiens. Atq; haec via est inuestigandi defini-tiones vt prius rei communes proprietates inquirantur. Se-cunda vero parte capitis explicatur propria felicitatis definitio, nempe quod sit in actione praestantissima hominis, quae ab optima illius virtute pro-ficiscatur. Tertia vero & ultima pars multa continet de genere ac forma notitia, qua definitionem hanc felicitatis possimus habere perspectam. Sed iam eam partem interpretandam sumamus, quæ primo loco nobis occurrit. Primum in ea videbimus Aristotelem connectere quæ nunc sunt dicenda his quæ hactenus tradidit, & cum disputationem de ideis & prolixam & molestam interposuerit, ait se velle redire ad inuestigationem definitionis boni, quam coeperat inuestigare, quod ut faciat commodius & apertiore methodo, quibusdam utitur hypothesibus, quæ nihil aliud sunt quam repetitiones strictæ ac summa illorum quæ ab initio dixerat. Et ante omnia proponit in omni actione atq; arte non idem imo diuersum reperiri bonum. Quod, inquit, testatur ars medica et actio militaris, & in aliis idetidem ostendi possit: quibus verbis innuit suam hanc hypothesim posse inductione probari. Quæ hic dicuntur cum ab initio libri huius explicata satis fuerint, modo non oportet repetere, ac res ipsa tam perspicua est, ut Aristoteles eam non iudicauerit accuratiore confirmatione opus habere.
units.tr: This chapter has three main parts. First, certain chief properties of happiness are set out, namely that it is one and supreme, then that it is most perfect, and lastly that it is self-sufficient. This is the method of seeking definitions: first the common properties of the thing are investigated. In the second part of the chapter the proper definition of happiness is explained, namely that it is the most excellent activity of man, proceeding from his best virtue. The third and last part contains much knowledge of the genus and form, by which we may have this definition of happiness clearly before us. But let us now take up the part that comes first before us. In it we shall see Aristotle connecting what he is now going to say with what he has taught so far. After a long and tedious digression on the Ideas, he says he wishes to return to the inquiry into the definition of the good, which he had begun. To do this more conveniently and by a clearer method, he uses certain hypotheses, which are nothing other than brief restatements and a summary of what he had said at the beginning. And first he sets out that in every action and art the good is not the same but different. This, he says, is attested by the art of medicine and by military action, and it can be shown again and again in other cases. By these words he hints that this hypothesis of his can be proved by induction. What is said here need not be repeated, since it was sufficiently explained at the beginning of this book; and the matter is so plain that Aristotle did not judge it to need more careful confirmation.

units.la: Quod igitur cuiusque bonum est? an id cuius gratia cætera aguntur? hoc autem in medicina ualetudo, in arte militari uictoria, in architectura domus, & in alio aliud.
units.tr: What, then, is the good of each thing? Is it that for the sake of which everything else is done? In medicine this is health; in military art, victory; in architecture, the house; and in each other thing, something else.

units.la: Secundam hic habemus hypothesin, quam statuit, bonum cuiusq; artis ac-tionis illud esse cuius causa omnia ea fiunt quæ prius aguntur, quod idem circa initia huius libri fuerat expositum. Et tamen id nobis inductione quadam confirmat, ostendens in medicina, in arte militari, nec non in architectura, & in aliis hoc facile deprehendi. Atque nos hæc eadem superius interpretando hanc finis descriptionem diligenter examinauimus: quare nunc ipsa duntaxat assumptione Aristotelis acquiescimus. Quare ad tertiam veniendum est hypothesin, ea vero sic habet:
units.tr: Here we have a second hypothesis, which he lays down: that the good of every art and action is that for the sake of which all the things done earlier are done, which was also set out near the beginning of this book. Yet he confirms this for us by a kind of induction, showing that it is easily recognised in medicine, in military art, in architecture too, and in other cases. We examined this end-definition carefully when we explained the passage above, so now we simply accept Aristotle's assumption. We must therefore come to the third hypothesis, which runs thus:

units.la: In omni autem actione ac delectu finis: huius enim gratia reliqua omnia agunt omnes.
units.tr: In every action and choice there is an end, for all men do everything else for its sake.

units.la: Cum iam sumpserit aliud atq; aliud esse bonum in aliis actionibus & artibus: & illud esse, cuius causa fiunt alia, propius ad rem accedit, & praetermissis artibus, de actione ipsa & delectu ait, Hæc quoque suum habere bonum, nempe finem: atque hoc ita probat, quoniam propter illud bonum reliqua omnes faciunt. Itaq; si quis est omnium rerum agendarum finis, hic erit bonum ipsum agendum. Sin autem plures, hi ipsi. Et oratio digrediens eodem peruenit. Hoc autem ut magis explicetur, danda est opera.
units.tr: Having now assumed that the good is one thing in one action or art and another in another, and that it is that for the sake of which the other things are done, he comes closer to the matter. Leaving the arts aside, he says of action itself and of choice that these too have their own good, namely an end. He proves this because all men do the other things for the sake of that good. So if there is one end of all things to be done, this will be the good to be done. But if there are several, these will be the goods. And his discourse, wandering off, arrives at the same point. But to make this clearer, effort must be given.

units.la: Ex assumptis vel hypothesibus iam allatis concludit, actionum humana- narum vel unum esse finem, qui erit bonum πρακτὰ[?], vel si plures erunt fines, ut revera sunt, hi ipsi fines erunt bona plura πρακτὰ[?]. Connexio firma est, quia finem oportet esse bonum: ista enim licet (ut diximus) non reciprocentur, quia bonum latius patet ac manat quam finis, attamen finium multitudo plura quoq; bona esse demonstrat. Proinde si multa bona erunt, in quae nostrae actiones ac delectus ferantur, quod nam illorum statuetur esse felicitas? Hic Aristoteles inquit iam suam orationem eodem redijsse, unde antea fuerat digressa. Nam superius cap. 2. proposuerat inter multas fines humanarum actionum, unam concedendam esse summam, ne appetitiones in immensum abirent. Et ostendit bonum huiusmodi non posse ad aliam facultatem pertinere, quam ad civilem, quae suprema est omnium, quandoquidem optimus finis assignandus est omnino facultati praestantissimae. Atq; hic digressio interposita fuit, qua examinata sunt varia hominum sententiae, qui bonum hoc aut in voluptate, aut in divitiis, aut in honoribus, aut in virtute collocarunt, & deniq; Platonis opinio, de idea boni, est confutata. Modo vero per hypotheses quas declarauimus, eo ventum est, ut si multi sint fines, multaq; bona delectus & actionum nostrarum, ut quaeratur, quis nam istorum finium quodue horum bonorum caeteris sit praeponendum, & ita praeponendum ut summum habeatur. Atque hoc est quod inquit orationem suam aliquandiu vagatam eodem redijsse. Quoniam ut istam quaestionem expediret, multorum & memorauit & confutauit opiniones, quod cum fecerit, id iam restat ut ipse suum exponat sensum, quo ad ordinem horum finium & bonorum, ut deniq; videamus, quod nam eorum sit caeteris omnibus praeferendum.
units.tr: From the assumptions or hypotheses already brought forward he concludes that human actions have either one end, which will be the good [πρακτά], or, if there are several ends, as there really are, these very ends will be several goods [πρακτά]. The connection is sound, because an end must be good; for although (as we have said) these are not convertible, since the good extends more widely and spreads further than the end, nevertheless the multitude of ends shows that there are also several goods. Therefore, if there are many goods towards which our actions and choices are directed, which of them shall be declared to be happiness? Here Aristotle says that his discourse has now returned to the point from which it had strayed. For in the second chapter he had proposed that among the many ends of human actions one must be granted as supreme, lest our appetites go on without limit. And he showed that a good of this kind cannot belong to any faculty other than the civil faculty, which is the highest of all, since the best end must necessarily be assigned to the most excellent faculty. And here a digression was inserted, in which the various opinions of men were examined, who placed this good in pleasure, or in riches, or in honours, or in virtue, and finally Plato's opinion about the Idea of the good was refuted. Now, by the hypotheses we have explained, we have come to this: if there are many ends and many goods of our choices and actions, then the question is which of these ends, or which of these goods, is to be preferred to the others, and preferred in such a way as to be held supreme. This is what he means when he says that his discourse, having wandered for a while, has returned to the same point. For to settle this question he first recalled and then refuted the opinions of many; having done that, what remains is for him to set out his own view about the order of these ends and goods, so that finally we may see which of them is to be preferred to all the rest.

units.la: Quoniam vero plures videntur esse fines, & eorum quosdam propter alios expetimus, ut divitias, tibias & omne genus instrumenti: perspicuum est, non omnes esse perfectos, Qui autem optimus est, quiddam perfectum uidetur. Si quis igitur unus ac solus perfectus est, is fuerit id quod quaerimus. Sin uero plures, eorum perfectissimus.
units.tr: But since there seem to be several ends, and some of them we desire on account of others, such as riches, flutes, and every kind of instrument, it is plain that not all are perfect. But that which is best seems to be something perfect. If, then, there is one only and single perfect end, this will be what we are seeking. But if there are several, it will be the most perfect of them.

units.la: In extremo fine inuestigando nunc docet, qui fines ab eius natura sint amouendi nimirum imperfectiores: ij vero sunt, qui propter alios expetuntur: & ratio sic explicatur:
units.tr: In investigating the final end, he now teaches which ends must be set aside as, by their nature, more imperfect: these are the ones that are desired for the sake of others. The argument is explained thus:
No imperfect end ought to be posited as supreme.
But many ends of this kind are found.
Therefore not all of them can be ultimate.

units.la: Minor propositio declaratur exēplis earū rerū q propter aliud expetuntur. Etenim instrumenta omnia propter aliud expetuntur, nam eo spectant, ut per illa coparemus nobis aliquod aliud bonū, quod magis optemus. Diuitiae tales perhibentur, quas nemo diligit, nisi ut per illas commoda vitae, dignitates aut voluptates consequatur. Tibiarum quoq; natura eadem est: musicis quippe inseruiunt, ut illis canant, quemadmodum libuerit. Maior autem propositio potest ex eo confirmari, quod quaecunq; propter aliud petuntur, ea inde perfectionem trahant, quam si haberent ex seipsis, in ea minime tenderent ad quae diriguntur. Vtq; hoc ostendat Aristoteles, dixit optimam illam finem, quam inuestigamus perfectam esse oportere. Quo sic posito distinctionem subiecit. Finis perfectus aut unus est aut plures, quod si unus fuerit, nō alius erit quaerendus, cum is bonum illud sit quod peruestigamus: Sin uero plures fuerint perfecti fines, inter hos vt summum, eum diligimus, qui fuerit omnium perfectissimus.
units.tr: The minor premise is made clear by examples of things that are desired for the sake of something else. For all instruments are desired for the sake of something else, since they serve to help us obtain some other good that we wish for more. Riches are of this kind: no one loves them except so that through them he may obtain the conveniences of life, dignities, or pleasures. The nature of flutes is the same: they serve musicians, so that these may play on them as they please. The major premise can be confirmed by this: whatever things are sought for the sake of something else get their perfection from that other thing, and if they had it in themselves they would not tend to the things towards which they are directed. And so that Aristotle may show this, he said that the supreme end which we are investigating must be perfect. Having laid this down, he added a distinction: a perfect end is either one or several. If it is one, no other is to be sought, since that is the good we are looking for. But if there are several perfect ends, we choose as the supreme among these the one that is the most perfect of all.

units.la: Perfectiorem uero dicimus eum, qui propter seipsum, quam propter alium persequendus est: quicq; nunquam propter alium diligitur, his qui & propter seipsos & propter hunc expetuntur: & omnino perfectus est, qui per seipsum diligitur, & nunquam propter alium.
units.tr: We call that end more perfect which is pursued for its own sake rather than for the sake of another; and that which is never loved for the sake of another is preferred to those which are desired both for their own sakes and for the sake of this one. And altogether that is perfect which is loved for its own sake and never for the sake of another.

units.la: Docemur his uerbis qua regula uti debeamus ad praestantissimum finem internoscendum, cum sint plures perfecti, & qui propter seipsos optentur. Et ait, Esse inter hos fines perfectos no paucos q licet expetatur per seipsos: attamen etiam propter alios diligitur. Hi sane perfecti sunt, sed praecipuo loco haberi non debent: quandoquidem illis praestabilior est ille finis, qui tantum propter seipsum est persequendus, & nunquam in alium potest dirigi.
units.tr: From these words we are taught by what rule we ought to recognise the most excellent end, when there are several perfect ends that are desired for their own sakes. And he says that among these ends there are not a few perfect ones, which, although they are desired for their own sakes, are nevertheless also loved for the sake of others. These are indeed perfect, but they ought not to be held in the first place; for that end is more excellent than they which is to be pursued for its own sake alone and can never be directed to another.

units.la: Eiusmodi sane felicitas maxime videtur: etenim illam diligimus propter seipsam perpetuo, nec unquam propter aliud.
units.tr: Such happiness seems to be the greatest of all, for we always love it for its own sake and never for the sake of anything else.

units.la: Hic iam concludit perducitq; ad exitum quod instituerat, nempe illud bonum summum esse felicitatem. Quod ista ratione confecit, quoniam perfectissima est, cum propter seipsam tantum desideretur. Quod tamen quibusdam non videretur ita esse: nemo enim felicitatem persequitur, nisi sui ipsius gratia nimirum ut per illam sit felix, et quam commodissime habeat. Verum his respondemus ea distinctione finium, qua superius usi sumus, dum quaereremus, finis quilibet an sit praestantior efficienti. Et diximus finem illum qui ab Aristotele 2.lib.de Anima dicitur [?], non esse praestantiorem, sed illum quem ipse appellat [?]. Nam si recta pergatur linea in finibus persequendis, extremus ille qui datur, est, quem Aristoteles affirmat, ipsa felicitas: at si postea flectamus animum ad id cui finem ipsum volumus, semper is praestabilior erit efficiente causa. Aristoteles itaq; nunc de priori genere finis agit, non de posteriori. Quapropter in hoc ordine finium beatitudo postrema collocatur. Instantia vero quae affertur ad alterum genus vel ordinem finium pertinet, de quo si loqueremur, fatendum esset, felicitatem non extremam esse. Atq; per hoc dissoluitur, quod itidem posset obyci de Deo, cui, si pie velimus agere, omnia nostra bona & felicitatem ipsam debemus velle, hoc est, ad nominis eius gloriam & laudem, quod tamen Aristoteles nunquam diserte scripsit: quod si potuisset, secum non pugnaret, quoniam (ut dixi) de eo genere finis hoc loco non tractat. Et quod modo utatur hoc verbo videtur, non id facit, quasi ambiguum sit, vel parum certum quod tradit, sed quia hoc vult esse sumptum a communi hominum sensu: etenim omnes ita iudicant, ut ipse docuit.
units.tr: Here he now concludes and brings to an end what he had set out to show, namely that happiness is the highest good. He reaches this conclusion by the argument that it is most perfect, since it is desired only for its own sake. Yet this might not seem so to some, for no one pursues happiness except for his own sake, namely so that by it he may be happy and have things as conveniently as possible. To these objections we reply with the distinction of ends that we used above, when we asked whether any end is more excellent than the efficient cause. We said that the end which Aristotle calls [?] in the second book of De Anima is not more excellent, but that which he himself calls [?]. For if we follow the line straight through in pursuing ends, the last end reached is the one Aristotle affirms, happiness itself. But if we afterwards turn our mind to that for whose sake we want the end itself, that will always be more excellent than the efficient cause. Aristotle therefore is now treating of the first kind of end, not the second. Hence in this order of ends, blessedness is placed last. The objection that is brought against the other kind or order of ends belongs to that second order, and if we were speaking of that, it would have to be admitted that happiness is not the last end. This also resolves what could likewise be objected about God, to whom, if we wish to act piously, we ought to direct all our goods and happiness itself, that is, to the glory and praise of his name. Aristotle never wrote this expressly, but if he could have, he would not be at odds with himself, since (as I said) he is not treating of that kind of end in this place. And that he uses this word here does not mean that what he hands down is ambiguous or not quite certain, but that he wants it taken from common human sense, for all judge in this way, as he himself has taught.

units.la: Honorem autem & voluptatem, & mentem, omnemq; virtutem, & propter seipsa diligimus: (quia eorum unumquodq; petimus, quamuis inde nihil aliud sequeretur.) Sed etiam diligimus propter felicitatem. Et quia opinamur propter illa feliciter nos acturos. Felicitatem uero nullus expetit horum causa, neque omnino propter aliud.
units.tr: We love honour, pleasure, the mind, and every virtue for their own sakes (because we seek each of these even if nothing else followed from them). But we also love them for the sake of happiness, because we think that through them we shall live happily. No one, however, desires happiness for the sake of these things, nor indeed for the sake of anything else.

units.la: Quod statuerat, confirmat ex collatione felicitatis cum his bonis, quae modo recesset: Et ait, honorem quidè, voluptatè, uniuersamq; virtutem eius esse naturae ut per se amabilia sint, sed ita ut nihilominus illa etiam persequamur felicitatis causa. Per se profecto expetenda sunt: nam etsi sola & nil haberent adiunctum aliud bonum, alliciunt homines ut se cupiant, sed tamen adhuc in ipsam felicitatem diriguntur. At è diuerso nunquam fit, ut propter haec ipsa optetur felicitas. Ex ista itaq; collatione perspicuum euadit, felicitatem his omnibus esse praestabiliorem, quòd nunquam propter aliud expetatur. Quod verò hic memorat de mente, non accipiendum quasi animi substantiam vel eius naturalem vim intelligat, quoniam de his bonis loquitur quae nostro delectu & optione acquirimus, id verò neq; animae substantiae neq; naturali facultati cognoscendi tribui potest, quare per mentem accipiemus virtutes quas nobis vendicamus intelligedo, quemadmodum sunt prudentia, & sapientia, & ita rem habere demonstrat, quod statim subiiciuntur caeterae virtutes.
units.tr: He confirms what he had laid down by comparing happiness with those goods which he has just gone over. He says that honour, pleasure, and virtue in general are by their nature lovable in themselves, yet we pursue them also for the sake of happiness. They are indeed to be desired for their own sakes, for even if they stood alone and had no other good attached to them, they would attract people to desire them; yet they are still directed to happiness itself. But on the other hand it never happens that happiness is desired for the sake of these very things. From this comparison it is plain that happiness is more excellent than all of them, because it is never desired for the sake of anything else. As for what he mentions here about the mind, it should not be understood as the substance of the soul or its natural power, since he is speaking of those goods which we acquire by our own choice and will. This cannot be ascribed either to the substance of the soul or to its natural faculty of knowing. So by mind we shall understand the virtues which we claim for ourselves by understanding, such as prudence and wisdom, and that this is the case he shows by what immediately follows, the other virtues.

units.la: Atque idem uidetur euenire, propterea quod sufficiat: perfectum etenim bonum sufficere uidetur.
units.tr: And the same seems to happen because happiness is sufficient, for the perfect good seems to be sufficient.
