units.la: Alia quoq; ratione probat felicitatem esse bonum perfectissimum quod quaerimus, quod sit sufficiens, & sibi ipsi satis quod in aliis bonis dici non potest: nam iis omnibus cum seorsim accipiuntur, aliquid deest. Sed felicitas satis habet & seipsa est contenta: quare illam oportet esse bonum perfectissimum. Non tamen praetereundum est, id quod perfectissime sufficit, & satis habet, tantummodo esse Deum, nec posse quicquam aliud inueniri, cui aliquid non desit. Verum de illo Aristoteles non agit, sed de bono quod à nobis parari & possideri queat, in quo genere vel ordine tantummodo felicitas est, quae sufficiat.
units.tr: He also proves by another argument that happiness is the most perfect good we seek, because it is sufficient and enough in itself, which cannot be said of other goods. For when each of those is taken separately, something is lacking. But happiness has enough and is content in itself; therefore it must be the most perfect good. Yet it must not be passed over that what most perfectly suffices and has enough is only God, and nothing else can be found to which nothing is lacking. But Aristotle is not treating of that, but of the good which can be procured and possessed by us, and in this kind or order happiness alone is what suffices.

units.la: Dicimus autem quod sufficit non soli ipsi, qui uitam solitariam exigat, sed et parentibus & liberis et uxori, atq; omnino amicis & ciuibus: quoniam homo natura sit ad societatem factus.
units.tr: We say, however, that what suffices is not for the one who lives a solitary life alone, but also for parents, children, wife, and in general for friends and fellow citizens, since man is made by nature for society.

units.la: Quod sufficit, posset bifariam intelligi, Vel quoad ipsum tantũ, quę felicē appellamus, vel ut respiciatur ipsamet felicitas, quòd ea sibiipsi sit satis nec aliunde quippiam expectet. Posterior hic sensus quadrat, non aut prior. Non enim ea, inquit Aristoteles, est beatitudo, quæ uni tantum habenti eâ suppeditet quantum est satis, quando vitam solitariam degit, sed eam opor tet sufficere illis etiam qui cum ipso coniuncti fuerint, ut sunt parentes, liberi, &c. Et ratio attingitur ex propria hominis natura, quòd sit ciuilis, et ad societatem factus. Quiq; huiusmodi est, actione communicat cum his quos habet cōiunctos. Quamobrem ut actio eius perfecta sit, opus habet multi-plicibus & variis bonis, quibus rectè valeat cum illis communicare: quia si nequeat id facere, non poterit non dolere, atque ita felicitas eius vitiabitur. Hinc fit ut ad felicitatem pertineant animi bona, quibus alios doceat eisq; consulat ac regat prudenter. Bona etiam corporis habenda sunt: nam sine viribus ac robore tueri patriam non possumus, et publica obire munera. Externa etiam bona, quæ fortunæ vocât, adhibenda sunt: nam citra illa re-[?]luare, fouere, ac iuuare necessarios minimè possumus.
units.tr: What suffices could be understood in two ways: either in regard to the one who is called happy alone, or with respect to happiness itself, that it is sufficient in itself and expects nothing from elsewhere. The latter sense fits here, not the former. For, says Aristotle, that is not blessedness which supplies enough to one person alone who has it, when he lives a solitary life; rather it must suffice also for those who are joined with him, such as parents, children, and so on. And the reason is drawn from the very nature of man, that he is civil and made for society. One who is of this kind shares in action with those whom he has joined to himself. Therefore, for his action to be perfect, he needs many and various goods, by which he may be able to share well with them; for if he cannot do this, he will inevitably grieve, and so his happiness will be spoiled. Hence it follows that goods of the mind belong to happiness, by which he may teach others, counsel them, and rule them prudently. Goods of the body must also be had, for without strength and vigour we cannot defend our country or discharge public duties. External goods, which they call goods of fortune, must also be used, for without them we can by no means relieve, cherish, and help our necessary friends.

units.la: Eustratius hoc loco expendens rationem Aristotelis, qua dixit, Hoc i-deo fieri, quòd homo sit natura ciuilis, Hoc inquit, ideo ponitur quod quidā sint non ciuiles, sed qui tantum contemplationi vacent, atq; ij segregant à se curas domesticas & ciuiles, turbamet societate fugiunt, quin & à sua ipsorum carne seiungi quàm maximè studeant, qui fit, ut tanta bonorum varietate non opus habeant: tantum satis est animum ad intelligendum & contemplandum accommodare. Atq; horum, ut inquit, difficillima est felicitas: quia cum natura quodammodo bellum gerunt, non quidem corpus aut carnem quærentes extinguere, sed illud prouidentes, ne ipsorum contemplationi sint impedimento. Proinde cum sit hæc vita simplicior, non ita multis indiget. Sed Aristotelem ait de his modò non loqui hominibus, quod testatur quum inquit, natura hominem ciuilem, quiq; sunt huiusmodi, nisi suis maioribus ac parentibus quæ necessaria fuerint sufficiant, nec non posteris, vxori, amici s, & ciuibus, claudam & mancam habent felicitatem, licet multis bonis instructi fuerint. Et diminutio felicitatis eorum & maior & minor est, vt magis vel minus bona quæ commemorauimus defuerint. Incumbit itaq; felici, omnium eorum quos memorauimus curam gerere: quòd si facere commodè queat, satis habet, ac poterit esse contentus: sin minus, felix non reputabitur. Hæc è doctrina Eustratij libuit referre, cuius equidem sententiæ minimè subscribo. Quòd enim aliquis ita velit solus agere, vt vni contemplationi vacet, abdicando se à cæterorum hominum consuetudine, atq; officia charitatis ac cæterarum virtutū erga illos deserendo, tam Philosophiæ quàm diu nis linis literis aduersatur. Philosophi quippe vulgò clamitant, homines minimè sibiipsi natos, & eam prædicant eius naturam, vt alios iuuet, atq; ab alijs vicissim adiuuetur. Deinde literarum diuinarum testimonia non desunt, à quibus tale genus vitæ damnatur. Dicebat Paulus, nullos debere quærere sua, verùm omnia facienda esse ad proximorum ædificationem. Et Deus legesanxit, Honorandos parentes, quod sanè præceptum sustentatione illorum tubet. Et parentib. mandatur, vt liberos diligenter & accuratè instituant. Neq; leges desunt de coniugio, de amicis & egenis conseruandis atq; tuendis. Quin et Paulus ad Timot. aiebat, Qui suorum ac præsertim domesticorum abiecit curam, is porrò abnegauit fidem atq; infideli est deterior. Quamobrem nemini fas est ita solitariam vitam sibi diligere, vt à se cæterorum hominum curam segregeret. Verum quidem est, Aristotelem seorsim de vita & functione ciuili agere, nec non de contemplante, sed non isto consilio, vt aliquis totum se se vni vitarum istarum addicat: sed vt sciat, quicunq; ad felicitatem aspirat, se non posse illam obtinere, nisi vtriusq; huius vitæ particeps egregiè fiat. Duæ quippe sunt nostræ naturæ proprietates: nam & intelligentes & ciuiles natura ipsa nos fecit. Quamobrem vtriq; conditioni debemus nostris actionibus respondere, nimirum vt cùm agendo occurrunt, quemadmodum oportet & ex virtute illa exequamur. Deinde vt cùm se offert aliquid ocij vel aliquo casu impedimur à rebus agendis, vt in contemplationem diuinarum & humanarum rerum magna cum voluptate occupemur, ita vt hæ actiones quæ ita genere videntur diuersæ mutuò sese inuent. Nam si quis moralibus ac ciuilibus exerceatur virtutibus in familia & repub. gubernanda, vt suis necessarijs iuuandis ac soluendis animum habet paratiorem, magisq; sedatum, ita fit vt ad contemplationem reddatur aptior. Et vicissim cùm quis per oblatum ocium diuina & humana fuerit attentius contemplatus, is deinde creditur ad agendum multò promptior. Hoc scimus inter Ethnicos fecisse Tullium, Catonem, Pompeium, Lucullū, & horum similes summos viros. Et legimus in sacris literis Christum serua-torem nostrum secessisse aliquando in montes & sylvas, vt oraret, & diuina meditaretur: sed mox redibat ad turbas & omnibus modis iuuabat humanum genus. Istud idem præstitit Ioannes Baptista, Elias, & cæteri prophetæ. Quin & idem Iesus Dominus noster Apostolos prius in solitudine doc[?] postea illos per Iudeam ad prædicandum & sanandos ægrotos emisit. Sunto itaque duo vitæ genera, sed ita vt non vni eorum perpetuò aliquis addicatur.
units.tr: Eustratius, weighing Aristotle's reason, by which he said this happens because man is by nature civil, says: this is set down because some men are not civil but devote themselves only to contemplation. These men separate from themselves domestic and civic cares, shun the company of crowds, and strive as much as they can to be cut off even from their own flesh. So it comes about that they have no need of such a variety of goods; it is enough to fit the mind for understanding and contemplating. And for these men, as he says, happiness is most difficult, because they wage war against nature in a way, not indeed seeking to extinguish the body or flesh, but taking care that it not be an impediment to their contemplation. Therefore, since this life is simpler, it does not need so many things. But he says Aristotle is not speaking now of such men, which he shows when he says that man is civil by nature, and that those of this sort, unless they supply what is necessary to their elders and parents, and likewise to descendants, wife, friends, and fellow citizens, have a maimed and crippled happiness, although they have been furnished with many goods. The diminution of their happiness is greater or less as the goods we have mentioned are lacking more or less. It therefore falls to the happy man to take care of all those we have mentioned. If he can do this conveniently, he has enough and will be able to be content; but if not, he will not be reckoned happy. I have chosen to set down these things from the teaching of Eustratius, though I by no means subscribe to his opinion. For that someone should wish to live alone so as to devote himself only to contemplation, renouncing the company of other men and abandoning the duties of charity and the other virtues toward them, is opposed as much to philosophy as to divine and human letters. For philosophers commonly cry out that men are not born for themselves alone, and they proclaim that it is man's nature to help others and in turn be helped by them. Then, too, the testimonies of the divine writings are not lacking, by which such a kind of life is condemned. Paul said that no one should seek his own, but that all things are to be done for the edification of one's neighbours. And God by law commanded that parents be honoured, which precept surely requires that they be supported. And parents are commanded to instruct their children diligently and carefully. Nor are there lacking laws about marriage, and about preserving and protecting friends and the needy. Indeed Paul also said to Timothy that whoever has cast off the care of his own, and especially of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. Therefore it is by no means right for anyone to so love a solitary life that he separates himself from the care of other men. It is true that Aristotle treats separately of the civic life and function, and likewise of the contemplative life, but not with this purpose: that someone should devote himself entirely to one of these lives. Rather, he wants us to know that whoever aspires to happiness cannot obtain it unless he becomes a thorough participant in both of these lives. For there are two properties of our nature, since nature itself has made us both intelligent and civil. Therefore we ought to answer to both conditions in our actions: when they come up in acting, we should carry them out as is fitting and from that virtue. Then, when some leisure presents itself, or we are hindered by some chance from doing things, we should occupy ourselves with great delight in the contemplation of divine and human things, so that these activities, which seem so different in kind, mutually help one another. For if someone is exercised in moral and civil virtues in governing his household and commonwealth, he has a mind more ready and more calm for helping and relieving his dependants, and so he is made more apt for contemplation. And conversely, when someone has contemplated divine and human things more attentively through the leisure offered him, he is then believed to be much readier for acting. We know that Tully, Cato, Pompey, Lucullus, and men like these, the greatest men, did this among the heathen. And we read in the sacred letters that Christ our Saviour at times withdrew into mountains and woods to pray and meditate on divine things, but soon returned to the crowds and in every way helped the human race. John the Baptist, Elijah, and the other prophets did the same. Indeed, our Lord Jesus himself first taught the apostles in solitude and afterwards sent them through Judea to preach and heal the sick. Therefore there are two kinds of life, but in such a way that no one is perpetually devoted to only one of them.

units.la: Sed horum certus terminus est constituendus. nā extendenti hoc ad Parentes, ad posteros & amicorū amicos, in infinitum progreditur. Sed hoc aliâs consyderandum.
units.tr: But a fixed limit must be set for these. For if this is extended to parents, to descendants, and to the friends of friends, it proceeds to infinity. But this should be considered elsewhere.

units.la: Quoniam posuerat felicitatem sufficere oportere non uni soli, sed eius omnibus necessariis, modo veritus ne progrediatur nimium, & fundatur latius haec administratio quam ferri possit, fine aliquo hanc rem coercēdam iudicat. Nam revera non potest fieri ut aliquis unus nimis multis sufficiat. Quare ne videatur felicitatem describere quae haberi non possit, eam finibus quibusdam terminandam censuit. Sed qui nam sint illi fines minimè nunc prodit, sed alibi ait hoc esse tractādum, innuens Politicorum libros.
units.tr: Since he had laid down that happiness ought to suffice not for one person alone but for all of that person's necessities, yet feared that this provision might go too far and spread more widely than it can be carried, he judges that the matter must be restrained by some limit. For in truth it cannot happen that one person suffices for very many. Therefore, lest he seem to describe a happiness that cannot be had, he thought it must be bounded by certain limits. But he does not now declare what those limits are, and says instead that this must be treated elsewhere, pointing to his books on Politics.

units.la: Caeterum nos Philosophis hoc relinquemus, quandoquidem Christiana charitas nullos fines praescribi sibi patitur, sed erga omnes benigna est, & proximus nobis, cui nimirum prodesse debemus, quando possumus, non est certo numero aut gradu comprehensus: imò Christiana dilectio vel ad ipsos inimicos extenditur. Quodq; attinet ad facultates & opes, quantum illae patiuntur, sunt extendendae: modum tantum modo Paulus hunc adiecit ad Corinthios, id non requiri, uti per nos aliis bene sit & commode, & ipsi versemur in angustia, sed quod facultatibus praestare non possumus, aliis charitatis officijs pro viribus debemus compēsare, atq; id ad quoslibet, ut illos Deus nobis obtulerit, quamuis, ut idem Apostolus docuit, qui sunt eiusdem fidei nobiscum, ceteris praeferri debeant.
units.tr: For our part, we shall leave this to the philosophers, since Christian charity does not allow any limits to be prescribed to it, but is kind toward all. The neighbour to whom we ought to do good whenever we can is not comprehended within a fixed number or degree. Indeed, Christian love extends even to enemies themselves. As for means and wealth, they are to be extended as far as they allow. Paul added only this qualification to the Corinthians: that it is not required that others be made well and comfortable through us while we ourselves are reduced to straits; but what we cannot provide from our means we ought to make up for, as far as our powers allow, by other offices of charity, and this toward whomever God has put before us. Yet, as the same Apostle taught, those who are of the same faith as we are ought to be preferred to the rest.

units.la: Id vero sufficere statuimus, quod vel per se solum vitam facit expetendam, & nullius indigam, cuius generis felicitatem esse arbitramur.
units.tr: We hold that that is sufficient which by itself alone makes life desirable and needs nothing else, and we judge happiness to be of this kind.

units.la: Paucis exponit quid intelligat sufficiens esse, atq; ait, illud bonum hoc nomine dignum, quod seorsim ac per seipsum vitam reddit expetendam. Un-de repetit, quod antea dixerat, Felicitatem huiusmodi esse. Quod sane de-monstrat alia ratione, dum inquit,
units.tr: In a few words he sets out what he understands by "sufficient," and says that the good worthy of this name is that which, taken separately and by itself, makes life desirable. Hence he repeats what he had said before, that happiness is of this kind. This he indeed demonstrates by another argument, when he says,

units.la: Quamuis non alio cum bono numeretur. Quod si numeretur, non est dubium quin cum minimo bono iuncta magis sit expetenda. Nā quod additur, accessio est bonorum: & quod maius fuerit bonum, magis est semper expetendum. Felicitas igitur videtur quid perfectum & sufficiens, ut quę sit omnium agendorum finis.
units.tr: Although it is not counted together with any other good. But if it were counted with another, there is no doubt that it would be more desirable when joined with even the smallest good. For what is added is an increase of goods, and what is greater as a good is always more to be desired. Happiness therefore appears to be something perfect and sufficient, as being the end of all actions.

units.la: Ratione quadam confirmat adhuc, felicitatem sufficiens esse bonum: quia etsi sola esset, neque ei aliquid aliud adiungeretur, maximè foret diligenda. Attamen subiicit, si ei fortasse aliquid aliud adderetur, efficeretur adhuc magis expetenda. Quod ut magis perspicuum fiat, scicendum est felicitatis tres esse præcipuas partes, Bona inquam animi, corporis, & fortunæ. Quamuis harum partium non sit omnium æqualis dignitas: etenim in bonis animi præcipua felicitatis ratio sita est. Deinde quodlibet horum bonorum aliquam sæpius recipit accessionem, atq; hinc fit quod Aristoteles dicit, utipsi felicitati si qua fiat additio, tunc reddatur expetibilior. Quod hac ratione probat,
units.tr: By a further argument he confirms that happiness is a sufficient good, because even if it were alone, with nothing else joined to it, it would be most of all to be loved. Yet he adds that if something else were perhaps added to it, it would become still more desirable. To make this clearer, it must be known that there are three principal parts of happiness: goods of the soul, goods of the body, and goods of fortune. Yet these parts do not all have equal worth, for the chief ground of happiness lies in the goods of the soul. Moreover, each of these goods often receives some increase, and hence comes what Aristotle says, that if any addition is made to happiness itself, it is then rendered more desirable. He proves this by the following argument:

units.la: Unumquodq; bonum quo maius est, eo magis expetitur,
units.tr: Each good is the more desired the greater it is.

units.la: Sed felicitas, cum additio accesserit, maius bonum efficitur.
units.tr: But happiness, when an addition has come to it, becomes a greater good.
Therefore it will then be more to be wished for.

units.la: Dixit autem id euenire, si quod numeretur cum aliquo minimo bono: & minimum bonum intelligit, quod sanè pertineat ad illa tria genera quæ iam recensuimus, sed ad nullum eorum maximum habeat momentum. Verùm sit eiusmodi, ut felix eo carere possit, cùm tamen si accesserit nonnihil habeat secum plus commodi vel ornamenti: multi enim possunt esse felices, quibus fortasis non contigerunt illustres & celebrata victoriæ, neq; gesserunt amplissimos magistratus. Talia & horum similia non sunt ex præcipuis bonis quibus constet felicitas, quamuis nonnihil ipsis augeatur.
units.tr: He says that this happens if something is counted together with some smallest good; and by the smallest good he means one that certainly belongs to those three kinds we have just recounted, but has no great weight in any of them. Yet suppose it is of such a kind that the happy person could do without it, while still, if it has been added, it brings some further advantage or ornament. For many people can be happy who perhaps have not gained illustrious and celebrated victories, nor held the highest magistracies. Such things, and things like them, are not among the principal goods of which happiness consists, although something is added to it by them.

units.la: At duo se dubia nunc offerunt, Quorum unum est, Non videri felicita-tem constare tribus illis bonorum generibus, cùm definienda sit ab Aristotele ita, ut dicatur hominis actio perfectissima iuxta illius absolutissimam virtutem: in qua definitione (ut liquet) neq; bonorum corporis, neque fortunæ ulla fit mentio. Verùm ad hoc respondemus, ita quidem felicitatem esse definiendam: sed in allata definitione licet de illis bonis nil memoretur expressis verbis, attamen ea sine illis non potest constare, ut suo loco declarabitur. Nam perfectissima hominis actio, & perfectissima eiusdem virtus bonis corporis & fortunæ pro instrumentis utitur, quibus cum penitus fuerit destituta, non potest consistere. Altera dubitatio est, Non videri consentaneu, vt felicitati aliqua possit fieri additio, cùm fit summum bonum, & summo nil maius dari queat. Ad hoc autem dicimus, verum quidem esse alicui sum-mo nil addi posse quod sit extra suum genus, & ita felicitas in hoc genere bonorum tenet eum locum, vt summa sit: quoniam vltra illam non est ali-quod bonum propter quod expetatur, sed in ipso genere felicitatis nil obstat quin vna possit aliqua esse maior. Et maior ac minor felicitas in eade sub-stantia seu ratione consentiunt. Vt omnia alba in ratione candoris: quod ta-men non impedit quin alius candor sit alio purior & melior.
units.tr: But two doubts now present themselves. The first is that happiness does not seem to consist of those three kinds of goods, since Aristotle must define it as the most perfect activity of a human being in accordance with his most complete virtue. In this definition (as is clear) no mention is made of goods of the body or of fortune. But to this we reply that happiness is indeed to be defined in this way; yet in the definition given, although nothing is said about those goods in express words, nevertheless happiness cannot exist without them, as will be shown in its place. For the most perfect activity of a human being, and his most perfect virtue, use goods of the body and of fortune as instruments, and without these altogether they cannot subsist. The other doubt is that it does not seem fitting that some addition can be made to happiness, since it is the highest good, and nothing greater can be given than the highest. To this we say that it is true that nothing outside its own kind can be added to the highest good; and so happiness holds that place within this kind of good that it is the highest. For nothing beyond it is a good on account of which it is desired. But within the very kind of happiness there is nothing to prevent one happiness from being greater than another. Greater and lesser happiness agree in the same substance or nature, just as all white things agree in the nature of whiteness, although this does not prevent one whiteness from being purer and better than another.

units.la: Itaque felicitas cùm sit agendorum finis, videtur quid perfectù ac sufficiens.) Hic habemus conclusionem rationum iam inductarum, quibus probata sunt quaedam communia de felicitate, quae vt praeambula fuerunt investigationis propriae illius naturae ac substantiae. Ita enim consuevit Aristoteles, & mos est peritorum artificum, vt ante propriam & veram definitionem communia quaedam ostendantur, de quibus omnes consentiant.
units.tr: Therefore, since happiness is the end of actions, it appears to be something perfect and sufficient. Here we have the conclusion of the arguments already brought forward, by which certain common points about happiness have been proved. These served as preliminaries to the investigation of its own nature and substance. For Aristotle is accustomed to proceed in this way, and it is the custom of skilled craftsmen, to show certain common points, on which all agree, before the proper and true definition.

units.la: At forsan si dixerimus felicitatem quid optimum esse, concessum id ab omnibus videtur, desydera-turq; ut exponamus euidentius quid ea sit.
units.tr: But perhaps, if we say that happiness is something best, this seems to be granted by all, and it is required that we explain more clearly what it is.

units.la: Hac sententia ostendit in confesso esse omnibus quae probata sunt: quae li-cet vtcunq; aperiant quid sit felicitas, desyderatur attamen, vt euidentius ac proprie definiatur. Atq; hic initium capit altera pars huius capitis. Etenim Aristoteles iam se accingit ad explicandam propriam definitionem.
units.tr: This sentence shows that those things which have been proved are agreed by all. Although these things in some measure disclose what happiness is, it is nevertheless required that it be defined more clearly and properly. And here begins the second part of this chapter. For Aristotle now sets himself to explain the proper definition.

units.la: Hoc uero fortasis fiat, si hominis opus deprehensum fuerit. Nam quemadmodum tibicini, & statua-rio aliisq; artificibus, & denique omnibus quorum opus aliquod & actio est, in opere bonum ipsum & id quod bene, videtur consistere: ita homini quoq;, si modo eius aliquod opus est, videretur.
units.tr: But this may perhaps be done if the work of a human being has been grasped. For just as for the flute-player, the sculptor, and other craftsmen, and finally for all whose work and activity is something, the good and what is well done seem to consist in the work, so too for a human being, if indeed he has some work, the good would seem to lie in it.

units.la: Primum quod quaeritur, quando aliquid est definitione aperiendum, ge-nus esse debet. Ideo Aristoteles inde iam initium capit.
units.tr: The first thing sought, when something is to be made clear by definition, must be the genus. Therefore Aristotle begins at once from this.

units.la: Propositio confirmanda est, opus hominis qua homo est, genus esse felici-tatis. Et probatur similitudine, atq; argumentum sic exponitur. Si tibicini, statuario & aliis artificibus, bonum consistit in opere quando rectum est: ita & hominis bonum in eius opere proprio reperietur.
units.tr: The proposition to be confirmed is that the work of a human being, insofar as he is a human being, is the genus of happiness. It is proved by likeness, and the argument is set out thus: if for the flute-player, the sculptor, and other craftsmen the good consists in the work when it is done rightly, then the good of a human being will likewise be found in his proper work.

units.la: Sed tibicini, statuario, & cæteris artificibus bonum consistit in opere eorum perfecto.
units.tr: But for the flute-player, the sculptor, and the other craftsmen, the good consists in their work when it is perfected.

units.la: Igitur & hominis bonum in eius erit opere.
units.tr: Therefore the good of a human being will also be in his work.

units.la: Ab artibus ideo principium sumpsit Aristoteles: quoniam illarum effecta perspicua sunt ac euidentia, passim nobis occurrunt, & probationes (uti sæpius est dictum) à notioribus nobis oportet ut proficiscantur.
units.tr: Aristotle therefore took his starting point from the arts, because their effects are plain and evident, and they meet us everywhere; and proofs (as has often been said) ought to proceed from things better known to us.

units.la: Præter argumenti explicationem illud notandum videtur, fatendum quidem esse ab homine pendere ac deriuari omnes artes, quæ licet omnes sint hominis alios tamen habent fines, ac diuersos à fine & operatione hominis qua homo est. Multum enim differt, si dixeris hominem simpliciter, aut grammaticum hominem, aut tibicinem hominem. Vtq; ista differunt, opus etiam & bonum aliud habent. Nec frustra est adiectum ab Aristotele, Et[?] deniq; omnibus quorum opus aliquod & actio exstitit: nam po-tuit verbis his naturalia respicere, vel, ut inquit Eustratius, additamenta quibus artes perficiuntur.
units.tr: Besides the explanation of the argument, this seems worth noting: it must be admitted that all the arts depend on and derive from the human being, and although all of them belong to a human being, they nevertheless have different ends, distinct from the end and activity of the human being insofar as he is a human being. For it makes a great difference whether you say simply "a human being," or "a human being who is a grammarian," or "a human being who is a flute-player." And as these differ, so their work and good are also different. Nor is it without purpose that Aristotle added "and finally for all whose work and activity exists." For he could have had in view by these words natural things, or, as Eustratius says, the additions by which the arts are perfected.

units.la: An igitur fabri & sutoris opera sunt aliqua & actiones, hominis vero opus est nullum, sed natura homo otiosus est?
units.tr: Are there then works and activities of the smith and the cobbler, while man has no work at all, but by nature is idle?

units.la: Quoniam ratio iam allata conclusit bonum hominis in opere ipsius proprio situm, & quispiam fortasis ambigeret, An hominis dandum[?] sit aliquod proprium opus: idcirco istud modo confirmat argumento duplici. Primum ab artibus hoc pacto. Faber & sutor proprium habent opus. Homo itaque illo non destituetur. Similitudini ratio innititur. Potuit etiam esse argumen-tum à minori, si faber & sutor proprium habent opus, nonne magis id homi-ni concederetur, nempe cum sit artium author & inuentor?
units.tr: Since the reason already brought has concluded that the good of man lies in his own proper work, and someone might perhaps doubt whether a proper work should be granted to man, he therefore now confirms this with a twofold argument. The first is from the arts, in this way. The smith and the cobbler have their own proper work. Man therefore will not be deprived of one. The reasoning rests on likeness. It could also have been an argument from the lesser: if the smith and the cobbler have their own proper work, would not this be granted all the more to man, since he is the author and inventor of the arts?

units.la: An quemadmodum oculi, pedis, manus, & deinque unius cuiusque membri opus quoddam extat, sic etiam hominis præter omnia hæc opus aliquod statuere aliquis posset?
units.tr: Or, just as the eyes, feet, hands, and each single member has some work of its own, could someone also posit some work of man over and above all of these?

units.la: Idem quod antea cōcluserat, rursum probat à diuersis hominis partibus. Manus enim, inquit, oculorum & pedum licet assignare proprium opus: licebit etiam ipsius hominis qua homo est. Et firma erit ratio duobus modis: Vel à Simili, vt dictum est, Vel à minori. Et notandum quod prius dixerat Aristoteles, hominem fore otiosum & vanum, si hoc ei non contigisset vt proprium opus haberet. Quid vero dici posset absurdius, vt ipse vanus & otiosus esset, cùm partes ipsius & artes quas inuenit nō videamus otiosas, sed earum vnamquamq; suis ornatam operibus?
units.tr: He proves again, from the different parts of man, what he had concluded before. For, he says, one may assign a proper work to the hands, eyes and feet; it will also be allowed to man himself, insofar as he is man. The reasoning will be firm in two ways: either from likeness, as has been said, or from the lesser. And it is to be noted that Aristotle had said before that man would be idle and vain if he did not have a proper work. What indeed could be said more absurd than that he himself should be vain and idle, when we see that his parts and the arts he has invented are not idle, but each one is adorned with its own works?

units.la: Quid nam igitur hoc erit: nam uiuere commune etiam cum plantis uidetur: quod autem modo quaeritur proprium est, unde nutriendi augendiq; uita omnis separanda. Sequitur sentiendi uita. Sed ea quoque cum equo & boue, & omnibus demum animalibus communis uidetur. Reliqua est igitur uita quaedam agens eius quod praeditum sit ratione.
units.tr: What then will this be? For living seems to be common even to plants. But what is now sought is what is proper, so all life of nourishing and growing must be set aside. Next comes the life of sensing. But this too seems common to horse, ox, and all animals in general. There remains, therefore, a certain life of acting according to the reason that man possesses.

units.la: Quia omnium actionum quae ab homine vtcunq; fiunt initium & fundamentum est vita, & ea vt euidens est, in homine habetur multiplex, ideo videre oportet, iuxta quam vitam homo discernatur à caeteris viuentibus. Et ea erit, cuius opus homini proprie adscribetur. Primo loco vita se offert nutriens & augens corpus: at illam communem habemus cum plantis: nam & illae suis radicibus trahunt alimentum à terra, ex quo alantur & crescant. Seponetur itaque hoc vitae genus: nam cum non sit homini proprium, sed commune multorum, non valet esse initium proprij operis hominis qua homo est. Secundum gradum habet ea vita, qua sentimus & progredimur, incedendo quo visum fuerit. Sed hæc quoq; communis habetur nobiscum cum brutis: nam equi, boues, & caetera quae rationis sunt expertia sentiunt & mouentur. Proinde remouenda est etiam hæc vita: quod ab ea non possit oriri proprium hominis opus. Quamobrem restat ea sola vita quae agit cum ratione: ea discernitur homo à reliquis omnibus. Idcirco poterit inde nasci proprium nostrum opus. Habet sanè homo comprehensas has vitas in seipso: ast illarum vna tantum est ipsi propria. Nec tamen propterea dicimus, illum habere tres animos: vnus est satis. Nam hæc est eius natura, vt quo præstantior fuerit, vires comprehendat ignobiliorum. Sed hoc ad præsentem locum non facit. Argumentum adductum partitione constat. Cùm enim opus hominis sit eius vita & ea triplex habeatur, duabus remotis partibus necessariò tertia retinetur. Ad hæc meminisse debemus quæ hic traduntur ab Aristotele de triplici vita, quæq; dicentur mox de duabus animi partibus, huc transferri ex libro de anima secundo, ubi omnia ista luculenter explicantur & confirmantur. Neq; absurdum est, artificem quempiam ab altero sumere scientiæ suæ principia. Et est Aristoteles diligentissimus in hac definiendi methodo: etenim opportunas distinctiones minimè præterit, quæ res vnica mirificè ad perspicuitatem conducit. Nam quæ fuerint involuta seu confusa, nunquam dilucidè cognosci possunt, nisi quis prius accuratè illa partiatur.
units.tr: Since life is the beginning and foundation of all the actions that are done by man in any way, and since this life, as is evident, is found in man in many forms, we must see according to which life man is distinguished from other living things. That life will be the one whose work is properly ascribed to man. In the first place, life presents itself as nourishing and growing the body. But we have this in common with plants, for they too draw nourishment from the earth by their roots, by which they are fed and grow. This kind of life is therefore set aside: since it is not proper to man but common to many, it cannot be the beginning of the proper work of man as man. The life by which we sense and move, going wherever we please, holds the second rank. But this too we share with the brutes, for horses, oxen and other creatures lacking reason sense and move. Therefore this life too must be removed, because a proper work of man cannot arise from it. What remains, then, is that life alone which acts with reason; by it man is distinguished from all the rest, and so our proper work can arise from it. Man indeed has these lives comprised within himself, but only one of them is proper to him. Nor do we therefore say that he has three souls; one is enough. For this is his nature, that the higher power comprehends the powers of the lower. But this does not bear on the present place. The argument brought forward rests on division. For since the work of man is his life, and this life is found to be threefold, when two parts are removed the third is necessarily retained. In addition, we must remember that what Aristotle here hands down about the threefold life, and what will be said presently about the two parts of the soul, is carried over here from the second book of On the Soul, where all these things are clearly explained and confirmed. Nor is it absurd for an artisan to take the principles of his science from another. Aristotle is most diligent in this method of defining, for he by no means neglects the apt distinctions, a single thing that greatly contributes to clarity. For things that have been involved or confused can never be clearly known unless one first carefully divides them.

units.la: Huius autem hoc quidem tanquam obsequens rationi, hoc vero ut illam habens atque intelligens.
units.tr: Of this soul, the one part is as obeying reason, the other as having reason and understanding it.

units.la: Quandoquidem iam statuerat opus hominis esse vitam iuxta rationem, quia hoc bifariam contingere potest, ideò subiicitur hæc distinctio, Ratione tribui quidem animi parti quod ei pareat & obsequatur, quemadmodum videmus in facultate irascente vel cupiente. Hæc sanè non habent cognoscè di vim, sed tamen regi possunt ratione, at præstabilior animi portio ipsa rationem habet & intelligit. Utrinq; igitur oriri potest humanum opus: nam quandoq; rationis erit propria ac vera, interdum verò ipsam participabit. Et quod affertur de hominis opere, intelligendum est de felicitate: nam ea licet in ipso rationis opere præcipuè conseruetur, communicatur attamen illis quoq; actionibus, quæ rationi obsequuntur.
units.tr: Since he had already established that the work of man is life according to reason, and since this can happen in two ways, this distinction is added: reason is attributed to the part of the soul which obeys and submits to it, as we see in the irascible or concupiscible faculty. These do not have the power of knowing, but can nevertheless be governed by reason; the more excellent portion of the soul, however, has reason and understands. A human work can therefore arise in either way: sometimes it will be of reason proper and true, and at other times it will share in reason itself. And what is said of the work of man must be understood of happiness: for although happiness is chiefly preserved in the very work of reason, it is nevertheless communicated also to those actions which obey reason.

units.la: Cùm verò & hæc dicatur dupliciter, ponenda est ea quæ sit actu: hæc enim magis proprie dici videtur.
units.tr: Since this is said in two ways, we must set down the one that is in act, for this seems to be the more proper sense.

units.la: Distinctio hæc vulgata est in physicis, nimirum per actum & potentiam: ne igitur erremus in vita secundū rationem, seu dicatur per se, sive per parti- cipationem, rursus eam distinguit, quod quadam sit potentia & quæda actu. Atq; potentia reiecta decernit ad rem præsentem actu facere, quod is magis proprie ad vitam attineat, & perfectiorem illius conditionem exprimat: idq; maximè requirit felicitatis ratio, quæ (ut ostensum est) perfectionem sibi vendicat. Et cùm perventum est ad felicitatem, non debemus ulterius progredi, at si quod est in potentia sumeretur, adhuc expectaretur actus.
units.tr: This distinction is commonplace in natural philosophy, namely between act and potency. So that we do not go wrong about life according to reason, whether it is said to be through itself or through participation, he distinguishes it again: some of it is potency and some of it is act. He sets aside potency and determines that it is act in the present thing that matters more properly to life and expresses its more perfect condition. The account of happiness especially requires this, since (as has been shown) it claims perfection for itself. And when we have arrived at happiness, we ought not to go further; but if what is in potency were taken, we would still be waiting for act.

units.la: Si autem ita sit opus hominis, actio erit animae iuxta rationem, vel non sine ratione.
units.tr: If, then, the work of man is of this kind, it will be an action of the soul according to reason, or not without reason.

units.la: Hac sententia concludit Aristoteles quid sit genus definitionis explicandae, nimirum actionem animae iuxta rationem, vel non sine ratione. Hoc duplici membro est usus: Quia(ut exposuimus)opus hominis tam ab inferiori parte quàm à superiori potest proficisci. Et quidem verum est facultatem irascentem atq; concupiscentem in brutis etiam reperiri, ita ut actio inde orta possit existimari non propria hominis. Sed ad hoc respondemus, inferiorem hanc vim animi, quae in homine rationi potest obsequi, quo ad istam conditionem sic esse nobis propriam, ut in brutis locum non habeat.
units.tr: By this statement Aristotle concludes what the genus of the definition to be explained is, namely an action of the soul according to reason, or not without reason. He has used this double member because (as we have explained) the work of man can proceed from both the lower part and the higher part. It is true that the irascible and concupiscible faculties are also found in brutes, so that the action arising from them could be thought not to belong to man. But to this we reply that this lower power of the soul, which in man can obey reason, is so proper to us in this condition that it has no place in brutes.

units.la: Idem autem dicimus opus huius & huius perfecti, veluti citharoedi & boni citharoedi. Quemadmodum enim simpliciter in omnibus, si quod exuperat virtutis ad opus additur. Citharoedi enim est pulsare citharam, boni vero praeclare.
units.tr: We say, moreover, that the work of this and of that thing is the same, as, for example, of a harpist and of a good harpist. For just as in all things, if something surpasses, it is added to the work of the virtue. For it belongs to a harpist to play the lyre, but to a good one to play it excellently.

units.la: Genere sic expositio, ad differentias indicandas pergit: ea sunt autē duæ.Prima sane est, ut operi hominis quod est iuxta rationem addatur virtus, ut nimirum sit ex virtute, ac illa quidem praestantissima. Differentia vero altera est, ut duret huiusmodi actio, neque sit momentanea: nam oportet vitae absolutionem adiungere. Priorem autem differentiam ita venatur, quia communis fortis hominis opus, & studiosi atq; perfecti genere conveniunt. Quod ut facilius intelligatur, exemplo declarat. Ut enim studiosus ac perfectus et homo quivis genere sunt idem, sic opus perfecti, & non ita perfecti genere conveniunt. Exemplo aperitur, opus citharoedi, & boni citharoedi non differunt genere, sed tantum quod bonus citharoedus praeclare pulsat, alter quoq; licet pulsel, id tamen ut cunq; facit. Quid vero id sit quo bene aut praeclare accedat operi, demonstrat, cum inquit excessum vel excellentiam virtutis adiectam, id semper & in omnibus efficere ut reddantur meliora & perfectiora quae fiunt. Citharam in summa quoquo modo pulsare ac bene pulsare idem sunt genere: differentiae adduntur, quae speciem complent, ut cunq; pulsare & praeclare: pulsationem vero praeclaram facit virtutis seu artis adiecta excellentia.
units.tr: Having set out the genus in this way, he proceeds to indicate the differences, and there are two. The first, indeed, is that virtue be added to the work of man which is according to reason, so that it is from virtue, and that a most excellent virtue. The second difference is that such an action should last and not be momentary; for it is necessary to add the completion of life. He hunts out the first difference in this way: the work of the ordinary man, and of the studious and perfect man, agree in genus. To make this more easily understood, he explains it by an example. For just as the studious and perfect man and any man at all are the same in genus, so the work of the perfect and of the not-so-perfect agree in genus. The example makes clear that the work of a harpist and of a good harpist do not differ in genus, but only in that the good harpist plays excellently, while the other, although he plays, does so in whatever way he can. What it is that adds goodness or excellence to the work, he shows when he says that the added excess or excellence of virtue always and in all things makes what is done better and more perfect. To play the lyre in general, whether in any way or playing well, are the same in genus; differences are added which complete the species, such as in any way and excellently. But an excellent playing is produced by the added excellence of virtue or art.

units.la: Quod cùm ita fit, statuimus opus hominis, uitam quandam, hancq; animi actum, & cum ratione actionem. Est autem boni uiri hæc recte atque preclare.
units.tr: Since this is so, we set down the work of man as a certain life, and this an activity of the soul, and an action with reason. Now the work of a good man is this, done rightly and excellently.

units.la: Collegit his verbis Aristoteles genus cum sua priori differentia: & quæ dicuntur, adeò clara sunt, ut interpretatione haud indigeant. Sed Eustra-thius dubitat, an possit opus vel actio esse hominis iuxta rationem quæ non recte agatur, vel in qua reperiatur error: quod prima fronte inquit non videri: quicquid enim iuxta rationem agitur, videtur absq; errore fieri. At si hoc esset, nunquam homines peccarent, cum nihil faciant, animo decernente ac deliberante, qu'n[?] ratio interueniat, quæ sanè non solum errare potest, sed non parum sæpè errat, quod sensus & cupiditates habeat secum coniunctas. Non deficere, inquit, hominum non est, sed tantum mentium illarum quæ mole carnis & pondere corporis sunt liberæ. Hæc ille. Quibus ego addo, ne mentes quidem à materia corporea anulsas, natura sua esse absq; vllo errore, quod autem modo non peccent, id illis vi gratiæ ac fauoris diuini concedi. Iam verò inde ab initio peccasse, vt diuinæ literæ tradunt, nunc verò non sua, sed Dei vi stare[?] atq; seruari.
units.tr: Aristotle gathered the genus together with its first difference in these words, and what is said is so clear that it needs no interpretation. But Eustratius doubts whether there can be a work or action of man according to reason which is not done rightly, or in which error is found. He says that at first sight this does not seem so, for whatever is done according to reason seems to be done without error. But if this were so, men would never sin, since they do nothing with the mind deciding and deliberating, in which reason intervenes, which certainly can not only err but often errs not a little, because it has the senses and desires joined with it. Not to fail, he says, is not a thing of men, but only of those minds which are free from the bulk of flesh and the weight of the body. So he. To these things I add that even minds, not yet freed from corporeal matter, are by their nature without any error; but that they do not now sin is granted to them by the power of divine grace and favour. Indeed, from the beginning they sinned, as the divine letters teach, and now they stand and are preserved not by their own power but by the power of God.

units.la: Vnumquodq; autem à propria uirtute rectè perficitur. Quod cum ita sit, humanum bonum est animi actio cum uirtute. Quod si fuerint plures uirtutes, iuxta optimam & perfectissimam.
units.tr: Moreover, each thing is rightly perfected by its own virtue. Since this is so, the human good is an action of the soul with virtue. And if there are several virtues, it is according to the best and most perfect.

units.la: Ratio ista sic explicatur. Quicquid perficitur iuxta propriam virtutem perficitur. Opus hominis perficitur. Quare id habebit ex propria virtute. Maior propositio cum sit vniuersalis, ex multis singulis vera potest iudicari, si oratio perficienda sit, à propria virtute seu facultate perficitur, vt à rhetorica, ita disputatio à propria facultate, nimirum dialectica, sic cantus à musica, & ita de omnibus constitui potest. Quare vt dicebatur, quicquid est perficiendum, à propria virtute perficitur: per virtutem optimam & perfectissimam hoc loco intelligit prudentiam, quæ prima est inter omnes agentes facultates.
units.tr: This argument is explained thus. Whatever is perfected is perfected according to its proper virtue. The work of man is perfected. Therefore it will have its perfection from its proper virtue. Since the major premise is universal, it can be judged true from many single instances: if a speech is to be perfected, it is perfected by its proper virtue or faculty, as by rhetoric; so a disputation is perfected by its proper faculty, namely dialectic; so song by music; and it can be established in the same way for all things. Therefore, as was said, whatever is to be perfected is perfected by its proper virtue; by the best and most perfect virtue here he means prudence, which is first among all the faculties that act.

units.la: Et adhuc in vita perfecta. Una enim hirundo nō facit ver, neque una dies: ita beatum & felicem non facit una dies nec breve tempus.
units.tr: And yet in a perfect life. For one swallow does not make a spring, nor does one day: so one day, or a short time, does not make a person blessed and happy.

units.la: Hæc est altera differentia, quæ à circumstantia temporis accipitur, quia oportet felicitatem diuturnam esse. Probat id simili, conferendo felicitatem cum verno tempore, cuius nuntius est hirundo. Sed una minimè sufficit ad illud indicandum, nec una dies quæ fuerit clementior. In hyeme profectò sunt alcionij dies, nonnihil tepidi & benigni, qui tamen haud possunt fidem facere ver adesse. Neque ista cum illis pugnant quæ superius dixit, candorem unius diei non minus esse candorem diuturno, quoniam illa tum ad definitionem referebat: utriq; enim candores definitionem candoris participant. Sed non propterea negasset Aristoteles alterum eorum maiorem & meliorem altero quo ad gradum candoris, & quo ad perfectionem. At istud non potest modo dici de beatitudine: quoniam in eius definitione comprehenditur perfectio, quam temporis brevitas imminuit.
units.tr: This is the second difference, which is taken from the circumstance of time: happiness must be lasting. He proves this by a comparison, likening happiness to the spring, whose messenger is the swallow. But one swallow is by no means enough to signal it, nor is one day, however mild. In winter there are indeed halcyon days, somewhat warm and gentle, which nonetheless cannot make us believe that spring is at hand. Nor do these words conflict with what he said above, that the brightness of one day is no less brightness than that of a long period, since at that point he was referring to the definition: both kinds of brightness share in the definition of brightness. But Aristotle would not on that account deny that one of them is greater and better than the other, both in degree of brightness and in perfection. Yet this cannot be said in the same way of blessedness, since its definition includes perfection, and the brevity of time diminishes this.

units.la: Ambiguum quomodo sit accipienda vita perfectio. Si enim intelligamus per totam vitam, nemini mortalium euenire, cum omnia sunt exposita infortunijs. Satis est ut diu sic degatur, quo virtutes optimæ ac præstantissimæ actiones queant se prodere. Aut si per ante actam vitam non licuit, saltem ad extremum obtineatur felicitas. Certum est naturam hanc esse felicitatis, ut matura sit & diuturna. Cic. de finib. lib. 2. statuit, beatam vitam inquit in perpetuitate duci solere. Si enim vicissitudines fuerint ut quis miser ex beato fieri possit, nunquam erit quisquam felix: metuet enim semper ne suam amittat felicitatem. At sapientia semel parta, & optimæ virtutes acquisitæ calamitatibus intereunt? non quidem: retinentur, sed ibi non est tota felicitas, licet ibi maior & melior pars eius comprehendatur. Sed possūt accidere aduersi casus & infortunia per quæ felicitas obscuretur, & ita ut desinat esse felicitas, non tamen illi propterea erūt miseri, sed felices dici non poterunt. Non est iuxta sententiā Aristotelis expectanda mors, ut quis dicatur felix: quoniam satis est ut quis aliquamdiu degat agendo ex optima virtute, ac bonis externis mediocriter instructus: neque timor calamitatum in eo erit tantus ut felicitatem impediat. Vita vero perfecta dicitur, cum virtus quæ diligenter agit, perfecta est, nec aliqua grandi calamitate impeditur. Sed virtutē aiūt in aduersis maximè illustrari, Fateor, magis redditur splendida & magis laudatur. Sed neminem ista ducit beatum qui graviori laboret fortuna. Nos ita nō sentimus, quia post hanc vitam omnia speramus tranquillissima & suavissima, quod philosophi ignorant. Infortunis itaq; virtus quidem est illustrior, sed non reddit felicem.
units.tr: It is uncertain how the perfection of life is to be understood. If we take it to mean the whole of life, it happens to no mortal, since all things are exposed to misfortunes. It is enough that one lives so long that the best virtues and most excellent actions can show themselves. Or, if this was not possible over the preceding life, at least happiness should be secured at the end. It is certain that the nature of happiness is that it be mature and lasting. Cicero, in De finibus book 2, lays down that a blessed life, he says, is usually reckoned in its permanence. For if the vicissitudes were such that a man could pass from blessed to wretched, no one would ever be happy, since he would always fear lest he lose his happiness. But when wisdom has once been won and the best virtues acquired, do they perish in calamities? Certainly not: they are retained, but happiness is not wholly there, although its greater and better part is contained there. Yet adverse chances and misfortunes can occur through which happiness is obscured, so that it ceases to be happiness; nevertheless those people will not on that account be wretched, but they cannot be called happy. According to Aristotle's view, one does not have to wait for death before someone is called happy: it is enough that a man lives for some time acting from the best virtue, and moderately furnished with external goods; nor will the fear of calamities in him be so great as to impede happiness. A life is called perfect, however, when the virtue that acts diligently is perfect and is not hindered by any great calamity. But people say that virtue shines most brightly in adversity. I grant it: it is made more splendid and is praised more. But no one counts a man blessed for that reason, if he labours under worse fortune. We do not judge so, because after this life we hope for all things to be most tranquil and most sweet, which the philosophers do not know. Thus virtue is indeed more illustrious in misfortunes, but it does not make a man happy.

units.la: Tempus felicitati attribuitur multiplici ratione. Primum non potest actio humana perfici & absolui absq; tempore. Deinde quo magis crescit numerus bonarum actionum, felicitas etiam exeditur[?], & latior magis est expetenda. Postremo ad felicitatem quoq; bona exiguntur externa, interq; ea solet prolixa vita enumerari. Quo ad exemplum de hirundinibus quae vernuntiant, putat Eustrathius illas per hyemem jacere quodammodo in obscuris locis mortuas prae nimio frigore, meliori vero flante aura excitari, cū alii credant mare transmisso illas ad nos redire. Dies una vel altera itē[?] non facit ver, quia etiam per hyemem sunt aliquot dies placidiores, nempe alcionii[?]: qui cum sint pauci, non sunt fideles nuntii veris.
units.tr: Time is attributed to happiness for several reasons. First, human action cannot be brought to completion and finished without time. Second, the more the number of good actions grows, the more happiness also grows and the more widely it is to be sought. Lastly, external goods are also required for happiness, and among these a long life is usually counted. As for the example of the swallows that announce spring, Eustathius thinks that they lie hidden in obscure places through the winter, almost dead from excessive cold, and are revived when a better breeze blows, though others believe that they cross the sea and return to us. One day or another does not make a spring, because even in winter there are some calmer days, namely the halcyon days; since these are few, they are not trustworthy messengers of spring.

units.la: Ita igitur circumscriptum esto bonum. Oportet enim fortasis ipsum prius delineare, postea vero pingere.
units.tr: Let the good therefore be outlined in this way. For perhaps it is necessary first to sketch it, and afterwards to paint it.

units.la: Haec est tertia pars capitis. Primo quippe descripta est felicitas per com-munia. Deinde propius accessit definiendo. Nunc accedit ad partes explicandas. Primum dixerat illam esse optimā, expetendā per se, atq; perfectam. Genus ostendit: opus quippe humanum cum ratione vel non sine ratione, ac hominis vitam intelligi voluit actu, & cum virtute adiecta diuturnitate aliqua. Tota haec definitio ut magis fiat dilucida, est per partes excutienda, quia totum sine partium notitia est obscurum. Tria continet haec pars. Primo metaphoram inducit a pictura, ubi prius res delineatur, postea pingitur: ita prius rem oportuit describere, postea dissolui & per partes excuti. Secundo, quaerit utrum sit operosius, describere, an partes declarare: & in priori maiorem ostendit sitam difficultatem. Tertio, monstrat quid maxime juvet ad illud difficilius praestandum, nimirum tempus quo ita profecerint & auctae sint artes. Metaphora optime convenit. Ut enim quando figurae describuntur, aliqui constituuntur termini, quibus quantitas clauditur & ab aliis separetur, ita genus & differentia termini sunt quibus res finitur, & ab aliis prorsus discernitur. Figura est quae uno vel pluribus terminis clauditur. Dixit recte circumscriptum, hoc est, definitum. Visus est sua definitione quasi circulo quodam humanum bonum claudere. Hanc vocat hypothesim, hoc est informationem quandam & summariam descriptionē.
units.tr: This is the third part of the chapter. First, happiness was described by common features. Then he drew nearer by defining. Now he comes to explain its parts. He had said first that it is the best, to be sought for its own sake, and perfect. He shows the genus: he wanted the human work, with or without reason, and the life of man, to be understood as an activity, with virtue added, and with some duration. This whole definition, to be made clearer, must be examined part by part, because the whole is obscure without knowledge of the parts. This part contains three things. First, he introduces a metaphor from painting, where the thing is first outlined and afterwards painted; so the thing had to be described first and afterwards dissolved and examined part by part. Second, he asks whether it is more laborious to describe, or to declare the parts; and in the former he shows that the difficulty lies greater. Third, he shows what most helps to achieve this more difficult task, namely the time in which the arts have so advanced and been increased. The metaphor fits very well. For just as, when figures are described, certain boundaries are fixed by which the quantity is enclosed and separated from others, so genus and difference are the boundaries by which a thing is finished off and wholly distinguished from others. A figure is that which is enclosed by one or more boundaries. He rightly said "circumscribed," that is, defined. He seemed, by his definition, to enclose the human good as with a sort of circle. He calls this a hypothesis, that is, a certain outline and summary description.

units.la: Agit igitur de felicitatis definitione quasi sit quaedam statua eius & imago. Colores apertius exprimunt delineata & effigiata per partes. Definitio si habuerit suas partes notas, non opus habet ampliori explicatione: at si partium fuerit obscurarum, tum fit resolutio, & singula exponuntur. Ita fecit Galenus in [illegible, ~6 letters]. Definiuit statim ab initio medicinam quod esset sanorum, aegrorum & neutrorum. Deinde adiecit corpora, signa & causas. Et quoniam omnes hae partes fuerunt obscurae, illas singillatim exposuit, ita ut ad septuaginta distinctiones peruenerit. Item factum est in physicis, ubi natura primum est definita, quod sit principium motus & quietis: mox de causis egit, quid sit per se, quid per accidens: definiuit motum, deinceps & tempus & locum, dissoluendo primam definitionem a se positam. Hic similiter facit: definiuit felicitatem, dissoluit ad duo principia, nempe ad actiones humanas & ad virtutes, et de his per totum hunc librum disputat. Unde liber Ethicorum nil aliud comprehendit quam huius definitionis expositionem. Est itaque doctrina haec per definitionem & dissolutionem.
units.tr: He therefore treats the definition of happiness as if it were a certain statue or image of it. Colours express more clearly what has been outlined and shaped part by part. If a definition has its parts well known, it has no need of fuller explanation; but if its parts are obscure, then resolution takes place and each is set out. Galen did this in [illegible]. At the very beginning he defined medicine as being of the healthy, the sick and the neutral. Then he added bodies, signs and causes. And since all these parts were obscure, he set them out one by one, so that he came to about seventy distinctions. It was done likewise in the Physics, where nature was first defined as the principle of motion and rest; soon he treated of causes, what is per se and what is per accidens; he defined motion, then both time and place, by dissolving the first definition he had laid down. Here he does the same: he defined happiness, and resolves it into two principles, namely human actions and virtues, and he disputes about these through the whole of this book. Hence the book of the Ethics comprehends nothing other than the exposition of this definition. This teaching therefore proceeds by definition and resolution.

units.la: Videtur autem cuiusuis esse producere ac articulatim distinguere, quae recte fuerint descripta: & tempus talium inuentor aut adiutor idoneus esse. Unde et artium facta sunt incrementa. Cuiusuis enim est, id quod deest, addere.
units.tr: Now it seems to belong to anyone to produce and to distinguish articulately those things that have been rightly described, and that time is a suitable inventor or helper of such things. Hence the arts too have been increased. For it belongs to anyone to add what is lacking.

units.la: Nunc utrunq; modum inter se confert, & ait esse difficilius ab initio bene recteque definire, quam per membra definitionem examinare. Nam qui definiuit, nihil habet prius adiumenti nisi quantum sensu & cogitatione potest rem definitam comprehendere. At qui resoluit, habet definitionem iam allatam ceu radicem & fundamentum suae contemplationis. Quamobrem doctissimorum est hominum definire, ut inquit Arist. in 2 posteriorum Analyticorum. Et in imagine pictorum longe difficilior est imitatio, quam partium cuiusque examinatio. Esse hoc inquit videri cuiuslibet homi-nis: quod accipiendum est non prorsus ignari: qui enim omnino rudis est, non posset definitionem dissoluere, sed ex collatione multo plures dissoluere possunt definita, quam definire. Dissoluenti & addenti positis definitionibus, est satis, ut definitionem positam bene cognoscat, videat consequentia, & inducat consentanea.
units.tr: Now he compares the two methods with each other, and says that it is more difficult to define well and rightly from the beginning than to examine a definition by its members. For the one who defines has no prior aid except as much as he can grasp the thing defined by sense and thought. But the one who resolves has the definition already given, like a root and foundation for his consideration. Therefore it is the mark of the most learned men to define, as Aristotle says in the second book of the Posterior Analytics. And in the painter's image, imitation is far more difficult than the examination of each part. He says that this seems to belong to any man whatever, which must be understood as not wholly ignorant people; for one who is completely unskilled could not resolve a definition, but from comparison many more can resolve given definitions than can define. For one who resolves and adds to definitions already laid down, it is enough that he understands the definition laid down well, sees its consequences, and draws out what agrees with it.

units.la: Tempus est inuentor & adiutor.) non quidem natura sua, quia tempus nil agit, sed propter illa quae in tempore fiunt: complura enim eueniunt aliquo
units.tr: Time is the discoverer and helper, not indeed by its own nature, since time does nothing, but on account of the things that happen in time: many things come to light over some stretch of time.

units.la: { } Ratio methodi qua hic utitur Philosophus, aliquo spacio temporis, quae occasionem praebent, res exquisitius & plenius cognoscendi.
units.tr: { } The method of reasoning that the Philosopher uses here: over some span of time, which offers the occasion for knowing things more exactly and fully.

units.la: Unde & artium facta sunt incrementa.) Qui primi artes inuenerunt, parua quaedam & breuia tradiderunt, ad quae adjcere non vsq; adeo fuit difficile, praesertim succesu temporis, cum sit cuiusuis propemodum addere inuentis, non cuiusuis absolute, sed longe indoctioris. Vt parua & breuia fuerint artium principia quis facile viderit ex Hippocrate: facta postea sunt tot incrementa, vt Galenus magnam ediderit librorum cogeriem.
units.tr: Hence also the arts have grown. Those who first discovered the arts handed down certain small and brief principles, to which it was not so very difficult to add, especially as time went on, since it is almost anyone's business to add to the discoveries, though not just anyone's, but that of a far less learned man. That the principles of the arts were small and brief one may easily see from Hippocrates. Afterwards so many additions were made that Galen produced a great heap of books.

units.la: Eorum autem quae dicta sunt meminisse oportet, & absolutum ac perfectum non similiter in omnibus quaerere, sed in quaq; re pro subiecta materia, & quo ad patitur cuiusq; doctrinae proprietas. Etenim faber & geometres angulum rectum dissimiliter exquirunt, ille quidem ut ad opus est utilis, hic autem quid & cuiusmodi sit; nam spectator est veritatis.
units.tr: We must also remember what has been said: we should not seek what is complete and perfect in the same way in everything, but in each matter according to its subject matter and as far as the nature of each discipline allows. For the craftsman and the geometer seek a right angle in different ways: the one indeed as far as it is useful for the work, the other what it is and of what kind; for the geometer is a spectator of truth.

units.la: Tria sunt quae hic aguntur. Primo proponit modum excussionis ac examinis partium huius definitionis: nempe iuxta subiectam materiam & doctrinae genus. Secundo, non esse in principiorum peruestigatione causas inquirendas. Tertio, rationes varias indicat, quibus principia si fuerint ignota, possint cognosci. Solent saepius definitiones ab alijs adduci, quas deinde alij excutiunt, dilatant, & pingunt: at modo Aristoteles idem suam definiti one per partes vult applicare. Ideo affert quae de modo iudicat nos esse praemonendos, ac inprimis iubet, vt eorum simus memores quae dicta sunt, ne pe ab initio, cum de modo ac forma huius doctrinae in proemio egit. Subtilitas, perfectio et exquisita tractatio, diuersa est pro materia, uel pro methodo seu doctrina. De materia seu subiecto satis liquet: quoniam moralis, physicus, & mathematicus circa diuersam versantur materiam, ideo non eadem subtilitate in suis tractandis rationibus utuntur. At quandoq; fit vt idem sit subiectum ac materia, quia tum non eadem est forma & ratio doctrinae seu methodus, ideo perfectio & exquisita tractatio non eadè requiritur: sape quippe contingit vt res eadem consyderetur à variis artificib. at nō eodem fine atq; consilio. Geometra, inquit, & faber, angulu rectu spectant, sed longe diuerso animo. Faber vt opus faciat, nepe vt ligna iungat apti. Architectus, vt columnam erigat quae situ habeat rectu: aedificator, vt paries nō sit obliquus. At geometra, ut sciat, nempe veritatis est contemplator. Rectus est. angulus, inquit Euclides, quem recta linea continent vel efficiunt. Et id ma-qualis est, quando recta linea super rectam cadit & quidem ad perpendiculum, tum angulus utrinq; rectus est & adhæc æqualis. Ad rerum scientiam spectat non solum rei quæ tractatur naturam cognoscere, sed etiam quæ in ea sunt, quæq; illam consequuntur: ideo Geometra dicit esse, non tantum nosse quid sit angulus, sed qualis. nam definitione illius habita, vid: t an sit acutus vel obliquus, æqualis vel inæqualis. Quod item in Grammatica nominus evenire: ibi enim non solum consyderamus quæ sint partes orationis, nimirum an verba an nomina an adverbia, sed quæ consequantur proprietates, an actiua an passiua, propria vel appellativa, &c. Quamobrem tam faber quàm Geometra suum habent modum rem eandem consyderandi, neq; est utrobiq; perfectio & subtilitas eadem tractationis. Quin omnes artes suum habent modum, ut à materia vel magis vel minus dividunt & separant quæ ab ipsis tractantur. Physicus, moralis & medicus hominis naturam spectant, sed longè diuersis modis eam contemplantur: nam physicus ut materia sensibili constat & forma quæ sit ei principium motus & quietis: medicus, qua est vel sanus vel æger vel neuter: moralis, ut felicitatis vel miseriæ conspicitur capax.
units.tr: There are three things being dealt with here. First, he sets out the manner of examining and testing the parts of this definition, namely according to the subject matter and the kind of doctrine. Second, that causes are not to be sought in the investigation of first principles. Third, he indicates various reasons by which principles, if they are unknown, can be recognised. Definitions are often brought forward by others, which others then examine, expand and embellish; but here Aristotle wants to apply his own definition part by part. So he states what he judges we must be forewarned about in the method, and above all he bids us to be mindful of what has been said, lest we forget from the beginning, when he treated of the manner and form of this teaching in the preface. Subtlety, perfection and exact treatment differ according to the matter or according to the method or doctrine. About matter or subject there is enough clarity: since the moral philosopher, the natural philosopher and the mathematician are concerned with different matter, they do not use the same subtlety in handling their arguments. But it sometimes happens that the subject and the matter are the same, yet the form and rationale of the doctrine, or the method, are not the same; then perfection and exact treatment are not equally required. For it often happens that the same thing is considered by various craftsmen, but not with the same end and purpose. The geometer, he says, and the craftsman look at a right angle, but with a very different intention. The craftsman does so that he may make his work, namely that he may join timbers fittingly. The architect does so that he may erect a column that stands upright; the builder so that a wall is not slanting. But the geometer does so that he may know; he is a contemplator of truth. A right angle, says Euclid, is that which a straight line makes or forms with another. And when a straight line falls upon a straight line and indeed perpendicularly, then each angle is right and, moreover, equal. It belongs to the science of things not only to know the nature of the thing under treatment, but also what is in it and what follows from it. Therefore the geometer says that it is not enough to know what an angle is, but what kind it is: for once its definition is given, one sees whether it is acute or obtuse, equal or unequal. The same thing happens in grammar as well: there we consider not only what the parts of speech are, namely whether they are verbs, nouns or adverbs, but what properties follow, whether active or passive, proper or common, and so on. Therefore both the craftsman and the geometer have their own way of considering the same thing, and there is not the same perfection and subtlety of treatment in both. Indeed all the arts have their own way, dividing and separating from their matter, more or less, what they treat. The natural philosopher, the moral philosopher and the physician look at the nature of man, but they contemplate it in far different ways: the natural philosopher as it consists of sensible matter and of form, which is the principle of motion and rest in it; the physician as it is either healthy or sick or neither; the moral philosopher as it is seen to be capable of happiness or misery.

units.la: Eodem autē modo & in aliis faciundū, ut ne quæ sunt præter institutum plura fiant ipsis operibus.
units.tr: In the same way, we must act also in other matters, so that there are not more things added beyond the plan, which would be a distraction from the works themselves.

units.la: Vt sui moris est ab hypothesi ascendit ad thesim, & quod in uno mostrauit exemplo, dicit in cæteris quæ consimilia sint faciundum. Quæ verò particula adjicitur, Ne plura sint πάρεργα [?] ipsis operibus, duos potest habere sensus. Primus, ut excuset quare tantum uno exemplo sit usus, ne scilicet præter institutum nimium vagetur. Vel ne si eandem subtilitatem & exquisitam tractationem sequatur faber & geometer, prolixiorem quam oporteat sumat operam, & circa plura versetur quàm eius requirat facultas. Poetarum illud est, ut longè minus dicatur de hypothesi, quàm de ornamentis exterius accersitis. Vergilius & Homerus breues ceperunt thesis, nec rum tot accesserunt ornamenta, ut prolixa scripserint poemata.
units.tr: As is his custom, he ascends from hypothesis to thesis, and what he has shown in one example he says must be done in the other similar cases. The particle which is added, "lest there be extraneous matters [πάρεργα?] in the works themselves," can have two senses. The first is that he excuses why he has used only one example, lest he wander too far beyond the plan; or lest, if the craftsman and the geometer followed the same subtlety and exact treatment, they should take more trouble than is fitting and spend effort on more things than their ability requires. It is the habit of poets to say far less about the hypothesis than about the ornaments brought in from outside. Vergil and Homer took brief theses, and not so many ornaments were added to them that they wrote long poems.

units.la: Neq; causa in omnibus eodem modo est exigenda, sed satis est in quibusdam si aperte ostensum fuerit ea esse, ceu de principijs, primum atque initium est quod sint ostendisse.
units.tr: Nor must a cause be demanded in the same way in all cases, but it is enough in some cases if it has been plainly shown that they are; as for first principles, the first and the beginning is to have shown that they are.

units.la: Nunc secundo loco hæc annectit, quoniam definiendo felicitatem non de-monstrauit, quare, vel cur illæ particulæ definitionis in ea insint, neq; etiam quare ad eam constituendam definitionem sint adhibitæ, quod forsitan vel diligens vel curiosus lector potuisset desyderare. Illa tantum tradiderunt verisimili persuasione, ut scilicet vel multis vel sapientibus videbatur. At-que hoc non est propter quid & causam demonstrare, sed tantum ostendere illa esse. Verum dixerit quispiam, propositiones rationum semper oportet cau-sas continere: alioquin minimè posset quippiam concludi. Fateor, sed reti-nendum est, propositiones causas semper esse conclusionis, at nō semper eius rei quæ demonstratur, & de qua tunc agitur. Quod si propositiones rationis non continent causas rei quæ tractatur, habent in se nonnunquam effecta, quæ fiunt causa conclusionis, quoniam per illa conficimus & concludimus quod quæritur. Exēplis hæc demonstrantur. Si ex diuerso aspectu lunaris lu-minis Lunam demonstrarim Sphæricam habere figuram, ab effectu ad cau-sam progredior. Sin vero ex figura Spherica Lunæ ostendero illius luminis varios aspectus, tum ex causa concludo. Si ex igne fumus indicetur esse, causæ argumentum est, sin è diuerso per fumum ignis, ratio est ab effectis. E-clipsis Lunæ demonstratur quandoq; per terræ interpositionem, tanquam à causa, interdū ex defectu luminis, qui est effectus. Huiusmodi progressu ab effectis ad causam utimur, inquit, circa principia, quandoquidē illorū cau-sas non habeamus. A Geometra non quæritur causa quare punctum statuat indiuisibile. Vel cur linea tantum unam distantiam habeat, quæ in eius fa-cultate tanquam principia se habent. Non licet in omni materia & subiecto rerum habere causas, & quando ipsas habere non possumus, est satis, addu-xisse conclusionis causas.
units.tr: Now, in the second place, he adds the following: since in defining happiness he has not demonstrated why, or for what reason, those particular elements are contained in the definition, nor even why they have been employed in establishing the definition, which perhaps a diligent or curious reader might have desired. They have handed these down only by a plausible persuasion, namely as it seemed to many or to the wise. But this is not to demonstrate the reason why and the cause, but only to show that these things are. Yet someone may say: the premises of an argument must always contain causes, otherwise nothing could be concluded at all. I grant it, but it must be kept in mind that the premises are always causes of the conclusion, but not always of the thing that is demonstrated and under discussion at that time. But if the premises of an argument do not contain the causes of the thing treated, they sometimes contain effects, which become the cause of the conclusion, since through them we establish and conclude what is sought. These things are shown by examples. If from the different appearance of the moon's light I demonstrate that the moon has a spherical shape, I proceed from effect to cause. But if from the spherical shape of the moon I show the various appearances of its light, then I conclude from cause. If smoke is shown to exist from fire, the argument is from cause; if conversely fire is inferred through smoke, the reasoning is from effects. An eclipse of the moon is sometimes demonstrated by the interposition of the earth, as from a cause, sometimes from a lack of light, which is an effect. He says that we use this kind of progression from effects to causes, in dealing with principles, since we do not have their causes. The geometer is not asked the cause of why he posits a point as indivisible, or why a line has only one distance, things which stand in his discipline as principles. It is not permitted to have causes in every matter and subject, and when we cannot have them, it is enough to have brought forward the causes of the conclusion.
