units.la: Conferuntur inter se hi duo modi cognoscēdi propter quid, & quod ali-quid sit, & quæritur quis illorum sit prior, ac respondetur, Tempore antece-dere notitiam quod aliquid sit, quoniam principia sic noscuntur, & illa de-bent in qualibet facultate primum omnium sciri. Ratio vero distinctionis huius accepta est ex ipsa rerum natura: quoniā aliqua sunt quæ causas ha-bent, alia non habent. Quæ habent causas, per illas utiq; sciri queunt: at cū non habent, demonstratione quod sint sciuntur. Cæterum quid erit statuen-dū de illis quæ causas & effecta habent? Vtroq; demonstrationis genere quæ sic sunt doceri poterunt. Hoc tamen interea non est tacendum, Omne quod est rei causa esse quoq; causam conclusionis, quod tamen non reciprocatur: quia non quicquid est coclusionis causa, est itidē causa rei. Principia non ha-bere propter quid Aristoteles probat, quia ὅτι, id est quòd sint, est primum. & initium quod sumimus de illis. Hoc autem verum est aut simpliciter, ut in summis & praecipuis scientijs, aut si sint ut vulgo appellant subalternatae, in ipsa inferiori facultate, cuius non est per causam suum probare principium, sed illud accipit a superiori scientia probatum, quod tamen ab ipsa facultate inferiori probari non potest. Si ὅτι[?] hoc est, quod sint ipsa principia, non acciperemus ut primum initium in qualibet facultate, sed volumus semper quaerere causas & propter quid, esset in immensum progressus, atque ita ut inquit Eustratius, omnis periret scientia. At si contingat interdum principia esse occultiora, quid fiet? tribus inquit modis potuerunt doceri, aut inductione, aut sensu, aut consuetudine, aut aliqua alia ratione. Verba haec sunt.
units.tr: These two modes of knowing, the why (propter quid) and the that (quod) something is, are compared with each other, and it is asked which of them is prior; and the answer is that knowledge that something is goes before in time, since principles are known in this way, and these must be known first of all in any discipline. But the reason for this distinction is taken from the very nature of things: since some things have causes and others do not. Those that have causes can indeed be known through them; but when they do not, they are known by demonstration that they are. Yet what is to be determined about those things which have both causes and effects? These can be taught by either kind of demonstration. Still, this must not be passed over in silence: whatever is the cause of a thing is also the cause of the conclusion, but this does not convert, since not everything that is the cause of a conclusion is also the cause of the thing. Aristotle proves that principles have no why, because the that, that is, that they are, is first and is the beginning of what we take from them. And this is true either absolutely, as in the highest and chief sciences, or, if they are what they commonly call subalternate, within the inferior discipline itself, whose office is not to prove its principle through a cause, but receives it as proved by the superior science, though it cannot be proved by the inferior discipline itself. If ὅτι [that] meant that the principles themselves are what they are, we would not take them as the first beginning in any discipline, but we would always want to seek causes and the why; there would be an infinite progression, and so, as Eustratius says, all science would perish. But if it happens at times that principles are more obscure, what then? He says they could be taught in three ways: by induction, or by sense, or by custom, or by some other reason. These are his words.

units.la: Principiorum uero alia inductione, alia sensu, alia consuetudine quadam, alia uero aliter cognoscuntur.
units.tr: Some principles are known by induction, others by sense, others by a certain custom, and others in some other way.

units.la: Inductio, si Ciceronem sequimur, est, quum ex multorum similium collatione peruenimus quo uolebamus. Vel ut Aristoteles & dialectici aiunt, Quando post multa collecta singula universum concludimus. Hoc idcirco, quia notitia semper est a notioribus: & singula magis, ut alias docuimus, habentur ab omnibus nota. Ponunt Mathematici, quae sunt aequalia uni tertio, inter se quoque sunt aequalia. Et si aequalibus addas aequalia, ea quoque inter se erunt aequalia, & si ab eisdem aequalia demas, erunt aequalia. In numeris & magnitudinibus haec vera sunt, & cateris quae metiri possumus, atque si non statim his credatur principijs, inductione aliqua possunt ostendi: ut si aliquibus aequalibus numeris totidem utrinque addantur unitates, aequalia efficient.
units.tr: Induction, if we follow Cicero, is when, by comparing many similar things, we arrive at what we were aiming at. Or, as Aristotle and the dialecticians say, it is when, after many single instances have been gathered, we conclude the universal. This is so because knowledge always proceeds from what is better known, and single instances, as we have taught elsewhere, are known to everyone. The mathematicians lay down that things which are equal to a third thing are also equal to each other; and if you add equals to equals, the results will also be equal to each other, and if you take equals from equals, the remainders will be equal. These things are true of numbers and magnitudes, and of other things we can measure. And if such principles are not believed at once, they can be shown by some induction: for example, if equal numbers have the same number of units added to each side, they will make equal totals.

units.la: At primae elementorum qualitates usurpantur sensu, ut calidum, frigidum, humidum, siccum, nec non posteriores, ut molle, lene, asperum, colores. Consuetudine autem, honesta & virtutes: nam de his nullus recte iudicabit, qui se in eis non diu ac diligenter assuefecerit, atque abstinendo a voluptatibus, agnoscimus homines fieri temperantes, & cupiditates vinci abstinendo. Quum vero additur ab Aristotele in contextu, Et alia aliter, hoc propter experientiam dictum nonnulli arbitrantur, qua medicina ac aliarum artium principia comprehenduntur.
units.tr: The first qualities of the elements, such as hot, cold, moist and dry, are grasped by sense, and so are the later ones, such as soft, smooth, rough, and colours. Honourable things and the virtues, however, are grasped by custom: for no one will judge them rightly unless he has long and carefully accustomed himself to them, and we see that men become temperate by abstaining from pleasures, and that desires are overcome by abstinence. But when Aristotle adds in the text "and others in another way," some think this was said with regard to experience, by which the principles of medicine and of the other arts are grasped.

units.la: Est alius praeterea modus, cum sumuntur aliquae ipsorum principiorum descridescriptiones, vt punctus est cuius non est pars: & linea, longitudo sine latitudine, atq; horum similia. Quae sane descriptio demonstrari non potest licet eam nonnulli quadam verisimili ratione illustrarint, dicendo: Quicquid fit seu terminat aliquam magnitudinem, vna dimensione ab ea deficit. Quae propositio locum habet in superficie qua corpus terminatur: id vero cum habeat tres dimensiones, superficies duabus clauditur, nimirum longitudine ac latitudine. In linea hoc idem videmus quae superficiem finit, & idcirco dimensionis vnius est, nempe longitudinis, cum superficies duas habeat: sed puncto linea terminatur, quare nullam habebit extensionem, ac merito dicetur partibus carere. Ratio haec probabilis quidem est, sed non probat efficaciter. Solent etiam interdum confirmari definitiones ex contrario, vt si candor dissipat visum, nigror e diuerso congregat & vnit. Verum necesse [?] est demonstratio, sed argumentum verisimile.
units.tr: There is also another way, when certain descriptions of the principles themselves are taken, for example, that a point is that which has no part, and a line is length without breadth, and things like these. This description certainly cannot be proved, although some have illustrated it by a plausible argument, saying: whatever ends or bounds some magnitude falls short of it by one dimension. This proposition holds in the surface by which a body is bounded; but since a body has three dimensions, the surface is enclosed by two, namely length and breadth. In the same way we see that a line, which bounds a surface, therefore has only one dimension, namely length, since a surface has two; but a line is bounded by a point, so the point will have no extension, and it will rightly be said to lack parts. This reasoning is indeed probable, but it does not prove effectively. Definitions are also sometimes confirmed by their opposites: for example, if whiteness dissolves sight, blackness on the contrary gathers and unites it. But the proof is necessary, while this is only a probable argument.

units.la: Annitendum autem est singula principia tractare vt apta fuerint et studere oportet vt recte definiatur, quod magnum habeant momentum ad illa quae sequuntur. Videtur itaq; principium esse plus quam totius dimidium. Et complura videntur ex his quae inquirimus manifesta euadere per ipsum.
units.tr: Each principle must be handled with care, so that it is fit, and we ought to take pains that it be rightly defined, because principles have great weight for what follows. Hence a principle seems to be more than half of the whole. And many of the things we inquire into seem to become clear through it.

units.la: Postquam recensuit nonnullas vias, quibus principia cognosci possunt, inter eas praecipit vt habeatur delectus, & illa deligatur quae magis conue- niat. Vnumquodq; ait principium sic adeundum est & tractandum vt natura comparatum est: non enim omnia principia omnibus illis viis & modis comprehendi queunt. Ea itaque deligatur, ad quam principium quod habe- tur prae [?] manibus natura potest accommodari. Et ne industria haec sper- natur, curandum esse magno studio inquit, vt principia ipsa recte constituantur ac definiantur, quum maximi sint momenti. Nam sunt vt radix & fundamentum eorum quae sequuntur. Neque ab re definiendi mentio- nem fecit, quia principiorum magna pars sunt definitiones. Ad cuius rei cuidentiam [?] notandum aliqua principia esse coniuncta & connexa, vt De quauis re aut esse aut non esse dicitur. Omne totum quauis parte sua est maius: & consimilia, quae in demonstrationibus non accipiuntur, sed sunt instar summorum capitum ad quae omnes Demonstrationes resoluuntur. Alia vero principia sunt simplicia, ut Definitiones, quæ licet plures voces comprehendant, attamen propositiones minime sunt, & loco simplicis termini habentur, ponunturq; in Demonstrationibus ut medium.
units.tr: After he has recounted some of the ways by which principles can be known, he advises that a choice be made among them, and that the one more suited be selected. He says that each principle must be approached and handled in the way that its nature allows: for not all principles can be grasped by all those ways and methods. Therefore let that way be chosen to which the principle at hand can be adapted by its nature. And lest this diligence be despised, he says we must take great care that the principles themselves are rightly laid down and defined, since they are of the greatest importance. For they are like the root and foundation of what follows. Nor has he mentioned definition without reason, since a large part of the principles are definitions. To make this clear, we should note that some principles are joined and connected, such as: Of any thing it is said either that it is or that it is not; and, The whole is greater than any of its parts; and similar ones, which are not assumed in demonstrations but are like the highest headings to which all demonstrations are reduced. Other principles, however, are simple, such as definitions, which, although they contain several words, are by no means propositions, and are held in place of a simple term, and are put into demonstrations as the middle term.

units.la: Principia vero magnum habere momentum ad sequentia, ex vulgato proverbio confirmat, nempe quòd principium sit plus dimidio totius. Vt in aliis rebus verum sit, quo ad rem nostram ita potest explicari. Totum quod est demonstrandum agnoscimus esse conclusionem, quæ subiecto & prædicato constat. Definitio alterutrius harum partium non tantum comprehendit dimidium, hoc est vel subiectum vel prædicatum, sed etiam continet causam, cur affectio insit in subiecto. Quare plus complectitur quàm dimidium totius. Atque hoc dictum sit de his principijs quæ sunt definitiones. Axiomata verò, id est connexa principia, ideò sunt plus quàm dimidium, quoniam vi & efficacia sua omnia quæ vera sunt in aliqua scientia vel facultate continent. Quamobrem rectè dicit Aristoteles, De principijs rectè esse statuendum ac definiendum, cùm tanti sint momenti.
units.tr: He confirms from the common proverb that principles have great weight for what follows, namely that the principle is more than half of the whole. This is true in other matters too, and as regards our subject it can be explained thus. We recognise that the whole thing to be demonstrated is the conclusion, which consists of a subject and a predicate. A definition of either of these parts does not contain merely half, that is, either the subject or the predicate, but also contains the cause why the attribute belongs to the subject. Therefore it embraces more than half of the whole. And let this be said of those principles which are definitions. Axioms, however, that is, connected principles, are more than half because by their force and efficacy they contain everything that is true in any science or discipline. Wherefore Aristotle rightly says that principles must be rightly laid down and defined, since they are of such great importance.

units.la: Atque ista videtur ea de causa interponere, quoniam posset quispiam mirari cur tam multis agat de felicitatis definitione, quæ primo aspectu videtur minima res & breuis: hoc excusat, Quod magna sit eius vis & efficacia: nam primum est facultatis huius principium. At q; in seminibus idem contemplamur, quæ minima sunt corporis mole, sed maximarum viriū & incredibilis efficaciæ. Proverbium illud vulgò receptum nempe initium plus esse dimidio totius, refertur ad Pittacum Mytileneum, teste Diogene Laertio, ad quod vtcunq; allusit noster Horatius, dum inquit, Dimidium facti bene cœpit habet.
units.tr: He seems to insert this for the following reason: someone might wonder why he spends so much on the definition of happiness, which at first sight seems a very small and brief matter. He excuses this by saying that its force and efficacy are great, for it is the first principle of this discipline. We see the same in seeds, which are very small in bulk but have the greatest powers and incredible efficacy. That commonly received proverb, namely that the beginning is more than half of the whole, is referred to Pittacus of Mytilene, as Diogenes Laertius witnesses, and our Horace in some way alluded to it when he says: "He has begun well who has half done the deed."
CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Oportet de ipso consyderare non solum ex conclusione, et ex quibus est ratio, sed etiam ex his quæ dicuntur de eo.
units.tr: We must consider the matter not only from the conclusion and the reasons on which it rests, but also from what is said about it.

units.la: Allatam à se definitionem dictis atque sententijs aliorum philosophorum vult confirmare, atque ostendere, illa quæ ab aliis dicuntur ei probè conuenire. In tres partes istud caput secabitur. Primum id proponit, ex aliorum sententijs adductam definitionem esse probandam. Deinde illorum, qui secum faciunt, dicta sua definitioni accommodat, & eos qui male senserunt aut falsum dixisse ostendit, aut si quid veri attulerunt, id omnino secum facere.
units.tr: He wishes to confirm the definition he has offered by the sayings and opinions of other philosophers, and to show that what others say fits it well. This chapter will be divided into three parts. First, he proposes that the definition he has adduced is to be proved from the opinions of others. Then he fits the statements of those who agree with him to his definition, and shows that those who thought otherwise either said something false or, if they brought forward some truth, that it altogether agrees with his view.

units.la: Caeterum priusquam ad rem ipsam accedamus, operae pretium esse arbitror, ut cognoscamus quid cum sacris literis definitio haec Aristotelis aut consentiat aut dissentiat. Et primo cum in actu constituit humanum opus esse felicitatem, haud aliter statuit quam divinae literae, ubi ponitur, Beati qui ambulant in lege Domini. Beatus vir qui timet Dominum, & qui in lege Domini meditatur die ac nocte. Sunt omnia haec actus & exercitationes pro hac vita honestissimae. Sed obiicitur, Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates & quorum tecta sunt peccata. Beatus vir cui non imputavit Dominus peccatum: quae non pertinent ad opus hominum, sed ex mera liberalitate Dei fluunt. Ad hoc dicimus, Aristotelem non intellexisse neq; credidisse hanc iustificationem per Christum quam divinae scripturae nobis revelarunt, necnos interea de ista felicitate loquimur, sed tantum de illa quae iam primam consequitur, et sita est dum hic vivimus in recte agendo, & in alio seculo, in contemplando & fruendo summi numinis aspectu. Et nihilominus etiam si spectare velimus beatitudinem iustificationis, & nobis id ob oculos ponere per quod nobis applicatur, fidei opus occurret, quia credendo iustificamur, licet merito eius actionis haud iustificemur, neq; propter eius dignitatem in gratiam recipiamur. Verum uti dixi de hac felicitate modo non agimus. Et ea de qua loquimur, quamuis opus hominis est, non tamen ab eius viribus erumpit, sed vi Spiritus Dei ac coelestis numinis producitur. In futuro seculo perfecta erit haec felicitas, quae nunquam interpolabitur, sed erit actus unus atq; continuus: cum haec Aristotelis beatitudo, ut ipsius indicat definitio, saepius intercidat. Vult ille hanc actionem qua homo fit beatus, ex praestantissima virtute dimanare: idem quoque nos existimamus, ut qui praedicamus actiones fidelium non esse rectas & Deo gratas, nisi fidei, spei atq; charitatis sint germina, quas pro virtutibus praestantissimis habemus. De temporis quoq; diuturnitate convenimus: nam dum hic vivitur, perseuerantiam requirimus, & in patria, beatitudinis aeternitatem credimus. Tantum in postrema differentia est dissidium inter nos & Aristotelem: quoniam ille bona mundana requirit, at nos hic in terris non esse necessaria Christiano qui sit beatus contendimus.
units.tr: But before we come to the matter itself, I think it worthwhile to learn how this definition of Aristotle agrees or disagrees with the Sacred Letters. And first, when he states that the human work in action is happiness, he lays this down in no other way than the divine letters do, where it is said, "Blessed are those who walk in the law of the Lord," and "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, and who meditates in the law of the Lord day and night." All these are actions and exercises most honourable for this life. But it is objected, "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered," and "Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin"; these do not belong to the work of men but flow from the sheer liberality of God. To this we reply that Aristotle neither understood nor believed in that justification through Christ which the divine Scriptures have revealed to us; and when we speak of this happiness, we mean only that which first follows in this life, in acting rightly while we live here, and in the other age, in contemplating and enjoying the sight of the supreme deity. Nevertheless, even if we wish to consider the blessedness of justification, and to set before our eyes that by which it is applied to us, a work of faith presents itself, because we are justified by believing, although we are not justified on account of the merit of that act, nor received into grace on account of its worth. But, as I said, we are not now treating of that happiness. The happiness of which we speak, although it is a work of man, does not burst forth from his own powers but is produced by the power of the Spirit of God and of the heavenly deity. In the future age this happiness will be perfect, and it will never be interrupted, but will be one continuous act; whereas this Aristotelian blessedness, as its definition indicates, is often broken off. He wishes that action by which a man becomes blessed to spring from the most excellent virtue, and we think the same: for we who maintain that the actions of believers are not right and pleasing to God unless they are the offspring of faith, hope and love, hold these to be the most excellent virtues. We also agree about the duration of time: while we live here we require perseverance, and in our homeland we believe in the eternity of blessedness. The only disagreement between us and Aristotle lies in the last difference: he seeks worldly goods, whereas we contend that these are not necessary here on earth for a Christian who is to be blessed.

units.la: Caeterum his missis ad textu reuertamur. Causa definitionis adducta multa de principiis interposuit: nunc vero a tractatione illa de principiis generali redit ad ipsius definitionis consyderationem. Neque nunc sibi proponit conconfirmandam seu probandam definitionem, sed tantum antiquorum sententiam vult ad illam accommodare. Prima itaque parte huius capitis ait, Oportet autem περὶ αὐτῆς, nempe ἀρχῆ[?], de ipso principio. Illud pronomē demonstrativum non demonstrat felicitatem, quia non est proximè illius facta mentio: neq; definitionem, quia Græce masculei est generis: demonstratur igitur ἀρχὴ[?], quod nomen paulo ante positum ac scriptum legimus. Hoc itaq; principium, quod reuera est definitio, inquit, non tantum expendi debet quo ad cognitionem ut sciamus quid sibi velit aut quid proprie significent voces, neq; tantum ex ratione seu probatione, sed etiam quod msdò facimus, ex aliorum sententijs.
units.tr: But these things set aside, let us return to the text. Having given the cause of the definition, he has inserted much about principles; now he returns from that general treatment of principles to the consideration of the definition itself. Nor does he now propose to confirm or prove the definition, but only wishes to fit the opinion of the ancients to it. In the first part of this chapter, then, he says, "It is necessary to consider concerning it [περὶ αὐτῆς], namely of the principle [ἀρχῆς]." That demonstrative pronoun does not point to happiness, since no mention of it was made immediately before; nor to the definition, since in Greek it is of masculine gender. It therefore refers to ἀρχή [principle], a word we read was placed and written a little earlier. So this principle, which really is the definition, he says, must be weighed not only with regard to knowledge, so that we know what the words mean or what they properly signify, nor only by reason or proof, but also, as we are now doing, from the opinions of others.

units.la: Vero enim omnia quæ sunt consonant, à falso autem continuo dissentit uerum.
units.tr: For indeed all things that are agree with the true, but the true always dissents from the false.

units.la: Rationem subiicit, quare suam definitionem velit ad aliorum sententias examinare. Quoniam inquit ea quæ sunt, nempe ut perhibentur, statim consonant vero. Quare si quod ego dico & asserui ita sit, vero consonabit quod ueteres dixisse omnes fatentur, & affirmant, & vicissim à mendacio verum statim dissentit: propterea si quod affirmauit sit verum, à dictis falsis quorundam statim dissentiet. Hæc est vera doctrina probatio, ut cum recte opinantibus consentiet, & à falsis dogmatis continuo dissideat. Sunt qui arbitrentur sensum esse, res quæ existunt, vero scilicet sermoni continuo consonant, & verum à falso dissidet, quasi verum ipsas res habeat pro mensura. Quod quidem per se verum est, sed non facile videtur, quomodo rationem assignet cur Aristoteles velit suam definitionem ad aliorum sententias examinare. Nec desunt qui sententiam his verbis contineri putent universalem, Omne verum vero consonat, &c. quod verba profecto non significant, licet sensus non sit multum alienus ab eo quem assignauimus, quemque simpliciorem & veriorem arbitror.
units.tr: He gives the reason why he wishes to test his own definition against the opinions of others: since, he says, things that are, as they are reported, immediately agree with the true. So if what I say and assert is so, it will agree with the truth which all the ancients admit and affirm; and conversely, the truth immediately dissents from falsehood; therefore, if what he has asserted is true, it will at once dissent from the false sayings of certain men. This is the true method of proof: that it agrees with those who think rightly and dissents at once from false doctrines. There are those who think the sense is that things which exist agree at once with true speech, and that the true dissents from the false, as if the true had the things themselves as its measure. This is indeed true in itself, but it does not readily appear how it gives the reason why Aristotle wishes to test his definition against the opinions of others. Nor are there lacking those who think that a universal statement is contained in these words, "Everything true agrees with the true," etc.; these words do not really signify that, although the sense is not far removed from the one we have assigned, which I judge to be simpler and truer.

units.la: Cum igitur bona trifariam distribuantur, & hæc quidem dicta sint externa, hæc vero circa animum, & alia circa corpus: quæ animi sunt summa dicimus & maximè bona, & animi actiones et facta in animo ponimus, ideo recte diceretur iuxta opinionem hac uetustam & confessam à philosophis.
units.tr: Since goods are divided into three kinds, some of them being called external, some concerning the mind, and others concerning the body, we call those of the mind the highest and chiefly goods, and we place the actions and deeds of the mind in the mind. Therefore it would rightly be said, according to this opinion, which is ancient and acknowledged by the philosophers.

units.la: Iam secunda parte huius capitis eorum sapientum sententiæ referuntur, qui cum Aristotelis opinione consentiunt, & primum de Genere definitionis agitur, ac explicatur quomodo sit congruè positum. Actio quippe animi genus erat in definienda felicitate: quòd pulchrè congruit cum veteribus, qui bona tripartitè diuiserunt, & inter ea præcipuum summumq; locum bonis animi assignarunt. Quare cum felicitas sit summum bonum, recte constitutum est ad actiones animi pertinere. Distinctio illa bonorum ab Academicis est profecta, & prius à Socrate, vt lib.5. de legibus habetur. Quamuis postea secuti sunt Stoici, qui tantum vnum genus bonorum fecerunt. Verum de illis Aristoteles non loquitur: quoniam post cum floruerunt. Animi bona distinguuntur, quoniam vel ad intelligendum vel ad appetendum sunt comparata. Referuntur ad priorem partem, acumen ingenij, sagacitas, celeritas comprehensionis, & memoria tenax: prudentia, sapientia, nec non scientia, ac rectæ opiniones. Voluntatem verò & appetitum omnes virtutes morales ornant. Bona verò corporis distinguuntur, quoniam alia in vniuerso eo sunt dispersa, vt valetudo, vires & forma. Nam hac non in vna quadam parte corporis, sed in vniuerso resident. Alia verò quorundam membrorum sunt propria, Pedum inquam, celeritas cursus: Manuum, robur in apprehendendo, impellendo, trahendo ac deijciendo. Linguæ, volubilitas, & sensuum omnium. Externa bona distribuuntur in amicos, nobilitatem, honores, diuitias & consimilia. Cur autem animi bona primum locum habeant, multæ sanè possunt rationes adduci. Sed nunc satis erit dixisse melioris subiecti iure præstantiores esse proprietates. Argumentum verò Aristotelis ita potest colligi: Præcipua bona sunt quæ ad felicitatem attinet. Animi bona sunt præcipua: merito igitur comprehenduntur in definitione beatitudinis. Quare cum actiones animi primum locum obtineant inter eius bona, iustè posita sunt vt genus felicitatis.
units.tr: Now in the second part of this chapter the opinions of those wise men are cited who agree with Aristotle's view, and first there is discussion of the genus of the definition, and it is explained how it is rightly placed. For action of the mind was the genus in defining happiness; this agrees nicely with the ancients, who divided goods into three kinds and assigned the chief and highest place among them to the goods of the mind. Therefore, since happiness is the highest good, it is rightly laid down that it pertains to actions of the mind. That division of goods was derived from the Academics, and earlier from Socrates, as is found in book 5 of the Laws. The Stoics followed afterwards, but they made only one kind of good. Aristotle, however, does not speak of them, since they flourished after him. Goods of the mind are distinguished because they are fitted either for understanding or for desiring. To the former part belong acuteness of wit, sagacity, quickness of comprehension, and a tenacious memory; prudence, wisdom, as well as knowledge and right opinions. All the moral virtues adorn the will and the appetite. Goods of the body are distinguished, since some are spread through the whole body, such as health, strength and beauty; for these reside not in one particular part of the body but in the whole. Others belong to certain members: speed of running to the feet; strength in grasping, pushing, pulling and casting down to the hands; fluency to the tongue; and keenness to all the senses. External goods are distributed into friends, nobility, honours, riches and the like. Many reasons can indeed be adduced why the goods of the mind hold the first place, but for now it will be enough to say that by the right of the better subject its properties are more excellent. Aristotle's argument may be gathered thus: the chief goods are those that pertain to happiness; the goods of the mind are chief; therefore they are rightly included in the definition of blessedness. Hence, since actions of the mind hold the first place among its goods, they are rightly posited as the genus of happiness.

units.la: Recte autem actiones quoque nonnullæ ac facta dicuntur finis: ita enim ponitur in bonis animi non in rebus externis.
units.tr: Actions and deeds too are rightly called ends, for in this way the good is placed in the goods of the soul and not in external things.

units.la: Ad idem confirmandum proponit aliam rationem, nempe quòd veteres recte dixerint actiones humanas esse finem: à qua opinione, definiendo felicitatem Aristoteles non discessit, accipiendo pro genere felicitatis, quæ finis extrema est, actionem animi. Sed Aristoteles non sine ratione dixit actiones quasdam, contrahendo vocem ad certas aliquas: nam sunt nonnullæ vitiatæ ac corruptæ, quæ fines iure constitui nequeunt. Consonat etiam rationi, felicem bene uiuere ac bene agere: nam fere bona quaedam uita & actio recta dicitur.
units.tr: To confirm the same point, he offers another reason: the ancients rightly said that human actions are the end. In defining happiness, Aristotle did not depart from this opinion, taking as the genus of happiness, which is the ultimate end, an action of the soul. But Aristotle did not speak without reason when he restricted the word to certain actions, for some actions are vitiated and corrupt, and these cannot rightly be established as ends. It also agrees with reason that to be happy is to live well and act well, for a good life and right action are almost commonly said to be the same thing.

units.la: Tertia ratione adhuc utitur, quae accepta est, à vocibus ἂν πράττειν, ἂν ζῆν [?]. Quae verba notant actus. Et dixit fere, partim quia non omnes Philosophi, quod ad vocem attinet, dicunt felicitatem bonam vitam aut laudabilem actionem, sed alii nominarunt eam virtutem prudentiam, sapientiam, & alia huiusmodi. Aut ita loquutus est, quoniam nonnulli sunt iudicio peruerso affecti, & felicitatem putant corruptam ac depravatam vitam. Testatur autem Laertius Diogenes Pittacum Mytilenaeum interrogatum quid esset optimum in praesentia, respondisse benefacere. Et Epistolis Graecis praefigitur ἂν πράττειν vel ἂν ζῆν loco eius quod nos Latini scribimus, Salutem dicere. Veteres quoq; retulerunt inter Deos Herculem. Et mirati sunt Scipiones, Catones, Curtios, quòd multa praeclara gesserint. Et Euripides aiebat τὰς ζῶντας ἂν ἀρετήν. Epictetus adiecit, τὸ κακῶς [?] ζῆν τὸ τεθνάναι κρεῖσσον [?].
units.tr: He still uses a third reason, taken from the phrases εὖ πράττειν and εὖ ζῆν [eu prattein, eu zēn]. These words denote activity. He said "almost" partly because not all philosophers, so far as the wording goes, call happiness a good life or praiseworthy action; some named it virtue, prudence, wisdom, and things of that kind. Or he spoke thus because some people, affected by a perverse judgment, think that a corrupt and depraved life is happiness. Diogenes Laertius reports that when Pittacus of Mytilene was asked what was best in the present, he answered "to do well." Greek letters also begin with εὖ πράττειν or εὖ ζῆν [eu prattein, eu zēn] in place of what we Latins write, "Salutem dicere" (greetings). The ancients also counted Hercules among the gods. The Scipios, the Catos and the Curtii were admired because they accomplished many glorious deeds. Euripides said that the living have virtue (τὰς ζῶντας ἀρετήν [tas zōntas aretēn]). Epictetus added that to live badly is better than to be dead (τὸ κακῶς ζῆν τὸ τεθνάναι κρεῖσσον [to kakōs zēn to tethnanai kreisson]).

units.la: Sed sciendum est, bonam vitam ambiguam esse vocem. Etenim quan-doq; est secundis rebus frui, quod ad praesens negotium non spectat: quia beatitudo non collocatur in rebus externis. Deinde significat honestè probè ac iustè agere: & in hoc sensu nunc accipitur. Nec praetereundum vitam mul-tiplicem habere significatum. Quia interdum viuere, nil est aliud nisi esse: aliquando significat Agere: Tertio vita est modus & genus agendi: non enim omnes viuendo sequuntur idem institutum. Unde Aristoteles non multò antea triplicem constituit vitam, Pecuniam, hoc est, voluptuariam, Ciuilem & Contemplantem. Recte itaq; viuere tertio modo nunc sumitur. Et animaduertendum, Eustratium interpretari ἐνεργαξίαν, πράξιν ἐναντιώτατα [?].
units.tr: But it must be understood that "good life" is an ambiguous expression. Sometimes it means enjoying prosperous circumstances, which does not bear on the present business, since blessedness is not placed in external things. Then it means living honourably, uprightly and justly, and in this sense it is now taken. Nor should we pass over the fact that life has several meanings. Sometimes to live is nothing other than to be; sometimes it means to act; and thirdly, life is a mode and kind of acting, for not all people follow the same way of life while living. Hence Aristotle, not long before, set out a threefold life: the life of pleasure, the civic life, and the contemplative life. So "to live well" is taken here in the third sense. It should also be noted that Eustratius interprets ἐνέργειαν [energeian] as πρᾶξιν [praxin], the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning.

units.la: Videntur autem & in eo quod diximus omnia, quae de felicitate dicuntur, inesse: quibusdam enim esse uidetur uirtus, aliis prudentia, aliis sapientia quaedam, nonnullis autem haec uel horum aliquid cum uoluptate, uel non absque uoluptate.
units.tr: Moreover, all the things that are said about happiness seem to be contained in what we have said. For to some, virtue seems to be happiness; to others, prudence; to others, a certain wisdom; and to some, these or some of them together with pleasure, or not without pleasure.

units.la: Aggreditur modo tertiam partem, & de his loquitur philosophis qui vi dendetur ei diuersa scripsisse, & inquit, τῷ λεχθέντι, hoc est, definitioni à me recitatæ ac positæ videntur inesse quæcunque à philosophis ea de re sunt quæsita. Pronunciata illorum appellat ἐπιζητούμενα[?], quoniam de illis non constabat inter omnes, nam variarunt, neque cuncti eadem dixerunt. Per virtutem intelligit moralem, atq; omnia quæ commemorat ad animum pertinent. Nam virtutes & quidem morales perficiunt crassiorem animi partem, prudentia verò intellectum practicum, sapientia contemplantem: atq; conueniunt hæ tres virtutes quo ad philosophos, quia sic ponuntur esse hominis beatitudo, vt externum additamentum non misceatur: tantum in eo discrepat Aristoteles, quia felicitatem non habitum sed actum posuit, & ista substantiam felicitatis reuera non attingunt, sed quæ illam circumstant, vt inquit Eustrathius. Virtus authorem habuit Socratem in Gorgia, Prudentia Bionem, & Sapientia Biantem. Voluptatis idcirco sit hoc loco mentio, quoniam virtutes natura consequuntur vt corpus vmbram. Loquutio autem Aristotelis, qua dicit, uel cum uoluptate uel non sine uoluptate, spectat eò quia voluptatem aliqui vt felicitatis partem essentialem admiserunt, alij vero vt quid consequens, & sine qua virtus exerceri non possit. Atque vt hoc verum sit, accipi debet de voluptate honesta: quia si turpem respexerimus, id nullo pacto esset admittendum. Voluptatem autem cum honestate Dinomachus & Callipho copularunt de felicitate tractantes.
units.tr: He now takes up the third part and speaks of those philosophers who seem to him to have written differently. He says: "to what has been said," that is, to the definition recited and laid down by me, appear to belong all the things that philosophers have inquired into concerning this matter. He calls their assertions ἐπιζητούμενα [epizētoumena], "things sought after," because there was no agreement among all of them on these matters; they varied, and not all said the same things. By virtue he means moral virtue, and everything he mentions pertains to the soul. For moral virtues perfect the cruder part of the soul, while prudence perfects the practical intellect and wisdom the contemplative. These three virtues agree with the philosophers in this respect: they are held to make up human happiness without any external addition mixed in. Aristotle differs from them only in that he placed happiness not in a habit but in an activity; and these virtues do not truly reach the substance of happiness but merely surround it, as Eustathius says. Socrates, in the Gorgias, was the author of the view that virtue is happiness; Bion of the view about prudence; and Bias of the view about wisdom. Pleasure is mentioned here because the virtues naturally follow it, as the body casts its shadow. Aristotle's phrasing, "either with pleasure or not without pleasure," looks to the fact that some admitted pleasure as an essential part of happiness, while others regarded it as a consequence, without which virtue cannot be exercised. For this to be true, the pleasure must be understood as honourable pleasure, since if we looked to shameful pleasure, that could in no way be admitted. Dinomachus and Callipho joined pleasure with honesty when they treated of happiness.

units.la: Alij uero æternarum quoque rerum copiam unà complectuntur.
units.tr: Others, however, also embrace an abundance of eternal things together.

units.la: Quæres ad naturam felicitatis duæ accedunt, affluentia rerum bonorum externorum, & voluptas, hoc loco ab Aristotele commemorantur, et de altera sanè illarum priori loco agit, postea de reliqua fusius tractaturus. Certè verbum συμπαραλαμβάνεσθαι[?] diligenter est attendendum: etenim il-lo facile intelligimus, veteres non putasse, copiam bonorum externorum ad naturam felicitatis pertinere, sed eam tantum vt quippiam additum vocarunt in subsidium. Diuitiæ felicitatis naturam non constituunt, in eius definitione non ponuntur, in bonis animi vbi felicitas maximè sita dicitur, non ducuntur. Quid ergo est? Primum quidem ideò accersuntur, quod ad multas actiones felicis hominis sint conducibiles: non enim liberalis aut magnanimus aut magnificus ex virtute sua possunt agere, si defuerint pecuniæ, si copia rerum destituantur, si denique tenues & pauperes fuerint, Deinde, sine opibus non solum felix aliis esse non posset adiumento, sed sibi quoq; non vacaret, dum quotidianus victus labore parandus est ad con-templandum. Quod aliqui libri habent εὐπορίαν, Eustrathius legit εὐτη-ρίαν, quae vox idem significat.
units.tr: You may ask: two things are added to the nature of happiness, an abundance of external goods and pleasure. Aristotle mentions these here, and he treats the first of them now, intending to deal with the other more fully later. Certainly the word συμπαραλαμβάνεσθαι [symparalambanesthai] must be attended to carefully, for from it we easily understand that the ancients did not think an abundance of external goods belonged to the nature of happiness, but called it only something added for support. Riches do not constitute the nature of happiness; they are not included in its definition, and they are not counted among the goods of the soul, where happiness is said to lie chiefly. What then is their role? They are first of all sought because they are conducive to many actions of the happy man. For a liberal, magnanimous or magnificent man cannot act from his virtue if money is lacking, if he is destitute of means, or if, finally, he is poor and humble. Next, without resources the happy man would not only be unable to help others, but would also have no leisure for himself, since his daily sustenance must be won by labour so that he may contemplate. Some books have εὐπορίαν [euporian, "resources"]; Eustathius reads εὐτηρίαν [eutērian, "good preservation"], a word that means the same thing.

units.la: Ex his partem dicunt multi ac ueteres, partem uero pauci & illustres uiri: quorum neutros uerisimile est prorsus aberrare, sed quo ad aliquid, & quo ad multa recte dixisse.
units.tr: Of these opinions, many ancient writers and a few distinguished men hold one part or the other. It is likely that neither group has gone entirely astray, but each has said what is right in some respects and in many.

units.la: Opiniones iam allatae suasores habuerunt aut multos aut veteres aut illustres viros. Vulgus & multitudo hominum sectati sunt voluptates, ut hodie nos experientia docet. Veteres diuitias magni penderunt, quod Pindarus a principio suorum carminum testatur, ubi cum tribuisset multum aquae, multum igni, deniq; nimio plus dedit auro. Et Menandri celebris est sententia, quae sanxit beatum, cui mens esset & res copiosa, neq; paucis commemorari possent quae ab antiquis in laudem pecuniae ac diuitiarum sunt conscripta. Illustres viri, qui prudenter & attente sunt philosophati, non voluptatibus aut diuitiis primas dederunt, sed virtutis fulgorem prae bonis omnibus sunt admirati. Ab his personarum conditionibus aut circumstantiis conficit Aristoteles, horum sententias non esse modis omnibus contemnendas: quandoquidem ex illis argumenta quae ducimus ab authoritate, verisimilitudinem suam habeant. Et sane, ut inde incipiam, consentaneum non est, famam publicam, populi sermonem, id in quo universi propemodũ consentiunt, omnibus partibus esse falsum. Veteribus praeterea multum tri-buitur, propterea quod primis rerum exordiis admodum vicini fuerint, ideoq; rerum causas commodius videre potuerint. Iudicantur in hominum genere nescio quomodo posteriores degeneres, habenturq; perpetuo deteriores. Hinc est maiorum libros & dicta luculentiorem fere semper habere authoritatem. Quis denique studiosis ac praeclaris philosophis plurimum non deferat? Illi putantur non iniuria verum invenisse, qui eo inquirendo noctu diuq; magno acriq; studio laborarunt. Ex his condiscimus, ut libri & scripta hominum non temere reiicienda sint, sed eo potius consilio debent legi, ut ex illis nonnihil veri nobis comparemus, cum authores eorum non facile credendum sit omnibus modis errasse. Haec idcirco Aristoteles interpo-uit. nit, ne videatur inepte garrire, dum aliorum sententias tam diligenter commemorat.
units.tr: The opinions just cited had as their supporters either many people, or ancient writers, or distinguished men. The common people and the crowd have pursued pleasures, as experience teaches us even today. The ancients set great store by riches, as Pindar bears witness at the beginning of his songs, where, after giving much water and much fire, he finally gave far more than enough to gold. The saying of Menander is famous, which pronounced happy the man who has a sound mind and plenty of goods. Nor could the many writings of the ancients in praise of money and wealth be listed in a few words. Distinguished men who philosophised wisely and carefully did not give first place to pleasures or riches, but admired the splendour of virtue above all goods. Aristotle argues from the standing of these persons, or from their circumstances, that their opinions should by no means be despised, since the arguments we draw from authority have their own plausibility. And indeed, to begin there, it is not consistent that public report, the talk of the people, and that on which almost everyone agrees, should be false in every part. Moreover, much is attributed to the ancients because they lived very close to the beginnings of things and so could see the causes of things more readily. Somehow the later generations are judged degenerate in the human race and are always considered worse. Hence the books and sayings of our elders almost always carry greater authority. Finally, who would not defer greatly to eminent and learned philosophers? Those are rightly thought to have found the truth who laboured at inquiring into it by night and day with great and keen zeal. From this we learn that the books and writings of men are not to be rejected rashly, but ought to be read with the purpose of gaining from them some measure of truth, since it is not easy to believe that their authors erred in every way. Aristotle inserted this, lest he seem to babble foolishly while he records the opinions of others so carefully.

units.la: Sed quo ad aliquid & quo ad multa recte dixisse.) Non toto coelo errasse credendi sunt harum opinionum authores, verum de aliquibus, imo de compluribus recte sensisse. Quod in aliquibus libris legit, [illegible, ~5 letters], καὶ τὰ πλεῖστα, Eustrathius habet [illegible, ~12 letters] quod dixeris, verum unum quippiam recte sensisse, idque cum pudendum videretur, ut philosophi & veteres, unum aliquod, aut certum quid tantum recte dixerint, per [illegible, ~8 letters] corrigit, vel plurima subiciendo.
units.tr: "But right in some respects and in many." We must not believe that the authors of these opinions were altogether mistaken, but that they judged rightly about some things, indeed about several. In some books he reads [illegible], "and most things" [καὶ τὰ πλεῖστα]; Eustathius has [illegible], "what you might say," but that they had rightly judged one thing; and since it seemed shameful that philosophers and the ancients had rightly said only one particular thing or one certain matter, he corrects this by [illegible], or by adding a great many.

units.la: Porro qui affirmant omnem virtutem aut certam virtutem ratio consonat: actio enim iuxta ipsam eius est.
units.tr: Moreover, those who affirm that every virtue, or a certain virtue, is in accordance with reason: for action is according to it.

units.la: In aliis opinionibus examinandis, ab eo sermonem vel examen adhi-bendum orditur, quod philosophi & quidem illustres affirmarunt. Et dum felicitatem virtuti adscribunt, demonstrat omnibus modis non aberrasse. Quod actio illa quae revera felicitas est, cum sit ex virtute deducta, eius esse videatur, sed quia eo discrepant ab Aristotele, quod absolute virtutem felicitatem esse pronuntiant, ipse quod illi dixerunt imprudenter, prudenter admodum corrigit. Quod recte dixerunt collaudat, quantum vero ab eo quod est discesserint ostendit.
units.tr: In examining the other opinions, he begins a discussion or examination of them, which distinguished philosophers have indeed asserted. And while they ascribe happiness to virtue, he shows that in every way they have not gone astray. For that activity which is truly happiness, since it is derived from virtue, seems to belong to it; but because they differ from Aristotle in this, that they pronounce virtue absolutely to be happiness, he corrects very wisely what they said unwisely. He praises what they said rightly, and shows how far they have departed from what is.

units.la: Distat autem fortasse non parum in possessione an in usu, in habitu an in actu optimum ponere.
units.tr: Perhaps it makes no small difference whether the highest good is placed in possession or in use, in habit or in act.

units.la: Tametsi videntur hi nobiscum sentire, non tamen idem dicunt: quia tā distant quae ipsi afferunt a nostra sententia quam possessio & usus, habitus & actio. Quatuor ab Aristotele commemorata, hunc ordinem inter se habent, ut possessio ad usum, ita habitus ad actionem refertur. Possessio & usus res externas complectuntur: nam possidemus agros, pecunias, supellectilia, artium instrumenta. Sed habitus et actiones insunt in nobis ipsis, interdum quo ad animum, ut scientiae, virtutes & artes: nonnunquam vero quo ad corpus, & ita in nobis insunt ut ex eis non mediocriter perficiamur. Quare ut possessio absque usu vana est, ut declarat avari qui suis pecuniis non viuntur, opulenti homines qui multa supellectilia domi possident otiosa, et nonnulli indocti ad quos nonnunquam perveniunt, & multi & boni libri, quorum usum minime callet, ita quoque habitus, cum illis actiones ademeris, nulla comcommoditatem afferunt, omnia sane actionum causa sunt, & propterea Deus res produxit, ac eas incitat & monet assiduè ut agant: quare ocium rerum naturae atq; ordini vehementer aduersatur.
units.tr: Although these men seem to agree with us, they do not say the same thing, because what they assert differs from our opinion as much as possession and use, habit and action, differ. The four things mentioned by Aristotle stand in this order to one another: as possession is related to use, so habit is related to action. Possession and use concern external things, for we possess fields, money, furniture, and the instruments of the arts. But habits and actions inhere in ourselves, sometimes with respect to the mind, as knowledge, virtues and skills, and sometimes with respect to the body, and they inhere in us in such a way that we are perfected by them not a little. Hence, just as possession without use is vain, as the miser shows who does not use his money, or wealthy men who keep much idle furniture at home, and some unlearned men to whom there sometimes come many good books whose use they hardly understand, so too habits, when you remove the actions that go with them, bring no advantage. Certainly all things are for the sake of actions, and therefore God produced things, and constantly stirs and urges them to act; hence idleness is strongly opposed to the nature and order of things.

units.la: Habitum enim usu venit dum est, nil boni efficere, ut dormienti vel quoquo alio modo cessanti: quod fieri non potest de actione, quia necessario efficiet, & bene efficiet.
units.tr: For it happens that a habit, while it exists, accomplishes nothing good, as with a sleeping man or one who is idle in any other way. This cannot happen with action, because it will necessarily produce something, and produce it well.

units.la: Actionem ab habitu distare non probauerat, cum id iam posuerit, propterea id nunc aperta ratione confirmat. Habitui, ait, potest accidere, ut dormientibus usu venire scimus, & ob aliquam causam cessantibus, ut quic-quam boni non efficiat, quod in actionibus nequeas offendere. Id autem cum ita sit, porro sequitur habitum ab actione multum differre, atq; ita differre, ut actio sit omnino perfectior habitu. Neminem vero latet, felicitatem in re optima collocandam: quamobrem, actio si rectè iudicemus, non habitus fuerit. Hoc probè noui Stoicos dicere consueuisse, cum virtutem felicitatem esse praedicant, se non id accipere de ociosa & stertenti[?], verum de actuosa. Hi tamen pingant rem & fingant ut volunt, actionem inficiari non poterunt, habitu esse longe meliorem. Syllogismus ita extruitur.
units.tr: He had not proved that action differs from habit, since he had already assumed it; therefore he now confirms it by a plain argument. A habit, he says, may happen to be in a sleeping person, as we know it does, or in one who is idle for some cause, so that it accomplishes no good, which you cannot find in actions. Since this is so, it follows further that habit differs greatly from action, and differs in such a way that action is altogether more perfect than habit. Yet no one is unaware that happiness must be placed in the best thing; therefore, if we judge rightly, the highest good is action, not habit. I well know that the Stoics were accustomed to say this, when they proclaim virtue to be happiness: that they do not take it of an idle and sleeping state, but of an active one. Yet however they may paint and shape the matter as they wish, they will not be able to deny that action is far better than habit. The syllogism is constructed thus.

units.la: Quod non est optimum, felicitatis rationem habere non potest.
units.tr: What is not the best cannot have the nature of happiness.

units.la: Habitus non est res optima, praesertim cum ad actionem confertur.
units.tr: Habit is not the best thing, especially when it is compared with action.

units.la: Quare felicitas non in eo, sed actione iure collocabitur.
units.tr: Therefore happiness is rightly placed not in that, but in action.

units.la: Nec praetereundum, minus proprie Aristotelem esse loquutum, cum actionem inquit agere ex necessitate ac bene agere, quia revera ipsa actio non agit, sed id est quo homines agunt. Sed quia modo hoc discrimen ad id quod agitur momentum non habet, ideo licuit Aristoteli sic loqui.
units.tr: Nor should it be passed over that Aristotle has spoken less properly when he says that action acts of necessity and acts well, because in truth action itself does not act, but that by which men act is what acts. But since this distinction is of no importance for the matter at hand, Aristotle was allowed to speak thus.

units.la: Quemadmodum in Olympijs non pulcherrimi & robustissimi coronantur, sed certantes: quoniam ex his aliqui vincunt: ita bona & honesta humanae vitae, qui recte agunt, asequuntur.
units.tr: As at the Olympic games the most beautiful and strongest are not crowned, but those who compete, since some of these win, so those who act rightly obtain the good and honourable things of human life.

units.la: Primas non habitibus sed actionibus deberi, ut ratione prius confirmauerat, ita nunc eleganti similitudine ostendit. In honore Deorū veteres cele-brabant. brabat statos ludos, Olympios, Nemeos et Pythios, inter quos illustriores et solenniores Olympij semper sunt habiti. Fiebat ad fluuium Alpheum inter Hebem Pisas & Olympiam urbes. Ibi homines quadrigis & bigis currebant, nec non pedites: certabant disco, cestu luctabantur, in honorem Iouis Olympij: atq; victores oleastri corona donabantur. Ex his intelligimus, ut ille hominum status fuerit deplorandus, qui magis his Deum coli sint arbitrati. Ad id sunt antiquitus dies festi adinuenti ut populus de rebus diuinis instrueretur, precibus numen fatigaret, sacrisq; ceremonijs fidem suam & pietatem testaretur, quae omnia illi praeteribant, et ludicra haec duntaxat exercebant. Hoc unicum est diaboli studium, ut solidum cultum Dei ad ridicula inuenta hominum transferat. Et hoc Papistae faciunt qui puram religionem Christiani tam totam ad histrionicam missam contraxerunt: vbi nihil ab eis omissum est, quod faciat plurimum ad solidum cultum Dei corrumpendum. Sed haec obiter. Haec similitudo adeo elegans est, ut bis Paulus ea sit visus, ad Corinth. priore cap. 9. & ad Timoth. posteriore cap. 2. Ad rem praesentem sic est accommodanda, ut speciosi & robusti respondeant habitibus: certantes, actionibus. Ut robusti & formosi non coronantur, sed certantes: ita non obtinent praeclara & honesta vitae humanae habitus, verum actiones. Etenim qui recte agunt, compotes fiunt verae voluptatis, utilitatis, & honestatis, quae praeclarissima sunt bona, quibus hominum vita potest affici. Licet tamen pronuntiare, ut a veteribus qui de virtute sic loquuti sunt, prorsus non discedamus. Earum habitu felices homines reddi, non quidem actu sed potentia, quandoquidem perfecta & absoluta beatitudo actionem omnino exigit.
units.tr: He shows, by an elegant comparison, that the prize is owed to actions and not to habits, as he had earlier confirmed by reason. The ancients celebrated in honour of the gods the fixed games, the Olympic, Nemean and Pythian, among which the Olympic were always held as the more illustrious and solemn. They were held by the river Alpheus, between the cities of Hebe, Pisa and Olympia. There men raced in fours and twos, and also on foot; they competed with the discus, fought with the cestus and wrestled, in honour of Olympian Jove; and the victors were rewarded with a crown of wild olive. From these things we understand how deplorable that state of men was, who thought God was honoured more by these than by other means. From ancient times festival days were devised so that the people might be instructed in divine things, might weary the divine power with prayers, and might attest their faith and piety by sacred ceremonies; all of which they passed over, practising only these games. This is the sole concern of the devil, to turn the solid worship of God into the ridiculous inventions of men. The Papists do this too, who have reduced the pure religion of the Christian almost entirely to a theatrical Mass, where they have omitted nothing that contributes greatly to corrupting the solid worship of God. But this is an aside. This comparison is so elegant that Paul seemed to use it twice: in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 9, and in the second to Timothy, chapter 2. For the present matter it must be applied so that the strong and beautiful correspond to habits, and the competitors to actions. As the strong and handsome are not crowned, but those who compete, so the excellent and honourable habits of human life do not obtain the prize, but actions. For those who act rightly become partakers of true pleasure, usefulness and honour, which are the most excellent goods with which human life can be endowed. Nevertheless, it may be affirmed, without departing at all from the ancients who spoke of virtue in this way, that men are made happy by habit, not indeed in act but in potency, since perfect and absolute blessedness altogether requires action.

units.la: Habet haec sententia non tantum ex Aristotele authoritatem, sed ex di-uinis quoq; literis confirmatur, quae non semel vrgent pios, ut suam fidem operibus declarent. Et eam fidem ut bonam & cum primis Deo gratam commendat quae per dilectionem agit, suumq; Timotheum Paulus sedulo monebat, ut exercitaret gratiam & Dei praeclara dona quae in se habebat, ex impositione manuum presbyterij. Et inter seruos Domini grauissime is castigatur, qui ocio corruptus & ignauia, talentum sua fidei concreditum potius in terram defodit, quam ipso uti ad quaestum agendum voluerit. Ita habitu instructos non pronunciari beatos videmus, sed qui ex illis recte atque sedulo egerint.
units.tr: This opinion has authority not only from Aristotle but is also confirmed by the divine writings, which more than once urge the godly to show their faith by their works. Scripture commends that faith as good and especially pleasing to God which works through love. Paul diligently admonished his Timothy to stir up the grace and the excellent gifts of God that were in him, received through the laying on of the hands of the eldership. And among the servants of the Lord, he is most severely rebuked who, corrupted by idleness and sloth, buries in the earth the talent entrusted to his faith rather than wishing to use it to make gain. Thus we see that those who are furnished with the habit are not pronounced blessed, but those who have acted well and diligently from it.

units.la: Est quoque uita ipsorum per seipsam suauis. Etenim uoluptate affici ex earum genere rerum est quae ad animum pertinent. Et cuiq; id est iucundum ad quod refertur, & cuius nominatur cupidus, ut equus equorum studiosus, spectaculum ei qui spectaculorum est cupidus, eodemq; modo iusta ei qui iusta diligit, & ad summam quae sunt uirtutis, amatori uirtutum.
units.tr: Their life is also pleasant in itself. For to be affected by pleasure belongs to the kind of things that pertain to the soul. Each person finds pleasant that to which he is drawn and of which he is called a lover: a horse is pleasant to the lover of horses, a spectacle to one who is fond of spectacles, and likewise just things to one who loves the just, and, in sum, the things of virtue to a lover of virtues.

units.la: Sermonem transfert ad voluptatem, quae post virtutem inter sapientum dogmata prius commemorata est, atq; illam probat non habendam a felicitate alienam, quod & ipsa sit ex eorum bonorum genere quae ad animum attinent, nisi dicere velimus lapides aut truncos aut metallum gaudere aclamatari. Neq; clausula haec, ut iudico, aliam ob causam interponitur, nisi quia felicitas, ut expositum est, in bonis animi collocatur.
units.tr: He turns the discussion to pleasure, which was mentioned earlier, after virtue, among the doctrines of the wise, and he proves that it should not be considered alien to happiness, since it too belongs to that class of goods which pertain to the soul, unless we want to say that stones, logs or metal rejoice when they are praised. Nor, I judge, is this clause inserted for any other reason than that happiness, as has been explained, is located in the goods of the soul.

units.la: In hac ratione connectenda, quia ordiutur a generali sententia, ea explicanda imprimis est. Cuiq; id est iucundum ad quod dicitur, & cuius nominatur cupidus. Innuit his Aristoteles voluptatem ex eorum genere videri, quae mutuo inter se conferuntur. Nec mirum: quae enim suauia sunt, alicui iucunda ut sint necesse est. Quis vero sit is ad quem refertur voluptas, explicat ex affectione, dum inquit, Equus, spectaculu, iusta & virtutes, hos voluptate afficiunt, qui equorum, spectaculorum, iusti & virtutis cupidi fuerint. Omnium Syllogismorum est, ut causa prius in vniuersum proferatur. Deinde accommodari solet ad eam rem de qua dicitur. Ita nunc agitur. Causa communis proponitur, propter quam quicquam dulce alicui est ac suaue, nimirum quia eius est amans. Contrahitur causa haec ad felicem, qui amans est honestarum atq; pulcherrimarum actionum, ex quo necesse est ut conficiatur, illum eis vehementer delectari. Ad confirmandam illam communem causam, variis multiplicibusq; vtitur exemplis. Primum q; affert equestrem voluptatem, qu i vt nonnulli aliquando flui e ac vehementer moueantur, Strepsiades adolescens apud Aristophanem testatur. Producit quoque spectaculorum cupidos: ad quos philosophia, vini, atque p cunia studiosos licet adiungere, quos omnes affici mirifice videmus, cum optatis aliquando tandem potiuntur. His tam exemplis forma rationis quam Dialectici vocant inductionem, maior propositio quae causam communem comprehendebat, est luculenter confirmata & demonstrata. Quae statim ad rem praesentem accommodatur, cum inquit, iidem ut illorum esse rationem iusti & boxarum actionum & ad viros probos & felices: ea nimirum ab illis amalis amari, & illis haud mediocriter gaudere. Qui plane fit, ut beati probiq; viri si quos aut viderint aut audiuerint praeclare honesteq; agere, inde magnam voluptatem capiant: at proculdubio multo maiorem, dum ipsi actionibus iustis, probis & honestis sese exercent. Ex his iam intelligimus felicium vitam a voluptate non seiungendam, videmusq; non prorsus aberras-se, qui ad eam felicitatem adiunxerunt.
units.tr: In connecting this argument, since it begins from a general statement, that statement must first be explained: "each person finds pleasant that to which he is drawn, and of which he is called a lover." By this Aristotle hints that pleasure seems to belong to the kind of things that are shared among one another. Nor is this surprising: things that are agreeable must necessarily be pleasant to someone. Who it is to whom the pleasure is referred he explains from the affection, when he says that horses, spectacles, the just and the virtues give pleasure to those who have been lovers of horses, spectacles, justice and virtue. Every syllogism has this order: the cause is first stated in general and then applied to the matter under discussion. So it is done here. The common cause is put forward, on account of which anything is sweet and pleasant to someone, namely because he is a lover of it. This cause is narrowed down to the happy man, who is a lover of honourable and most excellent actions, from which it necessarily follows that he takes great delight in them. To confirm this common cause he uses various and manifold examples. First he brings forward the pleasure of horses, which, as the young Strepsiades testifies in Aristophanes, sometimes carries some people away and moves them vehemently. He also brings forward lovers of spectacles; to these may be added those eager for philosophy, wine and money, all of whom we see are wonderfully affected when at last they obtain their desires. By these examples the form of reasoning that the dialecticians call induction is clearly confirmed and demonstrated: the major proposition, which contained the common cause, is established. This is at once applied to the present matter when he says that the same is true of those for whom just and honourable actions are their nature, and of upright and happy men: they love those things, and rejoice in them not a little. It plainly follows that upright and blessed men, if they see or hear of others acting nobly and honourably, derive great pleasure from it; but without doubt much greater pleasure while they themselves exercise themselves in just, upright and honourable actions. From these things we now understand that the life of the happy is not to be separated from pleasure, and we see that those who joined pleasure to happiness were not altogether wrong.

units.la: Quae modo ex Aristotele collegimus, è sacris item literis discimus. Pios homines ut felices hortabatur Paulus ad veram solidamq; laeticiam, cum scriberet, Gaudete in domino semper, atq; iterum dico gaudete. Prouerbiorum quoq; cap. 21. habetur, Gaudium est iusto facere iudicium. Nec semel ad laeticiam & exultationem Dauid iustos & pios excitat. Atq; adeo vera est haec sententia, ut etiam illae probae actiones felices voluptate perfundant, quae natura, sensu & vulgi iudicio repellendae videntur. Idcirco legimus discessisse hilares & gaudentes a conspectu concilij Apostolos, quod habiti essent digni contumeliis pro Christi nomine. Neq; tantum scimus permultos Christianos laeto animo propter fidei testimonium oppetiisse mortem, sed etiam nō-nullos Ethnicos magno gaudio atque alacritate vitam ob patriam liberandam posuisse.
units.tr: What we have just gathered from Aristotle we also learn from the sacred letters. Paul urged the godly, as happy people, to true and solid joy when he wrote: "Rejoice in the Lord always; and again I say, rejoice." It is also written in Proverbs 21: "It is joy to the just to do judgment." And David more than once rouses the just and the godly to gladness and exultation. Indeed this opinion is so true that even those upright actions which nature, the senses and the judgment of the crowd seem to shun, flood the doers with pleasure. Hence we read that the apostles departed from the council rejoicing and glad, because they had been counted worthy to suffer insults for the name of Christ. Nor do we only know that very many Christians met death with a cheerful mind for the testimony of the faith, but also that some heathens, with great joy and eagerness, laid down their lives to free their country.

units.la: At dubium hic se offert dissoluendum, quod Aristoteles causam voluptatis propriam & veram non videatur demonstrasse. Quoniam ob id aliqua dicuntur et sunt cuipiam iucunda quod illius naturae apta sint, commoda & idonea, ut arescenti potus, exhausto cibus, ignaro doctrina, &c. Quin ex i-sta commoditate, consensu, aut proportione animantium substantia ac natura cum aliquibus rebus, amor seu cupiditas earum nascitur. Prima itaq; voluptatis origo ex illa conuenientia non ex amore fuit ducenda. Respondetur ad haec, verè quidem ex illa rerum aptitudine inter se voluptatem excitari, sed quia consensus ille aut conuenientia multo maior adhuc reddi-tur, cum amor & cupiditas intercesserint, ideo Aristotelem illam attigisse a-ptitudinem & conuenientiam, quae illustrior & validior esset. Hoc autem ita esse addiscimus ex eo, quod interdum amor seu cupiditas conuenientiam aliquam inter res nonnullas adducit, ubi caeteroqui ex natura nulla esset. Delectantur grauida mulieres nonnunquam edendo calcem, carbones aut argilla, prae quibus panem, carnes & saccarum respuunt, ubi cupiditatem conuenientiam ponere vides inter gustum & illa quae ab eo sunt aliena, si naturam[?] ipsam spectare voluerit. Et amantibus persepe suarum puellarum naevus aut aliqua foeditas (sit[?] nimio magna voluptati.
units.tr: But here a doubt presents itself to be resolved: Aristotle does not seem to have demonstrated the proper and true cause of pleasure. For some things are said to be, and are, pleasant to someone for this reason: that they are suited to his nature, convenient and fitting, as drink is to one who is parched, food to one who is exhausted, teaching to one who is ignorant, and so on. Indeed, from this convenience, agreement or proportion between the substance and nature of living things and certain things, love or desire for them arises. Therefore the first origin of pleasure should be derived from that agreement, not from love. To this it is answered: it is true that pleasure is excited by that fitness of things to one another; but because that agreement or convenience is made much greater when love and desire have intervened, Aristotle therefore touched upon that fitness and convenience which is more evident and stronger. We learn that this is so from the fact that sometimes love or desire brings about some agreement between certain things where, by nature, there would otherwise be none. Pregnant women sometimes take pleasure in eating lime, coals or clay, and spurn bread, meat and sugar for them; here you see desire creating an agreement between the taste and things foreign to it, if you care to look at nature itself. And to lovers, often the mole or some blemish of their girl is exceedingly pleasing.

units.la: Vulgarium igitur hominum suavia pugnant, quod natura huiuscemodi non sint, sed studiosis honesti suavia sunt, quae natura suavitatem habent: tales autem perpetuae sunt actiones ex virtute. Quare illis per se ipsas jucundae sunt.
units.tr: Therefore the sweetnesses of ordinary men conflict, because they are not so by nature; but to the zealous, the honourable things are sweet, which have sweetness by nature. Such actions that spring from virtue are perpetual. Therefore they are pleasant to them in themselves.

units.la: Per occupationem soluitur, quod haec audiendo posset in mentem venire, omnes ne voluptates habeant cum felicitate consortium? Quod si non oes, ut dicendum videtur, quas nam illi assciabimus?[?] Ad haec distinctione occurritur. Quaedam suavia sunt natura sua & per seipsa, nonnulla vero ut oblectent suapte proprietate non habent, sed ex aliqua eius corruptione aut vitio qui capitur his delectant. Suapte bonitate suavia sunt, sapientia, virtutes, probae actiones, recordatio recte factorum, administratio rerum prudens, inventio utilium consiliorum, doctrina, contemplatio, & consimilia. Quae si ab aliquibus aliquando non probentur, id ob illorum insciitiam & ruditatem contingit. At e diverso vinum immoderatum, spectacula, crapulae ac libidines natura sua non jucunda & suavia, sed tantum his placent qui huiusmodi per se capiuntur. Vulgus, inquit, est quod consectatur[?], quae sunt opte[?] ingenio suavia non sunt, varia sane ac multiplicia, sed pugnantia. Magnum voluptatum vulgarium esse numerum nemo ambigit: sunt enim permulti sensus & cuique sua voluptas adest, quae sane tum legitima non est, cum fines excedit suos, cumq; nimium homines circa se detinet, vel eius animum incitat & perturbat. Ista caeteraq; sensuum voluptates si finibus atq; terminis suis sese contineant, neq; illos egrediantur, & naturales sunt, & jure damnari nequeunt.
units.tr: Here an objection arises which might come to mind on hearing these things: do not all pleasures have fellowship with happiness? But if not all, as seems necessary to say, which ones shall we then assign? To this the distinction answers. Some things are sweet by their own nature and in themselves, but some do not have the power to delight by their own property; rather, those who are captivated by them are delighted through some corruption or vice of theirs. By their own goodness are sweet: wisdom, the virtues, upright actions, the recollection of good deeds, prudent administration of affairs, the discovery of useful counsels, learning, contemplation, and the like. If these are at any time not approved by some, this happens through their ignorance and rudeness. On the other hand, immoderate wine, spectacles, drunkenness and lusts are not pleasant and sweet by their nature, but please only those who are taken up with such things for their own sake. The crowd, he says, pursues what is by nature not sweet; these things are indeed various and manifold, but conflicting. No one doubts that there is a great number of vulgar pleasures: for there are very many senses, and each has its own pleasure at hand, which surely is not lawful when it exceeds its bounds, and when it holds men too much, or stirs and disturbs their mind. If those pleasures of the senses and the rest keep within their own limits and do not go beyond them, they are both natural and cannot rightly be condemned.

units.la: Quae vero pugna sit vulgarium voluptatum Eustrathius ita explicat. Is cibo delectatur salso, ille dulci: gaudet hic potu acerbiori, ille austero: quia sapores inter se contrarij sunt, neq; simul in eadem re possunt haberi. Verum hic dixeris inter voluptates quas naturales dicitis, idem potest videri: alii qui delectantur mathematicis, alij physicis, nonnulli Dialecticis, alij tantum prudentibus actionibus. Quare cum tam hic quam ibi sit varietas, discri-men hoc pugnae ea ratione interpretatum, non videtur inter voluptates distinctionem ponere, cum ex aequo in utraq; parte reperiatur. Nisi dixeris, vulgarium voluptatum eam esse multitudinem & varietatem quae pugnet, ut dulce & acerbum, austerum & lene adversantur mutuo sibi: quod non est in voluptatibus honestis quae jam sunt commemoratae; nam mathematiea non adversatur physicae, neq; Dialectica prudentia. Sed verius explica-tur discrimen si pugna in appetitu eiusdem hominis attendatur: nam ille i-dem in delitiis hanc habuit, mox illam odit, quiq; cibū expetebat, eius nunc laborat nausea. Unde Terentius: In amore haec omnia insunt vitia, iniuriae, suspiciones inimicitiae, inducia, bellum, pax rursum. Hic animadvertimus pugnam rerum inter se atque contra animum. Illa tandē vere suavia sunt quibus delectantur amantes honesti. Consilio quippe illi melioris iudicis utuntur, qui rationi non sensibus credunt. Videas praeterea illos constantes et unanimes, recta quae semel illis placuere nunquam displicent, neque patiun-tur sibi veram sententiam extorqueri. Deinde cum viris eiusdem ordinis i-dem dicunt: nam quotquot amantes honesti sunt eas-dem virtutes ac eas-dem actiones probant.
units.tr: Eustrathius explains the conflict among the common pleasures as follows. One man takes delight in salty food, another in sweet; one enjoys a sharper drink, another a dry one. These tastes are opposed to each other and cannot both be had in the same thing at once. But you could say that the same may be seen among the pleasures you call natural: some take delight in mathematics, others in physics, some in dialectic, others only in prudent actions. So since there is variety here as well as there, this explanation of the conflict does not seem to draw a distinction between pleasures, because it is found on both sides alike. Unless you say that the conflict among common pleasures lies in their multitude and variety, so that they oppose one another as sweet opposes sour and dry opposes mild. That does not hold for the honourable pleasures just mentioned, since mathematics is not opposed to physics, nor dialectic to prudence. The distinction is explained more truly if the conflict is looked for in the appetite of one and the same man. For he who once took delight in something soon hates it, and he who craved food now suffers nausea from it. Hence Terence: "In love all these faults are present: wrongs, suspicions, enmities, truces, war, and peace again." Here we notice a conflict of things among themselves and against the mind. Those pleasures are truly sweet in which honourable lovers delight. For they use the counsel of a better judge, one who trusts reason rather than the senses. Moreover, you may see them steady and of one mind; what once pleased them as right never displeases them, and they do not allow the true opinion to be wrested from them. Further, they say the same things as men of the same rank; for all honourable lovers approve the same virtues and the same actions.

units.la: Non itaque vita illorum voluptate indiget ut aliquo certo additamento, sed in seipsa voluptatem continet.
units.tr: Thus his life does not need pleasure as some added supplement, but contains pleasure within itself.

units.la: Cum declarauit voluptatem cum felicitate magnam coniunctionem habere, ac discrimen protulit voluptatum, ut legitimas & honestas à vulga-ribus segregaret, nunc eo transfert orationem, ut modum indicet, quo in beatitudine voluptas inhaeret. Atque hinc facile patefit, ut illi nonnihil à ve-ro deflectant, qui dixerunt, ut supra est commemoratum, felicitatem non es-se sine voluptate, quasi voluptas ut quid additum ad eam foris acce-dat. Qui sic dicunt, falli plurimum ex eo constat, quòd felix quicquid agit, nō invitō, sed libēti cupidoq; animo facit, unde illi dulcis ac suavis est quae-libet ipsius actio.
units.tr: Having shown that pleasure is closely joined with happiness, and having drawn a distinction among pleasures so as to separate the lawful and honourable from the common, he now turns his discourse to show the manner in which pleasure inheres in blessedness. From this it is easy to see that those err somewhat from the truth who said, as was mentioned above, that happiness is not without pleasure, as if pleasure came from outside and were added to it. It is clear that those who speak thus are greatly mistaken, because a happy man does whatever he does not unwillingly but with a glad and eager mind; hence every action of his is sweet and pleasant to him.

units.la: Praeter ea quae dicta sunt, nemo bonus est qui honestis actionibus non gaudeat. Nemo quippe iustum dixerit, qui iuste agendo non gaudeat, neque liberalem qui liberalibus actionibus non laetetur, itidemq; in aliis.
units.tr: Besides what has been said, no good man fails to rejoice in honourable actions. Indeed no one would call a man just who does not rejoice in acting justly, nor generous one who is not glad in generous actions, and so in other cases.
