units.la: Idem confirmat à communi hominum sensu atq; sermone: titulus enim viri boni aut iusti nullis plane conceditur qui iustis & bonis actionibus nō gau-deant. Proinde ista reciprocantur, adeo consentiunt, Vir bonus bonis actioni-bus gaudet, ac vicissim qui bonis actionibus gaudet est vir bonus.
units.tr: He confirms this from the common sense and speech of mankind: for the title of good or just man is granted plainly to no one who does not rejoice in just and good actions. Therefore these propositions are reciprocal, so closely do they agree: the good man rejoices in good actions, and conversely, he who rejoices in good actions is a good man.

units.la: Si res itaq; sic est, actiones ex uirtute per seipsas erunt iucundæ: uerum & bonæ & honestæ.
units.tr: If then the matter stands thus, actions that proceed from virtue will in themselves be pleasant, and both good and honourable.

units.la: Rationis hæc est conclusio. Si qua diximus concessa & data fuerint, euidens est. probas honestasq; actiones voluptatem non quasi externum additamentum suscipere, sed eam in seipsis comprehensam habere. Omnia tamē quæ dicta sunt ad illas accommodari debent actiones, quæ à uirtutibus proficiscuntur, quia priusquam habitus fuerit partus, actiones quibus quæritur, molestia & difficultate non carent, ideoq; non adeo suaues ut cæteroqui natura earum est existimari possunt. Si quis tamen hinc putaret uoluptatem felicitatis definitionem implere aut eius partem esse, mendose colligeret: nā ut foris ad eam non accedat, est illius proprietas, à natura ipsius distincta, ita nihilominus inserta ut iam ab ipsa generatione simul existant.
units.tr: This is the conclusion of the argument. If what we have said has been granted and conceded, it is evident that upright and honourable actions do not take on pleasure as some external addition, but have it comprised within themselves. Yet all that has been said must be applied to those actions which proceed from the virtues, because before a habit has been formed, the actions by which it is sought are not free from annoyance and difficulty, and therefore are not as pleasant as their nature otherwise allows them to be thought. If anyone should nevertheless conclude from this that pleasure fulfils the definition of happiness or is a part of it, he would reason wrongly. For although pleasure does not come to happiness from outside, it is a property of it, distinct from its nature, yet so inserted that they exist together from the very moment of its generation.

units.la: Verùm & bonæ & honestæ.) Probas actiones non modò vult suaues & voluptate perfusas, verum & honestas & utiles: nam per καλὰς honestas intelligo, per ἀγαθὰς utiles & commodas. Atq; ista sunt illa præcipua in vita humana quæ paulo ante monuit, eos qui agant, & præclaras edunt actiones, consequi.
units.tr: "Both good and honourable." He wants the upright actions not only to be pleasant and steeped in delight, but also honourable and useful. For by kalas I understand honourable, and by agathas useful and advantageous. And these are the chief things in human life which he said a little earlier that those who act and perform excellent actions attain.

units.la: Et quodlibet horum maximè, siquidē uir bonus de his rectè iudicet, iudicat autem ut diximus.
units.tr: And each of these especially, since the good man judges rightly about them, and he judges, as we have said, that they are so.

units.la: Non illi satis est rectas actiones dixisse iucundas, honestas & utiles, nisi addat inter hæc bona, illas gradum summum habere, quòd tametsi ratione posset cōfirmari, quia beatitudo statuitur bonum extremum, idcoq; illi quæcunq; adscribuntur bona, non possunt intelligi ei convenire nisi gradu supremo. Etenim si meliora possent haberi, iam præter felicitatem aliquid optandum restaret. Sed hac ratione præterita, viri boni iudicio est contentus, quoniam, inquit, boni viri sic iudicant. Id verò est ac si diceretur, si eorum existimatio falleretur, iam boni & recti esse desinerent, quod à communi sensu est alienum, ut rectum sit obliquum, & probum habeatur prauum.
units.tr: It is not enough for him to have called right actions pleasant, honourable and useful, unless he adds that among these goods they hold the highest rank. Although this could be confirmed by reason, since blessedness is established as the final good, the goods that are ascribed to it cannot be understood to belong to it except in the highest degree. For if better things could be had, something beyond happiness would still remain to be desired. But passing over this line of reasoning, he is content with the judgement of the good man, since, he says, good men judge thus. Yet this is as if one said that if their estimation were mistaken, they would then cease to be good and upright, which is foreign to common sense, as if the straight were crooked and the upright were thought crooked.

units.la: Discrimen hic mihi notetur inter Philosophiam moralem atq; nostram Theologiam: illa facit analysin ad arbitrium sapientum ac bonorum virorum, nostra verò ad leges & sermones Dei. Dubitabitur utra verisimilius dicat? an errent interdum sapientes & probi quantum voluerisin ferendo iudicio de humanis actionibus, an Deo qui semper verax est, summum potius arbitrium sit deferendum? Profectò regulam firmam certamq; esse oportet. Quare cū homini mendacių & inconstantia iam sit innata corruptio ne genuina, illi tanta dignitas citra controuersiam non est concedenda. Iam itaq; audiuimus, & quid felicitas, & quid in ea insit, nimirum voluptas et honestas & vtilitas, idq; supremo gradu & modo. Nunc cum ita conclusum & perfectum est, carmen Deliacum obiter taxat.
units.tr: Let this distinction be noted here between moral philosophy and our Theology: the former makes its analysis by the judgement of the wise and good men, but ours by the laws and words of God. It will be asked which of the two speaks more truly: whether the wise and upright may sometimes err, however much they wish, in passing judgement on human actions, or whether the highest authority should rather be granted to God, who is always truthful? Surely the rule must be firm and certain. Therefore, since lying and inconstancy are already innate corruption in man, such great authority is not to be granted to him without controversy. So now we have heard both what happiness is and what it contains, namely pleasure, honour and usefulness, and these at the highest degree and in the highest manner. Now that this has been concluded and completed in this way, he briefly censures the Delian poem.

units.la: Optimum itaque & honestissimum & suauissimum beatitudo: necp ista diuellenda sunt a se inuicem ut carmen Deliacum velle uidetur, quod iustissimum pronunciat honestissimum, utilissimum recte ualere, suauissimum uero id consequi quod quis expetat. Omnia enim haec in optimis actionibus insunt: has autem, seu earum unam quae optima sit, felicitatem esse arbitramur.
units.tr: Therefore blessedness is the best, the most honourable and the most pleasant; nor are these to be torn apart from one another, as the Delian poem seems to wish, which pronounces the most just to be the most honourable, good health to be the most useful, and the most pleasant to be the attainment of what one desires. For all these are found in the best actions, and we judge that these actions, or whichever one of them is best, are happiness.

units.la: Delos insula fuit vbi augustissimum Apollinis templum fuit, quo mortales innumeri accedebant, vt de suis negociis Deum consulerent: nam quae humana explicare ratione non poterant, consueuerunt ad Deum exponeda referre. Carmen reuera est Theognidis, quare autem Deliacum vocetur, nō una potest ratio adduci. Aut enim Theognis ab Apolline Deliaco sensum carminis a se compositi didicisse iactabat, aut Pythia quae responsa in Delo reddere solebat hoc Theognidis carmine delectata, illo est respondendo usa, & ipsum numini suo vt proprium adscribebat. Sed quicquid sit, hoc in eo reprehenditur, quod haec inter se quae coniunctissima diuelleret. Eius haec porro videbatur sententia, vt honestas iustitia, sanitati vtilitas, & adeptioni rerum concupitarum voluptas tribueretur. Carmina Graece sic habent.
units.tr: Delos was an island where there was a most venerable temple of Apollo, to which countless mortals came to consult the god about their affairs; for they were accustomed to refer to God what they could not explain by human reason. The poem is indeed by Theognis; why it is called Delian, however, cannot be explained by a single reason. Either Theognis boasted that he had learned the meaning of the poem he composed from Apollo of Delos, or the Pythia, who used to give oracles at Delos, delighted in this poem of Theognis, answered with it, and ascribed it to her god as her own. But whatever the case, this is what is faulted in it: that it tears apart things most closely joined. Its opinion, moreover, seemed to be that honesty should be assigned to justice, utility to health, and pleasure to the attainment of the things desired. The verses in Greek read thus:

units.la: κάλλιστον τὸ δικαιότατον, λῷστον δ' ὑγιαίνειν,
units.tr: κάλλιστον τὸ δικαιότατον, λῷστον δ' ὑγιαίνειν, [Most beautiful is what is most just, and best is to be healthy]

units.la: πρᾶγμα ἢ τερπνότατον ὅ τις ἐξ ἂν τυχεῖν. [?]
units.tr: πρᾶγμα ἢ τερπνότατον ὅ τις ἐξ ἂν τυχεῖν. [?] [and the most delightful thing is that which one could obtain (?)]

units.la: Aristoteles carmen integrum non refert, nam in pentametro priore partem solū quo ad sensum recitat. Vno autem verbo, ἡδύσον dicit, quod Theognis poeta ἡδὺ καὶ τερπνότατον scripsit [?]. Sed nil in his significatio discrepat. Ista inquit Aristoteles quando reuera in ipsa felicitate iunguntur, diuidi ac sepa rari a se inuicem non debent. Quod sane sic ego intelligendu arbitror, vt nihil honestum possit inueniri, quod idem voluptatem & utilitate coniuncta non habeat: qui tamen haud fit quin honesti ipsa ratio, a ratione voluptatis &
units.tr: Aristotle does not give the whole poem, for in the first pentameter he recites only the part that bears on the sense. He changes one word, saying ἡδύσον, whereas the poet Theognis wrote ἡδὺ καὶ τερπνότατον [?]. But the meaning does not differ at all. Aristotle says that these things, since they are really joined together in happiness itself, ought not to be divided or separated from one another. Which I think should be understood in such a way that nothing honourable can be found which does not also have pleasure and usefulness joined with it; yet it does not follow that the very reason of the honourable is not to be distinguished from the reason of pleasure and utility.

units.la: { } ne genuina: as printed. utilitatis non sit discernenda. Cicero hac de re non leuiter conqueritur, eosque iudicat de humanis rebus male meritos, qui honestatem ab utilitate seiunxerunt. Oraculum proinde seu Theognidis carmen, tria quodammodo videtur summa bona statuisse, utilia inquam, suauia, & honesta quae gradu extremo existant. Id ab eis non recte neque ordine factum ostendit Aristoteles, quod actio perfectissima viri boni omnia haec tria & quidem summa in se complectatur.
units.tr: Nor should honour be separated from usefulness. Cicero complains about this matter with some vehemence, and he judges that those who divorced honour from usefulness have done ill by human affairs. So too the oracle, or the poem of Theognis, seems to have set up three chief goods in a way: the useful, the pleasant, and the honourable, which hold the highest rank. Aristotle shows that they did this wrongly and out of order, since the most perfect activity of the good man embraces all three, and indeed these supreme goods in itself.

units.la: Videtur attamen bonis quoque externis indigere, quemadmodum diximus: non enim fieri potest, aut non est facile ut honesta exequamur, nisi alicunde suppeditetur.
units.tr: Yet it seems that happiness also needs external goods, as we have said. For it cannot happen, or is not easy, that we carry out honourable deeds unless they are supplied from somewhere.

units.la: De voluptate, honestate ac utilitate felicitatis est satis dictum: restat ut de bonis externis adhuc tractetur, quod modo luculeter fiet. Ad naturam beatitudinis duo accedunt, voluptas & externorum bonorum copia. Sed haec in ipsa felicitate diuerso modo & ratione insunt. Voluptas consequitur ex intimis felicitatis principijs. Opes causa sunt sine qua felicitas non potest esse perfecta, ut adminiculu & subsidiu accersuntur. Proinde conexionis ratio est diuersa. Atq; ut felicitas sit finis, eget opibus externis, in quarum cẽsu omnia bona collocantur, quae habemus extra animum & extra corpus. Non aut felicitas per se aut natura sua ista requirit, verum ob subiectam materia: nam iustae probæq; actiones interdum circa quaedam versantur, quae absq; opibus externis regi nequeunt, ut administrare rempub. bellum gerere, paupertatem egestatem subleuare: ad quas profecto res pecuniys, largis prouentibus, agris, seruis, amicisq; opus esse omnes intelligimus.
units.tr: We have said enough about the pleasure, honour and usefulness of happiness. It remains to treat of external goods, which will be done shortly and clearly. Two things belong to the nature of blessedness: pleasure and an abundance of external goods. But these are present in happiness itself in different ways and by different reasons. Pleasure follows from the innermost principles of happiness. Wealth is a cause without which happiness cannot be complete, and it is sought as a support and aid. Therefore the manner of connection is different. And so that happiness may be an end, it needs external wealth, in which all those goods are placed that we have outside the mind and outside the body. Happiness does not require these things either in itself or by its own nature, but because of the matter it is concerned with. For just and upright actions sometimes deal with certain things that cannot be governed without external wealth, such as administering the commonwealth, waging war, and relieving poverty and want. For all of us understand that such affairs certainly require money, ample revenues, lands, slaves and friends.

units.la: At quibusdam parum probatur, rem tam praestatem ut felicitas est, indigere bonis longe se inferioribus. At una distinctione is nodus dissoluitur. Per se & naturam suam opus non habet: nam si per se indigeret his, nil posset esse felix nisi abundaret his bonis: quod minime debet concedi, cum Deus & angeli absq; ope et adminiculo istorum bonorum sint beati. Ad felicitatem adiungitur haec indigetia, quae est hominis corruptibilis & mortalis. Quemadmodum nostra vis intelligendi, absq; sensibus & imaginibus quas contemplamur, cogitando nil potest agere, quod sane illi usu venit, non quo vel mens est vel intelligentia: nam si esset hoc pacto, neque Deus neque angeli absq; sensibus & imaginatione quicquam intelligerent. Illa igitur mens ac intelligentia requirunt non per se aut natura sua, sed qua sunt hominis. notandum praterea, subiectam materiam bifariam posse intelligi. Aut e-nim refert illam materiam circa quam nostrae versantur actiones, aut de quibus paulo superius exempla commemoraui. Aut est materia in qua no-ster animus est, nimirum corpus, ad quod fouendum, sustentandum & alen-dum bona haec externa prorsus exiguntur. Proinde felicitas his duobus mo-dis externis bonis opus habet.
units.tr: But to some it seems hard to accept that a thing so excellent as happiness should need goods far inferior to it. Yet this knot is untied by one distinction. Happiness has no need of these by itself and its own nature. For if it needed them in itself, nothing could be happy unless it abounded in these goods; and this ought by no means to be conceded, since God and the angels are blessed without the help and aid of these goods. This neediness is added to happiness, the neediness of corruptible and mortal man. Just as our power of understanding, without the senses and the images which we contemplate, can accomplish nothing in thinking, and this happens to it not because of the mind or intelligence as such; for if it were so, neither God nor the angels would understand anything without senses and imagination. Therefore that mind and intelligence require these things not by themselves or by their own nature, but because they belong to man. It is further to be noted that the subject matter can be understood in two ways. For it refers either to that matter with which our actions are concerned, or to those examples which I recalled a little above. Or it is the matter in which our mind is, that is, the body, for the nourishing, sustaining and feeding of which these external goods are altogether required. Therefore happiness needs external goods in these two ways.

units.la: Multa enim fiunt ceu per instrumenta, per amicos, diuitias, & ciuilem potentiam.
units.tr: For many things are done, as it were, through instruments, through friends, through riches and civil power.

units.la: Quod adfert, ita potest explicari. Cernimus in artibus complura fieri, non tantum arte, quae in animo artificum sita est & membris corporis, sed externorum quoque instrumentorum auxilio. Faber ferrarius, igne, forcipibus, malleo, & incude utitur. Faber lignarius regula, securi, serra & aliis consimilibus, idq; propter subiectam materiam. Neq; plerunque artificibus arte atq; corporis membris est satis. Ita de felicitate usuenit: tametsi animus sit praeclarissimis virtutibus ornatus, & velit positiq; actiones optimas edere, neq; destituatur corporis viribus, nihilominus amicis facultatibus, & ciuili potentia est opus. Per ciuilem potentiam intelligo honores, beneuolentiam, fauores, clientelas & horum similia. Diuitiae autem partiendae sunt in naturales & artificiosas. Naturales habentur quaecunq; nascuntur ex terra, & quae res pecuaria producit. Artificiosa vero numis constat, qui sane reperti sunt, ut sequestres quodammodo sint in permutationibus. Hæ vero cum utraq; dicantur facultates, ex vocis etymologia colligimus, ad faciendum valere plurimum, quod cum hac Aristotelis do-ctrina pulchre consentit.
units.tr: What he adds can be explained thus. We see in the arts that many things are done not only by the skill that lies in the minds of craftsmen and in the members of the body, but also with the help of external instruments. The smith uses fire, tongs, hammer and anvil. The carpenter uses a rule, axe, saw and other similar tools, and this because of the matter at hand. Nor for the most part is skill and the members of the body enough for craftsmen. So it happens with happiness: although the mind is adorned with the most excellent virtues, and wishes to put forth the best actions, and is not deprived of bodily strength, nevertheless it needs friendly resources and civil power. By civil power I mean honours, goodwill, favours, clienteles and things like these. Riches, however, are to be divided into natural and artificial. Natural riches are considered to be whatever springs from the earth and what livestock produce. Artificial riches, however, consist in coin, which indeed was invented so that it might in some way serve as a go-between in exchanges. Now, since both of these are called "faculties" (facultates), we gather from the etymology of the word that they are powerful for making things (ad faciendum), which agrees splendidly with this doctrine of Aristotle.

units.la: Qui nonnullis horum priuantur, felicitatem co-inquinant, ut nobilitate, multa & proba liberorum copia, forma. Nō enim admodum felix est, qui spe-cie prorsus deformis fuerit, ignobilis, solitarius, vel absque liberis: forte quoque minus, si cui liberi fue-rint & amici omnino praui, aut boni cum esent, ob-ierunt.
units.tr: Those who are deprived of some of these things spoil their happiness: for example, nobility, a large and good number of children, and beauty. For he is not very happy who is quite misshapen in appearance, ignoble, solitary, or without children; perhaps also he is less happy if he has children and friends who are altogether wicked, or who, though good, have died.

units.la: A forma incipit quod proposuerat demonstrare: neque hic, ut arbitror, speciem requirit suauissimam, sed ne quis omnibus modis sit turpis: atque hoc sibi vult παναίχμος[?], vt Græcè habetur. Huic[?] dicti ratio assignari potest, vt Eustrathius arbitratur, quoniam proni sunt hominum animi vt amet & admirentur quos aliqua specie uiderint cæteris mortalibus præstare: qua ex propensione porro nascitur, vt ita pulchris libenter pareant & obsequatur. Animos uero populi sic habere erga se affectos, proculdubio multum ad agendas res præclaras adiuuat: multa enim plebs efficit cum ultro incitatur, & nutum vnius vehementi dilectione ac ultronea voluntate facit. Ideoq; rex ille, quem primum Deus Israelitis præfecit, nimirum, Saulem, adeo statura fuit procera, vt alios Hebræos ab humeris & sursum longitudine vinceret. Ac de Dauide, quem eundem in regem vngi iussit, scribitur, Rufus erat & pulcher valde. Aliud præterea est, quo mouentur homines ad formosos amandos, quoniam species corporis imago quædam animi est, cumq; is ante omnia quæri debeat vt probus sit & bonus, neq; aspectu cerni queat, restat vt corporis formam vulgares sequantur. Qua sane ratione si adducerentur amantes corporum, non essent culpandi: ast hodie nil fere cum modo agitur, sed omnia turpitudine ac libidine geruntur.
units.tr: He begins with beauty, which he had proposed to demonstrate. Nor here, I think, does he require the most delightful appearance, but that one should not be ugly in every respect; and this is what the word παναίχμος [panaichmos] means, as it is found in Greek. A reason for this word can be given, as Eustathius thinks: because human minds are inclined to love and admire those whom they see excelling other mortals in some appearance. From this inclination it follows further that people willingly obey and comply with the beautiful. That the people should have such dispositions towards oneself undoubtedly contributes much to performing noble deeds; for the common people accomplish much when they are roused of their own accord, and they do the nod of one man with vehement affection and willing consent. And so that king whom God first set over the Israelites, namely Saul, was so tall that he surpassed the other Hebrews from the shoulders upward. And concerning David, whom God likewise ordered to be anointed king, it is written that he was ruddy and very beautiful. There is also another reason which moves men to love beautiful people, since bodily appearance is a certain image of the mind; and since the mind ought above all to be sought for, that it be upright and good, and cannot be seen by looking, it remains that ordinary people follow the form of the body. By this reasoning, indeed, if lovers were drawn to bodies, they would not be blameworthy; but today almost nothing is done with moderation, but everything is carried on with baseness and lust.

units.la: Nobilitatem quoq; ad beatitudinem requirit Aristoteles. Quia plebs nobiles obseruat et reueretur. Quia nobilitas in eo genere est ex quo multi illustres ac præclari prodiere: atque virtutes quæ fulserunt in maioribus, à posteris expectari solent. Scio quidem nonnullos putare nobilitatem esse antiquis temporibus conseruatas in aliqua familia diuitias: at mihi prior sententia longe magis placet. Addit præterea Eustrathius ideo ad ciuilem felicitatem splendorem generis esse conducibilem, quoniam homines nouos, quum emergunt, populus consueuerit non modo considerare ex præsentibus virtutibus aut præclaris gestis, sed ex eo quod paulo ante fuerunt. Vnde prior obscuritas nonnihil dum reputetur obscurat præsentem gloriam, quod eo fit magis quo sunt homines vehementer propensi ad obtrectandum.
units.tr: Aristotle also requires nobility for blessedness, because the common people observe and revere nobles, and because nobility is in that stock from which many illustrious and distinguished men have come forth; and the virtues which shone in the ancestors are usually expected from their descendants. I know indeed that some think nobility is wealth preserved in some family from ancient times; but the former opinion pleases me far more. Eustathius adds moreover that the splendour of lineage is conducive to civil happiness because, when new men emerge, the people are accustomed to consider them not only from their present virtues or distinguished deeds but from what they were a little while before. Hence the former obscurity, while it is still thought about, somewhat dims present glory, and this happens the more because men are vehemently prone to disparagement.

units.la: Εὐτεκνία vox ambigua, quia non tantum copiam liberorum quàm illorum probitatem significat. Et sane quo ad copiam prolis qui ea pollent, & ciuitati sunt grati, & ab aliis timentur. Grati quidem sunt, quoniam remp. augent. Vnde apud Romanos fuit ius trium, quinq; & septem liberorum. Et Lacedæmonius adolescês assurgere noluit seniori cæteroqui bene merito de repub. Quoniam, inquit, ille postse[?] non relinquit qui mihi cum senuero assurgat & caput aperiat. Sed tum demum liberi ad felicitatem faciunt, si recte fuerint instituti. Nam secus vomicæ sunt aut carcinomata, vt Octauius Augustus aiebat de filia & nepte cum impudicitia laborarent. Doluit quoq; Tyberius Caligulam se domi populo Romano alere natricem crudelissimam.
units.tr: The word εὐτεκνία [euteknia] is ambiguous, since it signifies not only an abundance of children but their uprightness [Greek: good children]. And indeed, as regards the number of offspring, those who excel in it are both pleasing to the commonwealth and feared by others. They are pleasing indeed, since they increase the commonwealth; hence among the Romans there was the right of three, five and seven children. And a Spartan youth refused to rise for an elder who was otherwise well deserving of the commonwealth, because, he said, that man had left no son who might rise for me and uncover my head when I grow old. But children contribute to happiness only if they have been rightly brought up; for otherwise they are like abscesses or cancers, as Octavius Augustus said of his daughter and granddaughter when they suffered from immorality. Tiberius too grieved that he was feeding at home, for the Roman people, a most cruel viper of a stepdaughter (Caligula).

units.la: Vt vero amicitia summis adiumentis ad vitam rectè degendam homi-nes communiat, ex optimis scriptoribus & humana consuetudine satis po-test colligi. Sed longè reprehensibilior est, qui prauos habeat amicos quàm corruptos filios: nam fieri quandoq; potest vt ob prauum ingenium vtut ad-hibeatur diligentia in educando, non possimus liberos habere quales volu-mus: at amicos, quia illos nobis deligimus & relinqui possunt, nulla est ex-cusatio si malos habuerimus. Quorum adhac honestorum inquam libero-rum & amicorum, iacturam multum beatitudini obesse testatur Aristote-les: quia sine magno dolore ac luctu obire non possunt. Et eam calamitatem tametsi æquo feramus animo, si virtute fortitudinis prædití sumus, absque damno tamen illi non subiacemus: quod profecto damnum haud leuiter se licitatem[?] inquinat.
units.tr: That friendship greatly strengthens people for living well may be gathered sufficiently from the best writers and from common human experience. But a man who has wicked friends is far more open to blame than one who has corrupt sons. For it can sometimes happen that, although diligence is applied in bringing up children, we cannot have them as we would like because of their bad disposition. But we choose our friends for ourselves, and they can be dropped, so there is no excuse if we have had bad ones. Aristotle testifies that the loss of these worthy things, I say of children and friends, greatly hinders happiness, because one cannot die without great grief and lamentation. And even if we bear that misfortune with an even mind, provided we are endowed with the virtue of fortitude, we are nonetheless not exempt from loss, and that loss certainly does not lightly stain [our] felicity.

units.la: Vt itaque diximus uidetur opus habere hac quoque prosperitate, unde quidam eodē loco habent prosperam fortunā & felicitatem, alij uero uirtutem.
units.tr: As we have said, happiness seems to need this prosperity too. This is why some place prosperous fortune and happiness in the same rank, while others place virtue there.

units.la: His vt rectè monet Eustrathius gradum facit ad ea quæ proximo capite sunt dicenda. Veteres, inquit, hoc animaduertentes absq; bonis fortunæ felicitatem non esse perfectam, eodem loco illam habuerunt cum bona fortuna. Sed alij putantes indignum, fortuitum ponere tantum bonum, virtute non fortunā in eodem loco habuerunt cum beatitudine, propterea quòd virtus non forte sed electione acquiritur. Hic iam res exigit vt annotentur aliqua. Primùm, Aristotelem non dicere harum rerum priuationem felicitatem omnino tollere aut funditus delere: at solum nonnihil coinquinare vel obfuscare. Nam qui probis actionibus ornantur, vt hi bonis externis interdū careant, miseri non sunt, quamuis perfectè beati haberi nequeant.
units.tr: Following this, as Eustathius rightly observes, he makes a step toward what is to be said in the next chapter. The ancients, he says, noticing this, held that happiness is not complete without the goods of fortune, and so placed it in the same category as good fortune. But others, thinking it unworthy to count so great a good as something accidental, placed it in the same category as blessedness, not fortune, on the ground that virtue is acquired not by chance but by choice. Here the matter requires that some points be noted. First, Aristotle does not say that the lack of these things utterly removes happiness or destroys it from the foundations, but only that it somewhat stains or clouds it. For those who are adorned with virtuous actions, although at times they lack external goods, are not wretched, even though they cannot be considered perfectly blessed.

units.la: Neq; dissentit scriptura de commendatione bonorum externorum. Quo enim ad liberos, promittuntur à Deo, Filij tui sicut nouellæ oliuarum. Et inter cæteras benedictiones ea numeratur, vt in Israel non sit abortio. Et passim timentibus Deum copia seminis repromittitur. Quod idē de diuitijs possumus facilè cognoscere. Ditauit Deus Abraamum, Isaacum, Iacobum, cæterosq; suos amicos. Salomoni qui sapientiam postulauerat, vltrò diuitias concessit. Et populum suum ita volebat, si benè se gereret, diuitijs abundare, vt ipsi aliis fœnerarent populis, non autem ab illis acciperent ad fœad fœnus. Nobilitas adeò cordi fuit populo Dei vt quaq; familia suas habe-ret genealogias, quib. in capita tribuũ duodecim filior. Israel, suos maiores referebant. Et sacerdotes Ezræ tempore qui hoc facere non potuerunt, sunt loco & gradu moti. Quin Euangelista Christi Genealogiam Lucas & Matthæus recensuerunt, ne ignobilis videretur secundum carnem. Et Apostolus ad Rom. 9. quæ nobilitas esset Israelitarum describit, Qui sunt Israel, quorum est adoptio, gloria, & legislatio, testamentum, cultus, & quorum sunt partes, ex quibus est Christus qui est super omnia, &c. Formam corporis antea demonstrabam primis duobus regibus Sauli & Dauidi concessam: postea nouimus in sacerdotibus adeò requisitam vt nemo claudus, cæcus, gibbosus aut aliqua fœditate insigni maculatus, potuerit administrare pontifi-ficatum. Atque amicitia vt coalesceret inter Hebræos, curauit Deus aprimè suis legibus: quæ omnes cum penitius consyderantur, plurimum faciunt ad homines vnà couiungendos. Proinde non sunt hæc quæ Aristoteles commemorauit abijcienda, quibus tamen, quo ad felicitatem, dare non oportet plus quam par sit. Dicitur quidem in libro Ecclesiastis cap. 10. Pecunia obediunt omnia. Sed refertur ea sententia, vt à vulgo accepta, nõ vt vera, sed qua taxetur humanus error, Imò alibi sacræ litera perhibent, nimirum in Prouerb. 13. Quid prosunt stulto diuitiæ, cùm sapientiam sibi non posit emere. Proinde rebus pressius & accuratius inspectis, dicimus hæc dona Dei non contemnenda, cùm plurimum faciant ad multa officia beatitudinis civilia bene rectè administranda: sed proram & puppim ibi ponere non oportet. Imò si quando his bonis careamus, haud propterea vera solidaq; felicitas quam sectamur aufertur. Atq; si ob Christi nomen & fidei eius confessionem, his fuerimus priuati, tantum abest vt vera beatitudo commaculetur, vt potius magis magisq; reddatur illustris. Primùm non obstare nobis paupertatem, liquet, cùm sanctorum non minima pars fuerit ex pauperib. conflata. Et Christus adolescenti iussit, vt sua diuenderet ac daret pauperibus, quem tamen indubitatò volebat felicem reddere, quod sanè minimè fieri potuisset. Quin etiam Antisthenes & Crates Thebanus, vt in suaphilosophia magis beati redderentur, pecunias suas ac thesauros abiecerūt. Et Dominus centuplum & æternam vitam pollicetur his qui sui causa omnia huius generis amiserint. De nobilitate quid dicemus ? Videte vocationem vestram, inquit Paulus, non multi sapientes, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles, &c. Defectus quoq; liberorum non obstat: nam Esa. 56. Eunuchi dicuntur habituri meliorem locum in domo Dei, non hoc nomine quòd eunuchi aut cælibes agant, sed quanto magis diligenter quàm cæteri mandata Dei servarint. Amicitia quoq; si desint, à vera felicitate non excludunt, cum aliquando usu venit, ut propter nomen Christi pij omnibus hominibus odiosi efficiantur. Quod tamen Aristoteli non aduersatur, cum de politica seu civili beatitudine scribat.
units.tr: Nor does Scripture disagree about the commendation of external goods. As for children, they are promised by God: "Your sons shall be like olive plants." Among the other blessings, this is counted, that there be no miscarriage in Israel. And throughout, abundance of seed is promised to those who fear God. The same can easily be recognised concerning riches. God enriched Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and his other friends. To Solomon, who had asked for wisdom, he freely granted riches as well. And he wished his people, if they conducted themselves well, to abound in riches, so that they would lend to other peoples and not borrow from them at interest. Nobility was so dear to the people of God that every family had its genealogies, by which they traced their ancestors to the heads of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel. And the priests in the time of Ezra, who could not do this, were removed from their place and rank. Indeed, the evangelists Luke and Matthew recounted the genealogy of Christ, lest he seem ignoble according to the flesh. And the Apostle, in Romans 9, describes the nobility of the Israelites: "Who are Israelites, to whom belong the adoption, the glory, the giving of the law, the covenant, the worship, and the promises, of whom are the fathers, and from whom is Christ, who is over all, etc." Earlier I showed that bodily form was granted to the first two kings, Saul and David; later we know that among the priests it was so required that no one lame, blind, hunchbacked, or marked by any notable deformity could exercise the priesthood. And that friendship might grow up among the Hebrews, God took care by his laws, which, when considered more closely, all greatly contribute to uniting people together. Therefore those things Aristotle mentioned should not be cast aside, yet as far as happiness goes one should not give them more than their due. It is said indeed in Ecclesiastes 10: "Money answers all things." But that saying is reported as received from the common people, not as true, and to censure human error. Indeed, the sacred letters elsewhere assert, namely in Proverbs 13: "What good are riches to a fool, since he cannot buy wisdom for himself?" Therefore, when matters are examined more closely and accurately, we say that these gifts of God are not to be despised, since they contribute greatly to the rightful and proper administration of many civil duties of happiness; but it is not right to place the prow and stern there. Indeed, if at any time we lack these goods, the true and solid happiness we pursue is not therefore taken away. And if we are deprived of them for the name of Christ and the confession of his faith, true blessedness is so far from being stained that it is rather made more and more illustrious. First, that poverty does not hinder us is clear, since no small part of the saints was made up of the poor. And Christ commanded the young man to sell his possessions and give to the poor, whom yet he undoubtedly wished to make happy, which certainly could not have happened. Indeed, Antisthenes and Crates of Thebes, that they might be made more blessed in their philosophy, cast away their money and treasures. And the Lord promises a hundredfold and eternal life to those who for his sake have lost all things of this kind. What shall we say about nobility? "Consider your calling," says Paul, "not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble, etc." The lack of children also does not stand in the way; for in Isaiah 56 eunuchs are said to be going to have a better place in the house of God, not on this account that eunuchs or unmarried men live as they do, but because they have kept the commandments of God more diligently than others. Friendship too, if it is lacking, does not exclude from true happiness, since it sometimes happens that, on account of the name of Christ, the godly become hateful to all men. Yet this does not conflict with Aristotle, since he writes about political or civil happiness.
CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Unde revocatur in dubium, an comparari possit, vel disciplina, vel consuetudine, vel alio quoquo modo, exercitatione, vel accedat juxta divinam quandam sortem, vel ex fortuna.
units.tr: Whence it is doubted whether happiness can be acquired by training, by habit, or by some other kind of practice, or whether it comes by a certain divine lot, or by fortune.

units.la: JAM cùm de felicitate luculenter sit actum quo ad ipsius naturam, de illius causa inquiritur. Caput distinguitur, quia primo narrat quae putari a nonnullis queant eius causae, atq; numero quinq; recenset. Deinde singillatim de his agit. Quinque hic annumeratae causae ad duo cogi possunt: nam aut interiores sunt aut externae. Interiores habentur, quod a nobis proficiscantur disciplina, consuetudo, & exercitium. Externae vero putantur, Deus & Fortuna. Inter consuetudinem & exercitium hoc interest, quia consuetudo refertur ad virtutes, quae crebris & frequentibus actionibus pariuntur. Exercitia vero, & labores, & industriae sunt adhibenda, ad divitias, ad honores, & ad valetudinem firmam consequendam & servandam: in quibus rebus nonnulli felicitatem, ut dictum est, collocarunt. Primum vero de disciplina, spectat eos qui virtutes existimarunt addisci doctrinis adhibitis. Unde si opus est disciplina, discendum esset: sin consuetudine, oportet non desistere a rectis actionibus: si exercitationi adscribatur, necesse est ut non parcatur laboribus. Si a Deo expectetur, orandus est. Sin vero a fortuna, cum circa ea nil possimus, ei utiq; totum erit permittendum. Stoici & praesertim Epictetus, distinguunt omnia quae reperiuntur, aut ἐφ' ἡμῖν aut οὐκ ἐφ' ἡμῖν. Per ea quae sunt in nobis, intelligunt quae possumus nostro consilio regere ac viribus assequi. Illa vero dicuntur οὐκ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, quae in potestate non habemus: ut, nobilitas, valetudo, divitiae.
units.tr: Now that we have spoken clearly about happiness with respect to its nature, we inquire into its cause. The chapter is divided, because first he sets out what some may think its causes are and enumerates five. Then he treats each one separately. The five causes listed here can be reduced to two, for they are either internal or external. Training, habit, and exercise are considered internal, because they come from us. God and Fortune are regarded as external. Habit and exercise differ in this way: habit refers to the virtues, which are produced by frequent and repeated actions. Exercise, labours, and diligence are applied to gain and keep riches, honours, and firm health, and in these things some, as has been said, have placed happiness. Now, as for training, it concerns those who have judged that the virtues are learned by the use of teaching. So if training is needed, one must learn; if habit, one must not give up right actions; if it is ascribed to exercise, one must not spare labour; if it is to be expected from God, one must pray; but if it is to be expected from fortune, since we can do nothing about such things, everything must be left entirely to her. The Stoics, and especially Epictetus, divide all things that are found into those that are ἐφ' ἡμῖν [in our power] and those that are οὐκ ἐφ' ἡμῖν [not in our power]. By the things that are in our power they understand those that we can govern by our own counsel and attain by our own strength. Those are called οὐκ ἐφ' ἡμῖν which we do not have in our power, such as nobility, health, and riches.

units.la: Si quid aliud est quod a Deo hominibus donetur, consentaneum est felicitatem quoque a Deo datam, & praesertim quanto rerum humanarum est optima. Sed hoc forte magis est proprium alterius tractationis.
units.tr: If anything else is given to men by God, it is consistent that happiness too is given by God, and especially since it is the best of human things. But this perhaps belongs more properly to another treatise.

units.la: A Deo auspicatur examen, ob eius quantum iudico dignitatem, verum de illo admodum perplexè loquitur atq; obscurè. Propositionem adducit hypotheticam, neq; absoluit argumentationem. Si quod, inquit, est donū Dei, felicitas ab illo dabitur. Et connexionis rationem monstrat, quod ipsa inter omnia humana potissimum locum habeat. Verum ad argumentum perficiendum duplex minor potest addi, una piorum est & nostra. Sed multa donantur hominibus a Deo, igitur ab eodem est felicitas expectanda. Multa vero dari hominibus a Deo, nos haudquaquam dubitamus qui prouidentiam eius de singulis quoq; rebus prædicamus, & cum ab eo vt a summo bono & fonte bonitatis, quicquid bonum est deriuetur, id citra eius arbitrium, voluntatem & electionem dimanare ne suspicamur quidem. At nō desunt alij & quidem Peripatetici qui de prouidentia Dei longe aliter suspicatur: nam putant, eius prouidentiam quo ad singularia non extendi nisi vsq; ad lunam, quia illuc vsq; omnia constanter & summo agantur ordine. Quo vero ad res inferiores, prouidentiam duntaxat ponunt quo ad genera, non quo ad singula. Quare illi pro minori propositione acciperent, Sed nulla dona ex Deo distribuuntur hominibus: igitur neq; felicitatem largitur. Hominibus autem a Deo minimè dari dona dicunt, non quòd illum non agnoscant primam causam efficientem, vnde omnia bona oriantur, sed vocem dandi aut donandi sumunt ex electione, voluntate ac iudicio libero. Bona quæ habemus & felicitatem fatebuntur a Deo pendere & a motu cœli, neque aliter posse haberi, at illa dari ab eo non sentiunt, certa distributione de qua cogitet, aut quam libera dispositione tribuat: nam Deum putant necessariò agere ac naturali impulsu. Quamobrè animadvertendum est eū hoc loco non affirmare neq; negare felicitatē dari a Deo. Non affirmat: quia inquit esse hoc negotium alterius facultatis, nempe metaphysici a quo tractatur de prouidentia Dei, sine qua doctrina quæstio hæc definiri non potest. Nec etiam negat illam a Deo dari, ne incidat in absurdum: videtur enim a ratione alienum, dona reliqua dari a Deo & felicitatem ab illo non dari. Ex conditione itaq; docet, si alia diuinitus habentur, & felicitas quoq; inde prouenit: at nil affirmat. Quàm vero in alterum locum tractationem hanc reiciat opportunè, haud video. Nam si pendet hæc definitio a prouidentia, nónne poterat a metaphysico interim tantum mutuare doctrinæ, quantum esset satis ad suam sententiam aperiendam? Hoc fecit de anima & a physico trantranstulit, quantum faciebat ad moralem doctrinam, & ait, animam, ut mox videbimus, habere diuersas partes. Itidem ut non probatum sed assumptum [?] scribere poterat, Deum prouidentia sua dare hominibus multa dona, quibus cum ipsa felicitas longe sit praestantior, eam quoq; inde spectare par esse: at hoc dissimulato praeterit, & ad aliam inquit spectare tractationem. At obsecro quisnam opportunior fuerat locus, cum de moribus & virtutibus hic sit agendum, quorum notitia ut a primo principio pendet omnino a cognitione felicitatis? Nunc fuit tempus de illa categorice affirmare, ut a Deo expectari non minus deberet quam cetera dona. Propterea dum sic loquitur, inuidiam conatur declinare impietatis, sed laudem non meretur aperta atq; candida confessionis. Si probe recte, sentiret, his ambagibus non erat utendum. Sed quid ille faceret? De voluntate Dei erga homines ex philosophia nil cognoscere potuit: nam quicquid de illa nouimus, id totum diuinis literis & praesertim Euangelio debemus.
units.tr: He begins the inquiry with God, because of God's dignity, as I judge, but he speaks of him very obscurely and ambiguously. He puts forward a hypothetical proposition and does not complete the argument. "If," he says, "there is any gift of God, happiness will be given by him." And he shows the connection of the reasoning, namely that happiness holds the chief place among all human things. But to complete the argument, a double minor premise can be added: one is that of the godly, and it is ours. "But many things are given to men by God; therefore happiness too is to be expected from the same source." That many things are given to men by God we do not doubt at all, we who proclaim his providence even in single things, and who do not even suspect that whatever is good flows from him as from the highest good and fountain of goodness without his judgement, will and choice. But there are others, and indeed Peripatetics, who think quite differently about the providence of God. For they think that his providence does not extend to individual things except as far as the moon, because all things there are carried on constantly and in the highest order. As for lower things, they posit providence only with respect to kinds, not to individuals. Therefore they would take as the minor premise: "But no gifts are distributed to men from God; therefore he does not bestow happiness either." They say that God does not give gifts to men, not because they fail to acknowledge him as the first efficient cause from which all good things arise, but because they take the word "to give" or "to bestow" from choice, will and free judgement. They will admit that the goods we have, and happiness, depend on God and on the motion of the heavens, and cannot be had otherwise; but they do not think that these are given by him by a fixed distribution about which he deliberates, or which he bestows by free disposition, for they think God acts necessarily and by natural impulse. Hence it must be noted that in this place he neither affirms nor denies that happiness is given by God. He does not affirm it, because he says that this matter belongs to another discipline, namely metaphysics, which treats of the providence of God, without which this question cannot be settled by doctrine. Nor does he deny that it is given by God, lest he fall into absurdity: for it seems alien to reason that the other gifts are given by God and happiness is not. So he teaches on condition: if other things are had by divine gift, happiness too comes from there; but he affirms nothing. How opportunely he rejects this treatment to another place, I do not see. For if this definition depends on providence, could he not in the meantime borrow from the metaphysician only as much doctrine as was enough to make his own opinion clear? He did this concerning the soul, and he transferred from the physicist as much as served moral doctrine, and says that the soul, as we shall soon see, has different parts. Likewise he could have written, without proving but assuming [?], that God by his providence gives men many gifts, and since happiness is far more excellent than these, it is fitting that it too be looked for from there. But he passes over this by dissembling, and says that it belongs to another treatise. But I beg you, what place could have been more fitting, since morals and virtues are to be treated here, whose knowledge, as it depends on the first principle, depends entirely on knowledge of happiness? Now was the time to affirm this categorically, that it ought to be expected from God no less than the other gifts. Therefore, while he speaks in this way, he tries to avoid the odium of impiety, but he does not deserve the praise of an open and candid confession. If he had felt rightly, he would not have needed these circumlocutions. But what could he do? He could know nothing from philosophy about the will of God towards men, for whatever we know about it, we owe entirely to the divine letters, and especially to the Gospel.

units.la: Videtur autem ut a Deo non mittatur, sed ex uirtute aut doctrina quada aut exercitatione accedat, res esse maxime diuina: nam praemium uirtutis & finis, optimum, diuinum, & beatum uidetur.
units.tr: It seems, however, that it is not sent from God but comes from virtue or some kind of teaching or practice, and that it is a most divine thing, since the reward of virtue and its end seem best, divine, and blessed.

units.la: Cum a Deo felicitatem proficisci propemodum negarit, quia id fateri non luit, hoc saltem dat, eam esse rem maxime diuinam, id est perfectissimam, qua Deus quoque fruatur: is enim tametsi non ut homines, tamen sua quadam certa ratione beatus est. Hic Eustrathius de suo adiecit, Deum felicitatem elargiri, at non sine commemoratis mediis, doctrina, inquam, consuetudine, ac exercitio. Et certe a Deo nobis quaedam concediuntur, citra vllum nostrum laborem & studium. Quid enim quisquam vnquam laborauit ut ingeniosus nasceretur, nobilis, aut firmo corpore, ac aequabili temperamento? certe nullus. Alia vero sic dat Deus, ut quibusdam mediis ad ea perueniamus. Sed est diligenter attendendum, si pie ac religiose velimus rem putare, ab ipso eodem Deo media nobis attribui: nemo quippe ad sanam doctrinam, nemo ad consuetudinem bonam, nemo ad exercitationem vtilem promouebitur capessendam, nisi diuino agatur impulsu. Verum ad Aristotelem redeamus. Non tantū felicitas, verum etiam honor praemiū ponitur virtutis. At honor est praemii externum, neq; situ est in eo qui afficitur honore, sed in honorante. Beatitudo praemium est internum, & in homine virtute praedito haret, neq; à virtute vel eius actione diuellitur. Rem diuinam beatitudinē
units.tr: Since he almost denies that happiness proceeds from God, because he was unwilling to confess it, he at least grants this, that it is a most divine thing, that is, most perfect, and one which God also enjoys: for God, although not as men are, is nevertheless blessed in his own certain way. Here Eustrathius added on his own that God bestows happiness, but not without the means mentioned: teaching, I mean, habit, and exercise. And certainly some things are granted to us by God without any labour or effort of ours. For who ever laboured to be born clever, noble, or with a strong body and an even temperament? Certainly no one. But God gives other things in such a way that we arrive at them by certain means. But we must attend carefully: if we wish to think the matter piously and religiously, the means are assigned to us by God himself, for no one will be advanced to sound doctrine, no one to good habits, no one to useful exercise, unless he is driven by divine impulse. But let us return to Aristotle. Not only happiness but also honour is set as the reward of virtue. But honour is external to the reward; it lies not in the one who is honoured but in the one who honours. Blessedness is an internal reward, and it clings to the man endowed with virtue, nor is it torn away from virtue or its activity. He calls blessedness a divine thing

units.la: ideò profert: quia præmium est virtutis ac eius finis: præmium verò & finē præstantiora esse his liquet, quibus redduntur. At cùm in rebus humanis quicquam non sit virtute præstantius aut melius, beatitudinem, superesse aliquid esse diuinum. Et quemadmodum intelligentia, sic quoq; illa perfectione homines Deum ipsum attingere videntur.
units.tr: therefore: because it is the reward and end of virtue; and it is clear that the reward and end are more excellent than the things to which they are given. But since in human affairs nothing is more excellent or better than virtue, it follows that blessedness is something divine, existing beyond. And just as understanding, so also by this perfection men seem to touch God himself.

units.la: Cur autem virtuti propositum sit præmium, facile fuerit videre, quòd res paratu sit laboriosa: propterea ne difficultate homines ab illa deterrean-tur, adeò nobili ac eximio præmio allicunt[?]. Sed hic ab Aristotele scire velim, quis nam fuerit ἄλλοτις[?], qui beatitudinis præmium ac finem hominibus proposuerit, qui virtutem ac probitatem sectentur: non sanè potest alius responderi atq; Deus. Id quoq; ipse non negabit. Cur ergo tam cunctabatur dare felicitatem à Deo expectandam? Quia (diceret) ut ut videam sic rerum naturam à Deo institutam, ut certa quadam connexione, felicitas virtutes comitetur, ut lux Solem, ut umbram corpus, ut calor ignem nunquam deserit: Nihilominus id mihi de singulis hominibus non constat, an à Deo impellantur incitenturq; ad virtutes consequendas, & ad beatitudinē obtinendam, & quia id video fieri doctrina, consuetudine ac exercitatione, ideò nolui diserte affirmare beatitudinem à Deo mortalibus mitti. Et hæc porrò causa est, cur in definitione felicitatis, nullam Dei mentionem fecit, dixit solum actionem esse animi præstantissimam à perfectissima virtute deriuatam. Plato verò in Timæo cum de philosophia loqueretur, inquit, ὁ μέιζον ἀγαθὸν ἔποτ' ἐλθεῖν εἰδ' ἔξει[?] [?]δντῶ γένεσ ἐκ θεῶν[?]. At hoc naturalis rationis ductu non dixit, nec physica κατ' ὀδέξει[?] vsus, verum probabili argumento: & quia peregrinando in Aegypto multa fortassis cognouerat veræ solidæq; religionis arcana. Sed Aristoteles, qui tantum humanæ rationis vim atq; acumen sequitur, tria quæ iam commemorauimus, beatitudinis causas facit. Quæ tamen non dicit sufficere: nam & alia quoq; requiruntur, oportet enim & integras nancisci cum animi tum corporis vires, vt mox declarabitur.
units.tr: Why a reward has been set before virtue, it will be easy to see: the thing is laborious to attain, so that lest men be deterred by the difficulty, they are enticed by so noble and outstanding a reward. But here I would like to learn from Aristotle who it was (ἄλλοτις?) who set before men the reward and end of blessedness, namely those who pursue virtue and uprightness: certainly no one else can be named than God. He too will not deny this. Why then did he hesitate so much to say that happiness is to be expected from God? Because (he would say), although I see that the nature of things has been established by God in such a way that happiness accompanies the virtues by a certain connection, as light accompanies the sun, shadow the body, and heat never leaves fire, nevertheless it is not clear to me in the case of individual men whether they are impelled and incited by God to attain the virtues and to obtain blessedness; and since I see this come about through teaching, habit, and exercise, I was unwilling to affirm plainly that blessedness is sent to mortals by God. And this is also the reason why, in his definition of happiness, he made no mention of God, saying only that it is the most excellent activity of the soul, derived from perfect virtue. But Plato in the Timaeus, when speaking of philosophy, says: ὁ μέιζον ἀγαθὸν ἔποτ' ἐλθεῖν εἰδ' ἔξει... [that the greatest good has come to men from the gods]. But he did not say this by the guidance of natural reason, nor using physical argument, but by a probable argument; and perhaps because in his wanderings in Egypt he had learned many secrets of true and solid religion. But Aristotle, who follows only the power and keenness of human reason, makes the three things we have just mentioned the causes of blessedness. Yet he does not say that these suffice, for other things are also required: it is necessary to obtain whole strength both of mind and of body, as will be shown presently.

units.la: Atque communis multis fuerit: nam doctrina diligentiaq; poterit ab his omnibus comparari, qui manci non fuerint, ad virtutem capessendam.
units.tr: And it will be common to many

units.la: Si felicitas habet illa tria pro causis ac certis principijs, facile poterit communis esse multis: illi enim tantum excipiendi erunt, qui capti, debiles aut manci nascuntur, et ob id ad felicitatem nequeunt pervenire. Nonnulli enim sunt qui stulti & malo temperamento corporis nascuntur, & propterea non possunt bonas artes & literas addiscere, surdi, muti, aut magnis doloribus ac debilitate summa fracti, neque ad exercitia neq; ad rectos mores sibi comparandos sunt idonei. Doctrina autem non ob morales virtutes admittitur, sed propter contemplantes facultates atque scientias, in quibus felicitas maxima ex parte sita est. Et quia dicitur felicitas communis pluri-bus, adduntur auditoribus ac lectoribus animi, ut putent si ab illa excide-rint id sibi imputandum: qui discere, assuescere bonis actionibus, & exerce-ri laboriosè noluerint.
units.tr: If happiness has those three as causes and certain principles, it can easily be common to many: only those will be excluded who are born captive, weak or maimed, and for that reason cannot attain happiness. For some are born foolish and with a bad bodily temperament, and therefore cannot learn good arts and letters; deaf, mute, or broken by great pains or extreme debility, they are fit neither for exercises nor for acquiring upright morals. Teaching, however, is admitted not for the sake of moral virtues but on account of the contemplative faculties and sciences, in which happiness mostly lies. And because happiness is said to be common to many, reminders are added for hearers and readers, so that they may think that if they have fallen from it, this is to be imputed to themselves: those who were unwilling to learn, to accustom themselves to good actions, and to exercise themselves laboriously.

units.la: Flacuit hæc sententia Pelagianis, qui iustitiam & regnum cœleste in viribus hominum posuere. Scholastici etiam placuit: nam ut Pelagiani gratiam inficiabantur, & naturam aiebant sufficere, ita isti nomine gratiam statuentes, re ipsa eam sustulerunt, ut qui eam communem ac omnibus expositam fecerunt, tanquam sit cuiusq; illam seu recipere seu à se depellere: cumq; rogantur quis det illam acceptantibus, ut ipsam expectant et oblatà capiant, ad liberum arbitrium confugiunt. Atq; horum omnium antefigna-nus est Pighius. Quamobrem si vel ab Aristotele, vel ab his quæras, cum fe-licitas ita fit, ut dicitis, communis, qui fit, ut eam tā pauci obtineant? Quoniam inquient, pauci volunt discere, pauci laborare, pauci rectis actionibus & sanctis assuescere. At nos hic notemus communem certamq; propositio-nem; Cuilibet naturæ seu speciei propositam esse finem, quam omnes in ea co-[?]prehensi possent assequi. Et sane quod Aristoteles de captis, mancis & debi-libus responderet, interrogatus cur ipsi non possent felicitatis participes ef-se, nempe ob ipsorum defectum naturale, quod sua propositio intelligatur, quando vires integræ fuerint: ita nos respondemus: homines modo per seipsos non posse beatos esse, quoniam ab ipsa origine vitiata fuit natura, neq; habemus vires tam animi quam corporis integras. Proinde cum modo hæc audimus, putemus nos Aristotelem, non Paulum aut Christum audire. Tria iambic, ut vocant, prædicata felicitatis habemus. Res est divina, Obtineri potest tribus iam commemoratis principijs, & Omnibus propemodum est communis.
units.tr: This opinion pleased the Pelagians, who placed justice and the heavenly kingdom in the powers of men. It also pleased the Scholastics: for as the Pelagians denied grace and said that nature suffices, so these, while setting up grace in name, in fact took it away, since they made it common and exposed to all, as if it were each person's to receive or to repel from himself. When they are asked who gives it to those who accept it, so that they wait for it and take it when offered, they flee to free will. And the standard-bearer of all these is Pighius. Therefore if you ask either Aristotle or these men, since happiness is, as you say, common, how is it that so few obtain it? They will answer: because few wish to learn, few to labour, few to accustom themselves to right and holy actions. But here let us note a common and certain proposition: for every nature or species an end is set which all comprised in it could attain. And indeed, what Aristotle answered about the captive, maimed, and weak, when asked why they could not share in happiness, namely on account of their natural defect, which his proposition understands when their powers are whole, that is how we answer: men cannot now be blessed by themselves, since nature was vitiated from its very origin, and we have neither mind nor body whole. Therefore when we hear these things, let us think that we are hearing Aristotle, not Paul or Christ. We have three so-called predicates of happiness: it is a divine thing; it can be obtained by the three principles already mentioned; and it is common to almost all.

units.la: Quod si melius est hoc modo quam ex fortuna beatum fieri, rem sic habere consentaneum est: nam quæ secundum naturam fiunt, optimè quàm possunt fiunt,nec non quæ ab arte & omni causa, præsertim optima.
units.tr: But if it is better in this way than for happiness to come about by fortune, it is consistent that things are so: for things that happen according to nature happen as well as they can, and likewise those that come from art and every cause, especially the best.

units.la: Fortuna restabat, quam his verbis à causis felicitatis remouet: hoc porrò nomine, quòd indigna sit quæ ad tantum munus prodendum mortalibus adsciscatur. Conabor autem, priusquam rationem ab Aristotele allatā expediam, quid nam fortuna sit aperire. Ut secundo physicorum scribitur, causa est per accidens, atq; tum se interponit, vel quando aliquid cuipiam adjungitur, qui verè author est effectus consequentis, ad quem effectum producendum id quod adjunctum est, nil efficit, sed tantum aliquando præbet occasionem, & absque illo posset effectus provenire. Hoc similitudine patefit. Si per febrim quis temperatus efficiatur, id fortuito evenisse dicemus. Est enim ut à causa propria temperantia ex voluntate, quæ frenet cupiditatis affectum: febris ut id fiat, occasio esse potuit, causa esse non potuit: & quia fortuito concurrunt hæc in eodem homine, voluntas agendi temperanter & febris, ideo ex febri temperantia oritur fortuito. Satis autem liquet febrim temperantia per se non esse causam, alioqui omnes febricantes evaderent temperati. Ad hanc dicendi rationem examinari & accipi debet Pauli sententia, Scientia inflat: fastus ex voluntate prodit quæ nostra præfert immodicè alienis: hinc inanes evadimus, & tumidi. Et quia id ut fiat, nonnullis occasionem scientia præbet, ideo illa, sed ex fortuna, dicitur inflare. Quia in eodem homine fortuito hæc duo junguntur, appetitus vincendi & excedendi cæteros, & rerum aliqua scientia: utque ista temerè junguntur, sic tumor inanis fortuito progreditur à scientia. Fit item quum illi effectui, quem per seipsum ac nostro consilio expetimus, aliquis alius temerè cohæret: is enim tum ex fortuna provenit, non ex proposito, quum nos revera quippiam aliud quæreremus. Ut aliquibus nonnunquam fossoribus, qui tantum vinearum aut arborum cultui studebant, occurrit in laborando thesaurus, hoc, inquam, ex fortuna evenit, quum fossor aliud quaesivisset. Neque fossio propria veraque causa est inveniendi thesauri: nam id si quis statuat, idem necesse habebit, omnes fossores ponere thesaurorum repertores. Accedit præterea, omnes fortuitos effectus raro admodum evenire, idque contrà quàm fiat in veris ac proprijs causis, quæ haud frequenter impediuntur à suis producendis effectibus. Quæ quum ita sint, apparet, & quidem manifeste, fortunam cum ratione atq; consilio pugnare. Unde non est fas illi productionem felicitatis attribuere. Ita concludit Aristoteles, cum felicitas melius deriuetur ex iam commemoratis causis, quàm ex fortuna, consentaneum est ut sic esse atq; habere constituatur: quia debet optimo quàm possit modo effici: natura enim ita consueuit, quae parit melior modo & ratione quàm possit facere. Ac inde illa oritur admiratio in naturalibus rebus, quia summam animaduertimus industriam adhibitam à natura, ut res optimis rationibus & modis à fe prodirent, quod identidem in omnibus artibus agnoscitur: nam faber id elaborat, ut suum opus quàm optimum exeat. Nec non id sibi qualibet causa pro viribus vindicat: neque id mirum, quandoquidem, ut ab initio dictum est, omnis ars & facultas & causa bonum expetunt, quifit ut quo melior est causa, eo ad praftantiorem tendat effectum. Merito itaq; subdit Ariftoteles, praesertim quae optima fuerit, hoc de virtute, seu anima rationis participe intelligens, quas felicitatis ponit causas. Etenim fi aliae causae id agunt, et ibi sunt ut modo quàm optimo sua faciant, maximè de virtute ac hominis animo credendum est.
units.tr: Fortune remained, which he removes from the causes of happiness in these words: moreover, on the ground that it is unworthy to be employed for bestowing so great a gift on mortals. Before I explain the reasoning brought forward by Aristotle, I shall try to make clear what fortune is. As is written in the second book of the Physics, it is a cause per accidens, and it intervenes when something is joined to someone who is truly the author of the consequent effect; and the thing joined does nothing to produce that effect, but only sometimes provides an occasion, and the effect could come about without it. This is made clear by a comparison. If someone becomes temperate through a fever, we will say this happened by chance. For proper temperance arises from the will, which restrains the affection of desire; the fever may be an occasion for this to happen, but it cannot be the cause; and because these two come together by chance in the same man, the will to act temperately and the fever, temperance therefore arises from the fever by chance. And it is clear enough that fever is not in itself the cause of temperance, otherwise all feverish people would turn out temperate. By this mode of speaking should be examined and received the saying of Paul: knowledge puffs up. Pride comes from the will, which excessively prefers its own things to others'; hence we become empty and swollen. And because knowledge provides an occasion for this to happen to some, it is said to puff up, but by fortune. Because in the same man these two come together by chance, the appetite to conquer and surpass others, and some knowledge of things; and just as these are joined at random, so empty swelling proceeds from knowledge by chance. It also happens when some other thing casually adheres to that effect which we seek of ourselves and by our own counsel; for that then comes from fortune, not from purpose, when we were really seeking something else. As sometimes to some diggers, who were studying only the cultivation of vineyards or trees, a treasure turns up in their labour: this, I say, happens by fortune, when the digger had sought something else. Nor is digging the proper and true cause of finding treasure; for if someone should maintain this, he would necessarily have to hold that all diggers are finders of treasure. Moreover, all fortuitous effects happen very rarely, and this is contrary to what happens with true and proper causes, which are not often hindered from producing their effects. These things being so, it appears, and indeed plainly, that fortune fights against reason and counsel; whence it is not right to attribute to it the production of happiness. Thus Aristotle concludes: since happiness is better derived from the causes already mentioned than from fortune, it is consistent to establish that it is and ought to be so, because it ought to be brought about in the best way possible; for nature is accustomed to produce what it brings forth in a better way and by better reason than it could make. And from this arises that admiration in natural things, because we notice the greatest diligence applied by nature, so that things come forth from it by the best reasons and methods; which is recognised again and again in all the arts, for the craftsman labours so that his work comes out as good as possible. Likewise every cause claims this for itself as far as its powers allow, and this is not surprising, since, as was said at the beginning, every art, faculty, and cause seeks the good, so that the better the cause, the more it tends toward a more excellent effect. Rightly therefore Aristotle adds "especially the best," understanding this of virtue, or of the soul sharing in reason, which he posits as the causes of happiness. For if other causes do this, and are there so that they make their works as well as possible, it must be believed most of all of virtue and of the human mind.

units.la: Neq; ratione caret, quod inquit Consentaneum. Quia eo verbo indicat rationem suam non ἀπόδειξιν[?], sed probabilem esse rationem: ut enim facile videmus, à minori ad maius est illius probatio. Si cetera causae atque principia conantur res quàm praestantissimas edere, cur non id etiam de virtute atq; intelligenti animo existimemus? Vt autem natura folerter summa-que industria in suis operibus procedat, ipse Ariftoteles docet de partibus animalium. Theophraftus de partibus plantarum, Plinius de historia naturali, sed prae omnibus Galenus in libro de vtilitate partium. Quod fi omnia facit natura tanto ordine tamq; accuratè ac frequentissimè agit eodem modo, non raro & in paucissimis, fortuitae illius actiones vocari non possunt. Ars quoq; naturam imitatur, ad quam vt non perveniat, ratione tamen agit & magna industria: constat enim multis praeceptis. At nemo ignorat nō opus esse praeceptis ad fortuitas actiones: quare non casu agunt, qui artificiosè quippiam elaborant. Alia quoq; causae, illae praesertim quae bonarum rerum sunt authores, prout nobiles ac praestantes habent effectus, etiam ipsae praeclarae sunt & insignes.
units.tr: It is not without reason that he says "consentaneum" (reasonable). By that word he indicates that his argument is not a demonstration [ἀπόδειξιν] but a probable reasoning, for, as we easily see, the proof proceeds from the lesser to the greater. If other causes and principles strive to produce the most excellent things possible, why should we not think the same of virtue and the intelligent soul? That nature proceeds skilfully and with the greatest diligence in her works, Aristotle himself teaches in his book on the parts of animals; Theophrastus in his book on the parts of plants; Pliny in his Natural History; but above all Galen in his book On the Usefulness of the Parts. And if nature does all things in such a well-ordered and exact way, and acts so frequently in the same manner, and often even in the smallest matters, her actions cannot be called fortuitous. Art also imitates nature, and although it does not reach nature's level, it nevertheless acts by reason and great industry, for it rests on many precepts. But no one is ignorant that precepts are not needed for fortuitous actions; therefore those who carefully work out something do not act by chance. Other causes too, especially those which are the authors of good things, are themselves also distinguished and remarkable insofar as they have noble and excellent effects.
The reasoning on which Aristotle rests is explained as follows:

units.la: Summum bonum in causam vilem & abiectam referri non debet.
units.tr: The highest good should not be referred to a base and abject cause.

units.la: Felicitas est summum bonum, & fortuna inter causas ignobilis.
units.tr: Happiness is the highest good, and fortune is an ignoble cause.

units.la: Quare beatitudo non debet in fortunam, indigniorem causam ceteris, reduci.
units.tr: Therefore blessedness should not be referred to fortune, a cause less worthy than the others.

units.la: Atq; argumenti huius vis ex eo pendet, quia tamctsi nobilis causa interdum vilem producat effectum, quemadmodum scimus Solem non tantu gignere hominem, sed etiam ranas, pulices, & muscas: attamen præclara esse-cta non queunt nisi à causis eximijs proficisci. Hic videmus ut disertis & a-pertissimis uerbis Aristoteles explodat fortunam, ut qui nolit eam inter cau-sas felicitatis commemorare: atq; mutuo sumit propositiones cum ex physi-cis tum ex prima philosophia: quod sanè idem facere poterat asserendo De-um beatitudinis humanæ causam. Ablegauit igitur & Deum & for-tunam ab hoc munere, Deum quidem ut nimis dignum & excelsum. For-tunam verò ut indignam & viliorem causam: inconstantissima enim res est, neq; vllam habet [illegible, ~9 letters]. Quæ tamen sic excluditur, ut circa natu-ræ et essentiam felicitatis nil faciat, at indubitatò aliquid potest in ea bona quæ iuuant felicitatem, & eius instrumenta sunt. Quod si potest in diuitias & honores & consimilia, quæ ut dictum est, ad beatitudinem haud parum faciunt, quare illius causam esse negant? Fatemur quidem ista explere at-que felicitati inseruire, & ita inseruire, ut abs illis nõ sit: at illam proprie facere pernegamus. Nõ enim ut defectus harum rerum queunt beatitudinem im-pedire, ita si adfuerint, illam præstant & efficiunt. Siquidem permultos vi-deris nobiles, diuites, robustos & in honoribus, quos tamen, cum prauisint, felices minimè dixeris: quod porrò non eueniret si hæc felicitatis essent per se causæ. Verum si bona eiusmodi subducantur probis & sapientibus, illos fe-lices esse non sinunt, quamuis (ut dictum est) ipsa beatitudinis causæ non sint. Quod si quæras an à fortuna quoq; proveniat corporis bona, facilè ne-gauerim: quoniam fortuna ex illis causis perhibetur, quæ ut raro & infre-quenter agunt. Vix enim intra centum annos contingit, ut fossor vinearum aut arator incidat in thesaurum: at frequentissimè datur nascentibus homi-nibus, ut temperamentum corporis tolerabile sortiantur, membraq; dentur integra, & vires idoneæ ad res agendas.
units.tr: The force of this argument depends on the fact that, although a noble cause sometimes produces a base effect, as we know the sun begets not only man but also frogs, fleas and flies, nevertheless excellent effects cannot come forth except from outstanding causes. Here we see how Aristotle, in plain and very clear words, rejects fortune, since he does not want it counted among the causes of happiness; and he borrows his propositions both from natural philosophy and from first philosophy, which he could certainly have done in asserting God to be the cause of human blessedness. He therefore banished both God and fortune from this office: God, indeed, as too worthy and exalted; fortune as an unworthy and baser cause, for it is a most inconstant thing and has no [illegible, about nine letters]. Yet it is excluded in such a way that it does nothing regarding the nature and essence of happiness, but undoubtedly it can do something with those goods which help happiness and are its instruments. But if it can do so with riches, honours and similar things, which, as has been said, contribute no little to blessedness, why do they deny that it is the cause of these? We grant that these things fulfil and serve happiness, and serve it in such a way that it does not exist without them; but we flatly deny that they properly produce it. For the lack of these things cannot hinder blessedness, and their presence does not bring it about and effect it. Indeed you may see many people who are noble, rich, strong and honoured, whom, when they are wicked, you would by no means call happy; which would not happen if these things were per se causes of happiness. But if such goods are taken away from the good and wise, they do not allow them to be happy, although (as said) they are not the causes of blessedness itself. But if you ask whether bodily goods also come from fortune, I would readily deny it, since fortune is ascribed to those causes which act rarely and infrequently. For scarcely within a hundred years does it happen that a vinedresser or ploughman stumbles upon a treasure; but it is very frequently given to people at birth to receive a tolerable constitution of body, sound limbs, and strength fit for doing things.

units.la: Quod vero maximum atque pulcherrimum est fortunæ permittere, oppido absurdum fuerit.
units.tr: But to entrust to fortune what is greatest and most beautiful would be frankly absurd.

units.la: His verbis minor iam allatæ rationis propositio explicatur, nempe felicitatem esse bonum summum & fortunam ignobilem causam esse. Vox autem Græca πλημμελὲς[?] inconcinnum significat, inconditum, dissonans aut discrepans.
units.tr: By these words the minor premise of the reasoning already given is explained, namely that happiness is the highest good and fortune a base cause. The Greek word πλημμελὲς [plemmeles] means ill-fitting, disordered, dissonant or discordant.

units.la: Quodcq;[?] modo quæritur, ex ipsa quoq; definitione planum est: nam dictum fuit actionem quandam esse secundum virtutem. Quod nunc adducitur, argumentum est multò firmius, nempe à definitione beatitudinis desumptum: & sensus est, Quia felicitas animi actio est, et non vulgaris, à fortuna expectari non debet, siquidem alia est animorum virtutis, natura quàm sit fortuna. Non aut absolutè ait beatitudinem esse animae actionem, sed certam quandam adiecit, nempè absolutissimam & perfectissimā, quandoquidē ab optima virtute proficiscatur. Vis argumenti ex eo pendet, quod neq; animus humanus neq; virtus fortuitò agant.
units.tr: The question just raised is also plain from the definition itself, for it was said that happiness is a certain activity according to virtue. What is now adduced is a much firmer argument, namely one drawn from the definition of blessedness; and the sense is: since happiness is an activity of the soul, and not a common one, it ought not to be expected from fortune, since the nature of the virtue of souls is other than that of fortune. He does not say absolutely that blessedness is an activity of the soul, but adds a certain qualification, namely the most complete and perfect, since it proceeds from the best virtue. The force of the argument depends on the fact that neither the human soul nor virtue acts by chance.

units.la: Ex reliquis autem bonis haec necessario insunt, haec vero adiuuant & utilia sunt quasi instrumenta.
units.tr: Of the other goods, some are necessarily present in happiness, while others help and are useful as instruments.

units.la: Per occupationem proculdubio ista dicuntur. Dixerit enim aliquis, Cùm statuas felicitatem actionem esse animi perfectissimam, quae deriuetur ex praestantissima virtute, quid in cosortium eius aduocasti cætera bona, si natura & definitio beatitudinis ex illis non constat, quare tandē adiunguntur? Tacitè huic obiectioni respondet, Quia si loquaris de corporis bonis, ut recta valetudo est, sensuum integritas et commodum temperamentum, necessaria sunt, et requiruntur ad beatitudinē, ac ita requiruntur ut absq; his nemo felix aut haberi aut esse possit. Vnde superius à felicitate illi sunt exclu-si, qui capti essent uiribus, aut manci vel debilitati. Externa vero bona exi-guntur ut utilia, & ceu instrumenta quaedam, ut per haec elicere possimus ex virtutibus honestas actiones, non tamen inde fit, ista vel ad naturam uel ad essentiam beatitudinis pertinere.
