Quemadmodum fabrilis ars, necessa-rio exigit vires, malleos & incudem, & absq; his nil à fabro ex arte sua po-test fieri. Quis tamen dixerit artem illam esse malleos, incudem et vires? nullus meo iudicio qui sapiat: valent haec multum ad naturam seu definitionē humanae felicitatis intelligendam.
units.tr: Those goods are doubtless called these by way of anticipation. Someone might object: since you hold that happiness is the most perfect activity of the soul, arising from the most excellent virtue, why have you brought in the other goods as its companions, if the nature and definition of happiness does not consist in them? He answers this objection tacitly. If you speak of goods of the body, such as good health, soundness of the senses and a well-balanced temperament, these are necessary and required for happiness, and they are required in such a way that no one can be or be thought happy without them. Hence earlier he excluded from happiness those who are maimed by their limbs, or crippled or weakened. External goods are required as useful, and as certain instruments, so that through them we may bring forth virtuous actions from the virtues. Yet it does not follow from this that these things belong either to the nature or to the essence of happiness. Just as the craft of the smith necessarily requires strength, hammers and an anvil, and without these the smith can do nothing by his craft, yet who would say that the craft is the hammers, the anvil and the strength? No one of sound judgment, in my opinion. These things count for much in understanding the nature or definition of human happiness.

units.la: Consentanea haec fuerint his quae ab initio diximus. Etenim posuimus optimum esse facultatis ciuilis finem. Ea vero maximam diligentiam adhibet, ut ciues aliqua praecipua qualitate ornet, bonos faciat, & honestarum rerum effectores.
units.tr: These things will agree with what we said at the beginning. For we laid down that the best end of civil science is... The civil science applies the greatest diligence so that it adorns citizens with some outstanding quality, makes them good, and makes them doers of honourable deeds.

units.la: Rursus confirmat felicitatem ex fortuna non esse: quoniam ab initio dixerat, summum hominis bonum finem esse ciuilis facultatis. Nemini vero est dubium illam nō agere casu aut fortuito. Optimū finē hominis ad eā facul-tatem pertinere probat ex eo quia in eo plurimū laborat ciuilis virtus, vt bonos reddat ciues. Quare si diligentia vtitur, fortuito agere dici non potest. Consilium enim, industria & diligentia cum fortuna oppido pugnant. Studet vero ciuilis ars bonos reddere ciues, & optimis conditionib. ac qualitatibus insignes: primum, bonas leges ferendo: postea, earum custodes atq; fideles obseruatores honoribus ac praemijs afficiendo, è diuerso transgressores puniendo ac deprimendo. Sunt itaq; ciuilis virtutis geminae partes, Una est bonas promulgare leges: Altera illis rempub. gerere atque administra-re. Quas duas partes Plato duobus & attigit, & eleganter absoluit libris, nempe de legibus & repub. Ex isto quoq; loco habetur, magistratus (cum enim ciuilis facultatis meminit, de eo loquitur) praecipuum munus id esse, vt ciues bonos faciat. Est sane aliquid subditos ditare: fines imperij amplia-re, moenibus & propugnaculis urbem munire: sed quod in magistratu maxime omnium conuenit, est, vt bonos ciues faciat. Quare admoti ad reip. gubernacula, nil a sua cura putare debent alienum quod huc spectet. Neq; vt nonnulli faciunt, religionum puram castamq; obseruationem, extra su-um officium positam arbitrantur. Atq; hoc cum ita sit, illi prudenter sen-tiunt, qui magistratus & ministrorum ecclesiae summam coniunctionem, salutarem esse Rebus publicis iudicat. Unde alioquin ij qui praesunt rebus, melius gubernandi viam & modum haurient? a quibus alijs regulas crediti sibi muneris habere poterunt? per quos aptius quae praecipiunt recte atque honeste populo suadebunt? Et denique unde melius quam ex diuinis oraculis earum rerum quas decernunt rationes reddent? Porro cum se a subditis ea requirere ostendent, quae diuinis verbis congruant, plebi pie instituta perse-[?]cto satisfecerint. Verum ad Aristotelem redeo, qui robuste conficit, beatitu-dinem a fortuna non expectandam, cum a virtute ciuili seu magistratibus oriatur, qui ratione, consilio, grauiq; deliberatione sua faciunt atque statu-unt, cum è diuerso fortuna, sine consilio, absq; ratione, ac mente quae facit a-gere perhibeatur. Neq; leuiter praetereunda sententia, quae hinc elicitur, Graue testimonium esse veritatis, quando posterius dicta prioribus consentiunt: nam dicit Aristoteles, quod modo fortuna a causis felicitatis remoueat, his pul-chre congruere, quae iam inde ab initio libri tradiderat. Quare his qui aliquod argumentum tractant, aut disputant, aut causam dicunt, id magno-pere cauendum est, ne secum dicendo pugnent. Itaq; nec bouem nec equum neq; ullum aliud animal beatum esse dicimus, quod eiusmodi actionis particeps esse nequeat.
units.tr: Again he confirms that happiness does not come from fortune, since at the beginning he had said that the highest good of man is the end of civil science. No one doubts that this science does not act by chance or accident. He proves that the best end of man belongs to this science because civil virtue labours most in this, to make citizens good. So if it uses diligence, it cannot be said to act by fortune. For counsel, industry and diligence fight hard against fortune. Civil science strives to make citizens good and distinguished by the best conditions and qualities: first, by enacting good laws; afterwards, by honouring and rewarding their guardians and faithful observers, and on the other hand by punishing and degrading transgressors. Civil virtue therefore has two parts. One is to promulgate good laws; the other is to conduct and administer the commonwealth by them. Plato touched on these two parts and treated them elegantly in two books, namely the Laws and the Republic. From this passage it is also held that the chief duty of the magistrate (for when he speaks of civil science, he is speaking of him) is to make citizens good. It is certainly something to enrich the subjects, to extend the boundaries of the realm, and to fortify the city with walls and bulwarks; but what above all befits the magistrate is that he make citizens good. Therefore those who are placed at the helm of the commonwealth ought to think nothing foreign to their care that bears on this. Nor, as some do, should they regard the pure and chaste observance of religion as lying outside their office. Since this is so, those are wise who judge that a close union of the magistrates and the ministers of the Church is salutary for commonwealths. For otherwise, from whom would those who govern draw the way and manner of governing better? From whom could they have rules for the office entrusted to them? Through whom would they more fittingly and rightly persuade the people of what they prescribe as honourable? And finally, from where would they render better reasons for the things they decree than from the divine oracles? Moreover, when they show that they require from their subjects things that agree with the divine words, they will have satisfied the people by duly instituting them in piety. But to return to Aristotle, who vigorously argues that happiness is not to be expected from fortune, since it arises from civil virtue, that is, from the magistrates, who act and decide by reason, counsel and serious deliberation; whereas fortune is said to act without counsel, without reason and without the mind that makes things. A sentence that follows from this must not be passed over lightly: that it is a weighty testimony to the truth when later statements agree with earlier ones. For Aristotle says that his remark, that fortune is removed from the causes of happiness, agrees finely with what he had taught from the beginning of the book. Therefore those who treat any argument, whether by disputing or by pleading a case, must take great care that they do not contradict themselves in what they say. Thus we do not call an ox, a horse or any other animal happy, since it cannot share in this kind of activity.

units.la: De causis felicitatis est abunde actum, modo statuitur de materia, subiecto, seu de personis quae capaces illius non censeantur. Quiq; ab ea excluduntur, ut allatae iam definitionis remouentur, quae statuit felicitatem actionem esse animi humani optimam, quae a praestantissima virtute oriatur. Hoc inquam si sic est, primo loco bruta eius participia non erunt, quum actionis eius generis minime sint capacia. Sed inter expertia rationis cur potissimum equi ac boues mentionem fecit? Quoniam haec animantia inter cetera non tantum sunt mitiora, sed etiam perfecta sunt, & nobiscum perpetuo versantur. Ea igitur tametsi disciplina non careant, a beatitudine nihilominus aliena ponit. Neque dubium est, si disciplinae tantum ratio habenda fuisset, quin elephantus adducendus fuerit, quum, ut ipsemet Aristoteles & Plinius testantur, id animal facillime quiduis doceatur. Id tamen tacuit, quia non tam passim ut bos & equus inter homines versetur. Non quidem inficiaretur haec animantia bruta, in sua natura seu specie bonum quoddam sibi proprium habere, quod sit illis praecipuum et summum: at id beatitudinem putare debemus non esse, quum eius id sit, ut citra rationem minime consistat.
units.tr: Enough has been said about the causes of happiness; now he settles the matter, the subject, or the persons who are not regarded as capable of it, and who are excluded from it, as the definition already given removes them. That definition holds that happiness is the best activity of the human soul, arising from the most excellent virtue. I say that if this is so, first of all the brute animals will not be its participants, since they are in no way capable of this kind of activity. But why did he mention horses and oxen in particular among the creatures lacking reason? Because these animals are not only gentler than the others but also are perfect of their kind, and they live with us constantly. Therefore, although they are not without some training, he nevertheless places them outside blessedness. Nor is there any doubt that, if only the training had been taken into account, the elephant should have been brought forward, since, as Aristotle himself and Pliny attest, that animal is most easily taught anything. Yet he passed over it, because it does not live among men as commonly as the ox and the horse do. Certainly these brute animals do not deny that in their own nature or species they have a certain good proper to themselves, which is pre-eminent and highest for them. But we ought not to think that this is happiness, since it belongs to a kind of good that cannot exist apart from reason.

units.la: Ob eamq; causam ne puer quidem felix est: quippe qui nondum per aetatem istas actiones possit effi cere, quiq; felices praedicantur propter spem beati cẽsentur. Opus est enim (ut diximus) et virtute perfecta, & vita perfecta.
units.tr: For this reason not even a boy is happy: indeed, since by his age he cannot yet perform those actions, and those who are called happy on account of hope are counted blessed. For (as we said) there is need both of perfect virtue and of a perfect life.

units.la: Nunc a beatitudine pueros identidem ob id remouet, quia per aetatem, quae in eis est admodum recens ac tenera, minime possunt actionem illam omnibus numeris absolutam edere. Quid vero iudicium & ratione puerorum impediat, illis videre difficile non est, qui secum reputent, cum in intelligendo phantasia sit opus & cogitatione: (quia ut ipse idem Aristoteles dicit oportet, intelligentem phantasmata contemplari:) ea in illa aetate propter humorem nimium redundantem inepta esse. Proinde cum eiusmodi vitio iudicare nequeat, eligere quoq; quae agat non possunt: unde satis imperfecta sunt, quae ab illis geruntur. Vulgus nihilominus interdum beatos dicit pueros, quoniam sic futuri sperātur, sapius enim accidit, ut indoles, ut maiores, ut corporis & membrorum constitutio, ut facilitas discendi hoc de illis pollicean-tur. Et videntur nonnunquam in ea ætate impetus ad honesta, & odium seu detestatio vitiorum, quare adducantur pædagogi & præceptores ac co-gnati, ut ipsos pueros fore beatos expectent. Sed rationem quam reddit, propter quam beati esse non possint, ut ab [?]Aristotele producitur, excutiamus. Opus, inquit, est ad felicitatem perfecta cum virtute tum vita. De vita minime controversia est, Quia ut una hirundo non facit ver, ita una dies felicem hominem non reddit. Quare longiori ætate ac productiori tempore vita danda est, si quis felix effici debeat. Virtus quoq; perfecta exigitur: quia nisi radices altius egerit, ut parum firma facile dilabetur. In summa vult Aristoteles felicem in eo esse statu ut inde non possit leviter deiici, ad quem omnes vident & consummata vita & absoluta virtute opus esse. Dumq;[?] pueros ita nunc amolitur, etiā illi senes intelligendi sunt pari ratione exclusi qui delirant, & præ senio iam nil recte iudicant. Et ut nominatim non sint expressi, ratione definitionis allata in hoc grege compre-hendenduntur.
units.tr: Now he removes boys from blessedness again, for this reason: because by reason of their age, which is very recent and tender in them, they cannot perform that action, which is complete in every respect. And it is not hard for those who consider it to see what hinders the judgment and reason of boys. In understanding, there is need of imagination and thought (for, as Aristotle himself says, the one who understands must contemplate images), and these are unfit at that age because of an excess of superabundant moisture. Therefore, since they cannot judge with such a faculty, they also cannot choose what they should do; hence the things they do are quite imperfect. Nevertheless the common people sometimes call boys blessed, because they are hoped to turn out so; for it often happens that their natural disposition, their ancestry, the constitution of their body and limbs, and their aptitude for learning promise this about them. And sometimes in that age they show impulses towards honourable things and a hatred or detestation of vices, so that tutors, teachers and relatives are brought in to expect that the boys themselves will be blessed. But let us examine the reason he gives why they cannot be blessed, as it is brought forward by Aristotle. A perfect life as well as perfect virtue, he says, is needed for happiness. There is hardly any dispute about life, because just as one swallow does not make a spring, so one day does not make a man happy. Therefore, if anyone is to be made happy, life must be given over a longer age and a more extended time. Perfect virtue is also required, because unless it has struck its roots deeper, it easily slips away as too unstable. In sum, Aristotle wants the happy man to be in such a state that he cannot easily be cast down from it; and everyone sees that for this a finished life and an accomplished virtue are needed. While he thus removes boys, those old men who dote and who by reason of their age no longer judge rightly must also be understood to be excluded by the same reasoning. And even if they are not named expressly, they are included in this class by the reason of the definition given.

units.la: Etenim multæ fiunt in vita mutationes, ac variæ fortunæ contingunt, fieriq; potest ut homo copiosus & iucundus, gravibus calamitatibus senex inuolvatur, ut de Priamo in heroicis fabulę narrant. Qui autem fortunis eiusmodi fuerit usus, ut vitam ita mi-fere obierit, eum nemo beatum dixerit.
units.tr: For many changes happen in life, and various fortunes befall people. A man who is wealthy and happy may in old age be overwhelmed by grievous calamities, as the stories of Priam in the heroic tales relate. But no one would call happy a man who has used such fortunes and ended his life miserably.

units.la: His quæ modo afferuntur, & confirmatur sententia de pueris a felicitate removendis, & via sternitur ad ea quæ proximo capite sunt disputanda. Iu-re puer felix esse non potest, cum multæ magnæq; mutationes illi immineant: est enim adhuc in ipsis vitæ carceribus. Deinde cum possint omnibus modo rectè beneq; habentibus eadem cuenire quæ Priamo contigerunt, ambiguum relinquitur an quispiam quam diu hic vixerit, cum his vicissitudinibus subiacet, felix rite dici possit: nedum id velimus puero dare, qui præ sene multo frequentioribus undis & fluctibus vitæ agitandus est. Et videtur aptè dubitari seclusis brutis & pueris, an quiuis homo illius beatitudinis particeps haberi debeat: quod non temerè videtur affirmandum, propter multipluces [?] varietates. Quod enim est fretum, quis euripus, quæ tot agitentur perturbationibus, tot moueantur æstibus atq; hominum vita, quam totam licet bene constitutam vnus dies vel vna nox infausta non parum sæpè omnino pessundat. Neq; tantum corpus mutatur, quod esset vtcunque tolerabile, sed etiam animus, quo nunc discimus, nunc percepta obliuiscimur, consilia capimus, cōsilia reijcimus, quæ modò statuebamus euertimus, quodque paulò ante placuit, nunc oppidò repudiatur. Hæc secum reputans Eustrathius, & videns omnium harum permutationum causam ex corpore deriuari, ait animum nostrum, quando ei admiscetur, esse perinde atq; si demit teretur in aquam concitam, quæq; rapidissimè curreret, cuius vorticibus tantum abest vt noster animus resistat, vt potius illis quàm maximè trahatur. Quæ sententia licet percipere animi humani magnam infirmitatem, quasi tenetur, vt vim rapidam mundanarum vicissitudinum haudquaquam possit gubernare.
units.tr: From what has just been said, the opinion is confirmed that children are to be removed from happiness, and the way is paved for the matters to be discussed in the next chapter. Rightly, a child cannot be happy, since many great changes hang over him: he is still at the very starting-gates of life. Then, since those who are altogether well and rightly placed may suffer the same things that befell Priam, it remains doubtful whether anyone who lives subject to these vicissitudes can properly be called happy. Much less should we grant this to a child, who is to be tossed by far more frequent waves and surges of life than an old man. And it seems fitly to be doubted, setting aside brutes and children, whether any man at all ought to be held a sharer in that blessedness. This should not be affirmed rashly, on account of the manifold variations. For what is a strait, what a whirlpool, that is stirred by so many disturbances and moved by so many tides, is human life, which, though altogether well established, one unlucky day or night often utterly overturns. Nor is only the body changed, which might be tolerable in some way, but also the mind: by it we now learn and now forget what we have perceived, we take counsels and reject them, we overturn what we had just decided, and what pleased us a little before is now utterly repudiated. Pondering these things, Eustratius, seeing that the cause of all these changes derives from the body, says that our mind, when it is mixed with the body, is just as if it were plunged into agitated water that runs most swiftly. Against its whirlpools our mind resists so little that it is rather drawn most of all by them. From this opinion one can perceive the great weakness of the human mind, which is, as it were, held so that it cannot by any means govern the rapid force of worldly vicissitudes.

units.la: Poterat sanè Aristoteles tum corporis tum animi varium inconstantèq; statum commemorare, sed illam multiplicem rerum diuersitatem, quæ in externis rebus perpetuò cernitur, exposuit. Utq; quod dicebat magis liquidum esset, exemplum proposuit velipsis pueris notissimum, qui fabulas Poetarum audierint. Priamum nempe regem Asiæ opulentissimum, cui copiosa proles erat, vt qui pater fuerit quinquaginta liberorum, quorum septendecim nati sunt illi ex iustis coniugibus, abundauit amicis, militari vi clarus erat, sed quo magis per totam vitam fortuna illi perpetuò indulserat, sic ad finem vitæ omnia illi miserrimè abstulit. Quid hæc pluribus dicam, cum omnes ex Homero & Vergilio ista possint luculenter cognoscere? Carmina horum poetarum dicuntur heroica, quandoquidem illis heroum facta sunt exposita. Heroes dicti sunt, qui è hominibus illustribus in deos re-ferebantur, & ab ethnicis theologis, minores multò erant cum diis tum daemonibus, verùm cæteris hominibus multò maiores. Non tamen ex his Philosophi verbis colligendum est, neminem posse dici felicem nisi cùm obierit, vt Solon docuit. Potest quis cùm perfecta fuerit ætate atq; absoluta virtute instructus, ita vt fortunæ ictibus atq; vulneribus perferendis par sit, dici felix: nam licet deturbetur, variis obrutus calamitatibus, à felicitate, non tamen incidit in miseriam. Sed hac de re proximo capite fusius. Senem Pria-mum nunc adducit, partim vt illius ætatem pueris opponat, partim quia idoneus est ad quæstionem proximè tractandam, qui producatur. Cùm, inquit, talia quis patitur, à nemine felix prædicabitur, cùm magis dignus habeatur misericordia & lacrymis, quàm vt beatus celebrari possit. Quæ verò de Priamo referuntur, fabulosa sunt: at illis non multum dissimilia sacra nobis litera de Iobo referunt.
units.tr: Aristotle could indeed have recalled the varied and inconstant state of body and mind, but he set out that manifold diversity of things which is constantly seen in external affairs. So that what he said might be clearer, he proposed an example best known to boys themselves, who have heard the fables of the poets: namely Priam, the most opulent king of Asia, who had a plentiful offspring, being the father of fifty children, of whom seventeen were born to him from lawful wives. He abounded in friends and was famous for military might. But just as fortune had indulged him constantly throughout his life, so at the end of his life it took everything from him most miserably. Why should I say more, since everyone can learn these things clearly from Homer and Vergil? The poems of these poets are called heroic, since the deeds of heroes are set forth in them. Heroes were those who were raised from illustrious men to the gods, and among the pagan theologians they were far smaller than the gods and demons, yet far greater than other men. Yet it should not be gathered from the Philosopher's words that no one can be called happy unless he has died, as Solon taught. Someone who has reached mature age and is furnished with perfect virtue, so that he is equal to bearing the blows and wounds of fortune, can be called happy. For although he is cast down and overwhelmed by various calamities, he falls from happiness, yet he does not fall into misery. But this matter will be treated more fully in the next chapter. Now he brings forward Priam as an old man, partly so that he may set his age against that of boys, and partly because he is fit to be produced for the question to be treated next. "When," he says, "someone suffers such things, no one will call him happy, since he is deemed more worthy of pity and tears than of being celebrated as blessed." What is related of Priam is fabulous, yet the sacred letters relate things not very unlike these about Job.

units.la: Ad finem capitis cum expositio nostra deducta sit, par est ut de more, sed paucis tamen, examinemus quæ fuerunt allata, quantum cum diuinis literis congruant, vel ab ijsdem discrepent. Ambiguè loquitur Aristoteles de Deo, an sit felicitatis author: nos id constantissime asserimus. Ergo, inquit Dominus Abraamo, merces tua magna nimis. Et ne suspicemur hoc naturaliter verum esse, non autem ex ipsius Dei voluntate ac electione, ibi sequitur fœdus initum, quo ille sibi populum certum delegit, & credentibus pepigit se futurum Deum. Et Moses, qui probè intelligebat felicitatem in eo sitam, ut Deus intelligatur & videatur, id à Deo petijt, cum diceret, Ostende mihi faciem tuam: quod & impetrauit. Dauid quoque cecinit, Delectationes in dextera tua usque in finem. Et Christus seruator noster, noster inquam Deus, Venite, inquit, ad me omnes qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego reficiam vos. Idemq; de suis ouibus loquendo aiebat, Vocem meam audiunt, & ego vitam æternam do eis. Esto igitur id cuique nostrum persuasissimum à Deo ipso nostram felicitatem expectandam & petendam. Exercitia verò, consuetudines & doctrinæ quæ Aristoteles commemorat, nostra quoq; sententia non sunt aspernanda, imò passim in sacris literis nobis inculcantur. Non tamen ita ut sint nostræ felicitatis causæ: gratis enim iustificamur, non ex operibus, & gratis æterna vita nobis conceditur. Sed media quædam sunt, quibus nos Deus ad se ducit, & ad felicitatem quam optamus. Atque media hæc à Deo ipso habemus: quare à Paulo merito dicebatur, Deum esse qui & velle & perficere nobis elargiatur. Fortuna verò nos longè minus quam Aristoteles beatitudinem committimus, ut qui putemus omnia nostra Dei consilio & voluntate regi, ut absq; illa nec unus quidem capitis nostri capillus cadat. Atq; id longè salsissimum arbitramur quod ab Ethnicis passim dicitur, quenq; sapientem sibi suam fortunam fabricari. Paruulos felices esse posse Aristoteles negat: nos vicissim affirmamus, cum Christus de illis dixerit, Sinite ipsos ad me venire, atq; illos magna bonitate singulari, & clementia complexus est. Scimus quidem illos effectores adhuc esse non posse præstantissimarum actionum, sed per Christum & illis condonatur peccatum originis, & via in æternam vitam aperitur. Neq; illi damus, non posse felices dici qui gravibus afflictantur casibus, cum fieri possit ut gravia qui verè sunt beati ob Christi nomen patiantur, neq; illa dura & sæva quæ ferunt eam euertunt beatitudinem, quam dum hic vivimus nobis hominibus habere licet.
units.tr: At the end of the chapter, since our exposition has been carried through, it is fitting, as is customary, though briefly, to examine what has been said, how far it agrees with the divine writings, and where it differs from them. Aristotle speaks ambiguously about God, whether he is the author of happiness; we assert this most constantly. "Therefore," says the Lord to Abraham, "your reward is exceedingly great." And lest we suspect that this is true by nature, and not from God's own will and choice, there follows the covenant entered into, by which he chose for himself a certain people and promised to believers that he would be their God. And Moses, who well understood that happiness lies in this, that God be known and seen, asked this of God when he said, "Show me your face," and he obtained it. David also sang, "In your right hand are pleasures forevermore." And Christ our Saviour, our God I say, said, "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you." Speaking of his own sheep, he said the same: "They hear my voice, and I give them eternal life." Let each of us therefore be most firmly persuaded that our happiness is to be expected and sought from God himself. The exercises, customs and teachings which Aristotle mentions should not, in our view, be despised; indeed, they are inculcated upon us throughout the sacred letters. Yet they are not the causes of our happiness in such a way: for we are justified freely, not by works, and eternal life is granted to us freely. But they are certain means by which God leads us to himself and to the happiness we desire. And these means we have from God himself; wherefore Paul rightly said that God is the one who gives us both to will and to perform. But we commit our blessedness to fortune far less than Aristotle does, since we think all our affairs are ruled by God's counsel and will, so that without it not even one hair of our head falls. And we judge it very false what is commonly said by the pagans, that each wise man fashions his own fortune. Aristotle denies that children can be happy; we on the contrary affirm this, since Christ said of them, "Suffer the little children to come to me," and embraced them with great and singular goodness and mercy. We know indeed that they cannot yet be doers of the most excellent actions, but through Christ original sin is pardoned them too, and a way into eternal life is opened. Nor do we grant that those cannot be called happy who are afflicted by grievous misfortunes, since it can happen that those who are truly blessed suffer serious things for the name of Christ. Nor do the hard and cruel things they bear overturn that blessedness which, while we live here, we men are permitted to have.
CHAPTER X.

units.la: ANigitur neque alium quempiam hominem beatum praedicare oportet dum uixerit? Secundum Solonem quidem opus est finem spectare. Si uero ita, & hoc pacto statuendum est, an tunc felix est quispiam cum obierit? An hoc prorsus absurdum, praesertim nobis qui dicimus, felicitatem certam quandam actionem?
units.tr: Ought we then not to call any other man happy while he is alive? According to Solon, indeed, one must look to the end. But if so, and if it must be settled in this way, is someone happy once he has died? Or is this utterly absurd, especially for us who say that happiness is a certain activity?

units.la: Haec optimè iam dictis congruunt: nam de Priamo ac similibus eius affirmauit, eos felices nequaquam habendos, nempe quod fortuna tam varia & aduersa vel in ipso quidem fine vitae vsi fuerint. Vnde merito & iure quaerit, an quispiam felix habendus sit dum vixerit. Ac potest quaestio haec de tempore appellari: siquidem antea de causis beatitudinis quaesiuit: disputauit postea de materia, subiecto vel personis quae capaces illius essent, nunc inuestigat quando beatus quispiam sit aut dicatur. An, inquit, dum viuit aut post mortem hoc illi attribuetur? Quaestio est biceps, & ab Aristotele quo ad vtramq; partem tractatur. Priori loco de opinione agit, quae obitum vult expectari, quoniam ea falsa est, neq; illam nostrer sequitur, isq; semper falsa veris praeponit, vt illis confutatis, quae vera sunt magis constabilitantur. Authoritate Solonis, qui & sapiens erat vnus e septem totius Graciae, ac legislator celeberrimus, opinio probari videtur: is enim dixit neminem beatum esse aut dicendum ante mortem. Sententia haec ab eo dicta est Lydorum regi cui nomen Croeso erat, qui cum iactaret impotenter suas opes, fortunas, regni vires, delicias, & cetera quibus fruebatur bona, Ecquid, inquit, non tibi videor felix? Dicendo id philosophis videbatur insultare, qui cum suis doctrinis atque scientijs quodammodo egerent, cum ipse e Philosophia alienus, plenus atque distentus videretur sibi felicitate. Solon his auditis grauiresponso elati regis insolentiam repressit. Ante obitum, inquit, nemo felix: Philosophica libertate illum admonens, aduersa fortuna illa omnia facile sibi posse auferri, ita vt e tantis rebus ad extremam calamitatem detruderetur. Quod illu non fefellit, nā Croesus à Cyro victus, omnia sua euersa conspexit. Hanc huius Philosophi sententiam Ouidius expressit, Vltima semper Expectan-da dies homini, dicíq; beatus Ante obitum nemo supremaq; funera debet.Solonis dicti sensus duplex esse potuit. Primus est vt de ipsa re agatur, signi-ficetur, neminem beatum esse ante mortem, sed iam tandem post mortem homines felices dici. Haec in parte reprehenditur primo sententia vt absur-da, & allata definitioni felicitatis maximè repugnans. Nam si felicitas ac-tio est, & ea quidem perfecta, mortuis dari non debet: qui cum amplius nō sint, nil agere possunt. Locus iste grauis est ad testandum Aristotelem animūputasse mortalem: nam si post mortem maneret incolumis, vtiq; posset agere & multò expeditius quā coniunctus cum corpore. Quare non rectè neq; or-dine illi subtraheret actione, vt facit, dum talē rationem profert, quæ firma esse non poterit, nisi datū fuerit, eos qui obierint, nil agere. Videtur dicere, Hoc adeò absurdū esset, vt eosdē eodemq; tempore cogeremur dicere agere & non agere. Si felices ponentur, agunt: si mortui, non agunt. Neq; conue-nit, vt qui non sunt felices, felices dicantur. Scio quidē aliquos ita defende-re Aristotelē, quòd hoc loco de ciuili felicitate agat, cuiusmodi profecto à no-bis in alia vita non expectatur. Sed quæcunq; sit felicitas, siue ciuilis, siue solida & æterna, omnino actione esse necesse est. Deinde vno verbo si rectè sensit, poterat verum innuere, testando aliam quidē esse felicitatē post hanc vitam expectandam, de qua in præsentia non loquatur. Adhæc quando mox ostendet mortuos & bonis adhuc & malis subiacere, totam disputatio-nem ad bona & mala huius vitæ refert, vt mox videbimus. Non ita loquu-tus est Plato in vltimo libro de repub. vbi tum maximè puras actiones & felices nos manere demonstrat, cum ab hac vita fuerimus euocati. Et in Phædone ponit Philosophiam solidam & synceram meditationem esse mor-tis, nempè vt semper queramus à corpore mentem remouere, quam eius as-sensionem à sensibus tum denig; assequemur, quum hinc abierimus. At Ari-stoteles eius beatitudinis nunquam quod sciam vel vnum verbum fecit. Argumentum quod modò affert, vt videmus, à definitione sumitur.
units.tr: This agrees well with what has already been said. For he affirmed of Priam and men like him that they must by no means be counted happy, because fortune had been so varied and adverse to them even at the very end of their lives. Hence he rightly and justly asks whether anyone is to be counted happy while he lives. This question may be called one of time: he had earlier inquired into the causes of happiness, then discussed its matter, its subject, or the persons capable of it, and now he investigates when someone is or is called happy. Is it, he says, ascribed to a man while he lives, or after death? The question has two sides, and Aristotle treats it with respect to both. First he deals with the opinion that wants the end to be awaited. This opinion is false, and our school does not follow it; and Aristotle always puts false views before true ones, so that when these have been refuted, what is true is more firmly established. The opinion seems to be confirmed by the authority of Solon, who was both wise, one of the seven sages of all Greece, and a most celebrated lawgiver. For he said that no one is to be called happy before death. This saying was spoken by him to Croesus, king of the Lydians, who, while boasting immoderately of his wealth, fortunes, the power of his kingdom, his pleasures and the other goods he enjoyed, asked: "Do I not seem to you happy?" By saying this he seemed to mock the philosophers, who, as it were, made their living from their doctrines and sciences, while he himself, a stranger to philosophy, seemed full and swollen with happiness. Solon, hearing this, checked the king's arrogance with a grave reply. "Before death," he said, "no one is happy," warning him in the freedom of philosophy that adverse fortune could easily take all those things from him, so that he would be thrust from such great things into utter calamity. This did not escape Croesus, for when he was conquered by Cyrus he saw all his possessions overthrown. Ovid expressed this sentence of the philosopher: "The last day is always to be awaited by a man, and no one should be called happy before his funeral rites." The sense of Solon's saying could be twofold. The first is that the matter itself is being treated, meaning that no one is happy before death, but only at last, after death, are men called happy. In this part the opinion is first rebuked as absurd, and as most contrary to the definition of happiness. For if happiness is an activity, and indeed a perfect one, it must not be given to the dead, who, since they no longer exist, can do nothing. This passage is weighty for showing that Aristotle thought the soul mortal: for if it remained unharmed after death, it could certainly act, and far more readily than while joined to the body. Therefore he rightly and properly would not withdraw activity from it, as he does, when he puts forward a reason that cannot stand firm unless it is granted that those who have died do nothing. He seems to say: this would be so absurd that we would be compelled to say at the same time that they act and do not act. If they are called happy, they act; if they are dead, they do not act. Nor is it fitting that those who are not happy should be called happy. I know that some defend Aristotle by saying that at this point he is speaking of civil happiness, of the kind that is certainly not expected by us in the other life. But whatever happiness is, whether civil or solid and eternal, it must certainly consist in activity. Next, in a single word: if he thought rightly, he could have hinted at the truth, by testifying that there is indeed another happiness to be expected after this life, which he is not speaking of at present. Besides, since he will soon show that the dead are still subject to goods and evils, he refers the whole discussion to the goods and evils of this life, as we shall soon see. Plato did not speak in this way in the last book of the Republic, where he shows that we remain most pure in our actions and happy when we have been called away from this life. And in the Phaedo he holds that solid and sincere philosophy is a meditation on death, namely that we should always seek to remove the mind from the body, a withdrawal which we will then at last fully attain when we have departed from here. But Aristotle, so far as I know, never said even a single word about that happiness. The argument he now brings forward, as we see, is taken from the definition.

units.la: Si autem dixerimus defunctum nequaquam esse felicem, neq; Solon hoc uoluit. Sed quod quispiam tum felicem dixerit hominem tuto, qui quasi iam sit extra mala & infortunia. Verùm hoc quoque dubium habet: uidetur enim aliquod in mortuo inesse malum & bonum, siquidem & uiuenti, non autem sensentienti, hoc est, honores, ignominiae liberorum, & omnino posterorum prospera & calamitates.
units.tr: But if we say that the dead man is by no means happy, Solon did not mean this either. Rather, one may then safely call a man happy, as one who is already beyond evils and misfortunes. Yet this too is open to doubt. For there seems to be some good and some evil in the dead man, since honours and dishonours, and the prosperity and calamities of children and of all posterity, affect the one who lives, though not the one who feels.

units.la: Alterum nunc Solonis explicat sensum: nam inquit, Si dixerimus, defunctum non esse beatum, cum iam non sit & obierit, quod dicimus ita quispiam excipiet Solonem defendendo: neque hoc voluit suo apophthegmate Solon: is enim fatebitur re ipsa hominem felicem esse tantum dum vivit, sed a nobis pronunciari non debere felicem, nisi cum obierit. Quod revera aid tu tò dici posset quando is ita extra pericula & mala est. Discrimen est inter [?] & [?] Primum vitia significat, quae nostro delectu & iudicio adsciscimus. Alterum vero infortunia significat, quae vel nolentibus nobis accidunt. Ad hanc exceptionem defensorum Solonis, Aristoteles se opponit, & inquit, Quod ponitur, ambiguum est, nimirum mortuos iam extra mala & calamitates esse: nam & mortui subiacent adhuc & malis & bonis. Neque putandus est modo noster loqui de purgatorio & inferno. Sed de bonis & infortunijs huius vitae agit. Ratio eius ita ponatur:
units.tr: Now he explains the second sense of Solon. For he says: If we say that the dead man is not happy, since he is no longer and has died, then someone might defend Solon in the following way: Solon did not mean this by his saying. He will admit in fact that a man is happy only while he lives, but he ought not to be pronounced happy by us unless he has died, which indeed could be said of one who is in this way beyond dangers and evils. There is a distinction between [?] and [?]. The first signifies vices, which we take on by our own choice and judgement. The second signifies misfortunes, which befall us even against our will. Aristotle sets himself against this exception of Solon's defenders and says: What is posited is ambiguous, namely that the dead are now beyond evils and calamities; for the dead also are still subject both to evils and to goods. Nor should we think that he is speaking here of purgatory and hell. He is dealing with the goods and misfortunes of this life. His argument may be set out thus:

units.la: Qui non sunt extra bona & mala huius vitae, non sunt adhuc in tuto neque beati dici possunt.
units.tr: Those who are not beyond the goods and evils of this life are not yet in safety, and cannot be called happy.

units.la: Mortui adhuc non sunt ab his exempti, sed illis subiacent.
units.tr: The dead are not yet freed from these, but are subject to them.
Therefore they are not in safety.

units.la: Maior liquet. Minor patefit simili. Si quis enim viuens quidem absit & nō sentiat, potest aliquibus malis & bonis affici, ut si decernatur ipsi nescio honor, si ampla hereditas obueniat, si proles pulchra nascatur, &c. ista licet ipse non sentiat & absit procul, sunt eius bona, & vicissim queunt mala euenire, ut scilicet ignominia notetur, multetur, fiat exul, dispereant sua, &c. Quare licet mortui absint hinc & non sentiant, bonorum tamen & malorum quae hic fiunt possunt esse participes.
units.tr: The major premise is clear. The minor is shown by a similar case. For if someone who is alive, though absent and not feeling, can be affected by certain goods and evils, as when some honour is decreed to him, I know not what, or a large inheritance falls to him, or a fine child is born, and so on; though he himself does not feel these things and is far away, they are his goods. And conversely evils may happen to him: he may be marked with disgrace, fined, made an exile, lose his property, and so on. Therefore, although the dead are absent from here and do not feel, they can nevertheless be partakers of the goods and evils that happen here.

units.la: Lectio huius loci diuersa est: nam quidam textus habent, [?], & ita legit Argyropylus & Eustrathius: alij vero [?], & utraq; lectio consistit. Prior est magis plana & perspicua. Et exempla quae subiiciuntur partim bona sunt & partim mala, nempe honores, ignominia, prospera, & aduersa. Sin vero legamus [?] tum argumentum regulae satis certe nitetur, contrariorum eandem disciplinam seu rationem esse, ideoq; si mortui subiacent bonis, & malis quoq; erunt expositi, cum bona & mala inter opposita censeantur.
units.tr: The reading of this passage varies. For some texts have [?], and so Argyropylus and Eustratius read; others have [?], and both readings hold. The former is plainer and clearer, and the examples added are partly good and partly bad, namely honours, disgrace, prosperity and adversity. But if we read [?], the argument from the rule will rest quite securely, since contraries have the same discipline or reasoning; and so if the dead are subject to goods, they will also be exposed to evils, since good and evil are counted among opposites.

units.la: Sed quomodo absentium & non sentientium bona vel mala vlla esse di-cantur, videndum est: neque puto aliter hoc fieri, nisi quia referuntur ad illos illos & qui ea vident, aiunt & existimant illorum esse, quod aliqua eis animaduertant ex his quæ fiunt accedere vel adimi incommoda, seu commoda. Sed certè longè alia est ratio viuentium, licet absint & non sentiant, adesse nihilominus possunt & sentire, ac illis quandoq; renunciabuntur, mortuorum verò nullus aut rursus adesse aut sentire quæ hic fiant potest.
units.tr: But it must be examined how the goods or evils of the absent and the non-sentient can be called anything at all. I think this happens only because they are referred to those who see these things and think that those things belong to them, since they notice that inconveniences or advantages come to them from what is done. But the case of the living is quite different: although they are absent and do not perceive, they can nonetheless be present and perceive, and they will sometimes be told of these things. Of the dead, however, no one can either be present or perceive what happens here.

units.la: Sed & hæc afferunt dubitationem: nam fieri potest, ut ei qui beatè uixit ad usque senectutem, conue nienterq; rationi discessit, multæ posterorum mutationes accidant, & in iis alij boni sint, & pro dignitate genus uitæ consequantur, ac contra: nec dubium, quin interuallis temporum accidant, ut posteri multis modis uarient. Absurdum quidem sit, si una & is mutetur qui defunctus est, ita ut sit alias beatus, alias miser.
units.tr: But these points also raise a doubt. For it can happen that a man who lived happily up to old age and departed in a fitting manner sees many changes among his descendants, and that some of them are good and attain a way of life worthy of their station, and the reverse. And there is no doubt that the descendants vary in many ways as periods of time pass. It would indeed be absurd if the one who has died were himself changed, so that he was now happy and now wretched.

units.la: Intulerat contra Solonistas, si velimus varietates & mutationes fortunæ spectare, nec quidem mortuos posse dici felices, quòd & ipsi vicissitudinibus eiusmodi saltem propter superstites posteros subiaceant, quod à simili viuentium probauit, quia absentes licet non sentiant, & bonis & malis possunt assici. Nunc videmus hanc parum firmam rationem, eam videtur abÿcere hoc argumento, quod tamen cùm uariæ multiplicesq; sint posterorum mutationes nunquam diceretur defunctus quiescere. Quod vt magis ponat sub oculos, quendam inducit qui vsq; ad extremam senectam felicitER vixerit, & in eodem tenore vitæ mortem oppetierit, is porrò propter istam vicissitudinem posterorum multis varysq; modis subinde mutabitur, & è felici miser fiet, & ex miseria ad felicitatem assurget. Nec immeritò scribit, Vsq; ad senectutem, vt ostendat, quo ad felicitatis perfectionem illi dum viueret non defuisse constantiam. Quæ vt requiratur ad beatitudinem, & superius dictum est, & hic Eustrathius ostendit Achillis exemplo, qui licet in Troiana illa expeditione admodum floruerit, et omni bonorum genere suffultus fuerit, non tamen beatus dici potuit, cum iuuenis obierit. Multas fore in posteris rerum vicissitudines, Aristoteles vt manifestissimum accepit: nam Hesiodus ait, ἄλλοτε μὲν τρέχη ἡμέρη, ἄλλοτε μὲν τε...
units.tr: Earlier he had argued against the Solonians that if we look to the variations and changes of fortune, the dead cannot even be called happy, because they too are subject to such vicissitudes at least on account of their surviving descendants. He proved this from the likeness of the living, who, although absent and not perceiving, can be affected by good and evil. Now we see that he sets this rather weak argument aside and rejects it with this reasoning: since the changes among descendants are varied and manifold, a dead man would never be said to rest. To set this more clearly before our eyes, he introduces a certain man who lived happily up to extreme old age and died in the same tenor of life. This man, because of the vicissitudes of his descendants, will be changed again and again in many and varied ways: from happy he will become wretched, and from misery he will rise again to happiness. He rightly writes "up to old age," to show that, as far as the perfection of happiness goes, there was no lack of constancy in him while he lived. That constancy is required for blessedness, as was said above; and here Eustratius shows it by the example of Achilles, who, although he flourished greatly in that Trojan expedition and was supported by every kind of good, could not nevertheless be called happy, since he died young. Aristotle took it as most evident that there will be many vicissitudes of affairs among descendants. For Hesiod says: [ἄλλοτε μὲν τρέχη ἡμέρη, ἄλλοτε μὲν τε...] "at one time the day runs one way, at another time another..."

units.la: Deinde per hanc vocem χωρισμοί nil aliud intelligit quàm spacia seu interintervalla temporis, quae annis aut mensibus voluentibus claudantur. Con-sequi vult ex his, hominem eiusmodi quem pinxit infinitis vicibus modo felicem, modo miserum fore. Haec dicuntur, ut monstretur ad mortuos, quae hic aguntur, non pertingere, cum tamen prius id visus fuerit affirmare, ut diximus a simili: nunc illud negat ratione quae ad absurdum perducat. Et absurditas ex eo magis fiet perspicua, quod tunc neque in vita, neque post mortem quispiam poterit felix dici, propter eandem causam, nempe ob mu-tationes imminentes, quae tam vivum quam mortuum impedient ne sit beatus.
units.tr: Next, by this word [χωρισμοί] he understands nothing other than the spaces, or intervals of time, which are closed off as years or months roll by. He wishes to infer from these that a man of the kind he has portrayed will be, through infinite turns, now happy and now wretched. These things are said so that it may be shown that what is done here does not reach the dead, although he had earlier seemed to affirm this from a likeness, as we said. Now he denies it by a line of reasoning that leads to an absurdity. And the absurdity will become clearer from the fact that then no one could be called happy either in life or after death, for the same cause, namely the changes that threaten, which hinder the living and the dead alike from being blessed.

units.la: Hoc quoque videtur absurdum, res propinquo-rum nequaquam ad parentes, ne ad ullum quidem tempus, attinere. Sed redeundum est ad id de quo prius dubitatum est: ex illo enim & id quod modo quaerimus fortasse cognoscetur.
units.tr: This also seems absurd: that the affairs of one's kin should not pertain to one's parents at any time whatever. But we must return to the point about which doubt was raised earlier, for from that the question we are now asking will perhaps also become known.

units.la: Nec etiam in eo quod postremo confecit potest acquiescere: nam inquit perabsurdum videri, ut res posterorum nullo quidem tempore ad parentes pertineant. Quomodo vero istud absurdum sit, non demonstrat, ut satis notum reliquit, & ita notum, ut vulgo ita sentiatur. Omnes fere putarunt mortuos de his quae aguntur apud nos sollicitari. Hinc fabulae poetarum de Palinuro & de Achille, qui suos manes placari voluit praestantissima hostia. Cur autem dixerit, Vel ad ullum tempus, ratio est, quoniam illi potuissent excipere ad superiorem rationem, haud se ponere infinitu progressum, ita ut omnes omnium posterorum vicissitudines ad mortuos perveniant, sed tantum propinquorum, ut puta usq; ad quartam generationem. Ideo nunc ait Aristoteles videri absurdum, si res mortuorum vel nullo tempore ad defunctos pertingant. Rationem absurdi non explicat. Sed Eustrathius ait, videri hoc esse inhumanum seu ἄσπλαγχνοι[?], quasi omnis repente inter nos & defunctum abrumpatur communio. Motam quaestione in praesentia non ulterius prosequitur. Sed redeundum inquit ad dubium, quod ab initio fuit propositum, nempe an in vita quispiam dicendus felix sit an post mortem: nam ex illa quaestione dissoluta, id etiam fortasse patebit, quod modo investigamus[?].
units.tr: Nor can he rest content with what he finally accomplished. For he says that it seems most absurd that the affairs of descendants should in no time pertain to their parents. But he does not demonstrate how this is absurd, leaving it as something sufficiently well known, and so well known that it is commonly thought so. Almost everyone has supposed that the dead are concerned with the things that are done among us. Hence the fables of the poets about Palinurus and about Achilles, who wished his shade to be appeased by a most excellent victim. But the reason why he said "or at any time" is that they could have objected to his earlier argument, and he did not wish to posit an infinite progression, so that all the vicissitudes of all descendants would reach the dead; rather only those of kin, say, up to the fourth generation. Therefore Aristotle now says that it seems absurd if the affairs of the dead reach the departed at no time. He does not explain the reason for the absurdity. But Eustratius says that this seems inhuman, or [ἄσπλαγχνοι], as if all communion between us and the dead were suddenly broken off. He does not pursue the question raised at present any further. But he says that we must return to the doubt that was proposed at the beginning, namely whether someone is to be called happy in life or after death; for once that question has been resolved, what we are now investigating will perhaps also become plain.

units.la: Si itaq; oporteat spectare finem, atq; tunc unumquenq; beatum affirmare, non quasi tunc sit beatus, sed quia prius fuerit, quo pacto id non est absurdū, si dum beatus est, quod inest illi uere de ipso affirma re non licet, propterea quod nolint uiuentes felices dicere, ob mutationes, & quod opinentur felicitatē maximè stabilem esse, nec facilè mutabilem, & casu circa eosdem frequenter conuertantur.
units.tr: If, then, we ought to look to the end, and so affirm each man happy then, not as though he were happy at that time but because he was happy before, then it is not absurd that, while he is happy, what truly inheres in him cannot be affirmed of him. This is because the living are unwilling to call people happy on account of changes, and because they think happiness is most stable and not easily altered, and they are frequently overturned by chance in the same persons.

units.la: Tota vis huius rationis in hoc versatur, id perabsurdum esse vt aliquid non possit dum reipsa in quopiam inest de illo affirmari. Qui hoc negant, se aiunt id ob vicissitudines & mutationes facere. Sed falluntur, quia mutationes imminentes hoc efficere possunt, vt felicitas quae adest esse desinat. Verum id nunquam facient, quin dum adest de eo affirmari queat cui adfuerit. Et cum statuant aliquem posse dici felicem quod fuerit, id multo magis concedere debent dum est actu: quia ex eo quod fuit, iuxta eos dici potest beatus: ergo multo magis dum erat: quia, Propter quod vnumquodque tale est, id maxime tale affirmatur. Vt{q} Dialectici aiunt, Nulla propositio praeteriti temporis vera esse potest, nisi ei respondens vera quandoq{ue} fuerit de praesenti tempore. Istorum sententia duobus innititur principiis, Primum, felicitatem esse quid firmum & stabile: Alterum, eam à fortuna pendere. Primum est verum: non enim facile mutatur beatitudo, ideo à virtutibus pendet, quae sunt habitus confirmati nec leuiter mobiles. Vnde Cicero 2. de finibus ideo aiebat felicitatem à sapientia pendere, quod ea fixa & constanter animo haereat. Fortunas subinde mutari atq{ue} conuerti dubium nullum est: vnde patet quam isti aberrent quo ad alterum caput, quod putent fortunam sequendam in beatitudine constituenda. Propterea sequitur:
units.tr: The whole force of this argument turns on this: that it is utterly absurd that something cannot be affirmed of someone while it really inheres in him. Those who deny this say they do so on account of vicissitudes and changes. But they are mistaken, because impending changes can bring it about that the happiness which is present ceases to be. Yet they will never do so without its being possible to affirm of the person in whom it was present that it was present. And since they hold that someone can be called happy because he was so, they ought to concede this all the more while it is actually so; for if, according to them, someone can be called blessed from what he was, then much more so while he was. For, as the dialecticians say, "on account of which each thing is such, it is most of all affirmed to be such." Likewise the dialecticians say: no proposition about past time can be true unless a corresponding proposition about the present time was at some point true. The view of these men rests on two principles: first, that happiness is something firm and stable; second, that it depends on fortune. The first is true: blessedness is not easily changed, and therefore it depends on the virtues, which are confirmed habits not lightly moved. Hence Cicero, in the second book of the De finibus, said that happiness depends on wisdom because wisdom is fixed and clings constantly to the mind. That fortunes are from time to time changed and overturned is beyond doubt; from this it is clear how far these men go astray on the second head, namely that they think fortune must be followed in establishing blessedness. Therefore it follows:

units.la: Manifestum igitur, si casus fortunae sequamur, nos eundem hominem felicem saepius & miserum uicissim esse dicturos, felicem statuentes ceu quendam chamaeleontem, & parum stabiliter collocatum.
units.tr: Clearly, then, if we follow the chances of fortune, we shall have to say that the same man is happy and wretched by turns, making happiness like some chameleon, poorly fixed in place.

units.la: Quantum aberrent qui fortunā sequuntur, ex eo comonstrat, quod varium instabilemq{ue} felicem coguntur ponere instar chamaeleontis. De hoc animali mali scribit Plinius lib.8.cap.33. multas illius proprietates colligit: sed quae huc spectat, est variatio coloris ad res quascunq; obiectas: refert quippe illud animal omnes colores citra rubrum & candidum. Est etiam herba, cuius meminit Dioscorides chamaelea, sic dicta quod & ipsa colores mutet, quamuis alii putent, quod soluat aluum grauissimis torminibus, ita vt videatur instar leonis viscera dilacerare. Sed animantis Aristoteles non herbae meminit, & sensus eius est, non esse committendum, ut nostrum beatum faciamus aliquem chamaeleontem, qui subinde mutetur. Hoc vero vsuueniet si fortunam sequamur, quae nil firmitatis aut constantiae habet. Sic enim mundana bona constituta sunt, vt eundem habitum seruare nequeant. Et quod ait, parum stabiliter collatum, metaphora est à basibus vel à fundamentis putridis, debilibus & marcidis. Nam super ista siue parietes aedifices, siue statuas colloces, nil est solidi aut firmi ad remanendum: ita de felici erit si à fortuna pendeat, nam ex felici facile miser fiet, si aduersa inciderint, imo in ipsis prosperis non erit vere beatus, cum vacare timore non possit amittendarum fortunarum.
units.tr: How far those are wrong who follow fortune is shown by the fact that they are forced to make happiness changeable and unstable, like a chameleon. Plinius, in book 8, chapter 33, writes about this animal and gathers many of its properties. The one that bears on our point is its change of colour to match whatever things are placed before it; the animal, he says, shows every colour except red and white. There is also a herb, which Dioscorides mentions, called chamaelea, so named because it too changes colour, though others think it is so called because it loosens the bowels with very severe gripes, so that it seems to tear the viscera like a lion. But Aristotle does not mention the herb, only the animal, and his meaning is that we must not make our happy man a chameleon who changes from time to time. This would happen if we followed fortune, which has no firmness or constancy at all. For worldly goods are so constituted that they cannot keep the same state. And when he says "placed rather unsteadily," it is a metaphor from bases or foundations that are rotten, weak and crumbling. For whether you build walls or set up statues upon such foundations, nothing solid or firm will remain. So it will be with the happy man if he depends on fortune. For from happy he will easily become wretched if adversities befall him; indeed, even in prosperity he will not be truly blessed, since he cannot be free from fear of losing his fortunes.

units.la: An casus fortunae sequi rectum non est? in ipsis enim neque bene neque male positum est. Verumtamen horum indiget humana vita, quemadmodum diximus. Dominae autem sunt felicitatis actiones ex virtute, atque contrariae contrarij.
units.tr: Is it wrong to follow the chances of fortune? For they are neither well nor badly placed in them. Nevertheless human life has need of these things, as we have said. But actions that proceed from virtue are the masters of happiness, and their contraries are the masters of the contrary.

units.la: Incipit quaestionem soluere [?] atq; ait, non sequendam fortunam, cum de felicitate agitur: cum in ea bonū & malum hominis non sit positum. Grauissima profecto haec sententia est, Bonū et malum hominis in rebus fortuitis non esse posita. Inquit Eustrathius, quid prodesset simpliciter esse, si bene ac feliciter esse à fortuna & non à nobis ipsis penderet? Horum tamen inquit Aristoteles humana vita indiget, occurrens tacitae obiectioni. Diceret enim quis, Tu cum dicas in his fortuitis bonis hominis felicitatem non esse positam, cur illa expetimus? Cur ea requirebas? Quoniam, inquit, his humana vita indiget. At revera dominatum & praecipuum locum obtinent in felicitate virtutes, illarumq; actiones.. Ac ratio afferri potest, quoniam beatitudo non ab his pendet quae non sunt in nobis, cuiusmodi fortuna est, sed sua principia in nobis ipsis habet posita. Vtq; actiones ex virtute principia sunt felicitatis, ita contrariae nempe quae sunt ex vitijs, effectus contrarij sunt, principia nimirum calamitatis & miseriae. Concluditur proinde felicitatem a fortuna non esse, quoniam ibi in his nos aut eligimus aut deliberamus. At in his actionibus quae a virtute proficiscuntur, & electio & deliberatio nostra locum habent. Quod si vulgus in bonis putet felicitatem collocandam, non est audiendum, cum in plerisq; aliis rebus erret: & id tantum a Solone accipiemus, felicitatem stabili ac firmae rei inniti, cumq; tam perfectam tamq; absolutam res sit, a causis per se, non ab his quae per accidens appellantur est petenda.
units.tr: He begins to resolve the question and says that fortune is not to be followed when happiness is in question, since a man's good and evil is not placed in it. This is indeed a most weighty saying: that a man's good and evil are not placed in chance events. Eustathius says: what would it profit simply to exist, if living well and happily depended on fortune and not on ourselves? Yet, Aristotle says, human life has need of these things, meeting an unspoken objection. For someone might say: "Since you say that happiness is not placed in these external goods, why do we desire them? Why did you seek them?" Because, he says, human life has need of them. But in truth the virtues and their actions hold the chief and dominant place in happiness. And a reason can be given: blessedness does not depend on things that are not in us, such as fortune is, but has its principles placed in ourselves. And just as actions from virtue are the principles of happiness, so their contraries, namely those that come from vices, are contrary effects, the principles, that is, of calamity and misery. It follows, therefore, that happiness does not come from fortune, since in these things we either choose or deliberate. But in those actions that proceed from virtue, both choice and deliberation have their place. And if the common people think happiness should be located in goods, we ought not to listen to them, since they err in many other things. We shall take from Solon only this: that happiness rests on a stable and firm thing, and since it is so perfect and complete a thing, it must be sought from causes in themselves, not from those called incidental.

units.la: Huic vero rationi adstipulatur & id quod modo in dubium est revocatum: ex rebus quippe humanis in nulla sic inest firmitas, quemadmodum in actionibus quae sunt ex virtute: ipsę quippe vel scientijs videntur esse stabiliores, & ex his praestantiores firmiores quoq; sunt, eo quod beati & maxime & assiduissime [?] in eis viuunt: atq; haec videtur causa quod in his obliuio non intercedat.
units.tr: This reasoning is also supported by what has just been called into doubt. For among human things none has such firmness as actions that come from virtue. Indeed the sciences themselves seem more stable, and those things which are more excellent than these are also firmer, because the blessed live in them most of all and most constantly. And this seems to be the reason why forgetfulness does not creep into them.

units.la: Ad confirmandum fortunam non consectandam in adipiscenda felicitate, adducit quaestionem paulo ante motam: de eo enim maxime dubitatum est, an quispiam in vita dici queat felix, quia mutationes ac vicissitudines fortunae spectabantur. Quamobrem si fortuna remota hinc fuerit, ea dubitatio prorsus liquida fiet. Monetur itaq; Philosophus a hac sententiam statuendam, quod nil fortuna videatur instabilius. Quamobrem ex ipso Solone probari potest, in ea felicitatem non collocandam: quoniam ille sentit omnino firma esse debere. Nil aut firmius atq; constantius est in vita quam sint actiones ex virtute. Quod argumento deducto ex comparatione demonstrat: Sunt, inquit, firmiores virtutes quam scientiae, cum tamen illae inter humana admodum videantur constantes. Fundamentum rationis est, Quoniam quae sunt constantiora his quae videntur valde constantia, in eo genere pro firmis egregie habenda sunt. Et quidem scientiae si species circa quae versentur, nempe necessaria, & quae aliter se habere nequeunt, & species assensus, quoniam per demonstrationes paratur firmissimus, inter humana videntur constantiam habere maximam. Sed tamen non ita est: quia non ita ut virtutes in suos actus frequenter erumpunt. Si perpetuo contemplandum esset, ut perpetuo dum vivimus est aliquid agendum, tam firmae scientia profecto essent atque virtutes: at contemplatio sæpissimè intermittitur. Et qui mathematici sunt, dum studium remittunt, multarum demonstrationum obliuiscuntur. Sunt quidem tamen istæ quàm illæ habitus animi: & habituum natura est, ut difficillimè deleantur: attamen illi citius delentur circa quos frequenter non exercemur. Natura sua utrique habitus ex dissue-tudine possent excidere, at dissuetudo non potest ita euenire virtutibus & scientiis: in omnibus enim actionibus prudentia opus est, in periculis forti-tudine, in commerciis iustitia, in cibo, potu & Venere temperantia: in conuersatione cum hominibus, amicitia, comitate: ac denique in quouis opere mediocritate. Cum itaque semper beatis hominibus pateat usus virtutum, non autem scientiarum, patet illarum posse citius accidere oblivionem quam istarum: nam scientiæ plerunque sunt de his rebus quas nos minimè faci-mus. Virtutes verò sunt de his in quibus beati degunt. Quodq; dicitur de scientijs, de artibus quoq; affirmare licet. Si quis enim quantumuis nobilis artifex, longo spacio temporis à suo quiescat opere, facilè in rudem & imperitum abibit. Eo firmamento ratio hæc tota nititur, haud fas esse rei solidæ atque constantis causam assignare volubilem: quod porrò fieret si beatitudinis, quæ stabilis esse debet, causam poneremus fortunam, cum ea varia sit & eodem habitu fere nunquam constet.
units.tr: To confirm that fortune is not to be pursued in attaining happiness, he adduces the question raised a little earlier. For the question chiefly was whether anyone can be called happy in life, since the changes and vicissitudes of fortune were in view. So if fortune is removed from here, that doubt will become quite clear. The Philosopher is therefore warned to set down his opinion on this point, since nothing seems less stable than fortune. Hence it can be proved from Solon himself that happiness is not to be placed in it, since he holds that happiness must be wholly firm. Nothing in life is firmer or more constant than actions from virtue. He demonstrates this by an argument drawn from comparison: the virtues, he says, are firmer than the sciences, although the sciences among human things seem very constant. The foundation of the reasoning is this: those things which are more constant than those that seem very constant are to be counted outstandingly firm in their kind. Now the sciences, if we consider the objects with which they deal, namely necessary things that cannot be otherwise, and the kind of assent they give, since they are acquired through demonstrations and are most secure, seem among human things to have the greatest constancy. But it is not so, because they do not break out into their acts as frequently as the virtues do. If one had to contemplate continuously, just as something must be done continuously while we live, the sciences and the virtues would indeed be equally firm. But contemplation is very often interrupted. And mathematicians, when they relax their study, forget many demonstrations. These habits of the mind are indeed of one kind, and the nature of habits is that they are very hard to destroy; yet those that we do not frequently exercise are destroyed more quickly. By their nature both kinds of habit could fall away through disuse, but disuse cannot happen in the same way to the virtues and the sciences. For in all actions prudence is needed, in dangers fortitude, in dealings justice, in food, drink and love temperance, in conversation with men friendliness and courtesy; and finally in every work, moderation. Since, therefore, the use of the virtues is always open to happy men, but not the use of the sciences, it is clear that forgetfulness of the former can come more quickly than of the latter. For the sciences are for the most part about those things which we do not practise. The virtues, however, are about those things in which the blessed live. What is said of the sciences may also be said of the arts. For if any artisan, however noble, rests from his work for a long time, he will easily sink into the crude and unskilled. On this support the whole argument rests: it is not right to assign a changeable cause to a thing that is solid and constant. And this is what would happen if we placed the cause of blessedness, which ought to be stable, in fortune, since fortune is changeable and scarcely ever remains in the same state.

units.la: Hic dixerit aliquis, Hæc doctrina quî cū his consentit quæ ab initio libri posita sunt? ibi profecto assumptū est felicitatè causam esse virtutū & actionū, ideoq; ante omnia fuisse de illa constituendū, ut de summa præci-puaq; omniū rerū moraliū causa. Hic verò ponitur ob id beatitudinè à fortuna minimè pendere, sed à virtutib.ctrectè factis produci, quod ista firma sint atq; constantia, fortuna verò incerta & varia? Videntur sanè ista parūm congruere, beatitudinem causam esse virtutis & iustarum actionum, ac è diuerso ab his felicitatem produci. Sed optimè pugna ista componetur, si cau-sas distinxeris. Externarū duo facienda sunt genera, seponendaq; sunt finales ab efficientibus: tumq; dabitur, felicitatem inter finales causas præcipu-am esse: quam tamen ab his effici, quorum finis est, nemo debet mirari, cum inter finem & efficientem hæc vicissitudo semper cernatur. Nam ut finis ab efficiente producitur, ita efficiens à fine movetur. At quæ nam erunt illæ virtutes præcipuæ inter morales, quas Aristoteles maximè firmas & pro-pè immobiles pronunciauit? non alias, me iudice, nisi quatuor illæ vulgò celebratæ prudentia, iustitia, fortitudo, & temperantia: nam hæ omnes propemodū actiones humanæ vitæ comprehendunt: ideò à felice obliuioni tradi ne-quit. Aliud hoc loco in dubiū revocatur, nempe hominē aliquē posse inueniri, qui & rei familiaris curam negligat, & rempub. nunquam attingere decreuerit, sed tantum degere solus, & sese in variis scientys quas didicerit exercere. Is, quia natura paucis contenta est, in paucissimis admodum actionibus versabitur, totusq; in contemplationibus et scientijs erit: qui fiet ut virtutum facile obliuiscatur, aut illis citius careat, quàm vel scientias obliuio deleat, aut illas magno studio sibi non comparet. Propterea quo ad hūc, minimè constabit quod Aristoteles inquit, scientias facilius obliuioni tra-di quàm virtutes. Ad hoc dixerim: raro, neq; facile inueniendum hominē, qui etiamsi quandoq; reperiatur, non tanti faciendum, ut propter ipsum cōmunis hominū conditio mutetur. Quod hic traditur, plerunque hominibus vsuuenit, neque potest de his haberi scientia quae raro accidunt. Addemusq; non ad naturam hominum tales mores congruere, ut quis ita in soli-tudine vitam exigat, ut ferè nihil agat, sed totus in contemplando & addiscendo versetur.
units.tr: Here someone might say: how does this teaching agree with what was laid down at the beginning of the book? There it was surely assumed that happiness is the cause and end of virtues and actions, and therefore that it had to be settled first of all, as the chief and principal of all moral matters. But here it is laid down that happiness depends least of all on fortune, but is produced by virtuous and just deeds, because these are firm and constant while fortune is uncertain and changeable? These claims seem scarcely to agree: that happiness is the cause of virtue and just actions, and conversely that happiness is produced by these. But this conflict will be settled very well if you distinguish the causes. Two kinds of external causes must be made, and final causes must be separated from efficient causes. Then it will be granted that happiness is among the final causes the most important; yet that it is produced by those whose end it is, nobody should wonder, since this interchange is always seen between end and efficient cause. For just as the end is produced by the efficient cause, so the efficient cause is moved by the end. But which will be those chief virtues among the moral virtues, which Aristotle declared most firm and almost immovable? In my judgment they are none other than those four commonly celebrated: prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance. For all of these embrace nearly all the actions of human life, and therefore cannot be handed over to forgetfulness. Another point is called into question here, namely that a certain man can be found who both neglects the care of his household and has decided never to touch public affairs, but lives alone and exercises himself in the various sciences he has learned. Since by nature he is content with few things, he will be occupied in very few actions, and will be wholly given to contemplation and the sciences. So it will come about that he easily forgets the virtues, or lacks them more quickly than the sciences are destroyed by forgetfulness, or does not acquire them with great zeal for himself. Therefore, in regard to such a man, what Aristotle says will scarcely hold: that the sciences are more easily handed over to forgetfulness than the virtues. To this I would reply: such a man is rare and hard to find, and even if he is sometimes found, he is not to be counted so highly that the common condition of men should be changed on his account. What is here described happens for the most part to men, and no science can be had of things that happen rarely. And we add that such a manner of life does not agree with human nature, so that a man should spend his life in solitude in such a way that he does almost nothing, but is wholly absorbed in contemplating and learning.

units.la: Itaque beato quod quæritur inerit, ac in ipsius vi-ta talis erit. Semper enim uel maximè omnium aget & contemplabitur ex uirtute, casusq; quosuis pulcherrimè, ac usque quaque decenter feret, isq; ceu uerè bonus ac quadratus absque reprehensio-ne erit.
units.tr: Therefore the good thing we are seeking will belong to the blessed man, and his life will be of that kind. For he will always, or most of all, act and contemplate in accordance with virtue, and he will bear whatever chances befall him most beautifully and in every respect with decorum, and he will be, as one who is truly good and "four-square," without reproach.

units.la: Causa iam erroris detecta & sublata, contra quam Solon decreuerit, af-firmat, nimirum beatum etiam dum hic viuit felicitatem in se habere, atq; ab illa posse nominari, nilq; varios euentus & casus impedire. Atq; sua sen-tentia hanc rationem reddit, Beatum hominem semper aut maximè omni-um & acturum & contemplaturum ex virtute. Postquam Semper dixe-rat, adiecit Vei omnium maxime, quoniam fieri non potest ut semper quis agat aut contempletur: dormiendum aliquando est, & vigilantes non-nunquam animi causa, vel cogitationes doctrinarum et agendi studium se-ponunt. Appositè cum actionem tum contemplationem recensuit: quoniam in hac duo tota humana vita distribuitur. Per occupationem additum est quod sequitur: quoniam dixisset aliquis, Nihil dicis de infortunijs: quid si tuum beatum grauis aliquis casus impetat? Respondet, ista pulcherrimè feret ac decentissimè: non enim illi quod vulgaribus accidit, qui si calamitate premantur, frangantur, perturbatur illorum animus, ut nihil fermè videre queant, velut quando fortunæ sunt secundæ inflantur, de studio consueto remittunt, & prorsus negligentes efficiuntur. Non ita erit felix, sed perpetuo fere seruabit eundem animi tenorem.
units.tr: Having detected and removed the cause of the error, he now affirms, against what Solon decided, that the blessed man, even while he lives here, has happiness within himself and can be named blessed from it, and that various events and accidents cannot hinder it. And he gives the reason for his opinion: the blessed man will always, or most of all, act and contemplate in accordance with virtue. Having said "always," he adds "most of all," since it is impossible for anyone always to act or contemplate: sometimes we must sleep, and sometimes, for the sake of recreation, we set aside both our thinking about learning and our eagerness to act. He appropriately listed both action and contemplation, since the whole of human life is divided between these two. By the word "occupied" he added what follows: someone might say, "You say nothing about misfortunes: what if some grave calamity strikes your blessed man?" He answers that he will bear such things most beautifully and most decorously. For it is not like the common run of people, who, if they are oppressed by calamity, are broken, and their minds are so disturbed that they can scarcely see anything; just as, when fortune is favourable, they are puffed up, give up their usual study, and become utterly careless. The blessed man will not be like this, but will keep almost constantly the same tenor of mind.

units.la: Vtuere bonus, inquit. Hoc additur propter fucatos, arbitror. Vere, inquit, bonus & quadratus, hoc est, perfectus & firmus. Metaphora v-sus est, quam etiam indicauit in 3. Rhetoricorum, dicens, [illegible, ~24 letters] In numeris, in figuris & corporibus quadratus reperitur. Numerus qui resultat ex se ductus in seipsum, quadratus dicitur & cubus. vt Sexdecim, quia numerus quaternarius in seipsum ductus eu parit: Quater enim quatuor efficit sexdecim. Figura quoq; reperitur quadra, quæ constat quatuor lineis rectis, habetq; quatuor angulos rectos. Corpus vero cubum seu quadratum firmissimum est, habet quippe sex facies, quarum quaelibet quadratam habet figuram & quatuor angulos, unde quocunq; modo iaciatur firmum stat. Sine reprehensione additur: quod non intelligas, ulla, quia nunquam momenti desunt vel ipsi Deo optimo maximo, qui citra controuersiam est beatissimus, verum accipito quo ad sanos iudices, cæterorum dicta & sententiæ momentum non habent. Notandum præterea ex his non posse felicem esse nisi virum bonum, is í cùm sit prudentissimus, & reprehensione iusta carebit, & semper quocunq; modo res cadant firmiter stabit.
units.tr: "Be good," he says. This is added, I think, on account of pretenders. "Truly good and four-square," he says, that is, perfect and firm. He uses a metaphor, which he also pointed out in the third book of the Rhetoric, saying [passage illegible in the scan]. In numbers, in figures and in bodies, the square is found. A number which, multiplied by itself, results in a product is called square, and cube; for example, sixteen, since the number four multiplied by itself produces it: four times four makes sixteen. A square figure is also found, which consists of four straight lines and has four right angles.
