A body, indeed, the cube or square, is very firm, for it has six faces, each of which has a square shape and four right angles, so that however it is thrown it stands firm. "Without reproach" is added so that you do not take it to mean "without any flaw," since there are never lacking flaws even in God the best and greatest, who beyond controversy is most blessed; rather, take it with respect to sound judges, for the words and opinions of others do not carry weight. It should be noted besides, from these things, that no one can be happy except a good man, who, since he is most prudent, will lack just reproach and will always stand firm, however things turn out.

units.la: Cùm uero multa casu fiant, & inter sese uel magnitudine differant uel exiguitate, quæ uel ex rebus felicibus uel ex contrarijs parua sunt, non dubiu est quin momentum ad uitam non habeant. Quæ itaq; tum plura tum magna feliciter eueniunt, beatiorem uitam reddunt, ut quæ idonea et apta sint ad illā ornandam atque tum honestus tum præclarus est. Quæ uero secus ceciderint, beatitudinem & premunt & inquinant: nam tum dolores inferunt, tum permultis actionibus impedimento sunt: & nihilominus in his ipsis honestum resplendet, postquam quis multas & magnas calamitates pertulerit, non sane per indolentiam, sed quod generosus atque magnanimus existat.
units.tr: But since many things happen by chance, and differ among themselves either in magnitude or in smallness, and those things which are small, whether from happy or from adverse circumstances, undoubtedly have no weight for life. Therefore those things which happen favourably, both in number and in greatness, make the life more blessed, as being suitable and apt for adorning it; and in this way the honourable and the excellent is both. But those things which fall out otherwise both oppress and stain blessedness: for they both bring pains and are an obstacle to many actions. Nevertheless, even in these very things the honourable shines forth, when a man has endured many and great calamities, not indeed through insensibility, but because he is noble and magnanimous.

units.la: Sententia iam allata de infortunijs & constantia felicitatis, in eo qui beatus fuerit magis distinctè ac dilucidè traditur. Quod vt apte fiat, adhibetur distinctio, & ea quadripartita. Quæ nobis eueniunt aut prospera sunt aut aduersa, & tam aduersa quàm secunda vel magna sunt vel parua. His ita positis, parua sumit cum in genere aduersorum tum felicium, & illa inquit nullum habere momentum ad vitam immutandam, vel à suo statu deturbandam. Quod porrò debemus accipere quo ad beatos & virtute prædi tos: alioqui vulgares homines, quiq; sunt nihili facilè ac propemodum leuissimis de causis commouentur atque turbantur, quod probi & graues homines non item faciunt.
units.tr: The opinion already offered concerning misfortunes and the constancy of happiness is set out more distinctly and clearly in the case of the one who is blessed. So that this may be done aptly, a distinction is employed, and a fourfold one. The things that happen to us are either prosperous or adverse, and both adverse and favourable things are either great or small. With these points laid down, he takes the small things, both of the adverse and of the favourable kind, and says that they have no weight for changing one's life or for casting it down from its state. This we must understand with respect to the blessed and those endowed with virtue; otherwise ordinary men, who are worth nothing, are moved and disturbed easily and almost by the slightest causes, which upright and serious men do not do.

units.la: Deinde alterum membrum accipit, Facito, inquit, gra uia esse quæ accidunt: ea si prospera fuerint, augebunt proculdubio vitæ beatitudinem. Rationem affert, quia facta sunt ad illam ornandam. Felicitas extra genus suum augeri non potest, cùm sit extremum bonum: at in beatitudine sui generis, & maior & minor esse potest. Sed quia mentionem ornamenti facit, videtur beatitudo cum forma seu specie eximia posse conferri: quæ per seipsam licet iucunda sit, est attamen suauior, si decenter aliquod ornamentum fuerit adiectum. Et ars fabrilis, cùm instrumenta nanciscitur aptiora, maiores explicat vires, quàm cùm tantùm rudia illi conceduntur.
units.tr: Next he takes up the other member: "Make it your business," he says, "that the things which befall you are weighty. If they are prosperous, they will undoubtedly increase the blessedness of life." He gives the reason: they are made to adorn it. Happiness cannot be increased beyond its own kind, since it is the highest good; but within the kind of blessedness both greater and lesser are possible. But because he mentions ornament, blessedness seems to be able to be compared with an outstanding form or appearance: which, though pleasant in itself, is nonetheless more agreeable if some ornament has been fittingly added. And the craftsman's art, when it obtains more suitable tools, displays greater powers than when only rough ones are given to it.

units.la: Sin verò è diuerso grauia sint & multa infortunia quæ contingant, premunt, inquit, beatitudinem atq; contaminant. Et subijcit, quæ nam illa sit oppressio vel contaminatio. Dolores, inquit, ista inferunt, & impedimento sunt præclaris actionibus. Impedimentum ex duplici causa oritur: Primùm qui vehementer dolent, inepti redduntur ad res agendas. Et instrumenta cùm fuerint amissa, non possumus absq; illis agere vt volumus: ita obest amissio bonorum externorum felici. Mitigat nihilominus hanc oppressionem scu maculam. Quia, inquit, etiam in his aduersis honestum quoquo modo splendere, vt res lucidæ solent in obscuris locis. Proinde tenebræ aduersæ fortuna non ita felicitatem extinguunt, quin suos vel in eo statu edat fulgores, quod indicio est honestatem adhuc retineri quæ in beatitudine præcipuas habet partes: alioqui nō posset suos mittere splendores. Et vt à iam proposito exemplo non discedam, ceu si vir aut mulier speciosissima suis ornamentis nudata, pannis obsita & illuuie sordida esse cogeretur, fieri sanè haud posset, quin eo habitu sese aliquo pacto forma illa proderet. Nec tacet quàm in re sui sint illi splendores, inferendo patienter & æquo animo duros casus, non quidem Stoicè per quandam indolentiam, sed ex animi generositate atque praeclara fortitudine. Iam ista sunt satis ad quæstionem diluendam, An beatitudo in hac vita de quoquam affirmari queat. Et ex his posset commodè responderi ad ea quæ prius de mortuis adducta fuerunt. Et in summa colligimus bona externa, siue prosperam fortunam reuera non incidere in propriam & intimam felicitatis definitionem, sed adhiberi solum vt instrumenta & auxilia quædam. Quemadmodum nec ars fabrilis, ex instrumentis quibus vtitur, definiri debet, quauis nequeat sine illis quicquam agere. Per fortunam igitur aduersam felicitas contrahitur & clauditur, vt parum admodum in actum erumpat: nam dolore quem secum affert mens offuscatur, et uires quodammodo concidunt. Remouet attamen Aristoteles ἀναλγησίαν[?]: qui in ea non est virtus, sed potius quædam stupiditas. Neque oportet homines aut truncos aut lapides esse, qui dum impetuntur grauibus ictibus, nihil sentiant. Sed in eo virtus est, vt quæ sentimus ita regamus & moderemur, ne a statu mentis recto nos deturbent. Scio hic Stoicos Aristotelem flagellare, qui nullis aduersis putent felicitatem & virtutem vel impediri vel contaminari. Sed arbitrantur, vel in ipso Phalaridis tauro beatitudinem perfectam retineri. Et Epicuri tanquam è suis narthecijs illam suam præclaram consolationem promebant, vt habet Cicero de finibus bonorum & malorum, In doloribus, si longus facilis, si grauis brevis. Ista nihilominus dicuntur facilius quam probentur, & aliena sunt admodum ab hominis ingenio. Quæ vero Aristoteles tradit, non tantum rationi congruunt & naturæ nostræ, verum etiam cum vsu & experientia pulchrè consentiunt.
units.tr: But on the contrary, if the things that befall are grave and many misfortunes, he says, they oppress and stain blessedness. And he adds what that oppression or staining is. "They bring pains," he says, "and are an obstacle to noble actions." The obstacle arises from a twofold cause. First, those who grieve vehemently become unfit for doing things; and when the tools have been lost, we cannot act as we wish without them: so the loss of external goods hinders the happy man. Nevertheless, he softens this oppression or stain: because, he says, even in these adverse circumstances the honourable shines forth in some way, as bright things do in dark places. Therefore the darkness of adverse fortune does not so extinguish happiness that it does not put forth its own splendours even in that state, which is evidence that honour is still retained, and that honour has the chief parts in blessedness; otherwise it could not send forth its splendours. And, not to depart from the example just proposed, suppose a most beautiful man or woman were stripped of their ornaments, covered in rags and foul with filth: it could certainly not be that their beauty did not in some way show through that condition. Nor does he pass over how those splendours are in their own right, in that they bear hard chances patiently and with an even mind, not indeed Stoically through a certain insensibility, but from nobility of spirit and distinguished fortitude. Now these things are enough to resolve the question whether blessedness can be affirmed of anyone in this life; and from them one could fittingly answer the things that were previously adduced about the dead. And in sum we conclude that external goods, or prosperous fortune, do not really fall within the proper and intimate definition of happiness, but are employed only as certain instruments and aids; just as the craft of the builder ought not to be defined by the tools it uses, although it cannot accomplish anything without them. Through adverse fortune, therefore, happiness is contracted and enclosed, so that it bursts forth into action very little; for the mind is clouded by the grief that it brings with it, and the powers are in some measure broken down. Nevertheless Aristotle removes [ἀναλγησίαν] freedom from pain, which is not a virtue in it, but rather a certain stupidity. Nor ought men to be stumps or stones, who, while they are struck with heavy blows, feel nothing. But virtue consists in this: that we rule and moderate what we feel, so that it does not drive us from a right state of mind. I know that here Aristotle is lashing the Stoics, who think that happiness and virtue are neither hindered nor stained by any adversities. But they hold that perfect blessedness is retained even in Phalaris' bull. And the Epicureans drew forth, as from their own storehouse, that famous consolation of theirs, as Cicero has it in On the Ends of Good and Evil: "In pains, if long they are easy, if severe they are brief." Nevertheless these things are said more easily than they are proved, and they are very far from the character of man. But what Aristotle teaches not only agrees with reason and our nature, but also accords beautifully with use and experience.

units.la: Si aut quemadmodū diximus vitæ principatum obtinet actiones, nullus felix efficietur miser: nūquā enim faciet quæ odiosa sunt & nihili.
units.tr: If, as we have said, the leading principle of life governs actions, no one who is happy will become miserable, for he will never do things that are hateful and worthless.

units.la: Contra Solonis dictum, ponit felicitatem non subesse, dum hic viuitur, mutationi, quod à re firma & stabili pendeat, nimirum ab actione, quæ recta sit & ex virtute, in quam fortuna quæ inconstantissima est nihil potest. Aliqua sanè illi potest mutatio accidere, sed non ea qua efficiatur miser: nam infelicitas ex actionibus vitiosis nascitur, vt antea diximus, quarum actionum beatus author non erit. Facta inhonesta & turpia vocat μισητὰ καὶ φαῦλα[?] friuola enim sunt & nihili, quoniam à iusto veroq; fine hominum deflectunt. Odiosa vero merito appellantur, quia noxia, cum aliis non committentibus,
units.tr: Against Solon's saying, he holds that happiness does not lie open to change while one lives here, since it depends on something firm and stable, namely action that is right and springs from virtue, over which fortune, the most inconstant thing there is, has no power. Some change can indeed befall him, but not the kind by which he is made miserable: for unhappiness arises from vicious actions, as we said before, and the blessed man will not be the author of those actions. Shameful and disgraceful deeds he calls hateful and base [μισητὰ καὶ φαῦλα]; for they are worthless, since they turn men aside from the true and just end. They are rightly called hateful because they are harmful, while others do not commit them,

units.la: Eum vero qui sit bonus & prudens, arbitramur oes fortuitos eventus decenter ferre, ita ut pulcherrima perpetuo faciat, ex his quæ suppetunt.
units.tr: Moreover, we judge that the man who is good and prudent bears all chance events becomingly, so that from what is at hand he always makes the most beautiful things.

units.la: Nunc docet quid felix noster sit acturus quando in aduersa fortassis inciderit. Ex his, ait, quæ illi dantur, optima faciet, & omnino eorum quæ præstari queant nihil intermittet. Id porrò est optimorum artificum, vt licet semper instrumenta idonea, & materiam aptam non habeant, nunquam tamen committunt, vt quæ illis concediuntur vllo absq; operæ precio sinant perire. Et certè in isto defectu materiæ ac instrumentorum, industria eorum vehementer elucet. Quod item de felice superius docuimus, in medijs calamitatibus virtus quæ illi reliqua est, emicabit. Hic si dixeris, Quare igitur aduersa non dicuntur potius felicitatem illustrare quam inquinare? Ad id respondemus, Quia tametsi calamitates non totam obruant felicitatem, aliquo modo tamen premunt & obfuscant: quod autem in eis virtus nonnihil splendeat, non est ex vi calamitatum, neque quod eò non conspirent vt impediatur, sed quia non sunt tantarum virium vt eam penitus extinguant. Neque cùm aliquæ ibi relucent bonæ actiones illæ vt omnibus modis perfectæ commendantur, sed ex collatione ac respectu ad præsentem statum. Vt, ne discedamus ab artibus, si qui manibus carent, quemadmodum interdum fit, pedibus scribant aut suant, admirabuntur omnes ac prædicabunt eorum & scripturam & suturam, non quidem vt perfecta vel numeris omnibus absoluta, qualia esse non possunt, sed pro instrumenti ratione. Vnde Aristoteles in Rhetoricis, cum amplificare atq; commendare aliqua docet, non solum temporis, loci, societatis & similium docet rationem habendam, sed instrumentorum quàm maximè. Vnde hæc cernens Diabolus, & putans Iobum non daturum congrua & decentia facta, si organa externa felicitatis ei subtraherentur à Deo, facultatem petijt, vt sibi ad suam libidinem ea illi permitteretur eripere.
units.tr: Now he teaches what our happy man will do when he has perhaps fallen into adversity. From the things given to him, he says, he will make the best, and he will leave nothing undone of what can be achieved. This is the mark of the best craftsmen: although they always lack suitable instruments and fitting material, they never allow what is granted to them to perish without some worthwhile result. And indeed, in this lack of material and instruments, their skill shines out greatly. As we taught above concerning the happy man, the virtue that remains to him amid the greatest calamities will shine forth. Here, if you should say: why then are adversities not said rather to illuminate happiness than to defile it? To this we reply: although calamities do not overwhelm happiness entirely, yet they press upon and obscure it in some way. That virtue shines somewhat in them is not due to the power of the calamities, nor because they do not conspire to hinder it, but because they are not of such strength as to extinguish it utterly. Nor, when some good actions shine out there, are those actions commended as perfect in every respect, but in comparison and in relation to the present state. For example, not to depart from the arts: if people who lack hands, as sometimes happens, write or sew with their feet, everyone will marvel at them and praise both their writing and their sewing, not indeed as perfect or complete in every respect, which they cannot be, but according to the measure of their instrument. Hence Aristotle, in the Rhetoric, when he teaches how to amplify and commend certain things, teaches that account must be taken not only of time, place, company and the like, but above all of instruments. Hence the Devil, perceiving this, and thinking that Job would not produce fitting and decent deeds if the external instruments of his happiness were taken from him by God, asked for permission to be allowed to snatch them away at his own pleasure.

units.la: Quemadmodum & bonum imperatorem putamus, exercitu præsenti uti aptissimè ad bellum: & sutorem coriariū ex datis corijs pulcherrimum calceū facere, ac itidem omnes alios artifices.
units.tr: As we also think a good general makes the most suitable use of the army at hand for war, and a shoemaker who works leather makes a most beautiful shoe from the hides given to him, and likewise all other craftsmen.

units.la: Duo exempla quibus adductam sententiam illustrat, ita pronuntur, ut vnum eorum ad instrumenta & alterum ad materiam pertineat. Sunt vero hæc haud parum inter se coniuncta: imo cum instrumentum genus peculiare causæ non constituat, ad materiam potest referri, quamuis non sim nescius quosdam illud ad efficiens reducere. Sed priori sententiæ potius videtur subscribendum, quoniam vt in motu materia formam recipit, ita instrumenta ipsa motum & agitationem ab efficiente proficiscentem substinent, & per ea in materiam efficientis actio transfit. Vt itaq; ad instrumenta se habet materia, sic instrumenta sunt erga efficientem causam à qua immediatè mouentur. Militariter imperator exercitu suo vtitur qualicunq; quādo prudenter acies instruit, loca præoccupat opportuniora, nec sinit rei bene gerendæ occasionem præterire, atq; alia huius generis bene ac sapienter curat. Præsenti exercitu dicitur vti, quia illū quem habet, oportet ipsum probè nosse, tam quo ad numerum quàm quo ad vires, & illo qualis qualis est bene vti, nec meliorem optare: quando ad rem gerendam est ventum, si meliorem aut copiosiorem habere non potuit, iam ab eo non exigitur nisi vt præsenti rectè vtatur. Quæ de imperatore dicta sunt, in sutorem coriarium quoq; conueniunt, tantum discrimen inter eos est, quòd in vno ratio habetur instrumenti, sed in altero materiæ. Vt enim sutori pelles & coria sui artificij materia sunt, ita exercitum imperator pro instrumento victoriæ habet.
units.tr: The two examples by which he illustrates the opinion put forward are set out so that one pertains to instruments and the other to material. These are indeed not a little bound up with each other: indeed, since an instrument does not constitute a special kind of cause, it can be referred to the material, although I am not unaware that some reduce it to the efficient cause. But it seems rather that the former opinion must be subscribed to, since just as in motion matter receives form, so instruments themselves sustain the motion and agitation proceeding from the efficient cause, and through them the action passes into the matter. Thus as matter stands to instruments, so instruments stand to the efficient cause by which they are moved immediately. A general uses his army, of whatever quality, in a military manner when he prudently arrays the battle line, occupies more advantageous positions, does not let the opportunity for doing the business well slip by, and wisely attends to other things of this kind. He is said to use the army at hand, because he ought to know well the army he has, both as to number and as to strength, and to use well whatever sort it is, and not to wish for a better one. When it has come to fighting, if he could not have a better or more numerous army, nothing more is required of him than that he use the present one rightly. What has been said of the general applies also to the shoemaker; the only difference between them is that in the one case account is taken of the instrument, and in the other of the material. For just as hides and skins are the material of the shoemaker's craft, so the general holds his army as the instrument of victory.

units.la: Inter hæc verò hæc est differentia, materia fit, instrumenta non fiunt quando aliquid producitur: deinde ex materia constat quod efficitur, non itidem ex instrumentis cum illa effectum non ingredian-tur. Denique materia est in potentia ad formam recipiendam, & priusquam illam obtineat, priuationi eius est obnoxia, quæ omnia ita materiæ conueniunt vt instrumentis attribui non possint. Ex dictis efficitur, artificis cuiusq; opera non simpliciter æstimanda, sed ex commoditate atque proportione vel materiæ vel instrumentorum. Quod haud secus de actionibus felicis qui iam in aduersos casus inciderit sentiendum est: ea enim iudicanda sunt iuxta præsentem authoris statum. Atq; tum id sequitur quod superius dictum est, ea vel in ipsis calamitatibus suum quendam habere fulgorem.
units.tr: Between these, however, there is this difference: matter becomes the thing when something is produced, whereas instruments do not become it; next, what is effected consists of matter, but likewise not of instruments, since they do not enter into the effect. Finally, matter is in potency to receive form, and before it obtains that form it is subject to the privation of it; all of which belong to matter so that they cannot be attributed to instruments. From what has been said it follows that the work of any craftsman is not to be judged simply, but according to the convenience and proportion either of the matter or of the instruments. The same must be thought of the actions of the happy man who has already fallen into adverse circumstances: for they are to be judged according to the author's present state. And then there follows what was said above, that even in the calamities they have a certain brilliance of their own.

units.la: Quod cùm ita fit, felix nunquam miser efficietur, non tamen beatus erit, cùm in Priamicos casus incidêrit.
units.tr: Since this is so, the happy man will never be made wretched, yet he will not be blessed if he falls into the misfortunes of Priam.

units.la: Si vel afflictus fortuna felix ex his quæ suppeditatur pulcherrima semper faciet, non poterit miser effici. Cùm itaq; illa mutatio fortunæ acciderit, quid nā erit iste felix? quis dicetur? Hic premitur Aristoteles, dumq; nimis urgetur, denique statuit, partim felicem esse, partim non, quia felicitatem plenam non habet, licet illam omnino non amiserit. Medium quiddam in summa statuit, inter beatum & miserum, & eo loco felicem habet, qui gra-uibus ærumnis obruatur. Fuerunt sanè aliqui putantes differre beatum à felici, quòd beatus is dicatur, qui plenè ac omnibus modis sit absolutus & perfectus, at felix qui cùm virtutem & bonas actiones habeat, externis tamen bonis & adiumentis & opibus careat. Sed non ea de re disputo, id tamen dico, distinctionem hanc ad Aristotelis verba non posse accommodari: nam paulo post dicet, ex illis Priamicis ærumnis non facilè posse quempiam sic emergere, ut fiat rursus εὐδαίμων. Ubi apparet illum non discrimen ponere in εὐδαίμων & μακάριος, sed in eandem significationem his duabus vocibus uti. Erit itaq; medius: nec miser iudicari poterit cùm radicem ipsius beatitudinis adhuc retineat. At cùm possit beatus alicui mutationi subesse, quomodo tum firmus ac stabilis dici poterit? Quia non mutabitur, nisi casus acciderint, qui & maximi sint et plurimi. Unde Priamicarum fortunarum opportunè meminit, quæ cùm numero tum gravitate regem illum oppresserunt. Deinde firmus & stabilis est appellatus, quoniam non ita mutatus est, ut in contrarium cadat ac miser efficiatur. Sed quæritur, an fieri ullo modo possit ut tandem in miserum felix euadat. Certè reperti sunt nonnulli qui sic oppressi ærumnis ita cum fortuna mutati sunt, ut etiam tandem socordia ac vitijs & ijs quidem gravibus succubuerint, & à virtutibus quas habuerunt antea, defecerint. Sed crediderim illos dum florerent externis opibus potius visos fuisse probos, quàm revera fuerint: nam sæpè fit in his potentibus atq; illustribus, ut species quædam virtutis sit, non autem solida & syncera probitas, & vitia sub splendore dignitatis & opum facilè occultentur, quæ postea detracta fortuna reteguntur. Sed quare virtutes veræ non facilè transeant in vitia ex eo liquet: quoniam sunt habitus, & hi (ut definiuntur ab Aristotele in categoriis) difficilè amouentur. Et est deniq; firmus, cùm velin ipsis infortunijs radicem ac fundamentum felicitatis habet, eximiam virtutem ac ex ea præstantissimam actionem.
units.tr: If the happy man, even when afflicted by fortune, always makes the most beautiful things out of what is supplied to him, he cannot be made wretched. Since, then, that change of fortune has happened, what will this happy man be? Who will be called happy? Here Aristotle is pressed, and when pressed too hard he finally determines that he is partly happy and partly not, because he does not have full happiness, although he has not altogether lost it. He sets up a certain middle state between blessed and wretched, and in that place he puts the happy man, who is overwhelmed by grievous calamities. Some have indeed thought that the blessed differ from the happy, in that he is called blessed who is complete and perfect in every way, but happy is he who, though he has virtue and good actions, lacks external goods, aids and resources. But I do not dispute that matter. I say only that this distinction cannot be fitted to Aristotle's words, for shortly after he says that from those Priam-like calamities it is not easy for anyone to emerge so as to become again happy [εὐδαίμων]. Here it appears that he does not draw a distinction between happy [εὐδαίμων] and blessed [μακάριος], but uses the two words in the same sense. He will be middle: he cannot be judged wretched, since he still retains the root of blessedness itself. But since the blessed man can be subject to some change, how can he then be called firm and stable? Because he will not be changed unless calamities fall upon him which are both very great and very many. Whence he rightly mentions the fortunes of Priam, which oppressed that king both in number and in gravity. Then he is called firm and stable because he has not been changed so as to fall into the contrary and become wretched. But it is asked whether it can in any way come about that the happy man at last turns into a wretched one. Certainly there have been some who, so oppressed by calamities and so changed by fortune, at last succumbed even to sloth and vices, and grave ones at that, and fell away from the virtues they had before. But I would believe that they, while they flourished with external resources, were seen to be upright rather than truly were. For it often happens with these powerful and illustrious men that there is a certain semblance of virtue but not solid and sincere uprightness, and vices are easily hidden under the splendour of dignity and wealth, which are afterwards uncovered when fortune is removed. But that true virtues do not easily pass into vices is clear from this: because they are habits, and these (as Aristotle defines them in the Categories) are removed with difficulty. And finally he is firm when, even in misfortunes, he has the root and foundation of happiness, an outstanding virtue and from it a most excellent action.

units.la: Non itaq; uarius erit ac facilè mutabilis, non enim à felicitate facilè depelletur: nec à quibusuis infortunijs, uerùm ab ingentibus atque compluribus. De hac proprietate felicis deniq; concludit, & illum ait non esse varium ac facile mutabilem, vt Solon existimabat, qui ob istam causam putauit, neminem in vita felicem esse dicendum. Possumus autem in his Epithetis ποικίλος & ὑμπταβόλος[?] ad id respicere quod prius dixerat de chamaeleonte. Neque obstat his quae modo Aristoteles dicit, aliqua mutatio, quae nonnunquam felicibus accidit, quoniam ea (vt dictum est) perraro vsu venit: & quae raro contingunt, minime propositiones falsas reddunt, quae ad artes atq; scientias pertinent. Potest enim aestas dici calida, quamuis nonnulli dies in ea im ponantur frigidi aliquando. Non a quibusuis infortunijs inquit mutatur.) Quod pulchrè congruit cum eo quod iam dixerat, ea quae leuia sunt, tam aduersa quàm felicia paruum aut nullum ad vitam felicis habere momentum. Fatetur attamen illum mutandum, si calamitates & plurimae fuerint & ingentes. Vnde apparet actionem illam perfectam non esse satis ad plenam felicitatem, praesertim si de illa cuiusmodi agatur. Et mirantur aliqui cur fiat, vt si turpes actiones & vitia sufficiunt ad miseriam, virtus & ac-tio probata non sit satis ad felicitatem, cùm videatur contrariorum eandem esse rationem. Verùm ad id responderetur nequaquam in contrarijs perpetuò argumentum valere: quoniam quisq; seipsum potest occidere, at nemo se a mortuis valet reuocare. Deinde ad sanitatem omnium humorum temperatura & aequalitas exigitur, cùm ad morbum sit satis vt vel unus humor a sua naturali constitutione discedat.
units.tr: He will therefore not be variable and easily changed, for he will not be driven easily from happiness, nor by any misfortunes whatever, but only by great and many ones. He concludes finally about this property of the happy man, and says he is not variable and easily changed, as Solon thought, who for this reason held that no one should be called happy in life. We may, however, in these epithets poikilos [ποικίλος] and easily changed [εὐμετάβολος] refer to what he said earlier about the chameleon. Nor does what Aristotle has just said stand in the way, that some change which sometimes befalls the happy man, since (as has been said) it very rarely occurs; and things that rarely happen by no means make false the propositions that pertain to the arts and sciences. For summer can be called hot, although some cold days are sometimes included in it. He says he is not changed by any misfortunes whatever.) This agrees beautifully with what he had already said, that things which are light, whether adverse or fortunate, have little or no weight for the life of the happy man. Nevertheless he confesses that he would be changed if the calamities were both many and great. Whence it appears that that perfect action is not enough for full happiness, especially if it is of such a kind as is being treated. And some marvel why it is that, if shameful actions and vices suffice for wretchedness, virtue and approved action are not enough for happiness, since the reasoning about contraries seems to be the same. But to this it would be answered that an argument from contraries does not always hold: since each man can kill himself, yet no one can recall himself from the dead. Furthermore, for health the tempering and equality of all the humours is required, whereas for disease it is enough that even one humour depart from its natural constitution.

units.la: Post haec autem non efficietur denuo felix breui tempore, sed si diuturno quodam uiuat & perfecto, in quo fiat compos & magnarum & honestarum rerum.
units.tr: After these things, however, he will not become happy again in a short time, but only if he lives for some lasting and complete period, in which he comes to possess great and honourable things.

units.la: Quia de vna mutatione loquutus erat, cùm ex felici quis deturbatur, non quidem in miseriam, sed eò vt neque miser sit neque felix: nunc de altera mutatione vicissim agit, quaerendo an quispiam ex his ingentibus & plurimis infortunijs emergens, reuerti queat ad pristinam felicitatem. Vbi primum notes ὑπ' αὐτῷ[?] hic accipi pro absoluté atq; perfectè beato. Nam quaeritur an ab illis aerunis & gravibus casibus reditus sit concedendus ad pristinam felicitate, vnde beatus deciderat, vt Priamus vel Croesus, vel tales qui prius vere beati fuerint. Ad quaestionem respondet Aristoteles, id posse quidem fieri, sed non paruo tempore. Opus enim multis est, quae nō statim possunt acquiri & comparari, praesertim ab oppressis fortunae iniurijs. Utq; vir beatus in-star quadrati lapidis non facile movetur, sic deturbatus non facile restitui-tur. In historijs talia non legimus passim, neq; ego scio quenquam magnate euersum qui perfecte ad pristinum statum redierit. Divinae litera unum Io-bum nobis proponunt: qui revera ostentui fuit, et singulari Dei providentia est restitutus. Ac si qui huiusmodi sunt, revera ceu quaedam admiranda & rara opera haberi possunt. Quamq; hoc facto fit difficile, potest luculenter ostendere iam propositum exemplum Priami. Esto, aliquando e tantis malis emersisset, quando unquam civitatem euersam instaurasset? quando regnum ad pristinam formam atq; splendorem restituisset? quando abolevisset dolorem tot filiorum qui occisi fuerant, tot cognatorum qui iam misera captivi-tate adducti erant & Graecis serviebant? Perfectum tempus hic nil aliud quàm plenam vitam significat. Et in ipso tempore, inquit, vitae reliquo usq; ad finem oporteret ut ingentium & permultorum bonorum fieret compos, alioquin denuò non efficietur felix.
units.tr: He had spoken of one change, when someone is cast down from happiness, not indeed into misery, but to the point of being neither wretched nor happy. Now he treats in turn of the other change, asking whether someone who emerges from these huge and numerous misfortunes can return to his former happiness. Here first you should note that ὑπ' αὐτῷ[?] is taken to mean one who is absolutely and perfectly blessed. For the question is whether a return to his former happiness is to be granted after those grievous and severe calamities, from which he had fallen while blessed, like Priam or Croesus, or others who had truly been blessed before. Aristotle answers that this can indeed happen, but not in a short time. For much is needed, and that cannot be acquired and obtained at once, especially by those oppressed by the injuries of fortune. Just as the blessed man is not easily moved, like a square stone, so one who has been cast down is not easily restored. In histories we do not read of such things everywhere, nor do I know of any great man overthrown who returned fully to his former state. The divine letters set before us one Job, who was indeed a spectacle and was restored by the singular providence of God. And if there are such people, they can truly be regarded as admirable and rare works. How difficult this is, the example of Priam already proposed can clearly show. Granted that he had at some time emerged from so many evils, when would he ever have restored the overthrown city? When would he have restored the kingdom to its former form and splendour? When would he have ended the grief for so many sons who had been killed, and for so many kinsmen who had been led into wretched captivity and were serving the Greeks? "Complete time" here means nothing other than a full life, he says. And within that very remaining time of life, he says, up to its end, it would be necessary that he come to possess great and very many goods; otherwise he will not become happy again.

units.la: Quid igitur prohibet illum felicem dicere, qui agat ex uirtute perfecta, quicq; bonis externis copiose abundet, non quouis tempore sed perfecta uita, an addendum & ita uicturum & moriturum ratione, quandoquidem nobis futurum est incognitum, felicitatem autem & finem & perfectam usquequaque ponimus.
units.tr: What then prevents us from calling happy the one who acts from perfect virtue and abounds in external goods, not at any time but over a complete life? Or should we add that he will also live and die in this way, in accordance with reason, since the future is unknown to us, while we hold happiness to be an end and perfect in every respect?

units.la: Putat Eustrathius non de felici absolute ac simpliciter hic sermonem fi-eri, sed de restituto & qui ex malis ac infortunijs emerserit. Ideoq; non mi-rum, si ceu dubius loquitur, cum res illa sit & rara & parum explorata.
units.tr: Eustratius thinks the discussion here is not about the happy man absolutely and simply, but about one who has been restored and has emerged from evils and misfortunes. Hence it is no wonder if he speaks as if in doubt, since that matter is both rare and little examined.

units.la: Quia posuerat Βίος τέλειος [?], interpretationem eius quodammodo subiecit, dubitando, An vitam perfectam sic intelligamus, ut eodem tenore semper vivat & tandem eadem ratione ac in eodem statu moriatur. Quod ideo requiri videtur, quoniam felicitatem ponimus finem & usq; quaq; perfectam.
units.tr: Since he had posited [βίος τέλειος], he subjoined somewhat of an interpretation of it, doubting whether we understand a perfect life so that he always lives in the same tenor and at last dies in the same manner and state. This seems to be required, because we hold happiness to be an end and wholly perfect.

units.la: Sed ego potius iudicarim epilogum hic adjici, quo breui descriptione ostendit, quis nam sit felix: & id agit primum, quo ad ea quae perspicua sunt & in controversiam non revocantur.
units.tr: But I would rather judge that an epilogue is added here, by which in a brief description he shows who is happy; and he does this first with regard to those things which are clear and are not called into controversy.

units.la: Deinde, nonnihil subdubitat, an quic-quam in hac re sit gratificandum Soloni, & ostendit quid ei dari utcunque possit. posset. Primùm igitur, felicem illum dicit qui ex virtute perfecta agat, & externis bonis copiosè abundet, idq; vita perfecta nō quovis tempore, nam ætate confirmata est opus, ut superius est demonstratum, & si moreretur nimis iuvenis aut immatura morte, decederet nonnihil ex ratione verae felicitatis. Hæc ex iam dictis certa sunt & indubitata. Nunc addit, sed quodā-modo incertus & dubitans, & inquit, An addendum ut felix in his bonis & vivat & hoc modo se habens moriatur? Quod si adiiciatur, duplici de causa fit: tum quia nos felicitatem finem constituimus & rem perfectam, quæ videntur exigere durationem æquabilem in his usq; ad terminum vitæ: tum quia nobis incerta sunt, quæ impendent, & in futurum expectantur. Dubitatio hæc inducitur ob sententiam Solonis iam tractatam, cui etsi dare nolumus hominem dum hic vivit non posse dici felicem, tamen utcū-que non grauaremur ita loqui. Notabis etiam Aristotelem uti hoc loco εὐ-δαίμονα voce, ubi procul dubio de vero beato loquitur, utq; statum subdetur, pro eodem ponit μακάριον.
units.tr: Then he somewhat doubts whether anything in this matter should be conceded to Solon, and he shows what might in any case be granted to him. First, then, he calls happy the one who acts from perfect virtue and abounds in external goods, and this over a complete life, not at any time; for the work needs a settled age, as was shown above, and if he should die too young or by untimely death, something would be lost from the reckoning of true happiness. These things are certain and undoubted from what has been said. Now he adds, but in a somewhat uncertain and doubting way, and says: Or should it be added that he lives in these goods and dies in this condition? If this is added, it happens for a twofold reason: both because we set happiness as an end and a perfect thing, which seems to demand an even duration in these goods up to the term of life, and because what will impend and is awaited in the future is uncertain to us. This doubt is raised on account of Solon's opinion already treated, to which, although we are unwilling to grant that a man cannot be called happy while he lives here, nevertheless we would not be much troubled to speak in that way in any case. You will also note that Aristotle here uses the word εὐδαίμονα, where he undoubtedly speaks of the true blessed man, and that, to lay down the state, he puts μακάριον in its place.

units.la: Quod cum ita sit, ex iuventibus illos beatos dicemus, in quibus & insunt & inerunt iam commemorata bona, beatosq; dicemus, sed homines. Et hæc huc usq; sunto definita.
units.tr: Since this is so, we will call those happy among the young in whom the goods already mentioned are and will be present; and we will call them happy, but as men. Let these matters be defined so far.

units.la: Si velimus aliquid Soloni dare atque gratificari, sic esset dicendum, beatos hic esse & dici, sed addita conditione ut sic maneant in posterum: nec refragari videtur Aristoteles, quin hoc detur, ita ut futurum tempus cum præsenti consentiat: Soloni minimè datur ut felix quis non sit aut dici non possit dum vivit, quasi mors expectanda sit. Sed fortassis cum dicitur felix, addenda erit conditio. Sed notandum illum dicere istos non esse beatos simpliciter, sed tanquam homines: innuens quandam aliam beatitudinem perfectissimam esse, quæ non possit ullo modo commutari, neq; adiecta conditione de futuro opus habeat, & illa Dei est non hominum: sunt beati, sed beati homines.
units.tr: If we wish to grant something to Solon and oblige him, it should be said that they are, and are called, happy here, but with the added condition that they remain so in the future. Nor does Aristotle seem to object to this being granted, so that the future time agrees with the present. It is by no means granted to Solon that someone is not happy, or cannot be called happy, while he lives, as if death had to be awaited. But perhaps when we say "happy," a condition must be added. Yet note that he says these people are not happy absolutely, but as men, hinting that there is another, most perfect happiness, which cannot be changed in any way and needs no added condition about the future. That belongs to God, not to men: they are blessed, but they are blessed men.

units.la: Nunc reliquum est ut de his quæ in hoc capite dicta sunt paucis agam quomodo sacris literis consentiant vel ab eis desient. Primùm distinximus de beatitudine, ut quædam esset huius seculi, altera vero in futurum expectanda: de illa futura cum Solone facimus, nam assentimur in hoc seculo non habendam: sed altera quæ sita est in condonatione peccatorum, & instauranda vita per bonos mores, hic haberi potest. Quomodo autem quis dici queat felix ex ea, statuemus cuique de seipso id esse persuasum: nā quisque potest nosse an credat an non credat. Et hoc est, Probet seipsum homo, ac de pane illo edat & de calice bibat. Et habemus testem spiritum, qui testimonium reddit spiritui nostro, quòd sumus filii Dei. Adest et conscientia ac bona vitae testimonium. De aliis nil scire possumus, cùm eorum animus & gratia sit nobis incognita: sed quàm diu rectam fidem profitentur, & in ecclesia tolerabiliter vivunt, de illis est bene sperandum. Neq; statuere felicitatem esse actionem, quicquam impedit quin post mortem hi qui obierunt ea frui possint, cùm vel tunc expeditiores habenda sint à nobis actiones. Ut autem felicitas nostra firma sit & stabilis, ex eius principiis, ut Aristoteles fecit de sua, expendamus. Pendet nostra felicitas à prædestinatione, spiritu & fide, quæ longè præstabiliora sunt, quàm ullæ humanæ virtutes aut actiones. Et multò minus in his fortuna potest quàm in illis principiis Aristotelicis. Deinde nos quicquid Aristoteles in sua felicitate ponit, habemus in nostra: quia & iustificatos volumus recte agere, atq; sese veris & solidis virtutibus instaurare, ac præter illa, sublimia principia quæ naturam vincũt ponimus, nimirum divinam electionem, spiritum & fidem. Nec minus cum illo in eo consentimus, quòd principia miseriæ his contraria statuimus, hoc est, reprobationem Dei, spiritus destitutionem, & infidelitatem. Qui subiicitur his malis, miser & infelix omnino habendus est. De collatione virtutum & scientiarum, nullo pacto dissentimus: imò virtutes damus humanis scientiis magis constantes & firmas. Estq; tanta stabilitas nostra beatitudinis, ut dixerit Paulus de prædestinatione, Firmum stat firmamentum, novit Dominus qui sint sui. Et ex fide ac gratia nos voluit Deus iustificari, non ex operibus, ut firma sit promissio, & ne in illa tutebemur[?] ad nostram respiciendo infirmitatem. Atq; Paulus ait, Scio cui credidi & certus sum. Quiq; nostra fruitur beatitudine, is ictus fortunæ & quidem graues pulcherrimè fert. Dicebat Paulus se scire humiliari & excellere, esurire & sitire, abundare ac penuriam pati. Estitem noster felix ut quadratus lapis, Quis, inquit Paulus, nos à charitate Dei separabit? tribulatio? angustia? persequutio? fames? gladius? periculum? nuditas? &c. & subiicit se persuasissimum esse, neq; vitam, neq; mortè, neq; angelos, neq; principatus, neq; potestates, &c. Non laeditur noster felix fortuitis, sed omnia diligentibus Deum procedunt in bonum. Imò resplendet maximè in adversis. Tribulatio patientiam operatur, patientia probationem, probatio spem, spes autem nō confundit. Utq; Aristoteles ab insensibilitate abhorret, nos etiam illam non ponimus: imò fleuit Christus, fleuerunt prophetæ ac sancti: & iubemur condolere dolentibus. Dicit Aristoteles felicem suum nunquam commissurum vitia[?] & prava, nos de nostro hac non pronuntiamus: quoniam lapsus est graviter David, & Petrus graviter. Suos ille habet non posse citò reparari, nos verò pharmacum habemus pœnitentiæ promptissimum ac semper ad manum. Et potest etiam noster ex his quæ suppeditantur, facere pulcherrima, pro statu & conditione quam est nactus. Vnde minutum illud quod offerebat vidua, tam pulchrum, gratum & acceptum Deo erat, vt opulentorum oblationes vicerit. Postremò casus & infortunia temporaria quæcunq; fuerint, magis impellunt pios homines ad Deum, & à mundo abstrahunt. Non e-nim possunt nostri esse beati, nisi pauperes spiritu fuerint.
units.tr: It remains now to say briefly how the things said in this chapter agree with Holy Scripture, or depart from it. First, we distinguished between happiness of this age and another to be expected in the future. About the future happiness we agree with Solon, for we grant that it is not to be had in this age. But the other, which consists in the forgiveness of sins and in a life renewed through good morals, can be had here. How anyone may be called happy from this, we will leave for each to be persuaded of himself, for each can know whether he believes or does not believe. And this is what is meant: "Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup." And we have the Spirit as a witness, who bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God. Conscience and the testimony of a good life are also present. We can know nothing of others, since their mind and grace are unknown to us; but as long as they profess the true faith and live tolerably in the Church, we ought to hope well of them. Nor does anything prevent those who have died from enjoying happiness after death, even if we hold that happiness is an activity, since then our activities will be held to be freer. But so that our happiness may be firm and stable, let us weigh it by its principles, as Aristotle did with his. Our happiness depends on predestination, the Spirit and faith, which are far more excellent than any human virtues or actions. And in these things fortune has much less power than in those Aristotelian principles. Next, whatever Aristotle places in his happiness, we have in ours, since we who are justified want to act rightly and to renew ourselves by true and solid virtues; and besides these we posit the sublime principles which surpass nature, namely divine election, the Spirit and faith. Nor do we agree with him any less in this, that we set down as principles of misery the contraries of these, that is, the reprobation of God, the desertion of the Spirit and unbelief. Whoever is subject to these evils must be held wretched and wholly unhappy. We do not in any way dissent from his comparison of virtues and sciences; indeed we grant that virtues are more constant and firm than human sciences. And our happiness has such stability that Paul said of predestination: "The firm foundation stands, the Lord knows who are his." And God willed that we be justified by faith and grace, not by works, so that the promise may be firm, and so that we do not waver by looking to our own weakness. And Paul says: "I know whom I have believed, and I am certain." He who enjoys our happiness also bears the blows of fortune very finely, and indeed most beautifully. Paul said that he knew how to be brought low and how to abound, to hunger and thirst, to have plenty and to suffer want. Our happy man is like a square stone. "Who," says Paul, "will separate us from the love of God? Tribulation? Distress? Persecution? Famine? The sword? Danger? Nakedness?" and so on. And he adds that he is most fully persuaded that neither life nor death, neither angels, nor principalities, nor powers, etc. Our happy man is not harmed by chance events, but "to those who love God all things work together for good." Indeed he shines most brightly in adversity: "tribulation works patience, patience proof, proof hope, and hope does not disappoint." And just as Aristotle shrinks from insensibility, we too do not set it down; rather Christ wept, the prophets and the saints wept, and we are commanded to mourn with those who mourn. Aristotle says his happy man will never commit vices and wicked deeds; we do not pronounce this of ours, since David fell grievously, and Peter grievously. Aristotle's man has wounds that cannot be quickly healed; but we have the most ready remedy of repentance, always at hand. And our man can also make the most beautiful things out of what is supplied to him, according to the state and condition he has been placed in. Hence that little mite which the widow offered was so beautiful, pleasing and acceptable to God that it surpassed the offerings of the rich. Finally, whatever temporary calamities and misfortunes there are, they drive pious men more towards God and draw them away from the world. For our people cannot be blessed unless they are poor in spirit.
CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Posterorum autem fortunas & amicorum omnium nihil attinere, omnino ab amicitia est alienum, & contra opiniones uidetur. Cum uero quæ accidunt, & multa sint, & multiplices differentias habeant, aliaq; magis, alia minus nos attingant, singula distinguere longum & infinitum uidetur. At si uniuersè & crassius dicatur forte satis fuerit.
units.tr: That the fortunes of descendants and of all friends are no concern of ours is wholly foreign to friendship and seems contrary to common opinion. But since what happens is both numerous and has many different aspects, and some things touch us more and some less, to distinguish each one would seem long and endless. If it is said in general and in a rougher way, perhaps that will be enough.

units.la: QVia Solon voluerat neminem dum viueret felicem appellari, atq; id ob fortunæ multiplicem varietatem, contra quam sententiam obiecerat Aristoteles fortassis ne mortuos etiam extra fortunæ aleam omnino esse, nisi velimus decernere posterorum casus ad suos non attinere, seu mortui fuerint seu viui, quod inhumanum est & non dicendum videtur. Et relicta est sanè tunc utraque pars quæstionis absq; definitione. Quod tum expediri posse crederetur, cum patefactum esset, an quis dum hic viuit posset vocari felix, vt ut fortuna illius mutaretur? Et revera, dissoluta est quæstio ex dictis: nam si beatitudo, veluti dictum est, à fortuna minimè pendet, & reddi non possumus ex nostris aduersis miseri, neque propinquorum neque amicorum calamitatibus ita tangemur, vt à nobis felicitas prorsus eripiatur. Attamen vt nil à studiosis desyderetur, priuatim ad quæstionem respondetur. Et primùm ad fortunatos ait propinquorum & amicorum casus attinere: quod in universum dicitur. Deinde aliquod ostenditur discrimen inter mortuos & vivos: non enim tam istos quam illos ex aequo attingunt. Esto igitur propositio, Amicorum & propinquorum res euenta etiam ad nos pertinent. Ea duobus argumentis confirmatur: Alterum est, quia statuere secus, amicitia sanctas leges violat. Nam quis ignorat amicum haberi quasi eundem alterum oportere? quod non custoditur, quando ad me non puto attinere, quae illi qui sit alter ego accidant. Si amicitia est una eademq; anima in duobus corporibus, fieri non potest quin ab amico sentiatur quae amico suo contigerint. Et certè amicus haberi non potest, quisquis amici eventa sua esse non putauerit. Decreto Pythagoreorum id usq; adeò verum est, ut ab eis pronunciatum sit, amicorum omnia esse communia. Alterum quo eadem propositio stabilitur, est, Nisi hoc pacto sentiamus, receptae ab omnibus opinioni adversabimur: nullus enim ita rusticus & rerum imperitus est, qui suos tueri nō studeat, & suorum iniurias non ducat suas esse, atq; in secundis rebus amicis atque propinquis non gratuletur, vicissimq; in adversis una cum eis non doleat. Hinc mutuo conuiuia, nuptias, & exequias celebrant. Quamobrem dicendum, res posterorum seu cognatorum & amicorum ad nos attinere, ut ne vel in leges amicitiae, vel in receptas opiniones iniqui simus. Valet porro ac vera est in universum sententia tam quo ad viuos quàm quo ad mortuos: quod si quid sit discriminis, posteà indicabitur. Ponitur ad haec quaedam occupatio. Quiuis enim intelligit, in his quae coniunctis atque necessarijs nostris accidunt, non esse quo ad omnia aequabilitate: nam propinquitatis varij multiplices q; sunt gradus, cum habeamus parentes, avos, proavos, tritavos, & abavos: habemus item fratres, consobrinos, fratrueles, neq; tantum amicos verum etiam amicorum amicos, recentes quoq; ac veteres amicos: & ex his quae accidunt, nonnulla scimus levia, & alia gravia. Unde ab Aristotele videretur exigi posse ut inter haec distingueret, indicando, quibus tangi & quibus non moveri beatum oporteat. Ad id per occupationem respondet, hoc fieri non posse quod aut nimis longum aut infinitum esset: quorum utrunq; cum artes tum facultates respuunt: nam quae nimis longa seu infinita sunt, certis praeceptis, aut ratione definita comprehendi nequeunt. Ideò, inquit suscepto instituto satis erit, si universe atq; rudiori Minerva dixerimus. Non itaq; singula quaeq; persequetur, sed quod in universum indicandum sit aperiet: quae etiam ratione qui leges conscribunt uti videmus. Hi enim cum oēs casus nō valeat exprimere, communib. verbis praecipiunt quod visum fuerit. τύπω[?] quoq; vult dicere, nō subtiliter: quia facilia tradet & apertiora, omittedo nimis obscura et perceptu difficillima. Proinde subdit.
units.tr: Because Solon had held that no one should be called happy while still alive, on account of the manifold variability of fortune, Aristotle perhaps objected to this opinion, lest the dead also be entirely outside the lottery of fortune, unless we wish to decide that the misfortunes of descendants do not concern their forebears, whether these are dead or alive. That is inhuman and does not seem to be a thing one should say. Indeed both parts of the question were then left without definition. It might have been thought resolvable if it had been made clear whether someone who is living here could be called happy, even if his fortune were to change afterwards. In truth the question is dissolved by what has been said. For if blessedness, as has been said, depends least of all on fortune, and we cannot be made wretched by our own adversities, then we will not be so moved by the misfortunes of relatives or friends that happiness is utterly snatched from us. Nevertheless, so that nothing is left unanswered for students, the question is answered in particular. First he says that the misfortunes of relatives and friends concern the fortunate; this is said in general. Then some distinction is shown between the dead and the living, for these things do not touch the one as much as the other. Let the proposition therefore stand: the events that befall friends and relatives also pertain to us. This is confirmed by two arguments. The first is that to think otherwise violates the sacred laws of friendship. For who does not know that a friend ought to be regarded as another self? This is not observed if I think it does not concern me what happens to one who is my other self. If friendship is one and the same soul in two bodies, it cannot be that what happens to a friend is not felt by the other. Certainly no one can be considered a friend who has not thought his friend's affairs to be his own. The Pythagoreans' decree is so true that they declared all things of friends to be common. The second argument, by which the same proposition is established, is this: unless we feel in this way, we shall be opposed to the opinion received by all. For no one is so rustic and ignorant of affairs that he does not strive to protect his own, and does not count the injuries of his own as his own, and does not rejoice with friends and relatives in prosperity, and in turn grieve with them in adversity. Hence they celebrate banquets, weddings and funerals together. Wherefore it must be said that the affairs of descendants, kinsmen and friends pertain to us, so that we are not unjust either to the laws of friendship or to received opinions. Moreover the judgment is sound and true in general, both for the living and for the dead; but if there is any difference, it will be shown afterwards. Here also a certain preliminary point is laid down. Anyone understands that in what happens to our close and necessary kin there is not an equal measure in everything. For degrees of kinship are various and manifold: we have parents, grandparents, great-grandparents, great-great-grandparents and great-great-great-grandparents; we likewise have brothers, cousins and second cousins; and not only friends but friends of friends, recent as well as old friends. Among the things that happen, we know some to be light and others grave. Whence it might seem that Aristotle ought to be required to distinguish among these, indicating by which things the blessed man ought to be touched and by which he ought not to be moved. To this he responds, as a preliminary point, that this cannot be done, since it would be either too long or infinite. Both arts and skills reject these: for things that are too long or infinite cannot be comprehended by fixed precepts or defined reason. Therefore, he says, once this undertaking is accepted it will be enough if we speak universally and in a rougher manner. He will not, therefore, pursue each thing singly, but will set out what is to be indicated in general, as we see those who write laws also do. For since they cannot express every case, they prescribe in common words what seems fitting. He also wishes to speak [τύπῳ], roughly, not subtly, since he will hand down things that are easier and clearer, omitting what is too obscure and very difficult to grasp. Accordingly he adds.

units.la: Enimuero quemadmodum adversa quae accidunt, quaedam pondus habent ac momentum ad vitam, & alia videtur leviora: ita quae amicis omnibus eveniunt se habent.
units.tr: Indeed, just as adverse events have some weight and moment for life, while others seem lighter, so it is with whatever happens to all friends.

units.la: His verbis mensuram quandam praescribit, ut promiserat, sed universae ac pinguiori 〈Minervae: & accipitur haec regula ex iam allatis superius. Ac respicit magnitudinem aut paruitatem euentuum, cum inquit, Necessariorum nostrorum casus, fortuna ac eventa, non sint a nobis aliena, sed etiā ad nos attineant. Ea meticmur[?], ut de nostris ipsorum iam est dictum. Quaedā infortunia levia sunt, & illis nil movetur felix: alia vero quae pondus & momentum ad vitam habent, non faciunt quidem miserum ex beato, sed illius felicitatem nonnihil coinquinant & obscurant. Ita sane de his quae amicis accidunt, existimandum est.
units.tr: Here he prescribes a certain measure, as he had promised, but a general and rougher one; and this rule is taken from what has already been said above. He looks to the magnitude or smallness of the events when he says that the misfortunes, fortunes and happenings of our kinsmen are not alien to us but pertain to us as well. We measure these as has already been said about our own. Some misfortunes are light, and the blessed man is not moved by them at all; others, which have weight and moment for life, do not indeed make a wretched man out of a blessed one, but they somewhat stain and obscure his happiness. So indeed should we judge concerning what happens to friends.

units.la: Refert autem an quisq; casus uiuentibus an mortuis accidat, multoq; magis interest, quam iniusta ne ac grauia prius extiterint quae in tragoediis referuntur, an reipsa committantur. Itaq; hoc pacto discrimen inter ista colligendum est.
units.tr: It makes a difference whether a misfortune befalls the living or the dead, and much more does it matter whether the unjust and grievous crimes that are recounted in tragedies previously existed, or whether they are actually committed. Therefore the difference between these must be gathered in this way.

units.la: Casus atq; fortunae amicorum ac propinquorum licet ad nos quoq; atti-neat, mensuraq; et regula iam allata sint consyderanda: nihilominus eodem modo non se habent ad vivos & ad mortuos. Et certe longe aliter afficiebatur Priamus dum viueret, cerneretq; suum regnum suamq; familiam miserè cadere, quàm Pelops aut Tantalus, qui iam obierant, mouerentur & angerentur ob posterorum, Thyestis inquam & Atrei scelera. Tantumq; inter ista discrimen ponit, quantum inter flagitia quae actu patrantur, & iam longe antea commissa in tragoediis recitantur. Hoc ille in re ista utitur simili, quo plane indicatur defunctos aut nihil, aut parum admodum vivorum fortunis moveri. Nec mirum: Siquidem a morte vel nihil superest, vel si adhuc manent defuncti, neque ita sunt infirmi, neque sensibus amplius quemadmodum prius vtuntur: qui fit vt non inflar viuentium afficiantur. Vnde si aut nihil aut ita leuiter his tanguntur, apertum est illorum felicitatem neque his in miseriam verti, neque maculari aut contaminari, nisi fortasis viuorum existimatione. Quod vero attulit argumentis & rationibus adiunctis non confirmat, vel quod hic locus ad id tractandum non sit idoneus, vel quia ut potius credo, nil de statu atq; conditione alterius vitae compertum habuerit. Quare si modo suum morem custodit, quo solet in his aut mutus, aut saltem non multus esse, qui certis ac firmis rationibus nō va-leat probare, id mirum haberi minime debet. Quae vero iniqua & grauissima scelera e tragœdijs referri solerent, nemo versatus in poetis cum Græcis tum Latinis ambigit. Ibi Medea fratrem dilacerat & filios obtruncat. Ibi Atreus & Thyestes infando incestu & funestissimis dapibus contaminantur. Ibi Theseus filium Hippolytum ab equis discerpi curat. Ibi denique nihil, quod atrocissimum, detestabile, atque crudelissimum non fuerit, haud consueuit introduci.
units.tr: Although the misfortunes and fortunes of friends and relatives also concern us, and the measure and rule just given must be considered, nevertheless they do not stand in the same way for the living and for the dead. Indeed Priam, while he was alive and saw his kingdom and his family falling miserably, was affected far differently than Pelops or Tantalus, who had already died, would be moved and vexed by the crimes of their descendants, namely Thyestes and Atreus. And he places as great a difference between these as between the crimes that are actually perpetrated and those long committed that are recited in tragedies. In this matter he uses this comparison, by which it is plainly indicated that the dead are moved by the fortunes of the living either not at all or very little. Nor is this surprising: since after death either nothing remains, or if the dead still exist, they are neither so weak nor do they use their senses as they did before; so it happens that they are not affected as strongly as the living. Hence, if they are touched by these things either not at all or so lightly, it is clear that their happiness is neither turned into misery by these, nor stained or contaminated, except perhaps in the opinion of the living. But what he brought forward he does not confirm with arguments and supporting reasons, either because this place is not suitable for treating it, or, as I rather believe, because he had found nothing certain about the state and condition of another life. Therefore, if he keeps his usual manner, in which he is accustomed to be silent or at least not verbose on such matters when he cannot prove them by certain and firm reasons, this ought by no means to seem strange. What unjust and most grievous crimes are wont to be recounted from tragedies, no one versed in the poets, Greek or Latin, doubts. There Medea tears her brother apart and cuts down her sons. There Atreus and Thyestes are defiled by unspeakable incest and most dreadful feasts. There Theseus has his son Hippolytus torn apart by horses. Finally, there is customarily introduced there nothing that is most atrocious, detestable and cruel.

units.la: Sed animaduertere operæpretium est, similis propositi duplicem intelligi posse collationem. Nam vel accipiemus, ita fortunas & casus viuentium parum mouere defunc-tos, ut spectatores tragœdiarum non multum sceleribus & immanitate rerum, quas audiunt narrari, afficiuntur. Aut sicut quæ in tragœdijs exprimuntur, de his heroibus qui iam obierint, illos eos de parum aut nihil attingunt, cum aut nihil sint, aut à nobis valde remoti: Ita nostris infortunijs aut casibus nil aut omnino tenuiter permoueri defun-ctos: quasi necessariorum & propinquorum eventa ad mortuos conferan-tur, veluti tragœdia quæ de illis interdum referuntur, atque ipsorum vi-cunque par eademque ratio haberi debeat. Quanquam alius intellectus non minus quadrat, si hac ita permisceamus, ut contraria contrarijs reddan-tur, quemadmodum res mortuorum parum mouent vivos quando repræ-sentantur in tragœdijs, haud secus fortuna vivorum parum aut nihil mor-tuos feriunt.
units.tr: But it is worth noting that a similar proposition can be understood in two ways. We may take it that the fortunes and misfortunes of the living move the dead so little that spectators of tragedies are not much affected by the crimes and monstrous events they hear recounted. Or else, just as the things expressed in tragedies concerning those heroes who have already died touch those men little or not at all, since they are either nothing or very remote from us, so the events of our misfortunes or calamities move the dead little or not at all. It is as if the happenings of our kinsmen and relatives were brought to the dead, like those tragedies which are sometimes recounted about them, and as if the same reasoning ought to apply to their fortunes in turn. Yet another interpretation fits no less well, if we put these things together so that opposites are matched with opposites: just as the affairs of the dead move the living little when they are represented in tragedies, so the fortunes of the living strike the dead little or not at all.

units.la: Ac fortasse magis de mortuis dubitandum, sint-ne alicuius boni contrariorumq;[?] participes. Ex his quippe videtur, licet ad eos pervenire quicquam si-ve bonum sive contrarium, tenue quiddam & par-vum aut simpliciter aut illis esse.
units.tr: Perhaps it is still more doubtful whether the dead themselves share in any good or in their opposites. For from what has been said it seems that, whether something good or something contrary reaches them, it is either something slight and small, or else it is simply nothing to them.

units.la: Cum videat dubium & quidem non leve adhuc remanere de ipsis defunctis, an à morte boni maliue sint participes, id non omnino dissimulat, et inquit hoc magis forte superesse inquirendum. At modo, quemadmodum videmus, non fecit, vel ignorationis suæ sibi conscius, vel quod noluerit impietatis accusari, si post mortem nil superesse diceret: quare non est quod in praesentia illius nodi solutionem expectemus. Verum ex dictis inquit planum esse, nimirum ex prolato simili tragœdiarum, admodum tenue ac paruum esse quod hinc ad mortuos attinet, si quid tamen ista nostra illos tangant. Loquitur ut audimus, non affirmando absolute, sed conditione interposita, ex qua dicendi formula nemo possit certa ratione colligere eu de alterius vita statu quicquam affirmare: quod enim nunc tradit, est, dato seu concesso nostra pertingere ad mortuos, quanti momenti erga eos esse queant? Quod vero adiecit, aut simpliciter aut illis, hunc habet intellectum. Si quae viuis accidunt, eiusmodi sunt, ut leuia, & momentum seu pondus ad vitam immutandam non habeant, tum simpliciter ac natura sua tenuia & exigua sunt, quod si grauia per seipsa essent, saltem ipsis, hoc est mortuis, ob illorum statum atq; conditionem tenuia & parua essent.
units.tr: Since there is still a doubt, and not a slight one, about the dead themselves, whether they share in good or evil after death, he does not altogether conceal this, and says that this is perhaps something to be investigated further. But now, as we see, he has not done so, either because he was conscious of his own ignorance, or because he did not want to be accused of impiety by saying that nothing remains after death. Therefore there is no reason for us to expect the untying of that knot at present. But from what has been said, he says, it is plain, namely from the comparison with tragedies just made, that what reaches the dead from these things of ours is very slight and small, if indeed our affairs touch them at all. He speaks, as we hear, not by affirming absolutely but with a condition attached; by this form of speech no one could reasonably infer anything certain about the state of another's life. For what he now teaches is this: granted or conceded that our affairs reach the dead, what weight could they have for them? As for what he adds, "either simply or for them," his meaning is this: if the things that happen to the living are of such a kind that, being light, they have no weight or moment for changing life, then they are slight and small in their own nature. But if they were serious in themselves, they would still be slight and small for the dead themselves, on account of their state and condition.

units.la: Alioqui tale tantum, ut neq; beatos faciat eos qui non erant, neq; à beatis auferat felicitatem.
units.tr: Otherwise such things have only this effect: they neither make happy those who were not happy, nor take happiness away from those who are blessed.

units.la: Iam inquit, parum & tam exiguum id est, quod ad mortuos negotia huius vitæ faciant, ut illis neque beatitudinem afferat neque adimat. Imò potius nostra hacideo videntur ad mortuos spectare, quod aliquo respectu & quidem per viuentes ad ipsos videantur referri. Passim enim sceleratis dicitur, Magno dedecore atque ignominia vestros maiores afficitis: ac è diuerso bene atque præclarè se gerentibus, Beati profectò sunt parentes, à quibus in lucem editi estis.
units.tr: Now, he says, what affairs of this life do for the dead is so little and so trivial that it neither brings them blessedness nor takes it away. Indeed, our affairs seem rather to concern the dead, since in some respect they are, after all, referred to them through the living. For it is commonly said to the wicked, "You bring great dishonour and disgrace upon your ancestors"; and on the other hand to those who conduct themselves well and nobly, "Truly blessed are the parents from whom you were brought into the light."

units.la: Itaque ad mortuos pertinere videntur secundæ res, nec non aduersæ, sed ita & eatenus, ut nec ex beatis non beatos, nec aliud quippiam huiusmodi efficiant.
units.tr: Therefore the successes and also the failures of life seem to pertain to the dead, yet only in such a way, and to such an extent, that they do not make the blessed unblessed, nor produce anything of that kind.

units.la: Epilogo satis aperto rem concludit. Res nostras ad mortuos quidem pertinere, tamen ita ut illos non vehementer afficiant, atque in hac sententia ii.caput absoluit. Modò superest, ut de more spectemus quantum ista cum divinis literis consentiant.
units.tr: He concludes the matter with a summary that is clear enough: our affairs do indeed pertain to the dead, but in such a way that they do not greatly move them; and with this opinion he completes the second chapter. It remains only that, as is customary, we consider how far these things agree with the divine writings.

units.la: In summa quod res amicorum & necessariorum ad nos pertineant, diuina literæ assentiuntur. Quare iure meritoq; damnatur vox Cain, qua se negabat fratris custodem, tanquam minus ad illum pertineret quæ ipse ageret. Imò divina oracula indicant, lōgè arctius à Deo iunctum ac deuinctum humanum genus genus quando adstringimur ad proximos diligendos ut nosmetipsos. Atq; nomine proximi non amici tantum & necessarij comprehenduntur, sed nobis quoquo modo coniuncti, vel inimicitiarum occasione. Unde pie admodum scribebat Paulus, Quis scandalizatur, & ego non uror? Ad hæc Christus quoq; agnovit hanc vulgò receptam opinionem, & sensum communem omnibus inditum, ut sibi coniunctos putent amicos & necessarios. Unde inquit, publicanos & peccatores mutuo inter se salutare, iuuare ac benefi-cos esse: Quare à suis discipulis multum ultra hoc requirit: nempe ut charitatem suam vel ad hostes ipsos extendant. Nostra etiam spectare ad maiores qui iam obierint, scriptura docent. Nam Deus amicis suis posteroru pol-licitus est prosperitate, & impijs comminatus graues etiam in nepotes cala-mitates. Ac epulo diues ille in Luca descriptus, noluisset fratres ita perditè atq; corrupte viuere, ut ijsdem tandem poenis una secum afficerentur. Ad hæc si viuentium cum mortuis omnis funditus praecisa & abrupta esset communicatio, non vocati fuissent Iudaei filij Abrahami post illius obitum, neque adhuc à morte cognatorum gradus affinitatis, quæ per illos inducta est, custodirentur. Atque id ut verissimum quod hic subditur debet con-cedi, nempe defunctos ob ea quæ hic à nobis gerantur, haud statum seu conditionem mutare. Nam dives ille cuius paulo ante mentionem fecimus, ob cognatorum seu fratrum probitatem, ex misero non potuisset beatus fieri. An vero propter illorum prauam doctrinam, si magis indies grassetur per viuos, aut propter illorum corrupta & detestanda inventa seu exempla, cum iam obierint, ipsis poenæ accrescant, non ausim affirmare. Video sanè ob unum peccatorem resipiscentem ad angelos magnum gaudium redundare: at id non mirum, quando illi ad nos assiduè se conferunt, & quæ hic agatur non ignorant. Quod non possumus de animis nostris identidem constitu-ere, qui nostra suapte vi cognoscere nequeunt, nisi Deus illis voluerit patefacere, quod ab eo fieri diuinis literis non constat, imò potius demonstratur longè secus euenire. Hoc tamen si Deus faceret, ut mortuos nostra ignorare non sineret, non tamen ex eorum notitia, vel sic dolore tangerentur ut eorum felicitas imminueretur aut inquinaretur, nec ita lætarentur ut eorum miseria in beatitudinem abiret. Quæ omnia ut verè ac ex fide orthodoxa dicuntur, ita cum his quæ Aristoteles hic dicit facilè congruunt. At Papistæ qui animas in purgatorio degentes volunt actionibus viuorum liberari, ita ut ex grauissimis poenis atq; supplicijs ad summam requiem & optatissimam beatitudinem transeant, non modò literarum diuinarum oraculis, verùm authoritate quoq; Aristotelis grauissimè premuntur.
units.tr: In sum, that the affairs of friends and kinsmen pertain to us, the divine writings agree. Therefore the saying of Cain is rightly and justly condemned, by which he denied that he was his brother's keeper, as if what he himself did pertained less to his brother. Indeed the divine oracles show that the human race is joined and bound to God far more closely, since we are obliged to love our neighbours as ourselves. And by the name of neighbour are comprehended not only friends and kinsmen, but also those connected to us in any way, even by the occasion of enmities. Hence Paul wrote very piously, "Who is offended, and I do not burn?" Christ also recognised this commonly received opinion and common sense implanted in all, that men think their friends and kinsmen are joined to them. Hence he says that publicans and sinners greet one another, help one another and do good to one another; yet from his disciples he requires much more than this, namely that they extend their charity even to their enemies themselves. Scripture also teaches that our affairs pertain to our ancestors who have already died. For God promised prosperity to his friends' descendants, and threatened even grave calamities upon the grandchildren of the impious. And that rich man described in Luke, would not have wished his brothers to live so recklessly and corruptly that they would at last be punished by the same penalties along with him. Moreover, if all communication between the living and the dead had been utterly cut off and broken, the Jews, sons of Abraham, would not have been called so after his death, nor would the degree of kinship which was introduced through them still be kept after the death of relatives. And this which is added here must be granted as most true: namely that the dead do not change their state or condition because of what is done here by us. For that rich man of whom we spoke a little earlier could not have been made blessed out of his misery because of the piety of his kinsmen or brothers. But whether, if their wicked teaching spreads more widely among the living day by day, or because of their corrupt and detestable inventions or examples, punishments increase for them after they have died, I would not dare to affirm. I indeed see that over one repentant sinner there is great joy among the angels; but this is no wonder, since they constantly turn towards us and do not ignore what is done here. We cannot likewise determine the same about our souls, which by their own power cannot know our affairs, unless God is pleased to reveal them to them; and it is not established by the divine writings that this is done, but rather it is shown that things turn out quite otherwise. Yet even if God were to do so, so as not to let the dead be ignorant of our affairs, they would not on that account be touched with grief so that their happiness would be diminished or stained, nor would they so rejoice that their misery would pass into blessedness. All these things are said truly and in accordance with sound faith, and so they agree easily with what Aristotle says here. But the Papists, who want souls dwelling in purgatory to be freed by the actions of the living, so that they pass from the gravest penalties and torments to supreme rest and most desired blessedness, are pressed most heavily not only by the oracles of the divine writings, but also by the authority of Aristotle.
CHAPTER
CHAPTER XII.

units.la: His definitis, de felicitate consyderemus, reponenda ne sit inter laudabilia uel inter honoranda: siquidem perspicuum est, illam ad facultates non pertinere.
units.tr: Having made these definitions, let us consider whether happiness should be placed among things praiseworthy or among things to be honoured. For it is clear that it does not belong to faculties.

units.la: Saepius audivimus & liquet abunde, felicitatem bonum quid esse, ideo non iniuria modo quaeritur, cuiusmodi sit bonum, atq; id agitur, nempe his quae iam allata sunt definitis. Constitutum enim iam est illam esse, atque vera illius patefacta est definitio, causa demonstrata, illi remoti qui eius non sunt capaces, ac deniq; tempus expositum, quo quis dici debeat felix, in vita ne an post mortem. Quare nunc in dubium revocatur, honoranda ne sit felicitas, an laudanda sive praedicanda encomio.
