Haec tria sunt quae hoc 12.cap. comprehenduntur, quamuis ab initio duorum tantum capitum fit mentio: ad finem enim ponuntur quae ad ipsum encomium pertinent. Sed operaepretium iudico ut a nobis tria haec ex ipso Aristotele definiantur primo Rhetoricorum. ἡ δ' ἐπαινῶν λόγος ἐμφανίζων μέγεθος ἀρετῆς[?] ἀλλ' ἐν ταῖς πράξεις ἐπιδεικνύναι[?]. Laude itaq; magnitudo virtutis explicatur, sed quia latet, actiones celebrantur unde virtus ostendi certo argumento queat. τόδ' ἐγκώμιον τὴν ἔργων δή[?]. Tunc sane adhibentur encomia, cum ipsa opera sunt celebranda, sive maneant, ut colossi, Labyrinthi, statuae, sive iam praeterierint, ut victoria certaminis, patefactae coniurationes, & consimilia. Honor vero est σημεῖον δ' ὀξὺς ἐνεργείας[?]. atq; signa ista in sacrificiis constituunt, monimentis, vel metrica vel soluta oratione scriptis, praemiis, lucis dedicatis, primis accubitibus, sepulchris, imaginibus, victo publico, & adoratione ritu barbarico. Haec de his definitionibus breviter diximus.
units.tr: We have often heard, and it is abundantly clear, that happiness is some good. So it is not unreasonable to ask what kind of good it is, and this is what is being treated, namely by means of the definitions already given. For it has now been established what it is, its true definition has been laid out, its cause has been shown, those who are not capable of it have been excluded, and finally the time has been set out at which someone ought to be called happy, in life or after death. Now, therefore, it is put in doubt whether happiness is to be honoured, or praised with an encomium. These three things are comprehended in this twelfth chapter, although at the beginning mention is made of only two, for at the end are placed the things that pertain to the encomium itself. But I judge it worthwhile that these three be defined by us from Aristotle himself in the first book of the Rhetoric: ἡ δ' ἐπαινῶν λόγος ἐμφανίζων μέγεθος ἀρετῆς[?] ἀλλ' ἐν ταῖς πράξεις ἐπιδεικνύναι[?]. So praise explains the greatness of virtue, but because virtue is hidden, actions are celebrated, by which virtue can be shown with certain proof: τόδ' ἐγκώμιον τὴν ἔργων δή[?]. Encomia are indeed then employed when the works themselves are to be celebrated, whether they remain, like the colossi, the Labyrinth, and statues, or have already passed away, like a victory in a contest, conspiracies brought to light, and the like. Honour, however, is a sign of ὀξὺς ἐνεργείας[?]. And these signs consist in sacrifices, monuments written in verse or in prose, prizes, dedications in light, the first places at table, sepulchres, images, a public feast, and adoration in the barbarian manner. We have said these things briefly about these definitions.

units.la: Nunc vero bona sunt partienda: quaedam enim humana sunt, & quaedam divina. De divinis in praesentia parum agitur. Humana vero adhuc dividuntur: nam quaedam certa sunt & finita, quaedam incerta & non definita. Primi sane ordinis sunt virtus atq; beatitudo: nam ista sic certa sunt atq; finita ut illis nemo possit male uti, & ita prosunt ut nunquam obsint. Incerta vero se omnino secus habent, quia interdum iuuant, interdum nocent, atq; tam bene quam male homines illis utuntur. Huc vero pertinent naturales facultates tes animi, ut vis irascens, nec nō illa quæ cupimus voluptas & consimiles. Illa etiam quæ ratione ac usu parantur, ceu navigandi peritia, pugnandi & dicendi. Potest harū rerū malus esse usus: nec minus interdum nocumentum quam adiumentum afferunt: Cumq; res huiusmodi laude aut honore non existimantur digna, ideo quæstione proponendo illa particula de felicitate interiecta est, siquidem perspicuum est illam ad facultates non pertinere: ac si per occupationem tacita responderet obiectioni. Nam dixisset aliquis, Beatitudo neque laude neque honore afficienda est: quare abs te frustra quæritur, utrum duorum illi conveniat. Non ita est, inquit, quoniam beatitas & in numero bonorum est, neque adnumeratur illis quæ [illegible, ~8 letters] uti sunt facultates, quarum usus est et abusus, quæ nonnunquam prosunt & interdum nocent. Idcirco restat ut vel honore vel laude ipsam omnino prosequamur. Inter laudabilia non collocabitur, quoniam illa (ut dicetur) ad aliud referuntur. Unde in bonis honoratis manebit, ut Deus & illi qui maximis beneficiis nos cumulant: nam honor ad ipsa proprie pertinet. Propositio qua respondetur ad quæstionem, est: Felicitas non est ex genere laudabilium. Confirmat eam prius ratione, deinde authoritate philosophi Eudoxi.
units.tr: Now the goods must be divided. For some are human and some divine. Of the divine goods little is treated at present. The human goods are divided further: for some are certain and finite, others uncertain and not defined. Of the first order indeed are virtue and blessedness, for these are so certain and finite that no one can use them badly, and they so benefit that they never harm. The uncertain goods, however, are wholly otherwise, because they sometimes help and sometimes harm, and men use them both well and badly. To these belong the natural faculties of the mind, such as the irascible power, and also pleasure, which we desire, and similar things. Also those things which are acquired by reason and practice, such as skill in sailing, fighting and speaking. The use of these things can be bad, and they bring harm no less than help at times. Since things of this kind are not thought worthy of praise or honour, the particle about happiness was therefore inserted in proposing the question, since it is clear that it does not pertain to faculties; as if by anticipation he were answering a tacit objection. For someone might say: blessedness is to be honoured neither with praise nor with honour, so why do you ask in vain whether it belongs to one of the two? It is not so, he says, for blessedness is among the number of goods, and is not counted among those things [illegible] which are faculties, whose use and abuse both exist, which sometimes benefit and sometimes harm. Hence it remains that we pursue it altogether with honour or with praise. It will not be placed among praiseworthy things, since those (as will be said) are referred to something else. Therefore it will remain among honoured goods, such as God and those who heap great benefits upon us, for honour properly pertains to these. The proposition by which the question is answered is: Happiness is not of the genus of praiseworthy things. He confirms this first by reason, then by the authority of the philosopher Eudoxus.
The argument can be comprehended in a syllogism of this kind.

units.la: Quæ certa qualitate sunt affecta & referuntur ad aliud, sunt laudanda.
units.tr: Things that are affected with a certain quality and are referred to something else are to be praised.
Blessedness is not of this kind.
Therefore it is not praiseworthy.
But first let the words of Aristotle be inserted.

units.la: Id omne sane quod est laudabile, laudari videtur, quod aliqua sit prædita qualitate, & ad aliquid quodammodo referatur. Virum enim iustum, probum, fortem, ut in summa dicam, et ipsam virtutem, propter opera actionesq; laudamus. Robustū quoque & celerem cursu, & alium quemuis ob id laude afficimus, quod sit certæ qualitatis, et ad aliquid bonii honestiq; referatur.
units.tr: Indeed, everything that is praiseworthy seems to be praised because it is endowed with some quality and is in some way referred to something. For we praise the just man, the upright, the brave, to sum up, and virtue itself, on account of works and actions. We also bestow praise on the strong man and the swift runner, and on any other man, for this reason: that he is of a certain quality and is referred to something good and honourable.

units.la: Primo loco maior syllogismi expositi propositio traditur, quæ tum indu-ctione, tum alio argumento confirmatur. Inductione allata ostenditur quæ certa qualitate affecta sunt & ad aliud referri nimirum ad o-pera & actiones. Idcirco enim sunt laudabiles iustus, fortis et probus, quia istarum istarum virtutum habitibus ornantur, & actionum iustarum, fortium & honestarum sunt authores. Atq; in ista inductione, simplicia & con-iuncta numerantur, id est, vnà cum iusto viro, forti et probo virtus ipsa, ita vt non tantum præditi virtute, sed etiam ea per se ipsa laudetur. Deinde non tantum recensentur animi habitus, verum corporis quoq; adjiciuntur vtrūque velocitas. Referuntur inquit ista ad ἔργα & πράξεις, Forte πράξεως ad animam, & ἔργα ad corpus pertinent: quamuis hoc inter ista discrimen haud perpetuum sit & certum.
units.tr: In the first place is set out the major proposition of the syllogism expounded, which is confirmed both by induction and by another argument. By the induction adduced it is shown that things affected by a certain quality and referred to something else, namely to works and actions, are of this kind. For the just, brave and upright man are praiseworthy because they are adorned with the habits of these virtues and are the authors of just, brave and honourable actions. And in this induction simple and conjoined things are enumerated, that is, along with the just man, the brave and the upright, virtue itself, so that he is praised not only as endowed with virtue but also for that virtue itself. Next, not only the habits of the mind are listed, but bodily ones are added, such as speed. He says these are referred to ἔργα and πράξεις; perhaps πρᾶξις pertains to the soul and ἔργον to the body, although this distinction among them is not perpetual and certain.

units.la: Id deorum laudes perspicuè demonstrant: nam quum referuntur ad nos, ridiculæ videntur: quod profectò inde oritur, quòd laudes, ut diximus, ex collatione petantur.
units.tr: These praises of the gods make the point clearly. When they are referred to us, they seem ridiculous, and this surely arises from the fact that praises, as we said, are drawn from comparison.

units.la: Ratione adhuc maior probatur, quæ docet ex eo non posse Deos laudari, quia oporteret illos ad aliud quiddam referre: Quod sanè perabsurdum est, cū ea sit Dei bonitas & dignitas, vt non aliunde sit petenda, sed in seipsa ple-na satis & solida constet. Nil Deus habere potest se melius quo perficiatur, quod in his requiritur quæ laudantur. Virtutum laus actionibus cōstat, quæ actiones habitibus sunt meliores & illos perficiunt. Quod si quippiam hoc pacto de Deo tentaremus dicere, laudem ridiculam institueremus: nam illa Deus potius dehonestaretur quàm commendaretur. Neq; ista dicuntur, quasi Deus actiones non habeat erga nos beneficas, quæ à Dauide atq; hymnis Orphei commemorantur, eas plane habet, sed illarum celebratio ad honorem non ad laudes pertinent, quia tales non sunt actiones quasi absq; ipsis Deus sua dignitate careret, aut veluti ex illis eius perfectio pendeat. Bene quidem meretur Deus de hominibus: at id non est eius finis, nisi fortassis quo ad cui, quæ de re superius abundè sumus loquuti. Scio equidem locum hunc ab aliquibus exponi, ridiculas fore Dei laudes, dum ab isdem laudaretur à quibus homines laudantur, nimirum à parentibus, à forma, ab armis, à patria, & huiusmodi. Est sanè hoc verum, sed ad rem propositam nil facit, quoniam Aristoteles, ex eo Deos non posse laudari statuit, quod extra se nihil habeat ad quod referantur, & à quo perficiantur. & fortassis hoc dicendo poetas perstrinxit & aliquos ineptos, qui deos imprudenter laudauerint.
units.tr: A stronger argument is also offered, which teaches that the gods cannot be praised because they would have to be referred to something else. This is utterly absurd, since God's goodness and dignity are such that they are not to be sought from elsewhere but stand full and firm in themselves. God can have nothing better by which he might be perfected, and that is what is required of things that are praised. The praise of virtues consists in actions, which are better than habits and perfect them. If we tried to say anything of this kind about God, we would be instituting a ridiculous praise, for God would be dishonoured rather than commended by it. Nor is this said as though God had no beneficent actions toward us, which David and the hymns of Orpheus record. God certainly has them, but the celebration of them belongs to honour, not to praise, because they are not such actions that God would lack his dignity without them, or as though his perfection depended on them. God indeed deserves well of men, but this is not his end, except perhaps as to the "to whom," about which we have spoken fully above. I know that some expound this passage as meaning that the praises of God would be ridiculous if he were praised by the same things by which men are praised, namely parents, beauty, arms, country and the like. This is true, but it has no bearing on the matter proposed, since Aristotle laid down that the gods cannot be praised because they have nothing outside themselves to which they may be referred and by which they may be perfected. Perhaps in saying this he also struck at the poets and some foolish men who had praised the gods carelessly.

units.la: Quod si laus talium est, nemini dubium quin opti
units.tr: If praise belongs to such things, no one doubts that it does not suit the best things.

units.la: mis non non congruat. Sed aliud quiddam maius atque melius, ut uidetur: deos enim ut beatos & felices praedicamus, & quos habemus ex hominibus diuinissimos, beamus.
units.tr: But something greater and better, it seems: for we call God blessed and happy, and we bless the most divine of the men we have.

units.la: Non docuit Deos & beatitudinē non esse laudanda, quasi vellet quippiam eis detrahere: imò inquit illis quippiam laude maius & melius debetur, id vero est honor, cum deos ac diuinos homines non laudamus, tamen beamus. Vnde sciendum Aristotelem in Rhetoricis iam adducto loco, non tantum habere ἐπαίνος[?], γνώμια[?] & τιμῶ[?], sed has duas voces μακαρισμοὶ[?] & ὑπερδαιμονισμὸς[?], quae sane cum Deo tum viris diuinis conueniunt. Praedicare itaque possumus Deum vt principium, fontem, ac plenitudinem quandam bonorum omnium, quae cum de illo dicimus & celebramus, nonad ἔ-παινος[?], sed ad μακαρισμὸν[?] attinet. Quod ait de Deo, itidem de hominibus maxime diuinis affirmandum censet. hi autem sunt benefici, qui ad naturā prope diuinā exsiliimantur accedere, vt qui cum Deo penè ipsa natura communicant, iidem à Deo non discrepent hac honoris proprietate.
units.tr: He did not teach that the gods and blessedness are not to be praised, as though he wished to take something away from them. Rather, he says that something greater and better than praise is owed to them, namely honour. For we do not praise God and divine men, yet we bless them. Hence it should be noted that Aristotle, in the Rhetoric, in the passage already cited, has not only ἔπαινος [praise], γνώμια and τιμή [honour], but also the two words μακαρισμός [blessing] and ὑπερδαιμονισμός [extolling beyond happiness], which certainly suit both God and divine men. We can therefore call God the beginning, fountain and a certain fullness of all good things. When we say and celebrate these things about him, they belong not to praise but to blessing. What he says of God, he judges should likewise be affirmed of men most divine. These are the beneficent ones, who are thought to approach an almost divine nature, sharing in a way nature itself with God; they do not differ from God in this property of honour.

units.la: Ita quoque de caeteris bonis res se habet: nemo quippè felicitatem, quemadmodum iustitiam laudat, sed ut quippiam diuinius & melius beat.
units.tr: It is the same with the other goods. No one praises happiness as he praises justice; rather, one blesses it as something more divine and better.

units.la: Quod de Deo & hominibus prope diuinis pronuntiauerat, idem quoq; de beatitudine affirmat, cuius causa mota fuit quaestio. Quia felicitas nō est habitus, neq; actio imperfecta quae ad meliorem referatur, ideo scribitur nō esse capax laudis. Virtutem autem vt quae inter bona summum locum non occupat, laudare proprie licet.
units.tr: What he had said of God and of men nearly divine he also affirms of blessedness, which was the occasion of the question. Because happiness is neither a habit nor an imperfect action that is referred to something better, it is written that it is not capable of praise. Virtue, however, since it does not hold the highest place among goods, may properly be praised.

units.la: Eudoxusq; uidetur pulcherrima usus defensione, pro voluptatis praemiis & honoribus. Quod enim quum bona sit, non laudaretur, indicare putauit iis quae laudantur eam esse praestantiorem, cum Deus & ipsum bonum sint eiusmodi: nam ad haec alia referuntur.
units.tr: Eudoxus also seems to have used a most beautiful defence in favour of the rewards and honours of pleasure. For he thought that the fact that pleasure, though it is good, is not praised shows that it is more excellent than the things which are praised, since God and the good itself are of that kind: other things are referred to these.

units.la: Suam sententiam Eudoxi authoritate confirmat. Is enim voluptatem summum bonum statuerat, cui cum patrocinari deberet, quod a cateris philosophis non laudaretur, Jure inquit abstinent ab eius laudibus, quia inter bona dum summum locum obtinet, illam non queunt laudare. Cum bona inquit sit, hoc adiecit, ne quis ob id putet eam illaudatam, quod ex bonorum albo sit exclusa. Ex his non putetur Eudoxi opinio de voluptate confir-mari, quasi pro summo bono sit habenda. Sed eius commendatur acumen, qui ex eo quod sibi ab adversarijs obiciebatur, suam magis constabiliuit opinionem, recte a se id non esse laudibus ornandum, quod extremum bonum fuerit.
units.tr: He confirms his own opinion by the authority of Eudoxus. For Eudoxus held pleasure to be the highest good, and when he had to defend this, since the other philosophers did not praise it, he said: "Rightly they abstain from its praises, for while it holds the highest place among goods, they cannot praise it." Since it is good, he added this, lest anyone think it unpraised because it has been excluded from the roll of goods. From these words it should not be concluded that Eudoxus's opinion about pleasure is confirmed, as though it were to be held as the highest good. Rather, his acuteness is commended, for from what his opponents objected to him he confirmed his opinion more firmly: that it was rightly not to be adorned with praises, because it was the ultimate good.

units.la: Laus enim virtutis: nam honestorum authores ex ea evadimus. Encomia vero sunt operum, ut corporis, ita & animi.
units.tr: For the praise belongs to virtue, since through it we become the authors of honourable things. Eulogies, however, are of works, of the body as well as of the soul.

units.la: Cur virtus sit laudabilis modo exponitur, quia inde fit perfectior, quod nos actionum honestarum efficientes reddit, & ita reddit ut ipsa ex eis per- ficiatur. Ut virtuti laus proprie attribuitur, ita operibus encomium, neque refert an ea sint vel corporis vel animi, neque si transeant aut maneat. Cum autem encomii definitio sit prius allata, plura de eo loqui desinam.
units.tr: Why virtue is praiseworthy has now been explained: it becomes more perfect because it makes us the doers of honourable actions, and so is itself perfected by them. As praise is properly attributed to virtue, so a eulogy is attributed to works; nor does it matter whether they are of the body or of the soul, or whether they pass away or remain. But since the definition of eulogy was given earlier, I will stop speaking more about it.

units.la: At de his exquisitè agere, ad eos magis attinet, qui circa encomia laborāt. Nobis vero hinc liquet, felicitatem inter honorata bona & perfecta esse ha-bendam.
units.tr: To treat these matters exactly, however, pertains more to those who labour over eulogies. For us, it is now clear that happiness must be held among honoured and perfect goods.

units.la: Qui circa encomia exercentur & laborant, sunt ipsi Rhetores & Sophi-stæ, ut fuit Protagoras & Isocrates & horum similes. Huius philosophiæ non est de his exquisitè loqui, quoniam obiter in eorum mentionem incidi-mus. Atq; ista tantum ideo commemorata sunt, quia ostendendum erat, fe-licitatem ipsam, quod summum bonum esset, non posse laudari, sed tantum honore celebrandam.
units.tr: Those who are occupied and labour with eulogies are the rhetoricians and sophists themselves, such as Protagoras, Isocrates and their like. It is not the business of this philosophy to speak exactly of them, since we have come upon mention of them only in passing. These things were recalled only for this reason: it had to be shown that happiness itself, since it is the highest good, cannot be praised but only celebrated with honour.

units.la: Et ita quoque videtur habere, cum sit principiū: cætera enim omnia huius gratia omnes facimus. Quod vero principium & causa est bonorum, ho-norandum & divinum arbitramur. Noua ratione propositionem suam communit. Idcirco inquit felicitas est honorata, quia principium & causa est bonorum: neq; causa est quæcunque, sed finis. Quod sanè genus causæ est summum: nam materia pendet[?] à forma, ea inducitur ab efficienti, finis vero agentem causam incitat, ultra finem quo ipsa moueatur haberi non potest. Quare Aristoteles in 2. Physicorum non immeritò pronunciauit finem causam causarum esse.
units.tr: And so it seems also to hold, since happiness is the beginning: for we do all other things for its sake. Yet we judge that which is the beginning and cause of goods to be honoured and divine. He strengthens his proposition by a new line of reasoning: happiness is therefore honoured, he says, because it is the beginning and cause of goods. And it is not any cause, but the end. This is indeed the highest kind of cause: matter depends on form, form is induced by the efficient cause, but the end moves the agent, and beyond the end by which it is moved nothing further can be had. Wherefore Aristotle, in the second book of the Physics, not without reason pronounced that the end is the cause of causes.

units.la: Quæ in isto capite sunt allata, diuinis literis per omnia non consentiunt. Nam homines vt ut benefici & perfecti, atq; ipsa felicitas, non ita summa & eximia bona sunt, vt alio referri non debeant: hoc suadet pietas, hoc rei dignitas exigit, hoc diuina lege imperatur. At Aristoteles nusquam quod sciam, istam nostrorum bonorum relationem in Deum commendauit. Præterea id minus placet, quòd felicitatem ac eximios homines honore dicitor[?] nanda vt Deum, quasi pro meritis laudari nequeant, & Deo ipsi comparentur. Deo quidem dabimus, quòd verè non possit laudari, vt in Psal. 65. dicit, Tibi Deus laus silet in Zion, alij verterunt, Te expectat, Hebraicè scribitur דומיה[?] tacita est. Et Rabbi Dauid sequitur hanc expositionem, quòd Deus pro dignitate laudari non possit, quia omnia nostra protinus excedit. At id vel de vllis hominibus vel de humana felicitate non existimauerim posse piè dici.
units.tr: What is set out in this chapter does not agree in every respect with the divine writings. For men, however beneficent and perfect, and happiness itself, are not so supreme and outstanding goods that they ought not to be referred to another. Piety suggests this, the dignity of the matter requires it, and divine law commands it. Aristotle nowhere, so far as I know, commended this relation of our goods to God. Moreover, it is less pleasing that he says happiness and outstanding men are to be honoured as God is, as though they could not be praised for their merits, and as though they were compared with God himself. To God indeed we grant that he truly cannot be praised, as is said in Psal. 65: "Praise is silent for thee, O God, in Zion." Others rendered it "Thee doth wait for," but in Hebrew it is written dumiyah [דומיה], that is, silent, he is silent. Rabbi David follows this exposition, that God cannot be praised in proportion to his dignity, because he immediately surpasses all our powers. But I would not have thought this could be piously said of any men, or of human happiness.
CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: Quia vero beatitudo est actio quædam animi ex virtute perfecta, de virtute utiq; agendum est, atque ita fortasis felicitatem spectabimus.
units.tr: Since happiness is an action of the soul proceeding from perfect virtue, we must indeed treat of virtue, and so perhaps we shall come to consider happiness.

units.la: Tria[?] sunt quæ isto capite potissimum agiuntur. Primum statuitur de virtute pertractandum. Deinde animi partes distinguuntur. Iuxta quam diuisionem postremo virtutes quoq; separantur. Propositio prima est, Tractandum est de virtutibus: quod ratione duplici confirmatur: tum quia melius ipsa beatitudo intelligetur, tum quia ciuiles circa virtutem potissimum occupantur. Sciendum vero in methodo librorum Aristotelem hunc morem seruare, vt sub finem alicuius libri submoneat, de quibus proximo libro sit dicendum, quod modo licet apertissimè cognoscere: nam quia secundo libro de virtute in uniuerso agendum est, ideo in calce huius, causam ostendit quare id facere oporte. porteat, & quomodo partienda sint virtutes ostendit. Ratio prior qua pro- batur tractatio de virtutibus necessaria, sumitur à felicitatis natura, quae iam toto isto libro est explicata. Et certè cum in eius definitione virtus adhibita sit, ea non poterit perfectè intelligi nisi virtutis quoq; iusta notitia interponatur. Nam quae in definitione quauis accipiuntur, eius quod definitur partes esse quasdam non ambigitur, & nemo ignorat, ipsum totum nos latere, nisi partes illius patefiant. Et finis cùm pendeat à medijs quibus conse-qui possit, eo demonstrato necesse est, ut media etiam quibus habeatur ofte[?]n dantur. Quare beatitudine definita, de virtute iure tractandum est, quo ad illam ut medium necessarium refertur. Dixit ex virtute perfecta, non ut actuosam significaret non in potentia seu in habitu: quoniam id satis ex definitione liquebat, cùm actio ponatur ut genus, quod efficit, ne etiamsi uelimus, queamus virtutem in habitu accipere. Sed intellexit perfectā, quae tam radices egerit, sitq; firma & admodum constans. Vel innuit gradum inter virtutes esse. Quare felicitas dicitur actio virtutis, at non cuiusuis, sed melioris atq; praestantioris, ut est prudentia & sapientia.
units.tr: There are three things principally treated in this chapter. First, it is laid down that virtue must be discussed. Then the parts of the soul are distinguished. In accordance with this division, finally the virtues too are separated. The first proposition is: virtues must be discussed. This is confirmed by a twofold reason: both because happiness itself will be better understood, and because civil men are chiefly occupied with virtue. It must be noted that in the method of his books Aristotle observes the custom of indicating, near the end of one book, what is to be said in the next, which can now be seen most clearly. For since in the second book virtue must be treated in general, he therefore at the close of this one shows why this must be done, and how the virtues ought to be divided. The first reason, by which the treatment of virtues is proved necessary, is taken from the nature of happiness, which has already been explained throughout this whole book. And indeed, since virtue is employed in its definition, it cannot be understood perfectly unless a sound knowledge of virtue is also interposed. For there is no doubt that the things taken up in any definition are certain parts of what is defined, and no one is unaware that the whole itself remains hidden from us unless its parts are made plain. And since the end depends on the means by which it can be attained, once the end has been shown it is necessary that the means by which it is obtained are also given. Therefore, with happiness defined, virtue rightly must be treated, inasmuch as it is referred to that as a necessary means. He said "from perfect virtue", not to signify active as opposed to potential or in habit, since this was sufficiently clear from the definition, when action is put as the genus that produces it, so that even if we wished, we could not take virtue as a habit. But he understood "perfect" as that which has struck such deep roots and is firm and very constant. Or he hints that there is a degree among the virtues. Hence happiness is said to be an action of virtue, but not of any virtue, but of the better and more excellent, such as prudence and wisdom.

units.la: Videtur autem quisquis vere civilis fuerit, circa ipsam quam maxime laborare: vult enim cives bonos efficere, ac legibus obtemperantes. Atq; Cretensium Lacaedemoniorumq; legislatorum hac de re habemus exempla, & si qui alij huiusmodi fuere.
units.tr: Moreover, whoever is truly civil seems to labour chiefly about virtue itself, for he wishes to make citizens good and obedient to the laws. And we have examples of this in the legislators of the Cretans and the Lacedaemonians, and in whoever else there have been of this kind.

units.la: Iam ratione altera confirmatur par esse ut de virtute agatur, quando- quidem ad civilem facultatem, cuius haec philosophia vel pars vel initium est, maximè spectat. Sic poterit Syllogismus componi: Facultas civilis debet de virtute agere. Moralis philosophia est civilis facultas. Quare illius est de virtutibus tractare.
units.tr: Now it is confirmed by a second reason that it is fitting that virtue be treated, since it looks chiefly to civil science, of which this philosophy is either a part or the beginning. Thus a syllogism can be framed: civil science ought to treat of virtue; moral philosophy is civil science; therefore it belongs to moral philosophy to treat of the virtues.

units.la: Minor ut hactenus probata siue posita relinquitur. Maior exemplis con-firmatur legumlatorum cum Cretensium tum Lacaedemoniorum, id est, Mi-nois & Lycurgi. Et si qui alij huiusmodi fuere, addit: quoniam per haec exempla inductionis argumento est usus, quod sane infirmum est, nisi om-nia singula recesseamus, vel addatur particula quae illa omnia indicet se habere. Nec dubium est permultos alios fuisse legislatores, qui iure à pru-dentia & bonis institutis laudari debeant. Commemoratur enim Solon, Draco, Charondas, Numa Pompilius atq; consimiles. Dubitat Eustrathius an his Moses accenseri queat, videturq; id negare, quod populum non humana via, sed omnino divinitus instituerit. At mihi, pace illius dixerim, non ita videtur. Quia pertinent ad hunc numerum omnes legislatores, qui studuerunt homines bonos efficere, non autem refert an divinis an humanis rationibus id praestiterint. Siquidem Lycurgus ab Apolline, Minos à Ioue, Numa vero ab Aegeria se doctos finxerunt, leges tulisse quas promulgarunt. Civilem autem non simpliciter dicit, sed vere: quod ut inveniuntur quo ad doctrinam Sophista ac impostores, ita in disciplina publica administrationis occurrunt sæpe fucati & adulterini magistratus, qui scientiam bene regendi Rempub. vel non tenent vel uti nolunt, aliudq; consilium sequuntur, quàm ut cives bonos fieri cupiant. His vero iam addatur, si magistratui curæ debeat esse ut populi ex virtute agant, & inter eas pietas primas habeat. Ad bonum itaq; magistratum spectabit omnino providere, ut pura syncerąq; religio in suis ditionibus colatur. Quod qui non faciunt, veram gubernandæ Reipub. rationem non retinent. Quomodo autem ex instituto faciendi bonos cives conficiatur virtutem adhibendam, facile intelligitur, quoniam virtutes probitatis sunt causæ.
units.tr: The minor premise is left as already proved or assumed. The major is confirmed by examples of legislators, both of the Cretans and of the Lacedaemonians, that is, Minos and Lycurgus. And whoever else there have been of this kind: he adds this because by these examples he has used an argument from induction, which is certainly weak, unless we go through each single case, or a particle is added which indicates that these contain all of them. Nor is there doubt that there were very many other legislators who ought rightly to be praised for their prudence and good institutions. For Solon is mentioned, Draco, Charondas, Numa Pompilius and the like. Eustathius doubts whether Moses can be counted among these, and seems to deny it, because he established the people not by human means but wholly by divine direction. But to me, with his leave be it said, it does not seem so. For all legislators who have striven to make men good belong to this number, and it does not matter whether they achieved this by divine or by human reasons. For Lycurgus feigned that he had been taught by Apollo, Minos by Jupiter, and Numa by Egeria, and that they had brought in the laws which they promulgated. He does not say "civil" simply, but "truly civil", because just as among sophists and impostors there are found those who are false in their teaching, so in the public management of affairs there often occur counterfeit and spurious magistrates, who either do not hold or do not wish to use the knowledge of governing the commonwealth well, and who follow another plan than desiring that citizens become good. To these let it be added that if it ought to be the care of the magistrate that the people act from virtue, and that among the virtues piety holds the first place, then it will belong entirely to a good magistrate to provide that pure and sincere religion is cultivated in his dominions. Those who do not do this do not keep the true method of governing the commonwealth. Now how the making of good citizens by institution is to be accomplished, by which virtue is to be employed, is easily understood, since the virtues are the causes of uprightness.

units.la: Quod si tractatio civilis est facultatis, manifestum erit, inquisitionem iuxta nostrum ab initio institutum fore.
units.tr: If civil discussion belongs to the faculty of politics, it will be clear that our inquiry will proceed according to the plan we set at the beginning.

units.la: Ista modo interponuntur & quidem obiter, ut indicetur sic de virtutibus tractandum, ut exquisitæ rationes expectari non debeant, sed quales in facultate civili haberi solent: quandoquidem ista philosophia vel principium est vel pars civilis facultatis. Hæc duo sunt ab initio libri huius fusè declarata, nempe doctrinam hanc de moribus civilem esse, atq; demonstrationes ibi mathematicas haberi non posse.
units.tr: These matters are introduced only in passing, and so briefly, to indicate that virtues are to be treated in such a way that exact demonstrations should not be expected, but only those customary in civil science, since this philosophy is either the principle or a part of civil science. These two points were set out at length at the beginning of this book: namely, that this doctrine of morals is civil, and that mathematical demonstrations cannot be had here.

units.la: De virtute autem agendum, humana videlicet: etenim bonum humanum inquirimus, & felicitatem humanam.
units.tr: But we must speak of virtue, namely human virtue, for we are inquiring into human good and human happiness.

units.la: Ne putetur Aristoteles virtutem quamuis doctu-rus, de humana tantum se loqui velle testatur. Innuit Eustrathius hoc dici, quòd varie multiplicesq;[?] sint virtutes, reperitur quippe ciuilis, purgans, contemplans, & vti-tur exemplis: at hæc non multum ad rem faciunt, quoniam hæ omnes virtutes, quas recensét, humanæ sunt: & Aristoteles non humanas à tractati-one sua, verùm si quæ ab homine alienæ sint, excludit. Unde alij dixerunt, non esse hic de virtutibus Dei, quæ tanquam omnium virtutum exempla sunt, agendum, neq; de virtutibus mentium cœlestium, aut stellarum, aut e-lementorum aut naturæ, sed tantùm de humanis. Possent hæc, fateor, accom-modari, sed verior meo iudicio sensus est, ut hic putemus virtutes humana-nas intelligi, quæ ad animum attinent, ita ut de virtutibus corporis nil sit expectandum. Atque hunc sensum quæ proximè dicet Aristoteles confir-mabunt.
units.tr: Lest anyone think that Aristotle, though about to teach about virtue, wishes to speak only of human virtue, he bears witness that this is so. Eustathius hints that this is said because virtues are various and manifold: there is civil virtue, purgative, contemplative, and so on, and he uses examples. But these do not greatly bear on the matter, since all the virtues he lists are human, and Aristotle excludes from his treatment not human virtues but any that are alien to man. Hence others have said that the virtues of God, which are the examples of all virtues, are not to be treated here, nor the virtues of heavenly minds, or of the stars, or of the elements, or of nature, but only human virtues. I admit these could be accommodated, but in my judgment the truer sense is that we should understand human virtues here, those that pertain to the soul, so that nothing is to be expected about bodily virtues. And what Aristotle says next will confirm this sense.

units.la: Virtutem quidem humanam dicimus non corporis sed animi, & felicitatem quidem animi actionem dicimus.
units.tr: We say that human virtue belongs to the soul, not to the body, and we call happiness an activity of the soul.

units.la: Hic apertissimè videmus quæ ab hac tractatione virtutes excludantur corporis inquam: illæ autem 4. numerantur, sanitas, forma, sensuum perspi-cacitas, & robur: sub quo comprehenduntur, vis currendi, saltandi, trahendi, comprimendi & proceritas, vt in Rhetoricis ab eodem Aristotele dicitur: Et illas tantùm esse tractandas quæ in animo inhæreant. Quod cùm ita sit, gradus iam positus est, per quem ad partes animi distinguendas veniatur, cùm omnes virtutes haud sint in eadem animi parte. Ratiõem subdit, quare virtutem humanam illam dicat quæ animi sit: quoniam & felicitas, ad quam virtus refertur, animi actio est. Nec obscurum, oportere medium cum fine iustam habere conuenientiam. Unde si felicitas, quæ animi actio est, habeatur (vt haberi debet) pro fine, virtus quoq; per quam ad illam itur in animo erit. Nec ista sic accipienda sunt, quasi virtutes corporis ad felicitatem nil faciant. Faciunt quidem, sed non ita vt sint eius præcipuæ ac intimæ partes, verùm inter instrumenta censeri debet, & multò sanè præ-stantiora quàm diuitiæ.
units.tr: Here we see very clearly which virtues are excluded from this treatment, namely the virtues of the body. These are numbered as four: health, beauty, keenness of the senses, and strength; under strength are included the power of running, leaping, pulling, and gripping, and height of stature, as Aristotle himself says in the Rhetoric. And he says that only those virtues which inhere in the soul are to be treated. Since this is so, a step has now been laid down by which we come to distinguish the parts of the soul, since not all virtues are in the same part of the soul. He gives the reason why he calls it human virtue, the one that belongs to the soul: because happiness, to which virtue is referred, is also an activity of the soul. It is not obscure that the means ought to have a fitting correspondence with the end. Hence if happiness, which is an activity of the soul, is held as the end (as it ought to be), virtue too, through which one goes to it, will be in the soul. Nor are these things to be taken as if bodily virtues contributed nothing to happiness. They do contribute, but not so as to be its principal and inner parts; they must rather be counted among the instruments, and certainly far more excellent than riches.

units.la: Si autem hæc ita se habent, liquet oportere ciuile nosse aliquo modo quæ ad animum spectant, quæ-admodum uel oculos uel corpus uniuersum sanatu-rus, atque hoc magis quanto & honoratior & me-lior est ciuilis facultas quam medicina.
units.tr: If these things are so, it is clear that the civil man must know in some measure the things that pertain to the soul, just as the physician who is about to heal the eyes or the whole body must; and this all the more, since civil science is more honourable and better than medicine.

units.la: Quoniam animus virtutum est subiectum, ideò prius de illo quaedam videnda sunt, quàm de illius accidentib. agatur. Simili hoc suum consilium Aristoteles confirmat. Quia medicus idem agit: is enim ante naturam corporis & oculi speculat, quàm ad ista curanda manus admoueat. Augetur verò argumenti vis, quàdo in ista similitudine à minori ad maius pro-ceditur. Medica enim facultas ciuili habetur longè inferior: quare si medicus non ignorat qua tractaturus et sanaturus est membra, ciuilis multò ma-gis erit, animum, in quo sunt virtutes, cognoscere. Appositá est & commodissima similitudo medici & ciuilis. Vt enim ille medetur corpori, sic iste a-nimum bonis institutis curare satagit. Et est propemodum ac si cernamus hominis duas praecipuas partes à duplici facultate regendas & instaurandas: ciuili creditur animus, corpus medico. Vtq; medicus ante omnia de vnaquaq; corporis parte scire curat, quae illi ex natura propria conueniant, deinde intuetur, quid morbus incidens afferat eius naturae contrarium: quibus perspectis de remedijs prospicit, quibus illa corporis partes ad pro-priùm naturae statum reuocet. Atque cùm haec ad corpus pertineant, quod animo notius est, rationem argumentandi à similibus pulchrè obseruauit, quandoquidem ex his quae notiora sunt & apertiora similitudinem duxit. Nec sine ratione speciatim oculi mentionem fecit: vel quia is etiam finis est moralis doctrinae, vt mentis oculus non obscuretur aut flectatur ad errores ex animi affectibus immoderatis aut perturbatione vehementiori: vel quod inter catera corporis membra, oculorum notitia sit difficilior, cùm multiplicibus varijsq; rebus constent: ibi enim sunt membrana complures, humores varij, nervi, ac venae permultae. Vnde si medicus non perterreretur ea difficul-tate, neq; ciuilis à notitia quadam animi se minimè debet subtrahere. Duo sunt quae medico attribuit, notitiam oculi & corporis: quibus innuit duo medicum oportere nosse, totum quidem hominis corpus, & particulam illam priuatam quam sanat: quae si ad ciuilem transtuleris, oculos ad animum, corpus ad omnes partes & ordines Reipub. referes. Ideò addidit aliquo modo, quoniam ciuili non vult vniuersam de animo scientiam obtrudere, quàm quatenus ad virtutes accommodatur.
units.tr: Since the soul is the subject of the virtues, some things about it must be examined before we treat its accidents. Aristotle confirms his plan by a similar case: the physician does the same, for he studies the nature of the body and of the eye before he applies his hand to curing them. The force of the argument is increased when, in this comparison, one proceeds from the lesser to the greater. For the medical art is held to be far inferior to civil science; so if the physician does not ignore the limbs he is going to treat and heal, the civil man will much more need to know the soul, in which the virtues are. The comparison of the civil man and the physician is also very apt. For as the one heals the body, so the other labours to care for the soul by good institutions. It is almost as if we saw that man has two principal parts, to be governed and restored by a twofold art: the soul is entrusted to the civil man, the body to the physician. And as the physician takes care above all to know what belongs to each part of the body by its own nature, then looks at what disease brings that is contrary to that nature, and having seen these things, provides remedies by which he may restore those parts of the body to their proper natural state, so likewise the civil man must do for the soul. And since these things pertain to the body, which is better known to us than the soul, he has rightly observed the method of argument from like things, since he drew the comparison from what is better known and clearer. Nor without reason did he mention the eye especially: either because this too is the aim of moral teaching, that the eye of the mind may not be darkened or turned aside to error by immoderate affections of the soul or by more violent disturbance; or because among the other members of the body, knowledge of the eyes is more difficult, since they consist of many and varied things: for there are several membranes, various humours, nerves, and very many veins. Hence if the physician is not deterred by that difficulty, neither should the civil man withdraw himself at all from some knowledge of the soul. He attributes two things to the physician, knowledge of the eye and of the body, by which he hints that the physician must know two things: the whole body of man, and that particular part which he heals. If you transfer this to the civil man, you will refer the eyes to the soul and the body to all the parts and orders of the commonwealth. He added "in some way" because he does not wish to force upon the civil man a complete science of the soul, but only so far as it is suited to the virtues.

units.la: Et qui utique sunt inter medicos elegantes, plurimùm circa corporis notitiam laborant.
units.tr: And indeed, among physicians, those who are elegant labour much over knowledge of the body.

units.la: Ne putes illum de quibusuis medicis agere, τὰς χαρίεντας[?] nominatim exprimit, ut qui non ignoret, aliquos crassiores facile notitiam huiusmodi corporis corporis & oculorum præterire, ac tantum quibusdam experimentis vti. Propterea inquit, elegantiores medicos circa notitiam corporis plurimum laborare. Quamobrem quod illi magno studio ac labore sibi vendicant, ciuili turpissimum erit negligere. Vim hic sermo profecto habet adhortandi, vt quæ mox de animo dicenda sunt prompte atq; alacriter accipiantur. Medici elegantiores, qui modò commemorantur, fuere Machaon, Podalirius, Aesculapius, Hippocrates, Erisistratus atq; consimiles qui ætatem Aristotelis præcesserunt.
units.tr: Do not think he is speaking of physicians of any kind: he names expressly "the elegant ones", as one who knows that some cruder practitioners easily pass over knowledge of this kind of body and of the eyes, and use only certain experiments. Therefore he says that the more elegant physicians labour much over knowledge of the body. Wherefore, what they claim for themselves with great zeal and labour, it will be most shameful for the civil man to neglect. This statement certainly has the force of exhorting that what is about to be said of the soul be received promptly and eagerly. The more elegant physicians just mentioned were Machaon, Podalirius, Asclepius, Hippocrates, Erasistratus, and similar men who preceded the age of Aristotle.

units.la: Viro itaque ciuili de animo consyderandum est, sed ita consyderandum est, ut horum gratia id fiat, et quantum satis fuerit ad ea quæ inquiruntur: nam penitius & exquisitè ista cognoscere, operosius fortasse est, quàm quæ modò sunt proposita.
units.tr: The civil man must therefore consider the soul, but in such a way that this is done for the sake of these matters, and as far as is sufficient for the things being inquired into; for to know these things more thoroughly and exactly is perhaps more laborious than what has now been set forth.

units.la: Non vniuersam de animo doctrinam seu scientiam huc transferendam censet, sed quantum ad ea quæ modò aguntur satis fuerit. Nam quæ obiter in aliqua facultate sumenda interdum sunt, non debent ceu ex professo tractari, alioqui libri in immensum crescerent, & superfluis compluribus lectores onerarentur. Hoc est quod inquit operosius id fore, quàm sit res proposita. Quis ignorat scientiam de animo integram & perfectam tota philosophia de moribus esse difficiliorem multò? Si quis innumeras eas quæstiones videre cupiat, librum primum eius tractationis perlegat. Non vult Aristoteles vt quisquam auditorum labore deterreatur, quo minus his attendat, quæ de animi natura statim est interpositurus. Id obiter notabimus o-mnium facultatum seu scientiarum quosdam esse præscriptos fines, eosque non par esse excedere: unde quæ obiter accesserunt, curandum est vt parce inducantur, ne παρέργα institutis vel plura vel paria fiant. Et quia illa quæ per seipsa tractantur, non eadem sunt cum iis quæ propter aliud spectantur, ideò vt ut in illis prolixè agamus, in iis haud immorandum est nisi quantum ipsa necessitas coegerit. Possumus etiam ex his quæ nunc dicuntur intelligere, vt scientiæ sibi mutuò inseruiant, neq; vlla earum propemodum reperitur, quæ alterius opera in aliqua sui parte non indigeat. Est enim mira bonarum rerum connexio, neq; minus quàm virtutes ipsæ quoque scientiæ inter se coniunctæ sunt.
units.tr: He judges that a whole doctrine or science of the soul is not to be brought in here, but only so far as is enough for the matters now in hand. For things that are taken up in passing in some discipline ought not to be treated as if professedly, otherwise books would grow immensely and readers would be burdened with many superfluities. This is what he means in saying that it would be more laborious than the matter proposed. Who does not know that a complete and perfect science of the soul is far more difficult than the whole philosophy of morals? If anyone wishes to see those countless questions, let him read through the first book of that treatise. Aristotle does not want any of his hearers to be deterred by the labour from attending to those things which he is about to insert concerning the nature of the soul. We will note in passing that every faculty or science has certain prescribed limits, and it is not fitting to exceed them; hence whatever has incidentally come in must be introduced sparingly, lest digressions become as large as, or larger than, the main subject. And because those things which are treated for their own sake are not the same as those which are regarded for the sake of something else, therefore, just as we should deal at length with the former, so in the latter we should not linger beyond what necessity itself compels. We can also understand from what is now said that the sciences serve one another, and there is hardly any of them which does not in some part need the work of another. For there is a wonderful connection among good things, and the sciences are joined together no less than the virtues themselves.

units.la: Dicuntur autem de ipso nonnulla & in externis sermonibus abundè satis, & ijs modo est utendum.
units.tr: Some things are said about it in his external discourses, quite sufficiently, and it is only these that we need to use.

units.la: Quæ de animo faciant huc, indicat, ex quo loco sumi queant, nempè ex illis eius scriptis quæ vocat ἐξωτερικὰ [?]: ibi enim quædam se ait copiosè tradidisse, quibus in præsentia utendum censet, ea verò mox ipse referet. Ad quæ priusquam accedamus dicendum est, quòd sit ponendum discrimen inter ea scripta Aristotelis quæ ἀκροάματα [?] & quæ ἐξωτερικὰ [?] nominantur. Putant Eustrathius illa fuisse ἀκροάματα [?], quæ auditoribus proponebantur legenda, & ab ipso eodem explicabantur: ἐξωτερικὰ [?] verò fuisse, quæ requirebant de aliquo argumento ad quempiam scripsisset. Cicero verò 5. de Finibus habet: Duo genera librorum sunt, unum populariter scriptum quod ἐξωτερικὸν [?] appellabant, Alterum limatius quod in commentarijs reliquerunt. Gellius 2. lib. cap. 4. Exoterica dicebantur quæ ad rhetoricas meditationes, facultatem argutiarum, ciniliumq; rerum notitiam conducebant: Acroamatica autem vocabantur in quibus philosophia remotior subtiliorq; agitabatur, quæq; ad naturæ contemplationes, disceptationesve Dialecticas pertinebant. Ex his ut arbitror liquet, Exoterica illa fuisse quæ vulgabantur, facilius q; intelligi poterant, ut quæ non tantum haberent acuminis, methodi subtilisq; tractationis. Acroamata verò quæ tantùm in scholis retinebantur, neque poterant nisi ab exercitatis & bene doctis facilè cognosci. Cùm itaque nunc Aristoteles agat cum ciuilibus hominibus & de moribus tractet, lectores non ad libros suos de Anima remittit, qui sanè, ut iudico, acroamatici sunt, quandoquidem ibi methodus absolutissima conseruatur, & omnia multò subtilissimè atq; acutissimè scribuntur, sed ἐξωτερικὰ [?] ut faciliora & quibuslibet peruia. Et in eis non omnia de animo se scripsisse ait, sed quædam, innuens ibi non contineri perfectam tractationem. Atq; dicit, Et in externis, innuens rem alibi quoq; tractatam & perfectius: quæ tamen inde sumenda sint, ipse (ut audiemus) recitabit.
units.tr: What he says about the soul bears on this, and he indicates the place from which they may be drawn: namely from those of his writings which he calls exoterical [ἐξωτερικὰ]. For there he says he has set out certain things at length, which he thinks should be used for the present, and which he will himself soon recount. Before we come to these, it must be said that a distinction is to be drawn between those writings of Aristotle which are called acroamatic [ἀκροάματα] and those called exoterical [ἐξωτερικὰ]. Eustratius thinks the acroamatic were those set before hearers to be read and explained by Aristotle himself, while the exoterical were those he wrote for someone who asked him about a subject. Cicero, in book 5 of De Finibus, says: there are two kinds of books, one written popularly, which they called exoterical, and another more polished, which they left in their commentaries. Gellius, book 2, chapter 4: those were called exoterical which served rhetorical exercises, the faculty of cleverness, and knowledge of civic matters; but those were called acroamatic in which a more remote and subtle philosophy was treated, and which pertained to the contemplation of nature or dialectical disputations. From these, as I think, it is clear that the exoterical were those which were published, and could be understood more easily, since they had less sharpness, method and subtle treatment. But the acroamata were kept only in the schools, and could not easily be recognised except by the practised and well taught. Since, therefore, Aristotle now deals with civil men and treats of morals, he does not send his readers back to his books On the Soul, which are surely, as I judge, acroamatic, since there the most complete method is kept and everything is written most subtly and acutely; he sends them to the exoterical works, as easier and open to anyone. And in them he says he has not written everything about the soul, but only certain things, hinting that a complete treatment is not contained there. And he says "in the external [writings]", hinting that the matter is treated elsewhere too, and more fully. What he will recite from there, however, he will himself set out, as we shall hear.

units.la: Ut unam partem eius esse rationis expertem, alteram uero eam habere. Hæc uero utrum distincta sint ceu particulæ corporis, & omne quod diuidi potest, seu duo sunt ratione, cùm alioqui suapte natura nequeant à se mutuo diuelli, quemadmodum in ambitu conuexum & concauum, ad id quod agi-tur, nihil interest.
units.tr: That one part of it is devoid of reason, and the other has it. Whether these are distinct like parts of a body, and whatever can be divided, or are two only in reason, since by their nature they cannot be torn apart from each other, as in the circumference of a circle, convex and concave, makes no difference to what is being discussed.

units.la: Partitio quae adhibetur est, partium animi vnam esse quae rationem habeat, alteram quae non habeat. Atq; hic, ne simus id nescij, secunda huius capitis pars tractatur, qua distinguuntur animi partes quantum ad virtutes attinet, quae in illis haerent. Sed animaduertendum vtrunq; allatae diuisionis membrum adhuc partiendum, quia quod ratione caret, aut illa omnino vacuum est, vt vires alendi augendiq; corpus & id genus aliae: aut ratione caret, quod eam ex seipso non habet, sed tamen eius gubernationis atq; regiminis est vtcunq; capax: tales autem habentur, vis quae irascitur vna cum illa quae cupit.
units.tr: The division employed is: of the parts of the soul, one has reason, the other does not. And here, lest we be ignorant of it, the second part of this chapter is treated, in which the parts of the soul are distinguished as far as the virtues that inhere in them are concerned. But it should be noted that each member of the division given must be divided further. What lacks reason is either entirely empty of it, like the powers of nourishing and increasing the body and others of that kind; or it lacks reason, which it does not have from itself, but is nonetheless in some way capable of being governed and ruled by it. Such are held to be the power that is angry and the power that desires.

units.la: Quod item rationem habere dicitur, bifariam distin-guendum est. Nam aut est rationem per seipsum obtinens, cuiusmodi vis intelligendi seu mens esse non dubitatur. Aut rationis duntaxat capax est, quod ei obtemperat, & ab illa se gubernari patitur. Qui fit vt in facultate irascè te atque cupiente fortitudo, temperantia & id genus virtutes queant collo-cari: quod minimè liceret, si partes istae animi crassiores à ratione prorsus essent vacuae. Atque hoc animus noster quo ad illam partem inferiorem ab anima brutorum interest, quod ibi nos à ratione possumus regi ac ex virtute duci, quod feris non potest vsu venire. Non quasi & ipsa aliqua ratione non agantur: aguntur quippe ratione, at naturae seu Dei moderatoris naturae, at non ea ratione quae sit animis eorum coniuncta, vt nostram nobis adesse compertum habemus.
units.tr: Likewise, what is said to have reason must be distinguished in two ways. For either it has reason through itself, such as the power of understanding, or mind, which no one doubts. Or it is merely capable of reason, in that it obeys it and allows itself to be governed by it. Hence in the faculty that is angry and desires, fortitude, temperance and such virtues can be placed; which would by no means be allowed if those cruder parts of the soul were wholly empty of reason. In this our soul differs from the soul of brutes in that lower part: we can be ruled by reason and led by virtue, which cannot happen to wild beasts. Not as if they too were not governed by some reason: they are indeed governed by reason, but by the reason of nature, or of God the governor of nature, not by that reason which is joined to their souls, as we know ours is present to us.

units.la: Quomodo autem vna istarum partium ab altera differat, ratione inquâ vel separatione in reipsa, inquit ad praesens negotium nil referre. Distin-guuntur ceu particulae corporis animi vires, quando varia & loco separatae, taillarum[?] subiecta ponerentur, quasi ratio in cerebro, vis irascendi in corde, cupiendi in epate resideret. Etenim quae sic inter se se subiecto differunt, reipsa diuidi compertum est. Per id autem quod diuidi potest, corpus quodlibet ac illius partes intelligit: quandoquidem non sunt simul, neq; in eode loco seu puncto vniuersae habentur. Quod sanè proprium est spiritus, vt simul sit totus vbicunque fuerit: in his vero quae molem habent, res hoc modo non est, imò quaedam partes vt aliis iungantur atque continuentur, extra eas nihilominus iacent, alioquin diuidi ac secari non possent. Vnde colligimus quaedam reipsa distingui, alia vero mente seu cogitatione se interponente, cum suapte natura iuncta sint & indiuulsè copulata. Exemplis hoc patefacit, conuexi & concaui, quæ figuræ ambitus manifestæ sunt proprietates. Etenim, ut Euclides inquit, κύκλῳ δὲ σχῆμα ἐπίπεδον, οὗ μιᾶς γραμμῆς περιεχομένου [?] ἡ καλεῖται περιφέρεια [?]. Circulus siue orbis est figura plana, quam linea una complectitur, quæ vocatur ambitus. In figura huiusmodi conuexum & concauum actu & reipsa diuidi non potest, cum lineis constet, quæ cum latitudine tum altitudine carent. Ratione igitur ista solum differunt: quia linea eadem qua exteriorem partem respicit, conuexum, quæ verò interiorem, concauum in circulo appellabitur. Quòd si de figura non agatur, sed de corpore sphærico, id est de globo, Conuexum ibi & concauum reipsa poterit diuidi. Nam globus Lunaris, parte sua concaua ignis elementum attingit, deuexa globum Mercurij quem supra se habet.
units.tr: As to how one of these parts differs from another, whether in reason or in separation in fact, he says it makes no difference to the present business. The powers of the soul are distinguished as parts of a body when they are placed in various subjects, separated in place, as if reason resided in the brain, the power of anger in the heart, and desire in the liver. For those which thus differ from each other in subject are known to be divided in fact. Through what can be divided we understand any body and its parts, since they are not all together, nor are they all held in the same place or point. This is indeed proper to spirit, that it is wholly present wherever it is; but in things that have mass it is not so. Rather, some parts, in order to be joined and connected with others, nevertheless lie outside them; otherwise they could not be divided or cut. Whence we gather that some things are distinguished in fact, others only when the mind or thought interposes, though by their nature they are joined and inseparably coupled. He makes this plain by examples: convex and concave, which are manifest properties of a circumference. For, as Euclid says, "a plane figure of a circle, which is contained by one line, which is called a circumference" [κύκλῳ δὲ σχῆμα ἐπίπεδον, οὗ μιᾶς γραμμῆς περιεχομένου ἡ καλεῖται περιφέρεια]. A circle or orb is a plane figure which one line encloses, called the circumference. In a figure of this kind the convex and the concave cannot be divided in act and in fact, since it consists of lines, which lack both breadth and height. They differ therefore in reason only: the line that looks towards the outer part in the circle will be called convex, and that which looks towards the inner part, concave. But if we are not dealing with a figure but with a spherical body, that is, a globe, the convex and concave there can be divided in fact. For the lunar globe touches the element of fire with its concave part, and its convex part slopes down onto the sphere of Mercury which lies above it.

units.la: Quamuis Aristoteles quæstionem hanc in præsentia reiicit, pauca tamen ipse interponam. Diuisio hæc subiecti est in accidentia: quandoquidem ista animi partes nil aliud quàm vires eius dici debent, neque anima corpus est, quæ instar eius discerpi queat. Videtur autem notari Plato, cum dubitatur an possit animus distingui ut particulæ corporis: nam is (ut diximus) vi sus est, diuersis membris partes eius attribuere. Qui tamen à suis ipsius familiaribus defenditur, quòd non ita crasse, ut eum insimulat, animi partes per diuersa membra sit partitus: at id fecit ostendens in quibus potissimum corporis partibus hæ animi vires vigeant & sese aperiant. Proinde ratione di-stingui affirmantur, quòd reipsa & subiecto non differant, non tamen ita ut ratio vires istas aut illarum definitiones, cum in re non inueniantur, af-finxerit. Natura quippe sua citra nostras cogitationes distinctam inter sese substantiam vel essentiam habent.
units.tr: Although Aristotle here sets this question aside, I shall add a few words. This division is of subject into accidents, for these parts of the soul ought to be called nothing other than its powers, and the soul is not a body, which could be torn apart like that. But Plato seems to be noted, when it is asked whether the soul can be distinguished like parts of a body: for he, as we said, was blamed for assigning parts of it to different limbs. Yet he is defended by his own followers, who say that he did not divide the parts of the soul among different limbs so crudely as he is accused of doing, but did so by showing in which principal parts of the body these powers of the soul flourish and show themselves. Accordingly they are said to be distinguished in reason, because they do not differ in fact and subject; yet not so that reason has framed those powers or their definitions, since these are not found in the thing. For by their nature, apart from our thoughts, they have a substance or essence distinct from one another.

units.la: Quod autem ratione caret, partim communis animæ simile est, & illi quo stirpes vigent, id autem di-co nutriendi & augendi facultatem: talem autem animi vim in omnib. quæ alūtur, & in fœtibus immaturis quis posuerit, & hanc eandem in absolutis. Hanc enim magis quàm ullam aliam consentane-um est.
units.tr: What lacks reason is partly like the common soul, and like that by which plants flourish; I mean the faculty of nourishing and increasing. Who would not ascribe such a power of the soul to all things that are nourished, to immature offspring, and the same to mature ones? For it is more consistent to hold this than any other.

units.la: Alterum allatæ diuisionis membrum Aristoteles rursus distinguit, nem-pe illud quod ratione caret: quia partim ei potest obtemperare, licet ea non vtatur: Partim verò ea omnino vacuum est, quod à nostra tractatione reiicitur, quòd ad hominem, quà homo est, non pertineat, imò non absimile sit communis cuiusdam animæ, quā cum bruta tum planta communicent: viuunt enim stirpes, & aliqua facultate animæ sunt prædita. De hac itaq; animæ parte nunc agit, quæ ad istam doctrinam minimè pertinet, cū ea non sit hominis quà homo & probus censetur. Vis porrò hæc vegetandi non tantum in plantis, sed in brutis & in hominibus quoq; inest, sed qua viuunt et aluntur. Et in homine tum ea vis tum sentiendi facultas requiritur, quoni-am perista fit gradus ad rationem. Sic enim hominis materia præparatur, vt ad rationem explicandam seu recipiendam possit accommodari. Sciendum nihilominus, isti facultati non eadem instrumenta, quando in animan-tibus atq; cum in stirpibus est, inseruire. Vt enim species ac natura sunt diuersæ, sic diuersa organa sunt adhibita. Necminus ista vi prædití sunt fœtus adhuc immaturi: quandoquidem in ipsis nullum aliud natura opus appa-ret. Adiecit prætereà vegetantem facultatem in absolutis esse, ne for-tassis arbitraremur e fœtibus iam maturis & natis illam discedere: manet enim & in eis augendis & alendis laborat. Differunt autem inter se nonni-hil augere ac nutrire: nam alimentum instaurationem amissæ substantiæ spectat, incrementum verò non solum magnitudinem quæ prius aderat conseruat, verum etiam substantiam nouam adjicit, quà fœtus aut recens ani-mal ad iustam progrediatur staturam. Perfecta verò seu absoluta intelligit ex collatione, ad immaturos fœtus qui adhuc in vtero matrum delitescant. Imò inquit absolutis atq; perfectis viuentibus sive bruta fuerint siue homines, longè magis hæc ipsa facultas inest: quia cum aliæ illorum vires ab opere suo cessent, hæc nunquam agere definit, vt mox ostenditur.
units.tr: Aristotle now divides the other part of the division given above, namely that which lacks reason. Part of it can obey reason, although it does not use reason. The other part is entirely without reason. This part is set aside from our treatment, because it does not pertain to man as man. Indeed it is not unlike that common soul which both beasts and plants share, for plants live and are endowed with a certain power of the soul. So he now deals with this part of the soul, which has little to do with the present teaching, since it is not what makes man man, nor what is considered good in a man. This power of growth is present not only in plants but also in beasts and in men, by which they live and are nourished. In man both this power and the faculty of sensing are required, since they form a step towards reason. For thus the matter of man is prepared so that it can be adapted to receive or develop reason. Nevertheless, we should note that this faculty does not serve through the same instruments in animals as it does in plants. For just as the species and nature are different, so different organs are employed. Nor are unborn foetuses without this power, since in them no other work of nature is evident. Aristotle has added that the nutritive faculty is present even in the fully formed, so that we might not suppose it departs from foetuses that are now mature and born. For it remains in them and labours at their growth and nourishment. Yet to nourish and to augment differ somewhat. For nourishment aims at the restoration of substance that has been lost, whereas growth not only preserves the magnitude that was already there, but also adds new substance, by which a foetus or a newly born animal advances to its proper stature. He understands "perfect" or "complete" by comparison with immature foetuses, which still lie hidden in the wombs of their mothers. Indeed, he says, this very faculty is present far more in complete and perfect living things, whether beasts or men, because while their other powers cease from their work, this one never stops acting, as will soon be shown.

units.la: Eius autem quædam virtus communis esse videtur & non humana: nam in somnis potius hæc pars atq; virtus agere videtur, probusq; vir atque malus per somnum minimè discernitur.
units.tr: Yet some power of this part seems to be common and not human. For this part and power seems to act rather in sleep, and a good man and a bad man are by no means distinguished during sleep.

units.la: Id prius docuerat, quo satis cognosci potuit vim illam vegetandi ad sci-entiam ist am non attinere, quòd nimirum sit communis & plantis & brutis animātibus, ac fœtibus immaturis: modò tradit aliud, quod eodē fermè spectat, Quia, inquit, ꝑ ista animi parte homo pbus a prauo nō discernitur, ideo non est dicenda humana virtus. Quod sumpserat hac ratione ostendit, Quoniam inquit, potius in somnis agere huiusmodi virtus consuevit, et per somnum bonus ab iniusto viro non internoscitur. Ratio igitur est:
units.tr: He had taught the first point, by which it could be sufficiently known that this power of growth does not belong to this science, because it is common to plants, beasts and immature foetuses. Now he delivers another point, which aims at much the same thing: because, he says, a good man is not distinguished from a bad one by this part of the soul, therefore it should not be called a human virtue. He demonstrates by the following reasoning what he had assumed: since, he says, this kind of virtue is accustomed to act rather in sleep, and a good man is not discerned from an unjust man through sleep. The argument therefore is this:

units.la: Ea virtus non censetur homini propria quae magis per somnum quàm per vigiliam operatur.
units.tr: That virtue is not held to be proper to man which operates more through sleep than through waking.
Such a part of the soul is what quickens the body.
Therefore it should not be reckoned proper to men.

units.la: Complura facultatis huius opera enumerantur: cibum in vētriculo coquit, immutat in eum humorem quem chilum vocat, transmittit ad epar et cor, ut inde sanguis & spiritus habeatur, (sanguis enim in epate, spiritus in corde producuntur ex chilo:) in reliquam membra distribuitur, ibi applicatur & unitur, atq; in substantiam quae membro congruat vertitur, atque illi quantum fieri potest assimulatur. Sunt haec porrò munera vegetantis animi, quae cum vi caloris praesertim efficiantur, isq; dormiendo robustior quàm vigilando fit, hinc rectè dicitur, hanc vim magis per somnum quàm per vigiliam efficacem esse. Potest esse ratio à contrarijs:
units.tr: Many works of this faculty are enumerated: it cooks food in the stomach, changes it into that moisture which they call chyle, sends it on to the liver and heart, so that blood and spirits may be obtained from it (for blood is produced from chyle in the liver, and spirits in the heart); it is then distributed to the remaining members, where it is applied and joined, and turned into a substance that suits each member, and is made as like it as possible. These are the functions of the vegetative soul, which are effected chiefly by the power of heat; and since this power becomes stronger in sleep than in waking, it is rightly said that this power is more effective through sleep than through waking. There may be an argument from contraries:

units.la: Vis qua valentior est in somno quàm in vigilia non est hominis propria.
units.tr: A power which is stronger in sleep than in waking is not proper to man.
The faculty by which we are nourished is of this kind.
Therefore it is not human.

units.la: In hac ratione subintelligitur, hominem, quam homo est, in vigilia maximè agere. Quod verò somni opus non sit homini proprium, id ex eo confirmat, quòd iustus & iniustus à se invicem tum temporis non differunt.
units.tr: In this argument it is implied that man, as man, acts chiefly in waking. That the work of sleep is not proper to man, he confirms from the fact that the just and the unjust do not differ from one another at such times.

units.la: Quare aiunt dimidio temporis vitae felices à miseris nil distare: id autem iure accidit, est enim somnus otii animi quae vel probus vel prauus dicitur, nisi si aliqui motus parumper interveniant, atque ita meliora fiant proborum vita quàm quorumcunq;.
units.tr: Hence they say that for half of life the happy and the wretched do not differ at all. This happens rightly, for sleep is a rest of the soul, which is called either good or bad, unless some movements intervene for a little while; and so the life of good men becomes better than that of anyone else.

units.la: Suam propositionem, prauos et bonos dormiendo à se invicem non internoscI, vulgari sententia communiq; prouerbio confirmat, quo passim aiunt, miseros à felicibus dimidio vitae quicquam nõ differre. Fundamentum rationis huius ex natura probabili constat: nam quod omnib. videtur, id probabile est. Vulgatae vero sententiae atq; proverbia, inde porrò sunt orta, quod passim ita esse omnes indicarunt. Et hanc vulgarem sententiam esse id quoq; testatur, quòd somni spacium haud propria decentiq; mensura temporis est descriptum. Cùm enim in quemq; diem vel octo vel septem horas dormimus, tertia potius vitæ pars quàm dimidium oportuit dici: at more vulgi sermo est accipiendus, à quo res ad amussim non æstimantur, & quod reuera tertia pars est dimidium putatur.
units.tr: He confirms his proposition, that good and bad men are not distinguished from one another while asleep, by the common opinion and popular proverb, by which people everywhere say that the wretched differ from the happy in nothing for half of their life. The ground of this argument rests on a probable premise, for what seems so to all is probable. Now common opinions and proverbs have arisen from this, that everyone everywhere has indicated that it is so. And that this is the common opinion is also shown by the fact that the span of sleep has not been fixed by a proper and fitting measure of time. For since we sleep either eight or seven hours each day, it should rather have been said that a third part of life, not a half, is spent in sleep. But speech must be taken according to common usage, by which things are not measured precisely, and what is really a third is thought to be a half.

units.la: Ratione confirmat, bona vitæ parte, somni tempore inquam, bonos et pravos non differre, quoniam tum animus noster est otiosus, præsertim quà vel boni vel mali sumus. Non est hæc accipienda, vt somni propria definitio, quòd sit animi otium, sed tamen ita vtcunq; describitur. Ociatur quippè a-nimus dormiendo, tametsi non desinat interea virtutum habitibus ornari, qui tamen in homine quamdiu dormit haud agnoscantur. fructiferæ arbores à sterilibus non discernuntur, nisi suos fructus edi-derint, tametsi per hyemem dum fructibus carent sylvestribus atque steri-libus facultate longè meliori sint præditæ. Non absolutè posuit animi otium somnum esse, verùm adiecit, qua bonus vel malus dicitur: quia reuera dormiendo animus non omnibus partibus otiatur. Etenim tum (vt diximus) facultas illa vegetandi quàm maximè laborat. Neq; felices à mise-ris dormiendo nil differre, vsq; quaq; verum est: nam vtriusq; illorum insomnia, phantasmata inquam seu visa multò inter sese discrepant. Parū quiddam vel Parumper ait, ex collatione: nam discrimen hoc, si magnam actionum differentiam spectes quibus se vigilando exercent, paruum admodum est. Ἐπιεικεῖς modò illos vocat, qui à recto seu decenti non recedunt, τυχόντας vero intelligamus quosuis, qui vt occurrit, vtq; impelluntur se ge-runt. Nec mirum esse debet, proborum visa cùm dormiunt meliora & tran-quilliora esse quàm improborum: quoniam imagines spectraq; versantur in imaginatione seu phantasia earum rerum quas vigilando gessimus. Hoc idem Plato de Repub. docuit.
units.tr: He argues by reason that for a large part of life, namely the time of sleep, good and bad men do not differ, since then our soul is at rest, especially insofar as we are either good or bad. This should not be taken as the proper definition of sleep, namely that it is rest of the soul, but nevertheless it is described in this way in some sense. For the soul is at rest in sleep, although in the meantime it does not cease to be adorned with the habits of virtues, which, however, are not recognised in a man as long as he sleeps. Fruitful trees are not distinguished from barren ones unless they have produced their fruit, although during winter, when they lack fruit, they are endowed with a far better faculty than wild and barren trees. Aristotle did not state absolutely that sleep is rest of the soul, but added "insofar as one is called good or bad", because in truth in sleep the soul is not at rest in all its parts. For then, as we have said, that faculty of growth labours as much as possible. Nor is it entirely true that the happy and the wretched differ in nothing while asleep. For the dreams of each, that is, their phantasms or visions, differ greatly from one another. He says "a little" or "somewhat" by comparison, for this difference, if you look at the great difference of the actions by which they occupy themselves when awake, is very small. He calls them only [ἐπιεικεῖς] "decent," those who do not depart from what is right or seemly; but let us understand [τυχόντας] "ordinary" to mean any chance people, who conduct themselves as they happen to meet things and as they are driven. Nor ought it to be surprising that the visions of good men are better and calmer when they sleep than those of the wicked, since images and spectres move in the imagination or fantasy about those things which we did while awake. Plato taught the same thing in the Republic.

units.la: Non debemus ex his colligere somnum proprium esse affectum vegetan-tis facultatis, nam si hoc existimaremus, plàtas quoq; dormire dandu esset, quod non tantum primo aspectu absurdum videtur, sed etiam experientia refellitur. non enim vegetans vis tunc ociatur, neq; particulæ seu membra corporis quæ illi seruiunt, imò tum efficaciter exercentur. Cùm itaq; somnus dicatur ocium animi, non potest arborum esse, cùm illarum vegetadi facultas, qua dicuntur animatæ, nunquà à munere suo cessat. Est itaq; somnus affectus quidam sensuum, isq;, ut fiat ab Aristotele de somno et vigilia pulchrè traditur, à calore animantibus innato vapores quidam ex cibis assumptis feruntur ad superiores partes, nimirum ad caput, vbi cerebrum est natura frigidum, cumq; vapores eò peruenerint frigore quod ibi reperiunt crassescunt, vt nubibus in aere cernimus vsuuenire: redditi verò densiores, atq; ob id graues, pondere suo ruunt, & per vias meatusq; redeundo quibus ascenderunt, illos oppilant & sua densitate obstruunt, unde calori nostro interno facultas effundendi se ad sensus externos præripitur, non enim obscissis[?] viis a frigidis illis humoribus calidi spiritus possunt ad sensus mcare[?] imagines quoq; seu spectra quæ sensus exterius feriunt, ad cor vel ad cerebrum penetrare non valent, ideo sic sensus (ut videmus) dormientibus alligantur, eorumq; motus & actiones impediuntur. Est itaq; somnus vinculum sensuum, quo ratione ea expositæ impediuntur.
