Noua itaq; per sensus externos visa non transeunt solum circa præsentia, & prius in memoria conservata phantasia ipsa ut occurrunt, versatur, unde contingunt insomnia. Quod itaq; in dormientibus vegetandi facultas operetur valentius quam in vigilia, ex eo est, quod aliæ vires animi tum quiescunt, dumq; ad alia non distrahitur, maiori vi facultatis eius munera possunt effici, quam cum circa multa & varia opera vigilantes occupantur. Non igitur ideo per somnum vegetans anima roboratur, quod is vel ad ea pertineat vel sit illius affectus, verum quia tum vires aliæ vacant, neq; illius opus ulla ex parte impeditur.
units.tr: We ought not to conclude from these things that sleep is a proper affection of the vegetative faculty. For if we thought so, then plants too would have to be said to sleep, which seems absurd not only at first sight but is also refuted by experience. For the vegetative power is not then at rest, nor are the parts or members of the body that serve it; rather, they are then exercised effectively. Since, therefore, sleep is called rest of the soul, it cannot belong to trees, since their vegetative faculty, by which they are said to be animate, never ceases from its work. Sleep, therefore, is a certain affection of the senses, and, as Aristotle teaches beautifully in his work on sleep and waking, from the heat innate in animals certain vapours from the food taken in are carried to the upper parts, namely to the head, where the brain is by nature cold. And when the vapours arrive there, they thicken by the cold they find there, as we see happen with clouds in the air. Once they have become denser and therefore heavy, they fall by their own weight, and returning through the passages and channels by which they ascended, they block them and obstruct them by their density. Hence the faculty of our inner heat to pour itself out into the external senses is snatched away, for when the paths are blocked by those cold humours, the warm spirits cannot reach the senses; nor can the images or spectres which strike the external senses penetrate to the heart or to the brain. Thus, as we see, the senses are bound in those who sleep, and their motions and actions are impeded. Sleep, therefore, is a bond of the senses, by which the aforesaid functions are impeded. New things seen through the external senses therefore do not pass away; rather, the phantasy, which holds fast to what is present and what was previously preserved in memory, is itself occupied as things occur to it, and from this dreams arise. That the vegetative faculty therefore works more strongly in those who sleep than in waking is because the other powers of the soul are then at rest, and since it is not drawn away to other things, its functions can be performed with greater force than when we are occupied with many and various works while awake. The vegetative soul is therefore not strengthened through sleep because sleep pertains to it or is its affection, but because the other powers are then idle, and its work is hindered in no way.

units.la: Cæterum de his satis multa. Et facultas quidem alendi mitteda est: quod uirtutis humanæ sit expers. Alia uero animi natura esse uidetur, ratione quidem uacua, sed eius quoquo modo particeps. Continentis quippe ac incontinentis rationem, partem uidelicet animi quæ rationem habet, laude afficimus: nam recte atq; ad meliora hortatur: in ipsisq; aliud etiam apparet, quod est præter rationem, quodq; cum repugnat, tum resistit rationi.
units.tr: Enough has been said on these matters. The nutritive faculty is to be set aside, since it has no share in human virtue. But there seems to be another part of the soul, lacking reason yet in some way sharing in it. For we praise the reason of the continent and of the incontinent, that is, the part of the soul that possesses reason, since it exhorts rightly and towards better things. And in these people there also appears something else beyond reason, which, when it resists, also opposes reason.

units.la: Membrum alterius diuisionis, qua rationis expertem vim distinxerat, nimirum vegetantem facultatem, vt communem & minime propriam homini reiecit: destituitur quippe omnino ratione, atq; a notitia virtuteq; humana quam longissime abest. Oportet autem humanas virtutes, vt nos hoc minime lateat, semper cum notitia seu ratione coniunctas esse: nam cuiusq; naturæ seu speciei uirtutes opus est vt ad summum gradum perfectionemq; illius quoquo modo attingant. Cùm aliam vim animi esse inquit de qua modo agetur, aperte indicat animi tres facultates reperiri. De illa quae compos est rationis, tam a princi-pio, cum animus distingueretur, prima partitione constat: de alente vi nunc est visum: quare cum modo alia inducatur, tres Animi vires esse confectu est, nimirum Altricem, Sentientem atq; Intelligentem. Istam vero mediam, quae nempe ad sensum pertinet, a ratione ipsa differre, continentis atq; incontinentis experientia demonstratur. Is porro continens est, qui aduersus animi crassiores cupiditates dimicat & ita dimicat ut deniq; superior evadat. Incontinens e diuerso post diuturnam pugnam victus cupiditate voluptatum succumbit. Vnde ita continentia describitur, [illegible, ~40 letters]. Proinde utroq; horum tam in ipso continente quam in incontinente ratione laudamus, qua in ambobus prauis cupiditatibus repugnet. Qua vero fit pugna, in eo demonstratur, quod inquit, rationem ipsam ad meliora hortari: quia ex notitia, quam cum innatam tum comparatam habet, discrimen honestorum turpiumq; tenet. Quare consilio valet, & ob id ad honesta impellit & a turpibus revocat. Laudari ea de causa meretur, quoniam facultas est, & ad actionem refertur: nil autem (ut prius diximus) laude dignum est, quod ad bonum ulterius non ordinetur. Haec autem vis de qua modo agimus, ideo ratione differre asseritur, quod aduersus illam pugnet. At de ista pugna nec non continente & incontinente libro septimo Ethicorum copiose agitur, ubi etiam absolute scribitur de temperantia & intemperantia. Et Plato de Republica ista eadem ratione demonstrat discrimen inter superiorem animi partem & inferiorem, nec bellum esse potest nisi inter plura quae distincta sint, & minimum duo. Vnde veteribus dictum est duellum.
units.tr: The member of the other division, by which he had set apart the power that lacks reason, namely the vegetative faculty, he rejected as common and not at all proper to man: for it is wholly without reason and is as far as possible from knowledge and human virtue. Moreover, human virtues, so that this may not escape us, must always be joined with knowledge or reason: for the virtues of each nature or species must in some way attain its highest grade and perfection. When he says there is another power of the soul, which will be discussed presently, he plainly indicates that three faculties of the soul are found. The faculty that is endowed with reason was established by the first division, made when the soul was first distinguished; the nutritive power has been dealt with just now. So, since another is now introduced, it is clear that there are three powers of the soul: the nourishing, the sentient, and the intelligent. That this middle power, which pertains to sense, differs from reason itself, is shown by the experience of the continent and the incontinent. The continent man is one who fights against the grosser desires of the soul and fights in such a way that in the end he comes off the victor. The incontinent man, on the other hand, after a long struggle is overcome and succumbs to the desire for pleasures. Hence continence is described thus: [illegible]. Therefore we praise reason in both of them, in the continent and in the incontinent alike, because it resists the wicked desires in each. That reason does fight is shown by the fact that he says reason itself exhorts towards better things: because, from the knowledge which it has both innate and acquired, it holds the distinction between the honourable and the base. Hence it has counsel, and for this reason it drives towards honourable things and calls back from base ones. It deserves praise for this cause, since it is a faculty and is directed to action; but nothing (as we said before) is worthy of praise that is not ordered to some further good. Now this power of which we are speaking is said to differ from reason because it fights against reason. But about this struggle, and about the continent and the incontinent, he treats at length in the seventh book of the Ethics, where he also writes absolutely about temperance and intemperance. And Plato in the Republic shows by this same reasoning the distinction between the higher and the lower part of the soul; nor can there be a war except between several things that are distinct, and at least two. Hence the ancients called it a duel.

units.la: Profecto quemadmodum particulae corporis eorum qui volunt eas dextrorsum moueri, si dissolutae fuerint contra sinistrorsum feruntur: Ita in animae partibus est, incontinentium appetitus in contraria feruntur. Sed in corporibus, quod praeter voluntatem feratur uidemus, in animo vero non uidemus. Fortasis nihilominus putadum est, in animo quiddam inesse, quod rationi aduersetur atque contra ipsum veniat. Ut autem sit diversum, nihil refert.
units.tr: Indeed, just as the parts of the body, when they have been loosened, are carried in the opposite direction, to the left, though those who wish them moved to the right intend otherwise, so it is in the parts of the soul: the appetites of the incontinent are carried in contrary directions. But in bodies we see that a part is moved against the will, whereas in the soul we do not see this. Nevertheless it must be supposed that something is present in the soul which opposes reason and comes against it. Whether it is different, however, makes no difference.

units.la: Quomodo ista vis, de qua nunc agit, cum ratione pugnet ac illi resistat, cum ad honesta hortatur, & aliquid recti iubet, simili probat à membris corporis translato. Nam ibi statim ut animans aliquas particulas vult aliquo flectere ac movere, parent quæ sanæ fuerint, at dissolutæ suo pondere in contrarium nituntur. Contingit vero ista nervorum membrorumque dissolutio, cum superfluus humor eo redundat, præsertim frigidus: illo enim meatus & via oppilantur, ne spiritus movéntes eo queant accedere: vel aliqua violenta laesione, qua nervus incidatur aut compago dissolvatur. Particulæ igitur laxatæ cum appetitus animantis nituntur eas pro arbitrio trahere, feruntur in contrarium: quod item in parte animi cupiente ac irascente usu venit, nisi fuerint virtute domitæ, rationi perpetuo adversantur. Proinde imperium appetitus erga partes corporis, ad eas movendas confert cum adhortatione rationis, qua vim concupiscentem ad meliora & honestiora incitat. Atq; in ista similitudine perinde est sive continentem sive incontinentem spectes, nā eorū utrq; adversus cupiditates pugnat. Hoc tantum interest, alter duorum vincit, alter superatur. Similitudine inquit probè constare, licet corporis vitium in oculos incurrat, animi vero turpitudo visum subterfugiat. Attamē ipsa quoq; non omnino latet, quia prudentium virorum iudicio deprehenditur. Discamus hinc, eos qui possunt hæc animi nostri vitia nosse, haud minus iudicare turpe quod ratio succumbat cupiditatibus, quam quod os vel aliqua corporis pars in contrarium distorqueatur. Quamobrem cum utrq; istorū pugnet, continens inquā & incontinens, pars ista cupiditatibus obnoxia demonstratur apta sua natura esse ad parendum rationi, si quemadmodum à continente fieri videmus, in officio diligenter contineretur.
units.tr: He proves by a comparison taken from the members of the body how that power of which he now speaks fights against reason and resists it when reason exhorts towards honourable things and commands something right. For there, as soon as the living creature wills to bend and move some parts in a certain direction, those that are sound obey, but those that are loosened strive in the opposite direction by their own weight. This loosening of the sinews and limbs happens when superfluous humour flows into them, especially cold humour: for by it the passages and ways are blocked, so that the spirits moving them cannot reach them; or by some violent injury, by which a sinew is cut or a joint dislocated. Therefore the loosened parts, when the appetite of the living creature strives to draw them at its pleasure, are carried in the opposite direction; and in the same way it happens in the part of the soul that desires and is angry, unless it has been subdued by virtue, that it is constantly opposed to reason. Accordingly, the command of the appetite over the parts of the body, for moving them, is compared with the exhortation of reason, by which it urges the concupiscent power towards better and more honourable things. And in this comparison it makes no difference whether you look at the continent or at the incontinent, for each of them fights against the desires. Only this differs: one of the two conquers, the other is overcome. He says that the comparison agrees well, although a defect of the body falls under the eyes, while the baseness of the soul escapes sight. Yet it is not wholly hidden even so, because it is detected by the judgment of prudent men. Let us learn from this that those who are able to know these faults of our soul judge it no less shameful for reason to yield to the desires than for the mouth or some other part of the body to be twisted in the opposite direction. Wherefore, since both of them fight, I mean the continent and the incontinent, this part of the soul, liable to the desires, is shown to be by its nature fit to obey reason, if, as we see is done by the continent man, it is diligently kept within its duty.

units.la: Duæ voces in lectione Græca notari debent, ἀπλῶς[?] quod hoc loco nil aliud est nisi Certè, profectò. Unde inquit Eustrathius, ἀπλῶς αὐτὸ τὸ λίων[?]. Deinde quod inquit ἴσως, ἐστὶ πάντως[?]: non enim ea voce nunc utitur quicquam ambigat, sed id quod adducit, firmiter atq; constanter affirmat. Et apud hunc philosophum huius vocis in hunc intellectum est frequentissimus usus. Concludit deniq;, Ut in corpore læsæ particulæ voluntati quæ motum aliquem imperat resistunt, ita in animo quandam esse portionem, quæ cum ratione interdum pugnet.
units.tr: Two words in the Greek reading ought to be noted. The first is haplōs [ἀπλῶς], which here means nothing other than "surely" or "certainly." Hence Eustratius says, haplōs [ἀπλῶς] ... the thing itself. Next, what he says, isōs [ἴσως], is "altogether" [ἐστὶ πάντως]: for he does not use this word to signify that he doubts anything, but he affirms firmly and constantly what he adduces. And with this philosopher the use of this word in this sense is very frequent. He concludes finally that, as in the body, when a damaged part resists the will which commands some motion, so in the soul there is a certain portion which sometimes fights against reason.

units.la: Ut autem fit diversum, nihil refert.) Particulæ huius geminus affertur sensus. Putat Eustrathius esse quidem certum quoddam discrimen inter pugnā partis huius animi adversus ratione, & partiū corporis dissolutarum contra vim animi aliquem certum motum imperantem: sed id perse-qui discrimen, ipsumq; modo prodere ac explicare, ad rem quae in praesenti agitur nihil facere. Alter intellectus horum verborum est, ut differentia quae nunc relinquitur, cuiusq; tractatio non esse praesentis negotij dicitur, sit ea, quae ratio & vis ista quae apta est ad obediendū illi à seipsis distant. Quare idem nunc dicitur atq; superius, ubi priori distinctione animi partium allata, scribitur ad hanc rem quam paramus non opus esse scire, quo discrimine illae facultates inter sese differant. Et certe scire quomodo cum sit unus idemq; animus, partes ita secum pugnantes habeat, & difficillimum cognitu est, neq; hoc loco potest opportune doceri.
units.tr: "But that it is different makes no difference." This clause is taken in a twofold sense. Eustratius thinks that there is indeed a certain distinction between the struggle of this part of the soul against reason, and the loosened parts of the body against some definite motion commanded by the power of the soul; but to pursue that distinction and to set it forth and explain it does nothing for the matter now under discussion. The other meaning of these words is that the difference which is now left aside, and whose treatment is said not to belong to the present business, is the difference in which reason and this power that is apt to obey it are distinct from one another. Hence the sense is the same as above, where, after the earlier division of the parts of the soul was given, he writes that for the matter we are preparing it is not necessary to know by what distinction those faculties differ from one another. And indeed, to know how, since the soul is one and the same, it has parts so at war with each other, is most difficult to learn, and cannot be taught opportunely at this point.

units.la: Hoc quoq;, sicuti diximus, rationis esse particeps videtur: nam rationi continentis paret.
units.tr: This too, as we have said, seems to share in reason: for it obeys the reason of the continent man.

units.la: Prius partem hanc mediam extare demonstrabat, quae à ratione distinguretur, quod illi resisteret: nunc vero quòd rationis particeps quoquo modo existimari debeat, inde confirmat, quia rationi continentis hominis obediat. Idcirco (quemadmodum ante ea est dictum) continentis ratio laudatur, quòd suo studio, sedulitate ac diligentia super hanc partem victrix evadat. Rationis itaq; pars ista non est omnino expers, quia etsi propriam non habet, aliena utitur, ut Luna, quae ob fulgorem Solis quem admittit, lucere dicitur, & inter luminaria coeli connumeratur.
units.tr: Earlier he showed that there is a middle part of the soul, which is distinguished from reason because it resists reason. Now, however, he confirms that it must in some way be considered to share in reason, because it obeys the reason of the continent man. Accordingly (as was said before) the reason of the continent man is praised because by his zeal, diligence and care it emerges victorious over this part. This part of reason is therefore not altogether without a share in it, since although it does not have reason of its own, it uses another's, as the Moon, which is said to shine because of the brightness of the Sun that it receives, is counted among the lights of heaven.

units.la: Ac etiam illi fortasis magis obedit viri tempe-rantis & fortis appetitio: nam omnia rationi consentiunt.
units.tr: Indeed, perhaps the appetite of the temperate and brave man obeys it even more: for all things agree with reason.

units.la: Obedientiam huius facultatis animi quam deprehendi ostenderat in homine continente, nunc longe inquit evidentius apparere in viris tempera-tis & fortibus. Unde sciendum est, ita naturam hominum comparatam ef-se, ut morum summam perfectionem non uno momento, sed variis gradi-bus adipiscatur. Primo quidem nonnulli occurrunt, qui pravis cupiditati-bus omnino delectantur, cum ab illis tantum abest ut pugnent, ut se ab ipsis agi permittant quocunque velint. Sunt alij qui turpitudinem illarum ani-madvertant, damnosas non ignorent, fugiendasq; intelligant, & idcirco pugnam contra eas capessunt: at cum usum belli huius non habeant, sint debiles, & imperiti certaminis, vincuntur subinde, attamē pugnam redintegrant, donec ex victis aliquando victores euadant. Est nihilominus in his rationis principatus inquietus ac turbidus: obstrepunt enim cupiditates, & passim aduersus rationem seditiones mouent. At dum ipsa ratio vincendo pergit, debellatur tandem, & cupiditates protinus rationi traduntur captiuae, nihilq; vlterius mouere audent quam ab ea praescriptum fuerit, nō aufertur quidem earum natura, sed turbare, seditiosè agere & ferocire desinit. Atq; hic summa est affectionum obedientia erga rationem, de qua modo Aristoteles loquitur. Et hoc interesse in 7. huius Philosophia scribit Aristoteles inter incontinentem & intemperatum. Temperatus his qua praeter rationem sunt non gaudet, continens vero gaudet quidem, sed illis abduci se non sinit.
units.tr: Having shown that this faculty of the soul obeys reason in the continent man, he now says that this obedience appears far more clearly in temperate and brave men. Hence it must be understood that human nature is so constituted that it attains the highest perfection of character not in a single moment but by various degrees. At first, indeed, there are some who take sheer delight in base desires, and are so far from fighting them that they allow themselves to be driven by them wherever they wish. There are others who perceive the baseness of those desires, do not ignore that they are harmful, and understand that they must be avoided, and so they take up the struggle against them; but since they do not have experience of this warfare, they are weak and unskilled in the contest, and they are overcome from time to time. Yet they renew the fight until at last they emerge from the vanquished as victors. Nevertheless, in these men the rule of reason is restless and turbulent: the desires clamour and on all sides stir up rebellions against reason. But while reason itself keeps on conquering, the desires are at last subdued and handed over to reason as captives, and they dare to move no further than reason has prescribed. Their nature is not indeed taken away, but they cease to disturb, to act seditiously and to rage. And this is the highest obedience of the passions to reason, of which Aristotle has just spoken. And in the seventh book of this Philosophy Aristotle writes that this is the difference between the incontinent man and the intemperate man: the temperate man does not delight in those things which are contrary to reason, while the continent man indeed delights in them but does not allow himself to be drawn away by them.

units.la: Omnia, inquit, nempe in fortibus ac temperatis hominibus, rationi consonant. Orationis huius metaphora elegans à musicis deducta est, quorum arte sic temperantur voces & soni, vt quamuis natura inter se longè differant, attamen quo ad harmoniam mirificè consentiunt. Ita fortis ac tempe-rata virtute ratio & pars hæc animi crassior vt reipsa distinguantur, atta-men ad honesta magno studio simul conspirant. Non accepit Aristoteles exemplum temperati & fortis, verum incontinentis & continentis, quando hanc distinctionem à principio induxit, quoniam extare hanc partem ostendere voluit, & à ratione sua ipsius natura differre, quod in homine tempe-rato non valuisset demonstrare, vbi huic probè cum ratione conuenit. Ibi vero differentia est manifesta, cum pugnam inter vtramq; cernamus. Duarum virtutum exempla posuit, temperantiae ac fortitudinis, vt indicet partem hanc tum esse cupientem tum irascentem. Frenat harum altera cupidi-tates noxiarum voluptatum: altera vero metum cohibet, ne refugiat labo-riosa, dura, & periculosa, quando causa honesta tuenda est: & audaciam, ne ruat praeceps, & pericula inutilia seu non necessaria temere subeat.
units.tr: "All things," he says, that is, in brave and temperate men, agree with reason. This elegant metaphor is taken from musicians, by whose art voices and sounds are so tempered that, although by nature they differ widely from one another, yet with respect to harmony they agree wonderfully. So in the brave and temperate man, reason and this grosser part of the soul, although they are really distinct by virtue, nevertheless join together with great zeal in pursuing what is honourable. Aristotle did not take the example of the temperate and brave man but of the incontinent and continent man when he first introduced this distinction, because he wished to show that this part exists and differs in its own nature from his reason; this he could not have demonstrated in the temperate man, where it agrees thoroughly with reason. There, however, the difference is clear, since we see a struggle between the two. He has given examples of two virtues, temperance and courage, to indicate that this part is both desiring and irascible. The one of these two restrains the desires for harmful pleasures; the other checks fear, lest a man shrink from toilsome, hard and dangerous things when an honourable cause is to be defended, and restrains rashness, lest he rush headlong and recklessly undergo dangers that are useless or unnecessary.

units.la: Videtur itaque facultas rationis expers duplex quoque esse. Partim vegetans, quæ nullo modo ra-tione communicat. Partim cupiens & in universum appetens, quæ particeps eius est, quatenus illi obe-dit atque ipsius imperio paret.
units.tr: It seems therefore that the faculty devoid of reason is also twofold. Partly vegetative, which in no way shares in reason. Partly desiring and appetitive in general, which shares in reason insofar as it obeys it and submits to its command.

units.la: Epilogo, vt liquet, ex dictis colligit, duplicem esse partem illam animi quam ἄλογον appellauit. Adiecit, καὶ ὅλως ὀρεκτικὸν [?] vt non solum concu-piscentem, sed simul irascentem partem comprehenderet.
units.tr: In his summary, as is clear, he gathers from what has been said that the part of the soul which he called alogon is twofold. He added "and appetitive in general" [?], so that he would include not only the concupiscent but also the irascible part.

units.la: Hoc itaque modo patris & amicorum dicemus quempiam habere rationem, non ut rerum mathe-maticarum.
units.tr: In this way we shall say that someone has regard to reason as a father's or friends' [counsel], not as one has regard to mathematical things.

units.la: Ita inquit ista uis animi se habet ad rationem, vt filij ad parentes, atque amici ad amicos. Dum enim illorum monitis obtemperant, dicuntur eorum rationem habere, vt quod sua non vident, per illorum mentem intelligere dicantur. Mathematicos vero non audimus admonentes vel adhortantes, verum quae docent ipsi & nosse & scire volumus. Dum obedimus aut patri aut amico, rerum quae imperantur causas persepe haud nouimus. Ita pars animi quae appetit dum bene se gerit, rationem causamq; ignorat eorum quae agit, sed tantum menti quae imperat auscultat. Vt demonstraret quo-modo hae vires differant, exemplo est vsus partium corporis dissolutarum: nunc vero quomodo vna alteram audiat, nouo simili patris & fi-lij declarat.
units.tr: He says: this power of the soul stands towards reason as children towards parents, and friends towards friends. For while they obey their admonitions, they are said to have regard for their reason, so that, what they do not see for themselves, they are said to understand through the mind of others. We do not, however, listen to mathematicians admonishing or exhorting us; rather, we ourselves wish to know and understand the things they teach. When we obey either a father or a friend, we very often do not know the reasons for what is commanded. So the part of the soul that desires, when it behaves well, does not know the reason and cause of what it does, but merely listens to the mind that commands it. To show how these powers differ, he used the example of the parts of a dismembered body; now, however, he makes clear how one hears the other by a new comparison, that of father and son.

units.la: A ratione suaderi quoquo modo facultatem quę illa caret, indicio est admonitio, & omnis obiurga-tio atque adhortatio.
units.tr: That the faculty which lacks reason can be persuaded by reason in any way is shown by admonition, all rebuke, and exhortation.

units.la: Hanc obedientiam quam ostenderat in animi parte inferiori erga rationem, ex continentibus, fortibus atque temperatis, rursus demonstrat a ra-tione admonitionis, obiurgationis, & adhortationis. Nam quandoque fit, vt quispiam victus vel ira vel cupiditate quo ad propriam rationem, se a-gendum permittat ab his crassioribus animi partibus quo voluerint, mo-nenti postea vel patri vel amico cedat. Particulam illam πῶς [?] interposuit, quia non vnus, imo varij sunt modi, quibus hi frenantur impetus: atque hi modo recensentur suis nominibus, admonitionis, obiurgationis, & adhor-tationis. Haecque inter se ita differunt. Admonitio per doctrinam fit, qua dirigimus exorbitantem animi affectum. Correctio vel obiurgatio est sermo quo potestate quadam seu authoritate perterrefacimus eos qui labu-tur, & caecum illorum impetum reprimimus. Adhortatio vero seu παρά-κλησις oratio est blande ac leniter adhibita, vt infirmiores a prauis atque turpibus abducamus. Pars animi altrix, qua homines vegetantur, harum rerum non est capax: nemo quippe hominum ventrem suum unquam monuit, obiurgauit aut est adhortatus. Nam surdus est venter, ut Cato inquit. Ratio item haud monenda videtur, quando ipsa notitia non caret, eiusq; iubere est ac imperare. Proinde ista tria tantum ad mediam animi partem pertinebunt.
units.tr: He now shows again, from admonition, rebuke, and exhortation, the obedience that he had shown in the lower part of the soul towards reason, in the case of the self-restrained, the brave, and the temperate. For it sometimes happens that someone, overcome by anger or desire, so far as his own reason goes, lets himself be carried wherever those cruder parts of the soul want, and afterwards yields to a father or friend who admonishes him. He inserted the particle πῶς [?] because there are not one but several ways in which these impulses are restrained, and these are listed here by their own names: admonition, rebuke, and exhortation. These differ from one another in this way. Admonition is given through teaching, by which we direct an affection that has gone astray. Correction or rebuke is speech by which we frighten, with a certain power or authority, those who are slipping, and check their blind impulse. Exhortation, however, or παράκλησις [paraklēsis], is speech applied gently and mildly, so that we may lead the weaker away from wicked and shameful things. The nourishing part of the soul, by which human beings are kept alive, is not capable of these things: for no one has ever admonished, rebuked, or exhorted his own belly. For the belly is deaf, as Cato says. Likewise reason does not seem to need admonishing, since it does not lack knowledge itself and it is its office to command and order. Therefore these three things pertain only to the middle part of the soul.

units.la: Quo'd si opus fuerit dicere hanc quoque partem rationem habere, duplex erit pars compos rationis, Una quidem proprie ac in seipsa: altera vero ut quispiam patri audiens.
units.tr: But if it is necessary to say that this part too has reason, the part that partakes of reason will be twofold: one which has reason properly and in itself, and another which listens to it as a son to his father.

units.la: Non ita partem istam animi appetentem, illi quæ rationis expers est subjcit, ut neget sub altero membro contineri: imò scribit, id quoq; si quis voluerit posse fieri duplex, ita ut una pars dicatur proprie ac per seipsam rationem habere: alteram verò, non aliter eius esse participem ac puer sit rationis patris cui obedit particeps. Prius hoc nitebamur explicare simili deducto a Luna quæ alieno lumine lucet: hic possumus caeci hominis exemplum adhibere, qui ut ut lumine proprio careat, quando se duci ab alio patitur, eius utcunq; oculis utitur: Ita pars hæc propriam non habet rationem, sed mentis iudicio dum se regi sinit, eius lumine ut ipsius natura fert perfun-ditur. Cur verò animus hominis ex adeò variis diversisq; partib. sit conflatus, quæ inter se tam evidenter pugnent, ratio alia reddi non potest, nisi quòd homo esse debuit in ipso medio posítus inter substantias intelligentes & brutas. Quamobrem non modò est rationis particeps, qua cum substantijs intelligentibus communicat, verùm etiam affectuum, quibus bruta laborant. Potest hæc ratio utcunq; ferri. Sed quia hoc fraudi hominibus fuisse videtur, ut si discordantes animi partes hominibus dederit, existimari possit illorum saluti obiecisse impedimentum, rei huius causam à philosophis, tametsi non latuerit eos hoc genus incommodi, nunquam videmus redditam fuisse. Nobis verò est quàm apertissima: dedit enim Deus homini ab initio inferiores has animi partes, moderatas & rationi obsequentes, quarum deinde licentia ob primorum parentum scelus erupit. Quamobrem quod conqueramur de ipso non habemus, cùm ex nobis ipsis quicquid hic mali est profectum fuerit.
units.tr: He does not so subject that part of the soul which desires, to the part that is without reason, as to deny that it is contained under the other member. Rather, he writes that this too, if anyone wishes, can be made twofold, so that one part is said to have reason properly and through itself, while the other is a partaker of reason no differently than a child is a partaker of the reason of the father whom he obeys. We tried to explain this first by a comparison drawn from the moon, which shines with borrowed light. Here we can use the example of a blind man, who, although he lacks his own light, when he allows himself to be led by another, uses that man's eyes in whatever way he can. So this part does not have its own reason, but while it allows itself to be governed by the judgment of the mind, it is filled with the light of that mind, as its nature brings it about. But why the human soul has been compounded from such varied and diverse parts, which fight among themselves so plainly, cannot be explained in any other way, except that man had to be placed in the very middle between intelligent and brute substances. Therefore he is a partaker not only of reason, by which he shares with intelligent substances, but also of the affections with which brutes are afflicted. This reason can be borne in some way. But since it seems to have been a disadvantage to men that he gave them soul-parts at odds with one another, so that it could be thought he had placed an obstacle in the way of their salvation, we never see the cause of this matter given by the philosophers, although this kind of inconvenience did not escape them. But for us the cause is most clear: for God gave man from the beginning these lower parts of the soul, moderate and obedient to reason, whose license then broke out through the sin of our first parents. Therefore we have no reason to complain about God, since whatever evil there is here has come from ourselves.

units.la: Dividitur autem & virtus hac differentia. Ex illis enim alias dicimus intellectuales, alias vero morales. Sapientiam quidem solertiam et prudentiam intellectuales, Liberalitatem autem & temperantiam morales.
units.tr: Virtue is also divided by this difference. For from these we call some virtues intellectual, others moral. Wisdom, skill, and prudence are intellectual; liberality and temperance are moral.

units.la: Non alia de causa partes animi sunt inuestigatae nisi ut denique ad vir-tutum distinctionem peruenireturde qua modo succincte agitur. Illas quip-pe Aristoteles diuidit per sua subiecta. Vt enim in diuersis animi partibus habentur, sunt a se inuicem separatae. Partem vegetantem ab hac tractatione remouit, ut qua virtutum capax minime sit, in duas vero facultates residuas virtutes distribuit. In mente seu ratione intellectuales collocans, morales vero in ea parte, quae rationi potest obtemperare. Facultatem rationalem, in qua locum habent sapientia, solertia & prudentia, eam intelligimus, quae suopte ingenio, suaq;ipsius natura intelligit. Altera vero pars vbi morales virtutes collocantur est quae a ratione ceu a quodam paedagogo ducitur.
units.tr: The parts of the soul were investigated for no other reason than to arrive at the distinction of the virtues, which is treated briefly here. For Aristotle divides them according to their subjects. Since they are found in different parts of the soul, they are separated from one another. He removed the nourishing part from this treatment, since it is not at all capable of virtues, and he distributed the virtues among the two remaining faculties: placing the intellectual virtues in the mind or reason, and the moral virtues in that part which can obey reason. We understand the rational faculty, in which wisdom, skill, and prudence have their place, to be that which understands by its own talent and by its own nature. The other part, where the moral virtues are placed, is the one led by reason as by a kind of tutor.

units.la: Cum enim de more loquimur, neque sapientem neque solertem quenquam appellamus, sed clementem aut temperatum.
units.tr: For when we speak in the ordinary way, we do not call anyone wise or skilful, but merciful or temperate.

units.la: Distinctio iam allata ex communi hominum sermone probatur. Cum e-nim de more agunt cuiuspiam, semper has virtutes, quas morales vocamus, verba sua referunt, non ad sapientiam vel prudentiam. Id vero est, quoniam illud genus virtutum, morale, inquam, exercitio & usu constat. Non quod etiam sapientia, cum sit habitus, exercitatione non indigeat, sed quia doceri potest, quod moralibus virtutibus non usu venit, ut quae tantum exercitatione, minime vero doctrina vsurpentur. Exempla duarum virtutum adduxit, quarum clementia irascentis est facultatis, temperantia cupientis.
units.tr: The distinction just given is confirmed by the common speech of men. For when they speak of someone's conduct, they always refer these virtues, which we call moral, not to wisdom or prudence. And this is because that kind of virtue, moral, I say, consists in practice and use. Not that wisdom too, since it is a habit, does not need exercise, but because it can be taught, which does not happen with the moral virtues, since these are practised only by exercise and not at all by teaching. He has brought forward two examples of virtues, of which mercy belongs to the irascible faculty and temperance to the concupiscible.

units.la: Laudamus quidem sapientem ex habitu: ex habitibus vero, eos qui sunt laudati, virtutes dicimus.
units.tr: We praise the wise man for his habit; and from habits, we call those that are praised virtues.

units.la: Habitus intellectuales virtutes esse ostendit, quod laudentur: nam sapientem, inquit, virum propter illius præclarum habitum laudamus. Habi-tus verò illi qui sunt laudabiles, virtutes & dicuntur et sunt. Probatio hæc à proprio deducta est: id enim virtutis esse tradit, vt laudetur. Visq; ratio-nis huius in eo sita est, quòd ex multis habitibus, ij qui laude digni haben-tur sunt virtutes. Qua de re superius, quæ opportuna fuerunt, & Aristote-les dixit, & nos interpretati sumus. Quædam enim ex bonis honorata po-nebantur, & alia laudabilia. Illa honore afficienda statuebantur, quæ per seipsa expetenda erant, ita vt alio non referrentur. Deo quippe ac diuinis rebus honor defertur. Vnde conficiebatur felicitatem bonum esse honore dignum, quòd non in alia dirigeretur. Illa verò bona statuebantur laudanda, quæ alio referrentur: idq; potissimum virtutibus tribuebatur. Syllogismus eiusmodi esse in his Aristotelis verbis apparet:
units.tr: He shows that intellectual habits are virtues because they are praised: for we praise a wise man, he says, because of his excellent habit. Those habits which are praiseworthy are both called virtues and are virtues. This proof is drawn from what is proper: for he teaches that it belongs to virtue to be praised. And the force of this reasoning lies in this, that among many habits, those which are held worthy of praise are virtues. On this matter, Aristotle said earlier what was fitting, and we have explained it. For some of the goods were set as honourable, and others as praiseworthy. Those were established as deserving honour which were to be sought for their own sake, so as not to be referred to anything else. For honour is paid to God and to divine things. Hence it followed that happiness, being a good that is not directed to another, is worthy of honour. But those goods were established as praiseworthy which are referred to another, and this was attributed chiefly to the virtues. That this is a syllogism is clear from Aristotle's words:
Every habit of the soul that is praiseworthy is a virtue.

units.la: At sapiens propter habitum laudatur, id est, Sapientia est habitus lau-dabilis.
units.tr: But the wise man is praised because of his habit; that is, wisdom is a praiseworthy habit.

units.la: Proinde sapientia est virtus: & si ea sit, cateri quoq; intellectuales habi-tus sunt virtutes.
units.tr: Therefore wisdom is a virtue; and if it is, the other intellectual habits are also virtues.

units.la: Notabimus postremò has virtutes, tam intellectuales quàm morales, e-arum partium animi perfectiones esse in quibus fuerint: nam moralibus habitibus craßiores animi partes absoluuntur, intellectualibus verò mens, quæ animi pars præstantißima est.
units.tr: Lastly, we shall note that these virtues, both intellectual and moral, are perfections of those parts of the soul in which they are found: for by moral habits the cruder parts of the soul are perfected, but by intellectual habits the mind, which is the most excellent part of the soul.

units.la: Restat modò, vt quæ in isto capite sunt allata, ad regulam diuinarum li-terarum expendamus. Virtutes ab initio ait in definitione felicitatis positas, ideò de illis tractandum esse: hoc nos minimè dedimus, qui felicitatem ponimus in reconciliatione cum Deo per Christum, vt dicitur, Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates. Ad quam primam felicitatem consequitur hominis instauratio, donec in eo imago Dei restituatur, quo virtutes requiruntur: nam id inchoant vtcunq; dum hic viuimus, quod in alio seculo absolutè perficiendum est. Ad ciuilem facultatem spectare ait, de virtutibus agere: quandoquidem legislatores hoc maximè suis decretis volunt, vt ciues ornentur virtutibus: tametsi diuina Lex aliam finem præstantiorem habet, vt peccata & infirmitates ostendat, vnde postea homines ad Christum adducat. Adhæc si qui sunt legislatores qui veras virtutes præceperint, Lex Dei per Mosem lata, primas iure sibi vendicat, ibi verè sancta, iusta & honesta traduntur. Sed agendum prius, inquit, de anima. Fateor: nam & ante vllum præceptum in Genesi dicitur, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram. Satis est de anima nostra intelligere illam ima-ginis. ginis Dei capacem, nimirum ut eum intelligat, amet, & suis actionibus ex-primat. Non subtilis vel absoluta tractatio animi exigetur, sed breuis & quæ diuinis literis sit conformis. Iure vegetantem animi partem reiicit, ut quæ virtutum non sit capax: neq; Deus unquam præcepit non esuriendum, non sitiendum, non dormiendum, non somniandum, & consimilia quæ à in-dicto & voluntate nullo modo pendent. Somnia vero proborum virorum nos etiam dabimus esse quietiora, & addemus, Deum persæpe illis dormien-tibus ac somniantibus futura demonstrare, licet aliquando & impijs hoc largiatur. Hoc tamen inter nos bene congruit, Propter somnia ipsa nullos aut meliores aut deteriores esse. Quod vero pars animi crassior cum ratio-ne pugnet, quando bene instructa est, & verbo Dei formata, satis experi-mur. Vnde matrimonium datum est, ad istos cupiditatis impetus comprime-dos, ne homines passim scortentur, aut vagis libidinibus ignoscant. Hinc il-la Pauli verba, Melius est nubere quàm uri. Et ne priuatis ultionibus sæui-atur, positi sunt magistratus qui ius dicant, ut saltem his iustis modis ac vi-is affectus violenti, quib. ratio non posset moderari, certis & legitimis finibus coerceantur. Idem quoq; Apostolus dicebat, Caro concupiscit aduersus spiri-tum, & spiritus aduersus carnem, ut non quæ vultis ea faciatis: &, Sentio aliam legem in membris meis repugnantem legi mentis mea. Quæ tametsi reuera intelliguntur de natura non regenerata, cuiuscunq; partis animi sit: attamen quando ratio verbo Dei & spiritu formata est, impedimentum & quidem non paruum ex affectibus experitur. Possunt etiam hæ partes ani-mi inferiores obedire menti verbo Dei bene instructæ. Unde præcipitur, Di-ligito Deum toto corde, tota anima, & omnibus viribus. Quod quidé in hac vita non præstatur, sed in alia fiet. Cùm vero probat partem animi inferiorem quodammodo rationis esse capacem, alioquin admonitiones, correctiones, et consimilia essent inania & cassa, & ita hoc dicit, quasi ratio ipsa non his op-pus habeat: illi nō assentimur. Non enim ille uidit mentis corruptionem, pro-inde sic loquitur. Verum & ipsa cum uitiata sit, et monitis, & correctionib. & adhortationibus opus habet, quæ passim in diuinis literis proferuntur.
units.tr: It remains only that we weigh what has been brought forward in this chapter by the rule of the divine letters. He says at the beginning that the virtues are placed in the definition of happiness, and that therefore they must be treated of. We do not grant this at all, since we place happiness in reconciliation with God through Christ, as it is said: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven. To this first happiness there follows the restoration of man, until the image of God is restored in him, for which virtues are required: for these are begun in some measure while we live here, and are to be brought to complete perfection in the other age. He says that to treat of the virtues belongs to the civil faculty, since legislators especially wish by their decrees that citizens be adorned with virtues; although the divine Law has another and more excellent end, namely to show sins and infirmities, whence it afterwards leads men to Christ. Moreover, if there are any legislators who have prescribed true virtues, the Law of God given through Moses rightly claims first place for itself, for there the truly holy, just, and honourable things are handed down. But, he says, we must first treat of the soul. I agree: for even before any precept, it is said in Genesis, Let us make man in our image and likeness. It is enough to understand of our soul that it is capable of that image of God, namely so that it may know him, love him, and express him by its actions. A subtle or complete treatment of the soul is not required, but a brief one that agrees with the divine letters. He rightly rejects the nourishing part of the soul, since it is not capable of virtues: nor did God ever command us not to hunger, not to thirst, not to sleep, not to dream, and similar things that in no way depend on judgment and will. Yet we shall also grant that the dreams of upright men are more restful, and we shall add that God very often reveals future things to them while they sleep and dream, although sometimes he grants this even to the wicked. Still, we agree well on this point: that on account of dreams themselves no men are either better or worse. But that the cruder part of the soul fights against reason, when reason is well instructed and formed by the Word of God, we learn well enough from experience. Hence marriage was given to restrain those impulses of desire, lest men play the harlot everywhere or give way to wandering lusts. Hence those words of Paul: It is better to marry than to burn. And so that people do not rage with private revenges, magistrates have been set up to give judgment, so that at least by these just means and forces, violent affections which reason could not moderate may be checked within certain lawful limits. The same Apostle also said: The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do what you wish; and: I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind. Although these things are truly understood of nature not yet regenerate, whatever part of the soul it may be, yet when reason is formed by the Word of God and the Spirit, it still experiences no small hindrance from the affections. These lower parts of the soul can also obey the mind well instructed by the Word of God. Hence the command: You shall love God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength. This indeed is not achieved in this life, but will be in the other. But when he proves that the lower part of the soul is in some way capable of reason, otherwise admonitions, corrections, and the like would be empty and vain, and he says this as if reason itself had no need of them: we do not assent to that. For he did not see the corruption of the mind, and so he speaks in this way. But reason too, since it is corrupted, needs admonitions, corrections, and exhortations, which are set forth everywhere in the divine letters.

units.la: Diuisio autem virtutum in morales & intellectuales approbatur: nam utrasq; in sacris libris numerantur. In Isaia scribitur cap.11. Et requiescet super eum spiritus sapientiæ, intelligentiæ, &c. Pertinet utiq; dona ista ad par-tem animi intelligentem. Postea subditur, Spiritus fortitudinis & timoris, &c. quibus morales habitus exprimuntur. Sed quod Aristoteles non vi-dit, id est, omnia hæc spiritum sanctum habere authorem, præsertim si vera & perfecta fuerint. Sapientiam laudari, ut ipse dicit, facile dabimus, quamuis illa eius distinctio laudabilis & honorati boni haud concede-retur: nam ille putat felicitatem non esse laudandam, vt superius dictum est, quod alio non referatur: quod veritati aduersatur, nam & ipsa felici-tatis natura, quaecunq; tandem ea sit, in Deum referenda est. Habet praeterea in iis Aristoteles, partem hanc, nempe rationem semper inuitare ac adhor-tari ad meliora. Qua sententia illi abutuntur qui plus aequo libero arbitrio tribuunt. Quare non illi est simpliciter assentiendum, quasi mens & voluntas non habeat sua vitia. Damus quidem, multas adhuc notitias honestarum rerum Dei beneficio in mente humana conseruari. Vnde ibi possumus in hac sententia σωτήρησιν [?] concedere, quae non sit aliud quam istarum notitiarum conseruatio. Neque inde aliquas honestas σοφία [?] excludemus. Quae tamen vt natura sua sint bonae res, non regeneratis tamen sunt peccata. Verum notitiam voluntatis Dei qua per Christum seruandi sumus, vbi situm est Euangelium Christi, naturaliter non habemus. Et addendum est, naturali vitio sic laborare homines, vt illis notitijs honestarum rerum non queant obtemperare prae affectuum impetu & resistentia. Vnde aiebat illa Medea, Video meliora probóq, Deteriora sequor. Proinde verba Aristotelis ad notitiam tantum referenda videntur, quod adhuc in mente reliquum sit aliquod honestorum iudicium, unde nomine λόγῳ [?] vtitur, & verbo παρακαλεῖν [?]. Neque ob hoc putare debemus hominum mentes absque Christo rectas & iustas esse. Ac vt daremus, ceu dictum est, aliquas voluntati σοφίας [?] honestas, illas in non regeneratis, peccata ponimus, & debiles admodum, vt qui à prauis affectibus vincantur. Cogitate legislatorem quempiam vos audire, qui roget honestas & bonas leges, an illum, quia recte monere potest & nouit, ilico bonum virum putabitis? Non arbitror. Fieri enim potest, vt sit Vlpianus, Diocletianus, qui mali viri permultas leges utiles tulerunt. Neque semper bonarum legum authores illis obtemperant. Omnis enim homo mendax: ita de ratione statuendum, licet ad bona & honesta interdum hortetur: attamen non propterea ipsa bona est & incorrupta: neque peccata non sunt, quae faciunt Ethnici, dum rationi suae obtemperant. Quamuis & id praestare debent vt illi obtemperent: alioqui grauius peccabunt, si ea quoque negligant, quae à ratione vt honesta & iusta proponuntur. Minusque Deus temporariis externisque flagellis eas Respub. affligit, in quibus ciuilis disciplinae aliqua ratio habetur.
units.tr: The division of the virtues into moral and intellectual is approved, for both kinds are listed in the sacred books. In Isaiah 11 it is written: "And the spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him," and so on. Those gifts certainly pertain to the intelligent part of the soul. Then it is added: "The spirit of fortitude and of fear," and so on, by which moral habits are expressed. But what Aristotle did not see is that all of these have the Holy Spirit as their author, especially if they are true and perfect. We will readily grant that wisdom is praised, as he says, although that distinction of his and his notion of the honourable good could not be conceded, for he holds that happiness is not to be praised, as was said above, because it is not referred to anything else. This is contrary to the truth, for the very nature of happiness, whatever it may be, must be referred to God. Moreover, Aristotle holds that this part, namely reason, always invites and exhorts to better things. Those who ascribe more to free will than is right abuse this opinion. Therefore one should not simply assent to it, as if the mind and the will had no faults of their own. We grant indeed that, by God's benefit, many notions of honourable things are still preserved in the human mind. Hence in this sentence we can concede a "conservation" [συντήρησιν] which is nothing other than the preservation of those notions. Nor will we exclude from this some honourable "wisdom" [σοφία]. Yet although by their nature these are good things, in the unregenerate they are nonetheless sins. But the knowledge of God's will by which we are to be saved through Christ, where the gospel of Christ is set forth, we do not have by nature. And it must be added that human beings labour under a natural corruption so that they cannot obey those notions of honourable things, because of the onslaught and resistance of the passions. Hence that Medea said: "I see the better things and approve them, but I follow the worse." Therefore Aristotle's words seem to refer only to the notion, in that some judgement of what is honourable still remains in the mind; hence he uses the term "reason" [λόγῳ] and the verb "to exhort" [παρακαλεῖν]. Nor, because of this, should we think that the minds of men apart from Christ are upright and just. And even if we were to grant, as has been said, some honourable "wisdom" [σοφίας] to the will, we still count these as sins in the unregenerate, and very weak, since they are overcome by depraved affections. Consider that you are hearing some lawgiver who asks for honourable and good laws: will you at once think him a good man because he is able to give sound advice and knows how? I do not think so. For it can happen that there is a Ulpian or a Diocletian, wicked men who nonetheless passed many useful laws. Nor do the authors of good laws always obey them. For "every man is a liar" [Psalm 116:11]; so reason must be judged in the same way, even though it sometimes exhorts to good and honourable things; yet it is not therefore itself good and incorrupt, nor are the deeds of the heathen sins any less when they obey their reason. Although they ought to do even this, that they obey it; otherwise they will sin more gravely if they also neglect those things which reason sets before them as honourable and just. And God afflicts those commonwealths less with temporal and external scourges, in which some account is taken of civil discipline.

units.la: At illud modò prouidendum est, vt confirmemus rationis iudicium & mentem seu voluntatem per originis peccatum, corruptione, labefactam contraxisse. In epistola ad Romanos habetur, Qui sunt filij Dei ÿ [?] spiritu Dei aguntur. Et qui spiritum Christi non habent ij nō sunt eius. Qua duo loca spiritu Dei opus esse indicant si ad filiorum adoptionem, & communionem Christi si-mus euchendi [?]: ad quae si vires humanae sufficerent, Dei spiritus non esset vel accersendus vel expectandus. Ad Corinthios deinde habetur, Animalis homo non percipit ea quae sunt spiritus Dei: nec enim potest, quandoquidem illi stultitia sunt. Et nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & spiritu, non intrabit in regnum coelorum. Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater meus traxerit eum. Oes erunt docti a Deo. Absq; me nihil potestis facere. Quib. et illud possumus addere, Prudetia carnis inimica est Deo: Legi enim Dei nō est subiecta neq; potest. Et, Prudentia carnis mors est, cui testimonio aliqui resistunt: nam cùm humana prudentia doceat non furandum, non committendum adulterium non occidendum, siquidem hæc iniusta esse naturæ lumen ostendit. Quare, inquiunt, hæ notitiæ mors essent, quod tam absurdum videtur quàm legem Dei condemnare. At quid hoc dare cunctabimur? Ipsa Dei lex ad nostram cupiditatem & infirmitatem relata mors a Paulo dicitur. Sed non per se, nā suopte ingenio vita est & iustitia, sed incurrens in animum corruptum & mortem & peccatum operatur. Ad hac Paulus nō intelligit per prudentiam solummodo notitiam, sed unà comprehendit prauam cupiditatem & contractum naturae vitium. Quae iam recensui possunt liquidò pateface-re, ut accipienda sit ea sententia. Rationem semper ad meliora hortari.
units.tr: But this only must be taken care of: that we confirm that the judgement of reason and the mind or will have been weakened and corrupted by the sin of origin, which they have contracted. In the epistle to the Romans it is written: "For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God" [Romans 8:14]. And: "If any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his" [Romans 8:9]. These two passages indicate that there is need of the Spirit of God, if we are to be brought to the adoption of sons and to communion with Christ; and if human powers were sufficient for these things, the Spirit of God would neither need to be sought for nor to be waited for. Then in the Corinthians it is written: "The natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them" [1 Corinthians 2:14]. And: "Unless a man is born again of water and the Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven" [John 3:5]. "No man can come to me, unless my Father draw him" [John 6:44]. "They shall all be taught of God" [John 6:45]. "Without me you can do nothing" [John 15:5]. To these we may also add: "The wisdom of the flesh is enmity against God, for it is not subject to the law of God, nor can it be" [Romans 8:7]. And: "The wisdom of the flesh is death" [Romans 8:6]. Some resist this testimony, saying that since human wisdom teaches that one should not steal, not commit adultery, not kill, inasmuch as the light of nature shows these to be unjust, these notions would then be death; and they say this seems as absurd as condemning the law of God. But why should we hesitate to grant this? The law of God itself, when referred to our lust and weakness, is called death by Paul. Yet it is not so in itself, for by its own nature it is life and righteousness; but, falling upon a corrupt mind, it works both death and sin. Moreover, Paul does not understand by "wisdom" merely the notion, but at once includes in it depraved lust and the inherited corruption of nature. These things I have now recounted can plainly show that this sentence is to be understood thus: that reason always exhorts to better things.
END OF THE FIRST BOOK.

units.la: IN SECVNDVM LIBRVM ETHICORVM NICOMACHIORVM ARISTOTELIS D.Petri Martyris Vermilij, Florentini Commentaria. CAPVT PRIMVM▸
units.tr: ON THE SECOND BOOK OF ARISTOTLE'S NICOMACHEAN ETHICS, commentaries by Master Peter Martyr Vermigli of Florence. CHAPTER 1

units.la: Cum autem duplex sit virtus, mentis inquam & moris, quæ mentis est maiori ex parte à doctrina ortum & incrementum habet: idcirco experientia & tempore opus habet. Sed quæ moris est, à consuetudine paratur. Vnde nomen habuit, parum ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔθους[?], deflectens.
units.tr: Since virtue is twofold, that of the mind and that of character, the virtue of the mind arises and grows for the most part from teaching, and so it needs experience and time. But the virtue of character is produced by habit. Hence it got its name, slightly deviating from ethos [ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔθους].

units.la: QVIA felicitatis definitio, quæ allata est priori libro, Virtutem vt differentiam quandam habuit, ideo quo planior fiat melius q;[?] intelligatur, de virtute agendum est. Felicitas & Virtus inter se omnino coniunguntur. Quandoquidem Felicitas vel est virtutis effectus vel causa. Effectus est, cum ab ea ceu à fine pendeat: Causa vero, quia illam tandem nobis efficit. In ista de virtute tractatione, per hunc quem auspicamur librum methodus huiusmodi seruabitur. Primo loco inuestigantur eius causæ, Secundo quid ipsa sit demonstratur, Postremo vero in suas partes ac species distribuitur.
units.tr: Because the definition of happiness given in the previous book made virtue a kind of difference, we must treat of virtue so that the definition may become plainer and be better understood. Happiness and virtue are wholly joined together, since happiness is either the effect of virtue or its cause. It is an effect, since happiness depends on virtue as on its end; it is a cause, since in the end it brings happiness about for us. In this treatment of virtue, the method will be as follows, through this book which we are beginning. First, its causes are investigated; second, what virtue itself is is shown; last, it is divided into its parts and kinds.

units.la: Caput vero quod primum iam occurrit, tria præsertim complectitur: Primo diuisio prius allata virtutum repetitur. Secundo, eas non ingenerari hominibus à natura demonstratur, sed potius more. Idcirco tertio & vltimo loco admonet, educationi magnam diligentiam adhibendam, vt quisq; prudenter consideret, quibus nam actionibus assuescat. Hanc virtutis distinctionem superius Aristoteles memorauerat, sed ita vt membrorum eius materiam ac sedem ostenderit. Virtutem quippe aliâs dixit in ratione seu mente mente collocandas, alias vero in partibus animi crassioribus quæ à ratione gubernantur, inhærere. Hic vero materiam vel sedem virtutum non pate-facit, sed illarum effectrices docet causas, à quibus differentiam utilissimā scitu nanciscuntur: quandoquidem earum nonnullæ doctrina, & aliæ consuetudine acquiruntur. Oportuit vero nos haud latere utrumq; discrimen, materiæ inquam & efficientis causæ: non enim omnes virtutes in eisdē sedi-bus collocari possunt, neq; omnes ab ijsdē causis haberi. Nam si quo ad ista principia, inter sese non variarent, ijs distinctionib. supersedendum fuisset. Zeno quidē omnes virtutes in ratione collocauit, sed is potius prudentiā, earū initiū inquā unde pendent universæ, spectauit: nam eam in ratione sitā dubitat nemo, qui singularum naturam formamq; integram respexerit.
units.tr: The chapter that now comes first contains three things in particular. First, the division of virtues given earlier is repeated. Second, it is shown that virtues are not implanted in men by nature, but rather by custom. Therefore, third and last, he advises that great care be taken in education, so that each person may prudently consider which actions he gets accustomed to. Aristotle had mentioned this distinction of virtue earlier, but in such a way that he showed the matter and seat of its parts. For he said that virtues are in one place located in reason or the mind, and in another adhere to the grosser parts of the soul that are governed by reason. Here, however, he does not disclose the matter or seat of the virtues, but teaches their efficient causes, from which they receive a difference most useful to know: for some of them are acquired by teaching and others by custom. But we ought not to be ignorant of either distinction, that of matter and that of efficient cause. For not all virtues can be located in the same seats, nor all derived from the same causes. If they did not differ in these principles, the distinctions would have been unnecessary. Zeno indeed located all virtues in reason, but he looked chiefly to prudence, the beginning from which all the others depend; for no one who has considered the nature and complete form of each will doubt that prudence resides in reason.

units.la: Virtus mentis doctrina comparatur. Maiori ex parte idcirco adiectum est, quoniam & naturæ bonitas, animus docilis, & mentis perspicacitas requiritur. Meminit etiam experientiæ, siquidem complura scientiarum prima elementa per sensuum experimenta comprehendimus. Medici obseruarunt quid reubarbarum possit, quid scamonia, & ex huius experientijs, præceptiones varias collegerunt, ex quibus ars eorum perfecta euasit: Quod idem in Astronomia euenisse facile intelligimus. Nos adhæc id non prætereat virtutes mentis alios per seipsos acquirere, alios vero iam inuentas addiscere. Quo ad inuentores, experientia illis usui fuit. Qui vero ab aliis instructi sunt, doctrina sibi virtutes mentis pepererunt. Idcirco earum duo Aristoteles principia posuit: quamuis experientia, non tantum ad inuentionem artium valuit, sed etiam ad eas perficiendas plurimum est utilis: nam quæ didicimus peritos ac doctissimos viros audiendo, magis confirmantur & expoliuntur, quando id quod ante mente concepimus, variis experimentis ita esse deprehenderimus. Experientia ita cum initia, tū expolitionem virtutum mentis attribuimus. Quamuis ut monuimus in his natura quoque partem non paruam habet: si quis enim stolidus & hebes fuerit, iis admini culis parum iuuatur.
units.tr: The virtue of the mind is acquired by teaching. It is added "for the most part" because a good natural disposition, a docile spirit and a keen mind are also required. He also mentions experience, since we grasp many first elements of the sciences through experiments of the senses. Physicians observed what rhubarb can do and what scammony can do, and from their experiences they gathered various precepts, from which their art came to be perfected. We easily understand that the same happened in astronomy. Moreover, we should not overlook that some acquire the virtues of the mind by themselves, while others learn those already discovered. For those who discovered them, experience was their use. But those who were instructed by others obtained the virtues of the mind for themselves through teaching. Hence Aristotle laid down these two principles of them. Yet experience is useful not only for the invention of arts but also for perfecting them very much: for what we have learned by listening to skilled and very learned men is more confirmed and refined when we find by various experiments that what we first conceived in the mind is indeed so. Thus we ascribe both the beginning and the refinement of the virtues of the mind to experience and teaching. Although, as we have noted, nature also plays no small part in these things: if someone is dull and slow, he is little helped by these aids.

units.la: Tempus item requiritur: Quia nec experientia statim colliguntur, neq; doctrina breui momento percipitur. Egent quidem & morales virtutes aliquo tempore, verùm non usq; adeò prolixo. Experimentum verò seu experientia est obseruatio, qua per sensus conamur facultates ac vires & naturas rerum deprehendere: at ad id faciūdum tempore ideò indigemus (quoniam, ut inquit Hippocrates) experimentum est fallax.
units.tr: Time is also required, since neither experience is gathered at once, nor is teaching grasped in a short moment. Moral virtues also need some time, though not such a long time. Now experience, or experiment, is observation by which we try through the senses to discover the faculties, powers and natures of things. But we need time for this, because (as Hippocrates says) experiment is deceptive.

units.la: Atq; discrimen est inter experimentum & morē seu consuetudinē. Quia experientia circa externa uersatur: Physici enim herbarum vires, lapidū et metallorum experiuntur:obseruant etiam Astronomi effecta motus & aspectum stellarum. Sed mos et assuetudo est quo ad proprias nostrum cuiusq; actiones: agendo quippe assuescimus, & habitum nobis ipsis comparamus. Sunt fortasis etiam qui volent experientiam illud studium appellare, quo virtutes mentis, hoc est, sapientiam & scientias tractamus: quod qui sequuntur, a proprietate vocum discedunt. Dubium uero id non est, longam diutur namq; rerum experientiam homines prudentes ac sapientiores reddere.
units.tr: There is also a difference between experience and habit or custom. Experience concerns external things: natural philosophers test the powers of herbs, stones and metals; astronomers also observe the effects of the motion and aspects of the stars. But habit and custom concern our own individual actions: for by acting we become accustomed, and we acquire a disposition for ourselves. Perhaps there are also some who would like to call experience that study by which we handle the virtues of the mind, that is, wisdom and the sciences; but those who follow them depart from the proper meaning of words. Yet there is no doubt that a long experience of things makes men prudent and wiser.
Which Euripides pointed out when he said:

units.la: Ἀλλ' ἐμπειρίᾳ ἔχει τι λέξαι τὴν νέων σοφώτερος[?]
units.tr: But the one who is wiser through experience has something to say, more than the young. [Ἀλλ' ἐμπειρίᾳ ἔχει τι λέξαι τὴν νέων σοφώτερος]

units.la: Per doctrinam uero intelligit Aristoteles, non solùm quæ à præceptoribus nobis traduntur, sed totum illum progressum, quo à simplicibus ad propositiones, ab illis ad conclusiones, & à prioribus conclusis & perfectis ad posteriora ducimur.
units.tr: By teaching, however, Aristotle means not only what is handed down to us by teachers, but the whole progress by which we are led from simple things to propositions, from these to conclusions, and from earlier conclusions that are established and perfect to later ones.

units.la: Hucusq; vidimus quæ principia & ortus habeant virtutes mentis. Nunc de causa moralis virtutis agit, eamq; dicit à consuetudine vel vsu gigni, & rationem ex nominis Etymologia inducit. Vnde nomen habuit parum ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔθους deflectens. Si vertatur ε in η, quod Græcis est familiare, pro ἔθος habebis ἦθος, unde τὰ ἠθικά. Græca scholia hoc loco monent ἔθος actionem esse, ἦθος vero qualitatem, quaper ipsas energias & actiones parti animi affectuosæ accedit.
units.tr: So far we have seen what the principles and origins of the virtues of the mind are. Now he treats the cause of moral virtue, and says that it is born from custom or use, and he draws the reasoning from the etymology of the name. Hence it got its name, slightly deviating from ethos [ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔθους]. If ε is changed into η, which is familiar to the Greeks, then instead of ἔθος [ethos] you will have ἦθος [ēthos], whence τὰ ἠθικά [ta ēthika]. The Greek scholia at this point note that ἔθος [ethos] is an action, but ἦθος [ēthos] is a quality, which is why it attaches to the energies and actions themselves in the affective part of the soul.

units.la: Ex hac Aristotelis doctrina probare possumus euidenti ratione virtutes mentis & moris differre. Quæcunq; habent diuersam generationem inter se, non sunt eadem. Propositio ista probabilis est, & in Topicis traditur, Mentis virtus habet diuersam generationem à virtute moris. Igitur ab ea differt. Minor explicata est, indicando utriusq; virtutis initia.
units.tr: From this teaching of Aristotle we can prove by a clear argument that the virtues of the mind and of character differ. Things that have a different origin from one another are not the same. This proposition is probable, and it is laid out in the Topics: the virtue of the mind has a different origin from the virtue of character. Therefore it differs from it. The minor premise has been explained by indicating the beginnings of each virtue.

units.la: Vnde planum fit nullam moralem uirtutem natura nobis ingenerari. Quia nihil eorum quæ natura insunt, aliter assuescit. Vt lapis qui natura deorsum fertur, nunquam ut ad superiora feratur, assuescat, nec quidem illum assuescet quispiam si millies sursum proiiciat: neque ignis deorsum, neque aliud quicquam potest aliter assuescere quam natura fit comparatū.
units.tr: From this it is plain that no moral virtue is implanted in us by nature. For nothing of what is in us by nature becomes accustomed otherwise. As a stone, which by nature is carried downward, never becomes accustomed to being carried upward, nor would anyone make it accustomed to this even if he threw it upward a thousand times; and fire cannot become accustomed to move downward, nor can anything else become accustomed otherwise than as it has been made by nature.

units.la: Propositio huius loci est, Virtutes nobis natura non ingenerari. Quam tribus rationibus, imò quatuor confirmat. Hanc rem ideo diligentius tra-ctat, stat[?], quia duas virtutum causas iam dederat: quod incassum fuisset positum, si virtutes natura essent hominibus insitæ. Nam tum initia longè alia naturæ penetralibus eruenda essent, atq; ista quæ simpliciter iam sunt expositæ. Videreturq; tractatio ista, si sic esset, non ad moralem Philosophum pertinere sed ad naturalem spectare.
units.tr: The proposition of this passage is that virtues are not implanted in us by nature. He confirms it by three reasons, or rather four. He treats this matter more carefully because he had already given two causes of the virtues. That would have been pointless if virtues were implanted in men by nature. For then the beginnings would have to be drawn from the depths of nature, far different from those already set out simply. And this treatment, if it were so, would seem to belong not to the moral philosopher but to look toward the natural philosopher.

units.la: Causarum quas possemus virtutibus assingere, quinarius numerus se offert. Deus, casus, natura, doctrina, exercitatio. Duas has postremas Aristoteles recipit. De Deo nihil modo scribit: at superius, cùm de felicitateageretur, parum dixit. Sed nos prolixè id edocuimus, & ad finem huius capitis repetemus. Casus & fortuna explosa sunt, neque vt felicitatis causæ receptæ, partim quòd non sunt causæ per se, partim quòd rerum præstantissimarum non reddendæ sunt adeò viles causæ, tum deniq; quòd raro ex iis causis effecta proficiscuntur. Solum natura superest inspicienda, ne forte virtutes ab ea oriantur. Id negat, vt audiuimus. Quare aliis remotis causis, iam tantum aliæ duæ supererunt, doctrina inquam & consuetudo.
units.tr: The number five presents itself among the causes we could assign to the virtues: God, chance, nature, teaching, and exercise. Aristotle accepts these last two. He writes nothing now about God; but earlier, when happiness was being discussed, he said little about him. We have taught this at length, and will repeat it at the end of this chapter. Chance and fortune have been rejected, and are not accepted as causes of happiness, partly because they are not causes in themselves, partly because causes so base should not be assigned to the most excellent things, and finally because effects rarely proceed from such causes. Only nature remains to be examined, lest perhaps the virtues arise from it. He denies this, as we have heard. Therefore, with the other causes set aside, only two others will remain: teaching, I mean, and custom.

units.la: Propositionem verò non est mirum si de morali virtute solùm enuntiaSrit, cùm & de mentis virtute nihilominus vera sit, quia de morali nunc est agendum. Præterea hæ morales notiores sunt aliis & communiores: illisque oportet à teneris ornare homines. Id verò inscientiis tradendis perpetuò seruatur, vt à notioribus & communioribus auspicemur. Sed tamen ita res ab Aristotele tractatur, vt de moralibus agendo, vnà demonstret, se idem quoq; de virtute mentis intelligere. Quia non solum exemplis vtitur iustitiæ, fortitudinis, ac temperantiæ, verum & artium, quæ ad vim animi intelligentem pertinent. Postremò de virtutibus mentis erat minus obscurum, illas acquiri & natura non inesse, cùm permultos videamus rudes & indigere prorsus instructione. Verùm de moralibus magis dubitari potuit, cùm aliqui videantur ad illas natura comparati. Proinde cœpit de illis ante omnia dicere, de virtutibus mentis loco suo postea scripturus. Plato diuersum existimauit: nam illi animi ad corpora veniunt perfecti & absoluti, atq; omnibus virtutibus instructi, qui ex coniunctione corporis ita graventur & lædantur, vt oblivio scientiarum ac virtutum mentis eos rapiat: vnde opus est ipsis doctrina, & iustis interrogationibus, vt oblitorum denuò reminiscātur. Indiget etiam exercitatione ac vsu bonarum actionum, vt morales virtutes, quæ sunt in eis obliterata, in lucem emergant. Sed nunc non est locus aduersus hæc disputandi, cùm & ille fateatur doctrina & exercitatione opus esse, vt reparentur uirtutes, neq; ad rem præsentem permultum interest, an virtutes in animo acquirantur, vel prius ingenitæ patefiant, & cum alius opportunior locus huic disputationi iure debeatur. Ratio vero qua primum Aristoteles propositionem confirmat, ita explicatur.
units.tr: It is no wonder that he states the proposition only about moral virtue, since it is equally true of the virtue of the mind, but he is now concerned with the moral. Besides, these moral virtues are better known and more common than the others, and people must be trained in them from childhood. In teaching the disciplines this order is always kept, so that we begin with what is better known and more common. Yet Aristotle handles the matter in such a way that, while treating the moral virtues, he shows at the same time that he understands the same thing about the virtue of the mind. For he uses examples not only of justice, courage and temperance, but also of the arts that belong to the intellectual power of the soul. Finally, it was less obscure about the virtues of the mind that they are acquired and are not present by nature, since we see many who are untaught and wholly in need of instruction. But about the moral virtues there could be more doubt, since some seem to be naturally fitted for them. Therefore he began by speaking of them before all else, intending to write about the virtues of the mind afterwards in their proper place. Plato thought otherwise: for he held that souls come to bodies complete and perfect, furnished with all virtues, but that through their union with the body they are so burdened and harmed that forgetfulness of the sciences and of the virtues of the mind seizes them; hence they need teaching and searching questions, so that they may recall what they have forgotten. They also need practice and the exercise of good actions, so that the moral virtues, which have been obliterated in them, may emerge into the light. But this is not the place to dispute against these views, since Plato too admits that teaching and practice are needed to restore the virtues, and it matters little to the present question whether the virtues are acquired in the soul or are first innate and then revealed; and another, more suitable place is rightly reserved for this discussion. But the argument by which Aristotle first confirms the proposition is explained as follows.
Whatever is natural is not changed by custom.
Manners and virtues are changed by custom.
Therefore they are not present in us by nature.

units.la: Maior confirmatur exemplis lapidis et ignis. Lapis millies iactatus sursum, non mutabitur consuetudine, ut per seipsum moveatur sursum. Neq; ignis ita poterit assuefieri, ut deorsum sponte descendat. Adiecit, Neq; aliud quic-quam potest secus acquiescere atq; natura fuerit comparatum. Quia indu-ctio non est plena fidemq; non facit, si duobus tantum constet exemplis. Ad-dendum igitur, Neq; aliter invenitur, vel Sic de aliis, ut vulgo dicitur.
units.tr: The major premise is confirmed by the examples of the stone and of fire. A stone thrown upward a thousand times will not be changed by custom so as to move upward of its own accord. Nor can fire be so accustomed as to descend spontaneously. He adds: nor can anything else come to rest otherwise than as its nature has made it. For induction is not complete and does not produce faith if it rests on only two examples. So he adds: nor is it found otherwise, or: so it is with the rest, as is commonly said.

units.la: Non itaq; natura neq; præter naturam virtutes insunt, sed nobis aptis ad eas recipiendas iamq; per-sectis & paratis consuetudine adveniunt.
