units.tr: Therefore virtues are neither present in us by nature nor against nature, but they come to us by custom, in us who are fitted to receive them and already perfected and prepared.

units.la: Per occupationem, tacitæ interrogationi respondet. Quæreret enim quispiam, Si natura nobis non insunt, an contra naturam dicendæ sunt nobis inhærere? Respondet: Neq; natura eas habemus, neq; præter naturam. Quia cum illis non nascimur, ut cum oculis, manibus, pedibus, & animi viribus: neq; post nativitatem, ut barba & dentes proveniunt. Sed tamen haud contra naturam vendicantur: quia se habent ad animum nostrum, ut forma ergà materiam. Est materia propesa[?] per se ad eam accipiendam, sed efficiente causa indiget. Sic animus noster parandus est consuetudine ac doctrina, quibus excultus virtutes assequitur.
units.tr: By anticipation he answers an unspoken question. For someone might ask: if virtues are not present in us by nature, are they to be said to cling to us against nature? He answers: we have them neither by nature nor against nature. For we are not born with them, as we are with eyes, hands, feet and the powers of the mind; nor do they come after birth, as the beard and teeth do. Yet they are not claimed against nature, because they stand to our soul as form to matter. Matter is by itself inclined to receive it, but it needs an efficient cause. So our soul must be prepared by custom and teaching, and once trained by these it attains the virtues.

units.la: Adhæc, quæcunque natura nobis ingenerantur, earum vires prius accipimus, postea vero actiones edimus: quod in sensibus perspicuum est. Non e-nim quia frequenter videmus, aut sæpius audimus, sensus adepti sumus: verum è diverso, cum sensus haberemus, illis usi sumus: non quia usi sumus, accepimus. At virtutes adipiscimur postquam nos exercuerimus, quemadmodum & in aliis artibus: quæ enim postquam didicerimus oportet facere, ea discimus faciendo: ut ædificando fabri euadimus, & citharoedi citharam pulsando. Identidem iusta facientes iusti, temperata temperati, fortia fortes euadimus.
units.tr: Moreover, whatever faculties are engendered in us by nature, we first receive their powers and afterwards put forth actions; this is plain in the case of the senses. For we did not acquire our senses because we often see or often hear; rather, on the contrary, since we had the senses we used them; we did not receive them because we used them. But we gain the virtues after we have exercised ourselves, as also in the other arts. For what we must do after we have learned it, we learn by doing: as builders become builders by building, and lyre-players by playing the lyre. By doing just acts we become just, by temperate acts temperate, by brave acts brave.

units.la: Altera confirmat ratione propositam quæstionem. In ijs quæ natura obtinentur, agendi facultas actiones antecedit, quòd sensuum indicio probat: nam prius oculos, aures, facultatem quoq; videndi & audiendi sortimur, quàm videre aut audire liceat. Neq; quisquam est qui sibi visum peperit assiduis cernendi actionibus, & nemo frequenter audiendo, vel aures vel auditum sibi comparauit, sed potius quod omnino diuersum est usu venit, Animantes prius hæc beneficio naturæ cum oriuntur habere, postea eorundem usum percipere. Hucusque rationis Aristotelicæ maiorem habemus propositionem, testimonio sensuum confirmatam. Minor sic habet, Virtutes verò adipiscimur, cum prius nos exercuerimus: proinde ipsæ non insunt in nobis à natura. Ratio ista petitur ab efficienti causa: nam cum ista non easdem causas habeant, inter se nō sunt confundenda, sed discernenda. Virtutes ex actionibus proficiscuntur, naturalia verò ex illis ortum non habent. Quare virtutes nobis naturales esse, dici non potest. Quæ non eodem procreantur modo, eadem inter se minimè sunt. Minor ista propositio quo ad virtutes morales inductione suadetur. Iusta faciendo iusti, temperata temperati, fortes euadimus. Atque poterat sufficere ista probatio, nisi (quod antea monui) voluisset Aristoteles quæstionem de moralibus propositam ad virtutes quoque mentis applicare. Ideo nunc in probatione minoris, artium etiam mentionem fecit, quæ ad rationem pertinent, neque illarum simplici nudo què nomine fuit contentus, sed inductione ipsam earum appendi eam [?] confirmauit, ostendens architectos & citharoedos assiduis actionibus ædificandi atque pulsandi citharam, artifices tandem effici, non ex artibus quas nascendo perceperint aut ædificasse aut citharam pulsasse. Ista itaq; altera Philosophi ratio, sic virtutes morales probat à natura non esse, vt de virtutibus mentis idem confirmet. Sed iam tertiam auspicabimur.
units.tr: He confirms the question proposed by another argument. In those things which we possess by nature, the power of acting comes before the actions, as the evidence of the senses proves; for first we receive eyes, ears, and also the faculty of seeing and hearing, before it is possible to see or hear. Nor has anyone gained sight for himself by constant acts of looking, nor has anyone by frequent hearing acquired for himself ears or hearing; but rather the thing happens which is quite the reverse: living creatures at birth first have these by the gift of nature, and afterwards perceive their use. So far we have the greater premise of Aristotle's argument, confirmed by the testimony of the senses. The minor premise runs thus: but we acquire the virtues after we have first exercised ourselves; therefore they are not present in us by nature. This reasoning is drawn from the efficient cause: for since these things do not have the same causes, they must not be confused with one another but distinguished. Virtues arise from actions, whereas natural things do not have their origin from actions. Therefore virtues cannot be called natural to us. Things that are not produced in the same way are by no means the same. This minor premise, as regards the moral virtues, is supported by induction: by doing just acts we become just, by temperate acts temperate, we become brave. And this proof might have sufficed, except that, as I said before, Aristotle wished to apply the question proposed about moral matters to the virtues of the mind as well. So now, in proving the minor premise, he also mentioned the arts, which pertain to reason, and he was not content with their bare names, but confirmed the point by induction, showing that architects and lyre-players become craftsmen by the constant acts of building and playing the lyre, and not from the arts which they had from birth, by which they built or played. So this second reasoning of the Philosopher proves that the moral virtues are not from nature, in such a way that it confirms the same about the virtues of the mind. But now we shall begin the third.

units.la: Huic rei fidem facit & id quod in urbibus agitur, etenim legis latores ciues assuefaciendo bonos reddunt: atque hoc est cuiusq; Legislatoris consilium.
units.tr: This is also borne out by what happens in cities: for lawgivers make citizens good by accustoming them, and this is the aim of every lawgiver.

units.la: Quiq; id non recte faciunt aberrant. Et hoc Respu-blica Reipublicæ, bona inquam, prauæ præstat.
units.tr: And those who do not act rightly in this go astray. And this is how one commonwealth excels another, namely in good over bad, I mean.

units.la: Ratio hæc ab authoritate colligitur. Ex iudicio quippe legumlatorum quæstio proposita confirmatur. Illi iudicant cives fieri bonos, cum honestis legibus paruerint, & ad illarum præscriptum se fideliter exercuerint. Quod sane ipsorum studium atq; consilium superuacaneū esset, vbi natura virtutes ingenerarentur. Quid enim legibus & bonis & exercitijs quære-re oportet, quod natura cuiq; iam inde ab ortu fuisset concessum? Exercent iubendo populos boni principes, obsequentibus præmia proponendo: ea vero sunt, honores, statuæ, victus ex publico, atq; consimilia. Quin & seruis libertas & manumissio promittitur si bene se gesserint, è diuerso comminan-tur supplicia transgressoribus. Hæ bonæ sunt exercendorum ciuium ratio-nes: Hoc quoq; discrimine inquit Rempub. Reipublicæ præstare, bonamq; à mala posse discerni. In hoc vero legumlatorum & principum munere duplex defectus obseruatur. Interdum enim leges ad id institutum feruntur inutiles: interdum vero leges rectæ sunt & honestæ, at vt salvæ sint & obseruentur non datur opera. Vnde cum dicat Aristoteles, hanc debere voluntatem esse legumlatorum, pro legitimis legibus, & veris legislatoribus non habebuntur, qui alia sibi quærunt. Plato etiam & Cicero scribunt, pro legibus non esse habendas quæ aliquid iniusti vel inhonesti præceperint. Dumq; scribitur illos aberrare qui hoc non recte fecerint, ponitur aperte ob oculos ad quem scopum Principes collimare oporteat. Licet etiam hinc videre vt in oligarchia res peruerse geratur, vbi diuitiæ ac potentia paucorum sunt fines, ad quas & leges & exercitationes omnium dirigūtur: vtq; in popularis administratione tumultuaria erretur, vbi omnia spectant eo vt facile res innouentur, semperq; iniusta quædam isonomia quæratur. Quod Romæ sæpius vsuuenie-bat, leges agrarias promulgando, aut cum tribunitius furor æstuabat. Et pessime omnium in tyrannide res fit comparata, vbi leges atq; conatus omnes nil aliud quærunt, quàm ipsius tyranni commoda, securita-tem & incolumitatem, nulla prorsus ciuium habita ratione. Hi omnes errores hoc vno Aristotelis argumento confutantur, quo leges ita statuit condendas, vt eis honeste exerceantur cives, & virtutibus comparatis probi euadant. Bonas itaq; leges vitia emendare, ac virtutes commendare opor-tet. Et ea est beata Respublica, vbi neq; res neq; virtutes defuerint.
units.tr: This argument is drawn from authority. The question proposed is confirmed by the judgment of the lawgivers. They judge that citizens become good when they have obeyed honourable laws and faithfully trained themselves according to their prescriptions. Indeed, their zeal and purpose would be superfluous if virtues were engendered by nature. For why should one seek laws, good institutions and exercises, if nature had granted each person these things from birth? Good princes train peoples by commanding and by offering rewards to the obedient: these rewards are honours, statues, maintenance at public expense, and the like. Indeed, freedom and manumission are promised to slaves if they behave well, while punishments are threatened against transgressors. These are the good methods of training citizens. By this distinction, he says, one commonwealth excels another, and good can be distinguished from bad. In this office of lawgivers and princes, a twofold failure is observed. For sometimes laws are enacted for this purpose which are useless; sometimes laws are right and honourable, but no care is taken that they be kept and observed. Hence, since Aristotle says that the will of lawgivers must be this, those who seek other things will not be held to be legitimate laws or true lawgivers. Plato and Cicero also write that laws which have prescribed something unjust or dishonourable are not to be regarded as laws. And while it is written that those who do not do this rightly go astray, it is plainly set before our eyes at what goal princes ought to aim. One can also see here how affairs are conducted perversely in an oligarchy, where the riches and power of a few are the ends to which the laws and exercises of all are directed; and how one errs in a tumultuous way in a popular administration, where everything aims at making things easily changed, and some unjust equality is always sought. This happened at Rome more often, by proposing agrarian laws, or when the fury of the tribunes raged. And in a tyranny the worst of all arrangements is made, where the laws and all endeavours seek nothing but the advantage, security and safety of the tyrant himself, with no regard at all for the citizens. All these errors are refuted by this one argument of Aristotle, by which he lays down that laws are to be framed so that citizens may be honourably trained by them and, having acquired virtues, become upright. Good laws therefore ought to correct vices and commend virtues. And that is a happy commonwealth where neither resources nor virtues are lacking.

units.la: Adhæc ab ijsdem rebus & per easdem omnis vir-tus & nascitur & interit. Similiterqz omnis ars: nam ex pulsatione citharæ cum boni tum mali citharœ-di euadunt. Eademqz ratione fabri, cæterisqz omnes: ex recta enim ædificatione boni architecti, & ex pra-ua mali fient. Nam si res ita non haberet, præcepto-re non opus fuisset, verum omnes aut boni aut pra-vi nascerentur. Eodem quoque modo & de virtuti-bus se habet: nam dum circa humana commercia exercemur, alij iusti, alij iniusti efficimur. Dumqz in rebus periculosis versamur, assuefcimusqz vel time-re vel cõfidere, alij fortes, alij timidi euadimus. Nec secus est quo ad cupiditates & iram: alij temperati & alij clementes, alij intemperati alijqz iracundi effi-ciuntur, ex eo quod ij hoc vel illo modo alij atque alij circa ista versantur. Atque ut uno verbo dicam, ex actionibus consimilibus habitus fiunt.
units.tr: Moreover, every virtue both arises and perishes from the same things and through the same things. So too with every art: for by playing the cithara both good and bad cithara-players come to be. By the same reasoning with carpenters and all the rest: for from right building come good architects, and from bad building bad ones. For if things were not so, there would be no need of a teacher, but all would be born either good or bad. The same holds for the virtues: for while we are engaged in human dealings, some of us become just, others unjust. While we are involved in dangerous matters and accustom ourselves either to fear or to trust, some become brave, others timid. It is no different with regard to desires and anger: some become temperate and others mild, others intemperate and others irascible, because they are exercised in these matters in this way or that, one or another. And, to say it in one word, habits arise from like actions.

units.la: In hoc Aristotelico argumento primùm ponitur, Eodem plane modo & artes & virtutes morales comparari. Quod illud omnino confirmat à me prius commemoratum, ita hic Aristotelem de moralibus virtutibus agere, vt virtutes mentis vnà complectatur. Quod inquit ex ijsdem & per eadem gignitur & interit non inest natura in nobis. Quæ hic appellat eadem, genere conueniunt, & materia sunt eadem, siue (vt loquuntur) subiecto: eadem quippè actio & recta & prava esse potest, & consuetudo vel vsus tam bonus quàm malus esse potest: non itaq; intelligit eadem esse specie aut nume-ro, sed tantum genere. Ex ijsdem inquit & per eadem.) Possunt hæ particulæ sic accipi, vt idem significent, quamuis Græca scholia putent, ex ijsdem ad actiones referendum, per eadem verò ad vsum, frequentiam & consuetudinem. Virtutes ex ijsdem & per eadem producuntur & intereunt: igitur à natura non inseruntur animis hominum. Minor ista propositio ex artibus confirmatur. Quoniam & citharœdorum ars & fabrorum, pulsan-do citharam & ædificando [?] vel producuntur vel intereunt. Si enim ista reele[?] fiant, boni vel mali citharœdi & fabri euadunt. Nam si res aliter habe-ret, homines doceri non opus fuisset: cuncti enim vel boni vel praui artifi-ces nascerentur. Utq; in artibus videmus fieri, ita de virtutibus moralibus usuenit. Nec mirum videri debet, si eadem sint genere, actiones & consuetudines, siue bonæ siue malæ fuerint: quoniam hæc est natura contrariorum, vt ad idem genus pertineant. Habitus enim contrarij sunt eiusdem generis, quin & albor & nigror, dulce & amarum atque consimilia. Ut autem Aristoteles usus fuerit quo ad artes quibusdam exemplis citharœdi & fabri, sic modo quod dixerat, ostendit quo ad iustitiam, fortitudinem, temperantiam & clementiam. Circa humana commercia cum homines exercentur, aut iusti aut iniusti fiunt, dumq; in rebus periculosis aut fortes aut timidi, circa cupiditates vel temperantes vel intemperantes, & denique circa irā[?], prout nos exercemus, aut clementes aut iracundi efficimur. De clementia vero, iracundia, temperantia, intemperantia, iustitia & iniustitia, postea suo loco dicemus. Iustitia quoq; in Philosophia quædam species ostendetur, quæ circa humana commercia versatur.
units.tr: In this Aristotelian argument, first it is laid down that arts and moral virtues are acquired in exactly the same way. This wholly confirms what I mentioned earlier, that Aristotle here treats the moral virtues so as to include the virtues of the mind along with them. When he says that these things arise from the same things and through the same things and perish likewise, he does not mean that they are inborn in us by nature. The things he here calls "the same" agree in genus, and are the same in matter or, as they say, in subject: for the same action can be both right and wrong, and custom or practice can be good as well as bad. So he does not understand "the same" as the same in species or in number, but only in genus. "From the same things and through the same things," he says. These particles may be taken to mean the same thing, although the Greek scholiasts think that "from the same things" refers to actions, while "through the same things" refers to use, frequency and custom. Virtues are produced and perish from the same things and through the same things; therefore they are not implanted in the minds of men by nature. This minor proposition is confirmed from the arts. For both the art of the cithara-players and that of carpenters, by playing the cithara and building, either come into being or perish. For if these things are done rightly, cithara-players and carpenters become good; if wrongly, bad. For if things were otherwise, there would be no need for men to be taught; all craftsmen, good or bad, would be born so. And as we see happen in the arts, so it happens with the moral virtues. Nor should it seem strange if actions and customs, whether good or bad, are the same in genus; for this is the nature of contraries, that they belong to the same genus. Contrary habits are of the same genus; indeed whiteness and blackness, sweet and bitter, and the like. Just as Aristotle made use of certain examples from the arts, the cithara-players and carpenters, so he now shows what he has said in the case of justice, fortitude, temperance and mildness. When men are exercised in human dealings, they become either just or unjust; while they are involved in dangerous matters, either brave or timid; with regard to desires, either temperate or intemperate; and finally with regard to anger, as we exercise ourselves, we become either mild or irascible. But concerning mildness, irascibility, temperance, intemperance, justice and injustice, we shall speak later in their proper place. Justice too will be shown in philosophy to be a certain kind, which is concerned with human dealings.

units.la: Discrimen hoc loco consyderandum nobis occurrit, inter naturam & vim, à qua humanæ proficiscuntur actiones. Natura enim semper eadem modo operatur: voluntas autem varia est, & modo in hanc, modo in alteram partem flectitur. Pravis actionibus virtutes interire, sic accipiendum est, quòd nonnunquam cum inessent abolentur, interdum verò ne oriantur obstatur. Hoc in summa rebus quæ perperam aguntur debemus, per illas & partæ[?] iam virtutes auferuntur, & impedimentum ne oriantur interponitur. Humanæ actiones vniuersæ genere quidem congruunt, at specie differunt: contrahuntur enim per differentias boni & mali: unde humanarum actionum alias bonas, alias malas dicemus. Bonum verò & malum humanorum actuum respectu quodam constat: ut enim rationi consentiunt seu ab ea discrepant, vel bonæ vel malæ dicuntur. Ut virtutes igitur fiant, & præceptione atq; consuetudine opus habemus: at plus (ut audiemus) consuetudini ac usui quàm præceptionib. tribuitur. Syllogismus ita conecti[?] potest.
units.tr: Here we must consider the distinction that presents itself to us between nature and the force from which human actions proceed. For nature always operates in the same way; the will, however, is varied, and is bent now in this direction, now in the other. That virtues perish through bad actions is to be understood thus: sometimes, when they were present, they are destroyed, and sometimes they are prevented from arising. In sum, from things done wrongly we must hold that virtues already acquired through them are removed, and an obstacle is placed in the way lest they arise. Human actions all agree in genus, but differ in species: for they are distinguished by the differences of good and bad; hence we shall call some human actions good and others bad. The goodness or badness of human acts consists in a certain relation: for insofar as they agree with reason, or depart from it, they are called good or bad. So in order that virtues come about we need both precept and custom; but more (as we shall hear) is attributed to custom and practice than to precept. The syllogism can be constructed thus.

units.la: Quæcunq; per eadem & iisdem intereunt & producuntur, non insunt nobis natura.
units.tr: Whatever things both perish and are produced through the same things and by the same, are not inborn in us by nature.

units.la: Maiori huic propositioni hæc additur confirmatio, quia natura semper eodem modo agit: ideo ex iisdem & per eadem contraria non efficit, vt sunt ortus & interitus. Lapis ita sua graui natura deorsum ruit, vt sursum nunquam feratur, atq; ignis ita præleuitate sibi natiua sursum impellitur, vt ad inferna inclinare nequeat. Altera propositio subiicitur:
units.tr: To this major proposition is added a confirmation, because nature always acts in the same way; therefore it does not produce contraries, such as birth and death, from the same things and through the same things. A stone by its heavy nature falls downward, so that it is never carried upward; and fire, by its natural lightness, is driven upward so that it cannot incline toward the depths. The minor proposition is added:

units.la: At virtus iisdem atq; per eadem nascitur ac perit.
units.tr: But virtue is born from the same things and through the same things, and it perishes in the same way.
Therefore it does not arise from nature.

units.la: Minor ab artium similitudine confirmatur, & inductione cum architecturæ tum musicæ. Colligit deniq; omnes habitus ex consimilibus actionibus haberi. Et propterea infert, quæ sequuntur:
units.tr: The minor premise is confirmed by the likeness to the arts, and by induction from both architecture and music. Finally he concludes that all habits are had from like actions. And so he infers what follows:

units.la: Quapropter certæ quædam actiones edendæ sunt: quandoquidem habitus earum differentias consequuntur. Non itaq; parui refert, sed permultum, imo potius in eo totum situm est, an hoc an illo modo consuescamus.
units.tr: Therefore certain actions must be performed, since habits follow their differences. It matters not a little but very much; indeed the whole matter lies in whether we accustom ourselves in this way or that.

units.la: Monet ob ea quæ iam confecta sunt, ut non agatur fortuito, sed certæ quædam edantur actiones, & quisq; id quod agit, apud seipsum diligenter expendat: non enim actio humana res levis est, sed tanti profecto momenti, ut ex illius conditione, suam naturam habitus adipiscantur. Magnamq; iubet attentionem & diligentiam adhiberi, cum inde magna vis, imo fere tota colligatur, ad habitus quales quis voluerit sibi vendicandos. Cum iam hæc pars conclusa sit, statuamus Aristotelem, cum inficiatur virtutes in no-bis a natura inesse, haud propterea docere violenter ingenerari, cum dixerit, præter naturam virtutes non esse: at id tantum ostendere voluit, nos cum illis non nasci, sed industria ac frequenti usu bonarum actionum erum pere. Datur quidem nobis a natura facultas animi, voluntas inquam, unde possimus agere, at virtutes ex ipsa natura non oriuntur. Quia ut superius iam positum est, longe diversa est natura ac voluntatis ratio agendi: illa semper eodem modo, voluntas autem non item agit. Neq; fieri posset quin virtutes omnibus communes essent, si a natura prodirent. Virtus est (ut dicitur) ex actionibus, actiones ex voluntate, voluntas autem a natura est data: sed non quia voluntas a natura est, ideo virtus ex natura erit, quando natura ac voluntatis (ut dictum est) non est par agendi ratio. Non tamen putandum, actiones totam integramque causam esse virtutum: alioqui effectus dignitate causam vinceret. Quis enim non intelligat habitum firmum atque constantem esse, actionem vero præsertim qua ante habitum editur, incertam, dubiam & infirmam? Sed plena causa virtutis est voluntas, imo & Deus & actio: quibus etiam ratio addenda est, cui oportet ut recte actiones consentiant. Cumulus itaque iis omnibus ex causis sis collectus plenam perfectamq; comprehendit bonorum habituum effici-entem causam.
units.tr: On account of what has already been established, he warns that we should not act by chance but perform certain actions, and that each person should carefully weigh what he does within himself. For human action is not a light matter but of such great moment that habits acquire their nature from its character. He bids that great attention and diligence be applied, since a great force, indeed nearly the whole of it, is gathered from this for claiming for oneself whatever habits one wishes. Since this part is now concluded, let us hold that Aristotle, though he denies that virtues are inborn in us by nature, does not thereby teach that they are generated by force, since he said that virtues are not against nature. He wished only to show that we are not born with them, but that they are brought to perfection by diligence and frequent use of good actions. Indeed a faculty of the mind is given us by nature, namely the will, by which we can act; but virtues do not arise from nature itself. For, as was said above, the manner of acting of nature and that of the will are far different: nature always acts in the same way, but the will does not. Nor could virtues be common to all if they came from nature. Virtue comes (as it is said) from actions, actions from the will, and the will is given by nature. But it does not follow that, because the will is from nature, virtue will be from nature, since the manner of acting of nature and of the will is not equal (as has been said). Yet it should not be thought that actions are the whole and complete cause of virtues; otherwise the effect would surpass its cause in dignity. For who does not understand that a habit is firm and constant, but an action, especially one performed before the habit is formed, is uncertain, doubtful and weak? But the full cause of virtue is the will, indeed God too, and action; to these reason must also be added, with which actions ought to agree rightly. Thus the sum gathered from all these causes comprehends the full and perfect efficient cause of good habits.

units.la: Cognoscimus etiam hinc discrimen inter virtutem moralem atq; scien-tiam, Quod scientia interdum una inspectione unoq; cognoscendi actu acquiritur, ut in mathematicis videmus. Ut enim quis viderit quomodo triangularis figura ducatur, ἀπόδειξιν[?] habet, & eius rei scientiam est consecutus. At virtutem moralem quis non adipiscitur, nisi frequentes actus prius intercesserint. Actiones praeterea quae habitum producunt, quandoquidem sint oportet in eodem subiecto, in quo & virtutes sunt sitae, ideo sciendum virtutes ab interioribus non ab externis actionibus gigni. Sunt autem externae actiones indicia voluntatis bonae aut pravae, atq; interdum habitu-um bonorum aut malorum, non autem sunt causae. An vero per actiones externas habitus vel in corpore vel in membris acquirantur, quaestio est. Quidam id affirmarunt. Sed prudentiores Philosophi arbitrantur id quod acquiritur in corpore aut membris, scribendo, luctando, certando.potius es-se qualitates passibiles, ut caliditas, siccitas & huiusmodi, quam habitus.
units.tr: We recognise from this also the difference between moral virtue and knowledge: knowledge is sometimes acquired by a single inspection and one act of knowing, as we see in mathematics. For when someone has seen how a triangular figure is drawn, he has a demonstration [ἀπόδειξιν] and has attained knowledge of that thing. But no one acquires moral virtue unless frequent acts have gone before. Moreover, since the actions that produce a habit must be in the same subject in which the virtues are situated, it must be understood that virtues are born from inner, not external, actions. External actions are indications of a good or bad will, and sometimes of good or bad habits, but they are not causes. Whether habits are acquired through external actions, either in the body or in the limbs, is a question. Some have affirmed this. But the more prudent philosophers judge that what is acquired in the body or limbs by writing, wrestling and contending is rather passible qualities, such as heat, dryness and the like, than habits.

units.la: Quæ hucusque ab Aristotele sunt allata, prius oportet ad sacrarum literarum examen revocare, quàm ad alterum caput interpretandum accedamus. Quod primum dicitur virtutem mentis acquiri doctrina & experientiis, in universum non est suscipiendum. permulti enim fuerunt Apostoli, Prophetae, atq; alii viri boni qui sapientes ac docti afflatu spiritus statim evaserunt. Neq; illud recipimus, virtutem moralem usu atq; consuetudine acquiri. Deus hic praeteritur, qui est potissima & praecipua omnium virtutum causa, et scribitur, neminem posse castum cor habere, nisi Dominus dederit, aitq; Paulus, Quid habes quod non accepisti? Atq; si accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? Deus enim causa est impellens ad honeste agendum, idemq; largitur, ut perseverantia qui probi sunt evasuri, iustis actionibus insistant. An vero natura virtutes insint hominibus, dubitatum est. Sed si de homine loquamur, ut à Deo creatus est (quandoquidem omnia quae ille fecit, maximè bona erant) dubitari non potest quin & virtutibus instructus creatus fuerit. Ut enim caelum absque suis ornamentis non man-sit, & terra herbis statim fuit cooperta, ita homo cum creatus est, virtutibus se decentibus non caruit. Caeterum de natura vitiata & corrupta vera sunt quae dicuntur usitato cursu, & ratione consueta. Sed hanc naturae nostrae corruptionem Aristoteles videre non potuit, ut qui fide ac lumine divinarum literarum fuerit destitutus. Praeterea naturam nostram, uti nunc est, aptatam esse, idoneam, & capacem seu propensam ad virtutes recipiendas, est verum, si loquamur de his ciuilibus atq; moralibus, quamuis non omnes eodem modo se ad eas habent, sed varie pro temperamento corporis, educatione ac ingenio. De veris autem virtutibus, ut est fides, spes, charitas atq; consimiles, dicendum est naturam nostram ut corruptam non repugnare, quin talibus ornetur charismatis, modo ipse Deus dignetur afflare. Sed hoc illi repugnat ut suis viribus ac per se illas acquirat. Deinde nos prius habere actiones quam virtutes adipiscamur, in universum non est verum, cum propter primum hominem tum propter illos quibus Deus a sua conuersione statim virtutes infundit. Non dubitamus civilium legumlatorum hac esse voluntatem, consilium atque propositum, quod Aristoteles commemorat. Sed lex Dei habet alias quasdam fines, ut peccatum nempe ostendat, iram operetur, & ad Christum adducat. Ex hac legum dispositione ac legislatorum proposito respublicas inquit a se invicem differre, ac bonas malasque internosci. Quod sane ita verum est, ut Deus de suis legibus dixerit, fore ut si Iudaei eas servassent, omnes aliae nationes ipsorum Rempublicam sint ut beatam atq; felicissimam admiraturae. An vero ex ipsdem & per eadem virtutes intereant & gignantur, civiliter est verum, sed non in universum. Adamus enim virtutes accepit a Deo statim datas, corrupit autem prauo fastu: quare non ex ipsdem & per eadem fiunt, & pereunt. Idemque de iis est dicendum, qui eas a Deo statim habent & impetrant. Iusta faciendo iusti efficimur. Sed hoc non nisi de iustitia civili dabitur, & inhaerente: at de iustitia qua iustificamur, longe aliter sentiendum est. Atq; de fortitudine haud semper verum est, illos qui dum in periculis versantur & assuefuerunt non timere, illam adipisci: nam multis repente datum est, ut martyres fuerint constantissimi, qui antea sic molles fuerant, ut ne tantillum quidem perferre voluissent. Quare non recipimus in universum, habitus ex consimilibus fieri. Salutaris vero est admonitio, ut certa reddantur actiones, non tantum civiliter cuiq; videndum est ut ad rationis praescriptum agat, sed pie ac religiose quemlibet certum esse oportet suas actiones & instituta Deo placere. Neque inficiamur educationem tam multum ad virtutes acquirendas conducere. Dicit enim Solomon, adolescentem iuxta viam suam etiam cum senuerit profecturum. Et Paulus ad Eph. & Colos. tam multa mandat parentibus quae ad illorum institutionem spectant.
units.tr: What Aristotle has so far brought forward must first be brought back to the examination of the sacred letters before we come to interpret the second point. As for what is said first, that virtue of mind is acquired by teaching and experience, this must not be accepted in general. For there were very many Apostles, Prophets and other good men who at once became wise and learned by the breath of the Spirit. Nor do we accept that moral virtue is acquired by practice and custom. Here God is passed over, who is the chief and principal cause of all virtues; and it is written that no one can have a chaste heart unless the Lord gives it, and Paul says: "What have you that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" For God is the cause impelling us to act honourably, and he also grants that those who are upright should persevere in just actions. Whether virtues are in men by nature has been disputed. But if we speak of man as he was created by God (since all the things he made were very good), it cannot be doubted that he was created also furnished with virtues. For as heaven would not remain without its ornaments, and the earth was at once covered with herbs, so man, when he was created, did not lack the virtues that befitted him. As for nature in its corrupted and depraved state, what is said is true in the usual course and by the customary reasoning. But Aristotle could not see this corruption of our nature, since he was destitute of the faith and light of the divine letters. Besides, that our nature, as it now is, is fitted, suitable and capable, or inclined, to receive virtues is true, if we speak of those civil and moral virtues, although not all are disposed to them in the same way, but variously according to bodily temperament, upbringing and talent. But concerning true virtues, such as faith, hope, love and the like, we must say that our nature, being corrupted, does not resist being adorned with such gifts, provided God himself deigns to breathe upon it. But it does resist acquiring them by its own powers and of itself. Next, that we first have actions before we obtain virtues is not true in general, both on account of the first man and on account of those to whom God from their conversion at once infuses virtues. We do not doubt that this is the will, counsel and purpose of civil lawgivers, which Aristotle recalls. But the law of God has certain other ends, namely to show sin, to work wrath and to lead to Christ. From this arrangement of laws and purpose of lawgivers, he says, commonwealths differ from one another, and good and bad ones are distinguished. This is indeed so true that God said of his laws that, if the Jews kept them, all the other nations would marvel at their commonwealth as most blessed and happy. But whether virtues perish and are generated from the same things and through the same things is true civilly, but not in general. For Adam received virtues given at once by God, but corrupted them by depraved pride; therefore they are not made and destroyed from the same things and through the same things. And the same must be said of those who have them at once from God and obtain them. We become just by doing just things. But this holds only of civil justice, and inherent justice; concerning the justice by which we are justified, we must think quite otherwise. Nor is it always true of fortitude that those who, while in dangers and accustomed not to fear, acquire it; for to many it has been given suddenly that they became most steadfast martyrs, who before had been so soft that they would not endure even the slightest thing. Wherefore we do not accept that habits in general arise from like things. But the admonition that actions should be made certain is wholesome: not only must each person see civilly that he acts according to the precept of reason, but each one ought, piously and religiously, to be certain that his actions and institutions please God. Nor do we deny that education contributes greatly to acquiring virtues. For Solomon says that a young man, according to his way, will make progress even when he is old. And Paul, in Eph. and Col., enjoins on parents so many things that pertain to their children's instruction.

units.la: Non tamen (ut dicit Aristoteles) omnia illi tribuenda, quoniam ut docuimus, alia quoq; causae interveniunt ad virtutum productionem.
units.tr: Yet not all things (as Aristotle says) are to be attributed to it, since, as we have taught, other causes also intervene in the production of virtues.
CHAPTER II.

units.la: Quoniam hæc tractatio, non quemadmodum aliæ, contemplandi causa instituta est (non e-nim quo intelligamus quid sit virtus hæc perscruta mur, sed ut efficiamur boni, alioqui eius nulla esset utilitas) necesse est de actionibus videre, quo nam pacto sint exercendæ. Nam principes causæ sunt, unde habitus certi cuiusdam generis prodeunt, quem-admodum iam diximus.
units.tr: Since this treatise, unlike others, is undertaken not for the sake of contemplation (we are not investigating what virtue is so that we may know it, but so that we may become good, for otherwise it would be of no use), we must see in what way actions are to be performed. For actions are the originating causes from which habits of a certain kind arise, as we have already said.

units.la: AD ea quæ dicta sunt, hæc quæ modo scribuntur quàm aptissimè quadrant. Ex actionibus definiuerat habitus nasci, pro-pterea ut de ipsis videatur consentaneum est. Tria verò præ-cipua sunt quæ isto cap. sunt comprehensa. Primo quippe loco proponitur de quare sit modo agendum, & forma doctrinæ monstratur, quæ ad hæc tradenda sit idonea. Secundo, quia de actionibus est disputandum, quales hæ debeant esse, dicitur. Postremo denique nonnihil inducitur de illis actionibus quæ partos iam habitus consequuntur.
units.tr: These things just said fit very well with what is now written. We said that habits arise from actions, and so it is fitting to speak of actions. There are three main points in this chapter. First, it is stated what manner of teaching should be used, and the form of teaching suited to these matters is shown. Second, because we must discuss actions, it is said what sort they ought to be. Last, something is introduced about those actions that follow upon habits already acquired.

units.la: Propositio itaq; loci huius est, Oportere iam de actionibus disputare. Du-abus rationibus confirmatur. Prima, quia hæc scientia non est ad notitiam ordinata, sed ad ipsos actus perpetuò spectat. Non enim ut sciamus hæc di-scimus, verùm ut boni efficiamur. Unde cùm ista facultas eum scopum ha-beat, circa ipsas actiones par est ut maximè versetur. Quare sciendum con-templantium facultatum finem esse notitiam, sed practicarum actionem: comprehendunt quidem ipsa quoq; notitiam, sed ipsa non est præcipuus fi-nis. Altera verò ratio, qua confirmatur inducta propositio, est, id maximè in ea scientia quæ de felicitate ac virtutibus agit considerandum esse, quod i-psos habitus ad certum genus cõtrahit, & eos producit. Neq; dubium est cui-quam actiones huiusmodi esse: quare de illis est tractandum. Syllogismi ho-rum argumentorum ita connecti possunt.
units.tr: The proposition of this passage, then, is that we must now discuss actions. It is confirmed by two reasons. The first is that this science is not ordered toward knowledge but always looks to the actions themselves. For we learn these things not so that we may know them but so that we may become good. Since this discipline has that aim, it ought to be concerned chiefly with the actions themselves. For it must be recognised that the end of the speculative faculties is knowledge, but the end of the practical ones is action; the practical sciences do include knowledge, but knowledge is not their chief end. The second reason, by which the proposition is confirmed, is that in the science which treats of happiness and the virtues, the thing to be considered above all is that these actions bring the habits into a certain kind and produce them. And no one doubts that such actions exist; therefore we must treat of them. The syllogisms of these arguments can be connected thus.

units.la: In ea scientia quæ notitia non est contenta, sed eò spectat ut boni efficia-mur, de actionibus potissimum agitur.
units.tr: In the science that is not content with knowledge but aims at making us good, actions are chiefly treated.
Ethics is a science of this kind.
Therefore it treats of actions.

units.la: Maior propositio est euidens, quia non efficimur boni nisi actionibus, & quaelibet facultas circa suam finem praesertim versatur. Minor declaratur, quoniam scientia alioqui nulla est vtilitas. Sed hoc dubium nonnihil videtur, quandoquidem notitia quarumuis rerum sua natura expetenda est. Vnde licet quis vti nolit, non videretur sua vtilitate carere virtutum notitia. Respondetur: Esse quidem notitiam illam, qua iustum ab iniusto, & honestum a turpi discernitur, pulchram, & iucunditate afficere suopte ingenio. Sed tamen cum agendum non instituitur, propria caret vtilitate: non enim hic agitur de communi dignitate notitiae, qua communicant inter se vniuersae scientiae, sed de propria nunc loquimur huius facultatis vtilitate.
units.tr: The major premise is evident, since we become good only through actions, and every faculty is especially concerned with its end. The minor is proved because otherwise the science would be of no use. But this seems somewhat doubtful, since knowledge of any things is by its nature to be desired. Hence, even if someone does not wish to use it, the knowledge of the virtues would not seem to lack its own usefulness. The answer is: that knowledge by which the just is distinguished from the unjust and the honourable from the base is indeed fine, and by its own nature delights. But when action is not undertaken, it lacks its proper usefulness. For we are not here speaking of the general worth of knowledge, which all sciences share with one another, but now of the proper usefulness of this faculty.
The second syllogism is:

units.la: Ea potissimum tractanda in Ethicis quae causae sint virtutum:
units.tr: Those things are chiefly to be treated in Ethics which are the causes of the virtues.

units.la: Actiones autem causas esse virtutum non dubitamus.
units.tr: But we do not doubt that actions are the causes of the virtues.
Therefore we must treat of them.

units.la: Maior liquet, quod omnis scientia causis innitatur. Minor est iam in primo capite declarata. Hae sunt duae rationes, quarum prior causae finali innititur, altera vero efficienti.
units.tr: The major is clear, since every science rests on causes. The minor has already been shown in the first chapter. These are the two reasons: the former rests on the final cause, the latter on the efficient cause.

units.la: Rationi rectae conuenienter agere commune sit, ac ponatur.
units.tr: Let it be assumed that acting in accordance with right reason is common.

units.la: Quiddam accipit, vt commune humanis actionibus, non quidem omnibus, verum his tantum a quibus virtutes producuntur. Multa alioqui sunt hominum actiones, quae a recta ratione dissentiunt, sed ad ea sermo est contrahendus de quibus modo proposita est disputatio.
units.tr: He takes something as common to human actions, not indeed to all of them but only to those from which the virtues are produced. For there are many human actions that depart from right reason, but our discourse is to be confined to those about which the present discussion is proposed.

units.la: Dicetur autem postea de ipsa, & quid sit recta ratio, & quo pacto se ad alias virtutes habeat.
units.tr: What right reason is, and how it stands in relation to the other virtues, will be discussed later.

units.la: Ne quis expectet vt modo agat de ratione vel eius rectitudine, ista in aliud tempus dicenda reiecit: nam in sexto tractabuntur, cum de ipsa prudentia disputatio instituetur, ibique luculenter tradetur quid recta ratio sit, & prudentiam quae maxime ad eam spectat, scribet caeterarum virtutum esse condimentum, & illarum sal quam maxime necessarium.
units.tr: Lest anyone expect him to deal now with reason or its rightness, he has put off these matters to another time. For they will be treated in the sixth book, when the discussion of prudence itself is undertaken, and there it will be clearly set out what right reason is; and he will write that prudence, which is chiefly concerned with it, is the seasoning of the other virtues and their most necessary salt.

units.la: Id autem in confesso habeatur, rationem omnem de agendis forma quadam pinguiori non exquisitè tractandam, uti jam inde ab initio diximus: quoniam pro materia subiecta petendæ sunt rationes. Sed actiones humanæ, quæcunq; ad vitam utilia sunt, nil firmi atque constantis habent, ceu salubria. Cumq; ratio sit huiusmodi quæ circa genera versatur, quæ circa singula versatur, magis adhuc exquisita ratione caret: siquidem neque sub artem neque sub præce-ptionem ullam cadit.
units.tr: It must, however, be taken as granted that every account of things to be done should not be treated exactly in a rather rich form, as we said from the beginning; since reasons must be sought according to the subject matter. But human actions, whatever is useful for life, have nothing firm and constant, like healthful things. And since reason of this kind is concerned with genera, while that which is concerned with particulars has even less exact reason, since it falls under no art or precept.

units.la: Cùm de actionibus hominum dicendum sit, qua forma doctrinæ uti oporteat exponit, ne quis accuratam & subtilem expectet, nëue si crassiore audiuerit, indignetur. Dicit itaq; semper docendi rationem accommodatam esse debere materiæ, quæ tum præ manibus fuerit: actiones autem humanas inconstantes esse, ut quæ per tempora, loca, ætates, personarumq; conditiones, vicissitudines multas subeunt. Quemadmodum in rebus salubribus usuenit: non enim eadem omnibus conducunt, neque semper ad cunctos morbos eadem pharmaca, victusq; ratio sunt congrua. Et ad vitam utilia variantur, bellum, pax, conventiones, perceptio aut repudiatio voluptatū. Ista omnia interdum conveniunt, interdum vero sunt damnosa. Ista eadem Aristoteles 1. lib. commemorauit: nunc autem causa est cur repetat, quòd hic nouum quodammodo rerum ducedarum[?] principium faciat. Syllogismus componetur:
units.tr: Since we must speak about human actions, he sets out what form of teaching ought to be used, so that no one may expect precision and subtlety, nor be indignant if he hears something rather coarse. He therefore says that the manner of teaching must always be suited to the matter at hand; human actions are inconstant, since they undergo many changes according to times, places, ages and the conditions of persons. It is as with healthful things: the same things do not suit everyone, nor are the same medicines and regimens fitting for all diseases. Things useful for life also vary: war, peace, agreements, the acceptance or rejection of pleasures. All these sometimes agree and sometimes are harmful. Aristotle mentioned these same things in the first book, but now there is a reason for him to repeat them, because here he makes in a way a new beginning of the matters to be treated. The syllogism is composed thus:

units.la: Quæcunq; facultas circa materiam inconstantem ac mutabilem versa-tur, firmis & exquisitis rationibus uti non potest.
units.tr: Whatever faculty is concerned with inconstant and changeable matter cannot use firm and exact reasons.
The science of Ethics has matter of this kind.
Therefore it does not use exact and subtle reasons.

units.la: Maior propositio ex eo fidem habet, quòd rationes ad materiam non mi-nus accommodari debeant quàm calcei ad pedes vel ad corpus vestes. Minor idcirco probatur, quia ex circumstātiis varis actiones humanæ immutantur. Quod & simili confirmatur salubrium rerum & utilium: nam in-ter se plurimum congruunt. Ethica facultas & medica gubernatrix.
units.tr: The major premise is credible because reasons ought to be fitted to their matter no less than shoes to the feet or clothes to the body. The minor is proved because human actions are altered by various circumstances. This is confirmed by the similar case of healthful and useful things, which agree very much with one another. Ethics is a faculty like medicine, which guides.

units.la: Quod vero interponitur de generali doctrina & singulari, eo spectat, ne quis putet inconstantiam hanc ex methodo Aristotelica cuenire, quasi pos-set euitari, si non ita voluisset à generalibus auspicari. Per occupationem ad hoc respondet: Esse quidem in ratione naturali Ethicorum hanc materiam inconstantiam, sed longe maiorem adhuc positam in singulis: quandoquidem illa sic varia sunt & incerta, ut neq; arte neq; praeceptione vlla comprehendi queant. Cur autem id hoc pacto se habeat, duae rationes videntur posse adduci. Prima est, quod infinita sint numero, atq; ideo non valeant animo percipi. Altera quod exigua & praesua [?] tenuitate inconstantia fugiat mentis comprehensionem. Genera dividi possunt in species, composita in partes: verum haec singula, & propter numerorum exiguitatem et inconstantiam non ita solui possunt & distingui.
units.tr: What is inserted about general and particular teaching is meant to prevent anyone thinking that this inconstancy arises from Aristotle's method, as if it could have been avoided had he not chosen to begin from general principles. By way of anticipation, to answer: there is indeed this inconstancy in the natural reason of the Ethics, but it is far greater still in particulars, since these are so varied and uncertain that they cannot be grasped by any art or precept. Why this is so, two reasons may be adduced. The first is that they are infinite in number and therefore cannot be grasped by the mind. The second is that the inconstancy escapes the mind's grasp by reason of its slight and subtle nature. Genera can be divided into species, and composites into parts; but these particulars, on account of the smallness and inconstancy of their numbers, cannot be so resolved and distinguished.

units.la: Qui res gerunt semper oportet occasionē spectare, ut in medica facultate atque gubernatrice usu venit. Verum licet hæc ratio ita se habeat, attamen elaborandum est ut adiumentum afferamus.
units.tr: Those who conduct affairs must always look to the occasion, as happens in the medical art and in the art of government. Yet although this is so, we must labour to bring help.

units.la: Probat adhuc alia ratione materiae huius facultatis inconstantiam. Quoniam qui res gerunt, ad occasiones oportet esse attentos. Qui Respub. administrant, occasiones ferendarum legum captant, puniendorum scelerum, muniendi arces, delectum habendi, pacis & belli, & deniq; si sapiant nihil agunt in Respub. sine observata diligenter opportunitate temporis. Ut rusticus [?] tempore certo serit, certa parte anni metit, alia vero arat. Esto Syllogismus huius formae: Quæcunq; facultas pendet ab occasionibus, varia ea est, & firmitatem subiecti non habet. Scientia Ethica pendet ab occasionibus (quoniam qui res agunt opportunitatem agendi captare debent). Ergo scientia Ethica varia est, & subiecti firmitatem non habet. Id iubebat Pittacus inter Graecos iudicatus multo sapientissimus, ut in omnibus occasio bene perpenderetur. Atq; Hippocrates occasionem aiebat praecipitem esse, ideoq; diligentissime captandam. Non tamen hac de causa inquit Aristoteles desperandum, aut ab incepto desistendum, sed potius industria et labore adhibito est inconstantia atq; varietati subiecti succurrendum.
units.tr: He proves the inconstancy of the matter of this faculty by another reason: those who conduct affairs must be attentive to occasions. Those who administer the commonwealth seize opportunities for enacting laws, for punishing crimes, for fortifying citadels, for levying troops, for peace and war; and finally, if they are wise, they do nothing in the commonwealth without carefully observing the opportunity of the time. As a farmer sows at a certain time, reaps at a certain part of the year, and ploughs at other times. Let there be a syllogism of this form: Whatever faculty depends on occasions is varied and does not have the firmness of a fixed subject. The science of Ethics depends on occasions (since those who conduct affairs must seize the opportunity of acting). Therefore the science of Ethics is varied and does not have the firmness of a fixed subject. Pittacus, judged by the Greeks to be by far the wisest, bade that the occasion be carefully weighed in all things. And Hippocrates said that occasion is headlong, and therefore must be seized most diligently. Yet for this reason, says Aristotle, we must not despair or give up what we have begun; rather, by applying diligence and labour, we must meet the inconstancy and variety of the subject.

units.la: Primum itaq; attendendum, quae sunt huius generis, ea natura esse, ut & ab excessu & a defectu perdantur, uti uidemus fieri de robore & sanitate: oportet enim ad obscura quam manifestissimis probationibus uti. Exercitia enim uel contetiora uel remissiora fiora debilitant uires. Poculenta itidē & esculenta, si maiora uel minora fuerint, sanitatē uitiant. Modera-ta uerò illam producunt, augent & seruant. Ita de tē-perantia, fortitudine, aliisq; uirtutibus est.
units.tr: First, then, we must notice that things of this kind are destroyed by excess and by deficiency, just as we see happen with strength and health. For we must use the most evident proofs for what is obscure. Exercises that are either too strenuous or too slack weaken the strength. Likewise drink and food, if taken in greater or lesser amounts, spoil health. Moderate amounts, however, produce, increase and preserve it. So it is with temperance, courage and the other virtues.

units.la: Hic iam huius capitis secundam partem aggreditur, & naturam illarum actionum ostendit à quibus virtutes producantur. Propositio est, Illas temperatas ac moderatas esse debere, illam autem propositionem volens confirmare, praefatur, manifestis vtedum probationibus: quòd sane rationi doctrinae admodum consentaneum est, quia semper à notis ad ignota progredimur. Quae vero haec nota sint demonstrat, nempe exercitia & cibos. Si modum excesserint aut deficiant, nocent: moderata vero iuuant atq; conseruant.
units.tr: Here he now begins the second part of this chapter, and shows the nature of those actions from which the virtues are produced. The proposition is that these actions ought to be tempered and moderate. To confirm this proposition he first makes the point by means of evident proofs, which is certainly very consistent with the method of teaching, since we always proceed from the known to the unknown. He then shows what these known things are, namely exercises and foods. If they exceed or fall short of the measure, they harm; moderate amounts help and preserve.
The syllogism is:

units.la: Quacunq; defectu aut excessu corrumpuntur & intereunt, mediocrita-te seruantur.
units.tr: Whatever is corrupted and perishes by deficiency or excess is preserved by the mean.
So are actions and habits.
Therefore they are preserved by the mean.

units.la: Maior propositio demonstratur, cibis & exercitijs. Minor, temperantia & fortitudine. In his vero collationibus id obseruandum, medicam facultatem & ethicen plurimum conuenire. Quandoquidem quod est corpori sanitas, est animo felicitas. Quod in corporibus est robur & vires, in animo ipsa sunt virtutes. De notioribus agit, cibis inquam exercitijsq;, nec non de sanitate ac robore. Sunt haec magis cognita, quandoquidem in sensum incurrunt: alia vero quae ad animum pertinent, non ita cognoscuntur ab omnib. Vnde longe plures inuenias, qui morbos corporis exponere ac referre possint de illis interrogati, quàm qui aegritudines animi vel intelligant vel queant exprimere. Quare Plato verissimè dixit, Sapientiam si conspicua esset & ab omnibus cognosceretur, facile posse admirandos amores hominum erga se conciliare: at quia non videtur, ideo erga illam homines obstupescunt, quidus potius aliud quàm ipsam curando. Mi to Aristotelis exempla de cibis & exercitijs valere obiter ad frugalitatem commendandam & reprehendendam ignauiam.
units.tr: The major premise is proved by food and exercises. The minor by temperance and courage. In these comparisons, however, it must be observed that medical skill and ethics have very much in common, since what health is to the body, happiness is to the soul. What strength and power are in bodies, the virtues themselves are in the soul. He deals with the more familiar things, namely food and exercise, and likewise with health and strength. These are better known, since they fall under the senses; but the things that pertain to the soul are not so well known to everyone. Hence you will find far more people who can describe and report the diseases of the body when asked about them than people who understand or can express the sicknesses of the soul. Therefore Plato spoke very truly when he said that if wisdom were visible and known to all, it could easily win admiring love from people towards itself; but because it is not seen, people are astonished at it in a way that leads them to care for other things rather than for it itself. It is not surprising that Aristotle's examples of food and exercise serve incidentally to commend frugality and to rebuke idleness.

units.la: Nā qui fugit atq; timet omnia, nihil perfert, timidus efficitur. Quiq; nihil omnino metuit, sed adit omnia, fit audax. Similiter q; fruitur qualibet uoluptate, nullamq; non admittit, intemperans. Qui omnes fugit ut agrestes, fit stupidus ac sensus expers. Etenim ceu temperantia, sic fortitudo a mediocritate servatur: excessu vero ac defectu perit.
units.tr: For the one who shuns and fears everything, and endures nothing, becomes timid. And the one who fears nothing at all, but rushes at everything, becomes rash. Likewise the one who indulges in any pleasure whatever and admits none without exception becomes intemperate. The one who shuns all pleasures like a boor becomes dull and insensible. For just as temperance, so courage is preserved by the mean, and is destroyed by excess and by deficiency.

units.la: Minorem propositionem iam adductam confirmat. Ea erat, Fortitudi-nem, temperantiam, caeterasq; virtutes excessu defectuque perire. Probatio inde sumitur, Ex consuetudine usuq; timendi, homines fieri timidos: & dum frequenter adeunt pericula, fieri audaces. Dumq; omnibus absq; delectu fruuntur voluptatibus, euadunt intemperantes: & cum omnes refugiunt, agrestes & stupidi fiunt. Ergo si mediocritas conservetur in actionibus, virtus erit salua. His aduersari a nonnullis creditur, quòd non exercitio timor audaciaq; comparantur, sed natura videntur inesse, ut cùm sanguis friget: & in quibusdam animalibus id experientia quàm manifestissime docet. Nam timidissimos cuniculos, damas & lepores videas. In hominibus etiā propensiones quasdam naturales ad hos affectus quisq; potest vel in seipso experiri & sentire: quas utiq; propensiones cum ad corporis temperaturam, tum ad cælum, tum verissime ad ipsum Deum referre possunt. Hæc ut non negamus, ita statuimus usu ac educatione aut omnino vinci, aut saltem posse mitigari. Nonne Amazones mulieres erant ob sexus infirmitatem natura imbelles? at exercitatione (si poetis aut Historicis credamus) reddita sunt bellicosissimæ. Græci vicissim dum res eorum floruerunt, & penes illos fuit imperium, fortes erant atq; in armis strenui. Verum cum Romani sunt rerum potiti, armis positis, redditi sunt effœminati & ignavi. Illos præterea spectemus, qui sunt in aliquarum ditionum limitibus: ȳ[?] quoniam perpetuo cum hostibus dimicandum est, cæteris qui habitant in interioribus, atq; ob id tu-tioribus partibus, & fortiores & ad bellum maximè instructi euadunt. Ostendunt hæc omnia exercitatione inclinationes naturæ superari, aut sal-tem, quemadmodum est dictum, leniri.
units.tr: He now confirms the minor premise adduced above. That premise was that courage, temperance and the other virtues perish by excess and by deficiency. The proof is drawn from this: from the habit and practice of fearing, men become timid; and while they often encounter dangers, they become bold. And while they indulge in all pleasures without discrimination, they turn intemperate; and when they shun them all, they become boorish and dull. Therefore, if the mean is kept in actions, virtue will be safe. Some think these claims are contrary to this, because courage and boldness are not acquired by exercise but seem to be present by nature, as when the blood runs cold; and experience teaches this most plainly in certain animals. For you may see rabbits, deer and hares to be very timid. In humans too, anyone can experience and feel in himself certain natural inclinations towards these emotions; and these inclinations can rightly be referred to the temperament of the body, to the heavens, and most truly to God himself. As we do not deny these things, so we maintain that they can either be wholly overcome, or at least be moderated, by practice and upbringing. Were not the Amazon women by nature unwarlike because of the weakness of their sex? Yet by training (if we believe the poets or historians) they became most warlike. The Greeks in turn, while their affairs flourished and rule was in their hands, were brave and vigorous in arms. But when the Romans gained control of affairs, they laid down their arms and became effeminate and cowardly. Moreover, let us consider those who live on the borders of certain realms; since they must always fight with enemies, they become both stronger and better equipped for war than those who live in the interior and so in safer regions. All these things show that the inclinations of nature are overcome by practice, or at least, as has been said, softened.

units.la: Eodem inquit modo res habet quo ad voluptates. Qui nullam non ad-mittit, efficitur intemperans: & qui omnem fugit, euadit agrestis ac stupi-dus. Accipienda sunt non de quouis genere voluptatis, verùm de illis tantum quæ sunt crassiores, & ad sensus externos pertinent. Nam quæ sunt animi, non efficiunt intemperantem. Temperantiam ac fortitudi-nem perire tâ excessu quàm defectu bifariam debet accipi: nempe duobus iis extremis, cùm habetur, facilè corrupi: et quàdo nō habetur impediri, ne acquiratur. Similiter conservari mediocritate dicitur, quoniam etsi habita prius fuerit, retinebitur: & cum abfuerit, acquiri poterit.
units.tr: He says that the matter stands in the same way with respect to pleasures. The one who admits every pleasure becomes intemperate, and the one who shuns every pleasure turns rustic and dull. These things must be understood not of every kind of pleasure, but only of the grosser ones that pertain to the external senses. For the pleasures of the soul do not make a man intemperate. Temperance and courage must be understood to perish both by excess and by deficiency in two ways: namely, that when they are possessed, they are easily corrupted by those two extremes; and when they are not possessed, they are prevented from being acquired. Similarly, they are said to be preserved by the mean, since if they have been possessed before, they will be retained; and when they are absent, they can be acquired.

units.la: Sed non solum ortus atq; accesiones & interitus ex iisdem & ab iisdem fiunt, sed actiones in iisdem erunt. Sic enim in aliis quae magis aperta sunt, res habet, quemadmodum in ipso robore. Accedit enim cum cibus fuerit copiosus, & multi perferuntur labores: quicq; fuerit fortis, haec maxime potest facere. Ita sunt & virtutes. Efficimur enim temperati, dum a voluptatibus abstinemus: & cum temperati fuerimus, ab illis maxime possumus abstinere. Neque secus est de fortitudine: dum enim assuescimus terribilia despicere ac ea perferre, fortes evadimus: fortes autem jam effecti, maxime valemus terribilia perferre.
units.tr: But not only do their origin, growth and destruction come from the same things and by the same things, but the actions too will be the same in them. The matter stands in this way in other things that are more manifest, just as with strength itself. For it happens that when food is plentiful, and many labours are endured, the one who is strong can do the most. So it is with the virtues too. We become temperate while we abstain from pleasures; and once we are temperate, we are best able to abstain from them. It is no different with courage: while we become accustomed to despising terrible things and enduring them, we become brave; and once we have become brave, we are most able to endure terrible things.

units.la: Tertiam hic ingredimur capitis huius partem, qua nonnulla de iis actionibus dicuntur quas virtutes jam partas in lucem edunt. Actiones, inquit, ex quibus virtutes gignuntur, cum illis eadem sunt quae postea ex virtutibus oriuntur. Confirmatq; sententiam suam adducto simili a corporis viribus. Quod est a notioribus ea quae minus sunt nota constabilire. Ut enim ex cibo & exercitiis contrahitur robur corporis, & qui jam robusti evaserunt, copiosiori cibo uti possunt, & exercitia graviora queunt subire: ita ex abstinentia voluptatum oritur temperantia, & qui temperatus est maxime abstinet. Et perferre labores & difficiles casus aggredi frequenter fortitudinem parit. Quique fortis evasit, & frequentius & facilius dura perfert. Ista planissima sunt: nam ex habitu facilius agitur, cum ipsum natura vires & facultates perficiantur, & saepius ab eodem operamur, quoniam inclinat & adducit nos ad agendum. Unde Aristoteles in libro 3. de anima 18. textu scribit, nos habitu quando volumus & absque difficultate agere.
units.tr: Here we enter the third part of this chapter, in which some things are said about those actions which, once the virtues are acquired, bring them into the light. He says that the actions from which virtues are born are the same, as to their kind, as those which afterwards arise from the virtues. He confirms his opinion by a comparison with the strength of the body. This is establishing what is less known by means of what is better known. For just as strength of body is gained from food and exercise, and those who have already become strong can use more copious food and can undergo heavier exercises, so temperance arises from abstinence from pleasures, and the one who is temperate abstains most. And enduring labours and undertaking difficult hazards often produces courage; and the one who has become brave endures hardships both more often and more easily. These things are quite plain: for a thing is done more easily from a habit, since the powers and faculties are perfected by nature itself, and we operate from the same habit more often, because it inclines and draws us to act. Hence Aristotle writes in the third book On the Soul, text 18, that we act from habit whenever we wish and without difficulty.

units.la: At oritur grauis difficultas, qua ne ratione sint eadem actiones quae antecedunt virtutem, quaeq; illam consequuntur. Numero eadem esse nequeunt, cum simul non existant. Eadem esse genere non dicitur: nam identitas illa nimis laxa est. Etenim rectae prauaeq; actiones genere conveniunt. Superest it aq; ut eadem specie seu forma dicantur: at id non videtur posse fieri, cum eadem non habeant sui ortus principia. Nam quae praecedunt virtutes, à voluntate gubernata intelligentia fiunt: quae vero sequuntur, ex habitu prodeunt. Quaeque sunt eiusdem formae ac speciei, solent eodem modo communicari. Atq; si eorum varia interdum principia traduntur, unum e-orum erit per se, alterum vero temere seu per accidens, ut loquuntur, erit. Caeterum nos illud assumptum minime damus. Quae sunt eiusdem formae seu speciei, eodem modo communicari non ponemus. Calor enim à motu, à luce atque ab igne producitur. Quin & ignis interdum ex motu, non-nunquam ex luce, aliquando ex altero igne prodit. Et animantia eiusdem speciei à parentibus & à calore caeli ex putri materia generantur. Sci-entia quoque tam per doctrinam quàm per inuentionem acquiritur. At-que in Metaphysica lib.7.textu.23. eadem ex arte ac sine arte fiunt. Plantas etiā videmus alicubi per semen, alicubi sponte nasci, quae tamen diuersa for-mae aut speciei dici non possunt. Neq; si duo sunt aut tria originis principia, illi-co sequitur unū eorū esse per se, aliud vero per accidens: quoniam possunt e-iusdem esse facultatis & earundem virium. Ut calor feminis & calor caeli ac Solis quo fouetur putris materia, & praeparatur ad gignedum animalia imperfecta: at de imperfectis nominatim loquor. Nam quae perfecta sunt, ut recte Auerroes contra Avicennam sensit, non possunt ex putri materia gi-gni. Plures enim praeparationes in materia exiguntur ad illorum ortum quàm ad imperfectorum procreationem. Sunt ergo calor parentum & caeli stis in imperfectarum rerum productione virium earundem: ideò potest e-orum virtumq; principium per se appellari. Sed quando principia ortus ita di-stinguuntur, ut in una ratione communi copulari non queant, illa quae fiunt tum diuersa forma ac speciei esse dicuntur, ut esse videmus inuentionem & doctrinam quibus intelligentiae virtutes parantur, si ea conferatur cum usu & exercitio per quae virtutes morales conquiruntur. Sic habitus, ut à re praesenti non discedamus, haud à viribus animi permultum dissentit, sed il-larum est perfectio: ideò si eis coniungatur, speciem & formam effectus non mutat, imò absoluit, & reddit perfectiorem. Proinde affirmo Aristotelem rectè dicere, actiones quae habitum praecedunt & sequuntur, easdem esse: nam si ut intra eadem continentur extrema defectus & excessus, utq; con-sentiunt cum recta ratione, ambae sunt eiusdem forma ac speciei. Ut si quis reddat depositum ex virtute iustitiae, alterq; idem faciat suasu rectae ratio-nis absq; virtutis habitu, restitutiones ambae iuxta causas tam adductas, e-adem forma & specie comprehenduntur. Quamuis quo ad causas efficientes aliquam habeat varietatem, sed ea est per accidentia. Nā sine habitu illa est, difficultas & molestia in agendo: cum habitu facilitas, voluptas, & tranquillitas. Et in summa distinctio solum est penes magis & minus perfectum. Magis autem perfectum & minus perfectum, in accidentibus non mutant formam, sed in gradibus substantiae mutant: nam ex illis differentiae substantiales accipiuntur. Candor enim perfectior & minus perfectus eiusdem sunt naturae: homo tamen qui magis perfectus est equo, ad eandem speciem non attinet, quia hic discrimen perfectionis ad rei substantiam attingit.
units.tr: But a serious difficulty arises: how can the actions that precede a virtue and those that follow it be the same? They cannot be the same in number, since they do not exist at the same time. Nor are they said to be the same in genus, for that identity is too loose; for right and wrong actions agree in genus. It remains, then, that they be called the same in species or form; but this does not seem possible, since they do not have the same principles of origin. For the actions that precede the virtues are performed by intelligence governed by the will; but those that follow come forth from the habit. Things that are of the same form and species are usually produced in the same way. And if at times their principles of origin are various, one of them will be per se, and the other will be by chance, or, as they say, per accidens. However, we do not grant this assumption at all. We will not hold that things of the same form or species are produced in the same way. For heat is produced by motion, by light and by fire. Indeed fire sometimes comes from motion, sometimes from light, and sometimes from another fire. Animals of the same species are generated from parents, and from the heat of the heavens out of putrid matter. Knowledge too is acquired both through teaching and through discovery. And in Metaphysics book 7, text 23, the same things come about both by art and without art. We also see plants sometimes grow from seed and sometimes spontaneously, yet these cannot be called different in form or species. Nor, if there are two or three principles of origin, does it immediately follow that one of them is per se and another per accidens, since they can be of the same faculty and of the same powers. Thus the heat of the seed and the heat of the heavens and of the sun, by which putrid matter is warmed and prepared to generate imperfect animals (but I am speaking here specifically of imperfect things), are of the same kind. For perfect things, as Averroes rightly held against Avicenna, cannot be generated from putrid matter, since many more preparations are required in matter for their origin than for the production of imperfect things. Therefore the heat of the parents and of the heavens are of the same powers in producing imperfect things, and so their principle can be called per se. But when the principles of origin are distinguished in such a way that they cannot be joined under one common account, the things that are produced by them are said to be of different form and species; as we see with discovery and teaching, by which the virtues of the intellect are acquired, when these are compared with practice and exercise, by which the moral virtues are gained. Thus habit, so as not to stray from the matter at hand, differs little from the powers of the soul, but is their perfection; therefore, if it is joined to them, it does not change the species and form of the effect, but rather completes it and makes it more perfect. Accordingly I affirm that Aristotle is right to say that the actions which precede and those which follow a habit are the same. For if the extremes of deficiency and excess are contained within the same limits, and the actions agree with right reason, both are of the same form and species. For example, if someone restores a deposit from the virtue of justice, and another does the same at the urging of right reason without the habit of virtue, both restitutions, according to the causes adduced, are comprehended under the same form and species. Although with respect to efficient causes there is some variety, this is only accidental. For without the habit there is difficulty and trouble in acting; with the habit there is ease, pleasure and tranquillity. And in sum, the distinction lies only in the more and less perfect. But the more and less perfect do not change the form in accidents; they do change it in the degrees of substance, for substantial differences are taken from these. Thus whiteness that is more perfect and less perfect is of the same nature; yet a man, who is more perfect than a horse, does not belong to the same species, because this difference of perfection touches the substance of the thing.

units.la: Superest modo ut huius capitis doctrinam componamus cum diuinis literis. Scientiam hanc dicit Aristoteles non esse ut discamus sed ut boni efficiamur. Idem sacri libri docent, Quia Paulus inquit scientiam inflare, charitatem vero aedificare: atque hypocritis opponebatur eos tulisse clauem scientiae, sed non introisse. Nec non ille dicebatur super arenam aedificare, qui audiuisset & non fecisset: isq; vero qui audita implecuisset opere, super petram & quidem firmam dicebatur extruere. Commune statuitur esse omnibus rectis actionibus hominum ut rationi rectae congruant, quod a diuinis literis minimè conuellitur. Sed hoc addere oportet, nunquam humanam rationem fore sanam & rectam, nisi verbo Dei formetur. Crassiori etiam doctrina scribitur scientiam hanc tradendam: quod & in Sacris libris fieri videmus, vbi Dominus parabolis populos docet. Et Paulus lacte pascit eos qui solidum cibum non ferunt: nostraq; ab eodem notitia diuinarum per speculum et in aenigmate haberi dicitur. Deinde facultatem hanc asserit occasiones rerum obseruare. Quod in negocio pietatis etiam est obseruandum. Circumcidit Paulus Timotheum, Titum vero noluit circumcidere, cum vtrinque longe diuersa esset occasio. Idemq; Apostolus data occasione de ignoto Deo coepit Atheniensib. concionari: sic enim viderat illorum aram inscriptam. Mediocritas actionibus adhibenda est ad virtutes comparandas. Dicitur etiam ad Romanos, no plus sapere quam oportet. Viaq; nobis regia proponitur, a qua declinare non licet neq; ad dextram neq; ad sinistram. Iudicanda vero non est haec mediocritas nisi testimonio Spiritus & diuinarum literarum. Non semper autem virtutes acquiri frequentibus actionibus rectis, sed a Deo interdum inspirari, superius fuse docuimus.
units.tr: It remains now that we compare the teaching of this chapter with the divine writings. Aristotle says that this science is not for us to learn so much as that we may become good. The sacred books teach the same thing. Paul says that knowledge puffs up but love builds up; and hypocrites were rebuked for having taken the key of knowledge but not having entered in. Likewise, he who heard and did not act was said to build upon the sand, while he who heard what was taught and carried it out in work was said to build upon a rock, and indeed a firm one. It is agreed that it is common to all right human actions that they agree with right reason, and the divine writings by no means overturn this. But this must be added: human reason will never be sound and right unless it is shaped by the word of God. This teaching is also written in a cruder form, as we see done in the sacred books, where the Lord teaches the people by parables. Paul feeds with milk those who cannot bear solid food, and he says that our knowledge of divine things is had through a mirror and in an enigma. Next, Aristotle asserts that this faculty observes the occasions of things. This must also be observed in the business of piety. Paul circumcised Timothy but was unwilling to circumcise Titus, since the occasion in each case was far different. The same Apostle, given an occasion, began to preach to the Athenians about the unknown God, for he had seen the altar inscribed to them. Moderation must be applied in actions in order to acquire the virtues. It is also said in the Epistle to the Romans: not to be wiser than one ought to be. And a royal road is set before us, from which it is not lawful to turn aside either to the right or to the left. But this mean cannot be judged except by the testimony of the Spirit and the divine writings. Moreover, we taught at length above that virtues are not always acquired by frequent right actions, but are sometimes inspired by God.
CHAPTER III

units.la: SIgnū uero oportet obseruari habituum, uoluptatem & dolore, si ad actiones accesserint. Nā qui à corporeis uoluptatib. abstinet, & hoc ipso gaudet, est temperās: qui uero grauiter id fert, intemperans. Et qui res graues perfert ac gaudet, uel non dolet, fortis est: Qui uero dolorem capit, est timidus.
