units.tr: We must also observe the signs of habits in pleasure and pain, when these accompany actions. He who abstains from bodily pleasures and rejoices in that very abstinence is temperate; but he who bears it with grief is intemperate. And he who endures grievous things and rejoices, or does not grieve, is brave; but he who feels pain is timid.

units.la: Nisto[?] cap. principia moralis virtutis indicata sunt, frequentes actiones mediocres, quae neq; defectu neq; excessu laborent. Ideo posset quispiam rogare, quot nam eae actiones mediocres requirantur ad virtutem comparandam? Ad quam interrogationem haud numerus certus definitusq; reddi potest, ob ingeniorum varietatem. Nam sunt nonnulli duriores, quibus longa exercitatione opus est, priusquam virtute formentur: alij vero sunt faciles. Ideo praeter-missa numeri alicuius assignatione, iudicium profert quo possit quisq; nosse an virtute adhuc sit praeditus, an vero illa careat. Signumq; à voluptate atque dolore assumit: in secunda capitis parte occasione allati signi, Moralem virtutem circa voluptatem & molestiam esse docet, atq; suam hanc propositionem multis rationibus confirmat. Hac huius capitis est summa.
units.tr: In the previous chapter the principles of moral virtue were indicated: frequent intermediate actions, which suffer neither defect nor excess. So someone might ask how many such intermediate actions are required to acquire a virtue. To this question no certain and definite number can be given, because of the variety of natures. For some people are harder and need long exercise before they are formed in virtue, while others are easy. So, passing over any fixed number, he gives a judgement by which anyone may know whether he is already endowed with virtue or lacks it. He takes his sign from pleasure and pain. In the second part of the chapter, using the sign offered, he teaches that moral virtue concerns pleasure and annoyance, and he confirms this proposition with many reasons. This is the summary of the chapter.

units.la: Quod ad priorem partem, doctrina quae monstratur ex effectu est & à posteriori, ut Dialectici aiunt. Non enim ostenduntur causae acquisitionis vir-tutum: nam de iis iam satis est dictum: sed signum producitur. Quando cum voluptate quis recte agit, virtute iam est praeditus: sin vero doleat, adhuc virtutem non est assequutus. Exemplis rem declarat fortitudinis atq; tem-perantia. Vbi animaduertendum illum qui abstinet à corporeis voluptatibus, & agre fert, intemperantem dici. Quod non proprie accipi potest: nam qui recte facit cum molestia & dolore proprie appellandus est continens. Quia intemperans proprie is est qui non recte agit, & iudicat bonum esse i-ta agere, nam iudicium corruptum habet, incontinens autem male quidem agit, sed pungitur, reclamat, luctatur, sed in lucta succumbit. Accipit ergo Aristoteles hic ἀκόλασον[?], pro eo qui caret temperantia. Neque sem-per timidus est, qui dolet in rebus grauibus & duris: fieri enim potest ut labatur, non tamen adhuc vitij habitum contraxerit. De corporeis voluptatibus nominatim loquitur, quoniam alia quaedam ad mentem & voluntatem sunt pertinentes, à quibus non est abstinendum: neq; hoc illarum genus ad temperantiam attinet. Neq; significatione vacat, quod fortem inquit in rebus duris & asperis gaudere, vel non dolore. Quia saepe dum mortem aliqui oppetunt pro patria, vel ob aliquam aliam causam, vi cruciatus impediuntur ne gaudiū queant præse ferre, sed tamen haud sunt tristes non turpiter dolent, neq; muliebres lamentationes edunt: obfuscatur quidem nonnihil animi gaudium, ob externam afflictionem, haud tamen cedit animus dolori. Et credendus est Aristoteles hoc dicere, quasi consulat affectui non indulgendum, nam, qui fortis est, in medio cruciatu licet gaudium præse ferre non queat, non tamen dolet.
units.tr: As for the first part, the teaching is shown from its effect and from what comes after, as the dialecticians say. For the causes of acquiring virtues are not shown, since that has already been sufficiently discussed; rather a sign is produced. When someone acts rightly with pleasure, he is already endowed with virtue; but if he grieves, he has not yet attained virtue. He illustrates the matter with examples of courage and temperance. Here it should be noted that he who abstains from bodily pleasures but bears it with difficulty is called intemperate. This cannot be taken strictly, for he who acts rightly with discomfort and grief should properly be called continent. The intemperate, properly speaking, is one who does not act rightly and judges it good to act so, for he has a corrupt judgement; the incontinent, however, acts badly but is pricked, protests, struggles, and yet succumbs in the struggle. Aristotle therefore here takes [ἀκόλαστον] for one who lacks temperance. Nor is he always timid who grieves in grave and hard matters: for it can happen that he wavers, yet he has not yet contracted a habit of vice. He speaks specifically of bodily pleasures, because certain other pleasures pertain to the mind and will, and from these we must not abstain; nor does this kind of pleasure belong to temperance. Nor is his phrase idle, when he says that the brave man rejoices in hard and harsh matters, or at least does not grieve. For often, when some men face death for their country or for some other cause, they are prevented by the force of torment from being able to show their joy; yet they are not sad, they do not grieve basely, nor do they utter womanish lamentations. Indeed, their joy is somewhat dimmed by external affliction, yet the mind does not yield to pain. And Aristotle is to be believed to say this as one who counsels that the emotion should not be indulged: for the brave man, though in the midst of torment he may be unable to display joy, nevertheless does not grieve.

units.la: Circa voluptates autem & molestias moralis virtus.
units.tr: Moral virtue, however, is concerned with pleasures and pains.

units.la: Quomodo circa eam versatur? An tractat voluptatem ut propriam suam amq; materiam? Non videtur. Nam partim ut comitem sui subiecti, vel ut suam causam & quibusdam aliis modis, qui rationibus patefiant modo asse-rēdis. Quid sit voluptas & quid sit dolor, aliàs diximus & satis fusè, neque hoc loco ea sunt repetenda.
units.tr: How is it concerned with them? Does it treat pleasure as its own proper matter? It seems not. For it deals with it partly as the companion of its subject, or as its cause, and in certain other ways which become clear through reasons, which we need only assert. What pleasure and pain are we have said elsewhere, and at sufficient length; they need not be repeated here.

units.la: Nam voluptatis causa flagitia committimus, & propter dolorem ab honestis rebus abstinemus.
units.tr: For we commit disgraceful deeds for the sake of pleasure, and abstain from honourable things because of pain.

units.la: Prima hæc ratio à causa finali deducitur. Circa illa debet versari quaelibet facultas, à quibus fit & corrumpitur. Sed corrumpitur virtus à voluptate in genere causa finalis. Turpia enim homines agunt, & à virtute desistunt voluptatis causa: perduntur etiam à dolore, quoniam permulti desistunt à rectè agendo, ut molestias & dolores euitent. Quamobrem uterq; affectus ad virtutes morales attinet. Sed in hac ratione spectandum est, duo genera voluptatum constituenda. Quaedam enim male sunt & crassa, ac propter eas turpia committimus. Alia verò bona sunt & honesta, quae ad vitia homines non alliciunt. Et dolores etiam nonnulli sunt boni, propter quos homines ad rectè agendum permouentur, ut sunt poenae, de quib. paulo post sumus dicturi. Sed Aristotelis ratio non est naturalis, imò potius dialectica, quae in utramq; partem potest habere locum, præsertim quoad propositiones de incitando ad vitia vel revocando à virtutibus.
units.tr: This first reason is drawn from the final cause. Any faculty must be concerned with those things by which it is produced and corrupted. But virtue is corrupted by pleasure, as a final cause in general. For men do base things and desist from virtue for the sake of pleasure; they are also ruined by pain, since very many desist from right action in order to avoid discomforts and pains. Wherefore both affections belong to the moral virtues. But in this reasoning we must observe that two kinds of pleasure must be distinguished. For some are bad and gross, and it is on account of these that we commit base deeds. Others, however, are good and honourable, and these do not entice men to vice. Some pains too are good, on account of which men are moved to act rightly, such as punishments, of which we shall speak a little later. But Aristotle's reasoning is not natural; it is rather dialectical, which can have place on either side, especially with regard to propositions about enticing to vice or recalling from virtues.

units.la: Quapropter omnes iam inde à pueris, ut ait Plato, sic educatos esse par est, ut quibus debent rebus & gaudeant & doleant. Hæc enim recta disciplina.
units.tr: Therefore, as Plato says, all men from boyhood ought to be so brought up that they rejoice and grieve in the things they should. For this is right discipline.

units.la: Locus iste 4.de Legibus habetur, ubi nō tantum hoc scribit, verum addit, si nonfuerint iuuenes à teneris bene educati, non posse in bonos viros euadere. Deinde ab eodem 1.de Repub. scribitur, legislatores maximè debere ad voluptates atq; dolores aspicere, quòd sint duo fontes, à quibus homines cùm hauriunt quemadmodum oportet, in se omnia quodammodo bona deriuant: at si hauriant secus quàm deceat, implentur malis.
units.tr: This passage is found in Plato's fourth book of the Laws, where he writes not only this but adds that if young people have not been well brought up from tender years, they cannot turn out to be good men. Again, in the first book of the Republic, it is written that lawgivers ought chiefly to look to pleasures and pains, because they are two sources, from which men, when they draw as they ought, derive in some sense all good things into themselves; but if they draw otherwise than is fitting, they are filled with evils.

units.la: Præterea si uirtutes circa actiones & affectus uer-fantur, omnemq; affectum & omnem actionem vo-luptas & dolor comitatur, ob id etiam uirtus circa dolores & uoluptates erit.
units.tr: Moreover, if the virtues are concerned with actions and affections, and pleasure and pain accompany every affection and every action, then virtue will also be concerned with pains and pleasures.

units.la: Quæ modo ratio additur, à consequentibus deriuatur. Nam primùm accipit quod est indubitatum, virtutes in affectibus & actionibus versari. Deinde subdit ad hæc perpetuò sequi voluptates & dolores. Vnde confici-tur, virtutes morales etiam de ijs agere. Quando ait omnes actiones & affectus comites habere adiunctos dolores & voluptates: non accipit volu-ptates priuatim pro crassioribus atq; corporeis. Nam illæ non comitantur omnes actiones, neq; se ad omnes affectus adiungunt.
units.tr: This reason which has just been added is derived from consequences. For first it takes what is undoubted, that the virtues are concerned with affections and actions. Then it adds that pleasures and pains always follow these. Hence it is concluded that the moral virtues also deal with these. When he says that all actions and affections have pains and pleasures attached as companions, he does not take pleasures in a private sense as the grosser and bodily ones. For these do not accompany all actions, nor attach themselves to all affections.

units.la: Ostendunt id animaduersiones quæ per ista fiùt. Sunt enim medicinæ quædam. Solent autem medi-cinæ fieri ex contrarijs.
units.tr: This is shown by the corrections that are made through these. For there are certain remedies, and remedies are usually made from contraries.

units.la: Demonstrat aliter eandem propositionem. Ideo virtutes esse circa volu-ptates & dolores, quoniam doloribus reprimant vitia. Ergo de his agit quibus vtitur ad vitiorum correctionem. Quod verò pœnis à virtutibus corri-gantur peccata, confirmat à simili, Quoniam se habet virtus ad animum, vt medicina erga corpus. Et medicinæ constant rebus contrarijs. Ratio su-mitur à proprietate virtutum moralium, quæ est mederi vitiosis affectibus & actionibus. Medicatio verò contrarijs fit, nimirum pœnis: nam homines peccant voluptatem sectando magis quàm conueniat, ideò contrario re-primuntur, id est dolore. Nemo autem ignorat contrariorum eandem esse facultatem. Quare medicina constent rebus contrarijs, ratio in promptu est, Quia morbus fit ex declinatione à mediocritate in alterum extremorum, sed ab illo extremo, unde fit morbus, non reuocatur corpus nisi per alterum contrarium. Virtutes tamen cùm ab hominibus non separentur, cùm vitia dicuntur corrigere, non sic res accipi debet quasi actio virtutibus ipsis tribuatur, sed hominibus qui ex virtute illam habent facultatem vt vitia emē-dent. Interdum hoc officium quisq; praestat sibi ipsi. Nam cùm intempera-tus efficitur temperatus, castigat seipsum, & reprehendit quae male à se ce-mittuntur, aut olim commissa fuerunt. Aliquando munus illud praestant paedagogi, amici & parentes, qui reprehendunt in discipulis, in amicis, & in filijs quae videntur à recto aberrasse. Postremo in id magistratus incum-bit, qui disciplina ciuili variis poenis afficit peccantes. Poena vero graviores aut leniores adhibenda sunt pro peccantium ingenio, & peccatorum pondere. Nonnullos obiurgatione seu reprehensione leui satis est perstringere. Alios oportet externis bonis multare, pecunia, patria & consimilibus. Tertiò eò venitur vt corpore luant, quod turpiter & praue commiserunt.
units.tr: He demonstrates the same proposition in another way: the virtues are concerned with pleasures and pains, because by pains they restrain vices. Therefore they deal with those things which they use for the correction of vices. That sins are corrected by punishments through the virtues he confirms by a comparison: the virtue stands to the soul as medicine does to the body, and medicines consist of contrary things. The reasoning is taken from the property of the moral virtues, which is to heal vicious affections and actions. Healing, however, is effected by contraries, namely by punishments: for men sin by pursuing pleasure more than is fitting, so they are restrained by the contrary, that is, by pain. No one, moreover, is ignorant that contraries have the same power. Why medicines consist of contraries is readily explained: disease arises from a departure from the mean into one of the extremes, but the body is not brought back from that extreme where the disease arose except by the opposite extreme. Yet since virtues are not separated from men, when they are said to correct vices, the matter must not be understood as if the action were attributed to the virtues themselves, but to men who have from virtue that capacity to amend their vices. Sometimes a person performs this office for himself: when the intemperate becomes temperate, he chastises himself and reproves what he has committed wrongly, or what was done in the past. At other times tutors, friends and parents perform that duty, who rebuke in their pupils, friends and sons whatever seems to have strayed from the right. Lastly, the magistrate is charged with this, who by civil discipline punishes offenders with various penalties. Penalties, however, must be applied more severely or more leniently according to the disposition of the offenders and the weight of their offences. For some it is enough to rebuke them with a light reproof. Others must be punished with external goods: money, country and the like. In the third place, we come to the point where they must atone with their body for what they have shamefully and wickedly done.

units.la: Praeterea uti prius diximus, omnis habitus ani-mi ad ea spectat, & circa ea suapte vi & natura se ha-bet, à quibus deterior aut melior fieri consuevit. Vo-luptatibus autem & doloribus pravi fiunt, quod has persequantur & illas fugiant, aut quas nō licet, aut quando & quomodo fas non est, aut quot aliis modis haec negocia à ratione praescribuntur.
units.tr: Moreover, as we said before, every habit of the mind is directed toward those things, and is by its own power and nature related to them, by which it is usually made worse or better. Men become depraved by pleasures and pains because they pursue some and flee others, either those they ought not to have, or at the wrong time or in the wrong way, or in any of the other ways in which reason prescribes these matters.

units.la: Haec ratio ita extruitur: Quilibet animi habitus circa illa versatur, ex quibus vel melior vel deterior efficitur. Virtutes sunt habitus animi. Ergo circa ea versantur unde vel meliores vel deteriores fiunt. Illa vero, vt iam est dictum, sunt voluptates & dolores. Id fuit dictum prius in prima omnium iam adductarum rationum. Innititurq; praesens argumentum à causa, sed videtur attingi efficiens, cum antea spectare viderentur ad causam finalem. Erga ea & circa ea dixit, non ociosè, nam Erga relationem denotat, & relativa sunt πρός τι [?]. Circa indicat quodammodo materiam. Cur autem habitus deteriores fiant voluptatibus & doloribus, ostedit memorando πεϱισάσεις: qua si praetermittantur, actionem vitiosam reddunt, eaq; vitiata citra controuersiam habitus læditur. Accidit, inquit, vitium persequendo & fugiendo: persequendo inquam voluptates, fugiendo molestias, non habita circumstantiarum vlla ratione.
units.tr: The argument is built thus: every habit of the mind is concerned with those things by which it is made either better or worse. Virtues are habits of the mind. Therefore they are concerned with those things by which they become either better or worse. These, as has now been said, are pleasures and pains. This was said earlier, in the first of all the arguments already adduced. The present argument rests on the cause, but it seems to touch on the efficient cause, whereas before they seemed to look to the final cause. Towards them and concerning them he said not idly, for towards denotes a relation, and relatives are πρός τι [?]. Concerning indicates in a way the matter. Why habits become worse through pleasures and pains he shows by mentioning circumstances [περιστάσεις]: if these are left out, they make the action vicious, and when the action is vitiated, beyond controversy the habit is harmed. It happens, he says, that vice arises by pursuing and fleeing: by pursuing, I say, pleasures; by fleeing, discomforts, with no account taken of any circumstances.

units.la: Vnde uoluptates definiunt uacuitates quasdam affectuum et tranquillitates, non recte quidem: nam simpliciter dicunt, non autem quemadmodum oportet, at sicut non oportet, & quando & alia quaecunq; adiiciuntur.
units.tr: Hence some define pleasures as certain freedoms from the emotions and as tranquillities, not correctly. For they speak simply, not as one ought, but as one ought not, and without the addition of when and the other qualifications.

units.la: Confirmat virtutes, ut dixerat, deteriores ijs affectibus fieri, quod aliqui definierint illas esse ἀπαθείας, vacuitates quasdam affectuum. Nam si aliqui superstint affectus, ut ij homines arbitrabantur, fuissent animi perturbati. Virtutes aut iudicabant quasdam esse tranquillitates. Qui sic excluserunt affectus erant Stoici: at de illis modo non intelligit Aristoteles, quoniam illi post eum floruerunt. Sed iam illius tempore clari erant nonnulli, quorum etiam Cicero meminit De finibus, qui sic opinabantur. Non recte illos fecisse dicit Aristoteles, quia simpliciter auferebant affectus, cum potius debuissent secundum quid eos tollere, nimirum quo ad illorum summum & intensum gradum.
units.tr: He confirms that virtues, as he had said, are made worse by those feelings, since some have defined them as apatheiai [ἀπαθείας], certain vacuities of the emotions. For if some feelings remained, as those men thought, the minds would have been disturbed. Others judged that virtues are certain tranquillities. Those who excluded the feelings in this way were the Stoics; but Aristotle does not mean them here, since they flourished after him. Yet already in his time there were some famous men, of whom Cicero too makes mention in De finibus, who held this opinion. Aristotle says they did not rightly do so, because they simply removed the feelings, whereas they ought rather to have removed them in some respect, namely as to their highest and most intense degree.

units.la: Ponitur itaq; uirtus ea quae uoluptatibus & doloribus sit effectrix pulcherrimarum rerum. Vitium uero contra.
units.tr: Virtue is therefore posited as that which produces the most beautiful things through pleasures and pains. Vice is the contrary.

units.la: Iam allatis rationibus hoc ponendum statuendumq; ait, virtutem circa voluptates & vitia effectricem esse rerum pulcherrimarum. Sed priusquam hinc discedamus, videndum est quid istos permouerit, qui a virtute prorsus excindi affectus voluerunt. Putabant ij virtutem perfectam, appetitu superare, perfectiorem adhuc illum magis vincere, perfectissimam vero omnino ita vt illi non amplius relinqueretur locus. Putarunt q; virtute contrariā esse affectui. Omnes aut scimus ea esse contrariorum natura, vt cum alterum summum fuerit, alterum secum non patiatur in eodem subiecto, idcò concludebant virtutem perfectissimam in homine in quo esset, affectui ut- pote contrario suo locum non relinquere. Atq; semper cogitabant secum asse- ctus impedimenta quaedam esse virtutum, & idcirco perfectissimam virtu- tem reperiri non posse, nisi omnia impedimenta sublata penitus fuerint. Po- stremo, illud proprium virtutis esse accipiunt, ut animum repurget: nil au- tem videtur in eo repurgandum esse, nisi prauos affectus: quare nulla vir- tus perfectissima erit, ut ex cuius actione felicitas oriatur, nisi omnem asse-ctum extruserit ex animo, illumq; absolutissime repurgauerit. Haec sunt quibus isti sunt adducti, ut sic definirent virtutes. In qua forma definien- di omnino hallucinati sunt. Debet enim definitio adhiberi, quae omnibus definiti partibus conueniat. Verum multae sunt virtutes quae circa affectus non versantur, neq; quicquam habent cum illis quod agant: Nam totae sunt in actionibus, ut iustitia, magnanimitas, liberalitas, & aliae huius generis, quae cum affectibus non luctantur. Quamobrem definitio ista si danda es- set, non ut universalis, verum ut particularis reciperetur. Quod in defini- endo quam sit graue vitium, quiuis per seipsum intelligit. Deinde, si verum est quod omnes propemodum concedunt, virtutes esse affectuum moderatrices, ab illis ut a suis correlatiuis nequeunt avelli & separari. Neq; verum est virtutes oppositionem contrariam ad affectus habere: non enim cum af- fectu pugnant, sed cum eius extremis. Unde potius dicendi sunt affectus fra- gi seu mitigari a virtutibus, quam tolli. Et mirifice quadrat loquutio scri- pturarum diuinarum, ut dicantur non occidi, sed potius mortificari. Quiq;
units.tr: Now that the arguments have been brought forward, he says this must be laid down and established: that virtue, concerning pleasures and pains, produces the most beautiful things. But before we leave this point, we must see what moved those who wished the feelings to be utterly cut off from virtue. They thought that perfect virtue surpasses appetite, that more perfect virtue conquers it still more, and that most perfect virtue does so entirely, so that no place is left for it. They also thought that virtue is contrary to the feeling. We all know that contraries are of such a nature that when one is at its highest, the other does not suffer itself to be in the same subject; so they concluded that in a man in whom the most perfect virtue is present, it leaves no place for the feeling, as being its contrary. And they always reasoned to themselves that the feelings are certain impediments to the virtues, and therefore the most perfect virtue cannot be found unless all impediments have been wholly removed. Lastly, they take it as the proper function of virtue to purge the mind; yet nothing seems to need purging in it except depraved feelings. Therefore no virtue will be most perfect, from whose action happiness arises, unless it has thrust every feeling out of the mind and purged it most thoroughly. These are the reasons that led them to define the virtues in this way. In this form of definition they were utterly mistaken. For a definition ought to fit all the parts of what is defined. But many virtues are not concerned with the feelings and have nothing to do with them, for they lie wholly in actions, like justice, magnanimity, liberality, and others of this kind, which do not struggle with the feelings. Wherefore, if that definition were to be given, it should be accepted not as universal but as particular. How grave a fault this is in defining, anyone understands for himself. Next, if it is true, as almost everyone concedes, that virtues moderate the feelings, they cannot be torn away and separated from them, as from their correlatives. Nor is it true that virtues stand in contrary opposition to the feelings: for they do not fight with the feeling itself but with its extremes. Hence the feelings should rather be said to be broken or softened by the virtues than destroyed. And the manner of speaking in the divine Scriptures fits remarkably, that they are said not to be killed but rather mortified. And those

units.la: praediti sunt virtute non se patiuntur ab affectibus impelli, ut quippiam aduersus rationem faciant: & ea est vis praeclarissima virtutis, ut non si- nat homines affectibus duci. Ac fieri fortasse potest, ut sicuti passim aliqui reperiuntur, qui more belluino degunt, totiq; sequuntur affectus, nullum rationi dantes locum, ita vicissim aliqui sint, qui spretis affectuum stimulis & illecebris, ex ratione prorsus virtutibusq; viuant. Repurgant igitur vir- tutes animos non ab affectibus quibusuis sed ab extremis. Neq; impedian- tur, nisi a defectu & ab excessu.
units.tr: endowed with virtue do not allow themselves to be driven by the feelings to do anything against reason; and this is the most splendid power of virtue, that it does not allow men to be led by the feelings. It may perhaps happen that, just as there are everywhere some who live in a brutish manner, wholly following their feelings and giving no place to reason, so conversely there are some who, despising the goads and enticements of the feelings, live entirely by reason and the virtues. Virtues therefore purge minds not of any feelings whatever, but of the extremes. Nor are they hindered except by defect and by excess.

units.la: Et de ijsdem potest nobis dilucidum fieri ex his. Cum tria sint quae ad expetitiones, & totidem quae ad evitationem spectent, honestum inquam utile & iucundum, & e[?] diverso turpe, inutile ac molestum, & in ijs omnibus vir bonus rectus est, malus autem pravus, tum maxime in voluptate. Communis enim ea est animantibus, & ijs omnibus quae comitantur electionem. Etenim quod est honestum & utile, jucundum esse videtur.
units.tr: These same things can also be made clear to us from what follows. Since there are three things that look to pursuit, and as many that look to avoidance (the honourable, I mean, the useful and the pleasant, and on the contrary the base, the useless and the painful), and in all these the good man is right while the bad man is depraved, the case is especially so with pleasure. For it is common to animals, and to all the things that accompany choice. For what is honourable and useful also seems to be pleasant.

units.la: Ratio ista videtur à communiori bonitate & quae latius pateat deduci, ac si dicatur, Virtus moralis circa bonum quod generalius est atq; commu-nium versatur. Jucundum bonum est communius: Ergo, circa illud est mora-lis virtus. Minor probatur: Primò, quia cùm sint tria bona expetenda, ho-nestum, utile, ac jucundum: Et mala è diverso tria sint fugienda, turpe, in-utile, & molestum: Ex illis tribus bonis, jucundum omnibus animantibus est commune. Nam non omnia quaerunt animalia quod honestum est & u-tile, sed jucunda spectant, & illa sectantur. Deinde, jucundum comitatur semper electionem. Quicquid enim homines electione sua expetunt, jucundum est: nam quicquid est honestum ac utile, jucundū[?] est. Non tamē propositio recurrit: multa enim sunt jucunda, aliena nihilominus ab utilitate & hone-state. Notandum tamen honestum, utile, atq; jucundum saepius in eandem rem incidere, cùm rationes eorum nihilominus diversa sint: id enim est ho-nestum quod rationi consentit, utile quod alterius causa expetitur, jucun-dum vero quod allubescit.
units.tr: This argument seems to be drawn from the more common good, which extends more widely, as if one were to say: moral virtue is concerned with the good that is more general and common. The pleasant is the more common good; therefore moral virtue is concerned with it. The minor premise is proved thus. First, since there are three goods to be pursued, the honourable, the useful and the pleasant, and on the contrary three evils to be fled, the base, the useless and the painful, of those three goods the pleasant is common to all animals. For not all animals seek what is honourable and useful, but look to pleasant things and pursue those. Next, the pleasant always accompanies choice. For whatever men desire by their choice is pleasant, since whatever is honourable and useful is also pleasant. Yet the proposition does not convert: for many things are pleasant that are nonetheless foreign to usefulness and honesty. It should be noted, however, that the honourable, the useful and the pleasant often fall upon the same thing, although their definitions are nonetheless different: for that is honourable which agrees with reason, useful that which is desired for the sake of something else, and pleasant that which delights.

units.la: Præterea jam inde à puero nobis omnibus coalu-it: unde difficile est hanc affectionem vitę illitam ex-trudere.
units.tr: Moreover, from boyhood this affection has grown into all of us, so that it is difficult to drive out this feeling which has been smeared into our life.

units.la: A tempore idem concludit, Nobiscum nutrita est à pueris ac simul educa-ta voluptas. Igitur, circa eam laborandum est ut corrigatur, & ne modum excedat: quod proprie munus est moralis virtutis. Omnibus sanè periculis occurrendum est, sed ijs præsertim in quibus perpetuò versamur.
units.tr: From time he draws the same conclusion: pleasure has been nurtured with us and brought up alongside us from boyhood. Therefore we must labour to correct it, and see that it does not exceed its measure, which is properly the office of moral virtue. Certainly all dangers must be met, but especially those in which we are constantly engaged.

units.la: Dolore atq; molestia alij quidem minus, alij ve-rò magis actiones metimur, & idcirco necesse est hanc facultatem circa res huiusmodi esse.
units.tr: Some of us measure our actions by pain and discomfort more than others do, and so this faculty must be concerned with such things.

units.la: Confirmat idem ex ipsius voluptatis dolorisq; conditione. Quod illis u-tamur ut regula quadā in aggrediendis actionibus: cogitamus enim sem-per nobiscū, quidnā molestia, quidue[?] voluptatis actio quā incœptamus secum habeat. Quod tamen fatetur aliquos magis, aliquos minus facere: non enim omnes homines ex æquo ijs mouentur affectibus. Videmus itaq; non parum momenti habere ad actiones, aut bene aut male gaudere siue dolere. Si enim ista ut regulæ quædam earum adhibentur, magnum ad ipsas momentum habent.
units.tr: He confirms the same from the very nature of pleasure and pain: we use them as a kind of rule in undertaking actions. For we always consider with ourselves what discomfort or what pleasure the action we are beginning will bring. He admits, however, that some people do this more and some less, since not all men are moved by these feelings equally. So we see that it matters a good deal to actions whether we rejoice or grieve well or badly. For if these feelings are used as rules for them, they have great weight in the actions themselves.

units.la: Præterea difficilius est cum voluptate quàm cum ira pugnare, quemadmodum inquit Heraclitus. Circa id autem quod est difficilius, & ars & virtus perpetuo versatur. Quod enim recte est, in eo melius se habet. Vnde omnis huiusmodi facultas hac de causa circa voluptates & molestias est, atque hoc tã quo ad moralem quàm quo ad civilem virtutem. Quicunque enim ijs recte utitur, probus est: qui autem male, prauus.
units.tr: Moreover, it is harder to struggle against pleasure than against anger, as Heraclitus says. Yet art and virtue are always concerned with what is more difficult, for what is right is better when it is done in that case. Hence every such faculty is concerned with pleasures and pains for this reason, and this holds as much for moral virtue as for civil virtue. For whoever uses them rightly is upright, but whoever uses them badly is wicked.

units.la: Circa difficiliora versatur moralis virtus. Resistere voluptati est admodum difficile. Igitur, circa voluptatem moralis virtus versabitur. Maior propositio patet à simili. Nam & ars circa id quod est difficilius tota videtur esse: in communibus enim & vulgaribus rebus, non solemus artificium admirari, sed in arduis & difficilioribus. Quicquid recte agitur, quando in re difficili est, maximè commendatur. Minor authoritate Heraclitii confirmatur: is enim dixit multò difficilius esse luctari cum voluptate, quàm cum iracundia. Quod non sic intelligendum est, quasi non habeat ira suos impetus & quidè vehementes, quemadmodum voluptas, sed voluptas præter impetus, quos & ipsa suos habet, licet remissiores, à multò pluribus partibus nobis insidiatur. A tactu enim, à gustu, olfactu, cæterisq; sensibus inuadit, & habet permultas occasiones, nosq; latenter & blandè ad se allicit. Deinde perpetuo nos aggreditur. Quod nõ facit iracundia: nisi enim afficiamur iniuria seu contumelia, nosq; videamus contemni, non irascimur.
units.tr: Moral virtue is concerned with what is more difficult. To resist pleasure is very difficult. Therefore moral virtue will be concerned with pleasure. The major premise is clear from a parallel. For art too seems wholly concerned with what is more difficult: we do not usually admire skill in common and ordinary things, but in hard and more difficult ones. Whatever is done rightly, when the matter is difficult, is most commended. The minor premise is confirmed by the authority of Heraclitus, for he said that it is far harder to wrestle with pleasure than with anger. This should not be understood as though anger does not have its own impulses, and quite strong ones, as pleasure does; but pleasure, besides its impulses, which it also has though they are milder, lies in wait for us from far more parts. For it assails us through touch, taste, smell and the other senses, has very many opportunities, and draws us to itself secretly and enticingly. Then too it attacks us continually. Anger does not do this: unless we are hurt by an injury or insult, and see ourselves held in contempt, we do not get angry.

units.la: Quod itaque circa voluptates & molestias fit uir-tus, dictum esto, & alijs augeri atque corrumpi ex quibus producitur, cum non eodem modo fiunt, & circa illa operari ex quibus fit.
units.tr: What virtue is in regard to pleasures and pains has been said. It is increased and destroyed by the same things from which it is produced, since these are not made in the same way, and it works about the things from which it is made.

units.la: In calce capitis epilogo satis lucido & aperto utitur, quo comprehendit summam eorum quae sunt dicta.
units.tr: At the end of the chapter he uses a summary, quite clear and open, in which he sums up the things that have been said.

units.la: SED quia de voluptate atq; dolore multa sunt allata, conuenit vt non-nulla de affectuum natura interseramus, praesertim quia voluptas & dolor inter omnes affectus praecipuum locum habent. Affectus vis quaedam est seu facultas, qua propositá nobis obiecta vel persequimur vel fugimus. Atq; in animantibus quae sunt animantes & sentiunt, cognitionem sequitur:& alij quidem affectus contactum sequuntur, alij vero cogitationem vel opinionem comitantur. Qui sequuntur contactum, statim vt sensus incidit in obiectum congruum vel incommodum, aut persequuntur aut fugiunt. Est enim voluptas, quando inter se congruunt sensus & obiectum: cum vero secus, dolor habetur. Dumq; nervi laeduntur, magnus oritur cruciatus, qui sane non est opinio vel cogitatio, vt permulti stulte finxerunt. Nam citra cogitationem vel opinionem corpus ipsum male afficitur, neq; in nostra opinione vel imaginatione situm est, vt obiecta huiusmodi commutemus. Nam quae sunt dolorifica, semper nervos ad sensum pertinentes male afficient atq; corpus vexabunt, & vicissim quae natura sua iucunda sunt semper delectabunt, modo ex aliqua prava qualitate corpus non sit male affectum. Qui vero affectus tactum non sequuntur, ex cogitatione vel imagina-tione ortum habent, & excitantur, licet obiectum extremum non adsit praesens. Et sunt motus cordis, quibus persequimur vel fugimus obiecta, prout vere aut falso cogitatio illa vel commoda vel incommoda ostendit. Vocantur ý affectus πάθη[?]. Non itaque sunt cogitationes, verum ex illis oriuntur.
units.tr: BUT since much has been said about pleasure and pain, it is fitting to insert some remarks on the nature of the affections, especially because pleasure and pain hold the chief place among all the affections. An affection is a certain power or faculty by which we pursue or flee from objects set before us. In animals, which are living and have sensation, cognition follows. Some affections follow contact, while others accompany thought or opinion. Those that follow contact, as soon as the sense meets an agreeable or disagreeable object, either pursue it or flee from it. There is pleasure when the sense and the object agree with each other; when it is otherwise, we have pain. And when the nerves are injured, a sharp torment arises, which is certainly not an opinion or thought, as many have foolishly imagined. For without any thought or opinion the body itself is badly affected, and it does not lie in our opinion or imagination whether we change objects of this kind. Things that cause pain will always afflict the nerves that serve sensation and torment the body, and conversely, things that are pleasant by their nature will always delight us, provided the body is not badly disposed by some bad quality. Those affections which do not follow touch arise from thought or imagination and are stirred up even when the extreme object is not present. These are movements of the heart by which we pursue or flee from objects, according as that thought shows them to be truly or falsely advantageous or harmful. They are called passions [πάθη]. Therefore they are not thoughts, but arise from them.

units.la: Sunt vero ý multiplices[?]: aliqui enim sunt simplices, alij compositi. Sim-plices numerantur quatuor, Laetitia, Tristitia, Spes & Metus. Nam obiectu[?] quod offertur, aut bonum est aut malum. Et illud ostenditur a cogitatione vel vt praesens, vel vt mox venturum. Si bonum ostenditur praesens, oriturLaetitia, quae motus est cordis, quo se dilatat & extendit, amplectendo suaviter praesens bonum. Sin vero non adest bonum, sed expectatur, Spes na-scitur, motus cordis quo se dilatat, praeparatq; seipsum ad illud bonum amplectendum cum venerit. Malum vero praesens ostensum, a corde fugitur: nam Tristitia motus est cordis quo sese contrahit, vt malum praesenscuitet. Quod si ostendatur futurum malum, metuimus: & est is affectusmotus. motus cordis quo se contrahit, ne à malo venturo prematur. Ii sunt affectus simplices, dati animantibus ut non tantum ad salutem suam vtantur cognitione, sed si adiumentum illud esset debile, sint adiuncta huiusmodi calcaria quae nos incitent ad salutem & ab incommodis revocent. Sunt quasi venti quibus navis impellitur. In tertia specie qualitatis reponuntur. Et licet prima species & secunda valeant plurimum ad animantia gubernan-da & regenda, ÿ tamen sunt fortiores gubernatores, & maiori agunt impetu quam habitus, aut naturales potentiae. Verum sunt alij huius generis affectus, non simplices: nam componuntur ex pluribus, ut ira quae dolorem simul & laetitiam comprehendit: & alij eius consimiles.
units.tr: Affections are, however, many. Some are simple, others compound. Four simple ones are counted: joy, sorrow, hope and fear. For the object presented is either good or bad, and this is shown by thought either as present or as about to come. If a good is shown as present, joy arises, which is a movement of the heart by which it expands and extends itself, embracing the present good with delight. But if the good is not present and is awaited, hope is born, a movement of the heart by which it expands and prepares itself to embrace that good when it comes. A present evil shown is fled by the heart, for sorrow is a movement of the heart by which it contracts itself so as to avoid the present evil. If a future evil is shown, we fear; this affection is a movement of the heart by which it contracts, lest it be overwhelmed by the evil to come. These are the simple affections, given to animals so that they use cognition not only for their own safety, but, since that aid would be weak, these goads are added to urge them on to safety and to call them back from harms. They are like the winds by which a ship is driven. They are placed in the third species of quality. And although the first and second species are of the greatest use in guiding and governing animals, yet these are stronger governors and act with greater force than habits or natural powers. There are, however, other affections of this kind that are not simple: for they are compounded of several, as anger, which combines pain and joy at once, and others like it.

units.la: Modò superest ut videamus quae sint organa seu loca istorum affectuum. Plato iram in corde, cupiditatem & laetitiam in iecore posuit. At Aristoteli secus visum est, qui tam iram quam dolorem, laetitiam, & consimiles in corde collocauit, tametsi naturales affectus, nempe qui pertineant ad vim vegetantem in organis ei facultati propriis. Aristoteles etiam collocarit. Huiusmodi vero sunt, fames, sitis, & impetus ad liberos procreandos. Nec inficiaretur inter huiusmodi viscera iecur obtinere principatum, quia in eo prima est sanguinis officina, & is humor cùm alimonia est, tum seminis propria materia. Sed missis ijs naturalibus affectibus, qui notitiae non sunt coniuncti, de ijs agamus, qui adiunguntur aut sensuum apprehensioni aut co-gitationi. Et cum eos iuxta opinionem Aristotelis in corde constituamus, nostram hanc sententiam probemus argumentis. Certè sicubi collocanda sunt, aut in cerebro aut in corde aut in epate iderit faciundum. In cerebro non ponentur, quandoquidem ibi vigent actiones & facultates quae ijs affectibus aduersantur, nempe iudicium & ratio. Eadem vero facultas pugnantes actiones eodem tempore non producit. Actiones vero affectuum & iudicij seu rationis inter se pugnare, vel illa Medea testatur apud Ovidium, quae aiebat, Video meliora probóq, Deteriora sequor. Atq; ista eadem ratione apparet, affectus istos, ut putarunt Stoici, non esse cogitationes aut opiniones, cùm ista actiones in cerebro consistant. Proinde reliquum est si non sint in cerebro, ut vel in corde vel in epate ponantur. Non quidè epati queunt adscribi, quia illi affectus qui eò spectant, iudicio & ratione haud regi queant, ut fames, sitis, impetus ad procreationem. Potest quidem iudicium seu ratio imperare facultati moventi, ne cibum capiat, ne bibat, ne generet: at ne se prodat, ne incitet, perturbet ac exitimulet, non potest efficere. Illi vero affectus qui notitiam seu cognitione sequuntur, ratione ac iudicio cohibere queunt. Igitur nō sunt eiusdem rationis cum ijs qui ponūtur in epate: quare non ad illam corporis partem, sed ad cor attinebunt: Atq; cum ista sententia quae (ut putamus) Aristotelis est, divina litera faciunt, quae inquiunt, Diligas Dominum Deum tuum toto corde, tota anima & omnibus viribus, of-fensiones eius metuas.
units.tr: It remains only to see what are the organs or seats of these affections. Plato placed anger in the heart, and desire and joy in the liver. But Aristotle thought otherwise, and he located both anger and grief, joy and the like, in the heart, although natural affections, namely those that belong to the vegetative power, he placed in the organs proper to that faculty. Such are hunger, thirst and the impulse to beget children. Nor would he deny that among such viscera the liver holds the first place, because in it is the first workshop of the blood, and this humour is both nourishment and the proper matter of seed. But setting aside those natural affections that are not joined to knowledge, let us deal with those that are joined either to the apprehension of the senses or to thought. And since we place them in the heart, according to the opinion of Aristotle, let us prove this view of ours by arguments. Certainly, wherever they are to be placed, it must be either in the brain, or in the heart, or in the liver. They will not be placed in the brain, since there the actions and faculties that oppose those affections are at work, namely judgement and reason. The same faculty does not produce contrary actions at the same time. That the actions of the affections and of judgement or reason fight against one another, Medea bears witness in Ovid, who said: "I see the better and approve it, but I follow the worse." By the same reasoning it is clear that these affections are not thoughts or opinions, as the Stoics thought, since those are actions that consist in the brain. Therefore it remains that, if they are not in the brain, they are placed either in the heart or in the liver. They cannot be assigned to the liver, because those affections that look to it cannot be ruled by judgement and reason, such as hunger, thirst and the impulse to procreation. Judgement or reason can indeed command the moving faculty not to take food, not to drink, not to beget; but it cannot prevent it from betraying itself, from stirring, disturbing and rousing it. Those affections, however, which follow knowledge or cognition, can be restrained by reason and judgement. Therefore they are not of the same kind as those placed in the liver; so they belong not to that part of the body but to the heart. And we agree with this view, which (as we think) is Aristotle's, with the words of Scripture, which say: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your strength," and "fear to offend him."

units.la: Sed notandum famem, sitim, quandoque accipi pro ipso defectu quan-do sumus exhausti. At hoc modo a iudicio & ratione minime possunt regi, neq; inde ortum habent. Sed is dolor qui consequitur, ad cor attinet, quum prior exinanitio sit in organis quae vegetanti facultati serviunt. Quo ad af-sectus qui sensum tactus consequuntur, duo sunt consideranda[?]. Solutiones continui, dilacerationes & combustiones, illa fiunt in carnibus & nervis: dolores vero qui sequuntur, sunt motus cordis. Neque praetereundum, cor ipsum alios praeter affectus habere motus, nimirum pulsus: verum de illis in praesentia non agendum, ideo redeo ad affectus. Quos quum dixerimus cordis motus, eos non credendum est esse violentos, quum ex ipsa natura principium habeant: oriuntur enim a cordis viribus. Sciendum tamen hunc esse naturae cursum, ut quae vehementiora sunt, noceant, imo vitient et corrumpant. Ut si nimia sit lux, perdit oculos: nimius calor nimiumq; frigus animantia extinguunt: quae vero sunt moderata, prosunt & servant. Quod idem est de affectibus censendum. Vehemens dolor, timor aut laetitia sunt noxia: cum vero adhibetur modus, permultas utilitates habent & commoda.
units.tr: But it should be noted that hunger and thirst are sometimes taken for the very lack we feel when we are exhausted. In that sense they can by no means be governed by judgement and reason, nor do they arise from them. The pain that follows, however, belongs to the heart, since the prior emptying takes place in the organs that serve the vegetative faculty. As for the affections that follow the sense of touch, two things are to be considered. Solutions of continuity, lacerations and burnings take place in the flesh and sinews; the pains that follow them are motions of the heart. Nor should it be passed over that the heart itself has other motions besides the affections, namely its pulses; but these are not to be treated at present, so I return to the affections. Although we have called them motions of the heart, we must not think they are violent, since they have their principle in nature itself, for they arise from the powers of the heart. Yet it must be known that this is the course of nature: whatever is more vehement does harm, and indeed spoils and corrupts. If light is excessive, it destroys the eyes; excessive heat and excessive cold extinguish living things; but what is moderate benefits and preserves. The same must be judged of the affections. Vehement pain, fear or joy are harmful; but when moderation is applied, they bring very many uses and advantages.

units.la: Iam de causa formali est satis dictum: docuimus enim motus esse cordis, qui sequantur notitiam sensuum, aut cogitationem vel opinionem, qui tamen sint naturales, non violenti. Quid etiam de materia vel subiecto statuendum, ostendimus. Id modo superest, ut de efficiente causa dicamus. Illa vero est obiectum, quo sensus aut cogitatio movetur. Illud nempe bonum aut malum sive praesens sive futurum, quod se offert. Est etiam causa efficiens, vis cordis, quae illud statim movet ad persequendum vel ad fugiendum quod offertur. Verum inter obiectum & vim cordis excitatam media intercedit notitia: non enim ab obiecto vis cordis excitatur, nisi per cognitionem. Ilico enim ut obiecta vel per sensum vel per cogitationem sunt apprehensa, spiritus qui cognitioni serviunt, cor ipsum feriunt, excitaturq; vis cordis, unde vel ad fugam vel ad persequutionem movetur. Notandum tamen pro vario temperamento corporis, motum hunc cordis aut tardum aut celerem incitari: atque ob affectus in aliis sunt vehementiores, in aliis vero languidiores. Humores calidi & sicci facile ac vehementer excitant: qui vero sunt frigidi & humidi, sunt aliquanto tardiores a quibus est necesse ut affectus nonnihil remissi proficiscantur. Deinde pro affectuum natura seu conditione humores mouentur. In dolore seu timore atra bilis, in lætitia sanguis, in ira flaua bilis excitatur. Motus deinde sunt, aut contracti-onis, aut profusionis. Quando obiectum quod offertur bonum fuerit, effun-dit sese cor ad excipiendum: Sin vero malum fuerit, ad interiora se retra-hunt humores. Hinc pallores in facie, hinc rubores, prout sanguis ad interi-ora refugit, vel ad partes exteras sese effundit. Atq; tantum de causis eorum dictum esto.
units.tr: We have now said enough about the formal cause: we have shown that these are motions of the heart which follow the knowledge of the senses, or a thought or opinion, and which are nonetheless natural, not violent. We have also shown what must be decided about the matter or subject. It remains only to speak of the efficient cause. This is the object by which the sense or thought is moved, namely the good or evil, whether present or future, that presents itself. The efficient cause is also the power of the heart, which at once moves the heart to pursue or flee what is offered. Yet between the object and the excited power of the heart there intervenes knowledge; for the power of the heart is not aroused by the object except through cognition. As soon as objects are apprehended, either by sense or by thought, the spirits that serve cognition strike the heart itself, and the power of the heart is roused, whereby it is moved either to flight or to pursuit. It must be noted, however, that according to the varying temperament of the body this motion of the heart is stirred either slowly or quickly, and so in some people the affections are more vehement, in others more sluggish. Warm and dry humours excite easily and vehemently; but those that are cold and moist are somewhat slower, and from these the affections must arise somewhat more relaxed. Next, the humours are moved according to the nature or condition of the affections: in pain or fear black bile, in joy blood, in anger yellow bile is stirred up. The motions are then either of contraction or of effusion. When the object offered is good, the heart pours itself out to receive it; but if it is evil, the humours draw back inward. Hence pallor in the face, and hence redness, according as the blood flees inward or pours itself out to the outer parts. And let this be said enough about their causes.

units.la: Nunc duo videnda restant. Primùm, hos affectus non esse vel cogitatio-nes vel opiniones, ut Stoici senserunt. Deinde haud omnes ceu vitiosos & malos accusandos. Primùm demonstrari potest: facile in illis qui naturales vocantur, ut fames est & sitis, affectus ij absq; vlla cogitatione nos inuadunt. Quis etiam cogitationem dixerit aut opinionem, cùm affligimur solutione continui, neruorum dilaceratione, aut flammæ seu ignis combustione? Possunt & idem suadere σοφοὶ φυσικῶς[?] parentum in liberos, quæ non modo in hominibus, verù & in brutis acerrimæ sunt. Verù quia res clara est non multum in ea iudico immorandum. Quoad secundum igitur, nonnullos affectus vitium adiunctum habere non diffitebor. Sed permultos bonos ostendam, & illos qui mali sunt hominum culpa non sua natura malos esse. Potest primùm interponi error iudicij: non enim semper de obiectis, quæ sese offerunt, bene iudicamus. Quod malum est pro bono interdum accipitur, & quod est bonum existimatur malum. Comitantur autem affectus hæc animi iudicia, ut demonstrauimus. Unde vitium à iudicio transit in affectu.
units.tr: Two things remain to be examined. First, that these affections are not thoughts or opinions, as the Stoics thought. Second, that they are not all to be accused as vicious and bad. The first can be shown: in those called natural, such as hunger and thirst, these affections attack us easily without any thought at all. Who would call it a thought or an opinion when we are afflicted by a solution of continuity, by the laceration of a sinew, or by the burning of a flame or fire? The wise by nature [σοφοὶ φυσικῶς] can also show the same in the affection of parents towards their children, which is most keen not only in humans but also in brutes. But since the matter is clear, I judge that we should not dwell on it much. As to the second point, I will not deny that some affections have a vice attached to them. But I will show that very many are good, and that those which are bad are bad through the fault of men, not by their own nature. First, an error of judgement can intervene: for we do not always judge well about the objects that present themselves. What is evil is sometimes taken for good, and what is good is thought to be evil. Now these judgements of the mind accompany the affections, as we have shown. Hence the vice passes from the judgement into the affection.

units.la: Apostoli contumelias quas pro Christi nomine patiebantur, ut sibi honorificas iudicabant, ideo læti & gaudentes à concilio recedebant. E diuerso cum à filio pelleretur Dauid è regno, dolebat, quia suam deiectionem videbat scandalo esse hominibus, qui sciebant quid per prophetas Dominus Dauidi promisset. Suo deinde vitio ista videbat euenire[?]: atque quum hæc mala essent, non poterat non dolere. Utriq; Dauid & Apostoli de rebus obiectis recte iudicabat, licet diuersis rationib. quæ accidebant existimarent. Uani homines adulationes vera bona existimant, ideoq; illis delectatur. Alij rectius de illis statuunt: videt enim ludibria esse atq; ob id auersantur. Gaudent boni solidis virtutibus, quia de illis recte iudicant. Alios videas eas odisse, cùm iudicio corrupto laborent. Vitium itaq; aut rectitudo affectuum proucnit ex vera seu falsa rerum obiectarum æstimatione. Non autem æquum est omnes affectus vitiosos dicere quia multi homines abducti errore, in prauos istos motus animi impingunt: nam qui non errant, affectibus erroris non laeduntur.
units.tr: The apostles, regarding the insults they suffered for the name of Christ as honourable to themselves, therefore departed from the council glad and rejoicing. On the other hand, when David was driven from his kingdom by his son, he grieved, because he saw that his overthrow was a scandal to men, who knew what the Lord had promised to David through the prophets. Moreover, he saw that this was happening through his own fault; and since these were evils, he could not but grieve. Both David and the apostles judged rightly about the objects, although they reckoned the events that befell them by different reasons. Vain men think flatteries are true goods, and therefore take delight in them. Others judge these more rightly: they see that they are mockeries, and therefore turn away from them. The good rejoice in solid virtues, because they judge rightly about them. You may see others hating them, since they labour under a corrupt judgement. Vice or rectitude of the affections therefore arises from a true or false estimation of the objects. But it is not fair to say that all affections are vicious, because many men, led astray by error, fall into those perverse motions of the mind; for those who do not err are not harmed by the error of the affections.

units.la: Aliud vitium est in affectibus non quidem ex errore, sed quia nonnulli sunt qui rectæ rationi aduersantur. Vt cupiditas rerum alienarum, caedis, adulterij, & consimilium. Hi debent affectus iure damnari, sed non propter eos est in universum sententia proferenda, quoniam & alij sunt rectæ rationi sanoq; iudicio consentanei, vt amor erga virtutes, odium vel ira cōtra peccata, qui affectus rationi congruentes, non tantum honesti sunt ac laudabi-les, verum etiam vehementer vtiles: nam dati sunt vt calcaria quædam ad bene viuendum. Non enim satis est nosse bona, sed ad illa oportet vehementer impelli. Sunt autem affectus ceu nervi, quorum contentione aut remissione leuius aut incitatius commouemur. Quis non videat illud esse verissimum, iracundiam esse cotem quandam fortitudinis? Admodum essemus ad actiones & quidem honestas ignaui, nisi adhiberentur hæc incitamenta. Essemus vt navis in mari destituta vento. Quamobrem non est natura ipsa affectuum vitiosa, cum permulti sint valde vtiles ac honesti. Certe Deus organa dedit istorum affectuum, adiecit humores qui cis inseruiat, & notitias quas comitatur. Quare negari non possunt opera Dei, & præsertim cum affectus huiusmodi lege sua exigat. Vult enim vt Deum amemus, timeamus, vt diligamus proximos, vt serui dominos timeant. Sunt q; refer-te diuinæ literæ huiusmodi præceptis. Quare ἀπάθεια illa Stoicorum, quaq; Basilius Nazianzenus, & huiusmodi patres interdum videntur prædicare, omnino est repudianda. Christus fleuit, tristis fuit vsq; ad mortem, misericordia mouebatur: quamobrem non fuit sine affectibus. Non itaq; perfectioni humanæ affectus aduersantur. Vitia quidem sæpè accedunt corruptæ naturæ culpa, sed opera danda est, vt vitiosos affectus corrigamus, bonos autem & qui rationi sunt consentanei confirmemus & instauremus. Quod fecisse legimus sanctos viros & pios heroas in utroque Testamento: Non quidem illi affectus vt duces sequebantur, sed illis ad virtutes & egregia facta, quæ Deus imperabat, vtebantur. Neque in sacris literis obscurum est, heroicos illos viros fuisse diuinitus percitos quibusdam vehementiori-bus affectibus.
units.tr: There is another vice in the affections, not indeed from error, but because some are opposed to right reason: such as the desire for other people's goods, murder, adultery and the like. These affections must rightly be condemned; but judgement must not be pronounced on the affections in general because of them, since there are others that agree with right reason and sound judgement, such as love of virtues, and hatred or anger against sins. These affections, being in harmony with reason, are not only honourable and praiseworthy but also very useful; for they are given as spurs to living well. For it is not enough to know good things; one must be strongly driven towards them. Affections are like sinews, by whose tightening or loosening we are moved more gently or more vigorously. Who does not see that it is most true that anger is a kind of whetstone of courage? We would be very sluggish in actions, and indeed honourable ones, if these incitements were not applied; we would be like a ship on the sea left without wind. Therefore the nature of the affections is not itself vicious, since very many of them are most useful and honourable. Surely God gave the organs of these affections, added the humours that serve them, and the knowledge that accompanies them. Hence the works of God cannot be denied, especially since he requires such affections by his law. For he wills that we love and fear God, that we love our neighbours, that servants fear their masters. And the divine letters refer to precepts of this kind. Therefore that Stoic [ἀπάθεια] apatheia, which Basil of Nazianzus and such Fathers sometimes seem to preach, is wholly to be rejected. Christ wept, was sorrowful unto death, was moved by compassion: therefore he was not without affections. Affections, then, are not opposed to human perfection. Vices indeed often attach through the fault of corrupt nature, but care must be taken to correct the vicious affections, and to confirm and restore the good ones, which agree with reason. We read that holy men and pious heroes in both Testaments did this: they did not indeed follow those affections as leaders, but used them for the virtues and excellent deeds which God commanded. Nor is it obscure in the sacred letters that those heroic men were divinely stirred by certain more vehement affections.

units.la: At dubium esse potest unde vitiosi excessus affectuum aut in aliquibus [?]tanta dissensio à ratione, vt est cupiditas rerum alienarum, cædis, stupri, adulterij, quæ nullo modo probari possunt, ortum habuerint. Ad quam quæstionem ex diuinis literis facillimum est respondere: quia per vnum hominem, id est per Adami lapsum peccatum intravit in mundum. Philosophi vero qui hoc non intelligunt, ad temperamenta corporum & stellarum aspectus ac motus confugiunt. Sed ut res ipsa declarat, ex illis causis nequeunt perfectè rationem reddere.
units.tr: But it may be asked where the vicious excesses of the affections arose, and where some have departed so far from reason as to commit theft, murder, fornication and adultery, which can in no way be approved. To this question the divine writings give a very easy answer: through one man, that is, through the fall of Adam, sin entered into the world. The philosophers, who do not understand this, flee to the temperaments of bodies and to the aspects and motions of the stars. But, as the matter itself shows, they cannot give a full account of it from those causes.

units.la: Superest modo ut videamus, quomodo ij affectus regi atq; corrigi possint. Prima via civilis est per morales virtutes. Illæ quippe redigunt eos ad mediocritatem, & si tantum spectaremus præsente vita satis essent: at revera coram Deo non sunt satis, neq; ad eius tribunal ista civilis iustitia sufficit. Ideo alia est adhuc opus regula, nimirum divinarū literarū, quæ nihil prosunt, nisi fide fuerint apprehensæ. Regula ista duplex commodum secum affert. Primum est id quod verae iustitiæ deest, cū solū in morali statu sumus non imputatur, & ex plenitudine Christi complementum adscribitur. Deinde vires adduntur maiores ad resistendum cupiditatibus. Ac denique per fidem ipsæ virtutum actiones & boni affectus referuntur in Deum syncere, quod absque fide minimè fieri potest. Ideo in alienis hominibus à Christo ij moderati affectus ut ut speciosi fuerint, peccata sunt, non quidem sua natura, sed nostro natiuo vitio. Sumus enim ut infecta dolia, quæ vinum quamuis bonum in nos infusum corrumpimus. Proinde cum Deus omnis creaturæ sit author, nihilq; quod non sit bonum, neq; substantias nudas nulloq; adminiculo instructas condidit, sed cuiq; dedit propensiones & inclinationes ad ea quæ salutaria & utilia sint: conficitur non solum naturas atq; substantias esse bonas, verum etiam affectus à Deo illis insitos. Quamuis in hominibus impijs duo vitia hæc, quæ alioqui per se bona sunt contrahant. Primum ob peccatum originis adeo natura corrupta est & debilitata, ut boni affectus non ita sint efficaces ut esse deberent. Deinde non diriguntur in Deum ut oportuit, sed potius ad voluptates & terrenas delectationes captandas. Unde videre licet quatuor hominum gradus. Primi sunt infimi, qui neq; virtutibus moralibus, neq; pietate sunt præditi: in iis omnia videas perturbatione ac ἀταξία referta. Sunt alij deinde à pietate quidem adhuc alieni, sed tamen civiles, qui habitu quodam affectus ad mediocritatem utcunq; revocarunt. Tertij sunt credentes in Christum, qui etsi peccato ut reliqui mortales non carent, illis tamen haud quod peccant imputatur. Quarto & extremo loco ij ponendi sunt qui vel ab initio sunt à Deo conditi, vel hinc soluerunt & iam sunt cum Christo: ij utiq; vitiosos non habent affectus, neq; secunda neq; tertia de causa, verum illos omnino habent bonos, absolutos atq; perfectos. Non tamen in natura sunt ulli affectus adeo corrupti, adeoq; vitiosi, quin ibi videre liceat aliquid boni. In omnibus quippe aliquid institutionis divinæ apparet. paret. Prima enim illa inchoatio, vel (vt ita dixerim) facultas et vis harum qualitatum, diuinitus ortum habuit: sed ἀταξία vel imperfectionis vel obliquitatis, quæ à peccato est, corrupit.
units.tr: It remains only to see how those affections may be governed and corrected. The first way is civil, through the moral virtues. These indeed bring the affections back to the mean, and if we looked only at the present life, they would be enough. But in truth they are not enough before God, and this civil righteousness does not suffice before his tribunal. Therefore another rule is still needed, namely that of the divine writings, which profit nothing unless they are grasped by faith. This rule brings a double benefit. First, what is lacking to true righteousness, since we are only in a moral state, is not imputed to us, and the completeness of Christ is credited to us. Second, greater strength is added to resist the desires. And finally, through faith the very actions of the virtues and the good affections are referred sincerely to God, which cannot be done without faith. Therefore in men who are apart from Christ, those moderated affections, however fair they may appear, are sins, not indeed by their own nature, but by our native vice. For we are like jars that have gone bad, which corrupt even good wine poured into them. Accordingly, since God is the author of every creature, and nothing is not good, and since he did not create bare substances lacking any aid, but gave to each its inclinations and propensities toward what is wholesome and useful, it follows that not only natures and substances are good, but also the affections implanted in them by God. Yet in impious men these two faults, which in themselves are otherwise good, contract. First, because of original sin, nature is so corrupted and weakened that the good affections are not as effective as they ought to be. Second, they are not directed to God as they should be, but rather to seize pleasures and earthly delights. Hence one may see four grades of men. The first are the lowest, who have neither moral virtues nor piety; in them you will see everything filled with disorder and ataxia [ἀταξία]. Others are next, still foreign to piety, but nevertheless civil, who by a certain habit have somehow brought their affections back to the mean. The third are believers in Christ, who, although they are not free from sin like the rest of mortals, nevertheless the sin they commit is not imputed to them. In the fourth and last place are to be placed those who were either created by God from the beginning, or have been released from this life and are now with Christ. These certainly have no vicious affections, neither for the second nor the third reason, but they have altogether good, complete and perfect ones. Yet in nature there are no affections so corrupted and vicious that something good cannot be seen in them. For in all of them some trace of divine institution appears. That first beginning, or (as I may call it) the faculty and power of these qualities, has arisen from God; but the disorder [ataxia] or imperfection or crookedness, which comes from sin, has corrupted it.

units.la: Neq; ÿ[?] praui affectus nocent ipsi tantum animæ crassiori parti, verùm etiam voluntati & rationi. Sic enim Deus reuinxit & colligauit has animi vires, vt sibi mutuò inseruiant, nempe affectus rationi pareant, vtq; ratio affectus regat et moderetur, ac motus cordis temperet. At secus agitur, voluntatisq; tanta infirmitas est, vt collata cum affectibus, videri possit puer, isq; timidus, insidens equo ferocissimo. Proinde nostræ huius facultatis authores hunc sibi proposuere scopum, vt virtutibus affectus lenirent, atq; rationem imbecillem corroborarent.
units.tr: Nor do the depraved affections harm only the grosser part of the soul, but also the will and the reason. For God so bound and joined these powers of the mind that they serve each other: namely, that the affections obey reason, and that reason governs and moderates the affections and tempers the movements of the heart. But it goes otherwise, and the will is so weak that, compared with the affections, it may seem like a boy, and a timid one, sitting on a very fierce horse. Therefore the authors of our faculty set themselves this aim: to soften the affections by the virtues, and to strengthen the feeble reason.

units.la: Quæ verò ea sint animi partes, quæ vehementius instructæ affectibus rationem perturbent ac debilitent, Plato monstrauit, qui primo loco ἡγεμονικὸν statuit, inferius verò ἐπιθυμητικὸν atq; θυμοειδὲς. In ijs itaq; posterioribus animi partibus affectus collocantur. Has verò animi vires, vt antea dictu est, in capite, in epate atq; corde esse arbitratus est. Aristoteles verò vt genus accepit ὀρεκτικὸν, quod in partes diduxit ἐπιθυμίαν, θυμὸν, et βούλησιν. Quæ partes quoniam per se patent non opus est fusius explicare. Hoc tamen addam, iuxta rectum ordinem à facultate illa superiori quæ βούλησις est inferiores appetitus debere moueri, gubernari & regi vt sphæra suprema inferiores ducit, quemadmodum in 3. lib. de Anima scribitur. Et certè ita res habet. Inferiores vires, cùm excitantur, & ad aliquid faciundum impellunt, reguntur cogitatione, & cogitatio à ratione. Ac experitur quislibet in seipso, aliqua ratione naturali adhibita sedari cömotos affectus, ceu venti ab Aeolo finguntur comprimi. Patent ergo in homine affectus ipsi voluntati, cùm in brutis ad affectuum impulsum ilico actio consequatur: nostræ verò affectiones imperium voluntatis perpetuò expectant, nisi aliquod sese interposuerit impedimentum, vt in pueris & furiosis videmus euenire. Hic fortasse dixeris, In incontinentibus, nonne videmus voluntate inuita moueri affectus? Respondemus, tumultuari quidem contra voluntate, sed nihil efficere quo ad motum & actiones, nisi voluntas insferit: eam sanè affectiones oppugnant & turbant & vincunt deniq;, ac illam in suam traducunt sententiam, quæ cum fuerit assensa & imperauerit, sequuntur actiones non vtiq; quemadmodum ab initio decreuerat, sed vt victa insferit.
units.tr: Which parts of the mind these are, which, being more strongly equipped with affections, disturb and weaken reason, Plato showed, who placed the ruling part [hēgemonikon, ἡγεμονικὸν] first, and below it the desiring part [epithumētikon, ἐπιθυμητικὸν] and the spirited part [thumoeidēs, θυμοειδὲς]. In those latter parts of the mind, therefore, the affections are lodged. And these powers of the mind, as was said before, he thought to be located in the head, in the liver and in the heart. Aristotle, however, took the appetitive faculty [orektikon, ὀρεκτικὸν] as a genus and divided it into desire [epithumia, ἐπιθυμίαν], spirit [thumos, θυμὸν] and wish [boulēsis, βούλησιν]. Since these parts are plain in themselves, there is no need to explain them at greater length. I will add this, however: according to the right order, the lower appetites ought to be moved, guided and ruled by that higher faculty which is the wish, just as the highest sphere leads the lower ones, as is written in the third book On the Soul. And indeed the matter stands so. When the lower powers are roused and impel us to do something, they are governed by thought, and thought by reason. And anyone may experience in himself that, by applying some natural reasoning, the stirred affections are calmed, as winds are said to be checked by Aeolus. The affections, then, are plainly subject to the will in man, whereas in brutes an action follows at once upon the impulse of the affections. Our affections, however, always await the command of the will, unless some hindrance has intervened, as we see happen in children and madmen. Here perhaps you will say: in the incontinent, do we not see the affections move against the will? We reply that they indeed riot against the will, but accomplish nothing as regards motion and actions, unless the will consents. The affections assail it, disturb it and at last overcome it, and draw it over to their own opinion; and when this has been assented to and has given its command, actions follow, not in the way it had first decided, but as one conquered, it has yielded.

units.la: Sed arbitrati sunt aliqui, Vim cupientem et irascentè eandem esse, quia contraria pertinent ad eandem facultatè. Conuenientia verò naturæ, quæq; illi nocent, contraria sunt. Ergo sunt obiecta a eiusdem partis animi, vt albu & nigrum visus, linea recta & obliqua eiusdē est scientiæ, nēpe mathescos, sanum & ægrotum medicinæ. Ad hoc respōdemus, Obiectla[?] irascentis & cupientis facultatis non ita distinguí per conuenies et noxiū, sed vtrang̃ harū partium bonum & malum spectare, verum non eadem ratione. Quæ concupiscit vis, in bonū & malū respicit absolutè, nempe vt hoc assequatur, & illud euitet. At nonnunquā interdū se interponunt impedimenta & corrumpentia, ita vt difficile sit hoc obtinere, vel illud effugere. Ibi se vis irascens exerit ad istas difficultates superandas, pugnat & impedimentis acriter resistit, quo vel apprehendamus bonū, vel effugiamus malū pro vt cupimus. Obiectū itaq; facultatis irascentis est bonū & malū, vt difficile atq; arduū sese offert. Spes maximè affectus est irascentis: nam fertur in bonum, sed absens, ad quod obtinendum, impedimentū est deuorandum expectationis, & impedimentorum vis & difficultas vincenda est. Quo aut ordine facultates ex inter se ordinentur, hinc apparet, Quia irascentis impetus inchoat à cupiente et in eam definit. Cum enim quispiam afficitur iniuria, tristatur: tristitia verò affectus cupiētis est facultatis. Malū hoc quo tristatur lœsus vt euitetur, ira se interponit, quæ vltione malum cupit depellere, vltio verò (vt omnes nouimus) ardua est, sed cum perfecta fuerit, succedit lætitia, quæ pertinet ad vim cupientem, atq; ibi desinimus irasci. Vis itaq; irascēs tutatrix est & pugnax, et cupiēti parti aduersatur: illa enim labores & dolores refugit, hæc superat, perfert, ac ea inuita subit: & quando earum altera suam actione contendit, altera vicissim remittit. Qui depereunt vehementer mulieres, illis non irascuntur: & qui eis irati sunt, minus illarū cupiditate flagrant. Proinde obiectū irascibilis offendit cupiente partem, quoniam (vti iam diximus) labores & difficultates refugit, ad quæ irascens occurrit, & sese paratum ad superandum exhibet. Neq; obscurum est ex ijs duabus animi viribus, Irascentem magis ad rationem accedere: illius enim adiutrix est ad salutaria consilia exequenda. Cupiens autem sensui propior est. Vtq; in re iam satis (vt existimo) perspicua exemplis agamus, Audacia & Metus huius animi partes sunt affectus: nam Audacia bonum difficile affectat, Metus verò malum refugit euitatu difficile: nam quæ non urgent & facile possunt eludi mala, non metuimus. Hæc de affectibus in universum, de quibus non solum philosophus moralis disputat, sed & naturalis & medicus & rhetor.
units.tr: But some have thought that the concupiscible and the irascible power are the same, because contraries belong to the same faculty. But things agreeable to nature, and things that harm it, are contraries. Therefore they are objects of the same part of the mind, just as white and black belong to the sight, and straight and oblique lines to the same science, namely mathematics, and healthy and sick to medicine. To this we reply that the objects of the irascible and the concupiscible faculty are not distinguished by the agreeable and the harmful, but each of these parts regards good and evil, yet not in the same way. The concupiscible power looks at good and evil absolutely, namely to attain the one and avoid the other. But sometimes obstacles and hindrances intervene, so that it is difficult to obtain the one or escape the other. There the irascible power puts itself forth to overcome these difficulties; it fights and resists the hindrances sharply, so that we may either lay hold of the good or flee from the evil, as we desire. The object of the irascible faculty is therefore good and evil as something difficult and hard to reach. Hope is especially an affection of the irascible part, for it is directed to a good that is absent, and to obtain it the obstacle of expectation must be devoured, and the force and difficulty of hindrances must be overcome. In what order the faculties are ranked among themselves is clear from this: the impulse of the irascible begins from the concupiscible and ends in it. For when someone is affected by an injury, he is saddened; and sadness is an affection of the concupiscible faculty. To avoid the evil by which the injured man is saddened, anger intervenes, which seeks to drive the evil away by vengeance; but vengeance (as we all know) is hard. When it has been carried out, however, joy follows, which belongs to the concupiscible power, and there we cease to be angry. The irascible power, then, is a guardian and a fighter, and opposes the concupiscible part; for the one shrinks from labours and pains, the other overcomes them, bears them and undergoes them against its will; and when one of them strives by its action, the other in turn relaxes. Those who love women to distraction are not angry with them; and those who are angry with them burn less with desire for them. Therefore the object of the irascible power offends the concupiscible part, since (as we have already said) the latter shrinks from labours and difficulties, to which the irascible power runs and presents itself as ready to overcome them. And it is not unclear from these two powers of the mind that the irascible is nearer to reason, for it helps to carry out wholesome counsels; but the concupiscible is closer to sense. And that we may act in this matter, which I think is already sufficiently clear, by examples: boldness and fear are affections of this mind's parts. For boldness aims at a good that is hard to get, but fear flees from an evil that is hard to avoid; for we do not fear evils that do not press upon us and can easily be escaped.
