These things are said of the affections in general, about which not only the moral philosopher disputes, but also the natural philosopher, the physician and the rhetorician.

units.la: Atq; vt missis naturalibus philosophis & medicis de rhetoribus aliquid dicam, Illi vt Aristoteles in 2. Rhetoricorū testatur, primum quidā curāt vt argumentis fidem faciant, ea vera esse quæ affirmant. Deinde animos & affectus iudicum audientiumq; consyderant. Id enim magnum habet ad cau-sampondus. Nam qui reum amant, aut non peccasse aut quàm minimum pec-casse credunt: è diuerso autem si oderint, aut non innocentem omnino esse, aut maximè sontem apud se statuunt. Hos affectus nisi orator immutet, le-niat, aut in contrarium vertat, nihil prorsus efficiet. Docet itaq; ibi Aristo-teles tria esse attendenda. Primum, qui nam sint proni vt hoc vel illo modo afficiantur. Secundo, erga quos eiusmodi affectus induere soleant. Deniq; ob quas causas ita vel ita moueantur affectibus: quo ijs cognitis possint fa-cile inseruire causæ. Verum nonnulli sunt, qui arbitrentur non esse hoc iustu aut permittendum, vt in causis dicendis affectus moueantur, cum Iudicū mentes in decernendo tranquillas esse oporteat: quod non fiet si affectibus perturbentur artificiosa rhetorum oratione. Sed qui hoc dicunt, mihi non videntur affectuum naturam ab illorum vsu distinguere: quia natura quidem affectionum bona est, licet vsus interdum bonus, interdum malus sit. Gladij quoq; cùm ferro consistent, quod est Dei creatura bona, quandoq; iusto, quandoq; iniusto vsui seruiunt. Quid obsecro peccabit orator, si cùm vide-rit in bona instaq; causa iudicem malo affectu erga reum inflammatum, ora-tionis artificio illum demulceat, in contrarios affectus trahat, imò incitet e-ius cordis motus ad seueriter iusteq; decernendum? Hic certè nulla erit cul-pa, sed humani affectus ad finem illis prescriptam dirigentur. Sunt enim aliquando auditores & iudices qui frigeant, quibusq; non fuerit satis ofte-[?]disse quid agendum, nisi vehementiori affectu excitato eo pertrahantur. Il li sunt reprehendendi & coerceri debent, qui artificia orationis quo ad asse-ctus commouendos eò dirigunt, vt animi Iudicum perturbentur, & minus quod sit iustum videant: non tamen propter istorum prauitatem vtile illud artificium est ex rebus humanis explodendum. Sacræ alioqui literæ debe-rent accusari, quibus Dei spiritus non solum quæ agenda sunt & quæ cauen-da monet, sed affectus incitat, quo magis ad obediendum impellamur. Hæc de ista re iam velim satis esse.
units.tr: And, setting aside the natural philosophers and physicians, let me say something about the rhetoricians. As Aristotle testifies in the second book of the Rhetoric, they first take care to make their arguments convincing, to show that what they assert is true. Then they consider the feelings and dispositions of the judges and the audience, for this matters greatly to the case being pleaded. Those who love the accused believe either that he has not sinned or that he has sinned as little as possible. On the other hand, if they hate him, they hold either that he is not innocent at all or that he is the most guilty. Unless the orator changes, softens or turns these feelings to the opposite, he will achieve nothing at all. So Aristotle teaches there that three things must be attended to. First, who are prone to be moved in this or that way. Second, towards whom such feelings are usually directed. Third, for what causes they are stirred in one way or another. Once these are known, the orator can readily serve his cause. Yet some think that it is neither right nor permissible for the emotions to be stirred in pleading cases, since the minds of judges ought to be calm in deciding, and this will not happen if they are disturbed by the artful speeches of the rhetoricians. But those who say this do not seem to me to distinguish the nature of the emotions from their use. For the nature of the affections is good, although their use is sometimes good and sometimes bad. Swords too, while they remain iron, which is a good creature of God, sometimes serve a just use and sometimes an unjust one. What, I ask, would the orator do wrong if, seeing that the judge is inflamed with bad feeling against the accused in a good and just cause, he soothed him by the art of speech, drew him to contrary feelings, or indeed roused the movements of his heart to decide severely and justly? Here there will certainly be no fault, but human feelings will be directed to the end prescribed for them. For there are sometimes listeners and judges who are cold, and who have not been sufficiently shown what must be done unless they are drawn along by a more vehement emotion stirred up in them. Those who use the artifices of speech to stir the emotions in order to disturb the minds of judges, so that they see less of what is just, are the ones who should be rebuked and restrained. Yet the useful art is not, on account of their wickedness, to be driven out of human affairs. Otherwise the Holy Scriptures would have to be accused, since by them the Spirit of God not only tells us what is to be done and what to be avoided, but also stirs our affections, so that we may be more driven to obey. Let this now be enough on this matter.

units.la: NVNC superest vt quæ in isto capite sunt commemorata, demonstrem vt diuinis literis congruant, vtúe ab illis dissentiant. Signum, primò inquit, virtutis adeptæ aut nondum partæ inde vult accipi à dolore ac voluptate. Qui læto animo iusta faciunt vel temperata, illi iustitiam & temperanti-am nacti sunt. Qui vero hæc tristes faciunt, huiusmodi virtutibus carent. Diuinæ quoque literæ indicant, ea quæ recte aguntur, cum lætitia esse agen-da, & minus Deo placere, quæ tristi animo fiunt. Deutero. cap. 28. scribitur: Eò quòd non seruieris Domino Deo tuo cum lætitia, &c. Prius commemorauerat execrationes, cur autem illæ inducendæ in populum Israeliticum essent, verbis adductis monstratur. Proverb. 21. Gaudium iusto est, facere iudicium. 2. Cor. 9. Non ex tristitia vel ex necessitate. Nec nō hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Et ad Romanos, Qui miseretur in hilaritate. Ad Philipp. Gaudete in Domino semper, Iterum dico gaudete. Modestia vestra sit nota omnibus hominibus. Et adeo perfectam virtutem charitatis in Euangelium Paulus adeptus erat, ut in eadem Epistola diceret: Sive per veritatem, sive per occasionem annuncietur Christus, in hoc gaudeo. Et ad Colos. 1. Gaudeo in passionibus meis pro vobis. Et supplere aiebat quæ deerant, passionum Christi in carne sua pro corpore Christi, quod est Ecclesia. Et Petrus prior, cap. 1. Communicantes passionibus Christi gaudete. In Actis: Ibant gaudentes à conspectu concilij. Ad Galat. 5. inter fructus spiritus numeratur pax & gaudium. Iuuenis autem qui adhuc pietatis virtute non erat ornatus, quum audiuisset quæ Christus illi mandauit, abijt tristis. 2. Corint. 6. Quasi tristes semper aut gaudentes. Locus iste indicat, esse quidem aliquam carnis tristitiam in retinenda pietate, sed tamen semper animi adesse gaudium, quia Spiritus Domini consolatur, & lætitiam intimam parit. Inquit ad-hæc Aristoteles, Propter dolorem & voluptatem homines prava committe-re, nempe ut voluptatem assequantur, & dolorem fugiant. Idem sancta scriptura docet: quoniam Luc. 8. voluptates vocantur spinæ, quibus verbum Domini præfocatur. Et ad Timoth. posteriori, Erunt homines postremis temporibus magis φιλήδονοι quam φιλόθεοι. Atqʒ Israelitæ sequebantur Mosen, imò Dominum, inuiti ad terram promissionis: ideo subinde obloquebantur & murmurabant. Multique reperiuntur qui voluptatum nimia cupiditate, atque horrore doloris nolunt resipiscere, & ad Deum iusta pœnitentia redire. Plato quoque in isto capite laudatur, qui propter insitam nobis voluptatem ab incunabulis censuit bene pueros educan-dos, ut rebus gauderent & dolerent quæ digna gaudio vel tristitia essent. Pravitatem itemque istam sectandæ voluptatis & doloris fugiendi, & in-sum-ma ut contra Deum quæramus nostra, scribitur in Genesi, nobis à prima pueritia esse innata. Dicitur enim ab ipsa prima pueritia cor hominis esse pravum. Et Paulus de filijs in timore Domini educandis, ad Philippēses & Colossenses pulchrè docuit. Habuimus præterea pœnas esse medicinas, quod E-pistola ad Hebræos non tacuit, ubi dicitur, Deum illos quos amat corrigere ac castigare. Nec nō Deus plagis Iudæos ad se frequentissimè revocavit. Iudi-cia, incipit à domo sua, quæ non effundit in electos, quasi eos præ cæteris oderit, sed ut in viam revocentur, aut per illorum flagella corrigantur alij. Scripsit ad hæc Aristoteles esse perdifficile voluptates à nobis ipsis extrude-re, quod nobis innatæ sint & nobiscum creverint. Quod cum ita sit, merito Christus prædicabat sui abnegationem et mortificationem veteris hominis. Et adeo voluit istas cupiditates pravas & corruptas à nobis eradicatas, ut lege non tantum prohibuerit, ut declaratur in Matthæo, externi actus peccatum, sed etiam animi perversos impulsus: nam illos qui viderint seu aspexerint ad concupiscendum alienam mulierem, iam dicit mœchatos in corde suo. Vult itaq; reprimi damnatarum voluptatum non solum actiones, verum sensus & animi deliberationes atq; motus.
units.tr: Now it remains for me to show whether the things recorded in this chapter agree with the divine writings or dissent from them. First, he says that the sign of virtue already acquired, or not yet gained, is to be taken from pain and pleasure. Those who do just or temperate deeds with a glad mind have obtained justice and temperance; but those who do these things sadly lack such virtues. The divine writings also indicate that what is rightly done must be done with joy, and that what is done with a sad mind pleases God less. It is written in Deuteronomy 28: "Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy," etc. Earlier it had mentioned the curses, and why these were to be brought upon the people of Israel is shown by the words cited. Proverbs 21: "It is joy to the just to do judgment." 2 Corinthians 9: "Not out of sadness or necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver." And in Romans: "He who shows mercy, with cheerfulness." To the Philippians: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your moderation be known to all men." And Paul had so attained the perfect virtue of charity in the Gospel that in the same Epistle he said: "Whether by truth or by occasion, Christ is proclaimed; in this I rejoice." And to the Colossians 1: "I rejoice in my sufferings for you." And he said that he filled up what was lacking of the sufferings of Christ in his flesh for the body of Christ, which is the Church. And Peter in his first chapter: "Rejoice in sharing the sufferings of Christ." In Acts: "They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council." Galatians 5: among the fruits of the Spirit peace and joy are numbered. But the young man, who was not yet adorned with the virtue of piety, when he heard what Christ commanded him, went away sad. 2 Corinthians 6: "As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing." That passage indicates that there is indeed some sadness of the flesh in keeping piety, but that joy of the mind is always present, because the Spirit of the Lord comforts and brings forth inner gladness. Aristotle adds that men commit wicked acts because of pain and pleasure, namely to obtain pleasure and to flee pain. Holy Scripture teaches the same: Luke 8 calls pleasures thorns, by which the word of the Lord is choked. And in the second letter to Timothy: "Men will be in the last times more lovers of pleasure [φιλήδονοι] than lovers of God [φιλόθεοι]." Indeed the Israelites followed Moses, and indeed the Lord, unwillingly toward the promised land; therefore they continually grumbled and murmured. And many are found who, through an excessive desire for pleasures and a horror of pain, are unwilling to repent and to return to God by a just repentance. Plato too is praised in this chapter, who thought, because pleasure is implanted in us, that boys ought to be well brought up from their cradle, so that they might rejoice and grieve at things that deserve joy or sadness. The wickedness likewise of pursuing pleasure and fleeing pain, and in short of seeking our own things against God, is written in Genesis to be innate in us from earliest childhood: for it is said that the heart of man is wicked from his very youth. And Paul, concerning children to be brought up in the fear of the Lord, taught this beautifully to the Philippians and Colossians. Moreover, the Epistle to the Hebrews does not pass over the fact that punishments are medicines, where it is said that God corrects and chastises those whom he loves. Indeed God often called the Jews back to himself by blows. "Judgment begins at the house of God," which does not pour out upon the elect, as if he hated them above others, but so that they may be called back to the way, or that others may be corrected through their scourges. Aristotle also wrote that it is very difficult to drive pleasures out of ourselves, since they are innate in us and have grown with us. Since this is so, Christ rightly preached the denial of self and the mortification of the old man. And he so willed that these depraved and corrupt desires be uprooted from us that he forbade by the law not only the external act, which is declared in Matthew to be sin, but also the perverse impulses of the mind: for he says that those who have seen or looked upon a foreign woman to lust after her have already committed adultery in their heart. Thus he wills that not only the actions of condemned pleasures be restrained, but also the sensations, deliberations and movements of the mind.
CHAPTER IIII

units.la: Dubitaverit forte quispiam, quomodo dica-mus, oportere iusta facientes effici iustos, ac tē-perata tēperātes. Si enim iusta faciunt, iam sunt iusti ac temperati: quemadmodum qui grammatica & musica faciunt. Grammatici & Musici.
units.tr: Someone might perhaps ask how we can say that by doing just deeds people become just, and by doing temperate deeds they become temperate. For if they do just things, they already are just and temperate, just as those who do grammar and music are grammarians and musicians.

units.la: Disputabatur ab initio libri huius quo pacto virtutes acquire-rentur, & dictum est inter cetera, id fieri frequenti usu bona-rum actionum: quod cum usque adeo clarum non sit, nunc tractat. Suo loco id non facit, quod multa inciderint magis ne-cessaria dictu. Nunc id repetit, & primo loco dubitationem interponit. De-inde eam dissoluit. Tertio demum opinionem à vero alienam removet.
units.tr: At the beginning of this book it was discussed how the virtues are acquired, and among other things it was said that this happens through the frequent practice of good actions. Because this is not so clear, he now takes it up again. He does not deal with it in its proper place, because many more necessary matters came up to be discussed. Now he repeats it, and first he raises an objection. Then he resolves it. Third, at last, he removes an opinion foreign to the truth.

units.la: Dubitatio oritur. Quod iusti putantur esse qui faciunt iusta, & temperantes qui temperata faciunt. Quod si iusti sunt, quare iustitiam quaerant, quum eam sint assequuti? Probatur, hoc quod obijcitur, artium similitudine. Prius enim videtur ars in animo haberi, quam eius artificium queat produci. Quare sic isti[?] putant de virtutibus esse statuendum, ut antea quam illarum opera fiant, in animo præsint. A iustitia & temperantia sumit exempla, quod ex virtutes præ ceteris conspicuæ sint & illustres: & nemo ignorat exempla quàm maxime oportere conspicua esse. Argumentum vero quod obijcitur, est à simili, ac si diceretur:
units.tr: The objection arises: people are thought to be just when they do just things, and temperate when they do temperate things. But if they are just, why do they seek justice, since they already possess it? The objection is supported by the similarity with the arts. For the art seems to be held in the mind before its product can be made. Therefore these men think that the virtues must be judged in the same way: that they must be present in the mind before their works are done. He takes his examples from justice and temperance, because these virtues are more conspicuous and illustrious than the others, and nobody doubts that examples ought to be as conspicuous as possible. The argument that is raised is one from likeness, as if one said:

units.la: Sicuti se habent virtutes ad sua opera, ita & virtutes ad suas actiones:.
units.tr: Just as the virtues stand in relation to their works, so the virtues stand in relation to their actions.

units.la: At artes prius adsunt quàm sua edantur opera: Igitur & virtutes antecedunt suas actiones. Duplex autem ratio est diluendi similium argumenta. Vna, quando negatur id esse in simili, quod aduersarij in eo sumunt inesse. Altera, quando non consentimus esse similia, quæ ut similia proferuntur. Prima igitur diluendi utitur ratione ab initio, cum inquit,
units.tr: But the arts are present before their works are produced. Therefore the virtues also precede their actions. There are two ways of refuting arguments from likeness. One is when we deny that the thing the opponents assume to be in the likeness is in fact there. The other is when we do not agree that the things offered as alike are alike. Therefore he uses the first way of refuting, from the beginning, when he says:

units.la: An uero ne in artibus quidem sic est. Etenim usu-uenit ut aliquis fortuito aut aliquo suggerente non-nihil grammaticum faciat. Tum uero grammaticus erit, si & grammaticum aliquid & grammaticè fecerit, hoc est, ex ea quæ in eo grammatica fuerit.
units.tr: But indeed, it is not so even in the arts. For it happens that someone, by chance or at someone's suggestion, does something grammatical. Then he will be a grammarian only if he has done something grammatical and done it grammatically, that is, out of that which is grammar in him.

units.la: Dissolutio hac interemptione minoris constat. Artes enim ita comparatas esse, ut prius adsint, quàm earum opus edatur, negat. Et instantiam profert. Sic enim solet vniuersalis propositio euerti per instantiam. Fieri enim potest ut quispiam aliquid loquatur aut scribat, quod reuera grammaticum est: nam qui grammaticus esset, ita loqueretur aut scriberet. At is casu sic agit, aut alio suggerente, neque rationem aut causam vllam suæ loquutionis aut scripturæ posset reddere: quod non est ex habitu agere. Fortunam & alienam suggestionem recte opponit habitui artis, quia neque in fortuitis, neque in iis quæ tantum alio submonente facimus, possumus operis aut facti rationes reddere.
units.tr: The solution rests on denying the minor premise. For he denies that the arts are so constituted that they are present before their work is produced. And he offers an instance, for a universal proposition is usually overturned by an instance. It can happen that someone says or writes something that is really grammatical; for one who was a grammarian would speak or write in that way. But he acts in this way by chance, or at another's suggestion, and cannot give any reason or cause for his speech or writing; and this is not to act from a habit. He rightly sets chance and another's suggestion against the habit of the art, because in chance events, and in those things which we do only at another's prompting, we cannot give the reasons for the work or deed.

units.la: Adde in artibus & virtutibus non similem esse rationem. Nam quæ ab artibus fiunt, perfectionem in seipsis habent. Quare satis est sic effici ut certo quodam modo se habeant. At quæ per virtutes aguntur, licet certo quodam modo se habeant, non tamen vel iustè ilico vel temperanter fiunt. Sed tamen quando is qui agit certo quodam modo se habet, primo si sciens, deinde si ex delectu, ita ut propter ipsa deligat quæ facit, tertio si qui agit, constanter & immobiliter se habeat. Hæc autem præter ipsam scientiam non iis adnumerant, quæ ad exer-cendas alias artes faciunt. Ad virtutes quidem scien-tia ipsa vel parum vel nihil valet: in cæteris vero nō parva, sed omnis est facultas.
units.tr: Add that in the arts and the virtues the case is not similar. For the things that are made by the arts have their perfection in themselves. Therefore it is enough that they are brought about so as to be in a certain fixed condition. But the things that are done through the virtues, although they are in a certain fixed condition, are not done justly or temperately at once. But when the one who acts is in a certain fixed condition, first if he acts knowingly, then if he acts from choice, so that he chooses the things he does for their own sake, and third if he who acts is disposed constantly and immovably. Now these conditions, apart from knowledge itself, are not counted among those that help in exercising the other arts. Knowledge itself is worth little or nothing for the virtues, whereas in the other things it is not a small but a complete faculty.

units.la: Hic aliter affertur diluendi modus, & negatur maior, quod non similis ratio sit de artibus & scientiis. Et discrimen ostenditur, quia opera quæ ab artibus eduntur. Satis absoluta sunt, cum suas qualitates, formas, & pro-prietates fuerint assequuta. Neq; spectatur quo pacto artifex animo sit asse-ctus, modo gladius commode stringi possit, apte incidat, & sit firmus, est sa-tis. Ac sufficit medicina, si queat purgare, aut male affectis partibus corporis subuenire: De animo vero & voluntate fabri aut seplasiarij [?], nemo est solli-citus, qui hæc sibi comparat. In actionibus virtutum non similiter vsuenit: nam tametsi ad mediocritatem peruenant, sint officiosa, & certas quas-dam in sese habeant qualitates, non tamen ob id vel temperanter vel iuste fiunt. Quandoquidem in eo qui agit, vt sit iustus & temperans, tria exigun-tur. Primum, vt non agat fortuito seu temere, vt qui bene alicui facit pro- bo viro, sed casu, quia illum probum esse ac bonum ignorauit. Agat præte-rea ex delectu, & quæ facienda suscipit non propter extremum alienumq; [?] finem deligat. Sunt quippè nonnulli qui cupiam bene faciant, non sane hoc nomine quòd eo genere officij delectentur, sed quòd ea via quærunt ma-iora & plura lucrari, quam dederint. Exigitur postremò vt constanti & fir-ma voluntate quæ bona & recta sunt agantur. Quod illi sane haud præ-stant, qui parati sunt eundem hominem siue prauus sit siue bonus odisse & amare, vt sibi commodius fuerit. Cicero Clodium quandoque amauit, quandoq; odio habuit, cum tamen ille perpetuò fuerit malus. Infinita sane illorum exempla sunt qui iusta fecerunt, cum ipsi iusti non essent. Spurius Melius curabat summa diligentia frumentū populo Romano, cum annona esset difficilis: verum non propter seipsum bonum publicū amauit, sed quia imperiū affectabat. Iusta ergo faciebat, sed nō iuste. Catilina quoq; tolerans fuit laborū, famis, & sitis, & multa sæpe faciebat quæ potuisset quiuis lau-dare: at nō iuste agebat, cum sibi corruptissima fine præstituisset. Dauid nu-meravit populū, quod potuisset rectè fieri: sed quoniā animo nō syncero fe-cit, idcirco et reprehenditur à Deo, et punitur. Nebucadnezar euertes Iudæa, Hebræis iustas pœnas irrogauit, nō tamen iuste, cum ipse inde tantū quæreret vt suo animo satisfaceret ambitioso. Ex illis trib. q ad actiones virtutis exigitur, unum tantum requirunt artes, nimirum scientiam: illum enim qui operatur ex arte, scire oportet quid agat, & rationem tenere, quantum satis est, eorum quae facit. At istud in actionibus moralibus minimum est: nam permulti sunt qui noverunt, & causas virtutum atque bonarum actionum tenent, non tamen volunt recte vivere, imo sunt pravi & perditissimi. Scientia parum aut nihil valet ad virtutes: nam ea in artificibus est magna, in Mathematicis & Physicis admiranda, quae nihilominus illis non elargitur virtutum moralium actiones.
units.tr: Here another way of refuting is set out, and the major premise is denied, namely that the case of the arts and the sciences is not similar. And a difference is shown, because the works that are produced by the arts are complete once they have acquired their qualities, forms and properties. Nor is it looked at how the craftsman was disposed in his mind, provided the sword can be sharpened properly, cuts well and is strong; that is enough. And medicine suffices if it can purge, or help the badly affected parts of the body. But nobody is concerned about the mind and will of the smith or the carpenter who gets these things for himself. It is not the same with the actions of the virtues: for although they reach the mean, and are dutiful, and have certain qualities in themselves, they are not on that account done temperately or justly. For in the one who acts, if he is to be just and temperate, three things are required. First, that he not act by chance or rashly, as one who does a good turn to an upright man but by accident, because he did not know that he was upright and good. Then, that he act from choice, and choose the things he undertakes to do not for an ulterior and foreign end. For there are some who do good deeds not truly because they take pleasure in that kind of duty, but because by this route they seek to gain more and greater things than they have given. Lastly, it is required that the good and right things be done with a constant and firm will. Those people certainly do not manage this who are ready to hate and to love the same man, whether he is wicked or good, as it suits them better. Cicero at one time loved Clodius and at another time hated him, although Clodius was always wicked. There are indeed countless examples of those who did just deeds while they themselves were not just. Spurius Maelius took the greatest care to supply grain to the Roman people when food was scarce; but he did not love the public good for its own sake, but because he aimed at power. So he did just things, but not justly. Catiline too was able to endure labours, hunger and thirst, and often did many things that anyone could praise; but he did not act justly, since he had set before himself the most corrupt ends. David numbered the people, which he could have done rightly; but because he did it with an insincere heart, he was therefore rebuked and punished by God. Nebuchadnezzar, when he overthrew Judea, inflicted just punishments on the Hebrews, yet he did not act justly, since he sought from it only what would satisfy his ambitious spirit. Of those three conditions which are required for the actions of virtue, the arts require only one, namely knowledge. For the one who works from an art must know what he is doing and hold the reason of the things he makes, as far as is enough. But this is the least in moral actions. For there are very many who know, and hold to the causes of the virtues and of good actions, yet are unwilling to live rightly, and indeed are wicked and utterly depraved. Knowledge is worth little or nothing for the virtues. For it is great in craftsmen, and admirable in mathematicians and natural philosophers; yet nevertheless it does not confer on them the actions of the moral virtues.

units.la: Hic tamen diligenter attendendum est, non loqui Aristotelem de scientia seu notitia seorsim. Ita enim res est praeclara & magnis laudibus praedicanda. Sed illam adducit quae spectat ad morales virtutes, eiusq; vim par-vam esse scribit: nam facile est, nosse temperantiam in eo sitam esse, ut volu-ptates cibi & potus & Veneris frenentur, non tamen hoc praestare facile fuerit. Neq; praetermittendum est, sermonem hoc loco de virtutibus moralibus institutum, non autem de prudentia & aliis facultatibus ad mentem seu rationem pertinentibus. Eo spectant morales virtutes ut boni efficiamur, quod ipsa scientia seorsim accepta non proprie curat.
units.tr: Here, however, we must pay careful attention that Aristotle is not speaking of knowledge or notion taken separately. For that is an excellent thing and deserves great praise. But he is bringing in that knowledge which concerns the moral virtues, and he writes that its power is small. For it is easy to know that temperance consists in restraining the pleasures of food and drink and of love; yet it is not easy to achieve this. Nor must it be passed over that the discussion here is about the moral virtues, and not about prudence and the other faculties that pertain to the mind or reason. The moral virtues aim at making us good, which knowledge taken by itself does not properly care about.

units.la: Tria vero illa quae iam recensuit Aristoteles, ad virtutum moralium actiones necessaria, ita se habent, Scietia pertinet ad mentem seu rationem, delectus ad appetitum, constantia vero & immobilitas ad habitum, &c. Cum autem inquit, Reliqua non parum, sed totum possunt accipias dicta haec ex collatione: quia simpliciter vera non essent. Ista enim reliqua duo, nempe agere cum delectu, & constanter, non ita omnia possunt in moralibus virtutibus, ut absq; notitia illas perficiant: at scientia in hoc negocio tam parvi momenti est ut prae illis dicantur reliqua posse totum.
units.tr: Those three things which Aristotle has just listed as necessary for the actions of the moral virtues stand in this relation: knowledge belongs to the mind or reason, choice to the appetite, and constancy and firmness to the habit, and so on. When he says, "the rest can do not a little but everything," take these words in comparison with one another, because they would not be simply true. For those other two, namely acting with choice and acting constantly, do not so contribute to the moral virtues that they bring them to completion without knowledge. Knowledge, however, is of such little weight in this matter that, in comparison with those two, the rest are said to be able to do everything.

units.la: Quae quidem ex actione frequenti rerum iusta-rum & temperatarum conualescunt.
units.tr: Which indeed grow strong through the frequent practice of just and temperate actions.

units.la: Duo ista, quae (ut dictum est) ad virtutes comparandas plurimum valent, & propter quae iusti dicimur & temperantes, ex frequentibus actionibus iustarum rerum & temperatarum corroborantur: atq; ita virtutes acquiruntur, quando principia earum fuerint comparata.
units.tr: These two things, which (as has been said) contribute most to acquiring the virtues, and on account of which we are called just and temperate, are strengthened by frequent actions of just and temperate deeds; and thus the virtues are acquired, once their principles have been put in place.

units.la: Iusta igitur & temperata dicuntur, cum talia fiunt, qualia iustus & temperatus faceret. Iustus vero ac tempetemperatus est, non qui hæc agit, sed qui certo modo agit, nempe ut iusti atque temperati faciunt. Recte itaque dicitur, eum qui agit iusta, iustum fieri: & qui temperata, temperantem. Ex istis vero prætermittendis nullus unquam futurus est probus.
units.tr: Things are therefore called just and temperate when they are done in the way a just and temperate person would do them. A person is just or temperate not because he does these things, but because he acts in a certain manner, namely as just and temperate people act. So it is rightly said that one who does just things becomes just, and one who does temperate things becomes temperate. Indeed, no one will ever become upright who neglects these things.

units.la: Sæpius mentionem facit iustarum ac temperatarum actionum: at nunc definit quænam iusta vel temperata dicat, nempe illa quæ & iusti & temperantes facerent. Quæ talia sunt, ea sic nominantur: at non qui hæc faceret, statim iustus aut temperans dicetur, sed quisquis certo quodam modo ea fecerit, nimirum quemadmodum iusti ac temperantes facerent, nempe tribus illis quas antea numerauimus conditionibus. Proinde sunt tres hominum gradus aut genera. Quidam enim adeo perditi sunt, ut nihil iusti aut temperati aut probi unquam faciant. Alii faciunt quidem, at non sunt iusti aut temperati. Postremi vero & recta faciunt, & ex virtute faciunt. Proinde recte ab initio dictum fuit, Homines iusta faciendo effici iustos: quoniam ex illis frequentibus actionibus ad bonos laudabilesq; habitus perveniitur.
units.tr: He has often mentioned the actions that are just and temperate, but now he defines what he means by just or temperate actions, namely those which a just and temperate person would perform. Such actions are so named when they are of that kind. But a person who does them is not at once called just or temperate. Rather, whoever does them in a certain way, namely as just and temperate people would do them, that is, under those three conditions we listed earlier. Accordingly there are three grades or kinds of men. Some are so depraved that they never do anything just, temperate, or upright. Others do such things, but are not just or temperate. The last do right things, and do them from virtue. Hence it was rightly said at the beginning that men become just by doing just things, since by those frequent actions one arrives at good and praiseworthy habits.

units.la: Sed hæc plerique non faciunt: ad sermones autē confugientes, se philosophari & bonos fore arbitrãtur, ægrotorum illorum similes, qui medicos utique studiosè audiunt, sed nihil eorum quæ imperantur faciunt. Vt cꝗ ij[?] corpore non bene habebunt, ita qui sic philosophantur, animo non convalescent.
units.tr: But most people do not do these things. Taking refuge in words, they think they are philosophizing and will become good, like those sick people who listen carefully to their doctors but do nothing that is prescribed. Just as such people do not get well in body, so those who philosophize in this way do not grow strong in soul.

units.la: Quid plerunq; accidat, adeo apertis verbis expressit, ut explanatione minimè sit opus. Pertinet autem quod modo agitur ad tertiam huius capitis partem: nam explodit atq; taxat hoc loco nonnullorum peruersam opinionem, qui solum verbis ac nomine Philosophiam sibi vendicabant. Et argumento à simili eam damnat
units.tr: He has expressed so plainly what usually happens that no explanation is needed. What is now being discussed belongs to the third part of this chapter, for here he rejects and censures the perverse opinion of some who claimed philosophy for themselves merely in words and by name. And by an argument from likeness he condemns it.

units.la: ID modo tantum superesset, ut quæ dubia sunt in isto capite proferam & dissoluam. Primum, cum tria memorasset, quæ adid exiguntur, ut quis iustus & temperans sit, ait, Hęc autem ad exercendum uel habendū alias artes, non requiruntur. His verbis innuit virtutes esse artes. Respondetur, non esse quidem virtutes morales artes, attamen in genere habitus cum illis convenire. Conferuntur itaq; virtutes ista cum artibus, quae tamen ista quam illae sunt habitus.
units.tr: There remains only that I set forth and resolve the doubtful points in this chapter. First, when he had mentioned the three things required for someone to be just and temperate, he says, "These, however, are not required for practicing or possessing other arts." By these words he implies that the virtues are arts. The reply is that moral virtues are indeed not arts, yet in the genus of habit they agree with arts. So the virtues are compared with arts, though these are habits in the same way as those are.

units.la: Deinde, cum ista inquit ab artibus non exigi, an artes ipsas exspoliat prorsus omni rectitudine morali? Artem quidem priuat, sed non artifice.
units.tr: Next, when he says these things are not required of the arts, does he strip the arts themselves entirely of moral rectitude? He deprives the art, but not the artist.

units.la: Nam quod attinet ad artem, illa perficiet opus, quamuis non sit in animo artificis cum virtute coniuncta. Artifex attamen ea quae facit, iusto & recto animo facere debet, illa nempe instituens ad Reipub. utilitatem, & ventium commoda, sed tamen ista praestabit, non qua artifex, sed qua probus est vir. Unde bonitas artis & moris, ut distincta est, ita debet seorsim spectari. Verum dixeris, Imo ad artem ipsam probitas moris exigitur. Si enim perturbato sit animo artifex, facile aut perdetur aut minus bonum sum opus efficiet. Sed ad componendum animum virtus moralis est necessaria. Ergo debet arti omnino adiungi. Fateor animo perturbato interdum opus artificis corrumpi; sed hoc est casu, vel (ut schola loquuntur) per accidens, in doctrina vero per se quae sunt, traduntur. Non autem hoc est perpetuo, ut artifices turbato sint animo, ideoq; absq; virtute morali poterunt bene operari, nempe cum fuerint animo tranquillo. Neq; solum per virtutes morales animus redditur serenus, quia fieri potest ut id vel tempore impetretur, vel rationis imperio, cum tamen adhuc virtus moralis non sit acquisita.
units.tr: As far as the art is concerned, it will bring the work to completion even if the artist's mind is not joined with virtue. Yet the artist ought to do what he makes with a just and upright mind, directing it to the advantage of the commonwealth and the benefit of the citizens. But he will accomplish these things not as an artist but as an upright man. Hence the goodness of the art and the goodness of character, being distinct, ought to be considered separately. You may say, "On the contrary, the uprightness of character is required for the art itself. For if the artist's mind is disturbed, he will easily either ruin his work or produce a less good product. But moral virtue is necessary for composing the mind; therefore it must be wholly joined to the art." I grant that the work of an artist is sometimes spoiled by a disturbed mind, but this happens by chance, or (as the schools put it) accidentally, whereas in the teaching of the art, what belongs to the art is handed down in itself. Yet it is not always so that artists are of troubled mind, and therefore without moral virtue they can work well, namely when their minds are calm. Nor is the mind made serene only through the moral virtues, since this can be obtained at times either by chance or by the command of reason, even when moral virtue has not yet been acquired.

units.la: Quodq;[?] habetur, Iustum & temperantem operari oportere constanter & animo immobili, non sic est accipiendum, quasi non queat iustus & temperans mutari, & quidem in habitus contrarios. Nam ut ratio imperando actus iustos & temperatos, habitum iustitiae ac temperantiae inducit: ita si praecipiat vel ex ignoratione vel ex cupiditatum vehementia iniustas & intemperatas actiones, idq; frequenter faciat, non solum priores nobiles & boni habitus delebuntur, sed contrarii inducentur. Verum id intelligitur ex collatione ad illum qui habitu careat semperq; in agendo sit varius absque ulla constantia.
units.tr: As for what is held, that the just and temperate person ought to act constantly and with an unmoved mind, this is not to be taken as though a just and temperate person cannot be changed, and indeed into contrary habits. For just as reason, by commanding just and temperate acts, induces the habit of justice and temperance, so if it commands unjust and intemperate actions, either from ignorance or from the violence of desires, and does this frequently, not only are the earlier noble and good habits destroyed, but contrary ones are introduced. But this is to be understood in comparison with the man who lacks the habit and is always varying in his actions without any constancy.

units.la: Dubitamus etiam quomodo tam parum Aristoteles videatur notitiae tribuere, quo ad morales virtutes: cum tamen prudentia, quae in notitia sita est, virtutum moralium sit rectrix, moderatrix & gubernatrix. Ad hoc respondetur, Prudentiam notitiam quidem comprehendere, sed non simplicem ac puram, verum illam quae ab appetitu pendeat, tum superiori tum inferiori. Non solum enim ad prudentiam pertinet consulere de iis quae ad finem sunt, verum consultatione conclusa imperare & quidem efficaciter, ut hoc hoc vel illud fiat. Non tantum enim concludit hoc aut illud faciundum, sed imperat ut fiat: quod non potest fieri sine voluntate, eaq; non ad id adduce-retur, nisi appetitus inferior ut cunq; domitus esset. Proinde quo modo tradit Aristoteles, non de prudentia, sed simplici notitia sunt intelligenda, ut si quis librum Ethices contemplatione quadam teneret.
units.tr: We also wonder how Aristotle seems to attribute so little to knowledge in regard to the moral virtues, since prudence, which consists in knowledge, is the director, moderator, and governor of the moral virtues. To this it is answered that prudence does indeed comprise knowledge, but not simple and pure knowledge; rather it is that which depends on appetite, both higher and lower. For it belongs to prudence not only to deliberate about the things that are toward the end, but, once deliberation is concluded, to command, and that effectively, that this or that be done. For prudence does not merely conclude that this or that ought to be done, but commands that it be done. This cannot happen without the will, and the will would not be brought to it unless the lower appetite were in some way subdued. Therefore Aristotle's account must be understood not of prudence but of simple knowledge, such as one would have by a kind of contemplation of a book of Ethics.

units.la: Præterea mirum videtur, cum ad virtutes morales, vel ad id ut quispi-am iustus & temperans dicatur, etiam circumstantiæ nimirum loci, temporis & aliarum huiusmodi rerum exigantur, Quare Aristoteles modo solum illorum trium, quæ commemorauimus, meminerit. Ad id dicimus, Quia circumstantiæ ad actionem ipsam potius videntur spectare quam ad animum, ideo non est de illis loquutus: verum ista solum tria recensuit, ut quæ ad personam magis quam ad actionem pertineant.
units.tr: Moreover, it seems strange that, for the moral virtues, or for someone to be called just and temperate, circumstances are also required, namely of place, time, and other such things, yet Aristotle mentions only those three that we have recounted. To this we say: because circumstances seem to bear upon the action itself rather than upon the mind, he did not speak of them. Rather, he listed only these three, as those that pertain to the person more than to the action.

units.la: IAM id superest, ut quæ in isto Capite habuimus, videamus an cum di-uinis literis congruant. Primum inquit posse illos qui non sunt musici & grammatici, musica & grammatica facere. Idem ostendi superius de Dauide numerare populum, & Nebucadnezare affligente Israelitas. Possumque modo istud idem confirmare, quod Pharao & Nebucadnezar prophetica somnia viderint, quamuis ipsi prophetæ non fuerint. Et Caiaphas propheticum edidit oraculum, cum tamen ipse propheta non esset. Ut illi verè iusti sunt & grammatici, qui ex habitu agunt, ita hi verè pij sunt & sancti, placentq; Deo, qui spiritu Dei ad recte agendum incitantur. Tria præterea illa quæ Aristoteles exigit, ut civiliter quispiam sit iustus & temperans, divina quoque literæ postulant. Primum oportet ut non casu sed prudenter agamus. Nam ad Romanos habetur 12. cap. Ut probetis quæ sit voluntas Dei bona, beneplacens & perfecta. Et ad Ephes. Propterea ne sitis imprudentes, sed intelligentes quæ sit voluntas Domini. Alterum, ut cum delectu agamus, & actiones bonas propter seipsas, & felicitatem ad quam natura sua sunt institutæ, non autem propter extraneas fines expetamus divina scriptura monstrat: cum Dominus dixerit Ioan. 6. quosdam se ideo sequutos, ut panibus vescerentur. Constantiam quoque animi in recte agendo exigit Deus: cum illi [illegible, ~8 letters] taxentur in Euangelio, quod instar seminis inter petrosa delapsi fructum non ferant, sed æstu Solis arescant, cum radices non egerint. Et sapientem ædificatorem Christus requirit, qui domum super petram ædificet, quam neque torrentes neque venti diruant. Inconstantes quoque vicissim confert cum iis qui ædificant in arena. Notitiæ quoque à sacris oraculis parum tribuitur. Nam sapientia hominum stultitia dicitur apud Deum. Et Paulus pronuntiat scientiam inflare, charitatem autem ædificare. Nec minus ipsam notitiam longè inferiori loco habent, quàm delectum & in agendo constantiam, cùm dicatur ad Romanos, Non auditores legis, sed factores iustificabuntur. Quæ verba confirmant quod Aristoteles dicit, eos euadere[?] quoad animum, qui tantum ad sermones conferunt sese cum agere quæ iusta sunt & temperata detrectant. Nosq; fide iustificari dicimur, sed ea fide quæ sit efficax, non ocio-sa, quaeq; (ut scribitur ad Galatas) per dilectionem operetur.
units.tr: It now remains to see whether what we have held in this chapter agrees with the divine writings. First, he says that those who are not musicians and grammarians can make music and grammar. The same thing was shown above in the case of David numbering the people, and of Nebuchadnezzar afflicting the Israelites. And I can confirm the same point: Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar saw prophetic dreams, although they themselves were not prophets. And Caiaphas uttered a prophetic oracle, although he himself was not a prophet. As those are truly just and grammarians who act from a habit, so those are truly pious and holy, and pleasing to God, who are moved by the Spirit of God to act rightly. Furthermore, the three things that Aristotle requires for someone to be just and temperate in a civic sense, the divine writings also demand. First, we must act not by chance but prudently. For in Romans 12 it is written, "That you may prove what is the good, acceptable, and perfect will of God." And in Ephesians: "Therefore do not be unwise, but understand what the will of the Lord is." Second, that we act with choice, and desire good actions for their own sake, and for the happiness for which they are by nature instituted, and not for external ends, the divine Scripture shows: the Lord said in John 6 that certain people followed him because they wanted to eat bread. God also requires constancy of mind in acting rightly, since in the Gospel those are rebuked who, like seed fallen among stones, bear no fruit but wither in the heat of the sun because they have not put down roots. And Christ seeks the wise builder who builds his house upon a rock, which neither torrents nor winds can overturn. In turn he compares the inconstant with those who build on sand. Knowledge too is little valued by the sacred oracles. For human wisdom is called foolishness before God. And Paul declares that knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. Nor do they hold knowledge in a much lower place than choice and constancy in acting, since it is said in Romans: "Not the hearers of the law, but the doers will be justified." These words confirm what Aristotle says, that those who merely bring themselves to discourse, and shrink from doing what is just and temperate, are in their soul no better off. And we are said to be justified by faith, but by a faith that is effective, not idle, and which (as it is written to the Galatians) works through love.

units.la: CAPUT V. POST hæc videndum est quid sit virtus.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. AFTER these things it must be examined what virtue is.

units.la: IAM[?] est declaratum Virtutem non inesse naturaliter in animis nostris. Adhæc principia eius patuerunt, nimirum frequentes actiones, & illæ quidem bonæ ac rationi rectæ consentientes. Et commonstratum est indicium virtutis iam partæ. Quamobrem id modo superest, ut definitio eius inquiratur. Ea vero genere constat ac differentia. Principio itaque Genus reperietur. Deinde agemus de differentia. Proponit verbis iam allatis quid tractare instituat, nempe: Quid sit Virtus.
units.tr: It has now been shown that virtue is not naturally present in our minds. Moreover, its principles have been laid open, namely frequent actions, and indeed good ones that agree with right reason. And the sign of virtue already acquired has been shown. What remains, therefore, is to inquire into its definition. A definition consists of genus and difference. First, then, the genus will be found; afterwards we shall deal with the difference. In the words already cited he sets out what he proposes to treat, namely: what virtue is.

units.la: Cum tria sint quæ oriuntur in animo, affectus, facultates, & habitus, ut aliquid horum sit virtus necesse est. Affectus appello, cupiditatem, excandescentiam, iram, metum, fiduciam, invidiam, gaudium, amicitiam, desyderium, odium, æmulationem, misericordiam: ad summam, quæ sequitur voluptas aut dolor. Facultates, ex quibus harum rerum patibiles appellamur, ut qui eis prædíti, aut irasci aut dolere aut misereri possumus. Habitus, per quos circa affectus vel bene vel male nos habemus. Quemadmodum ergo iram, si quidem vehementer aut remisse à nobis feratur, male habemus: si autem mediocriter, bene. Et ad alios affectus eodem modo.
units.tr: There are three things that arise in the mind: affections, faculties, and habits. Virtue must be one of these. By affections I mean desire, anger, rage, fear, confidence, envy, joy, friendship, longing, hatred, emulation, and pity; in short, whatever is followed by pleasure or pain. Faculties are those by which we are called capable of these feelings: we are able to be angry, to grieve, or to pity because we are endowed with them. Habits are those by which we stand well or badly with respect to the affections. Thus, if anger is directed by us too vehemently or too weakly, we stand badly; if moderately, we stand well. The same holds for the other affections.

units.la: Quoniam virtutes ad animum pertinere constat, ideo methodo pulcherrima incipit recensere quae sunt in animo. Genus n. aptissime inuenitur per diuisionem. Huius via nempe partitionis maximus est usus in inueniedis particulis definitionum, quibus inuentis compositione utimur, atq; ita uniuersa definitio explicatur. Syllogismus est a diuisione, qua ponuntur aliquot membra seu partes. Unde si duae aut tres tollantur, confirmatur quae superest. Syllogismus ita componetur.
units.tr: Since it is agreed that virtues pertain to the mind, he therefore rightly begins, by a most excellent method, to enumerate what is in the mind. For the genus is most aptly found by division. Its use, namely the method of partition, is very great in finding the parts of definitions; once these are found, we use composition, and so the whole definition is explained. A syllogism is made from division, in which several members or parts are laid down. Hence, if two or three are removed, the remaining one is confirmed. The syllogism will be composed thus.

units.la: Si virtus ad animum pertinet, aut erit affectus, aut facultas, aut habitus.
units.tr: If virtue pertains to the mind, it will be either an affection, or a faculty, or a habit.
But it is neither an affection nor a faculty.
Therefore it is a habit.

units.la: Quo ad antecedens, quod virtus ad animum pertineat, non est dubium, neq; quod illa tria sint in animo. Restant duo declaranda. Primum, An ista tria tantum sint in animo. Deinde, Assumptum est demonstrandum, virtutem neq; affectum neq; facultatem esse. Hoc secundum late prosequitur Aristoteles.
units.tr: As for the antecedent, that virtue pertains to the mind, there is no doubt, nor that those three things are in the mind. Two things remain to be shown. First, whether those three alone are in the mind. Then, the assumption must be demonstrated, that virtue is neither an affection nor a faculty. Aristotle pursues this second point at length.

units.la: Primum ergo declarabo: sed antea videtur expediendum quid ista tria sint. Primum definit Aristoteles per enumerationem partium. Declarando enim affectum, complures recesset, quod est species definitionis. Excandescentia dixi θυμὸν, Ciceronę sequutus, qui excandescentia in Tusculanis esse inquit, iram nascentem, & quae modo existat, quae a Graecis dicitur θύμωσις. Facultas est vis animi, quam vulgo in Scholis potentiam vocant. Definitur hic a causa. Quod ea instructi & adiuti, dicamur horum affectuum patibiles. Non enim possemus irasci, nisi animi vim irascentem haberemus: neque possemus cupere, nisi vi illa cupiente effemus praediti. Habitum vero declarabat ex proprio. Quod boni aut mali dicuntur, prout ad affectus se habent. Sic ordinem harum rerum contemplemur. Animus est subiectum omnium istorum trium: unde haec diuisio dicitur subiecti in accidentia. Ex animo primum pullulat quodammodo & erumpit vis aut facultas: in ea sunt deinde affectus: ad affectus adiunguntur habitus.
units.tr: I shall therefore first declare the first point, though it seems necessary first to explain what those three things are. Aristotle defines the first by enumerating its parts. For in describing the affection, he sets aside several things, which is a kind of definition. I have rendered thumos as excandescentia, following Cicero, who in the Tusculans says that excandescentia is anger arising and just now coming into being, which the Greeks call thymosis. A faculty is the power of the mind, which in the Schools is commonly called potentia. He defines it here by its cause: that we are called capable of these affections because we are equipped and aided by it. For we could not be angry unless we had a power of the mind that is angry, nor could we desire unless we were endowed with a power that desires. He described the habit from its own nature: that people are called good or bad according as they stand with respect to the affections. Let us thus consider the order of these things. The mind is the subject of all three; hence this division is called the division of subject and accidents. From the mind there first springs up and breaks forth, in a manner, the power or faculty; in it afterwards are the affections; to the affections are added the habits.

units.la: Nunc videamus an ista tantum tria sint in animo. Videtur omisisse Aristoteles conceptus, notiones, ac primos motus. Verum de toto animo in uniuersum non loquitur, sed tantum de illo qui capax est moralium virtutum, nempe inferiori appetitu. Unde si quis recte intueatur, pulcherrima methodo procedit. Pertinet virtus ad praedicamentum qualitatis: cius vero quatuor sunt genera sive species. Quartum huc non pertinet, quia est solum corporeorum, Figura inquam & forma. Supersunt igitur tres species. Prima continet habitum & διάθεσις [?], id est animi commutationem: & est fere idem quod habitus, nisi quòd inchoata est, imperfecta & inconstans. Secundum est δύναμις καὶ ἀδυναμία φυσικὴ. Et in hoc genere collocantur res, cum animi tum corporis. Corporis, vt sentiendi vis & audiendi. Ventriculus vim habet coquendi cibos. Epar faciendi sanguinem. Cor calefaciendi corpus. Inanimata quoq; sunt viribus huiusmodi praedita. Vt elleborū purgat, Herculeus lapis ferrum trahit. Atq; de iis facultatibus abundè luculenterq; loquutus est Galenus de vtilitate partium, & in lib. de naturalibus facultatibus. Atq; iste vires animi sunt instrumenta: vt enim corpore vtimur variis organis ad aliquid agendum, sic animus iis facultatibus vtitur. Quibus opposita est ἀδυναμία: Ea verò est illarum priuatio. Spectat etiā ad hanc speciem Qualitatis Proprietas, vt risibilitas, capacitas disciplinae, & similia: nam ista reuera sunt eadem cum prioribus. Tertia species est ποιὸν τῆς παθητικῆς καὶ πάθος [?]. Qualitates patibiles illæ sunt, quæ vel animum vel corpus afficiunt. Corpus, vt calor, frigus, sic cum, humidum, &c. Animum verò, vt tristitia, læta, terribilia. Aut ex affectu oriuntur, quo ad animum, vt insania ex magna tristitia: quo ad corpus, vt nigror in Aethiope, ab æstu. Ista enim animum grauiter afficiunt. πάθος huc facit, & est subitus, siue quo ad corpus siue quo ad animum. In animo, vt metus, spes, laetitia. Quoad corpus, vt pallor ex metu, rubor ex verecundia. Ergo τὰ πάθη sunt motus animi subiti, vt laetitia, tristitia, gaudium. Ista tres species Qualitatis huc spectant, & eas Aristoteles commemorauit. Reliquit conceptiones, notiones, et collationes: quoniam illæ sunt partis animi intelligentis. Actiones non nominauit, quia non sunt firmæ, sed transeunt: neq; sunt in praedicamento qualitatis, sed Actionis. Primi autem motus renocantur ad affectus, siue ad τὰ πάθη.
units.tr: Now let us see whether these three alone are in the mind. Aristotle seems to have omitted concepts, notions, and first motions. But he does not speak of the whole mind in general, only of that part which is capable of the moral virtues, namely the lower appetite. Hence, if one regards this rightly, he proceeds by a most excellent method. Virtue belongs to the category of quality, and of this there are four kinds or species. The fourth does not belong here, since it applies only to bodily things: shape and form, I mean. There remain therefore three species. The first contains the habit and disposition (diathesis), that is, a change of the mind; it is almost the same as habit, except that it is incipient, imperfect, and inconstant. The second is power and natural impotence (dynamis kai adynamia physike). In this kind are placed things both of the mind and of the body. Of the body, such as the power of sensing and of hearing. The stomach has the power of digesting food; the liver of making blood; the heart of warming the body. Inanimate things too are endowed with powers of this kind: hellebore purges, the Herculean stone attracts iron. Galen has spoken abundantly and clearly of these faculties in his work On the Usefulness of the Parts and in the book On the Natural Faculties. And these powers of the mind are instruments: just as we use the body's various organs to do something, so the mind uses these faculties. Opposed to them is impotence (adynamia), which is their privation. To this species of quality also belongs property, such as the capacity for laughter, the capacity for learning, and the like; for these are in fact the same as the former. The third species is quality of the passible and passion (poion tes pathetikes kai pathos). These are the passible qualities, which affect either the mind or the body. Of the body, such as heat, cold, moisture, and so on. Of the mind, such as sadness, gladness, and terrors. Or they arise from an affection, as far as the mind is concerned, as madness arises from great sadness; as far as the body is concerned, as blackness in the Ethiopian arises from heat. For these affect the mind gravely. Passion (pathos) belongs here too, and it is sudden, whether with regard to the body or to the mind. In the mind it is such as fear, hope, and gladness; in the body, such as pallor from fear, redness from shame. Therefore the passions (ta pathē) are sudden motions of the mind, such as gladness, sadness, and joy. These three species of quality pertain here, and Aristotle has mentioned them. He has left out conceptions, notions, and comparisons, since these belong to the intellectual part of the mind. He did not name actions, because they are not stable but pass away; nor are they in the category of quality but of action. First motions, however, are referred to the affections, or to the passions (ta pathē).

units.la: Iis ita expositis, nunc videndæ sunt rationes, quibus probatur virtus & vitium non esse affectus. Rationes sunt quatuor.
units.tr: With these things thus set out, we must now consider the reasons by which it is proved that virtue and vice are not affections. There are four reasons.

units.la: Atq; adeò neque uirtutes neque uitia sunt affectus: quoniā propter has perturbationes neq; probi neque praui dicimur: at ex uirtutibus & uitijs ita uocamur. Et ob istos affectus neq; laudamur neq; uituperamur: nam qui timet aut irascitur, nō laudatur, sed qui certo modo. Ex uirtutibus autē & uitijs laudamur & uituperamur. Præterea irascimur & metuimus absque delectu. Virtutes autem electiones quædam sunt, aut non citra electionē. Ad hęc ex affectibus moveri dicimur: at ex virtutibus & vitiis non moveri, sed quodammodo affici.
units.tr: And so neither virtues nor vices are affections, since on account of these perturbations we are not called good or bad; but we are called so from virtues and vices. And on account of these affections we are neither praised nor blamed; for one who fears or is angry is not praised, but one who is so in a certain way is. We are praised and blamed for virtues and vices. Moreover, we are angry and afraid without choice, whereas virtues are certain choices, or at least not without choice. Again, we are said to be moved by affections, but not moved by virtues and vices; rather, we are said to be affected by them in a certain manner.

units.la: Primaratio est bonos & pravos nullos dici affectibus, cùm tamen ex virtutibus vel pravi vel recti prædicemur.
units.tr: The first reason is that good and bad people are not called such from their affections, whereas we are called bad or upright from our virtues.

units.la: Secunda, Ob istos affectus non laudamur neq; vituperamur. Ex virtutibus autem aut vitiis aut laudamur aut vituperamur. Ergo, Virtutes & vitia non sunt affectus. Mirum videtur ita loqui Aristotelem, cùm de inuenibus dicatur eorum pudorem laudari. Erubuit, salua res est. Laudantur etiam audentes, nec non aliquando irascentes. Ad hoc respondemus, cum si quis recte intelligat, recte scribere: nam fatetur laudari cum qui timeat & irascatur certo modo, at non simpliciter vel timeat vel irascatur. Nec illi affectus certi sunt aut moderati, nisi ex virtute. Ideo irascens aut timens certo modo, laudatur non simpliciter ex affectu, sed ex modo. Consentiunt quae hic dicuntur de laude, cum 12.cap. primi lib. Vbi laus iis datur, quae idonea sunt ad finem adipiscendam. Non enim laudantur dii aut beatitudo sed honore afficiuntur, & beati dicuntur. Virtus praecipuè digna laude judicatur. Stoici non laudarent irascentem aut metuentem certo modo, quandoquidem omnem affectum à sapiente viro excludunt. Tertia ratio est. Affectus non subiiciuntur electioni, virtus autem aut electio est, aut non citra electionem. Hic obiter attendendum, virtutem nō esse electionem, quum electio sit actio, & virtus (vt modò probatur) sit habitus. At non citra electionem est: quia per virtutem sequimur media, & vitamus extrema, quod fit deligendo. Prius enim adiuti prudentia, consultamus: deinde adhibita electione agimus.
units.tr: Second: on account of these affections we are neither praised nor blamed. But from virtues or vices we are either praised or blamed. Therefore virtues and vices are not affections. It seems strange that Aristotle speaks thus, since it is said of young men that their shame is praised: "he blushed, so the thing is safe." Those who dare are also praised, and sometimes those who are angry. To this we reply, if one understands rightly, that he writes rightly: for he admits that one who fears or is angry in a certain way is praised, but not one who simply fears or is simply angry. Nor are those affections certain or moderate except through virtue. Therefore one who is angry or afraid in a certain way is praised not simply for the affection, but for the manner. What is said here about praise agrees with chapter 12 of the first book, where praise is given to those things that are fit for attaining the end. For gods and blessedness are not praised, but are honoured, and are called blessed. Virtue is judged especially worthy of praise. The Stoics would not praise one who is angry or afraid in a certain way, since they exclude every affection from the wise man. Third reason: affections are not subject to choice, whereas virtue is either a choice or not without choice. Here we must note in passing that virtue is not a choice, since choice is an action, and virtue (as has just been proved) is a habit. But it is not without choice, because through virtue we pursue the means and avoid the extremes, which is done by choosing. For first, aided by prudence, we deliberate; then, having applied choice, we act.

units.la: Quarta ratio. Affectibus movemur: nam illi sunt animi quidam motus & impulsus. At virtute non movemur, sed potius dicimur illa affici. Hoc ideo scribitur, quoniam virtutes tranquillitates potius quaedam sunt animi, quàm motus: illum quippè serenant & pacatum reddunt. Ideo forma loquendi obtinuit, ut virtutibus affici dicamur, non moveri. Nam illis inclinamur, & propensi reddimur ad honesta, non impellimur.
units.tr: Fourth reason: we are moved by the affections, for these are certain motions and impulses of the mind. But we are not moved by virtue; rather we are said to be affected by it. This is written because the virtues are rather certain tranquillities of the mind than motions, since they calm it and make it peaceful. Hence the form of speech has prevailed that we are said to be affected by the virtues, not moved. For we are inclined by them and made disposed to what is honourable; we are not impelled.

units.la: Ob easdem causas non sunt facultates. Nec enim boni dicimur nec mali, neque laudamur neque vituperamur, quod simpliciter insit nobis agendi facultas. Insuper facultas in nobis a natura, non ite bonitas et prauitas, quod ante diximus. Quod si virtutes neque sint affectus neque facultates, relinquitur ut sint habitus. Quod nam sit genus virtutis ostendimus.
units.tr: For the same reasons, virtues are not faculties. For we are not called good or bad on account of them, nor are we praised or blamed, since the capacity to act is simply innate in us. Moreover, faculties are in us from nature, but goodness and wickedness are not, as we said before. If virtues are neither affections nor faculties, it remains that they are habits. What kind of genus virtue belongs to we have shown.

units.la: Eadem, inquit, rationes quae demonstrarunt virtutem non esse affectum probant etiam illam non esse vim aut facultatem naturalem animi. Quia nullus aut prauus aut bonus dicitur, quod has facultates habeat, neque dan-tur nobis ex delectu quopiam. Sed aliam peculiarem probationem hac de re producit. Quoniam, inquit, has vires a natura sortimur. Non autem probi nascimur, sed efficimur. Idq; se ait antea dixisse. Nam in principio 2. huius libri, demonstrauit virtutes non inesse a natura hominibus: quoniam si natura essemus virtute praediti, non possemus aliter assuescere. Concludit vir-tutem esse habitum, quum neque sit affectus, neque naturalis animi facultas. Cumq; oppositorum sit idem genus, probatum etiam est vitium ad habitum reuocari, tanquam ad genus. Patuit etiam ex his virtutem moralem de qua in praesentia loquimur, versari circa affectus, ut qui sint eius quodammodo materia.
units.tr: "The same reasons," he says, "which proved that virtue is not an affection also prove that it is not a natural power or faculty of the mind, since no one is called wise or wicked because he has these faculties, and they are not given to us by any choice. But he brings forward another, peculiar proof of this matter. Since, he says, we receive these powers from nature. But we are not born good; we are made so." And he says he had said this before: in the beginning of the second book of this work he showed that virtues are not present in men by nature, since if we were endowed with virtue by nature we could not become accustomed to it otherwise. He concludes that virtue is a habit, since it is neither an affection nor a natural faculty of the mind. And since opposites belong to the same genus, it has also been proved that vice is traced back to habit as to its genus. It is also clear from these things that moral virtue, of which we are speaking at present, is concerned with the affections, as they are in some sense its matter.

units.la: Nunc videndum est quomodo Aristotelis hac dicta cum divinis literis vel consentiant vel dissentiant. Collocauit in animo tria quae ad virtutem pertineat, affectum, vim naturalem, & habitū: at praeterijt dona spiritus sancti, nempe spiritum fortitudinis, spiritum timoris, & afflatus Dei, quibus ad recte agendum incitamur. Hęc naturam vincunt: ideo ab Aristotele non fuere cognita. Nos vero quum illa simus edocti, precibus a Deo ipsa ef-flagitemus. Virtus non est illa duo, affectus inquam & naturalis vis. Er-go erit habitus acquisitus, ut ille intelligit, bonis actionibus, quum frequen-tes fuerint. Non est firma hæc illatio. Nam fides, spes, charitas, & multa a-lia virtutes non sunt eiusmodi habitus, verum a Deo repente afflantur re-generatis. Statuit praeterea nos ex affectibus non dici prauos neque vituperari. Quod non conceditur. Quia non tantum affectus, imo etiam primi motus, quando feruntur contra legem Dei, peccata sunt: nam peccatum est quicquid illi summae regulae aduersatur. Unde Paulus ad Rom. conquereba-tur, se aliam legem sentire in membris, quae pugnaret cum lege mentis, dolebatque se venundatum sub peccato, seque infelicem clamabat, quod ita ca-ptiuaretur ptiuaretur sub eiusmodi lege. Vnde illud etiam liquet, non esse verum, motus illos prauos & malos affectus non esse vitia: quia cadunt sub electione.
units.tr: Now we must see how the sayings of Aristotle agree or disagree with the divine letters. He placed in the mind three things that pertain to virtue: affection, natural power, and habit. But he passed over the gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely the spirit of fortitude, the spirit of fear, and the inspiration of God, by which we are stirred to act rightly. These overcome nature, and therefore they were not known to Aristotle. But we, since we have been taught them, ask God for them in prayer. Virtue is not those two things, affection and natural power, I mean. Therefore it will be an acquired habit, as he understands it, arising from good actions when they have been frequent. This inference is not firm. For faith, hope, charity, and many other virtues are not habits of this kind, but are breathed into the regenerate suddenly by God. He further asserts that we are not called wicked or blamed on account of our affections. This is not granted, because not only the affections but even the first motions, when they are carried against the law of God, are sins; for sin is whatever opposes that supreme rule. Hence Paul in Romans complained that he perceived another law in his members, which fought against the law of his mind, and he grieved that he was sold under sin, and cried out that he was wretched, because he was held captive under such a law. Hence it is also clear that it is not true that those evil motions and bad affections are not vices, because they fall under choice.

units.la: Quia si virtus hominis esset quæ deberet, non solum plenas actiones, verùm etiam perfectos illos motus in nostra potestate haberemus, & ob peccatum ἀταξίᾳ[?] hæc inuecta fuit, qua deficimus à præcepto, quo iubemur diligere Deum tota corde, toto anima, & omnib. viribus. Paulus sq; ab iis motibus ceu à vitiis liberari cupiebat. Virtutibus, inquit, non mouemur, sed potius afficimur, cùm affectibus potissimum moueamur. Ista facile dabimus, si tamen concedatur probos, pios & sanctos viros Dei spiritu moueri: siquidem Apostolus dicit, Qui Dei spiritu aguntur, hi sunt filij Dei. Virtutes postremò tradit in nobis à natura non inesse, eò quòd efficiamur boni, non nascamur. Hæc uera sunt. si tamè addideris nos à Deo effici bonos, præsertim quo ad primam regenerationem. Ille quoque verarum virtutum est elargitor: hæc à natura non habemus. Neque nunc, quando per peccatum omnia propemodum corrupta sunt, neque à prima institutione, quia etiam tunc Deus ipse fauore ac gratia sua veras dedit Adamo virtutes, & donis suis cumpulcherrimis ornauit. Instaurati nihilominus ac regenerati gratiæ ac spiritui Dei cooperamur, & habitus istos virtutum acquirimus, unde reparamur & reddimur quotidie meliores, quare Paulus Philipp. hortabatur, ut su-amipsorum salutem operarentur.
units.tr: For if human virtue were such as it ought to be, we would have not only complete actions but also those perfect motions in our power; but through sin this disorder (ataxia) was introduced, by which we fall away from the precept by which we are commanded to love God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and all our strength. Paul also longed to be freed from those motions as from vices. "We are not moved by virtues," he says, "but rather affected, when we are chiefly moved by affections." We will readily grant these things, if it is nevertheless conceded that the upright, pious and holy men of God are moved by the Spirit of God, since the Apostle says: "Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God." Lastly, he teaches that virtues are not present in us by nature, because we are made good, not born so. These things are true, if you add that we are made good by God, especially as to the first regeneration. He is also the bestower of true virtues; these we do not have from nature, neither now, when almost all things have been corrupted through sin, nor from the first institution, because even then God himself gave Adam true virtues by his favour and grace and adorned him with his most beautiful gifts. Nevertheless, restored and regenerated, we cooperate with the grace and Spirit of God, and we acquire those habits of virtue, by which we are repaired and made better every day; wherefore Paul in Philippians exhorted that they work out their own salvation.
CHAPTER VI.

units.la: AT non modo sic dicendum, uirtutem esse habi-tum, sed qualis nam sit. Dicendum quidem uirtutem omnem efficere, ut id cuius est, bene habeat, & opus suum bene præstet. Vt oculi uirtus, & oculum ipsum, & opus eius bonum facit, nam uirtute oculorum bene uidemus: identidem uirtus equi, bonum facit equum idoneum quie ad currendum & ad gestandum sessorem, & expectandos hostes. Atque hoc quum in omnibus ita se habeat, & hominis itaque uirtus habitus erit, per quem homo bonus evadat, & per què opus suum bonum præstet. Quomodo autem id contingat, iam diximus, & adhuc i-ta fiet manifestius.
units.tr: But it is not enough to say that virtue is a habit; we must also say what kind of habit it is. It must be said that every virtue makes the thing it belongs to be in good condition and perform its work well. Thus the virtue of the eye makes the eye itself good, and its work too, for by the virtue of the eyes we see well. Likewise the virtue of a horse makes the horse good and fit for running, for carrying a rider, and for facing enemies. Since this holds true in all things, human virtue will also be a habit through which a man becomes good and through which he performs his work well. We have already said how this comes about, and it will become clearer still.

units.la: DIducitur in quatuor praecipua membra istud caput. Primo, quādam virtutis proprietatem exponit. Secundo, circa mediocritatem illam versari statuit. Tertio definitionem eius concludit. Postremo aliquos affectus esse ostendit, qui mediocritatem non recipiant. Quod attinet ad primum, iam genus virtutis est deprehensum, nunc debet contrahi differentia, ut materia forma clauditur, & definita continetur. Ad hanc differentiam inquirendam, conducit virtutis ipsius communis generaliter accepta proprietate cognoscere: nam proprietates ad ipsas differentias nos adducunt. Virtutis, ut omnibus est communis, hoc est proprium, ut id in quo est reddat bonum & opus eius absoluat, perficiat & expediat. Probatur genere quodam inductionis, quo ad oculum & equum, & in caeteris omnib. sic se habere dicitur. Quare concluditur & in homine ita esse debere. Quibus verbis definitionem quandam generalem virtutis aut potius descriptionem ad hominem accommodat seu ad virtutem humanam, de qua in praesentia sermo est institutus. Et ait hominis virtutem esse, quae illum probum faciat & reddat eius opus rectum. Antea, inquit, quomodo fiat [?] hoc diximus, nempe superius, quando virtutem ipsam oriri dixit ex actionibus, non quibusuis, verum mediocribus, capite secundo. Ubi declarauit quomodo actiones humanae exuperantia & defectu corrumpantur, mediocritate vero seruentur. Mirum tamen videri potest, si declarauit hoc eo loco, quomodo nunc id repetendum censeat. Id ob eam causam repetit, quia tum commemorauit solum, at non explicuit. Mediocritas etiam ipsa tunc non est distincta, ut alia sit quo ad rem, & alia quo ad rationem si-ne quo ad nos. Id nunc est faciundum, ut videamus quod nam genus medii virtus capiet. Et certe si medium sumitur e definitione virtutis, ea nunquam euadet clara et dilucida, nisi et mediocritas definiatur. At cum sit mul-tiplex, prius fuit distinguenda.
units.tr: This chapter falls into four principal parts. First, it sets out a property of virtue. Second, it establishes that virtue lies in that mean. Third, it concludes the definition of virtue. Last, it shows that some affections do not admit of a mean. As to the first part, the genus of virtue has already been grasped; now the difference must be drawn out, so that the form is enclosed as the matter is, and the defined thing is contained. To inquire into this difference, it helps to know the property of virtue taken generally, as common to all virtues, for properties lead us to the differences themselves. The property common to all virtue is this: that it makes good the thing in which it is, and completes, perfects and facilitates its work. This is proved by a kind of induction, in the case of the eye and the horse, and it is said to hold likewise in all other things. Hence it is concluded that it must be so in man too. In these words he adapts a general definition, or rather description, of virtue to man, that is, to human virtue, which is the subject now under discussion. He says that human virtue is that which makes a man upright and renders his work right. Earlier, he says, we stated how this happens, namely above, when he said that virtue arises from actions, not from any actions but from moderate ones, in the second chapter. There he showed how human actions are corrupted by excess and defect, but preserved by moderation. It may seem strange that, having explained this there, he now thinks it must be repeated. He repeats it for this reason: then he only mentioned it and did not explain it. Moreover, the mean itself was not then distinguished, so that it is one thing in itself and another in relation to us. This must now be done, so that we may see what kind of mean virtue will take. Certainly, if the mean is taken from the definition of virtue, that definition will never become clear and plain unless the mean is also defined. But since the mean is manifold, it had first to be distinguished.

units.la: In omni utiq; continuo ac diuisibili sumere licet quod maius est, quod minus, quod aequale, idque uel quo ad rem ipsam, uel quo ad nos. Aequale medium quiddam est exuperantiae ac defectus. Medium itaque rei appello, quod ab utroq; extremorum æqualiter distat, quod & unum est & idem omnibus. Quo ad nos vero, quod neque redundat, neque deficit plus quam oporteat: atque hoc neque unum est neque idem apud omnes. Quemadmo-dum si decem multa fuerint, duo vero pauca, sex accipient media quo ad rem: nam ex æquo excedunt et exceduntur. Est autem hoc medium iuxta proporti-onem arithmeticam. At medium quo ad nos, non ita sumendum est. Non enim si decem minas edere multum est, & duas parum, sex minas imperabit ali-ptes: nam sumpturo vel nimium vel parum fortas-sis esset. Miloni enim parum esset, illi vero qui se in-cipit exercere, nimium esset. Similiter q; res habet in cursu & palæstra.
units.tr: In every continuous and divisible thing one may take what is greater, what is less, and what is equal, and this either in the thing itself or in relation to us. The equal is a kind of mean between excess and defect. I call the mean of the thing that which is equally distant from either extreme, and which is one and the same for everyone. In relation to us, the mean is that which neither exceeds nor falls short more than is fitting, and this is neither one nor the same for everyone. For example, if ten is many and two is few, six will be the mean in the thing itself, since it exceeds and is exceeded by equal amounts. This mean accords with arithmetical proportion. But the mean in relation to us must not be taken in this way.
