For if ten minae of food is much and two is little, a trainer will not prescribe six minae, for that would be either too much or too little for the one who is to take it. It would be too little for Milo, but too much for someone just beginning to train. It is the same in running and wrestling.

units.la: Quod medium in rerum natura dandum sit, ex eo probat, quòd in continuo quouis & diuisibili reperitur maius & minus & æquale. Hoc tanquam perspicuum & clarum accipit, & quod probatione minime indigeat, ipsum autem æquale vocat medium. Ita componatur syllogismus:
units.tr: He proves that a mean must exist in the nature of things from the fact that in any continuous and divisible thing one finds the greater, the less and the equal. He takes this as plain and clear, needing no proof, and he calls the equal itself the mean. The syllogism is composed thus:

units.la: Sicut in continuo & diuisibiles habet, ita in affectibus humanis & habitibus.
units.tr: As it is in the continuous and divisible, so it is in human affections and habits.

units.la: Sed in continuo est maius, minus & medium.
units.tr: But in the continuous there is the greater, the less and the mean.

units.la: Igitur ista eadem reperiuntur in affectibus & habitibus.
units.tr: Therefore the same things are found in affections and habits.

units.la: Non tantum dixit in continuo, sed etiam adiecit diuisibili, ut unà cum continuo etiam numeros comprehenderet, nam & illi diuidi possunt: imò Aristoteles (ut videbimus) de numeris exempla sua desumet. Methodo Aristoteles utitur admodum congrua, quia ex rebus quæ sentiuntur, ut sunt magnitudines & numeri, ostendit quæ sensu non possunt attingi.
units.tr: He did not say only "in the continuous" but also added "divisible", so that along with the continuous he might include numbers too, for these also can be divided. Indeed Aristotle (as we shall see) will take his examples from numbers. Aristotle uses a very apt method, since from things that are perceived, such as magnitudes and numbers, he shows what cannot be grasped by the senses.

units.la: Distinguitur autem medium, in id quod sit rei, & medium quo ad nos. Rei medium est, quod æqualiter ab utroque distat extremorum. Medium vero quo ad nos definitur, quod neque redundet neque deficiat plusquam oporteat. Prius medium, nempe rei, unum est idemq; apud omnes, quia nostra intelligentia rem ipsam non mutat: utcunque enim referas illam, eadem est. Hoc autem genus proportionis, medij inquam ad extrema secundum rem, appellat arithmeticam, hac de causa (vt arbitror) quia numeri sunt inuariabiles, neque vnquam suam vel naturam vel definitionem mutant. Proportio autem nihil aliud est, quam collatio inter se magnitudinum aut numerorum. Exemplum Aristotelis numeris constat. Nam in denario videre licet maius & minus. Vt decem & duo, inter ista medium secundum rem sunt sex: nam excedunt duo quaternario, & vincuntur itidem à decem, quaternario: atq; proportio haec arithmetica est, nō potest mutari, neq; vnquā variabitur. Nam sex ad duo & ad decem aeternum sic se habent. Sed medium quo ad nos, haud est huius generis: quoniam inter se conferuntur duae rationes, seu duae proportiones, magnitudinum & numerorum. Vt quemadmodum se habet sex ad tria, ita se habent 4. ad 2. nam vtrobique ratio est vel proportio dupla. Eademq; proportio est inter nouem & tria, & inter quatuor & duodecim: nam vtrobique tripla. Ita trium ad duo, & nouem ad sex proportio eadem: quia vtrobiq; sexquialtera. Dicitur ista proportio Geometrica. In arithmetica consyderatur paritas seu imparitas interualli ab extremis. Geometra vero similitudinem rationis aut proportionis diuersorum numerorum inter se.
units.tr: The mean is distinguished into the mean of the thing and the mean in relation to us. The mean of the thing is that which is equally distant from either extreme. The mean in relation to us is defined as that which neither exceeds nor falls short more than is fitting. The former mean, that of the thing, is one and the same for all, because our understanding does not change the thing itself: however you regard it, it is the same. This kind of proportion, I mean that of the mean to the extremes according to the thing, he calls arithmetical, for this reason (I think), that numbers are invariable and never change either their nature or their definition. Proportion is nothing other than the comparison of magnitudes or numbers with one another. Aristotle's example is drawn from numbers. For in the number ten one can see the greater and the less. Thus, of ten and two, the mean according to the thing is six: two exceeds four by four, and is likewise exceeded by ten by four. This arithmetical proportion cannot be changed and will never vary, for six stands in the same relation to two and to ten for ever. But the mean in relation to us is not of this kind, since two ratios or two proportions of magnitudes and numbers are compared with each other. As six is to three, so four is to two, for in both cases the ratio or proportion is double. The same proportion holds between nine and three, and between four and twelve, for in both it is triple. So the proportion of three to two is the same as that of nine to six, since in both it is sesquialtera (one and a half times). This proportion is called geometrical. In arithmetic one considers the equality or inequality of the interval from the extremes; the geometer considers the similarity of the ratio or proportion between different numbers.

units.la: Atq; hac ratione, inquit, vtuntur in gymnasijs. Cibus ijs qui se exercebant dabatur diuersis mensuris, pro vt robore ac viribus illi praditi erant, qui sumpturi essent. Consueuisse autem veteres ad pondus certum panes dare, Cato de re rustica testatur, qui iussit vt compeditis darentur quatuor pōdo panis in diem per hyemem, sed quando vineam fodere inciperent quinq; pondo darentur, quo ad ficus maturuissent, tum iubebat vt ad quatuor redi retur. Mina vero medica, qua etiam aliptae vtebantur, sexdecim vncias habuit, cum libra communis comprehenderet duodecim. Dicitur autem hoc genus medij quo ad nos, quia non aestimatur quo ad extrema vel magnitudinis vel numeri, sed quo ad nos, id est, ad nostras uires, vel ad nostrum temperamentum. Vt sicut se habet robur athletarum, ita cibus est illis ministrandus. At robur Milonis vincit duplo robur tyronis. Ergo cibus eius debet esse duplo copiosior. Idē quoq; in re medica seruari debet, vt pharmaci vis ad aegroti robur temperetur. Virtutis autem medium hoc modo statuet Aristoteles captandum, sicut mox audiemus.
units.tr: And, he says, they use this method in the gymnasia. Food for those who trained was given in different measures, according to the strength and vigour of those who were to take it. Cato, in his work on agriculture, testifies that the ancients were accustomed to give bread by a fixed weight. He ordered that those in fetters be given four pounds of bread a day through the winter, but when they began to dig the vineyard, five pounds were to be given, and when the figs had ripened he ordered a return to four. The Median mina, which trainers also used, had sixteen ounces, whereas the common pound comprised twelve. This kind of mean is called relative to us, because it is not estimated with respect to the extremes of magnitude or number, but with respect to us, that is, to our strength or to our constitution. So just as the strength of athletes is, so must their food be provided. But Milo's strength is twice that of a beginner, so his food should be twice as abundant. The same must be observed in medicine, that the force of a drug be tempered to the strength of the patient. Aristotle will prescribe that the mean of virtue be sought in this way, as we shall hear presently.

units.la: Nunc vero quod ad verba & exempla spectat, Aliptem appellauit magistrum gymnicum, à verbo ἀλείφω, quod est ungo. Nam huius praeceptoris e-rat athletas suos vngere, cum ad certandum erant progressuri. Et Milo Crotoniata satis est celebratus ab omnibus propemodum bonis scriptoribus. Vicit saepius. sæpius in Olympiacis certaminibus & Pythijs. Supposuit humeros parieti schola Pythagoræ cùm iam rueret, ne magister cum discipulis ruina obrueretur. Sed tandem cùm aperire vellet fissam quercum, miserè periit, vt Val. Maximus lib. 9. & alij tradunt. Quamuis Cicero hanc sententiam de senectute minimè sequitur, imò illum ait senem, cùm spectaret gladiatores certantes, respexisse suos lacertos & ingemuisse, dicendo, At ij mortui sunt. Plura quoq; alia de illo eodem tradit Plinius lib. 7. quæ in præsentia non referam: nam ibi Lectores ea per seipsos poterunt cognoscere.
units.tr: Now as to the words and examples: he called the gymnastic trainer the "aliptes," from the verb ἀλείφω, which means to anoint. For it was this trainer's duty to anoint his athletes when they were about to go into the contest. Milo of Croton is celebrated by almost all the good writers. He won many times at the Olympic and Pythian games. When the school of Pythagoras was already collapsing, he propped his shoulders against the wall, so that the master and his disciples would not be crushed by the ruin. But at last, when he tried to split an oak tree open, he perished wretchedly, as Valerius Maximus (book 9) and others relate. Cicero, however, does not follow this account in his book on old age. On the contrary, he says that the old man, watching gladiators fight, looked at his own arms and groaned, saying, "But these men are dead." Pliny (book 7) relates many other things about the same man, which I will not report here, since readers can learn them for themselves from that place.

units.la: Sed cùm affectus humani sint in prædicamento qualitatis, animiq; acti-ones vel sint in eodem, vel in categoria actionis, mirum quomodo ab Aristotele cum magnitudinibus & rebus partibilibus conferantur. Quandoquidem partitio seu diuisio proprietas est quantitatis. Ad hoc respondet Græcus interpres, ista similia esse magnitudini, & habere maius & minus & medium: propter tempus ergo ea metimur: ipsum enim ad quantitatem spectat, & est partibile. Sed hoc non est satis. Fieri enim potest vt quis momento temporis irascendo vehementer, plus à medio recedat, grauiusq; pec-cet quàm alter, qui vel triduo irascatur aliquanto remissius. Ideò sciendum quasdam esse qualitates, quæ rationem quandam subeant magnitudinis: possunt enim vel contentiores vel remissiores fieri: habent suos gradus, per quos incrementum aut diminutionem accipiunt: suntq; affectus hoc pacto maiores aut minores. Ad hæc penes circumstantias loci personæ aut ætatis, medium variis modis æstimatur, atque defectus & excessus iuxta easdem variantur, vt non semper sint idem. Non itaq; absurdum est, iis rationibus qualitates actionésue parturi posse ac diuidi.
units.tr: But although human affections belong to the category of quality, and the actions of the mind belong either to the same category or to the category of action, it is strange how Aristotle compares them with magnitudes and divisible things, since partition or division is a property of quantity. To this the Greek interpreter replies that these things are similar to magnitude, and have a greater, a lesser, and a mean; therefore we measure them by time, for time pertains to quantity and is divisible. But this is not enough. For it can happen that someone, by being angry violently for a moment, departs further from the mean and sins more gravely than another who is angry for three days, but more mildly. So we must recognise that some qualities take on a certain kind of magnitude: they can become more intense or more relaxed, they have their degrees by which they receive increase or decrease, and in this way affections are greater or less. Moreover, the mean is judged in various ways according to the circumstances of place, person, or age, and the deficiencies and excesses vary in accordance with these, so that they are not always the same. It is therefore not absurd that qualities or actions can be measured and divided by these standards.

units.la: Ita quemadmodum est scientia prædītus, exupe-rantiam & defectum euitat, & quod medium est quæ-rit ac deligit, medium inquam non quo ad rem, sed quo ad nos. Si itaque omnis scientia medium spe-ctando, & in ipsum opus dirigendo, illud absoluit. (Unde consueuerunt de operibus dicitare quæ be ne habent, neque illis adimi posse neque addi quic-quam, quasi exuperantia & defectus quod bene ha-bet corrumpant, mediocritas uero conseruet:) Siq[?] boni artifices, ut dicimus, ad hoc ipsum intuentes operantur:virtusq;[?] arte quauis praestantior & melior est, quemadmodum & natura, medii utiq; sectatrix erit. De morali autem virtute loquor.
units.tr: Thus, just as one who possesses knowledge avoids excess and deficiency, and seeks and chooses the mean, the mean I say not with respect to the thing but with respect to us, so every science, by looking to the mean and directing its work toward it, completes that work. (Hence they are accustomed to say of works that are well made that nothing can be taken from them or added to them, as if excess and deficiency corrupt what is well made, while mediocrity preserves it.) If good craftsmen, as we say, work with this very aim in view, and virtue is more excellent and better than any art, just as it is than nature, then virtue too will be a pursuer of the mean. I am speaking of moral virtue.

units.la: Probaturus est, virtutem sectari medium quo ad nos, & non secundum rationem. Quod primo concludit argumento a minori.
units.tr: He is going to prove that virtue pursues the mean with respect to us, and not according to reason. He first concludes this by an argument from the lesser.

units.la: Si ars & natura medium huiusmodi quaerunt, & virtus moralis idem quaeret.
units.tr: If art and nature seek a mean of this kind, then moral virtue will also seek it.
But art and nature do this.
Therefore virtue will pursue a mean of this kind.

units.la: Argumentum a minori firmum est: quia & ars & natura sunt virtute indigniores. De natura, quod medium sequatur, haud obscurum est in cibo & potu, nam exuperantia horum & defectus perdunt animantia. Often-dunt haec quoq; temperamenta corporum. Si enim calor aut frigus, humor aut siccitas superauerint, illico aegrotamus. Et naturam arte maiorem esse, certissimum est, cum haec sit illius imitatrix. Nunc videndum quare sit inferior virtute. Virtus est natura perfectio: nam virtus, ut audiuimus, id cuius est virtus, bonum reddit, & illius opus perficit. Adhaec nullus virtutibus male uti potest, cum permulti naturalibus facultatibus pessime abu-tantur. Artem vero sequi medium, calceator demonstrat, qui calceum curat neq; maiorem neq; minorem pede facere. Itidem faber maiore minoremue do-mu non facit quam architectus constituerit. Arator neq; plus neq; minus quam par sit, aratrum sub terram demittit. Dicitur nihilominus ars non tantum sequi medium, sed optimum: medium quidem sectatur inter exuperantiam & defectum. Sed quo ad opus, optimum conatur & praestantissimum illud efficere. Neq; ista inter sese pugnant. Virtutem autem esse arte longe melio-rem multis modis probatur. Primo perficit quidem ars quoquo modo animum, sed non ut virtus: quod ipsum non reddit meliore. Imo permulti sunt aliquando viri prauii atq; impij, qui optimas artes apprime callent. Virtus vero bonos reddit illos, quorum est virtus, & in malis hominibus non potest locum habere. Praeterea materiam artes praeparant virtuti. Nam sutor vestes facit, quibus prudenter utamur. Coquus cibos condit, quibus tempe-ranter utamur. Et denique commercia & opera omnia quae spectant ad artes, materia sunt iustitiae. Proinde cum artes ancillae sint virtutis, ab illius dignitate longe distant. Adhaec virtutibus nemo potest ut artibus male uti. Et ad artes est satis cognitio, ut superius vidimus: at ad virtutem notitia minimam habet vim, cùm requiratur delectus ac constantia. Neq; pariunt hominibus artes bona tam praclara, ut virtutes: nam ex virtutibus oritur tandem felicitas. Omnia tamen haec tria, virtus inquam, natura & ars, commune hoc habent, ut mediocritatem sectentur, & citra vel supra illam corrumpantur.
units.tr: The argument from the lesser is sound, because both art and nature are less worthy than virtue. That nature follows the mean is clear enough in the case of food and drink, for excess and deficiency of these destroy living creatures. Likewise the temperaments of bodies are harmed: if heat or cold, moisture or dryness, prevail, we immediately fall ill. And that nature is greater than art is most certain, since art is its imitator. Now we must consider why it is inferior to virtue. Virtue is the perfection of nature, for virtue, as we have heard, makes that of which it is the virtue good, and brings its work to completion. Moreover, no one can misuse virtues, whereas very many misuse natural faculties most badly. That art follows the mean is shown by the shoemaker, who takes care to make a shoe neither larger nor smaller than the foot. Likewise the carpenter does not make a house larger or smaller than the architect has laid down. The plowman drives the plough into the ground neither more nor less than is fitting. Nevertheless, it is said that art follows not only the mean but the best: it pursues the mean between excess and deficiency, but as regards the work, it strives to produce the best and most excellent thing. Nor do these fight with each other. That virtue is far better than art is proved in many ways. First, art does indeed form the mind in some way, but not as virtue does, for art does not make the mind better; indeed, there are sometimes very many wicked and impious men who are thoroughly skilled in the best arts. But virtue makes good those whose virtue it is, and cannot have a place in bad men. Besides, the arts prepare material for virtue: for the tailor makes garments which we use prudently; the cook seasons foods which we use temperately; and finally, commerce and all the works that pertain to the arts are the matter of justice. Therefore, since the arts are the handmaids of virtue, they are far removed from its dignity. Moreover, no one can misuse virtues as one can misuse arts. For the arts, knowledge is enough, as we saw above; but for virtue knowledge has very little force, since choice and constancy are required. Nor do the arts bring to men goods so splendid as the virtues do, for happiness ultimately arises from the virtues. Yet all these three, I mean virtue, nature and art, share this in common: they pursue mediocrity, and are corrupted both by falling short of it and by going beyond it.

units.la: Confirmat insuper Aristoteles quod probavit, vulgato proverbio, quo de operibus artium recte confectis dici solet, Neque addi neque imminui quic quam potest. Cumque scientias hoc loco Aristoteles nominat, intelligere debemus artes: quamuis etiam in scientijs contemplantibus aliqua mediocritas apparet: resecant enim superuacanea, deinde subiectum suum ita certis finibus terminant, ut scientia doctrinam extra eos vagari non patiatur. Attamen Scholiastes Graecus, per scientias omnino artes intelligit: nam in ijs contemplantibus scientijs, exuperantiam inquit non esse metuendam: imo conari debemus, ut quàm maximè fieri potest sciamus, neque periculum est ut nimium intelligamus. Unde subiecit Aristoteles, loqui se de non quouis, sed tantum morali, nimirum ut reliqui habitus intellectus aut mentis excludantur, in quibus haec mediocritas non exigitur.
units.tr: Aristotle further confirms what he has proved by the common proverb, by which it is usually said of works of art rightly made that nothing can be added to them or taken from them. And when Aristotle here names the sciences, we must understand arts; although even in the contemplative sciences some mediocrity appears, for they cut away superfluous matter, and then they bound their subject by such fixed limits that the science does not allow its teaching to wander beyond them. Nevertheless, the Greek scholiast understands by "sciences" arts altogether; for he says that in the contemplative sciences excess is not to be feared, rather we ought to strive to know as much as possible, and there is no danger that we may know too much. Hence Aristotle added that he is speaking not of any sort of science but only of the moral, namely so that the other habits of the intellect or mind are excluded, in which this mediocrity is not required.

units.la: Haec autem circa affectus & actiones versatur, atque in his exuperantia, defectus & medium invenitur, ut metuere, confidere, cupere, irasci, miserari, atque in universum laetari atque tristari. In ijs inquã & maius & minus inest, & utraque haec non recte se habent: medium vero & optimum quod est in virtute, cum quando, quamobrem, in quos, cuius causa, & quomodo oportet, agitur. Identidemq; circa actiones est exuperantia, defectus & medium. Virtus vero cum in affectibus tum in actionibus versatur, ubi exuperatia peccat, & defectus vituperatur, medium laudatur & ad officium dirigitur: quae duo maximè sunt virtutis. Mediocritas igitur quaedam est virtus, estq; sectatrix medij.
units.tr: This, however, is concerned with the affections and actions, and in these excess, deficiency and the mean are found, such as fearing, being confident, desiring, being angry, pitying, and in general rejoicing and grieving. In these, I say, there is more and less, and both of these are not as they should be; but the mean, and the best, which is in virtue, is when one acts at the right time, on account of the right things, toward the right people, for the right purpose, and in the right way. Likewise, in actions there is excess, deficiency and the mean. Virtue, moreover, is concerned both with affections and with actions, where excess sins and deficiency is blamed, while the mean is praised and directed to duty; and these two things are chiefly the marks of virtue. Mediocrity, therefore, is a certain virtue, and it is a pursuer of the mean.

units.la: Circa quae versetur moralis virtus, de qua nunc agendum est, ostendit, nimirum circa affectiones & actiones. Affectus quosdam recensetur, ut ex ea connumeratione intelligamus, qui sint affectus. Atq; post censum quorun-dam, Et in summa laetari ac tristari: ut intelligamus hos duos affectus laetitiae atq; tristitiae quodammodo capitales esse: adeo quippe late patent, ut omnes alios comitentur. Ne autem dubitemus quomodo virtus moralis etiam in actionibus versetur, exemplo esse potest liberalitas, quae in largiendo consistit, quibus, quomodo, & quando par est: iustitia quoq; regi gubernat actiones. Attingit etiam obiter circumstantias, quando, quorum causa, cur, & quomodo. In affectibus & in actionibus plus & minus & me-dium esse affirmat ut superius expositum. Notandum adhæc duas virtutis esse proprietates, cum laudari, tum ad officium dirigi. Proinde concludi-tur, Virtutem mediocritatem esse, atq; medii sectatricem: quod ut sit accipi-endum, postea explicabimus.
units.tr: He shows what moral virtue, of which we are now to speak, is concerned with, namely affections and actions. He lists certain affections, so that from this enumeration we may understand what affections are. And after the listing of some of them, he adds "and in sum, to rejoice and to grieve," so that we understand these two affections, joy and sorrow, to be in some way the chief ones, for they extend so widely that they accompany all the others. Lest we doubt how moral virtue is also concerned with actions, liberality may serve as an example, which consists in giving, to whom, in what way, and when it is fitting. Justice also governs actions. He also touches in passing on the circumstances: when, for whose sake, why, and how. He affirms that in affections and in actions there is more, less and the mean, as was explained above. It should be noted besides that virtue has two properties: to be praised, and to be directed to duty. Therefore it is concluded that virtue is mediocrity and a pursuer of the mean; how this is to be understood we shall explain afterwards.

units.la: Præterea multis modis peccare usuvenit: quia malum infiniti est, ut Pythagorei coniciebant, sed bonum est finiti. Cumq; uno modo liceat benefacere, hinc id est facile, illud vero difficile. Nam est facile a scopo aberrare, consequi vero difficile. Igitur hac de causa tum exuperantia tum defectus ad pravitatem spectant. Virtutis vero est mediocritas. Boni enim fiunt simpliciter, varie autem multisq; modis mali.
units.tr: Moreover, it happens that people sin in many ways, because evil belongs to the infinite, as the Pythagoreans conjectured, but good belongs to the finite. Doing good is possible in only one way, so the one is easy and the other difficult. It is easy to miss the mark, but hard to hit it. For this reason both excess and deficiency tend toward wickedness, whereas virtue is the mean. Good people are good in a simple way, but bad people are bad in various ways and many modes.

units.la: Probat nunc idem, nempe virtutem sectari mediocritatem, aut medio-critatem esse. Rationem vero assumit, quod medium unum est, extrema vero sunt plura. Et si virtutem poneremus in extremis, tum multis modis virtus extaret. At id vitijs convenit, ut multiplicia sint, non virtutibus. Idq; confirmatur Pythagoreorum sententia, qui bonum aiebant finitum, malum vero infinitum. Fitq; hoc evidentius a simili sagittantium, quibus videmus longe facilius esse aberrare a scopo, quam assequi: nam multis modis aberrare possumus, uno tantum simpliciter modo illum ferire. Atq; de Pythagoreis inquit, Coniciebant: quoniam illi probabilia dixerunt, non accurate rem exquisite tractarunt. Ut alias est dictum, ij Pythagorei duos fecerunt principiorum ordines, Impar, vnum, dextrum, masculum, quietem, rectum, lu-men, & bonum, finitum & quadratum: quibus totidem opposita respon-debant, Par, multa, sinistrum, foeminam, motum, obliquum, tenebras, malum, infinitum, altera parte longius. At ex iis omnibus non facit ad rem praesentem nisi finitum & infinitum. Nam infinitum accommodat Aristoteles ad extrema quae plura sunt: non enim solum intelliguntur quae distant extremo loco, sed multa quae inter extrema & medium continentur. Ipsum vero medium quia est unicum, finitum seu terminatum appellatur, & virtuti congruit, quoniam uno tantum modo licet benefacere: obiterque notatur, facilius esse male facere, quam bene.
units.tr: He now proves the same point, namely that virtue pursues the mean, or is the mean. He gives the reason: the mean is one, but the extremes are many. If we placed virtue in the extremes, virtue would take many forms. But manifold forms belong to vices, not to virtues. This is confirmed by the opinion of the Pythagoreans, who said that good is finite and evil infinite. It is made clearer by the comparison with archers, for we see that it is far easier to miss the mark than to hit it: we can miss in many ways, but hit it in only one way. He says of the Pythagoreans, "they conjectured," since they spoke in probabilities and did not treat the matter with precision and exactness. As was said elsewhere, those Pythagoreans made two orders of principles: odd, one, right, male, rest, straight, light, good, finite and square; to which the same number of opposites corresponded: even, many, left, female, motion, crooked, darkness, evil, infinite, the other side being longer. But of all these, only the finite and the infinite bear on the present matter. For Aristotle applies the infinite to the extremes, which are many, since he understands not only those that lie at the outer limits but also the many that are contained between the extremes and the mean. The mean itself, because it is unique, is called finite or determinate, and it suits virtue, since one may act well in only one way. It is also incidentally noted that it is easier to do wrong than to do right.

units.la: Est itaque virtus, habitus cum electione in mediocritate consistens, quae est quo ad nos ratione definita, & ut prudens statueret. Medietas est duorum vitiorum, huius quidem iuxta exuperantiam, huius vero iuxta defectum. Et ad haec quod vitiorum hoc quidem exuperat, hoc deficit plus quam oportet, cum in affectibus tum in actionibus, & virtus medium & invenit & deligat.
units.tr: Virtue, then, is a habit, consisting in choice, lying in the mean, which is determined by reason as it applies to us, and as a prudent person would determine it. The mean lies between two vices, one by excess and the other by deficiency. Moreover, one vice exceeds and the other falls short of what is right, both in feelings and in actions, and virtue both finds and chooses the mean.

units.la: Concluditur absoluitur{?} jam virtutis definitio. Cum dicitur habitus,{3} ab omnibus diuiditur rebus, quae in animo quidem sunt, verum constantia non firmantur, ut opiniones, affectus, actiones, &c. Nam Habitus qualitas est firmissima. Etymon habet, vel ἀπὸ τῆς ἔχεσθαι[?] quod est inhaerere: nam firmiter habitus annectitur animis. Vel ἀπὸ τῆς ἔχειν[?] quod est habere: verè quippe habitus possidetur: nam catera facile transeunt. Cum electione.) ista particula notantur. Primum, ut illa moueamur ad agendum sponte ac ultro. Deinde, ut non casu, verum delectu adhibito. Excluduntur etiam naturalia & necessaria, quae non sunt in potestate nostra: nam eligimus quae putamus conducere ad finem, quem jam praestituimus nobis, quae arbitramur posse fieri. Hoc etiam differt virtus a scientiis: nam illae in rebus necessariis versantur, ideoque non interrogant (ut dicitur in posterioribus Analyticis) sed statim assumunt propositiones, cum in iis versentur quae aliter se habere nequeunt: unde aduersarij assensus de illis non est expectandus. Artes quoque non deliberant, cum certis praeceptionibus constent, quas artifices oportet sequi. Licet interdum Rhetor videatur deliberare, quo genere status causam suam velit tractare: et medicus inter multa pharmaca, quae aliquando uni morbo conducunt, delectum habet. Sed hoc est per accidens. Neque in aliis artibus usu venit: imo de iis etiam dicendum, ut viso quid nam sit utilius, eos illo debere, caeteris omissis, uti. Quod si quis medicus aut rhetor non fecerit, non habebitur utique bonus artifex. In mediocritate consistens.) Hoc discernitur virtus a vitiis. Nam illa quoq; sunt habitus & cum electione, sed in extremitatibus versantur. Mediocritas ea est quo ad nos: quoniam arithmeticum medium hic non retinetur, ut antea dictum fuit. Mediocritas vero quo ad nos ea dicitur, quae a ratione definita est: non autem a ratione cuiusvis hominis, sed prudentis.
units.tr: The definition of virtue is now complete. When it is said habit, this separates virtue from all those things that are in the mind but are not fixed by constancy, such as opinions, feelings, actions, and so on. For habit is the firmest kind of quality. Its etymology is either from ἔχεσθαι [echesthai], meaning to cling or adhere, since habit is firmly attached to the mind; or from ἔχειν [echein], meaning to have, since habit is truly possessed, whereas other things pass away easily. The phrase with choice marks two things. First, that we are moved to act willingly and of our own accord. Second, that the action is done by deliberate selection and not by chance. Natural and necessary things are also excluded, since they are not in our power, for we choose what we think conduces to the end we have already set for ourselves, and what we judge can be done. This also distinguishes virtue from the sciences, for these deal with necessary things, and therefore do not ask questions (as is said in the Posterior Analytics) but at once take up premises, since they concern things that cannot be otherwise; hence no assent from an opponent about them is to be expected. Arts also do not deliberate, since they rest on fixed precepts which craftsmen ought to follow. Although a rhetorician sometimes seems to deliberate about what kind of issue he should handle his case by, and a physician chooses among many drugs, some of which at times suit one disease, this is incidental. Nor does it happen in the other arts. Indeed, it must be said of these too that once it is seen what is most useful, craftsmen ought to use that and set the rest aside. If a physician or rhetorician fails to do so, he will certainly not be considered a good craftsman. Consisting in the mean distinguishes virtue from vices. For vices too are habits and involve choice, but they lie in the extremes. The mean is a mean with respect to us, since the arithmetical mean is not what is kept here, as was said before. The mean with respect to us is that which is determined by reason, not by the reason of any person whatever, but by that of the prudent.

units.la: His expositis, docet quare virtus sit mediocritas & medij sectatrix. Mediocritas est, quoniam est habitus medius inter duos habitus vitiosos. Deinde quia in actionibus & affectibus est circa medium, & non in extremis. Si quis ergo consyderet affectus & actiones, ut dictum est, in iis deprehendet extrema & medium: medij non extremitatum sectatrix est virtus. Ad haec si qualitas ipsa virtutis attendatur, iuxta naturam suam est mediocritas quaedam, habitus videlicet inter duos vitiosos habitus alios. Unde recte concluditur, & mediocritatem esse ac medij sectatricem.
units.tr: Having set these things out, he teaches why virtue is a mean and pursues the mean. It is a mean because it is a habit intermediate between two vicious habits. Then, because in actions and feelings it concerns the mean and not the extremes. If, then, one considers feelings and actions, as has been said, one finds in them both extremes and a mean; virtue pursues the mean, not the extremes. Moreover, if the quality of virtue itself is considered, by its nature it is a certain mean, namely a habit lying between two other vicious habits. Hence it is rightly concluded that virtue is both a mean and a pursuer of the mean.

units.la: Quamobrem quo ad substantiam & sermonem qui explicat quid sit res, virtus est mediocritas: quā-tum vero ad optimum, & id quod bene habet, ex-tremitas est virtus.
units.tr: Therefore, as to the substance and the account that explains what the thing is, virtue is a mean; but as to the best, and what is well disposed, virtue is an extreme.

units.la: Per occupationem obiectionis tacitae occurrit Aristoteles. Dixerit enim quispiam, quomodo virtutem in medio collocas, cum ea res perfectissima sit, & suum opus curet quam optime se habere, idcirco potius extremum videtur occupare? Ad hoc respondet, Illam quo ad essentiam & naturam, esse quidem mediocritatem, at diverso respectu nil obstat quin extremitas quaedam possit dici: nam moralia distinguuntur in bonum & malum. Virtutes collocantur in bonis: vitia vero in malis. Unde cum distinctione agitur, virtus in altero extremo collocatur, vitium vero in altero, quod postea rursus diducitur in exuperantiam & defectum. Nec dubium id est aliqua opposita posse rei eidem attribui, quando ratione ac respectu diverso consyderantur. Si definitio lineae attendatur, longitudo est profunditate ac latitudine carens:cui postea id etiam adiungitur ut recta sit aut obliqua. Græca Scho-lia notarunt hæc duo inter se collata, mediocritatem esse vel medium se-ctari, cum eo quod est optimum esse ac bene habere, instar causæ ac effecti esse. Nam ex eo quòd virtus est mediocritas, & medium captat, id assequi-tur ut optima sit, & opera nostra efficiat bene habere. Quapropter medio-critas pertinet ad substantiam, optimum verò & bene rectéque habere illi convenit ut proprietas.
units.tr: Aristotle meets an unspoken objection by anticipation. Someone might say: how do you place virtue in the middle, when it is the most perfect thing and takes care that its work be as good as possible? Does it not rather seem to occupy an extreme? To this he replies that virtue, as to its essence and nature, is indeed a mean, but in a different respect there is nothing to prevent its being called a kind of extreme, for moral things are distinguished into good and bad. Virtues are placed among good things, vices among bad. Hence, when the matter is considered with this distinction, virtue is placed at one extreme and vice at the other, and this again is divided into excess and deficiency. Nor is it doubtful that several opposites can be attributed to the same thing when it is considered under different reasons and respects. If the definition of a line is considered, it is length without breadth or depth, to which is afterwards added that it is straight or oblique. The Greek scholia noted that these two things, namely being a mean or pursuing the middle, and being best and well disposed, stand to each other as cause and effect. For from the fact that virtue is a mean and aims at the middle, it follows that it is best and makes our works well disposed. Therefore mediocrity pertains to the substance, while being best and rightly disposed belongs to it as a property.

units.la: Cur verò in optimis reponenda sit virtus, ita liquet. Partitio bonorum trita & peruulgata est, ut alia fortunæ, alia corporis, alia esse animi dican-tur. Atque inter hæc, animi bona præcipuum gradum obtinent, quæ cùm sint multiplicia, virtutes inter illa summum locum sibi vendicare omnes autumant, qui fit ut virtus hoc modo quid optimum dicatur. Adhæc ens ipsum, quod latissimè patet, omniaq; sua comprehendit amplitudine, per duas differentias quodammodo secatur, in bonum inquam & malum, quæ duo sunt quasi contraria. Contraria verò illa dicuntur, quæ sub eodem genere maximè distant. Ideoque cùm virtus in altero sit horum oppositorum, nimirum in bono, quod longissimè à malo distat, merito dici potest extremitas.
units.tr: Why virtue must be placed among the best things is clear as follows. The division of goods is common and widely known: some are said to be goods of fortune, some of the body, and some of the soul. Among these, the goods of the soul hold the first rank, and since they are many, all who think that virtues claim the highest place among them. In this way virtue is called something best. Moreover, being itself, which extends most widely and embraces all its contents within its breadth, is in a sense divided by two differences, good and bad, which are as it were contraries. Those are called contraries which are most distant from each other under the same genus. Therefore, since virtue lies in one of these opposites, namely the good, which is furthest from the bad, it may rightly be called an extreme.

units.la: Quod verò attinet ad voces, τί ἦν εἶναι [?] sciendum est illas Aristoteli esse familiarissimas, & est ac si diceres verbum de verbo expressum, quid sit esse, hoc est, quæ sit natura & essentia rei. Unde ipsa definitio si definienda sit, est sermo dicens τί ἦν εἶναι, quid sit esse, atque ita separatur à descriptione, ac explicatione quid nominis, ab etymologia & cæteris explicationum formis.
units.tr: As for the words τί ἦν εἶναι [ti ēn einai], it must be known that these were very familiar to Aristotle, and it is as if you said a word expressed from a word: "what it is to be", that is, what the nature and essence of a thing is. Hence the definition itself, if it is to be defined, is a phrase saying τί ἦν εἶναι, "what it is to be", and so it is separated from the description and explanation of a name, from etymology and the other forms of explanation.

units.la: At dixerit quispiam, cùm natura non sint præfixi termini extremi asse-ctuum vel actionum, quod ipsi sciamus: non enim dabitur adeò magnus ti-mor, quin putemus posse reperiri maiorem: Et audacia quamuis insignis, for-tè alia occurret aliquando vehementior. Neque secus est in defectu, Paruo timore ac tenui audacia, minor adhuc ac levior fortasis occurret. Quòd cùm ita sit, ut extremi termini cum actionum tum affectuum sint nobis ignoti, quomodo unquam poterimus deligere medium? Medium porrò quadam relatione conseritur cum extremis: et natura ea est relatiuorum, ut si alterum non noris, alterum quoq; nesciás. Ad hoc respondetur, argumentum esse firmissimum, neq; solui posse si medium quærendum esset iuxta rem. Sed cùm virtutis medium sit quo ad nos & rationis, extrema cognosci possunt: nō enim opus est, ut quisq; summum timore summámue audaciam, quantū ad ipsius affectus naturā cognoscat, sed quo ad seipsum, et quantū se deceat. Et satis est ut quis in universum sciat qui gradus affectus cuiuspiam pertinent ad unum vel alterum extremorum, ut illa euitet. Virtus enim captat medium cum ab extremis deflectit, non quod aliquid ex illis assumat, vel ex eis componatur, sed per abnegationem est medium. Nullum siquidem medium in quo sita est virtus, est aliquod extremorum. Quemadmodum lapis neque caecus est neque videns, sed inter ista medium est per abnegationem. Proinde qui virtutis medium quaerit, ut in arte agitur se gerit: illæ enim sua opificia, ut medium assequantur & bene habeant, nostrisq; u-sibus aptentur, vel detrahunt vel addunt. Unde tandem per istas accessiones & imminutiones artificia nostris commodis & institutis congruunt: non itaque rerum extrema spectant, sed quid nobis conveniat. Sicut etiam senarius numerus medium ponitur inter binarium & denarium, non quasi ex illis componatur, sed propter proportionem æqualem quam habet ad utrumque. Hoc itaque retinendum, mensuram medii virtutis ex circumstantiis esse metiendam, quia non est medium rei quod æque distat ab extremis rei: non est medium participationis quod ex extremis componatur, sed est medium quo ad nos seu rationis, & medium abnegationis vel ut ita dixerim deflexus. Et ad tale medium captandum & assequendum, satis est ut extremorum qualis qualis habeatur notitia.
units.tr: But someone might say: since no extreme limits of affections or actions are fixed by nature, so far as we know, there is no fear so great that we cannot think a greater can be found, and however remarkable a boldness, perhaps some more vehement one will sometime occur. Nor is it otherwise in deficiency: with a small fear and a slight boldness, something smaller and lighter will perhaps occur. Since this is so, and the extreme limits both of actions and of affections are unknown to us, how will we ever be able to choose the mean? Moreover, the mean is joined by a certain relation with the extremes, and it is the nature of relatives that if you do not know one, you do not know the other either. To this it is answered that the argument is very firm and could not be resolved if the mean were to be sought according to the thing itself. But since the mean of virtue is relative to us and to reason, the extremes can be known. For it is not necessary that each person know the greatest fear or the greatest boldness as to the nature of the affection itself, but as to himself and how far it becomes him. And it is enough that someone know in general which degrees of an affection pertain to one or the other extreme, so that he may avoid them. For virtue seeks the mean when it turns aside from the extremes, not because it takes anything from them or is composed of them, but by negation it is the mean. For no mean in which virtue lies is any of the extremes. Just as a stone is neither blind nor seeing, but between these is the mean by negation. Therefore one who seeks the mean of virtue acts as is done in an art: for craftsmen, that their works may attain the mean, be well disposed and fitted to our uses, either remove or add. Hence at last, by these additions and subtractions, artifacts agree with our conveniences and purposes. They therefore look not to the extremes of things but to what suits us. So too the number six is placed between two and ten, not as if it were composed of them, but on account of the equal proportion it has to each. Therefore this must be retained: the measure of the mean of virtue is to be judged from circumstances, because the mean of a thing is not that which is equally distant from the extremes of the thing; the mean of participation is not what is composed of the extremes, but the mean relative to us or to reason, and the mean of negation, or, as I may say, of deflection. And to seek and attain such a mean, it is enough that some knowledge of the extremes, of whatever sort, be had.

units.la: Sed omnis actio & omnis affectus non capit mediocritatem: nam quædam statim ut nominantur cum vitio connexa intelliguntur, ut malevolentia, impudentia, invidia: & in actionibus, adulterium, furtum, cædes. Hæc omnia & similia sic vocantur, quòd ipsa per se vitiosa sunt, non eorum exuperantiæ neque defectus. In iis igitur rectè agere nunquam licet, sed perpetuo peccare. Neque in iis est vel bene vel male factum, ut in adulterio committendo, quo ad licet, quando, & quomodo. Sed prorsus quiduis horum committere est peccare.
units.tr: But not every action and every affection admits of mediocrity. For some, as soon as they are named, are understood as joined with vice, such as malevolence, shamelessness and envy; and among actions, adultery, theft and murder. All these and similar things are so called because they are vicious in themselves, not because of any excess or deficiency in them. Therefore in these it is never permitted to act rightly, but one always sins. Nor is there in them a thing done well or badly, as there is in committing adultery as to whether it is permitted, when, and how. Rather, to commit any of these is simply to sin.

units.la: Postremam huius capitis jam habemus partem. Ubique dixerat virtu-tem moralem circa actiones & affectus versari in quibus maius, minus & medium effet. Nūc monet non omnes affectus omnesq; actiones ita esse com-paratas ut maius, minus & medium recipiant. Nam quaedam in hoc numero esse inquit, quae illico ut nominantur, vitiosa sunt, neq; mediocritate ulla recta iustaq; reddi possunt. Et affectus quosdam huiusmodi recenset satis notos. Maleuolentiam eleganter dicit ἐπιχαιρεκακίαν[?], cum quis alieno malo gaudet. Enumerat quoq; actiones quasdam, ut furtum, adulterium, cae-des. Ista enim ita mala suapte natura esse constat, ut circumstantijs ullis non-queant recta & iusta effici: nam quocunq; modo haec admiseris, pecca-bis. Duo tamenhic sunt notanda, quae annotarunt Graeca scholia, Videtur, inquiunt, nonnunquam adulteria iuste posse committi. Ut si quis cum uxore Tyranni rem habeat quo ad illum occidendum aditum faciliorem sibi paret. Item caedes fieri potest interdum iusta, Ut si quis alterum occidat defen-dendi sui causa. Respondent ad primum, Adulterium proprie non esse quod ita committitur cum uxore Tyranni: quandoquidem id non fit aut voluptatis turpis aut intemperantiae causa. Item de caede illius generis non agit nunc Aristoteles, verum de illegitima quae a sicarijs, rapacibus, turbulentis, se-ditiosis, & violentis hominibus admittuntur. De secundo non male iudicatur a scholijs. Non enim quoties homo interficitur peccatur ibi: sed quando priuata id fit authoritate. Nam tunc proprie caedem fieri constat, in quam non incurrit vel iudex, vel qui se defendit, vel qui iusto bello pugnat. At de adulterio non ita se habet: quia non debemus ad honestas fines per turpia media contendere.
units.tr: We now have the last part of this chapter. He had said throughout that moral virtue is concerned with actions and affections in which there can be more, less and a mean. Now he warns that not all affections and all actions are so constituted as to admit of more, less and a mean. For he says there are some in this class which, as soon as they are named, are vicious, and cannot be made right and just by any mediocrity. And he lists certain affections of this kind, well enough known. He elegantly calls malevolence ἐπιχαιρεκακίαν [epichairekakian], when someone rejoices in another's evil. He also enumerates certain actions, such as theft, adultery and murder. For it is agreed that these are so evil by their own nature that no circumstances can make them right and just: in whatever way you commit them, you will sin. Two points here are to be noted, which the Greek scholia remarked. "It seems," they say, "that adulteries can sometimes be justly committed, as when someone has relations with a tyrant's wife in order to make easier access for himself to kill him." Likewise murder may sometimes be just, as when someone kills another in defence of himself. To the first they answer that it is not properly adultery which is committed in this way with a tyrant's wife, since it is not done for the sake of base pleasure or intemperance. Likewise Aristotle is not now treating of murder of that kind, but of the unlawful murders committed by assassins, robbers, troublemakers, seditious and violent men. The scholia judge the second point not badly. For it is not sinful whenever a man is killed, but when it is done by private authority. For then it is agreed that murder properly occurs, into which neither a judge falls, nor one who defends himself, nor one who fights in a just war. But it is not so with adultery, because we ought not to strive for honourable ends through shameful means.

units.la: Idem quoq; est censere circa iniustitiam, ignauiã & intemperantiam, mediocritatem, exuperantiam, excessum et defectu nõ esse: nam hoc pacto exuperã-tiae ac defectus esset mediocritas, & exuperatiae exu-perantia, necnon & deficientiae defectus.
units.tr: It is likewise to be judged that there is no excess or deficiency in regard to injustice, cowardice and intemperance, or that there is no mean in them. For in that case the mean of excess and deficiency would be a mean, the excess of excess an excess, and the defect of defect a defect.

units.la: Alia hæc est ratio qua idem confirmatur, nempe in illis extremis non es-se mediocritatem quaerendam: quoniam tunc oporteret exuperantiæ concedere aliquam exuperantiam, & defectui alium defectum. Quod sane si daretur, nullus esset in huiusmodi terminis finis, imo semper ulterius progrederemur, & in immensum abiremus: quod absurdissimum est, & a rerum natura prorsus alienum.
units.tr: There is another reason by which the same point is confirmed: that in those extremes no mean is to be sought, since then one would have to grant some excess to excess and some defect to defect. And if that were allowed, there would be no end to such terms; rather we would always go further and proceed into the infinite. This is most absurd and wholly foreign to the nature of things.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem cum temperantiæ tum fortitudinis nō est exuperantia neq; defectus, quod medium quodammodo sit extremitas: ita neq; illorū nimirū extremorū est mediocritas, neq; exuperantia neq; defectus, sed quocunq; modo fiant, praue agitur. Quare in universum neque temperantiæ neq; defectus est mediocritas: neque mediocritatis vel exuperantia vel defectus.
units.tr: Just as neither excess nor defect belongs to temperance or to courage, because the mean is in a sense an extreme, so neither is there a mean in those extremes, nor any excess or defect, but however they occur, they are done badly. Therefore, in general, there is no mean of temperance or of defect, nor an excess or defect of the mean.

units.la: Postremò rationem aliam adducit, ex correlatiuo. Ideò in illis extremis non est mediocritas quærenda, quia in ipsa mediocritate non invenitur vel exuperantia vel defectus. Ac si dixeris,
units.tr: Finally, he adduces another reason, from the correlative. There is no mean to be sought in those extremes, because excess and defect are not found in the mean itself. As if you were to say:

units.la: Quemadmodum se habet mediocritas ad extrema, ita extrema ad mediocritatem.
units.tr: Just as the mean stands in relation to the extremes, so the extremes stand in relation to the mean.

units.la: Sed in mediocritate, ut in ipsa temperantia & fortitudine, non inveniuntur extrema, ita ut ibi sit vel exuperantia vel defectus.
units.tr: But in the mean, as in temperance and courage themselves, no extremes are found, so that there could be either excess or defect in it.
Therefore there will be no mean in the extremes either.

units.la: Et certè si esset in illis extremis vitiosis mediocritas, tum aliqua intemperantia esset laudabilis, & aliqua ignavia commendaretur: quod à vero longissime distat.
units.tr: And certainly, if there were a mean in those vicious extremes, then some intemperance would be praiseworthy and some cowardice would be commended, which is far from the truth.

units.la: Sed hic duo sunt cōsyderanda, Primum, Cū dicitur in extremis non esse mediocritatem, haud propterea magnitudinem et magnificentiam auferri, quæ circa extrema putantur versari: de quibus ut reuera in mediocritate sita sint, dicemus posthea suo loco. Alterum, quod annotamus est, Non propterea statui hoc loco vitia omnia esse paria, ita ut non debeant dari maiores et minores vel exuperantiæ vel defectus. Dantur enim, sed non ita, ut in ipsis mediocritas laudabilis, & quæ constituat virtutem, inveniatur.
units.tr: But two things are to be considered here. First, when it is said that there is no mean in the extremes, this does not take away the greatness and magnificence which are thought to lie about the extremes; we shall say later, in its proper place, that these really lie in the mean. Second, we note that it is not on that account asserted here that all vices are equal, so that there cannot be greater and lesser excesses or defects. For they do exist, but not in such a way that a praiseworthy mean, which constitutes virtue, is found in them.

units.la: NVNC superest ut videamus, quomodo istud caput ad vngulā [?] diuinarum literarum se habeat. Primò dictum est, Virtutem bonum reddere illum qui sit ea præditus, & eius opus perficere. Dei verbū ab hoc nō dissentit: nā fide iustificamur, ut Paulus testatur, & sancti per fidem præclarissima gesserunt, ut Epistola ad Hebræos testatur. Ad hæc spe salui facti sumus. Et beata dicitur spes in Epistola ad Titum, quod beatos nos faciat. Et ad Thessalonicenses, Nolo vos contristari de dormientibus, sicut cæteri, qui spem non habent. De charitate non est dubium, Quandoquidem illa omnia fert, omnia credit, omnia sperat. Hoc tamen addendum est, Deum ipsum nos perficere, sed ad nostram instaurationem huiusmodi virtutibus abuti. Secundo hic docet Aristoteles, virtutem hac praestare bona mediocritatem sectando, sed mediocritas etiam a divina scriptura commendatur. Paulus inquit ad Romanos non debere sapere plus quam oportet, sed ad moderationem. Non declines ad dextram neq; ad sinistram. Et medium hoc quo ad nos & secundum rationem est intelligendum. Unde nos conferimur ad Rom. cum membris, quae sunt in eodem corpore, quorum oportet unumquodq; suo constentum esse modo, & officio suo fungi, neq; aliena usurpare. Dominusq; laudavit pauperem viduam quae duo minuta offerebat, illamq; praetulit ditissimis, qui dona opima largiebantur. Et abnegatio suiipsius quo ad rem potest extremum videri, cum sit quo ad nos medium. Talis enim est nostra vitiata & corrupta natura, ut expediat ab ea recedere. Deinde inquit Dominus, potestis bibere calicem quem ego bibiturus sum? quod est vitam pro veritate ponere. Hoc videtur summum, si rem spectes: at quo ad nos & circumstantias iustas, medium est optimum ad felicitatem consequendam. Additur ab Aristotele, bonum simpliciter & uno quodam fieri modo, malum vero varie ac multipliciter committi. Et Christus ait latam esse portam & viamquae ad interitum ducit. Angustam e diverso portam & arctam viam quae ad salutem ducat. In definitione postea virtutis ponitur habitus. Unde constantia ostenditur necessaria in veris virtutibus. Et Dominus tradit non esse idoneum ad regnum coelorum, nisi quis perseveraverit, idque usque in finem. Et Ioannes idcirco laudatur, quod non sit arundo a vento agitata. Monetque Paulus ne simus ut parvuli, circumferamurq; omni vento doctrina. Et a Ieremia dicitur, bonum esse homini qui iugum ab adolescentia sua portaverit. Praeterea scribitur, virtutem esse cum electione. Laudatur etiam in sacris literis quod animo libero & voluntario agitur. In Psal. Populus tuus spontanearum, voluntatum scilicet. Et de Eleemosyna, inquit Paulus, Non ex tristitia, sed ex necessitate.
units.tr: NOW it remains for us to see how this chapter stands in relation to the divine writings, exactly as to the nail. First, it has been said that virtue makes the one who possesses it good and carries out his work. The word of God does not dissent from this: for we are justified by faith, as Paul testifies, and the saints by faith performed most excellent deeds, as the Epistle to the Hebrews testifies. By hope we have been made saved. And hope is called blessed in the Epistle to Titus, because it makes us blessed. And to the Thessalonians: I do not want you to be sorrowful concerning those who sleep, as the rest who have no hope. There is no doubt about charity, since it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things. Yet this must be added: God himself perfects us, but to use such virtues for our renewal. Second, Aristotle teaches here that virtue achieves its good by pursuing the mean, and the mean is also commended by divine Scripture. Paul says in Romans that one ought not to be wiser than he ought to be, but to be sober-minded. Do not turn aside to the right or to the left. And this mean is to be understood with respect to us and according to reason. Hence we are compared, in Romans, with the members that are in the same body, each of which must be content with its own measure and perform its own office, and not seize what belongs to others. And the Lord praised the poor widow who offered two small coins, and preferred her to the richest who gave lavish gifts. And self-denial, as regards the thing itself, may seem an extreme, yet as regards us it is a mean; for our nature is so corrupt and vitiated that it is expedient to withdraw from it. Then the Lord says: Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink? That is, to lay down life for the truth. This seems the highest if you look at the thing itself; but as regards us and just circumstances, it is the best mean for attaining happiness. Aristotle adds that good comes about simply and in one way, but evil is committed in various and manifold ways. And Christ says that the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, while on the other hand the gate is narrow and the way is strait that leads to salvation. In the later definition of virtue, a habit is posited; hence constancy is shown to be necessary in true virtues. And the Lord teaches that no one is fit for the kingdom of heaven unless he persevere, and that to the end. John is praised because he was not a reed shaken by the wind. And Paul warns us not to be like children, tossed about by every wind of doctrine. And Jeremiah says that it is good for a man to have borne the yoke from his youth. Moreover, it is written that virtue is with choice. In sacred letters it is also praised that it is done with a free and willing mind. In Psalm: Your people will be willing ones, that is, of free will. And concerning almsgiving, Paul says: not out of sadness, but out of necessity.

units.la: Medium quo ad nos & secundum rationem virtus sequitur, ut sapiens vir definiret. Hic nonnihil dissentimus. Non enim media virtutum quaerimus ex hominibus, sed ex verbo Dei. Nullus enim sapiens est qui non erret: unde illorum iudicio quo ad ista non est standum. Virtus dum consyderatur quatenus efficit ut res bene se habeat, & optimum quaerit, iam non medium, sed rationem extremi habet. Ita in sacris literis Dominus haud semel nos monuit, quum iubcret esse perfectos ut coelestis pater. Paulus quoque idem mandat, nec non se idem facere ostendebat, quum inquit ad Philipp. non adhuc se consecutum esse, verum ad ulteriora perpetuo tendere. Vbi declarat se non medium, sed quodammodo extremum quaerere. Postremo statuit Aristoteles, quosdam affectus & quasdam actiones, in quibus medium non sit quaerendum, nempe laude dignum, quodue faciat ad virtutem: sed statim ut nominantur omnia mala sunt. Sic ad Ephes. quaedam nominauit Apostolus, de quibus dixit, In vobis ne quidem nominentur. Et, qui talia faciunt, regnum Dei non possidebunt. Nil possunt in ijs circumstantiae.
units.tr: Virtue follows the mean in relation to us and according to reason, as the wise man defined it. Here we disagree somewhat. For we do not seek the means of the virtues from men, but from the Word of God. For no wise man is there who does not err; so in their judgment we ought not to stand as regards these matters. When virtue is considered insofar as it brings it about that a thing stands well, and seeks the best, it no longer has the character of a mean but of an extreme. Thus in the sacred letters the Lord has more than once admonished us, when he bids us be perfect as our heavenly Father is perfect. Paul also commands the same thing, and showed that he did the same when he said, in Phil., that he had not yet attained it, but always strives toward the things ahead. Where he declares that he seeks not the mean but in a way the extreme. Finally, Aristotle held that certain affections and certain actions, in which no mean is to be sought, namely those worthy of praise or which make for virtue, but as soon as they are named they are all evil. Thus in Ephesians the Apostle named certain things, of which he said, Let them not even be named among you. And those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God. In these there are no circumstances that can help.
CAPUT VII

units.la: HOc autem oportet non solùm in universum dicere, sed ad ea quae singula sunt adaptare. Nam in sermonibus, qui de actionibus tractant, ij qui de toto genere, communiores utiq; sunt: sed qui versantur circa partes, veriores. Actiones enim sunt in singulis, quare iis oportet concinere. Accipiendaigi-tur haec sunt ex descriptione.
units.tr: This, however, must be said not only in general but must also be adapted to the individual things. For in discourses that treat of actions, those that deal with the whole genus are indeed more common, but those that deal with the parts are more true. For actions exist in individual cases, so one must agree with them. These things are therefore to be taken from the definition.

units.la: Aput hoc in duo partiemur. Prius, quodnam sit suum consilium aperit, nimirum de virtutibus moralibus agere singillatim. Deinde numerum seu catalogum earum cōfusè describit, quo postea de illis queat subtilius exquisitiusq; docere. Quo ad primū, Non satis ait esse de virtute in universum et cōfuse dixisse, verum communem illius definitionem ad singulas ipsius formas & species adaptare. Hoc est enim quoddam probationis genus. Cum enim viderimus tem-perantiam consectari medium, fortitudinem quoque circa medium versari, ut iam est expositum, nec aliter ceteras eiusdem generis virtutes se habere viderimus, concludemus & quidem firmiter, definitionem virtutis in universum ita esse assignandam. Valebitque haec tractatio de singulis virtutum speciebus eo, ut certitudinem evidentiorem natura illius assequamur, & ob id ex doctrina fructum maiorem reportemus. Etenim sermones qui de toto genere sunt, maiorem habent amplitudinem, ac multo plura quam contractiores in se claudunt: at illi sunt veriores. Huc deinde accedit, scientias agetes evidentiam suam a singulis haurire, ideo par est ut [illegible, ~5 letters] lorum actionibus quam maxime agant: Quandoquidem actiones non sunt generum aut notionum communium, sed singulorum, neq; scientia πρὸς ἄλλῳ[?] alió quàm ad agendum sunt referenda. Unde notarūt Graeca scholia, Scientias contemplantes longè secus agere. Definit enim mathematicus triangulum neq; probationem definitionis allata à singulis triangulis disquirit, cùm in ipso vniuersali maiorem de eo notitiam habeat. Sensus enim docet ibi tres angulos esse, vbi duae lineae super alteram hoc modo cadunt. At nostra scientia agentes, vt nostra est moralis & medica, vniuersalem definitionem aut proprietatem de quapiam re concludere nequeunt, nisi quantum ex obseruatione singularium collegerint. Ita enim Galenus proprietates herbarum & medicamentorum congerebat.
units.tr: Here we divide the matter into two parts. First, he sets out his plan, namely to treat the moral virtues one by one. Then he describes their number or catalogue in a general way, so that afterwards he can teach about them more subtly and exactly. As to the first part, he says it is not enough to have spoken of virtue in general and confusedly; the common definition must be adapted to each of its forms and species. For this is a kind of proof. When we have seen that temperance pursues the mean, and that fortitude also lies in the mean, as has now been explained, and when we see that the other virtues of the same kind are not otherwise disposed, we will conclude, and indeed firmly, that the definition of virtue in general must be assigned in this way. This treatment of the individual species of virtue will serve so that we may attain a clearer certainty of its nature, and so gain greater fruit from the teaching. For discourses that concern the whole genus have greater breadth and contain far more within themselves than the narrower ones, but the narrower ones are more true. Moreover, sciences that act draw their evidence from singulars, and so it is fitting that they should be occupied especially with actions, since actions belong not to genera or common notions but to singulars, and knowledge is to be referred to nothing other than to acting. Whence the Greek scholia observed that those who contemplate the sciences proceed quite differently. For the mathematician defines a triangle and does not inquire into the proof of the definition from the individual triangles, since he has greater knowledge of it in the universal itself. For sense teaches there that there are three angles where two lines fall upon another in this manner. But we, who act in our science, as moral and medical science does, cannot conclude a universal definition or property of any thing except insofar as we have gathered it from the observation of singulars. Thus Galen used to collect the properties of herbs and medicines.

units.la: Dubitant aliqui quomodo sermonibus communioribus Aristoteles opponat veriores, & suspicio est in codice castigatiori fuisse scriptum κενότεροι[?], ac si diceres, inaniores sunt & minus utiles, aliy vero sunt veriores & fructuosiores. Verum etiam si scribatur κοινοτέροι[?] commodus erit sensus: nam rationes communes Aristoteli sunt minus certae, nempe probabiles: nam ἀποδεικτικὸς συλλογισμὸς[?] ex propriis concludere oportet, non ex communibus, vt in posterioribus Analyticis dicitur. Statuit ergo quasi descriptione quadam virtutes ante omnia esse describendas, à pictoribus deducta metaphora, qui prius crassius vel obscurius quae picturi sunt adumbrant, & illud idem postea coloribus idoneis ornant. Versabitur autem hac descriptio circa humanos affectus & actiones: quandoquidem virtutes morales in iis locum habere demonstratum est.
units.tr: Some doubt how Aristotle sets truer discourses against more common ones, and it is suspected that in a more correct codex it was written κενότεροι [kenoteroi], as if you were to say that they are emptier and less useful, while the others are truer and more fruitful. But even if κοινοτέροι [koinoteroi] is written, the sense will be fitting: for common reasons are less certain to Aristotle, that is, probable; for a demonstrative syllogism must conclude from proper premises, not from common ones, as is said in the Posterior Analytics. He therefore decides that, as it were by a certain description, virtues must be described before all else, a metaphor drawn from painters, who first sketch roughly or obscurely what they are going to paint, and afterwards adorn it with suitable colours. This description will concern human affections and actions, since it has been shown that the moral virtues have their place in these.

units.la: Fortitudo itaque circa formidines & ausus est mediocritas. Et inter eos qui exuperant, qui intrepiditate excedit caret nomine: in ijs enim permulta sunt absque nomine. Qui vero in confidendo superat, est audax. Quiq; timendo exuperat, & confidendo deficit, ignauus dicitur.
units.tr: Fortitude, then, is a mean concerning fears and daring. Among those who exceed, the one who exceeds in fearlessness has no name, for there are very many such cases without a name. But the one who exceeds in confidence is rash. And the one who exceeds in fearing and falls short in daring is called cowardly.

units.la: Iam catalogus quarundam virtutum describitur, & Fortitudo prima occurrit: cuius mediocritas est ipsa virtus. Ausus habet pro exuperantia, & Formidinem pro defectu. Sed exuperantiam partitur adhuc in duo: nam aliqui modum excedunt non timendo, alij autem audendo. Qui excedunt nō timendo traduntur esse qui prorsus omnem timorem exuerunt, et adeo sunt impa-
units.tr: Now the catalogue of certain virtues is described, and Fortitude comes first, whose mean is virtue itself. Daring takes the place of excess, and fear the place of deficiency. But the excess is further divided into two, for some exceed the mean by not fearing, others by daring. Those who exceed by not fearing are said to be those who have cast off all fear entirely, and are so

units.la: Fortitudo: marginal note to the first line of the paragraph "Iam catalogus". impauidi vt nec ad ea moueantur quæ omnino superant naturam, vt cæle-stia tonitrua, fulmina, terræmotus, & consimilia. Nec tamen ij excedunt au-dendo: non enim propterea se vltro periculis exponerent, vel aliquid honestum de causa tentarent arduum. Quiq; sunt eiusmodi, mania & furore quodam creduntur laborare. Nomine carent: quoniam pauci huiusmodi reperiuntur. Videtur quibusdam ita rem habere. Quicunq; audax est nil ti-met, & non e contrario: quandoquidem permulti queant intrepidi esse qui non audeant, neq; velint quicquam aut mouere aut tentare. At non ita res habet: quoniam audax no omnino est intrepidus, ita vt omne exuerit timorem: mouetur quidem illo aliquantisper, sed facile superat, & frequenter, imo saepius quam oportet, audet. A recto proinde & natura humana is magis discedit, qui superat intrepiditate, quam qui vincit audacia. Quamobrem sic est constituendum, fortem audere sed cum ratione: quando nimirum oportet, ac iussu rationis metum qui est in eo superante. Sed audax is est qui temere audet. Exponit quidem se periculis, verum absq; ratione, etenim metum omnem non abiecit, verum magna ex parte.
units.tr: Fortitude: marginal note to the first line of the paragraph "Now the catalogue". fearless that they are not moved even by those things that wholly surpass nature, such as heavenly thunder, lightning, earthquakes and the like. Nor do these exceed by daring, for they would not for that reason expose themselves voluntarily to dangers, or attempt something honourable and difficult for a cause. Those who are of this kind are believed to labour under a certain madness and frenzy. They lack a name, since few of this sort are found. To some it seems that the matter stands thus: whoever is bold fears nothing, and not conversely, since many can be fearless without daring, and without wishing to move or attempt anything. But the matter is not so, for the bold man is not wholly fearless, so as to have cast off all fear; he is indeed moved by it to some extent, but easily overcomes it, and frequently, indeed more often than he ought, he dares. Therefore he who exceeds by fearlessness departs more from what is right and from human nature than he who is overcome by audacity. Wherefore it must be established thus: the brave man dares, but with reason, namely when it is necessary, and by the command of reason he overcomes the fear that is in him. But the rash man is one who dares heedlessly. He indeed exposes himself to dangers, but without reason, for he has not cast off all fear, but only for the most part.

units.la: Sed quemadmodum in exuperantia diuersi ponuntur affectus, intrepidi (vt sic dixerim) & audacis, cur in defectu non item duo assignantur, sed vnus constituitur, quo dicimur ignaui seu timidi? Respondetur, duos quidem & ibi assignari modos defectus, cum dicatur aliqui deficere vel nimium timendo, vel non audendo: sed videntur simul in vno timidi vel ignaui nomine coniungi: quoniam a se inuicem non separantur. Nam quicunq; nimium est trepidus, nihil audet, & vicissim qui nihil audet, est nimium trepidus. Caeterum non ita res habet: quia fieri potest vt quispiam nil timeat, simulq; nil audeat. Coniunguntur potius ij duo modi ab Aristotele, quod eodem nomine ignaui seu timidi comprehendantur. At ille qui sic excedit non timendo, cur ἀφοβῶ non appellatur, & iste affectus quare non dicitur ἀφοβία? Quia nomina haec etiam forti conueniunt, necnon audaci: ideoq; illi quae appellauimus intrepidum non possunt esse propria. Vnde Aristoteles 3. Ethicorum cum de viro forti loquitur, inquit, ὁ οὖν ἀνδρεῖος πρὸς τοῦτο [?] ἔχει [?] ἀ-φοβῶς. At iam de altera virtute videndum est.
units.tr: But if in excess different affections are posited, of fearlessness and of boldness (so to speak), why in deficiency are not two likewise assigned, but one is set up, by which we are called cowardly or timid? It is answered that two modes of deficiency are indeed assigned there too, since it is said that some fall short either by fearing too much or by not daring; but they seem to be joined together under the one name of timid or cowardly, because they are not separated from each other. For whoever is excessively fearful dares nothing, and conversely whoever dares nothing is excessively fearful. Yet the matter is not so, because it can happen that someone fears nothing and at the same time dares nothing. Rather, those two modes are joined by Aristotle because they are comprehended under the same name of cowardly or timid. But why is he who thus exceeds by not fearing not called ἀφοβῶ [aphobo], and why is that affection not called ἀφοβία [aphobia]? Because these names also suit the brave man and the bold man, and so those which we have called fearlessness cannot be proper to the one. Whence Aristotle, in the third book of the Ethics, when he speaks of the brave man, says: "the brave man stands in relation to this without fear" [ὁ οὖν ἀνδρεῖος πρὸς τοῦτο ἔχει ἀφοβῶς]. But now we must consider the other virtue.

units.la: Temperantia est mediocritas circa voluptates & aegritudines, nō quidem oēs, nam in corporeis versatur, & inter has maxime tactu respicit: minus tamē circa aegritudines est. Excessus Intemperantia dicitur.
units.tr: Temperance is the mean concerning pleasures and pains, though not all of them, for it is concerned with bodily things, and among these it chiefly regards touch; it is less concerned with pains. Excess is called intemperance.

units.la: Qui uero circa uoluptates deficiunt, non ita multi sunt, ideo nomen non habuerunt: sunto uero stupidi.
units.tr: Those who are deficient with regard to pleasures, however, are not very many, and so they have had no name; they are called insensible.

units.la: Quare prius voluit Aristoteles de fortitudine agere quàm de temperantia? Quoniam inter animi partes ad rationem magis accedit vis irascens quàm cupiens: nam fere semper ea vis cum ratione facit, illam tuetur & illam defendit. Vnde cos rationis à sapientibus est dicta. Cumq; fortitudo in ista facultate animi sita sit, ac temperantia in illa quae cōcupiscit, ideo prior locus fortitudini est datus. Neq; arbitror adductam rationem esse necessariam: tantum probabilis est, & in praesentia magis verisimilis occurrit.
units.tr: Why did Aristotle wish to treat of fortitude before temperance? Because among the parts of the soul, the irascible power comes closer to reason than the appetitive power, for that power almost always acts with reason, keeps it and defends it. Whence it has been called the seat of reason by the wise. And since fortitude lies in that faculty of the soul, and temperance in the one that desires, the first place was given to fortitude. Nor do I think the reason adduced is necessary; it is only probable, and in the present case it appears more plausible.

units.la: Circa uoluptates & aegritudines mediocritas est temperantia: excessus intemperantia:defectus caret nomine. Sed quoniam voluptas est duum ge-nerum, quaedam animi eaq; ab omnibus collaudatur, ut cum quis gaudet Dei naturaeq; contemplatione, aut laetatur conscientia rectè factorum, vel delectatur iuuando, & beneficia quae potest in alios conferendo. Alterum vero genus voluptatis crassius est, & à sensibus non à ratione percipitur, dicunturq; voluptates ea corporea. Vnde Aristoteles ait hanc virtutem non circa priores versari: ratio potest afferri, quoniam illa cùm sint honestissima, non opus habent moderatione. Restat igitur vt in hoc posteriori genere temperantia collocetur. Neq; adhuc circa omnes corporeas locum habent, sed in iis tantum quae ad tactum pertinent. Sed cum tactu oportet ut gustum etiam intelligas. Sunt enim illi duo sensus, vt in lib. de Anima scribitur, admodū coniuncti. Erit itaq; temperantia mediocritas in voluptatibus cibi ac potus & Veneris. At quare moderatrix non est & voluptatum, quae per oculos, et per auditum sentiuntur? Quoniam illarum voluptatum non est tanta & tam vehemens cupiditas vt istarum, neque illae vt hae sunt noxiae: iis enim si fuerint immoderatae, homines quodammodo in bruta degenerant, non autem propter sonos, odores aut colores. At sit, etiam in hoc voluptatum genere quae ad alios sensus pertinent modum excedi, & opus esse aliqua virtute, exuperantia ciusmodi nunquam habita est aut dicta intemperantia. Sed qui sic peccant, alterius cuiusdam peccati non intemperantiae accusantur.
units.tr: Temperance is the mean concerning pleasures and pains; excess is intemperance; deficiency has no name. But since pleasure is of two kinds, one of the soul, which is praised by all, as when someone rejoices in the contemplation of God and of nature, or is glad in the consciousness of rightly done deeds, or takes delight in helping others and conferring benefits on them as far as he can; the other kind of pleasure is grosser, and is perceived by the senses, not by reason, and such pleasures are called bodily. Whence Aristotle says that this virtue is not concerned with the former; the reason can be given that, since those are most honourable, they have no need of moderation. It remains, therefore, that temperance be placed in this latter kind of pleasure. Nor does it yet have its place in all bodily pleasures, but only in those that pertain to touch. But with touch one must understand taste also, for those two senses, as is written in the book On the Soul, are very closely joined. Temperance will therefore be the mean in the pleasures of food and drink and of Venus. But why is it not also the moderator of the pleasures that are perceived through the eyes and through hearing? Because those pleasures do not have so great and so vehement a craving as these, nor are they as harmful; for if these are immoderate, men in a way degenerate into beasts, but not on account of sounds, odours or colours. But suppose that in this kind of pleasure too, those which pertain to the other senses are exceeded, and some virtue is needed; such an excess has never been called or named intemperance. But those who sin in this way are accused of some other sin, not of intemperance.

units.la: Cum itaq; temperantiae virtus cum in voluptatibus tum in aegritudinibus locum habeat, vtrā istarum affectionum est materia eius frequentius? Voluptates, inquit Aristoteles, quoniam in illis cohibendis magis laboramus & ad voluptatum exuperantia videmur à natura impelli. Neq; ita est difficile resistere ægritudini quàm sibi temperare à voluptate. Virtus verò maximè circa difficilia versatur. Deinde ægritudo animi quæ pertinet ad hanc virtutem, oritur ex defectu vel absentia voluptatis: at longè facilius est desiderium ferre absentis voluptatis, quàm præsenti non frui.
