units.tr: Since the virtue of temperance has its place both in pleasures and in pains, which of these two affections is its matter more often? Pleasures, says Aristotle, since we labour more in restraining them, and we seem to be driven by nature towards excess in pleasures. Nor is it so hard to resist pain as to restrain oneself from pleasure. Virtue, moreover, is concerned chiefly with difficult things. Then the mental distress that pertains to this virtue arises from the lack or absence of pleasure; but it is far easier to bear the longing for an absent pleasure than not to enjoy one at hand.

units.la: Defectus in hac materia nomen non habuit. Ratio affertur, quia non ita multi imò paucissimi sunt, qui omnino à voluptatibus abhorreant. Ea quæ raro accidunt, aut fere nusquam videntur, facilè nomine carent. Sint attamen inquit Aristoteles ἀναισθήτοι [?], hoc est, stupidi. Non tamen sic existimare debemus illos proprie appellari: nam ea vox etiam significat eos, qui ui morbi oppressi non sentiunt. Et fieri potest ut aliqui ex morbo vel aliqua neruorum dissolutione gustus voluptatis & Veneris non sentiant.
units.tr: Deficiency in this matter has no name. The reason given is that there are not many, indeed very few, who utterly shun pleasures. Things that happen rarely, or seem almost nowhere, easily lack a name. Yet, says Aristotle, there may be those who are anaisthētoi [ἀναισθήτοι], that is, insensible or stupid. We should not, however, think they are properly so called, for that word also means those who, overcome by disease, do not feel. And it can happen that some, through illness or some dissolution of the nerves, do not perceive the taste of pleasure and of sex.

units.la: In donandis autem & accipiendis pecuniis mediocritas est liberalitas: excessus verò & defectus, Effusio & Illiberalitas. Eæ verò contraria inter se ratione excedunt & deficiunt. Prodigus enim in largiendo exuperat: & in accipiendo deficit. Illiberalis verò in accipiendo modum excedit: at in elargiendo remissior est.
units.tr: In giving and receiving money, the mean is liberality; the excess and deficiency are prodigality and illiberality. These, by contrary reasoning, exceed and fall short of each other. For the prodigal man overspends in giving and falls short in receiving. The illiberal man, on the other hand, exceeds in receiving, but is too lax in giving.

units.la: Post fortitudinem ac temperantiam, de illis agit virtutibus, quæ sunt circa externa bona, ut facultates & honores. Ac in administrandis pecuniis, mediocritas vocata est Liberalitas: qui verò exuperat ἄσωτος [?], effusus & prodigus, non seruat res, imò perdit: nimium dat, & parum accipit. Auarus autem ab altero stat extremo, & plus æquo accipit, minus autem elargitur. Quamobrem exuperantia & defectus ijs modis inter se opponuntur.
units.tr: After courage and temperance, he treats of those virtues which concern external goods, such as wealth and honours. In managing money, the mean is called liberality; the one who exceeds is asotos [ἄσωτος], lavish and prodigal, who does not keep things but actually destroys them: he gives too much and receives too little. The miser, on the other hand, stands at the other extreme, receives more than is fair and gives less. Therefore excess and deficiency are opposed to each other in these ways.

units.la: De ijs autem nunc summatim dicitur & crasiori Minerua: nam de ijsdem postea exquisitius determinabitur. At quidam alij adhuc affectus circa pecunias habentur. Mediocritas enim quædam est magnificentia. nam magnificus à liberali distat, quod hic in magnis, alter verò in paruis versetur. Exuperantia dicitur ἀπειροκαλία [?] καὶ βαναυσία [?]. Defectus μικροπρέπεια [?]. Differunt autem hæ ab ijs quæ circa liberalitatem sunt. Quid uero differant, postea dicetur.
units.tr: Of these things a brief account is now given, and in a rather coarse manner; for they will be determined more exactly afterwards. But there are some other affections concerning money. For there is a certain mean, magnificence; for the magnificent man differs from the liberal in that the one moves in large matters, the other in small. The excess is called apeirokalia [ἀπειροκαλία] and banausia [βαναυσία]. The deficiency is mikropreperia [μικροπρέπεια]. These differ from those that concern liberality. What they differ in will be said later.

units.la: Nomen hoc ἀπειροκαλία deducitur ab ἄπειρον, quod indefinitum, & καλὸν: quòd sumptus vltra fines ac terminos honesti effundatur. Βαναυσία vocatur etiam hæc exuperantia: quoniam βάναυσοι, hoc est, sordidi artifi-ces, cùm sint rerum harum imperiti, dum volunt videri magnifici, non le-uiter in hoc impensarum genere peccant. Sutor semel factus diues epulum dedit Romano populo. Et Æsopus histrio volens epulari magnifice, lin-guas coemit pretiosissimarum auium. In popularibus porrò ciuitatibus adhi-bentur sæpius impensæ huiusmodi, quòd populus illis gaudeat. Vnde illi sor-didi artifices, qui mediocritatem ignorant, licet præ tenuitate non queant tales impensas facere, illis nihilominus delectantur. Quare Cicero aiebat non placere populo Romano priuatam luxuriam, sed publicam magnificen-tiam. μικροπρέπεια[?] est ex latere defectus, quando impensæ minores fiunt quàm operis magnitudo exigit. Sordes possemus dicere aut intempestiuam parsimoniam. A facultatum administratione transit ad honorum appe-titum.
units.tr: This name apeirokalia [ἀπειροκαλία] is derived from apeiron [ἄπειρον], meaning indefinite, and kalon [καλὸν], meaning fine or honourable, because the expense is poured out beyond the limits and bounds of what is honourable. This excess is also called banausia [βαναυσία], since the banausoi, that is, vulgar craftsmen, being ignorant of these matters, sin not lightly in this kind of spending when they wish to seem magnificent. A cobbler who became rich once gave a feast to the Roman people. And Aesopus the actor, wanting to feast magnificently, bought tongues of the most precious birds. In popular states such expenses are made more often, because the people take pleasure in them. Hence those vulgar craftsmen, who do not know the mean, although they cannot make such expenses because of their meagre means, nevertheless delight in them. Wherefore Cicero said that the Roman people did not like private luxury but public magnificence. Mikropreperia [μικροπρέπεια] is the defect on the other side, when the expenses are smaller than the magnitude of the work requires. We could call it meanness or untimely parsimony. From the management of resources he passes to the desire for honours.

units.la: Appello hic ignominiam ἀτιμίαν, non illam intelligens quæ ob aliquod admissum scelus incurritur, sed honoris carentiam seu vacuitatem, cùm quis ab honoribus abstinet, quos posset sibi vendicare, iustaque ratione ad illum attinent. Deinde χαυνότης est a verbo χαύνειν, quod est hiare: estque appe-titus nimius honoris, potestque appellari fastus ac superbia, cùm quis nimis al-tum sapit, de se magna æstimat, & ingentes spiritus concipit: hoc est hiare honoribus. Elatio alioquin animi posset à Latinis in bonam partem accipi. Vnde χαυνότητα superbiam interpretandam puto. Defectus autem qui di-citur μικροψυχία, est deiectio animi. Nonnulli enim ita se abiciunt, ut rei-publicæ prorsus reddantur inutiles.
units.tr: I call here "ignominy" [ἀτιμία], not understanding that which is incurred on account of some committed crime, but the lack or emptiness of honour, when someone holds back from honours which he could claim for himself and which rightly belong to him. Next, "vanity" [χαυνότης] comes from the verb χαύνειν, which means to gape open; it is an excessive appetite for honour, and it can be called haughtiness or pride, when someone thinks too highly of himself, esteems himself great, and conceives lofty notions: this is to gape open for honours. Otherwise, the elation of spirit could be taken in a good sense by the Latins. Hence I think χαυνότης should be rendered as pride. The defect, however, which is called "pusillanimity" [μικροψυχία], is dejection of spirit. For some so abase themselves that they become altogether useless to the commonwealth.

units.la: Verum quemadmodum ultra liberalitatem ha-betur quedam alia uirtus nempe magnificentia, quę à liberalitate distat penes magnum & paruum: ita supra magnanimitatem ponitur, quæ circa maximos non paruos honores uersatur. Est itaque ut diximus appetitus honoris quandoque maior, quandoque minor quam oportet. Qui exuperat, appellatur φιλότι-μῳ, qui autem deficit ἀφιλότιμῳ: medius uero caret nomine. Quin & affectiones ipsæ non habent nomen, nisi quod φιλοτίμως est φιλοτιμία tantum nominata. Hinc fit ut de media sede extremi certent. Et nos quoque medium interdum φιλότιμον uocamus, interdum ἀφιλότιμον. Et quandoque laudamus φιλότιμος, quandoque ἀφιλότιμος. Qua uero de causa hoc faciamus, in iis quæ sequentur, dicetur. Nunc de reliquis, eo modo quo cœpimus, dicamus.
units.tr: But just as beyond liberality there is another virtue, namely magnificence, which differs from liberality by reference to great and small, so above magnanimity is placed a virtue which concerns the greatest honours, not small ones. Thus, as we have said, the appetite for honour is sometimes greater, sometimes less than it ought to be. He who exceeds is called philotimos [φιλότιμος], he who falls short aphilotimos [ἀφιλότιμος]; the mean, however, lacks a name. Indeed, even the affections themselves have no name, except that philotimia is named only as philotimos. Hence it comes about that the extremes contend for the middle place. And we too sometimes call the mean philotimon, sometimes aphilotimon. And sometimes we praise the philotimos, sometimes the aphilotimos. Why we do this will be said in what follows. Now let us speak of the rest in the way we began.

units.la: φιλότιμον dicimus ambitiosum, & φιλοτιμίαν ambitionem, ἀφιλότι-μον honoris negligentem. Multos enim videas, qui careant honore, non quòd non possint consequi, sed quòd nolint & aspernentur. Cùm itaque medium careat nomine, hinc fit ut de media sede extrema certent. Nam quan-doque laudamus ambitiosum, quandoque negligentes honoris commendamus, quasi tam ista quam ille virtutem obtineat. Qua uero de causa hoc faciamus, suo dicetur loco. Si quis honores negligat, ne laboret, ne molestetur, vel ut impensis avare parcat, non laudatur, sed improbatur ut vitiosus. Si quis uero id faciat ob modestiam, vel quòd se non sentiat aptum, non vituperatur. Qui uero persequitur honores, quando id reipublicæ causa facit, & ad virtutem exercendam, non potest non laudari: at si captet propter opes, ac malis artibus sese ingerat, vituperatur.
units.tr: We call the philotimon ambitious, and philotimia ambition, and aphilotimon one negligent of honour. For you may see many who lack honour, not because they cannot obtain it, but because they are unwilling and scorn it. Since therefore the mean lacks a name, it comes about that the extremes contend for the middle place. For sometimes we praise the ambitious man, sometimes we commend those negligent of honour, as if both that one and this one possessed virtue. Why we do this will be told in its own place. If someone neglects honours so as not to labour or be troubled, or to spend sparingly out of avarice, he is not praised but disapproved as vicious. If someone does so out of modesty, or because he does not feel himself fit, he is not blamed. But he who pursues honours, when he does it for the sake of the commonwealth and for exercising virtue, cannot but be praised; but if he seeks them on account of wealth and thrusts himself forward by bad arts, he is blamed.

units.la: In exuperantia quoque iræ, est exuperatia, defectus, & mediocritas, & fere nomine carent: medium tamen appellamus mansuetum, & mediocritatem mansuetudine. Qui superatur esto iracundus, vitiumque dicatur iracūdia. Deficiens lentus, defectus vero lentitudo.
units.tr: In the excess of anger too there is excess, deficiency, and mean, and these mostly lack names: yet we call the mean mildness (mansuetus), and the mean state mansuetudo. The one who is overcome is to be called irascible, and the vice called irascibility. The deficient is lentus (slow to anger), and the deficiency slowness.
Thus Cicero calls it.

units.la: Sunt etiam aliæ tres mediocritates, quæ similitu-dinem quandam inter se habent, differunt tamen in-ter se. Omnes enim sermonum & actionum communitate versantur. Distinguuntur vero, quod una ea-rum veritatem sectatur, aliæ vero iucunditatem. Quod quidem iucundum partim in ioco, partim in omnibus vitæ commerciis consistit. Quamobrem de his etiam dicendum est, ut facilius intelligamus mediocritatem in omnibus laudandam, extrema vero neque recta neque laudanda, verum vitupe-randa.
units.tr: There are also three other means, which have a certain likeness among themselves, yet differ from one another. For all are concerned with the common intercourse of speech and action. They are distinguished, however, because one of them pursues truth, the others pleasantness. And this pleasant quality consists partly in jest, partly in all the dealings of life. Therefore these too must be discussed, so that we may more easily understand that the mean is to be praised in all things, but the extremes are neither right nor praiseworthy, but are to be blamed.

units.la: Sequuntur, ut inquit, tres aliæ virtutes, quæ hoc inter sese commune habent, quòd sunt circa sermones & vitæ conuersationem: habent enim locum quo homines inter se communicant. Distinguuntur vero, quòd vna earum veritatem sectatur, aliæ vero iucunditatem, quæ si fit in sermonibus, dicitur comitas & affabilitas. Sin vero in reliqua vitæ actione seu conuersatione, est amicitia. Conueniunt itaq; ac distinguuntur. Causa propter quam tractatur est, ut inductione quadam intelligatur, medium laudandum, extrema autem vituperanda.
units.tr: There follow, as he says, three other virtues, which have this in common among themselves, that they concern speech and the conduct of life: for they have a place in which men communicate with one another. They are distinguished, however, in that one of them pursues truth, the others pleasantness; which, if it is in speech, is called courtesy and affability; but if it is in the rest of life's action or conduct, it is friendship. Thus they agree and differ. The reason for which it is treated is that, by a kind of induction, it may be understood that the mean is to be praised, but the extremes are to be blamed.

units.la: Sed in iis plerisq; nomina imposita non sunt, verum curandum est ut imponantur: nam id faciet ad perspicuitatem, & ut quæ dicenda sunt melius asse-quamur. Circa verum igitur, qui medius est, verax: mediocritas vero veritas nominetur. Simulatio vero, quæ in maius tendit, Arrogantia, & qui ea affectus est, Arrogans: quæ vero in minus, dissimula-tio, & dissimulator.
units.tr: But for most of these no names have been imposed, yet care must be taken that they be imposed: for this will serve clarity and help us better grasp what must be said. Concerning truth, then, the one who is in the middle is truthful, and the mean may be named truthfulness. The pretence that tends to more is arrogance, and the one affected by it an arrogant person; but that which tends to less is dissimulation, and the dissimulator.

units.la: Virtus quæ circa veritatem est, vocabitur veritas, ac tum veritas nihil aliud significabit, nisi habitum, quo propensi reddimur & studiosi veritatis aut dicenda aut audienda. Simulatio autem vitium est ei oppositum, & merito vitijs adnumeratur, quòd veritatem adulteret, & sanum iudicium impediat. Non tamen omnis fictio vitiosa est, si tendat ad erudiendum, neque id quaerat ut homines fallantur. Habet autem duas partes simulatio, in quas distribuitur: Vna est exuperantia, & dicetur ἀλαζονία, Thrasonica iactantia: plura iis pollicentur, quàm velint aut queant praestare. ἀλαζόνες [?] aiunt Scholia Graeca, appellabant impostores praestigiatores, ideò iis etiam Thrasones, cùm eo tendant, ut decipiant & fucum faciant. E diuerso est imminutio & detractio de veritate, de suis inquam viribus & scientia, quando minus quàm sit dicitur. Socrates nihilominus laudatur, cùm maximus ἀξων [?] fuerit. Sed ille se nescire quicquam dicebat, ex collatione ad scientiam Dei. Sic Plato illum in Apologia excusat. Conferebat item illa quae sciebat, cum iis quae ignorabat, & ita collata poterant dici nihil. Adhaec non erat animus eius ut falleret, sed potius ut ostenderet aliis qui se plurima scire iactabant, quàm parum aut nihil scirent, atque suis illis interrogationibus quibus utebatur, quasi nescius, alios erudiebat.
units.tr: The virtue concerned with truth will be called truthfulness, and truthfulness will then signify nothing other than the habit by which we are made inclined and eager for the truth in speaking or in hearing. Pretence, on the other hand, is a vice opposed to it, and it is rightly counted among the vices, because it corrupts the truth and hinders sound judgement. Yet not every feigning is vicious, if it aims at instruction and does not seek to deceive anyone. Pretence has two parts into which it is divided. One is excess, called alazonia [ἀλαζονία], Thrasonic boasting: men promise more than they wish or are able to perform. The Greek Scholia say that alazones [ἀλαζόνες] were the name for impostors and tricksters, and so they are also called Thrasones, since they aim to deceive and to put on a false show. The opposite is diminution and detraction from the truth, namely about one's own powers and knowledge, when a man says less than is the case. Nevertheless Socrates is praised, although he was the greatest eiron [εἴρων]. But he used to say that he knew nothing, in comparison with the knowledge of God. Plato excuses him in this way in the Apology. He also set what he knew beside what he did not know, and so compared, they could be called nothing. Moreover, his purpose was not to deceive, but rather to show to others, who boasted that they knew a great deal, how little or nothing they knew; and by those questions which he used, as one who did not know, he instructed others.

units.la: Circa iucundum vero, quod in ioco cernitur, medius dicitur Comis siue urbanus & affectio Comitas. Exuperantia vero βωμολοχία: & qui eam exercet, βωμολόχος. Qui vero deficit, Rusticus: & habitus, Rusticitas.
units.tr: Concerning the pleasant in jest, the mean is called the witty or courteous man, and the disposition is courtesy. The excess is buffoonery [βωμολοχία], and the one who practises it is a buffoon [βωμολόχος]. The one who falls short is the boor, and the habit is boorishness.

units.la: Virtus quae sectatur iucunda in iocis est εὐτραπελία [?], comitas inquam & affabilitas. Res est quandoque necessaria: nam ut corpus opus habet requie, sic animus ut remittatur, aliqua voluptate. Cauendum tamen ne simus in iis nimiì, ne laedamus, ne obscaena vlla dicamus. Deinde ut seruentur circumstantia, quando, cum quibus, quomodo, & iis verbis aut actionibus quibus oportet. Exuperantia est βωμολοχία, cum homines dicaci scurrilitate vtuntur, obscaena dicunt, laedunt alios, rationem non habent loci, temporis, modi aut personarum. βωμὸς aram significat, & ibi circa aras epulae antiquitus habebantur, unde scurrae altaria obsidebant, ut sua dicacitate quae saepissime impudens erat homines exhilararent. Qui vero ab omnibus iocis abhorrent, rustici dicuntur ἄγροικοι. Vel ut faceti dici possunt urbani, sic iis dicentur inurbani.
units.tr: The virtue that pursues the pleasant in jests is eutrapelia [εὐτραπελία], that is, courtesy and affability. The thing is sometimes necessary, for as the body needs rest, so the mind needs to be relaxed by some pleasure. Yet we must take care not to indulge in it too much, not to hurt anyone, and not to say anything obscene. Then the circumstances must be observed: when, with whom, in what manner, and with those words or actions that are fitting. Excess is buffoonery, when men use biting, scurrilous wit, say obscene things, hurt others, and pay no heed to place, time, manner, or persons. Bomos means an altar, and in antiquity feasts were held around altars, whence the jesters besieged the altars so that they might cheer men with their sharp wit, which was very often shameless. Those who shrink from all jesting are called boorish [ἄγροικοι]. And just as those who are witty can be called urbane, so those who lack it will be called unurbane.

units.la: In altera uero iucunditate, quae in uitae commer-cijs est, qui ut decet iucundus est, φίλο: & mediocri-tas φιλία. Qui uero exuperat, siquidem absque causa id facit, ἀρεσκο: sin emolumeti sui gratia, κόλαξ. At qui deficit, & in omnibus inhumanus est, δύσχερης & δύ-σκολο.
units.tr: In the other kind of pleasantness, which lies in the dealings of life, the one who is pleasant as is fitting is friendly [φίλος], and the mean is friendliness [φιλία]. But whoever exceeds, if he does so without cause, is obsequious [ἀρεσκός]; if for the sake of his own gain, a flatterer [κόλαξ]. The one who falls short, and is unkind in everything, is surly [δύσχερης, δύσκολος].

units.la: In altera virtute quae iucunditatem sectatur, extrema quoq; sunt. Ipsa dicitur Amicitia, quae non proprie sic nominatur, quoniam illa virtus amici-tiae non solum fundatur in voluptate, sed modo sic nominatur quod ad amicitiam conciliandam valeat: posset autem dici humanitas. Exuperantia duplex est, quoniam homines interdum absq; causa nimium placere studet, atq; ij dicuntur ἀρεσκοι, omnibus sunt blandi, omnibusq; vellent gratificari, non reprehendunt vitia, nulla unquam volunt uti seueritate. At si faciant hoc pro suo commodo ac emolumento, sunt adulatores. Qui e diuerso, semper inhumani sunt & austeri: sunt enim δύσκολοι, hoc est, difficiles & morosi. Et δυσχερης litigiosus, etiam in hoc defecta est. Quicquid dixeris aduersantur, litigant & contendunt.
units.tr: In the other virtue that seeks pleasantness there are also extremes. The virtue itself is called friendliness, which is not properly so named, since that virtue of friendship is not founded only on pleasure, but is so named only because it serves to win friendship; it could also be called humanity. Excess is twofold, since sometimes people strive to please too much without cause; these are called obsequious [ἀρεσκοί]. They are fawning to all, wish to gratify everyone, do not rebuke vices, and never want to use any severity. But if they do this for their own convenience and gain, they are flatterers. On the other hand, those who are always unkind and austere are surly [δύσκολοι], that is, difficult and morose. And the quarrelsome [δυσχερής] are also defective in this respect: whatever you say, they oppose, quarrel and contend.

units.la: Sunt quoq; in affectibus, & in ijs quae circa affectus sunt, mediocritates. Verecundia enim uirtus quidem non est: ueruntamen laudatur is qui uerecundus est. Nam in his rebus medius dicitur, alius exuperans, ut καταπλήξ[?], stupidus, qui ad omnia erubescit. Qui uero deficit, quemq; nihil omnino pudet, ἀναίσχυντος[?] impudens: medius uero αἰδήμων[?], verecundus.
units.tr: There are also means in the affections and in the things that concern the affections. For modesty is indeed not a virtue; nevertheless the one who is modest is praised. In these matters the mean is called modest, while the other who exceeds is the stupefied [καταπλήξ], who blushes at everything. The one who falls short, whom nothing at all shames, is shameless [ἀναίσχυντος]; the mean is the modest [αἰδήμων].

units.la: Iam patuit in virtutibus quae sunt vel in affectibus, vel in actionibus, media esse laudabilia, extremaq; improbari. Nunc adhuc idem ostendit esse in ipsis affectibus, qui non sunt virtutes, nempe in illis quoq; medium laudari, & virtutem improbari. Verecundia quae medium est laudatur, non tamen est virtus: quia naturaliter homines illam incurrunt, & quandoq; nolentes: est enim dolor aut metus de aliquo dedecore quod immineat, vel in quod inciderimus. At dixeris, affectus non laudatur, aut vituperantur cum sint sint naturales, quomodo ergo verecundia laudatur & eius extrema damnantur? Respondeo. Non laudatur neq; vituperatur purus affectus, sed modi eius. Laudatur cum est medius, vituperatur si extremus fuerit. Exuperantia hic quoq; in verecundia reperitur: & qui ea laborat dicitur κατα-πλὴξ[?] id est attonitus, consternatus, qui ad omnia crubescit: e diuerso est impudens, qui etsi non omnino, tamen plus quam deceat, caret verecundia.
units.tr: It has now been shown that in the virtues, whether they lie in the affections or in actions, the means are praiseworthy and the extremes are condemned. Now he shows further that the same holds in the affections themselves, which are not virtues: namely, that the mean is praised in these too, and the excess condemned. Modesty, which is the mean, is praised, yet it is not a virtue, because people incur it naturally, and sometimes unwillingly; for it is a pain or fear about some disgrace that threatens, or into which we have fallen. But you may say that an affection is not praised or blamed, since they are natural; how then is modesty praised and its extremes condemned? I reply: it is not the pure affection that is praised or blamed, but its modes. It is praised when it is the mean; it is blamed if it is extreme. Excess is found here too in modesty: the one who suffers from it is called stupefied [καταπλήξ], that is, astonished and dismayed, who blushes at everything. On the other side is the shameless, who, though not wholly lacking modesty, has less of it than is fitting.

units.la: Nemesis uero mediocritas est inuidiae & maleuolentiae. Sunt autem circa aegritudinem & uoluptatem, quae suscipitur ex iis quae aliis contingunt: Qui enim Nemesi affectus est, dolet ob indignorum prosperos successus: inuidus hunc exuperans, de quibuslibet dolet. Maleuolus uero tantum abest ut doleat, ut potius gaudeat. Verum de iis quidem alibi dicetur opportunius. De iustitia uero, quoniam non simpliciter dicitur, deinceps diuisione adhibita de utraque dicemus quomodo mediocritates sint. Similiter & de uirtutibus rationis.
units.tr: Nemesis, however, is the mean between envy and malevolence. They are concerned with grief and with the pleasure taken from things that happen to others. For one affected by nemesis grieves at the prosperous successes of the unworthy; the envious man, exceeding this, grieves at whatever happens to anyone. The malevolent man is so far from grieving that he rather rejoices. But these matters will be discussed more fittingly elsewhere. As for justice, since it is not spoken of simply, we shall afterwards, with a division applied, speak of each of its kinds and how they lie in the mean. Likewise we shall speak of the virtues of reason.

units.la: Alius affectus medius est Νέμεσις[?], aegritudo ea est siue dolor, quem capimus ob sceleratorum prosperos successus. Exuperantiam complectitur inuidus: nam is de laeto prosperoq; successu cuiusuis dolet, nullo seruato discrimine probi vel improbi hominis. In defectu collocatur maleuolus, is tantum abest ut doleat, ut potius e diuerso gaudeat, cuicunq; mala euenerint. Scholia Graeca notarunt Aristotelem hic de isto affectu crasse loqui, sed reuera duos ordines esse constituendos, ita ut primo sit in medio [?] μέσοις, excessus inuidus, defectus is qui nullo pacto dolet, si videat indignos beari. Alter ordo medius qui gaudet si boni prosperentur, & mali affligantur. Exuperat maleuolus id est, πλεονεκτικῶς[?], qui gaudet vel etiam si mala cuiuis contigerint. Defectus, qui nullam capit voluptate de bonis aut malis quae aliis accidunt. Verum de iis alibi dicetur exquisitius. Conueniunt isti affectus, quoniam circa illa bona & illa mala versantur, quae aliis, non nobis accidunt. Cur vero de iustitia non sit loquutus, excusat, quoniam, inquit, ea non simpliciter dicitur. In distribuente & commutantem diuiditur, & de iis ambabus eius partibus dicetur postea suo loco, & de illis ostendemus quo nam pacto sint in mediocritate sita. Dicetur etiam de virtutibus rationis.
units.tr: Another affection that is a mean is nemesis [Νέμεσις]; it is the grief or pain which we feel at the prosperous successes of the wicked. Envy embraces the excess: for he grieves at the happy and prosperous success of anyone whatever, without regard to whether the man is good or bad. The malevolent man is placed in the defect: he is so far from grieving that on the contrary he rejoices whenever misfortunes befall anyone. The Greek scholia have noted that Aristotle speaks here crudely about this affection, but that in truth two orders should be set up: first, in the mean, the excess is envy, and the defect is the one who in no way grieves if he sees the unworthy blessed; the other order is the mean, who rejoices if good people prosper and bad people are afflicted. The malevolent man exceeds, that is, acts in a grasping way [πλεονεκτικῶς], since he rejoices even if misfortunes befall anyone. The defect is the one who takes no pleasure in the good or bad things that happen to others. But these will be discussed more exactly elsewhere. These affections agree, since they are concerned with those goods and evils which befall others, not us. Why he has not spoken of justice he excuses: since, he says, it is not spoken of simply. It is divided into distributive and commutative, and of both these parts we shall speak later in their proper place, and show how they lie in the mean. It will also be spoken of among the virtues of reason.

units.la: Modo superesset iuxta ordinem hactenus obseruatum, ut ostenderemus an ista diuinis literis consentiant. Sed quoniam de iis omnibus uirtutibus, quæ hic censu quodam breuissimo enumeratæ sunt, exquisitè ac subtiliter agetur posterius, ideò supersedeo, quia tunc locum habebunt opportunum, quæ ad hanc de diuinis literis methodum spectant.
units.tr: It only remained, following the order observed so far, to show whether these agree with the divine letters. But since all those virtues which have been enumerated here in a very brief survey will be treated exactly and subtly later, I forbear, because then they will have a fitting place for those matters which pertain to this method of the divine letters.
CHAPTER VIII

units.la: CUm autem sint tres affectiones, duæ quidē pra-uæ statuuntur, quarum altera uergit ad exupe-rantiam, & altera ad defectum. Una uerc[?] uirtute in mediocritate posita, omnes quoquo modo inter se-se opponuntur, & extrema ipsi mediocritati ac inter sese sunt contraria, & mediocritas extremis. Quem-admodum enim æquale maius est, si ad minus conferatur, & ad maius est minus: ita medij habitus defectum superant, ab exuperantia uero deficiunt, cum in affectibus tum in actionibus. Fortis enim comparatus ignauo uidetur audax, & aduersus audacem ignauus. Similiterq; temperatus dum stupido comparatur, intemperans uidebitur: & aduersus intemperantem, stupidus. Liberalis etiam collatus auaro prodigus habebitur, ad prodigum autem auarus. Idcirco medium extremi alterum in alterum extrudunt, & fortem ignauus appellat audacem, audax uero ignauum. Atq; in aliis est eadem ratio.
units.tr: Since there are three states of feeling, two of them are judged vicious: one tends to excess, the other to deficiency. Virtue, placed in the mean, is opposed in some way to both extremes, and the extremes are contrary both to the mean and to each other. For just as the equal is greater when compared with the lesser, and lesser when compared with the greater, so the middle state surpasses the deficiency and falls short of the excess, both in feelings and in actions. The brave man, compared with the coward, seems rash, and the coward, compared with the rash man, seems cowardly. Likewise the temperate man, compared with the insensible man, will seem intemperate, and the insensible man, compared with the intemperate. The liberal man, compared with the miser, will be thought prodigal, and the miser, compared with the prodigal. So the extremes thrust the mean out of its place, each towards the other: the coward calls the brave man rash, and the rash man calls him a coward. The same reasoning applies in other cases.

units.la: Tria[?] in hoc habemus Capite. Primum, uirtutem opponi extre-mis. Alterum, extrema inter se maximè distare. Tertiò, uirtutem magis cum uno extremo quàm cum altero pugna-re, & magis unius esse similem quàm alterius. Virtutem opponi extremis patet, quoniam inter illa est maius & minus, hæc autem relatiuè, vt notissimum est, opponuntur. Maius & minus i-bi esse declaratur inductione, quo ad fortitudinem, temperantiam & libe-ralitatem. Quî fit vt extrema impellant medium extra locum suum. Au-dax fortem facit timidum, timidus vero illum facit audacem. Hæc omnia inter se dicit opponi aliquo modo, non autem simpliciter. Est enim oppositio hic relatiua, maioris & minoris, parui & magni, mali & boni. Vt malum & bonum, virtus & vitium opponuntur: vt magnum & paruum, extre-ma inter se: vt maius & minus, virtus cum extremis. Et quia sunt, vt di-xi, varij modi oppositionum, ideò Aristoteles ait, Quodammodo. Virtus alioqui vicina est vtcunq; vtrique extremorum, & cum altero illorum ha-bet (vt dicetur) aliquam similitudinem. Quo itaq; ad ista, potest videri ex-tremis vitijs non multum opponi. Sed in eo est magna inter hæc diuersitas. Virtus est moderata: extrema sunt immoderata. Virtus finita: infinita verò neq; terminata sunt. Vitiorum extrema, facilius q[?] ex uno extremo ad alte-rum itur, quàm ad medium: imò extrema inter se quodammodo aduersus virtutem conspirant, facilius q; ignauus aliquod audax facinus committet, quàm actionem fortem edat. Ad hæc enucleanda videtur nonnihil facere locus in prædicamentis, vbi Aristoteles ait bonum opponi malo, vt morbum sanitati, fortitudinem ignauiæ, iustitiam iniustitiæ: quandoq; etiam malū malo opponi, vt excessum & defectum. Ecce iam hic duo genera magnarū oppositionum, quæ ad hunc locum spectant. Verum quidem est eundem Ari-stotelem scribere, vnum vni esse contrarium. Cùm enim ob res facilius con-seruandas noluit vni plura esse contraria, non posset aliquid corrumpenti-bus multis resistere. Verùm hoc nos intelligemus, quando agetur de oppositi-tione simpliciter, non secundum quid. Album nigro simpliciter opponitur, sed potest secundum quid opponi albo rubrum, ceruleum & flauum. Adhæc quando multa videntur vni opponi, ea multa pro vno habetur. Vnde cùm virtuti duo extrema opponuntur, ea duo loco sunt vnius extremi, quando-quidem vtrunq; illorum est vitium. Duplex igitur genus comparandi hic habemus. Vnum est quo ad spacij distantiam, alterum verò quo ad contra-rietatem boni & mali. Vt bonum & malum contraria sunt, virtus & vi-tium, sed vt maximè distantia: sunt inter se valde opposita duo extrema. Et hoc est quod modo Aristoteles dicit.
units.tr: We have three points in this chapter. First, virtue is opposed to the extremes. Second, the extremes are most distant from each other. Third, virtue fights more with one extreme than with the other, and resembles one more than the other. That virtue is opposed to the extremes is clear, since between them there is a greater and a lesser, and these are opposed relatively, as is well known. That there is a greater and a lesser among them is shown by induction, in the case of courage, temperance and liberality. Hence it is that the extremes drive the mean out of its place: the rash man makes the timid man, and the timid man makes him rash. All these are opposed to one another in some way, but not absolutely. For the opposition here is relative, that of greater and less, small and great, bad and good. As bad and good, virtue and vice are opposed; as great and small, the extremes are opposed to each other; as greater and lesser, virtue is opposed to the extremes. And since, as I have said, there are various modes of opposition, Aristotle says "in a certain way". Otherwise virtue is near to each extreme and, as will be said, has some likeness to one of them. So far as these things go, it may seem that the extreme vices are not much opposed to one another. But there is a great difference here. Virtue is moderate; the extremes are immoderate. Virtue is finite; the extremes are infinite and unbounded. Of the vices, it is easier to pass from one extreme to the other than to the mean; indeed, the extremes in a way conspire together against virtue, and a coward will more easily commit some rash deed than perform a brave action. To clarify these points, the passage in the Categories seems to help somewhat, where Aristotle says that good is opposed to bad, as sickness to health, courage to cowardice, justice to injustice; and sometimes too bad is opposed to bad, as excess to deficiency. Here, then, are two kinds of great opposition that pertain to this passage. It is true that Aristotle also writes that one thing is contrary to one thing. For since he did not wish one thing to have several contraries, for the sake of more easily preserving things, it would not be able to resist many corrupting things. But we shall understand this when we treat of opposition absolutely, not in a certain respect. White is absolutely opposed to black, but in a certain respect red, blue and yellow can be opposed to white. Moreover, when many things seem opposed to one, those many are taken as one. Hence, since two extremes are opposed to virtue, those two are in the place of one extreme, since each of them is a vice. There are therefore two ways of comparing here: one with respect to the distance of space, the other with respect to the contrariety of good and bad. As good and bad are contraries, virtue and vice are, but as most distant; the two extremes are very much opposed to one another. And this is what Aristotle now says.

units.la: Cùm autem ista sic opponātur inter sese, maior est contrarietas mutuò inter extrema, quàm cū medio: quia longius hæc à se mutuò distât, quàm à medio. Quemadmodum magnum a paruo, & paruum a magno, quàm utrunq; ab æquali. Est præterea quædam similitudo extremis quibusdam erga medium, quemadmodum audaciæ ad fortitudinem, & effusioni ad liberalitatem: sed extremorum erga se inuicem summa est dissimilitudo. Quæ vero à se mutuo plurimùm distant, contraria esse definiuntur. Quî fit, ut quæ magis distant, magis sint contraria.
units.tr: Since these are thus opposed to one another, the contrariety between the extremes is greater than between either extreme and the mean, because the extremes are further from each other than from the mean, just as the great is from the small and the small from the great, more than each is from the equal. Moreover, some extremes have a certain likeness to the mean: rashness to courage, and prodigality to liberality. But the extremes have the greatest unlikeness to one another. Things that are most distant from each other are defined as contraries. Hence it is that things which are further apart are more contrary.

units.la: Cùm dicitur maior contrarietas inter extrema, illam debemus penes distantiæ spacium metiri, non autem iuxta contrarietatem boni et mali. Sic enim virtus & vitium maximè opponuntur, & plus conuenit inter effusionem & auaritiam, quàm inter vtrumq; horum & liberalitatem. Consentiunt quippè illa in genere vitij, cum virtute autem in genere non congruunt. Plusq; conuenit equus cum cane, quàm vterq; illorum cum homine: siquidem vtrunq; illorum est brutum, & genere propinquiori conueniunt inter sese quàm cum homine. Superest nunc demonstrandum, extremum distare magis à se inuicem, quà à medio. Prima ratio est, quod extrema se habent vt magnum et paruum, medium verò vt æquale: at magnum & paruum magis opponuntur inter sese, quàm æquali ipsis. Ideò extrema sunt magis distantia & oppositas sibi ipsis quàm medio. Adhuc quia similitudo est nonnullorum extremorum cum medio, quæ cum extremis nulla est: consentit enim audacia cum fortitudine, ac effusio cum liberalitate: at extremis inter sese summa est dissimilitudo. Deinde ratio confirmatur ex contrariorum definitione, quæ statuit illa esse contraria, quæ plurimùm à se distant. Ex eo quod Aristoteles ait quædam extrema nonnullam habere similitudinem cum medio, regulâ rhetorum dimanauit, vt cum vitia cuiuspiam aut excusare aut commedare velimus, vel illa aliquo tempore persuadere, videamus cui virtuti similia sint, eaq; pro virtute commendemus.
units.tr: When it is said that the contrariety between the extremes is greater, we must measure it by the extent of the distance, not by the contrariety of good and bad. For in this way virtue and vice are most opposed, and prodigality and avarice agree more with each other than either does with liberality. For they agree in the genus of vice, but do not agree in the genus of virtue. A horse agrees more with a dog than either does with a man, since both are brutes and, belonging to a nearer genus, they agree with each other more than with man. It remains now to demonstrate that the extremes are further from each other than from the mean. The first reason is that the extremes stand to each other as great and small, but the mean as equal; and great and small are more opposed to each other than to what is equal to them. Therefore the extremes are more distant and more opposed to each other than to the mean. Again, since there is a likeness between some extremes and the mean, which is not found between the extremes themselves: for rashness agrees with courage, and prodigality with liberality, but the extremes to each other have the greatest unlikeness. Then the argument is confirmed from the definition of contraries, which holds that those things are contrary which are most distant from each other. The statement of Aristotle that some extremes have some likeness to the mean flowed from a rule of the rhetoricians: when we wish either to excuse or to commend someone's vices, or at some time to persuade people of them, we look to which virtue they resemble, and we commend them under that virtue.

units.la: Cumq; opponantur medio extrema, in nonnullis magis defectus, in alijs magis exuperantia opponitur. Fortitudini enim non audacia, quæ est exuperantia, sed ignauia, quæ defectus est, magis opponitur: nec non temperantiæ, haud stupiditas, quæ est defectus opponitur, sed intemperantia quæ est excessus. Idcirco propter duas contingit causas, unam quidem ex ipsa re, quod unum extremorum similius & proximius medio fit: unde nō hoc ei opponimus, sed potius eius contrarium: utcunque uidetur audacia similior fortitudini, dissimilior uero ignauia, ideo hanc potius fortitudini opponimus quam illam. Quæ enim plus a medio distant, magis uidentur esse contraria. Atque una hæc causa est ex ipsa re deducta. Sed altera est a nobis ipsis: nam ea uidentur medio magis aduersari erga quæ magis ipsi facti uidemur: ut quia ipsi natura magis proni sumus erga uoluptates, ideoque magis ad intemperantiam sumus procliues, quam ad modestiam. Hæc itaque contraria dicemus, ad quæ accessiones quo ad nos potius fiunt: idcirco intemperantia, quæ excessus est, magis contraria est temperantiæ quam stupiditas.
units.tr: Since the extremes are opposed to the mean, in some cases deficiency is opposed more, in others excess. For courage is opposed more to cowardice, which is a deficiency, than to rashness, which is an excess; and temperance is opposed not to insensibility, which is a deficiency, but to intemperance, which is an excess. This happens for two reasons. One comes from the thing itself: one extreme is more similar to and nearer the mean, so we do not oppose the mean to it but rather its contrary. Thus rashness seems more similar to courage, and cowardice more dissimilar, so we oppose cowardice to courage rather than rashness. For things that are further from the mean seem more contrary. This one cause is drawn from the thing itself. The other comes from ourselves: for those things seem more opposed to the mean to which we are more inclined. For example, since we are by nature more prone to pleasures, and so more apt to intemperance than to moderation, we call contrary those extremes towards which we more readily move. So intemperance, which is an excess, is more contrary to temperance than insensibility is.

units.la: Cur aliqua extrema vel magis opponantur vel magis similia sint medio critati, duas adducit rationes. Quarum vnam ex reipsa dicit sumi: quòd nimirum vtriusque ratio tam extremi quàm medij quoquo modo conueniat. Vt ratio liberalitatis & effusionis consistit in dando, magis liberalitati opponetur auaritia: quoniam eius ratio non in dando sed in retinendo & accipiendo ponitur. Temperantia vero quo ad rem magis conuenit cum stupiditate, quàm cum intemperantia: quoniam vtriusque illarum ratio in abstinendo habetur. Intemperantia vero in fruendo & percipiendo voluptates. Ex ijs patet, quare ista ratio ab ipsa re sumi dicatur. Altera ducitur ex naturali inclinatione, qua nos ipsi afficimur: virtuti enim magis illa opponuntur extrema ad quæ sumus natura magis propensi: & quia natura impellimur ad voluptates, ideo intemperantia magis quàm stupiditas est contraria temperantiæ. Sed Aristotelis doctrina videtur cum ijs pugnare quæ iam sunt allata. Si enim virtus est æquaæqualitas, quomodo magis ad vnum extremum quàm alterum accedit, vel quomodo magis ab vno quàm ab altero distat? Persuadetur adhuc idem ex natura medij, quod medium est, quia æqualiter ab extremis distat. Re-spondetur ad ista, in virtute non dici æqualitatem quo ad distantiam, sed quo ad rationem, & quo ad nos, non arithmeticam, sed geometricam. Concluderent argumenta, fi quo ad spacium seu distantiam accipe-rentur.
units.tr: He gives two reasons why some extremes are either more opposed or more similar to the mean. One is taken from the thing itself, namely that the account of both the extreme and the mean agrees in some way. Since the account of liberality consists in giving, avarice will be more opposed to liberality, since its account lies not in giving but in keeping and receiving. Temperance agrees more in the matter with insensibility than with intemperance, since the account of both of those lies in abstaining, whereas intemperance lies in enjoying and perceiving pleasures. From this it is clear why this reason is said to be taken from the thing itself. The other is drawn from the natural inclination by which we are affected: for the extremes to which we are naturally more inclined are more opposed to virtue; and since we are impelled by nature to pleasures, intemperance is more contrary to temperance than insensibility is. But Aristotle's teaching seems to clash with what has just been brought forward. For if virtue is equality, how does it approach one extreme more than the other, or how is it further from one than from the other? The same objection is pressed from the nature of the mean, that it is the mean because it is equally distant from the extremes. To these points the answer is that in virtue equality is not spoken of with respect to distance, but with respect to the ratio and to us; it is not arithmetical but geometrical. The arguments would be conclusive if they were taken with respect to space or distance.

units.la: Nunc superest vt videamus quo nam pacto ista diuinis literis confenta-neafint. Primum verissimum est, virtutem opponi vitijs & vitia virtuti-bus. Quæ enim conuentio lucis ad tenebras, & quæ societas Christo cum Be-lial? Et nemo potest duobus Dominis seruire. Nec non id vt verum admitti-tur, vitia inter sese pugnare. Isa. 57. Non est pax impijs, dicit Dominus. Vi-dentur quidem interdum conspirare in malum, sed tandé dissentiunt. Neq; id inficiandum est, cum virtute magis vnum extremum quàm alterum fa-cere in Ecclesiaste 7. cap. dicitur. Melior est fæueritas quàm risus. Et melior est tardus spiritu, quàm qui sublimem habet spiritum.
units.tr: Now it remains for us to see how these things agree with the divine writings. First, it is most true that virtue is opposed to vices and vices to virtues. For what agreement is there between light and darkness, or what fellowship between Christ and Belial? And no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6). It is also rightly admitted that vices fight among themselves. Isa. 57. "There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord." Indeed they sometimes seem to conspire in evil, but in the end they disagree. Nor is this to be denied: that one extreme is made more of a virtue than the other is stated in Ecclesiastes 7. "Severity is better than laughter, and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit."
CHAPTER IX

units.la: Quod itaque uirtus moralis mediocritas est, & quomodo, & mediocritas duorum uitiorum, huius quidem iuxta exuperantiam, illius uero iuxta defectum: Quodꝗ huiusmodi sit, quia medij coniectatrix est, cum in affectionibus, tum in actionibus, copiosè dictum est.
units.tr: That moral virtue is a mean, and in what way, and that it is the mean between two vices, one by excess and the other by defect, and that it is of such a kind because it aims at the mean, both in the affections and in actions, has been discussed at length.

units.la: Caput hoc in istas diducitur partes. Primo loco habetur Epilogus. Secundo proponitur, Difficile admodum esse medium inuenire. Tertiò, Quædam eius reperiendi ponuntur documenta. Quartò, Medium ipsum quantum respatitur, determinatur. Quo ad Epilogum, elegans est, paucis expeditur, sed significantibus vocibus. Dicit se loquutum de virtute, sed morali. Eam definiuit mediocritatem. Sed quomodo? non rei, sed quo ad nos vel rationis. Extrema etiam eius duo vitia ostendit, quorum vnum exuperet, alterum verò deficiat. Virtus autem mediocritas est ex effectu, quod illam sectetur. In quibus rebus? in affectibus & actionibus. Hac hactenus prolixè dicta sunt: nunc verò paucis perorata.
units.tr: This chapter is divided into these parts. First comes the epilogue. Second, it is proposed that it is very difficult to find the mean. Third, some rules for finding it are laid down. Fourth, the mean itself is defined as far as it can be. The epilogue is elegant and is dispatched in a few words, yet they are meaningful. He says that he has spoken of virtue, but of moral virtue. He defined it as a mean. But in what way? Not in the thing itself, but with respect to us, or to reason. He also showed the two extremes of that mean, the one of which exceeds it, while the other falls short. Virtue is called a mean because it follows from its effect that it pursues it. In what matters? In the affections and in actions. These things have been discussed at length up to this point; now they are summed up briefly.

units.la: Ideoq; difficile est in una quaque re probum esse: nam in omni negotio medium notare difficile est, ceu medium circuli non est cuiusuis deprehendere, sed periti. Sic & irasci cuiusuis est, & facile dare pecunias, & impendere. Sed cui, quantum, quando, & cuius causa, & quomodo oportet, necp[?] cuiusuis est, neque facile. Unde rectum rarum est, & laudabile quod est honestum.
units.tr: Therefore it is difficult to be good in any single matter. For in every business it is hard to mark the mean, just as it is not for anyone to find the middle of a circle, but only for the skilled. So too, to be angry is anyone's business, and to give money or spend it easily is anyone's business. But to be angry with the right person, to the right degree, at the right time, for the right cause and in the right way, is not for just anyone, nor is it easy. Hence rectitude is rare, and what is honourable is praiseworthy.

units.la: Difficultas rectitudinis & probitatis ex eo est, Quoniam (ut supra habuimus) uno tantum simplicitatis modo fit. Prauitas autem cum sit prope modum infinita, occurrit facilius. Ratio alia difficultatis est quae modo attingitur, Quod medium sit difficile inuentu. Et simile proponitur de circuli medio: non quiuis illud potest notare, sed tantum peritus mathematicarum. Euclides in 3. docet ut linea recta ducatur, quae medium circulum secet in partes aequales. Et centrum erit tum circuli, in eo puncto quod lineam tra-ctam diuidit in partes aequales. Verum exemplum adductum est medium rei seu magnitudinis. Nos autem nunc agimus de medio rationis, & quo ad nos: quare non videtur accommodatum. Sed argumentum reuera est a mi-nori ad maius. Si non cuiusuis est medium inuenire, quod facilius est & idem perpetuo manet: Quanto magis erit difficile, medium rationis & quo ad nos inuenire, quod non semper idem est, imo per omnes propemodum occasiones & circumstantias variatur? Quod ait Aristoteles, non eo spectat ut desperemus. Si non est id cuiusuis, est tamen aliquorum. In circulo exigitur aliqua peritia mathesEos. Hic requiritur exercitatio & usus. Valent ista quae modo scribuntur, ad animos auditorum inflammandos, ut sese in hoc cursu virtutum assequendarum exerceant. Non est Peripateticum dogma nihil posse sciri. Sententias istas relinquunt Democrito & Scopticis. Nonetiam[?] diffitemur hodie multos esse, qui tantum opinionibus regantur, quos tamen non laudamus, cum scientia, arte, bonisq; habitibus longe magis pra-stet res suas gubernare, quam vel opinione vel casu. Et ex ista peruersitate fit ut fit vt de virtutibus omnes fere velint iudicare, cum in eis nullum studium, nullum vsum, nullamue vnquam posuerint exercitationem. Liberalitatis fortè ac temperantiæ nomen audiuerunt: at non tenet rem, neq; vt tenerent vnquam operam dederunt. Est igitur in medio notando etiam magna difficultas ob numerum circumstantiarum. Et quia res in vniuersum (quemadmodū dicitur) tractari non potest, sed potius ad singula quodammodo pertinet, circumstantiæ non omnes hoc loco ab Aristotele commemorantur: de illis fusius agetur in Tertio. Continentur etiam omnes illo iactato versiculo,
units.tr: The difficulty of rectitude and uprightness arises from the fact that (as we had above) it comes about in only one way of straightness. Wickedness, however, since it is almost infinite in its forms, occurs more easily. Another reason for the difficulty, which is touched on now, is that the mean is hard to discover. And a similar case is put forward about the middle of a circle: not everyone can mark it, but only one skilled in mathematics. Euclid in book 3 teaches that a straight line is to be drawn which cuts the circle into equal parts; and the centre of the circle will be at that point which divides the drawn line into equal parts. But the example adduced is of the mean of a thing or a magnitude. We, however, are now dealing with the mean of reason, and with respect to us, so the comparison does not seem apt. Yet the argument is really from the less to the greater. If it is not for everyone to find the mean, which is easier and remains always the same, how much more difficult will it be to find the mean of reason and with respect to us, which is not always the same, but varies almost on every occasion and circumstance? When Aristotle says this, he does not aim at making us despair. If it is not for everyone, it is still for some. In the case of the circle some skill in mathematics is required; here practice and experience are required. What is now being written serves to inflame the minds of the hearers, so that they may exercise themselves in this course of acquiring the virtues. It is not a Peripatetic doctrine that nothing can be known. Those opinions are left to Democritus and the Sceptics. Nor do we deny that today there are many who are governed only by opinions, whom nonetheless we do not praise, since it is far better to manage one's affairs by knowledge, skill and good habits than by opinion or chance. And from this perversity it comes about that almost all men want to judge the virtues, though they have never applied any study, practice or exercise to them. They have perhaps heard the name of liberality or temperance, but they do not grasp the thing, nor have they ever taken pains to grasp it. Therefore there is also great difficulty in marking the mean because of the number of circumstances. And since the matter cannot be treated in general (as they say), but rather pertains in some measure to individual cases, not all the circumstances are mentioned here by Aristotle; these will be discussed more fully in book 3. All of them are also contained in that well-known little verse,

units.la: Quis, quid, vbi, quibus auxilijs, cur, quomodo, quando.
units.tr: Who, what, where, by what aids, why, how, when.

units.la: Deinde additur ex ista difficultate inueniendi medij id quod est rectum & honestum rarum esse: vitant quippe omnes plerig; laborem. Laudabile tamen est, quicquid rectum & honestum fuerit,
units.tr: Then, from this difficulty of finding the mean, it is added that what is right and honourable is rare, for almost everyone shuns the labour. Nevertheless, whatever is right and honourable is praiseworthy.

units.la: Ideoque oportet eum qui medium sectatur, ab eo extremo quod magis opponitur uirtuti discedere, quemadmodum & Calypso adhortabatur. ὡς τοῦ μὲν καπνοῦ [?] καὶ κύματος ἐντὸς ἐέργε νῦν [?]. Nam unum extremorum est in quo facilius peccatur, alterum vero in quo minus. Proinde quoniam summè asse-qui medium est difficile: secunda (utinquiunt) navigatione, ex malis assumenda sunt quæ minima fuerint. Hoc autem maxime fiet modo quem diximus.
units.tr: Therefore one who pursues the mean ought to steer away from that extreme which is more opposed to virtue, just as Calypso also urged: "Keep your ship away from that smoke and surge" [ὡς τοῦ μὲν καπνοῦ καὶ κύματος ἐντὸς ἐέργε νῦν]. For one of the extremes is that in which one sins more easily, and the other that in which one sins less. Therefore, since it is very difficult to attain the mean, one should take, as they say, the second voyage, choosing from among the evils the least.

units.la: Altera huius capitis parte profert Aristoteles documenta, quibus contra difficultatem inuentionis medij iuuemur. Vt virtuti magis vnum extremum quàm alterum aduersatur, aut rei natura aut ex nostra pronitate, ita documentum est duplex. Primo enim oportet deflectere ab eo extremo quod cum virtute magis pugnat: est enim periculosius. Doctrinam suâ confirmat Homeri testimonio, ad cuius euidentiorem lucè sciendum est duos esse scopulos in Siculo freto nempe inter Adriaticum & Tyrrhenum mare, quorum vnus dicitur Scylla, et alter Charybdis. Charybdis periculosior est: absorbetur enim aqua & reflatur. Vnde si nauis dum hoc fit ibi deprehendatur, omnino perit. Alter quoque scopulus perniciosus est, sed non vt alter. Quare versus illum collimandum est navigantibus, quo maius pe riculū euitetur. Quod tamē dū facimus, id cauendū est ut à nebula & vnda Scyllæ deflectamus, ne scilicet cupientes vitare Charybdim in Scyllā incidamus. Unde notandū est Græca scholia in Homero interpretando errare. Nā referūt καπνὸς et νύμφαι ad Charybdim, quod pertinet ad Scyllā. Nā illo carmine in ipso ii. lib. Odysseæ, Vlysses præcipit suo gubernatori vt versus Scyllā cat, cumq; eò peruenerit, nauim ab eius καπνὸς, id est nebula deflectat, et à fluctu quo percussa resonat. Est etiā notandū Aristotelem errare in nomine, quia hæc non dicuntur à Calypso: nā Circe hoc salutare consilium Vlyssi dedit. Carmen vero hic adductū nō à Circe recitatur, sed ab Vlysse memore præceptorū eius mandatur suæ nauis rectori. Neq; carmen habet, ὡς τ' μὲν καπνὸς, sed τοτὲ μὲν καπνὸς. Atq; post illa quæ hic recitantur, additur, σὺ δ' ἐκ σκοπέλης ἐπιμελέσθω, id est tu vero urge scopulum. Ratio cur hoc tanto studio faciundum sit, additur, nempe quod unum extremorum sit in quo facilius, alterum in quo minus peccatur. Cum vero tanta sit medij attingendi summa & ad amussim difficultas, secunda nauigatione assumenda sunt ex-malis minima.Secunda nauigatio hic non est prospera, vt aliqui falsò existimarunt, sed tum secundam nauigationem adhibemus cùm prima destituimur. Si enim venti non flauerint, tum remigum opera vtendum est. Appellatur hæc secunda nauigatio, quòd scilicet loco, nempe post felicem & optatam adhibeatur. Et hoc proverbio idem significatur, ac illo altero, Quando non licet vt volumus, vt possumus. Vellet quippe Aristoteles vt medium asequeremur: Sed quando id fieri non potest, ad extremum quod minus periculosum est tendamus. In Rhetoricis docuit minora mala boni loco haberi, si conferantur cum grauioribus. Et nos cùm legem ad amussim præ carnis [?] infirmitate non queamus obseruare, inchoatam nihilominus obedientiam potius exhibemus quam deflectamus ad peccata.
units.tr: The second part of this chapter sets out from Aristotle the rules by which we are helped against the difficulty of finding the mean. Whether one extreme is more opposed to virtue, either by the nature of the thing or by our own proneness, the rule is twofold. First, one must turn away from that extreme which fights more against virtue, for it is the more dangerous. He confirms the teaching by the testimony of Homer, and for a clearer light we must know that there are two rocks in the Sicilian strait, namely between the Adriatic and Tyrrhenian seas, one of which is called Scylla and the other Charybdis. Charybdis is the more dangerous: for the water is sucked in and thrown back. Hence, if a ship is caught there while this happens, it is utterly lost. The other rock is also dangerous, but not in the same way. Therefore sailors must aim toward that side, so that the greater peril is avoided. Yet while we do this, we must take care that we turn away from the mist and the wave of Scylla, lest, in wanting to avoid Charybdis, we fall into Scylla. Hence it should be noted that the Greek scholia err in interpreting Homer. For they refer "smoke" [καπνὸς] and "nymphs" [νύμφαι] to Charybdis, which pertains to Scylla. For in that very passage in book 12 of the Odyssey, Ulysses instructs his helmsman to steer toward Scylla, and when he has come there, to turn the ship away from her "smoke" [καπνὸς], that is, the mist, and from the wave by which it is struck and resounds. It should also be noted that Aristotle errs in the name, because these words are not spoken by Calypso: it was Circe who gave Ulysses this saving counsel. The verse quoted here is not recited by Circe but is delivered by Ulysses, mindful of her precepts, to the steersman of his ship. Nor does the verse read ὡς τ' μὲν καπνὸς, but τοτὲ μὲν καπνὸς. And after the lines quoted here there is added, σὺ δ' ἐκ σκοπέλης ἐπιμελέσθω, that is, "but you, see to the rock" [tu vero urge scopulum]. The reason why this must be done with such great care is added, namely that one of the extremes is the one in which one sins more easily, and the other the one in which one sins less. But since the goal of attaining the mean is so high and the difficulty of hitting it exact, one must take the least of the evils by a second voyage. The second voyage here is not a favourable one, as some have falsely thought, but we resort to the second voyage when we are deprived of the first. For if the winds do not blow, then the labour of the rowers must be used. This second voyage is so called because it is employed in place of the first, namely after the happy and desired one. And by this proverb the same thing is meant as by that other, "When we cannot do as we wish, we do as we can." Aristotle would certainly wish us to attain the mean; but when this cannot be done, let us aim at the extreme which is less dangerous. In the Rhetoric he taught that lesser evils are to be counted as goods when they are compared with graver ones. And since we cannot observe the law exactly because of the weakness of the flesh, we nonetheless offer an obedience begun, rather than turn aside into sins.

units.la: Nunquam tamen ob hoc documentum, quæ natura sua mala sunt debemus facere, vt bona nobis eueniant. Quomodo autem minima mala possimus accipere demonstrat, cùm inquit, Fiet id eo modo quem diximus, nimirum deflectendo ad extremum quod minus est periculosum, & in quo minus peccatur, & ex natura rei virtuti minus est contrarium.
units.tr: Yet we must never, on account of this teaching, do things that are evil in their own nature in order that good may come to us. He shows how we may take the smallest evils when he says: "It will be done in the way we have described, namely by turning aside to the extreme that is less dangerous, and in which less sin is committed, and which by the nature of the thing is less opposed to virtue."

units.la: Consyderare etiam oportet quæ nam ea sint ad quæ natura ipsi simus proclivióres [?]. Alij enim ad alia natura facti sumus. Hoc autem erit manifestum ex voluptate ac dolore quæ nobis euenerint, oportetqúe ut in contraria parte nosipsos subducamus. U-bi enim procul deflexerimus à peccando, ad medium pertingimus.
units.tr: We must also consider which things we are more naturally inclined to. For we are made by nature inclined to different things. This will be clear from the pleasure and pain that befall us, and we must withdraw ourselves toward the opposite side. For when we have turned far away from sinning, we reach the mean.

units.la: Alterum documentum sumitur ex natura ipsorum inclinatione. Illud enim quo ad nos extremum virtuti magis repugnat, ad quod natura sumus propensiores. Hic videmus agnouisse Philosophos naturæ morbum ac vitium. Iudicant enim nos non ad medium propensos esse natura, sed alterum extremorum vitiosorum: causam tamen huius natiui mali non intellexerunt. Quilibet, inquit, seipsum exploret: non enim omnes ad eadem facti sumus. Pronus est quisq; ad malum, sed non omnes eodem modo ad idem genus mali extimulantur, quisq; suos patimur manes. Vnde autem ea inclinatio possit deprehendi, commonstrat, nimirum ex dolore & voluptate. Videat quisq; præsentia cuius rei maximè delectetur, cuiusue rei absentia maximè doleat. Et aduersum inclinationem qua laborat maximè niti debet: nam dum magis à peccando recedit, magis ad medium accedit.
units.tr: The second teaching is taken from the inclination of the extremes themselves. For the extreme that is more opposed to virtue for us is the one toward which we are more naturally inclined. Here we see that the philosophers recognised the disease and fault of nature. For they judge that we are not by nature inclined to the mean but to one of the vicious extremes; yet they did not understand the cause of this innate evil. "Let each one," he says, "examine himself, for we are not all made for the same things. Each one is prone to evil, but not all are stirred to the same kind of evil in the same way; each of us bears his own ghosts." He shows how this inclination may be detected, namely from pain and pleasure. Let each one see in what thing he takes most delight, and at the absence of what thing he is most grieved. And he ought to strive most against the inclination with which he struggles, for the more he withdraws from sinning, the nearer he comes to the mean.

units.la: Quemadmodum faciunt qui distorta ligna corrigunt. In omni autem negotio maximè cauenda est voluptas & delectatio: non enim incorrupti de illa iudicamus. Quomodo igitur affecti erga Helenam fuerunt Senatores, ita nos oportet erga voluptatè esse affectos, & in omnibus illorum usurpare vocè, atque ita illam missam facientes minus peccabimus. Hæc itaq; faciendo, ut in summa dixerim maximè poterimus medium assequi.
units.tr: As those do who straighten crooked wood. In every matter, however, pleasure and delight are to be guarded against most of all, for we do not judge of them uncorrupted. Therefore, as the senators were affected toward Helen, so we ought to be affected toward pleasure, and in all cases to use their words, and so, by sending it away, we shall sin less. By doing these things, to put it in a sentence, we shall be able most of all to reach the mean.

units.la: Similiter adducit artificum dirigentium incurva ligna: nam illi ut recta ea faciant, in contrariam partem flectunt. Vnde sic probat, nostrum esse ad illam inclinare partem, in quam minimè propensi sumus, ita ut deflectamus quàm maximè ad extremum nostræ propensioni oppositum. At quispiam fortasse quærat: Illæ actiones vergentes ad alterum extremum nostræ inclinationi oppositum, quod alioqui per se vitiosum est, sunt ne secundum rectam rationem? Distinguimus, loquendo simpliciter, non sunt secundum rectam rationem: illa enim quantum potest fieri expetit medium: at secundum quid secundum rectam rationem dici possunt, quoniam illa iudicat sic facienfaciendo nos posse facilius ad medium pertingere. Non tamen istis actionibus oppositi vitij generatur virtus. Sed per istas actiones ad moderatas tandem peruenimus, & ex illis moderatis deniq; virtus gignitur. Docet hoc nos simile inductum, nunc exercitio maximè opus esse in corrigendis vitijs ac virtutibus acquirendis. Addit tertiò, cauendum esse à voluptate ac suauitatis illecebris omnibus modis. Rationem eiusmodi assignat, quia de illa non iudicamus incorruptè ac syncriter.
units.tr: He likewise brings in the craftsmen who straighten bent wood: for they, to make it straight, bend it toward the opposite side. Hence he proves that it is our task to incline toward that side toward which we are least inclined, so that we bend as far as possible toward the extreme opposed to our natural tendency. But someone may perhaps ask: are those actions which tend toward the other extreme, opposed to our inclination, and which are in themselves vicious, according to right reason? We distinguish: speaking simply, they are not according to right reason, for right reason seeks the mean as far as it can be done; but in a certain respect they can be called according to right reason, since reason judges that by so acting we can reach the mean more easily. Yet virtue is not generated by these actions opposed to the vice. But through these actions we come at last to the moderate, and from those moderate actions virtue is finally born. The simile which he introduces teaches us this, that now exercise is especially needed in correcting vices and acquiring virtues. Thirdly he adds that we must guard against pleasure and the allurements of sweetness by every means. He gives this reason: because we do not judge of it uncorruptly and sincerely.

units.la: Α᾽ δ᾽ ἐνκαεσο[?]: sunt illi, qui munera non accipiunt, ut secundum aliquos decernant: at rari & nulli propemodum sunt qui non voluptatis esca & blanditijs utcunque capiantur. Scientia Homeri confirmat quod dixerat. Helena cum duellum esset futurum inter Paridem & Menelaum, ascendit in turrim, ut spectaret, in qua item Priamus erat & eius proceres. Δυμνοί-[?]γοντες[?] sunt consiliarij & senatores, qui honoratissimi sunt in populo: ij animaduersa pulchritudine mulieris obstupuerunt, ac dixere non esse inuidiosum aut grauiter accusandum, quod Graeci Troianique fortissimæ nationes pro tali forma inter se tam acriter certarent: nam Helena vultu non homines, imò Deas ipsas refert: attamen vt sit, tam pulchra referatur ad naues & hinc asportetur, ne nobis aut liberis nostris sit damnosa. Ita nos voluptatem etsi miramur, eamq; fatemur iucundam & pulchram esse, nihilominus illam debemus ablegare: quoniam propter eam sæpissimè committuntur permulta iniusta & atrocia. Est poeta non vulgare artificium, quod hanc sententiam non iuuenibus sed senioribus attribuit, in quibus iam calores libidinum & perturbationum sunt propemodum restincti. Laudant quidem voluptatem, sed illam cum detrimento nolunt retinere. Vt detrimento sit iuuenibus facile fieri potest, ac illi etiam seipsos adiungunt, quoniam & senes quandoq; deturbat. Peruertit enim humanum iudicium. Nam Paris Minerua & Iunone spreta, sapientia inquam & ciuili virtute, sequutus est Venerem. Apparent hinc fructus Poeticæ lectionis. Quæ illi fabulose scripserunt grauia sunt, si allegoricè ad vitam instituendam trans-ferantur. Sed quod illi fecerunt, nempe Philosophi in Poetis, nos multo commodius in diuinis literis facere debemus, vbi nullæ sunt fictiones, nullæ fabulæ, sed omnia serio dicuntur.
units.tr: "Those who do not receive gifts, so that they may decide according to some men's opinion": but there are few, and almost none, who are not in some way captured by the bait and flatteries of pleasure. The learning of Homer confirms what he had said. When there was going to be a duel between Paris and Menelaus, Helen went up into the tower to watch, where Priam too was, with his nobles. The Demogerontes [Δυμνοί-[?]γοντες] are the counsellors and senators, who are most honoured among the people; these, when they saw the woman's beauty, were astonished and said that it was not blameworthy or to be harshly accused that the Greeks and Trojans, most valiant nations, should fight so fiercely with each other for such a form; for Helen in her countenance resembles not men but even goddesses themselves. Yet, however it be, let her, so beautiful, be sent back to the ships and carried away from here, lest she be harmful to us or to our children. So we, though we admire pleasure, and confess that it is agreeable and fair, must nevertheless send it away, since on account of it very many unjust and atrocious deeds are very often committed. It is no common artifice of the poet that he attributes this opinion not to young men but to old men, in whom the heats of lusts and passions are now almost quenched. They indeed praise pleasure, but do not wish to keep it at a cost. That it can easily be harmful to young men, and that they too join themselves to it, is because it sometimes overthrows even the old. For it perverts human judgement. Thus Paris, having scorned Minerva and Juno, that is, wisdom and civic virtue, followed Venus. From this appear the fruits of reading the poets. What they wrote fabulously are weighty matters if they are transferred allegorically to the ordering of life. But what the philosophers did with the poets, we ought to do far more profitably with the divine writings, where there are no fictions, no fables, but all things are said in earnest.

units.la: Difficile fortasis hoc & præsertim in singularibus: non enim est facile definire, quibus, qualibus, et quàm diu sit irascendum: siquidem & nos interdum eos laudamus qui deficiut, eosq; lenes appellamus, interdum vero acerbos, ut viriles commendamus. At qui parum a recto discesserit, minime vituperabitur, sive id fuerit ad exuperantiam, sive ad defectum: qui vero nimium, haud quaquam latebit. Quouf-que vero aut usque ad quantum vituperandus quis-piam sit, oratione definire non est facile, neque aliud quippiam sensibilium: nam huiusmodi sunt singula, & iudicium eorum penes sensus. Hoc vero tantum id manifestat, medium habitum in omnibus esse laudabilem, & oportere declinare interdum ad exupe-rantiam, interdum vero ad defectum. Sic enim facile rectum ac medium assequemur.
units.tr: This is perhaps difficult, especially in particular cases; for it is not easy to define toward whom, in what manner, and how long one ought to be angry. For we sometimes praise those who fall short and call them gentle, and at other times we commend as manly those who are harsh. But whoever has departed a little from the right will not be blamed at all, whether it be toward excess or toward deficiency; but whoever goes too far will by no means remain hidden. How far, or up to what point, someone is to be blamed it is not easy to define in words, nor anything else of sensible things; for particular things are of this kind, and judgement about them rests with the senses. This alone, however, makes clear that the mean state is praiseworthy in all things, and that one must sometimes incline toward excess, sometimes toward deficiency. For thus we shall easily attain the right and the mean.

units.la: Repetit adhuc inveniendi medij difficultatem, rationemq; affert, quòd in singulis non sit certitudo, neq; in actionibus facile sit circumstantias defi-nire. Imò inquit nos ipsi haud iudicamus eodem modo semper, imò quandoq; laudamus remissos iracundia, nonnunquam aut vehementes. Id vero nobis accidit vt sumus affecti, si oderimus illum in quem quispiam iracitur, vehementem eius iram laudamus: at si amemus illum cupiamusq; tractari mitius, remissam aduersus eum iram vt clementia & lenitate mirificè prædicamus. Excitantur vero affectus alioqui nobis innati, variis de causis: aut consuetudine, aut corporis temperamento, loco, tempore, ob commoda, incommoda, delectatione, molestia, &c. Quid ergo faciundum in tanta difficultate? Respondet, si parum a medio ipso deflexerimus, vel excedendo vel deficiendo, non erimus reprehensibiles. Est enim vt videtur medij quoddam latitudo, intra quam sese continentes bene agunt. At si quis e diverso longius a medio diuagetur, non latebit, sed reprehensioni multorum exponetur. Quousq; tamen a medio abire liceat, inquit non posse definiri: quoniam singularium iudicium non est rationis, verum sensus, & in rebus sensibilibus nihil definiri aut statui certi potest. Graeca scholia meminerunt hic argumenti acervalis aut Sorita, calvaria item, in quibus docent omnino nihil esse concedendum, sed tantum per indefinitam propositionem esse respondendum. Attamen ne videatur nihil dixisse, hoc tantum ait se declarasse, habitu mediocrem esse laudabilem, & declinandum interdum ad exuperantiam, interdum ad defectum, quo facilius medium assequamur.
units.tr: He still repeats the difficulty of finding the mean, and gives the reason that in particulars there is no certainty, nor is it easy in actions to define the circumstances. Indeed, he says, we ourselves do not judge in the same way always; sometimes we praise those who are slack in anger, and sometimes those who are vehement. And this happens to us according as we are affected: if we hate the one with whom someone is angry, we praise his vehement anger; but if we love him and wish him to be treated more gently, we extol his mild anger toward him as marvellous clemency and gentleness. Moreover, the affections naturally innate in us are roused for various reasons: by custom, or bodily temperament, place, time, advantages, disadvantages, delight, annoyance, and so on. What, then, is to be done in such great difficulty? He answers: if we have turned a little from the mean itself, whether by excess or by deficiency, we shall not be blameworthy. For there is, as it seems, a certain breadth of the mean, within which those who keep themselves act well. But if, on the other hand, someone wanders further from the mean, he will not remain hidden but will be exposed to the reproof of many. He says, however, that it cannot be defined how far it is permitted to depart from the mean, since the judgement of particulars belongs not to reason but to sense, and in sensible things nothing certain can be defined or established. The Greek scholia mention here the argument of the heap (acervus) or sorites, and also the bald man (calvaria), in which they teach that nothing at all is to be conceded, but that one must answer only by an indefinite proposition. Yet, lest he seem to have said nothing, he says only this, that he has explained that a moderate state is praiseworthy, and that one must sometimes incline toward excess, sometimes toward deficiency, so that we may more easily attain the mean.

units.la: Superest modo vt sententias huius Capitis ad diuinas literas exigamus. Quod dicitur difficile esse inuenire medium, admittimus, atq; id intelligentes ne erremus, ipsum medium à diuinis literis petemus. Quae ibi praecipiuntur, summae esse moderationis & aequitatis, non dubitamus. Laborare vero vt ratione humana inueniamus ipsi media in affectibus aut actionibus, vanum putamus, & iuxta Solomonis dictum, vanitatem vanitatum & afflictionem spiritus. Medium attingere, laudabile esse, & cum primis quærendum fatemur: quod tamen illi qui circa mediocritatem versantur sint magis reprehensibiles quàm extremi, est per accidens. Meretrices & publicani, qui sunt extremi, praecedunt Scribas & Pharisaeos, qui circa mediocritatem versabantur. Et in Apocalypsi dicitur, Vtinam calidus esses aut frigidus: sed quia tepidus es incipiam te euomere.
