Non inquam id est quod mediocritas mala sit, sed quia illi qui circa illam versantur, saepe laborant superbia, saturi sunt, & aliis bonis, praesertim coelestib. egere se non arbitrantur. Ob hoc itaq; accidens reprehenduntur, non propter mediocritatem. Ab extremo quod magis reipsa pugnat cum mediocritate, magis est deflectendum. Ideo in diuinis literis proponitur Decalogus, in quo crassa vitia ostenduntur vitanda, quae maximè contra virtutis medium pugnant, quae postea Christus est interpretatus & ostendit quomodo ad absolutas perfectas, q; virtutes deflexio illa pertineat, nempe vt vel in corde ipso talium vitiorum semina & initia restinguamus. Admonet deinde Aristoteles vt à nostra inclinatione caueamus, vultq; vt quisq; seipsum respiciat, & ea vitet ad quae se magis viderit propensum esse. Ita Paulus, quia infirmi sunt proni ad condemnandos & iudicandos firmiores: ipsis mandat ne id faciant. Et vicissim quia firmi & sapientes sunt proclives ad contemnendos infirmos, vrget ne id faciant. Diuites etiã quia sunt faciles ad fidendum opibus, & erigendos animos, ab ijs vitijs illos auocat. Quod vero statuit de voluptate, vt ab illa caueamus, hoc omnino suadent & diuinae literae, cum vbiq; à nobis exigant mortificationem. An vero theologicae virtutes medium sectentur, theologi scholastici negant, ego affirmo: sed earum medium est in diuinis literis praescriptum. Fides enim haud plus credere debet, quàm in sacris literis habeatur, neq; item minus quàm illa praecipiant. Peccant etiam qui plus sperant, quàm scriptura sancta praescribat, vt Chiliastae. Quiue [?] minus, vt Origenistae, qui resurrectionem sperant, sed non veram carnis. Describitur quoq; fines dilectionis Dei Sancta Scriptura. Plura voluit facere Petrus causa Christi, quàm ille vellet: at multi alij nolunt eius causa facere quae ille petit. Hoc sane modo potest recte defendi, Virtutes etiam theologicas medium sequi.
units.tr: It remains only for us to test the opinions of this chapter by the divine letters. We admit that it is hard to find the mean, and so that we do not go wrong in understanding this, we will seek the mean itself from the divine letters. We do not doubt that the precepts given there are of the highest moderation and fairness. But to labour to find the means in affections or actions by human reason, we think is vain, and according to the saying of Solomon, "vanity of vanities, and vexation of spirit." We confess that to attain the mean is praiseworthy and is especially to be sought; yet that those who are occupied with mediocrity are more blameworthy than the extremes is incidental. Harlots and publicans, who are at the extremes, go before the Scribes and Pharisees, who were occupied with mediocrity. And in the Apocalypse it is said, "I would that thou wert cold or hot; but because thou art lukewarm, I will begin to spew thee out." I say, this is not because mediocrity is evil, but because those who are occupied with it often suffer from pride, are full, and do not think they lack other goods, especially heavenly ones. Therefore they are rebuked for this incidental fault, not on account of mediocrity. We must turn away more from the extreme that fights more really against mediocrity. Therefore in the divine letters the Decalogue is set forth, in which gross vices are shown to be avoided, which most of all fight against the mean of virtue; which Christ afterwards interpreted and showed how that turning away pertains to absolute and perfect virtues, namely, that we extinguish in the very heart the seeds and beginnings of such vices. Aristotle then warns us to beware of our own inclination, and wishes each one to look to himself and avoid those things to which he sees himself most prone. So Paul, because the weak are prone to condemn and judge the stronger, commands them not to do this. And conversely, because the strong and wise are inclined to despise the weak, he urges them not to do this. He also calls the rich away from those vices, since they are easily given to trusting in riches and lifting up their minds. As to what he lays down about pleasure, that we should beware of it, the divine letters wholly urge this too, since everywhere they demand mortification from us. Whether the theological virtues pursue the mean, the scholastic theologians deny; I affirm it. But the mean of them is prescribed in the divine letters. For faith ought not to believe more than is contained in the sacred letters, nor likewise less than they enjoin. Those also sin who hope for more than Holy Scripture prescribes, as the Chiliasts do; or less, as the Origenists do, who hope for the resurrection but not of the true flesh. Holy Scripture also describes the limits of the love of God. Peter wished to do more for the cause of Christ than he was willing to; but many others are unwilling to do for his cause what he asks. In this way certainly it can rightly be defended that the theological virtues also follow the mean.
END OF THE SECOND BOOK,

units.la: IN TERTIUM LIBRUM ETHICORUM NICOMACHIORUM ARISTOTELIS D. Petri Martyris Vermilij, Florentini Commentaria. CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: IN THE THIRD BOOK OF ARISTOTLE'S NICOMACHEAN ETHICS, commentaries of Master Peter Martyr Vermigli of Florence. CHAPTER I.

units.la: CUM uirtus tam in actionibus quam in affecti-onibus versetur, cumq; sitæ sint laudes ac vitu-perationes in spontaneis: in coactis vero sit venia, & interdum misericordia: necessarium fortasis erit de virtute agentibus voluntarium & non voluntarium definire: erit etiam id utile legislatoribus, cum ob præmia tum propter pœnas.
units.tr: Since virtue is concerned as much with actions as with affections, and since praises and blames attach to voluntary acts, while pardon and sometimes pity attach to compelled acts, it will perhaps be necessary for those who treat of virtue to define the voluntary and the involuntary. This will also be useful to lawgivers, both for rewards and for punishments.

units.la: Quæ modo tractanda sunt, ita iam dictis cohærent. Ari-stoteles virtutis definitionem in universum definierat, illiusq; causas ostenderat: at deniq; singulas inductione quadam protulerat, pingui Minerua ostendendo, illas medium sectari. Nunc requirebatur, ut singillatim exquisita doctrina de omnibus ageret. Quod facturus est: sed illi videtur prius quaedam interponere de principijs humanarum actionum, agetq; de voluntario & non voluntario, de electione, consultatione ac voluntate, omniaq; ista tandem applicabit ad institutum quod tractandum suscepit. Partitio vero loci huius est, Primum proponet de quibus agendum. Secundo, à non voluntario auspicabitur, quod per vim fiat. Tertio loquetur de non voluntario per ignorationem. Quarto denique scribet de Voluntario.
units.tr: What is now to be treated coheres with what has already been said. Aristotle had defined virtue in general and shown its causes. Finally he had set out the individual virtues by a kind of induction, showing with plain common sense that they pursue the mean. It was now required that he treat each of them in detail with exact teaching. He will do so, but first he seems to wish to introduce certain points about the principles of human actions. He will treat of the voluntary and the involuntary, of choice, deliberation and will, and at last he will apply all these to the matter he has undertaken to treat. The division of this passage is as follows. First, he will set out what is to be treated. Second, he will begin with the involuntary that happens through force. Third, he will speak of the involuntary through ignorance. Fourth and finally, he will write about the voluntary.

units.la: Proponit agendum esse de voluntario & non voluntario. Cuius ratio est, Quia laus, vituperiu, venia, et quandoq; misericordia, sunt voluntarium. Est argumentum à consequentibus. Laudes & vituperia faciunt ad scien-tiam moralem: quia ut mores actionesq; laudabiles expetenda sunt, itavituperabiles euitandæ. At iudicari non possunt huiusmodi laudes & vituperia, nisi sciamus an volenti an inuito animo facta fuerint. Ergo de ijs est agendum. Aliam adijcit præterea causam, quòd sit hæc doctrina pars civilis facultatis, ad quam leges ferre spectat. Leges vero proponunt præmia & pœnas observatoribus & transgressoribus: propterea opus est ut quæ sint voluntaria sciant, quæue non voluntaria: nam inuiti non consequuntur præmia, & qui coacti peccarunt, non sunt afficiendi pœnis. Aliqui ratione hanc legumlatorum eo torquent, ceu cauere illi debeant, ne aliquid præcipiant necessarium, quodue præstari non possit, sed tantum quæ sint in nostra manu: ideoq; cognoscant oportet voluntarij & non voluntarij rationem. Scio equidem legis definitionem esse ut sit ratio præcipiens honesta & revocans ab inhonestis: at illud quod isti afferunt ut possibilia præcipiat, solùm de ciuilibus legibus concederem, non autem de diuinis: nam illa impossibilia exigunt, præsertim quo ad statum naturæ corruptæ ac vitiatæ. Sed tamen Aristoteles hac ratione non est vsus, illa solum attigit quæ de pœnis & præmijs ego memoraui.
units.tr: He proposes that we must treat of the voluntary and the involuntary. The reason is that praise, blame, pardon, and sometimes pity, concern the voluntary. This is an argument from consequences. Praises and blames bear on moral science: just as laudable morals and actions are to be sought, so blameworthy ones are to be avoided. But such praises and blames cannot be judged unless we know whether things were done with a willing or an unwilling mind. Therefore these matters must be treated. He adds another reason: this doctrine is part of the civil science, to which it belongs to make laws. Laws propose rewards and punishments to those who observe them and those who transgress them. Therefore it is necessary to know which things are voluntary and which involuntary, for the unwilling do not obtain rewards, and those who sinned under compulsion are not to be punished. Some by this reasoning press the lawgivers' concern, as if they ought to take care not to command what is necessary or what cannot be performed, but only what lies in our power. Therefore they ought to know the account of the voluntary and the involuntary. I indeed grant that the definition of law is that it is a reason commanding what is honourable and recalling from what is dishonourable. But I would concede that what they bring forward, that law commands only possible things, holds only of civil laws and not of divine ones, for the latter demand impossible things, especially in the state of corrupted and vitiated nature. Yet Aristotle did not use this argument. He touched only on what I have mentioned about punishments and rewards.

units.la: Sed cur meminit affectuum, cùm illi non sint voluntarij, sed naturaliter insint in animis nostris? Respondent Græca Scholia, Quia etsi quo ad substiam [?] & radicem à natura sint, voluntarij tamen possunt quoquo modo appellari, quoniam usu ac exercitio relaxari aut reprimi queant. Aut respondebimus utriusq; Aristotelem meminisse, affectuum inquam & actionum, sed voluntarium tantummodo ad actiones referendum. Quod si fiat, pertinebit etiam ad virtutes quæ versantur in affectibus: nam & illæ per actiones acquiruntur, quas cùm rectæ sint & laudabiles, oportet voluntarias ponere.
units.tr: But why does he mention affections, since they are not voluntary but are naturally present in our minds? The Greek scholia reply that although as to substance and root they come from nature, they can nevertheless be called voluntary in some way, since they can be relaxed or repressed by use and exercise. Or we shall answer that Aristotle mentioned both, affections and actions, but that the voluntary is to be referred only to actions. If this is done, it will also pertain to the virtues that are concerned with affections, for these too are acquired through actions, which, since they are right and laudable, must be posited as voluntary.

units.la: Ad hæc cur Aristoteles dixit, Interdum misericordia? Quia non semper illos misericordia prosequimur, quibus damus veniam. Etenim aliquis tuendo seipsum occidit eum qui se aggressus erat, non volens fecit, datur illi venia, sed illius non miseremur. Fortasse inquit necessarium est. Si necessarium est, quid oportuit addere forte? Dicunt Scholia Græca, hoc solum factum quo ad ordinem: nam fortassis potuissent hæc differri aut anticipari, licet necessario essent dicenda. Aut ἰω̃ς ἰστο [?] loco non est fortassis, sed æqualiter ac similiter, ac si sensus esset. Cùm res hoc pacto habeat, ut de illis diximus, pariter ac similiter de voluntario & non voluntario dicendum est. Potuit etiam Aristoteles more Academicorum loqui cum quibus assuetus erat, neque in Ethicis est in ijs loquendi formis plus quàm oporteat scrupulosus. Vt autem notitia voluntarij & non voluntarij faciat ad poenas legum moderandas, potest multis modis ostendi. In eos qui inuiti aut coacti aliquid admiserint non animaduertitur. Et in legibus ciuilibus permulti sunt tituli qui subueniunt ignorationi aut coactioni. Vt de ijs quae fiunt metus causa, & de dolo malo, & de minoribus 25.annis, &c. Insano quoq; ac furore percito ignoscitur: imo furiosus si fuerit parricida, non plectetur. Diuina leges absoluunt casorem lignorum qui casu & non volens alterum interfe-cerit, quod forte securis egressa fuerit manubrium, dabanturque ciuitates refugij. Plato etiam in 9.de Legibus multa ostendit esse condonanda, si voluntas defuerit. Proinde Legislatores & Legum custodes, ob poenas & praemia conferenda nosse voluntarium & inuoluntarium valde conducit.
units.tr: Again, why did Aristotle say "sometimes pity"? Because we do not always feel pity for those to whom we grant pardon. For someone who, defending himself, kills the one who attacked him, acts unwillingly, and pardon is given to him, but we do not pity him. "Perhaps," he says, "it is necessary." If it is necessary, why was it necessary to add "perhaps"? The Greek scholia say this was added only with regard to order, for these things could have been deferred or anticipated, although they would have to be said as necessary. Or the word here [ἴσως] is not "perhaps" but "equally and similarly," as if that were the sense. Since the matter stands thus, as we have said of those things, the same must be said equally and similarly of the voluntary and the involuntary. Aristotle could also have spoken in the manner of the Academics, whose company he was used to, and in the Ethics he is not more scrupulous about such forms of speech than necessary. But that knowledge of the voluntary and the involuntary helps to moderate the penalties of laws can be shown in many ways. No blame is attached to those who have done something unwillingly or under compulsion. In civil laws there are very many titles that come to the aid of ignorance or compulsion, such as those concerning things done through fear, through malicious deceit, and concerning minors under twenty-five years, and so on. The insane and the frenzied are also pardoned; indeed, a madman who has committed parricide will not be punished. Divine laws acquit the woodcutter who by chance and unwillingly killed another, because the axe head perhaps flew off the handle, and cities of refuge were given to such men. Plato too, in book 9 of the Laws, shows that many things are to be pardoned if the will was lacking. Therefore it greatly helps lawgivers and guardians of the laws, in conferring punishments and rewards, to know the voluntary and the involuntary.

units.la: Videntur autem non voluntaria, quę vel per vim vel per imprudentiam fiunt.
units.tr: But things are thought not voluntary when they are done either by force or through ignorance.

units.la: Incipit à non voluntario. Nam priuatio hic reipsa videtur notior. Ete-nim per tenebras melius cognoscitur lux: & morbus efficit magis conspicu-um sanitatis bonum. Definitio hæc non voluntarij constat partium eius enumeratione: unde potius partitio est quàm definitio, quamuis iusta plena-qúe diuisiones interdum definitionis locum habeant. Et illis potissimum tunc vtimur, quando id quod partibus est commune aliqua certa notione ac una explicari non potest. Sciendum tamen, Non voluntarium de ijs duabus formis aut speciebus univocè dici: nam & id quod fit per vim & per imprudentiam est non voluntarium. Probatur autem diuisionem duorum membrorum iuste esse factam, Quoniam voluntarium quod oppositum est non voluntario duobus constat, notitia & appetitu. Primum nouimus quod expe-tendum est, deinde motu appetitus in illud ferimur. Alterutrum autem horum duorum potest impediri. Ignoratio tollit notitiam, vis autem impedit appetitum. Voluntario igitur duo hæc merito opponuntur. Quid autem fit vis, hoc modo definitur. Est impetus vehemens, qui sustineri non possit, aut ægrè sustinetur. Sed mirabitur quispiam quomodo vni duo opponantur. Voluntario quippe opponitur quod fit per vim & quod fit per imprudentiam. Ad hoc r[?]spondetur, vnum reuera opponi vno, spontaneo seu voluntario inuitum (seu non voluntarium opponi. Sed istud inuitum seu voluntarium postea in duas partes distribuitur. Aliud enim est, quod fit per vim, aliud vero quod fit per imprudentiam. agens non inferret aliquam vim: at principium agendi & assentiendi est in ipso agente, ut Aristoteles monuit. Cum hæc relatiuè dicantur & referantur ad voluntatem, non simpliciter iudicanda sunt, verum pro respectu quem ad voluntatem habent. Unde cum voluntas in iis (ut declaratum est) locum habeat, voluntaria sunt dicenda.
units.tr: He begins with the non-voluntary, since privation is in this case the better known thing in itself. For light is better recognised through darkness, and sickness makes the good of health more conspicuous. This definition of the non-voluntary consists in an enumeration of its parts, so it is really a partition rather than a definition, although complete and proper divisions sometimes take the place of a definition. We use such divisions chiefly when what is common to the parts cannot be explained by one clear notion. It should be noted, however, that the non-voluntary is not predicated univocally of the two forms or species, for what is done through force and what is done through ignorance are both non-voluntary. The division into two members is shown to be rightly made, because the voluntary, which is opposed to the non-voluntary, consists of two things, knowledge and appetite. First we know what is to be sought, and then by the movement of appetite we are carried towards it. Either of these two can be impeded: ignorance removes knowledge, and force hinders appetite. Rightly, then, these two are opposed to the voluntary. What force is, is defined in this way: it is a violent impulse which cannot be endured, or is endured only with difficulty. But someone will wonder how two things can be opposed to one. For the voluntary is opposed both to what is done by force and to what is done through ignorance. To this it is answered that one is really opposed to one: the unwilling, or non-voluntary, is opposed to the spontaneous, or voluntary. But this unwilling or voluntary is afterwards divided into two parts. For one thing is what is done by force, and another is what is done through ignorance. The agent would not bring in any force; but the principle of acting and of assenting lies in the agent himself, as Aristotle warned. Since these things are said relatively and are referred to the will, they must not be judged absolutely, but according to the relation they have to the will. Hence, since the will has a place in them (as has been explained), they are to be called voluntary.

units.la: In eiusmodi autem actionibus quandoq; & laudantur homines cum turpe quippiam aut molestū tolerauerint pro magnis rebus & bonis consequendis: sin è diuerso, uituperantur. Turpissima quippe ferre pro nullo bono aut mediocri, prauum est.
units.tr: In actions of this kind, men are sometimes praised when they have endured something shameful or painful for the sake of achieving great and good things; but on the other hand, they are blamed. For to endure the most disgraceful things for no good or only a middling one is wicked.

units.la: Duabus rationibus hactenus probatum est, mixtas has actiones voluntarias esse. Prima, quod æstimari debeant ex natura temporis præsentis quæ fiunt. Altera, quoniā sunt in potestate facientis. Nisi enim voluntas organicas partes mouerent, non vtiq; fierent. Tertia modo ratio instituitur à laude & vituperio, quia homines interdū laudantur, interdum vituperantur, fœda & turpia ista patiendo, apparet id esse voluntariū: nō enim loquitur laus & vituperium nisi ad voluntaria. Ait interdum, quia non semper vt videbimus: nam aliquando non laus istis datur, sed venia concedi-tur. Sin è diuerso, inquit, uituperantur. Illud, è diuerso duo significat. Aut non volunt homines tolerare fœda pro magnis & honestissimis rebus: aut ferunt quidem talia, sed pro leuibus & indignis causis, in iis inquam reprehenduntur. Alterius autem istorum duorum tantum meminit Aristoteles, alterum tacet. Ista magna bona & honesta propter quæ patienda sunt molesta & dura, censentur ab interpretibus, Patria, parentes, liberi, uxor, iustitia et consimilia. Zopyrus Persa, ut refert Herodotus, truncauit sibi nares, aures, labra, ut Babyloniorum urbem proderet suo Dario. Vlysses, ut ab Homero dicitur, suū corpus passus est verberari ac fœdari vibicibus, aptauitq; sibi sordidas vestes, illoq; habitu quasi trásfuga esset seruus ad Troianos se contulit, & ut bem ingressus illam explorauit. Dolonem è diuerso vituperant omnes, quod ne tormenta ulla cogeretur pati, arcana suorum prodidit. Sed notandum, turpia cum dicitur interdum patienda, id non debet ad scelera referri vel[?] crimina: non enim ea committenda sunt pro quauis vtilitate vel honestate. Sed tantum illa dicuntur interdum ferenda quæ aliquam habeant molestiam & fœditatem. Ut si magistratus iubeatur instar seruorum per publiblicas plateas currere, aut stola muliebri publicè uti. Hac si maxima honestas & commoditas iustissima proponatur, facere non detrectabit. Oportet ergo maxima esse, quorum gratia ista fiunt, si quis inde velit laudem reportare. Non mihi probantur scholiarum exempla: nam turpia hæc ferenda cū declarant, mendacium proponunt dicendum, aut consuescedum cum vxore Tyranni vt maritus eius occidatur: ista enim vitiosa sunt, neque de iis (vt dixi) Aristoteles loquitur. Neq; talia possunt laudari, cum in primo libro habuerimus, virtutibus convenire laudationes, & vitijs vituperationes. Aliqui reperiuntur adeo abiecti animi & viles, vt merito vituperari debeant, cùm pro iusto & honesto nil omnino pati velint. Ita vituperantur milites qui deserunt stationem, quiq; dedunt non coacti arces & munitiones. Vituperantur & illi, qui ne cogantur soluere aliquam pecuniarum summam quiduis parati sunt facere..
units.tr: By two reasons it has so far been proved that these mixed actions are voluntary. The first is that they must be judged from the nature of the circumstances in which they are done. The second is that they are in the power of the doer. For unless the will moved the bodily parts, they would certainly not be done. The third reason is drawn from praise and blame: since men are sometimes praised and sometimes blamed for enduring these base and shameful things, it is evident that they are voluntary, for praise and blame apply only to voluntary things. He says "sometimes," because, as we shall see, praise is not always given to such people; sometimes pardon is granted instead. "On the other hand," he says, they are blamed. That phrase "on the other hand" has two meanings. Either men are unwilling to endure base things for great and most honourable ends, or they do endure such things but for trivial and unworthy causes; in those cases, I say, they are reproached. Aristotle mentions only one of these two, and passes over the other. The great and honourable goods for which hard and painful things are to be endured are, according to the commentators, country, parents, children, wife, justice and the like. Zopyrus the Persian, as Herodotus relates, cut off his own nose, ears and lips, so that he might betray the city of the Babylonians to his Darius. Ulysses, as Homer tells, allowed his body to be beaten and disfigured with weals, put on filthy clothes, and in that guise went to the Trojans as a runaway slave, and having been admitted, spied out the city. Dolon, on the other hand, is blamed by everyone, because, so as not to be forced to endure any torment, he betrayed the secrets of his own people. But it must be noted that when we say that base things are sometimes to be endured, this must not be applied to crimes or wrongdoing, for such things must not be committed for any advantage or honour whatever. Rather, only those things are said to be sometimes endurable which have some discomfort and disgrace attached to them: for example, if a magistrate were ordered to run through the public streets like a slave, or to wear a woman's stole in public. If the greatest honour and the most just advantage were set before him, he would not refuse to do it. It is necessary, then, that the ends for whose sake such things are done be very great, if anyone is to win praise from them. The examples of the schools do not please me, for when they illustrate enduring base things, they propose that one should tell a lie, or lie with the wife of a tyrant so that her husband may be killed. Such things are vicious, and Aristotle does not speak of them (as I said). Nor can such things be praised, since in the first book we have seen that praise belongs to virtues and blame to vices. Some men are found of such abject and mean spirit that they rightly deserve blame, since they are unwilling to endure anything at all for the sake of what is just and honourable. So those soldiers are blamed who desert their post, and those who hand over citadels and fortifications without being compelled. Those too are blamed who are ready to do anything whatever so as not to be forced to pay some sum of money.

units.la: In quibusdam autem rebus non laus sed uenia datur, quando propter ea quis fecerit quæ non de-cet, & ea sunt quæ naturam humanam uincunt, ne-que illa facile quis ferret: ad quædam uero fortas-se non licet pati se cogi, sed magis moriendum est grauissima patiendo: nam ridicula uidentur ef-se quæ Alcmæonem Euripidis coegerunt matrem interimere..
units.tr: In some matters, however, pardon is granted rather than praise, when someone has done what is not fitting because of things which overcome human nature and which no one could easily bear. For some things a man ought not to be forced to endure, but rather he must die enduring the most dreadful suffering; for the things which compelled Alcmaeon in Euripides to kill his mother seem absurd.

units.la: Nunc apparet euidenter cur superius dixerit interdum laudem se-qui tolerantiā molestissimarū rerū, quia id non est perpetuum: aliquando e-nim illis qui turpia ferunt neq; laus neq; vituperatio ex eo accidit, sed ve-nia datur. Id autem fit, quando illa comminantur Tyranni: aut subeun-da sunt, nisi turpia perferamus, quæ vim naturæ humanæ superant. Ibi A-ristoteles inquit veniā damus. Proponitur hominib. ut adurantur, secenter, vbi si succumbat vel arcana revelando vel aliquid turpe patiendo vel age-do, venia datur. Et quidam iis casibus putant licere mentiri. Addit Aristo-teles nihilominus quædam esse, ad quæ nullus debeat sinere se cogi. Potius quauis pati debet, et dum succubit, illi non dabitur venia, nec excusabitur. Vnde sapiunt nostri martyres, qui potius quauis pati decreuerunt, quā à pieta-te discedere. Exemplum sumitur ex Tragœdia Euripidis. Etenim Alc-maeonii orum opposita se conuertat, videatq; bona maiora esse, nempe vitam, pudi-citiam, libertatem, pietatem: intelligetq; magna esse mala, mortem, pudici-tiæ violationem, seruitutem, impietate, & consimilia: quæ adeo grauia sunt, vt nonnulla turpia sæpius ad illa euitanda committantur. Quam fœda sæ-pe fiant vt mors euadatur, facile potest cognosci. Cato se occidit ne seruiret. Regulus, ne falleret fidem, ad mortem redyt Carthaginem. Virginius filiam potius occidit quam illam violatam & seruam sineret viuere. Habent & sacræ literæ multa consimilia. Lotus potius obtulit consluprādas filias, quam vellet pati suis hospitibus iniuriam fieri. Filiæ vicissim eius potius incestu se polluerunt cum patre, quam vellent orbem deseri. Abrahamus ad mortem euitandam, Saram iussit dicere se fratrem illius esse, atque illius pudicitiam periculo exposuit. Iuditha quoque ad suum populum liberandum cum periculo castitatis ad Holoferne sese conferebat. Hic non disputatur an hæc recte vel perperam facta fuerint, sed solum quæritur an voluntaria vel nō voluntaria dici debeant. Et est magnum discrimen sceleratorum hominū, qui se ad ista vltrò facienda offerunt adulando tyrannis, vel quod prauis aut turpibus operibus delectentur: & illorum, qui ob probitatem non pos-sunt adduci vt ista committant, nisi magnis grauissimisq; malis propositis, aut magnis præmijs. Audiasq; nonnullos, qui sibi proposito aliquo magno bo-no dicant se cogi ad quoduis agendum, pro eo consequendo. Certè dicitur e-tiam alia ex parte à tyrannis, qua crudelissimè premunt populos, ac tantū sui causa imperant, multos cogi vt turpiter agant. Multiq; hodie sunt qui à Christiana veritate deficiant, crudelissima vi tyrannorum coacti. Adduci-tur quoq; simile de rerum eiectione quæ fit in naui tempestate vrgente, non quod hoc ad mores quicquam faciat, sed ex rei euidentia magis potest quod modo quæritur apparere.
units.tr: It now appears plainly why he said above that endurance of the most painful things is sometimes followed by praise: because this is not perpetual. For sometimes neither praise nor blame befalls those who endure base things, but pardon is given. This happens when tyrants threaten those things, or when they must be undergone unless we endure base things which exceed the force of human nature. In such cases, Aristotle says, we grant pardon. Men are set before the fire, as it were, and tortured; if they give way, either by revealing secrets or by enduring or doing something base, pardon is given. And some think that in such cases it is lawful to lie. Aristotle adds that nevertheless there are some things to which no one ought to allow himself to be forced. Rather, a man ought to suffer anything whatever, and if he gives way, he will not be granted pardon, nor will he be excused. Hence our martyrs have a sound understanding, who decided to suffer anything rather than depart from piety. An example is taken from the tragedy of Euripides. For Alcmaeon turns himself to the opposing considerations, and sees that the greater goods are life, chastity, liberty and piety; and he understands that the great evils are death, violation of chastity, slavery, impiety and the like, which are so grave that some base acts are committed quite often in order to avoid them. How shameful the things are that men often do so that death may be escaped, can easily be recognised. Cato killed himself so as not to be a slave. Regulus, so as not to break his faith, returned to Carthage to his death. Virginius killed his daughter rather than let her live violated and enslaved. Holy letters also contain many like cases. Lot offered his daughters to be violated, rather than allow an injury to be done to his guests. His daughters in turn polluted themselves with incest with their father, rather than see the world deserted. Abraham, to avoid death, ordered Sarah to say that she was his sister, and exposed her chastity to danger. Judith too went to Holofernes to free her people, at the risk of her chastity. Here the question is not whether these things were done rightly or wrongly, but only whether they ought to be called voluntary or non-voluntary. And there is a great difference between wicked men, who offer themselves of their own accord to do such things by flattering tyrants, or because they delight in depraved or base deeds, and those who on account of their uprightness cannot be brought to commit such things unless great and most grievous evils, or great rewards, are set before them. And you may hear some who say that, when some great good is set before them, they are compelled to do anything whatever in order to obtain it. Certainly it is also said, on the other side, that tyrants, who oppress their peoples most cruelly and rule only for their own sake, compel many to act basely. And today there are many who fall away from Christian truth, forced by the most cruel violence of tyrants. A similar case is also brought up about the throwing of goods overboard which happens in a ship when a storm presses; not because this contributes anything to morals, but because the clearness of the matter makes it easier to see what is being asked here.

units.la: Mixtæ igitur sunt huiusmodi actiones, accedunt uero magis ad uoluntaria, nam tunc expetēdæ sunt cum fiunt. Finis autem actionis ad temporis opportunitatem accömodatur: & utique uoluntarium ac non uoluntarium tum dicendum est, cum id quispiam agit: agit autem uoluntarius qui hæc agit. Etenim in huiusmodi actionibus principium mouendi organicas partes, in ipso est qui agit, quorū autem principium in ipso est agente, agere uel non agere est in eius potestate. Voluntaria itaque sunt huiusmodi simpliciter: at forte non voluntaria, nemo enim ullas eiusmodi actiones per se deligeret.
units.tr: Such actions are therefore mixed, though they come closer to voluntary ones, for they are to be desired at the time they are done. The end of an action is fitted to the opportunity of the moment. Something is to be called voluntary or involuntary when someone does it, and the one who does this is a voluntary agent. In such actions the principle of moving the bodily parts lies within the agent, and where the principle lies within the one acting, to act or not to act is in his power. Such actions, then, are voluntary in the absolute sense, but perhaps not voluntary in themselves, for no one would choose such actions for their own sake.

units.la: Mixtae dicuntur ea actiones quae commemoratae sunt: nam quae omitti possunt, & non ita sunt necessariae, ut illas omnino fieri oporteat, voluntaria videntur: quae vero eas nemo per seipsas eligeret, videntur non voluntariae.
units.tr: The actions just mentioned are called mixed. Those which can be omitted, and are not so necessary that they must be done at all, seem voluntary; but those which no one would choose for their own sake seem involuntary.

units.la: Magis tamen accedunt ad voluntariorum naturam: quia in illis est collatio quaedam malorum. Duo mala proponuntur, aut cum rerum iactura pauperies, aut cum illis substantiis mors praesens. Deligit voluntas minus malum & maius cupit evitare. Unde cum voluntas in ijs officio suo fungatur, non poterunt ista non dici voluntaria. Monuit deinde Aristoteles in Rhetoricis minus malum rationem boni habere, atque adeo expetendum esse, cum bonum id sit quod appetitur. Neque dubium est voluntatem esse quae finem deligit. Finis autem harum actionum, de quibus disputamus, accommodatur ad temporis rationem. Cum enim salus non possit haberi quam nautae optant, nisi iactis in mare facultatibus, voluntas eiectionem deligit. Est igitur tempus in hac tota re consyderandum, non quidem praeteritum aut futurum: quia nemo ante illum casum haec eligeret, & postea cum evaserunt nautae dolent, & illas eiectiones factas aegre ferunt. At res iudicari debet iuxta tempus praesens dum fit. Proinde cum ibi sit electio, resq; vocetur in deliberatione, & principium agendi sit in agente qui potest agere ac non agere, illa dicenda sunt voluntaria. Non possumus de actione iudicare in universum, sed ad circumstantiam temporis est respiciendum. Simpliciter dicuntur attamen ista non voluntaria: quoniam per se ipsa nemo illa expeteret. Sed tamen cum simpliciter non consyderantur, sed in isto casu sunt expetenda, & illi qui ea expetit non deest notitia: Scit enim quid agat, & voluntas vel appetitus haec deligens adest. Ideo sunt voluntariae actiones. Nam omnia debent iudicari ut acta sunt: acta autem non possunt esse nisi certo tempore: unde pro illo sunt iudicanda. Non autem ut ratione apprehenduntur. Sic enim non sunt voluntariae: nam dum simpliciter consyderantur, a tempore absolvuntur. Atque hoc est quod Aristoteles intelligit, cum inquit, simpliciter aut fortasis non voluntaria. Simpliciter hic est res absolute consyderata. Neque dubitandum est hic interuenire voluntatis assensum: non enim fierent, nisi voluntas assentiretur. Verum quidem est, neminem illa velle propter seipsa, sed propter aliud: at istud non efficit quin sint voluntaria. Si violenta essent,
units.tr: Yet they come closer to the nature of voluntary actions, because in them there is a kind of comparison of evils. Two evils are set before us: either the loss of property and poverty, or, with the loss of those things, present death. The will chooses the lesser evil and wishes to avoid the greater. Hence, since the will performs its office in these actions, they cannot fail to be called voluntary. Aristotle then warned in the Rhetoric that the lesser evil has the character of a good, and so is to be desired, since the good is what is desired. And there is no doubt that it is the will that chooses the end. The end of the actions we are discussing is fitted to the circumstances of time. For since the safety the sailors desire cannot be had unless their goods are thrown into the sea, the will chooses the jettisoning. So in this whole matter time must be considered, not indeed past or future: no one would choose these things before that peril, and afterwards, when the sailors have escaped, they grieve and bear badly the jettisoning that was done. But the matter ought to be judged by the present time, while it is being done. Therefore, since there is a choice there, and the matter is deliberated upon, and the principle of acting lies in an agent who can act or not act, those things are to be called voluntary. We cannot judge an action in general; regard must be had to the circumstance of time. Those things are said absolutely to be not voluntary, since no one would desire them of themselves. But when they are not considered absolutely, and in that case are to be desired, and the one who desires them is not lacking knowledge (for he knows what he is doing), and the will or appetite choosing them is present, then they are voluntary actions. For all things must be judged as they are done, and things done can only be done at a certain time; hence they are to be judged in relation to that time, not as they are grasped by reason. For thus they are not voluntary, since while they are considered absolutely they are abstracted from time. This is what Aristotle means when he says "absolutely, or perhaps not voluntary." "Absolutely" here means the thing considered in itself. Nor is it to be doubted that the assent of the will intervenes here, for they would not be done unless the will assented. It is true that no one wills them for their own sake, but for the sake of something else; but this does not prevent them from being voluntary. If they were violent...

units.la: Violentum est, cuius principium extrinsecum su-erit, cui quod agit & patitur nullum adiumentum affert. Quemadmodum si uentus aliquo nos asporta-ret, uel homines qui potestatem in nos habeant.
units.tr: Violent is that whose principle is external, and to which the thing it does or suffers brings no assistance: as when a wind carries us off somewhere, or men who have power over us.

units.la: Ab eo declarando auspicatur quod fit per vim. Principium, inquit, motionis eius exterius oportet esse: nam quæ mouentur ab interiori principio, naturaliter mouentur, non violenter. Sed aliqui putant posteriorem particulam, ita ut quod patitur aut agit non conferat illi principio vllum adiumentum. Dicunt enim, quando principium motus extrinsecus est, id consequitur ut quod agit aut patitur non afferat illi adiumentum. Sed qui sic dicunt, falluntur: nam ut videbimus de iactu qui fit in magna tempestate, principium eius extrinsecum est, nimirum sunt venti, fluctus & procellæ. Sed iactus non fieret, nisi etiam ipsi nautæ illa quæ iacienda sunt, e nauibus promerent. Et qui sub Tyranno est, adigiturq; ad turpia facienda, suarum actionum principium habet extrinsecum, nempe iussionem tyranni: at illa non fierent si & ipsi ad ea facienda non se accommodarent. Itaq; apparet ista principium exterius habere, ac nihilominus ei aliquod adiumentum conferre. Alij sunt qui frustra putent addi, agens: nam si principium sit exterius motus, tum patiens si diceretur, satis esset: id enim quod mouetur, patitur, non agit. Respondemus: Quæ mouentur violenter, potest fieri ut ipsa quoq; agant, ceu instrumenta: nam baculus a nobis motus mouet lapidem. Etiam aliqua turba conferta ubi premuntur homines, cum ibi aliquis præfocatur a circumstantibus comprimitur, ita ut illi dicantur in eum agere, quamuis agant non sponte, sed acti ab alijs & a reliqua turba impulsi. Exempla ab Aristotele adducta ita sunt, ut unum sit animatum, quando asportamur ab hominibus, in quorum potestate sumus, nolentes. Alterum est eorum quæ animi sunt expertia. Ut cum vento ferimur, quo nollemus, quod sæpe nau- gantibus accidit. Si quæsierit quispiam an voluntarium & spontaneum i-dem sit. Respondebimus spontaneum latius patere quam voluntarium, quia spontaneum etiam rebus animo carentibus conuenit, non autem voluntarium. Nec requiritur ut sit principium primum motus in nobis: nostra quippe notitia ex obiecto externo provenit, quamuis ille motus quo sensus ab obiecto efficitur est alterius ordinis. Principium de quo modo loquitur Aristoteles, causa est, & non quæuis, sed tantum efficiens. Et ea intelligitur quæ per se ad mouendum fuerit satis. Quæ autem ob timorem maiorum malorum fi-unt, vel ob aliquod honestum, ut si tyrannus quip-piam turpe iubeat nos facere, aut parentes nostros aut filios in potestate habens: ita qui fecerint, seruet, qui non fecerint, perdant : ambiguum est an huius-modi voluntaria sint, an involuntaria. Huiusmodi quippiam usu venit de iacturis quæ fiunt in tempe-statibus. Etenim simpliciter nemo est qui sponte ac volens abiiciat sua, propter salutem vero sui ipsius ac reliquorum, omnes qui sapiant, id faciunt.
units.tr: He begins by explaining what happens through force. The principle of its motion, he says, must be external, for things moved by an internal principle move naturally, not violently. But some think the latter clause, that what is suffered or done contributes no assistance to that principle, is to be taken thus. For they say that when the principle of motion is external, it follows that what is done or suffered brings no assistance to it. But those who say so are mistaken. As we shall see about the jettisoning that happens in a great storm, its principle is external, namely the winds, waves and tempests. But the jettisoning would not happen unless the sailors themselves threw out of the ships the things that must be thrown out. And one who is under a tyrant, and is driven to do base things, has an external principle of his actions, namely the tyrant's command; but those things would not be done if he did not also accommodate himself to doing them. So it is clear that these have an external principle, and yet contribute some assistance to it. Others think that the word "agent" is added in vain, for if the principle of motion is external, it would be enough to say "patient," since what is moved suffers and does not act. We reply: things moved violently may also act, as instruments do, for a stick moved by us moves a stone. Likewise, in some crowd packed together, where people are pressed, when someone is suffocated, he is squeezed by those standing around him, so that they are said to act upon him, although they do not act willingly, but are driven by others and pushed by the rest of the crowd. The examples adduced by Aristotle are such that one is of an animate thing, when we are carried off unwillingly by men in whose power we are; the other is of things devoid of soul, as when we are carried by the wind where we would not wish to go, which often happens to sailors. If someone asks whether the voluntary and the spontaneous are the same, we reply that the spontaneous extends more widely than the voluntary, because the spontaneous also applies to things lacking soul, but the voluntary does not. Nor is it required that the first principle of motion be in us, for our knowledge comes from an external object, although that motion by which the sense is affected by the object is of another order. The principle of which Aristotle speaks here is a cause, and not any cause, but only an efficient one; and it is understood as that which is by itself sufficient for moving. But those things which are done from fear of greater evils, or for some honourable end, as when a tyrant, having in his power our parents or our children, orders us to do something base, so that those who do it spare them and those who do not, they perish: it is doubtful whether such things are voluntary or involuntary. Something of this kind happens with the jettisoning in storms. For simply no one is there who would throw away his goods willingly and of his own accord; yet for the safety of himself and the others, all who are wise do so.

units.la: Mouetur quæstio de actionibus quibusdam quæ media videntur, dubi-tatq; an voluntariæ sint an involuntariæ. Quæstio autem proposita potest esse aut simplex, aut bimembris. Simplex est, si dixeris, Quæ fiunt ob timo-rem maiorum malorum, quàm ob aliquod bonum siue honestum consequen-dum, an sint voluntaria? Nam potest esse aut nota comparationis, aut nota disiunctionis. Si comparatio est, tum referetur ad comparatiuum μειζόνων[?] & scholia Græca lectionem hanc indicarunt: atq; talem rem euenisse pro-dunt Socrati, qui noluit parere triginta Tyrannis qui ab eo requisiuerunt, ut ciuem quendam Atheniensem occideret. Quod ille noluit facere, cum tamen illi comminati essent ei se patrem eius & liberos esse occisuros. Id autem quærebant, ut illum viderentur habere socium ac participem suorum crudelissimorum consiliorum. Posset etiam, quod mihi magis arridet, quæstio bimembris fieri: nempe an illa sint voluntaria quæ timore maiorum malorum fiunt, vel ob aliquod honestum consequendum, quæ alioqui non fierent. Ut mendacium quod sua natura est turpe si dicatur, dubium est an sit voluntarium vel non voluntarium, cum instituitur vel ad suam ipsius vel aliorum vitam tuendam. Adulterium quoque turpe est, quod per se ipsum nemo eligeret, sed ad Tyrannum interficiendum, si quis insinuaret se illius vxori & cum illa misceret, quo per eam paratum aditum haberet ad occidendum tyrannum, dubium est an illud adulterium dici deberet voluntarium. Atq; hæc exempla sunt honestorum finium. At καλὸν[?] potest etiâ utile commodum significare. Omnes scimus quanta tolerent mercatores, quæ ambitiosi, quæ voluptuarij ut suis fruantur finibus: illa vero quæ faciunt, non tolerarent, nisi propter suum commodum. Quare dubitatur an ea sint voluntaria. Quæ vero appellentur magna mala, si quis ambigat, ad e mæoni venia non est data, quòd parricidium admiserat cum leui aut potius ridicula causa fuerit ad tantum scelus adductus. Cùm istæ actiones, de quibus agimus (ut dictum est) mixtæ sint ex inuoluntario & voluntario, cũ voluntarium dominatur, aut laus aut vituperium illas consequitur: at si non voluntarium superet, videaturq; inuitus fecisse, datur venia. Quæ e-nim mixta sunt, ex duobus ita sunt comparata, ut alterutrum eorum, ex quibus componuntur, superet aut vincat. Rectè autem excepit Aristoteles grauia scelera, quibus venia non detur. Nam quis ignoscat ei qui condemnet innocentem, qui homicidium committat, adulterium, proditionem patriæ, pietatis abnegationem ob tormentorum asperitatem? Ista nullo pacto excusari possunt aut debent, Anaxarchus, ne tyranno gratificaretur, cũ in mortario tunderetur pistillis ferreis, aiebat, Fortiter tunde saccum Anaxarchi, tantum aberat ut voluntatem mutaret, aut tormentis succumberet. Et Zeno inter tormenta sibi linguam præcidit, ne vi doloris cogeretur prodere coniuratos.
units.tr: A question is raised about certain actions which seem intermediate, and it is doubted whether they are voluntary or involuntary. The question proposed may be either simple or double-membered. It is simple if you ask: are those things voluntary which are done from fear of greater evils rather than to obtain some good or honourable thing? For there may be either a sign of comparison or a sign of disjunction. If it is a comparison, it refers to the comparative [μειζόνων], and the Greek scholia point to this reading; they report that such a thing happened to Socrates, who refused to obey the Thirty Tyrants when they asked him to kill a certain Athenian citizen. He refused to do this, although they threatened that they would kill his father and children. They sought this so that they might seem to have him as an accomplice and sharer in their most cruel counsels. The question could also, and this pleases me more, be made double-membered: namely, whether those things are voluntary which are done from fear of greater evils, or to obtain some honourable end, which otherwise would not be done. As a lie, which is base by its nature, if it is told, it is doubtful whether it is voluntary or not, when it is undertaken either to preserve one's own life or that of others. Adultery too is base, and no one would choose it for itself; but if someone should insinuate himself into a tyrant's wife and have intercourse with her, in order to have through her a ready access to killing the tyrant, it is doubtful whether that adultery ought to be called voluntary. These are examples of honourable ends. But the honourable [καλὸν] can also signify useful advantage. We all know how much merchants endure, how much the ambitious and the pleasure-seekers endure, that they may enjoy their ends; yet they would not endure the things they do unless for their own advantage. Hence it is doubted whether these are voluntary. But as for what are called great evils, if anyone doubts it, pardon was not granted to Alcmaeon, because he had committed parricide, having been led to so great a crime by a slight, or rather ridiculous, cause. Since these actions, of which we speak (as has been said), are mixed of the involuntary and the voluntary, when the voluntary prevails, praise or blame follows them; but if the involuntary prevails, and he seems to have acted unwillingly, pardon is given. For things that are mixed are composed of two elements, so that one of those from which they are compounded prevails or overcomes. Aristotle rightly excepted grave crimes, to which pardon is not given. For who would pardon one who condemns an innocent man, who commits homicide, adultery, betrayal of his country, or renunciation of piety because of the harshness of torments? These can in no way be excused, nor ought they to be. Anaxarchus, so as not to gratify the tyrant when he was being pounded in a mortar with iron pestles, said, "Strike hard at the bag of Anaxarchus"; he was so far from changing his will or yielding to torments. And Zeno, amid torments, cut out his own tongue, lest by the force of pain he be compelled to betray his fellow conspirators.

units.la: De Alcmæone autem res ita se habet. Amphiaraus vates erat: uxorem autem habuit Eriphilem, ex qua filium Alcmæonem susceperat. Expeditionem Polynices aduersus Thebas instituebat: præuidit Amphiaraus fore, si eò accessisset, ut periret, ideoq; latebat. Sola uxor eius conscia fuit, latibuli, quo se celabat: sed adducta munere torquis aurei maritum prodit, & in casu ire cum rege coactus est. Id adeò ægrè tulit, ut inserit[?] filio, Cùm exitium meum audieris, matrem interficito: alioqui pessimis & crudelissimis diris te devoueo. Patris audita morte Alcmæo matre occidit, patris diras & execrationes metuens. Aristoteles pro leui ac ridicula istam causam habet. Ovidius Alcmæonem pium & impium vocat, pium in patrem, impium in matrem. Sunt itaq; quatuor genera hominum, quæ Aristoteles proponit. Unum est, eorum qui grauia ferendo laudantur. Secundum, eorum qui viiupe-rantur. Tertium, eorum qui veniam consequuntur. Quartum, eorum qui nec veniam consequuntur.
units.tr: As for Alcmaeon, the story goes like this. Amphiaraus was a seer. He had a wife, Eriphyle, by whom he had a son, Alcmaeon. Polynices was preparing a campaign against Thebes. Amphiaraus foresaw that if he went there he would perish, and so he hid. Only his wife knew the hiding place where he concealed himself. But she was won over by a gift of a golden necklace, betrayed her husband, and he was forced to go on the expedition with the king. Taking this very badly, he charged his son: "When you hear of my death, kill your mother, or else I curse you with the worst and most cruel curses." When his father died, Alcmaeon killed his mother, fearing his father's curses and execrations. Aristotle regards this cause as slight and ridiculous. Ovid calls Alcmaeon both pious and impious: pious towards his father, impious towards his mother. So there are four kinds of people that Aristotle sets out. One is of those who are praised for bearing grievous things. The second is of those who are blamed. The third is of those who obtain pardon. The fourth is of those who do not obtain pardon.

units.la: Est difficile interdum iudicare qualia pro qualib. expetenda sint, & quid pro quo tolerandum. At id est difficilius in iis, quæ decreta fuerint permanere. Etenim quæ expectantur sunt plerunque tristia, turpia uero quæ urgent; unde laudes & uituperationes illis eueniunt, qui vel cogi vel non cogi po-tuerunt.
units.tr: Sometimes it is difficult to judge which things are to be sought for which, and what should be endured for the sake of what. But it is more difficult to keep to what has been decided. For the things we look forward to are usually sad, while the things that press upon us are base. So praise and blame fall on those who could either be compelled or not be compelled.

units.la: In ferendis aut non ferendis rebus molestis aut turpibus honesta de cau-sa duo tradit occurrere difficilia. Primum ad facultatem iudicandi attinet, quòd sæpe ignoremus quæ ferri debeant alicuius rei gratia, an aliquid in bo-nis animis tolerandum sit, an in corpore, an in fortunis, et adhuc qualia fer-re qualiaue non ferre debeamus. Interdum recte ait, quoniam aliquando ista difficultas non occurrit. Omnes enim norunt scelera nō esse vlla de cau-sa ferenda. At dubitauit Achilles, an potius debuerit optare vitam longæ-uam sed inglorium domi latitando, an potius gloriam illustrem vna cum vi-ta breui certando ad Troiam. Dubitabit etiam filius, an tacere debeat, an prodere patrem, quem nouerit patriam expilare, in ærarium penetrare vel per cuniculos, & inde furari publicam pecuniam. Dubitabit etiam Dauid an illum oporteat simulare se fatuum, an potius ferre vt à rege barbaro tru-cidetur. Causa dubij animi est, quia tristia comparanda sunt cum turpi-bus: neque inter ista facile omnibus est iudicare aut discernere. Et virtus in rebus difficilibus sita est. Ideo hinc sunt laudes: aut si ad vitium à vir-tute deflexerimus, vituperationes. Auget hic difficultatem varietas circumstantiarum, quæ facit vt certas regulas non queamus in iis habere. Aliud genus difficultatis ex infirmitate virium oritur, non iudicij. Nam quum sumus extra periculum, aut dolorem, videmus quid sit eligendum, & recte sæpe decernimus. At quum venitur ad doloris, pœnarum atque tormentorum sensum ac experientiam, non manemus in sententia. Vnde e-tiam fit, vt cum valemus, recta consilia ægrotis demus: at nobis ipsis ægrotan-tibus non recte consulimus. Et illi vehementer laudandi sunt, qui sanis de-cretis & in bona sententia steterint: & è diuerso qui à sana defecerint sen-tentia, vituperantur. Themistocles mirifice commendatur, qui potius mori voluerit, quàm patriæ suæ arma inferre. At illi maximè è contra vituperra-tione sunt digni, qui potius abnegare pietatem voluerint, quàm vel tormen-ta vel mortem perferre.
units.tr: In enduring or not enduring painful or base things for an honourable cause, he says that two difficulties arise. The first concerns the faculty of judgement, because we often do not know what ought to be endured for the sake of something, whether something should be endured in the mind, or in the body, or in one's fortunes, and further, what kinds of things we ought to endure or not endure. Sometimes he rightly says so, since this difficulty does not always arise. For everyone knows that crimes must on no account be endured. But Achilles hesitated whether he ought rather to choose a long life, though inglorious, lurking at home, or rather an illustrious glory together with a short life, fighting at Troy. A son will also hesitate whether he should keep silent or betray his father, whom he knows to be plundering his country, breaking into the treasury, or by tunnels, and from there stealing public money. David too will hesitate whether he should pretend to be mad, or rather endure being slaughtered by a barbarian king. The cause of the doubtful mind is that sad things have to be weighed against base ones, and it is not easy for everyone to judge or distinguish between them in such cases. And virtue lies in difficult matters. Therefore praises arise from them, or, if we have turned aside from virtue into vice, blame. The variety of circumstances increases the difficulty here, and this makes it impossible for us to have fixed rules for such cases. The other kind of difficulty arises from weakness of strength, not of judgement. For when we are outside danger or pain, we see what ought to be chosen, and often decide rightly. But when we come to the feeling and experience of pain, punishments and torments, we do not hold to our opinion. Hence it also happens that when we are well we give sound counsel to the sick, but when we ourselves are sick we do not counsel ourselves rightly. And those who have stood firm in sound decisions and a good opinion are greatly to be praised, while on the contrary those who have fallen away from sound opinion are blamed. Themistocles is wonderfully commended, who preferred to die rather than bear arms against his country. But those are most worthy of blame on the other hand who have preferred to renounce piety rather than endure either torments or death.

units.la: Qualia vero ea sunt quę dicuntur violenta, an sim-pliciter quæ causam extrinsecā habuerint, & is qui agit nihil adiuuat? Quæ autem per seipsa quidem non voluntaria sunt, nunc vero præ quibusdam expetenda, & principium est in agente, magis accedunt ad uoluntaria, siquidem actiones sunt circa singula. Et haec sunt uoluntaria. Qualia autem pro qualibus expetenda sint, non est facile tradere, quoniam in singulis rebus plurimae sunt differentiae.
units.tr: But what are those things which are called violent: whether simply those which have an external cause, and the one who acts contributes nothing to them? Those things which are not voluntary in themselves, but are now to be chosen in preference to some things, and whose principle lies in the agent, come nearer to the voluntary, since actions concern particulars. And these are voluntary. But it is not easy to state which things are to be chosen in preference to which, since in individual cases there are many differences.

units.la: Nil hoc loco noui affertur, sed epilogo quodam perspicuo quae hactenus tradita sunt commemoratur: nempe illa esse non voluntaria simpliciter, quae principium extrinsecum habent, et id quod agit nullo ei est adiumento. Sed alia sunt non voluntaria per se quidem, at nunc & pro isto momento tempo-ris quo aguntur, pro quibusdam rebus durioribus expetuntur. Quin & principium earum actionum est in agente, magis accedunt ad voluntaria. Cum dicuntur per se non voluntaria, per se nil aliud est, quam si natura-liter consyderetur citra suas circumstantias. At in actionibus huiusmodi cogitatio est propemodum vana, cum actiones circa singula sint: at in singu-lis nostris actionibus dum aguntur, intrinsecum voluntatis principium deprehenditur esse in nobis. Unde concluditur istas actiones ad voluntariorum naturam accedere. Distinctio quaedam non voluntariorum ex iis verbis eli-citur: nam quaedam dicuntur non voluntaria, quod simpliciter huiusmodi sint, alia vero quod per se ac generaliter consyderata sint non voluntaria, licet non nihil habeant non voluntarij.
units.tr: Nothing new is brought forward in this place, but by a kind of clear summary what has been handed down so far is recalled: namely, that those things are not voluntary simply which have an external principle, and the thing that acts contributes nothing to it. But other things are not voluntary in themselves, yet at this moment of time in which they are done, they are chosen in preference to certain harder things. Indeed the principle of these actions lies in the agent, so they come nearer to the voluntary. When they are said to be not voluntary in themselves, this means only that they are considered naturally, apart from their circumstances. But in actions of this kind such consideration is almost idle, since actions concern particulars; and in each of our particular actions, while they are being done, an intrinsic principle of the will is found to be in us. From this it is concluded that such actions approach the nature of the voluntary. A certain distinction of the non-voluntary is drawn from these words: for some things are called non-voluntary because they are simply of this kind, while others are non-voluntary when considered in themselves and in general, though they have something of the voluntary in them.

units.la: Si quis uero dixerit, iucunda & bona uiolenta esse quod intrinseca sint, & quadam necessitate urgeant, omnia hoc pacto erunt isti uiolenta: nam horum gratia omnes omnia faciunt. Licet qui ui & inuiti, agre faciant: qui autem ob iucunditatem mala cōmittunt, cum uoluptate. Est uero admodum ridiculum, accusare quae sunt extrinsecus, & non seipsum, qui se facile ab iis capi sinat, & honestarum quidem actionum ipsum faciat authorem, turpium uero causam in iucunda reiciat.
units.tr: But if someone should say that pleasant and good things are violent because they are intrinsic and press on us by a certain necessity, then in this way all things will be violent, for everyone does everything for the sake of these things. Those who act under compulsion and against their will do so with reluctance; but those who commit wrongs for the sake of pleasure do so with enjoyment. And it is truly quite ridiculous to accuse what is external, and not oneself, who lets oneself be so easily caught by these things, and who makes oneself the author of honourable actions, but casts the cause of base ones upon pleasant things.

units.la: Duo genera inuoluntariorum hactenus enumeraverat: nunc illorum opinionem explodit, qui adhuc tertium genus faciebant non voluntariorum. Aiebant enim actiones pravas quas committimus ob voluptatem vel uti litatem[?] assequendam, esse violentas: & illas tantum actiones faciebant voluntarias, quæ rationi recte consentientes essent. Rationibus istis confutantur. Prima, Quia tunc omnes nostræ actiones essent violentæ: nam quicquid agimus, propter ista facimus, nimirum iucunditatem & utilitatem. Secunda ratio, quia violentum cum tristitia est coniunctum: at illi qui agunt ob voluptatem, læti agunt, non tristes. Quare apparet tales actiones non esse violentas. Tertia ratio, Quia tunc omnis pravus excusaret suas pravas actiones, culpam in res externas transferens, nimirum in iucunda, & utilia, à quibus se coactum diceret: quod est ridiculum. Quarta ratio, Non magis ratio cur honestarum actionum faciant ipsi[?] se authores, & turpium res iucundas aut commodas, quia tam istarum quam illarum in seipsis principium habent. Notandum aliquos textus habere: Si quis dixerit iucunda & mala violenta esse: ita ut non legatur καλὰ sed κακὰ. Atq; tunc sensus erit: Si quis dixerit violenta esse quæ agimus, ut iucunditatem consequamur, vel ut molestia seu mala effugiamus, illi profecto omnia humana violenta erunt: quoniam omnes agunt omnia propter ista duo, nimirum ut aliquam voluptatem assequantur, utq; fugiant & vitent incommoda. Sed quum vulgata lectio καλὰ obtineat, non videtur mutanda temere, præsertim quum illa idem significetur ac exprimatur, quod altera tradit. Euitare quippe molestia & incommoda est utile, atque inter τὰ καλὰ debet censeri. Ad summam si vera esset istorum sententia, nulla essent hominum peccata seu scelera, quæ non possent inuiti seu violenti prætextu excusari. Ratio est allata, quoniam omnes agunt ob istas causas, nempe iucunditatis & utilitatis. Quod utiq; verum est, si etiam sub voce καλὰ, honesta comprehendas: nam multi sunt qui multa honestatis causa faciunt. At dices, Adversarij non ita illud vocabulum usurparunt, ut notarint illo solum voluptuosa & utilia. Scio. Sed hoc Aristoteles arguit, & illos ait ridiculos, qui potius velint res iucundas & utiles accusare, quam seipsos, qui se tam faciles captu istis rebus exhibent. Hæc est illorum iusta reprehensio, quòd se tam facile ab ijs rebus capi sinant, & à iustis actionibus avocari. Quid oportet sibi ipsis attribuere honesta, & turpia rebus externis adscribere, quum & illa sint in potestate nostra? quemadmodum apparet in hominibus temperatis & continentibus qui ab istis facile sibi temperant. Et ad-hæc mirum est, quare non eadem ratione dicant se ab honestis rebus cogi, cùm illas deligunt, cùm & ipsa sint non minus externa, quàm uolupta-tes & utilia. Certè si nobis iure adscribimus honesta, turpia quoq; ad nos pertinebunt: nam contraria et ad idem genus pertinent, eadèq; regula sunt metienda. Videntur ista in Platonem dici: nam is in Memnone dicit, bonos non effici bonos natura, ac si diceret, voluntate fiunt boni & electione. E diuerso autem de malis in 9 de Legibus dixit, eos omnes quo ad omnia esse pravos, sed inuitos. Sed Aristoteles hoc loco affirmat, tam bonos quàm malos sponte ac voluntarijs actionibus fieri. Sunt enim tā probitatis quā malitiæ principia mouentia extrinseca, res nimirum quæ sese nostræ intelligentiæ offerunt, sed in utrisq; cùm fiunt, à nobis eligentibus ac decernentibus, auxilium adiumentumq; præstatur.
units.tr: Up to now he had listed two kinds of involuntary actions; now he refutes the opinion of those who still made a third kind of non-voluntary. For they said that wrong actions which we commit in order to obtain pleasure or advantage are violent, and they counted as voluntary only those actions which agree with right reason. These views are refuted by arguments. The first is that then all our actions would be violent, for whatever we do, we do for these things, namely pleasure and advantage. The second argument: violence is joined with sadness, but those who act for pleasure act cheerfully, not sadly. Therefore it is clear that such actions are not violent. The third argument: then every wrongdoer would excuse his wrong actions, transferring the blame to external things, namely pleasant and useful things, by which he would say he was compelled; which is ridiculous. The fourth argument: there is no more reason why they should make themselves the authors of honourable actions, and attribute base ones to pleasant or useful things, since both kinds have their principle in themselves. It should be noted that some texts read: "If someone should say that pleasant and bad [κακὰ] things are violent," not "good [καλὰ]." Then the sense will be: if someone should say that the things we do in order to obtain pleasure, or to escape pain or evils, are violent, then indeed all human actions will be violent, since everyone does everything for these two reasons, namely to obtain some pleasure and to flee and avoid discomforts. But since the common reading "good" [καλὰ] holds, it does not seem to be changed rashly, especially since it signifies and expresses the same thing as the other reading. For to avoid troubles and discomforts is useful, and ought to be counted among the good things [τὰ καλὰ]. In short, if their opinion were true, there would be no human sins or crimes which could not be excused under the pretext of being involuntary or violent. The reason given is that everyone acts for these causes, namely pleasure and advantage. This is certainly true, if you also include the honourable under the word "good" [καλὰ]; for there are many who do many things for the sake of honour. But you will say: the opponents did not use that word in such a way as to mark only pleasurable and useful things. I know. But Aristotle argues this point, and calls ridiculous those who would rather accuse pleasant and useful things than themselves, who so easily allow themselves to be caught by these things. This is their just reproof, that they let themselves be so easily captured by such things and diverted from just actions. Why should they attribute honourable actions to themselves, and ascribe base ones to external things, when these too are in our power? This is evident in temperate and continent men, who easily restrain themselves from such things. And moreover it is strange why they do not on the same principle say that they are compelled by honourable things when they choose them, since these are no less external than pleasures and advantages. Certainly if we rightly claim honourable things for ourselves, base things too will belong to us, for contraries belong to the same genus and must be measured by the same rule. These things seem to be said against Plato: for in the Meno he says that good men are not made good by nature, as if he were saying that they become good by will and choice. On the other hand, about bad men in the ninth book of the Laws he said that they are all wicked in every respect, but unwillingly. But Aristotle in this place affirms that both good and bad men are made so by spontaneous and voluntary actions. For there are external moving principles both of probity and of wickedness, namely things which present themselves to our understanding; but whenever these things come about in either case, help and assistance are supplied by us as we choose and decide.

units.la: Quicquid per ignorationem agitur, non est uoluntarium. Quod autem est inuitum, molestum est, & affectum poenitendi excitat. Qui enim per ignorantiam quippiam facit, neq; suam postea ægre fert actionem, nõ uolens facit quod prius non nouerat, & cum tristitia non afficiatur, non dicetur inuitus fecisse. Per ignorantiam alius agit cum poenitentia, & inuitus fecisse uidetur: alius uero quum fecerit ipsum non poenitet, qui quoniam à priori diuersus est, ideo non uolens aut non uoluntarius dicatur. Quia enim illo differt, præstat ut proprium nomen habeat.
units.tr: Whatever is done through ignorance is not voluntary. What is unwilling, however, is painful and provokes a feeling of regret. For someone who does something through ignorance and afterwards does not take the action badly, did not intend what he had not known, and is not affected with sorrow, it will not be said that he acted unwillingly. Another person acts through ignorance with regret and seems to have acted unwillingly. But the one who, having done it, feels no regret, since he differs from the first, is said to be not willing or not voluntary. Because he differs from the other, it is right that he should have a name of his own.

units.la: Hæc huius Capitis est altera pars, in qua cùm egerit de non voluntario quod per uim fit, nunc de nõ voluntario scribit, quod ab ignorantibus prodit. Et primùm ab eo quod fit per ignorantiam, aufert voluntarium: nihil enim quod ab ignorante fiat, potest dici voluntarium, quando id cognitionem eius quod agitur exigit. Sed proponit distinctionem quandam eorum qui agunt quippiam ignorantes: nam quidam eorum quum resciuerint postea quid egerint: eos poenitet, alios vero minimè poenitet, sed potius ratum habent quod actum fuerit. Duo ista ignorantium genera quia inter sese multum differunt, diuersas formas aut species ignorationis consti-tuunt, tnunt[?], & quia re distant à se inuicem, conuenit etiam vt diuerso nomine appellentur. Ille itaq; quem pœnitet, postquam resciuit errorem, dicetur ἀκών, id est, inuitus. Is vero quem minime pœnitet, dicetur fecisse nõ volès: nomen quippe generis retinebit, vt sit non voluntarius. Ab initio nostra actiones diuisæ sunt, quòd aliquæ sint voluntariæ, aliquæ non voluntariæ. A non voluntario est orsus membrorum partitionis huius declarationem, & non voluntarium distinxit rursus in inuitum seu violentum quod per vim geritur, & id quod sit per ignorationem. Violentum definiuit, cuius principium sit extra, & id quod agit aut patitur nullum adiumentum præstat. Alterum membrum, inuoluntarij nempe, quo agitur per ignorantiam, nunc tradit, idq; facit duplex, nimirum vel cum pœnitentia vel sine pœnitentia. Quod est cum pœnitentia simpliciter est inuitum, at illud quod ea caret ab initio non est voluntarium, sed post cognitionem facti quia non pœnitet, videtur nonnihil, imò plurimum distare ab inuito, imò potius aliquid habere voluntarij. Distinguentur igitur ista nomine. Primus dicetur inuitus, alter non voluntarius. Oedipus in fabulis inuitus occidit patrem & duxit matrem: nam quod fecerat resciscens, ita ipsum pœnituit, vt sibi oculos effoderit. E diuerso Tiberius ignorans torsit hospitem Rhodium, quem postea cùm agnouisset, illum interemit. Proinde ab initio cùm torquendo igno raret, non volens fecit, quia tamen postea illum non pœnituit, dici non potuit inuitus fecisse. Potest & aliud exemplum adduci. Inuitus facit qui occidit hominem, cùm feram esse putaret, si postea doleat. Verùm si aliquis cùm sibi deberetur æs accepit aurum, neq; illum erroris pœniteat, sed potius gaudeat, dicitur fecisse non volens, haud tamen inuitus. Ita ratio componi posset:
units.tr: This is the second part of this chapter. Having treated the non-voluntary that comes about by force, he now writes about the non-voluntary that proceeds from people acting in ignorance. First he removes the voluntary from what is done through ignorance: nothing done by an ignorant person can be called voluntary, since it requires knowledge of what is being done. But he sets out a certain distinction among those who act in ignorance. For some of them, when they afterwards learn what they have done, regret it; others do not regret it at all, but rather approve of what was done. Because these two kinds of ignorance differ greatly from each other, they constitute different forms or species of ignorance, and since they differ in fact, it is fitting that they also be called by different names. So the one who regrets it, after learning of the error, will be called unwilling [ἀκών], that is, unwilling. The one who does not regret it at all will be said to have acted nolens; he keeps the name of the genus, so as to be non-voluntary. At the beginning our actions were divided into those that are voluntary and those that are non-voluntary. He began the explanation of this division of parts with the non-voluntary, and again divided the non-voluntary into the unwilling or violent, which is done by force, and that which is done through ignorance. He defined the violent as that whose principle is outside, and in which the one who acts or suffers contributes nothing. Now he gives the other part, namely the involuntary that is done through ignorance, and he makes this twofold: either with regret or without regret. What is done with regret is simply unwilling, but what lacks regret from the start is not voluntary; yet after knowing the fact, since the agent does not regret it, it seems to differ somewhat, indeed a great deal, from the unwilling, and rather to have something of the voluntary. These are therefore distinguished by name. The first will be called unwilling, the other non-voluntary. In the fables Oedipus unwillingly killed his father and married his mother; for when he learned what he had done, he regretted it so much that he put out his own eyes. On the other hand, Tiberius, being ignorant, tortured a Rhodian guest, whom he afterwards recognised and put to death. Therefore, since at the time of the torture he did not know, he acted nolens; but because he did not regret it afterwards, he could not be said to have acted unwillingly. Another example can also be given. A man who kills another, thinking him a wild beast, acts unwillingly if he grieves afterwards. But if someone, when he was owed money, received gold instead of bronze, and does not regret the error but rather rejoices, he is said to have acted nolens, yet not unwillingly. The argument could be set out thus:

units.la: Quicquid violenter agitur aut inuite, dolorem seu pœnitentiam coniun-ctam secum habet.
units.tr: Whatever is done by force or unwillingly has pain or regret joined with it.

units.la: At non omnia quæ ab ignaro aguntur, pœnitentiam aut dolorem coniun-ctum habent.
units.tr: But not everything that is done by an ignorant person has regret or pain joined with it.

units.la: Ergo non sunt omnia huiusmodi violenta seu inuita.
units.tr: Therefore not all such things are violent or unwilling.

units.la: Aliud præterea uidetur per imprudentiam facere, & aliud imprudentem facere. Nam qui uel ebrius est uel iratus, non uidetur per imprudentiam facere sed propter aliquid eorum quæ diximus, non tamè prudens, & ignorans. Nam quilibet prauus ignorat quæ facere oporteat, quæue sint euitanda: atque propter huiusmodi errorem, iniusti atque omnino mali fiunt. Inuitum autem dici debet, non si quis ignoret quod est utile: quia ignoratio quæ est cum electione inuiti causa non est, sed potius malitiæ. Neq; ignorantia illa quæ uniuersalis est: nam homines propter illam uituperantur. At quæ de singularibus est, inuitum efficit, circa quæ singula est actio. Etenim in his misericordia est & uenia. Qui enim aliquid istorum ignorat, inuitus agit.
units.tr: It seems that to do something through lack of thought is one thing, and to be a thoughtless person who acts is another. For the one who is drunk or angry does not seem to act through lack of thought, but because of one of the things we have mentioned, and yet he is not without thought or ignorant. For every wicked person is ignorant of what he ought to do or what he ought to avoid, and because of this kind of error people become unjust and altogether bad. Yet one should not be called unwilling if he is ignorant of what is useful; for ignorance that accompanies choice is not the cause of unwillingness, but rather of wickedness. Nor is it the ignorance that is universal, for people are blamed on account of that. But ignorance concerning particulars, in which the action is about individual things, makes an act unwilling. For in these there is pity and pardon. For the one who is ignorant of any of these acts unwillingly.

units.la: Alia modò commemoratur distinctio. Aliud, inquam, esse agere per ignorantiam, & aliud ignorantem agere. Ex ignorantia vel per imprudentiam ij dicuntur agere, quibus causa est aliquo modo ignorantia quod agant. Ignorantes è diuerso multi agunt, qui errorem quodammodo sibi ipsis accer-sunt ob aliquam grauem perturbationem cuius ipsi sunt causa. Differunt hæc vt genus & species, late patens & contractum. Nam quicunque per ignorantiam agit, est ignorans: at non è diuerso quilibet ignorans per ignorantiam agit. Exempla ipse affert, primum ebrietatis: multa committuntur ab ebriis, in quibus nesciunt quid agant: non tamen per imprudentiam proprie dicuntur quid facere, quoniam abstinere potuerant à nimio vino, & plus æquo bibentes ignorationem sibi ipsis accersuerunt: unde tale vitium non efficit, vt dicantur inuiti fecisse. Alterum simile est de ira.
