Qui enim magno iræ furore perciti fuerint, ij sæpenumero quid agant ignorant, verùm non faciunt inuiti, quia oportuit eos temperare iram, & virtutem sibi comparare, quæ perturbationem eiusmodi compescerent. Quod cùm facere noluerint, de iis non excusantur quæ per iram male commiserint. Et in summa dicitur, ignorantiam eius generis non inuiti, sed prauitatis esse causam. Alioqui prauus quilibet est ignorans, nec tamen propterea excusandus. Pra-uos ignorantes esse id confirmat, quòd quæ sequenda sint quæue fugienda nesciunt. Nam decipiuntur suis cupiditatibus, propter quas ita falluntur, vt verè iucunda, verè vtilia, & è diuerso verè tristia verèq; damnosa nō intelligant. Sunt itaq; iudicio corrupti, & finis naturam propter quam ope-rantur ignorant. Ratio ita componatur:
units.tr: Another distinction is now mentioned: to act through ignorance is one thing, and to act while ignorant is another. Those are said to act through ignorance or lack of thought who have ignorance as a cause of their action in some way. On the other hand, many act while ignorant, who in some way bring error upon themselves because of some serious disturbance of which they themselves are the cause. These differ as genus and species, the broad and the narrow. For whoever acts through ignorance is ignorant, but conversely, not every ignorant person acts through ignorance. He gives examples himself, first of drunkenness: many things are committed by drunk people in which they do not know what they are doing. Yet they are not properly said to act through lack of thought, since they could have abstained from too much wine, and by drinking more than is right they brought ignorance upon themselves; so such a fault does not make them be said to have acted unwillingly. The other case is similar with anger. For those who are stirred by the great fury of anger often do not know what they are doing, yet they do not act unwillingly, because they ought to have restrained their anger and acquired virtue which would check such a disturbance. Since they were unwilling to do this, they are not excused for the wrongs they committed in anger. And in sum, it is said that ignorance of this kind is the cause not of unwillingness but of wickedness. Otherwise any wicked person is ignorant, and yet he is not for that reason to be excused. That wicked people are ignorant is confirmed by the fact that they do not know what ought to be followed or what ought to be avoided. For they are deceived by their desires, and because of these they are so misled that they do not understand what is truly pleasant, truly useful, and conversely what is truly sad and truly harmful. Therefore they are corrupted in judgment, and they do not know the end by which their actions are governed. The argument may be set out thus:
Not every wicked person acts through ignorance,
Every wicked person acts while ignorant.
Therefore, to act while ignorant and to act through ignorance differ.

units.la: Maior est manifesta: quoniam excusarentur praui (vt dictum est) si per ignorationem agerent. Quod vero, vt habetur in minori, sint ignorantes, paulo ante declarauimus. Ignorantia universalis, inquit, non excusat. Vniversalis dicitur quae non est circumstantiarum, sed totius ipsius rei. Vt si quis dicat ignorare se fornicationem aut adulterium esse peccata, non excu-satur: quoniam haec scire debuit. Imo potius ob hanc ignorationem grauius accusabitur. Particularis autem ignoratio, id est, circumstantiarum, excusat & meretur veniam, quia sciri non possunt: ij quandoq; casus eueniunt, vt nemo possit habere compertas huiusmodi circumstantias. At e diuerso uni-versalis ignorantia misericordiam non consequitur: quia in ignorantium potestate fuit discere. Unde si ignorant, per eos stetit quod non scirent, igno-rantiam q; suam videntur affectasse. Atq; si valeret excusatio ignoratiae u-niversalis, tum nulli praui homines possent accusari. Causa erroris eorum est, quod tantum voluptatem & utilitatem sectantur, virtutes autem & honestatem negligunt: quod tamen imprudentes faciunt. Unde Plato id probe exponit in suo Memnone. Primum accipit, Neminem esse qui velit esse miser atq; infelix. Quod cum datum fuerit, subiicit, Neminem igitur esse qui mala expetat: cum esse miserum atq; infelicem nihil aliud sit quam in malis versari, atque illis delectari. Quare patet prauos, quae mala sunt, sibi deligere imprudentes. Atque hunc errorem, vt inquit Cicero, suximus cum lacte nutricis. Causa vero cur ignoratio ista universalis non efficiat inuitum, est, quia non impedit electionem, imo cum illa est coniuncta. Eli-gunt enim mali potius furari quam laborare, potius ociari quam artem a-liquam exercere, potius crapulam quam abstinentiam. Fieri potest vt res tota quandoque in universum ignoretur, quandoq; scitur in universum, sed priuatim & particulariter ignoratur. Vt si quis dixerit, se nosse adulte-rium esse peccatum, ignorare autem seorsim hoc adulterium esse prohibitu, & neutra istarum ignorationum digna est venia. Quod si quis circumstan-tias ipsas in universum nesciat, putetq; non habendam rationem finis, non loci, neq; temporis, neq; materiae circa quam egerit, an erit iste misericordia seu venia dignus? Nequaquam. Scire enim debuit hoc. Pertinetq; communis ista notio ad scientiam universalem, quae omnino haberi debet. Sed igno-ratio singillatim huius aut illius circumstantiae potest excusare, cum illas ne-mo singillatim omnes aut queat aut valeat exploratas habere. Quare so-lum ignorantia earum actionem facit inuitam.
units.tr: The major premise is plain, since wicked people would be excused (as has been said) if they acted through ignorance. But that they are ignorant, as is stated in the minor premise, we have shown a little earlier. Universal ignorance, he says, does not excuse. That is called universal which concerns not the circumstances but the whole thing itself. For example, if someone says that he did not know that fornication or adultery is sin, he is not excused, since he ought to have known these things. Indeed, he will be accused more gravely on account of this ignorance. But particular ignorance, that is, of circumstances, excuses and deserves pardon, because such circumstances cannot be known; sometimes such cases happen that no one can have certain knowledge of these circumstances. On the other hand, universal ignorance does not obtain mercy, because it was in the power of the ignorant to learn. Hence, if they are ignorant, it is because they chose not to know, and they seem to have deliberately sought their ignorance. And if the excuse of universal ignorance were valid, then no wicked people could be accused. The cause of their error is that they pursue only pleasure and advantage, but neglect virtues and honour; yet foolish people do this. Hence Plato explains this well in his Meno. First he takes it that no one wishes to be miserable and unhappy. When this has been granted, he adds that therefore no one desires evil things, since to be miserable and unhappy is nothing other than to live among evils and to take delight in them. Hence it is clear that wicked people, not knowing, choose for themselves the things that are evil. And, as Cicero says, we sucked this error in with our nurse's milk. The reason why this universal ignorance does not make an act unwilling is that it does not hinder choice; rather it is joined with choice. For wicked people choose to steal rather than to labour, to be idle rather than to practise some craft, to gorge rather than to abstain. It can happen that a whole matter is at some time unknown in general, or at another time is known in general but is ignorant in particular and individually. For example, if someone says that he knows adultery to be a sin, but does not know in particular that this adultery is forbidden, neither of these ignorances deserves pardon. But if someone does not know the circumstances themselves in general, and thinks that no account need be taken of the end, the place, the time, or the matter with which he is concerned, would he be worthy of mercy or pardon? By no means. For he ought to have known this. And this common notion belongs to universal knowledge, which must altogether be had. But ignorance of this or that circumstance taken one by one can excuse, since no one can have all of them one by one investigated and known. Therefore only ignorance of these circumstances makes the action unwilling.

units.la: Fortasis igitur definire hæc non ab re fuerit, quænam & quot sint. Quis itaque, & quid, circa quid, vel in quo agat quispiam: quandoque autem et quo ceu organo, & cuius causa: quemadmodum salutis. Et quomodo, id est vehementer vel leniter. Omnia vero hæc nemo, qui non desipiat, ignoraverit. Cer-tum est illum non ignoraturum ipsum efficientem. Quomodo enim seipsum ignoret?
units.tr: Perhaps, then, it will not be out of place to define these: what they are and how many there are. Who, and what, about what, or in what someone acts; sometimes also by what, as an instrument, and for what purpose, as for safety. And how, that is, vehemently or gently. No one who is not out of his mind would be ignorant of all of these. It is certain that he will not be ignorant of the efficient cause itself. For how could he be ignorant of himself?

units.la: Quia circumstantiæ huiusmodi sunt magni ponderis, dant enim veniam & misericordiam cum ignorantur: ideo illas enumerat, ut explorate atque cognitæ habeantur. Sunt numero septem vel octo. Vulgatum est carmen in scholis:
units.tr: Because circumstances of this kind carry great weight, since they give pardon and mercy when they are unknown, he enumerates them so that they may be held as examined and known. There are seven or eight of them. A verse is commonly repeated in the schools:

units.la: Quis, quid, ubi, quibus auxiliis, cur, quomodo, quando.
units.tr: Who, what, where, by what aids, why, how, when.

units.la: Sunt istæ septem: sed una deest, Circa quid. Qua voce significatur mate-ria vel subiectum actionis. Et cum dicitur, in quo, ab Aristotele, duo significantur: nempe locus & tempus. Octo itaq; sunt si iustum velimus habere numerum: huiusq; summæ ratio hæc potest assignari. Quia vel causas actionis respicimus, vel ipsam actionis naturam vel substantiam consideramus. Causa si est efficiens, dicitur Quis: aut finis, & habemus Cuius causa: seu materia, ideo adiectum est Circa quid: vel instrumenta vel organa, quæ referuntur ad efficientem causam. Quod si actio ipsa consideretur, eius natura exprimitur per Quid. Cum vero mensura illius attenditur, habemus tempus & locum. Et postremo est mensura modi, qui ad qualitatem pertinet, & est Quomodo. Nemo potest, inquit, omnes istas circumstantias intelligito si-mul, ignorare. Privatim nesciri possunt, sed simul omnes minimè, nisi ab eo qui vehementer desipiat. Quomodo enim quis ignoraverit seipsum? Hoc nō est verum in universum: quoniam efficientem causam potest quispiam opti-mè ignorare. Si ipse fuerit efficiens, difficilius fateor seipsum nescire: at etiā hoc quandoq; fieri potest, ut aliquis interdum aliquid aliud agens nauim moveat, neq; se id facere animadvertit. Sed quod modo dicitur, est in pluri-bus: neq; in moralibus exigitur ista subtilitas.
units.tr: These are seven, but one is missing: About what (circa quid). This word signifies the matter or subject of the action. And when Aristotle says "in what," two things are meant, namely place and time. So there are eight, if we wish to have a full number, and the reason for this sum can be given as follows. We look either at the causes of the action or consider the nature or substance of the action itself. If the cause is efficient, it is called Who; if it is the end, we have For what purpose; if it is the matter, "about what" is added; or the instruments and organs, which relate to the efficient cause. If the action itself is considered, its nature is expressed by What. When its measure is attended to, we have time and place. And finally there is the measure of manner, which pertains to quality, and it is How. No one, he says, can be ignorant of all these circumstances at once. Individually they may be unknown, but all together not at all, except by one who is seriously out of his mind. For how could someone be ignorant of himself? This is not true universally, since someone can very well be ignorant of the efficient cause. If he himself is the agent, I grant that it is harder not to know himself; yet even this can sometimes happen, that someone, while doing something else, moves a ship and does not notice he is doing it. But what has just been said holds in most cases, and such subtlety is not required in moral matters.

units.la: Quis facilè id quod agit ignoraverit. Quemad-modum aiunt, qui dictitat sibi excidisse, vel minimè scire illa fuisse arcana, ut Aeschylus mysteria: siue qui voluerit ostendere iecerit, ut qui emittit catapultam. Potest etiam quis arbitrari filium esse hostem, uti Merope: aut hastam esse obtusam, quae fuerit acuto ferro munita: seu lapidem esse pumicem. Interficiatq; aliquis quempiam salutis causa: aut qui demonstrare voluerit, ut qui summis manibus aut digitis percutiunt. Itaq; circa omnia haec in quibus actio sita est, cum fuerit ignoratio, qui aliquid horum nesciuerit, invitus egisse videtur, & maxime in iis quae praecipua sunt: praecipua vero esse videntur, in quibus est actio, & cuius rei causa.
units.tr: Someone may easily be ignorant of what he is doing, as those who say that a word slipped from them, or that they least knew it was a secret, as with Aeschylus and the mysteries; or someone who wished to show something and let it fly, like one who fires a catapult. Someone may also think his son is an enemy, as Merope did; or think a spear is blunt when it has been fitted with a sharp iron; or think a stone is pumice. Someone may kill a man for the sake of his health; or one who wished to demonstrate something, as those who strike with the flat of their hands or fingers. Therefore, in all the things in which the action lies, when there is ignorance, the one who has not known any of these seems to have acted unwillingly, and especially in those which are principal. The principal circumstances, indeed, appear to be those in which the action lies and the cause for which it is done.

units.la: Exemplis res demonstratur. Circumstantia Quid excusauit Aeschy-lum Tragicum Poetam. Is tragoedia quadam sacra Cereris arcana visus est inuulgasse. Quod tantum excitauit tumultum in theatro, ut propemodum sit interfectus, ad aram Bacchi fugit, inde ad iudicium Areopagitarum ad ductus. Causam dixit, excusauit se nesciuisse illa fuisse mysteria: & quia ignorauit quid ageret, est absolutus. Alius item catapultam, machinam inquam iacientem lapides extruxerat, cuius effectum cum demonstrare vellet, iecit, & ictu quempiam occidit, excusauit se nesciuisse quid ageret. Circa quid, quod est materia siue subiectum actionis, exemplo Meropes exponitur: illa insidias filio struxit, & occidit, putans hostem esse, cum esset eius filius. Hic error fuit circa quid. Hoc autem dicitur habere apud Euripidem in Tragoedia Crespontis, quae non extat. Instrumentum interdum nescitur, id est quo: ut si putet quispiam hasta concurrere obtusa, & ea fuerit mucrone acuto munita. Vel existimans iacere se pumicem levem, emisit lapidem quo aliquis ictus aut vulneratus est aut interfectus. Aliquando ignoratur finis. Quispiam sanitatis aut salutis causa venam incidit, pharmacum dabit, aut percutiet, & contrarius consequetur effectus: aut morietur, aut laedetur: finis ignoratus excusat. Modus quoq; actionis, quando non volebat, excusat. Qui summis manibus aut digitis inter se pugnant (est genus luctae unusq; vult docere alterum, & putans leviter ferire, percutit gravius: excusatur. Quando in iis est ignoratio, invitum erit quod agitur, praefertim si ea circumstantiæ nos lateant, quæ sunt magis præcipuæ. Eæ verò sunt finis, & circa quid, vel in quibus. At noster Aristoteles in suis exemplis omisisse videtur circumstantiam loci ac temporis. Non mirum id est: quoniam sactis notæ potuerunt videri, vt quæ non egerent exemplis. Neq; id exigitur, cùm explicantur multa eiusdem generis, vt de omnibus afferantur exempla: namid satis est, vt aliqua ita esse demonstrentur. Nam exempla quæ aliqua illorum patefaciunt, aliis quoq; declarandis inseruiunt: ne tamen desyderentur, fieri posse dicimus: vt aliquis nesciat sacrum esse locum in quo aliquid mali committit, ignoratur etiam tempus, nonnunquam festum aut feriatum aut natalitium fuisse.
units.tr: The matter is shown by examples. The circumstance What excused the tragic poet Aeschylus. He was seen to have divulged the mysteries of Ceres in a certain sacred tragedy. This stirred up such a tumult in the theatre that he was nearly killed; he fled to the altar of Bacchus, and from there was brought before the judgment of the Areopagites. He pleaded his case and excused himself on the ground that he did not know those were mysteries; and because he was ignorant of what he was doing, he was acquitted. Likewise another man had built a catapult, a machine, I mean, that throws stones; wishing to demonstrate its effect, he fired it and struck someone, who died. He excused himself on the ground that he did not know what he was doing. "About what," which is the matter or subject of the action, is explained by the example of Merope. She laid a trap for her son and killed him, thinking he was an enemy, when he was her son. This error concerned "about what." This is said to occur in Euripides' tragedy Cresphontes, which is not extant. The instrument is sometimes not known, that is, "by what": as when someone thinks a spear is blunt for a bout, and it was fitted with a sharp point. Or thinking he is throwing a light pumice, he lets fly a stone by which someone is struck, wounded or killed. Sometimes the end is unknown. Someone opens a vein for the sake of health, or gives a medicine, or strikes, and the contrary result follows: he kills or injures. The unknown end excuses him. The manner of the action also excuses when one did not wish it. Those who fight with open hands or fingers (it is a kind of wrestling in which each wants to teach the other, and thinking to strike lightly, one strikes harder) are excused. When there is ignorance in these matters, what is done will be unwilling, especially if those circumstances which are more principal lie hidden from us. These are the end, and "about what," or "in what." But our Aristotle seems to have omitted the circumstance of place and time from his examples. This is no wonder, since they could seem known to all, as things that did not need examples. Nor is it required, when many things of the same kind are explained, that examples be given for all of them; for it is enough that some are shown in this way. For the examples that reveal some of them also serve to make the others clear. Lest these nevertheless be overlooked, we say it can happen that someone does not know the place where he commits some wrong is sacred; the time may also be unknown, as sometimes it was a festival, a holiday, or a birthday.

units.la: Cum itaque inuitum dicatur quod per hanc ignorationem agitur, oportet adhæc actionem molestiam esse.
units.tr: Since, then, that is said to be unwilling which is done through this ignorance, it must also follow that the action is unpleasant.

units.la: Inuitum si adscribi debeat actionibus quæ fiunt per imprudentiam, dum ignorantur istæ singulares circumstantiæ, requiritur præterea vt errore cognito ac retecto, actio sit molesta, doleatq; accidisse quod euenit nobis imprudentibus. Nam si molestia hæc non accesserit, actio quidem poterit dici non voluntaria, non tamen erit inuita. Sed hic operæprecium est videre, quo-modo ignoratio causa dicatur inuiti. Hoc ideò est, quia priuat notitiam, quæ si adfuisset, non admissum esset, quod iam factum est, aut si fuisset factum, actionem constituisset voluntariam. Vel ergo priuat notitiam à qua pendet voluntarium: vel eam notitiam, quæ si interuenisset, actio non esset conse-quuta. Et potest fieri, vt qui imprudens agit, ignorationem coniunctam ha-beat simul cum actione quam agit, non tamen id quod agitur nolit, sed po-tius cupiat. Vnde non sequitur postea dolor, cùm res cognita fuerit. Et hoc ignorantiæ genus non excusat, neq; parit inuitum. Vt cùm quis putat oc-cidere ceruum, hostem suum interfecit, quem antea voluisset occisum, et nunc interfectum gaudet, licet ignorauerit tum quid ageret. Est præterea quædam ignorantia, quam nonnulli de industria volunt: hoc enim sibi expetunt ac deligunt vt ignorent, ne perscientiam retrahantur à peccando vel à volu-ptatibus. Atq; ignorantia hæc grauiter accusanda est, nedum excuset. Alia est ignoratio, quæ fit vt aliquis sciens ius & fas, cùm ad actionem venitur, omittat cogitationè illam honesti ac rectitudinis, & vtilitatè potius aut vo-luptatè consyderet. Idq; fit vel ex animi vehementi perturbatione, vel ex prauo aliquo habitu: nec ista quoq; ignoratio excusat, quia sic ignorans ex incogiincogitantia non facit quod potuit & debuit efficere. Ignoratio interdum est ex eo quod quispiam addiscere negligit, vel quod labore fugiat, vel quod studium & diligentiam nullam adhibeat. Vniuersalia quippe iura quisque scire debet: cum itaq; neq; iste faciat quod potest ac debet, non est excu-sandus. Est attamen in ijs actionibus aliquid non voluntarium: nam ignorantia hæc anteuertit actiones seu motum voluntatis, qui si adesset, notitia minimè sequeretur. Postrema ignorantia est ea, de qua sumus loquuti. excu-sat, consequitur veniam & misericordiam, quod ignorentur circumstan-tia, atq; post actionem sequatur dolor & molestia.
units.tr: If things done through imprudence are to be counted as unwilling, while these particular circumstances are unknown, it is further required that, once the error is recognised and exposed, the action be unpleasant and that the person grieve that what happened without his knowing it has happened. For if this distress does not follow, the action may indeed be called not voluntary, but it will not be unwilling. But here it is worth seeing how ignorance is said to cause unwillingness. It does so because it deprives us of knowledge which, had it been present, would have prevented what has now been done, or, had it been done, would have made the action voluntary. Either, then, ignorance deprives us of the knowledge on which the voluntary depends, or of the knowledge which, had it intervened, would have stopped the action from following. And it can happen that someone who acts through imprudence has ignorance joined with the action he performs, and yet does not dislike what he does but rather desires it. Hence grief does not follow afterwards, once the matter is known. Such a kind of ignorance neither excuses nor makes an action unwilling, as when someone thinks he is killing a stag and has killed his enemy, whom he had wished dead before, and now rejoices that he is dead, although at the time he did not know what he was doing. There is also a certain ignorance which some people seek deliberately: they choose and desire to be ignorant so that they may not be restrained from sinning or from pleasures by knowing. This ignorance is to be severely condemned, far from excusing. There is another ignorance, which occurs when someone who knows what is right and lawful, when it comes to acting, sets aside the thought of what is honourable and upright and considers rather what is useful or pleasant. This happens either from a violent disturbance of the mind or from some depraved habit, and this ignorance also does not excuse, because such a person, through thoughtlessness, does not do what he could and ought to do. Sometimes ignorance arises from neglecting to learn, or from shirking the effort, or from applying no care and diligence. For each person ought to know the universal laws; since, then, such a person does not do what he can and ought to do, he is not to be excused. Yet in these actions there is still something not voluntary, for this ignorance comes before the action, or the movement of the will, which, had it been present, knowledge would not have followed. The last kind of ignorance is that of which we have spoken: it excuses, and obtains pardon and pity, that the circumstances are unknown, and that grief and distress follow the action.

units.la: Cum itaque inuitum fit aut quod per uim agitur aut quod per ignorantiam, uoluntarium esse uidebitur, cuius initium est in ipso efficiente, qui etiam nouerit singula in quibus actio consistit.
units.tr: Since, then, what is done unwillingly is either what is done by force or what is done through ignorance, the voluntary will be seen to be that whose beginning lies in the agent himself, who also knows the particulars in which the action consists.

units.la: Hæc est huius Capitis postrema pars, in qua de uoluntario agit, eiusq; (ut apparet) definitio duplici constat membro. Primùm, inquit oportere principium intrinsecum esse. Deinde, ut notæ sint circumstantiæ. Nam si voluntarium opponitur inuito, & inuitum duo habet membra, contraria earum necesse est, ut in definitione voluntarij ponantur. Hinc videmus præclaram Aristotelis methodum, nisi prius naturam violenti & ignorantiæ tradidisset, non tam facile fuisset ei nunc voluntarium definire.
units.tr: This is the last part of this chapter, in which he treats of the voluntary, and its definition, as is evident, consists of two members. First, he says the principle must be intrinsic; then, that the circumstances must be known. For if the voluntary is opposed to the unwilling, and the unwilling has two members, the contraries of these must necessarily be placed in the definition of the voluntary. Hence we see Aristotle's admirable method: unless he had first set out the nature of the violent and of ignorance, it would not have been so easy for him now to define the voluntary.

units.la: Fortasis enim non recte dicitur inuita esse, quæ uel per iram uel per cupiditatem fiunt.
units.tr: Perhaps, indeed, it is not rightly said that those things are unwilling which are done either through anger or through desire.

units.la: Ad hæc scribenda ideo adducitur Aristoteles, quoniam illa quæ ab iratis fiunt aut à cupientibus, in definitione voluntarij comprehenduntur: nã & principium agendi est in eo homine qui agit, & singula sciunt ac probè norunt: uiuntur enim deliberationibus et iudicio acri ad ulciscendum, vel ad consequendũ optata: quod minimè fieret, si laboraret ignoratione circumstantiarum. Ergo, concluditur ea voluntaria esse, atq; illos errare qui putauerint huiusmodi esse inuita. Sed cur dicit, ἴσως: fortasse, cum ratio ista sit ἀπόδεξις[?]? Quia voluit modestè agere: nõ imminuit hac loquutione vim suæ rationis, sed potius morato sermone uti voluit. Et quia fortasis aduersarij noluissent omnino assentiri definitioni ἀνεσεως[?] iam allatæ. Quid autem moüerit illos ut putarint ista inuita esse, facile potest intelligi. Viderunt dif-ficile omnino esse, ijs duobus affectibus, ut qui cæteris sint violentiores, resistere, ideò putarunt homines ab illis cogi. Vnde aiebat Heraclitus, χαλεπὸν θυμῷ μάχεσθαι. Et Plato 2.de Repub. ἀμαχόντε[?] ἀνίκητον θυμὸς. Quod si aduersus eam pugnari non potest, nec potest expugnari, videtur cogere atq; actiones inuitas reddere. Idcirco idem Plato de Legibus 9.dixit, Hominem iratum ὅμοιον τῷ ἀκρασίῳ[?]. Non quidem ait prorsus inuitum, sed similem ipsius. Atq; Cato Censorius iratum dixit à furente homine tempore solum differre. Quin & alij, ut Euenus, ausi sunt dicere, iram multò deteriorem esse insania. De cupiditate autem Plato in Cratilo scribens, eam vinculo firmissimo comparauit. Quare nos quoq; minimè dubitamus, hos duos affectus vehementes esse ac magnam vim habere, attamen non ita esse validos, ut ratione non frenari possint: quod fieri videmus in hominibus temperatis, ac lenitate cæterisq; virtutibus præditis. Haud tamen inficiarer, magis voluntarias esse actiones, quæ absq; impulsu talium affectuū fiant: quod tamen non efficit ut ista ab earum censu excludantur.
units.tr: Aristotle is brought in to write these things for this reason: those things done by angry men or by men who desire are included in the definition of the voluntary, for the principle of acting lies in the man who acts, and they know and understand each particular, since they live by deliberation and keen judgement in order to take revenge or to obtain what they wish; which would hardly happen if they laboured under ignorance of the circumstances. Therefore it is concluded that such things are voluntary, and that those err who have thought them unwilling. But why does he say ἴσως [perhaps], since this reasoning is a demonstration? Because he wished to speak modestly; by this way of speaking he does not weaken the force of his argument, but preferred to use a restrained manner of speech. And because perhaps his opponents would not have agreed at all with the definition already given. What moved them to think these things unwilling can easily be understood. They saw that it is altogether difficult to resist those two passions, since they are more violent than the rest, and so they thought men were compelled by them. Hence Heraclitus said, χαλεπὸν θυμῷ μάχεσθαι [it is hard to fight against anger]. And Plato in the second book of the Republic: anger is an invincible and unconquerable thing. If it cannot be fought against, nor overcome, it seems to compel and to make actions unwilling. For this reason the same Plato, in the ninth book of the Laws, said that the angry man is ὅμοιον τῷ ἀκρασίῳ [like the incontinent man]. He did not say he was altogether unwilling, but that he was like one. And Cato the Censor said that the angry man differs from a raving man only in time. Others too, such as Evenus, have dared to say that anger is far worse than madness. Concerning desire, Plato, writing in the Cratylus, compared it to the strongest bond. Wherefore we too have no doubt that these two passions are vehement and have great force, yet they are not so strong that they cannot be restrained by reason; as we see happens in temperate men, and men endowed with gentleness and the other virtues. Nevertheless I would not deny that actions done without the impulse of such passions are more voluntary; yet this does not bring it about that the former are excluded from the class of the voluntary.

units.la: Primùm quidem nullum cæterorum animalium sponte quicquam aget, nec pueri quidem.
units.tr: First, no other animal will act of its own accord, and not even children.

units.la: Propositio confirmanda est. Quæ aguntur per vim aut cupiditatem, sunt voluntaria. Declaratum id prius fuit definitione: nunc aliæ rationes adduntur, quarum prima est:
units.tr: The proposition must be confirmed: things done through force or desire are voluntary. This was declared earlier in the definition; now other reasons are added, the first of which is:

units.la: Si essent inuita, neq; bruta neq; pueri sponte quicquam agerent.
units.tr: If they were unwilling, neither brutes nor children would do anything of their own accord.
But they do many things of their own accord.
Therefore those things are not unwilling.

units.la: Syllogismus Hypotheticus est, à consequente sublato ad euersionem antecedentis. Connexio probatur, Quoniam bruta & pueri cum ratione carent ex ijs affectibus agunt quæcunq; faciunt. Vt verò consequens absurdum sit, inde patet, quòd videmus hæc animantia & pueros quædam inuitè facere, ut cùm vincuntur aut concludúntur in aliquo loco: è diuerso autem cùm soluta fuerint & libera, sponte atq; ultrò permulta faciút. Deligút sibi cibos, ingrediuntur sua cubilia & latibula, cum volunt: inde etiam cùm visum fuerit, egrediuntur, pullos tuentur, ad nidos sese recipiunt, & infinita huiusmodi sponte sua & ultrò faciunt. Gaudent libertate, ac è diuerso quando ad aliqua coguntur, dolent, ac tristitiam non paruam capiunt. Equus Alexandri Bucephalus aliū sessorem nullū admittebat, quàm Alexandrū quod proculdubio non invitus faciebat. Elephanti suos magistros amant, illis ob-temperant, imò genu flectunt, cum iussi fuerint. Sed quid Elephantos opor-tet spectare? canes domestici blandiuntur dominis, allatrant alienos, venan-tur alacriter, sequuntur illos qui se alunt, atq; omnia hæc sponte citra controuersiam agunt. Multa possent de auibus, piscibus, cæterisq; brutis huc spe-ctantia commemorari, quæ tā admiranda sunt, atq; tanta propensione fiunt ab illis, vt multi quandoque arbitrati sint in brutis esse voluntate, qua eligant quæ magis placuerint, alia seponendo quæ displicent. Neq; defuerunt qui aliquid rationis eis fuerint impartiti, quòd magna industria viderint ab eis agi quæ faciunt, quæ nos ex Aristotelis doctrina minimè concederemus, cum tamen vt audimus affirmandum sit ea sponte agere. Quod si dixeris feras dici, quod impetu quodam ferantur, non negabimus: & tamen asserimus appetitu non carere intrinseco, quo moueantur: vnde actiones quæ ab illis oriuntur spontaneas dicere oportet. Non autem mirum est pueros coniunctos fuisse hoc loco cum brutis: nam & ipsi per ætatis infirmitatem ratione non vtuntur, sed tantum affectibus, præsertim ira & cupiditate, mouentur. Quis tamen illos negauerit sponte agere? Excurrunt, ludunt, saltant, iocantur, parentibus blandiuntur. Quin si sponte non agerent, magna illis iniuria fieret, cum a præceptoribus cædantur. Quid enim illi aliud quarūt, nisi ut ab iis abstineant, a quibus illos posse sibi reperare norunt? Quod vero attinet ad appetitum, sciendum illum esse duplicem. Vnus quippe comitatur sensum, alter autem rationem. Bruta & pueri eo mouentur appetitu, qui sequitur sensum, non tamen in vtrisq; idem est huiusmodi appetitus. Diuersitas inde oritur, quia bruta omnino sunt ratione destituta, ideò illorum appetitus nunquam rationi obtemperat. Pueri vero habent rationem, sed non actu, imò potentia: ideò cùm per ætatem ratio erupit in actum, illorum appetitus rationi poterit obtemperare. Consyderandum quoq; hoc loco est, τὸ ἑκούσιον[?] latius patere, quàm voluntarium: nam ad bruta extenditur et pueros, ad quos voluntarium proprie non pertinet, cum voluntate careant, si proprie loqui velimus.
units.tr: This is a hypothetical syllogism, which by denying the consequent overturns the antecedent. The connection is proved thus: since brutes and children lack reason, they act from those affections in whatever they do. That the consequent is absurd is clear from the fact that we see these animals and children do some things unwillingly, as when they are bound or shut up in some place; but on the other hand, when they have been loosed and set free, they do very many things of their own accord and readily. They choose their food for themselves, they go into their lairs and hiding-places when they wish, and likewise, when it seems good to them, they go out, they look after their young, they return to their nests, and they do countless things of this kind of their own accord and willingly. They rejoice in liberty, and on the other hand, when they are forced to something, they grieve and feel no small sadness. Alexander's horse, Bucephalus, would admit no other rider than Alexander, which he doubtless did not do unwillingly. Elephants love their keepers, obey them, and indeed bend the knee when ordered. But why should we look at elephants? Domestic dogs fawn on their masters, bark at strangers, hunt eagerly, follow those who feed them, and without any dispute they do all these things of their own accord. Many things concerning birds, fish and other brutes could be mentioned here, which are so wonderful and done with such inclination by them that many have sometimes thought that brutes have a will by which they choose what pleases them and set aside what displeases them. Nor have there been lacking those who have attributed some reason to them, because they have seen them do what they do with great skill; we, following the teaching of Aristotle, would by no means concede this, although, as we hear, they must be said to act of their own accord. But if you should say that they are called wild because they are carried along by a certain impulse, we will not deny it; yet we assert that they are not lacking an inner appetite by which they are moved, and therefore the actions that arise from them must be called spontaneous. Nor is it strange that children are joined here with brutes; for they too, by reason of their weakness of age, do not use reason, but are moved only by the affections, especially anger and desire. Yet who would deny that they act of their own accord? They run about, play, leap, joke, and fawn upon their parents. Indeed, if they did not act of their own accord, a great wrong would be done to them when they are beaten by their teachers. For what else do these seek, except that they abstain from those things which they know can be restrained for them? As for appetite, it must be known that it is twofold. One accompanies sense, the other reason. Brutes and children are moved by that appetite which follows sense, yet this appetite is not the same in both. The difference arises from this: brutes are altogether destitute of reason, and therefore their appetite never obeys reason. Children, however, have reason, but not in act, rather in potency; therefore when reason breaks forth into act with age, their appetite will be able to obey reason. It must also be considered in this place that the voluntary [τὸ ἑκούσιον] extends more widely than the voluntary in the strict sense; for it extends to brutes and children, to whom the voluntary properly does not pertain, since they lack will, if we wish to speak properly.

units.la: Deinde an sponte nihil agimus eorum quæ per cupiditatē vel iram facimus? an honesta quidē sponte, invitē autem turpia? an id ridiculum est, cūm idē fit principium.
units.tr: Next, do we act of our own accord in nothing that we do through desire or anger? Or are honourable things done of our own accord, but shameful things against our will? Is this not ridiculous, since the same thing is the principle of both?

units.la: Ratio hæc disiunctiui syllogismi est, cuius utraq; pars destruitur, & inde quod assumebatur cōcluditur fuisse falsum. Id quod assumitur, est, aduersa-rios dicere, quae aguntur per iram vel cupiditatem inuita esse: tum sequitur oportere vel omnia eiusmodi esse inuita, vel honesta spontanea, & turpia inuita. Atqui neutrum horum dari potest. Ergo falsum id est unde haec de-ducuntur. Primum non conatur offendere falsum, partim quod inferius declarabitur, et iam definitione ac prima ratione patefactum est: partim quia non fuerunt aduersarij eius sententia. Sed potius membrum posterius tuebātur. Ideo ⌣Aristoteles illud euertit, et ait, Nonne ridiculum est, cum non minus turpia facta per iram vel cupiditatem, habeant idem principium cum honestis quae ab ijsdem affectibus procedunt, haec velle statuere spontanea, illa vero coacta & inuita? Ea porro quae habent idem principium, eodem ordine censeri debent.
units.tr: This reasoning is of a disjunctive syllogism, each part of which is destroyed, and from this it is concluded that the assumption was false. What is assumed is that our opponents say that the things done through anger or desire are against the will; then it follows that either all such things must be against the will, or the honourable ones are spontaneous and the shameful ones against the will. But neither of these can be granted. Therefore that from which these things are deduced is false. He does not first try to show the falsehood partly because it will be declared lower down and has already been made plain by the definition and the first reason, and partly because they were not opponents of this opinion; rather they defended the latter part. Therefore Aristotle overturns it and says: Is it not ridiculous, when shameful deeds done through anger or desire have the same principle as honourable deeds that proceed from the same affections, to want to establish that the former are spontaneous and the latter forced and against the will? Moreover, things that have the same principle ought to be judged in the same way.

units.la: Absurdum est fortasis inuita dicere, quae oporte-at expetere. Oportet autem & quibusdam irasci: & aliqua cupere, nempe sanitatem & doctrinam.
units.tr: Perhaps it is absurd to call things involuntary that we ought to desire. Yet we ought also to be angry at some things, and to desire some things, namely health and learning.

units.la: Est hoc argumentum a natura expetẽdarum rerum deductum, quarum proprietas est ut sponte agantur. At, inquit, hoc a nobis exigitur honestatis & iustitia lege, ut aduersus aliquos irascamur, nempe in vitia & viros improbos, quos nisi priuati homines corriperent, & magistratus punirent, accusandi essent. Sunt etiam multa quae nefas est non cupere, ac summo studio sibi vindicare, ut sanitas & doctrina. Dicemus igitur legem honestatis et iustitiae requirere a nobis inuita & coacta, quaeq; non possimus facere, vel a quibus non queamus abstinere? Hoc absurdum esset de ciuilib. legibus.
units.tr: This argument is drawn from the nature of things to be desired, whose property is that they are done willingly. But, he says, the law of honesty and justice requires us to be angry against some people, namely vices and wicked men, who would have to be accused unless private persons rebuked them and magistrates punished them. There are also many things it is wrong not to desire and to pursue with the greatest zeal, such as health and learning. Shall we say, then, that the law of honesty and justice requires of us things that are involuntary and coerced, things that we cannot do or cannot refrain from? This would be absurd even of civil laws.

units.la: Videnturꝗ inuita molesta esse, quae vero ex cupiditate aguntur, suauia sunt.
units.tr: Involuntary things seem to be painful, whereas things done from desire are pleasant.

units.la: Ducitur haec ratio a consequentibus. Quacunq; sunt inuita, molestiam doloremq; secum habent coniunctum. At quae per iram & cupiditatem fiunt, iucunda sunt: tantum abest, ut molestiam ac tristitiam secum afferant. De cupiditate hoc minime dubium erat: ideo Aristoteles hoc membrum expressè posuit. De ira vero quia dubium esse potuit, nihil dixit. Verum quod modo tacet, in Rhetoricis diserte verbis expressit, & dum tractaret illa quae voluptatem pariunt, & dum affectum irae describit, adducit q; Homeri carmen, qui scribit iram fuisse Achilli quasi mel quod sub lingua eius liquescebat. Neq; vero aliud est ira quam cupiditas ulciscendi.
units.tr: This reasoning is drawn from consequences. Whatever is involuntary carries pain and sorrow along with it. But things done through anger and desire are pleasant; so far are they from bringing pain and sadness with them. About desire there was no doubt at all, so Aristotle stated this clause expressly. About anger, since there could be doubt, he said nothing. But what he now passes over in silence he expressed plainly in the Rhetoric, both when treating of things that produce pleasure and when describing the emotion of anger, and there he cites the verse of Homer, who writes that anger was to Achilles like honey that melted under his tongue. Nor is anger anything other than the desire for revenge.

units.la: Ad hæc quid interest invita esse illa quæ secundum rationem, vel juxta iram perperam comissa fuerint? Evitabilia enim ambo sunt.
units.tr: Besides, what difference does it make whether things done in accordance with reason, or wrongly done through anger, are involuntary? For both are avoidable.

units.la: Videtur ista ratio constare peccati natura. Cum enim peccatum sit in iis quæ debent & possunt evitari, atq; ista conditio tam reperiatur in iis quæ male committuntur à ratione, quàm in iis quæ perperam ab ira cum cupiditate geruntur, utraq; dici debent voluntaria. Cur itaq; magis ista, quàm illa ponuntur ab adversariis esse invita?
units.tr: This reasoning seems to rest on the nature of sin. For since sin lies in those things which ought and can be avoided, and this condition is found as much in things wrongly done by reason as in things wrongly done through anger and desire, both ought to be called voluntary. Why, then, do the opponents posit the latter rather than the former as involuntary?

units.la: Videntur[?] quoque non minus esse humani irrationales affectus: & actiones hominis esse videntur, quæ ab ira vel cupiditate proficiscuntur. Absurdum igitur est hæc invita statuere.
units.tr: Moreover, the irrational affections seem to be no less human, and the actions of a man that proceed from anger or desire seem to be human. It is absurd, therefore, to posit these as involuntary.

units.la: Ratio est huiusmodi. Quia humanæ sunt affectiones irrationabiles quas habemus, humanæq; sunt actiones quæ ab ira vel cupiditate nascuntur, sunt etiam voluntariæ atq; spontaneæ. Quod enim humanum est, est voluntarium. Nemo autem dixerit cupiditates & iras non esse in animis hominum affectiones, quemadmodum ratio in illis eisdem est: unde si actiones humanæ sunt, quæ à ratione eliciuntur, quia ratio pars est animi nostri, sic illæ humanæ fuerint quæ ab ira vel cupiditate deriuantur. Nam vis irascës[?] & cupiens in animis hominum sunt. Potest fieri ut per occupationem tali occurratur objectione. Actiones quæ ab ira & cupiditate sunt, à parte irrationali proficiscuntur. Verum est, inquit. Sed tamen ista vires humani animi sunt. Ergo actus inde prodeuntes humani erunt. Et ista facultates, etsi per essentiam rationem non habent, illius tamen sunt participes & ab ea regi possunt: quod non accidit in brutis. Deinde spontanea sunt principia istæ affectiones & actiones quia possunt à voluntate coerceri. Neq; de illis est, ut de vi nutriente atq; alente quæ vel nobis nolentibus agit. Ideo concluditur absurdum esse statuere hæc invita seu coacta.
units.tr: The reasoning is of this kind. Because the irrational affections we have are human, and the actions that arise from anger or desire are human, they are also voluntary and spontaneous. For what is human is voluntary. No one would deny that desires and angers are affections in the minds of men, just as reason is in those same minds. Therefore, if the actions elicited by reason are human, because reason is a part of our mind, then those that derive from anger or desire are human too. For the irascible and the concupiscible powers are in the minds of men. Someone may anticipate this with an objection: actions that come from anger and desire proceed from the irrational part. True, he says. But nevertheless these are powers of the human mind, and therefore the acts issuing from them will be human. And these faculties, although in essence they do not possess reason, nevertheless share in it and can be governed by it, which does not happen in brutes. Further, these affections and actions are spontaneous principles because they can be restrained by the will. It is not so with them as with the nutritive and growth-producing power, which acts even against our will. Hence it is concluded that it is absurd to hold these to be involuntary or coerced.

units.la: ista cum sacris literis faciant, modo tractandum est. De voluntario & non voluntario agendum esse dixit Aristoteles, quòd laudationes & vituperia comitetur voluntaria, præmia, pœnæ ac misericordia. Ita in Psal. iii. laudantur fideles, quòd sint spontanei populus. Eunuchi etiam laudantur non facti vi, aut sic nati, sed qui se sponte castrauerint ob regnum cœ-lorum. Remittitur pœna cæsori lignorum, qui casu socium occidit: quoniam actio illa non fuit voluntaria. Diabolus cogitur verum dicere, cogitur disce-dere ab obsessis: non tamen ullam meretur laudem aut præmia. Balaam ab angelo cogitur gladio, ne populum Dei execretur: nulla est eius laus, quia non sponte fecit. Definitio violenti, ut principium sit extrinsecum, ita ut a-gens vel patiens non præstet adiumentum, declarat originis peccatum non esse rem violentam, quoniam intrinsecum nobis est vitium, et illud iuvamus prauitate illa quam quotidie addimus. Quod si dixerit quispiam, deesse scien-tiam seu notitiam quando contrahitur, idemq; causetur de primis moti-bus animi nostri prauis, in quibus nulla datur electio aut deliberatio. Respo-debimus, quæ Aristoteles ait de moralibus & actualibus actionibus esse in-telligenda: ista vero ille peccata minimè novit. Sed hoc nobis est satis, nō pos-se talia violeta dici, cum principium intrinsecum habeant. Mixtas quoq; a-ctiones concedimus, & statuimus eas accenseri debere voluntariis: ideo ad eas nos divinæ literæ hortantur, suadentes ut quiduis patiamur ne incurra-mus in peccata. Paulus inquit, nunquam facienda mala ut bona eveniant. Deo magis parendum est quàm hominibus. Vocamurq; ut nostram crucem accipiamus & Dominum sequamur. Et ille dicitur animam suam invenis-se, qui eam perdiderit. Neq; alio spectat suiipsius abnegatio. Mixtæ sunt hæ actiones, quia nemo extra casum hæc eligeret: sed ista volumus & facimus, partim ut evitemus peccata, partim ut Domino iungamur. At dixeris, hæc principium habent externum. Ergo potius violenta sunt. Nisi enim Deus in nobis ageret hæc, nullus nostrum faceret. Fatemur principium quo nostræ voluntates mutantur extrinsecum esse. At nostræ voluntates immutatæ à spiritu Dei nobis intrinsecæ sunt, & illarum iussu ad istas actiones movemur: ideo voluntariæ dici debent, non enim à Deo sine nobis fiunt. Imò lauda-mur & vituperamur ob istas mixtas actiones: nam Christus inquit se nega-turum coram patre illos, qui se coram hominibus negauerint. Nec, inquit, erubescam illum, qui de me non erubuerit coram hominibus. Et illi utiq; co-mendantur, qui Christi causa vexationes grauissimas patiuntur. Beati, qui persecutionem, inquit, patiuntur: nam illorum est regnum cœlorum. In quibusdam huiusmodi, ait Aristoteles, venia datur. Ut cum Dauid ne tru-cidetur, insanum se fingit coram rege Achis. Sed quædam sunt ad quæ commit-tenda nunquam adduci debemus. Quæ nam sunt ista? Peccata, Et dici solet usq; adeo. Iobus exemplo nobis est, ut execraretur Deum, nunquam ad-versis casibus, neq; uxoris petulantia & insultatione impelli potuit. Quid ad hæc impelluntur, tantum abest ut misericordiam inveniant, ut potius à spe illius excidant. Ut ad Hebræos de illis dicitur, qui ab agnita veritate resiluerunt. Ita contigit Spiera Italo, & iis qui se, cum Evangelium abiurassent, interemerunt. Duo difficilia proponit Aristoteles. Unum est, Quid nã pro quo sit patiendum: nos expedimur facile. Patienda sunt quævis, ne à Christo divinisq; mandatis recedamus. Quid prodest homini, si universum mundum lucretur, animi vero sui detrimentum patiatur. Nolite timere eos qui occidunt corpus, animam autem non possunt occidere, ait Dominus. Difficultatem alteram in nobis ipsis experimur, multosq; videmus temporari-os, qui solum ad tempus credunt. Et spiritus promptus est, caro autem infirma. Sed vicissim consolamur nosipsos, quia omnia possibilia sunt credenti. Et Paulus aiebat, se omnia in Christo posse, à quo confirmabatur. Iuste adhæc reprehendit Aristoteles illos qui honesta iustaq; censebant voluntaria, turpia vero statuebant non voluntaria. Secus omnino sentiendum est. Paulus dicebat, Scio quòd non habitet in me, id est, in carne mea, bonum. Imò si quid boni habemus, id totum Deo est transcribendum. Nam ad Philipp. habetur, Deum esse qui operetur in nobis & velle & perficere. Nunc de ignoratione videamus. Quædam est ad quam pœnitentia statim sequitur errore deprehenso, nonnunquam pœnitentia nulla sequitur. De posteriori membro Dominus ait, Ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid agant. Idem orauit Stephanus. Inter eos tamen pro quibus orabatur, aliquos pœnituit aliquādo, aliquos nunquam. Ionathas quoque mel gustauit, ignarus quid pater sanxisset, & cognito patris decreto, non doluit, sed potius illi succensuit. At Paulus detecto errore doluit. Dolucrunt & illi de quibus Petrus in Actis dixit, Scio quod per ignorantiam fecistis. Quod autem doluerint, ea declarant, quæ dixerunt, Viri fratres, quid oportet nos facere? Dolor qui sequitur, non semper indicat nullum peccatum interuenisse. Nam & qui Dominum crucifixerunt peccarunt, & Paulus peccauit: nam ignoraruntisti, quod scire debuerant. Sed si quædam ignoratio interuenisset circumstantiæ, quæ non potuissent nosci, ut in Noah cum est inebriatus, vinum antea non viderat, illius vim & proprietatem minimè nouerat. Ut q; Iacobo accidit, quando Lea loco Rachelis est commixtus. Nam uterque illorum ignorauit quid ageret, & sunt excusati. At legum universalia & summa capita qui nescit, non excusatur. Idcirco dictum est à Paulo in Epistola ad Corinth. priori, Qui ignorat, ignoret. Atque ista ignoratio quæ non excusat, interdum à Deo infligitur ut pœna, dum punit peccata peccatis. Ad Thessalonicenses posteriori scribitur, quia charitatem veritatis non receperunt, ut salui fierent, ideò immitimmittet Deus in illos efficaciam erroris. Et in Ezechiele: Si propheta seductus fuerit, ego seduxi eum. Rex quoque Achab est seductus à malo spiritu Deo volente. Habemus ergo quae ignoratio excusat & quae non excusat. Addit Aristoteles, quae fiunt per ebrietatem & iram, esse voluntaria, quod etiam nos affirmamus, quandoquidem accepimus de iis legem, Irascimini & nolite peccare. Sol non occidat super iracundia vestra, & prohibemus dicere alicui Fatue. Quo vero ad ebrietatem, dicitur à Domino, Cauete ne grauentur corpora vestra crapula vel ebrietate, Paulus quoque, Nolite inebriari vino in quo est luxuria. Quae itaque per iram vel ebrietatem fiunt, non excusant, cum ista vel non admitti vel frenari potuerint. Omnes vero prauos & impios ignorantes esse, licet non excusentur, scripturae ubique clamant: Dixit insipiens in corde suo, Non est Deus. Prouerbiorum septimo de illis qui trahuntur cupiditate ac voluptatibus habetur: Ut bos ducitur ad victimam, ut stultus in compedibus ad castigationem. Ad Romanos, dicentes se esse sapientes stulti facti sunt, et infatuatum est insipiens cor eorum. Ad Ephes. Non ambuletis ut caeterae gentes in vanitate mentis suae, alienati à vita Dei, propter ignorantiam quae est in ipsis, & obcaecationem cordis eorum. Imo ( ut inquit Isaias & omnes Euangelistae testantur ) Videntes non vident, & audientes non audiunt: quum sint in tenebris, nesciunt quo vadant. Inter circumstantias autem quae ignorate excusant, praesertim recensef finem & circa quid. Idque utique verum est. Dauid Absolomum dimisit ut iret in Hebronem, sed quo fine quoue consilio ille id ageret, scire non potuit: excusatur. Abimelech etiam uxorem alienam habuit, sed cum qua versaretur ignorabat: ideo dicere potuit Deo se fecisse quod egerat in simplicitate sui cordis: atque illi est ignotum. Quod etiam baptizatus fuerit Simon Magus, excusatur Ecclesia, quia consilium eius malum & fraudulentum ignoravit. Sed tamen in iis ignorationibus quae nos excusant, si non sequatur dolor, sumus rei: nam probamus quod actum est. Is qui sagittam emisit & casu interemit Achabum regem si resciuisset factum, non doluisset: neque invitè ob id ostenderetur fecisse quod actu est. Ac de morte Absolomi sequuta Dauid doluit, de morte item Abner & Amase: unde apparuit eo nolente atque invito eiusmodi evenisse. Voluntarium duo comprehendit, & ut principium sit intrinsecum, & non interveniat ignoratio eius quod agitur., Peccatum originis principium habet intrinsecum, & scimus talem corruptionem legi Dei & rectitudini adversari, quamuis ex nostra electione ipsum non accersamus: ideo voluntarium est. In paruulis tamen est ubi notitia deest. Sed hoc non refert:: fert:quoniam de actualibus hic agitur. Neq; Aristoteles aut moralis facultas ad id genus peccati potest pertingere. Voluntaria esse praeterea, quae per cupiditatem fiunt & iram, certis rationib. est demonstratum. Quod nos admittimus, quoniam de utroq; vitio leges accepimus. Non concupisces. Et no iubemur irasci fratri absq; causa. Accipit Aristoteles in suis argumentis, bruta sponte agere. Dixit quoq; Isaias, Cognouit bos possessorem suum, & asinus praesepe Domini sui. Ieremias q; ciconiam dixit tempus visitationis suae nosse, cap.8. Et de pueris idem sentimus. Nam Elizaei tempore puniti sunt per vrsos. Isaac quoq; dum ab Ismaele vexaretur, à Sara iubetur eiici. Sumit etiam requiri ac quadoq; à nobis exigi vt irascamur. Zelus domus tuae comedit me. Atq; Pinhas est à Deo commendatus, quòd sit vltus scortatores impurissimos. Deinde ponit: Quae fiunt ab inuitis, habere dolorem coniunctum. Paulus ad Romanos idem testatur: Infelix ego, idcirco quis me liberabit de corpore mortis huius? Cùm vero inquit, Et illa, quae committuntur per iram & cupiditatem, euitabilia esse, & illa quae per rationem seu voluntatem: id corrigimus, euitari quidem posse, adiecta Dei gratia: nam sine illa quis motus irae atq; cupiditatis cauebit? Possumus quidem ab externis actionibus temperare nobis, sed istos cordis motus in potestate nostra non habemus. Assentimur praeterea humanas actiones esse quae à cupiditate atque ira proficiscuntur: nam & de illis quoq; sumus rationem reddituri.
units.tr: Since these matters bear on the sacred letters, they must be treated here. Aristotle said that we must discuss the voluntary and the involuntary, because praise and blame, rewards, punishments and pity accompany voluntary acts. Thus in Psalm 110 the faithful are praised because they are a willing people. Eunuchs too are praised, not those made so by force or born so, but those who have castrated themselves willingly for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. The wood-cutter who killed his companion by accident is pardoned his punishment, since that act was not voluntary. The devil is compelled to speak the truth and compelled to depart from the possessed, yet he deserves no praise or reward for it. Balaam is compelled by the angel with a sword not to curse the people of God; there is no praise due to him, because he did not act willingly. The definition of the violent, that its principle is external, so that the agent or patient contributes no help, shows that original sin is not a violent thing, since the fault is within us, and we aid it by the wickedness we add daily. If someone should say that knowledge or awareness is lacking when it is contracted, and that the same can be said of the first evil motions of our minds, in which there is no choice or deliberation, we reply that what Aristotle says must be understood of moral and actual acts; he did not know such sins at all. For us it is enough that such things cannot be called violent, since they have an internal principle. We also concede mixed acts, and hold that they ought to be counted among voluntary ones; for this reason the divine letters urge us to them, persuading us to suffer anything rather than fall into sin. Paul says that evil must never be done that good may come of it. We must obey God rather than men. We are called to take up our cross and follow the Lord. And he is said to have found his soul who has lost it. Self-denial aims at nothing else. These acts are mixed, because no one would choose them apart from some compulsion; yet we will and do them partly so that we may avoid sin, and partly so that we may be joined to the Lord. But you will say that these have an external principle, and therefore are rather violent. Yet unless God worked these things in us, none of us would do them. We grant that the principle by which our wills are changed is external. But our wills, once changed by the Spirit of God, are internal to us, and at their command we are moved to these acts; therefore they ought to be called voluntary, for they are not done by God without us. Indeed we are praised and blamed for these mixed acts, for Christ says that he will deny before the Father those who have denied him before men, and: I will not be ashamed of him who has not been ashamed of me before men. And assuredly those are commended who suffer the gravest afflictions for Christ's sake: Blessed are they who suffer persecution, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Aristotle says that pardon is granted in certain acts of this kind, as when David, that he might not be slain, feigned madness before king Achish. But there are some things to which we must never be brought to consent. What are these? Sins. And it is commonly said: so far. Job is an example for us, that he cursed God; he could never be driven to it by adverse circumstances, nor by the wantonness and taunting of his wife. Those who are driven to such things are so far from finding mercy that they rather fall from the hope of it, as is said in Hebrews of those who fell back from the truth once known. So it happened to Spira the Italian, and to those who, having abjured the Gospel, killed themselves. Aristotle proposes two difficult matters. The first is what ought to be endured for the sake of what: we find this easy to settle. Everything must be endured rather than depart from Christ and the divine commands. What does it profit a man if he gain the whole world and suffer the loss of his soul? Fear not those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul, says the Lord. We experience the second difficulty in ourselves, and we see many who are temporary believers, who believe only for a time. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak. Yet in turn we comfort ourselves, because all things are possible to the believer. And Paul said that he could do all things in Christ, by whom he was strengthened. Aristotle rightly rebukes those who held honourable and just deeds to be voluntary, but shameful ones to be involuntary. We must think quite otherwise. Paul said: I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, there dwells no good. Indeed, if we have any good in us, the whole of it must be ascribed to God; for in Philippians it is written that God is the one who works in us both to will and to perform. Now let us consider ignorance. There is a kind of ignorance after which repentance follows at once when the error is detected; sometimes no repentance follows. Of the latter kind the Lord says: Forgive them, for they know not what they do. Stephen prayed the same. Yet among those for whom prayer was made, some repented at some time, and some never did. Jonathan too tasted honey, ignorant of what his father had decreed; and when the father's decree was known, he did not grieve but rather was angry with his father. But Paul, once the error was detected, grieved. Those of whom Peter spoke in the Acts also grieved, when he said: I know that you did it through ignorance. That they grieved is shown by what they said: Men, brethren, what ought we to do? Grief which follows does not always show that no sin has intervened. For both those who crucified the Lord sinned, and Paul sinned; for they were ignorant of what they ought to have known. But if an ignorance had intervened of circumstances which could not have been known, as in Noah when he became drunk, having not yet seen wine and not having known its power and nature at all; or as happened to Jacob when he was joined with Leah instead of Rachel: for each of them was ignorant of what he was doing, and they are excused. But one who does not know the universal laws and chief principles is not excused. Therefore Paul said in his first Epistle to the Corinthians: Let him who is ignorant remain ignorant. And that ignorance which does not excuse is sometimes inflicted by God as a punishment, when he punishes sins with sins. It is written in the second Epistle to the Thessalonians that, because they did not receive the love of the truth that they might be saved, God will therefore send upon them the efficacy of error. And in Ezekiel: If the prophet be deceived, I have deceived him. King Ahab too was deceived by an evil spirit, God willing it. We have therefore an ignorance which excuses and one which does not. Aristotle adds that what is done through drunkenness and anger is voluntary; we too affirm this, since we have received a law concerning them: Be angry and sin not; let not the sun go down upon your wrath; and we are forbidden to say to anyone, Fool. As for drunkenness, the Lord says: Take heed that your bodies are not weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness; Paul also: Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess. Therefore what is done through anger or drunkenness does not excuse, since such things could either not have been admitted or could have been restrained. Yet the Scriptures everywhere cry out that all wicked and impious men are ignorant, though they are not excused: The fool has said in his heart, There is no God. In the seventh chapter of Proverbs it is written of those who are drawn by lust and pleasures: as an ox is led to the slaughter, as a fool in fetters to the discipline. In Romans: professing themselves wise, they became fools, and their foolish heart was darkened. In Ephesians: Walk not as the other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, alienated from the life of God, because of the ignorance that is in them and the blindness of their heart. Indeed, as Isaiah says and all the Evangelists attest: Seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not, since they are in darkness, they know not whither they go. Among the circumstances which excuse ignorance, he especially mentions the end and the object of the act. And this is certainly true. David sent Absalom away to go to Hebron, but what end or what purpose he had in doing so, David could not know; he is excused. Abimelech also had another man's wife, but he did not know with whom he was living; therefore he could say to God that he had done this in the simplicity of his heart, and that was unknown to him. Likewise the Church is excused for baptizing Simon Magus, because it did not know his wicked and deceitful purpose. But in those ignorances which excuse us, if grief does not follow, we are guilty; for we approve what was done. The man who loosed an arrow and by chance killed king Ahab, if he had learned what he had done, would not have grieved; nor would he be shown to have done unwillingly what he did in fact. And David grieved over the death of Absalom which followed, and likewise over the deaths of Abner and Amasa; whence it appeared that such things happened against his will and unwillingly. The voluntary comprehends two things: that the principle be internal, and that no ignorance of what is done intervene. Original sin has an internal principle, and we know that such corruption is contrary to the law of God and to rectitude, although we do not summon it by our own choice; therefore it is voluntary. In infants, however, there is no knowledge, but this does not matter, since here we are dealing with actual sins. Nor can Aristotle or moral philosophy reach this kind of sin. Moreover, it has been demonstrated by sound reasons that those things done through lust and anger are voluntary. We admit this, since we have received laws concerning both vices: Thou shalt not covet; and we are not commanded to be angry with a brother without cause. Aristotle, in his arguments, takes it that brute beasts act willingly. Isaiah also said: The ox knows his owner, and the ass the crib of his master. Jeremiah said that the stork knows the time of its visitation, in chapter 8. We think the same of children; for in the time of Elisha they were punished by bears. Isaac too, when he was harassed by Ishmael, is commanded by Sarah to be cast out. Zeal is sometimes required, and sometimes demanded of us, that we be angry: The zeal of your house has eaten me up. And Phinehas was commended by God because he avenged the most impure fornicators. Next Aristotle lays down: what is done by unwilling men has grief joined with it. Paul testifies the same in Romans: Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death? When he says that those things which are committed through anger and lust are avoidable, and likewise those which are done through reason or will, we correct this: they can indeed be avoided, but with the grace of God added; for without it who will guard against the motions of anger and lust? We can indeed refrain from external actions, but we do not have these motions of the heart in our power. We further agree that human actions are those which proceed from lust and anger; for we shall also have to give an account of these.
CHAPTER II

units.la: CUM definierimus spontaneũ & invitum, proximũ est ut de electione tractemus. Etenim virtuti maxime propria esse videtur, & magis iudicat mores quàm actiones. Videtur autem electio esse spontaneum, non tamen idem cum eo est:nam spontaneum latius patet. Pueri quippe aliaq; animātia[?] spontanei participia sunt, non autem electionis.
units.tr: Having defined the voluntary and the involuntary, the next task is to treat of choice. Choice seems especially proper to virtue, and it judges character more than actions do. Choice seems to be the same as the voluntary, but it is not the same thing, for the voluntary extends more widely. Children and other animals are voluntary participants, but they do not take part in choice.

units.la: IN tres deducitur partes istud caput. Proponit primo de quo sit agendum. Deinde ipsius electionem definitionem inquirit. Postremò illam conclusam & absolutam ostendit. Est electio virtuti cognata, quoniā in illius definitione coprehenditur. Fusius patet spontaneũ quā electio. Cum de illa modo tractandũ sit ratione probat:
units.tr: This chapter falls into three parts. First it sets out what is to be discussed. Second it inquires into the definition of choice itself. Last it shows that choice is complete and perfect. Choice is akin to virtue, since it is included in the definition of virtue. More fully, the voluntary extends more widely than choice. Since choice is now to be treated, he proves it by reason:

units.la: De omnibus est agendum quae ad virtutem spectant.
units.tr: Everything that pertains to virtue must be treated.
Choice is especially proper to virtue.
Therefore it is right to treat of choice.

units.la: Alterum argumentum à minori ad maius deducitur. Si de actionibus humanis oportuit tractare: de electione multò magis agendum erit. Et probatur connexio, quòd magis indicantur mores electione quàm actionibus. An notandum quatuor in definitione virtutis esse comprehensa, nimirum Habitum, mediocritatem, spontaneum, & electionem. Hactenus est de omnibus tractatum, præterquam de ipsa electione. At cur prius de mediocritate scripsit, quàm de illa et de spontaneo? Quoniam mediocritas ipsam attingit substantiam virtutis. Est enim virtus habitus mediocris inter duos vitiosos habitus. Neque tantum ipse habitus est mediocris, sed mediocritatem in actionibus & affectionibus captat. Et quia oportuit ante omnia constitui obiectum, in quod ferretur et inclinaret habitus, ideò post habitus tractationem statim de mediocritate cœpit agere. Dicit electionem maximè propriam virtuti. Nam in definitione primò genus positum est, nimirum habitus. Differentia est adiecta, mediocritatis. Postea coniuncta fuerunt duo propria, nimirum quòd per virtutem sponte agamus, postea quòd ex electione. Verum ex iis duobus propriis electio magis est propria: neq; tantum si conferatur cum spontaneo, verum etiam collata aliis virtutis proprietatibus quæ sanè multæ sunt. Et eo nomine actiones ex virtute laudantur, quòd ex electione fiant. Mores, inquit, judicantur magis electione quàm actionibus. Verum quidem est, mores ex actionibus cognosci, ut arbos ex fructu. Et tamen fallax est illud iudicium. Nam hypocritæ sæpissimè fucum faciunt, & animo interdum agitur, quod videmus, longè alio quàm conueniat. Manichæi ab uxoribus abstinebant, item à carnium esu, non quasi essent castitatis aut sobrietatis cupidi, sed propter illorum erroneas & blasphemas opiniones. Tyranni aliquando leniter agunt cum ciuibus, at ut eos decipiant. Atq; homines facinorosi abstinent à sceleribus nonnunquam, timore pœnarum, non amore iustitiæ. Oderunt peccare mali formidinine pœnæ. Vnde in iudiciis, quando constat de facto, sæpè de voluntate, animo atq; consilio facientis quæritur. Neq; fortuna unquam exponitur electio quemadmodum actio. Imò qui deprehenduntur in aliquo crimine, frequenter ad[?] cere cõsueruerunt, se aliud voluisse facere, nec animo fecisse ut talia succederent. Et facile concedimus actiones euidentiores esse, cum aliorum oculis subjiciuntur: nō faciūt attamē iudiciū firmius ac certius. De morib. iudicatur à posteriori per opera, sed ex electione iudicium est à causa et (ut loquuntur) à priori. Et quādoq; fit vt quispiā nihil agat. Vnde non potest ex actionib. aut bonus aut malus iudicari, sed statim vt profert suam electionem, licet nihil egerit de eo fertur, vel quo ad malitiam, vel quo ad probitatem, iudicium. Sed quo nam pacto dicitur pueros electione carere, nec non & bruta, cum præferant cibos cibis, lusum disciplinæ, ac præ aliis alia vitent? Dicendum, ele-ctionem duplicem esse, quandam communem, qua una res anteponitur alteri, aut præ altera vitatur. Et hoc electionis genere neq; bruta neque pueri carent. Altera propria est electio, quæ habet consilium præcedens, & iudi-cio rationis dirigitur. Atq; hoc genus electionis neque bruta neq; pueri pos-sunt habere. Nam cum persequuntur aliquid præ alio, vel unum magis su-giunt quàm aliud vitent, non ratione sed sensu ducuntur. Illa etiam quæ repente ac subito facimus, carent electione: non quòd ratione careamus, sed quia illa committimus, sed quia spacium ad deliberandum non ponimus. Impeditur consilium iudiciumq; & deliberatio rationis vehementia perturba-tionis. Vnde tria numerantur quæ destituuntur electione. Primò bruta, quòd non sint rationis capacia. Secundò pueri, qui etsi ratione prædití sint, illa tamen per ætatem uti non possunt. Tertio sunt loco, animi subiti ac repentini motus: in quibus licet homines ratione polleant & ætatem habeant, spacio tamen deliberandi carent. Vnde solent qui alicuius impetu affectus quippiam agunt, dicere, se id ex proposito seu consilio non egisse.
units.tr: The second argument is drawn from the less to the greater: if it was right to treat of human actions, much more must choice be treated. The connection is proved because character is judged more by choice than by actions. Note that four things are included in the definition of virtue: habit, the mean, the voluntary, and choice. Up to now everything has been treated except choice itself. But why did he write about the mean before the voluntary and choice? Because the mean touches the very substance of virtue. For virtue is a habit lying in the mean between two vicious habits, and the habit is not only itself a mean, but it grasps the mean in actions and affections. And since it was necessary first to fix the object toward which the habit is carried and inclined, he began at once to treat of the mean after the treatment of habit. He says that choice is especially proper to virtue. In the definition, the genus is placed first, namely habit; the difference is added, namely the mean. Afterwards two properties are joined: that we act willingly through virtue, and that we act from choice. But of these two properties choice is the more proper, and not only when compared with the voluntary, but also when compared with the other properties of virtue, which are certainly many. For this reason actions are praised as virtuous because they come from choice. Character, he says, is judged more by choice than by actions. It is true that character is known from actions, as a tree is known from its fruit. Yet that judgment is deceptive. Hypocrites very often put on a false show, and sometimes the mind is driven in a direction far different from what we see. The Manichaeans abstained from wives and likewise from eating meat, not because they were eager for chastity or sobriety, but because of their erroneous and blasphemous opinions. Tyrants sometimes treat citizens gently, but in order to deceive them. Wicked men sometimes refrain from crimes out of fear of punishment, not out of love of justice. The bad hate to sin from dread of punishment. Hence in trials, when the deed is established, the will, intention and purpose of the doer are often inquired into. Choice is never exposed to chance in the way action is. Indeed, those who are caught in some crime often are accustomed to assert that they had wished to do something else, and that they did not act with the intention that such things should follow. And we readily grant that actions are more evident when they are set before the eyes of others: yet they do not make the judgment firmer or more certain. Character is judged a posteriori, through works; but judgment from choice is from the cause and, as they say, a priori. And sometimes it happens that a person does nothing. Hence one cannot be judged good or bad from actions; but as soon as he declares his choice, even though he has done nothing, judgment is passed on him, either as to wickedness or as to uprightness. But how is it said that children lack choice, and brute animals too, since they prefer one food to another, play to discipline, and avoid one thing rather than another? It must be said that choice is twofold: one kind is common, by which one thing is put before another or avoided in comparison with another, and neither brutes nor children lack this kind of choice. The other kind is choice properly so called, which has a prior counsel and is directed by the judgment of reason, and neither brutes nor children can have this kind. For when they pursue one thing before another, or flee one thing more than another, they are led by sense, not by reason. Those things also which we do suddenly and at once lack choice: not because we lack reason, but because we do not allow room for deliberation. Counsel, judgment and the deliberation of reason are impeded by the vehemence of passion. Hence three things are counted that lack choice. First, brutes, because they are not capable of reason. Second, children, who, although endowed with reason, cannot use it because of their age. Third, the sudden and abrupt movements of the mind, in which, although men have reason and are of age, they lack room for deliberation. Hence those who act under the impulse of some passion are accustomed to say that they did not do it by plan or counsel.

units.la: Qui autem dicunt illam esse cupiditatem, irā, aut voluntatem, aut opinionem, recte dicere non videntur: non enim electio communis est brutis, ut cupiditas & ira.
units.tr: But those who say that it is desire, anger, will, or opinion do not seem to speak correctly, for choice is not common to brute animals as desire and anger are.

units.la: Definitionem electionis inuestigat solito more, confutando prius aliorum falsas opiniones. Illas itaq; recenset, & quatuor ostendit fuisse. Possumus autem illa quatuor ista methodo digerere. Cum ad animum pertineat electio, aut est facultatis cognoscentis aut appetentis. Appetitus omnis est tripartitus: Aut est nobilioris partis animi, & cum ratione coniungitur, dicitur voluntas: Aut partis crassioris, iumq; diducitur in vim cupientem & irascentem. Hinc dixit Aristoteles, quosdam putasse electionem esse voluntatem, alios iram, alios cupiditatem. At si pertineat ad notitiam, occurrunt illi qui affirmarunt electionem esse opinionem: qui fortasse Stoici fuerunt. De cupiditate atq; ira primùm agit, & ratiocinatur id ineptè dici. Quia tñ oporteret electione concedere brutis, cùm ipsa & cupiditate & ira ducantur: quod ut absurdum & indignum reiicit.
units.tr: He investigates the definition of choice in his usual manner, first refuting the false opinions of others. He recounts them and shows that there were four, and we can arrange those four by this method. Since choice pertains to the soul, it belongs either to the faculty of knowing or to the faculty of desiring. All appetite is threefold: it either belongs to the nobler part of the soul and is joined with reason, and is called will; or it belongs to the grosser part and is divided into the desiring power and the irascible power.
