Hence Aristotle said that some thought choice was will, others anger, others desire. But if it pertains to knowledge, there come to mind those who affirmed that choice is opinion, who were perhaps the Stoics. He first treats of desire and anger and reasons that it is wrongly said. Yet one would have to grant choice to brute animals, since both are led by desire and anger, and he rejects this as absurd and unworthy.

units.la: Et incontinens ex cupiditate agit, non autem ex electione: continens uero è diuerso non ex electione agit.
units.tr: And the incontinent man acts from desire, not from choice; the continent man, on the contrary, does not act from choice.

units.la: Liquidò iam apparet Aristotelem mouere cupiditatem prorsus ab electione, quia nullo pacto dicere licet cupiditatem esse electionem: quod non ita sentiendum est de spontaneo. Differt quidem ab electione, sed ea non po-test ab ipso diuelli, cùm omnis electio spontanea est. Argumentum quo nunc utitur, est: Si cupiditas esset electio, quicquid agit ex cupiditate, utiq; ageret ex electione. At non quicquid ex cupiditate agit, ex electione agit. Destructio consequentis hinc apparet: quia incontinens ex cupiditate agit, non autem ex electione, quia illam non sequitur. Proposuit sibi recte agere, sed consilio non stetit. Ideò ex electione, quam in animo habuerat, non egit. Electio appetitio est consiliatrix. At incontinens dum rapitur cupiditate, consilium non audit. Continens è diuerso cupiditatem non audit, sed rectam electionem sequitur. Ratio hæc adaptari posset ad iram: nam & qui agit ex ira, non agit ex electione, quod in iracundis hominibus videre licet. Sed Aristoteles breuitati studens, id omisit. Uno tamen aut altero verbo postea id attinget. Quis autem sit continens quisue incontinens, quis intemperans & quis temperans, declarabitur suo loco. Hic sit satis dixisse, incontinentem non carere prorsus electione, sed illam quam in mente habet non sequi. Confertur dormienti, ebrio, & ciuitati cùm in ea bonæ leges iacent.
units.tr: It is now clearly evident that Aristotle separates desire entirely from choice, since it is by no means possible to say that desire is choice. This is not to be understood in the same way of the voluntary, which differs indeed from choice, but cannot be torn away from it, since all choice is voluntary. The argument he now uses is this: if desire were choice, whatever someone did from desire he would also do from choice. But not whatever he does from desire he does from choice. The denial of the consequent appears from this: the incontinent man acts from desire, not from choice, because he does not follow it. He had resolved to act rightly, but did not abide by his counsel; therefore he did not act from the choice he had in mind. Choice is deliberative appetite, but the incontinent man, while carried away by desire, does not heed counsel. The continent man, on the other hand, does not heed desire but follows right choice. This reasoning could be applied to anger, for one who acts from anger also does not act from choice, as can be seen in irascible men. But Aristotle, aiming at brevity, omitted this, though he will touch on it later with one or two words. Who the continent man is, or the incontinent, who the intemperate and who the temperate, will be declared in its place. Here it is enough to have said that the incontinent man does not lack choice altogether, but does not follow the choice he has in mind. He is compared to a sleeper, a drunk man, and a city in which good laws lie idle.

units.la: Et electioni cupiditas aduersatur, cupiditati uero cupiditas minime.
units.tr: And desire opposes choice, but desire by no means opposes desire.

units.la: Sic ratio componitur: Electio aduersatur cupiditati. Cupiditas non aduersatur cupiditati. Ergo, Cupiditas non est electio. In secunda figura. Ut quae sunt eadem uni tertio, sunt etiam eadem inter sese: ita quae non aduersantur cuipiam[?] tertio, non sunt eadem simul. At dubium oritur, Quia cupiditas cupiditati videtur aduersari. Est qui cupit famam & illustre nomen: idem laborat cupiditate pecuniarum. Una istarum cupiditatum cum altera pugnat. Augustus cupit dominatum, & cupit imitari Syllam abdicatione. Ista videntur pugnare. Pamphilus cupit esse cum sua Glycerio, & tamen desyderat gratificari patri. Ista declarant cupiditates esse contrarias. Est solutio lutio multiplex. Contraria debent perpetuo esse contraria: At ista perpetuo non sunt contraria, ut patet in Sophista, qui simul utraq; laborat cupiditate, nimirum gloria ac pecuniarum. Deinde contraria oportet ut idem spectent: At una istarum cupiditatum respicit famam, altera pecunias. Quae respiciunt idem opposita ratione, vere contraria sunt, & simul esse nequeunt: Vt, cupere famam & cupere non habere famam: esse illustre & non esse illustrem[?]: cupere ali & non ali. Ista sunt cupiditates contrariae, & non possunt simul esse. Non est sensus Aristotelis inter cupiditates non esse contrarietatem, sed contrarias cupiditates non esse posse simul in eodem homine. At sane electioni semper aduersatur in eodem homine ac eodem tempore prava cupiditas. Neq; semper omnis electio aduersatur cuiuis cupiditati: nam electioni qua statuat quispiam ditari vel iniuste, non aduersatur cupiditas furti. Et electioni tyrannidis non aduersatur cupiditas caedis. Verum (ut dictum est) sana electio semper aduersatur prauae cupiditati. At cuiusmodi est contrarietas ista cupiditatis ac electus: Non propria, sed qualis est oppositorum ventorum, aut duorum hostium. Quia propria contraria oportet ut possint in eodem subiecto esse, atq; ab eo sese mutuo depellant, ut album & nigrum, frigus & calidum, quod electioni atq; prauae cupiditati minime conuenit, in diuersis quippe animi partibus collocantur. Est enim electio in mente seu ratione sita, cupiditas vero in animi crassiore portione.
units.tr: The argument is framed thus: choice opposes desire; desire does not oppose desire; therefore desire is not choice. This is in the second figure: as things that are equal to a third thing are also equal among themselves, so things that do not oppose some third thing are not the same. But a doubt arises, because desire seems to oppose desire. One who desires fame and an illustrious name is also afflicted by desire for money; one of these desires fights with the other. Augustus desires dominion and desires to imitate Sulla by abdication; these seem to conflict. Pamphilus desires to be with his Glycerium, and yet wishes to please his father. These show that desires are contrary. The solution is manifold. Contraries must always be contrary, but these are not always contrary, as is clear in the Sophist, who labours under both desires at once, namely for glory and for money. Next, contraries must regard the same thing, but one of these desires regards fame, the other money. Things that regard the same thing under opposed aspects are truly contrary and cannot be together, as to desire fame and to desire not to have fame; to be famous and not to be famous; to desire to be nourished and not to be nourished. These are contrary desires and cannot exist together. Aristotle's meaning is not that there is no contrariety among desires, but that contrary desires cannot be together in the same man. Yet a wicked desire is always opposed to choice in the same man at the same time. Nor is every choice always opposed to every desire: to the choice by which someone resolves to grow rich even unjustly, the desire for theft is not opposed; to the choice of tyranny, the desire for murder is not opposed. But, as has been said, sound choice is always opposed to a wicked desire. Yet what sort of contrariety is this between desire and choice? Not a proper one, but like that of opposing winds or of two enemies. For proper contraries must be able to be in the same subject and drive each other out of it, like white and black, cold and heat. This does not suit choice and wicked desire at all, for they are placed in different parts of the soul. Choice is situated in the mind or reason, but desire is in the grosser portion of the soul.

units.la: Et cupiditas iucundi est atque molesti. Electio vero neque molesti neque iucundi, multo etiam minus ira: nam quae per iram fiunt, minime uidentur electione fieri.
units.tr: Desire is of the pleasant and the painful. Choice, however, is neither of the painful nor of the pleasant, and much less anger, for things done through anger seem by no means to be done by choice.

units.la: Postremum argumentum ex obiectis colligit. Quae aduersa cum sint, efficiunt ipsas facultates easdem non esse. Cupiditas fertur in ea quae iucunda sunt & tristia, nempe ut haec adsequatur, illa vero euitet. Electio vero ista non respicit, sed tantummodo turpe ac honestum, utile atq; damnosum. Sed hic scrupulus est, quia & iucundorum molestorumq; videtur esse electio. Proponitur adolescentibus virtus & voluptas, dicituráq; in biuio quodammodo statui, ut cum venerint ad annos pubertatis, vel ad dextram vel ad leuam flectant. Vnde illis optio datur, ut viam utram voluerint deligant: ita Pythagorici & poetae rem pinxerunt. Et Paridi est concessus delectus, offerebat ei Pallas doctrinam & bonas artes, offerebat Iuno ciuiles honores & Reipublicae felicem administrationem. Venus denique crassiores voluptates. Electio igitur Paridis fuit, & iucundum potius delegit. Quin & seruator noster proponit, viam latam & arctam, portam patentem & angustam. Quare molesti & iucundi videtur electio esse. Respondemus: Si per electionem intelligas actionem animi, qua res una praefertur alteri, non possumus negare, quin etiam iucundi & molesti sit electio, quando iucunditatem aegritudini anteponimus. At deliberatio propria non est de iucundis & crassis voluptatibus: non enim ad illas nati sumus. Unde qui præ-ferunt huiusmodi voluptates honestati austerae, aut quandoq; sensui molestae, non dicendi sunt eligere, sed potius ipsa duci & rapi cupiditate. Non tamen est negandum quandoq; fieri posse, ut honesta quae delegimus & vi-lia sint iucunda: verum id est temere vel (ut vulgo loquuntur) per accidens.
units.tr: He draws the last argument from the objects. Since they are opposite, they show that the faculties themselves are not the same. Desire is directed at things that are pleasant and painful, namely that it may attain the former and avoid the latter. But choice does not regard these, only the base and the honourable, the useful and the harmful. Yet here there is a difficulty, because choice also seems to be of the pleasant and the painful. Virtue and pleasure are set before young men, and it is said that they stand at a crossroads, so that when they come to the years of puberty they may turn either to the right or to the left. Hence they are given an option to choose whichever way they wish; so the Pythagoreans and the poets depicted it. Choice was also granted to Paris: Pallas offered him learning and good arts, Juno offered civic honours and the happy administration of the commonwealth, and Venus, finally, the grosser pleasures. Paris's choice was therefore his, and he chose the pleasant rather. Moreover, our Saviour also sets before us the broad and narrow way, the open and the narrow gate. Therefore choice seems to be of the pleasant and the painful. We reply: if by choice you understand an act of the mind by which one thing is preferred to another, we cannot deny that choice is also of the pleasant and the painful, when we put pleasure before distress. But proper deliberation is not concerned with the pleasant and the gross pleasures, for we were not born for these. Hence those who prefer such pleasures to austere honesty, or sometimes to sense that is painful, are not to be said to choose, but rather to be led and carried away by desire. Yet it must not be denied that sometimes the honourable things we choose may also be pleasant; but this happens by chance, or (as the common people say) accidentally.

units.la: Versatur itaq; electio circa bonum & malum: id enim quaerimus nostro de-lectu, ut bona assequamur, et evitemus mala. Quod si quaerat quispiam, an mali electio esse queat. Respondebimus id fieri non posse, quia nunquam mala deligimus: oportet enim quod eligitur, aut bonum esse, aut saltem specie aspectumq; boni præse ferre. At dixeris, Nonne saepius minora mala præ-gra-uioribus eliguntur? Fateor: at Aristoteles in Rhetoricis ait, minus malum eo casu boni rationem habere. Postremo de ira pauca scribit, illam quoque multo minus electionem esse, quia illa non videntur electione fieri quae per iram facimus. Hoc quia clarissimum est & vulgo receptum, ideo pluribus demonstrare noluit.
units.tr: Choice therefore is concerned with good and evil, for by our choice we seek this: that we may attain good and avoid evil. But if someone asks whether there can be a choice of evil, we reply that this cannot be, because we never choose evils: for what is chosen must either be good, or at least bear the appearance and aspect of good. But you may say: are not lesser evils often chosen over greater ones? I grant it, but Aristotle says in the Rhetoric that in that case the lesser evil has the character of good. Finally, he writes briefly about anger, that it is much less a choice, because the things we do through anger do not seem to be done by choice. Since this is most clear and generally accepted, he did not wish to demonstrate it at length.

units.la: Nec voluntas quidem, etiamsi ei sit affinis. Non enim est electio eorum quae fieri nō possunt. Quod si quispiam talia se fateatur eligere stolidus esse videbitur. At voluntas est eorum quae fieri nequeunt, ut immortalitatis.
units.tr: Nor is it will either, even though will is related to choice. For there is no choice of things that cannot be done. If someone claimed to choose such things, he would seem foolish. But will extends to things that cannot be done, such as immortality.

units.la: Duo nobis hic proponuntur, Unum est, voluntatem electioni affinem esse: nam utraq; in suprema sede animi collocatur. Deinde vulgus dicit se velle quae deligit, & nihilominus ut proxima sint, differunt a se invicem: nam voluntas fusior est ac liberior quàm electio, nam ad multa extenditur (quae admodum dicetur) ad quae non pertingit electio, ut ad finem, ad illa quae fieri nequeunt, ad ea quae per nosipsos non possumus praestare. Omnes itaq; istae rationes, quibus hic Aristoteles utitur, ab obiectis deductae sunt. Electionē eorum non esse quae fieri non possunt, ex communi omnium sensu probat. Insanus enim haberetur, qui talia deligeret. Voluntatem vero talium esse liquet ex eo, quòd multos facile reperias, qui vellent non mori, quod physicè non potest fieri. Sunt etiam qui vellent esse monarchæ totius orbis, & omnibus hominibus imperare: quod item esse non potest.
units.tr: Two things are proposed to us here. The first is that will is related to choice, for both are located in the highest seat of the mind. Second, the common people say that they will what they choose, and yet, although they are close to each other, they differ: will is broader and freer than choice, for it extends to many things (as will be said shortly) that choice does not reach, such as the end, things that cannot be done, and things that we cannot accomplish by ourselves. All these reasons that Aristotle uses here are drawn from the objects. He proves from the common sense of all that there is no choice of things that cannot be done, for a person who chose such things would be thought insane. That there is will of such things is clear from the fact that you can easily find many who would want not to die, which cannot physically happen. There are also those who would want to be monarchs of the whole world and rule over all men, which likewise cannot be.

units.la: Est etiā voluntas eorū quæ geri nō possunt ab eo, q ea voluerit. Ut aliquē histrionē vel athletā vincere. At nemo talia eligit, sed ꝙ putat ꝑ seipsū posse fieri.
units.tr: There is also will of things that cannot be brought about by the one who wills them, such as wanting to defeat some actor or athlete. But no one chooses such things, except what he thinks he can bring about through himself.

units.la: Argumento superiori probauit ista differre, Quod voluntas interdum sit eorum quæ nullo modo fieri possunt: at non electio. Hic addit voluntatem esse quandoq; illorum, quæ licet natura sua fieri possint, à volente nihilominus fieri nequeunt, vt quòd quispiam vel histrio vel athleta vincat. Histrio est qui in scena verbis, gestu & voce personas assimulat, & substinet quas voluerit. Athletæ vero certabant inter se. Vt autem vulgi studia essent propensa quandoq; vel in hos vel in illos, cum poeta tũ historici tradunt. Ista vero nemo deligat, cum videat à seipso minimè posse obiri.
units.tr: By the previous argument he proved that these differ, because will is sometimes of things that cannot be done in any way, whereas choice is not. Here he adds that will is sometimes of those things which, although they can be done by their nature, nevertheless cannot be done by the one who wills them, such as that some actor or athlete should win. An actor is one who, on the stage, imitates and sustains with words, gesture and voice the characters he wishes. Athletes, however, competed against one another. And historians and poets relate that the enthusiasms of the crowd were sometimes inclined toward these, sometimes toward those. But no one would choose such things, since he sees that they cannot at all be brought about by himself.

units.la: Adhæc voluntas est potius finis, electio vero eorū quæ ad finē pertinent: ut valere volumus, ea vero deligimus per quæ valetudine assequamur. Et felices esse, cum volumus, tum profitemur: non autem congruit ut nos dicamus id eligere. In universum autem videtur electio de iis esse quæ sita sunt in nobis.
units.tr: Moreover, will is rather the end, whereas choice is of those things that pertain to the end: we want to be well, but we choose those things by which we obtain health. And when we want to be happy, we profess it; but it does not fit that we say we choose it. In general, choice seems to concern those things that are within our power.

units.la: Voluntas est finis. Electio potius eorum quæ sunt ad finem. Igitur diffe-runt. Quare dixit, Electio potius? Quia vulgus etiam finem se dicit eligere. At si proprius sermo fuerit, non est dicendum. Cur adiecit illam clausulam, In universum electionem illorum esse quæ sunt in manu nostra? Quia finis, præsertim extrema, eius est natura, ut statim cum proposita fuerit, non possit refutari, ideoq; cum minimè sit in manu nostra ab ea resilire, non pertinet ad electionem: nam ea illorum est quæ sunt in nobis. Animadvertendum tamen, esse mediorum finium electionem. Proponitur enim sæpe adolescentibus optio aut bonarum literarum, aut artis militaris: aut ecclesiasticæ functionis, aut administrationis Reipub. Primum deligunt sibi unum istorum quod magis libuerit. Deinde media quoq; deligunt per quæ in iis excellunt. At respondemus electionem in illis finibus non habere locum, ut sunt fines sed ut media quædam ad felicitatem. Nam finis, qua finis est, ut Aristoteles dicit, non est electio.
units.tr: Will is of the end; choice is rather of those things that are toward the end. Therefore they differ. Why did he say "rather"? Because the common people also say they choose the end. But if the speech is proper, it should not be said. Why did he add that clause, "in general the choice of those things that are in our hand"? Because the end, especially the last end, is by its nature such that, once it has been set before us, it cannot be rejected; and therefore, since it is by no means in our hand to back away from it, it does not belong to choice, for choice is of those things that are in us. It must be noted, however, that there is also a choice of intermediate ends. For young men are often offered the option of either humane letters, or military art, or the ecclesiastical office, or the administration of the commonwealth. First they choose for themselves whichever of these they like best. Then they also choose the means by which they excel in them. But we reply that choice has no place in those ends insofar as they are ends, but insofar as they are certain means to happiness. For the end, as far as it is an end, as Aristotle says, is not a choice.

units.la: Neq; opinio quidem fuerit. Etenim opinio de omnibus esse uidetur, & nihilominus de æternis & quæ fieri nō possūt, q̄ de ijs quæ sunt in nobis posita
units.tr: Nor is it opinion either. For opinion seems to be about all things, and about eternal things and things that cannot be done no less than about those things placed in our power.

units.la: Quarta nunc sententia refutatur, nimirum, Electionem non esse opinionē
units.tr: Now a fourth view is refuted, namely that choice is not opinion.
And the argument is again drawn from the objects:
Opinion is about all things.
Choice is not about all things.
Therefore choice is not opinion.

units.la: Argumentum in secunda figura, à relatiuis: nam facultas ad obiectuū suū referētur. Nunc videamus quid sit opinio. Assensus mentis quo vnam contradictionis partem suscipimus at non intrepidè: uerum subdubitando, ne fortasse altera pars contradictionis vera deprehendatur. Et hoc differt opinio à scientia: ea enim firmissima et immobilis est assensio. Idcirco nemo tentat persuadere scienti aut mathematico aliter esse quàm sciat: id enim fieri non potest, vt persuadeatur ei, sed opiniones ex animis hominum euellere oratores maximè conantur, quando vident iudices vel auditores aliter sentire quàm ipsi velint. De omnibus esse opinionem probat, quoniam & circa aeterna versatur. Multa enim opinantur homines de Deo, de angelis, de coelo, & huiusmodi quæ pro æternis à philosopho habentur. Opinantur etiam homines ea quæ fieri non possunt, vt chimæras esse centauros, & huiusmodi. Et diametrum æqualem esse lateribus quadrati: quod fieri nequit. Necessaria quoq; interdum sub opinionem cadunt: nam fieri potest vt quod vnus percepit scientia, opinione alius credat. Cùm verò dicitur opinio esse de omnibus, id non est accipiendum quo ad simplices notiones sed quo ad propositiones quæ constant pluribus notionibus aut vocibus & aliquid aut esse aut non esse indicant. Neq; item de iis omnibus est opinio. Sunt enim quædam per seipsa nota aut sensui aut menti. Vt ignem calidum esse, sensus experimento certò nouimus, non opinamur. Ac totum esse maius parte sua: vel, De quolibet pronuntiatur esse aut non esse, (quæ axiomata dicuntur) minimè opinamur, cùm intelligentiæ nostræ sint per se nota. Igitur Aristotelem intelligimus, opinione de omnibus esse, nimirum propositionib. quæ per seipsas nota non fuerint. Distinguitur etiam opinio à Fide theologica, vt illud obiter attingam: quoniam Fides assensionem firmā significat verbo Dei adhibitā Spiritus sancti persuasione. Vnde minimè nutat aut vacillat, vt opinio. Minor propositio rationis huius probatur, quoniam electio est solum de iis quæ à nobis fieri possunt. Quare non est de omnibus, vt opinio. Et falso & uero distinguitur opinio, non prauo & bono: electio potius ijs.
units.tr: An argument in the second figure, from relatives: for a faculty is referred to its object. Now let us see what opinion is. It is an assent of the mind by which we accept one part of a contradiction, but not fearlessly; rather with some doubt, lest perhaps the other part of the contradiction be found to be true. This is what distinguishes opinion from science: for science is a most firm and unchanging assent. Therefore no one tries to persuade a man of science or a mathematician that things are otherwise than he knows them to be, for it cannot happen that he is persuaded of it; but orators most of all try to uproot opinions from men's minds when they see that judges or hearers think otherwise than they themselves wish. He proves that opinion is about all things, since it also concerns eternal things. For men hold many opinions about God, about angels, about heaven, and such things, which the philosopher regards as eternal. Men also hold opinions about things that cannot be done, such as that chimeras are centaurs, and such things; and that the diagonal of a square is equal to its sides, which cannot be. Even necessary things sometimes fall under opinion, for it can happen that one man believes by opinion what another has grasped by science. But when it is said that opinion is about all things, this is not to be understood with respect to simple notions, but with respect to propositions which consist of several notions or words and indicate that something is or is not. Nor is there opinion about all of them, either. For some things are known in themselves, either by the senses or by the mind. We know with certainty by the experience of the senses that fire is hot; we do not opine it. Likewise, that the whole is greater than its part; or, that of anything it is affirmed that it is or is not (which are called axioms), we by no means opine, since they are known in themselves to our understanding. Therefore we understand Aristotle to mean that opinion is about all things, namely about propositions that are not known in themselves. Opinion is also distinguished from theological faith, which I will touch on in passing: for faith signifies a firm assent, applied to the Word of God, by the persuasion of the Holy Spirit. Hence it by no means wavers or vacillates, as opinion does. The minor premise of this argument is proved, since choice is only of those things that can be done by us. Therefore it is not about all things, as opinion is. And opinion is distinguished by true and false, not by wicked and good; choice rather by these.

units.la: Aliud argumentum est à partibus. Non easdem partes habent, hæc duo tota, in quas diducātur. Ergo non sunt eadem. Partes enim electionis sunt praua & bona. Opinionis vero, falsa & vera opinio. Quod hic affertur, posset infirmum videri: quoniam vulgo multas opiniones prauas esse iactamus. Vt si quis opinetur animos nostros esse mortales: aut Deum non curare sua providentia humanas actiones. Quicunque ista opinantur, prauas opiniones habere dicuntur. Primum ad hoc respondetur, prauum hic accipi, vt ad mores pertinet. Ideoque Aristoteles dicit, opinionem non esse prauam aut bonam, quia inter mores haud numeratur. At vulgus opiniones dicit prauas, quoniam falsum est malum, quemadmodum verum est bonum. Ista enim quæ vulgo dicuntur transcendentia, ita inter se coniunguntur, ut verum sit bonum, & falsum sit malum. Possunt etiam ipsæ opiniones dici bonæ aut prauæ quandoque moraliter: quia ex illis falsis opinionibus aut veris homines vel ad bonos mores vel ad prauos incitantur.
units.tr: Another argument is drawn from the parts. Two wholes that are divided into parts do not have the same parts. Therefore they are not the same. For the parts of choice are wicked and good; but the parts of opinion are false and true opinion. What is said here could seem weak, since we commonly declaim that many opinions are wicked: for example, if someone opines that our souls are mortal, or that God does not care about human actions by his providence. Whoever holds such opinions is said to have wicked opinions. To this it is first replied that "wicked" is here understood as it pertains to morals. Therefore Aristotle says that opinion is neither wicked nor good, because it is not counted among the moral virtues and vices. But the common people call opinions wicked because falsehood is evil just as truth is good. For these things that are said in common are transcendentals, and are so joined together that truth is good and falsehood is evil. Opinions themselves can also sometimes be called good or wicked morally, because men are incited by those false or true opinions either to good morals or to wicked ones.

units.la: In uniuersum autem fortasis nemo dixerit, electionem idem esse cum opinione. Sed id neque potest dici cum aliqua: nam eligendo bona uel mala, certi quidam seu aliquales sumus, non autem opinando.
units.tr: In general, perhaps no one would say that choice is the same as opinion. But this cannot be said with any qualification, for in choosing good or bad things we become certain kinds of people, or people of some quality, whereas we do not become so by opining.

units.la: Nunc ex effectis argumentatur: Neq; particulariter dici posse aliquod genus opinionis esse idem cum electione. De parte aliqua idcirco se ait agere, quia iam demonstratum est in uniuersum, opinionem & electionem differre. Ne igitur aliquis dicat, Generaliter differunt, sed tamen fieri potest, vt aliqua opinio sit particularis electio: hoc probat fieri non posse, Quia, inquit, hic electionis effectus est, vt iusta causa aliqui efficiamur. At non id in opinione accidit. Ergo, nullo modo idem esse possunt. Quæ hoc loco dicuntur, maximè sunt euidentia in incontinente. Is enim quia male deligit, prauus dicitur, cum alioqui recte opinetur. De virtutibus enim recte iudicat, & opinatur bonum esse temperare sibi ab impudicitia & ebrietate, atq; id non eligit: minimè appellatur bonus. Non potest attamen quispiam negare, quin etiam opinando certa qualitate aliqua nos efficiamur, cum ipsa opinio sit qualitas, & ex ipsis opinionibus aliqui animi affectus oriantur. At de illa qualitate Aristoteles intelligendus est, qua opinamur & quam eligimus. Etenim eligendo casti, efficimur casti: fortia, fortes: iusta, iusti. Verum non ite in uniuersum ue verum est de opinione. Quia opinando æterna, non efficimur æterni: neq; opinando quippiam de iustitia, efficimur iusti. Verum quidem est ex veris opinionib. nos effici ad virtutes aptiores, & ex falsis procliniores ad vitia. Sed ipsa opinio statim cum adest, ex seipsa tales nobis formas aut denominatio-nes communicat: verum electionem interuenire oportet..
units.tr: Now he argues from the effects that no kind of opinion can be said to be the same as choice in particular. He says he is dealing with a part because it has already been shown in general that opinion and choice differ. So, lest someone say, "They differ in general, but it can still happen that some opinion is a particular choice," he proves that this cannot be. For, he says, the effect of choice is that by a just cause we are made just, but this does not happen with opinion. Therefore they can in no way be the same. What is said here is most evident in the incontinent man. For he, because he chooses badly, is called wicked, although otherwise he opines rightly. For he judges correctly about the virtues and holds it good to abstain from impurity and drunkenness, yet he does not choose this, and so he is by no means called good. Nevertheless, no one can deny that even by opining we are made to be of a certain quality, since opinion itself is a quality and certain emotions of the mind arise from opinions. But Aristotle must be understood to mean that quality by which we opine and which we choose. For by choosing chaste things we become chaste, brave things brave, just things just. But it is not so in general, nor is it true of opinion. For by opining about eternal things we do not become eternal, and by opining something about justice we do not become just. It is true that from true opinions we are made more apt for the virtues, and from false ones more inclined to vices. But opinion itself, as soon as it is present, communicates such forms or designations to us from itself; yet choice must intervene.

units.la: Et eligimus assumere aut euitare seu quippiā hu-iusmodi. Opinamur uero quid aliquid sit, cuiue cō-ferat, aut quomodo. Non autem admodum opina-mur, aut assumere aut fugere quippiam.
units.tr: And we choose to take up or avoid something or other of this kind. But we opine what something is, what it contributes to, or how. We do not, however, opine straight away whether to take up or flee something.

units.la: Quod referantur ad diuersa, modo etiam conficit illa duo inter sese differre. Versatur electio in prosequendo vel fugiendo, sed opinio non item. Aliqua enim re nobis oblata incipimus opinari quid nam ea sit, qua vtilitas eius haberi possit, aut quomodo sit ea vtendum: non autem admodum opinamur de illa, fugienda vel consequenda, quoniam ista pertinent ad electionem. Imo inter ista quidam videtur situs ordo. Prius enim quid aliquid sit opinamur, qua illius haberi possit vtilitas, aut quomodo inseruire queat vsui nostro. Quibus rebus opinione perceptis, ad illam rem vel persequendam vel euitandam procedimus.
units.tr: That they are directed to different objects also shows that the two differ. Choice is concerned with pursuing or fleeing, but opinion is not. For when some thing is presented to us, we begin to opine what it is, by what usefulness it may be had, or how it ought to be used. We do not at once opine about it, whether it is to be fled or sought, since these belong to choice. Indeed there seems to be a certain order among these. For first we opine what something is, by what usefulness it can be had, or how it can serve our use. With these things perceived by opinion, we proceed to pursue or avoid that thing.

units.la: Et electio quidem laudatur, quod eius rei fuerit quā deligi oportuit, uel recte fuerit delecta: opinio uero, quod sit uera.
units.tr: And choice is praised because it concerns the thing that ought to be chosen, or because it was rightly made; opinion is praised because it is true.

units.la: Pendet ista ratio a Secunda. Ibi ostensum fuit, distingui opinionem in veram & falsam. Electionem autem in bonam & malam. Ex eo istud oritur, quod modo explicatur. Vtrunq; laudatur, cum opinio tum electio: at diuer-so nomine ac titulo. Laudatur quippe a nobis electio, quod sit eius rei quam oportuit eligi, aut quod recte fuerit delecta. Comprehendit hoc sermone duas partes rectæ bonæq; electionis. Substantia & natura eius quod eligitur, oportet vt bona sit. Deinde vt recte id fiat, in loco & circumstantijs iustis. At inquit, opinio eo nomine laudatur quod sit vera.
units.tr: This reasoning depends on the second book, where it was shown that opinion is divided into true and false, and choice into good and bad. From this arises what is now being explained. Both are praised, opinion and choice, but under different names and titles. Choice is praised by us because it concerns the thing that ought to have been chosen, or because it was rightly made. This phrase comprises two parts of right and good choice: the substance and nature of what is chosen must be good, and then it must be done rightly, in a suitable place and circumstances. But he says that opinion is praised under the name that it is true.
